THE ELEVENTH DISSERTATION
IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiae Romanae dominantem Babylonem Magnam esse, probatur Sextò, quia populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu, ad sui & creaturarum cultum, salsámque religionem modis omnibus seducit.
units.tr: It is proved that the hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church ruling over the people, is the Great Babylon, because in every way it seduces the people subject to it from the true worship of the true God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to a false religion.
FIRST SECTION.
WHEREIN

units.la: Hierarchiam populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad falsam Religionem seducere ex erroribus ejusdem tyrannicis, in Christum & officia ejus arietantibus, demonstratur.
units.tr: It is shown that the Hierarchy, through its tyrannical errors which strike against Christ and his offices, leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God into false religion.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Argumentum principale sextum, inde petitum, quòd Hierarchia, cæteris paribus, populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad sui & creaturarum cultum, falsámque sámque religionem seducat syllogismo constringitur ; ejusque propositio probatur.
units.tr: I. The sixth main argument, drawn from this, that the Hierarchy, other things being equal, leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to false religion, is brought together in a syllogism, and its major premise is proved.

units.la: II. III. Assumptionis lemma alterum, quòd Hierarchia à vero Deo, Christóque ad falsam religionem & cultum creaturarum seducat, demonstrandum susci-pitur.
units.tr: II. III. The minor premise has two parts, and it is undertaken to demonstrate that the Hierarchy leads men away from the true God and Christ to false religion and the worship of creatures.

units.la: IV. Capitales sedis Romanæ errores, ex triplici Papæ diademate tripertiti, tyrannici, idololatrici & Magici constituuntur.
units.tr: IV. The chief errors of the Roman see are set out under the threefold tiara of the Pope: they are tyrannical, idolatrous and magical.

units.la: V. Tyrannici ii sunt, quibus Hierarchia tyranni instar, alienam Christi potestatem invadit, & usurpat ; triplex inprimis ejus officium, Propheticum, Sacerdotale & Regium impetit. Quod per singulas eas partes probatur.
units.tr: V. Those errors are tyrannical by which the Hierarchy, like a tyrant, invades and usurps the power of Christ alone; first of all it attacks his threefold office, prophetic, priestly and kingly. This is proved part by part.

units.la: VI. Christus solus N.T. Propheta est. Ejus revelatio seu verbum Propheticum Scripturis mandatum nunc extat.
units.tr: VI. Christ alone is the Prophet of the New Testament. His revelation, or prophetic word, committed to Scripture, now exists.

units.la: VII. Extra quas revelatio Prophetica Christi hodie nulla reperitur.
units.tr: VII. Outside of Scripture no prophetic revelation of Christ is found today.

units.la: VIII. Atque earundem sensus & interpretatio non aliunde quàm ex Scripturis ipsis arcessitur.
units.tr: VIII. The sense and interpretation of Scripture are derived from nothing other than Scripture itself.

units.la: IX. Quisquis ergo Scripturas impetit, Christi Propheticam authoritatem oppugnat. Quod Hierarchiam strenuè facere ostenditur.
units.tr: IX. Whoever therefore attacks the Scriptures attacks the prophetic authority of Christ. It is shown that the Hierarchy does this vigorously.

units.la: X. Oppugnat enim potentiam Scripturæ, quasuam ipsa Divinitatem cuiuis conscientiæ demonstrare valeat.
units.tr: X. For it attacks the power of Scripture, which can demonstrate its own divinity to any conscience.
XI. The blasphemies of the Hierarchs are noted.

units.la: XII. Divinitatem Scripturæ à testimonio Ecclesiæ, seu Papæ præsentis, suspendunt.
units.tr: XII. They make the divinity of Scripture depend on the testimony of the Church, or of the present Pope.

units.la: XIII. Idem Canonis Divini figendi refigendique authoritatem sibi rapiunt.
units.tr: XIII. They likewise seize for themselves the authority to fix and refix the Divine Canon.

units.la: XIV. Canonis Divini scripti sufficientiam nefariè lacessunt.
units.tr: XIV. They wickedly assail the sufficiency of the written Divine Canon.

units.la: XV. Versionem Latinam corruptam, ceu authenticam ipsismet fontibus præferunt. XVI. Sen-
units.tr: XV. They prefer the corrupt Latin version, as if it were authentic, to the sources themselves. XVI. Sen-

units.la: XVI. Sensum Scripturæ sui arbitrii, suaeque potestatis omnem faciunt. In quo securitatis eorum palladium consistit. .
units.tr: XVI. They make the sense of Scripture entirely subject to their own will and power. In this lies the bulwark of their security.

units.la: XVII. Tyrannidem sic exercent. Spiritum S. liberásque ejus operationes in ordinem redigendo.
units.tr: XVII. They exercise tyranny in this way, by reducing the Holy Spirit and his free operations to order.

units.la: XVIII. XIX. Adeóque facultatis prophetandi monopolium sibi vendicando.
units.tr: XVIII. XIX. And thus they claim for themselves the monopoly of the power of prophesying.

units.la: XX. Spiritus privati Scripturam ex Scriptura interpretantibus objecti opprobrium depellitur.
units.tr: XX. The reproach levelled at private spirits, who interpret Scripture from Scripture, is repelled.

units.la: XXI. In Scripturæ reddendo sensu infallibilitatem sibi nec quicquam arrogant ; etiam cùm diligentiam nullam adhibent.
units.tr: XXI. They claim for themselves no infallibility in giving the sense of Scripture, even when they use no diligence at all.

units.la: XXII. Eam à Cathedra S. Petri nullo jure arcessunt.
units.tr: XXII. They derive it from the Chair of St. Peter by no right.
XXIII. The monstrosity of that infallibility is demonstrated further.

units.la: XXIV. XXV. Et emblemate conspirantium Sacri Nemoris equitum, piraticam publicam prætextu infallibilitatis similis sibi arrogatæ, exercentium, exagitatur,
units.tr: XXIV. XXV. And by the emblem of the conspiring knights of the Sacred Grove, who under the pretext of an infallibility similarly claimed for themselves carry on public piracy, it is held up to censure.

units.la: XXVI. Ultimus Scripturas debellandi conatus, in hominibus ab ejus lectione vi & dolo arcendis consistit.
units.tr: XXVI. The final attempt to crush the Scriptures consists in keeping men from reading them by force and fraud.

units.la: XXVII. Papa Pseudopropheta Christi Prophetæ æmulus, sicut hic verbum suum Propheticum miraculorum sigillis confirmavit, ita ille pariter verbum suum Pseudopropheticum signis & miraculis stabilire annititur.
units.tr: XXVII. The Pope, a false prophet, is a rival of Christ the Prophet. Just as Christ confirmed his prophetic word with the seals of miracles, so the Pope likewise strives to establish his false-prophetic word by signs and miracles.
XXVIII. A specimen of the false-prophetic miracles is set forth.

units.la: XXIX. Sicut totus Papatus entibus fictis & pictis constat: sic miracula ejusdem fingi pingique debuerunt.
units.tr: XXIX. Just as the whole Papacy consists of fictitious and painted beings, so its miracles ought to have been feigned and painted.

units.la: XXX. Hierarchia veros Christi Prophetas occidendo, Christum Prophetam ipsum debellare conatur.
units.tr: XXX. By killing the true prophets of Christ, the Hierarchy tries to overcome Christ the Prophet himself.
XXXI. Progress to the priestly office of Christ.

units.la: XXXII. Ab Hierarchia illud oppugnari & infringi ex Sacerdotii Christi & Papæ antithesi demonstratur.
units.tr: XXXII. It is shown from the antithesis between the priesthood of Christ and the Pope that the Hierarchy attacks and undermines it.

units.la: XXXIII. Etenim 1. Christus Sacerdotium à Deo vocatus occupavit: Papa suum ἀυδαίρετω. Non ergo Papæ Sacerdotium Christi Sacerdotium est. XXXIV. 11. Christus Sacerdotio suo ceremonias veteres induxit: Papa suo eas postliminio restituit, & gravioriconscientias jugo premit. XXXV. Sacerdotii illius adulterini pompa externa perstringitur. XXXVI. Et cum præcepta adoratione Dei in spiritu & veritate comparatur. XXXVII. 111. Christus semel in ara crucis se ipsum obtulit, XXXVIII. Hierarchia eum creberrimè sacrificat. XXXIX. Et propitiatorio Christi unico Missaticum opponit. XL. Atque sic illud funditus destruit. XLI. XLII. Contumeliæ Christo in Missa illatæ. XLIII. Adductis etiam Francisci, Alex.de Ales, Thomæ; XLIV. Et Gabrielis Biel testimoniis confirmatæ. XLV. Unde de fructibus idolomaniæ Missaticæ proclive judicium est. XLVI. iv. Christus morte sua justitiam, salutem solus impetravit. XLVII. XLVIII. Hierarchia Justitiæ Christi persectissimæ justitiam propriam, seu inhærentis justitiæ infusum habitum. XLIX. Satisfactioni ejus absolutissimæ satisfactiones humanas tum proprias; L. Etiam post hanc vitam in purgatorio præstandas, LI. Tum alienas, indulgentiarum beneficio auxiliares manus porrigentibus impertiendas, LII. Quarum absurditas nimia ostenditur, LIII. Merito Christi consummatissimo merita justitiæ propriæ opponit. LIV. Fucus Hierarchiæ meretricius, quòd justitia, crux, satisfactio, meritum Christi justitiæ, satisfactioni, meritis humanis subordinentur, atque illa per hæc applicentur, abstergitur.
units.tr: XXXIII. For 1. Christ occupied the priesthood, being called to it by God; the Pope occupies his own, self-appointed [αὐθαίρετος]. Therefore the priesthood of the Pope is not the priesthood of Christ. XXXIV. 2. Christ introduced the old ceremonies into his priesthood; the Pope restores them by right of return and presses consciences under a heavier yoke. XXXV. The outward pomp of that adulterous priesthood is censured. XXXVI. And it is compared with the commanded worship of God in spirit and truth. XXXVII. 3. Christ offered himself once on the altar of the cross. XXXVIII. The Hierarchy sacrifices him very often. XXXIX. And it sets the Mass against the one propitiation of Christ. XL. And thus it utterly destroys that propitiation. XLI. XLII. The insults offered to Christ in the Mass. XLIII. The testimonies of Francis, Alexander of Hales and Thomas are also adduced; XLIV. and they are confirmed by the testimony of Gabriel Biel. XLV. Hence a judgment about the fruits of Mass-idolatry is easy to form. XLVI. 4. Christ alone obtained righteousness and salvation by his death. XLVII. XLVIII. The Hierarchy sets its own righteousness, or the infused habit of inherent righteousness, over against the most perfect righteousness of Christ. XLIX. Against his most complete satisfaction it sets human satisfactions, both one's own; L. to be performed even after this life in purgatory, LI. and those of others, to be imparted by the benefit of indulgences to those who stretch out helping hands; LII. the absurdity of which is shown to be excessive. LIII. Against the most complete merit of Christ it sets the merits of its own righteousness. LIV. The harlot's paint of the Hierarchy is wiped away, by which righteousness, cross, satisfaction and merit of Christ are made subordinate to righteousness, satisfaction and human merits, and the former are applied through the latter.

units.la: LV. v. Hierarchia Mediatori & Paracleto unico Christo innumeros Mediatores opponit.
units.tr: LV. 5. The Hierarchy sets innumerable mediators against Christ, the only Mediator and Paraclete.

units.la: LVI. LVII. Impietatis illius progredientis gradus notantur.
units.tr: LVI. LVII. The advancing stages of that impiety are noted.

units.la: LVIII. Fraus & periculum ingens ex multiplicatis Mediatoribus gliscens detegitur.
units.tr: LVIII. The great fraud and danger that arise from the multiplied mediators are laid bare.

units.la: LIX. Eadem impietate Hierarchia Officium Christi Regium impetit, unius Papæ imperio libidinique cuncta subjiciens.
units.tr: LIX. With the same impiety the Hierarchy attacks the kingly office of Christ, subjecting everything to the rule and lust of one Pope.
LX. Other specimens of this same attack are set forth.

units.la: LXI. Regno gratiæ per jactatas naturæ & liberi arbitrii vires immane quantum Hierarchia derogat.
units.tr: LXI. By boasting of the powers of nature and free will, the Hierarchy detracts immeasurably from the kingdom of grace.

units.la: LXII. Sub laudibus naturæ latent inimici gratiæ.
units.tr: LXII. Under praises of nature lie hidden the enemies of grace.

units.la: LXIII. Hierarchia raptæ potestatis Christi Regiæ spoliis ad horrendas fidelium Regni Christi subditorum vexationes abutitur.
units.tr: LXIII. The Hierarchy abuses the spoils of the kingly power of Christ, which it has seized, for dreadful vexations of the faithful, the subjects of Christ's kingdom.

units.la: LXIV. Christum & Christianam religionem ab Hierarchia his modis eversam esse, & eandem post Christum scortari, adeóque Babylonem Magnam esse, concluditur.
units.tr: LXIV. It is concluded that Christ and the Christian religion have been overthrown by the Hierarchy in these ways, and that the same Hierarchy has played the harlot after Christ, and so is the Great Babylon.

units.la: LXV. Objectioni, quòd Christum ejusque officia Hierarchia aperte profiteatur, occurritur.
units.tr: LXV. The objection, that the Hierarchy openly professes Christ and his offices, is met.

units.la: LXVI. Et Leonis X. contraria professione ex Maffæo producta eadem retunditur.
units.tr: LXVI. And it is refuted in the same way by the contrary profession of Leo X, quoted from Maffeo.

units.la: I. Nstitutæ demonstrationis nostræ caput, seu argumentum Sextum, inde videlicet petitum, quòd Hierarchia Romanæ Ecclesiæ populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad sui & creaturarum cultum, falsámque religionem modis omnibus seducat, succedit. Demonstratio ordine coepto & hucusque continuato, Syllogismo ἀκεραιότητος καὶ σωφροσύνης ἕνεκα constricta, hoc fere talo procedet:
units.tr: I. The head of our demonstration, or the sixth argument, namely that the Hierarchy of the Roman Church leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to false religion, in every way, now follows. The demonstration, continued in the order begun and carried on so far, is constrained in a syllogism of integrity and sobriety [ἀκεραιότητος καὶ σωφροσύνης ἕνεκα], and will proceed more or less in this form:

units.la: Is coetus Babylon Magna est, qui, ceteris paribus, populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu, ad sui & creaturarum cultum, falsámque religionem modis omnibus seducit.
units.tr: That assembly is the Great Babylon which, other things being equal, leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to false religion, in every way.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, ceteris paribus, populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad sui, & creaturarum cultum, falsámque religionem modis omnibus seducit.
units.tr: But the Hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, other things being equal, leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God to the worship of itself and of creatures, and to false religion, in every way.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans, est Babylon Magna.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, is the Great Babylon.

units.la: Propositionis nexus subjecti & attributi proprii nexu necessario & indivulso nititur. Etenim Babyloni M. attribuit Spiritus Dei, quòd sit πόρνη μεγάλη Meretrix Magna, ἡ μήτηρ τῶν πορνῶν Mater fornicationum & abominationum terræ, cum qua fornicati sunt Reges terræ, Apoc xvii. 2. 4. 5. &c. Scortationem porro intelligi inprimis spiritualem, eámque duplicem, tum qua Meretrix illa spiritualis ipsa religiosum cultum creaturis impertitur, & à Christo, unico fidelium sponso, ad alios abducit, falsámque religionem loco verae inducit, & homines ad eam seducit: tum qua Meretrix seipsam pro Numine venditans, ad cultum venerationémque sui Reges & incolas terrae invitat, iisque adeò procumbens satietatem cupiditatum, deliciarum, bonorum omnium promittit; jam supra Differt. III. 813. probare occupavimus.
units.tr: The connection of the proposition rests on a necessary and inseparable connection between the subject and its proper attribute. For the Spirit of God attributes to the Great Babylon that she is a great harlot [πόρνη μεγάλη], the mother of harlots and abominations of the earth, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication [ἡ μήτηρ τῶν πορνῶν], Apoc. 17. 2, 4, 5, etc. Moreover, that fornication is to be understood chiefly as spiritual, and that twofold: first, in that this spiritual harlot herself gives religious worship to creatures and draws men away from Christ, the one spouse of the faithful, to others, introducing false religion in place of the true and seducing men to it; second, in that the harlot, offering herself for sale as a divinity, invites the kings and inhabitants of the earth to the worship and veneration of herself, and, bowing down to them, promises them the satisfaction of all desires, delights and goods. We have already undertaken to prove this above in Differt. III, 813.

units.la: II. Assumptio duo membra habet. Prius est, quòd Hierarchia à vero Dei cultu ad sui cultum homines seducere conetur. Qua in re spiritualem fornicationem potissimùm consistere, supra quoque probavimus. Hic quoque demonstratione superiori diatriba defuncti abundè lumus. Posterius est, quòd Hierarchia populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad cultum creaturarum & falsam religionem modis omnibus seducat; adeóque fidem Deo & Christo, unico Domino datam, nefariè violans erroneum, falsum, idololatricum cultum præcipiat, exercéatque. Id verò solidis rationibus astruere, hoc nunc opus, hic labor erit.
units.tr: II. The assumption has two parts. The first is that the Hierarchy tries to lead men from the true worship of God to its own worship. That this consists chiefly in spiritual fornication we have also proved above. Concerning this, by the demonstration above and the discussion already completed, we have said enough. The second is that the Hierarchy, in every way, leads the people subject to it away from the true worship of the true God to the worship of creatures and to false religion; and so, wickedly violating the faith given to God and Christ, the one Lord, it prescribes and practises an erroneous, false and idolatrous worship. To establish this by solid reasons is now our task, and here is where the labour lies.

units.la: III. Ingens equidem heic dicendorum campus sese aperiret. Nos præcipua delibaturi, in pauca contrahemus, quæ diductiùs dici poterant. Cardo rei est, Hierarchiam rejecta doctrina Apostolica, qua Evangelium de Christo Salvatore unico, & veri Dei sanctè colendi ratio continetur, novum errorum capitalium corpus condidisse, fidem, quam Christo Domino suo intemeratam servare debuerat, & se servare verbis equidem profitetur, severéque pertendit, violasse denique in meritorium propudium, quod cruci veræ Christi valedicens, quæstum in mundo facere coccepit, & ipsam degenerasse, & ad eandem perfidiam populum sibi obnoxium venereo scilicet cestu suo, qui ad nationes ferocissimas subigendas, quàm veteris Romæ Martiale robur, efficacior fuit; seduxisse. IV. Capitales sedis Romanæ errores, quibus à verbo Dei, Christo & Evangelio ejus, & ipsa devia errat, & ad communem errorem alios secum abripit, ex triplici Papæ diademate, tripertiri commodè videmur in tyrannicos, idololatricos & Magicos. His enim fidei Apostolicæ & cultus unius ac solius veri Dei vis omnis resolvitur, depravatur & evertitur. Postremos illos, Magicos videlicet, seorsim explicabimus; tyrannicos in præsentiarum & idololatricos, auxiliante Domino, explicaturi, quantum instituto nostro satis erit.
units.tr: III. A vast field of things to be said would open up here. We shall touch on the chief points and gather them briefly, though they could have been discussed at greater length. The heart of the matter is that the Hierarchy, having rejected the apostolic doctrine, which contains the Gospel of Christ the sole Saviour and the way of rightly worshipping the true God, has founded a new body of capital errors. It has violated the faith that it ought to have kept inviolate for Christ its Lord, a faith it indeed professes in words and vigorously maintains. Finally, abandoning the cross of the true Christ, it began to make gain in the world by a shameful prostitution, thereby degenerating and seducing the people subject to it into the same faithlessness by its venereal allurement, which was more effective in subduing the fiercest nations than the martial strength of old Rome.

units.la: V. Errores ergo tyrannicos eos vocamus, quibus Hierar-
units.tr: V. We therefore call those errors tyrannical by which the Roman Hierarchy

units.la: Hierarchia Romana, tyranni instar, legitimi Domini jugum excutientis, & alienam potestatem invadentis usurpantisque, triplex Christi Mediatoris & Capitis nostri munus Propheticum, Sacerdotale & Regium impetit. Hoc ubi facere Hierarchiam Romanam demonstraverimus, non postrema Babylonicæ impietatis & fornicationis, qua falsam religionem falsumque cultum induci asseruimus, in propatulo erit. Nam characteres hi præcipui, & omnium clarissimi sunt, ex quibus de universa Hierarchiæ religione proclive judicium erit.
units.tr: The Roman Hierarchy, like a tyrant who shakes off the yoke of its lawful Lord and seizes and usurps another's power, assails the threefold office of Christ the Mediator and our Head: his prophetic, priestly and kingly office. When we have shown that the Roman Hierarchy does this, the chief part of the Babylonian impiety and fornication, by which we have asserted that a false religion and false worship are introduced, will be plain. For these are the principal marks, and the clearest of all, from which a ready judgment on the whole religion of the Hierarchy will be possible.

units.la: VI. Quoad munus Christi Propheticum, ut inde exordiar, satis constat, solum Christum Novi Testamenti Prophetam voce Mosis Deut. xviii. 18. ἀναστήσω, ante designatum, & Cœlesti voce, Hunc audite Matth. xvii. 5. proclamatum esse. Etenim Deum nemo vidit unquam. Unigenitus filius, qui est in gremio Patris, ille nobis edidit. Joh. i. 18. missus scilicet a Deo, ut verba Dei loqueretur, ib. cap. iii. 34. Dedit enim Deus הַמּוֹרֶה לִצְדָקָה Doctorem justitiæ, Joel. ii 23. & quidem docentem, ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων, ut potestatem habentem, non, uti scribæ solebant, Matth. vii. 29. Cumque Deus olim multis partibus, & multis modis locutus sit Patribus in Prophetis (per Spiritum scilicet ipsius etiam Magni illius Prophetæ, Christi ii. Pet. i. ii. iii. 18. 19. unde הַדָּבָר λαλῶν Loquentis & quidem τὴν ἀρχήν inde a principio nomine Esai. lii. 6. Joh. viii. 25. venit) in novissimis dierum locutus est in Filio, qui videlicet ceu λόγος verbum Dei caro factus est, & habitavit inter nos, plenus veritatis & gratiæ, Hebr. i. 1. Joh. i. 14. Ac Propheta ille Magnus in diebus quidem carnis suæ Apostolos, & una cum iis Ecclesiam docuit, non externo duntaxat affatu, & פֶּה אֶל פֶּה ore ad os; sed interiori inprimis vi
units.tr: VI. As to the prophetic office of Christ, to begin from there, it is well established that Christ alone was proclaimed the Prophet of the New Testament, first designated by the voice of Moses in Deut. 18:18 [ἀναστήσω, "I will raise up"], and then by the heavenly voice: "Hear him," Matt. 17:5. For no one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known to us, John 1:18, sent by God to speak the words of God, ibid. 3:34. For God gave him as the teacher of righteousness [הַמּוֹרֶה לִצְדָקָה], Joel 2:23, and indeed as one teaching "as one having authority" [ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων], not as the scribes used to, Matt. 7:29. Although God, having spoken of old in many parts and many ways to the fathers by the prophets (namely through the Spirit of that great Prophet himself, Christ, 1 Pet. 1:11, 3:18, 19, whence he came under the name of "the one speaking" [הַדָּבָר], Isa. 52:6, John 8:25, from the beginning [τὴν ἀρχήν]), in these last days has spoken in the Son, who, as the Word [λόγος], the Word of God, became flesh and dwelt among us, full of truth and grace, Heb. 1:1, John 1:14. That great Prophet, in the days of his flesh, taught the apostles and with them the Church, not only by outward speech, "mouth to mouth" [פֶּה אֶל פֶּה], but especially by an inward

units.la: ac potentia, qua apud animos hominum pollebat plurimum. Digrediens vero ex terris Ecclesiam orphanam non reliquit; sed reliquit eidem Spiritum suum ducem: dedit Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Pastores, Doctores, Joh. iv. 26. Ephef. iv. 11. הכבשרות Evangelizantium turbam magnam, Psal lxviii. 12. Horum erat testari de resurrectione Christi, Evangelium ex praescripto Domini sui praedicare in toto mundo, qua ore, qua scripto. Nam id ipsum, quod ore praedicârunt, inspiratione Divina nonnulli scribere debuerunt, ut Ecclesia Evangelium à Christo & Spiritu ejus dictatum in tabulis consignatum, adeóque invigilante pro verbo suo jugi Providentia Dei, ære fixo perennius haberet.
units.tr: and power by which he prevailed most among the minds of men. But departing from the earth, he did not leave the Church orphaned; he left his Spirit to it as its guide. He gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers, John 4:26, Eph. 4:11, [הכבשרות] "a great host of those who bring good tidings," Ps. 68:12. It was their task to bear witness to the resurrection of Christ and to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world according to the command of their Lord, both by word of mouth and in writing. For what they preached orally, some were bound by divine inspiration to write down, so that the Church might have the Gospel, dictated by Christ and his Spirit and recorded on tablets, more lasting than bronze, and thus under the ever-watchful providence of God for his word.

units.la: VII. Post Christi ergo in Cœlum ascensionem, & Apostolorum discessum, sic quidem Christus Magnus ille Propheta, intus Spiritus sui flexanima virtute corda hominum instruit, illuminat, flectit; ut tamen verbum ejus externum ἀξιόπιστον, verè Divinum, nisi in Scripturis nullum in mundo extet.
units.tr: VII. Therefore, after Christ's ascension into heaven and the departure of the apostles, Christ the great Prophet indeed instructs, enlightens and bends the hearts of men by the soul-moving power of his inner Spirit; yet in the world there exists no external word of his that is trustworthy [ἀξιόπιστον] and truly divine, except in the Scriptures.

units.la: Si quod enim extàret aliud, vel scriptum illud esset, vel non scriptum. Si scriptum, ubi illud extat? Si non scriptum, sed ore traditum, propagatum, vel illud idem est cum scripto, vel ab eo diversum. Si idem, omnis ergo revelatio Divina, omnis prophetia Christi in scriptura continetur. Si diversum, Dei igitur verbum non erit, tum quia in principii fidei, quod scripturis comprehenditur, virtute & foecunditate haud dubiè articuli fidei, qui copulativi sunt, continentur omnes: tum quia verbum scriptum sufficiens est instrumentum institutionis in rebus fidei & morum, neque adeò illi diversum quidquam addi potest, Deut. iv. 2. xii. 32. 1. Cor. iv. 6. Gal. 1. 8. Apoc. xxii. 17. Et quæ verbi Divini non scripti, sed à scripto diversi, & ore traditi propagatíque certitudo,
units.tr: For if there were any other, it would either be written or unwritten. If written, where is it? If unwritten, but handed down and propagated by word of mouth, then either it is the same as the written, or different from it. If the same, then all divine revelation and all prophecy of Christ is contained in Scripture. If different, it will not be the word of God, both because in the principles of faith, which are comprehended in the Scriptures, all the articles of faith, which are joined together, are undoubtedly contained in their power and fruitfulness; and because the written word is a sufficient instrument of instruction in matters of faith and morals, and nothing different from it can be added to it, Deut. 4:2, 12:32, 1 Cor. 4:6, Gal. 1:8, Rev. 22:17. And what certainty could there be of an unwritten divine word, different from the written and handed down by word of mouth,

units.la: Tom. II. quæ πληροφορία erit? Etenim notas certitudinis habet vel in se, vel in authentica aliqua norma. Non in se, quia manifestatione veritatis se conscientiæ omni hominum commendare nequit. Non in authentica norma, tum quia nullum habemus fidum ejus custodem, quomodo Scripturæ fidus comes est litera, pro qua Deus vigilaturum se recepit: tum quia recipit varietatem & contrarietatem: tum quia corruptioni obnoxium est, uti vel sola historia primorum temporum ante legem scriptam id evidenter ostendit.
units.tr: Vol. II. which would be full assurance [πληροφορία]? For it has marks of certainty either in itself or in some authentic norm. Not in itself, because by the manifestation of truth it cannot commend itself to the conscience of every man. Not in an authentic norm, both because we have no faithful guardian of it, as the letter is the faithful companion of Scripture, for which God has undertaken to watch; and because it admits variety and contrariety; and because it is liable to corruption, as the history of the earliest times before the written law alone clearly shows.

units.la: VIII. Neque tantùm in sola Scriptura omnis Christi prophetia, omne Dei verbum, omnis revelatio Divina continetur; verùm etiam eadem Christi prophetia & revelatio scripta sui ipsius in rebus dubiis interpres est, neque adeò ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως propriæ dissolutionis, interpretationis, 2.Pet.1.20. Nulla proin authoritas humana in mundo est, quæ Scripturam ex proprio motu, sine demonstratione sensus ex ipsa Scriptura infallibiliter interpretandi jus, charisma, potestatem sibi jure vendicare possit. Non tantùm enim Christus amandat ad Scripturas, non visibilem & infallibilem interpretem quenquam, Matth. xxii. 29. Luc. x. 26. Joh. v 39. Sed etiam Apostoli nulla habita proprii privilegii aut infallibilitatis ratione, non alium interpretem, quam Scripturam appellârunt, Act. xv. 6.7. &c. 2.Tim. iii.17. 2.Pet.i.19. 20. Cumque interpretatio, seu demonstratio genuini sensus Scripturæ ex Scriptura, sit Divinum charisma, liberè à Spiritu S. collatum, Ecclesiæ ad ædificationem Rom.xii.6.7.8. tyrannidem igitur exercet, & Spiritum Christi Propheticum in ordinem redigere conatur, quisquis eum ad coetum particularem, nedum unum hominem restringit, & talentum à Deo concessum in mercimonium spirituale erogari vetat. Quod nonnulli etiam in Tridentino Concilio Theologi, Cajetanum pro se allegantes, Suave Polano lib.11.138. teste, monuerunt.
units.tr: VIII. Nor is all the prophecy of Christ, all the word of God, all divine revelation contained in Scripture alone; the same prophecy and revelation of Christ, once written, is also its own interpreter in doubtful matters, and so has no [ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως] "private solution" or interpretation, 2 Pet. 1:20. Therefore there is no human authority in the world that can rightly claim for itself the right, gift or power of interpreting Scripture on its own initiative, without demonstrating the sense from Scripture itself with infallible certainty. For Christ not only sends us to the Scriptures, not to any visible and infallible interpreter, Matt. 22:29, Luke 10:26, John 5:39; but also the apostles, having no regard for any private privilege or infallibility, named no other interpreter than Scripture, Acts 15:6, 7, etc., 2 Tim. 3:17, 2 Pet. 1:19, 20. And since interpretation, or the demonstration of the genuine sense of Scripture from Scripture, is a divine gift freely bestowed by the Holy Spirit for the building up of the Church, Rom. 12:6, 7, 8, whoever restricts it to a particular assembly, let alone to one man, and forbids the talent given by God to be spent in spiritual trade, therefore exercises tyranny and seeks to bring the prophetic Spirit of Christ into subjection. Some theologians at the Council of Trent also warned of this, citing Cajetan in their favour, as Suave Polano testifies in book 11, p. 138.

units.la: IX. Consequens hinc est, contra Propheticum Christi munus aperto Marte insurgere, quisquis Scripturæ convitium facit, vel testandi authenticè officium ei eripere, & alió transferre conatur. Cujus sacrilegii ream esse Hierarchiam, pridem demonstratum est. Cui enim blasphemiæ ejus de verbi seu prophetiæ Christi sacris literis comprehensæ incertitudine, imperfectione & obscuritate: traditionum contra humanarum, ac verbi inprimis Papalis certitudine, perfectione & claritate, ignotæ sunt? Cui non dictus ille Hylas? Id unum quippe novi illi Papicolæ rerum satagunt, ut verbo & Prophetia Christi, quæ Sacris Scripturis continetur, veluti dubia, inerte, incerta & obscura, in ordinem redacta, Papæ verbum & Prophetia ἀὁηλος, tanquam fidei ac morum norma tutissima, ab omnibus acceptetur. Quod supra etiam, ubi de Regula & analysi fidei non uno loco actum est, demonstravimus.
units.tr: IX. It follows from this that whoever insults Scripture, or tries to take away from it the office of authentically bearing witness and transfer it elsewhere, openly makes war against the prophetic office of Christ. It has already been shown that the Hierarchy is guilty of this sacrilege. Who is not familiar with its blasphemies against the uncertainty, imperfection and obscurity of the word or prophecy of Christ contained in the holy letters, and against the certainty, perfection and clarity of human traditions, and above all of the Papal word? Who has not heard of that famous "Hylas"? These new Papal worshippers strive for one thing only: that the word and prophecy of Christ, contained in the Holy Scriptures, be reduced to the rank of something doubtful, inert, uncertain and obscure, while the word and prophecy of the Pope, [ἄδηλος] "manifest," be accepted by all as the safest norm of faith and morals. We have also shown this above, where the rule and analysis of faith were discussed in more than one place.

units.la: X. Ut strictius agamus, negat Hierarchia præfracte, Scripturæ, seu verbo scripto eam potentiam inesse, ut suam Divinitatem sensui hominum spirituali, sine Ecclesiæ, quæ unico tamen individuo constat, Papa videlicet, in quem omnis authoritas Ecclesiæ resolvitur, testimonio demonstrare valeat. Nota illa Eckii Enchir. sol.8. verba sunt: Scriptura non est authentica sine authoritate Ecclesiæ. Cui sententiæ ut verè aureæ ac nobili scilicet, in margine hic gratulantis ovantisque plausus adjicitur: Achilles pro Catholicis. Mitto Hermanni ac Hosii notas nimis blasphemias. Mitto horrendam glossematis illius turpissimi in Decretal. lib. 2. tit. 23. impietatem, quod Solomonis textum à canonizatione Papæ fidem suam mutuari docet. Quis non illos Divinitatis arbitros iis verbis compellaverit, quibus olim Tertullianus Apol. cap. 5. Ethnicos compellavit: Apud vos de humano arbitratu Divinitas pensitatur. Nisi homini Deus placuerit, Deus non erit. Homo jam Deo propitius esse debebit.
units.tr: X. To speak more strictly: the Hierarchy stubbornly denies that Scripture, or the written Word, has the power to demonstrate its own Divinity to the spiritual sense of men without the testimony of the Church, which nevertheless consists of a single individual, namely the Pope, into whom all the authority of the Church is resolved. Those are the well-known words of Eck's Enchiridion, chapter 8: "Scripture is not authentic without the authority of the Church." To this sentiment, truly golden and noble, the margin adds, in the manner of a triumphant and delighted round of applause: "Achilles for the Catholics." I pass over the notes of Hermann and Hosius, which are far too blasphemous. I pass over the horrible impiety of that most shameful gloss on the Decretals, book 2, title 23, which teaches that the text of Solomon borrows its faith from the canonization by the Pope. Who would not address those arbiters of Divinity with the words with which Tertullian once addressed the heathens (Apology, ch. 5): "Among you, Divinity is weighed by human judgment. Unless God is pleasing to man, God will not be. Man must now be made propitious to God."

units.la: XI. Quod est semen immortale 1. Pet. 1. 33. fecundissimum, Matth. xiii. 23. quod est ipsum Dei verbum vivum, efficax, & penetrantius quovis ancipiti gladio, Heb. iv. 12. quod est gladius, & quidem gladius Spiritus S. Ephes. vi. 17. quod est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti Rom. i. 16. quod est ipsum Dei brachium Esaj. liii. 1. id homines isti, vel ἄλογα potius ζῶα Jud. 10. nullam in se vim habere, sed sine vitali testimonio Ecclesiae, instar Alcorani, fabularum Æsopi, rami aridi, literae mortuae, navis sine remis, fundamenti arenosi, labyrinthi dubii (emblemata profecto Christianis auribus digna!) esse, dicere non erubescunt. Proh pudor! Proh scelus! Cicero singulos Euripidis versus singula vocat oracula. Idem Aristotelem aureum orationis flumen fundere testatur. Neutrum vidit, neutrum audivit; utriusque tamen scriptis non parum detulit. Isti vero sacras literas non tam aculeis, quam fulminibus adversus omnem impietatem instructas, nullam vim, potentiam nullam Divinitatem suam, sine testimonio Papae, demonstrandi habere calumniantur. Credunt Ecclesiae, vel potius Papae, nullo externo testimonio, nullis Divinitatis characteribus fidem sibi facienti. Verbo Dei scripto, sine externo testimonio humano, credere detrectant. Perinde facientes plane, ac si luna eo usque insolesceret, ut sibi potestatem arrogaret, in gratiam Solis testificandi, quod revera luceat; licet omnes, qui scotomate percussi non sunt, id videre possint, etiamsi luna sub horizonte delitesceret.
units.tr: XI. This is the "imperishable seed" (1 Pet. 1.33), "most fruitful" (Matth. 13.23), the very "living and effective word, and sharper than any two-edged sword" (Heb. 4.12), the "sword", and indeed "the sword of the Holy Spirit" (Eph. 6.17), the "power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes" (Rom. 1.16), the very "arm of God" (Isa. 53.1). These men, or rather "unreasoning animals" [ἄλογα ζῶα] (Jude 10), are not ashamed to say that it has no power in itself, but that without the living testimony of the Church it is like the Alcoran, the fables of Aesop, a dry branch, a dead letter, a ship without oars, a sandy foundation, a doubtful labyrinth (emblems indeed worthy of Christian ears!). Shame! Outrage! Cicero calls each single verse of Euripides an oracle, and he testifies that Aristotle pours forth a golden river of speech. Cicero saw neither of them and heard neither of them, yet he drew not a little from their writings. But these men slander the sacred letters, armed not so much with darts as with thunderbolts against all impiety, as having no power or strength to demonstrate their Divinity without the testimony of the Pope. They believe in the Church, or rather in the Pope, which gives faith to itself by no external testimony and no marks of Divinity. They refuse to believe the written Word of God without external human testimony. They act just as if the moon were so arrogant as to claim for itself the power of bearing witness, for the sake of the Sun, that it really shines, though all who are not struck with a scotoma can see it even when the moon is hidden below the horizon.

units.la: XII. Quaenam vero Ecclesia, seu quis potius Papa ille, Ecclesiae prora & puppis est, à cujus nutu & authoritate Scripturae Divinitas pendet? Non quaevis sane,
units.tr: XII. But which Church, or rather which Pope, is that prow and stern of the Church on whose nod and authority the Divinity of Scripture depends? Certainly not just any Church,

units.la: non Apostolica; non eæ, quæ primitus libros Divinos sibi traditos receperunt. Præsens est, inquiunt illi, præsens est. Sic plane Bellarminus, qui de num. & effect. Sacram. lib. 11. 15 septenarium Sacramentorum numerum Concilii Tridentini authoritate (hæc enim illis ἰεσὰ ἀγκύρεα est) suffulturus; Omnium, inquit, Conciliorum veterum, & omnium dogmatum firmitas pendet ab authoritate præsentis Ecclesiæ. Paulo ante: Si tollamus authoritatem præsentis Ecclesiæ, & præsentis Concilii; in dubium revocari poterunt omnium aliorum Conciliorum decreta, & tota fides Christiana. Ain vero, tota fides Christiana, dogmata omnia? Adeoque etiam, quæ digito Dei exarata, à Spiritu S. dictata sunt? Neque ea Divina erunt, nisi præsens Ecclesia, hoc est, Innocentius XI. qui, incertum est, an Biblia unquam legerit, (saltem non Scripturæ peritia, sed aleæ jactus aliquis fortunatior Cardinalem, adeoque etiam Pontificem scisse fertur) Divina esse affirmaverit? Nam si negaverit, de Scripturæ Divinitate, de dogmatum Christianæ fidei authoritate actum erit. Quid hoc aliud est, quàm Deum ipsum impuris hominibus emancipare, humanóque tribunali Cœli fabricatorem sistere? Quid aliud, quàm Christo Prophetæ exauctorato, & ad silentium damnato, Papam Prophetam, magnum certè Pseudo-prophetam substituere? Deus erit Deus, erit, quæ est Dei, Scriptura, quantumlibet reclamantibus Roma, Tridento, Orco.
units.tr: not the Apostolic one, nor those which first received the divine books entrusted to them. "It is present," they say, "it is present." So plainly says Bellarmine, who, in his work On the Number and Effect of the Sacraments (lib. 11, c. 15), seeks to support the septenary number of the sacraments by the authority of the Council of Trent (for this is their "sacred anchor" [ἰεσὰ ἀγκύρεα]). "The firmness of all the ancient councils and of all doctrines," he says, "depends on the authority of the present Church." A little before: "If we remove the authority of the present Church and of the present Council, the decrees of all other councils, and the whole Christian faith, may be called into doubt." Say, "the whole Christian faith, all doctrines"? And so even those things which were written with the finger of God and dictated by the Holy Spirit? Those will not be divine unless the present Church, that is, Innocent XI, affirms them to be divine. It is uncertain whether he has ever read the Bible (at any rate he is said to have known nothing of Scripture by skill, but to have been advanced to the cardinalate, and thus also to the Papacy, by some lucky throw of the dice). For if he were to deny it, the Divinity of Scripture and the authority of the doctrines of the Christian faith would be at an end. What is this other than to hand God himself over to impure men, and to set the Maker of heaven before a human tribunal? What is it other than to dismiss Christ the Prophet from his office, condemn him to silence, and put in his place the Pope as prophet, a great pseudo-prophet indeed? God will be God; what belongs to God, Scripture, will remain, however much Rome, Trent and Hell may protest.

units.la: XIII. Sed & hastam suam in Christum Prophetam
units.tr: XIII. But they also hurl their spear at Christ the Prophet

units.la: minaciter satis conjiciunt, eadem scilicet critica Divinitatis licentia Canonem ejus verbi scripti figentes, refigentes, & ei pro Papali authoritate sua inserentes libros velut Divinos, qui humana industria scripti sunt. Quis sic ferat ὑπόβλημα ῥάκος ἀγνάφῳ panno veteri adsui? Quid hinc nisi χεῖρον σχίσμα ruptura pejor? Quis ferat, ut contra Hebræorum fidelium, Christi Apostolorum, Concilii Laodiceni vetustissimi, Melitonis, Cyrilli, Athanasii, Origenis, Hilarii, Hieronymi, Rufini, Nazianzeni fidem & clarissima testimonia, contra testes medioxumos, nuperósque vel suos; sex integri libri, sub anathematis poena, Deo ipsi, Christo Prophetæ unico, ejusque Ecclesiæ à Tridentinis Paterculis, iisque primis imperiosius obtrudantur? Neque illis Divinitatis trutinatoribus obstabat, quòd aliqui magicas præstigias, alii ἀνηφονίας, mendaces planè fabulas alii, alii ritus Ethnicos, alii denique crudelia facinora, non sine publico quodam applausu lectoribus suis propinant. A doctoribus talibus quæ fides, qui mores disci imbibique possunt? Quod igitur olim Chius ille servus de Domino suo vinum vendente aliis, & vappam epotante dixit; Cùm adsunt bona, quærunt mala; id nos de infelicibus illis Divinitatis arbitris, dixerimus merito. Cùm enim adest Christi sermo Propheticus firmissimus, illi pro fœcibus & vappis hisce, velut pro aris & focis suis dimicare, & Deo Cœli, fœtus ingenii humani supponere non desinunt. Quid quod Canoni etiam antiquo decus omne detraxerunt pridem, utpote quem libidini Papæ, in quem, velut supremum Numen, Papistarum fides omnis, uti supra ostendimus, resolvitur, subjicere pensi nil habuere, nec habent adhuc.
units.tr: quite threateningly, with the same critical licence over the Divinity of the Word, fixing, re-fixing and inserting into its canon, by the authority of the Pope, books written by human industry as though they were divine. Who could bear such a patch of raw cloth sewn onto an old garment? What follows from this but a rent worse than the tear? Who could bear that, against the faith and clearest testimonies of the faithful Hebrews, the Apostles of Christ, the most ancient Council of Laodicea, Melito, Cyril, Athanasius, Origen, Hilary, Jerome, Rufinus and Nazianzen, against witnesses of the middle ages and recent times, or even their own, six entire books are forced on the Church more imperiously, under penalty of anathema, by the Tridentine Fathers (and those the most recent), as though they were God himself, Christ the sole Prophet and his Church? Nor did it hinder these weighers of Divinity that some present magical tricks, others the slaughter of men, others wholly fabulous lies, others heathen rites, and others finally cruel deeds, to their readers, not without a certain public applause. What faith, what morals can be learned and imbibed from such teachers? Therefore what that Chian slave once said of his master, who sold wine to others and drank the sour dregs himself, "When good things are at hand, they seek bad things," we may rightly say of those unhappy arbiters of Divinity. For when the most firm prophetic word of Christ is at hand, they do not cease to fight for these dregs and sour wine as though for their altars and hearths, and to set the products of human wit beneath the God of heaven. Why speak of how they have long since stripped even the ancient Canon of all its honour, since they have never thought it worth while, nor do they yet think so, to subject it to the lust of the Pope, into whom, as into a supreme Deity, the whole faith of the Papists is resolved, as we have shown above?

units.la: XIV. Neque Hierarchici, eorum, quæ scripta sunt inspiratione Divina, authoritatem suffodere, & quæ authore Deo scripta non sunt, Deo affingere, satis habent. Nam & scriptorum Deo authore sufficientiam lacessere audent, præcipientes scilicet, ut Traditiones cum ipsis Scripturarum libris pari pietatis affectu, pari veneratione suscipiantur. Ita Tridentini sanxere: ita Hierarchici uno ore omnes sustinent. Sunt quædam res mediæ, ritus adiaphori, in quibus aliquid Ecclesiæ traditiones vavalent. Quæ verò ad salutem scitu vel factu simpliciter necessaria sunt, ea vel per verba, vel per sensum in S. Scripturis non reperiri, merito quidem ἀθεόλογον vel iis, quæ supra recitavimus, aliisque argumentis inducti, censemus. Διαπυρώτες quædam publici ordinis ergo ab Ecclesia sunt: atque ὄφει quique necessarii ab unius foliúsque Dei voce petendi sunt. Lex Domini & perfecta est, & perfectum facit 2 Tim. iii. 17. Quid verò persecto addi potest? Aut quæ perfectio, ubi necessarium deest? Male sic edoctus, male locutus fuerit Constantinus M. cui tamen nemo Heroum illorum Tridentinorum vel aurem tetigit, dum ait: Evangelici & Apostolici libri, nec non antiquorum Prophetarum oracula plane instruunt nos sensu Numinis. Neque S. Patres ullam aliam fidei regulam aut agnoverunt, aut viderunt unquam. Putabimusne autem, vel invidisse humano generi Deum plenariam hanc voluntatis suæ perpetuis literarum monumentis consignationem; vel minus expedire censuisse, in communi illo veritatum conclavi (uti Roffensis appellat) necessaria quæque reponi; vel incertius esse, quòd literis fideliter mandamus, quàm quod vagis hominum rumoribus circumgestari, & æreo hoc flatu ad sera nepotum secula derivari solet? Hoc videlicet est, ut cum Irenæo lib. ii. 1. loquamur, Prophetarum, & Domini & Apostolorum relinquere vocem, & attendere nihil sani garrientibus. Cúmque Tridentini primi traditiones sine scripto recipiendas esse decreverint, neque tamen, quæ traditiones illæ sint, ubi reperiantur, & quomodo à falsis discernantur, quísve eorum sit numerus, definiverint, quæ alia fallacis & dolosæ hujus generalitatis crypsis esse potuit, quàm ut prætensa traditione Pseudo-propheta hic tueri possit, quicquid à vero Propheta Christo scriptum & præscriptum nuspiam est?
units.tr: XIV. Nor are the Hierarchs content to undermine the authority of those things which were written by divine inspiration and to attribute to God what was not written by God. For they dare also to attack the sufficiency of the writers who had God as author, prescribing, of course, that traditions be received with the same feeling of piety and the same reverence as the very books of Scripture. This the Tridentines decreed; this the Hierarchs all uphold with one voice. There are some matters indifferent, and rites adiaphorous, in which the traditions of the Church may have some value. But as for those things which are simply necessary to salvation, whether to know or to do, that they are not found in the Holy Scriptures, either in words or in sense, we judge rightly to be "godless" [ἀθεόλογον], led both by the arguments we have already recited and by others. Certain things "burning" [Διαπυρώτες] are indeed for the sake of public order, set by the Church; but whatever things are necessary "for help" [ὄφει] must be sought from the voice of the one and only God. "The law of the Lord is both perfect and makes perfect" (2 Tim. 3.17). But what can be added to the perfect? Or what perfection is there where something necessary is lacking? Constantine the Great was ill taught and spoke ill when he said, "The Gospel and Apostolic books, and also the oracles of the ancient Prophets, fully instruct us in the sense of the Deity," yet none of those Tridentine heroes so much as touched his ear with it. Nor did the Holy Fathers ever acknowledge or see any other rule of faith. But shall we think either that God envied mankind this full declaration of his will, consigned in perpetual written monuments, or that he judged it less expedient to store up in that common chamber of truths (as Rochester calls it) all things necessary; or that what we faithfully commit to letters is less certain than what is usually carried about by the vague rumours of men and handed down by this bronze breath to the late ages of our descendants? This, namely, is to speak with Irenaeus (book 2, ch. 1), to abandon the voice of the Prophets, the Lord and the Apostles, and to pay attention to those who babble nothing sound. And since the first Tridentines decreed that "traditions are to be received without writing," but did not define what those traditions are, where they are to be found, how they are to be distinguished from false ones, or what their number is, what other hiding-place of this deceitful and treacherous generality could there be, except that under the pretext of tradition this pseudo-prophet may defend whatever has nowhere been written or prescribed by the true Prophet, Christ?

units.la: XV. Neque levis adversus verbum Christi Propheticum scripto consignatum injuria est, quòd ejus versionem Latinam, eamque corruptissimam, authenticam definire, adeóque Augustissimis fontibus praeferre; quod non est χρύσεα χαλκέων, sed Divinis humana anteferre; Tridentini nulli dubitárunt. Etenim cùm Latina illa vulgata nec ἀυπήτιτος fit, sed humano studio adornata; nec ἀρχέτυπος, sed versio; neque fons, sed rivulus; etiamsi purissima versionum omnium esset (qualis tamen hodie habetur, forte impurissima omnium est) authentica esse non posset. Dixerat jam olim Cajetanus, & in Synodo Tridentina Catanæus repetierat, intelligere versionem Latinam, non esse intelligere verbum Dei, sed vocem Interpretis erroribus obnoxiam. Clarissimè quin etiam Isidorus Clarius Brixianus, Abbas Benedictinus asseverare solebat: nullam translationem cum sacri contextus lingua originali æquiparandam esse. Et Hebræos fontes, Græcos rivos, Latinos paludes bibere, scitè Reuchlinus, Hieronymi vestigia premens, dixit. Sed authenticam tamen Vulgatam, novitius ille Propheta declaravit, tum quia veritus est, ne non satis λατεινος Latinus videretur, nisi versionem Latinam, quàm plurimis vitiis scatentem, quam Hieronymus ipse non agnosceret amplius fontibus purissimis praetulisset: tum quia cùm Propheticum Christi verbum planè è medio tollere non potuit, adulterandum saltem, pro meretricia & Babylonica impietate sua putavit, Hebræo Veteris, & Græco Novi Testamenti Codici ruinam moliendo, quò sic Lydius versionum lapis, & cum eo certitudo Scripturæ funditus periret. Taceo causas alias hujus decreti parùm certè honestas, quas Suave Polanus Hist. Concil. Trident. lib. 11. p. 132. ex sententia cordatiorum fusiùs recitat.
units.tr: XV. It is also no small wrong against the prophetic Word of Christ, set down in writing, that the Tridentine fathers did not hesitate to declare the Latin version, and that a very corrupt one, authentic, and so to prefer it to the most venerable sources. This is not gold for bronze, but human things put before divine. The Latin Vulgate is not uncreated [ἀχειροποίητος] but made with human effort; it is not the archetype but a translation; it is not the spring but a stream. Even if it were the purest of all versions (though it is held to be today, perhaps it is the most impure of all), it could not be authentic. Cajetan had already said so long ago, and Catharinus repeated it at the Council of Trent: to understand the Latin version is not to understand the Word of God, but the voice of a translator liable to error. Isidorus Clarius of Brescia, a Benedictine abbot, used to assert very plainly: no translation can be equated with the original language of the sacred text. And Reuchlin, treading in the footsteps of Jerome, aptly said that the Hebrew sources are drunk, the Greek streams, and the Latin marshes. Yet that novice prophet declared the Vulgate authentic, partly because he feared that he would not seem Latin enough [λατεινος] unless he preferred a Latin version, teeming with so many faults, which Jerome himself would no longer have acknowledged, to the purest sources. And partly because, though he could not wholly remove the prophetic Word of Christ, he thought at least that it might be corrupted, in keeping with his harlot-like and Babylonian impiety, by undermining the Hebrew codex of the Old Testament and the Greek codex of the New, so that the Lydian touchstone of versions, and with it the certainty of Scripture, would perish utterly. I pass over the other causes of this decree, which are scarcely honourable, and which Paolo Sarpi (Suave Polanus) recounts at length from the judgement of the more sensible men, Hist. Concil. Trident. lib. 11, p. 132.

units.la: XVI. Cùm tamen ne sic quidem Scripturam, verbum Christi Propheticum, pessumdare Pseudopropheta posset, alia id via tentare aggressus, ejus interpretationem & sensum, qui verbi Divini anima est, sui arbitrii, suaeque potestatis facere totum conatus est. Quod ubi semel obtinuisset, jam utique verbum Dei, quod non in verborum corticibus, sed in sensus medulla consistit, sic debellaverat, ut nihil ex eo amplius extimescendum fuisset. Proclive enim fuerat cuique verbo sensum aptare, qui humanæ ejus libidini inserviret. Sic ergo Tridentina Synodus Seff. iv. decr. de usu librorum Sacrorum definit: Præterea ad coercenda petulantia ingenia decernit, ut nemo, suæ prudentiæ innixus, in rebus fidei & morum, ad ædificationem doctrinæ Christianæ pertinentium, Sacram Scripturam ad suos sensus contorquens, contra sensum, quem tenuit & tenet Sancta mater Ecclesia, cujus est judicare de vero sensu Scripturarum Sanctarum, aut etiam contra unanimem consensum Patrum, ipsam Scripturam Sanctam interpretari audeat.
units.tr: XVI. Yet even so the pseudo-prophet could not overthrow Scripture, the prophetic Word of Christ, so he set about attempting it by another way: he has tried to make its interpretation and sense, which is the soul of the divine word, subject to his own will and power. Once he had gained this, he had indeed so crushed the word of God, which lies not in the husks of words but in the marrow of the sense, that nothing more was to be feared from it. For it was easy for anyone to fit a sense to the word that would serve his human lust. Thus the Synod of Trent, Sess. IV, decree on the use of the sacred books, decides: Moreover, to restrain restless wits, it decrees that no one, relying on his own prudence, shall presume to interpret Sacred Scripture in matters of faith and morals pertaining to the building up of Christian doctrine, twisting Sacred Scripture to his own senses, against the sense which holy mother Church has held and holds, to whom it belongs to judge of the true sense of the Holy Scriptures, or even against the unanimous consent of the Fathers.

units.la: Corrupt line continues below. Qui contra venerint, per ordinarios declarentur, & pœnis à jure statutis puniantur. Per Sanctam Matrem Ecclesiam intelligit particularem Romanam, quam penes sic collocat jus supremum interpretandi Scripturas, ut ab ea nulla sit appellatio, ne quidem ad Scripturam ipsam. Et quamvis hic quatuor soleant erigere tribunalia, Ecclesiæ, Conciliorum, Patrum & Papæ, tamen subduētis ritè calculis solus restat Papa, seu privatus & Enthusiasticus Spiritus Papæ, qui dicis gratia Scripturam admittit, ut regulam, sed partialem, & ad nutum suum applicandam, flectendam, torquendámque.
units.tr: Those who act against this shall be declared by the ordinaries and punished with penalties established by law. By holy mother Church it means the particular Roman Church, in whose hands it places the supreme right of interpreting Scripture, so that there is no appeal from her, not even to Scripture itself. And although here they are wont to set up four tribunals, of the Church, of the Councils, of the Fathers and of the Pope, yet when the reckonings are duly cast up, only the Pope remains, or rather the private and enthusiastic spirit of the Pope, who admits Scripture as a rule for show, but a partial one, to be applied, bent and twisted at his nod.

units.la: XVII. Cùm verò interpretatio Scripturæ ex ipsa Scriptura, non voluntate, seu placito hominis peti debeat, nec fides nostra innitatur dicto hominum sua natura mendacium, adeóque caducum in parietem inclinet; atque insuper sit donum Dei, liberè à Spiritu S.
units.tr: XVII. But since the interpretation of Scripture must be sought from Scripture itself, not from the will or pleasure of man, and since our faith rests not on the word of men, which by nature is a lie and so leans toward a falling wall; and since, moreover, it is a gift of God, freely given by the Holy Spirit

units.la: Tom. II. c collacollatum ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ, Rom. xii. 6. 7. 8. tyrannidem ergo exercuit Synodus illa, & Spiritum S. liberásque ejus operationes in ordinem redigere ausa & interpretationem Scripturæ ad cœtum particularem Hierarchicum, imò hominem unum, Papam, contrahens; eique ejusmodi interpretandi privilegium impertiens ut nudè afferenti, dicantí, quem voluerit, sensum ; non demonstranti ex ipsa Scriptura, acquiescere omnis hominum fides & conscientia teneatur.
units.tr: to build up the Church (Rom. 12:6-8). That synod therefore exercised tyranny, and dared to bring the Holy Spirit and his free operations into order, and to bind the interpretation of Scripture to a particular hierarchical body, indeed to one man, the Pope, granting him the privilege of interpreting in such a way that all human faith and conscience must rest on what he merely asserts, saying whatever sense he pleases, without demonstrating it from Scripture itself. (Tom. II.)

units.la: XVIII. Profecto venditatum hujusmodi facultatis prophetandi monopolium Spiritus propheticilibertati, quæ Christi æternæ Dei Sapientiæ, donum est, è diametro repugnat. Nam Spiritus S donis omnem commeatum intercludit. Cùm tamen non aliunde Spiritus Dei liberè revelans & operans, nisi ex impuro & polluto corde, nisi ex animo peccandi consuetudini devincto excludatur, adeò ut penes Dynaftem nullum sit, eum sibi soli quasi addictum & circumscriptum mancipare. Liberior ergo est, quàm ut ad cathedram illam unius hominis alligari se patiatur: purior, quàm ut cum cathedra illa pestilentiæ commercium habeat.
units.tr: XVIII. Certainly the monopoly of this kind of prophesying faculty, pedalled about, is diametrically opposed to the liberty of the prophetic Spirit, which is a gift of Christ, the eternal Wisdom of God. For the Holy Spirit cuts off every passage to his gifts. Yet the Spirit of God, speaking and working freely, is excluded only by an impure and polluted heart, by a mind bound to the habit of sinning; so that it is not in the power of any dynast to take possession of him, as if he were made over and confined to himself alone. He is therefore too free to allow himself to be bound to that chair of one man, and too pure to have any dealings with that chair of pestilence.

units.la: XIX. Vera etenim Dei cognitio, verus de Numine sensus, vera Scripturæ intelligentia unius aut familiæ, aut gentis, aut sectæ propria esse nequit; sed quisquis sensu immortalitatis tangitur, & salutis suæ desiderio æstuat, ad se eandem pertinere, existimare debet. Poterat quidem Judæorum gens circumcisionem externam, Aaronis familia Sacerdotium, alias ceremonias sibi jure quodam vendicare. Sed Spiritus S. operationem & revelationem, Divinam & internam circumcisionem, vivas illas animi verásque hostias, æternas naturæ leges, quas in hominum animis Deus Optimus Maximus à principio insculpsit, omnium Mortalium sententiis comprobatas, sibi nec Judæi, nec Græci, nec Romani, nec ulla Natio ulla, nedum unus homo, quasi peculiaria vendicare potuerunt. Quomodo ergo summam quasi religionis hæreditariam ad unum aliquem sic venisse, ut pro libidine sua ipsummet Dei verbum, & notiones rationi humanæ insitas interpretari, addere, demere, mutare, statuere, abrogare possit, induci nos, ut credamus, patiamur? Neque enim iccirco leges Divinæ latæ, religio patefacta est, ut in eam Mortales jus ullum haberent, sed ut omni studio, cura, labore, diligentia pro se quisque annitatur, ut eam intelligat, colat, ejusque dignitatem tueatur.
units.tr: XIX. For the true knowledge of God, the true sense of the Deity, and the true understanding of Scripture cannot be the property of one man, or of a family, or of a nation, or of a sect. Rather, whoever is touched by a sense of immortality and burns with desire for his own salvation ought to think that it pertains to him as well. The Jewish nation could indeed claim for itself by a certain right the outward circumcision, the family of Aaron the priesthood, and other ceremonies. But the operation and revelation of the Holy Spirit, the divine and inward circumcision, those living sacrifices of the soul and true offerings, the eternal laws of nature which the best and greatest God engraved in the minds of men from the beginning, approved by the judgement of all mortals, these neither Jews, nor Greeks, nor Romans, nor any nation whatever, much less one man, could claim as peculiarly theirs. How then are we to be induced, or to allow ourselves to be induced, to believe that the chief inheritance of religion has come to one man in such a way that he can at his pleasure interpret, add, remove, change, establish or abrogate the very word of God and the notions implanted in human reason? For the divine laws were not given, nor religion revealed, so that mortals should have any right over them; rather, that each one should strive with all zeal, care, labour and diligence to understand it, to honour it, and to defend its dignity.

units.la: XX. Neque sic plus Spiritui privato, uti Pseudo propheta criminari solet, quàm Ecclesiæ tribuimus; sed Scripturæ intelligentiam ex demonstratione ipsius Scripturæ merè humano testimonio & arbitrio, sive unius, qualis Papa est, sive plurium, quicunque illi sint, & quocunque se nomine insigniant, præferimus. Quid enim, si Ecclesia, hoc est, jurato quodam cœtu, vel Papa aliud agente, privati illi, quos Tridentini petulantia ingenia petulanter appellant, in loci alicujus dubii interpretatione analogiam fidei sequantur? Quid si Scripturam per ipsam Scripturam locum obscuriorem per illustriorem interpretentur, adhuc ne plus tribuendum erit Papæ, non demonstrare quicquam, sed dictare, & placita sua ἀβαπτιστως recipienda obtrudere solito, quàm privatis illis? Utri Deo gratiores esse possunt, illine insolentes, qui Scripturam ἀυτόπνευστον de gradu authoritatis suæ dimovent, & fidem, quam voluerint, thrasonicè dictant: an verò pauperes & contriti spiritu, qui ad verbum Dei trepidant, qui S. literas honorificè tractant, & earum, invocato Numine, sensum studiosè indagant? Humiles enim isti Christi sunt oviculæ, quæ vocem Pastoris sui audiunt Joh. x. 27: parvuli ἐυδοχίας, quibus detecta Matth. xi. 25. & discipuli, quibus datum est nôsse mysteria Regni Cœlorum, Matth. xiii. 11. Hi critici sunt sacri, qui stylum Scripturæ noverunt optimè. Hinc adeò Gerson, Cancellarius Parisiensis, æquiorem se laicis & privatis illis præbens, Par. 1 de Exam. doctr. confid. 5. & 6. statuit, homini simplici, non authorisato, ut ipse loquitur, excellenter tamen in Scripturis versato, Evangelicam veritatem proponenti plus credendum esse, quàm Papæ vel Concilio, ex malitia vel ignorantia erranti. Neque præterea Spiritus ille fidei, qui singulis fidelibus datur, & judicio tum externo Scripturæ, tum interno Spiritus S. nititur, est privatus, sed publicus utique, & toti fidelium Ecclesiæ communis, adeóque quoad manifestationem veritatis, & donum fidei is ipse, quem habuerunt sancti homines, per quos Deus locutus est. Est enim Spiritus Dei, qui in Christo & toto ejus corpore, singulisque ejus membris agit, etsi diversa mensura, 1. Cor. 11. 12. Ephes. 1. 13 Sic revera Deus & Spiritus unus est Gal. 111. 20. 28. 1. Joh. 11. 27. qui eodem modo fidem operatur in omnibus.
units.tr: XX. Nor do we ascribe more to the private spirit, as the pseudo-prophet is wont to accuse us, than we ascribe to the Church; but we prefer the understanding of Scripture drawn from the demonstration of Scripture itself to a merely human testimony and judgement, whether of one man, such as the Pope, or of many, whoever they may be and whatever name they bear. For what if the Church, that is, some sworn assembly, or the Pope acting otherwise, or those private persons whom the Tridentine fathers wantonly call restless wits, follow the analogy of faith in the interpretation of some doubtful passage? What if they interpret the more obscure place by the clearer through Scripture itself: must more still be granted to the Pope, who is wont not to demonstrate anything but to dictate, and to force upon us his own decrees to be received [ἀβαπτίστως] without examination, than to those private persons? Which of them can be more pleasing to God: those insolent men who remove Scripture, which is inspired by God [αὐτόπνευστον], from the level of its authority and boastfully dictate whatever faith they like; or the poor and contrite in spirit, who tremble at the word of God, who handle the holy letters with reverence, and who diligently search out their sense, calling upon the divine power? For these humble ones are the little sheep of Christ, who hear the voice of their Shepherd (John 10:27); the little ones of good pleasure, to whom things are revealed (Matt. 11:25), and the disciples to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 13:11). These are the sacred critics who know the style of Scripture best. Hence Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, showing himself fairer to laymen and private persons, Par. 1 de Exam. doctr., confid. 5 and 6, decided that more credit is to be given to a simple man, not authorised (as he himself puts it), yet excellently versed in the Scriptures, who sets forth the Evangelical truth, than to the Pope or a Council that errs through malice or ignorance. Moreover, that spirit of faith which is given to each of the faithful, and rests both on the external judgement of Scripture and on the internal witness of the Holy Spirit, is not private but certainly public, common to the whole Church of the faithful; and so, as regards the manifestation of truth and the gift of faith, it is the very same that the holy men had, through whom God spoke. For it is the Spirit of God who works in Christ and in his whole body and in each of its members, though in different measure (1 Cor. 12; Eph. 1:13). Thus indeed God and the Spirit are one (Gal. 3:20, 28; 1 John 2:27), who works faith in the same way in all.

units.la: XXI. Quisquis Scripturæ authentice interpretandi jus sibi arrogat, infallibilitatis dote instructus sit opor- tet.
units.tr: XXI. Whoever claims for himself the right to interpret Scripture authoritatively must be endowed with the gift of infallibility.

units.la: Credendum enim ei est simpliciter, sine demonstratione alia, dictanti, definienti, proponenti. Fides autem non nisi infallibili teste nititur. Jam ergo Papæ, novo Prophetæ, uni scilicet solique authentico Scripturæ Interpreti, judicii quandam impeccantiam, detur venia Tertulliani verbo, adeóque infallibilitatem tribuere debuerunt. Tribuerunt post Concilium Tridentinum maximè. Tribuerunt Jesuitæ præ cæteris, neque in quæstionibus duntaxat juris, sed facti etiam. Cujus utriusque infallibilitatem inter articulos fidei Catholicæ referunt, ut in Historia Papatus, & supra quoque Differt. VIII. sect. 2. th. 34 &c. fusius narravimus. Memoratu certè digna sunt illa Gregorii de Valentia Anal. fid. fid. lib. 8. de vi & usu auctor. R. Pontif. in fide quaest. 6. verba: Respondeo, sive Pontifex in definiendo studium adhibeat, sive non adhibeat, modo tamen controversiam definiat, infallibiliter certò definiet, atque adeò reipsa utetur authoritate sibi à Christo concessa. Addit statim: Eadem fide credere debemus, illum, quando rem controversam definit, sufficientem adhibuisse diligentiam. Egregiè profecto! Dummodo dixisse, definivisse Papam aliquid constet, satis erit. Caeca fide amplectendum id omne est. Imò eo ipso, quòd dixit, definivit, diligentiam adhibuisse omnem censeri debet. Et si maximè non adhibuisset, dixisse, definivisse ad fidem sufficit. Nam Pythagoras est, ἀντὶ ἐφα. Quis contra mussitare ausit? Helena haec est, quam usque adeo delicatam habent Transalpini, ut eam sibi eripi passuri sint nunquam. Nullus Romanae fidei nunc apiculus, interpretatio nulla est, quin ab hoc ἀπλανείας Principio pendeat. Tuti jam plane sunt Hierarchici, neque verbi Divini Prophetiae. Christi religio eos abstterrere poterit, quò minùs quidvis ex animi sui sententia etiam sine cura & studio omni uti Valentia innuit, dicant, doceant, definiant. Novis articulis fidei nova norma, Statera nova debebantur. Lucifugae ergo Scripturarum monetam suam novam eorum, qui eam cuderunt, staterae dolosae sisterre, & pro eadem, ceu infallibili tanquam pro aris & focis suis propugnare non desinunt.
units.tr: One must believe such a man simply, without any further proof, when he dictates, defines and proposes. But faith rests on nothing except an infallible witness. Therefore the Pope, the new prophet, the one and only authentic interpreter of Scripture, ought to be granted a certain freedom from error in judgment (to use Tertullian's word), and so should be credited with infallibility. They have credited him with it, especially since the Council of Trent. The Jesuits have credited him with it above all others, and not only in questions of law but of fact as well. They count the infallibility of both among the articles of Catholic faith, as I have related more fully in the History of the Papacy, and also above in Dissertation VIII, section 2, thesis 34 etc. The words of Gregory de Valentia are certainly worth remembering, in Analysis of the Faith, book 8, on the power and use of the authority of the Roman Pontiff, question 6: I answer that whether the Pontiff applies diligence in defining or does not, provided he defines a controversy, he will define infallibly and with certainty, and so in fact he uses the authority granted to him by Christ. He adds at once: We must believe with the same faith that, when he defines a disputed matter, he has applied sufficient diligence. Admirable indeed! It is enough that it be established that the Pope has said or defined something. All of it must be embraced with blind faith. Indeed, from the very fact that he said or defined it, he ought to be considered to have applied all diligence. And even if he had applied none at all, that he said or defined it is enough for faith. For it is a case of ipse dixit [ἀντὶ ἐφα], as Pythagoras' followers said. Who would dare to mutter against it? This is the Helen whom the Transalpines hold so dear that they will never let her be snatched from them. There is now no scrap of Roman faith, no interpretation at all, that does not hang on this principle of infallibility [ἀπλανείας]. The hierarchs are now quite safe, and need not fear the prophecies of the Word of God. The religion of Christ can no longer frighten them from saying, teaching and defining whatever they please, as Valentia hints, without any care or study at all (omni). New articles of faith demanded a new rule, a new balance. So these enemies of the light of Scripture keep presenting their new coin, struck by those who minted it, to the deceitful balance, and they never cease to defend it as if it were infallible, as they would their altars and hearths.

units.la: XXII. Hanc vero infallibilitatis dotem à Cathe- dra S. Petri, stabili adeò, aeterna, plena prodigiosae virtutis arcessunt.
units.tr: XXII. They derive this gift of infallibility from the Chair of St Peter, which they hold to be so firm, eternal and full of prodigious power.

units.la: Olim quidem tabulae manu exaratae statim confractae perierunt. At cathedrae Petri tabulae aetatem non sentiunt, è quercu forte Hibernica dolatae, quam nulla tangit erroris aranea, quin occidat ilico. Vibius profecto Rufus redivivus hic nobis videtur, qui Xiphilino in Epitome, & Dione in Tiberio testibus, in sella semper sedebat, in qua Julius Cæsar, uxorémque duxit Ciceronis; de utroque gloriari solitus, quasi aut propter sellam Cæsar, aut propter uxorem Orator futurus. Sic omnis Papæ à cathedra Petri, in qua sedet & adoratur, virtus. Bene tamen est, quod reliqui proavorum ejus nihil huc contulere. Alias Alexander VI. successores suos in Cynædos; Clemens in sacrilegos; Julius in sicarios; Benedictus, Gregorius, Sylvester in Simoniacos; Paschalis in perjuros; Johanna Moguntina in fœminas; Martinus & Sylvester alter, aliique in Magos; Johannes uterque in Diabolos incarnatos transmutasset. Sic plane qui se olim in Paradisum insinuavit Serpens, idem in cathedram Petri surrepere callidè potuit.
units.tr: Of old, tablets written by hand were broken at once and perished. But the tablets of Peter's Chair do not feel the passage of time. They were perhaps hewn from Irish oak, which no spider of error touches without dying on the spot. Here Vibius Rufus seems to me to have come back to life, who, according to the witness of Xiphilinus in his Epitome and of Dio in the life of Tiberius, always sat in the same chair in which Julius Caesar and the wife of Cicero had sat. He used to boast of both, as if Caesar had become a dictator, or the orator were to become the husband, because of the chair. So too is the power of every Pope derived from the Chair of Peter, on which he sits and is adored. It is well, however, that his other forebears contributed nothing to this. Otherwise Alexander VI would have turned his successors into sodomites; Clement into sacrilegious men; Julius into assassins; Benedict, Gregory and Sylvester into simoniacs; Paschal into perjurers; Joan of Mainz into women; Martin and another Sylvester, and others, into magicians; and both Johns into incarnate devils. Thus clearly the Serpent that once crept into Paradise could also have stolen craftily into the Chair of Peter.

units.la: XXIII. Nusquam certè tale quid vel promisit, vel præstitit Christus.
units.tr: XXIII. Christ certainly neither promised nor performed anything of this kind anywhere.

units.la: Ubi enim hoc scriptum, uti merito Lutherus adv. falsò nom. Episc. jocatur, an forte Romæ apud Sanctum Petrum in camino quopiam? Dixit sanè Christus: Tu es Petrus: At Tu es Innocentius XI. successor Petri, infallibilis juris Divini & humani arbiter, nuspiam dixit. Dixit, Rogavi pro te, ne deficeret tibi fides. Sed dixit etiam: Vade post me Sathan, non sapis, quæ Dei sunt. Docet nos nunc Oraculum illud Cathedralitium, cur hæres promissi ex asse, illam censuram & ἀπῶλειαν abdicaverit? Nihil tale successoribus Christi & Petri ætati suboluit. Non Polycrati & Irenæo, qui Victori: non Cypriano, qui Stephano: non Chalcedonensibus, qui Leoni: non Orientalibus Episcopis, qui Julio: non Constantinopolitanis Patribus, qui Vigilio & Honorio cedere noluerunt. Sed & è recentioribus, qui nasum & frontem adhuc habuere, Johannes illle Cancellarius Parisiensis, Turrecremata, Almainus, Alphonsus de Castro, Hadrianus VI. Papa, Archiepiscopus Catharinus, Cardinalis Cajetanus, Fran-
units.tr: For where is it written, as Luther rightly jokes against the falsely named bishops? Perhaps in some hearth at Rome, at St Peter's? Christ indeed said: "You are Peter." But nowhere did he say: "You are Innocent XI, successor of Peter, the arbiter of infallible divine and human law." He said: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." But he also said: "Get behind me, Satan, you do not savour the things of God." Does that oracle of the Chair now teach us why the heir of the promise fully renounced that censure and perdition [ἀπῶλειαν]? Nothing of the kind grew up in the successors of Christ and Peter in the age that followed. It was not so for Polycrates and Irenaeus, who opposed Victor; nor for Cyprian, who opposed Stephen; nor for the Chalcedonian fathers, who opposed Leo; nor for the Eastern bishops, who opposed Julius; nor for the Constantinopolitan fathers, who refused to yield to Vigilius and Honorius. And among more recent writers, those who still had a nose and a forehead, namely John the Chancellor of Paris, Torquemada, Almain, Alphonsus de Castro, Pope Adrian VI, Archbishop Catharinus, Cardinal Cajetan, Fran-

units.la: infinibi-litatis illius monstrum amplius de-monstratur. Franciscus à Victoria, aliique complures non infimæ classis Theologi, à Bellarmino etiam de Rom. Pontif. lib. iv. 2. Cano Loc. Com. lib. vi. 8. aliisque citati, & à mequeTomo 1. Differt. xx. commemorati, palam illam Papalis iudicii impeccantiam negarunt. Instar omnium rationem huius rei Alphonsus Contra hær. lib. 1. c. 2. reddit: Multi, inquiens, Papæ adeo illiterati, ut Grammaticam penitus ignorent, qui fit, ut sacras literas interpretari possint? Non fugit profecto nos, quinam Pontificum Ario, qui Montano, qui Nestorio, qui Acacio, qui Monotheletis, qui Sadducæis, qui dæmonibus favere non dedignati fuerint; quæ sibi contraria edixerint, quæ Deo, quamque perforatam navim, Hieronymi verbis utor, debilis sæpe gubernator rexerit.
