Quasi etiam longinqua Pontificum serie, quæ portenta hominum, qui apostatici apostaticique olim fuerint (sic Platina, sic Genebrardus loquitur) lippis & tonsoribus notum non sit. Horum vita fabula mundi est.
units.tr: the monster of that infallibility is further exposed. Francisco de Vitoria, and several other theologians of no low rank, cited also by Bellarmine in On the Roman Pontiff, book 4, ch. 2, and by Cano in Loci Communes, book 6, ch. 8, and by others, and recalled by me in Tomo 1, Dissertation XX, openly denied that papal judgment is free from error. As the reason for this, Alphonsus, in Against Heresies, book 1, ch. 2, gives an answer that stands for all: Many popes, he says, are so unlearned that they are wholly ignorant of grammar. How then can they be able to interpret the sacred letters? Certainly it is not hidden from us which of the Pontiffs did not disdain to favour Arius, Montanus, Nestorius, Acacius, the Monothelites, the Sadducees and the demons; what contrary decrees they issued; and with what a leaky ship (I use Jerome's words), what a feeble helmsman often steered. Nor is it unknown to the blind and the barbers what monsters of men, who were once apostates and apostates again (so Platina and Genebrard speak), appeared in the long succession of Popes. Their life is a fable for the world.

units.la: XXIV. Sed placuit tamen Papæ hoc Papalis infallibilitatis dogma, & placuit se magno iudice, teste, reo & diffinitore. Non alia enim supererat ratio se liberandi à suspicione illa, quòd sit magnus Pseudopropheta & impostor, & S. Scripturam supplantandi, nisi audacter pronuntiando, & persuadendo hominibus, se esse infallibilem.
units.tr: XXIV. But the Pope nonetheless approved this Papal dogma of infallibility, and he approved of himself as the great judge, witness, defendant and definer. For there was no other way left for him to free himself from that suspicion, that he is a great pseudo-prophet and impostor, who wishes to supplant Holy Scripture, except by boldly declaring and persuading men that he is infallible.

units.la: Jam ergo fingamus (quod Celeb. Mori Theologi Angli Myst. Iniq. lib. 11. 17. emblema est, ad rem aprime faciens) numerosum hominum gregem, peculiari vestitu ornatum, qui ingens aliquod nemus incolat, & famæ Sanctitatis nescio cujus aucupandæ gratia, se Equites sacri Nemoris, vel Spiritus infallibilis Sacerdotes appellet, & obfirmatissimo consilio sibi in dictis factisque omnibus infallibilitatem arroget. Consentiant ergo illi determinéntque uno ore, tam inesse certæ verborum Magicorum formulæ à se usurpatæ, virtutem, ut si quis ex sacro suo ordine illam super uno ex puris, albis & rotundis, qui in obvio flumine reperiuntur, lapillis, pronunciaverit, ille eundem licet colorem, magnitudinem, figuram, duritiem retinens, repente in Aquilam mutetur, atque inde lapidis, quem Aetiten appellant, seu Lapidis Aquilini nomine veniat. Sed neget forte aliuseordatior & emunctiorum narium, Aquilam esse; &, quod res est, affirmet, lapidem album, rotundum fluviatilem, non aliud esse. Ast prosiliant mox Sacri Nemoris illi Equites, & per Sacrosanctam Ordinis sui dignitatem & infallibilitatem obtcestentur unanimiter, miraculum intercessisse, neque amplius, quod videtur, lapidem, sed Regium illum Jovis alitem esse. Instent nihilominus perspicaciores Aquilam esse non posse, cùm nec rostrum, nec ôs, nec caput, nec pedes, nec ungues, nec cauda, nec caro Aquilæ appareat, denique nil nisi vulgaris lapidis clarissima indicia abundent. Neque nudum affirmantis testimonium rei huic affirmatæ fidem facere posse pertendant. Ast occurrant hi Nemoris Equites & cum ratione licet restitantes adoriantur, fortunis omnibus exuant, denique occidant. Quid hic videbitur? Annon sani omnes Equites hos Spiritúsque infallibilis Sacerdotes, procul omni convitio, sanguinolentorum Impostorum subdolam Societatem, latronum denique turbam, piraticam exercentium, & viatores obvios quosque insestantium, esse, clamabunt merito?
units.tr: Now let us imagine (which is a picture most apt to the matter, drawn by the celebrated English theologian More in Mystery of Iniquity, book 11, ch. 17) a numerous flock of men, adorned with a peculiar dress, who dwell in some great grove and, in hunting for a reputation for I know not what sanctity, call themselves Knights of the Sacred Grove or Priests of the Infallible Spirit, and with most obstinate purpose claim infallibility for themselves in all they say and do. Let them then agree and declare with one voice that a certain power resides in the magic formula they use, so that if anyone from their sacred order pronounces it over one of the pure, white, round pebbles found in a nearby stream, that pebble, keeping the same colour, size, shape and hardness, will suddenly be changed into an eagle, and from this it will get the name of the stone called aetites, or the eagle-stone. But perhaps some other man, more clear-sighted and with a sharper nose, denies that it is an eagle, and affirms what is the truth, that it is a white, round river stone and nothing else. Then at once those Knights of the Sacred Grove will leap up and unanimously swear by the sacrosanct dignity and infallibility of their order that a miracle has intervened, and that what seems to be a stone is no longer a stone but that royal bird of Jupiter. Meanwhile the more perceptive will insist that it cannot be an eagle, since no beak, mouth, head, feet, talons, tail or flesh of an eagle appears, and, in short, nothing but the plainest signs of an ordinary stone abound. They will contend that the bare testimony of one who affirms cannot make this affirmed matter credible. But then the Knights of the Grove will rush at them, and, though these resist with reason, attack them, strip them of all their possessions and finally kill them. What will seem right here? Will not all sane people cry out, and rightly so, that these Knights and Priests of the Infallible Spirit, without any reproach intended, are a treacherous society of bloody impostors, a band of robbers practising piracy and harassing every traveller they meet?

units.la: XXV. Quid ergo nos quoque existimabimus de numerosis agminibus hujus se infallibilem venditantis Ecclesiæ, paratis ad insestandum atroeiter Christianum viatorem quentivis, in hac sua peregrinatione per mundi hujus eremum errantem, si forte, Scripturæ & sanæ rationi confisus, negaverit ille, album rotundúmque libum post certam verborum formulam à Sacrificulo super eo demurmuratam, in perfectum hominem conversum esse, eo quòd post exquisitissimum sensuum examen ne hilum quidem mutatum esse, deprehendere ille possit. Et tamen propter solam jactatam infallibilitatem vel paradoxum hoc <bl>?</bl> ei confitendum, imò & libum isthoc adorandum, vel crudelissimo mortis genere pereundum est. Quis coetum ejusmodi Christianum, & non potius verè Babylonicum, Dei, Scripturæ, sanæ rationis hostem juratissimum juraverit?
units.tr: XXV. What, then, shall we think of the numerous troops of this Church, which boasts of its own infallibility, and which are ready to attack any Christian traveller savagely while he wanders through this desert of the world on his pilgrimage? If he, trusting in Scripture and sound reason, should deny that a white, round wafer, after a fixed form of words has been muttered over it by the little priest, has been turned into a perfect man, since after the most careful examination of the senses he can detect that it has not changed in the least, then, on the strength of their boasted infallibility alone, he must either confess this paradox? and even adore that wafer, or perish by the cruellest kind of death. Who would not swear that such an assembly is not Christian but truly Babylonian, and a most sworn enemy of God, of Scripture, and of sound reason?

units.la: XXVI. Neque tamen hic vaframentorum Pseudopropheticorum finis est. Jus Scripturas interpretandi pro lubitu, & infallibiliter, quocunque demum modo interpretatio instituatur, ad se solum Papa pertraxit. Metus tamen adhuc erat, ne populo, cordatioribus saltem fraus suboleret, & nihil minus quàm vera & infallibilis verbi Christi Prophetici interpretatio videretur. Hoc ergo supererat, ut ad dirimendum Deum inter & homines commercium verbi Divini lux poneretur sub modio, & à Lectione Scripturæ populus astu quodam, imò adhibita etiam si opus foret, vi arceretur penitus. Prætextu uti placuit obscuritatis, periculi seductionis, quódque Scriptura sit lesbia regula, nasus cereus, farrago scriptorum fortuitorum & occasionalium, multos denique in hæreses certissimas præcipites dederit. Ergo eandem in usum populi vernaculo idiomate reddi, grave piaculum: legi vel in versionibus aliorum, vel in Vulgata etiam versione, ab iis, qui Latini idiomatis callentes essent, sine venia & dispensatione Ecclesiæ, nefas censeri voluit. Et ne forte loci cujuspiam Scripturæ, in publica liturgia occurrentis, vis homines à cæca illa obedientia, & ingeniorum tyrannide absolveret, summo studio cavit Pseudo-prophetæ, ne preces etiam publicæ, & Eucharistiæ celebratio à populo intelligi possent. Denique non raró sævitum in Codices, sævitum in eos, qui non consentientibus Præpositis Biblia legissent. Quæ omnia pluribus testimoniis Celeb. Rainoldus de R. Eccl. Idolol. lib. 1. cap. 18. Is. 14. 15. probata dedit. His artibus remoto candelabro omne lumen extinctum, scientiæ clavis abscondita, sides cum perfidia, lux cum tenebris facilè commutata est, factíque sunt cœci duces cœcorum. Neque profecto amplius mirum quòd omnibus nunc erroribus & hæresibus illi patent, idololatria & superstitionibus absorbentur, tyrannidi intolerandæ opportuni facti sunt clerus inferior & populus, similes idolis quæ colunt, vera mancipia præpositorum suorum. Quid enim contempto, neglecto, suppresso Dei verbo, quo deficiente semper nudatur populus, Prov. xxix. 18. aliud evenire poterat?
units.tr: XXVI. Nor does this trickery of the pseudo-prophets end here. The right to interpret the Scriptures as they please, and infallibly, by whatever method the interpretation is carried out, the Pope has drawn entirely to himself. Yet there was still a fear that the people, or at least the more discerning among them, might perceive the fraud and see that this was by no means a true and infallible interpretation of the prophetic word of Christ. What remained, therefore, was to put the light of the divine word under a bushel, so that the commerce between God and men should be cut off, and the people should be kept altogether from reading Scripture by a kind of cunning, and even by force if need be. They chose to use the pretext of obscurity, the danger of seduction, and the fact that Scripture is a Lesbian rule, a wax nose, a hodgepodge of chance and occasional writings, which has in many cases plunged men headlong into most certain heresies. Therefore, to have it rendered into the vernacular for the use of the people was a grave sacrilege; to read it, whether in the translations of others or even in the Vulgate version, by those who were skilled in the Latin language, without the permission and dispensation of the Church, they decided was an impious act. And lest the force of some passage of Scripture, met with in the public liturgy, should free men from that blind obedience and the tyranny of their minds, the pseudo-prophet took the greatest care that even public prayers and the celebration of the Eucharist should not be understood by the people. Finally, the codices were not seldom persecuted, and persecution was directed against those who had read the Bibles without the consent of their superiors. Celebrated Rainolds has proved all these things by many testimonies in De Romanae Ecclesiae Idololatria, book 1, chapter 18; Is. 14. 15. With these arts, the lampstand having been removed, all light was extinguished, the key of knowledge was hidden, faith was easily exchanged for faithlessness and light for darkness, and the blind became leaders of the blind. Indeed, it is no longer surprising that they now lie open to every error and heresy, that they are swallowed up in idolatry and superstitions, and that the lower clergy and the people have become convenient to an intolerable tyranny, like the idols they worship, true slaves of their superiors. For what else could follow when the word of God was despised, neglected, and suppressed, the word by whose lack the people is always laid bare, Prov. 29. 18?

units.la: XXVII. Quibus ergo gradibus, quibus modis Hierarchia Propheticum Christi verbum, dolosi lucratoris instar, supplantaverit, Pseudopropheta ille de Christo Propheta triumphos denique egerit; & suum verbum, velut ex quercu, populo suo, sublata lege Altissimi, obstruxerit, abunde jam colliquesc it. Sicut autem Christus Prophetico suo verbo per miracula omni exceptione majora fidem fecit, Deo juxta voluntatem suam signis, & prodigiis, multifariis virtutibus, & divisionibus Spiritus S. attestante illi Saluti, quæ initio prædicari cœpit per Dominum, & ab audientibus in nos sic confirmata est Hebr. 11. 3. 4. Sic Papa novello suo verbo Pseudoprophetico, hoc est, iis doctrinis, quæstus, commodi, potentiæ suæ stabiliendæ gratia protulit Miracula & Prodigia multa, ceu sigilla quædam appingi curavit. Si doctrinam Christi Propheticam Papa retinuisset, facilè iis, quibus olim illa per Apostolos & Apostolicos Viros Dei confirmata est, sigillis & miraculis ac-
units.tr: XXVII. By what steps and what methods the hierarchy has supplanted the prophetic word of Christ, like a crafty trickster, and how that pseudo-prophet has at last triumphed over Christ the Prophet, and has blocked up his own word to his people, the law of the Most High having been taken away, is now sufficiently plain. But just as Christ confirmed his prophetic word by miracles, greater than any objection, God also bearing witness with them, both by signs and wonders, and by divers miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to his own will, Heb. 2. 3. 4. So the Pope, for the sake of establishing his new pseudo-prophetic word, that is, those doctrines by which his profit, gain, and power might be secured, has caused many miracles and portents to be displayed, as it were seals to be stamped upon them. If the Pope had kept the prophetic doctrine of Christ, it would have been easy for him to rest content with those seals and miracles by which that doctrine was once confirmed through the Apostles and the apostolic men of God, sig-

units.la: Papa Pseudoprophera Christi Prophera annulus sicut hic verbum suum Propheticum miraculorum sigillis confirmavit, ita ille parituer verbum suum Pseudoprophetica signis & miraculis stabilire animitur. acquievisset. Nondum enim illa, vetera licet, senio suo confecta sunt, nedum fidem decoxerunt. Nunc verò novella Papæ Prophetia novellis scilicet miraculis statuminari debuit; licet Spiritus Dei novissimorum temporum, cujusmodi illa Papatus sunt, signa & miracula atro carbone notaverit, & diris notis, ceu signis scilicet Ἀρίωμ Ex legis illius, secundum operationem Sathanæ, in omni virtute, & signis, & prodigiis mendacibus adventantis, (2 Thess. II. 9.) compunxerit. Hic ergo ignem de Cœlo lapsum, ad Transsubstantiationis portentum confirmandum: hic statuas loquutas, sudorem, lachrimas, sanguinem emisisse, Pontificiorum historiæ testantur. Eodem videlicet veteratore, qui olim in Paradiso per Serpentem, Romæ per Fortunæ muliebris simulachrum locutus est; per imaginem Christi crucifixi, Thomam Aquinatem alloquente, ejusque scripta utroque pollice sic laudante: Bene scripsisti de me Thoma.
units.tr: The Pope, pseudo-prophet, who is Christ's prophet: just as the ring here confirmed his prophetic word with the seals of miracles, so that one strives to establish his pseudo-prophetic word with signs and miracles, would have acquiesced. For those ancient seals, though old, are not yet worn out by age, much less have they lost their credit. But now the novel prophecy of the Pope had to be buttressed by novel miracles, although the Spirit of God, in these last times, of which those papal things are a sign, has marked the signs and miracles with black charcoal and has pricked them with dire marks, namely as signs of that lawless one [ἄνομος], after the working of Satan, with all power, and signs, and lying wonders (2 Thess. 2. 9). Here, then, the fire fallen from heaven, to confirm the portent of transubstantiation: here the statues that spoke, that sweated, wept, and emitted blood, the histories of the Papists bear witness. It is the same old deceiver who once spoke in Paradise through the serpent, and at Rome through the image of the woman Fortune; who, through the image of the crucified Christ, addressed Thomas Aquinas and praised his writings with both thumbs: You have written well of me, Thomas.
XXVIII.

units.la: Et Spiritus, & calamus deficeret, si singula, quæ portentosi homines pro nova sua Prophetia in arce Divinitatis collocanda venditant, miracula heic recensere animum inducerem. Temperare tamen nequeo, quin nonnulla insuper delibem, ut ex iis de cœteris omnibus judicium fiat. Quis ergo nescit, populum illum acri thyrso percussum jam pridem pro Pontificiæ, quà talis est, doctrinæ, confirmatione, suetum talibus narrationculis oblectari, & Divinis veluti sermonibus pasci, quòd Sanctus quidam caput sibi amputatum manu propria tenens, per quatuor vel quinque milliaria ambulaverit, exacto quoque milliari semel interquiescendo, ut per apertam gulam respiraret: quòd Sanctus alius mensa hospitali exceptus, cum dispendio vitæ vaccæ & vituli, utrique post vitam restituerit, ut postero die denuo in pascuis domini fui oberrarent: quòd Sanctus alius viderit pone altare Diabolum peccata hominum pergameno inscribentem, atque illud, cùm angustum nimis esset, expandentem, & membrana lubrica dentium morsu elapsa, caput suum parieti allidentem: quòd fœmina Sancta à Dracone deglutita, cùm se cruce signâsseт, in ventre Draconis eundem fruftulatim laceraverit, atque sic salva ex ventre eo evaserit: quòd Episcopus quidam sibi propriam manum, fœminæ cujusdam tactu pollutam resecuerit, & precibus ad B. Virginem effusis ilico restituerit; & similiter Sanctus alius crura, tertius caput sibi amputatum reposuerit: quòd fœmina quædam Sancta, cùm funibus ad necem traheretur, cruce se signans, & B. Virginem in vota vocans, eo robore munita fuerit, ut integra boum quadriga ad locum supplicii trahi non potuerit: quòd Sancti nonnulli cum Deipara familiariter conversantes, adeò liberalem eam experti fuerint, ut lac è mamillis suis ori ipsorum decumbentium instillaverit: quòd camera ejusdem Deiparæ è Palæstina in Italiam manu invisibili per aera transportata fuerit: quòd crucifixum per idem elementum noctu quinquaginta milliarium iter confecerit: quod nescio quis Sanctus, Guerinus nisi fallor, postquam Comitis Filiæ vitium intulit, eámque occidit & sepeliit, à Papa damnatus in feram belluam conversus, diu oberraverit, donec captus à Comite, & ab ejusdem puero recens nato jussus esset sonora voce se in pedes rursus erigere, resurgente simul puella, ante plures annos stuprum & cædem ab eo perpessa, sed B. Virginis imploratæ ope incolumi & spirante in sepulchro servata: quòd cum fœminabus quibusdam Sanctis Christus, cum Viris Deipara, annulo pronubo extradito, matrimonium contraxerint: quòd infans recens natus ingeminaverit, Ad Missam, ad Missam: quòd ad singulorum nummulorum tinnitus intra málluvium in offertorio, totidem animæ è purgatorio exilierint: quòd hostia à quodam non jejuno deglutita eundem in porci formam mutaverit: quòd Christus è Cœlo cum magna Sanctorum & Angelorum turma descendens sacellum cum consuetis sacrificulorum cæremoniis solenniter consecraverit, & digrediens petræ digitorum suorum vestigia imprefferit: quòd fœmellam Sanctam inter & Christum tanta necessitudo intercesserit, ut alter alterius corda invicem gererent, Christi corde in corpus fœminæ, & fœminæ corde in corpus Christi transmisso. Hæc degustasse sufficiat, cùm similia infinita anilium fabularum hamaxarii prodiderint, sacra quadam cum reverentia à captis superstitione animabus excepta.
units.tr: Breath and pen would fail me if I set out here every single miracle that these monstrous men peddle to place in the citadel of divinity for their new prophecy. Still, I cannot refrain from touching on a few of them, so that a judgment may be formed from these about all the rest. Who does not know that that people, long since struck by the sharp thyrsus, is accustomed, for the confirmation of Papist doctrine as such, to be delighted by such little tales and fed as if on divine discourses: that a certain Saint, holding his own severed head in his hands, walked four or five miles, pausing once at each mile to breathe through his open throat; that another Saint, entertained at a hospitable table, restored a cow and a calf to life after he had eaten them, so that the next day they wandered again in his master's pastures; that another Saint saw the Devil behind the altar writing the sins of men on a parchment, and when it was too narrow, stretching it out, and the slippery membrane slipping from his teeth, dashed his head against the wall; that a holy woman, swallowed by a dragon, made the sign of the cross and, cutting the dragon to pieces from within its belly, escaped alive from that belly; that a certain bishop cut off his own hand, polluted by touching a woman, and with prayers poured out to the Blessed Virgin immediately restored it; and likewise another Saint replaced his legs, and a third his head, after they had been cut off; that a certain holy woman, when she was being dragged to her death with ropes, signing herself with the cross and calling upon the Blessed Virgin in her vows, was so strengthened that a whole team of four oxen could not drag her to the place of punishment; that some Saints, living on intimate terms with the Mother of God, found her so generous that she poured milk from her breasts into the mouths of those lying down; that the bedroom of the same Mother of God was carried through the air from Palestine to Italy by an invisible hand; that a crucified man travelled fifty miles by night through the same element; that a certain Saint, Guerinus unless I am mistaken, after he had violated the Count's daughter, and killed and buried her, was condemned by the Pope, turned into a wild beast, and wandered for a long time, until, caught by the Count and ordered by the Count's newborn son to rise to his feet again with a loud voice, the girl rose at the same time, who had suffered rape and murder from him many years before, but had been preserved alive and breathing in the tomb by the help of the Blessed Virgin, whom she had implored; that Christ married some holy women, and the Mother of God some men, a wedding ring being handed over; that a newborn infant kept repeating, "To Mass, to Mass"; that at the chink of each coin thrown into the basin at the offertory, just as many souls leapt out of purgatory; that a host swallowed by a man who had not fasted changed him into the shape of a pig; that Christ, descending from heaven with a great crowd of Saints and Angels, solemnly consecrated a little chapel with the usual ceremonies of the little priests, and, as he departed, left the prints of his fingers in the rock; that such close kinship existed between a certain holy little woman and Christ that they bore each other's hearts, Christ's heart being transferred into the woman's body and the woman's heart into Christ's body. It is enough to have tasted these, since the old wives' storytellers have related countless similar fables, which the superstitious, captive souls received with a certain sacred reverence.

units.la: XXIX. Dignum sane patella operculum est.
units.tr: XXIX. It is indeed a lid worthy of the dish.

units.la: Quale verbum Pseudo-prophetæ est, talia verbi sigilla sunt. Totus Papatus, qui Ecclesiam, sicut vermis pomum, infestat, Entibus constat fictis & pictis. Entia ficta sunt transsubstantiatio, thesaurus indulgentiarum, purgatorium, Sacrificium Missaticum, intercessio B. animarum in Cœlis, reliquiæ, Camera B. Virginis Lauretana, Decretales primorum Pontificum, donatio Constantini M. Monarchia Petri, primatus Papæ Hildebrandinus, &c. Picta sunt imagines Templorum, in quarum cultu summam pietatis collocant. Qualia ergo Papatus Entia, talia Entium illorum signa & sigilla sunt, ficta & picta. Aliud & pejus quid, quod possem, non addam.
units.tr: Such as the word of the pseudo-prophet is, such are the seals of his word. The whole of Papacy, which infests the Church as a worm infests an apple, consists of beings that are feigned and painted. The feigned beings are transubstantiation, the treasury of indulgences, purgatory, the Mass as sacrifice, the intercession of the blessed souls in heaven, relics, the Lauretan chamber of the Blessed Virgin, the Decretals of the early Popes, the donation of Constantine the Great, the monarchy of Peter, the Hildebrandine primacy of the Pope, and so on. The painted things are the images in temples, in whose worship they place the highest piety. Therefore, just as the Papist beings are, so are the signs and seals of those beings, feigned and painted. There is something else, worse, which I could add but will not.

units.la: XXX. Denique Ch. Prophetam unicum verissimumque haud dubiè inimico studio oppugnat quisquis veros C. Prophetas, fidelésque testes, perinde ut Pseudopropheta ille Michæam, percutit, similis Hierosolymæ Meretrici, quam sic Christus increpat Luc. xiii. 33. O Hierosolyma, Hierosolyma, quae occidis Prophetas, & lapidas eos, qui ad Te missi sunt. Qui vero sint pravi illi servi, qui tardante juxta mentem suam Domino, bacchari, inebriari, ac conservos suos verberare non cessant, tristis experientia nos docuit, docetque, & infra, ubi argumentum illud dedita opera σὺν Θεῷ prosequemur, amplius faciemus.
units.tr: XXX. Finally, whoever attacks with hostile zeal the one, true and most real Christ-Prophet without doubt, and strikes at the true prophets and faithful witnesses of Christ, just as that pseudo-prophet struck Micaiah, is like the harlot of Jerusalem, whom Christ rebukes thus, Luke 13:33: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who killest the prophets and stonest those who are sent to you. Who those wicked servants are, who, while the Lord delays according to their own thinking, do not cease to carouse, to get drunk, and to beat their fellow servants, sad experience has taught us and continues to teach us; and below, where we shall pursue that argument deliberately with God [σὺν Θεῷ], we shall say more.

units.la: XXXI. Non satis erat Prophetae Christo bellum indixisse. Indicendum etiam eidem Sacerdoti & cruci ejus fuerat.
units.tr: XXXI. It was not enough for the Prophet to declare war on Christ. He had to declare it on Christ's priesthood and cross as well.

units.la: Constat equidem inter fideles omnes Christum Coelestis Patris jussu ac vocatione factum esse Pontificem nostrum, imo jurisjurandi etiam religione accedente ut τὸ ἀμε‑ταθετον τῆς βουλῆς immutabile ejus consilium cognosceretur, confirmatum, Hebr. v. 5. v 11. 20. 21. 22. Obtulit ergo se ipsum, & proprium sanguinem libavit, eumque per Spiritum aeternum immolavit, immaculatum Deo, purificantem conscientias nostras, Hebr. ix. 14. ipse simul Sacerdos, victima & altare. Neque tantum sic se obtulit, sed etiam pro nobis, defuncturus fideliter ἀρχιερεύς Sacerdotali omni, intercessit, introiens in ipsum Coelum, ut nunc appareat faciei Dei pro nobis, ib. v. 24. Sic ergo solus Christus unico sacrificio sanguinis sui peccatores consummavit, peccata expiavit, delevitque, peccatores cum Deo reconciliavit; Coelum aperuit, tandemque Ecclesiam suam sibi uni solique acquisivit desponsavitque.
units.tr: Among all the faithful it is certainly agreed that Christ was made our High Priest by the command and calling of the heavenly Father, and that an oath was added to confirm it, so that his unchangeable counsel [τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς] might be recognised as his consilium: Heb. 5:5, 11, 20, 21, 22. He therefore offered himself, shed his own blood, and sacrificed himself through the eternal Spirit, without blemish to God, cleansing our consciences (Heb. 9:14), being at once priest, victim and altar. He did not offer himself only in this way; as faithful high priest [ἀρχιερεύς], about to die, he also interceded for us in the full priestly office, entering into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf (ib. v. 24). Thus Christ alone, by the single sacrifice of his blood, perfected sinners, expiated and blotted out sins, and reconciled sinners to God. He opened heaven, and at last acquired and betrothed his Church to himself alone.

units.la: XXXII. Jam vero Christum Pontificem nostrum Coelestem cum Pontifice Romano terrestri comparemus, ut liquido appareat omnibus, Sacerdotale illius munus hostiliter ubique ab hoc oppugnatum, infractum: denique, quantum in eo fuit, dissolutum, atque in Papam, ceu Babylonicae Ecclesiae Sacerdotem Summum, translatum esse.
units.tr: XXXII. Now let us set Christ our heavenly High Priest beside the Roman Pontiff on earth, so that it may plainly appear to everyone how this priestly office of Christ has been everywhere assailed by the Pope as by an enemy, broken, and, so far as lay in his power, dissolved, and transferred to the Pope as the chief priest of the Babylonian Church.

units.la: XXXIII. Primò Christus Sacerdotii sui honorem non nisi ex æterno Patris decreto inivit.
units.tr: XXXIII. First, Christ entered upon the honour of his priesthood only by the eternal decree of the Father.

units.la: Non enim seipsum glorificavit, ut esset Pontifex, sed qui locutus est ad ipsum: Tu es Filius meus, hodie genui te, eum glorificavit, Hebr. v, 5. Pontifex Romanus utriusque ιεραιας tum Melchisedecianæ tum Aaronicæ, qua Christi Sacerdotium adumbratum expressumque fuerat, dignitatem ἀνθαιρετης, & sine Divinis suffragiis capessivit, atque insuper, nulla vocatione Divina accedente alia, infinitas quotidie Sacerdotum cohortes inauguratur. Sacerdotium profectò Divinitus ordinatum & constitutum, & Sacerdotium voluntarium, Divinæ vocationis tabulis destitutum una consistere nequeunt. Illud si genuinum, hoc adulterinum est. Hoc si genuinum, illud firmum ratúmque esse nequit.
units.tr: Not because he glorified himself to be made priest, but he who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you, glorified him (Heb. 5:5). The Roman Pontiff has seized the dignity of both priesthoods, the Melchizedekian and the Aaronic, in which Christ's priesthood was foreshadowed and expressed, by self-appointment [ἀνθαιρετής] and without divine votes. Moreover, with no further divine calling, he inaugurates countless cohorts of priests every day. A priesthood ordained and established by God, and a voluntary priesthood lacking the tablets of divine calling, cannot stand together. If the one is genuine, the other is counterfeit; if the other is genuine, the one cannot be firm and valid.

units.la: XXXIV. Secundò Christus Leviticorum typorum & ceremoniarum umbras corpore suo, ipsàque veritate substulit & disspulit.
units.tr: XXXIV. Second, Christ by his body and by the truth itself removed and dispelled the shadows of the Levitical types and ceremonies.

units.la: Papa quasi inducta & abrogata illa χρηστότητα & liberalitate Christi, perinde ac si nondum advenisset tempus ἀνεθώσεως, neque Sacerdotio suo Christus umbras adhuc difflasset, egena illa mundi elementa postliminio revocavit, eáque insuper ethnicarum sordium teterrimo quasi quodam cinno cumulavit conspurcavitque. Neque illud innumerarum in cultu publico ceremoniarum choragium sic ille introduxit, ut liberè quisque obire vel negligere posset, sed ad rigidam earum observantiam conscientias hominum legibus plus quàm Persicis sic devinxit, ut jugum suum jugo illo, quod Patres Apostolorum portare non potuerunt, gravius longè reddiderit; haud dissimilis Rehabeamo, qui jugi paterni remissionem supplicitér implorantibus, sic ferociter respondit: Pater meus onus imposuit vobis jugum grave. Ego autem addam jugo vestro. Pater meus corripuit vos flagellis. Ego autem corripiam vos scorpionibus 1. Reg. xi 1. 14. Posset sanè, cui luberet, vel per otium, vel animi quadam levitate & laxitate, corpus inclinare, ut stramen de humo tollat, vel lutum coenúmque extremitate baculi in quadrata vel oblonga dispertiatur. Cui sic sordidè ludere vacat, libétque, nullum sibi impositum onus quiritabitur. Si tamen ad pensum ejusmodi severè aliquis urgeatur, imò sub anathemate, peccati mortalis noxa, urgeatur, nœis se condemnatum non tam ad vilem illam temporalem servitutem Ægyptiacam colligendi paleas, & conficiendi lateres, quàm ad servitutem spiritualem omnium turpissimam & perniciosissimam, adeóque Ægyptiaca temporali graviorem longè, quiritabitur merito; quando & conscientia sic onerabitur, & vel levissimæ rei transgressio peccati, imò & æternæ mortis rum faciet.
units.tr: The Pope, as though that kindness and generosity [χρηστότης] of Christ had been set aside and annulled, as though the time of restoration [ἀνόρθωσις] had not yet come, and as though Christ had not yet dispelled the shadows by his priesthood, has by a kind of postliminy revived those beggarly elements of the world, and has moreover heaped them up and defiled them with the foul soot, as it were, of heathen filth. Nor has he introduced the dance of countless ceremonies into public worship in such a way that each person may freely perform or neglect them. Instead he has bound men's consciences to their rigid observance with laws more than Persian, so that he has made his yoke far heavier than that yoke which the Fathers of the Apostles could not bear. He is not unlike Rehoboam, who answered fiercely those who humbly begged for relief from his father's yoke: My father laid a heavy yoke upon you. I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips. I will chastise you with scorpions (1 Kings 12:11, 14). Someone who has leisure, or who from some lightness and looseness of mind wishes to bend his body to lift a straw from the ground, or to cut mud and filth with the end of a staff into squares or oblongs, may do so; and whoever has the time and the pleasure to play at such filthy games will complain of no burden laid on him. But if someone is severely pressed to such a task, indeed pressed under anathema and the guilt of mortal sin, he will rightly complain that he has been condemned not so much to that vile temporal servitude of Egypt, gathering straw and making bricks, as to a spiritual servitude, the most shameful and most pernicious of all, and therefore far heavier than the Egyptian one. For his conscience is burdened in this way, and the transgression of even the slightest matter becomes sin, and makes him liable to eternal death.

units.la: XXXV. Quis verò novi illius Sacerdotii ceremonias, quæ pridem multitudine, splendore, pompa ritus Divinitus institutos obscurârunt, & tantùm non obrucerunt, ordine numeróque certo circumscripserit? Quis unctuiras, tonsuras, Sacerdotalem ornatum, ejúsque mysteria Fictitia singula, ut reliquarum ceremoniarum infinitum chaos silentio heic præteream; brevi sermone adæquaverit? Qua in re adulterinum isthoc Sacerdotium magnam equidem religionem collocat, cùm tamen histrionicis illis larvis vix aliud affectet, quàm ut Sacerdotes, rudi plebeculæ sese spectabiles, venerabiles & sacrosanctos reddant, eisque nescio quæ spiritualia beneficia, ceu Uncti Domini, & sacrata Divinitus capita promittant; feliciori longè æmulatione Urim, Thummim, & unctionem Summi Sacerdotis expresseuri, si illuminatione mentis, cordis integritate, & unctione illa, quæ manet, & omnia unctos docet, se Deo hominibúsque spectabiles redderent. Neque enim Spiritus Dei in consecratis vestibus, sed in mundo corde, homine interno, Deo uni solique per abnegationem sui, veram in Christo fiduciam, amorem Dei & proximi, dedicato hospitatur. Sicut autem periculum est, ne rudiores & simpliciores histrionia tali ad brutam quandam sacrificuli admirationem transversi abripiantur, ejúsque fraudibus undiquaque patent: sic natutioribus, qui mente sua ad altiora seducti, spectacula ejusmodi & oculiferia despicere consueverunt, offensam gravissimam & tantùm non Christiani nominis nauseam creent oportet.
units.tr: XXXV. Who has ever circumscribed, with fixed order and number, the ceremonies of that new priesthood, which long ago obscured, and almost overwhelmed, the rites divinely instituted, by their multitude, splendour and pomp? Who could sum up in a brief discourse the anointings, tonsures, priestly vestments, and each of its fictitious mysteries, not to mention the endless chaos of its other ceremonies, which I pass over in silence here? In this matter this counterfeit priesthood certainly sets great store by religion, though with those theatrical masks it hardly aims at anything except making its priests conspicuous, venerable and sacrosanct to the rude common folk, and promising them I know not what spiritual benefits as the anointed of the Lord and heads consecrated by God. It would express the Urim, Thummim and the anointing of the High Priest with a far happier emulation if it made itself conspicuous to God and men by illumination of mind, integrity of heart, and that anointing which abides and teaches all things. For the Spirit of God dwells not in consecrated vestments but in a pure heart, in the inner man, dedicated to God alone through self-denial, true trust in Christ, and love of God and neighbour. Just as there is danger that the ruder and simpler people may be swept away by such stage tricks into a dull wonder at the little sacrificer, and its frauds lie open on every side, so for the more acute, who are accustomed to look down on such spectacles and eye-catching shows because their minds are drawn to higher things, it must cause the gravest offence, almost a nausea at the very name of Christian.

units.la: XXXVI. Prædixit enim Christus, venire horam, & jam tum esse, cùm veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in spiritu & veritate; Patrem enim tales quærere, Joh.iv. 23.24. Jam nasuti ipectent mihi hominem Sacerdotalibus vestibus consecratis à capite ad calcem usque larvatum; manus capútque sacro oleo inunctum, in Ecclesia inuncta, cujus vel ipsum Cœmeterium aqua lustrali ad pellendos dæmonas aspersum, quin & Pyramidis campanæ baptizatæ & chrismatizatæ sint, ad truculentos aeris spiritus tinnitu suo propulsandos; consistentem, ad altare unctum cum unctu ealice & unctis utensilibus approximantem; in sacris suis stationibus nunc ad unum, nunc ad alterum altaris extremum, temulenti instar, præcipitantem; nunc faciem ad populum convertentem, eadem mox aversa tergum eidem ostentantem; manus subito attollentem, demittentémque iterum; mox pectori decussatim admoventem; nunc crucem manu sua singularem, nunc duas tresve describentem; interdum sedentem, interdum stantem, mox corpus inclinantem,& sanctum altare deosculantem; nunc elata voce proloquentem, nunc submissa mussitantem; denique tali lingua à principiad finem usque suæ ἱεραγλυφ, quæ nec à populo intelligi, nec à doctioribus, nisi aliunde de dramate hoc constet, percipi distinctè possit, sacra facientem. Spectaculum isthoc mirificum, si quod aliud, cum verbis Christi citatis de Patre in Spiritu & veritate adorando nasuti illi contendant. Annon animum illorum certissima cogitatio subibit, vel hos falsos Sacerdotes, falsos adoratores esse; vel praedictionem Christi jam pridem simplici illo Ecclesiæ primitivæ ævo completam, vel penitus falsam esse; vel potius, si ullos veros Patris adoratores usquam invenire velint, alibi quærendos esse; hic vero nec spiritum, nec veritatem, nec linguam intelligibilem; quin potius omnia tenebricosa, cæca, muta, magis quàm in media umbrarum Mosaicarum nocte, comparere? Denique in ea sententia mentem suam obfirmabunt, non aliud personatos hos Sacerdotes, ipsimet Christo vero Sacerdoti illudentes, histrionio & scenico ejusmodi apparatu intendere, quàm quòd cæteri histriones solent, quibus hoc unum curæ cordique est, ut populum pecuniis emungant, & ipsi se nitidiores unctiorésque reddant.
units.tr: XXXVI. For Christ foretold: The hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth; for the Father seeks such to worship him (John 4:23, 24). Now let the shrewd look at a man masked from head to foot in consecrated priestly vestments, his hands and head anointed with holy oil, in an anointed church, whose very cemetery is sprinkled with lustral water to drive away demons, and whose tower and bell are baptised and chrismated, so that their tinkling may repel the fierce spirits of the air. Let them see him standing at the anointed altar, approaching the anointed chalice and the anointed utensils, rushing now to one end of the altar, now to the other, like a drunken man, in his sacred stations; now turning his face to the people, soon showing them his back as he turns away again; suddenly raising his hands and lowering them again; soon bringing them crosswise to his breast; now making one cross with his hand, now two or three; sometimes sitting, sometimes standing, now bowing his body and kissing the holy altar; now speaking in a loud voice, now muttering in a low one. Finally, let them see him performing sacred acts from beginning to end in a tongue of this hieroglyphic kind, which cannot be clearly understood by the people, nor grasped by the more learned unless they are informed about this drama from elsewhere. Let the shrewd men contend, citing the words of Christ about worshipping the Father in spirit and truth, that this is a most marvellous spectacle if any ever was. Will not the most certain thought come into their minds, that either these are false priests and false worshippers; or that Christ's prediction, long since fulfilled in the simple age of the primitive Church, is wholly false; or rather that, if they wish to find true worshippers of the Father anywhere, they must seek them elsewhere? For here nothing appears: neither spirit, nor truth, nor an intelligible tongue, but rather everything dark, blind and mute, more than in the midst of the Mosaic night of shadows. Finally, they will fix their minds on this opinion: that these masked priests, mocking Christ himself, the true Priest, aim at such theatrical and stage display for no other reason than that other actors usually do, for whom this one thing is the care and desire of the heart: to fleece the people of their money, and to make themselves sleeker and more anointed.

units.la: XXXVII. Tertiò Christus, æternus Sacerdos, se- mel in ara crucis se ipsum obtulit, & unica oblatione in perpetuum consummavit eos, qui sanctificantur Hebr. x. 14.
units.tr: XXXVII. Thirdly, Christ, the eternal Priest, offered himself once on the altar of the cross, and by that single offering has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. Heb. 10. 14.

units.la: Neque enim, ut sæpe offerat seipsum, sicut Pontifex ingreditur in Sacrarium quotannis cum sanguine alieno; sed nunc semel in consummatione Seculorum ad abolendum peccatum per immolationem sui ipsius patefactus est, ib. cap. ix. 25. 26. Ea igitur oblationis Christi excellentia fuit, ea ad reconciliandum Deo mundum vis, ut ceu perfecta & numeris omnibus consummata, nulla omnino repetitione indigeat, sed ad omnia valens & efficax, sola plenissimè nos in paternæ gratiæ sinum restituat.
units.tr: For he did not enter in to offer himself often, as the high priest enters the sanctuary every year with the blood of others; but now once, in the consummation of the ages, he has been made manifest to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Heb. 9. 25, 26. So great was the excellence of Christ's offering, and so great its power to reconcile the world to God, that, being perfect and complete in every respect, it needs no repetition at all. Rather, being sufficient and effective for all things, it alone restores us most fully to the bosom of the Father's grace.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quid hæc Hierarchia, quid recentior ille Pontifex? Sacrificium Christi, nisi à se & sacrificu- lis suis quotidie innumeris in locis, oblatione exanimis &c
units.tr: XXXVIII. What of this Hierarchy, and what of that more recent Pontiff? Christ's sacrifice, unless by itself and by its countless little priests offered daily in countless places, lifeless in the offering, etc.

units.la: Hierarchia cum arcerrimè sacrificat. & furfuracei in Missa Numinis cujusdam, interpolatum continuatumque, ad salutem nostram proficere quicquam pernegat; ferro flammâque in eos, qui novo hoc sacrificio Babylonico Numini litare detrectant, sævit; atque sic incruentum illud suum, quòd vocat, sacrificium infinitorum Martyrum sanguine pridem longè cruentissimum effecit.
units.tr: The Hierarchy sacrifices most secretly, and in the Mass of some godling, interpolated and continued, it denies that anything profits our salvation. With fire and sword it rages against those who refuse to offer libations to this new Babylonian deity by this sacrifice; and so it has made that bloodless sacrifice, as it calls it, far more bloody than before, with the blood of countless Martyrs.

units.la: XXXIX. Sacrificium illud novum Christi Apostolis, veteribus tam incognitum fuit, quàm quod maximè. Ubi enim illi Eucharistiam esse sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum offerendum, pronuntiant? Sacrificium, fateor, veteres quandoque appellant; sed, ut vox sonat, Eucharisticum, non propitiatorium? in commemorationem unici Christi sacrificii, in cruce semel peracti, institutum
units.tr: XXXIX. That new sacrifice was as unknown to the Apostles and the ancients as anything could be. For where do they declare that the Eucharist is a propitiatory sacrifice to be offered for the sins of the living and the dead? The ancients sometimes do call it a sacrifice, I grant; but in the sense the word bears, it is a Eucharistic sacrifice, not a propitiatory one, instituted in remembrance of the one sacrifice of Christ, once accomplished on the cross.

units.la: 1 Cor. xi. 24. Est enim in Eucharistia, uti Chrysostomus homil. 17. in Hebr. loquitur ἀνάμνησις τῆς θυσίας, hoc est, interprete Augustino, memoria Dominicæ passionis, in Ecclesia celebrata. Ita Patres omnes sentiunt. Nec abnuit Lombardus lib. iv. dist. 12. ubi ad quæstionem: An quod facit Sacerdos, proprie dicatur Sacrificium vel immolatio? An Christus quotidie immoletur, vel an semel tantùm immolatus sit? Ex Patribus respondet, illud quod offertur & consecratur à Sacerdote, vocari sacrificium & oblationem, quia memoria est, & repræsentatio veri Sacrificii, & sanctæ immolationis factæ in ara crucis. Et semel Christus mortuus est in cruce, ibique immolatus in semetipso: quotidie autem immolatur in Sacramento, quia in Sacramento fit recordatio illius, quod factum est semel. Hactenus ille. Atque ita sacrificium Eucharisticum incruentum, unico sacrificio Christi propitiatorio cruento aptè subordinatur. Sed Hierarchia Romana propitiatorio unico missaticum opponit, æquè propitiatorium, ut theatrico lusu decepti homines, crucis Christi meritum súsque déque habeant.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11. 24. For in the Eucharist there is, as Chrysostom says in his seventeenth homily on Hebrews, an anamnesis of the sacrifice [ἀνάμνησις τῆς θυσίας], that is, as Augustine interprets it, a memorial of the Lord's passion, celebrated in the Church. So all the Fathers think. Nor does Lombard disown this, in book 4, distinction 12, where, putting the question Whether what the priest does is properly called a sacrifice or an immolation? Whether Christ is immolated daily, or was immolated only once?, he answers from the Fathers that what is offered and consecrated by the priest is called a sacrifice and an oblation, because it is a memorial and representation of the true sacrifice and holy immolation made on the altar of the cross. Christ died once on the cross and was immolated there in himself; but he is immolated daily in the sacrament, because in the sacrament there is a recollection of that which was done once. So far he. Thus the bloodless Eucharistic sacrifice is fittingly made subordinate to the one bloody propitiatory sacrifice of Christ. But the Roman Hierarchy sets against the one propitiatory sacrifice its own Mass, equally propitiatory, so that men deceived by this theatrical play treat the merit of Christ's cross as of no account.

units.la: XL. Quid enim? Idémne Sacerdos offert, quod Christus obtulit, an aliud? Si aliud, non ergo sacrificium propitiatorium offert. Solus enim Christus est ἱλασμὸς propitiatio pro peccatis mundi. Sin idem, non erit ἀναίμακτον incruentum. Cruentum enim erat Christi sacrificium. Tum naturale Christi esse denuo destruetur; & finiti erit valoris sanguis Mediatoris. Imò Christus non in mensa, sed in cruce sacrificavit. Etenim si perfectum in Coena sacrificium obtulit, plenéque propitiatorium, quid opus erat illi postmodum mori? Quorsum illi in cruce effusus est cruor, qui transsubstantiato illo nec dum emisso sanguine mundum prius redemisset? Quòd si incruentum est Sacrificium sacrificuli, propitiatorium non est, quia sine effusione sanguinis propitiatio, remissio nulla est, Hebr. ix. 22. Aut quæ demum oppositio est inter Melchisedeci ordinem & Aaronis, Christum & veteris legis Sacerdotes, si munus istud per longam Mortalium successorum seriem transeat æquè ac descendat? Quorsum iterata sunt toties sacrificia vetera legalia, nisi quia parùm perfecta extiterunt? Quod perfectissimum est, iteratione nulla planè indiget. Denique nihil planiùs & ἀπαραμύθητον dici vel cogitari poterat verbis Apostoli: "Απαξ προσενεχθεὶς, μία θυσία, μία προσφορά, semel oblatus, una victima, una oblatio, Hebr. ix. 28. x. 12. Et tamen adhuc Sacrificuli Pontificii, homines sacerrimi, Christum quotidie crucifigunt, immolant, dúmque Filium Dei Patri suo offerunt, rogant supplices, religiosa planè blasphemia, ut hostiam illam benedicere, & acceptam habere velit. Verbo alterutrum, vel Christi, vel Missatici Sacerdotis sacrificium ad propitiationem peccatoris pretii, valoris nullius est. Si Missaticum SaSacerdotium valet, Christi Sacerdotium inane prorsus, frustra ille pro nobis mortuus est.
units.tr: XL. For what then? Does the priest offer the same thing that Christ offered, or something else? If something else, then he does not offer a propitiatory sacrifice; for Christ alone is the propitiation [ἱλασμὸς] for the sins of the world. But if the same, it will not be bloodless [ἀναίμακτον]; for Christ's sacrifice was bloody. Then the natural body of Christ would be destroyed all over again, and the blood of the Mediator would be shown to have a limited value. Indeed, Christ did not sacrifice at the table but on the cross. For if he offered a perfect sacrifice at the Supper, and one fully propitiatory, why was it needful for him to die afterwards? Why was blood poured out on the cross, if by the transubstantiation of the bread and wine, before any blood had been shed, he had already redeemed the world? But if the sacrifice of the little priest is bloodless, it is not propitiatory, because without the shedding of blood there is no propitiation, no remission, Heb. 9. 22. Or what opposition, after all, is there between the order of Melchisedec and that of Aaron, between Christ and the priests of the old law, if this office passes down, and is handed on, through a long succession of mortal successors? Why were the old legal sacrifices repeated so often, except that they were not perfect? What is most perfect needs no repetition at all. Finally, nothing could be said or thought more plainly, or more without comfort, than the words of the Apostle: Once offered [Ἅπαξ προσενεχθεὶς], one sacrifice, one offering [μία θυσία, μία προσφορά], Heb. 9. 28; 10. 12. And yet still the Papist little priests, most sacred men, crucify and immolate Christ every day, and while they offer the Son of God to the Father, they beg him humbly, with a plainly religious blasphemy, to be pleased to bless that victim and accept it. In a word, if either Christ's sacrifice or the Mass-priest's sacrifice is of value for the propitiation of sin, the other is worth nothing. If the Mass-priesthood holds good, the priesthood of Christ is utterly empty, and he died for us in vain.

units.la: XLI. Perpendant quæso piæ mentes, rerum non iniqui arbitri omnes, quàm fœdis & plusquam barbaris contumeliis Missa Christi sacrificium exponat, & gloriosum Christi Pontificis, ad dexteram Majestatis illius excelsissimæ statum nefariè traducat. Quinque voculæ, Hoc enim est corpus meum, quacunque religione Sacrifex voluerit, demurmuratæ Christum ad dextram throni Majestatis in excelsis sedentem, denuo à Cœlesti sede revocatum prolabi cogunt in manus Sacrificuli peccatoris. Prolapsus eò indignioribus modis excipitur, quàm olim Jeremias, in cœnosum barathrum demissus. Abhorret enim imaginatio eò persequi, quo illi Christum, Regem gloriæ, viventem utique & spirantem, ablegant. Cui horridæ spurcæque servituti non semel atque iterum, nec in uno quopiam cœnoso barathro, sed eodem tempore in multis millibus, singulis forte diebus, per decursum plurium jam Seculorum mancipatur. Nitent splendéntque Templa, incensum & suffimenta adolentur, luculenta cuncta præparantur, ad excipiendum in iis Christum. Simul verò atque advenit, magnifico illo apparatu una cum reliquis frui neutiquam permittitur; quin potius inaudita contumelia & plusquam infernali ludibrio ilico in carcerem tenebricosum & squalidum magis, quàm fuit ille Jeremiæ, compingitur; vel certè, ubi cum eo paulo benigniùs agitur, pixidi, tanquam ampliatus reus includitur, mox occasione invitante, in foetulenta hominum moribundorum, imò quandoque etiam murium, vermium, porcorum, canum ora & corpora influxurus. Frustra sic Christus in cruce exclamavit, Consummatum est, cui non famosus ille decimus tertius Herculis, sed infiniti & sordidissimi labores cum praesentissima morte infinitis vicibus subeunda, exanclandi restabant.
units.tr: XLI. I beg pious minds, and all who are fair judges of things, to weigh how foul and more than barbarous are the insults which the Mass heaps on the sacrifice of Christ, and how wickedly it drags down the glorious priesthood of Christ, seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Those five little words, For this is my body, muttered by the priest in whatever manner he pleases, compel Christ, who sits on the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heights, to be called back from his heavenly seat and to fall into the hands of a sinful little priest. Having fallen, he is received in ways more unworthy than Jeremiah was when he was let down into the miry pit. For the imagination shrinks from following them to the point where they consign Christ, the King of glory, who is alive and breathing, to that place. He is enslaved to this foul and filthy servitude not once or twice, nor in one miry pit, but at the same time in many thousands, perhaps every day, over the course of many centuries. Temples shine and gleam, incense and perfumes are burned, all things are made splendid, to receive Christ in them. But as soon as he arrives, he is by no means allowed to enjoy that magnificent display together with the rest. Instead, with unheard-of insult and a mockery more than infernal, he is at once shut into a prison darker and more squalid than Jeremiah's was; or at least, where he is treated a little more kindly, he is enclosed in a pyx, like a condemned man who has been granted a reprieve, to be soon poured, when the occasion invites, into the mouths and bodies of foul, dying men, and sometimes even of mice, worms, pigs and dogs. In vain did Christ cry out on the cross, It is finished; for there remained for him not the famous thirteenth labour of Hercules, but endless and most sordid labours, with a most present death to be undergone again and again without end.

units.la: XLII. Turpia haec & indignissima adversus sanctissimum illud Deitatis tabernaculum molimina sunt. Molimina, inquam. Nam ut Christo Domino gloriae, & Omnipotenti gloriae suae vindici contumeliae hae revera contingant, nulla equidem humana potestate effici potest. Cum tamen se profiteantur haec facere, rei contumeliarum illarum sunt, & animum suum produnt; perinde atque illi, qui capite damnatum, e judicis manu elapsum licet, in effigie suspendere solent, aperte declarant mentem suam non minus, quam si reo poenam irrogassent. Accedit, quod adversus eos, qui molimina haec averruncant, vel reprehendunt etiam, hostilia quaeque tentant, eosque, cum suae ipsis vires satis placent, novissimis dirissimisque supplicis afficiunt; palam sic plane efficientes, quomodo erga Christum ipsum affecti sint, si exardescenti libidini suae satis quandoque facere possent.
units.tr: XLII. These are base and most unworthy contrivances against that most holy tabernacle of the Deity. Contrivances, I say. For that these insults should truly fall on Christ the Lord of glory, and on the Omnipotent who avenges his own glory, can by no human power be brought about. Yet since they profess that they do these things, they are guilty of those insults and betray their own mind. Just as those who, when a condemned man has slipped from the judge's hand, are wont to hang his effigy, clearly declare their mind no less than if they had inflicted the punishment on the man himself. Moreover, against those who turn aside or even rebuke these contrivances, they attempt every hostile act, and when their own strength is pleased enough with itself, they inflict on them the most extreme and dreadful punishments. In this way they plainly show how they are disposed toward Christ himself, if they could sometimes satisfy their raging lust to the full.

units.la: XLIII. Sed quam indigne gloriosum Christi corpus tractetur; eorum etiam, qui Ecclesiae Romanae patroni & doctores praecipui habentur, testimoniis confirmemus. Divus ergo ille Franciscus Conformit. lib. 1. par. 2. pag. 177. sic loquitur: Ut quid non cognoscitis veritatem, & creditis in Filium Dei, qui quotidie se humiliat, & sicut quando e Regalibus sedibus venit in uterum Virginis, quotidie venit ad nos ipse humilis apparens, quotidie descendit de sinu Patris super altare in manu Sacerdotis? Quam humiliationem sic Alexander de Ales Parte iv. quaest. 53. membro 2. exaggerat: Opinio quae dicit, quod corpus Christi, quocunque species deferantur, ut in ventrem canis vel suis vel in alia loca immunda, videtur vera. Salvo enim esse species non definit esse Sacramentum, nec Christus sub specie. Et Thomas Parte III. quæst. 8. art. 3. suffragatur his verbis: Quidam dixerunt, quod quamprimum Sacramentum sumitur à mure, vel à cane, definit ibi esse corpus Christi. Sed hoc derogat veritati hujus Sacramenti. Dicendum ergo, quod si mus aut canis hostiam consecratam manducet, substantia corporis Christi non desinat esse sub speciebus, quandiu species illæ manent. Sicut etiam si projiceretur in lutum.
units.tr: XLIII. But let us confirm, by the testimony of those who are held to be the chief patrons and teachers of the Roman Church, how unworthily the glorious body of Christ is treated. Thus the divine Francis, Conformities, book 1, part 2, page 177, speaks as follows: Why do you not know the truth, and believe in the Son of God, who humbles himself every day, and just as once he came from royal seats into the womb of the Virgin, so every day he comes to us, appearing humble, every day he descends from the bosom of the Father upon the altar, into the hand of the priest? This humiliation Alexander of Hales magnifies thus, in part 4, question 53, member 2: The opinion which says that the body of Christ, wherever the species are carried, as into the belly of a dog or pig or into other unclean places, seems to be true. For the species do not cease to be a sacrament, nor does Christ cease to be under the species. And Thomas, in part 3, question 8, article 3, lends his support with these words: Some have said that as soon as the sacrament is taken by a mouse or a dog, the body of Christ ceases to be there. But this detracts from the truth of this sacrament. It must be said, therefore, that if a mouse or a dog eats the consecrated host, the substance of the body of Christ does not cease to be under the species, as long as those species remain. Just as also if it were thrown into the mud.

units.la: XLIV. Ita Gabriel Biel Lect. iv. in Can. Missæ, Sacerdotum Papisticorum laudes ingenti cum Christi contumelia, extulit. Cæli Regina, inquit, & mundi domina, prolatis octo verbulis: Ecce ancilla Domini, mihi fiat secundum verbum tuum; semel concepit Dei Filium, & mundi Redemptorem. Isti autem à Domino consecrati quinque verbis contextam consecrationis formam cum debita intentione proferentes, eundem Dei Virginisque filium advocant quotidie corporaliter, in sacrificium & criminum purgationem. Et paulò post: Quis unquam vidit talia? Quis huic vidit similia? Qui creavit me (si fas est dicere) dedit mihi creare se, & qui creavit me sine me, creatur mediante me. Eadem lectione Biel probat creationem istam non fieri naturali potestate, vel meritoria operatione, sed assistente virtute: Secundum quem modum (NB) malefici & incantatrices quosdam effectus producere dicuntur, ut extrahere lac vaccarum de sedibus, seu manubriis securium: quod fit non virtute naturali maleficorum, neque ex eorum merito, sed virtute occulta sive bona, sive mala assistente. Pari furore Ludovicus Coelius Rhodiginus Antiq. Lect. lib. xvi. 14. scribit: Quæstio diu agitata veteribus est, insitne vis aliqua verbis certa quadam enuntiatis formula? Equidem Christianæ veritatis cultor qui possit inficiari? Quando Princeps ille rerum ac Summi Patris filius, ex vero verus Deus; praefatione Sacerdotis brevissima se vocetur eliciaturve a Caelesti sede. Cui simile quiddam & priscorum vana superstitio aut habuit, aut credidit: quando & Tullum Hostilium Pisonis tradidere monumenta, ex Numae libris eodem operatum sacro, Jovem elicere Coelo, quem & inde Elicium vocabant, quod in Fastis cecinit Poeta nobilis, conatum, &c.
units.tr: XLIV. So Gabriel Biel, in Lect. iv. on the Canon of the Mass, extolled the priests of the Papists with great insult to Christ: "The Queen of heaven and mistress of the world, having spoken eight little words, 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord, let it be done to me according to your word,' once conceived the Son of God and Redeemer of the world. But these men, consecrated by the Lord, uttering the form of consecration woven from five words, with due intention, summon the same Son of God and of the Virgin bodily every day, for sacrifice and the purging of sins." And a little later: "Who has ever seen such things? Who has seen anything like this? He who created me (if it is lawful to say so) has given me the power to create him, and he who created me without me is created through me." By the same reading, Biel proves that this creation is not effected by natural power or meritorious work, but by an assisting power. In this way (note it well) sorcerers and enchantresses are said to produce certain effects, such as drawing milk from cows' udders or from the handles of axes; this happens not by the natural power of the sorcerers, nor from their merit, but by some hidden power, good or bad, assisting them. With equal madness Ludovicus Coelius Rhodiginus, in Antiq. Lect. book xvi, chapter 14, writes: "The question has long been debated by the ancients, whether there is some power in words spoken in a certain fixed formula. Indeed, who among the worshippers of Christian truth could deny it, when that Prince of all things, the Son of the Highest Father, true God from true God, is called by the very brief preface of the priest and drawn down from his heavenly seat? Something similar to this the vain superstition of the ancients either had or believed, when the records also hand down that Tullus Hostilius, operating from the books of Numa with the same sacred rite, called Jupiter down from heaven, whom they then called Elicius, as the noble poet sang in the Fasti," and so on.

units.la: XLV. Hi sunt fructus idolomaniae Missaticae in Christum Sacerdotem, ejusque sacrificium contu-meliosissimi. Quinque vocula, H E. E. C. M. Christum ad dexteram Dei sedentem, denuo à Coelesti sede sevocatum humiliant, ut in magno periculo versetur, ne à canibus, suibus, muribus aut vermibus comedatur, vel in lutum etiam projiciatur. Humiliatum certè corpus legavit Dominus: non autem è Coelo, magicis demurmuratis vocalis devocandum, sed quale nobis in ipsa cruce vera fide amplectendum propositum fuit. In usu enim Coenae Dominicae fideles mortem Domini annuntiant, 1. Cor xi. 26.
units.tr: XLV. These are the fruits of Mass-idolatry, most insulting to Christ the Priest and to his sacrifice. By five little words, H. E. E. C. M., they bring down from the heavenly seat the Christ who sits at the right hand of God, and call him back, humbled, into great danger, lest he be eaten by dogs, swine, mice or worms, or even be thrown into the mud. Certainly the Lord bequeathed a humbled body, but not one to be summoned down from heaven by magic mumbling; rather it was set before us, to be embraced in true faith, as it was in the cross itself. For in the use of the Lord's Supper the faithful proclaim the death of the Lord, 1 Cor. xi. 26.

units.la: XLVI Quarto Christus, Coelestis Sacerdos noster, semet ipsum obtulit, ut nobis peccatoribus, quorum locum subvit, & peccata in se suscepit, justitiam Seculorum, remissionem peccatorum, redemptionem & glo-riam aeternam acquireret solus Purgationem enim peccatorum nostrorum δι' ἑαυτὸν per semet ipsum, non per alium quenquam fecit Hebr. 1. 3. Sanguis ejus purgat nos ab omnibus peccatis, 1. Joh. 1 7. Justificamur gratis, ejus gratia, per redemptionem in Jesu Christo; quem praestituit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ejus, ad demonstrationem justitiae propter remissionem praecedentium peccatorum, &c. Rom. iv. 24. 25. Haec crucis & Sacerdotii à Christo fidelissime obiti salutaris maxime planta, haec arbor vitae est, quam quisquis ex Paradiso Dei, quae Ecclesia est, extirpare conatur, ipsum Chriftum Sacerdotem, ejúsque meritum pretiosissimum inde, quantum in ipso est, exturbat.
units.tr: XLVI. Fourthly, Christ, our heavenly Priest, offered himself, so that for us sinners, whose place he took and whose sins he took upon himself, he alone might obtain righteousness for the ages, forgiveness of sins, redemption and eternal glory. For he made the purging of our sins through himself [δι' ἑαυτὸν], not through any other, Heb. 1. 3. His blood cleanses us from all sins, 1 John 1. 7. We are justified freely, by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the showing of his righteousness because of the remission of former sins, etc., Rom. iv. 24, 25. This is the most saving plant of the cross and of the priesthood faithfully discharged by Christ; this is the tree of life, and whoever tries to root it out of the Paradise of God, which is the Church, uproots Christ the Priest himself and his most precious merit, as far as lies in him.

units.la: XLVII. Hic verò, si uspiam, Hierarchia Sacrosanctum Christi Sacerdotium periculosissimè oppugnat, crucI, sanguini, & justitiæ Christi miscens venenum doctrinæ perniciosissimæ de justificatione hominis per habitum infusum justitiæ propriæ, de satisfactionibus propriis, nec non alienis per Papales indulgentias applicatis; de merito operum. Quod quidem præsentissimum venenum est, quod intimam Christianæ religionis medullam dulcedinémque non leviter arrodit, sed penitus excidit, ipsúmque Christi Sacerdotium non obiter offuscat, sed funditus pessúmdat.
units.tr: XLVII. Here, if anywhere, the Hierarchy most dangerously assails the most holy priesthood of Christ, mixing with the cross, the blood and the righteousness of Christ a poison of most pernicious doctrine: concerning the justification of man through an infused habit of his own righteousness, concerning his own satisfactions, and also those of others applied through Papal indulgences, and concerning the merit of works. This is indeed a most present poison, which does not merely gnaw lightly at the inmost marrow and sweetness of the Christian religion, but cuts it out entirely; and it does not merely dim in passing the very priesthood of Christ, but overthrows it from the foundations.

units.la: XLVIII. De Justificatione peccatoris quæ sententia sit Hierarchiæ, supra ex Tridentinis Patribus excsculpsimus. Pro inhærente justitia, ceu formali justificationis causa, tanquam pro aris, maximè autem pro focis, pugnant. Quo verò loco justitiam, meritum Christi & justificationem per fidem, sine operibus, habeant, testatur Index Expurgatorius Madriticus, qui clarissima quædam de sola fidei justificatione testimonia ex Indicibus & textu Chrysostomi, Hieronymi, Cyrilli, obelisco suo dedita opera confixit. A manibus liber est. Ecce Inquisitores sibi conscios erroris & fraudis! Quibus occinam ego merito, quod Arianis quondam Ambrosius de Spir. S. lib. iii. ii. occinuit: Literas quidem abolere potuistis, sed fidem non potuistis auferre. Plus vos illa litura prodebat, plus vos illa litura damnabat. Sed de justificatione per solam justitiæ Christi δικαίωμα alibi adversus Tridentinos, eorúmque hyperaspisten dicta uberiùs, huc sevocare non libet.
units.tr: XLVIII. What the Hierarchy's view of the justification of the sinner is, we have already set out from the Tridentine Fathers above. They fight for inherent righteousness as the formal cause of justification, as for their altars, and most of all for their hearths. In what place they hold righteousness, the merit of Christ and justification through faith without works, the Madrid Expurgatory Index bears witness, which, with deliberate care, fixed to its obelisk some very clear testimonies on the justification by faith alone, taken from the indexes and text of Chrysostom, Jerome and Cyril. It is set free from their hands. Behold the inquisitors, conscious of their own error and fraud! To them I may fittingly sing what Ambrose once sang against the Arians, in On the Holy Spirit, book iii, chapter 11: "You could indeed abolish the letters, but you could not take away the faith. That erasure betrayed you more; that erasure condemned you more." But I do not wish to set aside here what has been said at greater length elsewhere concerning justification by the sole δικαίωμα of Christ's righteousness, against the Tridentines and their hyperaspistes.

units.la: XLIX. Satisfactioni Christi omnibus numeris absolutissimæ Satisfactionum humanarum tum propriarum, tum alienarum molem infinitam Hierarchia non tam subordinat, quam opponit. Non displicuit equidem satisfactionis vocabulum Patribus; nec illorum sensus nobis displicet. Non de nomine, sed de re lis est. Dolemus nihilominus, incautas vocum Katachrestes, magno Ecclesiæ malo, rerum confusionem induxisse. Alias enim, uti licet Tertullianus de Præscript. loquitur: Fides nominum salus proprietatum est. Patimur tamen poenas ecclesiasticas seu canonicas, in Ecclesiæ, non Dei foro olim exactas, satisfactionum nomine venire. Sed hæpridem in Ecclesia Pontificia exoleverunt; atque iis, post absolutissimam Christi passionem, succéduriatæ sunt satisfactiones, seu, uti vocant, poenæ temporales, post remissa peccata, & peccatorum poenas æternas, hominibus vel à Deo, uti scitcunt illi, vel à Sacerdote, vel à semet ipsis impositæ, atque ab iis vel hic, vel in Purgatorio sic luendæ, ut justitiæ Divinæ in solidum satisfiat. Utramque hic paginam faciunt ἀφαδία τῆς σώματος, seu crudeles & barbaræ vexationes corporis, peregrinationes nudipedales ad reliquias Sanctorum, recitatio precularum superstitiosè toties, in lingua etiam peregrina, repetita, alienarum flagellationum substitutio, jejunia piscaria, multæ etiam pecuniariæ, eleemosynæ cleri ingluviem saturantes, aliæque ejusmodi, quæ operum laboriosorum nomine, veniunt. Annon hoc est universæ Oeconomiæ Christianæ dulcedinem in Stygiam quandam acerbitatem; lætum illum & illustrem Evangelii diem in nebulosam noctem Ægyptiacam, in qua nil nisi horridum, triste & servile dominetur; pacem animi in perturbationem ejusdem commutare, denique sanguinem Filii Dei utpote ad expianda supplicia temporalia, quorum metus & depulsio, quàm infernalium, longè præsentior & gratior homini carnali esse solet, ineptum nihilque pollentem, taurorum & hircorum sanguine viliorem reddere? Profecto uti pulchre Hieronymus
units.tr: XLIX. The Hierarchy does not so much subordinate the vast mass of human satisfactions, both one's own and those of others, to the satisfaction of Christ, which is most complete in every respect, as set them against it. Indeed the word satisfaction did not displease the Fathers, nor does their sense displease us. The dispute is not over the name but over the thing. Nevertheless we grieve that the careless use of words, a great evil for the Church, has introduced a confusion of things. For otherwise, as Tertullian says in De Praescriptione: the faith of names is the salvation of their proper meanings. Yet we suffer the penalties, ecclesiastical or canonical, which were once exacted in the forum of the Church and not of God, to be called by the name of satisfactions. But these have long since fallen into disuse in the Papist Church; and in their place, after the most complete passion of Christ, there have succeeded satisfactions, or, as they call them, temporal punishments, imposed upon men after sins are forgiven and their eternal punishments remitted, either by God, as they pretend, or by the priest, or by themselves; and these are to be paid off either here or in Purgatory, so that divine justice may be fully satisfied. Both of these make up the same page, [ἀφαδία τῆς σώματος], that is, cruel and barbarous mistreatments of the body; barefoot pilgrimages to the relics of the saints; the recitation of prayers, superstitiously repeated so often, even in a foreign tongue; the substitution of the flagellations of others; fish-fasts; many monetary payments; alms that satisfy the gluttony of the clergy; and other such things, which go under the name of laborious works. Is this not to change the sweetness of the whole Christian economy into a certain Stygian bitterness; to turn that joyful and bright day of the Gospel into a misty Egyptian night, in which nothing but the horrid, sad and servile holds sway; to exchange the peace of the mind for its disturbance; and, finally, to make the blood of the Son of God, as if it were for atoning temporal punishments, whose dread and removal are usually much more present and welcome to carnal man than the infernal ones, useless and powerless, and viler than the blood of bulls and goats? Surely, as Jerome says beautifully in Against Ctesiphon, there is no need to refute what is blasphemous by its own profession.

units.la: {a} factiones humanas tum propriias. mus adv. Ctesiph. loquitur, necesse non est convinci, quod sua statim professione blasphemum est.
units.tr: {a} human satisfactions, both one's own. Jerome, in his book against Ctesiphon, says: "There is no need to refute what is blasphemous by its own profession."

units.la: L. Auget horrorem dogmatis poenarum temporalium latitudo. Non satis enim erat hanc vitam earum metu distringere, nisi Poeticarum Furiarum instar cum flagellis facibusque suis excruciandos miseros in altero etiam Seculo, Purgatorio puta, quod temporaria quaedam Gehenna fingitur, insequerentur. Quasi scilicet macula quaelibet & erratum fragilis hujus vitae ne per aeterni quidem Filii Dei sanguinem expiari posset, sed quisque proprium suum debitum ad ultimum usque quadrantem solvere teneretur. An sic Christus is agnoscetur, de quo Esaias vaticinatus est cap. LIII.4.5. Sanè morbos ac dolores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros portavit. Castigatio pacis nostrae super eum, & vibicibus ejus sanati sumus. Non vibicibus Christi, si Hierarchiae fides est, sed propriis quisque vibicibus sanabitur. Exuetur peccator miser, coedetur, cutim cilicio induetur, longa & fastidiosa itinera suscipiet, nudis genubus per extantes silices conabitur, jejunabit, vigilabit non ad corrigendam vitam, sed ad satisfaciendum pro peccatis, perindeac si nunquam pro iis Filius Dei satisfecisset; demum post vitam flamma eum facerrima amburet, non extinguenda usque ad solutionem rigidam quadrantis novissimi. Mihi vero opportune hic illud Lutheri scomma μαισωνικὸν è Propheta excerptum occurrit: Domine, non possum vesci stercore humano.
units.tr: L. The breadth of the doctrine of temporal punishments increases its horror. For it was not enough to terrify men with the fear of these in this life, unless, like the Furies of the poets with their whips and torches, they were also pursued in another age, namely in Purgatory, which is imagined as a kind of temporary Gehenna, to be tormented there with miseries. As if, forsooth, any stain or error of this fragile life could not be expiated even by the blood of the eternal Son of God, but each person were bound to pay his own debt down to the last farthing. Is this the Christ whom Isaiah prophesied of, in chapter liii, verses 4 and 5? Surely he has borne our sicknesses and carried our sorrows. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. Not by the stripes of Christ, if the faith of the Hierarchy is true, but each one shall be healed by his own stripes. The wretched sinner will strip himself, be flogged, clothe his skin in hair-cloth, undertake long and tedious journeys, try to crawl with bare knees over jutting flints, fast, and keep vigil, not to correct his life, but to make satisfaction for his sins, just as if the Son of God had never made satisfaction for them; and at last, after this life, a most fierce flame will burn him, not to be quenched until the stiff farthing of the last penny is paid. To me here there comes, opportunely, that jesting remark of Luther's [μαισωνικὸν], taken from the Prophet: Lord, I cannot eat human dung.

units.la: LI. Neque tantum satisfactioni Christi satisfactiones proprias, sed alienas etiam, superogatorias inprimis Monachorum, indulgentiarum Papalium beneficio, auxiliares manus porrigentibus scilicet, impertiendas addunt, ut dum his umbris & quisquiliis stulti Mortales inhiant, canis Æsopici instar, nucleum satisfactionis Christi perdant. Olim quidem piè sic Leo pa Epist.83. locutus est: Accepere justi, non dedere coronas, & de fortitudine fidelium nata sunt exempla patientiæ, non dona justitiæ. Singulares quippe eorum mortes fuerunt: nec alterius quispiam debitum suo fine persolvit, cùm inter filios hominum unus solus Dominus noster Jesus Christus extiterit, in quo omnes crucifixi, omnes mortui, omnes sepulti, omnes etiam sunt suscitati. Si Leonis tempore Ecclesiæ satisfactiones verè Sanctorum reputit, quid de monachis modernis illa statuisset? An promeritis hypocritarum flagellis aliena debita solvi illa credidisset? Quorsum adhibendæ alienorum meritorum guttulæ vel umbræ, exundante & in usum nostrum immenso promeritorû Christi Oceano perenniter fluente?
units.tr: LI. Moreover, to Christ's satisfaction they add not only satisfactions of their own but also those of others, especially the supererogatory satisfactions of the monks, which they hand out by the benefit of papal indulgences, as if lending helping hands, so that while foolish mortals gape at these shadows and trifles, like Aesop's dog, they lose the kernel of Christ's satisfaction. Leo once spoke piously on this in Epist. 83: The just have received crowns; they have not bestowed them. Examples of patience were born from the courage of the faithful, not gifts of righteousness.
