Their deaths were individual, and no one paid another's debt by his end, since among the sons of men our Lord Jesus Christ alone has existed, in whom all were crucified, all dead, all buried, and all also raised. If in Leo's time the Church truly reckoned the satisfactions of the saints as such, what would he have decided about the monks of our day? Would he have believed that other people's debts could be paid by the merits of hypocrites' scourgings? Why should we use drops or shadows of others' merits, when the ocean of Christ's merits overflows, is immense, and flows forever for our use?

units.la: LII. Quis amabo nisi inebriatus nimiùm meretricis illius philtris, ferat, ut cùm imputatio perfectissimæ & indubitatæ Christi justitiæ, ad justitiam peccatoris, nobis à Deo facta, passim inter illos deridiculo sit, quin anathemate etiam feriatur; justitia tamen incerta & menstruata, merita & passiones Sanctorum hominum, è communi quodam thesauro ad levandas animarum pœnas ab homine imputentur? Quis ferat, ut Mortalium aliquis satis superque faciat Deo? Quis ferat prodigas indulgentiarum concessiones & nundinationes turpissimas? Quis ferat precularum quarundam supinæ obmurmurationi (neque enim, si Casuistis credimus, opus est vel intentione animi, vel devotione) concessam à Johanne XXII. annorum decies centenorum millium indulgentiam? Concessam tamen Hor. B. Virg. Rom. rythmic. testatur. Quis ferat, cùm non ultra mundi finem sævituram hanc flammam autument, uno tamen libello paulò minus, quàm annorum undecies mille millenorum indulgentiam credulis devotisque animis offerri? Oblatam tamen Hora B. Virg. ad usum Sarisb. testatur. Quinimò ímò inventus in Anglia est, uti Jos. Hallus alibi narrat, liber manuscriptus, membranaceus carie tincísque erófsus, in quo præter àlias absurdissimas & blasphemas pollicitationes uni perbrevi oratiunculæ facultas datur pœnas infernales in purgatorias; postmodum verò purgatorias in summa Cœli gaudia commutandi.
units.tr: LII. Who, pray, unless he were too much intoxicated with that harlot's love potions, could endure this? Although the imputation to the sinner of the most perfect and undoubted righteousness of Christ, which God makes over to us, is everywhere mocked by them and even struck with anathema, yet the uncertain and menstrual righteousness of holy men, their merits and sufferings, are imputed by man out of a certain common treasury to relieve the punishments of souls. Who could endure that any mortal should satisfy God fully and more than fully? Who could endure the lavish grants of indulgences and their most shameful marketing? Who could endure the indulgence of 30,000,000 years, granted by John XXII to a certain lazy mumbling of little prayers (for, if we believe the casuists, neither intention of mind nor devotion is needed)? The Roman rhythmic Hours of the Blessed Virgin attest that it was granted. Who could endure that, though they think this flame will rage until the end of the world, an indulgence of very nearly 11,000 million millennia should be offered to credulous and devout souls in a single little book? The Hours of the Blessed Virgin according to the use of Salisbury attest that it was offered. Indeed, as Joseph Hall relates elsewhere, a manuscript book was found in England, on parchment, eaten away by decay and stains, in which, besides other most absurd and blasphemous promises, the power is given to a single very short little prayer of changing infernal punishments into purgatorial ones, and afterwards purgatorial ones into the highest joys of heaven.

units.la: LIII. Restant humanorum operum merita;quibus quantum humanum supercilium arrogat, tantum merito Christi per summam ingratitudinem impietatém que derogat. Et bona quidem hominis justificati opera mereri secundum operis debitum Andradius Concil. Trid. orthod. explicat. lib.6. habere valorem condignum præmio Cœlesti, Theologus ille Anglo-Duacensis de trip. hom. offic. lib. 2. nec non convenientem proportionem æqualitatis & dignitatis cum præmio ipso vitæ æternæ, Pererius Comm. in Rom. 6. idque in se ipso absque ulla meritorum mortisve Christi regione, Suarez Tom. 1. in Thom. 3. d. 11. & Bayus de merit. oper. lib. 11. 9. contendunt.
units.tr: LIII. There remain the merits of human works; and as much as human pride claims for them, so much by the greatest ingratitude and impiety it takes away from the merit of Christ. Andradius, in Concil. Trid. orthod. explicat. lib. 6., explains that the good works of a justified man merit according to the debt of the work and have a value condign to the heavenly reward. That English-Douai theologian, in de trip. hom. offic. lib. 2., and Pererius, in Comm. in Rom. 6., hold a fitting proportion of equality and dignity with the very reward of eternal life. Suárez, in Tom. 1. in Thom. 3. d. 11., and Bayus, in de merit. oper. lib. 11. 9., contend that this happens in itself, without any regard to the merits or death of Christ.

units.la: Quod postremum blasphemiæ proximum mirum nì ipsis sanioribus Papistis videatur. Attamen quo loco Hierarchici nostri justitiam ac meritum Christi habeant, idem qui supra Index Hispanus Madriticus testatur. Ex libro enim, qui inscribitur Ordo baptizandi cum modo visitandi, Venetiis A. 1575. impresso, hæc verba: Credis non propriis meritis, sed passionis Domini nostri Jesu Christi virtute ac merito ad gloriam pervenire? Et paulò post: Credis, quòd Dominus noster Jesus Christus pro nostra salute mortuus sit, & quòd ex propriis meritis, vel alio modo nullus possit salvari, nisi in merito passionis ipsius? Verba, inquam, Christi & Apostolorum doctrinæ consentanea, fundamentum salutis continentia, deleri jubentur. Nimirum hi erant scorpiones & colubri veterum, quos inter incedendum fuisset lectori, nisi probè sic securitati nostræ Senatus Inquisitorius consuluisset.
units.tr: This last point, which is close to blasphemy, would seem strange even to the saner Papists themselves. Yet the Spanish Index of Madrid, mentioned above, testifies where our hierarchs place Christ's righteousness and merit. For in the book entitled Ordo baptizandi cum modo visitandi, printed at Venice in 1575, these words occur: Do you believe that you will reach glory not by your own merits, but by the virtue and merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? And a little later: Do you believe that our Lord Jesus Christ died for our salvation, and that no one can be saved by his own merits or in any other way, except in the merit of his passion? These words, I say, which agree with the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles and contain the foundation of salvation, are ordered to be erased. Surely these were the scorpions and serpents of old, among whom the reader would have had to walk, had the Inquisitorial Senate not so carefully looked to our safety.

units.la: LIV. Sed salvum & illibatum Christo Sacerdoti
units.tr: LIV. But Christ the Priest kept safe and unharmed

units.la: Summo, ejus justitiæ, cruci, merito honorem se ferre Hierarchici gloriantur eo prætextu, quòd sacrificium Missaticum, justitia inhærens, satisfactiones propriæ, indulgentiæ, merita humanorum operum, in quibusferè Evangelium Papisticum consistit, Sacrificio, justitiæ, satisfactioni, indulgentiæ, merito Christi perfectissimo vel subordinentur, vel virtutem certè efficaciámque suam omnem acceptam referant; vel quòd per illa hæc applicentur. Quis verò meretricium hunc Babylonis fucum non abstersterit facilè? Sic enim hæc omnia sacrificio & merito Christi subordinantur, & in eo fundantur ut cerea domus ardentibus prunis superædificatur, vel domus ex sale in medio flumine construitur. Nulla causarum subordinatio locum habere potest, ubi sic uni cuipiam soliquæ causæ omnis efficacia adscribitur, ut reliquæ omnes excludantur. Ita hic res se habet. Sanguini, sacrificio, justitiæ, satisfactioni, merito Christi soli salus & redemptio nostra sic in Dei verbo adscribitur, ut non nisi sanguini, & uni victimæ, uni oblationi remissio peccatorum accepta referatur, Esaj. LXIII. 3. Hebr. ix. 22. 28. x. 12. opera & justitia propria passim removeantur, Rom. III. 24. 25. 28. x. 3. satisfactio solius Christi causa remissionis peccatorum constituatur, Matth. xx. 28. Ephes. i. 7. Tit. iii. 5. 7. 1. Pet. i. 18. 1. Joh. ii. 2. iv. 10. & humana satisfactio, ceu impotens planè arceatur omnis, Psal. xlix. 8. 9. denique merita humana configantur omnia Rom. iv. 4. 5. xi. 6. Ephes. ii. 8. 9. Tit iii. 4. 5. Frustra ergo causarum ejusmodi subordinatio fingitur; frustra inter applicationis media deputantur, quæ gladius verbi Divini percutit. Peccata nostra, non justitiam, merita nostra, Christi sanguis tinxit. Meruitne Christus, ut perfecta sint, quæ nos facimus? Quomodo do ergo sic claudicant vel optimorum opera? Meruitne, ut dum imperfecta sunt, adhuc tamen justificent, mereantur? Quæ hæc Deo injuria, quæ terminorum contradictio est? Tot nunc erunt Salvatores, quot boni sunt. Quæ enim facio, mea sunt, mea sunt,quæ mereor, quisquis faciendi vel merendi facultatem dederit.
units.tr: The Hierarchs boast that they bear the honour of Christ's supreme justice, cross and merit, on the pretext that the Mass-sacrifice, inherent righteousness, their own satisfactions, indulgences and the merits of human works, on which the Papist gospel almost entirely rests, are either subordinated to the most perfect sacrifice, righteousness, satisfaction, indulgence and merit of Christ, and refer all their virtue and efficacy to it, or are applied through these. But who could not easily wipe away this harlot's paint of Babylon? For all these things are subordinated to the sacrifice and merit of Christ, and are founded on it, in the way a house of wax is built up over burning coals, or a house of salt is built in the middle of a river. No subordination of causes can hold where all efficacy is ascribed to one single cause and all the others are excluded. This is how the matter stands here. In God's Word, the salvation and redemption of us is ascribed to the blood, sacrifice, righteousness, satisfaction and merit of Christ alone, so that the forgiveness of sins is attributed to the blood, and the one victim, the one offering alone (Isa. 63:3; Heb. 9:22, 28; 10:12); our own works and righteousness are everywhere removed (Rom. 3:24, 25, 28; 10:3); the satisfaction of Christ alone is established as the cause of the remission of sins (Matt. 20:28; Eph. 1:7; Tit. 3:5, 7; 1 Pet. 1:18; 1 John 2:2; 4:10); and all human satisfaction is shut out as wholly powerless (Ps. 49:8, 9); finally, all human merits are overthrown (Rom. 4:4, 5; 11:6; Eph. 2:8, 9; Tit. 3:4, 5). So the subordination of causes of this kind is an invention made in vain; in vain are they reckoned among the means of application, which the sword of the divine Word strikes down. Our sins, not his righteousness, stained Christ's blood; our merits did not. Did Christ merit that the things we do should be perfect? How then do even the works of the best limp? Did he merit that, while they are imperfect, they should still justify and earn merit? What an injury this is to God, what a contradiction in terms! There will now be as many saviours as there are good men. For what I do is mine, and what I merit is mine, whoever has given me the power of doing or meriting.

units.la: LV. Quintò denique Sacerdotalis officii Christi partem alteram, quæ μεσιτέια intercessione & mediatione ejus apud Patrem constat, pari impietate Hierarchici oppugnant. Sicut Christum non nisi semel oblatum Scriptura, uti vidimus, testatur: sic ἑνα μεσίτην unum Mediatorem Dei & hominum: neque alium, quàm qui se redemptionis pretium pro omnibus dedit, hominem Christum Jesum eadem 1 Tim. 11. 5. 6. definit. Is ergo simul solus se victimam ἁμαρτὴν in ara crucis pro nobis semel immolavit: simul solus precum nostrarum thymiama, ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, odorem bonae fragrantiae in ara Cœli Patri suo jugiter offert, Rom. viii. 34. Hebr. vii. 25. ix. 24. 1 Joh. 11. 2.
units.tr: LV. Fifthly and finally, the other part of Christ's priestly office, which consists in his intercession and mediation before the Father (μεσιτεία), the Hierarchs attack with equal impiety. As Scripture testifies, as we have seen, Christ was offered only once; so too there is one Mediator between God and men (ἕνα μεσίτην), and the same 1 Tim. 2:5, 6 defines him as the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as the price of redemption for all, and no other. He therefore alone once sacrificed himself as the victim on the altar of the cross for us [ἅπαξ]; and alone he continually offers to his Father in heaven the incense of our prayers, a fragrant odour (ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας), on the altar of heaven (Rom. 8:34; Heb. 7:25; 9:24; 1 John 2:2).

units.la: LVI. Sicut ergo constitutis in cultu suo infinitis sacrificiis: sic introductis etiam innumeris Mediatoribus Christum Sacerdotem & Mediatorem unicum Hierarchici exauctorárunt. Non enim magis in hoc mundo crevit intercessorum numerus, quàm impietas invocandi. Modestius paulò prioris Scholæ acumen ita mediationis quandam distinctionem sibi finxit, ut alteram ejus speciem Christo eximiam; alteram Christo & Sanctis communem fecerit. At succedanei in omnia Mediatoris officia temere involárunt, & quicquid cuiquam sequestri quovis jure competere potuit, totum illud Sanctis suis tribuerunt. Alius B. Virgini inclamat, O servatrix salvame! Alius: Impetra veniam, applica gratiam, præpara gloriam. Alii, Cassandro teste, viri celebres dixerunt: Deum Regni sui, quod constat ex justitia & misericordia dimidium, hoc est, misericordiam, in B. Mariam transtulisse. Alii sic Franciscum cum Christo compararunt, ut uterque horum Jesus typicus fuerit, dubium reliquerint. En Turselllini apud Possevinum Biblioth. sel. p. 295. ἰδιωπαρμὸν;
units.tr: LVI. Therefore, just as they have multiplied sacrifices without end in their worship, so too, by introducing countless mediators, the Hierarchs have deprived Christ of his office as the unique Priest and Mediator. For the number of intercessors has not grown in this world any more than the impiety of invoking them. The subtler wits of a somewhat earlier school, with more restraint, invented a certain distinction within mediation, so that they made one kind of it peculiar to Christ and another common to Christ and the saints. But the substitutes have rashly rushed into all the offices of the Mediator, and whatever right of any kind could belong to a go-between, they have assigned all of it to their saints. One cries out to the Blessed Virgin, O saving mistress, save me! Another: Obtain pardon, apply grace, prepare glory. Others, according to the testimony of Cassander, celebrated men have said: God has transferred to the Blessed Mary the kingdom of his rule, which consists half in justice and half in mercy, that is, mercy. Others have so compared Francis with Christ that they have left it doubtful which of the two was the typical Jesus. Behold, from Tursellinus, quoted by Possevinus, Bibliotheca selecta, p. 295, a parody [ἰδιωπαρμόν]:

units.la: Qui Franciscus erat, jam tibi Christus erit.
units.tr: Whoever Francis was, now Christ will be to you.

units.la: Jam Franciscus erit, qui modo Christus erat.
units.tr: Now Francis will be, who only lately was Christ.

units.la: Idem Dominico praestitit pari blasphemia Archiepiscopus Florentinus. Alii Litanias, Psalteria, & quicquid ad Dei gloriam Spiritus Dei accommodavit, ad S. Virginis nomen ore sacrilego traduxerunt. Neque haec privatorum quorundam δαιμονία est. Nam etiam in Ecclesiis publice ejusmodi carmen decantatum Cassander testatur: O felix puerpera, Nostra pians scelera, Jure matris impera Redemptori. Haec similiaque a piissimis Ecclesiae Romanae censoribus, rigidis morum Magistris, ipsorumque Pontificum suffragiis comprobata, hodieque Jesuitae, curvae mentes, Bencius, Bonarscius, alii dicunt, scribunt, tuentur. Neque Bernhardini de Bustis, Antonini, Bartolomaei, Pisani, Turselllini, alii Mario-latrae,& Hagiolatrae, tot dictis factisque in Christum unicum Salvatorem & Mediatorem iniquissimi & blasphemi, digni (quod olim de Vigilantio Hieronymus minori longe ratione dixit) quorum praecideretur lingua, & per partes ac frusta dilaceraretur, criticum Inquisitorum vel expurgatorum veru hactenus subiverunt ulli.
units.tr: The Archbishop of Florence committed the same blasphemy with equal impiety towards the Lord's name. Others have transferred to the name of the Blessed Virgin, with a sacrilegious mouth, the litanies, psalters, and whatever the Spirit of God has fitted to the glory of God. Nor is this the mad notion of certain private individuals. For Cassander testifies that such a song was even sung publicly in the churches: O happy childbearer, who atone for our crimes, by a mother's right command the Redeemer. These and similar things, approved by the most pious censors of the Roman Church, strict masters of morals, and by the votes of the Popes themselves, are still said, written and defended today by the Jesuits, the crooked-minded Bencius, Bonarscius and others. Yet none of those Mary-worshippers and saint-worshippers, Bernardinus de Bustis, Antoninus, Bartholomaeus, Pisanus, Tursellinus and others, most unjust and blasphemous in so many words and deeds against Christ, the only Saviour and Mediator, deserving (as Jerome once said of Vigilantius, with much less reason) to have their tongue cut out and be torn apart piecemeal and in shreds, has up to now undergone the criticism of Inquisitors or expurgators.

units.la: LVII. Sed forte sobrie magis recentiores, Cassander inprimis, Polydorus Vergilius, Methodistae nuperi, dolosae generalitatis architecti sapiunt. Sed quocunque illi fuco publicum Ecclesiae suae decedus tegere conentur, neque tamen aperte blasphemias a nobis memoratas damnare audent; neque sic simpliciorum animas iis extricant, ut in magno salutis discrimine non versentur ampliùs: Quotus quisqueeorum prohibet Sanctos ceu Mediatores invocari? Quotusquisque Mediatores esse vi meritorum inficiatur? Qua verò fide preculæ ad beatos spiritus nitentur; nisi forte, quod Hosius concedit, credere etiam in sanctos debeamus? Qui fontem orationum, corda lustrare, qui simul semelque mille supplicum vota, locis totidem à se dissitorum, exaudire valet, omniscius omnino & omnipræsens sit oportet. Neque enim naturæ celeritas, sed vera ubiquitas, Bellarmino etiam de Beatitud. S. lib. 1. 20. fatente, ad preces percipiendas omnium ubique precantium requiritur.
units.tr: LVII. But perhaps the more recent writers are wiser, above all Cassander, Polydorus Vergilius and the recent Methodists, the architects of deceptive generality. Yet whatever fog they try to use to hide the public scandal of their Church, they do not dare openly to condemn the blasphemies we have mentioned; nor do they free the souls of simple people from them so that they are no longer in great danger of salvation. How few of them forbid the saints to be invoked as mediators? How few deny that they are mediators by virtue of their merits? By what faith then will prayers strive towards the blessed spirits, unless perhaps, as Hosius concedes, we ought to believe in the saints too? Whoever is able to search hearts, the fountain of prayers, and to hear at once and together the vows of a thousand suppliants, at as many places far apart from him, must be wholly omniscient and omnipresent. For, as Bellarmine also admits in De beatitudine sanctorum, book 1, chapter 20, it is not the swiftness of a nature but true ubiquity that is required to receive the prayers of all who pray everywhere.

units.la: LVIII. Nefas illud Sacerdotalis Christi μεσιτείας pollutæ auget non obscura. quam hic Hierarchia fraufa est, fraus, & manifestum periculum hominum. Fraus in eo consistit, quòd multiplicatis Mediatoribus oblationes cleri non parùm accrescunt; quando amplis pellecti largitionibus clientum suorum in Coelesti curia causam Fervidius acturi creduntur.
units.tr: LVIII. The impious usurpation of Christ's priestly mediation is no small increase of pollution, and this is the fraud of the Hierarchy and a manifest danger to men. The fraud consists in this: by multiplying mediators, the offerings of the clergy grow considerably, since men are thought to be won over by generous largesse and so to plead their clients' cause more fervently in the heavenly court.

units.la: Neque enim Babylonicus hic Sacerdos religioni ducit minori, vendere pecuniis officium Christi Mediatorium, quàm ipsius pretiosæ mortis ac passionis Christi efficaciam trapezitico fœnori suo exponere. Periculum verò ingens glisciit, dum rudis plebecula nænia hac soporifera sic delinita obdormit, ut Patroni Coelestis arbitrio suo delecti opera & intercessione potenti freta pensi nil habeat, quomodo vitam instituat, dummodo satis Patrono Coelesti suo facere videatur; atque adeò ejus mentes non rectà ad Deum eleventur, sed in Sanctulo suo Templo, altaribus, Sacerdotibus, diebus festis, oblationibus, aliisque inanibus ceremoniis colendo stupeant; denique omnem suam devotionem, affectum pium, amorem, fidem,
units.tr: For this Babylonian priest does not think it a lesser sin to sell Christ's mediatorial office for money than to put up the efficacy of Christ's precious death and passion at interest in his banking business. The danger, moreover, grows immense, while the rough common folk, lulled by this soporific lullaby, fall asleep, so that, relying on the powerful works and intercession of a patron chosen at their own discretion in heaven, they have no concern how they order their lives, provided they seem to give enough satisfaction to their heavenly patron. And so their minds are not lifted up straight to God, but they are dazed by worshipping in his little shrine, at altars, by priests, on feast days, by offerings and other empty ceremonies; and finally they turn all their devotion, pious affection, love and faith away from Christ and his cross into so many devious streams, which are of no moment for promoting the salvation and holiness of men, and they perish.

units.la: Tom. II. g 2 à Christo & cruce ejus in tot rivulos devios, qui nullius ad salutem & sanctimoniam hominum promovendam momenti sunt, detorqueant. perdántque.
units.tr: Tom. II. g 2 from Christ and his cross into so many devious streams, which are of no moment for promoting the salvation and holiness of men, and they perish.

units.la: LIX. Restat Officium Christi Regium, quod non inclementer minùs Hierarchica tyrannis invasit. Argumentum irrefragabile præbent, quæ Dissertationis Nonæ sectione Tertia integra de potestate spirituali, & sub prætextu hujus etiam temporali suprema, quam sibi Papa, ille Rex Regum, & Dominus dominantium, vindicat, & nefariè exercet, diximus. Testatur id ipsum inde à Bonifacii III. ætate perpetua Sedis Romanæ, quam in Historia Papatus fusiùs paulò exposituimus, praxis; affirmant Canonistarum blasphemiæ; contendunt Sophistarum indefessæ argutiæ. Christo enim Domino, Capite ac Rege Ecclesiæ unico, sedente ad dexteram Patris, & legibus Regni ejus fundamentalibus, quæ Scripturis sacris continentur, ausu Cyclopico, spretis, Papam, velut in demortuum Christi locum, Regem & Monarcham Ecclesiæ, eúmque æque ac Christum, infallibilem, judicio Mortalium nulli obnoxium, adeóque παντκρατορα & ἀνυπεύθυνον, constituunt, judicem supremum, & supremi judicii normam faciunt. Arma insuper undiquaque compilata ostentant, quibus pudendum hunc Monarcham tegant; arma, inquam, ficulnea, quæ nec ratio sana, nec sacra Scriptura, nec pia antiquitas ministrat, sed furor arripit, veritas confundit. Aut enim usurpationes afferunt Pontificum, ab optimis quibusque damnatas; aut mendacia à peritioribus detecta & convicta solidè. Sic nempe Absolones novi nefariis artibus hominum animas suffurari studeant, ut clavim Davidis, hoc est, supremam in Ecclesia & Republica potestatem majore licentia usurpent.
units.tr: LIX. There remains the Regal office of Christ, which the Hierarchical tyranny has invaded no less cruelly. The arguments we set out in full in the third section of the Ninth Dissertation, concerning spiritual power, and the supreme temporal power which, under this pretext, the Pope claims for himself and exercises unlawfully, as that King of kings and Lord of lords, provide an irrefutable argument. The unbroken practice of the Roman See from the age of Boniface III, which we set out more fully in the History of the Papacy, bears witness to this very thing; the blasphemies of the canonists affirm it; the tireless cleverness of the sophists contends for it. For with Cyclopean boldness, and despising the fundamental laws of his kingdom, which are contained in the holy Scriptures, they set up the Pope, as if in the place of the dead Christ, as King and Monarch of the Church, and, like Christ, infallible, subject to the judgment of no mortal, and therefore omnipotent and unaccountable [παντκρατορα, ἀνυπεύθυνον]; they make him the supreme judge and the rule of the supreme judgment. Moreover, they display weapons gathered from every side with which to cover this shameful Monarch; weapons, I say, of fig-leaves, which neither sound reason, nor holy Scripture, nor pious antiquity supplies, but which frenzy seizes and truth confounds. For they bring forward either usurpations of the Popes, condemned by all the best men, or lies thoroughly exposed and refuted by the more skilled. Thus, indeed, like the new Absaloms, they strive to steal men's souls by wicked arts, so that they may usurp, with greater licence, the key of David, that is, supreme power in the Church and the Commonwealth.

units.la: LX. Pertinent huc justi, quod Papæ Hierarchia vendicat, infallibiliter interpretandi leges Christi fundamentales ; novas etiam pro lubitu figendi, & conscientiis ipsis hominum obtrudendi ; leges Christi lingua peregrina velatas abstrudendi ; nec non notoria impietas illa, qua, uti supra ostendimus, legibus Christi robur, decus & pretium omne detrahit, atque minorem etiam transgressoribus suarum, quàm ipsius Christi legum, poenam dictat ; Legendas mendaces, & à ferreæ frontis hominibus scriptas legi Divinæ obscurandæ inducendæque substituit ; contra leges Divinas, perjurium etiam, incestum, adulterium, perduellionem, parricidium, Sodomiam, aliaque atrocissima crimina prohibentes, perinde ac si non praecepta, sed consilia liberæ hominum optioni relicta forent, liberè, retis sui Piscatorii implendi gratia, & cum praesentissimo aeterno etiam stolidorum Mortalium, Spirituali Patri confidentium, damno dispensat ; leges, pacta civilia, jurata etiam, quæ juxta leges Dei & naturæ κaθόλu universaliter cognitas, obligant, prout libido & res ejus ferunt, rata vel irrita reddit, & qualibet occasione rescindit. Quæ singula in loco discussa nihil hic repetere juvat. Sufficit infractæ Regiæ potestatis Christi non unum specimen indicasse.
units.tr: LX. To this head belong the things that the Papal hierarchy claims for itself: to interpret infallibly the fundamental laws of Christ; to frame new laws at will and impose them on people's consciences; to hide away Christ's laws under a foreign tongue; and that notorious impiety by which, as we have shown above, it strips Christ's laws of all their strength, dignity and value, and prescribes lesser penalties for those who break its own rules than for those who break the laws of Christ himself. It has substituted lying legends, written by men of brazen forehead, for the Divine law, to obscure and displace it. Against the divine laws, which forbid perjury, incest, adultery, treason, parricide, sodomy and other most atrocious crimes, it dispenses freely, as if these were not precepts but counsels left to human choice, in order to fill its fishing net, and to the eternal damage of foolish mortals who trust in their spiritual father. It makes civil laws and pacts, even sworn ones, which bind according to the laws of God and of nature universally known, valid or void as its lust and its interests dictate, and annuls them on any pretext. These matters have each been discussed in their place, and there is no point in repeating them here. It is enough to have pointed out one instance of the broken royal power of Christ, not the only one.

units.la: LXI. Accedit, quòd Hierarchia Christi Regis gratiæ infensam se gerens, quantum libero arbitrio, seu naturæ in rebus fidei viribus tribuit, tantum Regno gratiæ derogat. Jam olim quidem Concilium Arausicanum damnavit superbam vocem dicentium, liberè nos credere per vigorem naturæ. Neque malè S. Augustinus : Libere velle opus est naturæ : bene velle gratiæ ; male velle corruptionis. Sed tam hic sunt astuti Tridentini, quàm inconstantes Jesuitæ. Illud pro more ludens verborum cōthurnis Sess. VI. cap. 5. & can. 4. anathemate subjicit dicentes, liberum hominis arbitrium à Deo motum & excitatum nihil coopeperari, assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocanti, quòd ad obtinendam justificationis gratiam se præparet ac disponat. Potest etenim homo excitari à somno: potest à morte. Ibi vigor, hic vita restituitur. Sic plane liberi in spiritualibus arbitrii vel dormientis vigor, vel mortui vita excitatione & motu illo Divino restitui potest. Utrum verò hic contingat, verbis non expressit, sed verborum lubricitate illusit potius, quàm categoricè definivit quicquam. Bellarminus de Gratia lib. vi. 15. è Ruardo suo affert, opus pium, quatenus opus, ab arbitrio esse, quatenus pium, à sola gratia, quatenus opus pium, ab arbitrio & gratia esse. Ejusdem libri cap. 6. contra suos Catholico-Pelagianos docet, in rebus, quæ ad pietatem & salutem pertinent, nihil posse voluntatem humanam absque auxilio gratiæ. Sed prodit suum ὑπαλον cap. 15. ubi asserit conversionem esse in potestate liberi arbitrii, quoniam potest semper converti, quando voluerit. Addit, ante omnem gratiam habere nos liberum arbitrium etiam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia. Si ante omnem, ergo etiam, ante prævenientem, excitantem, moventem. Non ergo nunc, uti S. Augustinus lib. de correpț. & gratia, docuit, nos prævenit; ut velimus, sed nos Deum prævertimus, quia volumus. Sed ne crassè nimis Bellarminus locutus videatur, sic mitigat, ut dicat, ligatam quidem esse libertatem, & sic se habere, ut potentia videndi absente specie sensibili. Sicut ergo liberè videre possumus, absente objecto: sic liberè velle, absente gratia. Certè ne ad malum quidem liberiores sumus, neque pejus Pelagius ipse deliravit. Quale insuper Dei auxilium, qualis gratia est, quam Christus Rex Cœlestis miseris Spiritu suo dispensat? Prævenire, inquiunt Jesuitæ, inspirare, movere, excitare, vocare, adjuvare Dei est; voluntatem inclinare, hominis est. Quomodo nunc non plus sibi & libero arbitrio, quàm Deo & gratiæ homo debet?
units.tr: LXI. In addition, the hierarchy, which sets itself against Christ the King of grace, takes away from the kingdom of grace as much as it grants to free will, or to the powers of nature in matters of faith. Long ago the Council of Orange indeed condemned the proud saying of those who claim that we believe freely through the vigour of nature. And St Augustine rightly says: To will freely is the work of nature; to will well is the work of grace; to will badly is the work of corruption. But the Tridentines are as crafty here as the Jesuits are inconstant. The former, playing with the buskins of words as is their custom, Sess. VI. cap. 5 and can. 4, adds an anathema against those who say that the free will of man, moved and stirred by God, does nothing to co-operate by assenting to God who stirs and calls, so that he may prepare and dispose himself to obtain the grace of justification. For a man can be roused from sleep; he can be raised from death. There the vigour is restored, here the life. So clearly the vigour of free will in spiritual things, whether asleep or dead, can be restored by such stirring and movement of God. But whether this happens here, they have not said in words; they have rather mocked us with the slipperiness of words than categorically defined anything. Bellarmine, On Grace, book VI, ch. 15, cites from his Ruardus: a pious work, as a work, is from the will; as pious, it is from grace alone; as a pious work, it is from will and grace together. In the same book, ch. 6, he teaches against his own Catholic-Pelagians that in matters which pertain to piety and salvation, the human will can do nothing without the help of grace. But in ch. 15 he betrays his escape clause, where he asserts that conversion is within the power of free will, since it can always be converted whenever it wills. He adds that before all grace we have free will even for works of piety and supernatural works. If before all grace, then also before the grace that goes before, stirs and moves. Therefore, as St Augustine taught in the book On Correction and Grace, it is not that grace goes before us so that we may will; rather, we anticipate God because we will. But lest Bellarmine seem to have spoken too crudely, he softens it, saying that freedom is indeed bound, and is so disposed as the power of seeing is when the sensible species is absent. Just as we can see freely when the object is absent, so we can will freely when grace is absent. Certainly we are not freer even for evil, and Pelagius himself did not rave more wickedly. What sort of help of God, what sort of grace is it, which Christ the heavenly King dispenses to the wretched by his Spirit? To anticipate, the Jesuits say, to inspire, move, stir, call and help belong to God; to incline the will belongs to man. How then does man not owe more to himself and to free will than to God and to grace?

units.la: LXII. Profecto sub laudibus naturæ & liberi arbitrii latent inimici gratiæ. Tantum suffurantur Christo, gratiæ illud Regnum moderanti, quantum sibi, morticinam naturam hanc superbè decoraturi, tribuunt. Christus ipse, quicquid virtutum suarum habet, refert ad gloriam Patris. Et homo, cujus suum nihil est, sibi vendicare, quod per Christum resurrexit, laboret? Modestè quondam Tiberius, Xiphilino narrante, è multis, quæ restituerat perfecerátque ædificiis, nullum sibi vendicavit, sed nomina illorum, à quibus ædificari cœpta sunt, indidit. Isti vero sibi arrogant ædes, quibus ne tegulam quidem unam imposuerint. Deus & velle & facere in nobis ἐνεργεῖ operatur, non velle & facere excitat, Phil. ii. 13. Operatur ergo & quod primum est, velle, & quod ultimum, facere, perficere. Aufert cor lapideum, creat cor novum; aufert & creat non dispositis paratisque, sed non parum reluctante natura, carne, cujus φρόνημα σαρκὸς εἰς θεὸν studium omne inimicitia est adversus Deum, Ezech. xi. 36. Rom. viii. 7. Sunt inimicitiæ quædam intestinæ, quæ nunquam in nervum erumpunt. Contra studium illud carnis οὐχ ὑποτάσσεται legi non subjicitur. At parebit forte aliquando. Neque illud; ἃ δύναται non potest, uti ibidem Apostolus. Ecce rebellem usque quaque Deo conditionem! Sacrificent ergo sibi Hierarchici, quod Sejanum olim solitum Xiphilinus scribit: immolent suæ ligenæ: vim suam Deum suum faciant: regnent ipsi, Regia potestate exuto Christo. Sed ruat profecto Cœlum; nunquam nobis arrogabimus, quod soli Deo & Christo Regi sacra quadam ἀκοινωνησία competit.
units.tr: LXII. Truly, under the praises of nature and free will lie the enemies of grace. They steal from Christ, who governs that kingdom of grace, as much as they assign to themselves in order to adorn with pride this carrion nature. Christ himself refers whatever virtues he has to the glory of the Father. And should man, of whom nothing is his own, labour to claim for himself what has risen again through Christ? Tiberius once, as Xiphilinus relates, modestly claimed for himself none of the many buildings he had restored and completed, but inscribed on them the names of those by whom they had first been begun. These men, however, arrogate to themselves buildings on which they have not laid so much as a single tile. God both wills and works in us [ἐνεργεῖ operatur], not merely stirs us to will and to do, Phil. 2.13. He works, therefore, both what is first, the willing, and what is last, the doing and completing. He takes away the heart of stone and creates a new heart; he takes away and creates it not in men who are disposed and prepared, but while nature and flesh resist not a little, whose mind of the flesh [φρόνημα σαρκός] towards God is all enmity against God, Ezek. 11.19, Rom. 8.7. There are certain inner enmities that never break out into open strength. Against that mind of the flesh, it is not subject [οὐχ ὑποτάσσεται] to the law. Yet perhaps it will at some time obey. Nor is that so: it cannot [ἃ δύναται], as the Apostle says in the same place. Behold the condition, everywhere rebellious against God! Let the hierarchs then sacrifice to themselves, as Xiphilinus writes that Sejanus once used to do: let them offer sacrifice to their own ligeners; let them make their own strength their god; let them reign themselves, with Christ stripped of his royal power. But surely heaven would fall before we would claim for ourselves what belongs to God alone and to Christ the King by a certain sacred incommunicability [ἀκοινωνησία].

units.la: LXIII. Neque tandem silentio praetereundem est, quòd Hierarchia iis, quibus se exornavit, potestatis Regiae Christi spoliis, ad crudeles eorum, qui veri Christi Regis subditi sunt, eíque uni solique adhaerere, institutis ejus sanctis & indispensabilibus morem gerere constitutum habent, neque aliam profecto ob causam, quàm quia tales sunt, nulliusde coetero criminis comperti, caedes internecionésque abutitur. Cujus etiam animi nullo crudelitatis genere exsatiari possunt, id unicè in maximis votis habentes, ut, quod de Romano quondam populo tyrannus ille vovisse dicitur, fideles Christi subditi omnes unicum haberent collum, quò uno ictu feriri omnes possent. Atque id impietatem inprimis omnem superat, quòd sic adversus sincera Christi membra horribiliter grassantes, se ipsi Jesu Christo inservire, apud eos, quos nec Christi, nec membrorum ejus veram notitiam habere probè norunt, simulare non dubitant.
units.tr: LXIII. Nor finally must it be passed over in silence that the hierarchy, with the spoils of Christ's royal power with which it has adorned itself, has resolved to indulge in slaughter and mass murder against the cruel persecution of those who are true subjects of Christ the King and cling to him alone, obeying his holy and indispensable institutions, and that for no other cause than that they are such, having been found guilty of no other crime. Nor can their minds be sated by any kind of cruelty, having this one thing as their greatest wish: that, as that tyrant is said to have wished of the Roman people, all the faithful subjects of Christ should have a single neck, so that all might be struck down with one blow. And this surpasses above all impiety: that, while raging so horribly against the sincere members of Christ, they do not hesitate to pretend that they serve Jesus Christ himself, before those whom they know well do not have a true knowledge of Christ or of his members.

units.la: LXIV. Quæ cum ita sint, Hierarchiam Christum totum, Christianamque adeò religionem universam pridem sepelivisse, falsámque adeò, uti Meretricem illam Magnam Babylonicam, post Deum, Christum, Christianam religionem insatiabiliter scortantem maximè decebat, religionem invexisse, in propatulo est. Christus enim nomen officii est: & Dei veri verus cultus veri Christi cultu constat. Quisquis ergo Christi officia oppugnat, is Christum ipsum, & Christianam religionem oppugnat, & contra utrumque tyrannidem nefariè exercet.
units.tr: LXIV. Since this is so, it is plain that the Hierarchy long ago buried all of Christ, and indeed the whole Christian religion, and introduced a false religion, which is exactly what that Great Babylonian Harlot, who insatiably fornicates with Christ and the Christian religion after God, would most fittingly do. For Christ is the name of an office, and the true worship of the true God consists in the worship of the true Christ. Therefore whoever attacks the offices of Christ attacks Christ himself and the Christian religion, and wields tyranny against both.

units.la: LXV. In tam notoria tyrannide frustra mihi Hierarchia oggesserit, se Christum, ejúsque officia palam profiteri, verbo Dei, cruci Christi, merito & Regno ejusdem locum relinquere. Hic enim meretricius fucus Babylonis est, quam specie externa matrimonii & pro-
units.tr: LXV. In so notorious a tyranny, the Hierarchy will try in vain to tell me that it openly professes Christ and his offices, and leaves room for the Word of God, the cross of Christ, his merit and his Kingdom. For this is the harlot's disguise of Babylon, which, under the outward appearance of marriage and of the profession of fellowship

units.la: {a} Christum ejusque ... professionis societatis cum Christo Sponso, scortari cum incolis terræ & Regibus mundi, nos Prophetia, uti Dissertatione secunda demonstravimus, docet. Quid enim tum postea, si verbum Dei, crux, meritum & Regnum Christi verbis jactentur, at mox re ipsa sugillentur, supplantentur, deprimantur, & contra humanæ inventiones adornentur, peregrinum sacrificium introducatur, & homo ille peccati supra Deum & Christum efferatur, ut qui ex mysterio hoc se extricare nesciunt, maximo in salutis discrimine versentur? Annon sic de Hierarchia illud Hilarii adversus Auxentium usurpabitur merito: Sub specie Evangelicæ prædicationis Christi contrarii sunt: & Dominus Jesus negatur, cum ab iis prædicatur. Etenim non in verbis, sed in sensu fides est. Olim quoque Arius jussus à Constantino M. manu sua scribere, quid de fide sentiret, fidem sic Rufinus Hist. lib. 1. 11. loquitur, verbis nostram, sensu suam exaravit. Sed & omnes hæreses, inquit Irenæus lib. 1. 9. Deum unum dicunt, sed per sententiam immutant. Neque nos male Gratianus Decr. 22. 4. 5. Humana docuit, verba nemini curæ esse debere, cùm non intentio verbis, sed verba intentioni inservire debeant. Bestia illa Apocalyptica cornua habet similia cornibus Agni, sed loquitur ut Draco, Apoc. xiii. 11. Baronii nota illa monstra variam multiplicémque habent naturam: sicut Cicero Catilinam monstrum vocat, ex contrariis diversisque inter se pugnantibus naturæ studiis cupiditatibúsque conflatum. S. Apostolus Antichristum in Templo Dei sessurum vaticinatur: cujus regnum & doctrina mysterium sit iniquitatis. Per Templum Dei Ecclesiam intelligi, res ipsa loquitur. Non enim inter Diabolos, vel merè Ethnicos regnat Antichristus, sed ipsam occupat Ecclesiam: nec bona Ecclesiæ eximia, orationem Dominicam, symbolum, Decalocalogum, invocationem Trinitatis in Baptismo, aliáque ejusmodi prorsus abolet, sed nefariis suis traditionibus illa ita contaminat & corrumpit, ut mysterium iniquitatis manibus palpare liceat. Sanæ enim doctrinæ reliquiarum prætextu, iniquissimas suas constitutiones palliat, & observandas miserè seductis obtrudit. Neque enim aliter à plerisque qui principiis illis jam assueverunt, receptus fuisset, vel meditamenta sua fraudésque perfecisset.
units.tr: {a} with Christ the Bridegroom, fornicates with the inhabitants of the earth and the kings of the world, as the Prophecy teaches us, as we showed in the second Dissertation. For what follows if the Word of God, the cross, the merit and the Kingdom of Christ are bandied about in words, but are at once in fact disparaged, undermined and depressed, and human inventions are set up in their place, a strange sacrifice is introduced, and that man of sin is exalted above God and Christ, so that those who cannot extricate themselves from this mystery are placed in the greatest danger to their salvation? Will not that saying of Hilary against Auxentius be rightly applied to the Hierarchy: Under the appearance of evangelical preaching they are opposed to Christ, and the Lord Jesus is denied when he is preached by them. For faith lies not in words but in meaning. Long ago Arius too, when ordered by Constantine the Great to write in his own hand what he thought about the faith, wrote, as Rufinus says in his History, book 1, chapter 11, the faith in our words, but in his own sense. And Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 9, says that all heresies say that God is one, but change his meaning by their interpretation. Nor do we wrongly rely on Gratian, Decretum 22, 4, 5, who taught that words should be of no concern to anyone, since it is not the intention that should serve the words, but the words that should serve the intention. That Apocalyptic beast has horns like the horns of the Lamb, but speaks like a dragon, Apocalypse 13:11. Those monsters that Baronius noted have a varied and manifold nature, just as Cicero calls Catiline a monster, made up of contrary and mutually warring inclinations and desires of nature. The Apostle prophesies that Antichrist will sit in the Temple of God, and that his kingdom and doctrine will be the mystery of iniquity. That the Temple of God means the Church is clear from the matter itself. For Antichrist does not reign among devils or mere heathens, but occupies the Church itself; nor does he utterly abolish the Church's excellent goods, the Lord's Prayer, the creed, the Decalogue, the invocation of the Trinity in baptism and other such things, but defiles and corrupts them with his wicked traditions, so that the mystery of iniquity can be felt with the hands. For under the pretext of relics of sound doctrine he disguises his most unjust constitutions and wretchedly thrusts them upon the deceived to be observed. Nor would they otherwise have been received by most people, who are already accustomed to those principles, or have brought their own schemes and frauds to completion.

units.la: LXVI. Neque tamen sine Numine factum, quod Hierarchicis quibusdam voces exciderunt, quibus interior animi eorum notio clarè satis patefacta est. Nota enim satis est vox Leonis X. literarum monumentis consignata, qui, teste Christiano Maffæo historico, Bembo dixit, multas opes Collegio eorum conflatas esse jam diu (dicam molliter, quod Sathanicum illud os efflavit) postquam illa de Christo persuasio passim pervasit. Quid enim est Christi personam & officium crudè atque asla voce negare, si hoc non est? Licet ergo Hierarchia omnis disertis id verbis non profiteatur, tamen casu non evenit, ut infandum sedis illius caput ita non sentiret duntaxat, sed blasphemè etiam loqueretur. Crimine ab uno disce omnes.
units.tr: LXVI. It was not without the divine will that some of the hierarchs let slip words by which the inner sentiment of their minds was made clear enough. For the saying of Leo X is well known, recorded in the monuments of letters, who, according to the historian Christian Maffei, said to Bembo that great wealth had long since been amassed for their college (I will put it gently, though it was a Satanic mouth that breathed it out) since that belief about Christ had spread everywhere. For what else is it to deny the person and office of Christ crudely and openly, if this is not? Although, therefore, the whole Hierarchy does not profess this in explicit words, it has not happened by chance that the head of that unspeakable see not only thought thus but even spoke blasphemously. Learn all from the one crime.
Section Two of the Eleventh Dissertation
IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam populum sibi obnoxium à vero veri Dei cultu ad cultum creaturarum, falsamque religionem seducere, ex erroribus ejusdem idololatricis probatur.
units.tr: It is proved, from the idolatrous errors of the Hierarchy itself, that the Hierarchy seduces the people subject to it from the true worship of the true God to the worship of creatures and a false religion.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Progressus ad errores Hierarchiæ idololatricos. II. Idololatria ejus Syllogismo probata cujus propositio & assumptio strictim asseritur. III. Bellarmini & Greg. de Valentia adversus propositionem, quòd idololatria sit cultus Divinus creaturæ exhibitus, exceptiones proponuntur. IV. Bellarmini exceptio, quòd idololatria non sit nisi cultus Divinus idolis, seu simulachris falsorum Numinum exhibitus, oppositis similibus, Sexti Roscii à parricidio, & Johannis XII. Papæ ab adulterio simili ratione defensi utriusque diluitur. V. VI. Quid idololatria sit, optimè ex declaratione Dei ipsius cognoscitur. VII. Quicquid porro idololatriam esse Deus Judæis declaravit, pro tali etiam Christianis habendum est. Tom. II. h
units.tr: I. The progress to the idolatrous errors of the Hierarchy. II. The idolatry of the Hierarchy is proved by a syllogism, whose major and minor premises are briefly asserted. III. The objections of Bellarmine and Gregory of Valencia against the major premise, that idolatry is the divine worship paid to a creature, are set out. IV. Bellarmine's objection, that idolatry is only divine worship paid to idols, that is, images of false deities, is refuted by the similar cases of Sextus Roscius, defended against the charge of parricide, and of Pope John XII, defended in the same way against the charge of adultery. V. VI. What idolatry is is best known from the declaration of God himself. VII. Whatever God declared to the Jews to be idolatry must also be held by Christians to be such. Tom. II. h

units.la: VIII. Quicquid in Paganis idololatriæ censu venit, apud Christianos similia facientes eodem censu venire debet.
units.tr: VIII. Whatever among the Pagans counts as idolatry must count as idolatry among Christians who do similar things.

units.la: IX. Bellarminiana verò idololatriæ definitio nec idololatriam Judæis simul & Christianis prohibitam, nec in Gentilibus damnatam exhaurit.
units.tr: IX. Bellarmine's definition of idolatry embraces neither the idolatry forbidden at once to Jews and Christians, nor the idolatry condemned among the Gentiles.

units.la: X. Judæis Deus prohibuit non superstitionem tantùm falsi, sed etiam indebiti cultus; illius quo falsum Numen, hujus, quo verum Numen in imagine colitur. Neutram idololatriam cultu idoli, seu simulachri falsi Numinis absolvi, probatur.
units.tr: X. God forbade the Jews not only the superstition of a false god but also undue worship: the former, by which a false deity is worshipped, the latter, by which the true God is worshipped in an image. It is proved that neither kind of idolatry is absolved by the worship of an idol or image of a false deity.

units.la: XI. Idolum quandoque etiam veri Dei imago est; imò omne id, quod cum verus Deus non sit, Divino cultu afficitur.
units.tr: XI. An idol is sometimes also an image of the true God; indeed, anything that is not the true God is given divine worship.
XII. The Seventy Interpreters lend their support.

units.la: XIII. Et Dei ipsius idololatriam declarantis id omne, quo ad Zelum Deus provocatur, testimonio.
units.tr: XIII. And the testimony of God himself, who declares idolatry, includes everything by which God is provoked to jealousy.

units.la: XIV. Veri Dei in imagine cultum idololatricum esse, tum ex sensu legis Divinæ,
units.tr: XIV. That the worship of the true God in an image is idolatrous is shown both from the sense of the divine law,

units.la: XV. Tum exemplis vitulorum Aharonis & Jeroboami, nec non Teraphim Michæ cultorum liquidò probatur.
units.tr: XV. and clearly from the examples of Aaron's calves, of Jeroboam's calves, and of the teraphim worshipped by Micah.

units.la: XVI. Paganorum idololatria quandoque fuit cultus summi & veri Dei in imagine.
units.tr: XVI. The idolatry of the Pagans was sometimes the worship of the highest and true God in an image.

units.la: XVII. Greg de Valentia exceptio adversus propositionem majorem, quòd idololatria sit non quivis cultus Divinus creaturæ exhibitus, sed isdemum, qui eiut Deo exhibetur, discutitur.
units.tr: XVII. Gregory of Valencia's objection against the major premise, that idolatry is not every divine worship paid to a creature but only that which is paid to God, is examined.

units.la: XVIII. Ratio, qua Valentianus Hierarchiam ab idololatria defendit, prodit, meretricem Romanam antiquas lupas Romanas; & Jesuitas priscos causidicos impudentia & ingenio superare multum.
units.tr: XVIII. The reasoning by which Valentia defends the Hierarchy from idolatry is set out: it betrays the Roman harlot as surpassing the ancient Roman wolves, and the early Jesuit advocates in impudence and cleverness by a great deal.

units.la: XIX. Alterutrum duorum, quæ Valentia ad idololatriam requirit, scortum Babylonico-Romanum idololatriæ convincit.
units.tr: XIX. Either of the two things which Valentia requires for idolatry convicts the Babylonian-Roman harlot of idolatry.

units.la: XX. XXI. Absurditas definitionis Valentiæ ulterius ostensa.
units.tr: XX. XXI. The absurdity of Valentia's definition is further shown.

units.la: XXII. Omnes ii, quibus præter Deum verum Divinus honor exhibetur, alii Dii fiunt.
units.tr: XXII. All those to whom divine honour is paid besides the true God become other gods.

units.la: XXIII. Quicunque talibus Divinum honorem exhibent, idololatræ, Polythei & Athei sunt.
units.tr: XXIII. Whoever pays divine honour to such beings are idolaters, polytheists and atheists.

units.la: XXIV. Transitur ad assumptionis probationem, atque generali ratione docetur, Hierarchiam creaturis Divinum cultum exhibere, & exhibendum præcipere.
units.tr: XXIV. We pass to the proof of the minor premise, and it is taught by a general argument that the Hierarchy pays divine worship to creatures and commands that it be paid.

units.la: XXV. XXVI. Sicut inter excellentiam increatam & creatam media nulla: ita inter cultum Divinum seu religiosum & civilem medius, qui religiosus etiam sit, datur nullus. Et si daretur medius, civilis ille potius, quàm religiosus foret.
units.tr: XXV. XXVI. Just as there is no middle between uncreated and created excellence, so there is no middle between divine or religious worship and civil worship that is itself religious. And if there were a middle, that worship would be civil rather than religious.

units.la: XXVII. Religiosum cultum omnem Angelus præsens Apoc. xix. 10. repudiavit.
units.tr: XXVII. The angel present rejected every religious worship, Apoc. xix. 10.

units.la: XXVIII. Religiosus duliæ vel hyperduliæ cultus ad nullam Dei legem referri potest.
units.tr: XXVIII. Religious worship of the kind called dulia or hyperdulia cannot be referred to any law of God.

units.la: XXIX. Ejusdem vanitatem Christus Luc. iv. 8. & S. Paulus Hebr. 1. 6. demonstrant.
units.tr: XXIX. Christ, Luke iv. 8, and St Paul, Heb. 1. 6, demonstrate its vanity.

units.la: XXX. Religiosus cultus unicus, idémque Divinus est, quo Divinam excellentiam per signa propria eidem significandæ inservientia recognoscimus.
units.tr: XXX. The one religious worship, which is also divine, is that by which we acknowledge the divine excellence through the proper signs that serve to signify it.

units.la: XXXI. Propria religiosi cultus soli Deo debiti signa recensentur.
units.tr: XXXI. The proper signs of religious worship due to God alone are listed.

units.la: XXXII. Nil refert, qua σχέσει, amicorum an inimicorum Dei, creaturis cultus Divinus deferatur.
units.tr: XXXII. It makes no difference in what relation, whether as friends or as enemies of God, divine worship is paid to creatures.

units.la: XXXIII. Neque idololatriam purgat fucus ille, quòd cultus creaturarum non absolutus, sed relativus sit, & in prototypa transeat.
units.tr: XXXIII. Nor does that pretext clear idolatry, namely that the worship of creatures is not absolute but relative, and passes over to the prototype.

units.la: XXXIV. Ne quidem latria ad prototypa transfire potest.
units.tr: XXXIV. Not even latria can pass over to the prototypes.

units.la: XXXV. Et cultus ille relativus imaginibus proprius esse debet.
units.tr: XXXV. And that relative worship ought to belong to images.

units.la: XXXVI. Scholasticorum de cultu proprio imaginum dissidia.
units.tr: XXXVI. The disagreements of the Schoolmen about the proper worship of images.
XXXVII. The sinew of the general argument is drawn tight.

units.la: XXXVIII. Specialis demonstratio Assumptionis ubi Hierarchicorum idololatria juxta species creaturarum in ea expressas, in Papolatriam (de qua supra) Artolatriam, Hagiolatriam, Iconolatriam, Lipsano-latriam & Hierolatriam distinguitur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. A specific demonstration of the minor premise, in which the idolatry of the Hierarchicals, according to the kinds of creatures expressed in it, is distinguished into Papolatry (discussed above), Artolatry, Hagiolatry, Iconolatry, Lipsanolatry and Hierolatry.

units.la: XXXIX. Artolatria mare mortuum est. De Eucharistiae cultu definitio Tridentinorum ex qua idololatria Hierarchicorum demonstratur.
units.tr: XXXIX. Artolatry is a dead sea. The definition of the Tridentines concerning the worship of the Eucharist, from which the idolatry of the Hierarchicals is demonstrated.

units.la: XL. Eandem committi probatur, si maxime Eucharistiae Sacramentum in compositione ex speciebus, corpore & Divinitate Christi constituatur.
units.tr: XL. It is proved that the same idolatry is committed even if the sacrament of the Eucharist is held to consist of the species, the body and the divinity of Christ together.

units.la: XLI. Artolatriae fundamentum transsubstantiatio est. Quae si falsa fuerit, omnium turpissimos idololatras fore Pontificios, Cosierus fatetur.
units.tr: XLI. The foundation of Artolatry is transubstantiation. If that is false, the Papists will be the most shameful idolaters of all, as Cosier admits.
XLII. The Tridentine definition of it is attacked.
XLIII. By the circumstances of the Supper,

units.la: XLIV. Nec non principiis scientiarum, Physices, Metaphysices, Mathematices, Logices;
units.tr: XLIV. and also by the principles of the sciences: physics, metaphysics, mathematics, logic;
XLV. and it is contrary to all purer antiquity.

units.la: XLVI. Idololatrae proin hostiae adoratores certissimi sunt. Averroeis adversus eos, qui adorant, quod comedunt, apophtegma.
units.tr: XLVI. Therefore the worshippers of the host are most certainly idolaters. Averroes' apophthegm against those who worship what they eat.

units.la: XLVII. Non juvat artolatras persuasio, quod Christus praesens sit sub speciebus panis.
units.tr: XLVII. The belief that Christ is present under the species of bread does not help the artolaters.
XLVIII. And so they deny that bread is present.

units.la: XLIX. Si maxime transsubstantiationis dogma obtineret, non eo minus Hierarchici idololatria se polluerent, quia de conversione facta nunquam certi esse possunt; & tamen adorare non desinunt.
units.tr: XLIX. Even if the dogma of transubstantiation prevailed, the Hierarchicals would not for that reason be less polluted by idolatry, since they can never be certain that the conversion has taken place, and yet they do not cease to adore.

units.la: L. Artolatriam Hagiolatria, seu sanctorum cultus excipit, qui circumscribitur.
units.tr: L. Hagiolatry, or the worship of the saints, follows Artolatry, and it is circumscribed.
LI. It is proved that this worship is divine.

units.la: LII. Praetextus Hagiolatrarum, quod Sanctos ut amicos Dei, non ut summum Deum colant, & mediationem eorum ad intercessionem restringant, diluuntur.
units.tr: LII. The pretext of the Hagiolaters, that they worship the saints as friends of God, not as the supreme God, and restrict their mediation to intercession, is refuted.

units.la: LIII. A Sanctis perinde atque à Summo Deo maxima quaeque eos orare, ex invocationum formulis ad Sanctos, Cosmum, Damianum, Andream, Nicolaum, Agnetem, Brigittam, Catharinam, &c.
units.tr: LIII. That the saints are asked for the greatest things just as much as the supreme God is, from the formulas of invocation addressed to the saints Cosmas, Damian, Andrew, Nicholas, Agnes, Bridget, Catherine, etc.
LIV. This is shown chiefly from prayers addressed to the Mother of God.

units.la: LV. Colliguntur, quae de B. Mariae honore & cultu maxima quaeque & stupenda Mariolatrae prodiderunt. Atque ex iis, B. Mariam tantum non Deo & Christo praeferri colligitur.
units.tr: LV. Gathered together are the greatest and most astonishing things that the Mariolaters have put forth about the honour and worship of the Blessed Virgin Mary. And from these it is concluded that the Blessed Mary is preferred almost to God and Christ.

units.la: LVI. Absurditatum hagiolatriae ingens syrma. Divi in primis Chimaerici, non Sancti, quorum cultus omnem idololatriam superat.
units.tr: LVI. A huge heap of absurdities of Hagiolatry. Above all, the saints are chimeras, not saints, and their worship surpasses all idolatry.

units.la: LVII. Iconolatria succedit. De imaginum cultu definitio Tridentinorum; è diametro opposita Divinae legi.
units.tr: LVII. Iconolatry follows. The definition of the Tridentines concerning the worship of images, diametrically opposed to the divine law.

units.la: LVIII. LIX. Gentiles & Hierarchici iconolatrae pariter faciunt, dum utrique imagines à rebus, quarum imagines sunt aequè distinguunt.
units.tr: LVIII. LIX. The Gentiles and the Hierarchical iconolaters act alike, in that both distinguish images equally from the things of which they are images.

units.la: LX. Chaldaeorum veterum & Hierarchicorum iconolatria ex Jeremiae Epistola comparatur.
units.tr: LX. The iconolatry of the ancient Chaldeans and of the Hierarchicals is compared from the Epistle of Jeremiah.

units.la: LXI. Utrique ligno dicunt, Pater meus es; & lapidi, Tu genuisti me.
units.tr: LXI. Both say to the wood, "You are my father," and to the stone, "You have begotten me."

units.la: LXII. Utrorumque rudis populus statuas & imagines pro Diis habet.
units.tr: LXII. The uneducated people of both groups hold statues and images to be gods.

units.la: LXIII. Debitus juxta Hierarchicos imaginibus honor religiosus & Divinus est.
units.tr: LXIII. According to the Hierarchicals, the honour owed to images is religious and divine.

units.la: LXIV. Id quod colligitur ex definitione Concilii Nicaeni II.
units.tr: LXIV. This is gathered from the definition of the Second Council of Nicaea.
LXV. From the formulas of consecration of images.

units.la: LXVI. Et Theologorum Thomae inprimis, Bonaventurae, Bellarmini &c. sententia.
units.tr: LXVI. And from the opinion of the theologians, especially Thomas, Bonaventure, Bellarmine, etc.

units.la: LXVII. Prætextus Tridentinorum, quòd honor imaginibus exhibitus ad prototypa referatur, refellitur.
units.tr: LXVII. The pretext of the Tridentines, that the honour paid to images is referred to the prototypes, is refuted.

units.la: LXVIII. Relatio imaginum ad prototypa nec similitudinis imaginum cum prototypis; nec intentionis iconolatrarum, incurvatione coram imaginibus Christi & Sanctorum honorem intendentium, virtute obtinet.
units.tr: LXVIII. The relation of images to prototypes, neither by the likeness of the images to the prototypes nor by the intention of the iconolaters, who intend honour by bowing before images of Christ and the saints, has any force.

units.la: LXIX. Iconolatriæ haud postrema species Staurolatria, seu adoratio crucis est, quæ ex Pontificali R. ubi inprimis solennitatem, quæ Parasceve Antepaschali peragi solet, describit;
units.tr: LXIX. Not the least species of iconolatry is Staurolatry, or the adoration of the cross, which is described from the Roman Pontifical, where it first describes the solemnity that is usually celebrated on the Good Friday before Easter;

units.la: LXX. Nec non dedicationum & consecrationum formulis idololatriæ manifestæ convincitur.
units.tr: LXX. and it is shown to be manifest idolatry from the formulas of dedications and consecrations.

units.la: LXXI. De Lipsanolatria, seu Reliquiarum cultu definitio Tridentinorum subdola.
units.tr: LXXI. On Lipsanolatry, or the worship of relics: the definition of the Tridentines is deceptive.

units.la: LXXII. Reliquiis Divinos honores impendi, ex Concilio Nicæno II. Catechesi Tridentina Pontificali R. Vasquez, Thoma Waldensi, Baronio;
units.tr: LXXII. That divine honours are paid to relics is shown from the Second Council of Nicaea, the Tridentine Catechism, the Roman Pontifical, Vásquez, Thomas Waldensis and Baronius.
LXXIII. It is established chiefly by public practice.
LXXIV. A notable evasion of Bellarmine.

units.la: LXXV. Ex adorationis reliquiarum formulis, inprimis ea, quæ ad Sudarium Veronicæ dirigitur, eam absolutam, non relativam esse, ostenditur.
units.tr: LXXV. From the formulas of adoration of relics, especially that addressed to the Veil of Veronica, it is shown that this worship is absolute, not relative.

units.la: LXXVI. Lipsanolatriæ fœditatem prodit, quòd adorant id, quod quale sit, ignorant.
units.tr: LXXVI. The foulness of relic-worship is shown by the fact that they adore what they do not know the nature of.

units.la: LXXVII. Hierolatriæ species, quas inter cultus Agnorum Dei primas obtinet. Eorum consecratio describitur.
units.tr: LXXVII. Species of hierolatry, of which the worship of the Agnus Dei holds the first place. Their consecration is described.

units.la: LXXVIII. Virtutem iis plane Divinam tribui, tum ex consecrationis eorundem formula,
units.tr: LXXVIII. That divine power is plainly attributed to them, both from the formula of their consecration,

units.la: LXXIX. Tum ex carmine, cum quo Urbanus V. tres Agnos Dei Imperatori Græcorum transmisit, asseritur.
units.tr: LXXIX. and from the verses with which Urban V sent three Agnus Dei to the Emperor of the Greeks, is asserted.
LXXX. Conclusion of the argument.

units.la: I. Erroribus[?] Hierrachiæ capitalibus Tyrannicis succedunt Idololatrici, quorum lepra universum Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ corpus sic laborat, ut verus spiritualis Dei cultus in co propemodum oppressus jaceat. Hoc ergo probandum nunc suscipimus; palam sic facturi ampliùs, Hierarchiam Babylonem Magnam, scortationum & abominationum terræ Matrem illam merito à nobis haberi. Idololatriam enim esse scortationem spiritualem, corporali fœdiorem nocentiorémque longè, sic apud omnes, qui Scripturam & rationem consulunt, receptum est, ut de eo nemo sanus ambigere possit.
units.tr: I. The chief errors of the tyrannical hierarchy are followed by idolatrous ones, whose leprosy so afflicts the whole body of the Papal Church that the true spiritual worship of God lies almost crushed within it. We now undertake to prove this, so that it will be clearer still that we rightly regard that hierarchy as Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots and of the abominations of the earth. For that idolatry is spiritual fornication, far more foul and far more harmful than bodily fornication, is accepted by all who consult Scripture and reason, so that no sane person can doubt it.

units.la: II. [illegible, ~12 letters] II. Hierarchiam idololatriæ crimine ratione manifestissima, quam pro inst tuti nostri ratione Syllogismo arctare lubet, sic strictim arcessimus:
units.tr: II. [illegible, about twelve letters] II. We now bring the hierarchy under the charge of idolatry by a very plain line of reasoning, which, for the sake of our method, we wish to compress into a syllogism. We set it out briefly thus:

units.la: Quisquis creaturis Divinum cultum exhibet, & exhibere populum sibi obnoxium jubet, is idololatriam committit, & ad idololatriam populum sibi obnoxium seducit.
units.tr: Whoever pays divine worship to creatures, and orders the people subject to him to pay it, commits idolatry, and seduces the people subject to him into idolatry.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia Papam, Eucharistiam, Sanctos, imagines, Sanctorum reliquias & res consecratas religiose venerans, creaturis Divinum cultum exhibet, & exhibere populum sibi obnoxium jubet.
units.tr: But the hierarchy, religiously venerating the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, images, relics of the saints and consecrated things, pays divine worship to creatures, and orders the people subject to it to pay it.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia Papam, Eucharistiam, Sanctos, imagines, Sanctorum reliquias, & res consecratas religiosè venerans idololatriam committit, & ad idololatriam populum sibi obnoxium seducit.
units.tr: Therefore the hierarchy, religiously venerating the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, images, relics of the saints and consecrated things, commits idolatry, and seduces the people subject to it into idolatry.

units.la: Syllogismi hujus propositio è Scripturis manifesta est; utpote quæ idololatrarum nomine perstringunt omnes, qui Divinum cultum creaturæ, nominatim autem idolo, sive proprie dicto, veluti simulachro vituli, sive figurato, ut mammonæ, tribuunt; Exod. xxxii. 4. Matth. vi.24. Act. vii.41. Rom.i.25. 1 Cor.x.7. Ephef. v. 5. Sed & Assumptio fidem inveniet partim è Scripturis, docentibus, fiduciam Jerem. xvii. 7. invocationem Psal. l. 15. Joel. 11. 32. Rom. x. 14. vota Esai. xix. 21. sacrificia Exod. xxii. 20. denique adorationem Exod. xx. 5. Act. x. 26. Apoc. xix. 10. Divinum esse cultum: partim ex aliis testibus idoneis, Pontificiis ipsismet, non dissimulantibus, se horum quædam deferre Papæ, Eucharistiæ, Sanctis, Imaginibus, Reliquiis Sanctorum, & rebus consecratis. Uti quidem ex Missalibus, Pontificalibus, libris Ceremoniarum Romanæ Ecclesiæ, Concilio Tridentino, Theologis Scholasticis, Canonistis, Historicis, ipsa denique vulgari praxi, omni exceptione majori constat. Saltem religiosum esse, quo hæc, quæ dixi, prosequuntur, cultum, consentiunt omnes. Religiosum autem cultum eundem Divinum esse, soli que adeò Deo competere, supra probavimus. Ex præmissis his conclusio necessario sequitur. Concludant modò Hierarchici ipsi, ad se spectare, quod Israelitis à Deo dictum Hos. 11. 2. legimus: Contendite cum matre vestra, contendite, ipsam non esse uxorem meam, & me non esse virum ipsorum, ut amoveat scortationes è conspectu suo, & adulteria sua è medio uberum suorum, ne denudem eam plane, & statuam eam, ut die, quo genita fuit; disponensque eam velut in deserto, & redigens eam velut in terra siticulosa, extinguam eam siti; & filiorum ejus non miserear, eò quòd filii scorti sint.
units.tr: The major premise of this syllogism is plain from Scripture, which brands with the name of idolaters all who give divine worship to a creature, and especially to an idol, whether properly so called, like the calf-image, or figuratively, like those who give it to mammon: Exod. 32:4; Matt. 6:24; Acts 7:41; Rom. 1:25; 1 Cor. 10:7; Eph. 5:5. The minor premise also finds its proof partly in Scripture, which teaches that trust (Jer. 17:7), invocation (Ps. 50:15; Joel 2:32; Rom. 10:14), vows (Isa. 19:21), sacrifices (Exod. 22:20), and finally adoration (Exod. 20:5; Acts 10:26; Rev. 19:10) are divine worship; and partly from other credible witnesses, the Papists themselves, who do not conceal that they pay some of these things to the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, images, relics of the saints and consecrated things. This is beyond all exception, as is clear from the Missals, the Pontificals, the books of ceremonies of the Roman Church, the Council of Trent, the scholastic theologians, the canonists, the historians, and finally from common practice itself. All agree at least that the worship with which they honour these things is religious. We have already shown above that religious worship of this kind is divine and belongs to God alone. The conclusion follows of necessity from these premises. Let the hierarchs themselves conclude that what we read God said to Israel in Hos. 2:2 applies to them: Contend with your mother, contend, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband; let her put away her harlotries from her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts, lest I strip her utterly bare and set her as on the day she was born, and make her like a wilderness and a dry land, and slay her with thirst; and I will have no mercy on her children, for they are the children of harlots.

units.la: III. Sed Propositio major ante omnia à falsorum Jesu Sociorum, Bellarmini inprimis & Gregorii de Valentia tricis liberanda est.
units.tr: III. But first of all the major premise must be freed from the snares of the false companions of Jesus, especially Bellarmine and Gregory of Valencia.

units.la: Non diffitentur equidem illi, creaturam æquè colere ac Deum, esse idololatriam. Sed per cuniculos propositionem demoliri conantur, dum Bellarminus de Eccles. Triumph. lib.
units.tr: Certainly they do not deny that to worship a creature as much as God is idolatry. But they try to undermine the proposition by underground tunnels, as Bellarmine does in On the Church Triumphant, book

units.la: Bellarmini et Greg. de Valentia adversus propositionem, quod idololatria sit cultus Divinus lib. 1. cap. 5. idolum ab imagine distinguens, idololatram esse negat, quisquis creaturis Divinum honorem exhibet; sed eum demum, qui idolis, hoc est, falsorum Deorum simulachris Divinum honorem exhibet: Gregorius vero de Valentia de Idolol. lib. 11. 1. idololatras damnatos esse non quosvis creaturis Divinos honores exhibentes, sed creaturis eos exhibentes, sicut Deo; pertendit. Tali scilicet cataplasmate insignes adeo Medici Hierarchicorum causam indigere rati sunt. Quasi scilicet idololatriam non faciat simpliciter λατρεία τῆς κτίσεως παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα, cultus creaturæ præter creatorem Rom. 1. 25. sed cultus duntaxat hujus vel illius creaturæ; & exhibitus ei, ut Deo. Quæ distinctionum monstra ante omnia similitudine appositá duplici debellare lubet.
units.tr: Bellarmine and Gregory of Valencia, against the proposition that idolatry is divine worship, distinguish the idol from the image (Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 5). He denies that anyone is an idolater who gives divine honour to creatures; only one who gives divine honour to idols, that is, to images of false gods, is an idolater. Gregory of Valencia, in On Idolatry, book 11, contends that idolaters are condemned not for giving any divine honours to creatures, but for giving them to creatures as to God. Evidently these doctors, so eminent, thought the cause of the Hierarchs needed such a plaster. As if idolatry were not simply the worship of a creature besides the Creator [λατρεία τῆς κτίσεως παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα] (Rom. 1. 25.), but only the worship of this or that creature, and offered to it as to God! I wish first to overthrow these monstrous distinctions with a double comparison.

units.la: IV. Olim Sextus Roscius parricidii accusatus est hoc argumento: Quisquis patrem occidit, committit parricidium. Sextus Roscius Patrem occidit. Ergo Sextus Roscius parricidium commisit. Si Patronus S. Roscii Marcus Tullius negasset, parricidium ab omnibus committi, qui occidunt patres; dixissetque, eos damnat esse parricidas, qui rigidos & feroces patres, qualis Roscii pater non fuit, occidunt; adeoque assumptione refutanda clientis sui innocentiam non ostendisset, eccui Romanorum judicum putamus visum iri reum vacare omni culpa, quem tali patrocinio tutus orator egere judicasset? Similiter Johannes XII. Papa adulterio se contaminasse à Scriptoribus Pontificiis, Luitprando Ticinensi Rer. per Europamgestarum lib. vi. 11. aliisque arguitur. Argumentum vero struì ejusmodi poterat: Quisquis cum alterius uxore rem habet, adulterium committit. Atqui Johannes Papa rem habuit cum uxore alterius. Ergo Johannes Papa adulterium commisit. Si Parisiensis ille
units.tr: IV. Long ago Sextus Roscius was accused of parricide on this argument: Whoever kills his father commits parricide. Sextus Roscius killed his father. Therefore Sextus Roscius committed parricide. Had Marcus Tullius, Roscius's advocate, denied that everyone who kills fathers commits parricide, and said that only those who kill harsh and savage fathers, which Roscius's father was not, are parricides, then by refuting the minor premise he would not have shown his client's innocence. Do we think the Roman judges would have seen the accused as free from all guilt, when a careful orator had judged that such a defence was needed? Similarly, Pope John XII is charged with adultery by Pontifical writers, by Liutprand of Cremona in his History of the Deeds Done in Europe, book 6, chapter 11, and by others. The argument could be framed in this way: Whoever has intercourse with another man's wife commits adultery. But Pope John had intercourse with another man's wife. Therefore Pope John committed adultery. If that Parisian ...

units.la: {a} creatura exhibitus, exceptiones proponuntur. Bellarminus exceptio, quod idololatria non sit cultus Numinum falsorum exhibitus, oppositis melibus, Sexti Roscii à parricidio, & Johannis XII. Papa ab adulterio simili ratione defensi, uti dicuntur. ille Sorbonista, Margarinus de la Bigne, qui Præfat. Biblioth. S. Patrum ad Gregorium XIII. Ecclesiam in moribus errare posse negat, ad summum hoc Ecclesiæ caput à lapsu vindicandum, transmissa Assumptione, Majorem propositionem aggressus assereret, non quisquis alienam uxorem comprimit, eum adulterari; sed tantùm si quis laicus, clericúsque inferior, aut si quis maritali affectu non meretricio id perpetret, qui tam est imperitus rerum, quin existimaret, deploratam à Sorbonista illo causam susceptam esse, eúmque, conscientia teste, non veritatis atque innocentiæ tuendæ, sed parasitandi Papæ studio abreptum cavillari? Cùm ergo Syllogismi nostri propositio ex eodem fonte & firmamento idololatriæ damnandum statuat, quisquis creaturæ Divinum cultum exhibet; ex quo parricida, quisquis patrem occidit; adulter, quisquis alterius uxori consuescit, esse perhibetur: profectò aut perindulgens in Bellarminum aut parùm prudens sit oportet, qui Pontificiam causam non habeat suspectam, quam tali emplastro insignes illi seplasiarii curandam, neque alio curare posse arbitrantur. Atque id eò magis, quia Bellarminianum illud ex imaginis & idoli distinctione emplastrum multò putidius est, quàm si quis interfectionem clementis patris à parricida, aut clericum adulterum à laico discriminaret: Valentianensę verò, idololatram videlicet esse, qui creaturæ Divinum cultum, ut Deo exhibet, perinde adhibetur, ac si Sorbonista adulterum non alium esse diceret, quàm qui alienæ uxori maritale officium præstat, sicut maritus. Sed argumentis validioribus premamus utrumque.
units.tr: {a} ... the worship offered to a creature, exceptions are put forward. Bellarmine's exception, that idolatry is not the worship offered to false deities, is pressed with the same kind of argument used to defend Sextus Roscius from parricide and Pope John XII from adultery. That Sorbonist, Margarin de la Bigne, in his Preface to the Library of the Holy Fathers, addressed to Gregory XIII, denies that the Church can err in morals. To rescue the highest head of the Church from a fall, he attacked the major premise, once the minor had been let pass. He asserted that not everyone who lies with another man's wife commits adultery, but only if a layman or an inferior cleric does so, or if he does so with marital affection and not for lust. Who is so ignorant of affairs as not to think that this Sorbonist took up a desperate cause, and that, conscience being his witness, he was carried off to quibbling not by zeal for truth and defence of innocence but by a wish to flatter the Pope? Since the major premise of our syllogism holds that whoever gives divine worship to a creature is to be condemned as an idolater, from the same source and foundation as that, whoever kills his father is a parricide and whoever lives with another man's wife is an adulterer, it must surely be that either he is too indulgent towards Bellarmine or too imprudent, who does not regard the Papal cause as suspect, which those ointment-sellers think can be cured with such a plaster and by no other means. And this all the more so, because Bellarmine's plaster, resting on the distinction between image and idol, is much more rotten than if someone distinguished the killing of a merciful father from parricide, or a cleric who commits adultery from a layman.
