Valencia's view, namely that the one is an idolater who gives divine worship to a creature as to God, is brought forward just as if the Sorbonist said that an adulterer is none other than one who performs marital duty for another man's wife, as a husband does. But let us press both with stronger arguments.

units.la: V. Pertendo ergo, definitionem idololatriæ à Bellarmino allatam, ut videlicet ea dicatur idoli, seu imaginis fallorum Deorum cultus, angustam nimis, neque aliud quàm vimineam quasi ad depellendum propositionis nostræ telum validissimum, parmulani esse.
units.tr: V. I therefore contend that the definition of idolatry given by Bellarmine, namely that it is the worship of an idol or image of false gods, is far too narrow, and is nothing more than a little wicker shield, as it were, to ward off the most powerful weapon of our proposition.

units.la: VI. Constat satis, in Regno Dei idololatriam esse, quod in Republica seditio & perduellio est. Utrobique lædítur Majestas, & Principatus, ibi Rectorum humani generis, hic Dei ipsius, qui universitatis princeps est, in alium transfertur, cui neutiquam ille competit. Sicut ergo in Republica supremæ potestatis jus est, perduellionem, seu læsæ Majestatis crimen definire, &, qua in re illud consistat, quo pœnæ genere assiciendum sit, declarare: sic solius Dei omnipotentis jus est, definire & declarare suo populo, qua ratione idololatria, Divinæ Majestatis violatæ crimen committatur. Quicquid ergo Deus in verbo suo idololatriam definivit, id omne pro tali habendum est, licet vel lascivienti rationi & fugitivæ cognitioni hominis, vel vulgari captui & judicio talis non appareat, & vocabula ambiguæ significationis alia omnia suadere videantur. Non enim religio à phantasia, judicio, ratione, consiliis, nominibus humanis, sed à Divinæ voluntatis testificatione, & Divinitus intento sensu nominum pendet.
units.tr: VI. It is clear enough that in the Kingdom of God idolatry is what sedition and treason are in a commonwealth. In both, majesty and sovereignty are violated: in the one case the sovereignty of the rulers of the human race, in the other that of God himself, who is the prince of the whole universe, is transferred to another, to whom it in no way belongs. Just as in a commonwealth it belongs to supreme power to define treason, or the crime of injured majesty, and to declare in what it consists and by what kind of punishment it is to be visited, so it belongs to almighty God alone to define and declare to his people by what means idolatry, the crime of violated divine majesty, is committed. Whatever God has defined as idolatry in his word must therefore be held to be such, even if it does not appear so to a wanton reason and a fickle human knowledge, or to the common grasp and judgment, and even if all other words of ambiguous meaning seem to suggest otherwise. For religion depends not on fancy, judgment, reason, counsels or human names, but on the testimony of the divine will and on the sense of the words as intended by God.

units.la: VII. Constare pariter debet, quicquid Deus idololatriam esse, Judæis declaravit, à Christianis universis pro tali habendum, tum quia Christianorum cultus simplex & spiritualis magis est, quàm Judæorum, qui non minima sui parte carnalis fuit: tum quia Deus hac quidem in re mentem suam non aliter Judæis, aliter Christianis declaravit: tum quia, quid idololatria sit, Deus Judæis lege Decalogo, ejusque præceptis distinctis, primo & secundo, tradita revelavit; quæ lex cùm perpetua sit, quippe digito Dei tabulis lapideis inscripta, & Divinæ sanctitatis quædam effigies expressa; quin & ab ipso Christo consequendæ æternæ vitæ gratia inculcata, Marc. x. 18. 19. denique amoris Dei haud postrema species; perinde Christianos, uti olim Judæos obligat: tum denique quia apud Christianos alias, quæ vera idololatria sit, ambiguum plane esset, quia in Novo Testamento lex contra idololatriam à lege, in Decalogo expressa, distin�similia faciens eodem cesu venire debet. Quacunque ergo in re Pagani idololatriæ rei peragi possunt, in ea Judæi & Christiani, similia committentes. ejusdem rei potiori jure peragi possunt debéntque.
units.tr: VII. It must likewise be agreed that whatever God declared to the Jews to be idolatry must be held to be such by all Christians. This is so for several reasons: (1) because Christian worship is simpler and more spiritual than that of the Jews, which was not a little carnal in part; (2) because God has not declared his mind in this matter one way to the Jews and another way to the Christians; (3) because God revealed to the Jews what idolatry is through the law delivered in the Decalogue and its distinct precepts, the first and the second; and since this law is perpetual, written by the finger of God on tablets of stone, a certain expression of divine holiness, and urged by Christ himself for the sake of gaining eternal life (Mark 10:18-19), and finally no small form of the love of God, it binds Christians just as it once bound the Jews; (4) finally, because among Christians it would otherwise be quite unclear what true idolatry is, since in the New Testament the law against idolatry is not distinguished from the law expressed in the Decalogue. Whatever idolatry the pagans can commit in any matter, Jews and Christians who commit like things can and ought to be charged with the same offence, by a stronger right.

units.la: IX. His ritè & ἀναμφιτβητήτως suppositis receptisque, Bellarminianæ idololatriæ definitio, quòd sit cultus idoli, seu simulachri falsi cujuspiam Numinis, nullo negotio falsi convinci poterit; eo scilicet argumento, quòd nec Idololatriam Judæis simul atque Christianis prohibitam, nec à Gentilibus usurpatam, & communi omni consensu in iis damnatam, exhauriat.
units.tr: IX. With these things properly and indisputably supposed and received, Bellarmine's definition of idolatry, namely that it is the worship of an idol, or of a false image of some deity, can easily be shown to be false. The reason is that it does not cover the idolatry forbidden both to Jews and to Christians, nor that practised by the Gentiles and condemned in them by universal consensus.

units.la: X. Judæos enim quod attinet, illis Deus Decalogi præcepto primo, quo vetantur coram se habere אלהים אחרים Deos alios, Exod. xx. 3. idololatriam seu superstitionem falsi cultus, cùm falsum Numen colitur; secundo, quo vetantur facere imaginem vel sculptile, coram eo incurvari, ei inservire &c. idololatriam seu superstitionem indebiti cultus, quo Deus verus non eo, quo juxta præceptum ejus debet, cultu colitur; prohibuit. Neutra idololatria cultu idoli, seu simulachri falsi Numinis absolvitur. Non prior, quia in ea ne quidem est cultus idoli seu simulachri proprie dicti, sed falsi Numinis, qua talis, sive simulachro exprimatur, sive non. Non posterior, quia illa etiam cultum imaginis seu sculptilis veri, non falsi duntaxat Numinis sub se complectitur. Bellarmino autem idololatria non est nisi cultus simulachri falsi Numinis.
units.tr: X. As for the Jews, God by the first precept of the Decalogue, by which they are forbidden to have other gods [אלהים אחרים] before him (Exod. 20:3), forbade idolatry or superstition of false worship, when a false deity is worshipped. By the second, by which they are forbidden to make an image or carved thing, to bow down before it or serve it, and so on, he forbade idolatry or superstition of undue worship, by which the true God is worshipped not in the manner which his precept requires. Neither kind of idolatry is exhausted by the worship of an idol or of an image of a false deity. Not the former, because in it there is not even the worship of an idol or image properly so called, but of a false deity as such, whether it is represented by an image or not. Not the latter, because it also embraces under itself the worship of an image or carved thing of the true God, and not only of a false deity. But for Bellarmine, idolatry is nothing but the worship of an image of a false deity.

units.la: XI. Quoad prius, non obstat equidem, quòd εἴδωλον seu idolum proprie vocatur simulachrum; adeóque idololatria non videatur locum habere posse, ubi simulachri cultus nullus est. Nam missa voce res ipsa attenditur. Est enim cultus falsi Numinis, qui sive idololatria, sive cum Hebraeis עבודה זרה peregrina servitus appellatur, perinde est. Falsi enim Numinis cultus est. Quanquam propria magis significatione idoli latius extensa, idolum etiam dicitur, quicquid mens humana in locum veri Numinis substituit; quicquid, ut Deus, quod tamen Deus non est, adoratur, sive visibile, sive invisibile sit. Quo sensu Gregorius Nazianzenus Orat. Paneg. in Natal. Christi idololatriam definit μετάθεσιν τῆς προσκυνήσεως ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πεποιηκότος ἐπὶ τὰ κτίσματα, cultus seu adorationis translationem à creatore ad creaturas. Et Tertullianus de idolol. cap. 19. sic pronuntiat: Quicquid exaltatur uitra humani honoris modum, id est, cultu plusquam civili colitur, eo ipso idolum fit. Ibidem cap. 11. Idololatria, inquit, Deo fraudem facit, honores illi suos denegans, & conferens aliis, ut fraudi etiam contumeliam conjungat. Sed & Cyprianus ad Fort. in exhort. ad Mart. in universum: Idololatria, inquit, tunc committitur, cùm Divinus honor alteri datur. Itidem Ambrosius, seu potiùs Hilarius, Diaconus Romanus, in Ephef. cap. 5. Idololatria, inquit, Dei honorem usurpat, & creaturæ vindicat.
units.tr: XI. As to the former, it is indeed no obstacle that an idol (εἴδωλον) is properly called an image, and that idolatry therefore does not seem able to take place where there is no worship of an image. For the word being set aside, the thing itself is what is considered. It is the worship of a false deity, which is called either idolatry or, with the Hebrews, peregrine service [עבודה זרה], and it makes no difference which. For it is the worship of a false deity. Yet by a wider extension of the proper meaning of idol, whatever the human mind puts in the place of the true God is also called an idol: whatever is adored as God, though it is not God, whether visible or invisible. In this sense Gregory Nazianzen, in his Panegyric on the Birth of Christ, defines idolatry as the transfer of worship from the Creator to creatures [μετάθεσιν τῆς προσκυνήσεως ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πεποιηκότος ἐπὶ τὰ κτίσματα]. And Tertullian, in On Idolatry ch. 19, pronounces thus: Whatever is exalted beyond the measure of human honour, that is, is worshipped with more than civil worship, by that very fact becomes an idol. In the same book, ch. 11: Idolatry, he says, does a fraud to God, denying him his honours and conferring them on others, so that it adds insult to the fraud. Cyprian too, in his letter to Fortunatus in the Exhortation to Martyrdom, says in general: Idolatry, he says, is committed when divine honour is given to another. Likewise Ambrose, or rather Hilary the Roman deacon, on Ephesians ch. 5: Idolatry, he says, usurps the honour of God and claims it for the creature.

units.la: XII. Præiverunt Septuaginta Interpretes, qui passim voces אלילים, בעלים, & עצבים εἴδωλα idola reddiderunt, etiam ubi non de similachris falsorum Numinum, sed de ipsis Numinibus falsis, imò dæmonibus etiam sermo est. Sic planè 1. Paralip. xvi. 26. verba illa, כל אלהי העמים אלילים reddunt, πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα. Omnes Dii populorum idola sunt. Uti etiam Vulgatus convertit. Atqui populorum Dii non sola simulachra falsorum Numinum, sed Sol etiam, Luna, Saturnus, manes defunctorum, imagines non arte factæ, sed res naturales, fuerunt. Unde etiam אלילים quandoque Θεὸς, δαιμόνια, μιγιςάνες iidem reddunt. Qui posteriores manifeste ad ipsos invisibiles dæmones referuntur. Qui cùm juxta sententiam Scripturæ non sint nisi אלילים cultus etiam eorum non potest non idololatria esse. Cùmque per בעלים Baalim intelligantur falsa illa Numina ab imaginibus suis distincta, veluti 2. Paralip. xxviii. 2. tamen sæpe εἴδωλα idola redduntur. Siquidem Baalim sive Sol sint, sive manes defunctorum, non nisi idola sunt, quatenus pro veris Numinibus coluntur. Denique iidem עצבים quæ vox juxta quosdam dæmones, horrorem, à quo δαιμονία dicitur, incutientes, duodecies amplius εἴδωλα idola transtulerunt.
units.tr: XII. The Septuagint went before, who throughout rendered the words אלילים, בעלים and עצבים as idols (εἴδωλα), even where the discourse is not about images of false deities but about the false deities themselves, indeed even about demons. Thus plainly in 1 Chron. 16:26 they render the words כל אלהי העמים אלילים as All the gods of the peoples are idols [πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα], as the Vulgate also translates. Yet the gods of the peoples were not only images of false deities, but also the sun, the moon, Saturn, the shades of the dead, and natural objects not made by art. Whence the same translators sometimes also render אלילים as θεὸς, δαιμόνια, μιγιςάνες. The latter are manifestly referred to the invisible demons themselves. Since these, according to the judgment of Scripture, are nothing but אלילים, the worship of them cannot but be idolatry. And since by בעלים, Baalim, are understood the false deities distinct from their images, as in 2 Chron. 28:2, they are nevertheless often rendered idols. For the Baalim, whether they are the sun or the shades of the dead, are nothing but idols, insofar as they are worshipped as true deities. Finally, the same translators rendered עצבים, a word which some hold to denote demons who strike horror, from which the name δαιμόνια comes, as idols more than twelve times.

units.la: XIII. Quin ipse Deus ei rei Exod. xx. 5. testimonium perhibet, declarans, in eo maximè idololatriæ naturam consistere, quòd Divino cultu colitur id, quod non est Deus. Nam imaginum cultum interdicens, hac ratione utitur: Ego enim Jehova, Deus tuus, אל זנא Deus Zelotypus sum. Quomodo Deut. xxxii. 21. idem Deus dicit: הם קנאוני בלא אל Illi Zelare me fecerunt in non Deo. Non ergo imaginis cultus idololatricus aliam ob rationem est, quàm quia imaginem colens colit, quod non est Deus, adeóque non potest non hac ratione Deum Zelotypum, qui honorem suum alteri non dat, ad Zelum provocare. Verissima proin & generalis
units.tr: XIII. God himself bears witness to this matter at Exod. 20:5, declaring that the nature of idolatry consists chiefly in this, that what is not God is worshipped with divine worship. For in forbidding the worship of images he uses this reasoning: For I, Jehovah, your God, am a jealous God [אל זנא]. So in Deut. 32:21 the same God says: They have provoked me to jealousy with what is not God [הם קנאוני בלא אל]. Therefore the idolatrous worship of an image is for no other reason than that one who worships an image worships what is not God, and so cannot but provoke to jealousy, in this way, the jealous God, who does not give his honour to another.

units.la: {a} Et Dei ipsius idololatriam declarantis id omne, quo ad Zelum Deus provocatur, testimonio. ralis notio idololatriæ est, id colere, quod non est Deus. Hoc est, uti nostra definitio habet, creaturam Divino cultu colere. Hoc quippe solum illud est, quo ad æmulationem Cœlestę Numen non potest non provocari, & exardescere, quia rem sibi charissimam, gloriam Divinitatis soli sibi debitam, attentari videt. Et creaturæ igitur, & imaginis cujusvis, ad quodcunque exemplar relatæ, & rei cujusvis, quæ Deus non est, Divinus cultus idololatria est. Hoc est, quod Bellarminus ipse de Eccles. Triumph. lib. 11.24. dicit, creaturam æque colere ac Deum, idololatria est certe.
units.tr: {a} And of God's own testimony declaring idolatry, by which God is provoked to jealousy, everything of this kind is included. The general notion of idolatry is to worship what is not God. That is, as our definition has it, to worship a creature with divine worship. For this alone is the thing by which the heavenly Majesty cannot but be provoked to rivalry and blaze up, since he sees his dearest possession, the glory of divinity due to him alone, being assailed. Therefore the divine worship of any creature, and of any image whatever, however it is related to its prototype, and of any thing that is not God, is idolatry. This is what Bellarmine himself says in On the Triumphant Church, book 11, ch. 24: To worship a creature equally with God is certainly idolatry.

units.la: XIV. Ad posterius idololatriæ genus, quo verus Deus illicito modo, velut in imagine colitur, ut veniamus, certe & vera hæc, atque in verbo Dei damnata idololatria est, & cultus simulachri falsi Numinis non est. Non ergo idololatria tantum cultus est idoli, hoc est, simulachri falsi Numinis, quod Jesuita pertenderat. Verum, & in verbo Dei damnatam idololatriam esse, nulli certe dubitamus. Ita enim Deus Exod xx. 4. vetat sculptile vel similitudinem facere etiam ejus, quod est בשמים in Cœlo. Atqui in Cœlo potissimum Deus est, Cœli Rex & dominus. Tum eorum, quos verbum Dei idololatriæ reos peragit, exempla id ipsum clarissime demonstrant.
units.tr: XIV. As for the latter kind of idolatry, in which the true God is worshipped in an unlawful way, as if present in an image, this is certainly true idolatry, and it is condemned in the Word of God, even though it is not the worship of an image of a false god. So idolatry is not only the worship of an idol, that is, an image of a false god, as the Jesuit had argued. That idolatry is condemned in the Word of God, no one among us doubts. For in Exod. 20.4 God forbids us to make a graven image or any likeness even of that which is in heaven [בשמים]. Yet God is chiefly in heaven, the King and Lord of heaven. The examples of those whom the Word of God accuses of idolatry demonstrate this most clearly.

units.la: XV. Etenim idololatriæ accusantur μοσχολάτρεγ, seu ii, qui in deserto vitulum coluerunt, Exod. xxxii. 8. Psal. cvi. 20. Act. vii. 41. Et tamen non aliud egerunt, quam ut symbolum haberent veri Numinis, quemadmodum gentiles gaudebant: atque eo sine hoc exoptarunt, ut isto symbolo præsente & præeunte, præsentis & præeuntis Numinis Divini signum haberent. Certe Israelitas plerosque omnes, vel saltem non extrema stultitia occæcatos propositum habuisse in vitulo colendi verum Deum, inter alios etiam agnoscit. Jerus in. Act. vii. 41. ac probat ex ipsis Israëlitarum verbis: Hi sunt Dii tui, Israel, qui te eduxerunt de terra Ægypti, Exod. xxxii. 4. Indéque colligit, non in alieni Dei cultu peccasse, sed eo, quod contra Dei præceptum eum in idolo colere destinassent. Atque id ipsum peculiari de vitulo Aharonis diatriba, nos quoque pluribus argumentis in arce veritatis, destructis etiam contranitentium ratiunculis, collocavimus. Par ratio est vitulorum aureorum in Dan & Bethel, 1. Reg. xii. 28. Hos enim pro idolis habitos ostendunt verba de Jeroboamo cap. xiv. 9. Fecisti tibi Deos alienos & conflatiles, ut me ad iracundiam provocares. Me autem projecisti post corpus tuum. Quid his apertius? Et tamen verum Deum in vitulis seu Cherubinis similibus iis, qui Hierosolymis in Templo erant, coli Jeroboam justit. Neque enim alias populo Israëlitico, ut cultum hunc reciperet, persuasisset. Vaframentum ergo Jeroboami Politicum erat, ut non abdicato veri Dei cultu, sed imitatione quadam expresso, simul à Rehabeamo decem tribus abstraheret, simul in obsequio eosdem contineret. Quomodo enim aliàs sperare poterat, populum, qui ab ineunte ætate Deo Israelis inservivit, quasi in momento temporis sic mutatum, & à Numine tandiu cognito cultóque simul semélque, etiam sine aperta vi, abalienatum iri? Apertéque hoc innuitur 1. Reg. xvi. 31. 32. Et fecit Achab, filius Omri, malum in conspectu Domini super omnes, qui fuerunt ante eum. Nec suffecit ei, ut ambularet in peccatis Jeroboam, filii Nebat. Insuper duxit Jezabel, filiam Ethbaal, Regis Sidoniorum: & abiit, & servivit Baal, & adoravit eum. Et posuit aram Baal in templo Baal, quod ædificaverat in Samaria, & plantavit lucum &c. Apertè sic docetur, diversam esse rationem in vitulis adorantium verum Deum, & illorum lorum in simulachris colentium Solem, vel aliud Dei opificium. Atque discrimen hoc respexit etiam Elias Propheta, cùm 1. Reg. xviii. 21. ait: Quousque claudicaturi estis in duabus cogitationibus. Si Jehova est Deus, sequimini eum. Sin autem Baal, sequimini eum. Et Rex Jehu 2. Reg. x. 16. cùm Baalis servos necaret, ac statuas tolleret, Vide, inquit, Zelum meum pro Jehova. At idem, qui verum Deum in vitulis adorarent, non suftulit, sed v. 24. servos Jehovæ appellat, comparatè videlicet præ Baaliticis cultoribus, & æstimando eos ex humano propositò; quod etsi non tollebat idololatriæ crimen, multis tamen partibus levius reddebat, etiam Divina æstimatione. Non ergo falsum Numen inducendo, sed verum Numen illicita ratione per symbola ei non præcepta, & loco, in quo memoriam nominis sui Deus non posuit, colendo, adeóque ex symbolis illis idola & falsos Deos faciendo, Jeroboam peccavit. Denique idem judicium ferendum est de Idolo Michæ Jud. xvii. siquidem mater ejus argentum, unde factum erat simulachrum, sacrificasse dicitur Jehovæ: & Micham voluisse in eo colere Deum Israelis, satis arguitur v. 13. verbis istis: Nunc novi, Jehovam benefacturum esse mihi, eò quòd est mihi Levita in Sacerdotem. Et tamen vetus Interpres, quod Hebraicè תרפים Therafim, dicitur, interpretatur idolum.
units.tr: XV. The worshippers of the calf, that is, those who worshipped the calf in the wilderness, are accused of idolatry, and rightly so: Exod. 32.8; Psal. 106.20; Acts 7.41. And yet they did nothing else than have a symbol of the true God, as the Gentiles liked to do; and they desired it so that, with this symbol present and going before them, they would have a sign of the present and going-before Divine Majesty. Jerome, on Acts 7.41, acknowledges among others that almost all the Israelites, or at least those not blinded by extreme folly, had the purpose of worshipping the true God in the calf. He proves this from the very words of the Israelites: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, Exod. 32.4. From this he concludes that they did not sin by worshipping a strange god, but by having determined to worship him in an idol, contrary to God's command. We too have set out this same point in a special dissertation on Aaron's calf, in the stronghold of truth, with many arguments, and with the flimsy objections of opponents also refuted. The case is the same for the golden calves at Dan and Bethel, 1 Kings 12.28. The words about Jeroboam in chapter 14.9 show that these were regarded as idols: You have made yourself other gods and molten images, to provoke me to anger; but you have cast me behind your back. What could be plainer? And yet Jeroboam commanded that the true God be worshipped in calves, or cherubim like those that were in the Temple at Jerusalem. Otherwise he would not have persuaded the Israelite people to accept this worship. Jeroboam's device was therefore a political one: without abandoning the worship of the true God, but by a certain imitation of it, he would at the same time draw the ten tribes away from Rehoboam and keep them in his allegiance. For how else could he hope that a people who had served the God of Israel from their earliest age would in an instant be so changed, and would be estranged, without open force, from a God so long known and worshipped? This is clearly hinted at in 1 Kings 16.31-32: And Ahab, son of Omri, did evil in the sight of the Lord above all who were before him. And it was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. Moreover he took as wife Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians; and he went and served Baal and worshipped him. And he set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal, which he had built in Samaria, and planted a grove, etc. It is plainly taught here that there was a different reason for those who worshipped the true God in calves, and for those who worshipped the sun or some other work of God in images. Elijah the Prophet also noted this difference when he said, 1 Kings 18.21: How long will you halt between two opinions? If Jehovah is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him. And King Jehu, when he slew the servants of Baal and removed their statues, said, 2 Kings 10.16: Behold my zeal for Jehovah. Yet he did not remove those who worshipped the true God in calves, but in verse 24 he calls them servants of Jehovah, comparing them, of course, with the Baalite worshippers and judging them by human intention. Although this did not remove the crime of idolatry, it made it much lighter in many respects, even by divine judgment. Jeroboam therefore sinned not by introducing a false god, but by worshipping the true God in an unlawful manner, through symbols that God had not commanded, and in a place where God had not placed the memorial of his name. By making idols and false gods out of those symbols, he sinned. Finally, the same judgment must be passed on the idol of Micah, Judges 17. His mother is said to have sacrificed the silver from which the image was made to Jehovah, and that Micah meant to worship the God of Israel in it is sufficiently shown by the words of verse 13: Now I know that Jehovah will do me good, since I have a Levite as priest. And yet the old translator renders the Hebrew Therafim [תרפים] as idol.

units.la: XVI. Ex his liquidò constat, apud Judæos idololatriam fuisse non solùm cultum idoli, seu simulachri salsi Numinis; sed vel falsi cujusvis Numinis, vel veri Numinis non ita, uti Deus præcepit, culti; puta in imagine, quam diserte in cultu veri Dei adhiberi Deus prohibuit; neque idololatriæ rationem propriam alia in re magis, quàm in eo constitutam fuisse, quòd quamvis rem, quæ Deus non fuit, Divino cultu prosecuti fuerint. Atque id ipsum porro etiam Paganorum idololatria comprobat, quæ haud præcisè in eo consistebat, quòd falsi alicujus Numinis simulachrum coluerunt. Multi enim Gentiles idololatriæ rei habentur ab omnibus merito, qui nullis simulachris in cultu suo usi sunt. Veluti Persæ, qui Herodoto Histor. lib. 1. 131. teste, in fastigiis montium Cœlo visibili sub nomine Jovis, ut & Soli, Lunæ, terræ, aquæ, ventis, absque omni sensibili figura & repræsentatione, supplicârunt. Par veterum Romanorum ratio est, qui, si Varroni & Plutarcho fides est, Deorum fumorum multitudinem, absque omni idolo vel imagine, per ducentos fere annos continuos coluerunt. De prisciis quoque Celtis Tacitus libro de Germania: Neque cohibere parietibus Deos, neque in ullam oris humani speciem assimilare, ex magnitudine cœlestium arbitrantur. Lucos ac nemora consecrant, Deorúmque nominibus appellant secretum illud, quod sola reverentia videt. Et omnino antiquissima ac simplicissima omnium idololatria simulachris caruit, quando ἐμφανεῖς καὶ ἀόρατοι conspicui & visibiles illi Dii, uti à Græcis apud Origenem contra Celsum lib. 5. appellantur, rudem populum ad sui adorationem pellexerunt satis, priusquam vel arte, vel otio Templa Diis suis ædificand, statuásque erigendi pollerent. Quæ causa est, quòd seriò adeò Deus populo suo inculcavit Deut. IV. 19. ne, cùm sublatis in Cœlum oculis viderint Solem, Lunam, stellas, omnes denique Cœli copias, impelli se ad ea adoranda atque colenda sinerent. Tum qui inter Gentiles non plane πονηρῶς κόμματος, adeóque moratiores fuerunt, haud plane Deitatis unius summi Numinis, Creatoris Cœli & terræ expertes fuerunt, ejúsque unitatem, omniscientiam, omnipotentiam agnoverunt. Falluntur, ita Minutius Felix loquitur, in nomine, sed de una potestate consentiunt, qui Jovem principem volunt. Quàm verò Jovis nomen proximè ad illud ꟿ Jehovæ accedit? Et Thebaidos incolas Mundi conditorem coluisse, ipsa statua, per quam eum colebant, testatur, utpote quæ, uti Pierius Hieroglyph. lib. 59. docet, Hominis imago erat cum ovo ex ore ejus prodeunte, perinde ac si verbo Dei creatum esse, mundum insinuarent. Sed & Dio Chrysostomus Orat. 12. τῆς πρώτης τῶ θεῶ ἐικόιας, & Maximus Tyrius Dissert. 38. paganus uterque, apertè profitetur, se in simulachris aureis, argenteis, eburneis supremum rerum omnium conditorem conservatoremque colere. Summo autem illi Numini, quod generali saltem animi complexione intuebantur, religiosum cultum impertientes, altaria, Templa, imagines erigentes, sacrificia offerentes, vota nuncupantes, omnis retro antiquitas, ceu idololatriæ manifestos reos, damnavit
units.tr: XVI. From these things it is clear that among the Jews idolatry was not only the worship of an idol, that is, of an image of a false god, but the worship of any false god, or the worship of the true God not in the way God commanded, for example in an image, which God expressly forbade to be used in the worship of the true God. Nor was the proper nature of idolatry located in anything more than in this: that they paid divine worship to a thing that was not God. The idolatry of the pagans confirms this same point, since it did not consist strictly in worshipping an image of some false god. Many Gentiles are rightly held by everyone to be guilty of idolatry, though they used no images in their worship. For example, the Persians, according to Herodotus, Histories, book 1, 131, on the peaks of mountains offered worship to the visible heaven under the name of Jupiter, and likewise to the sun, moon, earth, water and winds, without any perceptible figure or representation. The case of the ancient Romans is similar, who, if we trust Varro and Plutarch, worshipped a multitude of gods without any idol or image for almost two hundred years in succession. Tacitus, in his book on Germany, says the same of the ancient Celts: They think it unworthy to confine gods within walls, or to represent them in any likeness of the human face, judging them by the greatness of the heavenly beings. They consecrate groves and woods, and call by the names of the gods that secret place which only reverence sees. And in general the most ancient and simplest of all idolatries lacked images, when those gods, conspicuous and visible [ἐμφανεῖς καὶ ἀόρατοι], as the Greeks call them in Origen, Against Celsus, book 5, drew the rude people to their worship well before they had the means, by skill or leisure, to build temples to their gods and set up statues. This is why God so earnestly impressed on his people, Deut. 4.19, that they should not, when they lifted up their eyes to heaven and saw the sun, moon, stars, and all the host of heaven, allow themselves to be driven to adore and worship them. Moreover, those among the Gentiles who were not wholly wicked in their sect, and so were more well-behaved, were not altogether without the knowledge of the one supreme Deity, the Creator of heaven and earth, and they acknowledged his unity, omniscience and omnipotence. Minucius Felix speaks thus: They are mistaken in the name, but they agree about one power, those who call Jupiter the chief. And how close the name Jupiter comes to that name Jehovah! That the inhabitants of Thebais worshipped the Maker of the world is shown by the very statue through which they worshipped him, which, as Pierius teaches in Hieroglyphica, book 59, was an image of a man with an egg coming forth from his mouth, as though they meant that the world was created by the word of God. Dio Chrysostom, Oration 12, [τῆς πρώτης τῶ θεῶ ἐικόιας], and Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation 38, both pagans, openly declare that they worshipped the supreme Maker and Preserver of all things in images of gold, silver, and ivory. And all antiquity, offering religious worship to that supreme Deity whom they at least grasped in a general way, and erecting altars, temples and images, offering sacrifices and making vows, it condemned as manifest guilty parties of idolatry.

units.la: XVII. Abunde sic, confido, Bellarmini adversus Propositionem nostram ἔνσαον imbellem planè & ficulneam esse demonstravimus. Nunc alio incedentem talo gregalem ejusdem, Gregorium de Valentia adoriamur. Is enim Bellarminiana latebra neglecta, imagines quasvis Christi, Sanctorum, non modo simulachra, sed etiam idola esse de Idolol. lib. 11. 7. haud dissimulans, effugium turpius, sed non minùs forte sustinendæ incliuatæ causæ necessarium quærit, atque, ut Tertulliani de carne Christi cap. 6. verbis utar, de calcaria in carbonariam pervenit, vel potiùs fumum, quod aiunt, fugiens, in ignem incidit. Negat nempe idololatram, damnatum scilicet (nam idololatriam quandam licitam ἀυτκαπ̃κεῖτης propugnat) esse, quisquis creaturæ Divinum cultum exhibet; atque ita lib. 11. 1. idololatriam definit, quòd sit impius cultus, quo creaturæ Divinus honor exhibetur, sic ut Deo. Quæ clausula inanis duntaxat esset repetitio rei significatæ vocabulo Divinum, si id simpliciter vellet, quod verba usitatè sonant. Idem enim est, honorem habere creaturæ sicut Deo, & creaturæ honorem Divinum habere. Unde Thomas Aquinas in 2. 2. quæst. 94. art. 1. definiens idololatriam, quòd sit superstitio, qua creaturæ Divinus cultus exhibetur, id confirmat verbis Augustini de Doctr. Christi lib. 11. 20. dicentis, creaturam in ea coli, sicut Deum. Et Catechismus Tridentinus Explicat. præc. 1. verbis idem sonantibus, modò, si idola colantur tanquam Deus, modò, si creatæ rei tribuatur honor Deo debitus, idololatriam committi docet. Sed Valentianus astutè aliud agit, &, ne idololatriæ definitio in Pontificios cadat, quos variis creaturis Divinum honorem impertiri negare non poterat, ad idololatriam necesse esse ait, ut duo concurrant; unum, ut quod honoris vel cultus creaturæ tribuitur, id soli Deo debitum fit; alterum, ut hoc, quicquid est honoris Divini, ita verè impendatur creaturæ, sicut Deo impendi oportebat. Eum porro dicit verè censeri Divinum cultum creaturæ conferre, tanquam Deo, qui eam Divino cultu sic prosequitur, ut eo, quantum in se est, velit illi opinionem talem conciliare, qualis revera in solam Dei Majestatem competit. Concludit ergo, cap. 7. Pontificios idololatriam minimè committere in imaginibus venerandis, quoniam in cultu Christi imaginum, atque adeò etiam crucis honorem quidem usurpant Divinum; sed non illum imaginibus ipsis deferunt, sicut Christo Deo ac Domino nostro. Nam ad Christum is honor pertinet, quatenus illi conciliat exístimationem Deo soli debitam; ad imagines verò, ut coram illis ejusmodi exístimatio concilietur Christo. XVIII. Qui hanc Hierarchiæ defensionem altiori mente penitaverit, is pro vero judicabit, tum antiquas lupas Romanas à meretrice Romana hodierna impudentia multùm superari: tum prisicis causidicis & oratoribus recentes Jesuitas ingenio antecellere. Juvenalis enim ostendens, quemadmodum Romanæ nuptæ olim, cùm in adulterio deprehenderentur, se defendderint, sic Sat. 6. canit:
units.tr: XVII. I trust that by this we have sufficiently shown that Bellarmine's answer to our proposition concerning ἔνσαον is feeble and fruitless. Now let us attack his fellow-soldier, Gregory of Valentia, who is marching on a different heel. He has set aside Bellarmine's hiding-place and does not conceal that any images whatever of Christ or the saints are not merely likenesses but idols (de Idolol. lib. 11. 7.). Seeking a more shameful escape, yet one he thinks necessary to defend his tottering cause, he moves, to use Tertullian's words (de carne Christi cap. 6.), from the lime-kiln into the charcoal-pit, or rather, as the saying goes, while fleeing the smoke he falls into the fire. He denies that a person is an idolater, meaning a condemned one (for he defends a certain lawful [ἀυτκαπ̃κεῖτης]), if he offers divine worship to a creature. Thus, in lib. 11. 1., he defines idolatry as an impious worship by which divine honour is paid to a creature, in such a way as to God. This closing clause would be an empty repetition of the thing signified by the word divine, if he meant only what the words ordinarily say. For to have honour for a creature as for God is the same as to have divine honour for a creature. So Thomas Aquinas, defining idolatry in in 2. 2. quæst. 94. art. 1. as a superstition by which divine worship is paid to a creature, confirms this with the words of Augustine (de Doctr. Christi lib. 11. 20.), who says that the creature is worshipped in it as God. The Catechism of Trent, in Explicat. præc. 1., teaches in words of the same sense that idolatry is committed both if idols are worshipped as God and if the honour due to God is given to a created thing. But Valentia cunningly does something else. So that the definition of idolatry does not fall upon the Papists, to whom he could not deny that they give divine honour to various creatures, he says that for idolatry two things must concur: first, that the honour or worship given to a creature is that which is due to God alone; second, that whatever is divine honour is truly bestowed on a creature in the way it ought to be bestowed on God. He further says that a person is truly judged to offer divine worship to a creature as to God when he so honours it that, as far as in him lies, he wishes to win for it an esteem of such a kind as truly belongs to the majesty of God alone. He therefore concludes, in cap. 7., that the Papists do not commit idolatry in venerating images, since in the worship of images of Christ, and even of the cross, they indeed employ divine honour, but do not pay it to the images themselves as to Christ our God and Lord. For that honour belongs to Christ, insofar as it wins for him the esteem due to God alone; but to the images, so that such esteem may be won for Christ in their presence. XVIII. Anyone who examines this defence of the hierarchy with a more penetrating mind will judge that the ancient Roman she-wolves are far surpassed by the present Roman whore in impudence, and that the recent Jesuits surpass the old Roman advocates and orators in cleverness. For Juvenal, showing how Roman wives once defended themselves when caught in adultery, sings in Sat. 6.:

units.la: Sed jacet in servi complexibus, aut Equitis, dic, Dic aliquem sodes hic Quintiliane colorem.Hæremus. Dic ipsa. Olim convenerat, inquit, Ut faceres tu quod velles; nec non ego possemIndulgere mihi: clames licet, & mare CæloConfundas, homo sum. Nihil est audacius illisDeprensis, iram atque animos à crimine sumunt.
units.tr: But she lies in a slave's embrace, or a knight's. Tell us, pray, Quintilian, some plea. We stick. Tell it yourself. She says: "We had agreed that you should do as you pleased, and that I too might indulge myself. Shout if you like, and confound sea with sky: I am only human. Nothing is bolder than women caught in the act: they take their anger and their spirit from their crime."

units.la: Jam verò Ecclesia Romana sponsa Christi jacens in complexibus imaginis aut crucis Christi, se spirituali adulterio polluit, dum alteri conjugale debitum præstat, & creaturæ honorem soli Deo debitum tribuit. Nisi ergo frontem Romanis illis lupabus veteribus, quibus tamen audacius nihil Juvenalis putavit; duriorem haberet, sic saltem se excusaret: Homo sum, errare possum, clames licet, & mare Cælo confundas. At se errare posse præfractè negat; imò Petrum Oxoniensem id negantem damnavit, uti Caranza Summ. Concil. in Sixto IV. & Canus Loc. Theol. lib. VI. 7. referunt; & quæ in Historia Papatus, atque superiùs etiam eam in rem narravimus, produnt. Et ad cujus causæ defensionem color nullus Quintiliano Rhetori acutissimo, excogitari posse videbatur. Ad suæ verò defensionem facilè colorem excogitavit Jesuita, dicendo, idololatriam esse, honorem Divinum habere creaturæ, sicut Deo. Infelicem verò Quintilianum causidicum, qui sic cœcutivit, ut non videret, pro uxore in alieni viri complexibus cubante responderi posse, hanc solam esse genuinam rationem adulterii, obsequium conjugale præstare alteri, ut conjugi, seu marito. Si ergo negasset illa, se obsequium conjugale alteri hac mente praestitisse, ut pro marito eum haberet; praetexens forte, intentionem suam fuisse, ut ex ipso memoriam mariti renovaret, aut in mariti gratiam liberos suscwithin;iperet; quemadmodum viro talem conjugem habenti quidam apud eundem Juvenalem Satyr. 9. dicit;
units.tr: Now indeed the Roman Church, the bride of Christ, lying in the embraces of an image or the cross of Christ, defiles herself with spiritual adultery, while she renders conjugal duty to another and gives to a creature the honour due to God alone. Therefore, unless she had a brow harder than those old Roman she-wolves, to whom Juvenal thought nothing bolder, she might at least excuse herself thus: I am human, I can err, shout if you like, and confound sea with sky. But she flatly denies that she can err; indeed she condemned Peter of Oxford for denying it, as Caranza (Summ. Concil. in Sixto IV.) and Canus (Loc. Theol. lib. VI. 7.) report, and as the History of the Papacy reveals, and as we have also related above on this matter. And for the defence of this cause no plea seemed to be devisable even for the most acute rhetorician Quintilian. But the Jesuit has easily devised a plea for her defence, by saying that idolatry is to have divine honour for a creature as for God. Poor Quintilian, the advocate, who was so blind that he did not see that a reply could be made for a wife lying in another man's embrace: this is the only true reason for adultery, to render conjugal duty to another as to a spouse or husband. If she had denied that she rendered conjugal duty to another with the intention of regarding him as her husband, perhaps pleading that her intention was to renew her husband's memory through him, or to bear children for her husband's benefit, as someone in the same Juvenal (Satyr. 9.) says to a husband who has such a wife:

units.la: Nullum ergo meritum est, ingrate, ac perfide, nullum,Quòd tibi filiolus, vel filia nascitur ex me?
units.tr: No merit then, ungrateful and faithless man, none, that a little son or daughter is born to you from me?

units.la: firmissimo sic argumento sibi, & alteri eam labem, quam utrique immerito Juvenalis aspersit, abstersisset, dum hunc adulteri, illam moechae nomine traducit.
units.tr: By this most solid argument she would have wiped away, for herself and for the other, the stain which Juvenal unjustly cast on both, since he calls the one adulterer and the other adulteress.

units.la: XIX. Alterum ergo duorum illorum, quae requiri ad propriam idololatriae rationem Valentia dixit, ut videlicet creaturae Divinus exhibeatur honos, sufficit ad scortum illud Babylonico-Romanum adulterii spirituali s convincendum, quòd Divinum se creaturis honorem impertiri, inficias ire non ausit: alterum verò, ut creaturae Divinus honos exhibeatur, sicut Deo, redundat, ut struma, qua exacta corpus definitionis integrum relinquitur. Sive proin quis adulteram defendat, cavillando, eam conjugali amore morigerari alieno viro, sed non sicut conjugi; dicent sani omnes, eam alienum virum amare sicut conjugem, sed non sicut conjugem: sive idololatra garriat, se Divinum honorem exhibere creaturae, sed non sicut Deo, helleborum ei ut parum sano optaturi sunt omnes, utpote dicenti, se creaturam colere sicut Deum, sed non sicut Deum. Haec Valentiae φλυαρίαν vertigo est.
units.tr: XIX. Therefore, of the two conditions which Valentia said are required for the proper account of idolatry, the first, namely that divine honour be given to a creature, is enough to convict that Babylonian-Roman harlot of spiritual adultery, since she does not dare to deny that she bestows divine honour on creatures. The second, that divine honour be given to a creature as to God, is superfluous, like a tumour which, once removed, leaves the body of the definition whole. So if anyone defends an adulteress by quibbling that she obeys another man with a wifely love, but not as a wife, all sensible people will say: she loves another man as a wife, but not as a wife. And if an idolater chatters that he gives divine honour to a creature, but not as to God, all will wish for hellebore for him, as for one not quite sound, since he says: I worship a creature as God, but not as God. This is the vertigo of Valentia's nonsense.

units.la: XX. Sed remisse nimis & molliter Jesuitam hunc habemus, pupillas ei duplices, bicipitisque monstri formam, aut struma m definitioni ejus objicientes. Nam & Vatinius ille apud Ciceronem ad Attic. lib. 11. Epist. 10. non obstante struma fuit verus: & vitulus ille biceps, Saturæ natus, apud Julium Obsequentem de prodigiis, fuit verus vitulus: & fœminæ duplicibus pupillis præditæ, veræ fœminæ sunt. Definitio autem Valentiani vera definitio non est, quia, prout appendice hoc, sicut Deo, augetur, non omni definito convenit. Idololatria enim in imaginum cultu à multis commissa est, qui Divinum tamen honorem imagini non tribuerunt ea mente, ut imagini ipsi existimationem conciliarent talem, qualis in Deum competit, sed ut rei per imaginem repræsentatæ: sive creaturæ, de qua talis opinio excitanda non est; sive creatori, qui eam hoc modo de se excitari Deut. iv. 15. vetuit. Ita Israelitas in deserto, & post decem tribus vero Deo existimationem cultu vituli, ceu simulachri, & Micham Teraphim suorum cultu, conciliare voluisse, supra astruximus. Dionem quoque Chrysostomum & Maximum Tyrium, Ethnicos ex eorum sapientum numero, quos S. Paulus Rom. i. 21. Deum cognovisse, non tamen ut Deum glorificasse, sed Dei cogniti gloriam in efformatam hominis imaginem mutasse, scribit, supra laudavimus asseverantes, Summum, primum, maximum Deum, Creatorem & Conservatorem omnium, à se in simulachris ex auro, argento & ebore factis coli. Illi ergo sua Jovis Olympici à Phidia effecti veneratione Deo, in quo vivimus, movemur & sumus, non Phidiacæ statuæ existimationem Divinam conciliare gestientes, non iccirco idololatriæ culpa vacárunt; verùm ceu idololatriæ rei, perinde ut Athenienses, aureis, argenteis, lapideis simulachris, verum Deum colentes Act. xvii. 16. 19. 23. damnabuntur. Etiam Alexandrum Severum Bellarminus de Eccles. Triumph. lib. ii. ii. idololatris accensuit, quoniam Divino honore imaginem Christi prosecutus est. Et tamen Alexander der ille, si Lampridio in ejus vita fides est, non de Christi imagine, sed de Christo ipso, velut animo sanctiore, & cui inter Divos recepto Templum facere cogitavit, exîstimationem soli Deo debitam conciliare voluit. Ipsa quoque Synodus Nicæna Act 7. epist. ad Synod. adConst. & Iren. anathematizat Nestorii idololatriam in homine, quia scilicet Christum Mariæ filium dicebat merum esse hominem, quem Divino cultu venerabatur. Unde etiam à Cyrillo ad Reg. de recta fide ἀνθρωπολατρείας arguitur. Et tamen Nestorius Christum opinione sua hominem tantùm Divinis honoribus afficiendo, talem de Mariæ filio opinionem excitare noluit, qualis in solum Deum competit. Par ratio eorum, qui quondam exercitum Cœli, Solem, Baalem in imaginibus coluerunt, qui opinionem soli Majestati Divinæ convenientem non de imaginibus, sed de rebus per imagines repræsentatis excitare voluerunt.
units.tr: XX. But we have treated this Jesuit too loosely and gently, objecting to his definition double pupils, the shape of a two-headed monster, or a tumour. For that Vatinius in Cicero (ad Attic. lib. 11. Epist. 10.) was a real man despite his tumour; and that two-headed calf born at Saturae, in Julius Obsequens (de prodigiis), was a real calf; and women with double pupils are real women. But Valentia's definition is not a true definition, because, as it is enlarged by this appendix, as to God, it does not fit every case defined. For idolatry in the worship of images has been committed by many who nevertheless did not give divine honour to the image with the intention of winning for the image itself an esteem of the kind that belongs to God, but as to the thing represented through the image: whether to the creature, for whom such an opinion ought not to be stirred up, or to the Creator, who forbade that he should be honoured in this way (Deut. 4:15). Thus we have shown above that the Israelites in the desert, and after the ten tribes, wished to win for the true God esteem by worship of the calf as an image, and Micah by the worship of his teraphim. We have also praised above Dion Chrysostom and Maximus of Tyre, Gentiles from the number of those wise men of whom St Paul writes (Rom. 1:21) that they knew God but did not glorify him as God, but changed the glory of the known God into the image of a fashioned man; they assert that the supreme, first, greatest God, Creator and Preserver of all, is worshipped by them in images made of gold, silver and ivory. Those, therefore, who, eager that the divine esteem of their Olympian Jupiter, made by Phidias, should not be won for Phidias's statue but for God, in whom we live, move and have our being, were not for that reason free from the guilt of idolatry; but, as guilty of idolatry, they will be condemned just as the Athenians were, who, worshipping the true God in golden, silver and stone images, are condemned (Acts 17:16, 19, 23). Bellarmine (de Eccles. Triumph. lib. ii. ii.) also reckons Alexander Severus among the idolaters, because he showed divine honour to an image of Christ. And yet that Alexander, if we trust Lampridius in his life, wished to win the esteem due to God alone not for an image of Christ but for Christ himself, as for a holier soul, and one whom he thought of building a temple for, received among the gods. The Nicene Synod itself (Act 7. epist. ad Synod. adConst. & Iren.) anathematizes the idolatry in a man of Nestorius, because he said that Christ, the son of Mary, was a mere man, whom he nevertheless worshipped with divine honour. Hence he is also charged by Cyril (ad Reg. de recta fide) with worship of man. And yet Nestorius, by honouring Christ, in his opinion a man only, with divine honours, did not wish to stir up in the Son of Mary such an opinion as belongs to God alone. The same reasoning applies to those who long ago worshipped the host of heaven, the Sun and Baal, in images, and who wished that the esteem belonging to the divine majesty should be stirred up not for the images but for the things represented by the images.

units.la: XXI. Nihil ergo verius Valentianus idololatriam definivit, quàm si quis hominem definiret animal rationale, à Jesuitis corruptum. Id sanè in hominibus multis nimis eheu! verum est. Quia tamen per Dei gratiam non omnes homines à Jesuitis corrupti sunt, vera hæc hominis definitio esse nequit. Auferr voces ultimas, à Jesuitis corruptum, relinquès veram ejus definitionem, animal rationale. Ita veram habes definitionem idololatriæ, creatura Divinum honorem tribuere, si appendicem Valentiani, sicut Deum, maximè dempseris.
units.tr: XXI. Valentinus therefore defined idolatry most truly when he defined man as a rational animal, corrupted by the Jesuits. Alas, that is indeed true of many men. Yet since by the grace of God not all men have been corrupted by the Jesuits, this cannot be a true definition of man. Remove the final words, corrupted by the Jesuits, and you keep his true definition, a rational animal. So you have a true definition of idolatry, a creature giving divine honour, if you especially remove the appendix of Valentinus, as God.

units.la: XXII. Cœterùm ii, quibus Divinus honos tribuitur, licet nec verus Deus sint, nec verum Deum eos esse, idololatræ profiteantur, communicatione tamen eorum, quæ Divina sunt, & soli Deo tribuenda fuerant, quantum in idololatris est, Dii efficiuntur, sed אלהי אחרים Dii alii, quos coram facie sua habere, lex Divina prohibuit. Deus autem alius, qui non sit Creator Cœli & terræ, est לא-יהוה Non-Jehova, NonDeus, Deut. xxxii.27. אליל res nihili, vanitas, nullitas, quomodo idola dici אלילים quasi אל אלים nonDeus nonnulli arbitrantur. Nullus enim alius verus Deus est, quàm qui φύσει θεὸς natura Deus est, Gal. iv. 8. At omnes alii Dii, non natura, sed tantùm opinione & attributione sunt Dii, id est, Dii precarii & λεγόμενοι. Hinc omnis idololatra necessariò divergit ab unitate ad multitudinem, & loco unius Dei asciscit multos. Verus enim Deus tantùm unus est. Qui autem Divinitatem alii, sive ille verè subsistat & existentiam habeat extra mentem, sive ut figmentum, ab homine pro arbitrio excogitatum, in sola mente stabuletur, attribuit, si una verum Deum colit, jam duos Deos habet, & πολύθεος est. Et quia in unica creatura abscessio hæc rarò, vel nunquam subsistit (uti ἐνὸς αὐτῶν δεῦρο τὰ ἴπρα ἴπ(ι) hinc illa πολυθεότης, multorum Deorum turba infelici satu humani ingenii nata est. Atque licet ille, qui omisso & præterito creatore creaturam tantùm colit, majoris se sacrilegii reum constituat, quàm qui juxta cum creatore, in creaturam præterea animum dividit; tamen & hic præter creatorem creaturam colens verè sacrilegus & idololatra est. Cùm enim summus gloriæ suæ Zelotes sit Deus, societatem, vel divisum imperium non fert, neque gloriam suam dat alteri, neque laudem suam sculptilibus, Esai.xlii.8. Gloria quippe ischæc excedit captum creaturæ, nullique communicabilis est. Unde qui alteri transcribit, quod soli Deo proprium est, Deum, quantum in se est, spoliat sua prærogativa, & facit non-Deum. Duobus enim tam disparibus dominis nemo unus simul servire potest, quin aut unum odio habeat, & alterum diligat; aut uni adhæreat, & alterum contemnat,
units.tr: XXII. Moreover, those to whom divine honour is given, although they are neither the true God nor (as idolaters profess) is the true God them, yet by sharing in what is divine, which ought to have been given to God alone, become gods so far as idolaters are concerned. But they are other gods [אלהי אחרים], whom the divine law forbade to have before his face. A god who is other, and who is not the Creator of heaven and earth, is Not-Jehovah, Not-God [לא-יהוה], Deut. 32.27. An idol [אליל] is a thing of nothing, vanity, nullity; and some think idols are called אלילים as if from אל אלים, not-God. For there is no other true God except the one who is God by nature [φύσει θεὸς], Gal. 4.8. But all other gods are gods not by nature but only by opinion and attribution, that is, borrowed gods and so-called gods [λεγόμενοι]. Hence every idolater necessarily departs from unity to multiplicity, and in place of the one God takes on many. For the true God is only one. Whoever ascribes divinity to another, whether that other truly subsists and has existence outside the mind, or stands only in the mind as a fiction devised by man at will, and yet worships one true God, already has two gods and is a polytheist [πολύθεος]. And since this defection rarely or never stops at a single creature (as [ἐνὸς αὐτῶν δεῦρο τὰ ἴπρα ἴπ(ι)]), hence that polytheism, the crowd of many gods, was born from the unhappy seed of the human mind. And although he who, omitting and passing over the Creator, worships only a creature, makes himself guilty of a greater sacrilege than he who divides his mind between the Creator and a creature alongside him, yet he too, who worships a creature besides the Creator, is truly a sacrilegious idolater. For since God is the supreme jealous guardian of his own glory, he does not bear a partnership or divided rule: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images, Isa. xlii.8. Indeed, that glory surpasses the grasp of a creature and cannot be shared with anyone. Hence whoever transfers to another what is proper to God alone strips God, so far as he is able, of his prerogative, and makes him a non-God. For no one can serve two such unequal masters at once, but he will either hate the one and love the other, or cling to one and despise the other,
Tom. II.

units.la: Matth. vi. 24. Quantum enim datur creaturæ, tantum Deo detrahitur, qui coli & amari non potest, nisi ex toto corde, tota anima, & omnibus viribus. Sicut enim Conclusio semper sequitur partem deteriorem: ita qui servitutem, quam vero domino debet, partitur cum peregrino, magis is contumelia, quàm honore Dominum afficit.
units.tr: Matth. vi. 24. For as much as is given to the creature, so much is taken from God, who cannot be worshipped and loved except with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all strength. For just as the conclusion always follows the weaker part, so he who divides the service he truly owes to his Lord with a stranger honours the Lord more by insult than by honour.

units.la: XXIII. Liquet hinc clarissimè, omnes eos, qui creaturis, vel præter Deum rei alii, sive verè subsistenti, sive fictæ, Divinum honorem, seu id, quod soli Deo & revelatio, & recta ratio tribuendum docet, impertiuntur; non tantùm idololatras, sed etiam polytheos & atheos esse. Idololatras quidem, stylo Scripturæ, & saniorum omnium judicio, uti abunde supra confirmavimus. Polytheos, quia præter vel Deum verum, vel fictitium aliquod Numen colunt Deos alios, res videlicet eas, quibus post verum Deum Divinitatem tribuunt. Denique Atheos, quia ii etiam, qui præter verum Deum res quascunque alias Divino cultu afficiunt, neque verum Deum colunt, sed gloriam ejus, utpote solius omnipotentis, Sapientis &c. delibando, ex eo idolum, vel non-Deum, Θεὸν λεγόμενον faciunt; adeóque verum Deum nullum colunt, & genuini in mundo Athei sunt. Qui idololatriæ fructus funestissimus est.
units.tr: XXIII. It is most clear from this that all those who impart divine honour to creatures, or to any other thing besides God, whether truly subsisting or fictitious, that is, to what revelation and right reason teach is due to God alone, are not only idolaters but also polytheists and atheists. Idolaters, indeed, in the style of Scripture and by the judgement of all sane people, as we have abundantly confirmed above. Polytheists, because besides either the true God or some fictitious deity they worship other gods, namely those things to which, after the true God, they ascribe divinity. Finally atheists, because those too who honour any other things whatever with divine worship, besides the true God, and do not worship the true God, but by diminishing his glory, which belongs to him alone as almighty, wise, and so on, make out of it an idol, or a non-God, so-called god [Θεὸν λεγόμενον]. Thus they worship no true God and are genuine atheists in the world. This is the most deadly fruit of idolatry.

units.la: XXIV. Asserta hactenus, & in arce veritatis collocata Propositione, assumptio demonstranda restat. Demonstrabimus autem tum ratione generali, tum specialibus, juxta objecta in propositione expressa distinctis. Ac generalis inde petita est, quòd vel omnia, vel nonnulla cultus Pontificii extra cultum unius Dei vagantia objecta, puta Papam, Eucharistiam, Sanctos, imagines, reliquias, res consecratas Hierarchia & colit & colenda scilicet adoratione, invocatione, fiducia, incurvatione, sacrificiis, libaminibus, suffitu, votis, juramentis, erectione Templorum, altarium, hymnis. Ille ergo cultus objectis his vel singulis vel nonnullis, per omnes illos, quos recensui modos, ab Hierarchia delatus vel civilis vel religiosus, adeóque Divinus est. Civilem esse, nemo Hierarchicorum sustinet. Religiosus ergo est, adeóque Divinus. Nam religiosum & Divinum cultum eundem esse, jam supra certis rationibus constituimus, atque eadem ratione Hierarchicos Papolatriæ convicimus. Sed ea de re heic exquisitius paulò agendum nobis fuerit, cùm idololatriæ Hierarchicorum demonstratio clarissima, addo & compendiosissima inde pendeat.
units.tr: XXIV. Having asserted the proposition so far and set it in the citadel of truth, what remains is to demonstrate the assumption. We will demonstrate it both by a general argument and by special ones, distinguished according to the objects named in the proposition. The general argument is drawn from this: either all or some of the objects of Papist worship, which stray outside the worship of the one God, namely the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, images, relics, and things consecrated by the hierarchy, are both worshipped and to be worshipped with adoration, invocation, trust, bowing down, sacrifices, libations, incense, vows, oaths, the erection of temples and altars, and hymns. That worship, then, offered by the members of the hierarchy to these objects, either singly or some of them, through all the modes I have listed, is either civil or religious, and so it is divine. That it is civil no member of the hierarchy maintains. It is therefore religious, and so divine. For that religious and divine worship are the same, we have already established above by certain arguments, and by the same reasoning we have convicted the hierarchists of Papolatry. But on this matter we must treat a little more carefully here, since the very clear demonstration of the idolatry of the hierarchists, and a most compendious one, depends on it.

units.la: XXV. Hierachici ergo ad palliandam idololatriam suam perbellam nobis historiam concinnârunt, nempe tot esse genera honoris, seu cultus, quot sunt excellentiarum. At genera excellentiarum tria esse, Divinum, Humanum & Medium, inter humanum scilicet & Divinum. Divinus illis cultus Latriæ, humanus civilis seu societatis, medius dulia nomine venit. Illum soli Deo, & relative ejus Vicario, Papæ, Vice-Deo, nec non ejus imaginibus; istum solis hominibus nondum Deificatis, hunc hominibus Deificatis, quos Sanctos appellant, eorúmque imaginibus relative, deberi pertendunt. Addunt recentiores Mariolatræ Medium principaliorem Hyperduliam, soli Deiparæ, & relative ejus imaginibus debitum. Quanto verò rectius & à fraudulentia remotius fuerat juxta distinctionem & oppositionem immediatam Creatoris & creaturæ, rei infinitæ & finitæ honorem omnem & cultum bipartiri, in religiosum & civilem; quorum ille Deo Creatori, hic creaturæ convenit. Sic enim, qualem cultum duliam vel hyperduliam facerent, cognoscere integrum suisset. Nam cultum civilem esse, utpote ab eo distinctum, pernegant. Religiosum ergo facere debuissent. Atqui ille non alius, quàm Divinus est, quia religio proprië est cultus Numinis, adeóque jure ad solum Deum pertinet, adeò quidem ut quoties alii, quàm Deo tribuitur, in superstitionem & idololatriam ilico degeneret. Quòd si mediam quandam excellentiam, adeóque medium etiam cultum constituere libuit, profectò ille civilis potiùs, quàm religiosus constituendus fuerat, quia duas excellentias, increatam & creatam, quas inter distantia infinita intercedit, longè absurdius esset uno communi religioso, quàm duas excellentias, puta Angelorum Sanctorúmque hominum, & hominum purorum, militantium adhuc, utramque finitam, adeóque ad se invicem infinito propiùs accedentem, uno communíque civilis cultus complexu jungere. Sicut infinita & finita excellentia miscéri nullo modo possunt, ita neque medius quidam cultus institui religiosus potest. Vel enim de extremis participaret, vel utrumque negaret. Non prius, quia Deus honorem suum vel universum vel partem ejus nemini alii dat. Non posterius, quia sicut nihil est, quod non finitum vel infinitum sit, ita medius cultus, neutra excellentia participans, excogitari nequit. Quinimò si media quaedam excellentia, & medius cultus daretur, is tum excellentiæ, tum cultus civilis nomine longè & concinniùs & tutiùs veniret, quia Sancti glorificatique Angeli & homines pii sunt συνδουλοι και συμμέτοχοι, conservi & concives ejusdem Hierosolymæ, quæ à Cœlo ad terram usque pertingit, juxta illud S. Pauli Hebr. xii. 22. 23. Accessistis ad Sion montem, civitatem Dei viventis, Hierosolymam Coelestem, Myriadas Angelorum, Spiritus hominum persectorum. Omnia enim in Christo recapitulata sunt, quæ in Cœlis, & quæ in terra sunt, Ephes. i.10. Per ipsum Deus reconciliavit omnia in ipsum, pace facta ta per sanguinem crucis ejus ; sive quæ in terra sunt, sive quæ in Cælis, Col. i. 20. Unde jam πολίτευμα, jus civitatis nostrum in Cælis est, Phil. iii.20. Unde planè constat, Sanctos & Angelos cœlites, Hominésque pios in terris militantes una politia, societate gaudere, cives esse ejusdem civitatis. Ast verò συμπολῖται concives sibi mutuò non religiosum utique, qualis Deo convenit, sed civilem honorem cultúmque, qui mutuæ dilectionis est, præstant.
units.tr: XXV. The members of the hierarchy, then, to cover up their idolatry, have devised for us a very fine story: that there are as many kinds of honour, or worship, as there are kinds of excellence. But there are three kinds of excellence, divine, human, and intermediate, that is, between the human and the divine. The divine worship they call latria, the human civil or social, and the intermediate goes by the name dulia. They contend that the first is owed to God alone, and relatively to his Vicar, the Pope, the vice-God, and to his images; the second to men not yet deified; the third to men who have been deified, whom they call saints, and relatively to their images. The more recent Mariolaters add a more principal intermediate, hyperdulia, owed to the Mother of God alone and relatively to her images. But how much more correctly, and how much further from deceit, it would have been, according to the distinction and the immediate opposition of Creator and creature, of infinite and finite being, to divide all honour and worship into two parts, religious and civil, of which the former belongs to the Creator God and the latter to the creature. For thus they would have been able to know in full what kind of worship they were making dulia or hyperdulia. For they flatly deny that it is civil. They ought therefore to have made it religious. But that is nothing other than divine, because religion is properly the worship of the divine power, and so it rightly belongs to God alone, so much so that whenever it is given to anyone other than God it at once degenerates into superstition and idolatry. But if they wished to establish some intermediate excellence, and so an intermediate worship, then surely it ought to have been established as civil rather than religious, because it would be far more absurd to join, under one common religious worship, two excellences, the uncreated and the created, between which lies an infinite distance, than to join under one common complex of civil worship two excellences, namely of angels and holy men, and of men still in the militant state, both finite, and therefore drawing much nearer to each other. Just as infinite and finite excellence can in no way be mixed, so neither can an intermediate worship be instituted as religious. For it would either share in the extremes or deny both. Not the former, because God gives his honour, whether the whole or a part of it, to no one else. Not the latter, because just as there is nothing that is not either finite or infinite, so an intermediate worship, sharing in neither excellence, cannot be conceived. Indeed, if some intermediate excellence and an intermediate worship were granted, it would be named far more fittingly and safely as both excellence and civil worship, because the saints, the glorified angels, and pious men are fellow-servants and fellow-partakers [συνδοῦλοι καὶ συμμέτοχοι], fellow-servants and fellow-citizens of the same Jerusalem, which reaches from heaven down to earth, according to that saying of St Paul, Heb. xii. 22, 23: You have come to Mount Sion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to myriads of angels, the spirits of perfected men. For all things in Christ are gathered up, both those in the heavens and those on the earth, Eph. i. 10. Through him God reconciled all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether those on earth or those in heaven, Col. i. 20. Hence our citizenship [πολίτευμα] is in heaven, Phil. iii. 20. Hence it is plainly clear that the saints and the angels of heaven, and pious men militant on earth, enjoy one commonwealth and fellowship, and are citizens of the same city. But fellow-citizens [συμπολῖται] render one another not religious honour, such as is fitting to God, but civil honour and worship, which belongs to mutual love.

units.la: XXVI. Addo inter Angelos, Sanctos & homines militantes maximam esse συγγένειαν, arctissimámque co- gnationem.
units.tr: XXVI. I add that between angels, saints and men still on earth there is the greatest kinship [συγγένεια] and the closest relationship.

units.la: Sancti enim homines glorificati & militantes præterquam quòd ejusdem speciei sunt; etiam gratiæ iisdem collatæ ejusdem generis, licet quoad mensuram earum varient. Utrique per unum spiritum in unum corpus baptizati filii Dei sunt, adeóque supernaturali conditione participant. Quomodo ergo honor iis debitus toto genere sic differre potest, ut glorificatis religiosus, militantibus civilis exhibeatur? Cúmque Angelum inter & glorificatum hominem nihil admodum discriminis intercedat, manifestum est, non magis Angelo, quàm glorificato homini à pio homine militante religiosum honorem deberi.
units.tr: For glorified saints and saints still on earth are not only of the same kind, but also have the same kind of grace bestowed on them, although they differ in its measure. Both, baptized into one body by one Spirit, are sons of God, and so share in a supernatural condition. How, then, can the honour due to them differ so much in kind that it is offered to the glorified as religious and to those on earth as civil? And since there is hardly any difference between an angel and a glorified man, it is plain that a godly man on earth owes religious honour no more to an angel than to a glorified man.

units.la: XXVII. Hinc adeò pii homines militantes Angelorum σύνδουλοι conservi dicuntur Apoc. xix. 10. ubi sic Angelus ad S. Johannem coram eo procidentem, & adoraturum: Vide, ne feceris, conservus tuus sum & fratrum tuorum, qui habent testimonium Jesu. Deum adora. Si religiosum cultum repudiavit Angelus præsens, ea ratione, quòd conservus sit, quanto magis absens repudiaturus eundem fuerat. Si cultus ille oblatus latria, non dulia fuit, cur non Angelus dicebat potiùs, Creatura sum sicut tu es, quàm,
units.tr: XXVII. Hence godly men on earth are called fellow-servants [σύνδουλοι] of the angels, conservi, in Rev. 19:10, where the angel speaks thus to St John, who fell down before him to worship: See that you do not do it; I am your fellow-servant and that of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God. If the angel who was present rejected religious worship on the ground that he was a fellow-servant, how much more would he have rejected it had he been absent. If the worship offered was latria, and not dulia, why did the angel not rather say, Creatura sum sicut tu es (I am a creature as you are), than

units.la: Religionem cultum omnem Angelus repudiavit. quàm, ego conservus tuus sum. Quo certè dicto aperte innuit, servum à confervo adorari, vel religiosè coli neutiquam debere. Quòd si putavit Angelus, duliam quandam religiosam sibi à confervo præstari posse, (quanquam absurdissimum est,confervum alterius confervi servitutem pacisci vel admittere velle,) an putabimus Angelum illum non ea charitate polluisse, ut ἐπικωδ interpretaretur honorem à S. Johanne sibi delatum de honore licito duliæ? Inprimis cùm coram Angelis prosterni, ab honore duliæ haud alienum esse, adversarii pertendant. Sed distinctio profecto duliæ & latriæ adeo quidem subtilis est, ut etiam Angelus ἐχυδερεύεων in cultu religioso rimam vel fissuram tenuissimam videre non potuerit, qua sic ille disrumpi dividique posset, ut vel minimam sibi, utpote non Deo, sed creaturæ, particulam vendicare posset. Manifestissimè ergo tum ex sensu Scripturæ, tum ex infinita inæqualitate ac distantia inter Creatorem & creaturas, exiguáque inter creaturas ipsas, liquet, cultum illum, quem sibi mutuò creaturæ deferunt, merè civilem, non religiosum esse.
units.tr: The angel rejected all religious worship. than, ego conservus tuus sum (I am your fellow-servant). Surely by these words he plainly hints that a servant should not be worshipped or given religious honour by a fellow-servant at all. But if the angel thought that a certain religious duliam could be rendered to him by a fellow-servant (though it is most absurd for one fellow-servant to wish to agree to or admit the servitude of another), shall we suppose that the angel did not in his charity [ἐπικωδ] interpret the honour offered to him by St John as the lawful honour of duliam? Especially since our adversaries maintain that prostration before angels is not foreign to the honour of dulia. But the distinction between dulia and latria is indeed so subtle that even the angel, [ἐχυδερεύεων], could not see in religious worship a crack or fissure so fine that it could be split and divided, so that he might claim for himself even the smallest part, as one who is not God but a creature. Therefore it is most manifest, both from the sense of Scripture and from the infinite inequality and distance between the Creator and the creatures, and from the slight difference between the creatures themselves, that the worship which creatures pay to one another is merely civil, not religious.
XXVIII.

units.la: Accedit; quòd religiosus quispiam duliæ cultus ad legem Dei, qua cultus religiosus haud duliè determinatur, referri nequit. Vel enim refertur ad legis Divinæ tabulam priorem, vel posteriorem. Atqui referri non potest ad priorem, quia ejus objectum solus Deus est. Creaturæ autem nullæ Deus sunt. Et sanè tam non priore tabula cultus ille præcipitur, ut potiùs interdicatur verbis: Non habebis Deos alios coram me. Non facies tibi sculptile. Ego Zelotes sum. Neque etiam referri potest ad posteriorem, quæ officia erga proximum complectitur. Quòd si verò Angeli Sanctique proximi nostri sunt, quo jure religiosum cultum vel depacisci, vel admittere, vel iis talis offerri potest?
units.tr: Moreover, a religious kind of dulia cannot be referred to the law of God, by which religious worship is not determined as dulia. For it is referred either to the first table of the divine law or to the second. But it cannot be referred to the first, since its object is God alone, and no creature is God. Indeed that worship is so far from being prescribed by the first table that it is rather forbidden in words: You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image. I am a jealous God. Nor can it be referred to the second, which embraces duties towards our neighbour. But if angels and saints are our neighbours, by what right can religious worship be bargained for, admitted, or offered to them?

units.la: Religiosus duliæ vel hyperduliæ cultus ad nullam Dei legem referri potest? Necessum ergo fuerit tertiam quandam comminisci tabulam, adeóque legi Divinæ, ceu impersectæ, ἐπιδιαπίσσσθαι, adjicere; atque eundem in finem quoddam etiam tertium objectum legis, quod nec Deus, nec proximus, nec Creator, nec creatura sit, confingere.
units.tr: Can a religious worship of dulia or hyperdulia be referred to no law of God? It would then be necessary to devise some third table and, as though the divine law were imperfect, to add to it; and for this purpose to invent also a third object of the law, which is neither God, nor neighbour, nor Creator, nor creature.

units.la: XXIX. Denique & Christus, & S. Paulus religiosi cultus unitatem demonstrant.
units.tr: XXIX. Finally, both Christ and St Paul demonstrate the unity of religious worship.

units.la: Christus enim Diabolo προσκύνησιν seu adorationem postulanti respondit: Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & ei soli servies, Luc. iv. 8. Certè adorationem non petiit Sathanas, ceu Supremum Numen, qualem latriæ nomine Hierarchici venditant. Satis enim ipse Sathanas professus est, quòd supremum Numen haberi neutiquam desideret, dicens v. 6. ὅτι ἐμοὶ παραδέδοται, quia mihi datum est, Regna scilicet distribuere pro lubitu. Datorem ergo se superiorem, Deum videlicet, agnoscit. Talem ergo adorationem, talem cultum religiosum à Christo stipulari voluit, qualem præstari noverat multis Diis gentium, citra notionem Supremi. Christus verò ejusmodi etiam cultum detestatus, & solum Deum adorare jubens, manifestè illum duliæ cultum rejicit, & adorationem universam ad unum solúmque Deum contrahit. S. Paulus quoque Divinitatem Christi demonstraturus, illa Psalmi repetit: Et adorent eum omnes Angeli, Hebr. 1. 6. Si duo sunt adorationis, & cultus religiosi genera, parùm certè, vel nihil pro Divinitate Christi verba illa strinxissent. Neque etiam vel Ariani, vel Nestoriani, Christum filium Mariæ merum hominem confessi, simulque adorantes, à veteribus Conciliis, ceu ἀνθρωπολάτραι jure damnati essent, siquidem religiosa quædam adoratio creaturæ locum habere posset. Satis enim constat, illos Christum ut hominem, non ut Deum adorasse.
units.tr: For Christ, answering the devil who demanded προσκύνησιν, that is adoration, said: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone, Luke 4:8. Certainly Satan did not ask for adoration as the Supreme Deity, such as the hierarchs peddle under the name of latria. For Satan himself sufficiently professed that he did not at all desire to be regarded as the Supreme Deity, saying in v. 6, ὅτι ἐμοὶ παραδέδοται (for it has been given to me), that is, to distribute kingdoms at his pleasure. He therefore acknowledges that the giver is superior to him, namely God. Therefore he wished Christ to pledge such adoration, such religious worship, as he knew was paid to the many gods of the nations, without any notion of a Supreme Being. But Christ, rejecting such worship too, and commanding that God alone be worshipped, manifestly rejects that kind of dulia worship and confines all adoration to the one God alone. St Paul too, wishing to demonstrate the divinity of Christ, repeats that passage of the Psalm: And let all the angels of God worship him, Heb. 1:6. If there are two kinds of adoration and of religious worship, those words would have proved little or nothing for the divinity of Christ. Nor would the Arians or the Nestorians, who confessed Christ to be a mere man, the son of Mary, and at the same time worshipped him, have been justly condemned by the ancient Councils as anthropolatrae (man-worshippers), if some religious adoration could be given to a creature. For it is well established that they worshipped Christ as man, not as God.
XXX.

units.la: XXX Unicus ergo cultus religiosus est, uni solique Deo in quem religio omnis ferri debet, praestandus, qui nihil aliud est, quàm devota quaedam recognitio Divinae excellentiae, Majestatis, Nominis, & proprietatum, per signa propria recognitioni eidem significandae inservientia. Quae signa, si quando, praeter animi sententiam, per vim metúque adacti aliis, quàm soli Deo, nonnulli exhibuerunt; uti sanè quondam Christiani thurificati fecerunt, & hodiéque nonnulli, idolo Panaceo litare coacti, faciunt, crassissimae idololatriae crimine sese obstrinxerunt, & obstrinxisse se, merito crediti sunt, & hodiéque creduntur. Alioquin enim ad idololatriae crimen compelli nemo posset, cùm interior animi sententia, & Divinae Majestatis recognitio vim pati externam minimè possit. Sicut blasphemiae damnas censeretur, quisquis vocem hanc sibi extorqueri pateretur, Christum filium Dei impostorem esse, licet horribilem vocem interiore animi sensu quàm maximè detestaretur: ita idololatriae reus non minùs censebitur, quisquis signa recognoscendae Divinae excellentiae propria, etiam praeter animi sententiam, vi externa subactus, non Deo applicaret.
units.tr: XXX. There is therefore only one religious worship, to be rendered to the one and only God, to whom all religion must be directed. It is nothing other than a certain devout acknowledgement of the divine excellence, majesty, name, and properties, by means of proper signs serving to signify that acknowledgement. If some people, against their own inner conviction and compelled by force and fear, have offered these signs to anyone other than God alone, as Christians once did when they burned incense and as some still do today, forced to sacrifice to the idol Panaceus, they have bound themselves to the crime of the grossest idolatry. They have rightly been believed to have done so, and are still believed to have done so. For otherwise no one could be compelled to the crime of idolatry, since the inner conviction of the mind and the recognition of divine majesty cannot suffer external violence.
