Just as a man would be judged guilty of blasphemy if he were forced to utter the words that Christ, the Son of God, is an impostor, even though in his inner mind he most heartily detests that dreadful utterance, so the one who, under external force, does not apply to God the proper signs of recognizing divine excellence, even against his inner conviction, will be considered no less guilty of idolatry.

units.la: Unde plane consequens est, nullos esse gradus vel species religiosi cultus, sic ut alius dulia, alius hyperdulia, alius latria censeatur; sed unicum esse cultum religiosum, latriam. Signa enim externa Divinae Majestati recognoscendae idonea, qualia sunt adoratio, invocatio, incurvatio, juramenta, vota, sacrificia, templa, &c. propria esse debent; adeóque, quod in dulia & hyperdulia fit, in creaturam nullam transferri possunt. Alioquin enim cùm de recondita animi notione nemini certò constet, nullum unquam de idololatria ferri judicium posset. Et si signa talia religioso affectu Deo & creaturae praestari, adeóque communia esse possent, jam in cultu saltem externo inter venerationem Dei & creaturæ nulla prosecto differentia statui posse. quod quantum honori & Majestati supremæ Dei deroget, pii omnes judicent.
units.tr: Hence it plainly follows that there are no degrees or kinds of religious worship, such that one is called dulia, another hyperdulia, another latria. There is only one religious worship, latria. For the external signs suited to acknowledging divine majesty, such as adoration, invocation, bowing down, oaths, vows, sacrifices, temples, and so on, must be proper to God, and therefore they cannot be transferred to any creature, as happens in dulia and hyperdulia. Otherwise, since no one can know for certain the hidden notion of another's mind, no judgement of idolatry could ever be pronounced. And if such signs could be offered to God and to a creature with religious affection, and so be common to both, then in external worship at least no real difference could be established between the veneration of God and the veneration of a creature. How much this detracts from the honour and supreme majesty of God, all the pious will judge.

units.la: XXXI. Propria porro religiosi cultus, soli Deo, ad infinitam ejus Majestatem recognoscendam, debiti signa haud dubiè ea sunt, quæ Divina declaratio, accedente vel omnium gentium consensu, vel particularium consuetudine, vel ipsius rei naturali significatione, religioso Dei cultui vendicat. Sacrificia quidem libamina & suffitus Divini cultus signa propria esse, gentium consensus esse voluit. Quæ tamen propriè dicta cùm pridem exoleverint, neque apud Christianos unquam obtinuerint, reliqua signa tantò arctius uni soliqúe Deo devincient evehéntque altiùs. Juramenta soli Deo præstanda esse, tum ex Deut. vi. 13. x. 20. Esai. lxv. 15. 16. Jerem. iv. 2. v. 7. tum ex gentium consensu constat. Parem esse votorum, ut & invocationis, adorationis, petitionisque adeo Spiritus S. remissionis peccatorum, & vitæ æternæ, rationem supra ostendimus. Sicut enim ex eo, quòd Deus solus author & largitor est beneficiorum spiritualium universorum, is, qui res adeò sublimes à creatura poscit, virtutes Dei in ea creatura agnoscit: ita etiam is, qui absentem Angelum vel Sanctum invocat, in utroque omniscientiam & omnipræsentiam, Deo soli eximias proprietates, agnoscit. Addo etiam petitionem earum rerum, quas creaturæ largiri possunt, si in Templo & apud altare, vel à Sanctis & Angelis absentibus, atque in vota vocatis, deposcantur, idololatriæ crimine non vacaturam, quia & Divina & humana jura Templorum atque altarium erectionem pro precibus, votis & sacrificiis, Divini cultus signa propria constituunt. Incurvatio civili & religiosa cultui communis, signum tamen proprium religiosi & Divini cultus evadere potest. Puta si dirigatur velut versus spiritum quempiam invisibilem, etiam dum invisibilis est, quia sic ubiquitas, incommunicabilis Dei excellentia, in illo agnosceretur (ubique enim Deo incurvare nos possumus non aliam ob causam, quam quia ubique praesens est) vel versus imaginem cuiusvis creaturae, praesertim in Templo, vel super altare, erectam, ex sententia Infallibilis Dei, vetantis incurvare nos imagini, eamque colere; nec non gentium etiam, quando incurvatio fit Spiritus alicujus invisibilis repraesentationi visibili in imagine, vel simulachro. Denique &hymni, seu cantica in honorem rei decantatae sic composita, ut epitheta, incommunicabiles Dei excellentias significantia inserantur, cultus Divini signa propria fiunt.
units.tr: XXXI. Furthermore, the proper signs of religious worship, due to God alone for acknowledging his infinite majesty, are without doubt those which divine declaration claims for the religious worship of God, together with either the consensus of all nations, or the custom of particular peoples, or the natural meaning of the thing itself. Sacrifices, libations, and incense were indeed, by the consensus of the nations, meant to be the proper signs of divine worship. But since these, strictly speaking, have long since fallen into disuse and never prevailed among Christians, the remaining signs bind us all the more tightly to the one God alone and raise us higher toward him. Oaths are to be sworn to God alone, as is clear both from Deut. 6:13, 10:20; Isa. 65:15-16; Jer. 4:2, 5:7, and from the consensus of nations. We have shown above that the same reasoning applies to vows, to invocation, to adoration, and to petition, including petition for the remission of sins by the Holy Spirit and for eternal life. For just as, because God alone is the author and giver of all spiritual benefits, one who asks such lofty things of a creature acknowledges the powers of God in that creature, so too one who invokes an absent Angel or Saint attributes omniscience and omnipresence, the peculiar properties of God alone, to that being. I add also that a request for those things which creatures can grant, if sought in a temple and at an altar, or from Saints and Angels who are absent and called upon in vows, will not be free of the crime of idolatry. Both divine and human law establish the erection of temples and altars as the proper signs of divine worship, for prayers, vows, and sacrifices. Bowing, which is common to civil and religious reverence, can nevertheless become a proper sign of religious and divine worship. For example, if it is directed as toward some invisible spirit, even while that spirit is unseen, because in this way God's ubiquity, his incommunicable excellence, would be acknowledged in it (for we can bow down to God everywhere for no other reason than that he is present everywhere); or if it is directed toward the image of any creature, especially one erected in a temple or over an altar, contrary to the judgement of the infallible God, who forbids us to bow down to an image and worship it; and also among the nations, when bowing is made to a visible representation of some invisible spirit in an image or statue. Finally, hymns or canticles in honour of the thing sung, composed so that epithets signifying God's incommunicable excellences are inserted, become proper signs of divine worship.

units.la: XXXII. Neque quicquam hic refert, qua ex ista signa haec religiosi & Divini cultus creaturis applicentur. Quomodo Hierarchici idololatriam suam hac fere cerussa incrustare solent, quod non utique Venerem, Neptunum, Martem; sed amicos Dei Deiparam, St. Petrum, S. Paulum colant. Quid enim? An Bilhah Jacobi uxor adulterii & incestus rea non fuit, quia non cum inimico quopiam Jacobi, sed cum filio ejus Rubene, qui Patris imago viva fuit, rem habuit, Genef. xxxv. 22. An iccirco Jacobus torum conjugalem non profanatum esse censuit? Aliter ipsi visum esse, ex Genef. xlix. 4. plane constat. Ponamus etiam, potentem Principem quempiam adversus adulterium severam legem sanxisse, atque adulterii reum sic apud Principem defendere: Equidem, auguste Princeps, fateor, me adulterio me polluisse. Caeterum expendas rogo, quam excusate peccaverim. Non enim cum profligati pudoris proprofiibulo rem habui, sed cum Filia, Sorore, nepte tua. Annon defensio ejusmodi animum Principis ad majorem indignationem adversus insignitam adeò impudentiam accenderet? Sed de eo quicquid sit, religiosum cultum nulli omnino creaturæ, qualiscunque ea sit, citra læsæ gloriæ & Majestatis Divinæ crimen præstari posse demonstravimus.
units.tr: XXXII. Nor does it matter here by what means these signs of religious and divine worship are applied to creatures. Thus the Hierarchy are wont to plaster over their idolatry with this sort of whitewash: that they do not worship Venus, Neptune, or Mars, but friends of God, the Mother of God, St. Peter, St. Paul. For what? Was not Bilhah, Jacob's wife, guilty of adultery and incest, because she had relations not with some enemy of Jacob but with his son Reuben, who was a living image of his father? (Gen. 35:22). Did Jacob therefore judge the marriage bed not profaned? That it seemed otherwise to him is plain from Gen. 49:4. Let us also suppose that some powerful prince had enacted a severe law against adultery, and that an accused adulterer defended himself before the prince thus: "Indeed, august Prince, I confess that I have polluted myself with adultery. But please consider how excusably I sinned. For I did not have relations with a shameless prostitute, but with your daughter, your sister, and your granddaughter." Would not such a defence kindle the prince's mind to greater indignation against so notorious an impudence? But whatever the case there, we have demonstrated that religious worship can in no way be rendered to any creature, whatever it may be, without the crime of injuring God's glory and majesty.

units.la: XXXIII. Neque etiam Hierarchicos à fœda idololatriæ labe purgat pervulgatus ille, & verè Babylonicus fucus à Nicænis & Tridentinis Patribus, iconolatriam statuminantibus, obductus, quòd omnis creaturæ cultus ad Dei, & Prototypi honorem referatur; adeóque illi cultu creaturarum non absoluto & terminativo, sed relativo & transitivo (hoc enim peregrino idiomate peregrina mulier loqui amat) defungantur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Nor does that widely spread and truly Babylonian veil, cast over by the Fathers of Nicaea and Trent, who uphold the worship of images, cleanse the Hierarchy from the foul stain of idolatry. The veil is this: that all worship of a creature is referred to the honour of God and of the Prototype, and so they discharge their worship of creatures not as absolute and terminative, but as relative and transitive. (For a foreign woman loves to speak in this foreign idiom.)

units.la: Hæc quidem defensio cultum imaginum Dei & Christi tangit; ad cultum Sanctorum adeóque etiam imaginum eorum non tangit. Manebit ergo saltem in Sanctorum & imaginum, reliquiarúmque eorum cultu idololatria. Sed judicent etiam omnes sana ratione præditi ex communi sensu & pervulgata hominum omnium intelligentia, an cultus per se illicitus, verbo Dei interdictus, & objecto indebito præstitus, ob solam relationem ad objectum debitum & congruum excusari possit? Quid quæso indignum magis quàm cultum Divinum, etiam qui latriæ est, stipiti lapidíque, qui imago vel idolum vulgo vocatur, tribuere? Quæ latria imagini vel idolo exhibita maximè proprié idololatria vocatur. Si ergo latria idolo, objecto adeò impense incongruo, cum relatione ad objectum congruum, ritè exhiberi potest, jam idololatria vel iconolatria relativa licita erit. Quod perinde est; ac si quis diceret, homicidium, vel adulterium relativum licitum esse. Jam ergo fas piumque fuerit innocentem occidere eo consilio, ut iram adversus nocentem, qui mortem meruerat, evomas: cum mulicre aliena consuescere, ut absentis conjugis suavem scilicet memoriam recolas. An hoc homicidium, adulterium relativum crassum & nefarium homicidium, adulterium esse desinet? An destinata ejusmodi relatio specificam facti turpitudinem tollit, quò minùs idololatria γνώσος committatur?
units.tr: This defence indeed touches the worship of images of God and Christ; it does not touch the worship of Saints, and so does not touch even the images of Saints. Idolatry will therefore remain at least in the worship of Saints and of their images and relics. But let all who possess sound reason judge, from common sense and the widely shared understanding of all men, whether worship that is in itself unlawful, forbidden by the word of God, and rendered to an improper object, can be excused merely by its relation to a proper and fitting object. What, I ask, is more unworthy than to ascribe divine worship, even latria, to a stock or stone, which is commonly called an image or idol? Latria exhibited to an image or idol is most properly called idolatry. If, then, latria can rightly be offered to an idol, a most incongruous object, with a relation to a congruous object, then relative idolatry, or relative image-worship, will be lawful. This is just as if someone were to say that homicide or adultery is lawful in a relative sense. Would it then be right and pious to kill an innocent man with the intention of venting anger against a guilty one who deserved death; or to consort with another's wife so as to recall the sweet memory of an absent spouse? Will this homicide or adultery cease to be a gross and wicked homicide or adultery? Or does an intention of this kind remove the specific baseness of the deed, so that true idolatry is not committed?

units.la: XXXIV. Addo ne quidem latriam in cultu tali ad prototypon transfire, sed in idolo terminari, adeóque planè absolutam esse, quia latria ultra transire verè ac realiter nequit, sed illicsinitur, in relatione ad Deum latria esse definit, speciémque cultus mutat, & contumeliæ, inobedientiæ, ignominiæque adversus Deum, qui coram imagine incurvari, eámque colere vetuit, actus evadit. Neque potest intentio colentis naturam actus vetiti mutare, quò minus actus sit ignominiæ adversus Deum. licet evitari nequeat, quin Deus actus illius obje&tum sit, sed sub ignominiæ specificatione, quod ajunt. Perinde ut in Medico fit, qui propinata potione lethifera ægrotum curare intendit, at revera perimit. ubi ægrotus, quicquid etiam Medicus intenderit, Medici quidem objectum est. at perimentis, non curantis. Unus nempe idémque actus contrarias respectu diversorum objectorum specificationes, adeóque etiam terminationes contrarias habere potest. Quomodo idem rosæ odor uni suavis, insuavis alteri contingere potest. ubi unus actus est, diversum objectum, contraria terminatio. Præterea cultum vitulorum Aharonis & Jeroboami, nec non Teraphim Michæ relativum, non absolutum fuisse constat. Nam in vitulis & Teraphim unum verúmque Jehovam, Deum Israelis coluerunt. Quo quidem non obstante idololatriæ reos cos Spiritus Dei peragit, quia symbola cultus, & specialiter præsentis cum iisdem Numinis solus Deus constituere potest. Constituta autem ab homine ut per eadem religiosè Deus colatur, cùm non recipiat Deus, idola sunt, & qui per ea Deum religiosè colit, idololatra est. Atque gentilium plurium cultum relatum fuisse ad Supremum Numen, ceu Prototypon, supra probavimus! Neque tamen ideo crassæ idololatriæ culpa illi vacarunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. I add that the worship of latria in such a cult does not pass over to the prototype, but stops at the idol, and is therefore wholly absolute, because latria cannot truly and really go beyond that point. There it halts, and in relation to God it ceases to be latria and changes its kind of worship. It becomes an act of contumely, disobedience and dishonour against God, who forbade bowing down before an image and worshipping it. The intention of the worshipper cannot change the nature of a forbidden act so that it is not an act of dishonour against God. Although it cannot be avoided that God is the object of that act, He is the object under the specification of dishonour, as they say. It is like a physician who intends to cure a sick man by giving a deadly drink but in fact kills him. Whatever the physician intended, the sick man is the physician's object, but as one whom he kills, not as one whom he cures. One and the same act can have contrary specifications with respect to different objects, and so contrary terminations too. The same smell of a rose is pleasant to one person and unpleasant to another. Here there is one act, different objects and contrary termination. Moreover, it is established that the worship of Aaron's and Jeroboam's calves, and of Micah's teraphim, was relative and not absolute. For in the calves and the teraphim they worshipped the one true Jehovah, the God of Israel. Nevertheless, the Spirit of God counts them guilty of idolatry, because only God can establish the symbols of worship and, in particular, the presence of the Deity with them. But when man establishes things by which God is to be worshipped religiously, and God does not accept them, they are idols, and whoever worships God religiously through them is an idolater. Indeed, we have already proved above that the worship of many Gentiles was referred to the Supreme Deity as the prototype. Yet they were not therefore free of the guilt of gross idolatry.

units.la: XXXV. Accedit, quòd cultus ille relativus imaginibus proprius esse debet. Nam prototypi certè cultus juxta adversarios ipsos non est relativus, sed absolutus. Atque cultum relativum ejusmodi si imaginibus non deputassent, sed eo solo cultu, qui iis ad prototypon non relatis debitus est, afficiendas statuissent, quàm quæso cultus ille exilis vilisque, ludicrus, imò nullus foret? Non potuerunt non ergo iconolatræ relativum imaginibus cultum decernere. Sed non potest non etiam is cultus relativus imaginum esse proprius. Cúmque sic & religiosus, & Divinus statuatur, idololatria pura atque puta est. quippe cultus Divinus, religiosus, relativus, creaturis appropriatus.
units.tr: XXXV. Add to this that such relative worship must belong to the images. For the worship of the prototype, according to the adversaries themselves, is not relative but absolute. And if they had not assigned such relative worship to the images, but had decided that the images should be honoured with only that worship which is due to them when they are not referred to the prototype, what, I ask, would that worship be? It would be meagre, cheap, trifling, or indeed nothing at all. The image-worshippers could not but assign relative worship to the images. But that relative worship cannot fail to be proper to the images. And since it is thus established as both religious and divine, it is pure and simple idolatry, for it is divine, religious worship, relative and yet given to creatures.

units.la: XXXVI. Denique Theologi Scholastici de cultu imaginum disputant. Quorum alii, velut Alexander Dürandus, Alphonsus, Castrensis &c. non imagines, sed coram imaginibus exemplar ; alii, Thomas Cajetanus, Bonaventura, Marsilius, Capreolus, &c. crassius eodem, quo prototypon, cultu imagines colendas sciscunt. Hodie plerique, Bellarminum secuti, cultum imaginum proprium paulò minorem esse, quàm exemplaris, ejusmodi tamen, qui analogicè reductivè ad cultum exemplaris referatur. Nulli horum ab idololatriæ crimine se purgaverint unquam. Non primi, quia contra interdictum Divinum coram imaginibus se incurvant tamen, & Sanctos saltem coram imagine prostratos exaudire, adeóque omnisciōs vel omnipræsentes esse supponunt. Non secundi, quia eodem cultu Deum & imagines
units.tr: XXXVI. Finally, the Scholastic theologians dispute about the worship of images. Some of them, such as Alexander Dürandus, Alphonsus, Castrensis and others, hold that not the images but the prototype is to be worshipped in the presence of the images. Others, such as Thomas Cajetanus, Bonaventura, Marsilius, Capreolus and others, more crudely decree that images are to be honoured with the same worship as the prototype. Today most of them, following Bellarmine, hold that the worship proper to images is somewhat less than that of the prototype, yet of such a kind that it is referred analogically and reductively to the worship of the prototype. None of these has ever cleared himself of the charge of idolatry. Not the first group, because although they bow down before images against the divine prohibition, and assume that the saints, prostrate at least before an image, hear them, and so suppose that the saints are omniscient or omnipresent. Not the second, because to honour God and images with the same worship is plainly idolatry. Not the third group, because whatever inferior and analogical worship is laid down for images, in the opinion of the worshippers themselves it is never civil but always religious and therefore divine. But religious and divine worship of images is idolatry.

units.la: m prosequi, palpabilis idololatria est. Non tertii, quia qualiscunque ille cultus inferior & analogicus imaginum statuitur, opinione ipsa colentium non civilis, sed religiosus adeoque Divinus semper est. Atqui cultus religiosus & Divinus imaginum idololatria est.
units.tr: …with the same worship God and images; it is palpable idolatry. Not the third group, because whatever inferior and analogical worship is laid down for images, in the opinion of the worshippers themselves, is never civil but always religious and therefore divine. But religious and divine worship of images is idolatry.

units.la: XXXVII. Jam ergo Hierarchicos creaturis qui- busdam Divinum cultum exhibere, quod assumptio nostra statuit, generali argumento, hactenus deduc- to, plane ad liquidum perduximus.
units.tr: XXXVII. Now, then, we have brought to full clarity, by the general argument deduced so far, the proposition of our Assumption: that the Hierarchy gives divine worship to certain creatures.

units.la: Fatentur enim, ut nervum argumenti colligam, Hierarchici, cultum illum, quem creaturis nonnullis, Papæ, Eucharistiæ, Sanctis, reliquiis, rebus consecratis exhibent, non civilem, sed religiosum esse. Cultum porro religiosum eundem Divinum, solique Deo debitum esse, atque insuper externa cultus illius signa ceremoniasque cultus Divini, quo solus Deus prosequendus est, proprias esse, argumentis irrefragabilibus firmavimus; denique suum etiam meretrici peregrinæ fucum abstersimus. Quis ergo cultum ab Hierarchicis creaturis nonnullis exhibitum Divinum esse, inficias ire amplius ausit? Cum proin omnem cultum Divinum creaturis exhibitum idololatriam esse, firmissimis quoque rationibus præoccupaverimus, Hierarchiam idolatriam committere, & populum sibi obnoxium ad eandem seducere, Jubare meridiano clarius est.
units.tr: For the members of the Hierarchy admit, to sum up the sinew of the argument, that the worship they give to certain creatures (the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, relics, and consecrated things) is not civil but religious. We have also established by unanswerable arguments that this same religious worship is divine and due to God alone, and moreover that the external signs and ceremonies of that worship are proper to the divine worship by which God alone is to be honoured. Finally, we have wiped away the paint with which the foreign harlot disguises herself. Who, then, would dare any longer to deny that the worship given by the Hierarchy to certain creatures is divine? Since we have also settled, with the firmest reasons, that all divine worship given to creatures is idolatry, it is clearer than the noonday sun that the Hierarchy commits idolatry and seduces the people subject to it into the same.

units.la: XXXVIII. Poteramus sane in generali demonstratione Assumptionis nostræ, utpote omni exceptione majore, & convincendæ Hierarchicorum idololatriæ efficacissima, acquiescere. Lubet tamen abundantioris certitudinis gratia, ad species idololatriæ Hierarchicorum descendere, atque eadem strictim exponere. Et tanta quidem est Hierarchicorum idolatria, ut omnes idolomaniasin Ecclesia Romana vigere, verissime affirmemus. Non quod ei vel portentorum Ægypti, Specialis demonstratio assumptionis ubi Hierarchicorum idololatria juxta species creaturarum in ea expressas, in Papolatriam (de qua supra) gypti, vel idolorum omnium, quæ olim hodiéque Iudæi & gentes coluerunt, cultum attribuamus. Hoc unicè contendimus merito, nullam esse idololatriæ speciem, quâ se Ecclesia Romana non polluat fœdissimè. Is enim idololatricus cultus est, vel quo Deus verus in imagine colitur; quomodo Judæi in deserto, & Jeroboam cum asseclis suis Deum verum in vitulis coluerunt: vel quo falsus colitur Deus; quomodo peccato Jeroboami etiam Baalis cultum populus adjecit, & veteres pagani sidera Cœli coluerunt: vel quo falsus Deus insuper in imagine colitur; qui cultus fuit statuæ Nebucadnezaris. Omnes hæ idololatriæ species apud Hierarchicos in usu sunt. Deum in imaginibus colunt: falsos colunt Deos, partem Eucharisticum, crucem, Papam, Sanctos, qui verus Deus non sunt: denique crucem in imaginibus crucis, Sanctos in statuis adorant. Nos juxta species creaturarum in Assumptione expressas, puta Papam, Eucharistiam, Sanctos, imagines, reliquias Sanctorum & res consecratas, Hierarchicorum idololatriam commodè in Papolatriam, Artolatriam, Hagiolatriam, Iconolatriam, Lipsanolatriam & Hierolatriam partimur. De Papolatria satis superque supra nobis actum. Reliquas species paucis perstringere juvabit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. We could certainly rest content with the general demonstration of our Assumption, since it is beyond all exception and is the most effective way of convicting the Hierarchy of idolatry. Nevertheless, for the sake of greater certainty, we are pleased to descend to the species of the Hierarchy's idolatry and set them out briefly. Indeed the idolatry of the Hierarchy is so great that we may most truly affirm that all kinds of idolatry flourish in the Roman Church. Not that we ascribe to it the portents of Egypt, or all the idols that the Jews and the nations once worshipped and still worship. We contend only this, that there is no kind of idolatry by which the Roman Church does not most foully pollute itself. For that is idolatrous worship in which either the true God is worshipped in an image, as the Jews in the wilderness and Jeroboam with his followers worshipped the true God in the calves; or a false god is worshipped, as by the sin of Jeroboam the people also added the worship of Baal, and the ancient pagans worshipped the stars of heaven; or a false god is worshipped moreover in an image, which was the worship of Nebuchadnezzar's statue. All these species of idolatry are in use among the members of the Hierarchy. They worship God in images; they worship false gods, which are not the true God: the Eucharistic host, the cross, the Pope, the saints. Finally, they adore the cross in images of the cross and the saints in statues. Following the species of creatures expressed in the Assumption, namely the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, images, relics of the saints and consecrated things, we conveniently divide the idolatry of the Hierarchy into Papolatry, Artolatry, Hagiolatry, Iconolatry, Lipsanolatry and Hierolatry. We have already dealt with Papolatry above, more than enough. It will be helpful to touch briefly on the remaining species.

units.la: XXXIX. Artolatriam, seu adorationem Panacei Numinis in Eucharistia, ejusmodi idololatriam esse, in quam, ceu Mare quoddam mortuum, omnes superstitiones Pontificiæ sese exonerant, scitè Anglus Dunelmensis Episcopus quondam dixit. Est enim cultus Pontificii externi apex, prora & puppis. De quo Concilii Tridentini Patres Sess. xiii. cap. 5. sic loquuntur, definiúntque: Nullus dubitandi locus relinquitur, quin omnes Christi fideles, promore in Catholica Ecclesia semper recepto, latriæ cultum, qui vero Deo debetur, huic Sanc-
units.tr: XXXIX. That Artolatry, that is, the adoration of the supposedly Divine Being in the Eucharist, is a kind of idolatry into which, as into a dead sea, all the superstitions of the Papists discharge themselves, was wisely said long ago by the English Bishop of Durham. For it is the summit, prow and stern of the external worship of the Papists. On this the Fathers of the Council of Trent, Session 13, chapter 5, speak and define thus: There is no room for doubt that all the faithful of Christ, according to the custom always received in the Catholic Church, give to this Sanc-

units.la: Artolatriam mare mortuum est. De Eucharistia cultu definitio Tridentinorum ex quo idololatria Hierarchicorum demonstratur. prosequi, palpabilis idololatria est. Non tertii, quia qualiscunque ille cultus inferior & analogicus imaginum statuitur, opinione ipsa colentium non civilis, sed religiosus adeóque Divinus semper est. Atqui cultus religiofus & Divinus imaginum idololatria est.
units.tr: Artolatry is a dead sea. From the Tridentine definition of the cult of the Eucharist the idolatry of the Hierarchy is demonstrated. …with the same worship God and images; it is palpable idolatry. Not the third group, because whatever inferior and analogical worship is laid down for images, in the opinion of the worshippers themselves, is never civil but always religious and therefore divine. But religious and divine worship of images is idolatry.

units.la: XXXVII. Jam ergo Hierarchicos creaturis qui- busdam Divinum cultum exhibere, quod assumptio nostra statuit, generali argumento, haftenus deduc- to, plane ad liquidum perduximus.
units.tr: XXXVII. Now, then, we have brought to full clarity the claim we set out, namely that the Hierarchy gives divine worship to certain creatures, a point established by the general argument deduced so far.

units.la: Fatentur enim, ut nervum argumenti colligam, Hierarchici, cultum illum, quem creaturis nonnullis, Papæ, Eucharistiæ, Sanctis, reliquiis, rebus consecratis exhibent, non civilem, sed religiosum esse. Cultum porro religiosum eundem Divinum, folíque Deo debitum esse, atque insuper externa cultus illius signa ceremoniásque cultus Divini, quo solus Deus prosequendus est, proprias esse, argumentis irrefragabilibus firmavimus; denique suum etiam meretrici peregrinæ fucum abstersimus.
units.tr: For the Hierarchy admits, to gather the sinew of the argument, that the worship which they offer to certain creatures (the Pope, the Eucharist, the saints, relics, consecrated objects) is not civil but religious. We have further established, by unanswerable arguments, that religious worship of this kind is divine and due to God alone, and that the external signs and ceremonies of such worship are proper to the divine worship by which God alone is to be honoured. Finally, we have wiped away the paint of the foreign harlot, which the Hierarchy also used to disguise it.

units.la: Quis ergo cultum ab Hierarchicis creaturis nonnullis exhibitum Divinum esse, inficias ire ampliùs audit? Cùm proin omnem cultum Divinum creaturis exhibitum idololatriam esse, firmissimis quoque rationibus præoccupaverimus, Hierarchiam idololatriam committere, & populum sibi obnoxium ad eandem sedu-
units.tr: Who, then, still dares to deny that the worship which the Hierarchy offers to certain creatures is divine? Since we have also already settled, by the firmest reasons, that every divine worship offered to creatures is idolatry, it follows that the Hierarchy commits idolatry and drives the people subject to it into the same error,

units.la: Argumenti generalis nervus adstringitur. cere, Jubare meridiano clarius est.
units.tr: and the sinew of the general argument is tightened. That is clearer than the midday sun.

units.la: XXXVIII. Poteramus sanè in generali demon-
units.tr: XXXVIII. We could indeed rest content with the general demon-

units.la: stratione Assumptionis nostræ, utpote omni exceptione majore, & convincendæ Hierarchicorum idololatriæ efficacissimæ, acquiescere. Lubet tamen abundantioris certitudinis gratia, ad species idololatriæ Hierarchicorum descendere, atque easdem strictim exponere. Et tanta quidem est Hierarchicorum idololatria, ut omnes idolomanias in Ecclesia Romana vigere, verissimè affirmemus. Non quòd ei vel portentorum Ægypti, gypti, vel idolorum omnium, quæ olim hodieque Judæi & gentes coluerunt, cultum attribuamus. Hoc unicè contendimus merito, nullam esse idololatriæ speciem, quæ se Ecclesia Romana non polluat foedissimè. Is enim idololatriæ cultus est, vel quo Deus verus in imagine colitur, quomodo Judæi in deserto, & Jeroboam cum asseclis suis Deum verum in vitulis coluerunt: vel quo falsus colitur Deus, quomodo peccato Jeroboami etiam Baalis cultum populus adjecit, & veteres pagani sidera Cœli coluerunt: vel quo falsus Deus insuper in imagine colitur, qui cultus fuit statuæ Nebucadnezaris. Omnes hæ idololatriæ species apud Hierarchicos in usu sunt. Deum in imaginibus colunt: falsos colunt Deos, partem Eucharisticum, crucem, Papam, Sanctos, qui verus Deus non sunt: denique crucem in imaginibus crucis, Sanctos in statuis adorant. Nos juxta species creaturarum in Assumptione expressas, puta Papam, Eucharistiam, Sanctos, imagines, reliquias Sanctorum & res consecratas, Hierarchicorum idololatriam commodè in Papolatriam, Artolatriam, Hagiolatriam, Iconolatriam, Lipsanolatriam & Hierolatriam partimur. De Papolatria satis superque supra nobis actum. Reliquas species paucis perstringere juvabit.
units.tr: stration of our Assumption, since it is beyond all exception and most effective for refuting the idolatry of the Hierarchs. Nevertheless, for the sake of greater certainty, it pleases us to descend to the species of the Hierarchs' idolatry and to set them out briefly. The idolatry of the Hierarchs is indeed so great that we may most truly affirm that every kind of idolomania flourishes in the Roman Church. Not that we ascribe to it the worship of the portents of Egypt, or of all the idols which the Jews and the Gentiles once worshipped and still worship. We contend only, and rightly, that there is no species of idolatry which the Roman Church does not most foully pollute. For idolatry is either a worship in which the true God is honoured in an image, as the Jews did in the wilderness and Jeroboam with his followers worshipped the true God in calves; or a worship in which a false god is honoured, as the people, by the sin of Jeroboam, also added the worship of Baal, and the ancient pagans worshipped the stars of heaven; or a worship in which a false god is further honoured in an image, which was the cult of Nebuchadnezzar's statue. All these species of idolatry are in use among the Hierarchs. They worship God in images; they worship false gods, namely the Eucharistic bread, the cross, the Pope, and the Saints, who are not the true God; and finally they worship the cross in images of the cross, and the Saints in statues. Following the kinds of creatures set out in the Assumption, namely the Pope, the Eucharist, the Saints, images, relics of the Saints and consecrated things, we conveniently divide the Hierarchs' idolatry into Papolatry, Artolatry, Hagiolatry, Iconolatry, Lipsanolatry and Hierolatry. We have already dealt with Papolatry above, and more than sufficiently. It will be helpful to touch briefly on the remaining species.

units.la: XXXIX. Artolatriam, seu adorationem Panacei Numinis in Eucharistia, ejusmodi idololatriam esse, in quam, ceu Mare quoddam mortuum, omnes superstitiones Pontificiæ sese exonerant, scitè Anglus Dunelmensis Episcopus quondam dixit.
units.tr: XXXIX. That Artolatry, that is, the adoration of the all-powerful Deity in the Eucharist, is a kind of idolatry into which all Papist superstitions discharge themselves, as into a dead sea, was wisely said long ago by the English Bishop of Durham.

units.la: Est enim cultus Pontificii externi apex, prora & puppis. De quo Concilii Tridentini Patres Sess. XIII. cap. 5. sic loquuntur, definiúntque: Nullus dubitandi locus relinquitur, quin omnes Christi fideles, pro more in Catholica Ecclesia semper recepto, latriæ cultum, qui vero Deo debetur, huic Sanctissimo Sacramento in veneratione adhibeant. Postea Canone VI. Si quis dixerit, inquiunt, in Sancto Eucharistiae Sacramento, unigenitum Dei filium non esse cultu latriae etiam externo adorandum, &c. & ejus adoratores esse idololatras, anathema sit. Quae duo non sonant idem. Non enim idem est, Sacramentum esse adorandum, & Christum in Sacramento esse adorandum; cùm cap. V. Synodus Sacramentum adorandum à Christo distinguat. Asserit enim, in Sacramento illo cultu latriae venerando, Christum Dominum ac Deum nostrum praesentem adesse. Atqui in quo quid praesens est, non potest idem esse cum eo, quod in ipso praesens adest. Cùm igitur si à Christo discesseris, ex Hierarchicorum hypothesi non aliud sit in Eucharistiae Sacramento, quàm visibilia panis & vini accidentia, tam tenui videlicet & levi rei, qua vix quicquam in tota rerum universitate longiùs à Deo distat, imò quae, si recte rem putemus, nihil est (accidentia enim à subjecto separata nihil sunt) Divinissimum illum latriae cultum decernunt. Neque satis Synodum purgat Pallavicinus Hist.Conc.Trid.lib.xi.7: 6. afferens, Christum in Sacramento esse dici, non ut aquam in vasculo, sed ut partem in toto cujus pars est. Quia Synodus Christum in Sacramento non esse simpliciter, sed praesentem adesse dicit; quae verba non partis in toto, sed contenti in continente, locati in loco exist-entiam sonant. Si ergo verba capitis quinti, uti manifestè sonant, accipiantur, non aliud Synodus decreverit, quàm ut Sacramentum Eucharistiae, quatenus à Christo, qui in eo praesens adesse dicitur, illud distinguitur, hoc est, accidentia panis & vini, quae ipsa etiam formalem Sacramenti hujus rationem facere, Vasquez, Soto, Fieinus, alii pertendunt; latriae cultu adorentur. Qua idololatria tetrior foediorque nulla excogitari potest.
units.tr: For it is the summit, prow and stern of the external worship of the Papists. Concerning this, the Fathers of the Council of Trent speak and define thus in Sess. XIII. cap. 5.: There is no room for doubt that all the faithful of Christ, according to the custom always received in the Catholic Church, offer to this most holy Sacrament in veneration the worship of latria, which is due to the true God. Afterwards, in Canon VI., they say: If anyone shall say that the only-begotten Son of God is not to be adored in the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist with the worship of latria, even external, etc., and that its worshippers are idolaters, let him be anathema. These two statements do not mean the same thing. For it is not the same to say that the Sacrament is to be adored and that Christ is to be adored in the Sacrament, since in cap. V. the Synod distinguishes the Sacrament to be adored from Christ. For it asserts that Christ the Lord and our God is present in that Sacrament, to be venerated with the worship of latria. But that which is present in something cannot be the same as that which is present in it. Therefore, if you take away Christ, then according to the hypothesis of the Hierarchicals there is nothing in the Sacrament of the Eucharist but the visible accidents of bread and wine, a thing so thin and light that scarcely anything in the whole universe is further removed from God; indeed, if we think rightly, it is nothing at all (for accidents separated from their subject are nothing), and yet they decree that this most divine worship of latria be given to it. Nor does Pallavicini clear the Synod enough when he asserts in his Hist. Conc. Trid. lib. xi. 7: 6. that Christ is said to be in the Sacrament not as water is in a vessel, but as a part is in the whole of which it is a part. For the Synod does not say simply that Christ is in the Sacrament, but that he is present; and these words express not the existence of a part in a whole, but of a thing contained in a container, of a thing placed in a place. So if the words of the fifth chapter are taken as they plainly sound, the Synod has decreed nothing other than that the Sacrament of the Eucharist, insofar as it is distinguished from Christ, who is said to be present in it, that is, the accidents of bread and wine, which Vasquez, Soto, Ficinus and others maintain even constitute the formal character of this Sacrament, are to be adored with the worship of latria. No more foul and horrible idolatry can be imagined.

units.la: XL. Sed consistat sane Sacramentum Eucharistiae in compositione quadam ex speciebus & corpore Christi, uti quidem Suarez, Becanus, Bellarminus, & plerique hodie pertendunt; ne sic tamen efficietur, ut totum Sacramentum sit Christus Deus, qui solus adorandus, & latriæ cultu prosequendus est. Nam Gabrielem Biel, qui Sacramentum per Synecdochen solum Christum esse, seclusis speciebus, statuit, omnes hodie repudiant. Frustra vero nuper retiarius meus, Abbas vicinus A. Redingius, consuetis præcisionibus suis, species, humanitatem seu corpus Christi, & Divinitatem ejusdem sic distinxit, ut species adorari non per se, sed qua conjunctas cum corpore Christi, verbo Divino hypostaticè unito: humanitatem seu corpus Christi realiter in Sacramento subsistens, adorationem in Sacramento terminare, sed ejus motivum non esse: denique Divinitatem solam per se primò adorabilem esse, per modum objecti formalis motivi, & latreaticæ adorationis specificativi, pertendat. Has certè subtilitates Tridentini Patres vel ignorarunt, vel pensi non habuerunt, simpliciter Sacramentum, etiam prout à Christo distinctum est, adorandum proponentes definientésque. Cumque species Eucharisticæ à subjecto separatæ nihil sint; & humanitas Christi, qua talis, unita licet hypostaticè verbo, sit creatura; quisquis species sive propter se, sive propter aliud adorat, is idolum fictitium, non entia Deificata scilicet adorat: & quisquis humanitatem Christi, sive ut motivum, sive ut objectum terminans adorationis, adorat, ab idololatriæ crimine absolvi nequit. Et quocunque se artolatræ vertant, certè Sacramentum adorantes, verum, solum, summum Deum non adorant, adeóque idololatriæ commissæ manifesti sunt. Fuit enim verus solus, summus Deus, antequam Sacramentum esset.
units.tr: XL. But let the Sacrament of the Eucharist indeed consist in a certain composition of the species and the body of Christ, as Suárez, Becanus, Bellarmine and most today maintain; yet even so it will not follow that the whole Sacrament is Christ the God, who alone is to be adored and worshipped with the worship of latria. For Gabriel Biel, who held that the Sacrament is Christ alone by synecdoche, the species being excluded, all now reject. But my net-man, the neighbouring Abbot A. Redingius, with his customary precisions, has vainly maintained that he distinguishes the species, the humanity or body of Christ, and the Divinity of the same, in such a way that the species are not adored in themselves, but as conjoined with the body of Christ, hypostatically united to the Divine Word; the humanity or body of Christ, subsisting really in the Sacrament, has the adoration terminate in the Sacrament, but is not its motive; finally, the Divinity alone is in itself primarily adorable, by way of the formal motive object and that which specifies latreutic adoration. The Fathers of Trent either were ignorant of these subtleties or took no account of them, simply proposing and defining that the Sacrament, even as distinguished from Christ, is to be adored. And since the Eucharistic species separated from their subject are nothing, and the humanity of Christ as such, though hypostatically united to the Word, is a creature, whoever adores the species, whether for their own sake or for the sake of something else, adores a fictitious idol, that is, non-beings deified. And whoever adores the humanity of Christ, whether as the motive or as the object at which the adoration terminates, cannot be absolved of the crime of idolatry. And whichever way the Artolaters turn, certainly in adoring the Sacrament they do not adore the true, only, and highest God, and so they stand manifestly guilty of idolatry. For the true, only, highest God existed before the Sacrament did.

units.la: XLI. Artolatria omnis transsubstantiatione niti- tur. Hac enim panem Eucharisticum Deificant scilicet.
units.tr: XLI. All artolatry rests on transubstantiation, for by it they deify the Eucharistic bread.

units.la: Si igitur transsubstantiatio panis nulla contingit, idololatriam omnium maximam à se committi, Hierarchici omnes fateantur oportet. Fassus est ingenuè Franciscus Costerus Jesuita Enchir. Controv. cap. 12. ubi sic ille: Tolerabilior est error eorum, qui pro Deo colunt statuam auream, aut argenteam, aut alterius materiæ imaginem, quomodo Gentiles Deos suos venerabantur; vel pannum rubrum in hastam elevatum, quod narrat de Lappis; vel viva animalia, uti quondam Ægyptii: quam eorum, qui frustum panis, quod hactenus per universum orbem tot annis fecere Christiani, nisi verasit doctrina transsubstantiationis. Sic profectò est, nec pro merito satis crimen exaggerari potest. Nam ne panem quidem verum, nutriendi facultate præditum, sed spumam panis, rem pœne nihil, adorabunt. Atqui, audi Costere, vera doctrina Transsubstantiationis non est: dogma est monstrosum, verbo Dei & sanæ rationis principiis universis contrarium, piæ antiquitati prorsus incognitum.
units.tr: If, then, there is no transubstantiation of the bread, all the Hierarchs must admit that they commit the greatest of all idolatries. The Jesuit Franciscus Costerus has frankly confessed as much in his Enchiridion of Controversies, chapter 12, where he writes: The error of those who worship as God a golden or silver statue, or an image of some other material, as the Gentiles worshipped their gods; or a red cloth raised on a spear, which is said of the Lapps; or living animals, as the Egyptians once did, is more tolerable than the error of those who worship a morsel of bread, which Christians throughout the whole world have done for so many years, unless the doctrine of transubstantiation is true. So it certainly is, and the crime cannot be exaggerated enough in proportion to its guilt. For they will worship not even true bread, endowed with the power of nourishing, but the froth of bread, a thing that is almost nothing. Yet, hear Costerus, the true doctrine of transubstantiation does not exist: it is a monstrous dogma, contrary to the Word of God and to all the principles of sound reason, and wholly unknown to pious antiquity.

units.la: XLII. Transsubstantiationem illam his ferè verbis Tridentini Sess. XIII. 4. definiverunt:
units.tr: XLII. The Tridentine Council defined that transubstantiation in roughly these words, Session 13, chapter 4:

units.la: Quoniam Christus Redemptor noster corpus suum, id quod sub specie panis offerebat, verè esse dixit, ideo persuasum semper in Ecclesia Dei fuit, idque nunc denuo Sancta hæc Synodus declarat, per consecrationem panis & vini conversionem fieri totius substantiæ panis in substantiam corporis Christi Domini nostri, & totius substantiæ vini in substantiam sanguinis ejus. Quæ conversio convenienter & proprie à Sancta Catholica Ecclesia Transsubstantiatio est appellata. Ubi verò corpus suum sub specie panis Christum obtulisse Scriptura testatur? Obtulit in cruce pendens, non sub specie panis latens. Obtulit, postquam verba illa: Hoc enim est corpus meum, pronuntiavit. Hoc verò, quod corpus suum esse dixit, panis erat, uti series textus, & λεγεγραμμένη ἀνάγκη evincit.
units.tr: Since Christ our Redeemer said that what he offered under the appearance of bread was truly his body, it has therefore always been held in the Church of God, and this holy Synod now declares it again, that by the consecration of the bread and wine there takes place a conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord, and of the whole substance of the wine into the substance of his blood. This conversion the holy Catholic Church fittingly and properly calls transubstantiation. But where does Scripture testify that Christ offered his body under the appearance of bread? He offered it hanging on the cross, not lying hidden under the appearance of bread. He offered it after he had pronounced those words, This is my body. But what he said was his body was bread, as the sequence of the text and the written necessity [λεγεγραμμένη ἀνάγκη] make clear.

units.la: Tridentinorum de ea definitio oppugnatur. cit. Aliud certè longè est dicere: Hoc est corpus meum; aliud dicere: Sub specie panis verè est corpus meum. Ex adversariorum hypothesi verbis, H. E C. M. pronunciatis demum fit transsubstantiatio. Quomodo igitur verbum Hoc speciem panis notare potest, quæ talis, subjecto suo exuto, demum per transsubstantiationem contingere putatur? Cúmque in omni conversione, qualem esse transsubstantiationem fingunt, sint duo termini, unus à quo, alter ad quem, & terminus ad quem in prædicato propositionis illius existat, terminus à quo, qui non species duntaxat, sed ipsa substantia panis est, in subjecto sit oportet. Hoc ergo substantiam panis significabit. Addo, verba illa ne quidem conversiva esse; tum quia non dixit Christus, Hoc fiat corpus meum, sed Hoc est corpus meum: tum quia dici supponit esse; adeóque Hoc dici corpus Christi non potuit, nisi ante fuit. Quale etiam fuit corpus, in quod substantiam panis conversam asserunt, integrum, an fractum? Cùm corpus illud pro nobis datum Christus ipse dixerit, integrum esse nequit. Fractum igitur erit. At in gloria Christi ejus corpus ἀπαθὲς frangi proprie dici non poterit. Neutrum ergo est. Taceo, quòd transsubstantiatio tum pugnat cum institutione Cœnæ & præcipuis fidei articulis: tum Cœnæ Dominicæ essentiam penitus destruit, perimendo & signum, quia panis & vini substantiam abolet relictis speciebus, quæ absque proprio subjecto spectra potius fallacia, quàm rerum Divinarum infallibilia testimonia sunt; & rem signatam, quia corpus Christi spoliat sua quantitate & dimensionibus, pro uno multiplex spirituum proprietates mentiens, inducit, & pro nucleo Eucharistiæ substituit ejusmodi carnem, quam Christus ipse vel prodesse, vel vivificare negat; & analogiam Sacramentalem, quia relationis Sacramentalis fundamentum tollit, & ubi signum in rem signatam convertitur, omnis inter illa similitudo definit.
units.tr: The Tridentine definition of it is attacked. It is one thing to say This is my body; it is quite another to say Under the appearance of bread is truly my body. On the hypothesis of our opponents, transubstantiation comes about only when the words HOC EST CORPUS MEUM have been pronounced. How, then, can the word This signify the appearance of bread, which, with its subject stripped away, is supposed to come into being only through the transubstantiation? And since in every conversion, such as they imagine transubstantiation to be, there are two terms, one from which and the other to which, and since the term to which is in the predicate of that proposition, the term from which, which is not merely the appearance but the very substance of the bread, must be in the subject. This, therefore, will signify the substance of bread. I add that those words are not even conversive: first, because Christ did not say Let this become my body, but This is my body; second, because is presupposes existence, and so this could not be said to be the body of Christ unless it already existed. Again, what kind of body was it into which they claim the substance of the bread was converted: whole or broken? Since Christ himself said that the body given for us was whole, it cannot be whole; it will therefore be broken. But in the glory of Christ his body, impassible [ἀπαθὲς], cannot properly be said to be broken. Therefore it is neither. I pass over the fact that transubstantiation both conflicts with the institution of the Lord's Supper and with the chief articles of faith, and that it entirely destroys the essence of the Lord's Supper: it destroys the sign, because it abolishes the substance of bread and wine while leaving the appearances, which without a proper subject are deceptive phantoms rather than infallible testimonies of divine things; and it destroys the thing signified, because it strips the body of Christ of its quantity and dimensions, bringing in many properties of spirits while lying of one body, and it substitutes for the kernel of the Eucharist a kind of flesh which Christ himself denies to profit or to give life; and it destroys the sacramental analogy, because it removes the foundation of the sacramental relation, and where the sign is converted into the thing signified, every likeness between them ceases.

units.la: XLIII. Quomodo quæso induci Christianum nomen profesi potuerunt, ut crederent, Christum suum ipsius corpus altera manu gestasse,porrexisse deglutiendum sanctis hospitibus, qui illum & inter manducandum, & post sacrum illud fruftulum piè devoratum,præsentem intuiti sunt,alloquentem audiverunt? Christum se totum simul devorasse, integrum tamen & incolumem præterea discubuisse? Gloriosum Christi corpus in rancidulos ventriculorum meatus migrasse;ut vel in corporis nostri substantiam inibi demum convertatur, vel putredinem sentiat;vel in nihilum evanescat;vel in Cœlum illud,in quo erat,antequam rediit,dum rediit revertatur? Quæ hæc ineptiarum portenta sunt, Christianam religionem universam probris & sannis infidelium objicientia? XLIV. Ad principia sanæ rationis & scientiarum omnium exactum isthoc dogma monstrosum pariter approbabit. Etenim principium Physices est: Internum spatium, quod corpus uno tempore occupat, corpori illud occupanti æquari. Si igitur unum idemque corpus duo istiusmodi loca & spatia interna eodem tempore occupet (corpus autem Christi occupabit plurima) corpus his duobus spatiis illis erit æquale,utpote quod utraque eodem tempore replet, quæ tamen alterutrius spatiorum sunt duplum. Quam ob rem & corpus illius corporis in spatio alterutro siti duplum est, ac proinde unum idemque corpus duplum sui ipsius. Quæ manifesta contradictio est. Metaphysices principium est: Unum quodvis individuum est in se, & divisum ab omni alio. Corpus autem Christi unum, cùm sit tum in Cœlo, tum etiam sine ulla ejusdem corporis continuatione simul in terra, totum corpus dividetur à toto corpore,ac proin unum & plura erit. Mathematices principium Euclideum est: Totum majus est sua parte. Tridentini vero sanxerunt, sub unaquaque specie, vel sub singulis cujusque speciei partibus, separatione facta totum Christum contineri. Cum vero corpus Christi eodem tempore sibi æquale sit, annon sic pars æquabitur toti, neque totum majus erit parte? Logices principium est: Partes cum toto consentiunt, & inter se dissentiunt. In hostiæ autem seu Sacramenti divisione partes adeo inter se consentiunt, ut una omnino eademque res sint. Cumque divisio quævis sive Logica, sive physica sit divisio unius alicujus in multa, hæc divisio est unius in unum, idque seipsum. Denique principium Catholicum est: Unumquodque est, vel non est: Idem non potest esse simul & non esse. Posita autem μετρσία & μαλυπερσία corporis Christi idem erit & non erit eodem tempore. Res enim individua quævis permanens, nec, postquam extiterit, unquam desitura, quæ fieri potest, suturumque est, ut fiat ex re aliqua, illa nondum exstitit. Individuum vero Christi corpus incorruptibile fieri potest, futurumque est, ut fiat ex pane consecrato, quippe qui in corpus ejus individuum convertitur. Corpus autem ejus individuum & incorruptibile indesinenter erat ante hanc consecrationem. Erat ergo, & non erat, eodem tempore. Plures λεγόμενοι λογίας alibi à me fusius discussas, manifestásque contradictiones omitto. Quid est non fidei duntaxat, sed rationi etiam omni, Cœlo indignante, ridentibus Ethnicis, reluctante tamdiu vera Ecclesia, bellum indicere, & humanitatem exuere, si hoc non est?
units.tr: XLIII. I ask, how could men who professed the Christian name be led to believe that Christ carried his own body in one hand and offered it to his holy guests to swallow, guests who saw him present while they ate and heard him speaking to them, and who, after they had devoutly devoured that sacred morsel, still saw him reclining whole and unharmed? That Christ had devoured himself entirely at once, and yet remained whole and unhurt besides? That his glorious body had migrated into the rancid passages of the stomach, there to be turned into the substance of our body, or to undergo putrefaction, or to vanish into nothing, or to return, when it returned, to that heaven in which it had been before? What monstrous absurdities are these, which expose the whole Christian religion to the reproaches and jeers of unbelievers? XLIV. This monstrous dogma will equally fail to meet the principles of sound reason and of all the sciences, if examined exactly. For the principle of physics is: The internal space which a body occupies at one time is equal to the body occupying it. If, then, one and the same body occupies two such internal places and spaces at the same time (and the body of Christ will occupy very many), the body will be equal to these two spaces, since it fills each of them at the same time, and yet each of the spaces is one of the two. Therefore the body of that body, situated in either space, is double, and consequently one and the same body is double itself. This is a plain contradiction. The principle of metaphysics is: Every single individual is in itself and divided from every other. But the body of Christ, being one, since it is in heaven and at the same time on earth without any continuation of that same body, the whole body will be divided from the whole body, and so it will be both one and many. The principle of mathematics, the Euclidean one, is: The whole is greater than its part. But the Tridentines decreed that under each species, or under the separate parts of each species, the whole Christ is contained, when separation has been made. Yet since the body of Christ is at the same time equal to itself, will not the part be equal to the whole, and the whole not be greater than the part? The principle of logic is: Parts agree with the whole and disagree among themselves. But in the division of the host, or of the Sacrament, the parts agree among themselves so completely that they are altogether one and the same thing. And since every division, whether logical or physical, is the division of one thing into many, this division is of one into one, and that into itself. Finally, the Catholic principle is: Each thing either is or is not: the same cannot at once be and not be. But if the metousia and the metapoiesis of the body of Christ are posited, the same thing will both be and not be at the same time. For any individual thing that is permanent, and that will never cease after it has come into existence, cannot have come into being from another thing, which is still to come about; yet the individual body of Christ, incorruptible, can come into being, and will come into being, from the consecrated bread, into which it is converted as an individual body. But his individual and incorruptible body was continually existing before this consecration. Therefore it both was and was not at the same time. I pass over the many so-called logical propositions, and the manifest contradictions, which I have discussed at more length elsewhere. Is this not declaring war not only on faith but on all reason, with heaven indignant, the Gentiles laughing, and the true Church for so long resisting, and putting off humanity itself?

units.la: XLV. Neque veterum quisquam dogma isthoc credidit; nisi forte Eutychiani, qui apud Theodoretum Dialogo II. qui ἀσύγχυτος inscribitur, à transmutatione panis & vini in corpus & sanguinem Dominicum, argumentantur ad mutationem corporis Domini in Divinam essentiam. Sed negat ille Pater Orthodoxus, Symbola mystica propriam naturam amittere. Nec manere duntaxat
units.tr: XLV. None of the ancients believed this dogma; except perhaps the Eutychians, who, in Theodoret's Dialogue II, which is entitled Inconfusus [ἀσύγχυτος], argue from the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of the Lord to a change of the Lord's body into the divine essence. But that orthodox Father denies that the mystical symbols lose their own nature. Nor does he say that they merely remain

units.la: Et anti-quitati pu-tori omni repugnat. priorem speciem & formam, sed etiam substantiam priorem asserit. Ita enim libro primo, qui Ἀλεχανδρος dicitur, Christus, inquit, visibilia signa appellatione corporis & sanguinis honoravit, ὁ τὴν φύσιν μὴ μεταβαλὼν, ἀλλὰ τὴν χάριν τῇ φύσει προσεθηκώς, non transmutans symbolorum naturam, sed naturæ symbolorum adjiciens gratiam. Idem Gelasius Papa lib. de duabus in Christo naturis, panem & vinum ita transfire in corporis & sanguinis Christi substantiam dicit, ut tamen substantia panis & vini esse non desinat. Et clamat omnis Patrum Senatus, in Cœna panem & vinum esse symbola, ἀντίτυπα, signa, exemplar, similitudinem, figuras corporis & sanguinis Domini. Docuerunt sane idem μεταβολὴν καὶ μετατροπὴν, transmutationem & conversionem quandam symbolorum, sed relativam illam, non essentialem; officii & usus, non substantiæ vel naturæ respectu; ut quæ ante in sedanda fame & siti usum communem habuerunt, accedente verbo corporis & sanguinis Dominici Sacramenta fiant. Constat enim, res quoad substantiam non mutari. Neque fando auditum est unquam, relatum esse correlatum. Demum à Concilio Lateranensi, obstetricante barbarie & ignorantia, horrendum μετουσίας seu transsubstantiationis (alii οὐσιώσεως potius autumant) monstrum in ipsa naturæ principia, rerum ordinem, Servatoris humanitatem, Sacramenti veritatem, constantem Scripturæ sententiam, Theologiæ fundamenta omnia arietans; exclusum, & à Monachis mendicantibus, novis itidem naturæ monstris, avidissimè exceptum fuit: ex quo cum aliæ hæreses ingruere, tum ἀρτολατρείαν, seu panis adorationem, ab Honorio III. primùm sancitam, & ab Urbano IV. instituto festo corporis Christi auctam, consequi necesse fuit.
units.tr: And this is wholly repugnant to antiquity: he asserts that not only the former appearance and form remain, but also the former substance. For in the first book, which is called Alexander [Ἀλεχανδρος], Christ, he says, honoured visible signs with the name of body and blood, who did not change the nature [ὁ τὴν φύσιν μὴ μεταβαλὼν, ἀλλὰ τὴν χάριν τῇ φύσει προσεθηκώς], but added grace to the nature; not transforming the nature of the symbols, but adding grace to the nature of the symbols. Gelasius the Pope likewise says, in his book on the two natures in Christ, that the bread and wine pass over into the substance of the body and blood of Christ, yet so that the substance of bread and wine does not cease to be. And the whole senate of the Fathers cries out that in the Supper the bread and wine are symbols, antitypes [ἀντίτυπα], signs, copies, likenesses, figures of the body and blood of the Lord. The Fathers certainly taught a certain change and conversion [μεταβολὴν καὶ μετατροπὴν], a transmutation and conversion of the symbols, but a relative one, not an essential one; with respect to office and use, not to substance or nature. Before the word of the Lord's body and blood is added, the elements have a common use in relieving hunger and thirst; once it is added, they become sacraments. For it is agreed that the thing is not changed as to its substance. Nor has it ever been heard in speech that a correlate was passed on. At last, by the Lateran Council, with barbarism and ignorance acting as midwife, that horrible monster of transubstantiation [μετουσίας], or (others think rather) essentiation [οὐσιώσεως], was brought forth, battering the very principles of nature, the order of things, the humanity of the Saviour, the truth of the sacrament, the constant sense of Scripture, and all the foundations of theology. It was rejected, and then most eagerly embraced by the mendicant monks, who were themselves new monsters against nature. From this it was bound to follow that, while other heresies pressed in, idolatry of bread [ἀρτολατρείαν], that is, the adoration of bread, was also established, first sanctioned by Honorius III and increased by the feast of Corpus Christi instituted by Urban IV.

units.la: XLVI. Quæ cùm ita sint, atque omnino prodigiosum sum illud transsubstantiationis dogma, uti non frustra ὁ δὲινα asseruit, unum tot in se absurdos errores contineat, quot momenta temporis ab ejus prima nativitate, id est, à Concilio Lateranensi, unde dogmatis istius æra auspicanda est; ad hanc usque horam intercesserunt; ipso utique Jesuita Costero ἑαυτὸν πμωρχμένα, judice, Pontificii idololatriæ adeò turpis & detestabilis rei sunt, ut illa longè tolerabilior omnis Gentilium idololatria fuerit. Adorant enim maximè solenniter & devotè non tam panem, quàm spumam panis; & quod sic adorant, mox horribile dictu! devorant. Quibus proin jam olim falsè admodum Averroes objecisse fertur, satius esse ut permaneat anima sua cum Philosophis, quàm cum illis Christianis, qui adorant quod comedunt, & comedunt, quod adorant. Quod merito Theodoretus ἰσχάπην αβελπίαν esse dixit.
units.tr: XLVI. These things being so, and that dogma of transubstantiation being wholly monstrous, as the Jesuit who said it not without reason, contains in itself so many absurd errors as there have been moments of time from its first birth, that is, from the Lateran Council, from which the era of this dogma must be dated, until this very hour; by the judgement of the Jesuit Costerus himself, who [ἑαυτὸν πμωρχμένα] — the Papists are guilty of an idolatry so shameful and detestable that every idolatry of the Gentiles is far more tolerable by comparison. For they adore most solemnly and devoutly not so much the bread as the foam of bread; and what they so adore, horrible to say, they soon devour. Hence Averroes is said to have objected to them long ago, quite falsely, it would be better for his soul to remain with the philosophers than with those Christians who adore what they eat, and eat what they adore. Theodoret rightly called this an impious and foolish hope [ἰσχάπην αβελπίαν].

units.la: XLVII. Neque profecto artolatras persuasio, quòd sub specie panis & vini corpus & sanguis Christi, adeo que totus Christus θεάνθρωπος præsto sit, atque ei, ceu Regi suo præsenti, honor adorationis omnino exhibendus sit; ab idololatriæ culpa absolvit. In cultu enim Dei non falsa persuasio, sed vera fides regnat. Stultorum est putare: sapientum & prudentum scire, & teste Deo credere. Si prætextus talis juvaret, jam omnem ferè gentium idololatriam nitrum lomentúmque facere liceret. Potior longè ratio erat, ut Gentiles Solem verum illum æternúmque Deum, creatorem ac gubernatorem omnium esse, uti in Liturgiis eorum habetur, crederent, quàm ut Christianus panis, seu spumæ consecratæ, frustulum supremum Numen esse, ut credat, inducatur. Neque dubitare licet, quin Pagani æquè firmiter crediderint, Solem Deum esse, quàm Christianus quivis credere possit, Panem Eucharisticum esse corpus Christi. Cui tamen sano in mentem venit, propte- adoratores certissimi Non juv.ut artolatras persuasio, quòd Christus præsens sit sub specie panis propterea Solis cultores verissimos idololatras non esse? Accedit, quòd erronea hæc persuasio & canoris vocibus, & scriptis irrefragabilibus ex Dei verbo & sana ratione toties convicta est, plurimis ad ravim usque clamantibus, imò sanguinem proprium expuentibus, ut veritati contra palpabilem adeò idololatriam fidem facerent. Unde verbo Dei ubique expositò, & ex eodem clarissimè demonstrata veritate,errori explosissimo Πρόφασις nulla amplius esse potest.
units.tr: XLVII. Nor indeed does the persuasion of the bread-worshippers, that under the species of bread and wine the body and blood of Christ, and indeed the whole God-man Christ, is present, and that adoration must be fully offered to him as to a present King, absolve them from the guilt of idolatry. For in the worship of God it is not false persuasion but true faith that must reign. It is the mark of fools to think; of the wise and prudent to know, and to believe on God's testimony. If such a pretext helped, it would be possible to make nearly all the idolatry of the nations into lye and soap. A far better reason was that the Gentiles should believe the sun to be that true and eternal God, the creator and governor of all, as is held in their liturgies, than that a Christian should be led to believe that a crumb of consecrated bread or foam is the supreme Deity. Nor can it be doubted that the pagans believed the sun to be God as firmly as any Christian can believe the eucharistic bread to be the body of Christ. Yet does it not come into any sane mind: are the most certain adorers of the bread not idolaters, just as the true worshippers of the sun are not idolaters, because the persuasion that Christ is present under the species of bread does not help them? Moreover, this erroneous persuasion has been refuted so often, by sweet-sounding voices and by irrefutable writings drawn from God's word and sound reason, many crying out even to hoarseness, indeed spitting out their own blood, in order to make the faith true against such a palpable idolatry. Therefore, with the word of God set out everywhere, and the truth clearly demonstrated from it, the error, utterly exploded, can have no further pretext [Πρόφασις].

units.la: XLVIII. Frustra ergo Hierarchici inclamant, se artolatras, seu panis adoratores non esse, eò quòd panem adesse, ne quidem agnoscunt. Sufficit enim, nil nisi panem, vel panis potiùs spumam adesse. Quin etiam gravior idololatria fuerit, si cassa accidentia, quæ à subjecto avulsa nihil sunt, & adesse, & à se adorari agnoverint. Præterea Pagani, qui Solem adorabant, non eam rem, quæ non aliud quàm Sol; res inanimis, sensus & intelligentiæ expers erat, illic adesse ; sed Supremum potiùs Numen in Sole mundo præsidere autumabant. Neque tamen opinio falsa idololatriæ labem à fama eorum abstergere potuit.
units.tr: XLVIII. Vainly therefore do the hierarchs cry out that they are not artolatrists, that is, worshippers of bread, because they do not even acknowledge that bread is present. For it is enough that nothing but bread, or rather the foam of bread, is present. Indeed their idolatry would be even graver if they acknowledged that bare accidents, which are nothing when torn from their subject, are both present and adored in themselves. Moreover, the pagans who worshipped the sun did not suppose that the thing which is nothing other than the sun, an inanimate thing lacking sense and understanding, was present there; they held rather that the Supreme Deity presided over the world in the sun. Yet a false opinion could not wipe the stain of idolatry from their reputation.

units.la: XLIX. Sed esto sanè, fidem nonnullam transsubstantiationis dogma mereatur, ut consecratione legitimè facta, præsens sit in Eucharistia corpus & sanguis Christi. Ne sic quidem idololatriæ crimine sese Hierarchici exsolverint. Tridentini enim, uti supra ostendimus, Eucharistiam à Christo distinctam adorandam sanxerunt. Tum qui adorat Christum infallibili fide statuat oportet, Deum esse, quem ut Deum & Christum adorat. Papistæ autem infallibiliter certi esse nequeunt, Christum esse, quem adorant. Quippe domestica illorum principia sunt, ut transsubstantiatio fiat triticeum, non corruptum esse debere panem: vinum ex uvis maturis expressum : pronuntiationem consecrativam fieri debere, nec addendo, nec detrahendo, nec mutando, nec transponendo: Sacerdotem consecrantem oportère rite esse baptizatum & ordinatum: eundem Sacramentum non aliter conficere, quàm si adsit intentio faciendi, quod facit Ecclesia. De conditionibus autem istis alterutram in partem quotusquisque προφητικῶς certus esse potest? Qui autem nescit quid adoret, & tamen adorat perinde ac si sciret, verum Deum esse, quod adorat, purus criminis idololatriæ haberi nequit. Produnt anceps periculum disputationes perplexæ Pontificiorum, quorum proin multi hoc veluti pharmaco idololatriæ suæ sensum sopientes, ad adorationem requirunt conditionem expressam vel tacitam: Adoro te, si Deus es. Adorant interim absolutè, hoc est, id quod vero Deo debetur, objectio illi, veluti Θεῷ ἀγνώστῳ Deo incognito impendunt; & tamen cum conditione si Deus sit. Hoc scilicet est juxta viam illam adulterae Prov. xxx. 20. comedere, & tergere os suum, & dicere: Non sum operata iniquitatem.
units.tr: XLIX. But grant, certainly, that the dogma of transubstantiation deserves some faith, so that, with consecration lawfully performed, the body and blood of Christ are present in the Eucharist. Even so the hierarchs will not free themselves from the crime of idolatry. For the Tridentine fathers, as we showed above, decreed that the Eucharist, distinct from Christ, is to be adored. Then whoever adores Christ must hold with infallible faith that he is God whom he adores as God and Christ. But the Papists cannot be infallibly certain that the one they adore is Christ. Indeed their own principles are these: that for transubstantiation to take place the bread must be of wheat and not corrupted; the wine must be pressed from ripe grapes; the consecratory pronouncement must be made without adding, subtracting, changing, or transposing anything; the consecrating priest must have been rightly baptized and ordained; and he cannot effect the sacrament unless there is the intention of doing what the Church does. But of these conditions, how few can be certain, in either direction, by prophetic [προφητικῶς] insight? And one who does not know what he adores, yet adores as if he knew that what he adores is the true God, cannot be held free of the guilt of idolatry. Their perplexed disputations reveal a dangerous uncertainty, so that many of them, as if soothing the feeling of their idolatry with this sort of remedy, require an expressed or tacit condition for adoration: I adore you, if you are God. Meanwhile they adore absolutely, that is, they offer to that object what is due to the true God alone, as if to the unknown God [Θεῷ ἀγνώστῳ]; and yet with the condition, if he is God. This is clearly the way of that adulterous woman in Prov. 30:20: she eats, and wipes her mouth, and says: I have done no wickedness.

units.la: L. Succedit Hagiolatria, seu Sanctorum Angelorum & Hominum Cœlitum cultus. Tridentini quidem Sess. xxv. simpliciter Sanctorum invocationem commendant. Sed cultus eorundem tam varius, tam multiplex est, ut in eo narrando non copia, sed modus dicendi quærendus sit. Honorantur nempe Sancti aris, imaginibus, radiatis capitibus, Templis, Missis, cereis, festis, juramentis, votis, quorum nonnulla ad cultum latriæ referri solent. Invocantur imo adorantur, uti Catechesis Tridentina in præceptum 1. aliique plures, alibi à nobis producti loquuntur. Etquid sunt Orationes ad Sanctos aliud quàm adoratio Sanctorum? Ante imagines Sanctorum quorundam procumbentibus mos est orare, Pater noster. probante etiam Catechesi Tridentina capite de oratione: Cum ad imaginem Sancti quis orationem Dominicam pronuntiat, ita tum sentiat, se ab illo petere ut secum oret. Cofterus Jesuita Enchir. de Venerat. Sanctorum sic scribit: In honorem Sanctorum recitannus orationem Dominicam. Salmeron in 1. Tim. 11. Disp. 7. eò impietatis processit, ut diceret, orationem fusam per Sanctos meliorem esse ea, quae Deo funditur, non adhibita intercessione. Creduntur Mediatores & intercessores apud Deum, utpote magis ἐντρόπωι, ut sic per gradus & via obliqua ad Deum veniatur: cordium inspectores, omnisciì, omni praesentes, sine quibus doribus omnes omnium orationes earumque integritatem dijudicare non possent. Nec tantùm creduntur pro nobis supplicare, sed etiam pro nobis satisfacere, & aliis salutem mereri. Nam quod Deo supererogaverunt, creditur aliis cedere in solutionem, Papa sic dispensante, quomodo Clemens VI. Extravag. Unicus dicit, ad cumulum thesauri electorum merita adminiculum praestare. In Missa Sacerdos petit remissionem peccatorum & salutem non tantùm per preces Sanctorum, sed etiam per eorum merita. Unde Bellarminus de Indulg. lib. 1. 4. non dubitavit dicere, Sanctos aliquo modo esse Redemptores nostros. Denique eo usque supersistitio excrevit, ut rudis plebecula vix Christum à Sanctis distinguat, & in ipsa Missa Maria Christo praeponatur. Ibi enim Missa instituta dicitur inprimis ad commemorationem Virginis Mariae, Christo inferiorem in locum projecto. Et Sacerdos peccata sua confitetur Michaeli & Sanctis, Christo insuper habito.
units.tr: L. Next comes hagiolatry, that is, the worship of the holy angels and the heavenly inhabitants among men. The Tridentine fathers, in Session 25, simply commend the invocation of the saints. But the worship of these is so varied and manifold that in describing it the question is not one of abundance but of the manner of speaking. Saints are honoured with altars, images, haloed heads, temples, Masses, candles, feasts, oaths and vows, some of which are usually referred to the worship of latria. They are invoked, indeed adored, as the Tridentine Catechism speaks under the commandment, and several others, as we have cited elsewhere. And what are prayers to the saints but the adoration of the saints? It is customary to pray before the images of certain saints, to say the Our Father; the Tridentine Catechism too, in the chapter on prayer, approves: When someone says the Lord's Prayer before the image of a saint, he should think that he is asking him to pray with him. The Jesuit Costerus, in his Enchiridion on the Veneration of the Saints, writes thus: In honour of the saints we recite the Lord's Prayer. Salmeron, on 1 Tim. 2, Disputation 7, went so far in impiety as to say that a prayer poured out through the saints is better than that which is poured out to God without the intercession of the saints. The saints are believed to be mediators and intercessors before God, as being more approachable, so that by degrees and an oblique way one comes to God; inspectors of hearts, all-knowing, present everywhere, without whose gifts they could not judge all the prayers of all and their integrity. Nor are they believed merely to plead for us, but also to make satisfaction for us, and to merit salvation for others. For what they have done beyond what was owed to God is believed to be transferred to others in payment, the Pope so dispensing, as Clement VI says in the Extravagant Unigenitus, that the merits of the elect provide a help to the treasury's surplus. In the Mass the priest asks for forgiveness of sins and salvation not only through the prayers of the saints but also through their merits. Hence Bellarmine, in On Indulgences, book 1, chapter 4, did not hesitate to say that the saints are in some way our redeemers. Finally, superstition has grown so far that the rude common folk scarcely distinguish Christ from the saints, and in the Mass itself Mary is put before Christ. For the Mass is said to have been instituted chiefly in commemoration of the Virgin Mary, with Christ thrust into a lower place. And the priest confesses his sins to Michael and the saints, with Christ set aside.

units.la: LI. Quis sic Sanctis religiosum & Divinum cultum praestari, negare ausit? Quisquis enim invocatur, adoratur, pro Mediatore & intercessionis & satisfactionis habetur; omnisciius, omni praesens per invocationem & & adorationem constituitur; aris, Templis, Sacrificiis, juramentis, votis, incurvatione honoratur, ei religiosus & Divinus honos exhibetur. Cuncta enim hæc non cadere nisi in Deum & Christum, supra probavimus; & Scriptura, adeóque res ipsa sonorè loquitur. Ei enim qui sic colitur, Divina quædam πλεονεκτήματα, Excellentiæ Divinæ competant necesse est. Atqui Sanctos sic coli, ne ipsa quidem impudentia negare ausit.
units.tr: LI. Who would dare to deny that such religious and divine worship is paid to the saints?
