Whoever is invoked and adored, and is regarded as a mediator of both intercession and satisfaction, who is believed to be present everywhere and to know all things through invocation and adoration, and who is honoured with altars, temples, sacrifices, oaths, vows and bowing down, is given religious and divine honour. For we have already shown above that all these things belong only to God and Christ, and Scripture and the thing itself speak plainly. For one who is worshipped in this way must necessarily possess certain divine advantages [πλεονεκτήματα], that is, divine excellences. But that the saints are worshipped in this way not even impudence itself would dare to deny.

units.la: LII. Atque frustra Hagiolatræ distinctionum suarum præstigiis evadere, & à cultu Divorum suorum idololatriæ aspergines amoliri satagunt. Neque enim quicquam illi proficient, nisi ea, quæ recensuimus, signa esse cultus communis, & non Divini propria demonstraverint. quod nunquam præstare illi possunt.
units.tr: LII. The Hagiolaters try in vain to escape by the sleight of their distinctions, and they labour to remove from the cult of their divinities the stain of idolatry. For they will gain nothing unless they can show that the signs we have listed belong to a common cult and not to the proper cult of God, which they can never do.

units.la: Quocunque ergo loco Sanctos habeant, sive Dei summi, causæ primæ, omnium bonorum largitoris, sive Divorum subalternorum; satis est, quòd ea iis tribuunt, quæ soli Deo eximia sunt, nec ulli creaturæ impertiri licet. Sic enim, Divina iis tribuendo, quantum in ipsis est, Divos subalternos suos in Deum summum convertunt & transsubstantiant. Præextextus quinetiam ille, quòd universus ille Sanctorum cultus non aliud sit, quàm bonorum, quibus indigemus, à Deo per Filium Christum impetrandorum ratio, neque efficit, ut modus, quo impetrare conantur, idololatria esse desinat: & ad summum hoc efficit, ut Sancti ad conditionem Gentilium Deorum Medioxumorum, Dæmonúmque, hominum negotia cum Summo Numine transigentium, similitudinem propius accedant. Dulíæ & hyperdulíæ cultus à latriæ cultu distincti alexipharmacon abunde supra averruncavimus. Neque denique Mediationem intercessionis à mediatione redemptionis vel satisfactionis separantes, nitidiores se fa-
units.tr: Therefore, whatever place they give the saints, whether that of the supreme God, the first cause and giver of all good things, or that of subordinate divinities, it is enough that they ascribe to them what is peculiar to God alone and may not be imparted to any creature. For by ascribing divine things to them, they convert and transubstantiate their subordinate divinities, as far as in them lies, into the supreme God. That pretext too, that the whole cult of the saints is nothing other than a way of obtaining from God through the Son Christ the good things we need, does not make the manner in which they seek to obtain them cease to be idolatry; at most it makes the saints come closer to the condition of the Gentile gods, the intermediate beings and demons, who conduct the affairs of men with the supreme Deity. The distinction between the worship of dulia and hyperdulia and the worship of latria we have already sufficiently driven away as an antidote above. Finally, by separating the mediation of intercession from the mediation of redemption or satisfaction, they do not appear to be any the more refined, since

units.la: Prætextus Hagiolatrarum, quod Sanctos ut amicos Dei, non ut summum Deum colant, & mediationem eorum ad intercessionem referunt, dicunt. faciunt, tum quia nisi satisfactionis & redemptionis merito nixus, Mediatoris adinstar, intercedere nemo potest; quomodo Christus Mediator esse, nisi data redemptionis pretio (1. Tim. 11. 5. 6.) non potuit: tum quia eosdem Divos satisfactionis etiam Mediatores facere, jam probavimus.
units.tr: The pretext of the Hagiolaters is that they worship the saints as friends of God, not as the supreme God, and they refer the mediation of the saints to intercession. Against this we say: no one can intercede, like a mediator, unless he relies on the merit of satisfaction and redemption, just as Christ could not be Mediator unless the price of redemption had been given (1 Tim. 2:5, 6); and also because we have already shown that these same divinities are made mediators of satisfaction as well.

units.la: LIII. Inspectæ paulò altiùs Orationum ad Divos fusarum formulæ palam facient, Hagiolatras maxima quæque perinde à Sanctis, atque à Deo, si non magis, effl agitare. Ita enim Oratio ad S. Cosmum & Damianum, eos ceu Medicos piissimos, meritis clarissimos implorat, ut à peste, clade corporum præservent & operum ; Moribus, inquiunt oratores, ne langueamus, nec moriamur Spiritu, sed animæ ab obitu velociter surgamus ; & vivamus in gratia, Sacra Cœli palatia donec regrediamur. An altius à Deo quicquam petimus? Oratio ad S. Franciscum talis est: S. Francisce, prosperè veris ; Pater accelera ad populum, qui premitur & teritur sub onere, palea, luto, latere, & sepultos Ægyptio sub fabulo nos libera, carnis extinctio vitio. Annon hæc est liberationis à captivitate & servitute peccati imploratio ? Preces ad S. Andream gratiam tolerandi patienter crucem sic expetunt : Jam nos foveto languidos, curamque nostri suscipe, Quo per crucis victoriam Coeli petamus gratiam. S. Nicolaum in talia vota vocare solent : Ergo pie nos exaudi Assistentes tuae laudi, Ne subdamur hostis fraudi, Nobis fer auxilia. Nos ab omni malo ducas, Vita recta nos conducas, Post hanc vitam nos inducas Ad aeterna gaudia. Sic Nicolaus ille adversus omnes Sathanae insultus tutos incolumesque haud secus quam Deus ipse, praestare potis erit. S. Agnetem gratiam serviendi Deo in charitate perfecta : S. Brigittam gratiam periti Naucleri adinstar per omnes tempestates casusque súsque hujus mundi transfretandi, & in Cœlo feliciter appellendi: S. Catharinam gratiam cordis contriti, in bono immoti, vivendi Deo, ipsa regente, pura mente, de procella mortis salvandi; mundum superandi, decumbentem læva fovendi, & de morte sæva solvendi &c. supplice prece orant. Ubi illud animadversione dignum est, quòd inter viginti quatuor, quibus oratio ea comprehenditur, versus, tres duntaxat occurrunt, quibus Catharina illa ut pro supplice intercedat, oratur: reliquis omnibus ejus, tanquam bonorum spiritualium jugis fontis & scaturiginis, auxilium imploratur. Gemellas ad S. Martinum, Andræam, Jacobum, Bartholomæum, alios Sanctos Sanctásque formulas reperire est.
units.tr: LIII. If we look a little more deeply into the formulas of the prayers poured out to the divinities, they will make it plain that the Hagiolaters attribute the greatest things to the saints just as much as to God, if not more. Thus the prayer to Saints Cosmas and Damian implores them, as most pious physicians, most famous for their merits, that they should preserve us from plague and the destruction of bodies and of works; by their habits, as the petitioners say, let us not grow faint, nor die in spirit, but let our souls rise quickly from death; and let us live in grace until we return to the sacred palaces of heaven. Do we ask anything more from God? The prayer to Saint Francis is of this kind: Saint Francis, prosper true things; Father, hasten to the people who are oppressed and trodden down under the burden, chaff, mud and brick, and free us, buried under the Egyptian clay, from the death of the flesh by vice. Is this not an imploring of liberation from captivity and the servitude of sin? Prayers to Saint Andrew seek grace to bear the cross patiently in this way: Now cherish us who are weak, and take up our care, so that through the victory of the cross we may attain the grace of heaven. They are accustomed to call on Saint Nicholas for such vows: Therefore mercifully hear us, who attend your praise, lest we be subjected to the snare of the enemy; bring us help. Lead us away from every evil; guide us in a right life; after this life lead us into eternal joys. Thus that Nicholas will be able to keep us safe and unharmed against all the assaults of Satan no less than God himself. They pray with suppliant petition for Saint Agnes to grant the grace of serving God in perfect charity; for Saint Bridget, the grace of crossing over through all the storms and chances of this world like a skilled sailor, and of landing happily in heaven; for Saint Catherine, the grace of a contrite heart, of remaining unmoved in good, of living for God with herself as guide, of being saved with a pure mind from the storm of death, of overcoming the world, of cherishing the one who lies sick on the left, and of freeing from cruel death, and so on. Here it is worth noting that among the twenty-four verses that make up this prayer, only three occur in which Catherine is asked to intercede as a suppliant; in all the rest her help is implored as if she were a constant fountain and spring of spiritual goods. One may find similar formulas addressed to Saint Martin, Andrew, James, Bartholomew, and other saints, male and female.

units.la: LIV. Et tales quidem ad minorum gentium Divos Divásque orationum formulæ frequentantur. Longè flagrantior affectus se in cultu Deiparæ, ceu Matris Christi, adeóque Mariolatria, omnium devotissima exerit. In Rosario B. Virginis oratione prosa sic interpellatur: Peccatorum consolatrix, infirmorum curatrix, errantium revocatrix, justorum consummatrix, desolatorum spes, & auxiliatrix, atque mea promptissima adjutrix, tibi, Domina gloriosa commendo hodie & quotidie animam meam, ut me in custodiam tuam commendatum ab omnibus malis & fraudibus Diaboli custodias, atque in hora mortis constanter mihi assistas, & animam ad æterna gaudia perducas. Ad calcem Rosarii hæc occurrunt: Cor meum illumina, fulgens stella maris, & ab hostis machina semper tuearis. O gloriosa Virgo, libera nos ab omni malo, & pœnis inferni. Et sanè ante Reformationis tempora B. Virginis patrocinium tanto ardore precibus suis captæ superstitione animæ ambiverunt, ut Christi oblivio eos penitus cepisse videatur. Oratio recepta erat, & hodié-
units.tr: LIV. Such formulas of prayer are commonly used toward the lesser divinities, male and female. The more ardent devotion, however, shows itself most fervently in the cult of the Mother of God, as mother of Christ, and so Mariolatry, the most devoted of all, breaks out. In the Rosary of the Blessed Virgin the prose prayer entreats her thus: Consoler of sinners, healer of the sick, recaller of the wandering, perfecter of the just, hope and helper of the desolate, and my most ready helper, to you, glorious Lady, I commend my soul today and every day, that you may keep me, commended to your custody, safe from all evils and the deceits of the Devil, and that you may stand constantly by me in the hour of death and lead my soul into eternal joys. At the end of the Rosary these words occur: Illumine my heart, shining star of the sea, and always protect it from the machinery of the enemy. O glorious Virgin, free us from every evil and from the pains of hell. And indeed, before the time of the Reformation, souls captured by superstition ambitiously sought the patronage of the Blessed Virgin with such ardour in their prayers that the forgetfulness of Christ seems to have wholly taken hold of them. The prayer was received, and today

units.la: Imprimis ad Deiparam directis demonstratur. hodiéque est ejusmodi: Te, mater illuminationis cordis mei, te, nutrix salutis meæ mentis, te obsecrant quantum possunt cuncta præcordia mea. Exaudi Domina, adesto propitia, adjuva potentissima, ut mundentur sordes mentis meæ, ut illuminentur tenebræ meæ. O gloriosa Domina, Porta vitæ, Janua salutis, via reconciliationis, Aditus recuperationis, obsecro Te per salvatricem tuam fœcunditatem, fac ut peccatorum meorum venia, & vivendi gratia concedatur, & usque in finem hic servus tuus sub Protectione custodiatur. Mutato sexus genere cuncta hæc ad Christum Salvatorem mundi, & quidem magnificè satis, dirigerentur. Planè sicut in Psalterio Virginis Mariæ, quod Bonaventura authore prodiit, & inter opera ejus jussu Sixti V. edita extat; nec non in Bibliis Mariæ, quæ Alberto Magno authori tribuuntur, & Doctorum ac Professorum Theologiæ approbatione suffulta lucem publicam salutárunt; mutato sexus genere Mariæ cuncta ab Hieropsalte & in universis Bibliis Jehovæ Summo dicta horribili audacia vendicantur. In Litania Filia Dei, Illuminatrix cordium, Fons misericordiæ, Flumen Sapientiæ, Regina Cœli, Domina mundi, Domina Cœli & terræ insignitur. Neque aliud supererat, quàm ut in locum Christi Filii Dei, Christa, Filia Dei substitueretur, & Christæ potiùs Filiæ Dei, quàm Christi Filii Dei cultores Mariolatræ se profiterentur. Ut jam tenuiter nimis de ea Biel Lect. 80. in Can. Misse prædicaverit, quòd Rex Regum dimidium Regni sui huic Reginæ dederit; & ex potioribus Regni sui bonis, nempe justitia misericordiáque justitiam retinuerit sibi, misericordiam autem Matri reliquerit.
units.tr: It is shown especially by prayers directed to the Mother of God, and it is still of this kind today: You, mother of the illumination of my heart, you, nurse of the salvation of my mind, all the depths of my heart beseech you as much as they can. Hear me, Lady, be present and gracious, help me most powerfully, so that the filth of my mind may be cleansed, so that my darkness may be enlightened. O glorious Lady, gate of life, door of salvation, way of reconciliation, entrance to recovery, I beg you by your saving fruitfulness, grant that the pardon of my sins and the grace of living may be given, and that this your servant may be kept under your protection to the end. With the gender changed, all these things would be addressed to Christ the Saviour of the world, and indeed quite magnificently. Just so, in the Psalter of the Virgin Mary, which came out under the name of Bonaventure and is extant among his works, published by order of Sixtus V., and also in the Bible of Mary, which is attributed to Albert the Great and, supported by the approval of doctors and professors of theology, brought its light to the public; with the gender changed, all things said of Jehovah, the Supreme, are claimed by the Psalmist and in all the Bibles for Mary with dreadful audacity. In the Litany she is marked as Daughter of God, Illuminator of hearts, Fountain of mercy, River of wisdom, Queen of heaven, Lady of the world, Lady of heaven and earth. Nothing remained but that Christa, Daughter of God should be substituted in the place of Christ the Son of God, and that they should profess themselves worshippers of Christa, Daughter of God, rather than worshippers of Christ, Son of God. Biel, in Lect. 80 on the Canon of the Mass, has already spoken of her too feebly, saying that the King of kings gave half of his kingdom to this Queen; and that, of the better goods of his kingdom, namely justice and mercy, he kept justice for himself, but left mercy to the Mother.

units.la: LV. Possent de Mariolatria hac dici profecto innumera & stupenda. Et de ea multa nimis, taliáque, quæ Hierarchicorum in cultu B. Mariæ superstitionem omnes idololatriæ numeros implevisse planissimè produnt, duo Viri celebres, Augiæ hoc stabulum ingressi purgantésque, Andreas Rivetus, & Carolus Drelincurtius, cum Camusio Bellicensi Episcopo, contentionis sunem ducens, dixerunt. Ibi productos bona, & ne ab ipso quidem Camusio solicitata fide, testes & numero, & in Ecclesia Pontificia authoritate præstantes legere est, qui omni fronte posita & pudore prostituto, uti quidem Meretricis hujus lenones decebat,plenis, quod ajunt, tibiis decantant, B. Virginem esse Deam Deificatam, Divinizatam, Oceanum Divinitatis & Complementum Trinitatis, Infantem sive Infantinam Trinitatis; habere potestatem in omnes Gratias & beneficentias Dei, Hominumque salutem; plenam & supremam potestatem dispensandi de Gratiis Dei omnibus; esse depositariam vitæ æternæ, habentem innumera alba, nomine Dei subscripta, in quibus ipsa, quæ placuerit, scribat; Thesauriam esse generalis Sacri ærarii Dei & redituum Spiritus S. Cancellariam aulæ Cælestis, Gubernatricem Cælorum, Paradisi Rectricem, Inventricem, Authorem & Causam gratiæ, scaturiginem salutis, vitæ, Christianorum vitam; Librum vitæ, in quo scripti sint prædestinati; Canalem omnium gratiarum Dei; Solam & unicam causam, cur gratissimus Deo; Mediatricem, Propitiatricem, Redemptricem mundi; Fenestram Paradisi; Portam Cæli; Portam aureain firmamenti; Scalam Cæli; in cujus gratiam omnes liberationes & indulgentiæ sub V.T. contigerint, per quam, ceu tubam Opticum Deus omnes reliquos homines respiciat à Deo ad B. Virginem appellationem licitam esse; in celebri illa visione duarum scalarum Rubræ & Candidæ facilius esse in Paradisum ascendere per candidam quæ est Virginis, quàm per rubram, quæ est Christi; Monachos per rubram ascendere molientes præcipites interram actos esse, & per candidam ascensum tentantes Coelum intrasse; Improbos post abnegatos Deum & Christum, à morte liberatos esse, quòd B. Virginem confessi essent; fas esse orare Christum in nomine Mariae; esse eam Agnum Coeli, sustulisse maledictionem, condonare & delere peccata; reparatricem esse damnorum Adami, rectè eam Altare appellari; omnia peccata nostra in sanguine Christi & lacte B. Mariae submersa esse, homines à Christo damnatos per B. Mariam servari posse; saepius eam Christi decreta refigere; eundem effectum habere sanguinem Filii & lac Mariae, atque dubitare peccatorem meritò, ad utrum rectius se converat; ipsam contrivisse caput serpentis; esse eam supremam Dominam, Reginam, Imperatricem, Monarcham, Gubernatricem Coelorum, Paradisi, Angelorum, Seraphinorum, Reginam Reginarum, Principem Principum; Deum cum ea partitum esse regnum; esse judicem vivorum & mortuorum, absolutè eam dominari in totum universum, causam eam una cum Christo esse, cur Deus mundum creaverit; imò ipsam mundum aliquo sensu creasse; opera ejus æquè ac opera Dei perfecta esse; potestatem eam habere in Dominum Jesum Regiam, ita ut ei imperare pro lubitu possit; Deum ei debitorem & obstrictum esse; respectu generationis temporalis Christi, Deum Patrem nulla re praecedere Virginem; Christum, qua Deum & hominem B. Virginem imitatum esse; majora eam clementiae exempla dedisse, quàm Christum; Jehovam illam possedisse ab initio viae suae; esse eam adorandam, etiam adoratione latriae; adoratam esse ab Angelis in primo creationis ejus momento, posse nos baptizari in nomine B. Virginis; omnia nostra debere nos in nomine, & ad gloriam nominis ejus inchoare & finire. Quid videtur de his, & similibus infinitis floseculis; qui in hortis doctorum plusquam octoginta Episcoporum, Archiepiscoporum, Cardinalium, Jesuitarum ab eodem Drelincurtio, citatis totidem eorum verbis, laudatorum ejusmodi, qui publica authoritate Censorum Apostolicorum, praxi quinetiam publica, ex qua Ecclesiæ Romanæ fides cognoscitur optimè, muniti, neque unquam ab Inquisitorum spongiis vexati, talia in publicum protulerunt; nec non in Litaniis & Hymnis solennibus occurrunt? Quique etiam defensores vindicésque in Ecclesia Romana haud imæ cavæ Theologos nacti sunt? Annon belle admodum hæc Hierarchiæ, Babylonicæ Meretrici, & scorrationum Matri quadrare putabimus?
units.tr: LV. Many marvellous things could truly be said about this Mariolatry, and a great deal too much of it, of such a kind that it plainly shows the superstition of the Hierarchy in its worship of the Blessed Mary to have filled up every number of idolatry. Two famous men, Andreas Rivetus and Carolus Drelincurtius, entered this Augean stable to cleanse it, and they drew the rope of contention against Camusius, Bishop of Belley. There one can read witnesses produced there, outstanding both in number and in authority within the Papal Church, and not even solicited in good faith by Camusius himself. With brazen faces and shameless prostitution of their dignity, as the pimps of this harlot would fittingly do, they sing with full pipes, as the saying goes: that the Blessed Virgin is a Goddess deified and divinized, the ocean of the Divinity and the complement of the Trinity, the infant or little child of the Trinity; that she has power over all the graces and benefits of God and over the salvation of men; that she has full and supreme power of dispensing all the graces of God; that she is the depositary of eternal life, having countless blank sheets signed in the name of God, on which she may write whatever she pleases; that she is the treasurer of the general sacred treasury of God and of the revenues of the Holy Spirit, the chancellor of the heavenly court, the governess of the heavens, the ruler of paradise, the inventor, author and cause of grace, the fountain of salvation and of life, the life of Christians; the book of life in which the predestined are written; the channel of all the graces of God; the sole and only cause why she is most pleasing to God; the mediatrix, propitiatrix and redeemer of the world; the window of paradise; the gate of heaven; the golden gate of the firmament; the ladder of heaven; for whose sake all the deliverances and indulgences under the Old Testament came about; through whom God, as through an optic tube, looks upon all other men; that it is lawful to address the Blessed Virgin rather than God; that in that famous vision of the two ladders, the red and the white, it is easier to ascend into paradise by the white, which is the Virgin's, than by the red, which is Christ's; that monks who tried to climb by the red were thrown headlong to the earth, while those who attempted the ascent by the white entered heaven; that wicked men who had denied God and Christ were freed from death because they confessed the Blessed Virgin; that it is right to pray to Christ in the name of Mary; that she is the Lamb of heaven, that she has taken away the curse, that she forgives and blots out sins; that she is the restorer of the losses of Adam, and that she is rightly called the Altar; that all our sins are submerged in the blood of Christ and the milk of the Blessed Mary; that men condemned by Christ can be saved through the Blessed Mary; that she often annuls the decrees of Christ; that the blood of the Son and the milk of Mary have the same effect, and that a sinner may rightly doubt to which of the two he should turn; that she bruised the head of the serpent; that she is the supreme Lady, Queen, Empress, Monarch, Governess of the heavens, of paradise, of the angels and seraphim, the Queen of queens, the Prince of princes; that God has divided the kingdom with her; that she is the judge of the living and the dead; that she absolutely rules over the whole universe; that she, together with Christ, is the cause why God created the world; indeed that she herself in some sense created the world; that her works are as perfect as the works of God; that she has royal power over the Lord Jesus, so that she can command him at her pleasure; that God is her debtor and bound to her; that with respect to the temporal generation of Christ, God the Father precedes the Virgin in nothing; that Christ, as God and man, imitated the Blessed Virgin; that she gave greater examples of clemency than Christ; that she possessed that Jehovah from the beginning of his way; that she is to be adored, even with the adoration of latria; that she was adored by the angels in the first moment of her creation; that we can be baptized in the name of the Blessed Virgin; that all our actions ought to begin and end in her name and for the glory of her name. What think you of these things and of countless similar flowers, which were praised, with the same number of their own words cited by the same Drelincurtius, in the gardens of more than eighty doctors, bishops, archbishops, cardinals and Jesuits, who published such things with the public authority of Apostolic censors, and moreover with a public practice, by which the faith of the Roman Church is best known, and who were never troubled by the sponges of the Inquisitors; and which also occur in the solemn Litanies and Hymns? And who also found defenders and vindicators in the Roman Church, theologians of no low rank? Shall we not think these things fit quite well for the Babylonian harlot of the Hierarchy, and for the Mother of fornications?

units.la: LVI. Denique Hagiolatria isthæc luculentum maximè absurditatum syrma post se trahit. Hinc enim velut per posticam, sub canonizationis velo, Gentilium ἀνθρωπολατρείας incessit, ut jam Hierarchia non tam idololatriam eorum profligasse, quam novis fucis & cincinnis speciosius adornasse dicatur. Invaluerunt miraculorum impostura, oraculorum ludibria, Legendarum non aurerum, sed, uti Espencæus appellavit, ferrearum fabulæ; & quod præ cæteris Hierarchicos crassissimæ idololatriæ reos peragit, Divorum, qui nunquam Solem vel supra, vel infra se aspexerunt, larvæ, ejusmodi scilicet personæ, qualis illa fuit, quam narratur ab Æsopo vulpes in domum histrionis ingressa contemplasse, dicens: O quale caput, & cerebrum non habet! Ejusmodi Divi chimærici sunt Reges tres, Magorum trium pretextu, confiĉti, Magnus ille Christophorus, S. Georgius, ab ipso Baronio inter Non-entia abjectus, Hippolytus, Longinus, Diva Margarita, Catharina, Ursula, Petronilla, Martialis, Septem dormientes, aliáque ejusmodi Utopica Numina, quæ nihil unquam fuerunt in mundo, & tamen devotè diu in mundo adorata sunt. superstitione omnium Gentilium δεισιδαιμονίαν superante. Taceo Sanctos minimè Sanctos Dominicum, infamem Waldensium latronem; Thomam Beket perduellem, Raimundum de penna forti Ignatium, Xaverium, Philippum Nærium, Salesium, aliósque ejusdem commatis, à Celeb. Gisb. Voetio Disp. sel. p. iii. 520. &c. fusius recensitos. Hinc etiam domus Dei in latronum ementium & vendentium speluncas, prisci ritus in histrioniam theatralem, Agapæ in Bacchanalia, devotæ solennitates in Orgia, piorum eleemosynæ in hypocritarum aucupia degenerârunt. Perculitque inde idololatria hæc scandalo gravissimo Judæos & Turcas, qui in Thalmude & Alcorano Christianis idololatriam pleno gutture objectant. Denique sic tandem, uti solent exoletæ meretrices turpitudinis sensum exuere, decoxit pudor omnis, ut Vasquez de adorat. lib. iii. 1: 5. non erubuerit afferere, ipsum Diabolum posse sub lucis radio, ut & Judæ labia, Asinamque, cui Christus insidebat, absque culpa adorari. Valentianus quoque, uti supra vidimus, idololatriam aliquam licitam esse, agnoscit. Quin ad Gallum etiam, B. Petri monitorem, invocationem olim directam esse, vetusta satis in Bibliotheca Oxoniensi membranula ostendit. Hi scilicet Hagiolatriæ pudendi fructus sunt.
units.tr: LVI. Finally, this Hagiolatry drags behind it a most conspicuous train of absurdities. For through the back door, under the veil of canonization, the anthropolatry [ἀνθρωπολατρεία] of the Gentiles has crept in, so that the Hierarchy is now said to have not so much abolished their idolatry as adorned it more handsomely with new paints and curls. The impostures of miracles have prevailed, the mockeries of oracles, and legends which are not golden but, as Espencaeus called them, iron tales. And what, above all else, makes the Hierarchy guilty of the thickest idolatry is the phantoms of the saints, who never saw the sun either above or below them: persons of the sort that the fox in Aesop is said to have observed when she entered the house of an actor, saying: "What a head, and it has no brain!" Such chimerical saints are the three Kings, invented under the pretext of the three Magi; that great Christopher; St George, cast out among the non-entities by Baronius himself; Hippolytus, Longinus, Saint Margaret, Catherine, Ursula, Petronilla, Martial, the Seven Sleepers, and other such Utopian deities, which never existed at all in the world, and yet for a long time were devoutly adored in the world, with a superstition surpassing all the superstition [δεισιδαιμονία] of the Gentiles. I say nothing of the men who are by no means saints: Dominic, the infamous robber of the Waldenses; Thomas Becket, the traitor; Raymond of the strong pen; Ignatius, Xavier, Philip Neri, Sales, and others of the same stamp, which the celebrated Gisbertus Voetius has reviewed more fully in Disp. sel. p. iii. 520, etc. Hence also the house of God has degenerated into a den of robbers, the buyers and sellers; the ancient rites into theatrical play-acting; the agapes into Bacchanalia; the devout solemnities into orgies; and the alms of the pious into a snare for hypocrites. From this idolatry, too, a most grave scandal has struck the Jews and Turks, who in the Talmud and the Alcoran throw idolatry in the faces of Christians with full throats. Finally, at last, just as worn-out harlots are wont to shed all sense of shame, all modesty has so rotted away that Vasquez, de adorat. lib. iii. 1: 5., did not blush to assert that the Devil himself can be adored under a ray of light, and likewise the lips of Judas and the ass on which Christ sat, without sin. Valentianus too, as we saw above, acknowledges that some idolatry is lawful. Indeed, that an invocation was once addressed even to Gallus, the monitor of St Peter, an ancient little parchment in the Bodleian Library at Oxford shows. These, to be sure, are the shameful fruits of Hagiolatry.

units.la: LVII. Hagiolatriam hanc Iconolatria excipit, à qua quantum veteres initio Ecclesiæ abhorruerint, vel unus Lactantius Institut. lib. ii. 19. sic declarat: Non est dubium, quin religio nulla sit, ubi simulachrum est. Coetum non æquè Tridentini abhorruerunt, quorum hæc definitio Sess. xxv. extat: Imagines Christi, Deiparæ Virginis & aliorum Sanctorum, in Templis præsertim habendas & retinendas, eisque debitum honorem & venerationem impertiendam, non quòd credatur inesse aliqua iis Divinitas, vel virtus, propter quam sint colendæ; vel quòd ab eis sit aliquid petendum, vel quòd fiducia in imaginibus sit figenda; veluti olim fiebat à Gentibus, quæ in idolis spem suam collocabant; sed quoniam honos, qui eis exhibetur, refertur ad prototypa, quæ illæ repræ-sensentant: ita ut per imagines, quas osculamur, & coram quibus caput aperimus & procumbimus, Christum adoremus, & Sanctos, quorum illæ similitudinem gerunt, veneremur. Id quod Conciliorum, præsertim verò secundæ Nicænæ Synodi Decretis contra imaginum oppugnatores est sancitum. Dixit equidem Deus Legislator unicus inter tonitrua & fulmina: Non facies tibi sculptile, nec similitudinem illius, quod in Cœlo est. Contradicunt Tridentini inter anathemata: Imagines Christi, Deiparæ, Sanctorum, in Templis præsertim (adeóque cultu Dei) habendæ & retinendæ, adeóque etiam faciendæ sunt. Dixit Deus: Non coles eas. Contradicunt Tridentini: Imaginibus debitus honor & veneratio impertienda est. Dixit Deus: Non incurvaberis iis. Contradicunt Tridentini: Imagines osculandæ sunt, coram iis caput aperiendum, procumbendum est. Quid est digitum in Cœlum extendere, contra severum Dei præceptum idolis (omnis enim imago religiosè culta idolum est, uti supra ostendimus) inservire, si hoc non est? Conscientiam ipsorum iconolatrarum appello, qui secundum præceptum abscondere coacti sunt, ne populus idololatriam suam manibus palpare possit.
units.tr: LVII. Iconolatry follows this Hagiolatry, and how greatly the ancients abhorred it at the beginning of the Church, Lactantius alone declares, thus: Institut. lib. ii. 19. There is no doubt that there is no religion where there is an image. The Council of Trent did not abhor it equally, and this definition of theirs stands in Sess. xxv.: The images of Christ, of the Virgin Mother of God, and of the other saints are to be had and kept especially in the temples, and due honour and veneration are to be given to them, not because it is believed that any divinity or power is in them, on account of which they are to be worshipped, or because anything is to be asked of them, or because trust is to be placed in images, as was once done by the Gentiles, who placed their hope in idols; but because the honour which is shown to them is referred to the prototypes which those images represent: so that through the images which we kiss, and before which we uncover our heads and kneel down, we adore Christ, and venerate the saints whose likeness they bear. This has been sanctioned by the decrees of the Councils, and especially of the second Synod of Nicaea, against those who attack images. Indeed, God, the sole Lawgiver, spoke amid thunders and lightnings: "Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven image, nor the likeness of what is in heaven." The Tridentines contradict this in their anathemas: "The images of Christ, of the Mother of God, of the saints, are to be had and kept especially in the temples" (and so in the worship of God), and therefore they are also to be made. God said: "Thou shalt not worship them." The Tridentines contradict: "Due honour and veneration are to be given to images." God said: "Thou shalt not bow down to them." The Tridentines contradict: "Images are to be kissed, the head is to be uncovered before them, one is to kneel down." What is it to stretch out the finger toward heaven, if it is not to serve idols against the stern command of God (for every image worshipped with religious rites is an idol, as we have shown above)? I appeal to the consciences of the iconolaters themselves, who are compelled by the precept to hide them, lest the people should be able to touch their idolatry with their hands.

units.la: LVIII. Separare quidem Tridentini causam suam à Gentilium, in idolis spem suam collocantium, causa conantur. Conantur frustra. Neque enim tam stolidi Gentiles, idololatræ quamvis fuerunt, ut aurum, argentum, lapides, ligna Deos, atque in iis, ceu Diis, fiduciam collocandam esse, putarent. Mutârunt enim pro arbitrio simulachra, Deos semper eosdem animo retinentes. Ita Rhodii coluerunt Solem. Ejus antiquissimas imagines fecerunt capitis humani radiati forma: recentiorem colossum ad hominis totius similitudinem fabricati sunt. Mutârunt simulachra Solis; Solem eundem retinuerunt. Non ergo simulachra putârunt Solem, nec in illis, sed in hoc fiduciam, collocárunt. Multa dein uni Deo simulachra struxerunt,nec pro multitudine simulachrorum complures sibi Deos finxerunt.Præterea nova quotidie simulachra confecrárunt,nec putárunt novos se facere Deos. Legantur excusationes, quas ab idolõlatris sui seculi prætextas fuisse, S. Augustinus In Psal. cxiii. Conc. 2. refert. Nempe cùm arguerentur, respondebant vulgares, se non illud visibile colere, sed Numen, quod illic invisibiliter habaret. Qui vero purgatioris,ut ipse loquitur, religionis erant, nec simulachrum, nec dæmonium se colere ajebant, sed per effigiem corpoream ejus rei signum, quam colere deberent, intueri. Vetustissimi scriptores id ipsum testantur. Athenagoras enim Legat. pro Christ. refert,quosdam ex Sapientibus Gentilium dixisse, ipsa quidem idola imagines & simulachra tantùm fuisse, Deos non fuisse, quorum honori ea essent dicata; & quæcunque in ea conferuntur, reditus & sacrificia ad Deos referenda esse, & in eorum gratiam fieri. Origenes lib. vi. contra Cels. testatur, eosdem causari solitos, se simulachra adorare in honorem Dei; alios dixisse,hæc noñ esse Deos, sed Deitatis imitationem, & verorum symbola. Sic apud Arnobium lib. vi. Deos, inquiunt, per simulachra veneremur. Et: Neque nos, aiunt, aras, neque auri argentíque materias, neque alias, quibus signa confiunt, esse per se Deos, & religiosa credimus Numina: sed eos in his colimus, eos veneramur, quos dedicatio infert sacra. Quin & fuisse ait, qui confiterentur, signa nihil habere Numinis, neque ullum omnino inesse his sensum, neque hoc ignorâsse antiquos, sed propter indomitum atque imperitum vulgus (quæ pars in populis atque in civitatibus maxima est) salutariter ea consilióque formasse, ut velut quadam specie objecta his Numinum, abjicerent asperitatem metu, arbitratíque præsentibus sese sub Diis agere facta impia deponerent, & ad humana officia morum immutatione transirent. Quàm similis ergo iconolatriæ Ethnicæ Papistica est?
units.tr: LVIII. The Tridentines try, though in vain, to separate their cause from that of the Gentiles, who placed their hope in idols. The Gentiles were not so stupid, idolaters though they were, as to think that gold, silver, stones and wood were gods, or that trust should be placed in such things as in gods. They changed their images at will while keeping the same gods in mind. Thus the Rhodians worshipped the Sun. Their most ancient images had the form of a radiate human head; a later one was made as a colossus in the likeness of the whole man. They changed the images of the Sun, but they kept the same Sun. So they did not think the images were the Sun, and they placed their trust not in the images but in him. They also made many images for the one God, and did not invent several gods for themselves because of the multitude of images. Moreover they dedicated new images every day, and did not think they were making new gods. Let the excuses be read which, as St Augustine reports in In Psal. cxiii, Conc. 2, were put forward by the idolaters of his day. When they were accused, the common people replied that they did not worship that visible thing but the divinity which was present there invisibly. Those of a purer religion, as he himself calls it, said that they worshipped neither the image nor a demon, but looked through the bodily likeness to the sign of the thing they ought to worship. The oldest writers bear witness to the same. For Athenagoras, in Legat. pro Christ., reports that certain wise men among the Gentiles said that the idols themselves were only images and likenesses, not gods, and that the gods to whose honour they were dedicated were the ones; and whatever is brought to them, the offerings and sacrifices, are to be referred to the gods and made for their sake. Origen, in lib. vi. contra Cels., testifies that these same people were accustomed to plead that they worshipped images in honour of God; others said that these were not gods but an imitation of the Deity and symbols of the true ones. So in Arnobius, book 6: "We worship the gods," they say, "through images." And: "Nor do we believe, they say, that altars, or the materials of gold and silver, or the other things from which the statues are made, are gods or divine powers in themselves; but we worship in them, and venerate, those whom the sacred dedication brings in." Indeed he says there were some who confessed that the statues have nothing of divine power, nor any sense at all, and that the ancients did not fail to know this, but for the untamed and unskilled crowd (which is the largest part of peoples and cities) they shaped them wisely and for their good, so that, as if with some visible appearance of the divinities set before them, they would cast off their roughness through fear, and, thinking that the gods were present, would put aside impious deeds and pass over to human duties through a change of manners. How, then, is Papist image-worship so similar to Ethnic idolatry?

units.la: LIX. Cur verò, sic Bellarminus, aliíque Hierarchici quæserunt, omnes Prophetæ laborant, ut docéant, Gentilium idola aurea & argentea non esse Deos, atque inde probant, quia non loquuntur, non vident, & cœtera; nisi quia ipsa simulachra pro Diis, loquentibus, videntibus habuerunt, adeóque in iis fiduciam collocârunt? In promptu causa est, licet non hæc; quam illi allegant, quasi pro Diis proprièe, non metonymicè dictis habuerint. Nam Esai. xlvi. 6. Propheta dicens, Deum auro, argento à conflatore fieri, significat Dei nomine simulachrum Dei, uti apparet ex v. 5. ubi sic præfatur Deus: Cui assimilaretis me, aut æquaretis, aut compararetis me, ut essemus similes? Cui assimilabitis Deum, & quam similitudinem ei ordinabitis? Id ipsum etiam Catechismus Tridentinus in explicat. præc. 1. agnoscit. Ita Belum Chaldæi pro summo Numine habuerunt Baruch. vi. 4. atque eum hominem fuisse, pro Deo ab illis habitum post mortem, Bellarminus de verbo Dei lib. 1. 13. asserit. Ergo idola non videre non loqui Prophetæ dixerunt, non quòd ea loqui, videre Gentiles putaverint; sed ut innuerent, stultè Gentiles facere, qui muta simulachra tum Deos metonymicè (quomodo Israelitæ vitulum אלהי Deum suum appellârunt, licet in eo, ceu veri Dei simulachro, verum Deum coluerint) tanquam Dei scilicet similia nuncuparent: tum honore prosus, ut Deos, afficerent, ea colendo, adorando Esai. xlv. 6. iis sacrificando Baruch. v i. 20. ea invocando Habac. 11. 19. fiduciam & spem in illis reponendo Psal. cxv. 8. cxxxv. 18. Habac. 11. 18. Eequod enim luculentius documentum est, idola nec Divinis honoribus dignanda, nec similia Dei judicanda esse; quàm quia inclamantes nequeunt audire, Esai. xlvi. 7. os habent, sed non loquuntur; oculos habent, sed non vident; nasum habent, sed non odorantur; manus habent, sed non palpant, pedes habent, sed non ambulant; non mutiunt gutture suo Psal. cxv. 5. cxxxv16. nec est spiritus ullus in medio eorum, Habac. II. 19.?
units.tr: LIX. But why, as Bellarmine and the other Hierarchs ask, do all the Prophets labour to teach that the golden and silver idols of the Gentiles are not gods, and prove it because they do not speak, do not see, and the rest, unless because they regarded the images themselves as gods, able to speak and to see, and so placed their trust in them? The reason is obvious, though not the one they allege, as if the Gentiles had called them gods properly and not by metonymy. For in Isaiah 46:6 the Prophet, saying that God is made of gold and silver by the smith, means by the name God the image of God, as appears from verse 5, where God speaks thus: "To whom will you liken me, or make me equal, or compare me, that we should be alike? To whom will you liken God, and what likeness will you set up for him?" The Tridentine Catechism also acknowledges the same in its explanation of the first commandment. So the Chaldeans held Bel to be the supreme deity (Baruch 6:4), and Bellarmine, in de verbo Dei lib. 1. 13, asserts that he was a man who was regarded as a god by them after his death. Therefore the Prophets said that idols do not see and do not speak, not because the Gentiles thought that they spoke or saw, but to signal that it was foolish of the Gentiles, who called dumb images gods by metonymy (as the Israelites called the calf their God [אלהי], although in it, as an image of the true God, they worshipped the true God), as if they were like God; and who also honoured them with divine honour, as gods, by worshipping them (Isaiah 45:6), sacrificing to them (Baruch 6:20), invoking them (Habakkuk 2:19), and placing their trust and hope in them (Psalm 115:8; 135:18; Habakkuk 2:18). For what clearer proof is there that idols are neither to be honoured with divine honours nor judged to be like God, than that those who cry out cannot be heard (Isaiah 46:7), they have mouths but do not speak; they have eyes but do not see; they have noses but do not smell; they have hands but do not feel; they have feet but do not walk; they do not utter a sound from their throat (Psalm 115:5; 135:16), and there is no spirit at all in their midst (Habakkuk 2:19)?

units.la: LX. Quòd si Hierarchici Platonica, quam Plutarchus de audit. commendat; in alienis peccatis meditatione, Num ego talis sum? Epistolam Jeremiæ, quam Bellarminus inprimis hic legere & meditari jubet, perlegerent considerate, intelligerent plane, & conclusionem & argumenta, quibus scriptor ille utitur, iconolatriæ suæ exactè congruere. Nam ad singula argumenta sic Epistola illa concludit: Unde notum sit vobis, quia Chaldaeorum simulachra, Belum repræsentantia, non sunt Dii. Annon Hierarchici hic se ipsos vident, qui Divorum statuas Divos nuncupant; quanquam minùs Ethnicè, si vocarent tantùm, & non etiam Ethnicorum more colerent, & tanquam Deos venerarentur. Argumenta persimilia sunt. Illic enim Baruch. vi. 3. Chaldæi dicuntur Deos argenteos, aureos & ligneos humeris portasse. Id Hierarchici Divis consimilibus faciunt, ut Baronius Natal in Martyrol. Rom. Aug. 16. de Rocho; Sleidanus Comment. lib. ix. de Genoovefa; de aliis alii testantur. Illic v. 5. Chaldaeorum turba Deos adorasse dicitur. quod ad similes Divos Hierarchici, coram imaginibus Sanctorum venerabundi procumbentes, transferunt. Illic v. 10. Chaldaei Deos suos vestimentis induunt & ornant, ac si homines essent, quo deliramento Hierarchici in similibus Divis insaniunt, usque adeò ut ex ipsis moderatiores nonnulli Monlucius Episcopus Valantianus, Salignacus, Espencæus Hist. Eccl. Ref. in Gallia lib. iv. inter varios imaginum abusus hunc nominatim perstrinxerint, & aboleri optaverint. Illic v. 18. Chaldaei lucernas Diis accendunt, quarum nullam ipsi videre possunt. Videtne melius ligneus Hispanorum Jacobus suam candelam, aut alii Divi cereos, qui coram ipsis accenduntur? Illic v. 20. Chaldaeodæorum Dii atrantur facie suaex fumo, quem thura in eorum venerationem cremata emittebant. Hierarchici aureis, argenteis, æreis Divis similiter thura adolent. Denique ne singulis, quæ ejusmodi sunt, insistam, illic v. 30. Sacerdotes habentes capita barbásque rasas, similimi scilicet Papistarum Sacerdotibus; v. 48. ingruente bello consilium de Diis ineunt, ubi abscondantur simul cum iis. Hanc Divorum quoque, non sui duntaxat, curam Pontificiis Sacerdotibus esse oportere, apud Severinum de vita Hyac. lib. i. 13. Hyacinthum docuit B. Virginis statua, lamentabiliter conquerens: O fili Hyacinthe, effugis manus Tartarorum, & me diffecandam & conculcandam relinquis. Ad singula igitur argumenta, exemplo Epistolæ illius Jeremiæ, à Bellarmino hic commendatæ, cùm concludere mihi liceat: Unde notum sit Vobis, quia non sunt Dii; fateantur oportet Hierarchici, statuas ipsas pro Divis à se haberi, sii idola ipsa ab Ethnicis pro Diis habita hinc conficere velint.
units.tr: LX. But if the Hierarchs would read carefully, as a meditation on other people's sins, that Platonic saying which Plutarch commends in de audit., "Am I not such a one?", and above all the Epistle of Jeremiah, which Bellarmine here bids them read and meditate upon, they would clearly understand that the conclusion and the arguments which that writer uses fit their image-worship exactly. For the Epistle concludes each single argument thus: "Hence you may know that the images of the Chaldeans, representing Bel, are not gods." Do not the Hierarchs see themselves here, who call the statues of the saints Divos? It would be less Ethnic if they merely called them so and did not also worship them after the manner of the Gentiles and venerate them as gods. The arguments are very similar. There, in Baruch 6:3, the Chaldeans are said to carry gods of silver, gold and wood on their shoulders. The Hierarchs do the same with similar Divi, as Baronius reports in the Natal in Martyrol. Rom., 16 August, about Roch; Sleidanus in Comment. book 9 about Genevieve; and others testify about others. There, in verse 5, the crowd of the Chaldeans is said to have worshipped the gods; the Hierarchs transfer this to the like Divi, prostrating themselves reverently before the images of the saints. There, in verse 10, the Chaldeans clothe and adorn their gods with garments, as if they were men; this folly the Hierarchs rave about in the case of similar Divi, to such an extent that some of the more moderate among them, Monluc the bishop of Valence, Saliginac, and Espencaeus in Hist. Eccl. Ref. in Gallia book 4, have named this particular one among the various abuses of images and wished it abolished. There, in verse 18, the Chaldeans light lamps for the gods, none of which they can see themselves. Does the wooden James of the Spaniards see his candle better, or the other Divi to whom candles are lit in their presence? There, in verse 20, the gods of the Chaldeans are blackened in the face by the smoke which incense burnt in their honour sends out. The Hierarchs likewise burn incense before golden, silver and bronze Divi. Finally, not to dwell on each of the things of this kind, there in verse 30 are priests with shaven heads and beards, clearly most like the priests of the Papists; and in verse 48, when war threatens they plan about the gods where they may hide them along with themselves. That the Papist priests ought to have care not only of themselves but also of the Divi, is taught by Severinus in de vita Hyac. lib. 1. 13, where the image of the Blessed Virgin taught Hyacinth, lamenting piteously: "O son Hyacinth, you escape the hands of the Tartars and leave me to be cut in pieces and trampled underfoot." Therefore, taking each argument by the example of that Epistle of Jeremiah, commended here by Bellarmine, I may conclude: Hence you may know that they are not gods. The Hierarchs must confess that they regard the statues themselves as Divi, if they wish to draw from this the same conclusion about the idols that the Gentiles themselves held to be gods.

units.la: LXI. Sed forte Hierarchici non æquè ac Ethnici dicunt ligno Pater meus es, & lapidi, Tu genuisti me.
units.tr: LXI. But perhaps the hierarchists, unlike the Gentiles, do not say to the wood, "You are my father," and to the stone, "You have begotten me."

units.la: Jerem. 11, 27. Adeóque non æquè ac Ethnici imagines suas Deos esse putant. Sed paria facere Hierarchicos, constat. Nam cùm ad Imaginem Sancti alicujus pronuntiant orationem Dominicam, quod Catechismo Tridentino de Orat. tit. quis orandus sit, teste faciunt, dicunt sanè ligno, aut lapidi, Pater noster es. Nec enim, quia phrasi d.screpare videntur, dicere ligno, & dicere ad lignum, iccirco re differunt, quæ Jeremias & Catechismus notant. Siquidem & phrasi, qua Catechismus utitur, uti etiam potuit Jeremiæ interpres, uti passim consuevit, veluti Genes. vi. 13. vii. 1. ix. 13. ubi pro לנ ad Noe, לה ad eos habet; adeóque etiam illud Jeremiæ לץ ad lignum reddere potuit: & Bellarminus de Eccles. Triumph. lib. ii. 23. plenè ac perspicuè morem Pontificiorum oratorum explicans, Concionatores, inquit, alloquuntur imaginem crucifixi, eique dicunt, Tu nos redemisti, Tu nos Patri reconciliasti. Sicut autem, quemadmodum Bellarminus statim addit, ista non dicuntur imagini, nec ut lignum, nec ut imago est. sed ut accipitur loco exemplaris, id est, dicuntur Christo, cujus tamen imago vices gerit; sic Augustinus in Psal. cxiii. scribit, Ethnicos haud fuisse professos, se preces simulachris fundere, quatenus ligna aut simulachra erant, sed quatenus loco exemplarium accipiebantur, id est, prasse Deos ipsos, quorum vicem simulachra gerebant. An ovum ovo similius est, quàm Gentiles & Hierarchici iconolatræ sunt?
units.tr: Jer. 2:27. So they do not think, as the Gentiles did, that their images are gods. Yet it is plain that the hierarchists do the same thing. When they pronounce the Lord's Prayer to the image of some saint, as the Catechism of Trent teaches under the title De oratione, quis orandus sit, they are in effect saying to the wood or the stone, "You are our Father." Nor do they differ in substance from Jeremiah and the Catechism merely because they seem to differ in phrase, between "to say to wood" and "to say to the wood". The Catechism's phrasing could equally have been used by Jeremiah's translator, since the translators often do this, as at Gen. 6:13, 7:1, and 9:13, where for the Hebrew לנ [le], "to Noah", he has לה [lah], "to them". So he could have rendered Jeremiah's לץ [le], "to the wood", in the same way. Bellarmine, in De ecclesia triumphante II.23, explains the custom of the Papist orators fully and clearly: "Preachers address the image of the crucified Christ and say to it, 'You redeemed us, You reconciled us to the Father.'" As Bellarmine immediately adds, however, these words are not addressed to the image as wood, or as an image, but as it is taken in the place of the exemplar, that is, they are addressed to Christ, whose image takes his place. Likewise Augustine, in Psalm 113, writes that the Gentiles never professed to pour out prayers to statues as far as they were wood or images, but as far as they were taken in the place of the exemplars, that is, to the gods themselves, whose place the statues held. Is an egg more like an egg than the Gentiles and the image-worshipping hierarchists are alike?

units.la: LXII. Ast peritiores & cordatiores inter Ethnicos agnovisse, quòd preces simulachris fundendæ sint, ut sunt non ligna & simulachra, sed loco exemplarium; rudiores verò ipsis statuis, ut Numinibus supplicasse, Hierarchicus aliquis suggesserit.
units.tr: LXII. But the more skilled and sensible among the Gentiles recognised that prayers should be poured out to images not as wood and statues, but as standing in the place of exemplars. The cruder sort, however, prayed to the statues themselves as to divinities. So some hierarchist will have suggested.

units.la: Quid ergo tum fiet de rudi in Papatu plebecula? An minùs solemnia insanit? Non solam allegabo historiam unius illius Anglicanæ sub Papatu, quæ in Templo coram statua B. Virginis supplicans, interrogata quid faceret, respondit: Ego huic B. Dominæ preces fundo, ut apud Dominam nostram in Cœlo pro me intercedat. Quam responsionem cùm ex vultu subridentis illius, qui interrogaverat, minùs rectam esse misella conjecisset, retractavit, & Lapsa sum, dixit: Ego precor B. Dominam nostram in Cœlo, ut huic gratissimæ Dominæ me commendet. Non solùm Polydori Vergilii testimonium, sic de Invent. rer. lib. vi. 13. scribentis: Bene multi sunt, bene multi rudiores stupidioresque, qui saxeas, vel ligneas, marmoreas, æneas, seu in parietibus pictas, variisque coloribus litas imagines colant, non ut figuras, sed perinde quasi ipsæ sensum aliquem habeant: & iis (NB) magis fidant quàm Christo ipsi, cujus tamen imago vicem gerit. Hæc quidem Belgici Censores & Expurgatores deleri jusserunt, & recentiores editiones forte deleverunt. At nullis spongiis deleri poterit testimonium Papæ Pii II. Pontificiis approbantibus editum, qui Comment. Pii II. lib. 2. refert, in Ecclesia S. Mariæ Prunetanæ, agri Florentini, Virginis esse imaginem, quam mira religione populi venerantur, tanquam pluviæ serenitatisque donatricem, quum necessitas ingruit. Dives illic Templum est, inquit, & assiduis Mortalium votis insigne. Donator pluviæ ab Ethnicis habebatur Jupiter ipse pluvius, non ejus simulachrum. Unde, Pausania in Atticis teste, Athenienses volentes monumento testari siccitatem terræ, qua laboraverat regio, fecerunt simulachrum terræ supplicantis, non simulachro Jovis, sed Jovi, ut sibi plueret. Sive ergo Prunetani illi imagini, uti verba sonant, sive in imagine Mariæ, ceu pluviæ & serenitatis donatrici supplicârunt, vel paria cum Ethnicis fecerunt, vel eos superstitione sua superârunt.
units.tr: What, then, will become of the uneducated common people under the Papacy? Are they not raving just as wildly? I will not cite only the story of that one English woman under the Papacy who, praying in a church before a statue of the blessed Virgin, was asked what she was doing and replied: "I pour out prayers to this blessed Lady, that she may intercede for me with our Lady in heaven." When she gathered from the face of the man who had asked her, who was smiling, that her answer was not correct, she took it back and said, "I have fallen into error. I pray to our blessed Lady in heaven that she will commend me to this most gracious Lady." Nor shall I cite only the testimony of Polydore Vergil, who writes in De inventoribus rerum VI.13: "There are very many, very many cruder and more stupid people who worship images of stone or wood, marble or bronze, or painted on walls and coloured with various pigments, not as figures, but as though the images themselves had some sense; and they (note this) trust them more than Christ himself, whose image takes his place." The Belgian censors and expurgators ordered these words deleted, and perhaps later editions deleted them. But no sponge can wipe out the testimony of Pope Pius II, published with Papist approval, who in his Commentaries II relates that "in the church of St Mary of Prato, in the Florentine countryside, there is an image of the Virgin, which the people venerate with wondrous devotion as the giver of rain and fair weather when necessity presses. The place is rich," he says, "and notable for the constant vows of mortals." Among the Gentiles, the giver of rain was Jupiter himself, the rain-bringer, not his statue. Hence, as Pausanias reports in the Attica, the Athenians, wishing to mark by a monument the drought that had afflicted their region, made a statue of the earth supplicating, not to the statue of Jupiter, but to Jupiter, that he might send rain. So whether the people of Prato prayed to that image, as the words sound, or to the image of Mary as giver of rain and fair weather, they either did the same as the Gentiles or outdid them in their superstition.

units.la: LXIII. Cœterum imaginibus Christi, Deiparæ & Sanctorum debitum honorem & venerationem, adeóque honorem quendam propriam Tridentini decernunt. non constituentes tamen, qua in re ille consistat; nisi quòd apertionem capitis, & ante eas proftrationem exprimunt. Aliunde ergo honor ille erui debet. Neque rectius quâ ex Concilio Nicæno, cujus sententiam suam Tridentini fecere; consecrationum imaginum formis, & Doctorum in Papatu eminentium, eorum cum primis, qui in Sanctorum numerum relati sunt, sententia erui potest.
units.tr: LXIII. Moreover, the Council of Trent decrees the due honour and veneration to be paid to images of Christ, of the Mother of God, and of the saints, and so a certain honour of its own kind. Yet it does not say in what this honour consists, except that it mentions uncovering the head and prostrating before the images. That honour must therefore be drawn from elsewhere. Nor can it be drawn more correctly than from the forms of consecration of images in the Second Council of Nicaea, whose opinion the Tridentine fathers adopted, and from the opinion of the eminent teachers of the Papacy, especially those who have been enrolled among the saints.

units.la: LXIV. Concilium Nicænum II. quod attinet, simpliciter illud decrevit, imagines esse adorandas, & æque venerabiles eas esse atque Evangelia. Adorationem, honorem incensi, suffitus, cereorum imaginibus tribuit. Quàm de iisdem magnificè senserit, vel illud indicio est, quòd varia imaginum miracula, loquelam, curationem morborum, poenas
units.tr: LXIV. As for the Second Council of Nicaea, it simply decreed that images are to be adored and are to be held as venerable as the Gospels. It attributed adoration, honour, incense and candles to the images. How highly it thought of them is shown by the fact that it lavishly extols the various miracles of images, their speech, their healing of diseases, and the punishments

units.la: Tom. II. pœnas contemptorum prolixè extollit. Act. 2. citatur Basilii illa sententia suppositita. Sanctos Prophetas, Apostolos suscipiio. Quam ob causam & historias imaginum illorum honoro, & palam ADORO. Sed & confirmata in eo Concilio est sententia Tarasii Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, monitúsque ille, ut deinceps etiam σχῆμας venerandas imagines Christi, Deiparæ Virginis, & Sanctorum colere & adorare pergat. Photius quoque in Collectionibus suis inter alia: Hæc septima (Nicæna) Synodus imaginem Christi ἐπὶ τιμῇ καὶ σεβασμίῳ ἢ ὑκονιζομένῃ προσκυνεῖσθαι καὶ τιμᾶσθαι ad honorem & venerationem illius, quem ipsa refert, adorandam atque colendam suffragiis omnibus censuit & confirmavit; cùm adoratio nimirum, & honor adhibeatur καθ' ὃν τρόπον eodem modo, quo in aliis notis & formis sacris sanctissimæ latriæ utimur. Neque enim in illis consistimus, honorémque ac adorationem inibi concludimus, nec in diversos ac discrepantes fines diffrahimur, sed per cultum ipsarum ac adorationem, quæ discrepans ac divisa videri possit, nos sanctè ac indistrattè in divisam illam unámque ac unificam Deitatem sursum ferimur. Aperte sic declaratur, eum ipsum cultum, qui ad Deitatem transit, præstari prius aut simul imagini Christi, utpote qui revera cultus unus & ἀδιαίρετος indivisus sit; & quidem cultus latriæ, qualis soli Deo Altissimo competit. De cultu imaginum Sanctorum, eodem Photio teste, Synodus Nicæna decrevit, quòd colendæ & adorandæ sint καὶ ἀναλογίαν τῆς τῶν πρωτοτύπων ὑπεροχῆς καὶ σεβασμιότητος pro ratione excellentiæ & venerabilitatis prototyporum, utpote per quas in unitivam quandam conjunctivámque virtutem attollamur, cujus beneficio, Divino illo ac supernaturali congressu contactúque fruamur illius, qui rerum expetendarum summus est; ipsius utique Dei. Imaginibus ergo Christi, juxta Nicænos, eadem devotio & cultus, quæ ipsi Deo, latriæ scilicet: cet: Sanctorum verò talis, qualis prototyporum est, atque ita ut, dum statuis & imaginibus eorum adhæremus, idonei sic ad communionem & contactum ipsius Dei evadamus, competit. An ad excitandam idololatriam, vesanúmque & rabidum imaginum ac idolorum amorem & desiderium, potentius aliquod philtrum, quàm Nicæna hæc Sanctio excogitari potuit? Imaginari nempe iconolatræ sic docentur, quòd dum Statuis inanimatis adhærent, & idola colunt, individuus ille actus, atque is ipse sit, quo amplexibus veri & æterni Dei constringantur uniantúrque. Idololatriæ autem universæ hoc κρηφύγιν est, quòd per idolorum cultum devotionis & affectuum cum Deo conjunctio intendatur.
units.tr: Vol. II. the punishments of those who despise them. In Act. 2 is cited that spurious saying of Basil: "I receive the holy prophets and apostles. For this reason I also honour the stories of their images and openly ADORE them." Moreover, in that council the opinion of Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, was confirmed, and he admonished that "from now on they should continue to honour and adore the venerable images of Christ, of the Virgin Mother of God, and of the saints," [σχῆμας] Photius too, among other things in his Collections, says: "This seventh Synod (of Nicaea) judged and confirmed by all votes that the image of Christ is to be adored and honoured for the honour and reverence of him whom it represents [ἐπὶ τιμῇ καὶ σεβασμίῳ ἢ ὑκονιζομένῃ προσκυνεῖσθαι καὶ τιμᾶσθαι], since adoration and honour are given in the same way [καθ' ὃν τρόπον] as we use in other holy signs and forms of most holy latria. For we do not rest in those things, nor do we confine honour and adoration there, nor are we drawn out towards divergent and discordant ends; but through the worship and adoration of these things, which might seem divergent and divided, we are lifted up holily and undividedly to the one undivided and unified Deity." This plainly declares that the very worship which passes on to the Deity is rendered first, or at the same time, to the image of Christ, since it is in truth one worship and [ἀδιαίρετος] undivided, and indeed the worship of latria, which belongs to the Most High God alone. Concerning the worship of images of the saints, the same Synod, according to Photius, decreed that they are to be worshipped and adored [καὶ ἀναλογίαν τῆς τῶν πρωτοτύπων ὑπεροχῆς καὶ σεβασμιότητος] in proportion to the excellence and venerability of the prototypes, since through them we are raised into a certain unitive and conjunctive power, by whose benefit we enjoy that divine and supernatural meeting and contact with him who is the highest of desirable things, namely God himself. So for the Nicene fathers the same devotion and worship that is due to God himself, that is, latria, is due to the images of Christ; while the images of the saints receive such worship as belongs to their prototypes, and so that, by clinging to their statues and images, we are made fit for communion and contact with God himself. Could any more powerful love-potion for stirring up idolatry, and for a mad and frenzied love and longing for images and idols, have been devised than this Nicene decree? For image-worshippers are taught to imagine that, while they cling to lifeless statues and worship idols, that single act, the very act by which they are bound and united in embraces with the true and eternal God, is taking place. Indeed this is the refuge of all idolatry: that through the worship of idols a union of devotion and affections with God is sought.

units.la: LXV. Imaginum cultum consecratio earundem const- ituit.
units.tr: LXV. The consecration of images establishes their worship.

units.la: Quomodo simili consecratione Deastros Gentilium factitatos sic apud Minutium Felicem Octavius narrat: Ecce funditur, fabricatur, sculpitur; nondum est Deus. Ecce plumbatur, construitur, erigitur, nec adhuc Deus est. Ecce ornatur, consecratur, oratur. tunc postremò Deus est. Talis imaginum Pontificiarum ratio est. Cœterùm consecrationum formulæ cultum earundem propalant. B. Virginis imago tali formula consecrari solet: Sanctifica, Deus, hanc imaginem B. Virginis, ut tuis fidelibus salutaris auxilii opem ferat, tonitrua aut fulmina, si valuerint, nocentia celeriùs expellantur, pluviarum quoque inundatio, aut civilium bellorum commotio, seu Paganorum devastatio ad præsentiam ejus comprimantur. Quis sic sub B. Virginis imagine, tanquam sub alis magni Jehovæ se non abscondat? Imago S. Johannis hac fere formula consecratur: Præsta, Deus, ut omnes cum reverentia illam intuentes, precésque coram illa fundentes, pro quacunque necessitate oraverint, exaudiantur. Sit hæc imago Dæmonum sanctla expulsio, Angelorum advocatio, fidelium protectio, ejúsque in hoc loco potenter
units.tr: In a similar way Octavius, in Minucius Felix, describes how the gods of the Gentiles were made: Behold, it is poured, fashioned, carved; it is not yet a god. Behold, it is leaded, built up, erected; it is still not a god. Behold, it is adorned, consecrated, prayed to; then at last it is a god. Such is the method for Papist images. Moreover, the formulas of consecration reveal their worship. The image of the Blessed Virgin is usually consecrated with this formula: Sanctify, O God, this image of the Blessed Virgin, so that it may bring the help of saving aid to your faithful; let thunderings and lightnings, if they have power to harm, be driven away more quickly; let floods of rain, or the stirring of civil wars, or the devastation of the Pagans, be held back at its presence. Who would not hide himself under the image of the Blessed Virgin as under the wings of the great Jehovah? The image of St John is consecrated almost with this formula: Grant, O God, that all who look upon it with reverence, and pour out prayers before it, may be heard, whatever their need. Let this image be a holy expulsion of demons, a calling of angels, a protection of the faithful, and let its intercession flourish powerfully in this place.

units.la: {consecrationem} Consecrationem imaginum formulis. tenter vigeat intercessio. Potens profecto incantamentum ad efficiendum, ut simpliciorum animæ ejusmodi imaginibus, perinde ac si ipsarum præsentia Divina protectio foret, addictissimæ hæreant stupéantque. Consecrationis imaginum in Ritùali Romano Pauli V. & Urbani VIII. authoritate, adeóque post Concilium Tridentinum recognito hæc formula narratur: Præsta, Deus, ut quicunque coram hac imagine Unigenitum Filium tuum vel beatissimam Virginem (prout imago fuerit, quæ consecratur) vel gloriosum Apostolum, sive Martyrem, sive Confessorem aut Virginem supplicìter colerit ac honorare studuerit, illius meritis & obtentu à te gratiam in præsenti, & æternam gloriam obtineat in futuro. Sic ergo Virgo Sanctique alii ante imagines suas pro gratia vel gloria supplicibus, una cum ipso Christo, & quidem ex propriis meritis, & propter cultum hunc, quo ante statuas eorum, ceu præsentias symbolicas, preces fundunt, gratiam & gloriam, ceu causæ sociæ, distribuunt, dispensántque. Hic ille debitus honos, hæc debita veneratio est imaginum, à Tridentinis insinuata. An majus quid Gentiles imaginibus suis deferunt? Etenim apud eos, inquit Octavius, imago ornatur, consecratur, oratur, tunc postremò fit Deus. Atque simili consecratione hic imagines fiunt Dii, utpote coram quibus religiosè & devotè incurvantur homines, simili supplicantium positura, qua pagani uti solebant; à quibus, cohærentibus quippe & conjunctis Divis ipsis, gratia & gloria postulatur; cerei iisdem accenduntur, incensi & suffimentorum oblationes fiunt; festa, Templa, altaria æquèac Divis ipsis fiunt; quæque antiquo etiam Paganorum ritu circumgestari solenniter solent.
units.tr: Consecration of images by formulas. flourish powerfully in this place. Surely it is a powerful charm for making the souls of simple people cling to and be struck with awe by such images, just as if the presence of the images were divine protection. In the Roman Ritual, revised on the authority of Paul V and Urban VIII and therefore after the Council of Trent, this formula is given for the consecration of images: Grant, O God, that whoever, before this image (whatever image is being consecrated, of your Only Begotten Son, or of the Most Blessed Virgin, or of a glorious Apostle, or Martyr, or Confessor, or Virgin), humbly worships and strives to honour it, may obtain grace in the present life and eternal glory in the future through its merits and intercession. So then the Virgin and the other saints, before their images, give grace and glory, as partners in causing them, to those who make supplication for grace or glory, together with Christ himself, and indeed on the strength of their own merits and because of this worship, by which people pour out prayers before their statues as symbolic presences. This is that due honour, this is the due veneration of images, recommended by the Tridentines. Do the Gentiles pay anything greater to their images? For among them, says Octavius, the image is adorned, consecrated, prayed to, and only then does it become a god. And by such consecration images here become gods, since men bow down before them religiously and devoutly, in the same posture of suppliants that the pagans used; from them, since the gods themselves are present and joined to them, grace and glory are asked; candles are lit before them, incense and offerings of smoke are made; festivals, temples and altars are made to them just as to the gods themselves; and they are solemnly carried about, even in the ancient pagan manner.

units.la: LXVI. De Theologorum, eorum etiam, qui Divorum in chorum cooptati sunt, puta Thomæ & Bonaventuræ (qui imagines eodem, quo prototypon, cultu, adéoque Christi & crucis etiam latriæ cultu venerandas pertendunt) sententia discordè non repetam hic, quæ supra thesi xxxvi, dicere occupavi. Certè Azorius Jesuita affirmat, constantem esse Theologorum opinionem, imaginem eodem honore cultúque honorandam coledámque, quo is, cujus imago est, honoratur & colitur. Quod à Nicæni Concilii, imaginibus cultum juxta analogiam (unde Bellarminus, aliquæ analogicum cultum vocant) excellentiæ prototyporum decernentis sententia nihil abludit. Bellarminus de Imag. lib. II. 21. Si, inquit, imago non est veneranda nisi improprie, quia nimirum coram illa vel in illa, aut per illam adoratur exemplar, certè licebit simpliciter negare, imagines esse venerandas. Quod enim non dicitur nisi improprie; simpliciter negari potest. uti patet. At Concilium VII. Act. 7. anathema dicit illis, qui negant imagines esse venerandas. Et quemcunque tandem imaginum honorem & cultum proprium faciunt, religiosum esse fatentur omnes. Religiosum autem cultum Divinum eundem esse, supra probavimus.
units.tr: LXVI. I will not here repeat, in discord, what I took pains to say above in thesis XXXVI about the opinion of the theologians, including those who have been enrolled in the choir of the saints, such as Thomas and Bonaventure, who maintain that images are to be venerated with the same worship as the prototype, and therefore with the worship of latria due to Christ and the cross. Certainly the Jesuit Azorius affirms that it is the constant opinion of theologians that an image is to be honoured and worshipped with the same honour and worship with which he whose image it is is honoured and worshipped. This does not differ at all from the judgment of the Council of Nicaea, which decrees worship for images according to analogy (whence Bellarmine and others call it analogical worship), in accordance with the excellence of the prototypes. Bellarmine, On Images, book II, ch. 21: If an image is not to be venerated except improperly, because, namely, the prototype is worshipped before it or in it or through it, then surely it will be allowed simply to deny that images are to be venerated. For what is said only improperly can be simply denied, as is plain. But the Seventh Council, Act 7, pronounces an anathema on those who deny that images are to be venerated. And whatever honour and worship of their own they give to images, all admit that it is religious. And we have already proved above that religious worship is the same as divine worship.

units.la: LXVII. Frustra ergo Tridentini honorem, qui ima- ginibus exhibetur, referri ad prototypa, quæ illæ repr- æsentant, prætexunt.
units.tr: LXVII. Therefore the Tridentines vainly pretend that the honour paid to images is referred to the prototypes which they represent.

units.la: Nam honorem quendam religiosum proprium imaginibus eo ipso deputant: iis capita aperienda, coram iis procumbendum sciscunt. Et quæ ex Concilii Nicæni II. sententia, consecrationum formulis, & Theologorum placitis allegavimus, honorem imaginum proprium, Divinum, haud inferiorem eo, quem suis Pagani idolis exhibuerunt, esse arguunt. Supra quoque Thesibus xxxiii. xxxiv. xxxv. illud cultus & honoris relativi, seu ad prototypa relati, quem non potuerunt non Nicæni & Tridentini sancire, non potuerunt non ipsi etiam pagani obtendere & revera obtenderunt semper, monstrum debellavimus, & ad viam adulterae pertinere, efficaciter demonstravi-
units.tr: For by that very fact they assign to images a certain proper religious honour: they decree that heads are to be uncovered before them and that men are to prostrate themselves before them. And the arguments we have drawn from the decision of the Second Council of Nicaea, from the consecration formulas and from the opinions of the theologians show that the honour proper to images is divine, and no less than that which the pagans paid to their idols. Above too, in theses XXXIII, XXXIV and XXXV, I have overcome that monster of relative worship, or worship referred to the prototypes, which the Nicene and Tridentine fathers could not help but sanction, and which the pagans themselves could not help but put forward, and did always put forward; and I have shown effectively that it belongs to the way of the adulteress.

units.la: Prætextus Tridentinorum, quod honor imaginibus exhibitus ad prototypa referatur, refellitur. stravimus. Dicant, sic Carolus M. & Synodus Francofurtensis in Capitularis lib. iii. 16. Nicænos iconolatras ferit, dicant igitur, quibus hoc tam peculiare est dicere, quòd imaginis honor in primam formam transit: dicant: ubi hoc legerint, aut quibus valeant approbare. Dominus namque & Salvator noster non ait: Quandiu fecistis imaginibus: sed quandiu fecistis uni de minimis istis, mihi fecistis. Nec ait, qui imagines, sed qui vos recipit, me recipit. Nec Apostolus ait: Diligamus imagines, sed, diligamus nos invicem. Addo illud Agobardi libro de Piƈturis & imaginibus: Summopere notandum est, quia si opera manuum Dei non sunt adoranda & colenda, nec in honore Dei, quanto magis opera manuum hominis non sunt adoranda, nec in honore eorum, quorum similitudinem gerunt. Cùm ergo Divina lex, quæ sim-plex, & ad facilem populi captum scripta est, neque adeò hominum argutorum subtiles evasiones & profundas latebras patitur; omnem imaginum cultum vetet; neque Christus testatus sit, gratum sibi esse honorem per imagines ad se transeuntem, relinquitur, honorem & adorationem, quæ in prototypon transire putatur, in imaginibus manere, quiescere, terminari, adeóque qui vel eas, vel coram iis adorat, etiam præter opinionem & intentionem suam, ex rei nimirum veritate opus manuum hominis, aurum, argentum, ligna, lapides, picturas adorare.
units.tr: The pretext of the Tridentines, that the honour paid to images is referred to the prototypes, is refuted. Let them say, so Charlemagne and the Synod of Frankfurt in the third book of the Capitularies, chapter 16, strike the Nicene image-worshippers. Let them say then, those for whom it is so peculiar to say that the honour of the image passes to the original form: let them say where they have read this, or by what authority they can approve it. For our Lord and Saviour does not say: As long as you have done it to images; but as long as you have done it to one of these least ones, you have done it to me. Nor does he say: whoever receives images, receives me; but whoever receives you, receives me. Nor does the Apostle say: let us love images, but: let us love one another. I add that passage of Agobard in his book on pictures and images: It must be carefully noted that if the works of God's hands are not to be adored and worshipped, nor in honour of God, how much less are the works of men's hands to be adored, or in honour of those whose likeness they bear. Since therefore the divine law, which is simple and written for the easy understanding of the people, does not admit the subtle evasions and deep hiding-places of clever men, and forbids all worship of images; and since Christ has not testified that the honour passing over to himself through images is pleasing to him, it follows that the honour and adoration which is thought to pass to the prototype remains, rests and ends in the images; and so those who adore the images, or adore before them, even apart from their own opinion and intention, in very truth adore works of men's hands: gold, silver, wood, stones, paintings.

units.la: LXVIII. Sed dicant adhuc iconolatræ, relatio imaginum ad prototypa obtineat ne virtute similitudinis imagines inter & prototypa intercedentis, an intentionis iconolatræ, aspectu imaginis, & incurvatione coram eadem intendentis colere Christum, Deiparam, Sanctos? Prius innuere Tridentini videntur, cùm imagines prototyporum similitudinem gerere dicunt. Cœterùm nec similitudo talis religiosi cultus fundamentum
units.tr: LXVIII. But let the image-worshippers still say: does the reference of images to their prototypes arise from the virtue of the likeness that lies between the image and the prototypes, or from the intention of the image-worshipper, who, in looking at the image and bowing before it, intends to worship Christ, the Mother of God, or the saints? The Tridentines seem to point to the former, when they say that images bear the likeness of the prototypes. But neither the likeness

units.la: {a} Relatio imaginum ad prototypa nec simi-litudinis imaginum cum proto-typis; nec intentionis iconola-trarum, incurvatione tum esse potest, tum quia externa lineamenta extra prototypa nihil venerabile & excellens habent; tum quia potissima prototypi pars, mens, sola venerabilis in imagine non repræsentatur: & Pontificiæ imagines ne quidem Prototyporum formas habent. Crux enim Christi, & Christus ipse usque ad Concilium vi. Generale non imagine aliqua, sed symbolo & typo, uti ex Paulino Cassander probat, exprimebantur. Et Christus quidem Agni, crux vero coronæ floribus undique textæ specie figurari consuevit. Unde ergo illa, quæ post Concilium Generale circumfertur Christi & crucis imago deprompta est? Quæ similitudinis cultum religiosum fundantis nota indubitabilis? Par ratio imaginum Deiparæ, Apostolorum, Sanctorum veterum; quas exactam prototyporum formam referre, nemo fidem faciet. Pleræque imagines non aliam quàm barbæ, insignium, habitus differentiam habent. Quin similes sæpe imagines sunt hominibus notis, heri & nudius tertius natis, quandoque insignitè improbis. quos sic honor & cultus ille continget. Quid quòd imagines statuuntur Sanctis Cœlitibus, cœlesti visione fruentibus? Illi verò in Cœlo non corpore, sed anima tenus degunt.
