Docet id ipsum praxis non tyrannorum duntaxat, sed etiam haereticorum veterum. De Nestorio Hist. Tripart. lib. xii. 4. memoratur, quod in prima sua inauguratione ad Archiepiscopatum Constantinopolitanum Imperatori dixerit: Da mihi, o Imperator, terram ab haereticis liberam: & ego Coelum tibi reddam. Tu mihi haereticos extirpa: & ego Persis delendis adero. Plane sic Papa Imperatori & Regibus pollicitus eadem ratione auxilium contra Turcas. Ita Donatistæ, Ariani, Eutychiani, alii summa crudelitate orthodoxos persecuti sunt. Eudoxius Arianus Imperatorem Valentem Arianum juramento adstrinxit ad defensionem Arianæ hæreseos, & diversum statuentium extirpationem per gladium & tormenta quævis. Dioscorus, Zonara Tomo iii. in Theodosio Juniore teste, cum defensionem Eutychianismi suscepisset, orthodoxos Episcopos stipatis militibus (audite Papales Episcopi) ad subscriptionem coegit.
units.tr: Things must be judged by what they are, not by the opinion, suspicion or unjust judgements of men who seek not what is Christ's but what is their own. Certainly the Babylonian harlot never calls saints and witnesses of Jesus those whom she hates and persecutes, nor do the saints and witnesses of Jesus ever call the Babylonian harlot a chaste virgin or an honourable matron. According to Augustine, in his book On the Usefulness of Believing, those are heretics who for the sake of some temporal advantage, and above all of glory and of their own supremacy, either devise or follow false and new opinions. Surely those are not such who oppose the Hierarchy. For in opposing it they seek neither temporal advantage, nor glory, nor supremacy; they are rather certain that by opposing it they suffer the loss of such things. Nor are those rightly considered to devise or follow new opinions who cling to the written Word of God and assent to the doctrines revealed in it, and are ready to yield to those who show from the Scriptures what is more correct. There is certainly no shortage of arguments by which we can show that we are more defamed than convicted as heretics. Long ago the Arians also dared to set the orthodox apart from the common herd of heretics. Let us hear Salvian speaking thus of the Arians: They are heretics, but they do not know it; and among us they are heretics, though among themselves they are not. For they judge themselves so Catholic that they brand us with the title of heretical wickedness. So what they are to us, we are to them. We know for certain that they do injury to the divine generation, since they say the Son is less than the Father. They think we do injury to the Father, since we believe that the Son is equal. The truth is with us, but they presume it is with them. The honour of God is with us; but they think the honour of the Godhead consists in what they believe. They are disrespectful, but to them this is the highest duty of religion. They are impious, but they think this is true piety. VI. Moreover, those whom the Hierarchy persecutes as disobedient to the Pope, and whose blood it drinks in drunkenness, are shown to be truly saints both by their right faith, love and patience, and by a certain lawful prejudgment. For by the very fact that the Hierarchy hates and persecutes them for the sake of religion, and because they refuse to bow their necks to the kingdom of the Pope, it openly shows itself to be the Babylonian harlot. The prophecy brands with the mark of Babylon the Great and of the harlot not those who suffer persecution but those who inflict it, and the same prophecy declares as saints and witnesses of Jesus those who faithfully and steadfastly endure persecution so inflicted. Isaac, the son of promise, was not persecuted by Ishmael, the son according to the flesh; rather Ishmael the fleshly persecuted Isaac the spiritual. The Canon Law itself, in Causa 23, can. 13, q. 4, pronounced this sentence: The spiritual never persecute the carnal; but the carnal persecute the spiritual. The practice not only of tyrants but also of ancient heretics teaches the same. It is recorded in the Historia Tripartita, book 12, chapter 4, about Nestorius, that at his first installation as Archbishop of Constantinople he said to the emperor: Give me, O Emperor, a land free from heretics, and I will give you heaven. You root out the heretics for me, and I will be present to destroy the Persians. Clearly the Pope, on the same principle, promised the emperors and kings help against the Turks. So too the Donatists, Arians, Eutychians and others persecuted the orthodox with the greatest cruelty. Eudoxius the Arian bound the emperor Valens, himself an Arian, by oath to defend the Arian heresy and to exterminate by the sword and every kind of torture those who held otherwise. Dioscorus, according to Zonaras, Tome 3, in the life of Theodosius the Younger, when he had taken up the defence of Eutychianism, forced the orthodox bishops to subscribe, with soldiers crowding around them (hear this, you Papal bishops).

units.la: VII. Religionem certè vi & armis adstruere, & pro-
units.tr: VII. To establish religion by force and arms, and to propa-

units.la: pagare, solius religionis causa, de coetero nullius criminis, blasphemiæ, perduellionis, maleficii compertos, infestare, non Christianum, sed Antichristianum, & proprie Babylonicum est. Pugnat id cum doctrina & praxi Christi, Apostolorum & priscæ Ecclesiæ: cum natura religionis: cum proportione culpæ & pœnæ: cum proprietate veræ Ecclesiæ: cum judicio saniorum omnium. Cum doctrina & praxi Christi, Apostolorum, EcEcclesiae priscæ id pugnare, testatissimum est. Christus quidem Servator Luc. ix. 54. 55. Apostolos suos ob intempestivi Zeli votum, ut ad exemplum Eliæ de Coelo cadens ignis Samaritas Messiam non recipientes absumeret, graviter increpuit, eósque ad Spiritus Evangelici mansuetudinem revocavit. Sed & S. Petrum idem Matth. xxvi. 52. severe castigavit, postquam Zelo percitus, æquissimo quidem illo, sed non secundum scientiam, Malcho aurem præcidisset; palam etiam denuntians perituros, quicunque pietatis obtentu, aut Zelo præfervido impulsi, perdere alios aggredientur. Apostoli quoque Magistri sui, nil nisi pacem spirantis, & præceptum & exemplum secuti, authoritate suadendi magis, quam jubendi potestate, nulla supplicium immanitate, prædicationis Evangelii prima per orbem terrarum fundamenta jecerunt; non carnalibus, sed spiritualibus militiæ armis usi, 2. Cor. x. 4.
units.tr: gate it, and to harass people who are found guilty of no crime, blasphemy, treason or sorcery, solely on account of religion, is not Christian but Antichristian, and specifically Babylonian. It conflicts with the teaching and practice of Christ, of the Apostles and of the early Church; with the nature of religion; with the proportion between fault and punishment; with the character of the true Church; and with the judgement of all sensible people. That this conflicts with the teaching and practice of Christ, of the Apostles and of the early Church is most fully attested. Christ our Saviour (Luke 9:54-55) sharply rebuked his Apostles when, in an ill-timed zeal, they wished that fire might fall from heaven, as it did through Elijah, and consume the Samaritans who refused to receive the Messiah, and he recalled them to the gentleness of the Gospel Spirit. Likewise in Matthew 26:52 he severely rebuked Peter, who, stirred by zeal, indeed a most righteous zeal but not according to knowledge, cut off Malchus's ear; and he openly declared that all who, moved by a pretext of piety or by a fiery zeal, undertake to destroy others will themselves perish. The Apostles too, following the precept and example of their Master, who breathed nothing but peace, laid the first foundations of the preaching of the Gospel throughout the world by the authority of persuasion rather than the power of command, with no cruelty of punishment, using not carnal but spiritual weapons of warfare (2 Cor. 10:4).

units.la: VIII. Secuti Apostolos veteris Ecclesiæ Patres, opus ab Apostolis feliciter cœptum urgentes, nullius se miscere morti (ita Gregorius M. loquitur) ne tum fas esse duxerunt, quando ad Christianos summa rerum pervenit. Nemo illorum religionem Christi aliquo inferre cupiens, armis rem gessit: nemo bellum cum ullo Principe suscepit; quippe qui probe meminissent, juxta Thucydidis illud, τὸν πάλεμον δίδασκαλον βίαιον bellum cen violentum magistrum in religionis negotio locum nullum habere. Longe enim, uti Lactantius Divinat. lib. v. 20. loquitur, diversa sunt carnificina & pietas: nec possunt aut veritas cum vi, aut justitia cum crudelitate conjungi. De Manichaeis audiamus eum, qui in illorum crassis sordibus diu hæsit, Augustinum sic contra Epist. fund. cap. 1. 2. differentem: Illi, sæviant in vos, qui nesciunt, quo cum labore verum inveniatur, & quam difficile caveantur errores. Illi in Vos sæviant, qui nesciunt, quam rarum & arduum sit carnalia phantasmata piæ mentis fere- sereserenitate superare. Illi in vos sæviant, qui nesciunt, quanta difficultate sanetur oculus interioris hominis, ut possit intueri fidem suam. Illi in vos sæviant, qui nesciunt, quantis gemitibus & suspiriis fiat, ut ex quantulacunque parte possit intelligi Deus. Postremò illi in vos sæviant, qui nullo tali errore decepti sunt, quali vos deceptos vident. Ego autem sævire in vos omnino non possum, quos sicut me ipsum illo tempore, ita nunc debeo sustinere, & tanta patientia vobiscum agere, quanta mecum egerunt proximi mei, cùm in vestro dogmate rabiosus & cæcus errarem. Ante ipsum Tertullianus ad Scapul. Non religionis est, inquit, cogere ad religionem, quæ sponte suscipi debet, non vi, cùm & hostiæ ab animo libenti expostulentur. Ita etsi nos compuleritis ad sacrificandum, nihil præstabitis Diis vestris, &c. Athanasius quoque Epistola ad Solitarios in Arianam hæresin acriter invehitur, quòd prima in contradicentes usa esset judicum potestate, & quos non poterat verbis inducere, eos plagis, vi, carceribúsque ad se pertrahere anniteretur. Aque ita, inquit, se ipsam, quàm non sit pia, nec Dei cultrix, manifestat. Similia Hilarius Oratione ad Constantium habet. Gregorius ad Constantinopolitanum Episcopum: Nova & inaudita est ista prædicatio, quæ verberibus exigit fidem. In Gallia jam olim damnati sunt Ecclesiæ judicio Episcopi, qui ut in Priscillianistas gladio, animadverteretur, curaverant: & in Oriente damnata Synodus, quæ in Bogomili exustionem consenserat. IX. Sed & cum natura religionis vis ob religionem facta pugnat. utpote quæ doctore, non tortore indiget. Animus enim externa & corporea violentia superior, per naturam suam velle, quod nolit; & nolle, quod velit, nequit. Adeò enim liber est, ut ne ab ipso quidem Deo cogatur nolle, quod vult, vel quod non vult, velle. utpote quæ contradictoria sunt. Locuples libertatis hujus coactioni oppositæ Scriptura passim testis est. veluti Deut. xxx. 1.9. Ioß.xxiv. 15. 2.Cor. 1.23. &c. Quis, inquit Lactantius Institit. lib. v. 14. imponat mihi necessitatem vel credendi, quod nolim, vel quod velim, non credendi. Et ut maximè te imposuisse credideris, quid aliud, quàm hypocrisin & simulationem, pietati validissimè contrariam induxeris, & fortasse, uti apud Socratem Hist.Eccl.lib.iii.14. Themistius loquitur, ἀλαρργίδα, ὁ ϑεὸν ϑεραπεύονζες purpuræ tuæ, non Dei cultores aliquot effeceris, si veram, aut idoli, si aliam religionem urgeas. Mentis Rex Deus est, quem Stephanus Poloniæ Rex Sapientissimus uni sibi hæc tria reservasse dixit: ex nihilo aliquid facere; scire futura, & dominari velle conscientiis.
units.tr: VIII. The Fathers of the ancient Church followed the Apostles and pressed forward the work they had so happily begun. They judged that it was not lawful for them to meddle with anyone's death (so Gregory the Great puts it), least of all once the highest power of affairs had come into Christian hands. None of them, wishing to bring the religion of Christ into any place, carried on the business with arms. None undertook war against any prince. They well remembered that, according to that saying of Thucydides, [τὸν πόλεμον διδάσκαλον βίαιον], war is a violent teacher, and that it has no place in the matter of religion. For, as Lactantius says in the Divine Institutes, book 5, chapter 20, butchery and piety are far apart; truth cannot be joined with force, nor justice with cruelty. Let us hear Augustine on the Manichaeans, for he had long stuck in their gross filth, arguing thus in Against the Fundamental Epistle, chapter 1: Let them rage against you who do not know with what labour the truth is found, and how hard it is to guard against errors. Let them rage against you who do not know how rare and difficult it is to overcome carnal fantasies with the calm of a pious mind. Let them rage against you who do not know by how great a difficulty the eye of the inner man is healed, so that it can look upon its own faith. Let them rage against you who do not know with what groanings and sighs God can be understood even in the smallest part. Last of all, let them rage against you who were never deceived by any such error as they see you deceived by. But I cannot rage against you at all; I ought to bear with you, as I was once borne with myself, and to deal with you with as much patience as my neighbours showed to me when I wandered, mad and blind, in your doctrine. Before him Tertullian, in To Scapula, says: It is not the business of religion to compel to religion, which ought to be taken up willingly and not by force, since even sacrifices are demanded from a willing mind. So even if you should compel us to sacrifice, you will gain nothing for your gods, and so on. Athanasius too, in his Epistle to the Solitaries, attacks the Arian heresy sharply, because it first used the power of judges against those who contradicted it, and, unable to win them over by words, strove to draw them to itself by blows, violence and prisons. And thus, he says, it shows itself how far from pious it is, and how far from a worshipper of God. Hilary has similar things in his address to Constantius. Gregory, writing to the bishop of Constantinople: This preaching is new and unheard of, which drives faith out with blows. In Gaul, long ago, bishops were condemned by the judgment of the Church for having taken care that Priscillianists should be punished by the sword; and in the East a synod was condemned which had consented to the burning of the Bogomils. IX. But also, the force used on account of religion fights against the very nature of religion, since religion needs a teacher, not a torturer. For the mind, which is superior to external and bodily violence, by its very nature cannot be made to will what it does not will, nor to refuse what it wills. It is so free that not even God himself compels it to refuse what it wishes, or to wish what it does not wish, since these are contradictories. Scripture, rich in this freedom, bears witness everywhere against such coercion, as in Deut. 30:19, Josh. 24:15, 2 Cor. 1:23, and so on. Who, says Lactantius in the Institutes, book 5, chapter 14, will impose on me the necessity either of believing what I do not want to believe, or of not believing what I want to believe? And even if you believe you have imposed it most effectively, what else have you brought in but hypocrisy and pretence, which are most strongly opposed to piety? And perhaps, as Themistius says in Socrates' Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 14, you will make a few worshippers not of God but of your purple, if you press one religion, or of an idol if you press another. God is the King of the mind, and the most wise King Stephen of Poland said that he alone had reserved three things for himself: to make something out of nothing, to know the future, and to wish to rule consciences.

units.la: Cæsar in has poterit juris habere nihil.
units.tr: Caesar can have no right over these matters.

units.la: Atque id etiam Calanus, Indorum vetustus Philosophus, agnovit, cùm ad Alexandrum, amicorum suasu, vim & manum Indorum Philosophis allaturum, hæc, Philone lib. quòd omnis probus liber, narrante, scriberet: Τὰ μὲν σώματα μεταβάσις ἐκ τῆς ἀς τῶν. Ψυχὰς δὲ ἀ ἐὐσαμαι ταῖν ἃ μὴ βάλοι, ἢ μᾶλλον πλήθυς καὶ ξύλα φωνὴν ἀφίεναι· ἐκ ἐςὶ βασιλεύς, ὅπ ἀρχων, ὡς ἀναγκάσαι ἡμᾶς ποιεῖν, ἃ μὴ πρεαιρέμεθα. Corpora quidem de loco in locum transferes: animos verò non coges, quæ nolint, facere: aut citiùs lapides & ligna vocem emittere. Non est Rex aut Imperator, qui adigat nos facere, aut credere ea, quæ non decrevimus. Sed fac, religionem violentia promoveri. Evangelii tamen illa militaris & cruenta prædicatio calamitatis iliada, etiam felici bellorum eventu, secum trahit: perfidiam, atheismum, rebellionem, excidia Rerumpublicarum & gentium, & quicquid honestati & sanctitati contrariatur. Sic pietas pietate perit; & sæpe, qui volunt hæresium nulla inter se esse Zizania, hoc efficiunt, ut nullum apud eos fit triticum. Et quàm denique fœdum illud, laudem prædicationis Apostolicam cum carnifice militibúsque communicare?
units.tr: Calanus, the ancient philosopher of the Indians, also recognised this, when, at the urging of his friends, he wrote to Alexander, who was about to bring force and violence against the Indian philosophers. Philo, in his book That Every Good Man Is Free, reports his words: [Τὰ μὲν σώματα μεταβάσις ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς, ψυχὰς δὲ οὐκ ἂν ἐξαναγκάσαι βάλοι, ἢ μᾶλλον πλήθυς καὶ ξύλα φωνὴν ἀφίεναι·] You may move bodies from place to place, but you cannot force souls to do what they do not will; you might as well make stones and wood utter a voice. There is no king or emperor who can compel us to do or to believe what we have not decided. But grant that religion is advanced by violence. Yet that warlike and bloody preaching of the Gospel drags behind it a whole iliad of calamities, even when the wars end well: treachery, atheism, rebellion, the ruin of commonwealths and nations, and whatever is contrary to honour and holiness. So piety perishes by piety; and often those who want there to be no tares among them bring it about that there is no wheat among them at all. And finally, how foul it is to share the praise of Apostolic preaching with the executioner and the soldiers!

units.la: X. Parùm etiam Religiosa hæc violentia cum culpæ & pœnæ proportione congruit. Ficri enim potest, ut erroneam in religione sententiam amplectatur insciusˌ cùm sua cuique religio videatur optima, utpote quæ à pluribus non ratione, sed affectu dijudicatur. Quis verò nomen unquam sceleris errori dedit, vel pœnam decrevit? Seneca in Herc.fur. sic quærente. Si verò pertinaci quis malitia peccaverit; cùm tamen Religionis jus non homini cum homine intercedat, sed inter hominem ac Deum conscium animi hominis versetur, ac proinde religionis diversitate jus hominum non lædatur, nec violentia, exceptis iis, quos supra designavimus, inferri errantibus, nec supplicia, quæ delictis publicam humanæ societatis destruentibus debentur, irrogari possunt.
units.tr: X. This religious violence also agrees very poorly with the proportion between fault and punishment. For it can happen that someone embraces an erroneous opinion in religion without knowing it, since each person's own religion seems best to him, and since most people judge religion not by reason but by emotion. But who has ever given the name of crime to error, or decreed punishment for it? Seneca says this in the Hercules Furens, when he asks. But if someone has sinned through stubborn malice, nevertheless, since the right of religion does not lie between man and man, but between man and God, who knows the mind of man, and therefore the rights of men are not harmed by a difference of religion, violence cannot be inflicted on those who err, except on those whom we have designated above, nor can the punishments that are owed to those who by their offences destroy public human society be imposed.

units.la: XI. Cum proprietate Ecclesiæ, cujus est non sævire ad sanguinem usque, vim facere, sed vim pati, violentiam isthanc pugnare supra adstruximus. Hæretici contra ( sic Hieronymus Orat in Auxent. ) quos non possunt sermone decipere, eos putant gladio esse feriendos. Cruentas leges ore dictant, manu scribunt, & putant, quòd lex fidem hominibus queat imperare. Probè equidem novimus, sacris literis edocti, non Ecclesiam, sed Hominem illum peccati, Filium perditionis interficere populum Sanctorum 2 Thess 11.3. Dan. viii. 24. xi. 41. & Bestiam, non Ecclesiam, facere bellum adversus testes Dei, & vincere illos, ac occidere Apoc. xi. 7. xiii. 7. 15. Sed & Prophetia nostra non Ecclesiam, sed Babylonem, non vestemagis, quàm innocentum cruore purpuratam; Sanctorum sanguine ebriam induciy.
units.tr: XI. We have said above that this violence conflicts with the character of the Church, whose part is not to rage to the point of bloodshed, nor to do violence, but to suffer violence. "Heretics," as Jerome says (in his Oration against Auxentius), "whom they cannot deceive by speech, they think should be struck down with the sword. They dictate bloody laws with their mouth, they write them with their hand, and they think that a law can command men's faith." Taught by the sacred writings, we know full well that it is not the Church but that man of sin, the son of perdition, who destroys the people of the saints (2 Thess. 2:3; Dan. 8:24, 11:41), and that it is the Beast, not the Church, that makes war against the witnesses of God, and conquers and kills them (Rev. 11:7, 13:7, 15). Moreover our Prophecy shows not the Church but Babylon, purple with the blood of the innocent, drunk with the blood of the saints.

units.la: XII. Denique cum judicio faniorum, Pontificiorum etiam, illam religiosam tyrannidem pugnare, plurium suffragiis probari potest. Pauca adscribam e quibus agmen ducat Theologus Hispanus, Petrus Ximenius, qui Epist. Belgic. Epist. 33. de turbulentissimo bello, quod contra Protestantes Religiosa Gallia superiori Seculo gestit, sic inter alia ad Cassandrum scripsit: Luimus hac in parte poenas stultitiae nostrae, quod ita animati sumus, ut a nobis in religione dissidentes ferre non possimus, nisi simul eos extinctos velimus, atque extinguere etiam studeamus. Addimus deinde incendio oleum ex aliis causis, quae non minus virium habent ad alendas has contentiones, quamvis religionis causa tegantur. Orandus ergo summis precibus Deus, ut arma, quae ipse certe non excitavit, eripere aliqua ratione dignetur manibus imprudentium, ne dicam furentium &c. Sic de Gallicis rebus Hispanus. Ipsa vero Gallia viros habuit sapientes, quibus istud ferro & flammis diversam religionem extirpandi consilium segniter placuit. Cujacius apud Alb. Gentilem de Jure belli cap. 10. negat religionem esse, quae calet in caedes civium, & perniciem patriae. Bodinus de Repub. lib. IV. 7. Si, inquit, Princeps aliquis certissimas de vera religione assensiones animo comprehensas habens, subditos opinionum varietate & multitudine distractos in suam velit pertrahere sententiam, vim amovere oportet. Nam quo majora supplicia irrogabis, eo minus prosicies: cum ea sit hominibus insita vis & natura, ut ad assentiendum aliquid sponte duci velit, cogi nolit. Inprimis Seculi nostri Livius, Jac. Augustus Thuanus, quid de suppliciis religionis causa illatis sentiat, non uno loco prodidit. veluti cum Histor. lib. LXVII. ex Leunclavio ostendisset, Turcas à
units.tr: XII. Finally, that religious tyranny can be shown to be opposed even by the judgement of the saner sort, Papists included, by the testimony of many. I will add a few passages. The Spanish theologian Petrus Ximenius leads the way. In Epist. Belgic. Epist. 33, writing to Cassander about the most turbulent war that Religious France waged against the Protestants in the last century, he wrote among other things: We pay in this matter the penalty of our folly, in that we are so inflamed that we cannot bear those who differ from us in religion unless we also wish them destroyed, and strive to destroy them. Then we add oil to the fire, from other causes that have no less power to feed these quarrels, though they are covered by the pretext of religion. Therefore God must be entreated with the highest prayers, that He may deign by some means to snatch the arms, which He certainly did not stir up, from the hands of the unwise, not to say the mad, etc. So the Spaniard on French affairs. France itself, however, had wise men, to whom the plan of rooting out a different religion by sword and flame was little pleasing. Cujacius, cited by Alberico Gentili in de Jure belli cap. 10, denies that there is any religion that burns for the slaughter of citizens and the ruin of the fatherland. Bodin, de Repub. lib. IV. 7: If some prince, holding in his mind most certain assent to the true religion, wishes to draw his subjects, split by the variety and multitude of opinions, into his own view, he must remove force. For the more severe the punishments you inflict, the less you will accomplish, since men have such an innate force and nature that they wish to be led to assent of their own accord, and do not wish to be compelled. Above all, Livius, Jacobus Augustus Thuanus, of our own age, has in more than one place revealed what he thinks of punishments inflicted for the sake of religion. For example, in Histor. lib. LXVII., after showing from Leunclavius that the Turks, persuaded by their Mufti

units.la: Muphte suo persuasos, existimare, gratius esse Deo, religionis Muhamedanæ causa, Persam unum trucidari, licet professione & ipse Muhamedanus sit, quàm si quis Septuaginta Christianos, à Muhamedanis in religione prorsus dissidentes, interficiat; hæc postea subjicit: Quam eandem sententiam quidem novi Theologi nuper tueri ausi sunt, cùm dicerent, bellum, quod communi Christianorum consensu contra Muhammedanos geri oportuit, utiliùs ad Dei gloriam contra Sectarios, qui inter nos sunt, omissis Turcis verti debuisse. Quod quàm pie & juxta mansuetudinem Christianam dicatur, ipsi, qui conscientiam aliorum moderantur (Jesuitæ) conscientiam suam rogent. Eodem facit, quòd idem lib. 11. Carolum V. scribit Summi Pontificis suasu sententiam mutasse, & arma in Turcam parata, vertisse in Germanos, pessimo, sed solenni & usitato Pontificis Romani consilio, qui eos è Christianis, qui niniam ipsorum potentiam in dubium vocant, capitaliori odio, quàm ipsos Christiani nominis hostes semper sunt prosecuti. In præfatione ad Henricum IV. ex professo & rationibus solidissimis, exemplísque clarissimis, Bellum non esse legitimum tollendæ ex Ecclesia scissuræ modum, demonstrat. Idem animus fuit Nicolao Fabro, Ludovici XIII. Præceptori, qui Balbo in vita ejus teste, & ipse religionem moderata ratione suadendam potiùs, quàm ferro & armis imperandam judicavit. Quin & Curia Suprema Parisiensis Ann. 1535. Regi Evangelicos extirpaturo, propositum dissuasit, æquum esse dictans, ut potiùs Ecclesiæ veteris vestigiis insistatur, quæ non ferro & flammis in religione constituenda, ac propaganda, sed puriore doctrina, & honestis vitæ Antistitum exemplis rem confecerit, Thuano eodem lib. xvi. narrante. Possem consentientes producere Seldum, Ferdinandi I. Procancellarium ; Lazarum Schwendium, Cæsari Maximiliano II. peculiari scripto præcipitia & πεφαχ​s-κινδυνευομένα in Protestantes consilia vehementer dissuadentem, alios; ipsum denique Turcarum Imperatorem, Gentileto in Anti-Machiavello narrante, Papæ A. 1453. Sacrum in Turcas bellum conflanti objicientem, Christum magnum & nobilem Prophetam fuisse, sed nunquam imperasse, ut homines ad suscipiendam suam legem vi & armis adigerentur: neque se quenquam cogere, ut Muhammedis legi credat.
units.tr: Persuaded by their Mufti that it is more pleasing to God for one Persian to be slaughtered for the sake of the Muhammadan religion, even though he is himself a Muhammadan by profession, than for someone to kill seventy Christians, who are wholly at odds with the Muhammadans in religion. He later adds: This same opinion certain new theologians have lately dared to defend, when they said that the war which ought to have been waged by the common consent of Christians against the Muhammadans would have been more usefully turned, for the glory of God, against the sectaries who are among us, the Turks being set aside. How piously and in keeping with Christian gentleness this is said, let the Jesuits, who regulate the consciences of others, ask their own conscience. To the same effect is what he writes in book 11 about Charles V: that at the urging of the Supreme Pontiff he changed his opinion and turned the arms prepared against the Turk against the Germans, by the very wicked but customary and usual counsel of the Roman Pontiff, who pursued with a deadlier hatred those of Christians who call into doubt their excessive power than the enemies of the Christian name have ever pursued them. In the preface to Henry IV, on purpose and with the most solid arguments and the clearest examples, he demonstrates that war is not a lawful means of removing a schism from the Church. The same mind was held by Nicolas Fabre, tutor to Louis XIII, who, as Balzac attests in his life, also judged that religion ought to be persuaded by moderate reason rather than enforced by the sword and arms. Indeed, the Supreme Court of Paris in the year 1535 also dissuaded the King, who was about to root out the Evangelicals, from his purpose, declaring that it would be fair to tread rather in the footsteps of the ancient Church, which accomplished the matter in establishing and spreading religion not by the sword and flames, but by purer teaching and the honourable example of the lives of its bishops, as Thuanus relates in the same book xvi. I could also produce others agreeing: Seld, Procancellor to Ferdinand I; Lazarus Schwendi, who in a special writing to Emperor Maximilian II vehemently dissuaded rash and hazardous counsels against the Protestants; and finally the Emperor of the Turks himself, who, as Gentillet relates in the Anti-Machiavel, when the Pope in the year 1453 was stirring up a sacred war against the Turks, objected that Christ was a great and noble Prophet, but never commanded that men be compelled by force and arms to take up his law; nor does he compel anyone to believe in the law of Muhammad. [προπετῆ καὶ κινδυνευόμενα]

units.la: XIII. Hæc cùm ita sint, tyrannidis & crudelitatis reus est, quisquis lege etiam lata vi religionem promovet, pœnis externis in corpora, honores, fortunas eorum, qui in alia omnia eunt, grassatur; conscientiæ dominatur; inprimis si vim eam proferat in Sanctos; & ut impune magis proferre possit, hæreticorum nomine eosdem traducat. Quid verò hic Hierarchici? Ratum apud eos, & legibus constitutum est, posse, imò debere vim inferri omnibus iis, qui Papam suum non agnoverint Dominum, ejúsque oraculis & definitionibus fidem adhibere & substringere neglexerint; Tros Rutulúsve suant. Quorum in numero non possunt non esse Sancti, utpote qui uni solique Deo adhærentes, nullius in humanæ authoritatis obsequium sese dedere, nulli homini religionem dictanti sacramento jurare possunt. Frustra sævitiæ suæ hæresin obtendunt, quæ nulla est. Non enim Papa & Hierarchici omnes adversus dissentientes, Protestantes inprimis, extinguendos amore Dei, vel religionis salutiferæ excitantur, sed importuno flagitatore, VENTRE & AMBITIONIS immensæ stimulis agitati. Hæ sunt veræ & germanæ causæ, quæ sub religionis & hæreseos dissentientibus impactæ velamento latitant.
units.tr: XIII. These things being so, he is guilty of tyranny and cruelty who, even by a law passed with force, promotes religion, and rages with external punishments against the bodies, honours and fortunes of those who go in other directions; who lords it over the conscience, especially if he brings that violence to bear upon the Saints; and who, in order to be able to do so with greater impunity, brands them with the name of heretics. But what do the hierarchical men say to this? It is accepted among them, and enshrined in law, that force can and indeed must be applied to all those who have not acknowledged their Pope as Lord, and who have neglected to give faith and submission to his oracles and definitions: whether he be Trojan or Rutulian, it makes no difference. Among these there cannot fail to be Saints, who, adhering to the one and only God, have given themselves over to obedience to no human authority, and cannot swear an oath to any man who dictates religion. They vainly put forward heresy as a pretext for their cruelty, though there is none. For the Pope and all the hierarchical men are not stirred up by the love of God to destroy those who dissent, especially the Protestants, nor by the love of saving religion, but are driven by the importunate goads of BELLY and of boundless AMBITION. These are the true and genuine causes, which lie hidden under the cloak of religion and heresy, thrust forward against those who dissent.

units.la: XIV. De pœnis hæreticorum Bellarminus de Laicis lib. III. 21. 22. disputat.
units.tr: XIV. On the punishments of heretics, as Bellarmine discusses them in De Laicis, book III, chapters 21 and 22.

units.la: Nos, inquit, ostendemus, hæreticos incorrigibiles ac præsertim relapsos posse ac debere ab Ecclesia rejici, & à Secularibus potestatibus, temporalibus pœnis, atque ipsa etiam morte multari. Inter alia argumento à legibus Ecclesiæ petito militans, Probatur, inquit, tertiò legibus Ecclesiæ, C. ad abolendum, & cap. Excommunicatus, extra de hæreticis, & in sexto de hæreticis, cap. super eo, definit Ecclesia, hæreticos incorrigibiles seculari potestati tradendos, ut ab eis debito modo puniantur. Item Constantiense Concilium Sess. 15. damnavit sententiam Johannis Huss, & ipsum Johannem, & Hieronymum de Praga tradidit Seculari potestati, à qua ambo exusti fuerunt. Denique Leo X. articulos Lutheri damnavit. Sed Canones & Decretales illæ, pœnas externas in hæreticos statuentes nullæ sunt in Ecclesia prisca pura & incorrupta. Quæcunque vero afferuntur, modernæ sunt, Ecclesiæ Babylonico fermento corruptæ, & Pontificum Papatum & Principatum suum per summam vim, ferro & flamma proferentium. Pertinet huc inprimis Bulla Pauli IV. qua ipsos Summos Reges & Principes in hæresin, hoc est, apostasiam à tyrannide Papæ lapsos, iisdem pœnis & ecclesiasticis & temporalibus immanis illa tigris subjecit, quibus subjicere quosvis alios solet. Horribilem Bullæ illius sententiam Histor. Pap. ff. 273. repræsentavimus.
units.tr: We will show, he says, that incorrigible heretics, and especially relapsed ones, can and must be rejected by the Church and punished by the secular powers with temporal penalties and even with death. Among other arguments drawn from the laws of the Church, he writes: It is proved, he says, thirdly by the laws of the Church, C. ad abolendum, and the chapter Excommunicatus, Extra de hereticis, and in the Sixth Book, De hereticis, chapter Super eo, that the Church has determined that incorrigible heretics are to be handed over to the secular power so that they may be punished in a due manner by it. Likewise, the Council of Constance, Session 15, condemned the opinion of John Huss, handed John himself and Jerome of Prague over to the secular power, by which both were burned. Finally, Leo X condemned the articles of Luther. But those canons and decretals, which impose external penalties on heretics, are not found in the pure and uncorrupted early Church. Whatever is cited for them is modern, and comes from a Church corrupted by Babylonian leaven, from popes who advance their papacy and their principate by extreme violence, by sword and by fire. Here belongs above all the bull of Paul IV, by which that monstrous tiger subjected the very kings and princes, who had fallen into heresy, that is, into apostasy from the tyranny of the Pope, to the same ecclesiastical and temporal penalties with which it is accustomed to subject anyone else. We have set out the dreadful sentence of that bull in the History of the Papacy, p. 273.

units.la: XV. Operæ pretium est, ex eodem Bellarmino cognoscere ordinem, quo Ecclesia Papalis in puniendis hæreticis procedit. Experientia (Babylonicorum furorum scilicet) inquit loc. cit. docet, non esse aliud remedium, hæreticorum coercendorum. Nam Ecclesia paulatim progressa est, & omnia remedia experta. Primo solum excommunicabat. Deinde addidit multam pecuniarum, tum exilium. Ultimo coacta est ad mortem veni-
units.tr: XV. It is worth learning from the same Bellarmine the order in which the Papal Church proceeds in punishing heretics. Experience (of course, of Babylonian furies), he says in the place cited, teaches that there is no other remedy for restraining heretics. For the Church advanced step by step and tried all remedies. At first it only excommunicated. Then it added a fine of money, then exile. Last, it was forced to come to death.

units.la: Note: the right-margin notes read: "De pœnis hæreticorum sententia Bellarmini, legibus Ecclesiæ Pontificia, & Conciliorum decretis inmixa."; "Ordo, quo Ecclesia Papalis in puniendis hæreticis procedit, expertus est, ex eo dem proposito ..."; "perstringi-tur." venire. Nam excommunicationem contemnunt haeretici, ac dicunt, esse fulmina frigida. Si mineris multam pecuniariam, nec Deum timent, nec homines reverentur, scientes, non defuturos stultos, qui illis credant, & a quibus alantur. Si in carcerem concludas, vel in exilium mittas, corrumpunt vicinos verbis, & longe positos libris. Ergo solum remedium est, mittere eos mature in locum suum. Hæc Draconis Romani lex est, sanguine non atramento scripta; neque adversus eos, qui Deum, Christum, verbum ejus, Sacramenta γνήσια contemnunt, lacerant, abnegant; (alias in ipsos Hierarchicos poenæ recciderent) sed adversus eos solos fere, qui Papalem Majestatem dedignantur, Sanctos, vel saltem jurium suorum, à Tarpejo illo Vulture invasorum raptorumque, defensores. Quanquam in puniendis veris etiam haeresibus Ecclesia nec potest, nec tenetur omnia remedia possibilia pro rebus spiritualibus, sed ea sola, quae in ejus potestate sunt, expedire. Cumque eo pervenerit, ut haereticum pro Ethnico & publicano declaraverit, suis jam partibus abunde defuncta, ovibus suis providit satis, dum eas, ut a lupo jam noto & manifesto caveant, sic praemuniit. Neque aliam in haereticos poenam praescripsit. Si tamen ille obstinatus nocere perrexerit, non amplius Ecclesiae, sed Principis fuerit, non belluina crudelitate grassari, sed moderatis remediis & ordine providere, ne Ecclesia, ne Respublica detrimentum patiatur. Neque enim Ecclesia dici potest, quae cruentis morsibus pascitur, & sanctorum sanguine & carnibus opimatur. dictum est Parmeniani, ab Optato Milevitano, contra Parmen. cap. 2. ceu verissimum, approbatum, & in ipsum Parmenianum retortum.
units.tr: Marginal notes: "The sentence of Bellarmine on the punishments of heretics, mixed in with the laws of the Church, the Papal decrees and the decisions of councils." "The order in which the Papal Church proceeds in punishing heretics, learned from this very proposal ..." "...is censured." ...come to death. For heretics despise excommunication and say that it is cold thunderbolts. If you threaten a fine, they fear neither God nor men, knowing that there will never be lack of fools who believe them and by whom they are fed. If you shut them in prison or send them into exile, they corrupt their neighbours with words and those far away with books. Therefore the only remedy is to send them promptly to their place. This is the law of the Roman dragon, written in blood, not in ink. It is not directed against those who despise, tear apart or deny God, Christ, his Word and his sacraments genuine (otherwise the penalties would fall back on the Hierarchs themselves), but almost only against those who scorn the Papal majesty, the defenders of the saints, or at least of their own rights, which have been invaded and seized by that Tarpeian vulture. Yet in punishing even true heresies the Church neither can nor is bound to use every possible remedy for spiritual matters, but only those which are in its power to employ. And when it has come to the point of declaring the heretic a heathen and a tax collector, already amply discharged from its own duties, it has sufficiently provided for its sheep, by forewarning them so that they may guard against a wolf now known and manifest. It has prescribed no other penalty against heretics. If, however, that man, obstinate, continues to do harm, it will no longer be the business of the Church but of the prince, not to rage with bestial cruelty, but to provide with moderate remedies and in good order, so that neither the Church nor the commonwealth suffers harm. For "that cannot be called a Church which feeds on bloody bites and grows fat on the blood and flesh of the saints": this saying was said of the Parmenians by Optatus of Milevis, against Parmenian, chapter 2, as most true, approved, and turned back upon Parmenian himself.

units.la: XVI. Idem porro Bellarminus loc. cit. cap. 22. objicienti, Fidem esse liberam, respondet, infideles quidem liberos esse ab obligatione juris humani ad suscipiendam fidem, neque puniendos, nisi à solo Deo, si non respiant. At vero qui jam per Baptismum fidem sunt professi, eos liberos esse ab obligatione juris vel humani, vel Divini non esse; idea cogi, ut eam obligationem servent, debere. At hæc quoad humanum jus obligatio fingitur certè, non probatur. Baptizatus sanè nec tacitam nec expressam sponsionem emittit, vel in se obligationem humanam ullam suscipit. Totum hoc negotium merè spirituale solum inter Deum & animam hominis transfigitur; & baptizatus sic jus acquirit ad bona Ecclesiæ spiritualia, ut ipsa tamen Ecclesia nullam in baptizatum jurisdictionem, nedum humanam & temporalem acquirat. Quòd si spiritualia ad opus externum exeant, jam propter opera illa externa jurisdictioni externæ baptizatus subjicietur. Si ergo in hæresin veram incidat, & declaret, se esse in ea sententia, quæ sit judicata hæresis, deest quidem suæ obligationi erga Deum; at erga hominem non deest, quia humanam obligationem nullam subivit.
units.tr: XVI. Again, Bellarmine, in the same place, chapter 22, answers the objection, Faith is free, as follows: Unbelievers are indeed free from the obligation of human law to receive the faith, and are not to be punished, except by God alone, if they do not repent. But those who have already professed the faith through baptism are not free from the obligation either of human or of divine law; therefore they ought to be compelled to keep that obligation. But this obligation, as far as human law goes, is certainly feigned, not proved. A baptized person surely does not make either a tacit or an express promise, nor does he take on any human obligation at all. This whole matter is purely spiritual and is carried on solely between God and the soul of man; and the baptized person thus acquires a right to the spiritual goods of the Church, while the Church itself acquires no jurisdiction over the baptized, much less a human and temporal one. But if spiritual matters issue in external action, then, on account of those external actions, the baptized person will be subject to external jurisdiction. If therefore he falls into true heresy and declares that he is in that opinion which has been judged heresy, he indeed fails in his obligation toward God; but toward man he does not fail, because he has undertaken no human obligation.

units.la: XVII. Haud alienum hic fuerit Hierarchicorum de vi dissentientibus, seu hæreticis, quos illi defectores à Papa & ejus lege faciunt, inferenda, ψηφισματα seu decreta in lucem proferre ex famosi illius agyrtæ, conducititii aulæ Romanæ mancipii, Caspari Sciopii Classico belli Sacri, in exemplum è multis, ut cujus Spiritus filii sint Hierarchici, cognoscatur. Prodiit liber feralis non sine publica approbatione Fr. Jacobi Martenisii, Vicarii Generalis Inquisitoris Papiæ, qui librum vulgari voluit justit. In eo dictis Scripturæ obtorto quasi collo in alium & diversum à vero sensum tractis, homo, ut Aristophanis illud de eo usurpem, δαιμονίως ἐνθυσιῶν καὶ κορυβαντιῶν furore ingenti, more Corybantum agitatus, cap. 1. ex Psal. CXLIX. 8. ait, alligandos Cæsari Protestantium Reges sive Principes in compedibus; & Nobiles eorum in manicis ferreis, non in eum finem, ut eos post paucis annis e captivitate liberet ac dimittat (Johannem Fridericum Saxoniæ Electorem, & Philippum Hassiæ Landgravium indigetat) sed ut faciat in eis judicium conscriptum apud Prophetam: (Esai. LX. 12.) Gens & Regnum, quod non servierit tibi, peribit, & gentes solitudine vastabuntur. Paulo post ex Esai. XLIX. 23. Si Reges, inquit, Principesque nolint vultu in terram demisso (NB) Pontificem adorare, & pulverem pedum ejus osculando lingere, iis necesse suturum, ut erubescant & conturbentur in Saeculum Saeculi, & confundantur & pereant. Utque appareat, quàm æger mora, & spei impatiens in maturandam eandem Protestantium inhiet, subjicit, & denique sæpe inculcat: Statim sæviendum in Protestantes esse. Barbaris nempe, Taciti Annal. VI. 32. verbis utar, cunctatio servilis: STATIM exequi Regium videtur Ergo Cæsarem jubet statim ipsos filios Belial & idololatras (Deut. XIII. 13. &c.) percutere in ore gladii, terramque eorum delere, & omnia, quæ in illa sunt, usque ad pecora, infantes & pueros, (1. Reg. XV. 3.) parvulum & lactentem. Eosdem (ex Num. XXV. 4. Jos. X. 26.) in patibulis contra Solem suspendi jubet. Neque curandum Cæsari ait, quo id animo cæteri Reges sint accepturi, quibus scilicet æquius videri queat, supplicio aut pœna corporis remissa, custodiam captivis poni Principe aut Rege dignam. Addit Theomachus ille ex 1. Reg. XV. 33. Deut. XIII. 13. Psal. C. 8. Protestantium Principes instar Agag Amalecitarum Regis in frusta concidendos, idque in honorem Dei. Omnes hæreticos & schismaticos, quippe homines Diis alienis servientes, in matutino, hoc est, statim interficiendos. Cap. 18. ex 1. Reg. XV. sic Cæsarem affatur: Hoc memorabili exemplo (Saulis Amalecitis parcentis) monitus, etiam atque etiam,
units.tr: XVII. It will not be out of place here to bring forth, to show whose sons the Hierarchs are, the decrees [ψηφίσματα] of that notorious quack, the hireling of the Roman court, Caspar Schoppe, his Classicum Belli Sacri, as an example out of many, concerning the violence to be inflicted on dissenters, or heretics, whom the Hierarchs make defectors from the Pope and his law. That deadly book appeared not without public approval, from Fr. James Martenius, Vicar General of the Inquisitor of Pavia, who wished the book to be published in the vernacular. In it, Scripture's sayings are twisted, as it were by the neck, into a sense other and different from the true one; the man, to borrow Aristophanes' phrase about him, possessed by a god and raving like the Corybantes [δαιμονίως ἐνθυσιῶν καὶ κορυβαντιῶν], driven with immense fury in the manner of the Corybantes, says in chapter 1, from Psalm 149:8, that the kings or princes of the Protestants are to be bound by Caesar in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles, not to the end that, after a few years, he should free and release them from captivity (he names John Frederick, Elector of Saxony, and Philip, Landgrave of Hesse), but that he should carry out upon them the judgment written down by the Prophet: (Isaiah 60:12) The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish, and those nations shall be laid waste with desolation. A little later, from Isaiah 49:23: If kings and princes, he says, will not, with face bowed to the ground (NB), adore the Pontiff and lick the dust of his feet with kisses, it will be necessary for them to be ashamed and confounded for ever and ever, and to be confused and perish. And so that it may appear how sick he is with delay, and impatient of hope, longing to hasten the same destruction upon the Protestants, he adds, and at last often repeats: Violence must be used against the Protestants at once. For in the barbarous manner, to use the words of Tacitus, Annals VI, 32, "slavish delay: to act AT ONCE seems royal." Therefore he orders Caesar at once to strike down those sons of Belial and idolaters (Deut. 13:13, etc.) with the edge of the sword, and to destroy their land, and everything in it, down to the cattle, infants and boys, (1 Kings 15:3) the little one and the suckling. He orders them (from Num. 25:4, Josh. 10:26) to be hanged on gibbets against the sun. Nor, he says, should Caesar care in what spirit the other kings will take it, to whom it might seem fairer that, the punishment or bodily torment being remitted, custody befitting a prince or king be given to the captives. That same god-fighter adds, from 1 Kings 15:33, Deut. 13:13, Psalm 100:8, that the princes of the Protestants, like Agag, king of the Amalekites, are to be cut into pieces, and that for the honour of God. All heretics and schismatics, namely men serving strange gods, are to be killed in the morning, that is, at once. In chapter 18, from 1 Kings 15, he addresses Caesar thus: Warned by this memorable example (of Saul sparing the Amalekites), again and again,

units.la: Imperator cavebis, ne si quando Tuos ac Dei perduelles, Divino ac humano jure mori jussos, in potestatem tuam redegeris, clementiæ famam aucupabundus, eis parcas, & gladium in vindictam malorum Tibi (NB) ab Ecclesia datum, sic feriatum geras. Denique, quod Israelitis de Cananæis occidendis Deus Deut. vii. 2. mandaverat, ad Protestantes accommodans, cum tradiderit, inquit, tibi Dominus gentes illas, percuties eas usque ad internecionem. Non inibis cum eis fœdus (Pacem Religionis) nec misereberis eorum, ne sint in ruinam tui. Hoc est, ne si clementius eos tractaveris, Papæ scitu Imperium & vitam amittas. Qui vitæ Protestantium, etiam Regum & Principum, adeo non parcendum statuit, multo minus fortunis eorundem parcit, quin eas universas prædæ exponit. Six enim habet: Deus hæreticorum bona Catholicis dedit occupanda. Ecquare? Si enim (inquit cap. 2. ex Esaj. i. 19. i. Tim. iv. 8.) audieritis me, inquit Dominus, bona terræ comedetis. Et Paulus: Pietas ad omnia utilis est, habens promissionem vitæ, quæ nunc est, & futuræ. Et Servator: Qui reliquerit domum, aut agros propter me, accipiet centuplum nunc in tempore hoc, & in Sæculo suturo æternam vitam. Alibi cap. 3. p. 12. Principes hæreticos ait non esse Principes, sed Tyrannos ac lupos, ac proin Regnis ac Provinciis hereditariis ejiciendos. Ibidem demonstrare conatur, Principibus hæreticis subditos ipsos, aut etiam alienos, nullam inimitiæ causam cum iis habentes imperium abrogare, sibique vindicare posse.
units.tr: Emperor, take care lest, if you ever bring under your power those who are enemies of you and of God, condemned to death by divine and human law, you spare them out of a greedy desire for a reputation for clemency, and so keep idle the sword that the Church has given you for the punishment of evildoers. Finally, applying to the Protestants what God commanded the Israelites about killing the Canaanites (Deut. 7:2), he says: When the Lord your God shall deliver those nations to you, you shall smite them until they are utterly destroyed. You shall make no covenant with them (no peace of religion), nor shall you show mercy to them, lest they become a snare to you. That is, if you treat them too leniently, you will lose your empire and your life at the Pope's pleasure. He decides that the lives of Protestants, even of kings and princes, must not be spared, and he is much less sparing of their property, since he hands all of it over to plunder. For Sixtus says: God has given the goods of heretics to the Catholics to seize. Why? For if you hear me (says the Lord, ch. 2, from Isa. 1:19; 1 Tim. 4:8), you shall eat the good things of the land. And Paul: Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. And the Saviour: Whoever has left house or fields for my sake shall receive a hundredfold now in this time, and in the age to come eternal life. Elsewhere, ch. 3, p. 12, he says that heretical princes are not princes but tyrants and wolves, and therefore must be driven out of their kingdoms and hereditary provinces. In the same place he tries to show that the subjects of heretical princes, or even outsiders who have no cause of enmity with them, may revoke their rule and claim it for themselves.

units.la: XVIII. Satis jam tum ex Bellarmino, Ecclesiæ decretis innixo, tum ex Ardelionis Sciopii, Viri Sanguinum & dolosi horrendo legis Draconicæ carmine (quibus etiam Suarezii, Marianæ, Bannes, Emanuelis à Sa, aliorum sanguinariæ voces, ab aliis pridem notatæ, addi possunt) constat, quæ Hierarchicorum de Religione Pontificia cœdibus rapinisque propaganda fides & sententia sit: & quàm pium Sanctúmque,& legibus congruens habeatur, atrociter persequi omnes qui adversus Papæ imperia vel hiscere sustinent. licet de cœtero illi de Deo, Christo convenienter verbo ejus credant,& puri scelerisque sanctique mundo vivant. Sed magis id etiam ex Sacerimo illo Officio, seu Tribunali Inquisitionis liquebit, de quo paucis nunc & planè ad rem nostram dicemus.
units.tr: XVIII. It is already sufficiently clear, from Bellarmine, who relies on the decrees of the Church, and from the fierce bloody-minded poem of Sciopius, that busy meddler, a man of blood and deceit, with its horrible Draconian law (to which may be added the bloodthirsty utterances of Suárez, Mariana, Bañez and Emanuel à Sá, already noted by others), what the faith and opinion of the hierarchs is concerning the propagation of the Papist religion by slaughter and plunder, and how they regard it as pious, holy and in agreement with the laws to persecute savagely all who dare to breathe a word against the commands of the Pope, even though in other respects they believe rightly about God and Christ according to his word, and live a pure, blameless and holy life in the world. But this will become clearer still from that most sacred institution, the Office or Tribunal of the Inquisition, about which we shall now say a few things, and plainly, to the point of our subject.

units.la: XIX. De Inquisitionis origine cùm alii, tum dedita opera P.Paulus Venetus, in Historia Inquisitionis, susius paulò egit. Summa huc redit. Christus & Apostoli contra hæresin non aliud reliquerunt remedium, quàm correptiones frequentatas errantium, & si callum ii obduxerent, declarationem, ut non secus ac Ethnici & Publicani vitarentur. Nec temporales iis pœnas decreverunt, nec forum pœnale erexerunt. Postquam Imperatores Christo nomen dederunt, ab Episcopis curam gerere Divinæ legis utriusque tabulæ; adeóque æquè vel magis blasphemias, hæreses, perjuria, quàm latrocinia & furta, latis legibus coercere edocti sunt. Hinc contra hæresin rogatæ leges frequentes, & post in Codicem Theodosii & Justiniani relatæ; & iisdem reis etiam pœnæ pecuniariæ, exilia, privationes partis bonorum, vel omnium, secundum delictorum circumstantias impositæ sunt. Executio verò Judicibus Secularibus demandari suevit. In judicio cognitio hæresœos foro ecclesiastico: cognitio facti & sententia politico competiit. Episcopi postquam opiniones hæreticas declarárunt, & pertinaces excommunicárunt, non amplius negotio huic se immiscuerunt, sed alii, ne adversus charitatem delinquere viderentur, ne quidem seculari Judici reos detulerunt: alii detulerunt quidem pertinaces (unde de quibusdam ob turbas potiùs quàm hæresin supplicia etiam capitalia sumpta sunt) attamen, ut sanguini parceretur, supplicârunt iidem. Sic causæ hæreseos in Imperio Romano oɗto fere integris Seculis tractatæ sunt ad divisionem usque Orientalis & Occidentalis Ecclesiæ. Et in Orientali quidem Ecclesia forma isthæc perseveravit. In Occidentali Papa regnavit, in quem omnes jam hæreses immeare coeperant. Non igitur per trecentos inde annos alii hæretici venerant: & si quis casus occurreret, Episcopi judicabant & castigabant etiam permissu Principum. Interea Papam inter & Imperatores dissensiones æstuare coeperunt. Unde Papæ judicio non alia hæresis gravior haberi coepit, quàm Politicorum, Majestatem Papalem dedignantium. Nec dum tamen Inquisitionis nomen innotuit. Demum Innocentius III. Seculo duodecimo exeunte, delegatæ Inquisitionis officium instituit, ad Episcoporum scilicet, uti Nicol. Eymbricensis Direct Inquisit. p. 3. n. 229. loquitur, nolentium aliis negotiis præferre fidei dogmata, negligentiam supplendam. Extant Innocentii ad Auxitanum Archiepiscopum datæ literæ Epist. Decret. Innocent. lib. 1. p. 49. in quibus de navículæ Petri in partibus Vasconiæ invalescentibus adversariis conquestus, de remedio adhibendo sic inter alia commonet: Ideóque fraternitati tuæ præsenti pagina indulgemus, per Apostolica Scripta firmiter injungentes, quatenus ad extirpandas hæreses universas, & eos, qui sunt hac polluti, de Provinciæ tuæ finibus excludendos, modis, quibus poteris tribuas efficacem: in ipsos & omnes illos, qui cum eis aliquod commercium contraxerint, sine appellationis obstaculo ecclesiasticæ districtionis exercendo rigorem, & etiam per Principes & populum eosdem facias virtute materialis gladii coerceri. Ubi ad marginem Scholiastes Pontificius, Fr. Pegna annotat: Hoc tempore nondum erant Inquisitores delegati constituti. Similes mox literas ad Archiepiscopos Aquensem, Narbonnensem, Viennensem, Arelatensem, Ebrodunensem, Tarraconensem, Lugdunensem, & eorum Suffraganeos scripsit, constituris etiam commissariis Rainerio & Guidone quodam, ad capiendum eos, qui Romanæ Ecclesiæ magisterium refugerent. quales Valdenses, Cathari, & Paterini erant. Postea, Episcopis in opere hoc remissioribus, officium delegatæ inquisitionis in Gallia Narbonensi Dominico commissum fuit. qui decem ibi continuos annos in oppugnandis Albigensibus desudavit, alibi etiam æmulo Dominici Francisco. Ac tum demum Inquisitionis nomen percrebuit, eo quod incumberet delegatis illis inquirere in omni loco, quo numero & quales essent hæretici; quis Zelus Episcoporum, & cuncta hæc Romam deferre. Nondum tamen tribunal erectum, sed interdum Judices eo perducti, ut exilio, aliáve pœna hæreticos mulctarent; interdum potentior aliquis inductus, ut armis eos coerceret; vel concitus populus ad excidendos eos conspiravit. Demum A. 1244. Fridericus II. Imperator Patavii quatuor edictis promulgatis, Inquisitores tutandos suscepit, & hæreticis obstinatis pœnam ignis, pœnitentibus perpetuorum carcerum decrevit; atque horum omnium examen Ecclesiasticis, Judicibus Secularibus condemnationem injunxit. Prima hæc lex fuit, quæ hæreticis pœnam mortis dictavit. Sed ipso post Imperatore cum tribus Pontificibus collisio, hæresis Papæ magisterium excutientium altiores radices egit. Post mortem Imperatoris Innocentius IV. in Longobardia, aliisque Italiæ partibus rerum arbiter, Dominicanos & Franciscanos fratres, ad prædicandum, cruce signatos congregandum, exequendásque extra ordinem leges misit, authoritatem stabilem, & tribunal perpetuum, in quo Inquisitori junctus erat Episcopus, sed dicis gratia; hac in re iisdem imperticiens. Ne vero Potestas secularis exclusa videretur, ei potestas nominandi Ministros Inquisitionis, è quibus quos vellet Papa eligeret, relinquebatur. Anno 1484. Rex Ferdinandus Catholicus, Muhamedanorum in Granata extirpato Imperio, ad expurganda à Judæis & Muhammedanis propria & uxoris Isabellæ Regna, Sixto IV. consentiente in omnibus Hispaniæ, Siciliæ & Sardiniæ Regnis, nec quicquam Arragoniis armata etiam vi resistentibus (nam victi occisorum sanguine tinctas leges recipere coacti sunt) tribunal Inquisitionis erexit ea forma, qua hodiéque extat, & in hæreses insuper seu veras, seu fictas grassatur. Forma autem ejusmodi est. Rex Inquisitorem generalem per omnia Regna sua nominat. Eundem Papa confirmat. Electus & confirmatus pro singulis locis Inquisitores particulares nominat. Eosdem Rex confirmat. Senatum etiam Rex in loco, ubi curia est, deputat, cujus Præses est Inquisitor supremus. Hic Senatus Summam potestatem exercet, leges condit, controversias inter Inquisitores dirimit, provocationes audit, soli Regi subest. In Regnum Neapolitanum & Belgium, quantumvis niterentur Hispani maximè, introducere non potuerunt. Venetiis A. 1289. Papa Nicolao IV. annitente, creatum fuit partim, ex Secularibus, partim ex Ecclesiasticis judicibus consistens; cujus leges longè ab Hispanicis diversas idem, qui supra, Paulus Venetus, collegit & exposuit. Romam Paulus IV. in oraculo Malachiæ Draco & Leo designatus, Phalaridis illum bovem intulit. non sine turbis gravissimis, moriente eo, consecutis. quas post Thuanum, Paulum Venetum, alios Pallavicinus Histor. Concil. Trid. lib. xiv. 9. 5 copiosè tradit.
units.tr: XIX. Many have written about the origin of the Inquisition, and Paulus Venetus, in his History of the Inquisition, has done so at some length and with deliberate care. The sum comes to this. Against heresy, Christ and the Apostles left no other remedy than frequent corrections of those in error and, if they hardened themselves, a declaration that they were to be shunned no differently than heathens and tax collectors. Neither did they decree temporal punishments for them nor set up a penal court. After the Emperors gave their name to Christ, the bishops were taught to take charge of both tables of divine law, and so to restrain by enacted laws blasphemies, heresies and perjuries, which are equal to or worse than robberies and thefts. Hence frequent laws were passed against heresy, later incorporated into the Codes of Theodosius and Justinian, and for the same offenders pecuniary penalties, exile, and deprivation of part or all of their goods were imposed, according to the circumstances of the offences. The execution, however, was usually entrusted to secular judges. In a trial, the investigation of heresy belonged to the ecclesiastical forum; the investigation of the fact and the sentence belonged to the civil power. After the bishops had declared heretical opinions and excommunicated the obstinate, they no longer mixed themselves in this business; but others, so as not to seem to offend against charity, did not even hand the accused over to the secular judge. Others did indeed hand over the obstinate (whence on some occasions capital punishments were taken, on account of disturbances rather than heresy), yet the same bishops entreated that blood be spared. Thus cases of heresy were handled in the Roman Empire for almost eight whole centuries, up to the division of the Eastern and Western Church. In the Eastern Church this form remained. In the Western, the Pope reigned, and into him all heresies had begun to flow. Therefore for three hundred years after that no other heretics appeared; and if some case arose, the bishops judged and punished, even with the permission of the princes. Meanwhile disputes began to seethe between the Pope and the Emperors. Hence, in the Pope's judgement, no heresy began to be regarded as graver than that of the politicians who disdained the papal majesty. Yet the name of the Inquisition was not yet known. At last Innocent III, at the end of the twelfth century, established the office of a delegated Inquisition, to supply the negligence of the bishops, as Nicolaus Eymericus says in his Directorium, Inquisit. p. 3. n. 229, of those unwilling to put the dogmas of faith before other business. There survives a letter of Innocent to the Archbishop of Auch, Epist. Decret. Innocent. lib. 1. p. 49, in which, complaining of the adversaries of the little ship of Peter growing strong in the regions of Gascony, he advises among other things a remedy in these words: Therefore we grant your brotherhood by this present writing, firmly enjoining by apostolic letters, that you should, by whatever means you can, bring about the uprooting of all heresies and the expulsion from the borders of your province of those who are polluted by them; that you should exercise the rigour of ecclesiastical discipline against them and all who have contracted any dealings with them, without the hindrance of appeal, and also cause them to be restrained by the princes and people by the power of the material sword. Here the Papist commentator Fr. Pegna notes in the margin: At this time the delegated inquisitors had not yet been appointed. Soon he wrote similar letters to the Archbishops of Aix, Narbonne, Vienne, Arles, Embrun, Tarragona, Lyons, and their suffragans, appointing commissioners, Rainerius and a certain Guy, to seize those who fled the teaching authority of the Roman Church, such as the Waldensians, Cathari and Paterines. Later, since the bishops were too slack in this work, the office of the delegated Inquisition was entrusted to Dominic in Narbonese Gaul, who sweated for ten continuous years there in assailing the Albigenses, and elsewhere also with his rival Francis. And then at last the name Inquisition became common, because those delegates were to inquire in every place how many and what sort of heretics there were; such was the zeal of the bishops, and they reported all this to Rome. Still no tribunal had been set up; but sometimes the judges were brought to exile or other punishment to fine the heretics, sometimes some more powerful man was induced to restrain them by arms, or the people, stirred up, conspired to wipe them out. At last, in 1244, the Emperor Frederick II, at Padua, issued four edicts, took the inquisitors under his protection, and decreed the penalty of fire for obstinate heretics and perpetual imprisonment for penitent ones; and he enjoined that the examination of all these should belong to the ecclesiastical judges, and the condemnation to the secular judges. This was the first law that prescribed the penalty of death for heretics. But after the Emperor's death, the conflict with three Popes allowed the heresy of those who shook off the Pope's teaching to strike deeper roots. After the death of the Emperor, Innocent IV, master of affairs in Lombardy and other parts of Italy, sent the Dominican and Franciscan friars, signed with the cross, to preach, to gather men, and to execute the laws outside the ordinary course; he established a fixed authority and a permanent tribunal, in which a bishop was joined to the inquisitor, but only for show; in this matter he yielded everything to the friars. Lest the secular power seem to be excluded, it was left with the power of nominating the ministers of the Inquisition, from whom the Pope might choose whomever he wished. In 1484, King Ferdinand the Catholic, after the Muhammadan empire in Granada had been destroyed, wanting to purge his own kingdoms and those of his wife Isabella of Jews and Muslims, with Sixtus IV consenting, set up in all the kingdoms of Spain, Sicily and Sardinia, and in Aragon also, where people resisted even by armed force (for the conquered, forced to accept laws stained with the blood of the slain), a tribunal of the Inquisition in the form in which it still exists today, and which rages against heresies, whether real or invented. The form of it is as follows. The King nominates a Grand Inquisitor for all his kingdoms. The Pope confirms him. The one elected and confirmed nominates particular inquisitors for individual places. The King confirms these. The King also appoints a Council in the place where the court is, whose president is the Supreme Inquisitor. This Council exercises supreme power, makes laws, settles disputes between the inquisitors, hears appeals, and is subject to the King alone. They could not introduce it into the Kingdom of Naples or Belgium, however much the Spaniards strove. At Venice, in 1289, with Pope Nicholas IV pressing, a court was set up consisting partly of secular and partly of ecclesiastical judges; its laws, far different from the Spanish ones, were collected and set out by the same Paulus Venetus mentioned above. At Rome, Paul IV, who was marked out as the Dragon and the Lion in the oracle of Malachi, brought in that bull of Phalaris; and when he died, very grave disturbances followed, which Thuanus, Paulus Venetus and others, and Pallavicini in his History of the Council of Trent, book 14, ch. 9, relate at length.

units.la: XX. Ere nobis visum est, erecti tribunalis hujus historiam paucis pertexere. ut vel ex ejus eruta origine haud certè Apostolica, sed novissima, quando in Ecclesiam apostasia & ὁ Ἀνομος Exlex ille incessit, confstet, stet, Pontificiæ dominationis & tyrannidis apicem esse. Verè dico, tyrannidis. Horribili enim immanitate, in Hispanico-Romana inprimis, per Dominicanos fratres, exerceri solet. Nam in speciem quidem ad extirpandas hæreses comparata, ut primùm Inquisitor comperit, aliquem in quodam Fidei capite à Romana Ecclesia dissentire, nova & sanguinaria disputandi ratione, & tortoribus, carnificibúsque magis, quàm Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, Pontificibúsque conveniente, confestim ei Syllogismum opponit, exigne, aqua aut laqueo confectum; qui fortiùs, quàm qui primæ figuræ, & modi Barbara dicuntur, stringat, & ubi mors necessario conclusionem ingrediatur. Revera tamen, ut sub malis olim Principibus, Tacito Annal. iii. 67. teste, Majestatis crimen: ita hæc vinculum est ac necessitas silendi; & Neapolitanorum ipsorum apud Thuanum lib. iii. judicio in id potissimùm inventa, ut eversis ista ratione omnium fortunis, liberis capitibus periculum creetur. Quàm impatiente rigidáque cervice Hispanico-Romani homines hoc immane jugum ferant, scimus. Non mittere ingenuam vocem, non ducere liberum spiritum cuiquam permittitur. Voluntas, ratio, cogitatio hominis, in quam nullus unquam tyrannus imperium tenuit, in vilis sacrificuli vel Monachi potestate hæret. Jubet ille vetátque quod videtur. Præscribit vivendi sentiendíque rationem quæ allubescat. Non inquirere in veritatem, non expendere religionis mandatæ certitudinem licet. Dispereas, si latum unguem à mente sensúque præscripto deflectas. Ad inferorum portas relegeris, si aut imperanti quicquam recuses, aut dicentis, vel distantis verba in dubium revoces. Non ita ullum mancipium fuit sub potestate domini; non ita quisquam dominantis servivit libidini, ac populus Christianus Capitolini tyranni edictis; suo exemptus arbitrio, & sub jura aliena missus. Sic Tibi, Libertas Ecclesiæ dotalis, os occluditur: Tibi, Sanctissime Prophetæ Christi Spiritus, frænum injicitur, ut alienæ mancipatus libidini, neque audeas liberè sentire, neque animi sensa profiteri!
units.tr: XX. It seems good to us to set out briefly the history of this tribunal, so that from its origin, which is certainly not apostolic but very recent (since apostasy and that Lawless one [ὁ Ἄνομος] crept into the Church), it may be established that it is the summit of Papal domination and tyranny. I say truly: tyranny. For it is usually exercised with horrible savagery, above all in the Spanish-Roman sphere, by the Dominican friars. In appearance it was devised to root out heresies. But as soon as the Inquisitor learns that someone dissents from the Roman Church on some article of faith, he at once confronts him with a new and bloody method of disputation, one suited to torturers and executioners rather than to teachers of the Church or to Popes: a syllogism made of fire, water or the noose. It presses harder than the figures and moods called Barbara in the first figure, and where death must enter as the conclusion. Yet in truth, as Tacitus testifies (Annals iii. 67) under the wicked princes of old, this was the crime of treason: so too this is a bond and a necessity of silence; and by the judgment of the Neapolitans themselves in Thuanus (book iii.), it was devised chiefly for this purpose, so that, with everyone's fortunes overturned by this method, danger is created for free heads. We know how impatiently and stiff-necked the Spanish-Roman people bear this monstrous yoke. No one is permitted to send forth a free voice or to draw a free breath. The will, reason and thought of a man, over which no tyrant has ever held sway, cling to the power of some wretched little priest or monk. He commands and forbids whatever pleases him. He prescribes whatever way of living and thinking he likes. One may not inquire into the truth or weigh the certainty of the religion handed down. You will perish if you deviate by a hair's breadth from the mind and opinion prescribed. You will be banished to the gates of hell if you either refuse anything he commands, or call into doubt the words of him who speaks or of him who dissents. No slave was ever so under the power of a master, no people ever so served the whim of a ruler, as the Christian people serve the edicts of the Capitoline tyrant, stripped of their own judgment and handed over to alien laws. Thus, O Liberty, the dowry of the Church, your mouth is stopped! Thus, O Spirit of Christ, most holy prophet, a bridle is put upon you, so that, enslaved to another's lust, you dare neither to think freely nor to profess what your mind feels!

units.la: XXI. Sed singula penitius lustremus. ut de tremendi tribunalis hujus injustitia & tyrannide melius constet. Judices ergo sunt non illi, quibus omnes animas Divina potestas, & omnis ratio subjecit; sed homines de claustris, Monachi, quorum erat plangere, non plangenda committere, plangúmque innocentum ciere. Et Monachi quidem tales, quos Jurisconsultos esse quàm Theologos, longè præstare, contra Michaelem Zanardum Diana Par. iv. Tract. 8. Resol. 52. severè pertendit. Illi habent carceres: habent torturas: habent patibula: habent ignes: habent falces & secures. Jam fraternosi Inquisitores facti sunt vel ipsis Principibus formidabiles. Hinc vires, hincque arma sumpserunt, quibus obvio cuivis, pro veritate contra Romanæ Curiæ errores & intolerandam idolomaniam vel hiscere auso, vim horribiliter inferrent. Papæ hæretici, quos pro sua libidine tales esse affirmat. Hos ergo ferro flammáque, Papæ & Inquisitoribus ejus à Principibus Divini juris ignaris, & humani negligentibus, ac forte etiam subditorum expilandis bonis, & diadematis peregrinorum Principum, quos Papa hæreticos declarat, capitibus excutiendis, intentis; in manus tradita persequi fas est.
units.tr: XXI. But let us examine the individual points more closely, so that the injustice and tyranny of this dreadful tribunal may be better established. The judges, then, are not those to whom divine power and all reason have subjected every soul, but men from the cloisters, monks, whose task was to lament and not to commit what is lamentable, and to raise the wailing of the innocent. And such monks, whom Michael Zanardus in Diana, Part 4, Tract 8, Resol. 52, severely maintains are far better jurists than theologians. They have prisons; they have torture; they have gibbets; they have fires; they have sickles and axes. Now the brother Inquisitors have become feared even by the princes themselves. From here they have taken up powers and weapons, by which they might horribly inflict violence on anyone at all who dared to open his mouth in defence of truth against the errors of the Roman Curia and its intolerable idolatry. Those whom the Pope declares heretics at his own whim: it is lawful to pursue these with sword and fire, once they have been handed over into the hands of the Pope and his Inquisitors by princes who are ignorant of divine law and careless of human law, and who are perhaps also intent on plundering their subjects' goods, and on striking the crowns from the heads of foreign princes whom the Pope declares heretics.

units.la: XXII. Quam vero Monachi illi, unde, à quo potestatem habent? Delegatam dicunt à Romano Pontifice; nonnulli etiam ordinariam dicunt; uti apud Dianam Par. iv. Tract. 8. Resol. 1. Barbosa, saltem quoad Inquisitorem generalem, pertendit; alii, uti ipse Diana Sanctarellum secutus, Valde accedentem ad ordinariam. Annon verò quilibet Episcopus vel pastor Ecclesiæ
units.tr: XXII. But from whom and from what source do those monks have their power? They say it is delegated by the Roman Pontiff; some also say it is ordinary, as Diana does in Part 4, Tract 8, Resol. 1. Barbosa maintains this, at least as regards the Inquisitor General; others, as Diana himself following Sanctarellus, say that it comes very close to being ordinary. But is not every bishop, or minister of the Church, the shepherd of his own flock?

units.la: y fiæ gregis sui pastor est? Annon pastoris cujusvis est, lupos cognoscere, & cos à grege suo convenientibus remediis abigere? Si quis negligentius rem agit, sunt vicini, sunt præpositi alii: & in Papatu quidem Metropolitani, Primates, Patriarchæ. Cur etiam, ubi diligentissimi & doctissimi Episcopi sunt, suos Papa Inquisitores Monachos habet? Cur in alienam falcem messem mittit? Si hæreses glisccunt, Pastores & Episcopi primi sunt, qui eas olfaciunt, Synodi Provinciales discutiunt, ac, si necessitas postulaverit, Nationales & Generales damnant: Principes legitimis mediis exterminant. Caruit Ecclesia Inquisitoribus ejusmodi, caruit tribunali mille integros ducentos annos. Quid igitur hoc monstri? Sed mirum profecto non est, ex Papatu monstro horrendo, monstra alia permulta indies gigni. Nam perpetuò jam non Africa, sed Roma portenta nova profert. Intererat etiam Papæ, Episcopis ejus crescentem potentiam pridem obliquis oculis limantibus, tales deligere, quibus, ceu dominationis suæ instrumentis, nexu & mancupio sibi devinctis turò confidere posset.
units.tr: Is it not the duty of any shepherd to recognise wolves and to drive them away from his flock by suitable remedies? If someone deals with the matter too carelessly, there are neighbours, there are other superiors: and in the Papacy, indeed, metropolitans, primates and patriarchs. Why too, where there are very diligent and learned bishops, does the Pope have his own Inquisitors, monks? Why does he put his sickle into another man's harvest? If heresies grow, the ministers and bishops are the first to scent them out, provincial synods examine them, and, if necessity demands, national and general synods condemn them; princes exterminate them by lawful means. The Church lacked inquisitors of this kind, and lacked such a tribunal, for a full twelve hundred years. What, then, is this monster? But it is certainly no wonder that from the horrible monster of the Papacy many other monsters are born every day. For now it is not Africa but Rome that constantly produces new portents. It was also in the Pope's interest, while his bishops were long watching the growing power with sidelong glances, to choose such men as, instruments of his dominion, bound to him by ties and bondage, he could rely on securely.

units.la: XXIII. Incompetens ergo planè tribunalis hujus judex est.
units.tr: XXIII. The judge of this tribunal is therefore plainly incompetent.

units.la: Sed cujusmodi ille judicii sui normam sequitur? Malo id Cornelii Agrippæ, testis idonei, utpote qui non semel cum monstris his conflixit, quàm meis verbis recitare. Sic autem ille de vanit. Scient. cap. 96. hanc in rem scribit: Inquisitorum jurisdictio cum tota in Theologicis traditionibus & sacris Scripturis fundata esse deberet, ipsi tamen hanc omnem ex jure canonico & Pontificiis decretis, ac si Papam errare impossibile sit, crudelissimè exercent, ipsam Scripturam Sacram velut mortuam literam, & non nisi umbram veritatis à tergo relinquentes, quin & veluti hæreticorum, ut ajunt, scutum & propugnaculum procul rejiciunt. Neque etiam antiquo-
units.tr: But what norm does he follow in his judgment? I prefer to recite it in the words of Cornelius Agrippa, a reliable witness, since he has more than once contended with these monsters, rather than in my own words. In de vanit. Scient. cap. 96. he writes on this matter as follows: The jurisdiction of the inquisitors, though it ought to be founded wholly on theological traditions and holy Scripture, they nonetheless exercise most cruelly from canon law and papal decrees, as if it were impossible for the Pope to err, leaving holy Scripture itself behind as a dead letter and only a shadow of the truth, and even casting it far away as the shield and bulwark, so they say, of heretics.
