Nor even the ancient-

units.la: Judicii illorum norma ex Cornelio Agrippa exponitur; non verbum Dei, vel recta ratio, sed Pontificum decreta Pontificia. tiquorum doctorum Patrumque traditiones recipiunt, dicentes: quia falli possunt & fallere; sed unam Romanam Ecclesiam, quæ, ut dicunt, errare non potest, cujus caput Papa est; ejusque curiæ stylum sibi scopum fidei præfigunt, non aliud cum inquirendo expostulantes, quàm si credat in Romanam Ecclesiam. Quòd si affirmárit, dicunt illico: Ecclesia Romana hanc propositionem aut hæreticam, aut scandalosam, aut piarum animarum offensivam, aut Ecclesiasticæ potestatis derogativam damnat, mox ad palinodiam & revocationem compellunt. Quòd si tunc inquisitus opinionem suam Scripturæ testimoniis, aliisve rationibus tueri conetur, interrumpentes strepitu iratis buccis dicunt, non esse illi negotium cum baccalaureis & Scholaribus, ad cathedram, sed cum judicibus ad tribunal: non esse ibi litigandum, & disputandum, sed simpliciter respondendum, si velit stare decreto Romanæ Ecclesiæ, & suam opinionem revocare. Sin minùs, fasciculos & ignem ostendunt, inquientes, cum hæreticis non argumentis & scripturis, sed fasciculis & igne decertandum, hominémque nec pertinaciæ alicujus convictum, nec meliora edoctum, contra conscientiam suam abjurare compellunt: quod si nolit, veluti desertorem Ecclesiæ Seculari foro tradunt, ut comburatur. En normam judicii hujus religiosi non verbum Dei, non sanam rationem; sed Romanæ Ecclesiæ Persica decreta, Romanorum Pontificum nil nisi malè parta tueri quærentium, oracula & sententias decretorias! En Argumentorum terminos, non scripturæ dicta, non rationis, non juris vel Divini vel communis humani scita, sed fasciculos, ignes!
units.tr: The norm of their judgment, as Cornelius Agrippa sets it out, is not the word of God or sound reason, but the decrees of the Popes. -ent doctors and the traditions of the Fathers they accept, saying that they can be mistaken and can mislead; but only the one Roman Church, which, they say, cannot err, and whose head is the Pope. They set the style of its court before themselves as the aim of faith, and in the inquiry they ask nothing else than whether he believes in the Roman Church. If he affirms it, they say at once: the Roman Church condemns this proposition as heretical, or scandalous, or offensive to pious souls, or derogatory to ecclesiastical power, and they immediately compel him to recant and retract. But if the one inquired into then tries to defend his opinion by the testimonies of Scripture or other arguments, they interrupt him with noise and angry mouths, saying that his business is not with bachelors and scholars at the chair, but with judges at the tribunal: there is no place here for contending and disputing, but he must simply answer whether he is willing to abide by the decree of the Roman Church and revoke his opinion. If not, they show him the faggots and the fire, saying that one must contend with heretics not with arguments and Scriptures but with faggots and fire; and they compel a man who has been convicted of no obstinacy, and taught nothing better, to abjure against his conscience. If he is unwilling, they hand him over to the secular court as a deserter of the Church, to be burned. Behold the norm of this religious judgment: not the word of God, not sound reason, but the Persian decrees of the Roman Church, and the oracles and decisive sentences of Roman Pontiffs who seek only to defend what they have ill-gotten! Behold the limits of their arguments: not the sayings of Scripture, not of reason, not the statutes of divine or of common human law, but faggots and fires!

units.la: XXIV. Modus procedendi in tribunali isthoc non religiosis, non Christianis, non hominibus, sed ingenuè, & quod res est, dicam, infernalibus furiis dignus est.
units.tr: XXIV. The mode of proceeding in this tribunal deserves not religious men, not Christians, not human beings, but, to speak frankly and as the matter really is, the infernal furies.

units.la: Exhorbitat enim ab omni jure communi, Divino & humano, ab æquitate & justitia omni. Si quos justitia, clementia, bonitas, circumspectio, simplicitas decuit, religiosum certè tribunal decuit. Has enim, aliásque virtutes similes vera religio dictat. A nullo tamen tribunali, quàm religioso isthoc longiùs eas virtutes exulare, comperiet certò, quisquis non dicam libros forte adversariis suspectos, cujusmodi sunt Eusebius Captivus Cœlii Secundi Curionis; Reginaldi Gonsalvii Inquisitionis Hispanicæ artes detectæ ac palàm traductæ; Betingerus de tyrannicâ Inquisitionis Hispanicæ mysterio; Cornelius Agrippa de Vanitate scientiarum cap. 96. aliíque similes, sed Eymerici Directorium Inquisitorum, cum Commentariis Francisci Pegnæ; Bernhardi Comensis Lucernam Inquisitorum cum notis ejusdem Pegnæ; & vel solius Antonini Dianæ Panormitani Resolutiones de Tortura in Sancto Officio suspectorum de hæresi: de pœnis delictorum pertinentium ad tribunal Inquisitionis; & de Officio ac Potestate Inquisitorum, quæ Operum ejus Parte IV. tract. 6, 7. & 8. extant, casibus pluribus & intricatis refertas, & dicta ab iis, quos modò citavimus, abundè confirmantes, perlustraverit. Dominicus Bannes, Salmanticensis, adeóque Hispanus Theologus celebris Comm. super Thom. 2. 2. q. 11. art. 2. paucis multa dixit, sic scribens: Inquisitores hæreticæ pravitatis procedunt ex præsumptione, & tenentur punire ut hæreticum eum, qui ex dictis & factis convincitur hæreticus, etiamsi revera non sit hæreticus. Sic ergo contingere potest, ut qui revera hæreticus non est, à religiosis illis Patribus horrenda & sævissima quæque patiatur, & vivus tandem comburatur.
units.tr: For it departs from all common law, divine and human, and from all equity and justice. If justice, clemency, goodness, circumspection and simplicity have ever become anyone, a religious tribunal certainly ought to have them, for true religion prescribes these and similar virtues. Yet whoever has perused, I will not say books perhaps suspect to their adversaries, such as Curio's Eusebius Captivus; Reginald Gonsalvius's Inquisitionis Hispanicae artes detectae ac palam traductae; Betinger's de tyrannica Inquisitionis Hispanicae mysterio; Cornelius Agrippa's de Vanitate scientiarum cap. 96. and others like them, but Eymeric's Directorium Inquisitorum with the commentaries of Francisco Peña; Bernard of Como's Lucernam Inquisitorum with the notes of the same Peña; and the Resolutions of Antoninus Diana of Palermo alone, de Tortura in Sancto Officio suspectorum de haeresi: de poenis delictorum pertinentium ad tribunal Inquisitionis, and de Officio ac Potestate Inquisitorum, which are found in Part IV, tracts 6, 7 and 8 of his works, filled with many intricate cases and abundantly confirming what those we have just cited say, will find that these virtues are exiled from no tribunal more certainly than from this religious one. The Salamanca theologian Dominic Bañez, a celebrated Spaniard, said much in few words in Comm. super Thom. 2. 2. q. 11. art. 2., writing thus: Inquisitors of heretical depravity proceed on presumption, and are bound to punish as a heretic the one who is convicted by his words and deeds of being a heretic, even if in truth he is not a heretic. So it can happen that one who is in truth not a heretic suffers the most horrible and savage treatment from those religious Fathers, and is at last burned alive.

units.la: XXV. Juvabit ex authoribus suprà citatis aliquot sacerimi fori hujus processum paucis repræsentare, fidemque omnibus facere, Tribunal illud, quanquam haud perinde justum, magis tamen severum & crudele esse eo, cui
units.tr: XXV. It will help to present, from the authors cited above, a few of the proceedings of this forum, and to make it credible to all that this tribunal, though not equally just, is nonetheless more severe and cruel than that over which those infernal judges, Minos and Rhadamanthus, preside.

units.la: Inquisitio crudelitas processus Gonsalvi, Diana, alii reprehenduntur. cui Infernales illi Judices, Minos & Rhodamantus, præsidént. Nam ut propiùs ad illud accedat, situm est in loco subterraneo, ne clamores gemitúsque eorum, qui torquentur, ad aures populi perveniant. Ibi omnia peraguntur in impuriori illo lumine ac fœtore tædarum lychnorúmque, quos manibus ministri tenuerint; inter vultus haud minùs torvos, quàm furiarum vultus Poetæ fingunt. Curiæ hujus definitiones & sententiæ injustiores longè sunt iis, quas apud inferos ferri, iidem comminisçuntur. Sancti enim Judices hi potestate nullis circumscripta limitibus gaudent. Non notorios duntaxat persequitur; sed suos habet coryzæos, qui facilè imprudentes, divites inprimis, in naßam ejus pertrahunt. Citare & capere iis licet reos in alieno territorio, sine litteris subsidialibus dominorum, uti Diana Tract. viii. Resol. 7. comprobat. Ex sola præsumptione condemnari posse reos in favorem fidei, ib. Resol. 36. non pauci tenent. Vilis persona quælibet pro teste contra suspectos admittitur. Perinde est, sive viva voce, sive mutis tessèris accusatio instituatur. Sine ulla enim personarum comparitione, mutuáve oppositione actio instruitur, sine parte, sine teste præsente, solo ferè Judicum spiritualium arbitrio. Licet etiam reis promittere impunitatem per simulationem, ut facilius capiantur; Flaminio Cartherio & Barbosa judicibus.
units.tr: The cruelty of the Inquisition: the proceedings of Gonsalvius, Diana and others are censured. For, to come closer to it, the tribunal is situated in an underground place, so that the cries and groans of those who are tortured may not reach the ears of the people. There everything is carried on in the dim, foul light and stench of torches and lamps, which the ministers hold in their hands, among faces no less grim than the faces of the Furies that the poets imagine. The decisions and sentences of this court are far more unjust than those the same poets invent as pronounced in the underworld. For these holy judges enjoy a power bounded by no limits. It does not pursue only the notorious; it has its own decoys, who easily draw the unwary, especially the rich, into its net. They may summon and seize the accused in another's territory without letters of assistance from the lords, as Diana proves in tract. 8, resol. 7. Not a few hold that the accused can be condemned on presumption alone "in favour of the faith," ibid. resol. 36. Any base person whatever is admitted as a witness against the suspected. It makes no difference whether the accusation is brought by living voice or by silent tokens. For the case is conducted without any appearance of the parties or mutual opposition, without a party and without a witness present, almost by the sole discretion of the spiritual judges. It is also lawful to promise the accused impunity by pretence, so that they may be caught more easily, with Flaminius Carterius and Barbosa as the judges.

units.la: XXVI. Quamprimum suspectus aliquis in has mortis umbras descenderit, atque ille, impatiens moræ, processus sui initium precibus suis impetraverit, exordiuntur judices à terrificis admonitionibus & comminationibus, protestantes interim, se innocentes fore à sanguine, si pertinacia sua rigorem reus provocaverit. Ita planè Diana Tract. vi. Resol. 28. citata etiam Congregatione Cardinalium, nuda testium dicta absque nominum publicatione, vel indicio circumstantiarum, ex quibus in notitiam testis veniri posset, judicium peragi debere, asserit. Quod si se ipsum tamen accusare captivus noluerit, ad tormenta impetus judicum fertur. Nam Diana loc. cit. Refol. 1. Torreblancam graviter increpat, negantem, quòd Inquisitores proniores ad torquendum suspectos esse debeant. Ratio illi est, quia heresis est crimen occultum, & difficilis probationis. Ergo, inquit, ad torturam judex debet esse promptior. Indicia quod attinet, Martinus Delrio, in causis fidei leviora indicia ad torturam sufficere asserit. Sanctarellus graviora requirit. Diana Refol. 2. ex sententia communi, sic ille ait, Doctorum in materia torturæ negat dari posse certam regulam ad cognoscendum, quæ indicia sufficientia sint; asseritque, totum illud ab arbitrio Inquisitoris pendere. Idem Diana Refol. 3. & ii, testes duos etiam non idoneos, puta familiares, infames excommunicatos &c. dummodo sint contestes; imò Refol. 6. unum etiam, & Refol. 13. juxta quosdam famam ad torquendum reum sufficere pertendit. Ex solo dicto socii criminis reum torqueri posse, ibid. Refol. 7. Petrus Caballus, aliíque asserunt.
units.tr: XXVI. As soon as any suspect has descended into these shadows of death, and he, impatient of delay, has obtained by his prayers the beginning of his trial, the judges open with terrifying admonitions and threats, protesting meanwhile that they will be innocent of his blood if the accused by his obstinacy provokes rigour. Diana, Tract. vi, Resol. 28, plainly asserts, citing also a decision of the Congregation of Cardinals, that the judgment must be carried out on the bare statements of witnesses, without publication of names or any indication of circumstances by which the witness could become known. But if the prisoner refuses to accuse himself, the judges' onslaught is directed to torments. For Diana, loc. cit., Resol. 1, sharply rebukes Torreblanca, who denied that inquisitors ought to be readier to torture suspects. His reason is: "because heresy is a hidden crime and hard to prove. Therefore," he says, "the judge ought to be more ready for torture." As for indications, Martin Del Rio asserts that in matters of faith slighter indications suffice for torture; Sanctarellus requires graver ones. Diana, Resol. 2, says that, according to the common opinion of the doctors, it is denied that any certain rule can be given for knowing which indications are sufficient, and he asserts that the whole matter "depends on the discretion of the inquisitor." The same Diana, Resol. 3, holds that even two witnesses who are not fit, such as household servants, the infamous, the excommunicated and so on, suffice, provided they agree with each other; indeed, Resol. 6 holds that even one suffices, and Resol. 13 maintains, according to some, that rumour is enough to torture the accused. Petrus Caballus and others assert that the accused can be tortured on the mere word of an accomplice in the crime, ibid. Resol. 7.

units.la: XXVII. Tam levibus de causis ad torturam Rhodamenti hi pergunt. Atque hic infernalium cruciatuum triste auspicium capitur. Adest truculentus carnifex à capite ad calcem terribili specie personatus, Diabolo quàm homini similior, qui torquendos, nullo discrimine virorum, fœminarum, virginum, nobilium, ignobiliumve, omnibus vestimentis exuit, manus à tergo revincit, certo orbium numero, ad octo decémque vices, præcipientibus judicibus, ut orbes singulos unum altero arctius constringat, pollicésque dein tenuiori chorda colliget, manúsque demum atque pollices vincti ad camelum, qui à trochlea pendet, alliget; postea plumbi ferríque massam pedibus, prima vice viginti quinque pondo, annectat, & in sublime eum fune rapiat, usque dum caput trochleam contingat. Sic pendentem inclamant & allatrant religiosi judices, ut in universum, quæ ad hæresin pertinent, omnia, circumstantias, socios, dicta, facta confiteatur; exquisito cruciatu per horam, sic Diana licere ait, extracto. Si nihil reus prima hac vice fatetur, secunda vice, annexo duplo ferri pondere, in sublime rapitur, præcipientibus carnifici judicibus, ut funis retro porróque currat crebro inhibitus retentúsque, donec pondus ferri omnes corporis articulos divulserit. Cunctanti confessionem edere & vociferanti barbari hi, ceu obstinato cani, insultant; & dimissum tertia vice, alligato pondere majore, in altum rapiunt, & afflictissimum corporis Christi membrum intolerandis his cruciatibus dirissimum in modum, non unius horæ spatio, quandiu libet, exercent. Triduo post, cùm articuli maximè dolent, easdem torturas repetunt, & tantisper frequentant, dum vita & spiritus miseri ægerrimè tractus finit.
units.tr: XXVII. Such slight grounds are enough for them to proceed to the torture of Rhodamentus. Here begins the grim omen of infernal torments. A brutal executioner, dressed from head to heel in a terrifying disguise and looking more like the Devil than a man, is present. He strips those to be tortured without distinction of men, women, virgins, nobles or commoners, and binds their hands behind their backs. At the judges' command he tightens a cord around the rope's loops, one tighter than the last, for eight or eighteen turns, then binds the thumbs with a thinner cord, and finally fastens the bound hands and thumbs to a pulley-hung hook. Next he attaches a mass of lead and iron weighing twenty-five pounds to the feet at the first stage, and hauls the victim aloft on the rope until the head touches the pulley. While he dangles, the pious judges shout and bark at him to confess everything that pertains to heresy: all the circumstances, accomplices, words and deeds. Diana says it is lawful to keep him hanging like this for an hour of exquisite torment. If the accused confesses nothing at this first stage, he is hoisted aloft a second time with twice the weight of iron attached. The judges order the executioner to run the rope back and forth, checked and held again and again, until the weight of iron has pulled apart every joint of the body. These barbarians mock the man who hesitates to confess and cries out, as if he were a stubborn dog. They let him down, and a third time they hoist him aloft with a heavier weight attached, and they keep up this most dreadful torment, which afflicts the most wretched member of Christ's body, for as long as they please, not merely for an hour. Three days later, when the joints ache most, they repeat the same tortures and continue them until the wretch's life and breath are drawn out with great difficulty and come to an end.

units.la: XXVIII. Sunt & alia torturarum genera, quibus has libidinis suæ victimas barbari hi excarnificant. Est enim, ubi iterum exutos vestibus, & manibus revinctos à tergo, à trochlea suspendunt, tibiis cruribúsque per chordas validas arctè constrictis, & chordis in carnem, ligno interposito tam profundè impressis, ut ad ipsa ossa facilè penetrent. Quandoque utrumque crus, tibias, brachia per tenues validásque chordas tam arctè constringunt, ut in carnem ilico fere ad ossa subsidant. Sic vinctum supinúmque imponunt scamno grandi, solido, excavato superna parte, baculum habente in medio transversum, in quem dorsum impositi cum ineffabili cruciatu recumbat. Post velo ex lino tenuissimo super jacentis os extenso, & naribus quoque obthuratis, aqua non guttatim, sed uno quasi continuo filo ex sublimi in os jacentis sic effunditur, ut velum suo lapsu in imum guttur propellat. Cujus tormenti extremam violentiam, non minorem anxietatem, quàm quæ est spiritum extremum trahentium, excitantem mollius illud machinamentum, velum tenue, quod ex ore retractum magna aquæ & sanguinis copia profluens sequitur, ut ipsa viscera cum eo è corpore evulsa putes, prodit. Denique, ne non omnia elementa improbis crudelitatum machinatoribus inservirent, olim, quando ob infirmitatem reus aliter torqueri non potuit, prægrandia prunaria ferrea, ignitis carbonibus plena adhibita sunt, ut admotæ iis pedum plantæ, lardo perunctæ, ut exquisitior dolor excitaretur, lentè ustularentur. Quia tamen, uti Diana Tract. vi. Resol. 35. narrat, praxis docuit, quòd plures rei ita torti consessionem nullam ediderint, ideo regulariter hoc tormentum, ceu tolerabile nimis, in Sacro tribunali Regni saltem Siciliæ, in desuetudinem abiit.
units.tr: XXVIII. There are also other kinds of torture with which these barbarians butcher their victims of lust. Sometimes they strip them again, bind their hands behind their backs, and hang them from the pulley, tying their shins and legs tightly with stout cords, and with the cords, with a piece of wood placed between, pressed so deeply into the flesh that they easily reach the bones. At other times they bind both legs, shins and arms with thin but strong cords so tightly that they sink into the flesh almost to the bone at once. They then lay the bound victim on his back on a large, solid bench, hollowed out on its upper side and having a transverse stick in the middle, on which the back is laid so that he rests on it with unspeakable agony. Afterwards a very fine linen cloth is stretched over the face of the one lying there, and the nostrils are also stopped up. Water is poured from above into the mouth of the one lying there, not in drops but in one almost continuous stream, so that the cloth is driven by its own fall into the bottom of the throat. The extreme violence of this torment, and no less anguish than that of men drawing their last breath, is shown by the softer device, the thin cloth which, pulled out of the mouth, follows along with a great flood of water and blood, so that you would think the very entrails were torn out of the body along with it. Finally, lest every element should fail to serve the wicked machinators of cruelty, at one time, when the accused could not otherwise be tortured because of weakness, very large iron braziers full of glowing coals were brought in, and the soles of the feet, smeared with lard, were slowly scorched by holding them over these, so that a more exquisite pain would be produced. Yet because, as Diana relates in Tract. vi, Resol. 35, experience has taught that many of those so tortured made no confession at all, this method, as too tolerable, has generally fallen into disuse, at least in the Sacred Tribunal of the Kingdom of Sicily.

units.la: XXIX. Torturæ plus quàm Cyclopicam hanc barbariem suppliciorum immanitas excipit. Quæ tamen pro reatu diverso ipsa quoque differentiam recipiunt. Sunt enim hæretici λεγόμενοι contumaces: sunt pœnitentes: sunt pœnitentes in hæresi rudiores, tyrones, molles: sunt proveçtiores, in quibus hæresis radices egisse videtur. Contumaces sunt, qui liberè Christum confitentur, & Papatum ejurant, neque ullis promissis, minis, monitis inflecti se patiuntur, ut mentem vel confessionem mutent. Hi vivi magna crudelitate comburuntur. Pœnitentes in hæresi proveçtiores palo alligati strangulantur, & strangulati comburuntur. Nota hæc sunt tum ex praxi: tum ex legibus Inquisitionis Belgis impositæ, uti eas Carolus V. A. 1550. contraxit, quas inter prima sic habet: Extra Theologos ab Universitate admissos de Scripturarum sensu sermonem nemo misceto &c. Qui secus faxit, perduellis, ex die criminis intestabilis esto, alienandi facultatem ne habeto. Pœnarum gradus sunto. Pœnitentia ducti, si viri, gladio plectuntur: Fœminæ in terram vivæ defodiuntur: Contumaces igne cremantur, bona universorum in siscum redigiuntur. Molliores & rudiores reconciliantur (hac enim voce uti solent) hoc est, ignominia publica affecti, & velut in triumphum ducti, publicè laqueos colla induti, togas ferales Sambeniticas gestantes, poenam promeritam sic confitentur, & vel ad certum tempus usque sic vestiti ingrediantur, vel carceribus sive perpetuis, sive arbitrio judicis ad certum tempus restrictis mancipentur, & bonorum vel magna parte, vel universis etiam multentur.
units.tr: XXIX. The cruelty of the penalties follows torture, a barbarity more than Cyclopean. These penalties, however, also differ according to the different degrees of guilt. There are heretics so-called [λεγόμενοι] who are obstinate; there are penitents; there are penitents who are less instructed in heresy, novices and the tender; and there are more advanced ones, in whom heresy seems to have struck root. The obstinate are those who freely confess Christ and renounce the Papacy, and who allow themselves to be moved by no promises, threats or admonitions to change their mind or their confession. These are burned alive with great cruelty. Penitents who are more advanced in heresy are strangled, tied to a stake, and then burned after being strangled. These things are known both from practice and from the laws of the Belgian Inquisition, as Charles V enacted them in the year 1550. Among the first of these it reads as follows: Let no one discuss the sense of the Scriptures, apart from the theologians admitted by the University. Whoever acts otherwise shall be a traitor, and from the day of the crime shall be incapable of making a will, and shall have no power to alienate property. Let there be degrees of punishment. Men who have repented shall be beheaded with the sword; women shall be buried alive in the ground; the obstinate shall be burned with fire, and the goods of all shall be confiscated to the treasury. The softer and less instructed are reconciled (for this is the word they usually use), that is, they are visited with public disgrace and, as if led in triumph, publicly with nooses around their necks and wearing the funeral robes called sanbenitos, they confess the penalty they deserve in this way. Either they go about dressed thus for a set time, or they are consigned to prisons, either for life or for a time fixed at the judge's discretion, and they are fined either a large part or even the whole of their goods.

units.la: XXX. Crudelitati suæ barbari Inquisitores Monachi ludibrium immane addunt, cum Pilato lavantes manus suas, dicentésque: Puri sumus à sanguine istorum, postquam nequitia & diritate sua cruciatus quæsitissimos, & morte quavis duriores miseris intulerunt. Nam judicatos à se hæreticos postquam brachio, uti loquuntur, Seculari, secum & conjunctissimo & consentienti tradiderunt, ficta intercessione miseris illudunt, & judicibus fucum faciunt, hac aut simili formula, quæ apud Guilhelmum Benedictum JC. in quæst. de homicidio extat: Domini Judices, rogamus Vos, cum omni affectu, quo possumus, ut amore Dei, pietatis & misericordiæ intuitu, & nostrorum interventu, miserrimo huic nullum mortis aut mutilationis periculum inferatis. Sic illi, eo ipso tempore, quo, eorum instigatu rogus accenditur, vel gladius stringitur, & quo sanguinem eorum, pro quibus se intercedere simulant, plus quàm infernaliter sitiunt. Causa huic histrioniæ prætexitur, quòd olim Idacius & Ithacius Episcopi incitantes Maximum Clementem, oppidum Trevirorum victorem ingressum, & impetrantes ab eodem, ut Priscillianum, haereticum impurum, supplicio afficeret, à Sulpitio Severo, aliisque graviter reprehensi, magnam invidiam conflârunt. Hinc Baronius ad A. 386 ff. 13. in Ecclesia Catholica usu receptum dicit, ut cùm quis à Magistratibus Secularibus adversus haereticos opem expetit, ne Ithacianæ partis consors & sectator esse videatur, contestationem illam consulte præmittat, nimirum sic se correctionem expetere incorrigibilium delinquentium, ut tamen citra poenam sanguinis puniantur. Sic illi sanguinarii Magistri, Idacio & Ithacio quovis afrociores longè, crudelitati suæ Babylonicæ ludibria addunt.
units.tr: XXX. To their cruelty the barbarous Monk-Inquisitors add an enormous mockery, washing their hands like Pilate and saying: We are innocent of the blood of these men, after they have inflicted on the wretched men the most exquisite tortures, by their wickedness and savagery, and torments harsher than death. For once they have handed over to the so-called secular arm, as they put it, the heretics they have condemned, to be with them and wholly in agreement, they mock the wretched men with a feigned intercession and deceive the judges with this or a similar formula, which is found in Guilelmus Benedictus, JC, in quaest. de homicidio: Lord Judges, we ask you, with all the affection we can, for the love of God, out of regard for piety and mercy, and at our intercession, not to inflict on this most wretched man any danger of death or mutilation. So they speak, at the very time when, at their instigation, the pyre is lit or the sword is drawn, and when they are more than infernally thirsty for the blood of those for whom they pretend to intercede. The reason given for this play-acting is that long ago the bishops Idacius and Ithacius, urging Maximus, who had entered the city of Trier as conqueror, and obtaining from him that Priscillian, an impure heretic, be put to death, were severely rebuked by Sulpicius Severus and others, and stirred up great hatred. Hence Baronius, ad A. 386 ff. 13, says that in the Catholic Church the custom has been received that when anyone seeks aid from secular magistrates against heretics, so that he may not seem to be a partner and follower of the party of Ithacius, he deliberately sends ahead that protestation: namely, that he seeks the correction of incorrigible offenders in such a way that they may be punished without the penalty of blood. So these bloodthirsty masters, far more savage than Idacius and Ithacius, add mockeries to their Babylonian cruelty.

units.la: XXXI. Non ergo Inquisitionis tribunal Sanctuarium Domini est, sed Babylonica fornax, Schola latronum, in qua injustitia, fraudes, avaritia & crudelitas dubio Marte certant, eademque scelera Hierarchia tum Magisterio, tum ferali exemplo omnibus iis, qui in Babylonicæ hujus Meretricis Sanctorum sanguine ebriæ, amplexibus hærent, instillat, spoliarium civium, cruentarum prædarum sævum receptaculum; denique sica in omnes literatos (sic apud Thuanum lib. xxxix. Palearius insignivit) nos addimus, in omnes Sanctos & testes Jesu, distrikta. Tale scilicet sacrum illud tribunal est, quo uno niti Sedis Apostolicæ auctoritatem, Paulus IV. moribundus, Onuphrio in ejus vita teste, Cardinalibus professus est; & cui Italiam (Hispaniam addere poterat) servatæ fidei integritatem acceptam referre debere. Pallavicinus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. xiv. 9. 5. pronuntiavit. Posset eadem ratione Turca in universo Imperio suo, quin ipsa quoque Italia, si ea potiretur, Musulmannicæ fidei juæ integritatem servare, & Christianam religionem radicitus extirpare. sed nondum eò immanitatis Barbari, quò Religiosorum illorum, qui Evangelicam perfectionem profitentur, animus præcipitavit.
units.tr: XXXI. The tribunal of the Inquisition, therefore, is not the Sanctuary of the Lord but a Babylonian furnace, a school of robbers, in which injustice, fraud, avarice and cruelty fight with doubtful battle, and the same wickednesses are instilled by the hierarchy, both by its teaching and by its deadly example, into all who cling to the embraces of this Babylonian harlot, drunk with the blood of the saints. It is a den for plundering citizens, a savage repository of bloody spoils; and finally it is a sword drawn against all men of letters (so Palearius named it, according to Thuanus, book 39), and we add, against all the saints and witnesses of Jesus. Such indeed is that sacred tribunal, on which alone, as Onuphrius, witness in his life, records, Paul IV, when dying, professed to the cardinals that the authority of the Apostolic See rests; and to which Italy (he could have added Spain) ought to ascribe the integrity of the faith preserved. Pallavicinus, in his History of the Council of Trent, book 14, chapter 9, section 5, has declared this. By the same reasoning the Turk could claim, throughout his whole empire, and Italy too, if he possessed it, to preserve the integrity of the Muslim faith and to root out the Christian religion. But the barbarians have not yet reached the point of savagery to which the mind of those religious men who profess evangelical perfection has plunged.

units.la: XXXII. Proximum crudelitatis Hierarchiæ do- cumentum est, quòd Papa per Emissarios, seu Legatos suos, fideles Regum Principumque indignationi & furori exponit.
units.tr: XXXII. The next proof of the cruelty of the Hierarchy is that the Pope, through his emissaries or legates, exposes the faithful of kings and princes to his indignation and fury.

units.la: Hoc certè non obscurè Babyloni Spiritus Dei Apoc. xvi. 13 &c. tribuit. Nam sexto Angelo phialam iræ Dei in fluvium Magnum Euphratem effundente, atque sic exsiccata aqua, ut via præpararetur Regibus ab Oriente Sole; S. Johannes vidit ex ore Draconis, & Bestiæ, & ex ore Pseudoprophetæ spiritus tres immundos, similes ranis. Sunt enim, inquit v. 14. Spiritus dæmonum, facientes signa, qui proficiscuntur ad (vel potius) in Reges terræ & totius orbis habitabilis, ut eos congregent in prælium diei illius magnæ Dei & Omnipotentis. Et congregárunt eos in locum, qui Hebraicè dictus est Harmagedon. Origo spirituum triplex os, vel antrum est, puta Draconis, Diaboli, qui ab initio mendax & homicida fuit; Bestiæ, populi animalis, veræ religionis expertis; & Pseudoprophetæ, falsi illius doctoris, qui Apoc. xiii. 11, 12. dicitur secunda Bestia, quæ ascendit ex terra, & habuit duo cornua similia agno, & locuta est, ut Draco, & potestatem prioris Bestiæ omnem coram illo fecit, &c. Spiritus vocat impuros, qualis Dæmon, & omnis homo irregenitus est; & quidem tres, non ob numerum eorum, quasi tres duntaxat, non plures futuri sint; sed vel quia ex trium ore exeunt, vel quia triplex operatio est, juxta qualitatem trium, à quibus exeunt, tanquam ex suis domibus. Draconis enim spiritus est homicidij; Bestiæ cupiditatis rerum temporalium: Pseudoprophetæ mendacii & falsæ doctrinæ cum omni artificio ejus incrustandæ. Spiritus vocantur δαιμονιον, dæmoniorum, sapientiam, scientiam multiplicem & astutiam artificiosè fallacitérque conficiendi res suas. Estenim δαίμων, quasi δαημὼν sciens, peritus, artifex. Ranis comparantur ob indefessas coaxationes, continuas vociferationes atque studia enixissima, quibus Reges & Principes ad bella instigant. Exeunt in ad, vel potiùs in Reges & Principes, hoc est, eos, veluti Spiritus quidam, animant ad religiosa bella, dum clamat in iis Bestia, & clamat Pseudopropheta, & Draco instigat, ad bellum inferendum iis, qui à Babylone recesserunt.
units.tr: Certainly the Spirit of God clearly attributes this to Babylon, Rev. 16:13 and following. When the sixth angel poured out the vial of God's wrath on the great river Euphrates, and the water was so dried up that a way was prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun, John saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet. For, he says in verse 14, they are spirits of devils, working miracles, which go forth to the kings of the earth and of the whole world, to gather them to the battle of that great day of God Almighty. And they gathered them into a place called in Hebrew Armageddon. The source of the spirits is a threefold mouth or den: that of the dragon, the devil, who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning; that of the beast, the animal people, ignorant of true religion; and that of the false prophet, that false teacher who is called the second beast in Rev. 13:11, 12, which rose out of the earth, had two horns like a lamb, spoke like a dragon, and exercised all the power of the first beast before him, etc. He calls them unclean spirits, as a demon is, and every unregenerate man is. There are three of them, not because their number is limited to three, as if there would be no more, but either because they come out of the mouths of three, or because their operation is threefold, according to the nature of the three from whom they go out, as from their own houses. For the spirit of the dragon is that of murder; that of the beast, of lust for temporal goods; that of the false prophet, of lies and false doctrine, with all the art of dressing it up. They are called δαιμονιον [daimonion], demons, that is, spirits of wisdom, of manifold knowledge, and of the cunning to carry out their schemes artfully and deceitfully. For δαίμων [daimōn] is as if from δαημών [daēmōn], knowing, skilled, expert. They are compared to frogs because of their tireless croaking, their constant shouting, and their most eager efforts by which they incite kings and princes to war. They go out to, or rather into kings and princes, that is, they animate them like spirits, inciting them to religious wars, while the beast cries out in them, the false prophet cries out, and the dragon urges them to make war on those who have withdrawn from Babylon.

units.la: XXXIII. Non puto, tacente etiam me, quenquam fore, cui non promptissimè in mentem veniant Hierarchiæ, Capitis ejus Papæ inprimis, Legati, Nuntii, Emissarii, Spirituales Patres, bellorum religiosorum incentores acerimi, à Papæ ad, & in Reges & Principes terræ missi, & velut in cor & conscientiam eorum intrantes, ut continuis suis clamoribus & coaxationibus eos ad vim faciendam iis, qui à Papæ obsequio deflexerunt, commoveant. Citius sanè in hac sublunari regione vacuum dabitur, quàm paulò celebrior Regis ac Principis aula, quam tripartita hæc spirituum phalanx non totam possideat, dum modo aditus eò illis vel per angustam rimulam pateat. Indicæ quoque relationes testes sunt, Spiritus hosce, quam primùm in Aridam excendunt, recta in Aulas & ad Reges tendere, ut hos primùm in potestatem redigant, & per eosdem deinceps subjectos populos infestent.
units.tr: XXXIII. I do not think, even if I say nothing, that anyone will fail to think readily of the Hierarchy, and above all of its head, the Pope: his legates, nuncios and emissaries, spiritual fathers, the most fierce instigators of religious wars, sent by the Pope to and among the kings and princes of the earth, and entering, as it were, into their heart and conscience, so that by their constant shouting and croaking they may stir them to use force against those who have turned aside from obedience to the Pope. Sooner, certainly, will an empty space be found in this sublunary region than a somewhat more famous royal or princely court which this threefold phalanx of spirits does not entirely possess, provided only that they have access to it, even through a narrow crack. The Indian accounts also bear witness that these spirits, as soon as they go up onto dry land, make straight for the courts and the kings, so that they may first bring these under their power and then, through them, harass the peoples subject to them.

units.la: XXXIV. Sunt hi Trifaces Spiritus duorum fere generum. Primi Legatorum Majorum est, quos Papa ἀπέστειλε & cum plena potestate pro expediendis negotiis suis mittit ad Aulas Regum & Principum, qui Legati à Latere & Nuntii Apostolici insigniri solent. Sunt enim orales Interpretes Papæ, Apparitores & Parmenonces nones Sanctæ Sedis proximi, qui post Reformationis, Concilii inprimis Tridentini, à quo propria & nativa æra calamitatis Europæ per trisulcos illos Spiritus concitatæ, incipit, tempus frequentiores longè & acriori cum delectu ad Reges mittuntur, quàm ante factitatum fuerat. Mandatis instruuntur talibus, 'qualia ad finem illum, quem Spiritibus his S Johannes tribuit, directa sunt; ut videlicet sublata fœderum, pactorum, juramentorum religione, Reges vel contra se invicem, vel contra subditos, vel hos in illos concitent, prout Papæ rationibus conducere visum fuerit, Conciliíque adeò Tridentini executionem sanguinariam persuadeant. Sùntque hi ceu Castrorum Commissarii, uti hodie loquuntur, seu ἐφοδιαςταὶ in sacra hac expeditione. Ad hoc Spirituum genus etiam totus Principum purpuratorum Senatus, in quibus, ceu cardinibus, Reip. Christianæ status versatur; Præsulum & Prælatorum Ordines, qui aulas Regum Principumque sectari, & consiliis suis moderari solent, pertinent.
units.tr: XXXIV. These three-faced spirits are of roughly two kinds. The first kind is that of the greater legates, whom the Pope sends forth (ἀπέστειλε [apésteile]) with full power to carry out his affairs, and who are usually called legates a latere and apostolic nuncios, sent to the courts of kings and princes. For they are the Pope's oral interpreters, attendants and Parmenones, the closest servants of the Holy See. After the Reformation, and above all after the Council of Trent, from which the proper and native era of the calamity of Europe, stirred up by those three-furrowed spirits, begins, they are sent to kings far more often and with far more keen selection than was done before. They are furnished with instructions such as are directed toward that end which John assigns to these spirits: namely, that, with the bond of treaties, pacts and oaths set aside, they should stir up kings either against one another or against their subjects, or the subjects against them, as the Pope's interests seem to require, and should persuade them to carry out the bloody enforcement of the Council of Trent. They are, as people now say, like commissaries of the camp, or ἐφοδιασταί [ephodiastai], in this sacred expedition. To this kind of spirit belong also the whole senate of purple-robed princes (the cardinals), on whom, as on hinges, the state of the Christian commonwealth turns, and the orders of prelates and bishops, who are accustomed to follow the courts of kings and princes and to guide them by their counsels.

units.la: XXXV. Posterius Spirituum illorum genus eorum est, qui religionem in claustris suis professi, relictis iis ceu paludibus suis, in aulas Regum & Principum penetrant, & causam Domini sui inprimis alacriter agunt. Referri huc possunt omnes Sophistarum familiæ, linguæ, calamique acie rem Romanam defendentes, omni artium & linguarum luce, ingeniorúmque præstantissimorum donis, ad fuganda, pallianda & excusanda Papatus σκύβαλα, eludendámque veritatem impiè abutentes; omnes religiosorum larvæ; inprimis autem Aulipetæ celebres Jesuitæ, à Lojola, quæ vox Hebraicè scripta (ללה) Nocturnum tenebriorem significat, originem ducentes, hominum genus vetustissimum, qui ingenii, dicendi, agendi dotibus excellentes, adeóque verè δαίμονες Scientes & periti, pro Regis gis sui imperio audacissimè callidissimèque velitantur.
units.tr: XXXV. The second kind of those spirits is of those who, having professed religion in their cloisters, leave those as their marshes and penetrate into the courts of kings and princes, and above all eagerly pursue the cause of their lord. Here may be placed all the families of Sophists who defend the Roman cause with the edge of their tongue and pen, abusing, with impious misuse, the light of all the arts and languages and the gifts of the most outstanding talents, to put to flight, cloak and excuse the dregs of Papacy and to mock the truth; all the masks of the religious orders; and above all the famous courtiers, the Jesuits, who take their name from Loyola (a word written in Hebrew as (ללה), signifying a dark night), a most ancient race of men who, excelling in the gifts of intellect, speech and action, and thus truly daimones, knowing and skilled, skirmish most boldly and most cunningly under the command of their king.
Ready for either,

units.la: Et versare dolos, & aperto tendere Marte.
units.tr: to weave tricks and to strive in open war.

units.la: Non enim arbitrio quodam, sed voto, quod quartum & Jesuitis proprium est, ad obeundam missionem obstriguntur. Formulam quarti hujus voti à Lojola, & decem primis Societatis Patribus oblatam Julius III. confirmavit, in qua inter alia sic primipilares illi decreverunt: Sciant omnes socii, & non solum in primis professionis suae foribus; sed quoad vixerint, quotidie animo volvant, hanc Societatem universam, & singulos, sub Sanctissimi Domini Papae nostri, & aliorum Romanorum Pontificum successorum ejus fideli obedientia Deo militare. Et quamvis Evangelio doceamur, & fide orthodoxa cognoscamus, ac firmiter profiteamur, omnes Christi fideles Romano Pontifici, tanquam capiti, ac Jesu Christi vicario subesse: ad majorem tamen nostrae societatis humilitatem, ac perfectam unius cujusque mortificationem, & voluntatum nostrarum abnegationem, summopere conducere judicavimus, singulos nos ultra commune illud vinculum speciali voto obstringi: ita ut QUICQUID Modernus, aliique Romani Pontifices pro tempore existentes jusserint, ad profectum animarum & fidei propagationem pertinens, & AD QUASCUNQUE PROVINCIAS (earúmque adeo Reges & Principes) nos MITTERE voluerit, sine ulla tergiversatione, aut excusatione, illico quantum in nobis fuerit, exequi teneamur; sive miserit nos ad Turcas, sive alios quoscunque infideles, etiam in partibus quas Indias vocant, existentes, adeóque Reges Orientis, quibus exsicato Euphrate aditus muniendus, juxta Phialae plagam, fuerat) sive ad quoscunque haereticos, sive schismaticos, sive etiam ad quosvis fideles. adeóque, uti eadem prophetia sonat, ad Reges terrae (hoc est fideles, Ecclesiæ addictos, nam prophetia terræ nomine Ecclesiam significare solet) & orbis habitabilis, puta reliquos infideles, hæreticos, schismaticos. Ipsa ergo Voti hujus Jesuitici formula ambigere neutiquam sinit, qui sint illi Babylonii spiritus, ex ore Draconis, Bestiæ & Pseudoprophetæ prodeuntes.
units.tr: For they are bound to undertake a mission not by some free choice but by a vow, which is the fourth vow and peculiar to the Jesuits. Julius III confirmed the formula of this fourth vow, offered by Loyola and the ten first fathers of the Society, in which those first-rank men decreed, among other things, as follows: Let all the members know, and not only at the threshold of their profession but every day as long as they live let them ponder in their minds, that this whole Society and each of its members serves God in militant obedience under our most holy Lord the Pope and his successors, the Roman Pontiffs. And although we are taught by the Gospel, and know by the orthodox faith, and firmly profess, that all the faithful of Christ are subject to the Roman Pontiff as to their head and to Jesus Christ's vicar, nevertheless, for the greater humility of our society and the complete mortification of each of us and the denial of our own wills, we have judged it most helpful that each of us be bound by a special vow beyond that common bond: so that whatever the present Pontiff and the other Roman Pontiffs who may be in office shall order, pertaining to the progress of souls and the propagation of the faith, and whenever he shall wish to send us TO WHATEVER PROVINCES (and to their kings and princes), we are bound to carry it out at once, as far as in us lies, without any shirking or excuse; whether he sends us to the Turks, or to any other unbelievers, even those in the parts called the Indies, and thus to the kings of the East (for whom the way was to be prepared by drying up the Euphrates, according to the plague of the vial), or to any heretics, or schismatics, or even to any of the faithful. And so, as this same prophecy says, the kings of the earth (that is, the faithful, attached to the Church, for prophecy usually signifies the Church by the name of earth) and the inhabited world, that is, the remaining unbelievers, heretics and schismatics. The very wording of this Jesuit vow therefore does not allow any doubt as to who those Babylonian spirits are that come forth out of the mouth of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet.

units.la: XXXVI. Nam ex ore certè Christi Legati & Missionarii hi prodire dici non possunt, eo modo quo prodierunt Apostoli, qui ex ore Christi sic instructi sunt: Sicut Pater me misit, ita ego mitto vos, Joh. xx. 21. Tametsi enim utrique Jesuitæ inprimis, quos Lusitani Apostolos etiam vocare solent; & Apostoli Christi, & Missionarii, in eo conveniunt, quòd utrique orali & immediata vocatione, illi à Christo afflati, hi ex ore Draconis, Bestiæ & Pseudoprophetæ missi currebant, currúntque: quodque non vocati ad eos utrique venerunt & veniunt, qui de iis cogitárunt nunquam, in ceteris tamen διὰ διὰ πνεῶν differunt. Apostoli enim evitatis Magnatum aulis, spretóque Mundi hujus supercilio ad plebem se conferebant: hi Regum domos & Gynecæa rectà petunt. Illi Schôlas & Synagogas frequentabant: hi Prætoria & Curias scrutantur. Illi in aulis, si quando eò abripiebantur, ut pecora mactabantur: hi Reges Principésque ipsos vel mactandos curant, vel Subditis apud eos perniciem machinantur. Illi populis Evangelium de Christo cum omni patientia & lenitate prædicabant: hi eosdem vel denuntiata, ni pareant, suprema Magistratus indignatione territant, vel prædicata Cruciata in Magistratum concitant. Illorum Evangelium à Sapientibus hujus seculi respuebatur, & ut inepta spermologia explodebatur: hi doctrinam suam rationi consentaneam esse, & ab ingeniosissimo quoque inter Barbaros præsertim (sic Surius alicubi) expeti dicti-
units.tr: XXXVI. For these certainly cannot be said to come forth from the mouth of Christ as legates and missionaries, in the way the apostles came forth, who were so instructed from the mouth of Christ: As the Father has sent me, so I send you, John 20:21. For although both the Jesuits, whom the Portuguese are accustomed to call even Apostles, and the apostles of Christ and missionaries agree in this, that both come by an oral and immediate calling, the former inspired by Christ, the latter sent, and running, out of the mouth of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet, and that both came and come, uncalled, to those who had never thought of them, yet in other respects they differ by a different spirit [διὰ διὰ πνεῶν]. For the apostles, avoiding the courts of the great, and scorning the pride of this world, went to the common people; these make straight for the houses and women's quarters of kings. The former frequented schools and synagogues; these search out the praetoria and the councils. The former, if at any time they were dragged into courts, were slaughtered like sheep; these take care either that kings and princes themselves are slaughtered, or they plot ruin for their subjects at their hands. The former preached the Gospel of Christ to the peoples with all patience and gentleness; these terrify the same peoples, either by threatening, unless they obey, the supreme anger of the magistrate, or by proclaiming crusades, they stir up the magistrate against them. The Gospel of the former was rejected by the wise men of this age and dismissed as foolish babbling; these claim that their doctrine agrees with reason and is sought by the most gifted of all, especially among the barbarians (so Surius somewhere says),

units.la: Legatorum & Missionarum Patrum & Apostolorum seu Legatorum Christi immane dif-crimen. dictitant; multo etiam de Regum, Principum, Magnatum favore jactantes. Illi cor Patrum ad filios, & filiorum ad Patres, quantum in ipsis erat, convertebant: hi liberos contra Parentes, & hos contra illos, adeóque proximos Agnatos contra se invicem concitant. Illi dulcissimum Christi jugum, & per hoc conscientiæ libertatem & pacem prædicabant: hi Romano-Hispanicæ Inquisitionis tyrannicum jugum fidelium cervicibus intentant. Illi spreta humana commendatione omni, propriæ conscientiæ testimonio, & legationis suæ authoritate contenti erant: hi supremi Magistratus mandatis, & severissimis edictis, adeóque militum cohortibus se muniunt, ut horum præsidio tuti perniciosas artes securius exercere queant, adeóque à subditis quod volunt, extorqueant; aut quod optatius illis est, apud eosdem illis contemptæ Majestatis invidiam conflent. Illi quocunque veniebant, nemini molesti aut graves erant: hi innocentes avitis suis sedibus variis artibus, ut easdem ipsi occupent, expellere conantur. Denique illi sentientes, secum Evangelio suo contemptui haberi, non aliam de contemnentibus poenam graviorem expetebant, quàm quòd excusso pedum pulvere abierunt, & res suas sibi habere jusserunt: hi semel recepti, vel semel ipsos per angustum foramen intrudentes, per patentissimas deinceps valvas vix ejiciuntur; ejecti aut læsi vindictæ rationes omnes tentabunt.
units.tr: The Legates and Missionaries, the Fathers and Apostles, or Legates of Christ, are in immense danger. They keep saying so, and they boast greatly of the favour of kings, princes and nobles. The former turned the hearts of fathers toward their children, and of children toward their fathers, as far as they could. These men set children against parents, and parents against children, and so set close kinsmen against one another. The former preached the sweet yoke of Christ and, through it, freedom of conscience and peace. These men hold over the necks of the faithful the tyrannical yoke of the Roman-Spanish Inquisition. The former, setting aside all human recommendation, were content with the testimony of their own conscience and the authority of their embassy. These men fortify themselves with the orders and most severe edicts of the supreme magistrate, and with companies of soldiers, so that under their protection they may practise their pernicious arts more safely, extort from the subjects whatever they want, or, what suits them better, kindle hatred of offended majesty against those same subjects. The former, wherever they came, were a burden to no one. These men try by various devices to drive out innocent people from their ancestral homes, so that they may occupy those homes themselves. Finally, when the former perceived that their gospel was held in contempt, they sought no heavier punishment for those who despised it than that they shook the dust from their feet and left, bidding them keep their goods. These men, once received, or once they have pushed themselves in through a narrow opening, are scarcely driven out through the widest doors afterwards; and if they are thrown out or harmed, they will try every means of revenge.

units.la: XXXVII. Missionariis his, turbarum & tempesta- tum in orbe Christiano Æolis, characteres, quibus na- tura illorum Spirituum in Prophetia exprimitur, aprimè quadrant.
units.tr: XXXVII. The characters by which the nature of those spirits is expressed in the Prophecy fit these missionaries, the stirrers of tumults and storms in the Christian world, most exactly.

units.la: Nam & Spiritus sunt, & quidem immundi: & similes ranis: & Spiritus dæmoniorum. Qui Spirituum Trifaucium characteres Apoc. xvi. 12. 13. 14. constituuntur. Spiritus sunt, quomodo πνεύματα Spiritus metonymicè appellantur, qui inusitato quodam, & minimè
units.tr: For they are spirits, and indeed unclean; they are like frogs; and they are spirits of demons. These are the marks of the three-mouthed spirits set out in Rev. xvi. 12, 13, 14. They are spirits, as spirits [πνεύματα] are called by metonymy, who burn with an unusual and by no means ordinary zeal, whether of true or false religion.

units.la: Sunt Spiritus, & quidem immundi. minimè vulgari religionis sive veræ, sive fictæ zelo flagrant. Sub religionis sanè obtentu jam dudum per illos Draconica truculentia, Bestialis malitia, & Pseudoprophetica impostura Orbem, & in eo Reges ac Respublicas præcipuè infestant. Hoc enim à longo jam tempore Spiritualium illa Patrum (sic enim dici amant) cohors ingenti, religionis zelo, qui quiddam ecstaticum, & furori lymphatico simile habet (quomodo Hos ix. 7. dicitur: אויל הנביא משגע איש הרוח Stultus est Propheta, & spirituales insaniunt, lymphantur, fanaticorum instar) agit, hoc scribit, hoc disputat, hoc voce contendit, hoc vigilans somniat, hoc omnes aulæ, omnia dicasteria, omnes Curiæ, omnia Gynecæa, Templa, Cathedræ personant: hoc armis, fuste, resti, ense, aqua, igni evincere & pervincere, magno tumultuum, sed exiguo veræ pietatis incremento, conatur, ut religio Papæ ubique locorum vel constituatur, vel restituatur. Ad furorem hunc accedunt dona ingenii, excitata vis animi, mens sagax, & innata quædam industria. Quæ insuper externo & affectato hypocriseos artificio fucantur; veluti virginali castitate, abstinentia, simulata paupertate, divitiarum contemptu, regulari vestitu, duro victu, tetrico vultu in propatulo μισογυνέα, precibus multis, extraordinariis revelationibus, Sanctorum jactatis apparitionibus; & si quid aliud ad larvæ religiosæ expolitionem, vel per Concilii Tridentini reformationem, vel per Lojolæ, aliorúmque recentium hypocritarum perfectiores regulas adjectum est. Si interiorem interrea Spirituum illorum habitum spectes, præter salsam doctrinam, furorem, hypocrisin, artes & consilia sanguinaria, nil nisi ambitionem, avaritiam, immunditiem, obscoenitatem, crapulam, detestandas libidines, aliáque ejusmodi produnt. Et πνεῦματα igitur
units.tr: They are spirits, and indeed unclean. They burn with no ordinary zeal. Under the pretext of religion, these men have long since attacked the world, and above all kings and commonwealths, with dragon-like savagery, bestial malice and prophet-like imposture. For a long time now this company of so-called spiritual Fathers (for they love to be called that) has acted with immense religious zeal, which has something ecstatic about it, something like frenzy, a fanatic's madness (as Hosea ix. 7 says: "The prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad" [אויל הנביא משגע איש הרוח]: they rave and go mad). They write this, they dispute this, they argue this aloud, they dream this even awake; this echoes through every court, every tribunal, every council chamber, every women's apartment, every church and every pulpit. By arms, clubs, halters, swords, water and fire they try to conquer and overcome, with much uproar but little real growth of piety, so that the religion of the Pope may be established or restored everywhere. To this frenzy are added natural gifts, a stirred-up force of mind, a shrewd intellect and a certain innate industry. These are further disguised by an outward and affected art of hypocrisy: by virginal chastity, abstinence, feigned poverty, contempt of riches, a religious habit, hard fare, a gloomy face, a conspicuous hatred of women, many prayers, extraordinary revelations, and boasted appearances of saints; and whatever else has been added to polish up the religious mask, whether through the reform of the Council of Trent or through the more perfect rules of Loyola and other recent hypocrites. If meanwhile you look at the inner disposition of those spirits, they reveal nothing but a corrupt doctrine, frenzy, hypocrisy, bloody arts and plans, and besides these ambition, avarice, uncleanness, obscenity, gluttony, detestable lusts and other things of that kind. And so the spirits [πνεύματα], who in the name of religion stir up all holy things, are unclean spirits [ἀκαθάρτα πνεύματα]. Such was Balaam, who by similar arts had won among the men of his age the belief that he held blessing and cursing in his own power; the Roman Arch-Balaam imitates him not unsuccessfully, and while he hands over the pious, excommunicated and devoted with curses here and there, to be pursued by his Balak.

units.la: Tom. II. aa igitur Spiritus religionis nomine omnia sacra commoventes; & ἀκαθάρτα πνεύματα impuri spiritus sunt. qualis Bileamus erat, qui similibus artibus id apud fui Seculi homines consecutus erat, ut benedictionem & maledictionem in sua habere potestate crederetur, quem Romanus Archi-Bileamus non infeliciter imitatur, dumque pios hinc inde excommunicatos, dirisque devotos Balako suo persequendos tradit.
units.tr: Tom. II. aa. Therefore the spirits who stir up all holy things in the name of religion are unclean spirits [ἀκαθάρτα πνεύματα]. Such was Balaam, who by similar arts won among the men of his age the belief that he held blessing and cursing in his own power; the Roman Arch-Balaam imitates him not unsuccessfully, and while he hands over the pious, excommunicated and devoted with curses here and there, to be pursued by his Balak.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ranis porro, & quidem Ægyptiacis similes esse novellos hosce Apostolos, quid dicere attinet? Sicut nempe ranæ Ægyptiacæ, præter generis sui naturam, relicto Nilo, defertisque paludibus primùm Pharaonis aulam, & ex hac deinceps Satraparum ejus, sicut & reliquorum Ægyptiorum domos appeticrunt, eásque inaudita, & in hac animantium specie planè prodigiosa agilitate, ad intima usque penetralia perreptárunt; cubilium strata, vasa farinaria, culinaria, cum clibanis & universa suppellectile defœdárunt; denique in ipsummet Pharaonem, ejúsque aulicos. & illorum vestes prodigioso ausu insilierunt, Exod. vii. 28. 29. sic planè Spiritus hi toti Oecumenico orbi faciunt. Nam quod Pharaoni Ægyptus fuit, hoc Draconi, Bestiæ & Prophetis, spiritus hosce exhalantibus, totus orbis est. Relictis ergo claustrorum suorum, in quibus impurissimam vitam ducunt, latebris, posito omni pudore, non alia quàm Præpositorum suorum, Papæ uni solíque inservientium, authoritate totum orbem pervagantur, in Principum omnium Curias, Regum palatia, Magnatum, Cancellariorum, Mareschallorum &c. domos prorumpunt, eósque importuna coaxatione sua in arenam deductos, ad decernendum magni illius diei prælium concitant. Vox porro à Mose usurpata Hebræa יְצְפַּרְדֵּעַ quæ ranam significat, mysterio non caret. Nam derivari illa potest à צְפַרְדֵּעַ quod Chaldæis & Arabibus Collegium, Communitatem, Seminarium significat, & רעה Scientia, cognitio, opinio. Atque sic argutum, omniáque perrimans infectum, vel infectorum cœtum notare potest. Certum autem est, nec ranas Ægyptiacas, uti res ipsa ostendit; nec spirituales hos Emissarios ab Etymologiæ hujus ratione abludere. Sic enim etiam Daniel viii. 23. Antichristus מבן הידות intelligens ænigmatum, vel potius catus & versipellis homo, quem nunquam ingenii versuti expedita facultas destituit, insignitur. Cujusmodi Protheum olim in Scholis Subtilistam; hodie vafrum Sophistam, in aulis Subtilem & exercitatum Politicum, Practicum; in castris Hannibalem appellare consueverunt. Testatur autem experientia, Pseudopropheticam hanc Emissariorum cohortem non solum omnem spem & fiduciam in captiosa Sophistica repositam habere, utpote qui aliter nec se, nec curiosam quam susceperunt, causam tueri queant: sed etiam hanc ipsam versutiam nunc demum Æquivocationis fallaciam, hoc est, versutissimum & subtilissimum mentiendi artificium in Cœlesti etiam veritatis Professore probare, ejúsque artem & usum publicè docere ac prositeri. Ut jam mirum non sit, quòd in aulis, ipsíque adeò castris vulpina astutia cum perfida crudelitate conjuncta omnia acta & consilia moderatur. Possent & aliæ ranarum & emissariorum comparationes institui. Etenim constat satis, totum ranarum genus esse ἀμφιβίου; Limo tamen palustri impensè gaudere; vivas aquarum scaturigines putredinem hanc non ferre; clamosos esse præsertim circa vesperam, ubi interdum vehementer tumultuantur, suisque coaxationibus totas paludes replent. qui coaxatus tum imminentis imbris certum omen habetur. Non puto cuiquam obscurum esse, vix ovum ovo similius esse, quàm hæc Emissariis, Jesuitis præprimis. Illi enim amphibii & in terra, hoc est, stylo Prophetico, Ecclesia; & in mari, seu aqua, hoc est, mundo, Seculo vivunt; inter Monachos Episcopi, inter Episcopos Monachi; orbem terrarum terra marique æquali facilitate peragrant: à limpidis Israelis fontibus, tanquam à suo naturali veneno aut refugiunt, aut non aliter ex iis, quàm ut canes ex Nilo potant; aut eosdem calumniis impetunt: contra suum illud Aristophanicum βρεκεκεκέξ & κοάξ, κοάξ per limosum traditionum cœnum, per insanos & insatiabiles illos clamores: Sanctissima Sedes, Beatissimus Pater; Sancta Romana Ecclesia: Non errat Sancta Romana Ecclesia: Audienda est Sancta Romana Ecclesia; qui non audiverit, hæreticus & schismaticus est, ferro & igni expiandus, &c. in Lacu Antichristi ceu colorando efformant: coaxatu suo ominosi sunt Regnis & nationibus multis, quibus non semel diem & horam calamitatis suæ certissimè prædixerunt, haud equidem futurorum scientia, sed quia consiliorum ipsimet architecti fuerunt. Denique, ut secundum hunc characterem claudam, caput ipsum Ranæ Jesuitici, Tulipanti, seu Capucii quadraturam exactè repræsentat.
units.tr: XXXVIII. As for these new apostles being like frogs, and indeed Egyptian frogs, what is the point of saying more? Just as the Egyptian frogs, going beyond the nature of their kind, left the Nile and the swamps and first sought out the court of Pharaoh, and from there the houses of his satraps and of the other Egyptians, and crept with unheard-of, and in this kind of creature quite prodigious, agility right into the innermost chambers; they defiled the bedding, the kneading-troughs, the cooking pots, the ovens and all the household furniture; and finally, with prodigious boldness, they leapt upon Pharaoh himself and his courtiers and their clothes (Exod. vii. 28, 29), so exactly do these spirits act toward the whole ecumenical world. For what Egypt was to Pharaoh, the whole world is to the dragon, the beast and the prophets who breathe out these spirits. So, leaving behind the hiding places of their cloisters, where they lead the most impure lives, and casting off all shame, they roam the whole world under the authority of their Superiors alone, who serve the one Pope; they burst into the courts of all princes, the palaces of kings, the houses of nobles, chancellors, marshals and so on, and by their unwelcome croaking they drive those rulers into the arena and stir them up to decide the battle of that great day. Moreover, the Hebrew word used by Moses for frog, יְצְפַּרְדֵּעַ (tzephardea), is not without mystery. For it can be derived from צְפַרְדֵּעַ, which in Chaldean and Arabic means college, community, seminary, and from רעה, knowledge, understanding, opinion. Thus it can denote the sharp-witted, the one who infects everything he touches, or a gang of the infected. It is certain, however, that neither the Egyptian frogs, as the thing itself shows, nor these spiritual emissaries differ from the sense of this etymology. For in the same way Daniel viii. 23 marks out Antichrist as מבן הידות, a man who understands riddles, or rather a crafty and slippery man, whom the ready facility of his cunning never deserts. Such a Proteus men used to call a subtle thinker in the schools, today a sly sophist, at court a subtle and practised politician, a practical man, and in camps they are accustomed to call him Hannibal. Experience, moreover, bears witness that this pseudo-prophetic company of emissaries not only places all its hope and confidence in captious sophistry, since otherwise they cannot defend either themselves or the cause they have taken up; but also that they now at last prove this very cunning by the fallacy of equivocation, that is, the most crafty and subtle art of lying, even in the Heavenly Professor of truth, and that they openly teach and profess its art and use. So it is no wonder that in courts, and indeed in camps, all their acts and plans are governed by foxlike cunning joined with treacherous cruelty. Other comparisons between frogs and emissaries could also be drawn. For it is well enough known that the whole genus of frogs is amphibious; yet they greatly delight in muddy swamp-slime, and cannot bear living springs of water to be putrid; they are noisy especially towards evening, when they sometimes make a great uproar and fill whole marshes with their croaking. The croaking of frogs at that time is taken as a sure omen of an approaching shower. I do not think anyone can fail to see that these emissaries, the Jesuits above all, are scarcely more alike than egg to egg. For they live amphibiously, on land, that is in the prophetic style the Church, and in the sea or water, that is in the world, the age; among monks they are bishops, among bishops they are monks; they roam the whole earth with equal ease by land and sea; from the clear fountains of Israel they either shrink back as from their natural poison, or drink from them no differently than dogs drink from the Nile, or they attack them with slanders; and against that Aristophanic croaking of theirs, brekekekex, koax, koax [βρεκεκεκέξ & κοάξ, κοάξ], through the muddy filth of traditions, by their mad and insatiable cries: Most Holy See, Most Blessed Father; Holy Roman Church: the Holy Roman Church does not err; the Holy Roman Church must be heard; whoever does not hear it is a heretic and schismatic, to be purged with sword and fire, and so on, they fashion themselves in the lake of Antichrist as if in colour. By their croaking they are ominous to many kingdoms and nations, to which they have more than once foretold with the greatest certainty the day and hour of their calamity; not indeed by any knowledge of the future, but because they were themselves the architects of their plans. Finally, to close this description of the character, the very head of the Jesuit frog, the Tulipant or Capuchin, exactly represents the outline of it.

units.la: XXXIX. Neque tertio Spirituum charactere, se- cundum quem πνεύματα δαιμονίων Spiritus dæmoniorum, seu Dæmoniaci insigniuntur, Legati hi & Emissarii de- stituuntur.
units.tr: XXXIX. Nor do these emissaries lack the third character of spirits, according to which they are designated spirits of demons (πνεύματα δαιμονίων), or demoniacs.

units.la: Etenim Dæmoniorum vox Hebrææ voci שדד vastavit, perdidit; respondens spiritus perniciosos, seu, uti Chaldæus reddit Psal. cvi. 37. מויקא nocivos notat. Rabbinorum alii sic dictos volunt, quòd aeris & aquæ dominio præsint, ventos & tempestates concitent: alii, quòd obsessos homines torqueant. Neque desunt, quia Caino prognatos esse, ac propterea humanis cœdibus delectari affirment, uti in Schalschel Hakab. tract. de Incantat. legere est. Sunt igitur
units.tr: For the Hebrew word for "demons," שדד [shadad], means to lay waste or to destroy, and corresponds to "destructive spirits." Or, as the Chaldee paraphrast renders it at Psalm 106:37, the word [מויקא, muyqa'] means "harmful." Some of the rabbis hold that they are so called because they rule over air and water and stir up winds and storms; others, because they torment men who are possessed. Nor are there lacking those who affirm that they are descended from Cain, and therefore delight in human slaughter, as may be read in Schalschel Hakab., tract. de Incantat. They are therefore

units.la: Sunt Spiritus damoniaci, crudelitate, afflutia, impuritate damoniaca praediti. igitur Spiritus sanguinolenti, vastatores, λυμαινόμενοι, πληγέυοντες; & quidem, uti R. Hiskias ad Deut. xxxii. 17. annotat, שרדים את רעת אדם vastantes, seu pervertentes intellectum humanum. David etiam Psal. cvi. 37. istam Israelitarum stultitiam, de qua ibi Moses loquitur, de liberorum immolatione interpretatur. Addunt Rabbini, eos mediæ Diabolos inter & homines substantiæ esse בני הבליעל salaces, lascivos supra modum, quorum Rex sit אשמדאי Asmodæus ille, conjugii, liberorumque, masculorum inimicus. Habet etiam vox שר cognationem cum זר Tumidus, superbus, insolens, in quarum affinium vocum permutatione multum Rabbini ludunt. Observandum insuper, Prophetam eos non directè Dæmonas, sed Dæmoniorum spiritus, hoc est, Spiritus dæmoniacos vocare, indicantem, non eos spectra, sed homines esse, malitia dæmoniaca præditos, furore & libidine dæmoniaca agitatos. Non puto equidem verbis opus me habere ad demonstrandum, exactè criterion isthoc congruere Emissariis, Jesuitis inprimis, quorum furores, strages abiis passim factas, parricidia, vel attentata vel perpetrata, vel commendata (uti ex Simanca, Mariana, Becano, aliis constat) veneficia, perjuria, proditiones, doctrinam dæmoniacam, conjugio casto inimicam, libidines fœdas, technas multifarias orbis universus Eous & Occiduus proh dolor! expertus est, atque experitur adhuc.
units.tr: They are demoniac spirits, endowed with demoniac cruelty, lust and impurity. They are therefore bloody spirits, destroyers, corrupters, smiters. And indeed, as R. Hiskias notes on Deuteronomy 32:17, they are שרדים את רעת אדם [sheradim et ra'at adam], laying waste, or perverting, the human mind. David also, at Psalm 106:37, interprets that folly of the Israelites of which Moses speaks there as the sacrificing of children. The rabbis add that these beings, who are of a substance midway between devils and men, are בני הבליעל [benei Belial], lewd, wanton beyond measure, whose king is אשמדאי [Ashmedai] (Asmodeus), that enemy of marriage and of children, and especially of males. The word שר [sar] also has kinship with זר [zar], proud, haughty, insolent, and the rabbis play much on the exchange of these related words. It should further be observed that the Prophet does not call them devils directly, but spirits of demons, that is, demoniac spirits, indicating that they are not phantoms but men endowed with demoniac malice, driven by demoniac fury and lust. I do not think I need many words to show that this mark fits the emissaries exactly, and the Jesuits above all: their furies; the slaughters carried out by them everywhere; parricides, whether attempted, perpetrated, or commended (as is clear from Simancas, Mariana, Becanus and others); poisonings, perjuries, betrayals; a doctrine of demons hostile to chaste marriage; foul lusts; manifold tricks. The whole world, East and West, has, alas, experienced these things and still experiences them.

units.la: X L. Sed & Spirituum istorum officia belle Emissariis quadrant. Tribus pariter illa capitibus Spiritus S. inclusit, dicens Apoc. xvi. 14. eos miracula facere, abire ad Reges terræ & totius mundi; & eosdem ad bellum congregare. Non sine causa primore loco miracula ponuntur. Eorum enim ostentatio usitatum Diaboli, quoties Dei verbo & digito ita premitur, ut præstigias suas aliter mundo obtrudere nequeat, artificium est. Et circa finem mundi hac impostura frequentius eum usurum, Scriptura Matth. xxiv. 24. 2. Thess. ii. 9. Apoc. xiii. 13. 14. testatur. Quo vero certiore charactere Emissarii suam Draconis, Bestiae & Pseudoprophetae clientelam nobis probare possent? In utraque enim India, (quas regiones Spiritus S. iis pro suo etiam campo attribuit) omnium efficacissime Miraculorum hic character operatus est; si modo vera sunt, quae in Epistolis Indicis & Japonicis referuntur. quarum vix ulla est, quae non insigne aliquod miraculum commemoret. Primis maxime Africae inventoribus stupenda miracula adscribuntur. uti apud P. Martyrem lib. vi. Dec. 2. videre est. Et sane splendidus ille character Spiritibus his inter Barbaros praesertim, & apud Reges, qui eis seducendi objiciuntur, speciem longe augustissimam conciliat, & Daemoniacam malitiam sic tegit, ut pro verae & ardentis pietatis zelo habeatur, & ipsi Daemones per eum in Angelos lucis transformentur. Tali fascino opus est iis, qui Reges excaecare, & cum Janne & Mambre veritati resistere debent.
units.tr: XL. But the functions of these spirits also suit the emissaries admirably. The Holy Spirit has likewise included those functions under three heads, saying at Revelation 16:14 that they perform miracles, go out to the kings of the earth and of the whole world, and gather them to battle. Not without reason are miracles put first. For such display is the usual trick of the Devil whenever he is so pressed by the Word and finger of God that he cannot otherwise thrust his juggling upon the world. And that near the end of the world he will use this deceit more often, Scripture testifies at Matthew 24:24, 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and Revelation 13:13-14. But what surer mark could the emissaries offer us to prove that their clientele belongs to the Dragon, the Beast and the False Prophet? In both Indies (regions which the Holy Spirit also assigns to them as their field), this mark of miracles has worked most powerfully of all, if indeed what is reported in the Indian and Japanese letters is true; there is hardly one of them that does not record some notable miracle. Stupendous miracles are ascribed above all to the first discoverers of Africa, as may be seen in Peter Martyr, book 6, Decade 2. And indeed that splendid mark, among barbarians especially and before the kings whom these spirits are set to seduce, gives them a far more august appearance, and so covers their demoniac malice that it is taken for the zeal of true and burning piety, and the demons themselves are transformed through it into angels of light. Such a charm is needed by those who must blind kings and, like Jannes and Jambres, resist the truth.

units.la: XLI. Alterum officium, eundi in ad, vel in Reges terrae & orbis habitabilis, non minus eos exequi strenue, jam supra dicere occupavimus. Sunt enim similimi Prophetis illis Achabi, in quorum ore mendacem se fore promisit Spiritus ille malus, ut Achabum ad bellum pelliceret; quem etiam efficacissime pellexerunt seduxerintque. Sic plane hi TOTORBIPE- RAMBULITECHNI, uti eos nonnemo scite insignivit, instincti a Spiritu, qui in ore illorum est, Regum limina terunt, ad Reges terrae & totius Mundi abierunt & abeunt, qui in eos & penetralia animi eorum descendunt, ut eos fraudibus & mendaciis suis obsequio Papae subjiciant, subjectos in eodem retineant, & & adversus Papæ immorigeros inflamment. Ut enim de utroque mundi cardine ab illis peragrato, turbato & devastato nil amplius dicam; de remotissimis illis orbis partibus, in quibus ante hanc exiccationem Euphratis vix hominis Europæi vestigium conspectum est, certum est, nullam ex eo tempore paulò celebriorem Legationem ex ulla Occidentis parte ad reliquos orbis Monarchas emissam esse, cui non Legati vel Emissarii hi se adjunxerint, ut sub Legationis pluteo eò penetrarent, & Papæ ibidem, à quo missi sunt, negotia curarent. Testantur id Jesuitarum de suis in India successibus Epistolæ & relationes historicæ: Matthæi Ricii de Societatis illius apud Sinas suscepta expeditione libri, à Nicolao Trigautio editi: Maffeii, à Costa, Martini, aliorum historiæ. Et Jesuitæ ab hac officii parte adeò non abhorrent, ut palam etiam profiteantur, Se pro istius rei symbolo geometricos suos pileos, quadricornuta capuciola gestare. quorum hoc mysterium pandunt: Quatuor anguli quatuor mundi plagas designant, ad quas vel à Pontifice ipso, vel à suo Generali, etiam non accepto viatico ablegantur. Neque soli Jesuitæ, sed alii etiam Monachi quadraturam illam inde à tempore non longo cucullis suis induxerunt; quin Episcopi quoque pileos hujus modi gestare coeperunt, ut similis officii admoneantur.
units.tr: XLI. We have already said above that the second function, going in to, or to the kings of the earth and the inhabited world, they perform no less diligently. For they are very like those prophets of Ahab, in whose mouth that evil spirit promised to be a lying spirit in order to entice Ahab to war; and these men too have enticed and seduced most effectively. Just so, these TOTORBIPERAMBULITECHNI, as someone has aptly named them, moved by the Spirit who is in their mouth, wear down the thresholds of kings; they have gone and still go to the kings of the earth and of the whole world; they descend into the inner recesses of their minds, so as to subject them by their frauds and lies to obedience to the Pope, to keep them so subjected, and to inflame them against the Pope's disobedient subjects. For I will say no more about the two hemispheres of the world which they have wandered over, disturbed and laid waste. Concerning those most remote parts of the world, where before this drying up of the Euphrates a trace of a European man was scarcely seen, it is certain that from that time no fairly notable embassy has been sent from any part of the West to the other monarchs of the world without these legates or emissaries attaching themselves to it, so that under the cover of the embassy they might penetrate there and attend to the Pope's business. The letters and historical reports of the Jesuits on their successes in India bear witness to this; the books of Matteo Ricci on the expedition undertaken by that Society among the Chinese, published by Nicolas Trigault; the histories of Maffei, Acosta, Martini and others. And the Jesuits shrink so little from this part of the office that they openly profess that, as a symbol of this matter, they wear geometrical caps, four-horned little hoods, whose mystery they explain thus: The four corners designate the four quarters of the world, to which they are sent out, whether by the Pontiff himself or by their General, even without receiving provision for the journey. And not only the Jesuits, but other monks too, not long since, have put that quadrilateral shape on their hoods; nay, bishops too have begun to wear caps of this kind, so that they may be reminded of a similar office.
