It is therefore a common doctrine that the sacred writers were not moved by any divine command, but were invited by chance occasions to set their hands to writing. This certainly weakens the authority of Scripture immensely. For who would call a document authentic if some writer had set it down by chance, not at the bidding of king and lord, but merely prompted by an occasion? Above all, if he ought to have put into writing not his own will but another's, and another's commands? Scripture is assailed with equal insult by those who deny its necessity. Bellarminus, indeed, in De verbo Dei, book 4, chapter 4, wishing to show that Scriptures were not simply necessary without traditions, declares his view thus: they were necessary not absolutely, but for well-being, that is, merely useful. Among other arguments he uses this one: that even when Scripture existed, the Jews used tradition rather than Scripture, because until the time of Ezra the Scriptures had not been brought together into the form of books, so that they could be easily and conveniently had, but were scattered in various annals and papers, and sometimes for a long time through the negligence of the priests they could not be found. This is an impious and blasphemous doctrine, forged in hell and brought forth with the midwifery of the hierarchs, which leads men who do not love the truth, with headlong speed, from divine revelation to human dictatorship; from the true rule to a counterfeit; from obedience to God to obedience to the devil; from the study of searching the Scriptures to contempt for them; from faith in the truth to ignorance and foolish opinions; from Christ to Antichrist; from the glorification of God to his blaspheming. What, I ask, can be heard that is more ill-sounding [δύσφημον] and more abhorrent to all faith than the claim that Scripture, divinely inspired, is not necessary? As if human wisdom, prudence [φρόνησις], vigilance, and zeal for a good conscience were such that Scripture is useful to some extent, but not necessary! Tradition is necessary, yet no divine certainty or full assurance [ἀληροφορία] can be had from it. The Pope's vicarious power and infallibility are necessary, so that all depend on the mouth of one man. But Scripture, whose revelation no other in the world surpasses in certainty, is not necessary!

units.la: XVIII. Neque minor blasphemia est humano verbo Divinitatem tribuentium, quia aliis tribuere, quod solius Dei est, omnium consensu est blasphemare Deum, gloriam Divinitatis ejus profanando dissipandóque. Atqui culpæ etiam hujus circa Materiam verbi Divini rei sunt Hierarchici, dum Divinitatem arbitratu suo, ut Tertulliani denuo verbis utar, pensitantes, eam non libris duntaxat Scripturæ Canonicis; sed verbo etiam tradito, quod merè humanum est, & libris aliis merè humanis liberali manu admetiuntur. Neque blasphemiæ reatu vacare hanc Doctrinam, ipsimet Hierarchici negabunt, si constiterit, Traditiones dogmaticas vel rituales non scriptas, necessitatis opinione & obtentu commendatas, nec non libros quoldam Ecclesiasticos, quibus utrisque illi Divinitatem arrogant, non Divinum, sed merè humanum verbum esse. De utrisque autem id liquidò à nostris frequentérque probatum est. Et traditiones non scriptas, quas Tridentini verbo scripto æquiparárunt, non Divinum, sed humanum verbum esse, inde fortiter asserimus, tum quia illæ verbo scripto addunt in diversis, detrahunt in contrariis: tum quia verbum scriptum suæ in causis fidei & morum sufficientiæ sic passim attestatur, ut omne verbum aliud non scriptum rejiciat, adeóque eo ipso humanum esse declaret: tum quia verbo scripto nihil vel diversum, vel contrarium addi potest; non diversum, quia articuli fidei copulativi sunt, & in solo fundamento fidei, quod Scripturis comprehensum esse, negari nequit implicitè reliqua continentur; non contrarium, quia alias Spiritus Dei foret ita & non, Spiritus non ordinis, sed confusionis: tum quia verbum traditum ἀπρόφευξα seu certitudinem fidei gignere nequit, cùm notas certitudinis & Divinitatis nec in se, nec in authentica norma habeat; fido custode destituitur; varietatem recipit; corruptioni obnoxium est; neque æ- qualiter omnibus fidelibus, sed alia quidem omnibus, alia solis Episcopis tradita putantur, (quæ lata porta est ad obtrudendum omne genus mendaciorum sub titulo traditionum) tum quia in V. T. traditionibus Divinis locus nullus fuit, Christo & Apostolis nullibi ad traditiones, ad verbum scriptum Mosis & Prophetarum ubique amandantibus: tum quia verbum aliquod Divinum ore duntaxat, & non scripto tradi, nec mysteriorum, quæ scribi non possint, sublimitas, nec alia quæpiam causa postulavit: tum denique quæ sint traditiones Divinæ, & quibus criteriis veræ à falsis discerni possint, quisve earum sit numerus, haftenus Hierarchici ipsi definire non sustinuerunt. Par ratio est librorum Ecclesiasticorum, quos Apocryphos vocamus. Nam & iis comprehensum verbum non Divinum sed merè humanum esse, fidem certis argumentis fecimus. Cujusmodi sunt, quòd scripti non sunt à Viris θεοπνεύστοις Divinitus inspiratis, quorum ultimus in V. T. fuit Malachias, post quem Apocryphi plerique omnes scripti sunt; quòd Ecclesiæ Judaicæ fideli, ad quam omne verbum Divinum pertinebat, traditi non sunt, neque proin ab iisdem accepti, vel à Christo & Apostolis commendati sunt: quòd Ecclesia vetus Christiana sive Græca, sive Latina eos in Canonicorum censu nunquam habuit, imò à proprie dictorum Canonicorum censu ad Concilium usque Tridentinum exclusit: quòd iis suspecta multa, frivola, ἀνυστα, mendacia, impia, fabulosa, magica comprehendantur, ut plura alia, alibi à me adversus capitales veritatis hostes Redingium Abbatem, & Othonem Lojolitam, asserta silentio præteream.
units.tr: XVIII. Equally great blasphemy is committed by those who attribute divinity to human words; for to give to others what belongs to God alone is, by universal agreement, to blaspheme God, profaning and scattering the glory of his divinity. Yet the hierarchs are also guilty of this in regard to the matter of the divine word, since they measure out divinity at their own pleasure (to use Tertullian's words again), and lavishly bestow it not only on the canonical books of Scripture, but also on the unwritten handed-down word, which is purely human, and on other purely human books. The hierarchs themselves will not deny that this doctrine is not free from the guilt of blasphemy, if it is established that the unwritten dogmatic and ritual traditions, commended under the pretext and opinion of necessity, and certain ecclesiastical books, to which they both ascribe divinity, are not a divine word but a merely human one. We have clearly and frequently proved this about both. And we strongly assert that the unwritten traditions, which the Tridentines placed on a par with the written word, are not a divine but a human word: first, because these traditions add things that differ from the written word, and take away things that conflict with it; second, because the written word attests its own sufficiency in matters of faith and morals so widely that it rejects every other unwritten word, and so by that very fact declares it to be human; third, because nothing either different or contrary can be added to the written word. Not something different, because the articles of faith are joined together, and in the foundation of faith alone, which cannot be denied to be contained in the Scriptures, the rest is implicitly contained. Not something contrary, because otherwise the Spirit of God would be "yes and no," a spirit not of order but of confusion. Fourth, because a handed-down word cannot produce the certainty of faith, since it has no marks of certainty or divinity either in itself or in any authentic standard; it lacks a faithful guardian; it admits variety; it is open to corruption; and it is not handed down equally to all the faithful, but some things are thought to have been given to all, and others to the bishops alone (which is a wide gate for thrusting every kind of lie under the name of tradition). Fifth, because in the Old Testament there was no place for divine traditions, and Christ and the Apostles nowhere send people to traditions, but everywhere to the written word of Moses and the Prophets. Sixth, because the sublimity of the mysteries, or no other cause whatever, did not require any divine word to be handed down by mouth alone and not in writing. Finally, the hierarchs themselves have not ventured to define which traditions are divine, by what criteria true ones can be distinguished from false, or how many there are. The same reasoning holds for the ecclesiastical books, which we call Apocrypha. For we have established by sure arguments that the word contained in them is not divine but purely human. Such arguments are: that they were not written by men divinely inspired [θεοπνεύστοις], the last of whom in the Old Testament was Malachi, after whom almost all the Apocrypha were written; that they were not handed down to the faithful Jewish Church, to which all the divine word belonged, and so were not received by it, nor commended by Christ and the Apostles; that the ancient Christian Church, whether Greek or Latin, never counted them among the canonical books, but indeed excluded them from the list of the strictly canonical books right up to the Council of Trent; that many suspicious, frivolous, useless, false, impious, fabulous and magical things are contained in them. I pass over many other points, which I have asserted elsewhere against the chief enemies of the truth, the Abbot Redingius and the Jesuit Otho.

units.la: XIX. Dogma illud Traditionum Scripturæ æquiparatarum, blasphemiam de imperfectione S. Scripturæ post se trahit necessario. Pudet equidem blasphemiæ hujus ipsosmet Hierarchicos, qui subinde perfectionem Scripturæ verbis asserunt, adeoque agnoscere videri volunt.
units.tr: XIX. That dogma of traditions made equal to Scripture necessarily carries with it the blasphemy that Scripture is imperfect. I am indeed ashamed of this blasphemy, even in the hierarchs themselves, who from time to time assert the perfection of Scripture in words and so seem willing to acknowledge it.

units.la: Setarius enim Proleg. cap. 24. q. 1. sic scribit: Biblia esse ad salutem hominibus conciliandam perfecta & perfectissima, nulli negant Catholici. Novissimè etiam Clerus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ inter calumnias, de quibus apud Regem Christianissimum questus est, hanc pag. 19. retulit; quòd Pontificios Scripturam imperfectionis insimulare nostri scripserint; quos inter allegat verba Georgii Dounami, Episcopi Dierensis in libro, cui titulus, Papa Antichristus; sic pag. 175. scribentis: Sacras Scripturas cum Marcionitis imperfectionis arguunt & insufficientiæ, quam certam esse notam hæreticorum Irenæus observavit. Putares,
units.tr: For Serarius in Proleg. cap. 24. q. 1. writes thus: That the Bible is perfect and most perfect for bringing men to salvation, no Catholics deny. Most recently too, the Clergy of the Gallican Church, among the calumnies of which they complained before the Most Christian King, reported this at p. 19.: that our writers have charged the Papists with accusing Scripture of imperfection. Among these they cite the words of George Downame, Bishop of Derry, in the book entitled Papa Antichristus, where at p. 175. he writes: They charge the Holy Scriptures, together with the Marcionites, with imperfection and insufficiency, which Irenaeus observed to be a certain mark of heretics. You would think...

units.la: Inprimis Scripturæ perfectionem seu sufficientiam oppugnant. Fuerunt Cleri Gallicani novissimè congregati, Serarii, aliorum, qui Scripturæ perfectionem negant, voluntatem dis-cuiuntur. res, rem confectam esse, neque Scripturam ab Hierarchicis, sed Hierachicos à nostris blasphemari. Sed fucum profecto Serarius; fucum se indignum Illustrissimus ille Clerus facit. Latet in cauda venenum. Praeterquam, inquit Serarius, in haereticorum sensu. Quis autem, Lojolita, haereticorum ille sensus est? Hic scilicet, Biblia esse perfecta relativè ad salutem; hoc est, uti ipse explicat; ita, ut ad res fidei nullo sit opus verbo Dei non scripto, seu traditione; nulla omnino interpretatione authentica alia, nullo alio controversiarum fidei judice, sed omnia solae per se ipsas efficiant Scripturae, sicque quoad efficientiam efficientiaeque modum perfectae sint, seu ad totum salutis negotium propemodum per se sufficientes. At ipse; ut dixi, Solus de Scripturae persectione ac sufficientia sensus à Catholicis negatur. Haec Serarius. Negatur ergo à Catholicis illis, Scripturam sine traditionibus ad salutem sufficere; affirmatur, alia extra Scripturam ipsam, authentica interpretatione, alio controversiarum fidei judice opus esse; negatur, Scripturas id efficere per se ipsas, hoc est, ad totum salutis negotium propemodum esse sufficientes. Ubi latet in verbis per se ipsas ambiguitas. Si enim sic intelligantur, quasi Ministerii in Ecclesia necessitas iis negaretur, calumniam continent: sin, nullo alio, quod proponatur ministerialiter, verbo opus esse, verum nobis sensum tribuunt; at suum insimul de imperfectione Scripturae sensum, ambiguis verbis, uti Sophistae solent, palliatum pandunt. Id paucis demonstremus.
units.tr: Above all, they attack the perfection or sufficiency of Scripture. The Clergy of Gaul were lately assembled, and Serarius and others who deny the perfection of Scripture are being refuted. The matter is said to be settled: it is not Scripture that is blasphemed by the hierarchs, but the hierarchs who are blasphemed by our people. But Serarius, I think, is putting on a disguise, and that most illustrious Clergy makes itself unworthy of such a disguise. The poison lies in the tail. Except, says Serarius, in the sense of the heretics. But what, Jesuit, is that sense of the heretics? It is this: that the Bible is perfect relative to salvation; that is, as he himself explains, in such a way that for matters of faith there is no need of the unwritten word of God, that is, of tradition; no authentic interpretation other than it, no other judge of controversies of faith; but that Scriptures alone, by themselves, effect everything, and so are perfect as to efficacy and the manner of efficacy, or are nearly sufficient in themselves for the whole business of salvation. But he himself, as I have said, alone denies that such a sense of the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture is held by Catholics. So Serarius. Therefore, by those Catholics, it is denied that Scripture without traditions suffices for salvation; it is affirmed that something outside Scripture itself, an authentic interpretation, another judge of controversies of faith, is needed; it is denied that Scriptures accomplish this by themselves, that is, that they are nearly sufficient in themselves for the whole business of salvation. Here lies an ambiguity in the words by themselves. If they are understood as though the necessity of a ministry in the Church were denied, they contain a calumny; but if it is meant that no other word is needed, beyond what is proposed through a ministry, they grant us the true sense, while at the same time they set forth, in ambiguous words, as Sophists are wont to do, their own disguised sense of Scripture's imperfection. Let us show this briefly.

units.la: XX. Initio quidem Serarius aliquam Scripturae sufficientiam tribuit; sed eam post ita coarctat, ut vel Caecus videre possit; Scripturae sufficientiam insufficientem, & perfectionem imperfectam tribui. Sunt, inquit, Biblia perfecta respectu rerum nobis ad salutem necessariarum dupliciter. Primò quia omnia earum genera docent & monstrant. Secundò, quia plures etiam res singulas. In explicatione generum illorum statim ulcus doctrinæ suæ aperit, tandémque aperte pronunciat; Scripturas hoc sensu esse perfectas, quia & quæ ad credendum, & quæ ad benè vivendum, necessaria sunt dogmata & præcepta dant, nófque ad Ecclesiam audiendam, traditiones Apostolicas, & Doctores Pastoresque nostros obligant. Si hoc sibi Serarius vellet, quòd non obstante eo, quòd in S. Bibliis cuncta ad salutem creditu factúque necessaria traduntur, tenea-ntur singuli audire Pastores & doctores, quos Deus in Ecclesia constituit, ut pro ratione temporum, locorum & personarum præcepta & dogmata ex Scripturis hausta nobis applicent, jam res transacta esset. Sed aliud intendit, quòd scilicet Scriptura in pluribus quidem articulis ad salutem necessarios singillatim explicet, quid credendum, faciendúmve sit; in aliis verò singillatim explicandis sic deficiat, ut ii extra Scripturam quærendi sint; sed per generalem tamen Scripturæ ductum; quatenus videlicet, uti idStapletonus Relect. Princip. Fid. cap. 5. quæst: 5. art. 1. explicat, Scriptura docens clarè & expresse, quæ sit vera Ecclesia, & ejus authoritas aliáque principia fidei doctrinalia docet tanquam in radice & principio omnia ad fidem necessaria, quia per Ecclesiam cætera dicuntur, quæ Scriptura tacet. Hæc illa Helena est, quam proci hi rapturiunt: hoc pigmentum, quo fœditatem blasphemiæ, qua Scripturam S. afficiunt, tegere conantur. Scriptura iis sufficiens est ad omnia salutis dogmata, quia ad illa omnia docet, Ecclesiam esse sufficientem: perfecta est, quia ad persectionem Ecclesiæ nos ablegat. XXI. Atqui sic haudquaquam evadunt, quò minùs juxta illos Scriptura sit imperfectissima. Cùm enim juxta eos ejus perfectio in eo consistat, quòd doceat, quæ sit illa
units.tr: XX. At first, indeed, Serarius grants some sufficiency to Scripture, but afterwards he so restricts it that even a blind man could see it: sufficiency is given to Scripture that is insufficient, and perfection to Scripture that is imperfect. There are, he says, the Bible is perfect with respect to the things necessary for us to salvation in two ways. First, because it teaches and shows all their kinds. Second, because it also gives several single things. In explaining those kinds he at once opens the sore of his doctrine, and at last openly declares that Scriptures are perfect in this sense because they give the dogmas and precepts necessary both for believing and for living well, and they bind us to hear the Church, the Apostolic traditions, and our Teachers and Ministers. If Serarius meant only this: that, although in the Holy Bible all things necessary to be believed and done for salvation are handed down, individuals are nonetheless bound to hear the ministers and teachers whom God has set in the Church, so that they may apply to us, according to the circumstances of times, places and persons, the precepts and dogmas drawn from Scripture, then the matter would already be settled. But he intends something else: namely, that Scripture indeed explains in detail, in many articles necessary to salvation, what is to be believed or done; but in others, which are to be explained in detail, it so fails that these must be sought outside Scripture, yet still by the general guidance of Scripture. That is to say, as Stapleton also explains in Relect. Princip. Fid. cap. 5. quaest. 5. art. 1.: Scripture, teaching clearly and expressly what the true Church is, teaches its authority and the other doctrinal principles of faith as in a root and principle, and all things necessary to faith; for the other things which Scripture is silent about are said through the Church. This is that Helen for whose sake these suitors go to war; this is the paint with which they try to cover the foulness of the blasphemy by which they stain Holy Scripture. Scripture is sufficient for them for all the dogmas of salvation because it teaches that the Church is sufficient for all of them; it is perfect because it sends us away to the perfection of the Church. XXI. But by no means do they thereby escape the charge that, on their own view, Scripture is most imperfect. For since, according to them, its perfection consists in this, that it teaches what that Church is...

units.la: Ecclesia, cui nos docendos tradere debemus, si id Scriptura facere non potest, certè manca & mutila erit. Stapletonus equidem ait, Scripturam docere clarè & expresse, quae sit vera Ecclesia. Sed quæ tum ille, tum alii de natura Scripturæ, Ecclesiæ & Traditionis disputant, often-dunt, ad id Scripturam non solùm sufficientem non esse, sed nec aptam, vel tantillum utilem. Ut Scriptura sit principium credendi ratione nostri, fieri per Hierarchicos non potest, nisi priùs id nobis Ecclesiæ testimonio constet. Testimonium autem Ecclesiæ non potest fidem facere, nisi id nobis certum sit, verum esse & fide credendum, quicquid Ecclesia docet tanquam tale. Non ergo id per Scripturam nobis primò innotescit, cùm id certum esse debeat, priusquàm credere quis possit, Scripturam esse Dei verbum. Hinc sanè sequitur, Scripturam peræos esse imperfectissimam; & articulum de Ecclesia & eius authoritate aliunde nobis innotescere, priusquam de eo fidem Scripturæ adhibere possimus. Tum ne sic quidem, postquam ex Ecclesiæ testimonio Scripturæ ἀνῳτιλία innotuit, clarè & expressè, quæ sit vera Ecclesia, ex Scriptura nobis innotescit. Nullibi enim expressè habetur, vel Ecclesiam Romanam esse & manere perpetim veram Ecclesiam; vel solam esse veram Ecclesiam. Id enim ex consequentiis quibusdam deducendum erit, in quibus propositionibus quibusdam extra Scripturam, quarum veritas ex sensu patebit, utendum erit. Unde sequetur, ex ipsorum hypothesibus, ex Scriptura non deduci conclusionem, quæ sit de fide, quòd Romana præsens Ecclesia sit vera Ecclesia, quam audire debemus, quia conclusio deteriorem partem sequitur. Ut autem ostendant id, quod de Ecclesia dicitur in Scriptura, ad Romanam Ecclesiam, quæ nunc est, pertinere, aliunde assumptio petenda erit. Proinde nec id Scriptura secundum eos aperte docet. Quomodo ergo, juxta eos, Scriptura perfectissima est, quia omnia rerum ad salutem necessariarum genera docet & monstrat? Sed esto etiam. Doceat Scriptura sufficienter, quæ sit vera Ecclesia, cujus in rebus fidei decretis standum sit. Sic certè Ecclesia persecta erit perfectione illa relativa; Scriptura verò erit imperfectissima, utpote quæ non ipsa docet, sed ad alium doctorem remittit, à quo ipsa pendeat, & sine quo non solum nullam apud nos authoritatem habebit, sed etiam, postquam precariam aliquam obtinuerit, non poterit de multis nos certiores reddere, sine quibus salus nostra periclitabitur. Quomodo ergo ratione salutis nostræ vel persecta, vel perfectissima erit? Implicitè, regerunt, quia etsi ipsa talia non habeat, ostendit tamen, unde peti possint. Sic ergo quilibet pauper dives erit implicitè, quia indicare potest, ubi divitiæ sint: quilibet illiteratus doctus, quia ostendere potest Academiam, in qua doctiores docent: is qui nutricem indicat, cujus ubera affluunt lacte, infantulo lac perfectè suppeditare dici poterit: is cibis abundabit, qui mensam opiparam & deliciis instructissimam ostendit: denique Samaritana illa mulier, vel Johannes Baptista pleni fuerint gratia & veritate, qui ostenderunt Messiam plenum gratia & veritate. Neque alia Scripturæ sufficientia competet, quàm quæ literis fiduciariis, quibus jubetur quis fidem habere verbis illius, qui eas reddituros est, competit: imò minor etiam, quia supponitur, eum qui tales literas accipit, notam habere manum & sigillum ejus, qui scribit; & fiduciariæ dicuntur, quia fidem conciliant ei, qui mandata ferre, & verbis suis exponere debet; cùm contra Pontificii vetent credere, quòd authoritas Ecclesiæ à Scriptura pendeat, & hujus potiùs authoritatem ab Ecclesiæ testimonio quoad nos totam suspendant. Quorsum denique attinebat tot libros V. & N. T. conscribi dictante Spiritu, cùm uno hoc verbo: Audite Ecclesiam, seu Papam
units.tr: ...to which we ought to be handed over to be taught, if Scripture cannot do this, it will surely be defective and maimed. Stapleton indeed says that Scripture teaches clearly and expressly what the true Church is. But what both he and others argue concerning the nature of Scripture, the Church and tradition shows that Scripture is not only not sufficient for this, but not even fit for it, or useful in the least. For Scripture to be a principle of belief for us, it cannot come about through the hierarchs unless it is first established for us by the testimony of the Church. But the testimony of the Church cannot produce faith unless it is certain to us that whatever the Church teaches as such is true and to be believed. Therefore this is not first made known to us through Scripture, since it must be certain before anyone can believe that Scripture is the Word of God. Hence it surely follows that Scripture is most imperfect for them, and that the article concerning the Church and its authority becomes known to us from elsewhere, before we can give faith to Scripture concerning it. Yet not even then, after the authority [αὐθεντία] of Scripture has become known to us from the testimony of the Church, is it made known to us from Scripture clearly and expressly what the true Church is. For nowhere is it expressly stated either that the Roman Church is and always remains the true Church, or that it alone is the true Church. For this would have to be deduced from certain consequences, in which some propositions outside Scripture, whose truth will be evident from their meaning, would have to be used. Whence it follows, on their own hypotheses, that from Scripture there is not deduced a conclusion that belongs to faith, namely that the present Roman Church is the true Church which we ought to hear, because the conclusion follows the weaker part. Moreover, in order to show that what is said of the Church in Scripture pertains to the Roman Church that now exists, the minor premise must be sought from elsewhere. Therefore, according to them, Scripture does not openly teach even this. How then, on their view, is Scripture most perfect, because it teaches and shows all the kinds of things necessary to salvation? But grant it even so. Let Scripture teach sufficiently what the true Church is, whose decisions in matters of faith are to be obeyed. Then surely the Church will be perfect with that relative perfection; but Scripture will be most imperfect, since it does not itself teach, but refers us to another teacher, on whom it depends, and without whom it will not only have no authority among us, but even when it has obtained some borrowed authority, it will not be able to inform us about many things without which our salvation will be in peril. How then, with respect to our salvation, will it be either perfect or most perfect? Implicitly, they reply, because even if it does not itself contain such things, it shows whence they may be sought. So then any pauper would be rich implicitly, because he can point out where riches are; any illiterate man learned, because he can show the Academy where the more learned teach; he who points out the nurse whose breasts overflow with milk could be said to supply the infant with milk perfectly; he will abound in food who shows a lavish table furnished with delicacies. Finally, the Samaritan woman, or John the Baptist, were full of grace and truth, because they pointed to the Messiah, full of grace and truth. Nor does Scripture have any other sufficiency than that which belongs to letters of trust, by which one is bidden to have faith in the words of him who is to deliver them. Indeed it has even less, because it is supposed that the one who receives such letters knows the hand and seal of the one who writes; and they are called letters of trust because they win faith for the one who must carry the orders and explain them in his own words. Whereas, on the contrary, the Papists forbid us to believe that the authority of the Church depends on Scripture, and rather make the authority of Scripture wholly dependent, so far as we are concerned, on the testimony of the Church. Finally, what was the point of so many books of the Old and New Testament being written under the dictation of the Spirit, when the whole matter could have been committed to and settled by this one word: Hear the Church, or the Pope

units.la: Tom. II. kk RomaRomanum è Cathedra docentem; res tota Ecclesiæ committi & expediri potuerit.
units.tr: Tom. II. kk Rome the Roman pontiff teaching from the Chair; the whole matter could have been committed to the Church and settled by it.

units.la: XXII. Quid verò multis? Cùm diu hostes Scripturæ heic lucem fugerunt, neque sine nebulis & fallaciis in conspectu hominum comparuerunt, tandem sibi larvam detrahunt ipsi, verbum traditum, ceu speciem oppositam, Scripturæ opponentes, & perfectionem Scripturæ palam oppugnantes. Roffensis art. 27. pag. 584. Falsum est, inquit, quòd omnia, quæ vel ad fidem pertinent, vel ad morum & operum legem, plenè sint in Scripturis exposita. Censura Coloniensis sol. 220. aperte contendit, Scripturam esse imperfectam, mutilam, mancam, quæ non continet omnia, quæ ad fidem & mores pìè vivendi pertinent. Hesselius in Catech. pag. 44. Non hoc ait, egerunt Apostoli scribentes, ut tutam fidei doctrinam scripto traderent, sed pro necessitate nata, quod verbo erga absentes præstare non poterant, hoc literis egerunt, contenti satisfacere difficultati occurrenti. Bellarminus de Verbo Dei lib. iv. 3. Asserimus nos, in Scriptura non contineri expresse totam doctrinam necessariam, sive de fide, sive de moribus; & proinde præter verbum Dei scriptum requiri etiam non Scriptum. quibus posterioribus verbis aperit, quid sibi velit adverbium illud expresse. nempe non illud, quòd omnia fidei & morum dogmata totidem verbis in Scriptura non inveniantur, sed per consequentiam inde deducenda sint; verùm quòd traditiones quædam non scriptæ dogmatis fidei & morum scriptis addendæ sint. Per traditionem hanc non scriptam nisi staret, nullæ apud eos Scripturæ momenti alicujus essent. Sic enim Lindanus lib. de Optimo genere interpretandi, Præfat. pag. 9. scribit: Traditio Ecclesiastica omnis planè nostræ Christianæ religionis est puppis & prora, indubitatùmque salutis & castrum & propugnaculum: quòd ea salva, omnis doctrina Scripturarum, rarum, rarum, etiam perditarum, adeoque exustarum & deletarum, consistat salva: quam Christus ille Christiano gregi à Christo Pastore Doctor promissus non modò suggeret, sed tuebitur etiam atque propugnabit, vero Christi sensu illustratam. In margine notat: Salvo traditionis Apostolica fundamento nihil noxæ inferetur Ecclesiæ, licet aboleantur Scripturæ: Addit paulò post: Neque Princeps neque primarium in Scripturarum salute positum est momentum. Denique Pighius Eccles. Hier. lib. i. 4. ad traditiones potiùs quàm Scripturas provocandum esse contendit: Cujus, inquit, doctrinæ si memores fuissemus, hæreticos non esse informandos seu convincendos ex Scripturis, meliore sanè loco essent res nostræ. Sed dum ostentandi ingenii & eruditionis gratia cum Luthero in certamen descenditur Scripturarum, excitatum est hoc, quod proh dolor! videmus incendium. Huic proin extinguendo incendio ex eo tempore nervos omnes intenderunt, ut Scripturæ omnem authoritatem & perfectionem derogarent, & ab earundem possessione & lectione suos viribus omnibus arcerent.
units.tr: XXII. But why say more? For a long time the enemies of Scripture have shunned the light here, and have appeared before men only amid clouds and deceptions. At last they strip off their own mask, setting unwritten tradition against Scripture as if it were a rival, and openly attacking Scripture's perfection. Roffensis (art. 27, p. 584): "It is false," he says, "that everything which pertains either to faith or to the law of morals and works is fully set out in the Scriptures." The Cologne Censure (sol. 220) plainly contends that Scripture "is imperfect, mutilated, maimed, and does not contain all that pertains to faith and to living piously in morals." Hesselius in his Catechism (p. 44): "He does not say that the Apostles, in writing, intended to hand down the safe doctrine of faith in writing, but that, from the necessity that arose, what they could not do for absent people by word, they did by letter, content to satisfy the difficulty that had occurred." Bellarmine (On the Word of God, bk. IV, ch. 3): "We assert that the whole doctrine necessary, whether concerning faith or morals, is not expressly contained in Scripture, and therefore, besides the written word of God, the unwritten also is required." By these last words he makes clear what he means by the adverb "expressly": not that all the dogmas of faith and morals are not found in Scripture in so many words, and must be deduced from it by consequence, but that certain unwritten traditions must be added to the written dogmas of faith and morals. Unless this unwritten tradition stood, Scripture would have no weight of any kind for them. So Lindanus (On the Best Kind of Interpreting, Preface, p. 9) writes: "All ecclesiastical tradition is quite plainly the stern and prow of our whole Christian religion, and the undoubted fortress and bulwark of salvation; while it stands safe, all the teaching of the Scriptures survives safe, even if rare or lost, and so burnt and destroyed. That Christ, the Teacher promised by Christ the Shepherd to the Christian flock, not only suggests this but also guards and defends it, illuminated by the true sense of Christ." In the margin he notes: "While the foundation of Apostolic tradition is safe, no harm will come to the Church, even if the Scriptures are abolished." A little later he adds: "Neither the Prince nor the chief point of salvation lies in the Scriptures." Finally Pighius (Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, bk. I, ch. 4) contends that appeal must be made to traditions rather than to the Scriptures: "If we had been mindful of this teaching," he says, "heretics would not have to be instructed or convicted from the Scriptures, and our cause would certainly stand in a better place." But while, for the sake of showing off wit and learning, people have entered into a contest over the Scriptures with Luther, this fire has been kindled, which, alas! we see. From that time on they have strained every nerve to put out this fire, to take away from Scripture all authority and perfection, and to keep men from its possession and reading by every means in their power.

units.la: XXIII. Alia, neque minùs impia blasphemia circa Scripturæ formam, seu genuinum sensum ernergit.
units.tr: XXIII. Another blasphemy, no less impious, arises concerning the form, or genuine sense, of Scripture.

units.la: Etenim Scripturæ forma interior & anima in Θεοπνευςία seu inspiratione Divina, adeoque sensu ejus Divinitus inspirato consistit. Cúmque Scripturæ cujusvis sensus, æquè atque forma, ei insitus sit; etiam Scripturæ Divinæ sensus eidem ceu anima quædam, insitus sit oportet. Qui ergo Scripturæ sensum aliunde arcessunt, & ab humano sensu & arbitraria interpretatione suspendunt; ii procul omni dubio Scripturam Divina inspiratione & Divino sensu, qui ejus anima est, suo defraudant, & humano arbitrio Scripturam pro lubitu interpretanti & animanti, quod solius Spiritus Divini est, tribuunt; adeóque Scripturam, & in Scriptura Deum blasphemant. Hoc autem Hierarchicos facere palam est. Nam sensum Scripturæ apertè negant ex ipsa Scriptura per spiritualem ἐπλωσιν & demonstrationem arcessendum esse; asserúntque, non aliunde quàm ex Ecclesiæ, quæ hominum coetus est, & verbum Dei ac sensum ejus non constituit, vel authenticè declarat, sed ab eo constituitur, arbitrio & infallibili interpretatione arcessendum esse. Tridentini enim Seff. iv. graviter vetant, ne quisquam Sacram Scripturam contra sensum, quem tenuit & tenet Sancta mater Ecclesia, cujus sit judicare de vero sensu & interpretatione Scripturarum Sacrarum; aut etiam contra unanimem consensum Patrum, interpretari audeat. Per Sanctam matrem Ecclesiam, intelligunt Ecclesiam Romanam, quæ particularis est. Planum ergo est, sensum Scripturæ ab hominum judicio suspendi; ac sine eo Scripturam, juxta definitionem Concilii, sensum nullum fundere: quin & humano illi judicio Divinitatem vendicari. Sensus enim Scripturæ Divinæ Divinus est. Cùm igitur à judicio interpretantis Ecclesiæ pendeat, ipsum etiam judicium hoc. Divinum sensum depromens, Divinum sit oportet.
units.tr: For the inner form and soul of Scripture consists in theopneustia [Θεοπνευστία], that is, divine inspiration, and so in its divinely inspired sense. Since the sense of any writing is inherent in it, just as its form is, the divine sense of Scripture must likewise be inherent in it, as a kind of soul. Therefore those who seek the sense of Scripture from elsewhere, and make it depend on human understanding and arbitrary interpretation, undoubtedly defraud Scripture of its divine inspiration and divine sense, which is its soul. They attribute to human judgment, which interprets and animates Scripture as it pleases, what belongs to the Divine Spirit alone, and so they blaspheme Scripture and, in Scripture, God. That the Hierarchists do this is plain. For they openly deny that the sense of Scripture is to be drawn from Scripture itself by spiritual explication [ἐπίλυσιν] and demonstration. They assert instead that it must be drawn from the arbitrary and infallible interpretation of the Church, which is an assembly of men, which does not establish the word of God and its sense or authentically declare it, but is itself established by it. For the Council of Trent, Session iv, sternly forbids anyone to dare to interpret Holy Scripture contrary to the sense which holy mother Church has held and holds, to whom it belongs to judge the true sense and interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, or even contrary to the unanimous consent of the Fathers. By holy mother Church they mean the Roman Church, which is only a particular church. It is therefore plain that the sense of Scripture is made to depend on human judgment, and that, according to the Council's definition, Scripture yields no sense at all without it. Indeed, divinity is claimed for that human judgment. For the sense of divine Scripture is divine. Since it depends on the judgment of the interpreting Church, that judgment itself, which brings forth the divine sense, must necessarily be divine.

units.la: XXIV. Ad cumulum blasphemiarum accedit, quòd probaturi Hierarchici necessitatem Scripturæ per Ecclesiæ definitiones interpretandæ, sibi temperare nequeunt, quò minùs multa adversus Scripturam inclementer effudiant. Accusant enim eam perfrictâ fronte ambiguitatis & obscuritatis; adeò quidem ut eam, ceu fidei articulum, propugnent, & in reddendis obscuritatis causis plurimùm desudent. uti apud varios Theologos eorum Polemicos videre est. Sine traditione & sententia Ecclesiæ eam & obscuram esse, & ambiguam, & nasi cerei instar flexibilem, sic Cardinalis Pighius Hier. Eccl. lib. j. cap. 4. & lib. v. 3. pertendit: Demonstramus authoritatem traditionis Ecclesiasticlesiasticæ magis idoneam, quàm Scripturarum, ad fidem certitudinémque faciendam in re dubia, etiam ubi id, de quo agitur, ex Scriptura constare posset. Cùm clarior sit, & magis aperta, planéque inflexibilis communis Ecclesiæ sententia, traditióque Ecclesiastica; cùm contra Scripturæ plurimum frequenter obscuritatis habeant, & horsum illorsúmque, velut nasus cereus, trahi se permittant, & velut plumbeam quandam regulam applicari impiæ cujusvis sententiæ. In Concilio Tridentino Pictavius Scripturam dixit esse rem inanimem atque mutam, eóque, sicut reliquæ leges Politicæ, judicis voce animandam. Pamelius ad Tertullianum de Præscript.num.237. Scripturam ipsʃ equoque vocat nasum cereum, ad res profanas & impias probandas flexibiliorem & faciliorem, quàm facile est ex pedibus aut semipedibus; aut penthemimeribus Virgilianis epithalamia, seu quidvis aliud congerere. Baronius ad A.34. num. 4.215. Scripturam lapidem offensionis, petram scandali esse affirmat omnibus iis, qui non per ostium (hoc est, ex præscripto Tridentinorum Patrum, veniam ab Episcopo impetratam) ingressi, se ad legendos libros sacros accinxerint. quo horribili carmine Christianos universo sà Scripturis abster rere conatur. Quomodo eadem blasphemia Gregorius de Valentia Annal. lib. iv. 4. Scripturam petram scandali vocat, ad perdendos omnes eos, qui ea sola nituntur. Cofterus in Enchirid. cap. eam ait esse vaginam, quæ gladium chalybeum, plumbeum, ligneum perinde recipit. Walenburgii Controv. iv. num. 26. blasphemant, absque Scripturæ interpretatione authentica per Ecclesiam, nullam Rempublicam stultius constituí potuisse, quàm Christianam; & prædicationem Apostolorum non aliud, quàm puerorum & psittacorum, qui sine mente dant & accipiunt sonos, prædicationem fuisse. Diceres, hos Scripturarum diabolos de Delphicorum oraculorum, aut Sybillinorum foliorum ambibiguitate agere.
units.tr: XXIV. To the heap of blasphemies is added this: the Hierarchists, wishing to prove the necessity of interpreting Scripture through the definitions of the Church, cannot restrain themselves from pouring out many harsh charges against Scripture. With brazen face they accuse it of ambiguity and obscurity, so much so that they champion this as an article of faith, and they sweat hard in assigning the causes of its obscurity, as can be seen in the various polemical theologians among them. That without tradition and the judgment of the Church Scripture is obscure, ambiguous, and bendable like a wax nose, Cardinal Pighius Hier. Eccl. lib. i. cap. 4. & lib. v. 3. maintains: "We show that the authority of ecclesiastical tradition is more suited than that of Scripture to produce faith and certainty in a doubtful matter, even where what is in question could be established from Scripture. For the common opinion of the Church and ecclesiastical tradition is clearer, more open, and plainly inflexible, whereas the Scriptures very often have much obscurity, and allow themselves to be dragged this way and that, like a wax nose, and to be applied like some leaden rule to any impious opinion whatever." At the Council of Trent, Pictavius called Scripture a lifeless and mute thing, which, like the other political laws, must therefore be animated by the voice of a judge. Pamelius, on Tertullian's De Praescriptione, also calls Scripture a wax nose, more pliable and easier to bend to prove profane and impious things than it is to gather epithalamia from Virgilian feet, half-feet, or penthemimers. Baronius, at A.D. 34 num. 4.215, affirms that Scripture is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to all who have girded themselves to read the sacred books without entering by the door (that is, by the prescription of the Fathers of Trent, having obtained permission from the bishop). With this dreadful verse he tries to keep Christians altogether from Scripture. In the same blasphemy, Gregory of Valencia, Annal. lib. iv. 4., calls Scripture a rock of offence, for the ruin of all who rely on it alone. Coster in the Enchiridion, cap., says it is a sheath which receives a sword of steel, lead, or wood alike. Walenburch, Controv. iv. num. 26., blasphemes, saying that without the authentic interpretation of Scripture by the Church no commonwealth could have been established more foolishly than the Christian one, and that the preaching of the Apostles was nothing but the preaching of boys and parrots, who give and receive sounds without mind. You would think these devils of Scripture were dealing with the ambiguity of the Delphic oracles or the Sibylline leaves.

units.la: XXV. Quòd Scripturam sic ambiguitatis & obscuritatis palam accusant, mirandum equidem non est, quia nihil eorum in ea inveniunt, quæ ad defensionem Papismi faciunt: sùntque perobscura, aut potiùs nulla præsidia, quæ ex Scriptura ad palliandos errores suos comminiscuntur. Non enim si lynceos oculos haberent, in ea invocationem Sanctorum, successionem Papæ in Apostolatum Petri, cultum imaginum, adorationem reliquiarum, sacrificium Missæ &c. invenirent. Ad quæ stabilienda utcunque Scripturam nasi instar cerei, pro quo illam venditant, torqueant, flectant, inflectant, nihil tamen extorquent. Nec dubium est, quin Hierarchici de Scripturæ obscuritate quæsti, eam cupiant esse centuplo obscuriorem, quotiescunque errores Papismi evidenter jugulat, & tenebras, quas ipsi offuderunt, multa luce perfundit.
units.tr: XXV. That they openly accuse Scripture of ambiguity and obscurity is indeed not surprising, because they find nothing in it that supports the defence of Papism. The proofs they devise from Scripture to cloak their errors are very obscure, or rather no proofs at all. For even if they had eyes like lynxes, they would not find in it the invocation of saints, the succession of the Pope to the apostolate of Peter, the worship of images, the adoration of relics, the sacrifice of the Mass, and so on. To establish these things they twist, bend, and bow Scripture, which they peddle as a wax nose, yet they wrest nothing out of it. Nor is there any doubt that the Hierarchists, when they complain of the obscurity of Scripture, wish it were a hundred times more obscure whenever it plainly strikes down the errors of Papism and pours much light over the darkness they themselves have spread.

units.la: XXVI. Restant blasphemiæ adversus Scripturæ finem, qui haud dubiè alius, Dei Scripturam inspirantis & Ecclesiæ tradentis respectu, esse non potuit, quàm ut esset fidei vitæque nostræ Canon sive regula, adeoque etiam Controversiarum omnium in Ecclesia oborientium arbitra & judex. Nam & diserte κανὼν Canon seu regula Gal. vi. 16. appellatur; & ad eam, ceu arbitram, ambigua litium fata dirempturam, omnes remittuntur, Esaj. viii. 20. Luc. xvi. 29. & κρίνειν judicare Joh. xii. 48. dicitur. Neque enim Scripturam & regulam, quatenus fidei & morum norma unica & amussis est: & simul judicem esse, quia fides, quæ veritatem recipit, nullam aliam judicis sententiam audit vel novit, nisi demonstrationem ex Scriptura: & nihil aliud in Ecclesia, in rebus fidei audiri debet, nisi revelatio Dei in Scriptura loquentis pugnat. Mitto argumenta πλανωτάια, quibus hoc fidei Christianæ principium à nobis alibi corroboratum est. Qui ergo hac Scripturam prærogativa defraudat, & eandem in aliud verbum ἀδηλον, & juratum quendam hominum coetum, vel ejus potius principem Papam transfert, is Scripturæ, quod suum est, eripit, & Divinum hoc ἀλειτύργημα non-Deo tribuit, adeóque Scripturam γομμῇ κεφαλῇ blasphemat.
units.tr: XXVI. There remain blasphemies against the purpose of Scripture. With respect to God, who inspired it, and to the Church, which received it, its purpose can undoubtedly be nothing other than to be the canon or rule of our faith and life, and therefore also the arbiter and judge of all controversies arising in the Church. For it is expressly called the canon, or rule [κανών] (Gal. 6:16), and all are referred to it as to an arbiter that will settle the uncertain outcome of disputes (Isa. 8:20; Luke 16:29), and it is said to judge [κρίνειν] (John 12:48). Scripture is the sole and exact norm of faith and morals, and it is also the judge, because faith, which receives the truth, hears and knows no other judgement than demonstration from Scripture. Nothing else should be heard in the Church in matters of faith, unless it contends with the revelation of God speaking in Scripture. I pass over the arguments [πλανωτάια] by which we have elsewhere confirmed this principle of the Christian faith. Whoever therefore deprives Scripture of this prerogative and transfers it to something obscure [ἄδηλον], to a certain sworn assembly of men, or rather to its head, the Pope, takes from Scripture what is its own and ascribes this divine office [λειτούργημα] to a non-God. In this way he blasphemes Scripture with bare head [γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ].

units.la: XXVII. Hoc autem facere Hierarchicos, ne ipsi quidem inficias ire, ausint. Quomodo enim norma, regula Divina esse potest, quod nasus cereus, regula Lesbia est? Quomodo Scriptura norma & judex fidei esse potest, si, quod Bellarminus de Verbo Dei lib. iv. i2. pronuntiat, Scriptura finis proprius & præcipuus non fuit, ut esset regula fidei, sed ut esset commonitorium quoddam utile ad confervandam & fovendam doctrinam ex prædicatione acceptam? Si, quod ibidem mox statuit, est regula fidei non totalis sed partialis? Nam vel totalis fidei regula est, vel plane regula non est. Si enim fides nostra est Scriptura latior, non poterit Scriptura esse fidei regula, quia regulam inter & regulatum æqualis fidei certitudo intercedat oportet; & regula quævis, nec oppositionem, nec diminutionem patitur. Nam judice Chrysostomo in Epist. ad Phil. homil. 12. 'O καιῶν ἐν πεισθῆναι, ἐν ἀφαιρέσει δίκῃ, ... Regula neque additionem, neque ablationem recipit, alioquin enim regula non esset. Varinus in voce κανὼν consentit, inquiens: Κανὼν ἐστι νόμος ἀπαράλλακτος ... Regula, seu Canon est lex perpetua, & mensura fallere & falli nescia, quæ nec additionem nec ablationem ullo modo recipit. Possent ex S. Patribus, gravissimè hoc urgentibus plurima afferri. XXVIII. Pari protervia Scripturæ partes judicis Hierarchici abjudicant, ut illas Papæ, terrestri judici, vindicent. dixerit licet Optatus Milevitanus lib. v. contra Parmen, men. verissimè, in terris de rebus fidei nullum posse repe-riri judicium; de Cælo quærendum esse judicem. Sed ut quid pulsamus, inquit, ad Cælum, cum hic habeamus in Euangelio testamentam. Sed alia nunc tempora vivimus.
units.tr: XXVII. The Hierarchists themselves would not dare to deny that they do this. For how can a norm or rule be divine if the Lesbian rule is a leaden measure? How can Scripture be the norm and judge of faith if, as Bellarmine states in de Verbo Dei lib. iv. 12, Scripture's proper and chief purpose was not that it should be a rule of faith, but that it should be a useful reminder for preserving and nourishing the doctrine received from preaching? And if, as he lays down a little later in the same place, it is a rule of faith not complete but partial? For either it is the complete rule of faith or it is no rule at all. If our faith is broader than Scripture, Scripture cannot be the rule of faith, since there must be an equal certainty between the rule and what is ruled, and no rule admits of addition or diminution. For, as Chrysostom judges in Epist. ad Phil. homil. 12: "The canon [ὁ κανὼν] admits neither addition nor subtraction [ἐν πεισθῆναι, ἐν ἀφαιρέσει δίκῃ], otherwise it would not be a rule." Varinus, in the word κανών, agrees, saying: "The canon [Κανὼν] is an unchanging law [νόμος ἀπαράλλακτος]... A rule, or canon, is a perpetual law and measure that cannot deceive or be deceived, and admits neither addition nor subtraction in any way." Very many passages could be cited from the holy Fathers, who press this point most seriously. XXVIII. With equal boldness the Hierarchists strip Scripture of the role of judge in order to claim that role for the Pope, the earthly judge. Optatus of Milevis, in book 5 against Parmenianus, rightly says that no judgement can be found on earth in matters of faith; the judge must be sought from heaven. "But why," he says, "do we knock at heaven, when we have the testament here in the Gospel?" But we now live in other times.

units.la: Papæ enim libuit omne ad se & cathedram suam judicium contrahere, tum ut textus Scripturæ manifestos, quibus ejus idololatria, hæreses & tyrannis oppugnantur, suæ interpretationis judicio sic inflectere posset, quò suis rationibus inservire cogantur: tum ut, ubi prorsus silet Scriptura, è latebris vel scrinio pectoris Papalis extrahatur non scripta traditio pari pietatis affectu cum Scriptura suscipienda, quæ ceu alter gladius Alexandri nodum secet, vel hoc quoque deficiente stet pro ratione voluntas, & judicis terrore ad Harpocraticum silentium partes adigantur.
units.tr: For it has pleased the Pope to draw all judgement to himself and his chair, so that, first, he may bend the manifest texts of Scripture, by which his idolatry, heresies and tyranny are attacked, to serve his own interpretation, so that they are forced to serve his arguments; and second, so that where Scripture is entirely silent, an unwritten tradition, to be received with the same reverence as Scripture, may be drawn from the hiding places or the chest of the Papal heart, to cut the knot like a second sword of Alexander; and if this too fails, his will stands as the reason, and by the terror of his judgement the parties are driven into Harpocratic silence.

units.la: XXIX. Bellarminus de Verbo Dei lib. iij. 3. de judice controversiarum, & authentico Scripturæ Interprete disputans, sic progreditur: Convenit inter nos & adversarios, Scripturas debere intelligi eo Spiritu, quo factæ sunt, hoc est, Spiritu S. Tota igitur quæstio est, ubi sit ipse Spiritus? Nos (Catholici Romanenses) exȉtimamus, hunc Spiritum, etsi multis privatis hominibus sæpe concedítur, tamen certò inveniri in Ecclesia, hoc est, in Concilio Episcoporum confirmato à summo Pontifice Pastore, sive in summo Pastore cum Concilio aliorum Pastorum.
units.tr: XXIX. Bellarmine, in de Verbo Dei lib. iij. 3, discussing the judge of controversies and the authentic interpreter of Scripture, proceeds thus: "It is agreed between us and our opponents that Scriptures must be understood by the Spirit by whom they were written, that is, the Holy Spirit. The whole question, therefore, is where that Spirit himself is. We Roman Catholics think that this Spirit, although it is often granted to many private persons, is nevertheless certainly found in the Church, that is, in a council of bishops confirmed by the supreme Pontiff as shepherd, or in the supreme shepherd together with a council of other shepherds."

units.la: Ideo dicimus, judicem veri sensus Scripturæ & omnium controversiarum esse Ecclesiam, hoc est, Pontificem cum Concilio, in quo omnes Catholici conveniunt. At hæretici omnes hujus temporis docent, Spiritum S. Scripturæ interpretem alligatum non esse Episcopis, vel ulli hominum generi &c. Non igitur Spiritus S. ei judex est Summus, prout in Scriptura loquitur, & sententiam ferre ex ipsâ Scriptura, ministeriali discretionis judicio à tota Ecclesia & singulis fidelibus demonstratur: sed prout loquitur in Ecclesia, & per eam, seu potiùs in Papa, & per eum, in quem omnia denique resolvuntur: ita ut solum Papæ dictum & oraculum, sive demonstratum ex Scripturis, sive non, habendum sit pro infallibili judicio, controversias omnes dirimente, & conscientias ad fidem definitionibus suis habendam obstringente. Annon hoc est Spiritum S. judicem à Scriptura, in qua loquitur & sententiam fert, abstrahere, & Papæ, hominis Itali talis qualis, certè Scripturam non amantis, nisi quatenus eam concupiscentiis suis inservire cogit, servituti mancipare? Etenim veræ Ecclesiæ & singulis ejus membris Spiritum S. sic affulgere, ut ejus gratia illuminatis oculis videant in Scripturis magnalia Dei, & genuinum earundem sensum percipiant, atque tum sibi, tum aliis eum demonstrent; denique judicium ejus in Scripturis propositum sequantur, ultra equidem fatemur. At Ecclesiam, hoc est, Papam cum Concilio, vel sine eo, sic Spiritum S. ceu peculium quoddam possidere, ut dicta quævis, sive ex Scripturis demonstrata, sive non; velut ab eo procedentia pro authoritate & imperio fidelibus, ceu subditis suis dictare posset, atque illi sic pro imperio dictata ἀδουμάσως & cœca quadam obedientia, haud aliter ac ipsius Dei effata recipere & exosculari teneantur; hoc inquam, est, Scripturæ, seu Spiritui S. in Scriptura loquenti & definienti judicium omne Divinum abdicare, & in hominem vel cœtum quempiam juratum, monopolium hoc Spiritus S. non pretio, sed vi rapientem, & solo nutu, non demonstratione necessaria, fidei dominantem non sine blasphemia atrocissima, transferre.
units.tr: "Therefore we say that the judge of the true sense of Scripture and of all controversies is the Church, that is, the Pontiff with a council, in which all Catholics agree. But all heretics of this time teach that the Holy Spirit, the interpreter of Scripture, is not bound to bishops or to any class of men, etc. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not the supreme judge of it as he speaks in Scripture, and pronounces sentence from Scripture itself, shown by the ministerial judgement of discernment to the whole Church and to each of the faithful; but he speaks in the Church and through it, or rather in the Pope, and through him, into whom all things are finally resolved. So that the mere word and oracle of the Pope, whether demonstrated from Scripture or not, must be held as an infallible judgement, settling all controversies and binding consciences to hold his definitions as faith. Is this not to tear the Holy Spirit as judge away from Scripture, in which he speaks and pronounces sentence, and to enslave him to the Pope, a certain Italian man who certainly does not love Scripture except insofar as it compels Scripture to serve his desires? Indeed we admit, beyond doubt, that the Holy Spirit so shines upon the true Church and on each of its members that, by his grace, with eyes enlightened they see the wonderful works of God in the Scriptures, perceive their genuine sense, and show it both to themselves and to others, and finally follow the judgement set forth in the Scriptures. But to hold that the Church, that is, the Pope with a council or without it, so possesses the Holy Spirit as a private property, that whatever is said, whether demonstrated from Scripture or not, as proceeding from him, can dictate as authority and command to the faithful as his subjects, and that they are bound to receive and kiss what is thus commanded [ἀδουμάσως] with a certain blind obedience, no differently than the very words of God; this, I say, is to renounce all divine judgement of the Holy Spirit speaking and defining in Scripture, and to transfer this monopoly of the Holy Spirit, which is seized not by price but by force, and which rules faith by mere nod and not by necessary demonstration, to a man or a certain sworn group, and this not without the most atrocious blasphemy."

units.la: XXX. Viderint ergo Walenburgii, annon Deo homi-nibúsque imponere conentur, quando Compend. Controv. cap. 7. ff. 5. sic loquuntur: Hinc patet, quanta injustitia accusetur Ecclesia Romano-Catholica, quasi homines con- Tom. II. 11 stitucstitueret judices Dei, & verbi ipsius; quasi homines supra S. Scripturæ authoritatem extolleret; cùm Spiritui S in Ecclesia præsenti Pastoribus tanquam organis suis utenti, & sensum suum fidelibus aperienti eam authoritatem tribuat. Aliud enim longè est dicere, Spiritum S. Ecclesiæ & fidelibus omnibus adesse, & tum immediatè, tum mediantibus Ministris sensum Scripturæ ejusdem gratia perceptum non dictantibus, vel conscientiis liberis obtrudentibus; sed ex ipsa Scriptura demonstrantibus, adeòque ex ipsa Scriptura aperire: aliud, dicere, Spiritum S. sic Ecclesiæ non universæ, nedum singulis fidelibus, sed repræsentativæ duntaxat, quæ calculis rite subductis in solo denique Papa consistit, adesse & præesse, ut sensum suum per Pastores tanquam organa, vel potiùs per solum Papam non organicè se, sensum Scripturæ ex ipsa Scriptura, eruendo & demonstrando, gerentem, sed αὐτεξουσίως proprio motu & ex plenitudine potestatis sine ulla institutione & demonstratione solida, definientem, dictantem, & ad obsequium soli Spiritui S. debitum, sine examine prævio definitionum suarum obligantem, aperiat. Illud dicere Christianum; hoc Antichristianum & Babylonicum est. Illud fidem hominum soli Spiritui S. hoc homini uni, quem dicta & facta Spiritus S. expertem testantur, subjicit: illud Dei, hoc hominum in fide servos facit.
units.tr: XXX. Let the Walenburgs see whether they are not trying to deceive God and men when they speak thus in Compend. Controv. cap. 7, "From this it is plain how unjustly the Roman Catholic Church is accused, as if it made men the judges of God and of his very Word, as if it exalted men above the authority of Holy Scripture; when it ascribes that authority to the Holy Spirit present in the Church, using the pastors as his instruments and revealing his sense to the faithful. For it is one thing to say that the Holy Spirit is present to the Church and to all the faithful, and that, both immediately and through the ministers, he opens the sense of Scripture which has been received by grace, not dictating it or forcing it upon free consciences, but demonstrating it from Scripture itself and so opening it from Scripture itself; it is another thing to say that the Holy Spirit is present and presides not over the universal Church, much less over individual believers, but only over a representative body which, once its counts are properly reckoned, finally consists in the Pope alone, and that he reveals his sense through the pastors as instruments, or rather through the Pope alone, who does not act organically, drawing out and demonstrating the sense of Scripture from Scripture itself, but acts of his own accord [αὐτεξουσίως], by his own motion and from the fullness of power, without any institution or solid demonstration, defining, dictating, and binding to the obedience owed only to the Holy Spirit, without prior examination of his definitions. The former is Christian; the latter is Antichristian and Babylonian. The former subjects the faith of men to the Holy Spirit alone; the latter subjects it to one man, whom the words and deeds of the Holy Spirit testify to be without the Spirit. The former makes men servants of God in faith; the latter makes them servants of men."

units.la: XXXI. Scripturæ Sacræ Divinum judicium abrogantium πρόφασις est, quòd Spiritus S. in ea visibiliter præsens non sit, ut proferat sententiam, adeóque sic judicis munere defungatur.
units.tr: XXXI. The pretext for those who abrogate the divine judgment of Holy Scripture is that the Holy Spirit is not visibly present in it to pronounce sentence, and so does not discharge the office of judge.

units.la: Hinc petulans illa & blasphema insultatio, qua Jesuita Gretserus in Ratisbonensi Colloquio sess. ix. pag. 292. os suum in Cœlum aperuit, atque sic Spiritui S. & Scripturæ insultavit: Sumus in conspectu Sacræ Scripturæ & Spiritus S. Pronuntiet sententiam, & si dicat: Tu Gretsere, malè sentis, cecidisti causa Tua; Tu Jacobe Heil
units.tr: Hence that insolent and blasphemous taunt with which the Jesuit Gretser opened his mouth to heaven at the Colloquy of Regensburg, sess. ix. pag. 292., mocking the Holy Spirit and Scripture in this way: We stand in the sight of Holy Scripture and of the Holy Spirit. Let them pronounce sentence, and if they say, "You, Gretser, think wrongly, your cause has fallen," you, Jacob Heilbrunner, have conquered.

units.la: Præterea impius Scripturæ Divinum judicium abrogantium est, quòd Spiritus S. in ea visibiliter præsens non sit, ut proferat sententiam: Gretseri concepta blasphemia. Heilbrunnere vicisti: tunc ego statim transfibo ad vestrum scammum. Adsit, adsit, adsit, & condemnet me. Et postea: Si potest, hoc faciat Spiritus S. in præsentia, ut omnes evidenter audiant, me errare. Sed non potest. Ergo non est judex, qualem Vos dicitis. Non thrasonicè magis impius Lamechus suis mulieribus; quàm impurus hic Lojolita ipsi Spiritui S. & Scripturæ insultavit. Ille absentis Papæ fui, ceu Judicis in terris Supremi, bullis & rescriptis haud ægrè fidem substringit. At Spiritus S. præsentissimi & verbo suo inspiratione ejusdem ab hominibus ϑεόπνευστος scripto animam hominis potentissimè efficacissimè & suavissimè alloquentis judicio fidem habere se posse negat, nisi Lojolitico ore pronuntiet, eum causa sua vel stare vel cadere. O blasphemiam inexpiabilem! Quantò verecundiores meliorésque fuerunt Judæi quamvis infideles, quorum nulli certè in mentem venit, ut Christo ad eos dicenti: Si crederetis Mosi, crederetis etiam mihi; de me enim ille scripsit. Item: Est qui Vos accusat Moses, in quo vos speratis, Joh. v. 45. 46. 47. simili blasphemia obstreperet: Accuset me Moses. En librum Mosis. Loquatur Moses & dicat: Tu Judæe, male facis, quòd Jesum pro Christo non habes. Adsit, adsit, adsit Moses, & condemnet me. Sed non potest. Ergo non est judex. Tanta blasphemandi libido nondum verpas pervicacissimas licet incesserat.
units.tr: Moreover, the impious abrogators of the divine judgment of Scripture say that the Holy Spirit is not visibly present in it to pronounce sentence. Gretser's blasphemy, conceived in these terms, was: Heilbrunner, you have won; then I will at once cross over to your bench. Let the Spirit be present, let him be present, let him be present, and condemn me. And afterwards: If he can, let the Holy Spirit do this in person, so that everyone may plainly hear that I am in error. But he cannot. Therefore he is not the judge you describe. Not even the impious Lamech boasted so arrogantly to his wives as this impure Jesuit mocked the Holy Spirit himself and Scripture. Lamech, I suppose, does not hesitate to rely on the bulls and rescripts of an absent Pope, as if he were the supreme judge on earth. But he denies that he can put faith in the judgment of the Holy Spirit, who is most present and who, through the Scripture inspired by himself (theopneustos [θεόπνευστος]), speaks to the soul of man most powerfully, most effectively and most sweetly, unless the Jesuit's mouth pronounces that his cause stands or falls. O inexpiable blasphemy! How much more modest and better were the Jews, though unbelievers, none of whom thought, when Christ said to them, If you believed Moses, you would believe me too, for he wrote of me, and again, There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope (John 5:45, 46, 47), to raise the same blasphemous clamour: Let Moses accuse me. Here is the book of Moses. Let Moses speak and say, "You, Jew, do wrongly in not holding Jesus to be the Christ." Let Moses be present, let him be present, let him be present, and condemn me. But he cannot. Therefore he is not a judge. Such was the lust for blaspheming that had already seized even the most obstinate, though they were still unbelievers.

units.la: XXXII. Viderint denique Hierarchici, annon blasphemiam manifestam spiret impium illud scomma, quo Spiritum S. per verbum Ecclesiam & fideles omnes docentem, qui est Spiritus gratiæ & revelationis 1. Cor. 11. 10. 1. Joh. 11. 27. tanquam Spiritum privatum, seu ἰδιογνώμονα ex proprio arbitratu & sensu de rebus fidei statuentem, traducere & irridere palam solent. Ille scilicet Spiritus, qui non toti Ecclesiæ, nec omnibus fidelibus, sed factioni Papæ & Concilii privatim & seorsim, solo afflatu, sine ulla demonstratione verbi, revelat docenda, & à verbo ac lege Dei ad verbum & legem humanam seducit; qui nec ab omnibus explorari, nec juxta eam regulam, quæ omnibus tradita est, se Spiritum lucis omni conscientiæ probare potest; Spiritus Dei, Spiritus publicus est. Ille contra Spiritus, qui ad verbum Dei adducit, & verum ejusdem sensum non prætoria potestate dictat, sed demonstrat & ab omni conscientia explorari potest; quique id præstat erga fideles omnes; eo solo nomine, quòd ad amusśim Papalis Spiritus verè ἀδηλα factus non est, privatus & ἰδίως Φηλίπως est! Atqui ii, qui credunt Scripturis, habent eundem Spiritum, quem habuerunt Sancti Dei homines, per quos Deus locutus est; & est idem quoad donum fidei & manifestationem veritatis ad omnes credentes. uti supra etiam ostendimus. Sed qui Papam privatim afflat & alloquitur, & alios subjicit in obsequium Papæ, quoad operationem fidei non est idem omnibus, & in omnibus adeóque verè privatus & Enthusiasticus est.
units.tr: XXXII. Finally, let the hierarchs consider whether that impious jibe does not breathe manifest blasphemy, by which they commonly openly distort and ridicule the Holy Spirit who teaches the Church and all the faithful through the Word (who is the Spirit of grace and revelation, 1 Cor. 11:10; 1 John 2:27), as a private spirit, that is, one who decides matters of faith by his own judgment and sense (idiognomona [ἰδιογνώμονα]). That spirit, they say, reveals what is to be taught not to the whole Church or to all the faithful, but privately and separately to the faction of the Pope and the Council, by mere inspiration, without any demonstration from the Word, and leads them away from the Word and law of God to human words and law. Such a spirit cannot be tested by all, nor can it prove itself by the rule delivered to everyone to be the Spirit of light to every conscience; this is the public Spirit of God. On the other hand, that spirit which leads to the Word of God and does not dictate its true sense by praetorian power, but demonstrates it and can be tested by every conscience, and which does this for all the faithful, is by that very fact called private and idiōs [ἰδίως] (Philippus?) because it has not become truly unclear [ἄδηλα] to the rule of the Papal spirit! Yet those who believe the Scriptures have the same Spirit that the holy men of God had, through whom God spoke, and he is the same as regards the gift of faith and the manifestation of truth to all believers, as we have also shown above. But he who privately inspires and addresses the Pope, and subjects others to obedience to the Pope, is not the same to all as regards the working of faith, and is therefore truly private and enthusiastic.

units.la: XXXIII. Hactenus fuerunt blasphemiæ adversus Nomen Dei.
units.tr: XXXIII. So far have been the blasphemies against the Name of God.

units.la: Sequuntur blasphemiæ adversus Tabernaculum Dei, Christum caput, & Ecclesiam corpus ejus, in quo utroque Deus habitat. Blasphemias adversus Christum errores Hierarchicorum Tyrannici, in officium ejus triplex Propheticum, Sacerdotale & Regium; nec non idololatrici, in officium ejusdem Mediatorium universum arietantes, & Dissertatione Undecima tota fusè & ex vero demonstrati propalant. Omnes enim errores illi Christo Tabernaculo Dei, quod suum est, sacrilegè auferunt, & in illud Vice-Dei seu Vice-Christi idolum conferunt. Tot ergo hic blasphemiarum adversus Christum, quot errorum illorum genera constitui possunt. Potissima illa sunt: quòd Christus non solus sit Ecclesiæ caput & fundamentum, Media-
units.tr: There follow the blasphemies against the Tabernacle of God, Christ the Head, and the Church his body, in which God dwells in both. The errors of the tyrannical hierarchs strike against Christ in his threefold office, prophetic, priestly and kingly, and the idolatrous errors against his whole mediatorial office, and these are fully and truly demonstrated in the Eleventh Dissertation. For all those errors sacrilegiously take away from Christ the Tabernacle of God, which is his own, and transfer it to the idol of the Vicar of God or Vicar of Christ. There are therefore as many blasphemies against Christ as there are kinds of those errors that can be distinguished. The chief ones are these: that Christ is not alone the head and foundation of the Church, Media-

units.la: Blasphemiæ adversus Tabernaculum Dei, Christum ex erroribus Hierarchicorum tyrannici cognuscuntur. Mediator, Paracletus, Salvator: quòd habeat Regnum aspectabile: quòd sit ἐν παμείω: quòd velit in Maozim, arcibus coli: quòd non invenerit sufficientem ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem, utpote quæ sacrificiis continuis, satisfactionibus, meritis perfici debeat. Quæ & plura ejusmodi alia superius dedita operâ prosecuti, repetere hoc loco supersedemus.
units.tr: Blasphemies against the Tabernacle of God, Christ, are recognised in the errors of the tyrannical hierarchs: that he is not the Mediator, Paraclete and Saviour; that he has a visible kingdom; that he is en pameiō [ἐν παμείω]; that he wishes to be honoured in Maozim, that is, in fortresses; that he did not find a sufficient redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν], since it must be accomplished by continual sacrifices, satisfactions and merits. These and many other such things we have already pursued with deliberate care above, and we shall not repeat them here.

units.la: XXXIV. Possent Hierarchicorum apertè blasphemæ adversus Christum voces notari. Sic enim Leo X. ad Cardinalem Bembum fabulas de Christo mussavit. Thomas Aquinas Opusc. 21. cap. 10. Christum importunum vocare non erubuit. Cardinalis Bellarminus de Monach. cap. 45. eundem Mendici convitio proscindit: Sed & indiscretum Bertrandus in Extravag. Bonif. VIII. de Majorit. appellat. Nicolaus IV. Cap. Exiit, de verb. signif. in sexto Christum & Franciscum comparans, Christum ait habuisse quædam infirma, quibus Franciscus caruerit. Fugisse enim eum, & loculos habuisse, quæ duo à Francisco abfuerint. Faciunt huc comparationes impiæ Christi cum Deipara, Francisco & aliis, in quibus toties palma Mariæ & Francisco, depresso Christo, delata est. Nonnulla superiùs quoque hanc in rem attulimus.
units.tr: XXXIV. The openly blasphemous words of the hierarchs against Christ could be noted. Thus Leo X, writing to Cardinal Bembo, sneered at the fables about Christ. Thomas Aquinas, Opusc. 21. cap. 10., did not blush to call Christ importunate. Cardinal Bellarmine, de Monach. cap. 45., tears him with the reproach of beggar. Bertrand, in Extravag. Bonif. VIII. de Majorit., calls him indiscreet. Nicholas IV, Cap. Exiit, de verb. signif. in sexto, comparing Christ with Francis, says: Christ had certain weaknesses that Francis lacked. For he fled, and had a purse, and these two were absent from Francis. To this belong the impious comparisons of Christ with the Mother of God, with Francis and others, in which the palm has so often been given to Mary and Francis while Christ is lowered. We have already brought forward some things to this effect above.

units.la: XXXV. Adversus Ecclesiam, quæ corpus Christi, & eatenus quoque tabernaculum & domus Dei viventis est, Hierarchicorum blasphemiæ si non graviores, certè apertiores & ferociores sunt. Ecclesiam intelligo, quæ ab iis separata, Ecclesiæ Romanæ jugum excussit, Vice-Deatum Papæ ejuravit, dominationi, tyrannidi, idolatriæ & capitalibus ejus erroribus nuntium remisit, denique humana omni in causa fidei authoritate, legibus, judiciis abdicatis, se totam ad normam verbi Divini, ejúsque scripti (quia excitra illam revelatio Divina certa in mundo nulla extat) comp osuit, denique μὴ τὶ ἡμᾶ omnem cogitationem, omnem fidem suam in obsequitum Christi captivam redegit. Quæ non ideo non est vera Christi Ecclesia, quia eam talem esse Hierarchici perfricta fronte & præfracta mente negant, & horribilibus maledictis proscindunt. Nam vel nullam in mundo Christus habet veram Ecclesiam: vel eam veram Ecclesiam habet, quæ vocem ejus, qualis extra Scripturam nulla hodie extat, audit, cum sequitur, se ipsam abnegat, animas suas in bonis operibus Christo committit, & in patientia tribulationem, ac sub cruce se humilians fraternæ ædificationi studet, quam in mundo contemptam licet & blasphemiis eorum, qui mundum in Ecclesiam invexerunt, appetitam, sic Christus, primus & ultimus, qui mortuus est & revixit, Apoc. 11. 9. alloquitur: Novi opera tua, & afflictionem & paupertatem (qualis non Hierarchicorum est, Regalibus opibus affluentium, sed eorum, qui per Regia edicta bonis suis spoliantur, pauperum de Lugduno, Geusiorum &c.) sed dives es: & blasphemiam eorum, qui se dicunt Judaeos esse (Christum confitentur verbis) & non sunt, & Synagoga Sathanæ.
units.tr: XXXV. Against the Church, which is the body of Christ and, in that respect also, the tabernacle and house of the living God, the blasphemies of the hierarchs are, if not graver, certainly more open and fiercer. I mean the Church which, separated from them, has thrown off the yoke of the Roman Church, has renounced the Papal vicariate of God, has sent back their domination, tyranny, idolatry and capital errors, and finally, having set aside all human authority, laws and judgments in matters of faith, has composed itself wholly to the norm of the divine Word and its written form (since outside that there is no certain divine revelation in the world), and has, in short, brought every thought and all its faith captive into the obedience of Christ. That body is not for this reason not the true Church of Christ, because the hierarchs deny with brazen brow and obstinate mind that it is such, and tear it with horrible curses. For either Christ has no true Church in the world, or he has a true Church which hears his voice, which is found today nowhere outside Scripture, which follows him, denies itself, commits its souls to Christ in good works, and in patience under tribulation, humbling itself under the cross, strives for the edification of brethren; a Church despised in the world and sought after by the blasphemies of those who have brought the world into the Church. Christ, the First and the Last, who died and came to life again, addresses it thus, Apoc. 11:9: I know your works, and your affliction and poverty (not the poverty of the hierarchs, who abound in royal riches, but of those who are stripped of their goods by royal edicts, the poor of Lyons, the Geuses, etc.), but you are rich; and the blasphemy of those who say they are Jews (they confess Christ in words) and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.
XXXVI.

units.la: Quotquot ergo piè in mundo vivere, & soli Deo inservire volunt, ab Hierarchicis blasphemè Hæretici, Schismatici, Novatores, impii, sacrilegi, Dei & Sanctorum contemptores, omnis Divini cultus hostes, Reipublicæ pestes, quibus salvis eam subverti necesse sit, purgamenta mundi, diris & anathematis ex Ecclesia, imo societate hominum ad tartara ablegandi, & quid non audiunt? Vix Waldenses quondam caput extulerunt, & imbellia sua castra Romanæ tyrannidi oppositerunt, cum Pontificiorum Fraterculorum mendicabula, de quibus id dici meritò potest, quod de Græcorum gente Cicero pro Flacco dixit: Testimoniorum religionem & fidem nunquam ista natio coluit; eos aggressi blasphemiis & calumniis obruerunt, ne sic infamatis & sideratis alii se associasociarent. Parùm erat, eos hæreticorum in censu reponere. Cùm in Euangelii historia maximâ infamiâ laborauerint Publicani, horum ergo nomine eos palam traducere placuit. Sic enim Rodulphus Cogeshalensis Monachus, Anglus, in Historia sua Ms. de iis scribit : Temporibus Ludovici Regis Franciæ, qui genuit Philippum, cùm error quorundam hæreticorum (Waldenses innuit) qui vulgò appellantur Publicani, per plures Galliæ Provincias proserperet, &c. Veris quibusdam eorum dogmatis nonnullis proditis, subjicit idem : Ajunt alii (qui de eorum secretis inuestigárunt) quòd isti non credunt, Deum res humanas curare : nec aliquam dispositionem vel potentiam in terrenis creaturis exercere ; sed Apostolum Angelum, quem & Lusabel nominant, universæ creaturæ corporali præsidere, & ad nutum ejus cuncta terrena disponi. Corpus à diabolo dicunt formari ; Animam verò à Deo creari, & corporibus infundi. Unde fit, ut semper quædam pertinax pugna inter corpus & animam geratur. Dicunt etiam nonnulli, quòd in subterraneis suis quædam nefanda sacrificia Lucifero suo, temporibus agant constitutis, & quasdam sacrilegas turpitudines operentur. Imperatorem à Papa non dependere, constanter prædicárunt. Ergo duo eos statuere principia, adeóque Manichæos esse, Monachi proclamárunt. Crustam farinaceam in Christi corpus conuersam esse, iidem valdè negárunt. Ergo Arianos esse, negantes Diuinitatem Christi, iidem asseruerunt. Taceo plusquam Diabolicas accusationes de incestis pollutionibus, usu mulierum promiscuo, adoratione barbarum, odio & contemptu Magistratuum, rejectione Veteris Testamenti, Pædobaptismi, juramenti, conjugii, resurrectionis corporum &c. qualia ex Rogerio in Annalibus Angliæ Baronium ad A. C. 1176. num. 3. &c. & ex Guidone Perpiniano Carmelita, ta, Antonino Florentino Archiepiscopo Ganderum Monarch. Vit. lib. vj. A. 1198. Coccium Thesaur. Tom. j. lib. viij. art. 3. denique ex Gabriele Prateolo & Bernhardo Lutzenburgio Rob. Parsonium de tribus Angliæ conversionibus p. 11. cap. 10. ff. 26. 27. ad invidiam innocentibus conflandam corradere non puduit. Quarum similiúmque blasphemiarum & accusationum vanitatem post alios viri Celeberrimi, Rainoldus adversus Vincentium & Bel forestum de Idolol. Eccl. Rom. lib. j. cap. 5. 31.
