Usserius Armachanus de Christ. Eccl. Succeff. cap. 6. collisis invicem nefariis eorum maledictis, & expensis sigillatim calumniis apertam in lucem protulerunt.
units.tr: Therefore all who wish to live piously in the world and to serve God alone are called heretics, schismatics, innovators, impious, sacrilegious, despisers of God and the saints, enemies of all divine worship, and pests of the commonwealth, whom it is necessary to overthrow if the state is to be safe, the filth of the world, to be cast out with curses and anathemas from the Church and indeed from human society to hell, by the hierarchs, who blaspheme freely. What do they not hear? The Waldenses had scarcely raised their heads once, and set up their feeble camp against Roman tyranny, when the beggarly mendicants of the Papist friars attacked them with blasphemies and calumnies and overwhelmed them, of whom what Cicero said in the Pro Flacco about the Greek nation can rightly be said: That nation never cultivated the religion and faith of witnesses; so that others, thus defamed and blighted, would not associate with them. It was not enough to place them in the roll of heretics. Since the publicans suffered the greatest infamy in the history of the Gospel, it pleased them to slander these people openly under that name. For so Rodulphus of Coggeshall, an English monk, writes about them in his manuscript history: In the time of King Louis of France, who begat Philip, when the error of certain heretics (he means the Waldenses), commonly called Publicans, spread through many provinces of France, etc. After some of their true doctrines had been revealed, the same author adds: Others say (who investigated their secrets) that these men do not believe that God cares for human affairs, nor that he exercises any providence or power over earthly creatures; but that an Apostle Angel, whom they also call Lusabel, presides over all bodily creation, and that all earthly things are arranged at his nod. They say that the body is formed by the devil, but the soul is created by God and infused into bodies. Hence a certain stubborn struggle always goes on between body and soul. Some also say that in their underground places they perform certain unspeakable sacrifices to their Lucifer at set times, and carry out certain sacrilegious obscenities. That the emperor does not depend on the Pope they preached constantly. Therefore the monks proclaimed that they posited two principles and so were Manichaeans. That the floury crust is turned into the body of Christ they strongly denied; therefore the same men asserted that they were Arians, denying the divinity of Christ. I pass over the more than diabolical accusations of incestuous pollutions, promiscuous use of women, worship of barbarians, hatred and contempt of magistrates, rejection of the Old Testament, of infant baptism, of oaths, of marriage, of the resurrection of the body, etc., such as they were not ashamed to gather to stir up envy against the innocent, from Roger in the Annals of England, Baronius ad A.C. 1176, num. 3, etc. and from Guido Perpinianus the Carmelite, from Antoninus of Florence, archbishop, Ganderum Monarch. Vit. lib. vj. A. 1198, Coccius Thesaur. Tom. j. lib. viij. art. 3, and finally from Gabriel Prateolus and Bernhard Lutzenburg, and Robert Parsons de tribus Angliae conversionibus p. 11, cap. 10, ff. 26, 27. The vanity of these and similar blasphemies and accusations, after other very famous men, Rainoldus against Vincentius and Belforest de Idolol. Eccl. Rom. lib. j. cap. 5, 31, and Usher of Armagh de Christ. Eccl. Succes. cap. 6, have brought to clear light by setting their wicked slanders against one another and weighing each calumny separately.

units.la: XXXVII. Ex propriis Papæ paludibus vix enatavit
units.tr: XXXVII. Scarcely anyone has emerged from the Pope's own swamps

units.la: quisquam paulò liberalioris oris aut ingenii, qui non sub hæretici ferè titulo insignem per calumniam & blasphemiam pipulo differretur. Hæreticus iis audit Petrus Abailardus. Quare? In Philosophicis scilicet erat aliquanto limatior, in Poëticis politior, in Theologicis liberior. quæ ad hæresis calumniam sufficiunt. Hæreticus & Magus audiebat Robertus Bacon. Quo errore? Mathematicus erat, & in linguis paulò versatior & acutior cæteris, quorum subinde stupendam insicitiam vellicat. quod satis erat ad hæresin. Hæreticus erat & Simoniacus Henricus IV. Imperator, & cum eo Henriciani omnes. Quæ causa hæreseos? Papæ de temporali potestate & investituris controversiam movebant. Hæreticus erat Arnoldus Brixiensis Episcopus. Quo jure? In clero civilem administrationem improbavit. Hæreticus erat Hieronymus Savanarola Florentinus, piacularibus flammis consumptus. Quis prætextus hæreseos erat? Negavit primatum Papæ, indulgentias damnavit, cleri scandala liberiùs paulò perstrinxit. Hæreticum erat ꝯ Claudio Espencæo teste, Hebraicè scire. Quamobrem verò? Timebant barbarici suæ ex fontibus cognitis.
units.tr: anyone of a somewhat more liberal mouth or intellect, who was not almost marked, under the title of heretic, with calumny and blasphemy and was handed about by the crowd. Peter Abelard is called a heretic. Why? Surely he was somewhat more polished in philosophy, more refined in poetry, and freer in theology, which were enough for the charge of heresy. Robert Bacon was called a heretic and magician. For what error? He was a mathematician, and more skilled and sharper in languages than the rest, whose astonishing ignorance he now and then mocks; that was enough for heresy. Henry IV, the Emperor, was a heretic and a Simoniac, and all the Henricians with him. What was the cause of the heresy? The Popes were stirring up controversy about temporal power and investitures. Arnold of Brescia, a bishop, was a heretic. By what right? He disapproved of the clergy's civil administration. Jerome Savonarola of Florence was a heretic, consumed by expiatory flames. What pretext of heresy was there? He denied the primacy of the Pope, condemned indulgences, and censured the scandals of the clergy somewhat too freely. To know Hebrew was, according to the testimony of Claude d'Espence, a heresy. Why indeed? Their barbarism feared being exposed by known sources.

units.la: {a} nec non ad-versus quosdam pie-tate, zelo, eruditione Romanæ curiæ su-spectos, quos illico haereti-corum in numerum reputat. cognitis. Hæreticus & excommunicatus moriebatur Robertus Grosteedus Lincolniensis Episcopus, Doctorum Seculi sui facilè princeps. Quæ <bl>πτόφανς</bl> hæreseos? Faltui & tyrannidi Papæ erat paulo infensior, neque dubitavit Bestiæ in os contradicere.
units.tr: {a} and also against certain men of piety, zeal and learning whom the Roman court suspects, and whom it at once counts among the heretics. Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, the foremost of the doctors of his age, died a heretic and excommunicate. What was the pretext [πρόφασις] of the heresy? He was rather hostile to the deceit and tyranny of the Pope, and did not hesitate to speak against the Beast to its face.
XXXVIII.

units.la: Quid verò cicatricibus illis pridem obductis vulnera refrico? Post Reformationem quibus non blasphemiis Reformatores & confessores ipsos ob attrectatam oculi Papæ pupillam; quibus non doctrinam Euangelicæ Ecclesiæ lacerárunt? Lutherum à Diabolo fuisse suffocatum, atque à suis, quos à putrescente & moriente cadavere fœtorem abegisse fingunt, in fossam injectum reli&túmque mentiti sunt. Heroicus tamen ille Christi athleta, quando talia Monachi prepalárunt, & vivebat, & valebat, & post dentatis scriptis ipse calumniam sepeliebat. Calvino ut apud incautiores infamiam conciliarent, conductitium quoddam & venale mancipium subornárunt, Hieronymum Bolfecum, qui quicquid irritata Sathanæ virulentia suggerere potuit, chartis illevit, & in ejus ignominiam evomuit. Cujus vomitum nuper Maimburgius homo ex mendaciis confutus, sorpsit, & sorptum denuo expulit tanta blasphemandi libidine, ut non puduerit in plena luce de Calvino aliisque splendidissimè quidvis mentiri. Cataphracti hac impudentiæ panoplia prodierunt contra Lutherum Cochlæus, Sleidanum Laurentius Surius, Reginam Elisabetham Sanderus & Parsonius; Jacobum Regem Jesuitæ Gretserus, Lessius, Becanus, Costeteau, Cccucus; & satelles eorum Sciopius. Denique nullus ferè nostrûm caput inter sidera condens, Papæ ulcera contrectavit, quem portentosis apud suos mendaciis dehonestare conati non fuerint. De calumniatoribus doctrinæ & vitæ suæ Zwinglius Oper.Tom. I. pag. 148. ad Cantones Bernæ congregatos multa questus, inter alia sic scripsit: Sunt qui hoc ipso anno quatuor liberos illegitimo thoro natos me genuisse dicant. Sunt qui noctu per plateas canentem, & aliis Musicis instrumentis ludentem discurrere asserant. Sunt qui aleæ plus nimio deditum, & publicum scortatorem una cum reliquis lenonum prostibula frequentare tradant. Sunt rursus, qui Principum muneribus corruptum omnia turbare iudicitient. Quæ & ipsa mendacissimorum hominum figmenta & calumnias impudentes esse respondemus. Quod ipsum quoque veris testibus probare possumus. Alia horribilia longè magis post mortem ejus de Viro Sancto, nulla specie veri, sola blasphemandi Diabolica libidine, de eo in vulgus sparserunt. Beza, si Diabolis his credimus, fuit præderastes; sepultus Romano-Catholicus septennio prius quàm moriebatur. Franciscus Junius pede ungulato deformis. Isaaci Casauboni pater, qui eodem loco, quo sidum Dei ministrum agebat, placidè obdormivit, ita mentiuntur illi, ceu nequam patibulo affixus est. Recentissima velut in cumulum afferre possem; ac me ipsum forte indignum licet, qui huic peplo inferar, quem ante plures annos mortuum, ex inferno cum ignitis manibus domesticis meis comparuisse, Missæque restitutionem suasisse (nam nisi ab infernali titione suaderi nequit) sacrificuli mendaciorum architecti pro suggestu putidissimè declamarunt. Taceo Ecclesias integras, infamatas; Anglicanas inprimis à Sandero; Helveticam, à Gothardo, Gretsero, Genevensem, aliisque, de quibus non tam publicè quàm privatim in Confessionum arcano suggestu infanda miseris & cæcis confessoribus suis suggerentes, atque inter illa hoc cumprimis, quòd Geneva omnium facinorosorum latibulum sit (quod credentibus quibusdam Hispanis, aliis pessimè cessit, aliis conversionem maturavit) Eduinus Santes de Statu Relig. cap. 37. non pauca memoratu dignissima prodidit. Sic planè pugnat, sic est metuendus Ulysses. Sic Ethnicum illud pro πανουργία sua veteratorie accommodant: Calumniare audaćter. Semper aliquid hæret, ut noctuas suas à luce abstrahant, ne Scripturas legant, concionesque audiant, rationes pensitent, & perspectis Bestiæ maculis ocyùs Babylonii nuntium mittant!
units.tr: But why do I reopen wounds that healed long ago? Since the Reformation, with what blasphemies have they not torn at the Reformers and confessors themselves, because they touched the pupil of the Pope's eye? With what lies have they not mangled the doctrine of the Evangelical Church? They have lied that Luther was strangled by the Devil, and that his own people, whom they pretend he drove off by the stench of his rotting and dying corpse, threw him into a pit and left him there. Yet that heroic athlete of Christ, when the monks spread such tales, was both alive and well, and afterwards with his biting writings he himself buried the calumny. To win infamy for Calvin among the more gullible, they suborned a certain hireling and mercenary creature, Hieronymus Bolsec, who smeared on paper whatever the provoked venom of Satan could suggest and vomited it out to his disgrace. Recently Maimbourg, a man refuted by his own lies, swallowed that vomit, and having swallowed it, expelled it again with such a lust for blaspheming that he was not ashamed to lie most splendidly, in full daylight, about Calvin and others. Against Luther, Cochlaeus came forth as a man in full armour of this impudence; against Sleidan, Laurentius Surius; against Queen Elizabeth, Sanders and Parsons; against King James, the Jesuits Gretser, Lessius, Becanus, Costeteau and Coccius; and their henchman Sciopius. In short, scarcely any of ours who holds his head among the stars has touched the Pope's sores without their attempting to dishonour him with monstrous lies among their own people. Concerning the slanderers of his doctrine and life, Zwingli, in his works vol. I, p. 148, complaining at length to the cantons gathered at Bern, among other things wrote thus: There are those who say that in this very year I have fathered four children born of an illegitimate bed. There are those who assert that I run through the streets at night singing and playing on other musical instruments. There are those who report that I, given excessively to gambling, frequent a public whore together with the rest of the brothel-keepers' harlots. There are again those who judge that I, corrupted by the gifts of princes, disturb everything. We answer that these are the most lying men's fictions and shameless calumnies. We can also prove this by true witnesses. After his death they spread other horrors far worse about this Holy Man, with no semblance of truth, moved only by the Devil's lust for blasphemy. Beza, if we believe these devils, was a pederast; Francis Junius was deformed with a cloven hoof; the father of Isaac Casaubon, who peacefully fell asleep in the same place where he served as a minister of God, they lie was hanged on a gibbet. I could bring forward the most recent examples as well, and perhaps I, unworthy though I am, who am being added to this cloak: the little priests, architects of lies, have loudly declaimed from the pulpit that a man who died many years ago appeared to my household from hell with burning hands and urged the restoration of the Mass (for this could only be urged by a firebrand from hell). I pass over whole Churches defamed: the English above all by Sanders; the Helvetic by Gotthard and Gretser; the Genevan and others, about which, not so publicly as privately, in the secret pulpit of confession they suggest unspeakable things to their wretched and blind confessors. Among these especially is the claim that Geneva is a hiding-place of all criminals (which turned out badly for some Spaniards who believed it, and for others hastened their conversion). Eduinus Santes, in On the State of Religion, chapter 37, has published not a few things worth recording. Thus he clearly fights, thus he is to be feared as Ulysses. Thus they adapt that heathen saying to their craftiness [πανουργία] with deceitful skill: Slander boldly; something always sticks, so that they may draw their owls away from the light, lest they read the Scriptures, hear sermons, weigh the reasons, and, having seen the spots of the Beast, send more quickly the messenger of Babylon!

units.la: XXXIX. Doctrinam ipsam Ecclesiæ, ex verbi Divini penetralibus depromptam licet, quibus non blasphemiis illi incessunt? Quærit Bailius, Lojolæ pullus, in Proœmio Catechismi: Quid judicas de Religione, quam prætendunt Reformati nostri? Respondet Catholicus Papista: Hant equo Trojano similem censeo, utpote cujus lateri inclduntur maxima pars hæresium antiquatarum. Crambem esse recoctam juxta Proverbium, repetitionem multorum errorum, qui antecedentibus Seculis vigebant. Cornicularum Horatianam, quæ plumis veterum hærestarcharum ornata gloriatur. Specimina nonnulla in medium proferre libet. Cum S. Scriptura fide, & non nisi fide, adeòque solâ peccatorem justificari profitemur. Ergo Bailio sumus Eunomiani. Peccatorem irregenitum esse mortuum in peccatis, adeóque destitutum viribus liberi arbitrii in spiritualibus, asserimus. Ergo sumus Simonis Magi affectæ. Conciliorum definitiones sic conscientias obligare, ut iis non exploratis ad verbi Divini regulam, assentiendum sit, negamus. Ergo sumus Nestoriani. Traditiones, seu dogmata non scripta ex verbo Dei rejicimus. Ergo sumus Sadducæi. Soli Deo peccata necessariò confitenda esse, cum Davide & Sanctis quibusque credimus. Ergo sumus Novatiani. Fidelium liberos ἀδαπίστως ob prærogativam fœderis cum Scriptura salvari posse, pronuntiamus. Ergo sumus Pelagiani. Confirmationem Sacramentum esse negamus, quia nusquam ei Sacramenti requisita S. literæ conferunt. Ergo Novatiani iterum sumus. Aquæ benebenedictæ insitam esse vim spiritualem negamus. Ergo sumus Flagellantes, hoc est, Papistæ. Monasteria hodie esse ignaviæ domicilia dicimus. Ergo sumus Petiliani assecla. Ecclesiæ Ministris liberum esse matrimonii usum cum S. Paulo pronuntiamus. Ergo sumus Circumcelliones. Cardinalium, Archiepiscoporum, Episcoporum Prælaturam Divini juris esse, Missæ histrioniam à Christo esse institutam negamus. Ergo sumus Acephali. Carnem Christi in Sacramento corporaliter præsentem, oraliter manducandam esse, cum Christo ipso inficiamur. Ergo sumus Capernaitæ. Exorcismorum post expirans charisma Divinum nullum esse usum, ex re ipsa conficimus. Ergo sumus Ulpiani Ethnici assecla. Satisfactiones proprias vel alienas humanas Christi satisfactioni derogare pertendimus. Ergo sumus Audiani. Licere post divortium legitimum ad se- cunda vota transfire, cum Christo & S. Paulo asserimus. Ergo sumus Ebionitæ. Omnia peccata esse mortalia, cum eodem S. Paulo statuimus. Ergo sumus Pelagiani. Dei circa peccatum providentiam esse efficacem cum Scriptura docemus. Ergo sumus Floriniani, & Deum esse authorem peccati, blasphemamus. Matrimonium Sacramentum esse, nulli agnoscimus, quia proprietatibus Sacramenti destituitur. Ergo sumus Carpocratiani, Gnostici. Crucis signo efficaciam quandam spiritualem inesse negamus. Ergo sumus Messaliani. Cleri Romani corruptos mores improbamus. Ergo sumus Donatistæ. Et quid non? Ferri æquiore animo hæ poterant blasphemiæ Hierarchicorum, qui ipsi deploratissimis hæresibus scatent toti, nisi per latus Ecclesiæ Deum viventem, & κυεῖας illas δόξας in verbo suo clarissimè docentem horribiliter ferirent. Accedunt blasphemiæ illæ, quibus per calumnias Ecclesiis nostris ejusmodi dogmata, à quibus planè illæ abhorrent, impingere Hierarchici non erubescunt, quas post alios plurimos Celeb. Altingius in Theologia sua Elenchtica Nova singulorum Locorum controversiis realibus præmisit, unde illæ arcesti possunt.
units.tr: XXXIX. Even the doctrine of the Church, though drawn from the innermost parts of the Divine Word, with what blasphemies do they not assail it? Bailly, the offspring of Loyola, asks in the preface of his Catechism: What do you judge of the religion which our Reformed people profess? The Catholic Papist answers: I judge it similar to the Trojan horse, since into its side are enclosed the greatest part of the ancient heresies. It is cabbage reheated, as the proverb goes, a repetition of many errors which flourished in earlier centuries. The Horatian jackdaw, which glories adorned with the feathers of the old heresiarchs. It is pleasing to bring forward some specimens. Since we profess that a sinner is justified by Scripture through faith, and through faith alone, and therefore by faith alone, we are Eunomians, says Bailly. We assert that the unregenerate sinner is dead in sins, and therefore destitute of the powers of free will in spiritual matters: therefore we are followers of Simon Magus. We deny that the definitions of councils bind consciences so that, unless they have been tested by the rule of the Divine Word, they must be assented to: therefore we are Nestorians. We reject traditions, or doctrines not written, as coming from the Word of God: therefore we are Sadducees. We believe with David and all the saints that sins must be confessed to God alone: therefore we are Novatians. We pronounce that the children of believers can be saved without baptism [ἀδαπίστως] by the prerogative of the covenant with Scripture: therefore we are Pelagians. We deny that confirmation is a sacrament, because the Holy Letters nowhere confer on it the requisites of a sacrament: therefore we are Novatians again. We deny that holy water has an inborn spiritual power: therefore we are Flagellants, that is, Papists. We say that monasteries today are dwelling-places of idleness: therefore we are followers of Petilian. We pronounce with St Paul that the ministers of the Church are free to use marriage: therefore we are Circumcellions. We maintain that the prelacy of cardinals, archbishops and bishops is not of divine right, and that the mummery of the Mass was not instituted by Christ: therefore we are Acephali. We confess with Christ himself that the flesh of Christ, corporeally present in the sacrament, is to be eaten orally: therefore we are Capernaites. We conclude from the fact itself that there is no use of the divine gift, now ceased, in exorcisms: therefore we are followers of the heathen Ulpian. We contend that human satisfactions, our own or another's, detract from the satisfaction of Christ: therefore we are Audians. We assert with Christ and St Paul that after a lawful divorce it is permitted to pass to second vows: therefore we are Ebionites. We maintain with the same St Paul that all sins are mortal: therefore we are Pelagians. We teach with Scripture that the providence of God is effective concerning sin: therefore we are Florinians, and blaspheme that God is the author of sin. We acknowledge that marriage is a sacrament to no one, because it lacks the properties of a sacrament: therefore we are Carpocratians, Gnostics. We deny that there is any spiritual efficacy in the sign of the cross: therefore we are Messalians. We disapprove of the corrupt morals of the Roman clergy: therefore we are Donatists. And why not? These blasphemies of the hierarchs, who themselves teem entirely with most desperate heresies, could have been borne with more equanimity, unless they were horribly striking at the side of the Church, which in its word clearly teaches the living God and those empty opinions [κυεῖας δόξας]. Added to these are those blasphemies, by which the hierarchs are not ashamed to impute by calumny to our Churches doctrines from which they utterly shrink; after very many others, the celebrated Altingius, in his New Elenctic Theology, placed these at the head of the real controversies of each locus, whence they may be drawn.

units.la: XL. Neque mihi Hierarchici crimini dent, quòd eorum adversus Ecclesiam blasphemias sic liberè perstringam, ut suæ tamen Ecclesiæ maxima, uti quidem interpretantur, blasphemia stigma Babylonicæ Meretricis incurere religioni neutiquam ducam. Nam, juxta notum illud Comici
units.tr: XL. Nor let the hierarchs charge me with crime because I so freely expose their blasphemies against the Church, while I by no means judge that my religion incurs the stigma of the Babylonian harlot, although they interpret their own Church's greatest blasphemy in that way. For, according to that well-known saying of the comic poet:

units.la: Indignis si maledicitur, maledictum id esse dico:
units.tr: If it is said to the unworthy, I call that a curse.

units.la: Verum si dignis dicitur, benedictum est, meo quidem animo.
units.tr: But if it is said to the worthy, it is a blessing, at least in my own mind.

units.la: Estque, Cicerone etiam judice, longè aliud maledicere, aliud accusare. Maledictio nihil habet propositi præter contumeliam: Accusatio verò crimen desiderat, rem ut definiat, hominem ut notet, argumento probet, teste confirmet. Non ego Hierarchicis maledico, sed eos accuso, & rem cum re, causam cum causa, prophetiam ἀψόδη, quæ impleri utique debuit, neque impleta alibi ostendi potest, cum eventu conspicuo in Hierarchia ipsa, contendo; denique dictorum à me rationes certas evidentesque, quas defendere me posse animi recti ἀπολογία mihi dictat, reddo; neque planè dubito, quin cordati omnes, veris pretiis res æstimare sueti, non blasphemandi œstro percitum, sed veritatis studio inflammatum me scapham scapham, & ligonem ligonem appellare, agnituri sint. Cæteris, quos ignoratio veri, & incrustatio falsi transversos ad omnia alia abripit, meliorem mentem precari satis erit.
units.tr: And, even by Cicero's judgement, it is quite a different thing to curse and to accuse. Cursing has no purpose beyond insult; accusation, however, requires a charge: to define the matter, to mark the man, to prove by argument, to confirm by witness. I do not curse the hierarchs, but I accuse them; and I set thing against thing, cause against cause, and I contend that the prophecy, which assuredly ought to be fulfilled and cannot be shown fulfilled elsewhere, has its conspicuous outcome in the Hierarchy itself. Finally, I render certain and evident grounds for what I have said, which the defence of an upright mind dictates to me that I can defend. Nor do I doubt that all discerning men, accustomed to weigh things by their true worth, will recognise that I am not driven by the gadfly of blaspheming, but inflamed by zeal for the truth, when I call a scaphe a scaphe and a ligo a ligo. As for the rest, whom ignorance of the truth and the encrustation of falsehood drag askew to everything else, it will suffice to pray for a better mind.

units.la: XLI. Parùm etiam movent me novissimæ Cleri Gallicani in Congregatione Generali A. M. DC. LXXXV. habita de calumniis Protestantium querelæ, Christianissimo Regi propositæ non eum in finem, ut de genuina & intima Religionis Pontificiæ in capitibus nonnullis sententia explicatam mm 3 tam animi sui notionem evolveret, (sic enim protinus de calumniis Protestantium affectatae querelae leves in auras abiissent) sed ut adhibitis Oraculis Delphicis, seu cothurnis Tridentinis, & recondita interiore, quam palam profiteri semper Pontificios puduit, & pudebit semper, sententia, oppositisque lacveris, truncatis, & a corpore suo avulsis nostrorum verbis potius quibusdam, quàm sententiis integris verissimis, Regis, apud quem nullum patere ad defensionem oppressae sanctissimae causae aditum noverat, animum ad excidium Protestantium accenderet propellerétque. Speciem μενυρίας illius supra jam vindicatis Dounami verbis, quibus ille Pontificiorum de sufficientia Scripturae sententiam procul omni calumnia expositit, exhibui. Integrum querelarum illarum subdolarum ιδιοpropedicm scrutabuntur excutientque alii; & Cleri fidem apricabuntur strenuè. Ego quae me concernunt, περίοχε ὄδεν, & strictim, pro ratione instituti, perstringam.
units.tr: XLI. I am also little moved by the recent complaints of the French Clergy, laid before the Most Christian King at the General Assembly held in 1685 concerning the calumnies of the Protestants. Their purpose was not to have the King, once the genuine and inner opinion of the Papist Religion on several heads was explained, form a notion of their mind (for in that case the affected complaints about the calumnies of the Protestants would at once have vanished into thin air). Their purpose was rather, by means of the Delphic oracles, that is the Tridentine buskins, and that hidden inner opinion which the Papists have always been ashamed to profess openly and always will be, together with our words, set against them, twisted and torn from their body (more fragments of our words than whole and most true sentences), to inflame and drive the King's mind to the ruin of the Protestants, whom they knew had no access to the king's ear for defending their oppressed and most holy cause. I have already displayed the appearance of folly in the words of Dounam, cited above, by which he set out the Papists' view on the sufficiency of Scripture free of all calumny. Others will examine and sift the whole peculiar bent of those crafty complaints, and will vigorously vindicate the faith of the Clergy. I shall touch on what concerns me, in summary, briefly, as the plan of this work requires.

units.la: XLII. De Traditionibus à Tridentinis Verbo Dei scri- pto aequiparatis sic inter alia Anat. Concil. Trid. pag. 87.
units.tr: XLII. On the Traditions which the Tridentines equated with the written Word of God, thus among other things Anat. Concil. Trid. p. 87.

units.la: scripsi: His gradibus perventum in Concilio ad Canonizationem Traditionum eo in sensu quem nunquam vera Ecclesia tenuit, imò quem in haereticis damnavit. Haec verba à corpore suo divulsa Clerus pag. 21. in censu calumniarum reponit. Quo vero jure? An quia per gradus itum esse ad Canonizationem Traditionum scripsi? Atqui non nudè sic scripsi, sed, gradibus illis ordine descriptis, demonstravi. An ergo qui demonstrat verissima, calumniae damnas est? An quia Tridentinos Traditionem canonizasse eo in sensu, quem nunquam vera Ecclesia tenuit, scripsi? Cedo ergo Concilium aliquod vetus, cedo unanimem Ecclesiae sententiam sub anathemate definitam, quòd dentur Traditiones tum ad fidem, tum ad mores pertinentes, ore tenus à Christo, vel à Spiritu S. dictatæ, & continua (inde à Christo) successione in Ecclesia Catholica conservatæ, pari pietatis affectu ac reverentia (cum libris scriptis; quos paulò supra sine scripto traditionibus Synodus oppositorat) suscipiendæ venerandaque. Quemodo cum verbo non scripto, dogmata fidei & morum non scripta complexo, Scripturæ plenitudo à Tertulliano contra Hermogenem acri adeò tibia decantata consistere: quemodo in sensu Tridentinæ definitionis Athanasius in Synopsi Scripturas τῆς πίστως ἀποδόσεως, ἄγχυσαν καὶ ἐρεισμα fidei primitias, anchoram & fulcrum vocare: Basilius M. in libro de Confessione fidei scribere: Φασιεὰ ἐκπλήξεως τῆς πίστεως καὶ ἐπιστήμης καὶ [illegible, ~6 letters] τῶν μὴ γεγραμμένων. Manifestum est infidelitatis & arrogantiæ crimen, vel rejicere aliquid, quod scriptum est, vel addere aliquid quod non scriptum est: Hieronymus in Matth. 23. pronuntiare: Quod de Scripturis authoritatem non habet, eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur: denique Augustinus de Doctr. Christ. ij. 9. afferere: In his, quæ aperte posita sunt in Scripturis, inveniuntur ea omnia, quæ continent fides, moresque vivendi; potuere? An quia Tridentinos canonizasse eo sensu, quem in hæreticis vetus Ecclesia damnavit? Atque Irenæus lib. 1. cap. 8. Simonianis, hæreticis utique tribuit, quòd gloriati sint de iis, quæ scripta non sunt; sed solum viva voce tradita. Idem cap. 2. Capocratianis impingit, quòd commenta sua hoc prætextu defenderint, Dominum Jesum Apostolis talia privatim in mysterio locutum esse; Apostolos autem non omnibus, sed dignis solummodo locutum esse. Et lib. iij. 2. de iisdem & Basilidianis: Cùm ex Scripturis arguerentur, in accusationem convertebantur Scripturarum, quasi non rectè haberent, neque sint ex auctoritate, & quia variè sint dictæ, & quia non possit ab bis inveinveniri veritas, qui nesciunt traditionem. Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem. Ob quam causam Paulum dixisse: Sapientiam loquimur inter persectos. Non ovo ovum simulius, quàm hisce hæreticorum scitis sunt scita Hierarchicorum. Vel ergo hæc Ecclesiæ veteris de propria & hæreticorum sententia dicta, Clerici Magnates, eradite, inducite: vel à calumnia me insontem absolvite, culpámque vestram ingenuè confitemini.
units.tr: I wrote: By these steps the Council arrived at the canonization of Traditions in that sense which the true Church never held, indeed which it condemned in heretics. The Clergy, on p. 21, places these words, torn from their context, among the calumnies. By what right? Because I wrote that the Council proceeded by steps to the canonization of Traditions? But I did not write this baldly; I set out those steps in order and demonstrated it. Is he who demonstrates the most true things to be condemned as a calumniator? Or because I wrote that the Tridentines canonized Tradition in that sense which the true Church never held? Then let them show me some ancient Council, let them produce a unanimous judgment of the Church, defined under anathema, that Traditions pertaining both to faith and to morals are given, handed down by word of mouth from Christ or from the Holy Spirit, and preserved by continuous succession (from Christ) in the Catholic Church, to be received and venerated with equal affection and reverence (alongside the written books, which the Synod had just set against traditions without writing). How can the fullness of Scripture, so sharply sung by Tertullian against Hermogenes, stand together with the unwritten word, which embraces the unwritten doctrines of faith and morals? How, in the sense of the Tridentine definition, could Athanasius in his Synopsis call the Scriptures the anchor and support, the first-fruits of the faith [ἄγκυραν καὶ ἐρεισμα τῆς πίστεως ἀποδόσεως]? How could Basil the Great write in his book on the Confession of faith: [Greek: ...] of faith and knowledge and [illegible] of things not written [Φασιεὰ ἐκπλήξεως τῆς πίστεως καὶ ἐπιστήμης καὶ [illegible, ~6 letters] τῶν μὴ γεγραμμένων]? It is a manifest crime of unbelief and arrogance either to reject anything that is written or to add anything that is not written. Jerome, on Matthew 23, pronounces: What has no authority from the Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is approved. Finally Augustine, in De Doctrina Christiana II.9, asserts: In those things which are plainly set down in Scripture are found all those things which contain faith and the rule of living. Could they have? Or is it because I wrote that the Tridentines canonized Tradition in that sense which the ancient Church condemned in heretics? Yet Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 8, attributes to the Simonians, surely heretics, that they boasted of things which are not written but were handed down by living voice alone. The same author, chapter 2, charges the Carpocratians with defending their inventions on the pretext that the Lord Jesus spoke such things privately in a mystery to the Apostles, and that the Apostles spoke only to the worthy and not to all. And in Book III, chapter 2, he says of the same people and the Basilidians: When they were refuted from the Scriptures, they turned to accuse the Scriptures, as though they were not rightly held nor authoritative, and because they were variously stated, and because the truth cannot be found in them by those who do not know the tradition. For that tradition was not handed down through letters but by living voice. For this reason Paul said: We speak wisdom among the perfect. No egg is more like an egg than these sayings of the heretics are like the decrees of the Hierarchs. Therefore, learned Clergy magnates, either produce and bring forward these sayings of the ancient Church about its own opinion and that of the heretics, or acquit me of calumny and frankly confess your own fault.

units.la: XLIII. De Attritione Clerus pag. 24. ea citat, quæ Anat. Concil. Trid. pag. 558. à me scripta sunt.
units.tr: XLIII. On Attrition. p. 24. The Clergy cites what I wrote, in the passage from the Anatomy of the Council of Trent at p. 558.

units.la: Ibi tamen non calumniâ ullâ, sed meris rationibus adversus impium Attritionis dogma à Jesuitis magno cum scandalo propugnatum, à Janssenitis aliisque oppugnatum, certavi. Neque verba exscripsit Clerus, quæ calumniam spirare putavit. De Confessione secreta his omnino verbis pag. 564. mentem meam explicavi: Secreta confessio est carnificina animi, desperationis laqueus. Hamus est Sacerdotum & Ecclesiæ, cujus hoc modo mirificè crescunt divitiæ, authoritas ac formidabilis potentia, procul omni libidine calumniandi. Dixi enim, quod res est, atque id ipsum non nudè asserui, sed argumentis pluribus firmavi. Citavi ibidem consentientes Rhenanum & Cassandrum, qui posterior Consult. art. 2. sic loquitur: Credo de hac re controversiam nullam fuisse futuram, si non salutaris hæc confitendi medicina ab imperitis & importunis Medicis multis inutilibus traditiunculis referta & contaminata fuisset, quibus conscientiis, quas extricare & levare debebant, laqueum injecerunt, & tanquam tormentis quibusdam excarnificarunt. An gravius aliquid à me dictum est? Esse quinetiam Confessionem vinculum Regni Papalis, hamum Sacerdotum & Ecclesiæ, quo illi divitias & formidabilem potentiam suam piscantur, exactiùs certiúsque Clerus ipse, quàm
units.tr: I did, however, contend there not with any calumny but with plain arguments against the impious doctrine of attrition, which the Jesuits defended with great scandal and the Jansenists and others opposed, I contended. The Clergy has not quoted the words that it thought breathed calumny. On the secret confession I explained my view in these very words, p. 564: Secret confession is the torture of the soul and a noose of despair. It is the hook of the priests and the Church, by which their riches, authority and formidable power grow wonderfully. I wrote this with no desire to slander. I said what is true, and I did not merely assert it but supported it with many arguments. There I cited in agreement Rhenanus and Cassander, the latter of whom speaks thus in Consultation, art. 2: I believe there would have been no controversy about this matter, had this salutary medicine of confession not been filled and polluted by unskilled and meddling physicians with many useless little traditions, by which they threw a noose around consciences that they ought to have freed and relieved, and tortured them as with certain instruments of torment. Was anything harsher said by me than this? That confession is the chain of the Papal kingdom and the hook of the priests and the Church, with which they fish for their riches and formidable power, the Clergy itself knows more exactly and more certainly than any of us, when it judges about attrition and confession.

units.la: de Attritione et confessione quàm nostrùm quisquam noverit. Sed Regni Papalis ejusmodi nervos & arcana palladia tegi, & Confessionis ipsius sacro sigillo, vix alium in finem cuso obsignari quàm maximè, é re sua judicat.
units.tr: Yet it judges it to its own advantage that the sinews and secret palladia of the Papal kingdom be covered, and that confession itself be sealed with its sacred seal, a seal struck for hardly any purpose more than this.

units.la: XLIV. Peccatum originale per Baptismum expungi penitus, Tridentini Sess. v. can. 5. decreverant. Ego Anat. Concil. Trid. pag. 131. observaveram, dogma isthoc ad avaritiæ & superbiæ incudem formatum esse. Id enim dare operam Clericos, ut Sacramentorum, quæ ab ipsis conferuntur, extollatur efficacia, & inde ministerio suo lucrum ac bonos accrescat. Hæc quoque verba in calumniarum catalogo Clerus pag. 32. recensuit, quo jure, quave injuria, viderit ipse. Si enim, quod non nudè asserui, sed Quæst. iij. ad Sess. vij. pluribus argumentis confirmavi, Tridentini Sacramentorum efficaciam præter & contra verbum Dei extulerunt: si, quod negari non potest, quæstum ex Sacramentis, eorúmque efficacia ultra modum meritúmque exaltata, Sacerdotes faciunt, atque inde ccu miraculi effectores (revera enim si Sacramenta inhærente virtute operantur supernaturalem gratiam, qui ea administrant, Thaumaturgi sunt) dignitatis & potestatis suæ peristromata dilatant; non calumnia est, quod dixi, sed res est, quam aperto pectore & citra fucum enuntiare mihi liberum fuit. Nam, ut ille ait Tragicus Veritatis oratio simplex est, & negligens sucos ficus ficus, ligonem ligonem appellat.
units.tr: XLIV. The Tridentine decrees, Session v, canon 5, declared that original sin is wholly wiped out by Baptism. I had observed in the Anatomy of the Council of Trent, p. 131, that this dogma was fashioned on the anvil of greed and pride. For the clergy labour to have the efficacy of the sacraments that they confer exalted, and so their ministry brings them gain and goods. The Clergy has also listed these words among its catalogue of calumnies at p. 32, and let it see for itself by what right or wrong it did so. For if the Council of Trent extolled the efficacy of the sacraments beyond and against the Word of God (as I did not merely assert but confirmed with many arguments in Question 3 on Session 7), and if priests, as cannot be denied, make a trade of the sacraments, with their efficacy raised beyond measure and merit, and thence, as makers of miracles (for if the sacraments work supernatural grace by an inherent virtue, those who administer them are wonder-workers), enlarge the tapestries of their dignity and power, then what I said is not calumny but the truth, which I was free to state with an open heart and without disguise. For, as that tragic poet says, The speech of truth is simple, and, neglecting ornament, calls a fig a fig and a spade a spade.

units.la: XLV. Majus quiddam est, quòd Clerus idem ex verbis meis, quibus Anat. Concil. Trid. pag. 130. Tridentinam Synodum sub anathemate decernentem, quòd concupiscentia etsi in Scripturis peccatum appelletur, proprie tamen peccatum non sit, videre jussi, annon sic Scripturam anathemate nefarie & veluti percusserit
units.tr: XLV. A greater matter is this: the same Clergy, from my words, in which I bade it see whether the Council of Trent, decreeing under anathema that concupiscence, though it is called sin in the Scriptures, is not properly sin (Anatomy of the Council of Trent, p. 130), had not in this way wickedly and as it were struck the Scripture with an anathema.

units.la: conficere non veretur pag. 33. scripsisse me de Synodo, quòd Scripturæ anathema dixerit, imò (une espece de Deicide) speciem aliquam Deicidii commiserit. Proh fidem Cleri! Quàm magni sæpe sunt hypocrifeos recessus! Scripturæ anathema Synodum dixisse, non scripsi; sed providere jussi, annon suam assertionem, suum anathema, Scripturæ assertioni è diametro, sola fictitia, certè non probata, non probabili peccati proprie & improprie dicti distinctione obtrusa, opponens, Scripturæ ipsi anathema dixerit. Et sanè anathema liquidò dixisse comperitur, ubi hoc unum confiterit, concupiscentiam regenitorum esse veri nominis peccatum, quod ego non simpliciter asserui, sed rationibus pluribus evidentibusque probavi. Nam quòd Synodus peccatum proprie non esse, licet peccatum Scriptura appellaverit, probare conatur eo argumento, quia in renatis nihil odit Deus, & concupiscentia nocere non consentientibus non potest, frivolum planè est, quia concupiscentiam, quæ, uti ipsa Synodus sciscebat, ex peccato est & ad peccatum inclinat, semper odit Deus, adeoque vel in concupiscente ipso, vel in Sponsore punit: atque etiam non baptizati infantes actu concupiscentiæ non consentiunt, quorum nihilominus concupiscentiam peccatum esse proprie dictum fatentur ìidem. Sed quid sibi vult species Deicidii? Petii ego, ut videat Synodus, annon anathemate feriens sententiam Scripturæ, ipsam Scripturam veluti συμαχίας, cum Deo, cujus verbum Scriptura est, pugnans, anathemate percusserit. An veluti συμαχῶν pugnare cum Deo, castra sua Scripturæ castris opponendo, est Deum occidere? Non sic profectò impotens Deus noster, Dominus exercituum est, ut se occidi patiatur ab iis, qui verbo ejus se opponunt. Omne instrumentum adversus Eum formatum non prosperabitur. Esaj. LIV. 17. Quanquam neque video etiam, quo jure calumniæ lummiz lumniæ crimine arcessere Clerus eos possit, qui Pontificios, quantum quidem in iis est, speciem Deicidii committere dictitant, cùm constet satis, eorum sententia Christum in Missa infinities sacrificari, adeóque etiam mactari, occidi.
units.tr: At p. 33 the Clergy does not hesitate to make out that I wrote that the Synod had pronounced an anathema on Scripture, and indeed that it had committed (a kind of deicide) some sort of deicide. Good faith, O Clergy! How deep the recesses of hypocrisy often are! I did not write that the Synod had pronounced an anathema on Scripture. I bade it see whether, by setting its own assertion, its own anathema, against the assertion of Scripture, which is diametrically opposed to it, and by forcing on us a distinction between sin properly and improperly so called that is merely fictitious and certainly unproved and not even probable, it had not pronounced an anathema on Scripture itself. And indeed it is clear that it did pronounce an anathema, when it asserts this one thing, that the concupiscence of the regenerate is sin in the true sense of the word. I did not merely assert this but proved it with many and evident arguments. For the Synod tries to prove that it is not sin properly, though Scripture calls it sin, by this argument, because God hates nothing in the reborn, and concupiscence cannot harm those who do not consent to it. This is plainly frivolous, because God always hates concupiscence, which, as the Synod itself decreed, comes from sin and inclines to sin, and so he punishes it either in the one who is concupiscent or in the Surety. Moreover, unbaptized infants do not actually consent to concupiscence, and yet these same men confess that in them concupiscence is sin properly so called. But what does the appearance of deicide mean? I asked that the Synod see whether, by striking down the judgment of Scripture with an anathema, it had not struck Scripture itself with an anathema, as if it were fighting in alliance [συμμαχίας] with God, whose Word Scripture is, fighting [συμμαχῶν] against him. Is it deicide to fight against God, as if in alliance, by setting one's own camp against the camp of Scripture? Our God is certainly not so weak that, being the Lord of hosts, he suffers himself to be killed by those who oppose his Word. No weapon formed against him shall prosper. Isaiah 54:17. Yet I do not see by what right the Clergy can bring the charge of calumny against those who keep saying that the Papists, so far as it lies in them, commit an appearance of deicide, since it is quite certain that by their doctrine Christ is sacrificed, and so also slain and killed, countless times in the Mass.

units.la: XLVI. Vix denique speciem calumniæ habet, quòd Tridentinorum de meritis doctrinam Anat. Concil. Trid. pag. 261. insignivi fastuosam; & pag. 131. Romanenses Pharisæos, suffarcinatos persuasione propriæ justitiæ scripsi, quæ Clerus genuino mordens ipse, per calumniam dicta pag. 35. interpretatur. Non calumniam certè hæc, sed simplicem & rusticanam veritatem spirant. Dicit enim clarissimè Spiritus S. Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur, Ephes. II. 9. Qui ergo ex operum merito, justitia propria justificari, salvari contendunt, ii gloriantur certè; & qui sic gloriantur, fastum & Pharisaicum supercilium produnt, sic cum Pharisæis gratiam Dei decantantes, ut confidant tamen sibi ipsis quòd justi sint (justitia propria) Luc. XVIII. 9. 11. 12. 13. &c. Etenim non potest non confidere operibus suis, qui per ea se mereri contendit; cùm justitia postulet, ut merces merito detur. Facit huc notatissimum illud Bellarmini: Homo justus duplici titulo jus habet ad eandem gloriam, uno ex meritis Christi, sibi per gratiam communicatis: altero ex meritis propriis, contrà quàm Spiritus S. Stipendia peccati mors: donum autem Dei vita æterna, Rom. VI. 23. In quæ paulò sanctius Cardinalis alter Cajetanus Comment. ad Rom. 6. Non dicit, quòd stipendia justitiæ vita æterna; sed Donum Dei vita æterna, ut intelligamus, non ex nostris meritis, sed ex gratuito Dei dono assequi nos pro fine vitam æternam: propter quod & subdit; In Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Ecce meritum, ecce justitiam, cujus stipendium est vita æterna, nobis autem donum ratione ipsius Christi. Nullus proin hic, Cajetano judice, meritis locus est: nec sine fastu plus quàm Campano & Pharisaico dari potest. Modestè quondam, Xiphilino teste, Tiberius è multis, quæ restituisset perfecisset-que, ædificiis, nullum sibi vendicavit, sed nomina illorum indidit, à quibus ædificari cœpta. At hi merita, justitiam propriam crepantes, sibi arrogant ædes, quibus ne tegulam quidem unam imposuerunt. An ergo sic à fastu, à supercilio Pharisaico se abhorrere, jure meritóque asseverabunt?
units.tr: XLVI. Finally, there is scarcely any appearance of calumny in my saying that I marked the Tridentine doctrine of merits as proud. The Clergy, biting its own genuine self, explains as calumny what it quotes at p. 35. I wrote at Anatomy of the Council of Trent, p. 261, and at p. 131, that the Roman Pharisees, stuffed with the persuasion of their own righteousness. These words breathe not calumny but plain and rustic truth. For the Holy Spirit says very plainly, Not of works, lest anyone should boast, Ephesians 2:9. So those who contend that they are justified and saved by the merit of works and their own righteousness certainly boast; and those who boast in this way reveal pride and a Pharisaical haughtiness, singing the grace of God with the Pharisees while they still trust in themselves that they are righteous (their own righteousness), Luke 18:9, 11, 12, 13, etc. For whoever contends that he merits by works cannot help trusting in his works, since justice demands that a reward be given for merit. To this belongs Bellarmine's notable saying: A righteous man has a double title to the same glory: one from the merits of Christ, communicated to him by grace; the other from his own merits, contrary to what the Holy Spirit says, The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life, Romans 6:23. On this the other cardinal, Cajetan, speaks more soberly in his Commentary on Romans 6: He does not say that eternal life is the wages of righteousness, but the gift of God, so that we understand that we attain eternal life as its end not from our merits but from the free gift of God. That is why he adds: in Christ Jesus our Lord. Behold the merit, behold the righteousness, of which eternal life is the wage; but to us it is a gift on account of Christ himself. Therefore, by Cajetan's judgment, there is no place for merits here, and it cannot be granted without more pride than the Campanian and Pharisaical. Once, as Xiphilinus bears witness, Tiberius, out of the many buildings that he had restored and completed, claimed none for himself but inscribed the names of those by whom they had been begun. But these men, crying up merits and their own righteousness, claim for themselves buildings on which they have not laid even a single tile. Will they then assert, rightly and justly, that they shrink from pride and Pharisaical haughtiness in this way?

units.la: XLVII. Sed ὀκ παρέδα, è diverticulo in viam ut redeamus, ad pertexendas Hierarchiæ adversus Ecclesiam blasphemias, hoc quoque ad extremum pertinet, quòd βλασφημεῖ κυριότητας blasphemat Dominationes, seu Majestatem dominantium, eorum maximè, qui Ecclesiæ Christianæ membra præcipua, imò & Nutritii sunt. Vaticinatur S. Petrus 2. Ep. 11. 10. fore quandoque falsos doctores κυριότητας καταφρονοῦντας dominationes contemnentes, audaces, sibi placentes, glorias blasphemare non reformidantes. Et S. Judas v. 8. surrecturos, qui dominationem rejiciant, gloriās autem blasphement. Id profectò Hierarchici faciunt, qui palam docent, eos, qui in summo gradu Majestatis collocati sunt, debere Papæ potestatem suam, & servire ei teneri in exequendis sententiis, denique judicio ejus sic subesse, ut nefas iis sit ab eo vel latum unguem discedere, vel populum suum in alio, quàm Papæ, Vicarii Christi nomine congregare, id nisi faxint, arbitrii ejus esse, eos deponere, anathemate ferire, excindere; Subjectos iis populos à jurejurando absolvere, & contra dominos suos concitare; idque propterea, quia ipsi potestas Divina competat in omnes populos & Regna terræ, ut edictis, sententiis, omníque vi sua faciat unum populum in mundo, qui Ecclesia vocetur; & cui ipse summo jure præsit. Talia dogmata & tale judicium haud dubiè blasphemia est, quia incurrit in ipsum Deum & Christum ejus. Huic enim Reges & Principes terræ inservire; in hujus civitatem gloriam & potentiam suam inferre debent. In Sapientia enim Reges regnant, & Principes ferunt leges justas. Prov. viii. 19. non in aliquo Capite Ecclesiæ terrestri.
units.tr: XLVII. But, to return from this digression to the main road and finish the Hierarchy's blasphemies against the Church, one more charge remains: they blaspheme dominations [βλασφημεῖ κυριότητας], that is, the majesty of rulers, above all of those who are the chief members of the Christian Church and even its nursing fathers. St Peter prophesied (2 Pet. 2:10) that false teachers would arise, despising dominion [κυριότητας καταφρονοῦντας], presumptuous, self-pleasing, and not afraid to speak evil of dignities. St Jude (v. 8) says the same of those who despise dominion and speak evil of dignities. The Hierarchists certainly do this when they openly teach that those who hold the highest rank of majesty must yield their power to the Pope, must be bound to serve him in carrying out his sentences, and must so submit to his judgment that it is wrong for them to depart from it by so much as a finger's breadth, or to gather their people under any name other than the Pope's as Vicar of Christ. If they do not comply, it is up to his judgment to depose them, strike them with anathema and cut them off. He releases subjects from their oath and sets them against their lords. They do this because divine power belongs to them over all peoples and the kingdoms of the earth, so that by their decrees, sentences and all their force they may make one people in the world, which is called the Church, and over which he presides by the highest right. Such doctrines and such judgment are undoubtedly blasphemy, because they strike at God himself and at his Christ. For kings and princes of the earth ought to serve him and bring their glory and power into his city. For by wisdom kings reign, and princes decree just laws (Prov. 8:15, 16), not in some earthly head of the Church.
XLVIII. The blasphemies of the Hierarchists that remain are directed against

units.la: eos, qui habitant, seu tabernaculum habent in Cœlo; à Deo scilicet, & tabernaculo ejus distincti. Sunt autem hi Sancti Cœlites, Angeli & homines, quibus utrisque per religiosum, uti supra diximus, cultum, in Deos, seu, ut illi loquuntur, Divos Divasque conversis, & sacrilegis titulis in Dei Christique locum subrogatis, eos blasphemare dicuntur merito. Atrocem enim iis injuriam faciunt, quando, ut mentitis eos laudibus & honoribus deforment, Deo, quod suum est, eripiunt; & Cœlitibus quod suum non est, quódque illi pro sua pietate, si conscii forent, despuerent maximè, arrogant. Sic ergo Sanctos sive verè, sive δοξασπὰς tales in idola commutant, vestientes eos titulis soli Deo competentibus. Fingunt enim eos corda hominum pervidentes adeóque omniscios: vota iis nuncupant, templa erigunt: per merita eorum in Canone Missæ salutem expetunt: denique nihil non soli Deo competens, in eos transferunt. Quod quid aliud est, quàm eos per speciem honoris in idola convertere?
units.tr: those who dwell, or have their tabernacle, in heaven, that is, who are distinct from God and from his tabernacle. These are the holy inhabitants of heaven, angels and men, to both of whom, through the religious worship we spoke of above, which turns them into gods, or as they put it, divi and divae, and which by sacrilegious titles puts them in place of God and Christ, they are rightly said to blaspheme. For they do them a grievous wrong when, by deforming them with lying praises and honours, they take from God what is his, and ascribe to the heavenly ones what is not theirs, which they, out of their piety, would most of all spit out if they were aware of it. So they change the saints, whether truly or merely in appearance, into idols, clothing them with titles that belong to God alone. For they imagine them seeing into the hearts of men and therefore knowing all things. They make vows to them, they raise temples to them, they seek salvation through their merits in the Canon of the Mass, and in short they transfer to them everything that belongs to God alone. What is this but turning them into idols under the appearance of honour?

units.la: XLIX. De Sanctis Cœlitibus honorificè tum sentien- dum, tum loquendum est, prout quisque eorum donis excelluit. In ambobus delinquunt Hierarchici cùm generatim erga universos Sanctos, tum sigillatim erga plurimos.
units.tr: XLIX. The holy inhabitants of heaven must be spoken of and thought of with honour, according as each has excelled in his gifts. The Hierarchists offend in both respects, both generally toward all the saints and specifically toward very many of them.

units.la: In Canone Missæ pro Sanctis mortuis orant, ut Deus locum refrigerii & pacis eis indulgeat, æternæque lucis beatitudine perfrui concedat. Addunt: Libera animas omnium fidelium defunctorum de pœnis inferni, & de pro-fundo lacu. Libera eas de ore Leonis, ne absorbeat eas imò in Tar-
units.tr: In the Canon of the Mass they pray for the dead saints, that God would grant them a place of refreshment and peace, and allow them to enjoy the blessedness of eternal light. They add: Deliver the souls of all the faithful departed from the pains of hell and from the deep lake. Deliver them from the lion's mouth, lest it swallow them up, nor let them fall into Tar-

units.la: Tartarus. Jam vero quod laudatur ab Augustino de verb. Apost. Serm. 17. dictum: Injuria est pro Martyre orare; aut, quemadmodum Papa Innocentius III. Cap. Cùm Marthae Extr. de Celebrat. Missae, è Sacra Scriptura citat, Injuriam facit Martyri, qui orat pro Martyre: hoc declarat idem Papa ratione consimili de aliis Sanctis sentiendum quia orationibus nostris non indigent, cùm sint perfectè beati. Ergo universis Sanctis Hierarchici detrahunt, & injuriam faciunt. Augetur injuria ex genere æ- rumnarum & periculorum, à quibus ut liberentur Sancti, orant. Etenim Absolon 2 Sam. xiii. 38. & xiv. 29. post triennium Gessure in exilio actum Hierosolymam redux, atque ibidem biennio à conspectu Regis patris sui exclusus, tantum inde dolorem concepit, ut palam significaverit, se malle adhuc exulem esse Gessure, imò morte, si ita meruisset, affici, quàm non videre faciem Regis. Si gratia terreni Regis & Patris præsentia orbari luctuosum adeò acerbúmque fuit filio degeneri; quid Sanctis morigeris Dei filiis erit é conspectu Cœlestis Patris, Regis Regum, & Dominî dominantium excludi? Ille tamen, exul licet, liber tamen perpetuò solutúsque vixit. Hoc Hierarchici in Purgatorium condunt; carcerem longè deteriorem eo, in quem Josephum Potiphar misit. Ille excepto unius rei desiderio, de cætero lætus egit. Sanctos Hierarchici gravius non damni duntaxat, sed etiam sensûs poena excruciant, quàm Urbanus VI. Cardinales suos, Theodorico Nyem de Schism. lib. i. 45. 50. &c. narrante, catenis, fame, frigore, siti, vermibus, equuleo excruciavit. Absolon quinquennio, non ampliùs afflictus est. Sed cùm Dominicus Soto. In 4. Sent. Dist. 19. q. 3. art. 2. dixisseт, credibile non esse, Deum longo tempore amicos suos in poenis detinere; & credere se, nunquam aliquem in Purgatorio viginti annis extitisse, imò nec decem; Bellarminus, improbataejus sententia, de Purg. lib. ÿ. 9. contendit ex Ecclesiæ Romanæ anniversariis sacris pro defunctis, & ex visionibus, quosdam qui centum annos, quosdam qui ducentos, etiam qui nongentos (tot enim effluxe:unt, ex quo Beda Eccl. hist. gentil. Angl. lib. v. 12. rem viso cujusdam probatam memorat) illic sunt detenti, tum detineri adhuc, tum ad diem usque judicii detentum iri. Quin & alios Sanctos poena duntaxat damni cruciatos, quòd in bonis operibus è vita excesserint, Bellarminus idem de Purgat. lib. ÿ. 7. pari ratione arcet à conspectu Dei, & à gaudiis Regni Cœlestis usque ad diem judicii. Quos porro iidem è cœtu fidelium defunctorum in Cœlitum choro locant, eos itidem Deo, ut Purgatorianos commendant. Nam Innocentius III. Cap. Apost. Extra. de Presbyter. non baptizato, agens de Presbytero non baptizato, quem mortuum quia in Sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ fide, & Christi nominis confessione perseveraverat, cœlestis patriæ gaudium esse adeptum asserit, incunctanter jubet juges preces hostiásque Deo pro illo offerri. Quod ulcus Panormitanus Comment. in cap. illud hoc emplastro curare conatur, quòd Presbyter dictus sit Cœlestis patriæ gaudium adeptus in spe, non in re. Sed Bellarminus de Eccl. Triumph. lib. ÿ. 1. agnoscit, Innocentium de re locutum esse. Eadem labe Dei param polluunt maximè, salutatione Angelica ad precandum utentes. Angelus certè sic salutando B. Virginem: Ave, vel, Pax Tibi; oravit sanè, ut Deus eam pace & gaudio cumularet. Fatetur autem Bellarminus de Missa lib. ÿ. 25. suos supplicantes, ut Deus locum pacis omnibus in Christo quiescentibus indulgeat, significatum velle, eos nondum Dei visione frui. Sic ergo Beatæ Virgini bene precando, dicentes: Ave Maria; eam nondum æternæ beatitudinis gaudium adeptam esse innuunt. Et tamen salutatione ea nihil in Hierarchicorum cultu frequentius, celecelebrius nihil est, postquam inprimis Rosarium & Psalterium B. Virginis, & Confraternitates Rosarii, atque Sodalitates invaluerunt.
units.tr: Tartarus. Now, what Augustine says in his de verbis Apostoli, Sermon 17, is praised: It is an injury to pray for a martyr; or as Pope Innocent III, citing Holy Scripture in Cap. Cum Marthae, Extra, de Celebratione Missae, puts it, He does an injury to a martyr who prays for a martyr. The same Pope declares that by similar reasoning this must be thought of the other saints, since they do not need our prayers, being perfectly blessed. So the Hierarchists detract from all the saints and do them an injury. The injury grows from the kind of miseries and dangers from which they pray that the saints be freed. Absalom, for instance (2 Sam. 13:38; 14:29), after three years in exile at Geshur, returned to Jerusalem and was there for two years excluded from the sight of his father the King, and he conceived such grief from this that he openly declared he preferred to remain an exile in Geshur, or even to suffer death if he had deserved it, rather than not see the King's face. If to be deprived of the presence of an earthly king and father was so grievous and bitter to a degenerate son, what will it be to the holy sons of God, who obey him, to be shut out from the sight of their heavenly Father, the King of kings and Lord of lords? Yet Absalom, though an exile, lived always free and unbound. The Hierarchists shut the saints up in Purgatory, a prison far worse than that into which Potiphar sent Joseph. Joseph, apart from the longing for one thing, lived happily in other respects. The Hierarchists torment the saints with a punishment not only of loss but also of sense, more severely than Pope Urban VI tortured his cardinals, as Theodoric of Niem relates (de Schismate, bk. 1, chs. 45, 50, etc.), with chains, hunger, cold, thirst, worms and the rack. Absalom was afflicted for five years, and no longer. But when Dominicus Soto (In 4 Sent., dist. 19, q. 3, art. 2) said it was not credible that God keeps his friends in punishment for a long time, and that he believed no one had been in Purgatory for twenty years, or even ten, Bellarmine, disapproving of his opinion (de Purgatorio, bk. 2, ch. 9), maintained, from the Roman Church's annual rites for the dead and from visions, that some had been detained there for a hundred years, some for two hundred, even some for nine hundred (for that many years have passed since Bede, in his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, bk. 5, ch. 12, recorded the proven vision of a certain man), and that they are still detained there and will be detained until the day of judgment. Moreover, Bellarmine himself (de Purgatorio, bk. 2, ch. 7) by the same reasoning keeps other saints, who were tormented only by the pain of loss because they departed this life with good works, from the sight of God and from the joys of the heavenly kingdom until the day of judgment. Furthermore, those whom the same writers place in the choir of the heavenly ones from the company of the faithful departed, they likewise commend as Purgatorial to God. For Innocent III, in the chapter Apostolicae, Extra, de Presbytero non baptizato, dealing with an unbaptized presbyter, whom he asserts to have obtained the joy of the heavenly fatherland after death because he had persevered in the faith of holy mother Church and in confession of the name of Christ, without hesitation orders that continual prayers and sacrifices be offered to God for him. Panormitanus, in his commentary on that chapter, tries to heal this sore with the plaster that the presbyter is said to have obtained the joy of the heavenly fatherland in hope, not in fact. But Bellarmine (de Ecclesia Triumphante, bk. 2, ch. 1) admits that Innocent was speaking of the actual thing. With the same blemish they very greatly defile God, using the Angelic Salutation in prayer. The angel, certainly, in greeting the Blessed Virgin, said Hail or Peace be with you; he indeed prayed that God would fill her with peace and joy. Bellarmine (de Missa, bk. 2, ch. 25) admits that his supplicants, in saying that God would grant a place of peace to all who rest in Christ, mean to signify that they do not yet enjoy the vision of God. So by praying well to the Blessed Virgin, saying Hail Mary, they imply that she has not yet obtained the joy of eternal blessedness. And yet there is nothing more frequent or more widely used in the Hierarchists' worship than that greeting, especially since the Rosary and Psalter of the Blessed Virgin, and the Rosary confraternities and sodalities, have taken hold.

units.la: L. Neque etiam parum dejusto honore & gloria Cœlitum Hierarchici delibant prohibente, vel paucis certè speciali indultu permittentes lectionem Scripturæ, in qua Angelorum, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Martyrum, aliorúmque Sanctorum dicta & facta, gloriæ & honoris eorum veri materies, Divinitus nonnullorum ex ipsis manu scripta sunt. Quid enim aliud gloria est, quàm frequens de aliquo fama cum laude, uti Cicero lib. ij. de invent. loquitur? Sapientiam & laudem Enochi, Noe, cæterorum, quibus palmam fidei ac pietatis Apostolus Heb. xi. 4. &c. tribuit, quàm pauci inter Pontificios Ecclesiæ Christianæ populos celebrárunt? Quorum plerique ex Pontificiis institutis in tanta ignorantiæ caligine custoditi sunt, ut non magis cognitas habuerint virtutes illorum hominum Dei, quam Virgilianum illum versum:
units.tr: Nor do the Hierarchicals take little from the just honour and glory of the heavenly ones, since they forbid, or at least permit to only a few by special indulgence, the reading of Scripture. In Scripture, divinely written down in part by some of their own number, are the deeds and sayings of Angels, Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs and other Saints, which are the true material of their glory and honour. For what else is glory than frequent fame about someone, with praise, as Cicero speaks in book 2 of De inventione? How few among the Papists have celebrated the wisdom and praise of Enoch, Noah and the rest, to whom the Apostle assigns the palm of faith and piety (Heb. 11:4 etc.)? Most of the peoples of the Christian Church who are kept under Papist institutions are in such thick darkness of ignorance that they know the virtues of those men of God no better than that line of Virgil: Scarcely does a thin breeze of fame drift to us.

units.la: Ad nos vix tenuis famæ perlabitur aura.
units.tr: Scarcely does a thin breeze of fame drift to us.

units.la: Quo pacto uxores fidelem obedientiam Saræ: fideles cuncti Abrahami vestigia sibi sequenda proponere, & Prophetas sumere pro lenitatis exemplari, quæ non sine insigni honore Sarae, Abrahami, Prophetarum 1. Pet. iii. 6. Spiritus S. præscribit possunt, cùm innumerabiles non modò fœminæ, sed & viri, Pontificiorum Pastorum, seu luporum potius sævitia sic è Scripturarum pascuis profligati sint, ut mirum sit, si nôrint, quod genus hominum Prophetæ sint, aut ecquis Abrahamus, ecquæ Sara fuerit unquam? Honorificum fore Matthæo, Lucæ, Jacobo, Johanni, cæterisque, ut à pluribus legantur & audiantur, quis ignorat? Nisi forte ad honorem Mariæ facere putabimus, quòd Matth. xxvi. 23. & Marc. xiv. 9. ejus erga Christum beneficentia commemoranda dicitur in quocunque mundo hoc prædicatum Euangelium fuerit: Euangelistis autem honori non esse, quòd & hujus, & reliquæ totius Divinissimæ Christi historiæ scriptores, in quocunque loco degit dispersa Ecclesia, celebrantur. Aut de Orationis Galbæ Epilogo Ciceronem de Clar. Orat. aptè pronuntiâsse: Tanto in honore, pueris nobis, erat, ut eum etiam edificeremus; at Apostolorum scripta si cujusvis ætatis, sexûs, ordinis homines legant, nedum edisc ant, ad honorem eorum nihil pertinere; dicemus.
units.tr: How can wives be set before them the faithful obedience of Sarah, and all the faithful be set before them the footsteps of Abraham to follow, and the Prophets be taken as the pattern of gentleness, which the Holy Spirit prescribes not without remarkable honour to Sarah, Abraham and the Prophets (1 Pet. 3:6)? Yet countless women and men alike have been so driven off from the pastures of the Scriptures by the savagery of the Papist shepherds, or rather wolves, that it would be remarkable if they knew what sort of men the Prophets were, or who Abraham or Sarah ever was. Who does not know that it would be an honour to Matthew, Luke, James, John and the others to be read and heard by many? Unless perhaps we think it does honour to Mary that her kindness to Christ is said to be recounted (Matt. 26:23; Mark 14:9) wherever this Gospel is preached in the world; but that it is no honour to the Evangelists that the writers of her history and of the whole most divine history of Christ are celebrated wherever the scattered Church dwells. Or should we say that Cicero, in De claris oratoribus, aptly pronounced of Galba's oration: It was held in such honour by us as boys that we even learned it by heart; yet if men of any age, sex or rank read the writings of the Apostles, let alone learn them by heart, that is nothing to their honour?

units.la: LI. Sed fortè si non plebeji in lingua vernacula; at certè Pastores in Officiis Ecclesiasticis Latinè; Theologi aliique viri docti in S. Scriptura Latinè, Græcè, Hebraicè talia legere, & populo tradere permittuntur. Atqui etiam Parochis tam pauca & pusilla Scripturarum frusta in Breviariis suis recitanda præscribunt, ut nec ipsi laudes Sanctorum, de quibus dixi, Abrahami fidem, Sarae obedientiam, Prophetarum lenitatem celebrare soleant. Quod etsi Cardinalis Quignonius observavit, & ex parte correxit in Breviario Romano à se reformato, ubi Præfat. ad Paulum III. conquestus est, discessum antea fuisse à Sanctissimis veterum Patrum institutis, propterea quia libri Sacræ Scripturæ, qui statis anni temporibus legendi erant more Majorum, (ut est in monumentis Gelasii & Concilii Romani LXX. Episcoporum) vix dum incepti omittuntur in alio Breviario; tamen Pius V. Brev. Rom. ex decreto Concilii Trid. restitut. Pii V. jussu edito, istam Cardinalis correctionem corrigens in Breviario novo, discessit rursum à veterum Patrum institutis, capitaque illa Sacræ historiæ de fide Abrahami, obedientia Sarae, & multa similia de Prophetis, quæ Quignonius restituerat, ex Parochorum libris & oculis removit. De Theologis verò Claudius Espenæus in cap. 1. ad Tit. testatur, inter Episcopos Pontificios esse, qui Scripturarum lectionem tam periculosam judicent, ut ab ea præ metu abstineant, caveántque sic, ne fiant hæretici, quasi verò, inquit, hæreses ex Scripturarum studio, ac non potiùs ex neglectu & ignorantia nascantur.
units.tr: LI. But perhaps, if not the common people, at least the ministers in the ecclesiastical offices are permitted to read such things in Latin, and theologians and other learned men to read and pass on to the people such things in Scripture in Latin, Greek and Hebrew. Yet they prescribe for parish priests to recite in their Breviaries so few and such tiny scraps of Scripture that they are not accustomed to celebrate the praises of the Saints I have mentioned, Abraham's faith, Sarah's obedience and the gentleness of the Prophets. Cardinal Quignonius observed this, and partly corrected it in the Roman Breviary which he reformed himself, where in the Preface to Paul III he complained that a departure had earlier been made from the most holy institutions of the ancient Fathers, because the books of Holy Scripture which were to be read at fixed times of the year according to the custom of our ancestors (as is in the records of Gelasius and of the Council of Rome of seventy bishops) were dropped in another Breviary hardly after they had been begun. Yet Pius V, in the Roman Breviary restored by decree of the Council of Trent and published by order of Pius V, correcting that correction of the Cardinal in the new Breviary, again departed from the institutions of the ancient Fathers, and removed from the parish priests' books and eyes those chapters of sacred history about Abraham's faith, Sarah's obedience and many similar things about the Prophets, which Quignonius had restored. As for the theologians, Claudius Espenaeus, in his commentary on chapter 1 of Titus, testifies that there are among the Papist bishops those who judge the reading of Scriptures so dangerous that they abstain from it for fear, and take care not to become heretics that way. As if, he says, heresies arose from the study of the Scriptures and not rather from neglect and ignorance.

units.la: LII. Quid quòd lectissimos illos Dei servos, quos Christus Matth. xix. 28. Sessuros in duodecim thronis, & judicaturos duodecim tribus Israël pollicitus est, Hierarchici tantùm non de supremo dignitatis suæ fastigio deturbant? Sic enim S. Petrum Orbis doctorem ad eas angustias redegerunt, ut ex Apostolo Ecclesiæ Romanæ particularis Pastor & Episcopus fieret. In Appendice Nili de Primatu Papæ extat initium disceptationis cujusdam Græcum inter & Cardinales Romanos habitæ, ubi Cardinalibus pertendentibus, Petrum fuisse primum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pastorem, respondet Græcus: Ἀν ὁγνώμονες ἀκεῖν ἐξίλεπ, τὸ πρὸς πιλεῖ πάχα ἔ ταυτοφαύς τῶν Ἀποστόλων τῶν παρ' ὑμῶν διαυγόμενον, ὡς τινα τον μάλιστα ὀξυτεριμένου ὄρρη. Πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι τ' ἐκκλησίης ὑπὸ διδάσκαλον ὑπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἀρξαμένου ἔ κηρύγματος, ἐν ἡ τῇ Ῥώμῃ τὴν τῆς ἀποστολῆς δρόμον πλείστος, ἀλλ' ἔ πιστὸ ἀποξληψμένος ὑμῶν μετῆς ἔ Ῥώμης ἀδιάκτωλον τῶν ψυχῶν καταγκάζων. Si equis animis audire velitis; id quod vos veluti honoris causa de coryphæo Apostolorum adfertis, in contrarium potiùs vergere intelligetis. Primùm quidem, quòd totius orbis doctorem & Magistrum, qui prædicationis suæ initium à Judæa fecit, Romæ autem Apostolatûs sui cursum peregit, tali vestra propositione solius Romæ magistrum fuisse statuitis, atque ita etiam Servatoris ad illum promissionem, quam Sancti Patres universaliter de omnibus qui credidissent, & credunt, interpretantur; vos ad solam Romam coarctatis, violentdque interpretatione torquetis. Quo concesso reliquum est omnino, eam quæ Romæ est tantùm, non autem universam fidelium Ecclesiam sibi adoptâsse Servatorem, ædificationémque hujus tanquam super petram Petri doctrinam promisisse. At verò qui ita & sentiunt & loquuntur, qualem honorem Apostolorum coryphæo deferant, ipsimet considerate. Plura addit Græcus, quibus non parum Romanos de honore S. Petri delibare & decerpere; atque velut Principis Apostolorum elogio cum ornent, revera tamen omni prorsus dignitate Apostolatûs exuere, liquidò probat.
units.tr: LII. What of the fact that the Hierarchicals almost cast down from the highest summit of their dignity those most choice servants of God whom Christ promised (Matt. 19:28) would sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel? For they have reduced St Peter, teacher of the world, to such narrow straits that from an Apostle he became the particular minister and bishop of the Church of Rome. In the Appendix to Nilus on the Primacy of the Pope there survives the beginning of a Greek dispute held between certain Roman Cardinals, in which, when the Cardinals contend that Peter was the first minister of the Church of Rome, the Greek replies: If you are willing to listen with an open mind, you will understand that what you put forward as honour to the leader of the Apostles tends rather to the contrary. First, because you make him teacher and master of the whole world, who began his preaching in Judea and completed the course of his apostleship in Rome, only the master of Rome, by your proposition; and so you confine to Rome alone, and twist by violent interpretation, the promise of the Saviour to him, which the holy Fathers interpret universally of all who had believed and believe. From this concession it follows entirely that the Saviour adopted only the Church which is at Rome, and not the universal Church of the faithful, and promised that his teaching would be built upon Peter's rock. But as for you who think and speak thus, consider for yourselves what honour you bestow on the leader of the Apostles. The Greek adds more, by which he clearly proves that the Romans take not a little from, and pluck away, the honour of St Peter, and while they adorn him with the praise of the Prince of the Apostles, in truth strip him of all the dignity of the apostleship.

units.la: LIII. Pari impietate Pius V. cœteros Apostolos omnes deprimit, quando sic Sent. Declar. contra Elisabetham loquitur: Regnans in excelsis, cui data est omnis in Cœlo & in terra potestas, unam Sanctam, Catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, extra quam nulla est salus, uni soli in terris videlicet Apostolorum Principi Petro, Petrique successori, Romano Pontifici, in potestatis plenitudine tradidit gubernandam. Christus equidem Apostolis omnibus delegavit suum officium his verbis: Sicut me misit Pater, ita & ego mitto vos; Joh. xx. 21. omnésque pariter jussit proficisci & docere omnes gentes Matth. xxviii. 18. Omnium gentium appellatione si notetur aliqua particularis, non universalis & Catholica Ecclesia, quanto minùs Papa Petro ostendere poterit traditam Catholicam ex cura ovium & agnorum ei demandata, sine appositione dictionis Omnium Joh. xxi. 15? In potestatis verò plenitudine commissam esse gubernandam ut Petro sic cœteris, adeò luculenter Christi verba declarant, ut disertè illinc Jansenius Comment. in concord. Euang. cap. 147. adstruat, Christum suam eis functionem tradidisse cum plena sibique propria potestate, quæ ad illam functionem Christi nomine obeundam erat necessaria; potestate scilicet remittendi & retinendi peccata; perinde atque Reges Legatis suis plenam potestatem committere solent, promittentes se ratum habituros, quicquid illi agerent rationabiliter. Sed multum scilicet Apostoli Pio Papæ debent, qui fui ipsius, atque sedis suæ Zelo, tanquam œstro percitus, majorem Lino, Cleto, Clementi, Episcopis Romanis, quàm Johanni Apostolo potestatem tribuit. Atque jam Eusebius virgulà censoriâ Sacrâ Congregationis Romanæ Expurgatorum castigandus fuerit, eò quòd in historia temporis Trajani Hist. Eccl. lib. iy. 16. scripserit, Clementem Romanum gubernâsse Ecclesiam: ac Johannem Apostolum, adhuc in Asia vitam traducentem, Ecclesias ibi administrâsse. Nam sine gravi periculo Papatus non amplius docebuntur homines; unius urbis Ecclesiam à Clemente Papa administratam esse: à S. Johanne autem plures, eâsque variarum Provinciarum. Corrigi Eusebiana debebant hunc in modum: Clemens solus unam Sanctam, Catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, extra quam nulla salus est, in potestatis plenitudine gubernabat: Ecclesiæ verò, quas Johannes Apostolus administravit, vel ab eo gubernabantur, ut Clementis Vicario in Diœcesi Asiana; vel hæretica aut schismaticæ erant.
units.tr: LIII. With like impiety Pius V depresses all the other Apostles, when he speaks thus in the Sentence of Declaration against Elizabeth: The Reigning One on high, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, has handed over one Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, outside which there is no salvation, to be governed in the fullness of power by one alone on earth, namely the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, and Peter's successor, the Roman Pontiff. Christ, to be sure, committed his office to all the Apostles in these words: As the Father sent me, so I send you (John 20:21), and likewise commanded them all to go forth and teach all nations (Matt. 28:18).
