If by the term of all nations some particular Church, not the universal and Catholic one, is marked out, how much less can the Pope show Peter to have been handed the Catholic Church to be governed, entrusted to him in the care of sheep and lambs without the addition of the word all (John 21:15)? That the Words of Christ make it so clear that the office was committed to be governed in the fullness of power, to Peter as to the others, Jansenius plainly asserts in his Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 147: Christ handed over his function to them with full power, and their own, which was necessary for undertaking that function in Christ's name, namely the power of forgiving and retaining sins; just as kings are accustomed to commit full power to their envoys, promising that they will hold valid whatever those envoys reasonably do. But clearly the Apostles owe much to Pope Pius, who, stung as by a gadfly by his own zeal for himself and his see, has attributed greater power to the Roman bishops Linus, Cletus and Clement than to the Apostle John. And now Eusebius deserves to be punished with the censor's rod of the Sacred Roman Congregation of Expurgation, because in his history of the time of Trajan (Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 16) he wrote that Clement the Roman governed the Church, and the Apostle John, still living his life in Asia, administered the churches there. For men will no longer be taught without grave danger to the Papacy that the Church of one city was governed by Pope Clement, but by St John several, and those of various provinces. The Eusebian text ought to be corrected in this way: Clement alone governed in the fullness of power the one Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, outside which there is no salvation; but the churches which the Apostle John administered were either governed by him as the Vicar of Clement in the Asian diocese, or were heretical or schismatic.

units.la: LIV. Deiparam præterquam quòd in idolum maxi- mum Hierarchici converterunt pridem, aliis etiam contu- meliis affecerunt iidem, uti Legendæ eorum locuples te- stimonium præbent.
units.tr: LIV. Besides the many insults that the hierarchs have long heaped upon the Mother of God, turning her into their chief idol, they have also inflicted other outrages on her, as their legends abundantly testify.

units.la: Monialis à Sacerdote compressæ, & postea in lupanar detrusæ vices & personam eam in Monasterio sustinuisse, Cæsarius de miraculis cap. 35. habet. Alanus de Rupe, Monachus putidissimus, jactare ausus est, sibi B. Virginem nupsisse, annulum sibi pronubum, fidei conjugalis Sacramentum, donasse, oscula sibi fixisse, mammas contrectandas, fugendásque exhibuisse, de quo memorantem in vita Sixti IV. Balæum videre est. Similia de Dominico Cæsario lib. vj. 52. de Hermanno Josepho, Viro Angelico, Jesuita Hautinus Angel. Cust. cap. 4. p. 158. ex Surio: de milite, qui uxorem heri sui deperibat, & ex consilio Eremitæ per annum centies de die Mariam salutabat, cui illa apparens dixit: Ego ero uxor tua; accede ad me, & da mihi osculum: & coëgit illum, dixitque. Modò initiatæ sunt nuptiæ, & mox perficientur; Cæsarius lib. vij. 33. tradidere. Sic ergo polygamam faciunt etiam Cœlitem illam. Eandem solis Hierarchis, hoc est, Missificis, in commissi mysterii executione concedere, Gabriel Biel Lect. 4. blasphemat. Miracula ei tributa planè contumeliosa ex legendarum & fabularum hamaxariis, Cæsario, Thoma Cantipratensi, Discipulo de Tempore, Trithemio, Pelbarto de Themes Waar, Bernhardino de Bustis, Alano de Rupe, aliis plura Cl. Rivetus Apol. pro B. Virgine lib. ij. 15. collegit. Denique merito Erasmus in Colloquio, quod Naufragium inscribitur, Papistas reprehendit simul & albis dentibus ridet, quòd in præfectura maris Mariam Veneri substituerint. Nam olim Venus agebat curam nautarum, quia nata credebatur ex mari. Ea quoniam desiit curare, inquit Erasmus, suffecta est (à nautis Pontificiis, qui ex Pontificiæ Scholæ disciplina Mariæ titulos Stellæ maris, Reginæ Cœli, dominæ mundi, portus salutis, dulcedinis, vitæ, spei nostræ) huic matri non Virgini Virgo Mater. Ita quod Pagani Venerem orabant: Sic te Diva potens Cypri &c. id nautas à Maria petere sub Papatu, Virginem lectissimam in præfectura maris turpissimo scorto substituentes, Erasmus indicat.
units.tr: Cæsarius, de miraculis cap. 35., reports that a nun, ravished by a priest and afterwards thrust into a brothel, took her place and role in the convent. Alanus de Rupe, a most foul monk, dared to boast that the Blessed Virgin had married him, had given him a ring as the pledge of marital faith, had fixed kisses on him, and had offered her breasts to be handled and sucked. Balaeus may be read on this, mentioning it in the life of Sixtus IV. Similar stories are told by Cæsarius, lib. vj. 52, about Dominicus Cæsarius; by Hautinus, Angel. Cust. cap. 4. p. 158, about Hermann Joseph, the angelic Jesuit, drawn from Surius: about a soldier who lusted after his master's wife and, on the advice of a hermit, greeted Mary a hundred times a day for a year, until she appeared to him and said: I will be your wife; come to me and give me a kiss. He was compelled, and she said: Now the marriage has begun, and it will soon be consummated; Cæsarius, lib. vij. 33, has handed this down. Thus they make that heavenly woman a polygamist. Gabriel Biel, Lect. 4., blasphemously grants the same power to the hierarchs alone, that is, to the celebrants of the Mass, in the performance of the committed mystery. The miracles ascribed to her are plainly insulting, drawn from the rubbish heaps of legends and fables: Cæsarius, Thomas Cantipratensis, the Disciple of the Time, Trithemius, Pelbartus de Themeswar, Bernardinus de Bustis, Alanus de Rupe, and others, which the illustrious Rivetus, Apol. pro B. Virgine lib. ij. 15., has gathered in quantity. Finally, Erasmus rightly rebukes the Papists in the colloquy entitled Shipwreck, and at the same time laughs with white teeth, because they have put Mary in charge of the sea in place of Venus. For Venus once had the care of sailors, because she was believed to have been born of the sea. "Since she has ceased to take care of them," says Erasmus, "she has been replaced" (by the Papist sailors, who, following the teaching of the Papist school, give Mary the titles Star of the Sea, Queen of Heaven, Lady of the World, Haven of Salvation, Sweetness, Life, Our Hope) "by this mother, not a virgin, the Virgin Mother." So Erasmus shows that, where the pagans prayed to Venus, Thus, powerful goddess of Cyprus, etc., under the Papacy sailors seek the same from Mary, setting the most chosen Virgin in charge of the sea in place of the most foul harlot.

units.la: LV. Inter Sanctos Cœlites etiam referendi sunt, qui Patrum nomine veniunt.
units.tr: LV. Among the saints in heaven must also be counted those who come under the name of Fathers.

units.la: Utut autem in honorem eorum multa Hierarchici garriant, ut simplicibus & incautis sucum faciant; revera tamen eos totos, quanti quanti sunt, unius Papæ, Deastri sui libidini subjiciunt, dedúntque mancupio & nexu, qui eos non aliter, quàm Mercatores suos solent calculos, usurpat. Aliquando enim ei denarium sunt loco, aliquando librarum, ut ad manum quosque proxiproximè ad rationes suas conficiendas habet. Episcopus Bitontinus in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 14. pag. 66. profitetur palam, se in his, quæ mysteria fidei tangunt, plus uni summo Pontifici credere, quàm mille Augustinis, Hieronymis, Gregoriis. Præterea eos invitos ad patrocinium doctrinæ Antichristianæ trahunt, lancinant, adulterant, interpungunt, veru critico, quoties lubet, notant. Indicio esse possunt Indices Expurgatorii, Romanus, Hispanus, certissimi eorum erga Patres irreverentiæ testes.
units.tr: However much the hierarchs chatter in their honour, in order to hoodwink the simple and the unwary, in truth they subject all of them, however many there are, to the lust of their one Pope, their little god, and hand them over in bondage and servitude, using them just as merchants use their counters. For sometimes they stand for pennies, sometimes for pounds, as he has them close at hand to make up his accounts. The bishop of Bitonto, in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 14. pag. 66., openly professes that in matters touching the mysteries of faith he trusts the one supreme Pontiff more than a thousand Augustines, Jeromes, and Gregories. Moreover, they drag them unwilling into the defence of anti-Christian doctrine, mangle them, adulterate them, punctuate them, and mark them with the critic's spit whenever they please. The Expurgatory Indexes, Roman and Spanish, can serve as evidence, the most certain witnesses of their irreverence towards the Fathers.

units.la: LVI. Denique Sanctorum defunctorum corpora falsis honoribus illi mactant, & veris defraudant. Nam ad honorem eorum pertinere, ut terræ communi matri mandata, ibidem quiescant, usque dum ad vitam à Deo revocentur; exempla corporum Sanctorum Patriarcharum, Mosis, piorum Regum, aliorum probant. Ipsius Eliæ ossa, quorum contactu mortuus resuscitatus est, Iosia 2 Reg. XXIII. 18. piè mandante, ne quidem commota, sed humi relicta sunt. Hi verò Sactorum ossa non tantùm commovent & è sepulchris suis effodiunt, adeóque sepulchra Sacrosancta violant, sed etiam circumgestata & publicè conspecta, alia quidem in sublimiore sepulchro condunt, alia verò penitus insepulta servant, eáque sepeliunt sepulturâ asini, uti Propheta Ierem. XXII. 19. loquitur: adeóque honoris scilicet causa faciunt, quod Pontificii ipsi, imò & Ethnici ignominiosum, profanum & impium esse docent. Bellarminus enim de Purgat. lib. ij. cap. ult. inter utilitates, quæ mortuis ex sepultura accedunt, hanc commemorans, quòd consulitur honori eorum, adhuc in hominum memoriis viventium. Non enim caret, inquit, ignominia quadam, quòd fœditas nostri corporis aliorum conspectui pateat. Et Cardinalis Borrhomæus Concil. Mediol. 4. tit. de Sacris reliquiis, Concil. Tomo 5. cum universa Synodo Mediolanensi vetat, ne tangantur Sacræ reliquiæ, quoniam hoc sacrilegium, ac minùs propterea ferendum esse S. Gregorius scribit. Gregorius autem Registr. lib. iy. epist. 50. scribens, intolerabile esse omnino atque sacrilegum, Sanctorum corpora tangere, addit; cùm sepulchrum Laurentii Martyris ignoranter ab operariis aliud agentibus apertum esset, eos, qui prasentes erant, & laborabant, Monachos & mansionarios, qui corpus Martyris viderunt, etsi tangere non præsumpserunt, omnes intra decem dies obiisse, ita ut nullus vitæ superesse posset, qui sanctum & justum illius corpus viderat. Denique insepultam sepulturam Cicero Philipp. I. pro dedecore habuit. Nec Tumus Virgilianus Æneid. lib. 10. largiens Pallanti, Quisquis honos tumuli est, mortuis honorificum putavit non humari. Et Horatius Epod. 16. bella civilia hoc incommodo maximum sui odium commotura speravit, quòd hostis, urbem occupans civibus orbatam, sepulchrum Romuli violaturus sit: Quæque carent ventis & solibus, offa Quirini, (Nefas videre) dissipabit insolens.
units.tr: LVI. Finally, they lavish false honours on the bodies of the dead saints and rob them of true ones. For it belongs to their honour that they be committed to the common mother earth and rest there until God calls them back to life; the examples of the bodies of the holy Patriarchs, Moses, pious kings and others prove this. The bones of Elijah, by whose touch a dead man was raised, were not even moved, but left on the ground, as Josiah piously commanded, 2 Kings 23:18. But these hierarchs not only move and dig up the bones of saints from their tombs, thereby violating sacred sepulchres, but also carry them about and display them publicly; some they lay in a higher tomb, others they keep wholly unburied, and bury them in the burial of an ass, as the prophet Jeremiah 22:19 puts it. Thus they do, for the sake of honour, what the Papists themselves, and even the pagans, teach to be shameful, profane and impious. For Bellarmine, de Purgat. lib. ij. cap. ult., listing among the benefits that accrue to the dead from burial this one, says: that their honour is consulted while they still live in the memories of men. For it is not free, he says, from a certain disgrace, that the foulness of our body should lie open to the sight of others. And Cardinal Borromeo, Concil. Mediol. 4. tit. de Sacris reliquiis, Concil. Tomo 5., forbids with the whole Milanese Synod that sacred relics be touched, since St Gregory writes that this is sacrilege and must for that reason be borne the less patiently. Gregory himself, writing in Registr. lib. iy. epist. 50, that it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious to touch the bodies of saints, adds: when the tomb of the martyr Lawrence was opened unknowingly by workmen busy with other things, all those who were present and labouring there, monks and custodians, who saw the body of the martyr, although they did not presume to touch it, died within ten days, so that no one was left alive who had seen his holy and righteous body. Finally, Cicero, Philipp. I., counted an unburied burial a disgrace. Nor does Virgil's Turnus, Æneid. lib. 10., when he grants to Pallas, say: "Whatever honour a tomb is, the dead have thought it honourable not to be buried." And Horace, Epod. 16., hoped that civil wars would stir up the greatest hatred of themselves by this inconvenience, that an enemy occupying the city, bereft of its citizens, would violate the tomb of Romulus: "and the bones of Quirinus, which are kept from winds and sun, the insolent man will scatter (a sacrilege even to see)."

units.la: Atqui Hierarchici Sanctorum ossa servant in capsis ostendenda populo, à Clericis attrectanda, gestanda in processionibus, in altaribus exponenda: nec ea vel à ventis, vel à Solis radiis remota esse sinunt, sed è sepulchris eruta conspectui tactuique hominum objiciunt, & quaquaversum dissipant. Cujus enim Sancti paulò celebrioris ossa non varias in oras disperserunt? Etenim Abundius & Abundantius neutiquam ex clarissimis Divis fuerunt. Eorum tamen, uti ex Hist. pass. invent. & translat. Sanctorum Abundii & Abundantii edit. à Colleg. Societ. Jesu Romæ A. 1584. liquet, corpora postquam è Cosmæ & Damiani Templo, in quo requiescebant, in novam Jesuitarum Basilicam Gregorius XIII. transferri jussisset, quædam eorum ossa relicta sunt in pristino hospitio Cosmæ & Damiani; quædam ad CœnoCœnobium Sanctimonialium Senas transportata; quædam in Japonum, novi orbis insulam, ultra Garamantas & Indos transmissa sunt. Licet ergo jactent Papistæ, se reliquias ita tractare ad Sanctorum honorem; atque id eo sensu, quo Cicero Philipp. i. quendam honorem contumeliosum nominat; atque idem Pro domo sua asserit Catonem ejectum esse à Clodio per honorem turpissimum; verum est: tamen eas tractant ignominiosè, exhumantes dissipantésque corpora, quæ in pace sepulta sunt: & quorum fœditatem, vel Bellarmino supra agnoscente, ratio, religio, jus humanitatis tellure tegi jubebat; ea partim intra capsas, partim extra hominibus videnda & tangenda exhibent.
units.tr: Yet the hierarchs keep the bones of saints in boxes to be shown to the people, handled by clerics, carried in processions, and displayed on altars. They suffer them to be kept neither from the winds nor from the rays of the sun, but dig them out of their tombs and expose them to the sight and touch of men, scattering them in every direction. For whose bones of any fairly famous saint have they not scattered to various regions? Abundius and Abundantius, for instance, were by no means among the most illustrious saints. Yet, as is clear from the Hist. pass. invent. & translat. Sanctorum Abundii & Abundantii edit. à Colleg. Societ. Jesu Romæ A. 1584., after Gregory XIII ordered their bodies to be transferred from the Temple of Cosmas and Damian, where they rested, to the new Basilica of the Jesuits, some of their bones were left in the former lodging of Cosmas and Damian; some were carried to a convent of nuns at Siena; and some were sent across to Japan, an island of the New World, beyond the Garamantes and the Indians. So although the Papists boast that they handle relics thus for the honour of the saints, in the sense in which Cicero, Philipp. i, calls a certain insulting honour, and the same man in Pro domo sua asserts that Cato was thrown out by Clodius with the most shameful honour, that is true. Nevertheless they treat them with dishonour, digging up and scattering bodies that were laid to rest in peace, and whose foulness, even Bellarmine acknowledged above, reason, religion and the law of humanity order to be covered by the earth; some of these they display within boxes, others outside, to be seen and touched by men.

units.la: LVII. Ex iis, quæ hactenus per summa capita attigi, jubare meridiano clarius constat, Hierarchicos honorem debitum multis modis detrahere Deo, ejus verbo, Christo, Ecclesiæ Dei, Sanctis Cœlitibus, Patriarchis, Apostolis, Deiparæ, omnibus denique Sanctis. Frigidius proin remissiúsque justo mihi agere videor, si Apostoli illud de Judæis dictum: Neque Deo placent, & omnibus hominibus adversantur, 1 Thess. ii. 15. iis accommodem. Nam & Dei Christíque honorem suâ idololatriâ spoliísque multifariis horribiliter lædunt, & Angelos hominésque electos contumeliis probrísque gravissimis afficiunt; adeóque se blasphemiis nefariè polluunt, quo suscepto demonstrationis octavo capite ritè nos defunctos confidimus.
units.tr: LVII. From what I have touched upon so far under the main heads, it is clearer than the noonday sun that the hierarchs take away the honour due to God in many ways: from his Word, from Christ, from the Church of God, from the heavenly saints, the Patriarchs, the Apostles, the Mother of God, and finally from all the saints. Therefore I think I would be acting too coldly and too leniently if I applied to them, as they deserve, what the Apostle said of the Jews: "They do not please God and are opposed to all men," 1 Thess. 2:15. For they both horribly wound the honour of God and Christ by their idolatry and manifold spoliations, and they heap the most grievous insults and reproaches on the angels and chosen men; and so they foully pollute themselves with blasphemies, which task, undertaken in the eighth chapter of the demonstration, I trust I have duly discharged.
DISSERTATIO DECIMA QUARTA

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem esse Babylonem Magnam probatur Nonò, quia luxuriâ & impuritate carnis se multis modis polluit. BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: IN WHICH it is proved that the Hierarchy, or the clergy ruling the Church of Rome, is the Great Babylon: Ninthly, because it pollutes itself in many ways by luxury and impurity of the flesh. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Ad habitum interiorem Babylonis M. pertinet etiam luxuria & impuritas carnis. II. Ejus Hierarchia rea peragitur demonstratione Syllogismo innexa. Cujus propositionis nexus & Assumptio per singula membra probatur. III. Hierarchia luxuriæ ansam ejusmodi præbet, ut eam ob carnis infirmitatem & eventum inevitabilem certò post se trahat. IV. Luxuriæ instrumenta Babylon habet divitias haud vulgares. V. Hierarchiæ in corradendis divitiis summa solertia exponitur. VI. Iisdem ad luxum & potentiæ exaltationem abutitur. VII. Prætextus acquirendarum divitiarum ad externi cultûs splendorem futilitas. VIII. Uti eam divitiis ad magnificentiam, superbiam, Tom.II. PP IX. in
units.tr: I. Luxury and impurity of the flesh also belong to the inner character of the Great Babylon. II. Its Hierarchy is charged with guilt, and the demonstration is bound together in a syllogism. The connection of the major premise and the assumption are proved member by member. III. The Hierarchy gives luxury such an occasion that, because of the weakness of the flesh and the inevitable outcome, it certainly draws luxury after it. IV. Babylon has no ordinary riches as the instruments of luxury. V. The Hierarchy's great skill in amassing riches is set out. VI. It abuses the same riches for luxury and the exaltation of power. VII. The pretext of acquiring riches, for the splendour of external worship, is shown to be trifling. VIII. That it uses the riches for magnificence and pride, IX. in

units.la: IX. inprimis luxuriam, idoneis testimoniis & documentis probatur.
units.tr: IX. especially luxury, is proved by fitting testimonies and documents.

units.la: X. Babylonis & Hierarchiæ exacta hac in re harmonia.
units.tr: X. The harmony of Babylon and the Hierarchy is exact in this matter.
XI. Idleness is the mother of luxury.

units.la: XII. Religiosum Hierarchiæ otium ex frequentia feriarum cognoscitur.
units.tr: XII. The religious idleness of the Hierarchy is known from the frequency of holidays.

units.la: XIII. Ad luxuriam otium illud inclinare demonstratur tum ex cultûs, qui festivo tempore peragitur, exercitiis, nihil ad mortificationem hominis facientibus;
units.tr: XIII. That this idleness tends toward luxury is shown both from the exercises of worship performed in festive time, which do nothing to mortify a man;

units.la: XIV. tum ex testimoniis Clemangis, Petri de Aliaco, Polydori Vergilii, Gravaminum Imperii, Urbani VIII. Papæ;
units.tr: XIV. and from the testimonies of Clemangis, Pierre d'Ailly, Polydore Vergil, the Gravamina of the Empire, and Pope Urban VIII;

units.la: XV. tum ex debacchationibus solennibus & festivis Bacchanalium;
units.tr: XV. and from the solemn and festive revelries of the Bacchanalia;

units.la: XVI. quorum impietas verbis Baptistæ Mantuani graphicè depingitur.
units.tr: XVI. whose impiety is vividly portrayed in the words of Baptista Mantuanus.

units.la: XVII. Impuritati Hierarchiæ ansam etiam lex cœlibatûs Sacerdotibus lata; & vota continentiæ Monastica præbent. Donum continentiæ non commune fidelibus universis, sed proprium quibusdam esse, ex 1 Cor. vÿ. 7. &c.
units.tr: XVII. The law of celibacy imposed on priests, and the monastic vows of continence, also provide an occasion for impurity. That the gift of continence is not common to all the faithful but proper to some is shown from 1 Cor. 7:7 and following.

units.la: XVIII. nec non Matth. xix. 10. 11. & natura ipsa demonstratur.
units.tr: XVIII. and from Matt. 19:10, 11, and from nature itself.

units.la: XIX. Cœlibatum lege vel voto suscipientes, vel jam mortificati, vel nondum mortificati sunt. Utrosque certissimo impuritatis periculo se exponere, probatur.
units.tr: XIX. Those who take up celibacy by law or by vow are either already mortified or not yet mortified. That both expose themselves to the most certain danger of impurity is proved.

units.la: XX. Preces & afflictatio certa obtinendæ in cœlibatu continentiæ remedia non sunt.
units.tr: XX. Prayers and affliction are not sure remedies for obtaining continence in celibacy.

units.la: XXI. Neque id ex promissionibus, iis, qui petunt, pulsant, quærunt, saltis comprobatur.
units.tr: XXI. Nor is this sufficiently shown from the promises made to those who ask, knock and seek.

units.la: XXII. Monachorum inprimis vota, vita, iners cultus, otium ad impuritatem omnem ducatum præbet, quod hypotyposi quadam ab Henrico Moro adornata ostenditur.
units.tr: XXII. The vows, life, idle worship and leisure of monks above all lead to every impurity, as is shown in an outline drawn up by Henry More.

units.la: XXIII. Summum ex lege & voto cœlibatús periculum augent tum immodica & falsa encomia cœlibatús;
units.tr: XXIII. The greatest danger from the law and vow of celibacy is increased both by immoderate and false praises of celibacy;

units.la: XXIV. tum contumeliæ, quibus matrimonium inprimis eorum, qui voto ad cœlibatum se prius obstrinxerunt, Hierarchici afficiunt.
units.tr: XXIV. and by the insults which the Hierarchy heaps upon marriage, especially the marriage of those who have previously bound themselves by vow to celibacy.

units.la: XXV. Experientia testis impuritatis ex lege & votis cœlibatús consecutæ inducitur;
units.tr: XXV. Experience is brought in as a witness to the impurity that follows from the law and vows of celibacy;

units.la: XXVI. atque testimoniis Gersonis, Pighii, Dominici à Soto suffulcitur.
units.tr: XXVI. and it is supported by the testimonies of Gerson, Pighius and Domingo de Soto.

units.la: XXVII. Concubinatus inprimis Cleri, Clemangis, Johannis Chemensis, Gravaminum Imperii, Alberti, Bavariæ Ducis, Espencæi confessionibus probatus, periculum legis & votorum cœlibatús clarissimè arguit.
units.tr: XXVII. Concubinage, especially among the clergy, proved by the confessions of Clemangis, John of Chemin, the Gravamina of the Empire, Albert Duke of Bavaria and Espencaeus, clearly argues the danger of the law and vows of celibacy.

units.la: XXVIII. Impuritas à Clero capite ad subjectum universum populum facilè promanat.
units.tr: XXVIII. Impurity easily flows from the head of the clergy down to the whole subject people.

units.la: XXIX. Bellarmini exceptio, quòd non lex & vota cœlibatús, sed eorundem abusus prodigiosus libidines peperit, diluitur.
units.tr: XXIX. Bellarmine's objection, that it is not the law and vows of celibacy but their monstrous abuses that bred lusts, is refuted.

units.la: XXX. Hierarchicorum prætextus, quòd ad vovendum & suscipiendum cœlibatum neminem impellant vel cogant, discutitur.
units.tr: XXX. The Hierarchy's pretext, that they compel no one to vow or take up celibacy, is examined.

units.la: XXXI. Eorundem functio Sacra concipiendæ impuritati ansam præbet; in confessione auriculari inprimis. Instructio Sacerdotum ad confessiones audiendas plena impudentiæ est, quod ex Casuistarum libris proditur; inprimis Sanchezii opere de matrimonio, de quo Petri Aurelii Sorbonistæ judicium gravissimum adscribitur.
units.tr: XXXI. Their sacred function provides an occasion for conceiving impurity, especially in auricular confession. The instruction of priests for hearing confessions is full of shamelessness, as is evident from the books of the Casuists, above all Sanchez's work on marriage, to which is appended the very weighty judgement of Pierre Aurel the Sorbonnist.

units.la: XXXII. Confessarii sic instructi quales confitentes efficiant.
units.tr: XXXII. What sort of penitents confessors so instructed make.

units.la: XXXIII. quomodo etiam se ipsi gerant, res loquitur, & testes Alvarus Pelagius, Erasmus patefaciunt.
units.tr: XXXIII. How they themselves behave, the matter itself speaks, and the witnesses Alvarus Pelagius and Erasmus make plain.

units.la: XXXIV. & Casuistarum casus circa denuntiationes Sacerdotum, qui pueros, puellas, fœminas pro arcano hoc tribunali solicitant; ex Diana Panormitano eruti demonstrant. celebrius nihil est, postquam inprimis Rosarium & Psalterium B. Virginis, & Confraternitates Rosarii, atque Sodalitates invaluerunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. and the Casuists' cases concerning the denunciations of priests who solicit boys, girls and women at this secret tribunal; drawn from Diana of Palermo, they demonstrate it. Nothing has become more famous since, above all, the Rosary and Psalter of the Blessed Virgin, and the Confraternities of the Rosary and sodalities, have grown strong.

units.la: L. Neque etiam parùm dejusto honore & gloria Coelitum Hierarchici delibant prohibentes, vel paucis certè speciali indulto permittentes lectionem Scripturæ, in qua Angelorum, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Martyrum, aliorúmque Sanctorum dicta & facta, gloriæ & honoris eorum veri materies, Divinitus nonnullorum ex ipsis manu scripta sunt. Quid enim aliud gloria est, quàm frequens de aliquo fama cum laude, uti Cicero lib. y. de invent. loquitur? Sapientiam & laudem Enochi, Noe, caeterorum, quibus palmam fidei ac pietatis Apostolus Heb. xi. 4. &c. tribuit, quàm pauci inter Pontificios Ecclesiæ Christianæ populos celebrárunt? Quorum plerique ex Pontificiis institutis in tanta ignorantiæ caligine custoditi sunt, ut non magis cognitas habuerint virtutes illorum hominum Dei, quam Virgilianum illum versum:
units.tr: L. Nor do the Hierarchy take too little from the honour and glory of the heavenly ones, by forbidding, or at most permitting to a few by a special indult, the reading of Scripture, in which the sayings and deeds of Angels, Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs and other Saints, the true material of their glory and honour, were written down by divine inspiration, some of them by their own hand. For what else is glory than frequent fame of someone with praise, as Cicero speaks in the second book of De Inventione? How few among the Papists, in the peoples of the Christian Church, have celebrated the wisdom and praise of Enoch, Noah and the others to whom the Apostle assigns the palm of faith and piety (Heb. 11:4 and following)? Most of them, kept under Papist institutions in such a fog of ignorance, know the virtues of those men of God no better than that Virgilian line:

units.la: Ad nos vix tenuis famæ perlabitur aura.
units.tr: Scarcely a thin breath of fame glides down to us.

units.la: Quo pacto uxores fidelem obedientiam Saræ: fideles cuncti Abrahami vestigia sibi sequenda proponere, & Prophetas sumere pro lenitatis exemplari, quæ non sine insigni honore Saræ, Abrahami, Prophetarum 1. Pet. iii. 6. Spiritus S. præscribit possunt, cùm innumerabiles non modò foeminæ, sed & viri, Pontificiorum Pastorum, seu luporum potiùs saevitia sic è Scripturarum pascuis profligati sint, ut mirum sit, si nôrint, quod genus hominum Prophetæ sint, aut ecquis Abrahamus, ecquæ Sara fuerit unquam? Honorificum fore Matthæo, Lucæ, Jacobo, Johanni, caeterisque, ut à pluribus legantur & audiantur, quis ignorat? Nisi forte ad honorem Mariæ facere putabimus, quòd Matth. xxvi. 23. & Marc. xiv. 9. ejus erga Christum beneficentia commemoranda dicitur in quocunque mundo hoc
units.tr: In what way can wives set before themselves the faithful obedience of Sarah, all the faithful propose the footsteps of Abraham to follow, and take the Prophets as the pattern of gentleness, which the Holy Spirit prescribes not without a notable honour to Sarah, Abraham and the Prophets (1 Pet. 3:6)? Countless women, and men too, have been so driven off from the pastures of Scripture by the savagery of the Papist pastors, or rather wolves, that it is astonishing if they know what sort of men the Prophets were, or whether there ever was an Abraham, or ever a Sarah. Who does not know that it would be an honour to Matthew, Luke, James, John and the rest to be read and heard by many? Unless perhaps we think it serves Mary's honour that her beneficence toward Christ is said to be commemorated (Matth. 23; Mark 14:9) wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world.

units.la: Sanctis: hoc est, ... (marginal notes, italic) hoc prædicatum Euangelium fuerit: Euangelistis autem honori non esse, quòd & hujus, & reliquæ totius Divinissimæ Christi historiæ scriptores, in quocunque loco degit dispersa Ecclesia, celebrantur. Aut de Oratione Galbæ Epilogo Ciceronem de Clar. Orat. aptè pronuntiàsse: Tanto in honore, pueris nobis, erat, ut eum etiam edifceremus; at Apostolorum scripta si cujusvis ætatis, sexûs, ordinis homines legant, nedum ediscant, ad honorem eorum nihil pertinere, dicemus.
units.tr: Sanctis: that is, ... (marginal notes, italic) that this gospel has been preached. But it brings no honour to the Evangelists that the writers of this and of the rest of the most divine history of Christ are celebrated wherever the scattered Church dwells. Or we may say that Cicero aptly spoke of the epilogue of Galba's speech in De Claris Oratoribus: So great was its honour among us, when we were boys, that we even learned it by heart; yet if men of any age, sex or rank read the writings of the Apostles, let alone learn them by heart, we shall say that this contributes nothing to their honour.

units.la: LI. Sed fortè si non plebeji in lingua vernacula; at certè Pastores in Officiis Ecclesiasticis Latinè, Theologi aliique viri doĉti in S. Scriptura Latinè, Græcè, Hebraicè talia legere, & populo tradere permittuntur. Atqui etiam Parochis tam pauca & pusilla Scripturarum frusta in Breviariis suis recitanda præscribunt, ut nec ipsi laudes Sanctorum, de quibus dixi, Abrahami fidem, Saræ obedientiam, Prophetarum lenitatem celebrare soleant. Quod etsi Cardinalis Quignonius observavit, & ex parte correxit in Breviario Romano à se reformato, ubi Præfat. ad Paulum III. conquestus est, discessum autem fuisse à Sanctissimis veterum Patrum institutis, propterea quia libri Sacræ Scripturæ, qui statis anni temporibus legendi erant more Majorum, (ut est in monumentis Gelasii & Concilii Romani xxx. Episcoporum) vix dum incepti omittuntur in alio Breviario; tamen Pius V. Brev. Rom. ex decreto Concilii Trid. restitut. Pii V. jussu edito, istam Cardinalis correctionem corrigens in Breviario novo, discessit rursum à veterum Patrum institutis, capitáque illa Sacræ historiæ de fide Abrahami, obedientia Saræ, & multa similia de Prophetis, quæ Quignonius restituerat, ex Parochorum libris & oculis removiт. De Theologis verò Claudius Espenæus in cap. I. ad Tit. testatur, inter Episcopos Pontificios esse, qui Scripturarum lectionem tam periculosam judijudicent, ut ab ea præ metu abstineant, caveántque sic, ne fiant hæretici, quasi vero, inquit, hæreses ex Scripturarum studio, ac non potiùs ex neglectu & ignorantia nascantur.
units.tr: LI. But perhaps, if not common people in the vernacular, at least the pastors in the offices of the Church are permitted to read such things in Latin, and theologians and other learned men to read them in Scripture in Latin, Greek and Hebrew, and to pass them on to the people. Yet they prescribe for parish priests such few and tiny scraps of Scripture to be recited in their breviaries that they are not accustomed to celebrate the praises of the Saints I mentioned: Abraham's faith, Sarah's obedience, the gentleness of the Prophets. Although Cardinal Quiñones observed this and partly corrected it in the Roman Breviary he reformed, where in his preface to Paul III he complained that they had departed from the most holy institutions of the ancient Fathers, because the books of Holy Scripture which were to be read at set times of the year, according to the custom of our ancestors (as in the records of Gelasius and of the Council of thirty Roman bishops), are scarcely begun before they are omitted in another breviary; nevertheless Pius V, in the Roman Breviary restored by decree of the Council of Trent and issued by order of Pius V, correcting that Cardinal's correction in the new Breviary, again departed from the institutions of the ancient Fathers, and removed from parish priests' books and eyes those chapters of sacred history about the faith of Abraham and the obedience of Sarah, and many similar things about the Prophets, which Quiñones had restored. As for theologians, Claude d'Espence testifies, in his commentary on chapter 1 of Titus, that among Papist bishops there are some who judge the reading of Scripture so dangerous that they abstain from it out of fear, and take care lest they become heretics, as if, he says, heresies arose from the study of the Scriptures, and not rather from neglect and ignorance.

units.la: LII. Quid quòd lectissimos illos Dei servos, quos Christus Matth. xix. 28. Sessuros in duodecim thronis, & judicaturos duodecim tribus Israël pollicitus est, Hierarchi-ci tantùm non de supremo dignitatis suæ fastigio deturbant? Sic enim S. Petrum Orbis doctorem ad eas angustias redegerunt, ut ex Apostolo Ecclesiæ Romanæ particularis Pastor & Episcopus fieret. In Appendice Nili de Primatu Papæ extat initium disceptationis cujusdam Græcum inter & Cardinales Romanos habitæ, ubi Cardinalibus pertendentibus, Petrum fuisse primum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pastorem, respondet Græcus: Ἀ' Ἀγνώμονες ἀκούειν ἐθέλετε, τὰ πρὸς πιστὰ τῶν τοιούτων ἀπορίαν ... Πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι ἡ ἐπιεικὴς ὕλη διδάσκαλον τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐξέλαμψε & κηρύγματος, ἐν ᾗ τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἦν τῆς ... Si æquis animis audire velitis; id quod vos veluti honoris causa de coryphæo Apostolorum adfertis, in contrarium potiùs vergere intelligetis. Primùm quidem, quòd totius orbis doctorem & Magistrum, qui prædicationis suæ initium à Judæa fecit, Romæ autem Apostolatùs sui cursum peregit, tali vestra propositione solius Romæ magistrum fuisse statuitis, atque ita etiam Servatoris ad illum promissionem, quam Sancti Patres universaliter de omnibus qui crediderunt, & credunt, interpretantur; vos ad solam Romam coarctatis, violentdque interpretatione torquetis. Quo concesso reliquum est omnino, eam quæ Romæ est tantùm, non autem universam fidelium Ecclesiam sibi adoptásse. optasse Servatorem, ædificationemque hujus tanquam super petram Petri doctrinam promisisse. At verò qui ita & sentiunt & loquuntur, qualem honorem Apostolorum coryphæo deferant, ipsimet considerate. Plura addit Græcus, quibus non parum Romanos de honore S. Petri delibare & decerpere; atque velut Principis Apostolorum elo-gio cum ornent, revera tamen omni prorsus dignitate Apostolatûs exuere, liquidò probat.
units.tr: LII. What of those most excellent servants of God whom Christ, in Matthew 19:28, promised would sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel? The Hierarchs all but strip them of the highest rank of their dignity. For they have reduced St. Peter, the teacher of the world, to such narrow limits that from an Apostle he has become the particular pastor and bishop of the Roman Church. In the Appendix to Nilus on the Primacy of the Pope there survives the opening of a Greek dispute held between certain Roman Cardinals. When the Cardinals insist that "Peter was the first pastor of the Roman Church," the Greek replies: "Ignorant men, if you are willing to hear with fair minds, [Ἀ' Ἀγνώμονες ἀκούειν ἐθέλετε, τὰ πρὸς πιστὰ τῶν τοιούτων ἀπορίαν ...] ... First of all, [Πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι ἡ ἐπιεικὴς ὕλη διδάσκαλον τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐξέλαμψε & κηρύγματος, ἐν ᾗ τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἦν τῆς ...] you will understand that what you bring forward as an honour to the leader of the Apostles tends rather to the opposite. For, first, by your proposition you make him who was the teacher and master of the whole world, who began his preaching in Judea and finished the course of his Apostleship at Rome, to have been the teacher of Rome alone. In this way you also twist the promise of the Saviour, which the holy Fathers interpret universally of all who believed and believe, by confining it to Rome alone and forcing it by a violent interpretation. Once this is granted, it follows that the Church which is at Rome alone, and not the whole Church of the faithful, has adopted him for itself. The Saviour wished, and promised that by the teaching of this man as upon the rock of Peter the edifice would be built. But you yourselves should consider what honour they pay to the leader of the Apostles, who both think and speak in this way." The Greek adds more, and plainly proves that the Romans, while they adorn him with the praise of the Prince of the Apostles, in fact strip him of all the dignity of the Apostleship, and pluck away and gnaw at the honour of St. Peter.

units.la: LIII. Pari impietate Pius V. cæteros Apostolos omnes deprimit, quando sic Sent. Declar. contra Elisabetham loquitur: Regnans in excelsis, cui data est omnis in Cælo & in terra potestas, unam Sanctam, Catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, extra quam nulla est salus, uni soli in terris videlicet Apostolorum Principi Petro, Petrique successori, Romano Pontifici, in potestatis plenitudine tradidit gubernandam. Christus equidem Apostolis omnibus delegavit suum officium his verbis: Sicut me misit Pater, ita & ego mitto vos; Joh. xx. 21. omnesque pariter jussit proficisci & docere omnes gentes Matth. xxviii. 18. Omnium gentium appellatione si notetur aliqua particularis, non universalis & Catholica Ecclesia, quantò minùs Papa Petro ostendere poterit traditam Catholicam ex cura ovium & agnorum ei demandata, sine appositione dictionis Omnium Joh. xxi. 15? In potestatis verò plenitudine commissam esse gubernandam ut Petro sic cæteris, adeò luculenter Christi verba declarant, ut disertè illinc Jansenius Comment. in concord. Euang. cap. 147. adstruat, Christum suam eis functionem tradidisse cum plena sibique propria potestate, quæ ad illam functionem Christi nomine obeundam erat necessaria, potestate scilicet remittendi & retinendi peccata; perinde atque Reges Legatis suis plenam potestatem committere solent, promittentes se ratum habituros, quicquid illi agerent rationabiliter. Sed multum & ex consilio Eremitæ per annum centies de die Mariam salutabat, cui illa apparens dixit: Ego ero uxor tua; accede ad me, & da mihi osculum: & coëgit illum, dixitque. Modò initiatæ sunt nuptiæ, & mox perficientur; Cæsarius lib. vj. 33. tradidère. Sic ergo polygamam faciunt etiam Cœlitem illam. Eandem solis Hierarchis, hoc est, Mistificis, in commissi mysterii executione concedere, Gabriel Biel Lect. 4. blasphemat. Miracula ei tributa planè contumeliosa ex legendarum & fabularum hamaxariis, Cæsario, Thoma Cantipratensi, Discipulo de Tempore, Trithemio, Pelbarto de Themes Waar, Bernhardino de Bustis, Alano de Rupe, aliis plura Cl. Rivetus Apol. pro B. Virgine lib. ij. 15. collegit. Denique merito Erasmus in Colloquio, quod Naufragium inscribitur, Papistas reprehendit simul & albis dentibus ridet, quòd in præfectura maris Mariam Veneri substituerint. Nam olim Venus agebat curam nautarum, quia nata credebatur ex mari. Ea quoniam desiit curare, inquit Erasmus, suffecta est (à nautis Pontificiis, qui ex Pontificiæ Scholæ disciplina Mariæ titulos Stellæ maris, Reginæ Cœli, dominæ mundi, portùs salutis, dulcedinis, vitæ, spei nostræ) huic matri non Virgini Virgo Mater. Ita quod Pagani Venerem orabant: Sic te Diva potens Cypri &c. id nautas à Maria petere sub Papatu, Virginem lectissimam in præfectura maris turpissimo scorto substituentes, Erasmus indicat.
units.tr: LIII. With equal impiety Pius V. degrades all the other Apostles when he speaks thus in the Sentence of Declaration against Elizabeth: "The King reigning on high, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, delivered the one, holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, outside which there is no salvation, to be governed in the fullness of power by one alone on earth, namely the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, and Peter's successor, the Roman Pontiff." Christ, to be sure, committed his office to all the Apostles in these words: As the Father has sent me, so I also send you; John 20:21. and he likewise ordered them all to go and teach all nations, Matthew 28:18. If by the name of "all nations" some particular Church is meant, and not the universal and Catholic Church, how much less will the Pope be able to show that the Catholic care of the sheep and lambs was handed to Peter, when the word all is not added, John 21:15? That the commission was to be governed in the fullness of power, as much for the others as for Peter, the words of Christ declare so clearly that Jansenius, in his Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 147, expressly asserts that "Christ handed over to them his function together with full and their own power, which was necessary for discharging that function in Christ's name, namely the power of remitting and retaining sins, just as kings are accustomed to entrust full power to their legates, promising that they will ratify whatever they do reasonably." But the Hermit, acting on his advice, greeted Mary a hundred times a day, and she, appearing to him, said: "I will be your wife; come to me and give me a kiss." And she forced him, and said: "The marriage has now begun, and will soon be consummated." Caesarius has handed this down, book 6, 33. Thus they make even that Heavenly Lady a polygamist. Gabriel Biel, Lecture 4, blasphemes that the same power of executing the committed mystery was granted to the Hierarchs alone, that is, the Priests. The miracles attributed to her, plainly insulting and drawn from the cauldrons of legends and fables, Caesarius, Thomas of Cantimpré, the Disciple of the Time, Trithemius, Pelbartus of Themeswar, Bernardinus de Bustis, Alanus de Rupe and others, are gathered in larger number by the illustrious Rivetus, Apology for the Blessed Virgin, book 2, 15. Finally, Erasmus rightly reproaches the Papists in his Colloquy entitled Shipwreck, and at the same time laughs with white teeth, because they have substituted Mary for Venus in the government of the sea. For formerly Venus took care of sailors, because she was believed to have been born from the sea. "Since she has ceased to care for them," says Erasmus, "she has been replaced" (by the Papist sailors, who, following the discipline of the Papist School, give Mary the titles Star of the Sea, Queen of Heaven, Lady of the World, Haven of Salvation, Sweetness, Life, Our Hope) "by this Mother, not a Virgin, a Virgin Mother." Thus Erasmus points out that under the Papacy sailors ask Mary for what the Pagans begged of Venus, "So may you, powerful goddess of Cyprus," etc., setting the most chaste Virgin in charge of the sea in place of the most shameless harlot.

units.la: LV. Inter Sanctos Cœlites etiam referendi sunt, qui nomine veniunt. Utut autem in honorem eorum multa Hierarchici garriant, ut simplicibus & incautis sucum faciant; revera tamen eos totos, quanti quanti sunt, unius Papæ, Deastri sui libidini subjiciunt, dedúntque mancupio & nexu, qui eos non aliter, quàm Mercatores suos solent calculos, usurpat. Aliquando enim ei denariorum sunt loco; aliquando librarum, ut ad manum quosque proximè ad rationes suas conficiendas habet. Episcopus Bitontinus in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 14. pag. 66. profitetur palam, se in his, quæ mysteria fidei tangunt, plus uni summo Pontifici credere, quàm mille Augustinis, Hieronymis, Gregoriis. Præterea eos invitos ad patrocinium doctrinæ Antichristianæ trahunt, lancinant, adulterant, interpungunt, veru critico, quoties lubet, notant. Indicio esse possunt Indices Expurgatorii, Romanus, Hispanus, certissimi eorum erga Patres irreverentiæ testes.
units.tr: LV. Among the holy Heavenly Ones must also be counted those who come in the name of the Lord. Although the Hierarchs chatter much in their honour, so as to make a profit out of the simple and the incautious, in reality they subject them all, however many there are, to the lust of one Pope, their little god, and hand them over in bondage and servitude, and he uses them no differently from the counters his merchants use. For sometimes they take the place of pennies, sometimes of pounds, as he has each one close at hand to make up his accounts. The Bishop of Bitonto, on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 14, page 66, openly confesses that in matters touching the mysteries of faith he believes the one Supreme Pontiff more than a thousand Augustines, Jeromes and Gregories. Moreover, they drag them against their will into the defence of anti-Christian doctrine, mangle them, adulterate them, punctuate them, and mark them with a critical spit whenever it pleases them. The Expurgatory Indexes, the Roman and the Spanish, may serve as evidence; they are most certain witnesses of their irreverence towards the Fathers.

units.la: LVI. Denique Sanctorum defunctorum corpora falsis honoribus illi mactant, & veris defraudant. Nam ad honorem eorum pertinere, ut terræ communi matri mandata, ibidem quiescant, usque dum ad vitam à Deo revocentur, exempla corporum Sanctorum Patriarcharum, Mosis, piorum Regum, aliorum probant. Ipsius Eliæ ossa, quorum contactu mortuus resuscitatus est, Iosiæ 2 Reg. xxiii. 18. piè mandante, ne quidem commota, sed humi relicta sunt. Hi verò Sanctorum ossa non tantùm commovent & è sepulchris suis effodiunt, adeóque sepulchra Sacrosancta violant; sed etiam circumgestata & publicè conspecta, alia quidem in sublimiore sepulchro condunt; alia verò penitus insepulta servant, eáque sepeliunt sepulturâ asini, uti Propheta Ieremi. xxii. 19. loquitur: adeóque honoris scilicet causa faciunt, quod Pontificii ipsi, imò & Ethnici ignominiosum, profanum & impium esse docent. Bellarminus enim de Purgat. lib. 2. cap. ult. inter utilitates, quæ mortuis ex sepultura accedunt, hanc commemorans, quòd consulitur honori eorum, adhuc in hominum memoriis viventium. Non enim caret, inquit, ignominia quadam, quòd fœditas nostri corporis aliorum conspectui pateat. Et Cardinalis Borrhomæus Concil. Mediol. 4. tit. de Sacris reliquiis, Concil. Tomo 5. cum universa Synodo Mediolanensi vetat, ne tangantur Sacræ reliquiæ, quoniam hoc fabot sacrilegium, ac minùs propterea ferendum esse S. Gregorius scribit. Gregorius autem Registr. lib. iij. epist. 50. scribens, intolerabile esse omnino atque sacrilegum, Sanctorum corpora tangere, addit; cùm sepulchrum Laurentii Martyris ignoranter ab operariis aliud agentibus apertum esset, eos, qui præsentes erant, & laborabant, Monachos & mansionarios, qui corpus Martyris viderunt, etsi tangere non præsumpserunt, omnes intra decem dies obiisse, ita ut nullus vitæ superesse posset, qui sanctum & justum illius corpus viderat. Denique insepultam sepulturam Cicero Philipp. I. pro dedecore habuit. Nec Turnus Virgilianus Æneid. lib. 10. largiens Pallanti, Quisquis honos tumuli est, mortuis honorificum putavit non humari. Et Horatius Epod. 16. bella civilia hoc incommodo maximum sui odium commotura speravit, quòd hostis, urbem occupans civibus orbatam, sepulchrum Romuli violaturus sit: Quæque carent ventis & solibus, ossa Quirini, (Nefas videre) dissipabit insolens.
units.tr: LVI. Finally, they bestow false honours on the bodies of the dead saints, and cheat them of true ones. For that it is an honour to them that, committed to the common mother earth, they rest there until they are called back to life by God, the examples of the bodies of the holy Patriarchs, of Moses, of pious kings and of others prove. The bones of Elijah, by whose touch a dead man was raised, were not even moved, but left on the ground, at the pious command of Josiah, 2 Kings 23:18. But these men not only move the bones of the saints and dig them out of their tombs, and so violate the sacred sepulchres, but also, carrying them about and displaying them publicly, they bury some in a more lofty sepulchre; others, however, they keep wholly unburied, and bury them with the burial of an ass, as the Prophet Jeremiah, 22:19, speaks. So they do, for the sake of honour, what the Papists themselves, and even the Pagans, teach is shameful, profane and impious. For Bellarmine, On Purgatory, book 2, last chapter, recalling among the advantages which accrue to the dead from burial this one, that "regard is shown for their honour while they still live in the memories of men. For," he says, "it is not free from a certain disgrace that the foulness of our body lies open to the sight of others." And Cardinal Borromeo, Council of Milan 4, title On Sacred Relics, in the Councils, Volume 5, together with the whole Milanese Synod forbids that "sacred relics be touched, since this would be sacrilege," and St. Gregory writes that it is less to be borne for that reason. But Gregory, writing in Register, book 3, letter 50, that "it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious to touch the bodies of the saints," adds that when the tomb of the martyr Laurence was opened unknowingly by workmen who were busy with something else, all those who were present and labouring there, the monks and the attendants who saw the body of the martyr, although they did not presume to touch it, died within ten days, so that no one who had looked upon that holy and just body could remain alive. Finally, Cicero, Philippics 1, regarded an unburied burial as a disgrace. Nor does Virgil's Turnus, Aeneid, book 10, when he bestows on Pallas, "Whatever honour there is in a tomb, he thought it an honour for the dead not to be buried." And Horace, Epode 16, hoped that the civil wars would bring the greatest hatred of himself by this inconvenience, "because the enemy, occupying the city bereft of its citizens, is about to violate the sepulchre of Romulus: and the bones of Quirinus, which lie free from winds and sun, (a sin to see) he will scatter in his insolence."

units.la: Atqui Hierarchici Sanctorum ossa servant in capsis ostendenda populo, à Clericis attrectanda, gestanda in processionibus, in altaribus exponenda: nec ea vel à ventis, vel à Solis radiis remota esse sinunt, sed è sepulchris eruta conspectui tactuique hominum objiciunt, & quaquaversum dissipant. Cujus enim Sancti paulò celebrioris ossa non varias in oras disperserunt? Etenim Abundius & Abundantius neutiquam ex clarissimis Divis fuerunt. Eorum tamen, uti ex Hist. pass. invent. & translat. Sanctorum Abundii & Abundantii edit. à Colleg. Societ. Jesu Romæ A. 1584. liquet, corpora postquam è Cosmæ & Damiani Templo, in quo requiescebant, in novam Jesuitarum Basilicam Gregorius XIII. transferri jussisset, quædam eorum ossa relicta sunt in pristino hospitio Cosmæ & Damiani, quædam ad CœnoCœnobium Sanctimonialium Senas transportata; quædam in Japonum, novi orbis insulam, ultra Garamantas & Indos transmissa sunt. Licet ergo jactent Papistæ, se reliquias ita tractare ad Sanctorum honorem; atque id eo sensu, quo Cicero Philipp. 1. quendam honorem contumeliosum nominat; atque idem Pro domo sua asserit Catonem ejectum esse à Clodio per honorem turpissimum; verum est: tamen eas tractant ignominiosè, exhumantes dissipantésque corpora, quæ in pace sepulta sunt: & quorum fœditatem, vel Bellarmino supra agnoscente, ratio, religio, jus humanitatis tellure tegi jubebat; ea partim intra capsas, partim extra hominibus videnda & tangenda exhibent.
units.tr: Yet the hierarchs keep the bones of the saints in cases to be displayed to the people, handled by the clergy, carried in processions, and set out on altars. They do not allow these relics to be kept away from the winds or the rays of the sun. They drag them out of their tombs and expose them to the sight and touch of men, scattering them in every direction. For whose bones of a fairly famous saint have they not scattered to various shores? Abundius and Abundantius were by no means among the most illustrious saints. Yet, as is clear from Hist. pass. invent. & translat. Sanctorum Abundii & Abundantii edit. à Colleg. Societ. Jesu Romæ A. 1584., after Pope Gregory XIII ordered their bodies moved from the Temple of Cosmas and Damian, where they rested, into the new basilica of the Jesuits, some of their bones were left in their former lodging at Cosmas and Damian, some were carried to the convent of nuns at Siena, and some were sent across to Japan, an island of the New World, beyond the Garamantes and the Indians. So let the Papists boast that they handle relics in this way to honour the saints, in the sense in which Cicero, in the first Philippic, calls a certain thing an insulting honour, and in Pro domo sua says that Cato was driven out by Clodius through a most shameful honour. It is true that they handle them with ignominy: they dig up and scatter bodies that were buried in peace, and whose foulness, as even Bellarmine acknowledges above, reason, religion and the law of humanity bid us cover with earth. Some of these they display inside cases, and some outside, for men to see and touch.

units.la: LVII. Ex iis, quæ hactenus per summa capita attigi, jubare meridiano clariùs constat, Hierarchicos honorem debitum multis modis detrahere Deo, ejus verbo, Christo, Ecclesiæ Dei, Sanctis Cœlitibus, Patriarchis, Apostolis, Deiparæ, omnibus denique Sanctis. Frigidiùs proin remissiúsque justo mihi agere videor, si Apostoli illud de Judæis dictum: Neque Deo placent, & omnibus hominibus adversantur, 1 Thess.11.15. iis accommodem. Nam & Dei Christíque honorem suâ idololatriâ spoliisque multifariis horribiliter lœdunt; & Angelos hominésque electos contumeliis probrisque gravissimis afficiunt; adeóque se blasphemiis nefariè polluunt, quo suscepto demonstrationis octavo capite ritè nos defunctos confidimus.
units.tr: LVII. From what I have touched on so far, under the main heads, it is clearer than the midday sun that the hierarchs rob God of the honour due to him in many ways: his Word, Christ, the Church of God, the heavenly saints, the patriarchs, the apostles, the Mother of God, and in short all the saints. I seem to myself to be too cold and too lenient if I apply to them what the apostle said of the Jews: Neque Deo placent, & omnibus hominibus adversantur, 1 Thess.11.15. For they both dreadfully wound the honour of God and Christ by their idolatry and by their many plunderings, and they load the elect angels and men with the gravest insults and reproaches; and so they defile themselves with blasphemies in an unspeakable way. Having undertaken this, I trust that I have duly discharged it in the eighth chapter of the demonstration.
DISSERTATION FOURTEEN

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem esse Babylonem Magnam probatur Nonò, quia luxuriâ & impuritate carnis se multis modis polluit.
units.tr: WHEREBY it is proved that the Hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church that rules, is the Great Babylon. Ninthly, because it pollutes itself in many ways by luxury and impurity of the flesh.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Ad habitum interiorem Babylonis M. pertinet etiam luxuria & impuritas carnis. II. Ejus Hierarchia rea peragitur demonstratione Syllogismo innexa. Cujus propositionis nexus & Assumptio per singula membra probatur. III. Hierarchia luxuriæ ansam ejusmodi præbet, ut eam ob carnis infirmitatem & eventum inevitabilem certò post se trahat. IV. Luxuriæ instrumenta Babylon habet divitias haud vulgares. V. Hierarchiæ in corradendis divitiis summa solertia exponitur. VI. Iisdem ad luxum & potentiæ exaltationem abutitur. VII. Prætextus acquirendarum divitiarum ad externi cultûs splendorem futilitas. VIII. Uti eam divitiis ad magnificentiam, superbiam, Tom.II. pp IX. in
units.tr: I. To the inner character of the Great Babylon belong also luxury and impurity of the flesh. II. Its Hierarchy is charged with guilt and carried out by a demonstration bound into a syllogism. The connection of this proposition and its assumption is proved member by member. III. The Hierarchy gives luxury such an occasion that, on account of the weakness of the flesh and its inevitable outcome, it certainly draws luxury after itself. IV. Babylon has, as instruments of luxury, riches that are not ordinary. V. The great skill of the Hierarchy in heaping up riches is set forth. VI. It abuses the same riches for luxury and for the exaltation of its power. VII. The pretext of acquiring riches, namely the splendour of external worship, is futile. VIII. That it uses its riches for magnificence, pride, Tom.II. pp IX. in

units.la: IX. imprimis luxuriam, idoneis testimoniis & documentis probatur.
units.tr: IX. especially luxury, is proved by fitting testimonies and documents.

units.la: X. Babylonis & Hierarchiæ exacta hac in re harmonia.
units.tr: X. The agreement of Babylon and the Hierarchy in this matter is exact.
XI. Idleness is the mother of luxury.

units.la: XII. Religiosum Hierarchiæ otium ex frequentia feriarum cognoscitur.
units.tr: XII. The religious idleness of the Hierarchy is recognised from the frequency of holidays.

units.la: XIII. Ad luxuriam otium illud inclinare demonstratur tum ex cultûs, qui festivo tempore peragitur, exercitiis, nihil ad mortificationem hominis facientibus;
units.tr: XIII. It is shown that this idleness tends towards luxury, both from the exercises of worship that are carried out in festive times, which contribute nothing to the mortification of the man;

units.la: XIV. tum ex testimoniis Clemangis, Petri de Aliaco, Polydori Vergilii, Gravaminum Imperii, Urbani VIII. Papæ;
units.tr: XIV. and from the testimonies of Clemangis, Peter of Ailly, Polydore Vergil, the Gravamina of the Empire, and Pope Urban VIII;

units.la: XV. tum ex debacchationibus solennibus & festivis Bacchanalium;
units.tr: XV. and from the solemn and festive revelries of the Bacchanalia;

units.la: XVI. quorum impietas verbis Baptistæ Mantuani graphice depingitur.
units.tr: XVI. whose impiety is vividly portrayed in the words of Baptista Mantuanus.

units.la: XVII. Impuritati Hierarchiæ ansam etiam lex cœlibatûs Sacerdotibus lata; & vota continentiæ Monastica præbent. Donum continentiæ non commune fidelibus universis, sed proprium quibusdam esse, ex 1 Cor. vij. 7. &c.
units.tr: XVII. The law of celibacy imposed on priests, and the monastic vows of continence, also provide occasion for the impurity of the Hierarchy. The gift of continence is not common to all the faithful, but belongs to some only, from 1 Cor. 7:7, etc.

units.la: XVIII. nec non Matth. xix. 10. 11. & natura ipsa demonstratur.
units.tr: XVIII. and also Matt. 19:10, 11, and nature itself, demonstrate this.

units.la: XIX. Cœlibatum lege vel voto suscipientes, vel jam mortificati, vel nondum mortificati sunt. Utrosque certissimo impuritatis periculo se exponere, probatur.
units.tr: XIX. Those who take up celibacy by law or vow are either already mortified, or not yet mortified. It is proved that both expose themselves to the most certain danger of impurity.

units.la: XX. Preces & afflictatio certa obtinendæ in cœlibatu continentiæ remedia non sunt.
units.tr: XX. Prayers and mortification are not sure remedies for obtaining continence in celibacy.

units.la: XXI. Neque id ex promissionibus, iis, qui petunt, pulsant, quærunt, factis comprobatur.
units.tr: XXI. Nor is this proved from the promises made to those who ask, knock and seek.

units.la: XXII. Monachorum imprimis vota, vita, iners cultus, otium ad impuritatem omnem ducatum præbet, quod hypotyposi quadam ab Henrico Moro adornata ostenditur.
units.tr: XXII. The vows of the monks above all, their life, their idle worship and their idleness lead to all impurity, as is shown by a sketch drawn up by Henry More.

units.la: XXIII. Summum ex lege & voto cælibatûs periculum augent tum immodica & falsa encomia cælibatûs;
units.tr: XXIII. The danger of the law and vow of celibacy is greatly increased both by immoderate and false praises of celibacy;

units.la: XXIV. tum contumeliæ, quibus matrimonium inprimis eorum, qui voto ad cælibatum se priûs obstrinxerunt, Hierarchici afficiunt.
units.tr: XXIV. and by the insults with which the Hierarchy assails marriage, especially of those who earlier bound themselves by vow to celibacy.

units.la: XXV. Experientia testis impuritatis ex lege & votis cælibatûs consecutæ inducitur;
units.tr: XXV. Experience is brought forward as a witness to the impurity that has followed from the law and vows of celibacy;

units.la: XXVI. atque testimoniis Gersonis, Pighii, Dominici à Soto suffulcitur.
units.tr: XXVI. and it is supported by the testimonies of Gerson, Pighius and Domingo de Soto.

units.la: XXVII. Concubinatus inprimis Cleri, Clemangis, Johannis Chemensis, Gravaminum Imperii, Alberti, Bavariæ Ducis, Espencei confessionibus probatus, periculum legis & votorum cælibatûs clarissimè arguit.
units.tr: XXVII. Concubinage, especially of the clergy, proved by the confessions of Clemangis, John of Chemensis, the Gravamina of the Empire, Albert, Duke of Bavaria, and Espence, clearly argues the danger of the law and vows of celibacy.

units.la: XXVIII. Impuritas à Clero capite ad subjectum universum populum facilè promanat.
units.tr: XXVIII. Impurity flows easily from the head clergy to the whole subject people.

units.la: XXIX. Bellarmini exceptio, quòd non lex & vota cælibatûs, sed eorundem abusus prodigiosus libidines pepererit, diluitur.
units.tr: XXIX. Bellarmine's objection, that it was not the law and vows of celibacy but the monstrous abuse of them that gave birth to lusts, is refuted.

units.la: XXX. Hierarchicorum prætextus, quòd ad vovendum & suscipiendum cælibatum neminem impellant vel cogant, discutitur.
units.tr: XXX. The pretext of the Hierarchy, that they compel or force no one to vow and undertake celibacy, is examined.

units.la: XXXI. Eorundem functio Sacra concipiendæ impuritati ansam præbet; in confessione auriculari inprimis. Instructio Sacerdotum ad confessiones audiendas plena impudentiæ est, quod ex Casuistarum libris proditur; inprimis Sanchezii opere de matrimonio, de quo Petri Aurelii Sorbonistæ judicium gravissimum adscribitur.
units.tr: XXXI. Their sacred function provides occasion for conceiving impurity, above all in auricular confession. The instruction of priests for hearing confessions is full of shamelessness, as is revealed from the books of the casuists; especially in the work of Sanchez on marriage, to which the very grave judgment of Peter Aurelius the Sorbonist is appended.

units.la: XXXII. Confessarii sic instructi quales confitentes efficiant.
units.tr: XXXII. What sort of penitents confessors so instructed make.

units.la: XXXIII. quomodo etiam se ipsi gerant, res loquitur, & testes Alvarus Pelagius, Erasmus patefaciunt.
units.tr: XXXIII. How they themselves also behave, the matter speaks for itself, and the witnesses Alvarus Pelagius and Erasmus reveal.

units.la: XXXIV. & Casuistarum casus, circa denuntiationes Sacerdotum, qui pueros, puellas, fœminas pro arcano hoc tribunali solicitant, ex Diana Panormitano eruti demonstrant.
units.tr: XXXIV. And the cases of the casuists concerning the denunciations of priests who solicit boys, girls and women at this secret tribunal, drawn from Diana of Palermo, demonstrate it.

units.la: XXXV. Musicam voluptuariam Babyloni Spiritus Dei tribuit. Eadem Hierarchicorum cultus perstrepit.
units.tr: XXXV. The Spirit of God ascribes voluptuous music to Babylon. The worship of the Hierarchy echoes with the same.
XXXVI. Abuses of music among the same:

units.la: XXXVII. De scenica & theatrali eorum Musica, voluptati potius quam cultui Dei inserviente, voces Erasmi, XXXVIII. Guilhelmi Lindani;
units.tr: XXXVII. On their scenic and theatrical music, serving pleasure rather than the worship of God, the words of Erasmus; XXXVIII. of Guilhelm Lindanus;

units.la: XXXIX. ipsius Thomae Aquinatis & Cajetani proditae.
units.tr: XXXIX. and those set forth by Thomas Aquinas himself and by Cajetan.

units.la: XL. De fornicatione, adulterio tenuiter Hierarchici sentiunt.
units.tr: XL. The Hierarchy thinks lightly of fornication and adultery.

units.la: XLI. Quin peccata Sodomae Johannes Casa, Archiepiscopus Beneventanus & Legatus Papae laudavit; nequicquam ab Hardingo, objiciente Jucllo, defensus;
units.tr: XLI. Indeed Johannes Casa, Archbishop of Benevento and Legate of the Pope, praised the sins of Sodom; he was in vain defended by Harding, against the objection of Jewel.

units.la: XLII. XLIII. Ex poenis criminum, quid de ipsis criminibus judex sentiat, colligitur. Hierarchici autem impuritati, fornicationi, adulterio &c. levissimas poenas constituunt.
units.tr: XLII. XLIII. From the punishments of crimes, one gathers what the judge thinks of the crimes themselves. But the Hierarchy assigns very light penalties to impurity, fornication, adultery, etc.

units.la: XLIV. Vetus Ecclesia scortatores a ministerio suo amovit.
units.tr: XLIV. The ancient Church removed fornicators from their ministry.

units.la: XLV. Secus longe Hierarchici; quorum Casuistae, Baunius, Mascarenhas quoslibet Clericos post quamvis pollutionem mortaliter peccaminosam, etiam contra naturam, adeoque a scelere recentes, praevia contritione sola, sacris defungi posse, scribunt.
units.tr: XLV. The Hierarchy thinks very differently. Their casuists, Baunius and Mascarenhas, write that any clergy, after any pollution, even one mortally sinful and even against nature, and therefore fresh from the crime, may perform sacred functions with contrition alone beforehand.

units.la: XLVI. Pii demum V. contra Clericos Sodomitas Bulla, eosdem clericali dignitate exuens; ne quidem, juxta Escobarium, in foro conscientiae obligat.
units.tr: XLVI. The bull of Pius V against Sodomite clergy, stripping them of clerical dignity, does not even, according to Escobar, bind in the court of conscience.

units.la: XLVII. Impuritatis ejusdem poenae per indulgentias & vilissima pro dispensationibus & absolutionibus pretia relaxantur.
units.tr: XLVII. The penalties for the same impurity are relaxed through indulgences and for the most paltry prices paid for dispensations and absolutions.

units.la: XLVIII. Taxae poenitentiariae impuritatis quasvis species pecuniae pretio aestimantis, extrema improbitas, ab ipso Claudio Espencaeo depicta.
units.tr: XLVIII. The penitentiary tax, which values every kind of impurity at a price in money, is extreme wickedness, as depicted by Claude d'Espence himself.

units.la: XLIX. Ex eadem, quo pretio olim incestus, actus Clericorum libidinosi qualescunque, contra naturam etiam; bestialitatis crimen ipsum saxari succuerint, ostenditur.
units.tr: XLIX. From the same source it is shown at what price incest of old, and whatever lewd acts of clerics, even against nature, and the crime of bestiality itself, were once bought off for a sum of money.

units.la: L. Indulgentiæ pro futuris peccatis, efficax luxuriandi illecebra, ex libello de stationibus Romæ, Romæ & Norimbergæ edito, expositæ.
units.tr: L. Indulgences for future sins, an effective enticement to lust, set out from the little book on the Station churches of Rome, published at Rome and at Nuremberg.

units.la: LI. Papales in gradibus Divinitus prohibitis dispensationes Romanam Ecclesiam incessant.
units.tr: LI. Papal dispensations in degrees forbidden by God assail the Roman Church.

units.la: LII. Lupanaria ab ipso Pontifice erecta, Hierarchiæ impuritatem quàm maximè insuper propalant.
units.tr: LII. Brothels erected by the Pontiff himself further openly proclaim the impurity of the Hierarchy most of all.

units.la: LIII. LIV. Prætextus Jesuitarum, quòd Papa lupanaria non probet, sed permittat permissione facti, & quadam etiam juris, diluitur; hac inprimis ratione, quòd constat, Papam ex lenonia hac quæstum facere.
units.tr: LIII. LIV. The pretext of the Jesuits, that the Pope does not approve brothels but permits them by a permission of fact, and in a certain sense also of law, is refuted; chiefly by this reason, that it is established that the Pope makes profit from this pandering.

units.la: LV. Prætextus alter, quòd eadem ad vitanda graviora mala permittat, ceu publica Babylonicæ impuritatis confessio exploditur.
units.tr: LV. The other pretext, that he permits the same to avoid greater evils, is exploded as a public confession of Babylonian impurity.

units.la: LVI. Majora mala iis locis, quibus lupanaria in usu non sunt, nec timentur, nec patrantur.
units.tr: LVI. In places where brothels are not in use, greater evils are neither feared nor committed.

units.la: LVII. Espencæi & Pici Mirandulani adversus lupanaria declamatio.
units.tr: LVII. The declamation of Espence and Pico della Mirandola against brothels.

units.la: LVIII. Lenoniæ huic Papæ neutiquam favet, quòd Lupanaria Papa, ut Episcopus, non probet, sed censuris Ecclesiasticis lupas notet.
units.tr: LVIII. This pandering by no means favours the Pope, since the Pope, like a bishop, does not approve brothels but marks the prostitutes with ecclesiastical censures.

units.la: LIX. Hierarchiæ denique omnimoda impuritas experientiæ & historiæ ipsius luce & testimoniis liquidò probatur.
units.tr: LIX. Finally, the utterly complete impurity of the Hierarchy is clearly proved by experience and history itself, and by testimonies.
LX. The impurity of the supreme Pontiffs.

units.la: LXI. Eadem decem Pontificum, continuo ferè ordine, intra Seculi unius decursum, sibi succedentium, puta Pii II. Pauli II. Sixti IV. Innocentii VIII. Alexandri VI. Julii II. Leonis X. Pauli III. Julii III. Pii IV. infamia libidinum laborantium, allato specimine & historia apertam in lucem profertur.
units.tr: LXI. The infamy of the lusts of the same ten Pontiffs, who succeeded one another in an almost unbroken order within the course of one century, namely Pius II, Paul II, Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII, Alexander VI, Julius II, Leo X, Paul III, Julius III and Pius IV, labouring under the infamy of their lusts, is brought into open light, with an example and history.

units.la: LXII. Cleri totius Romani impuritas testimoniis ex Scriptoribus Pontificiis octo retro Seculorum repetitis convincitur, ubi testes inducuntur ex Seculo Nono S. Huldrici Augustani Episcopi ad Nicolaum I. epistola. Cujus germanitas asseritur. LXIII. De Seculi Decimi impuritate Baronii confessio. LXIV. Ex Seculo Undecimo testes citantur Petrus Damiani, qui librum titulo Gomorrhæi scripsit, à Leone Papa suppressum. LXV. Ex Duodecimo Bernhardus, Rupertus Tuitiensis. LXVI. Ex Decimo tertio Guilhelmus Durandus, Hugo Cardinalis. LXVII. Ex Decimo quarto Alvarus Pelagius, Robertus Holkot. LXVIII. Ex Decimo quinto Johannes Gerson, Nicolaus Clemangis, Episcopus Chemensis author libri de Onere Ecclesiæ, Petrus de Aliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis, Stanislaus Orichovius, Nicolaus Tudescus, Polydorus Vergilius, Æneas Sylvius, Platina, Felix Malleolus. LXIX. Ex Decimo Sexto status Imperii Romani, Cardinalis Campegius, Antoninus Cornelius Lynnichanus, Ferdinandus I. Maximilianus II. Dux Bavariæ, Erasmus, Cassander &c.
units.tr: LXII. The impurity of the whole Roman clergy is proved from testimonies drawn from Popish writers going back eight centuries, where witnesses are cited from the ninth century: the letter of St Hildulf, Bishop of Augsburg, to Nicholas I; its authenticity is asserted. LXIII. The confession of Baronius concerning the impurity of the tenth century. LXIV. From the eleventh century the witnesses cited are Peter Damian, who wrote a book with the title Gomorrhian, suppressed by Pope Leo. LXV. From the twelfth, Bernard and Rupert of Deutz. LXVI. From the thirteenth, William Durand and Hugh the Cardinal. LXVII. From the fourteenth, Alvarus Pelagius and Robert Holcot. LXVIII. From the fifteenth, John Gerson, Nicholas Clemangis, the Bishop of Chemensis, author of the book On the Burden of the Church, Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, Stanislaus Orichovius, Nicholas Tudeschi, Polydore Vergil, Aeneas Sylvius, Platina and Felix Malleolus. LXIX. From the sixteenth, the estates of the Roman Empire, Cardinal Campeggio, Antoninus Cornelius Lynnichanus, Ferdinand I, Maximilian II, the Duke of Bavaria, Erasmus, Cassander, etc.

units.la: LXX. Adeò frequens paulò ante Reformationem Cleri scortatio & concubinatus fuit, ut in ludum & jocum abiverit, quod ex quodlibetari disputatione Heidelbergæ solenniter ventilata probatur. LXXI. Hierarchiam impuritate & luxuriâ carnis multis modis se polluere, adeoque Babylonem M. esse, concluditur.
units.tr: LXX. Shortly before the Reformation, the fornication and concubinage of the clergy were so common that they became a matter of sport and jest, as is shown by a quodlibetical disputation solemnly held at Heidelberg. LXXI. It is concluded that the Hierarchy defiles itself in many ways through impurity and carnal luxury, and so is Babylon the Great.

units.la: I. Ad habitum interiorem Babylonis Magnæ Spiritus S. haud obscurè luxuriam & impuritatem carnis refert. Nam & Meretricem, neque qualemcunque, sed μεγάλω Magnam Apoc.xvi.r. utramque propter scortationem spiritualem & corporalem, eámque non vulgarẹm, sed exquisitam, multifariam, horribilem; nuncupat; & eidem Ἰωάμιτ & φλὼς potentiam luxuriæ, qua scilicet ἐφλωίαν luxuriavit, Apoc. xviii. 3. 7. tribuit. Pertinent eodem χόμος seu Merces Babylonicæ, luxuriæ instrumenta, ib. v. 11. & quòd in ea vox Citharoedorum, Musicorum, tubicinum personuisse c. xviii. 22. commemoratur.
units.tr: I. The Holy Spirit clearly refers the inner character of Babylon the Great to luxury and carnal impurity. For he calls her a harlot, and not just any harlot but a great one [Rev. 16.], on account of both spiritual and bodily fornication, and that not common but refined, manifold and horrible. To her he also attributes the power of luxury [δύναμιν στρήνους], by which she indulged in luxury [ἐστρηνίασαν], Rev. 18:3, 7. To the same end belong the merchandise of Babylon [ἔμπορος], the instruments of luxury, ib. v. 11, and the mention that in her the voice of harpers, musicians and trumpeters was heard, c. 18:22.

units.la: II. Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ isthoc luxuriæ & impuritatis carnalis stigma jure meritóque inurimus, Syllogismo cjusmodi freti:
units.tr: II. We rightly and deservedly brand this stain of luxury and carnal impurity upon the hierarchy of the Roman Church, relying on a syllogism of this kind:

units.la: Ille cœtus se luxuria & impuritate carnis multis modis polluit, adeoque cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est; qui non tantum luxuriæ & impuritati carnis ansam præbet, dum luxuriæ instrumenta avidè nimis conquirit, otium religiosum cum inefficaci cultu & debacchationibus conjunctum sectatur; legem de cœlibatu Sacerdotum figit & pertinaciter tuetur; votum Cœlibatus perpetui laudat & commendat; opportunitatem impuritati concipiendæ & fovendæ in ipsa functione sacra suppeditat; Musicæ voluptuariæ amore & studio nimio tenetur: sed etiam de fornicatione, adulterio, aliisque impuritatibus tenuiter nimis sentit, eásque levibus pœnis afficit, & dispensationum indulgentiarúmque beneficio pœnis exsolvit; contra leges Divinas de incestu dispensat, lupanaria permittit; denique omnis generis libidinibus nefariè indulget.
units.tr: That body which in many ways defiles itself with luxury and carnal impurity is, other things being equal, Babylon the Great; one which not only provides an occasion for luxury and carnal impurity, while it eagerly seeks out the instruments of luxury, pursues religious leisure joined with unprofitable worship and revelry, enacts and stubbornly defends the law of clerical celibacy, praises and commends the vow of perpetual celibacy, supplies opportunity for conceiving and fostering impurity within the sacred office itself, is held by an excessive love and zeal for voluptuous music; but also thinks too lightly of fornication, adultery and other impurities, punishes them with slight penalties and, by the benefit of dispensations and indulgences, releases them from penalties; against the divine laws it grants dispensations for incest, permits brothels, and in short indulges shamelessly in every kind of lust.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans non tantùm luxuriæ & impuritati carnis ansam præbet, dum luxuriæ instrumenta avidè nimis conquirit, otium religiosum cum inefficaci cultu & debacchationibus conjunctum sectatur, legem de Cœlibatu sacerdotum figit & pertinaciter tuetur, votum perpetui cœlibatús laudat & commendat, opportunitatem impuritati concipiendæ & fovendæ in ipsa functione sacra suppeditat, Musicæ voluvoluptuariæ amore & studio nimio tenetur: sed etiam de fornicatione, adulterio, aliisque impuritatibus tenuiter nimis sentit, easque levibus pœnis afficit, & dispensationum indulgentiarúmque beneficio pœnis exsolvit; contra leges Divinas de incestu dispensat, lupanaria permittit, denique omnis generis libidinibus nefariè indulget.
units.tr: But the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, not only provides an occasion for luxury and carnal impurity, while it eagerly seeks out the instruments of luxury, pursues religious leisure joined with unprofitable worship and revelry, enacts and stubbornly defends the law of clerical celibacy, praises and commends the vow of perpetual celibacy, supplies opportunity for conceiving and fostering impurity within the sacred office itself, is held by an excessive love and zeal for voluptuous music; but also thinks too lightly of fornication, adultery and other impurities, punishes them with slight penalties, and by the benefit of dispensations and indulgences releases them from penalties; against the divine laws it grants dispensations for incest, permits brothels, and in short indulges shamelessly in every kind of lust.
