units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans sese luxuriá & impuritate carnis multis modis polluit, adeóque, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, defiles itself in many ways with luxury and carnal impurity, and so, other things being equal, is Babylon the Great.

units.la: Cùm utraque Propositio plura membra complectatur, juvabit singula ordine proponere, atque quoad singula, utrique propositioni fidem certam facere.
units.tr: Since each premise contains several parts, it will be helpful to set out the individual parts in order, and to establish for each of them, and for both premises, a firm proof.

units.la: III. Qui cœtus luxuriæ & impuritati carnis ansam non unam præbet, haud dubiè se luxuriâ & impuritate carnis polluere censebitur, si ansa illa luxuriam & impuritatem istam, sive ob carnis humanæ infirmitatem, sive ob eventum inevitabilem post se traxerit. Ejusmodi autem ansam præbere inter alia etiam membra illa in Propositione utraque commemorata, paucis nunc demonstremus.
units.tr: III. A body which provides not one occasion for luxury and carnal impurity will undoubtedly be judged to defile itself with luxury and carnal impurity, if that occasion has drawn these vices after it, either through the weakness of human flesh or through an inevitable outcome. That the aforesaid body provides such occasions, among the other parts mentioned in both premises, we shall now demonstrate briefly.

units.la: IV. Primò Luxuriæ instrumenta Babyloni Magnæ Spiritus S. Apoc.xviii.3.11.12.&c. non obscurè tribuit. Notat enim in ea v. 3. δύναμιν σφοδρὰν potentiam luxuriæ, seu instrumenta exercendæ luxuriæ potentia & prævalida. Vocem σφοδρᾶς Hesychius interpretatur διὰ πλῆθος ὑλῶν propter divitias contumeliis afficere. Arethas καταζωπλαλᾶν & ἀπρέπεις βίος, quod luxuriari est. Res ergo terrestres, divitiæ, luxuriæ instrumenta Babyloni Spiritus Dei vendicat. Est enim Babylon illustre emporium Apoc.xviii.17. Finis ejus est ditari, rebus terrestribus ad voluptates carnis nutriendas abundare. Sed & v.11.&c. inter Babylonis merces reponitur μύρων mercimonium auri, argenti, lapidis pretiosi, margaritæ, byssi, purpuræ, serici, coccini; omne lignum odoratum, vas eburneum, cinnamomum, odoramenta, myrrhâ, thus, vinum, oleum &c. Quæ omnia sive secundùm literam, sive allegoricè capiantur, eò tendunt, ut Babylonis divitiæ & abundantiam rerum terrestrium delineent. Si secundum litteram, nulla dubitatio erit. Sin allegoricè, ut v. 9. aurum sit emblema Dei; argentum puritas naturæ Christi humanæ; Lapis pretiosus B. Petrus &c. eodem res redit, quia Babylon spiritualia quæstui habet ad acquirenda corporalia corrogandas immensas opes quarum beneficio genio indulgere & in mundo luxuriari valeat.
units.tr: IV. First, the Holy Spirit does not obscurely attribute the instruments of luxury to Babylon the Great, Rev. 18:3, 11, 12, etc. For in v. 3 he signifies the power of luxury, that is, the instruments of exercising luxury with a strong and mighty power [δύναμιν σφοδρὰν]. Hesychius interprets the word σφοδρᾶς as meaning to treat with contempt on account of riches [διὰ πλῆθος ὑλῶν]. Arethas gives it as to revel in luxury and an unseemly life [ἀπρέπεις βίος], which is to live in luxury. Therefore the Spirit of God assigns earthly possessions, riches and the instruments of luxury to Babylon. For Babylon is a famous market, Rev. 18:17. Its purpose is to be enriched, and to abound in earthly things in order to nourish the pleasures of the flesh. But also in v. 11 etc. there are listed among the merchandise of Babylon gold, silver, precious stone, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet; every scented wood, ivory vessel, cinnamon, spices, myrrh, incense, wine, oil, etc. Whether these are taken literally or allegorically, they all tend to depict the riches of Babylon and the abundance of earthly things. If taken literally, there will be no doubt. But if allegorically, so that in v. 9 gold is an emblem of God, silver the purity of Christ's human nature, the precious stone St Peter, and so on, the matter comes to the same thing, because Babylon makes spiritual things a source of gain, in order to acquire and amass immense wealth, by whose benefit she may be able to indulge her nature and revel in the world.

units.la: V. Historia Ecclesiæ testis locuples est, Christum & Apostolos nihil minùs curæ cordique habuisse, quàm ut opes corraderent; & ex eo tempore ad Constantinum M. usque vix quicquam à divitiis magis alienum fuisse, quàm Ecclesiam. Inde paulò opulentior facta est, maximè inde à Caroli M. temporibus. Is enim exemplo suo non tantùm posteris præivit in ditanda Ecclesia; sed etiam ipsos Ecclesiasticos ad opes captandas liberaliter invitavit. Inde factum, ut tandem Prælatorum ii optimi censerentur, qui Ecclesiæ suæ opes augerent maximè. Sed hos multis post se parasangis Pontifices reliquerunt. Si enim reliquorum omnium solertiam, artes, dolos in unum conferas; longo intervallo distabunt ab horum vivida industria & solertia; quæ tandem Petro amplissimum acquisivit patrimonium; non sine miraculo quodam. Nam qui vivus possidebat omnino nihil, & quoad terrestres opes nec Iro nec Codro controversiam fecisset; is Successores suos ita ditavit, ut iis comparati Reges atque Imperatores, vix non vilia mendicabula dici queant. Cæterùm de Hierarchiæ divitiis, & modis acquirendi eadem ex professo pluribus infra, ubi argumentum undecimum prosequemur.
units.tr: V. The history of the Church is a rich witness that Christ and the Apostles had nothing less at heart than to amass wealth, and that from that time until Constantine the Great there was scarcely anything further from riches than the Church. Thereafter she became somewhat richer, chiefly from the time of Charlemagne. For he not only led the way for his successors in enriching the Church by his example, but also generously invited the clergy themselves to seize wealth. Hence it came about that at last those prelates were deemed the best who most increased the wealth of their Church. But the popes left these far behind, many parasangs. For if you were to compare together the cleverness, arts and tricks of all the rest, they would be far separated from the lively industry and shrewdness of these men, who at last acquired for Peter a very ample patrimony, not without a certain miracle. For he who, while alive, possessed absolutely nothing, and who in earthly wealth would not have contested the point even with Irus or Codrus, enriched his successors so greatly that kings and emperors, compared with them, could well be called almost worthless beggars. But concerning the riches of the Hierarchy and the ways of acquiring them, we shall treat them expressly in more detail below, where we pursue the eleventh argument.

units.la: VI. Hæc ergo luxuriæ instrumenta sic luxuriæ & impuritati carnis ansam præbent, ut eadem se Hierarchia nefarie polluat. Etenim divitiæ nunquam melius æstimantur quàm
units.tr: VI. These instruments of luxury therefore provide an occasion for luxury and carnal impurity in such a way that the Hierarchy thereby defiles itself wickedly. For riches are never better valued than for [the purpose of] enjoyment of luxury and pleasures.

units.la: Tom. II. quàm àluxu, & voluptatum fruitione. Non deesse autem Hierarchas supremos, medioxumos, imos, qui omnes Sardanapalos & Heliogabalos longè excedant, historiarum monumenta non loquuntur, sed clamant. Luxus ipse tantus est in Romanensibus, ut nusquam major: raro æ-qualis; etiam in profanis. Fictitia Constantini M. donatio supponit sedem Romanam gloriosius exaltandam, quàm Imperatoris sedem; atque adeò omnia ei concedit, quibus ad maximam pompam & luxuriam Imperatores uti solent.
units.tr: Tom. II. than from luxury and the enjoyment of pleasures. That the supreme, middling and lowest hierarchs are not lacking, who far surpass all the Sardanapaluses and Heliogabaluses, is not told by the records of history but cries out. Luxury itself is so great among the Romanists that nowhere is it greater, and rarely equalled, even among secular rulers. The fictitious donation of Constantine the Great assumes that the Roman see is to be exalted more gloriously than the emperor's seat, and so grants it everything with which emperors are accustomed to use for the greatest display and luxury.

units.la: VII. Nihil ego de Sacrarum opum usu nunc dicam, quòd (sic Erasmus Orat. de Virg. queritur,) nonnullis in locis offenditur Mariae deluhrum, sericis, argento, auro, gemmis differtum: ut, qui illic adorant Virginem, Mammonem adorare videantur: quae opes multò gratiores essent Mariae, si erogarentur & impenderentur fublevandis Christi membris, in quibus unà cum filio vel affligitur vel refocillatur mater: nihil quòd in caeterum (Aventini Histor. Bojor. lib. vij. gemella querela est) Templorum ornatum, cultum parietum atque pompam versa sunt, quae in alimenta pauperum antea distribuebantur. Licet enim cum calicibus ligneis aureos Sacerdotes reduci optimus quisque malit, optetque cum Isidoro Pelusiota lib. ij. Epist. 246. τῷ ἔντως ἐκκλησίαν veram potiùs Ecclesiam spiritualibus gratiis excoli; quàm τὸ ἐκκλησιαστικὸν Templum plusquàm par sit, exornari magnificè: cùm interim illa comicis cavillis incessatur: tamen is ipse praeposterus opum Sacrarum usus, partim Judaismi, partim Gentilismi καταξηλίας invectus excusari qualitercunque solet. Nec importunius objecto, quae sunt ab historicis annotata de ministris (sic Thuanus lib. j. Guicciard. lib. xiij.) Pontificis, qui per lustra & popinas cottidie sine pudore, in aleae lusum, usúsque turpissimos, potestatem extrahendi animas functorum functorum ex igne expiatorio promittentes, pecuniam à credulis emunctam profundebant. His enim ipsum nunc Clerum ob proditam nimia licentia tam utilem fabulam graviter irasci scio; beatis futuris, si corrasa indulgentiarum æruscationibus bona sua non jactâssent; si scivissent in sinu gaudere, & se ad clandestinam ganeam occultúmque luxum referre potiùs, quàm sermonibus & curiosulis istis in purgatorias indulgentias inquisitionibus occasionem dare.
units.tr: VII. I shall now say nothing about the use of sacred wealth, since (as Erasmus complains in his Oration on the Virgin) in some places the image of Mary is offended, filled with silks, silver, gold and jewels, so that those who worship the Virgin there seem to worship Mammon; these riches would be much more pleasing to Mary if they were bestowed and spent on relieving the members of Christ, in whom the mother with her son is either afflicted or refreshed; I shall say nothing of the other complaint, which is similar (in Aventinus, History of the Bavarians, book 7): the ornament of temples, the decoration of walls and display have been turned to what was formerly distributed for the food of the poor. For although every good man would rather see priests of gold led back to wooden chalices, and wishes with Isidore of Pelusium (Letters, book 2, letter 246) that the true church [τῷ ὄντως ἐκκλησίαν] be cultivated with spiritual graces rather than the ecclesiastical temple [τὸ ἐκκλησιαστικὸν] be adorned magnificently beyond what is fitting, while meanwhile the former is assailed with comic jibes, nevertheless this very absurd use of sacred wealth, introduced partly from Judaism and partly from Gentile rivalry [καταξηλίας], is usually excused in some way or other. Nor can what historians have noted about the ministers of the Pope be objected to more troublingly (so Thuanus, book 1, and Guicciard., book 13): who, every day without shame, through brothels and taverns, in gambling and most shameful practices, spent the money extracted from the credulous, promising to draw the souls of the dead out of the purgatorial fire. For I know that the clergy themselves now are sorely angry with them for betraying such a useful fable through excessive licence; they would have been happy in the future, if they had not squandered their goods gathered by the jingling of indulgences; if they had known how to rejoice in their bosom and to betake themselves to secret gluttony and hidden luxury, rather than give occasion for sermons and those nosy inquiries into purgatorial indulgences.

units.la: VIII. Illa verò, quæ moribus hodiernis tam usitata, quàm excusata, partim etiam ad decus ac splendorem dignitatis Ecclesiasticæ relata videas, quis est, quæso, qui, revocato ad rationem judicio, probare queat, quòd (cum Erasmo Adag. Sileni Alcibiad. loquor) Sacerdotes prædiis famulitio, luxu, mulis, equis, sumptuosis ædium, vel magis palatiorum substructionibus, ac reliquo vitæ strepitu Satrapas ipsos æquant, imò longè superant? Non unus Cardinalis Wolsejus erat, cujus (ita apud Stow. in Henrico VIII. legere est) palatio & sumptu Regis major & superbior esse non potuisset, dum omnia potiùs quàm semet ipsum vi sendum efficiebat. Non unus erat Nevillus, Eboracensis Archiepiscopus, cujus exquisita coenarum ingenia, & luxum mensæ, profusis inaudita magnificentia sumptibus exercitum eo præcipuè tempore, cùm Episcopen suam suscipceret, ab authoribus, inprimis Godwino de Præsul. Angl. pag. 65. memoriæ proditum cum stupore legimus. Non unus Sixtus V. est, qui otiosa & stulta pecuniæ ostentatione, in unius obelisci translationem & erectionem 37965. coronatos impendisse, à Cicarella in ejus vita scribitur. Adeò Clericalis ille luxus in immensum prorupit ad cuncta, queis pecunia prodigitur: nec id ævo superiore modò; sed nostris quoque temporibus, licet rebus multùm accisis, eadem illa, quæ erat in abundantia, libido permanet.
units.tr: VIII. As for those practices, which are as common today as they are excused, and which are partly ascribed to the honour and splendour of ecclesiastical dignity: who, I ask, could prove, with judgement brought back to reason, that (to speak with Erasmus in the adage Sileni Alcibiadis) priests equal the satraps themselves in their estates, their servants, their luxury, their mules, horses, sumptuous houses, and still more the building of palaces, and the rest of the noise of life, indeed far surpass them? There was not only Cardinal Wolsey, whose palace and expense (as one reads in Stow, in Henry VIII) could not have been greater or prouder than the King's, while he made himself into everything rather than himself a priest. There was not only Neville, Archbishop of York, whose refined banquets and table luxury, with lavish expense unheard of in its magnificence, we read with astonishment were recorded by authors, above all Godwin de Praesulibus Angliae p. 65, at the time when he took up his bishopric. There is not only Sixtus V, who, as Ciacconius writes in his life, spent 37,965 crowns on the translation and erection of a single obelisk, a vain and foolish display of money. Thus that clerical luxury has burst out without measure into everything on which money is squandered: and not only in the earlier age, but in our own times too, though things are much reduced, that same appetite which was once abundant remains.

units.la: IX. Et hæc forte æquo animo concoqui possent, nisi fructus longè nocentiores, & qui propiùs institutum nostrum contingunt, Clericalis isthæc opulentia produxisset. Nam ut nihil de intolerabili, & summis quibusque Principibus insultante superbia, indiscreta fidelium pedisequa, dicam: cui, quæso, rei nisi Regalibus illis Cleri opibus tribuemus, quòd (verbis Platinæ in vita Marcellini Papæ id effabor) alia quoque Cleri vitia usque eò creverunt, ut vix apud Deum misericordiæ locum reliquerint? Quanta sit avaritia Sacerdotum, & eorum maximè, qui rerum potiuntur; quanta libido undique conquisita; quanta desidia; quanta ignoratio tum sui ipsius, tum doctrinæ Christianæ: quàm parva religio, & simulata potiùs quàm vera; quàm corrupti mores, vel in-profanis etiam hominibus (quos Seculares vocant) detestandi, non attinet dicere; cùm ipsi ita aperte & palam peccent; ac si inde laudem quærerent. Qua morum impietate fit, ut (verba Erasmi in adagio eodem Sileni Alcibiadis mea faciam) Christi nomen infametur inter Ethnicos. Quid enim consentaneum est, Christianæ religionis hostes dicere, cùm in Euangelicis literis viderint, Christum ad opum contemptum, ad voluptatum abdicationem, ad gloriæ negletium hortantem: & è regione conspexerint, primores etiam ac duces Christianæ professionis ita vivere, ut opum accumulandarum studio, ut voluptatum amore, ut vitæ splendore, ut belli ferocitate, cæterisque ferè vitiis omnibus, ipsos superent Ethnicos?
units.tr: IX. These things perhaps might be borne with an even mind, were it not that this clerical opulence had produced more harmful fruits, which touch more closely on our undertaking. To say nothing of the intolerable pride that insults even the greatest princes, and of the indiscriminate following of the faithful, to what, I ask, should we attribute it, other than to those royal riches of the clergy? By these, to use Platina's words in the life of Pope Marcellinus, the other vices of the clergy have grown so much that they have hardly left any room for mercy with God. How great is the avarice of priests, and especially of those who hold power; how great the lust sought out on every side; how great the idleness; how great the ignorance both of themselves and of Christian doctrine; how small the religion, feigned rather than true; how corrupt the morals, detestable even in profane men whom they call secular, is not worth saying; since they sin so openly and boldly, as if they sought praise for it. By this impiety of morals it comes about that (I shall make Erasmus's words in the same adage, Sileni Alcibiadis, my own) the name of Christ is defamed among the heathen. For what are the enemies of the Christian religion likely to say, when they have seen in the evangelical writings Christ urging contempt of wealth, renunciation of pleasures, and neglect of glory; and on the other hand have observed that the leaders and chiefs of the Christian profession live in such a way that, in their zeal for piling up wealth, their love of pleasures, the splendour of their life, the ferocity of war, and almost all the other vices, they surpass the heathen themselves?

units.la: X. Quid verò multis? Luxuriæ instrumenta Babyloni Magnæ Spiritus S. tribuit. Eandem luxuriæ & impuritatis ipsius ream peragit. Luxuriæ instrumenta non modo, quod ajunt, nec trimodio, sed toto horreo Hierarchia possidet; plus quàm tertiam terrarum partem, & redituum prope dimidiam complexa; quam non immeritò quatuorillis infaturabilibus Solomonis Prov. xxx. 16. adjeceris. Luxuriam & impuritatem ipsam Cleri, instrumentis illis male quæsitis abutentis, infra domesticorum testium fide nullo negotio probabimus. Et probat S. Pagina, quæ Ezech. xvi. 49. iniquitatis Sodomæ causam inter alias superbiam & saturitatem panis לחם שבעת און perhibet. Plane igitur cum Babylone Magna Hierarchiæ convenit.
units.tr: X. But why say more? The Holy Spirit assigns the instruments of luxury to Great Babylon, and she is guilty of the same luxury and of impurity itself. The Hierarchy possesses the instruments of luxury not merely, as they say, by the peck, but by the whole granary, holding more than a third of the lands and almost half of the revenues; which one might not unjustly add to Solomon's four insatiable things (Prov. 30:16). The luxury and impurity of the clergy itself, abusing those ill-gotten instruments, we shall prove without any difficulty by the testimony of their own household. Holy Scripture also proves it, which in Ezek. 16:49 names, among other causes of Sodom's iniquity, pride and fullness of bread [לחם שבעת און]. Plainly, then, it agrees with Great Babylon of the Hierarchy.

units.la: XI. Luxuriæ carnis non postremam ansam Religiosum illud, quod in Feriis & festivitatibus Sacris anniversariis lege vel consuetudine receptis, agitatur otium; cum cultus inefficacis & exanimis exercitio conjunctum, suppeditat. Nam in universum Otium Diaboli pulvinar, & desidia spurcitiæ mater est; atque juxta tritum illud, Otia, si tollas, perière cupidinis arcus, Contemptæque jacent & sine luce faces. Hæc ut ames faciunt, hæc quæ fecēre tuentur, Hæc sunt jucundi causa cibúsque mali.
units.tr: XI. The religious idleness practised on the feasts and holy festivals received each year by law or custom, joined with a worship that is ineffective and lifeless, supplies no small occasion for fleshly lust. For in general idleness is the devil's pillow, and sloth is the mother of filth; and according to the familiar saying: Take away idleness, and the bows of Cupid perish, and his torches lie spent and without light. These things make you love, these things keep what they have made; these are the cause and food of pleasant evil.

units.la: Et sanè quid aliud est ἀεργία otium, quàm κακυργίας ἀρχή, maleficii principium, uti verissimè Basilius definit? quàm vitiorum plurium fœcunda parens & nutrix? Scilicet otiosus Diabolo semel à se digressus cor suum parat, ut avidiùs revertatur, & septem pejoribus assumptis latiùs & impotentiùs dominetur. Neque enim aditum promptiorem apud eos, qui jugum ejus excussisse videbantur, invenit, quàm si ipsos nulli bono operi intentos, sed ψυχαγωγοῦς, securos, otiosos inveniat. Unde Spiritus S. Ezech. xvi. 49. inter iniquitates Sodomæ etiam שלוה השקט abundantiam otii ejus & filiorum ejus refert. Nam otium quodvis cùm per se malum est, tum ad patranda alia mala invitat, quia nihil agendo malè agere discimus.
units.tr: And indeed what else is idleness [ἀεργία], but, as Basil defines it most truly, the beginning of wickedness [κακυργίας ἀρχή]? It is a fruitful parent and nurse of many vices. The idle man, once he has departed from himself to the devil, prepares his heart so that he may return more eagerly, and, taking seven worse spirits to himself, rules more widely and more powerfully. For he finds no readier access among those who seemed to have shaken off his yoke than when he finds them intent on no good work, but idle, secure, and given to amusements [ψυχαγωγοῦς]. Hence the Holy Spirit, in Ezek. 16:49, also reports among the iniquities of Sodom the abundance of ease [שלוה השקט] of her and of her daughters. For idleness is evil in itself, whatever else it may be, and it also invites the committing of other evils, because by doing nothing we learn to do evil.

units.la: XII. Religiosum isthoc otium ex frequentia feriarum sacrarum, & cultûs in iisdem ἀεργία inertia optimè cognoscitur. Olim quidem Ecclesiam, non ex Christi vel Apostolorum institutione, sed suo arbitrio, neque malo fine, festa quaedam instituisse, Socrates Histor. Eccl. lib. v. 22. memorat. Talia erant Epiphaniae, Paschatis, Ascensionis, Pentecostes. Paulatim pro varietate Regionum variae Martyrum memoriae liberè institutae, & absque superstitione celebratae sunt. Procedente tempore variis occasionibus numerus eorum auctus est, uti ex Canone 36. Concilii Moguntini, ac inprimis ex Concilio Lugdunensi A. M. CCXL. celebrato constat. Demum introducta sunt festa inventionis crucis, corporis Christi, quatuor Doctorum Ecclesiae, Visitationis, Praesentationis, Conceptionis Mariae, Antonii, Nicolai, Catharinae, aliorum, particularia inprimis sine numero, sine & modo. Adeò quidem ut inter Gravamina Imperii A. MDXXII. Norinbergae exhibita, haud postremum hoc fuerit, quòd feriarum festorumque tanta copia laicorum vulgus urgeatur, ut vix aegrè agricolis tempus suppetat, quo fructus agri tot sudoribus è terra pelleti, aliquando aqua pluvia immodicèque æstu non raro etiam grandine aliáve tempestate periclitantes, in horrea conferantur.
units.tr: XII. This religious idleness is best recognised from the frequency of the holy festivals and from the inactivity [ἀεργία] of the worship performed on them. Socrates, Hist. Eccl. lib. v, 22, relates that the Church once instituted certain festivals, not by the institution of Christ or the Apostles but by its own judgement, and not for a bad end. Such were Epiphany, Easter, Ascension and Pentecost. Gradually, according to the variety of regions, various memorials of martyrs were freely instituted and celebrated without superstition. As time went on, the number of these grew on various occasions, as is clear from Canon 36 of the Council of Mainz and especially from the Council of Lyons celebrated in A.D. 1240. At last there were introduced the feasts of the Finding of the Cross, of the Body of Christ, of the four Doctors of the Church, of the Visitation, the Presentation, the Conception of Mary, of Anthony, Nicholas, Catherine, and others, particular feasts without number or measure. So much so that among the Gravamina Imperii presented at Nuremberg in A.D. 1522, this was no small complaint: that the common people of the laity are so burdened by such a multitude of holidays and feasts that farmers scarcely have time in which to carry the fruits of the field, drawn from the earth with so much sweat, into the barns, while they are at times endangered by rainwater, excessive heat, not rarely also by hail or other storm.

units.la: XIII. Tolerari utcunque multitudo feriarum posset si cultus Dei verus vividúsque in iis celebraretur. Jam verò nefas equidem habetur eorum tempore saecularibus negotiis, & honestis quaerendi victus rationibus vacare. Ipse verò verus veri Dei cultus, & religionis salutaris exercitium friget, atque ejusmodi est, ut corda hominum neutiquam attingat penetrétque, nec timorem pium Nominis ei ingerat, vel carnis cupiditates in feriantibus mortificet. Quippe mutorum duntaxat spectaculorum arbitri & spectatores publicæque liturgiae, peregrina lingua, & in honorem non Dei, sed Sanctorum, adcòque sine solidæ pietatis incremento peractæ, auditores existunt; atque sic præclarè partibus suis se defunctos arbitrantur. Non iis religio verbum Dei legere, meditari, in succum & sanguinem convertere; sed reliquum tempus totum alia omnia sibi vindicant. Homines ergo qui nec mentes mortificatas habent, neque opportunitatem per intelligibilem, vivam, penetrantem Dei publicè colendi rationem, animarúmque convincendarum potens ad præmuniendos se adversus carnis tentationes ministerium adipiscuntur, & tamen per legem Ecclesiæ sic feriari coguntur, ut tutius iis sit in caupona aut lupanari deprehendi, quàm honestum eo tempore quæstum exercere; quò amabo, naturaliter magis, quàm in Cereris, Bacchi, Veneris sacra minimè sacra prolapsuri sunt? Non potest non ergo Dierum festorum numerositas cum inefficaci & exanimi cultu, multisque spectaculis conjuncta non turpitudinis schola, & libidinis ac impuritatis certissima nutrix existere.
units.tr: XIII. The multitude of holidays could be tolerated to some extent if the true and living worship of God were celebrated on them. But now indeed it is deemed wrong to devote their days to secular business and to honest means of earning a living. Yet the true worship of the true God, and the practice of saving religion, grows cold on them, and is of such a kind that it in no way touches or penetrates men's hearts, nor instils in them a pious fear of the Name, nor mortifies the lusts of the flesh on the feast days. Indeed, men merely act as judges and spectators of dumb shows and public liturgy, performed in a foreign tongue, in honour not of God but of the saints, and so without any increase of solid piety; and thus they think they have discharged their part splendidly. For them religion does not mean reading the Word of God, meditating on it, and turning it into juice and blood; rather all other things claim the rest of the time for themselves. Therefore men who have neither mortified minds nor the opportunity, through an intelligible, living and penetrating ministry, of a means of publicly worshipping God that is powerful to convince souls and to fortify them against the temptations of the flesh, and yet are compelled by the law of the Church to keep holiday in such a way that it is safer to be caught in a tavern or brothel than to carry on honest trade at that time: to whom, pray, are they more naturally going to fall, than into the rites of Ceres, Bacchus and Venus, which are by no means sacred? Therefore the multitude of festival days, joined with an unfruitful and lifeless worship and many spectacles, cannot fail to become a school of shame and a most certain nurse of lust and impurity.

units.la: . XIV. Falli sunt id ipsum haud postremæ in Papatu authoritatis viri. Nam Michaël Altiliodorensis Archiepiscopus, congregata Provinciali Synodo, pleraque festa abolevit. Credo, sic Nicolaus Clemangis, Magister Parisiensis, & Archidiaconus Bajocensis libello de Novis festis Ἀποκαλύψεων, offensum esse variis abusibus non solùm Epicureorum, ebriosorum, aliorumque flagitiosorum hominum, qui diebus festis toti effunduntur in omne nefas: sed quòd videret, tot Divorum festis homines induci ad cultum creaturarum, Deique veri, qui solus coli vult, oblivionem. In eodem libello Clemangis acerbè queritur, tam multa de Sanctis legi & dici in Templis, ut jam sacrarum literarum lectio planè omittatur. In antiqua Ecclesia planè diversum fuisse morem. Itaque jam Deum suo loco detrusum & deturbatum esse, & Sanctos pro eo in Templis regnare. Petrus de Aliaco, Cardinalis Cameracensis, libro Sigismundi Imperatoris jussu de Reformatione Ecclesiæ fiæ scripto, & Conftantienfi Concilio oblato, inter alia festorum dierum numerum minui suadet his verbis: Providendum effet, ne tot nova festa solennizarentur, & tot novi Sancti canonizarentur: ut praeterquam Dominicis & majoribus festis ab Ecclesia institutis liceret operari post auditum officium, cum quod in festis saepe magis multiplicantur peccata in tabernis, choreis & aliis lasciviis, quas docet otium: tum quia dies operabiles vix sufficiunt pauperibus ad necessaria vitae procuranda: item ut in hujusmodi festis Scripturae apocryphae, aut hymni novi, vel orationes, seu aliae voluntariae voluntates non legerentur omissis antiquis & authenticis, & jam in Ecclesia consuetis. Polydorus Vergilius de Invent. Rer. lib. vj. 8. scribit, quam olim ex religionis usu erat festa haec instituere, tam nunc praestare videri eadem antiquare, cum (NB) bona pars hominum otium illud festorum dierum non ad adorandum Deum, non ad Divina scripta audienda, cujus rei causa datum est, sed ad omnifariam bonorum morum corruptelam augendam, indies magis magisque impudenter consumat, dictitans, se id animi gratia facere, quasi plane sentiens cum Platone, qui ob illud ipsum, Deum ejusmodi festa sacra instituisse ajebat. Faxit Deus, ut Pontifices nostri tandem aliquando festos dies utiles reddant: quod facient, si minuendos & caste agitandos curarint. Gravamina Imperii supra laudata eandem querelam ingeminant, quod feriatis diebus innumera perpetrentur delicta, peccata & scelera potius, quam his omnipotens Deus colatur veneretúrque. Id quod, inquiunt, res ipsa notorium facit, tantum abest, ut testibus hoc egeat. Erasmus in cap. xj. Matth. Feriarum, inquit, nec finis nec modus: quae cum ad pietatis primitus vacationem paucae sint institutae, nunc ad scelerum exclusionem tolli debeant, nisi Sacerdotum avaritia suis rebus consuleret po-tiús, tiùs, quàm veræ religioni. Denique Urbanus VIII. in sua de obseruantia Festorum Bulla A. M D C XLII. edita, festorum numerositatem, uti vocat, restricturus, fatetur, quæ festa ad glorificandum Diuinum Numen primitus instituta fuerunt, ea temporis decursu inimicum hominem corrupisse, & in magnam illius offensionem, grauémque animarum jacturam convertisse.
units.tr: . XIV. Men of no small authority in the Papacy have also been mistaken about this very matter. Michael, Archbishop of Auxerre, when he had called a provincial synod, abolished most of the feasts. I believe that Nicolas Clamanges, Master of Paris and Archdeacon of Bayeux, was offended by the same things, as he says in his little book On New Feasts [Ἀποκαλύψεων]: by the various abuses not only of Epicureans, drunkards and other shameless men, who on feast days throw themselves wholly into every wickedness, but also because he saw that so many feasts of the saints lead people to the worship of creatures and to forgetting the true God, who alone wishes to be worshipped. In the same little book Clamanges bitterly complains that so many things are read and said about the saints in the temples that the reading of the sacred letters is altogether neglected. In the ancient Church the custom was quite different. And so now God has been pushed and thrust out of his place, and the saints reign in the temples in his stead. Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, in his book On the Reformation of the Church, written by command of the Emperor Sigismund and presented to the Council of Constance, urges among other things that the number of feast days be reduced, in these words: Care should be taken that so many new feasts are not celebrated and so many new saints are not canonized; so that, apart from Sundays and the greater feasts instituted by the Church, it would be permitted to work after the service has been heard, since on feast days sins are often multiplied in taverns, dances and other wantonness, which idleness teaches; and since working days scarcely suffice for the poor to procure the necessities of life; likewise so that on such feasts apocryphal Scriptures, or new hymns, or prayers, or other voluntary inventions are not read, the ancient and authentic ones, already customary in the Church, being set aside. Polydore Vergil, On the Discovery of Things, book 6, chapter 8, writes that just as it was once in keeping with religious practice to institute these feasts, so now it seems to be a matter of abolishing them; for (NB) a good part of mankind spends that leisure of feast days, which was granted not for adoring God or hearing the divine writings, but for increasing the corruption of good morals on every side, more and more shamelessly each day, saying that they do it for the sake of their spirits, as if they fully agreed with Plato, who said that God had instituted such sacred feasts for that very reason. May God grant that our Pontiffs at last make the feast days useful; they will do so if they take care to have them reduced and spent chastely. The Gravamina of the Empire, praised above, repeat the same complaint: that on holidays countless crimes, sins and wickedness are committed, rather than Almighty God being worshipped and honoured on them. The thing itself makes this notorious, as they say; so far is it from needing witnesses. Erasmus, on Matthew chapter 11: Of holidays, he says, there is neither end nor measure; though few were originally instituted for leisure devoted to piety, they must now be abolished to exclude wickedness, unless the greed of the priests were looking more to their own affairs than to true religion. Finally, Urban VIII, in his Bull on the observance of feasts, published in 1642, intending to restrict what he calls the multiplicity of feasts, confesses that the feasts which were originally instituted to glorify the divine Majesty, in the course of time the enemy of man has corrupted, and turned them to his great offence and the grave loss of souls.

units.la: XV. Pertinent huc solennes illæ debacchationes, festiuæ scilicet, quæ tribus primis Quinquagesimæ (sic enim festum, quo pœnitentiam & remissionem, nec non statum beatitudinis æternæ significari & repræsentari, Hierarchici docent, appellatur) diebus ab vniverso populo, & ipsa quinquagesimæ Dominica à Clero, imò à nonnullis inde à die Nativitatis Christi vsque ad quadragesimam frequentantur, adeò quidem flagitiosè, ut si quis Græcorum aut Romanorum veterum ad bacchantes illos rediret, Jovem lapidem juraturus sit, sua Bacchanalia & Lupercalia agitari. Pleraque enim sua reperiret, & pristinam insaniam furorémque suum superari multùm, cerneret. Hi enim non novis quibusdam, sed iisdem, certisque adeò ritibus & pompis, quas sibi ipsi præscripserunt, quotannis uti consueverant. Illi verò, Christi nomen præ se ferentes, singulis annis, singulis oppidis atque vicis novas pompas producunt. Hi, puta Romani, cognita Bacchicorum turpitudine, illa ex urbe sua totáque Italia exterminárunt. Scythæ quoque, gens barbarissima, ipsius naturæ instinctu ab illis vehementissimè abhorruerunt. Illi verò, Christiani scilicet Catholici, illa mordicitus retinent, illis mirum in modum delectantur, illo non minore, sed forte majore, quàm olim Ethnici, furore atque insaniâ, diurnis nocturnisque discursibus, ludis, spectaculis obscœnis, clamoribus atque vociferationibus infamis, helluationibus atque potationibus monstrosis, libidinibus vagis atque stupris agitant, ita ut non homines, sed Stygiæ illæ Bacchæ, Furiæ atque Erynnes cum ardentibus suis facibus ex inferis excitatæ passim discurfare videantur. Denique improbitatem turpitudinemque illam plusquàm gentilem, & qualemcunque effræits imaginationis suæ lascivia vel petulantia suggesserit, sub larvis & personis committunt, perinde ac si abscondito apud homines vultu, ipsi quoque Deo imponere, & sanctissimo conspectui ejus actiones suas detestabiles subducere possent. Quæ profectò recta methodus est homines cuivis improbitati & nequitiæ initiandi, cósque pestiferâ opinione imbuendi, quasi virtus & vitium essent inania nomina, neque Deus scelerum & impuritatis omnis inspector & judex esset.
units.tr: XV. To this belong those solemn debaucheries, the festivities, namely, which are kept with great frequency from the three first days of Quinquagesima (for so the feast is called, by which, as the hierarchs teach, repentance and forgiveness, and also the state of eternal blessedness, are signified and represented) by the whole people, and on Quinquagesima Sunday itself by the clergy; indeed by some from the day of the Nativity of Christ until Lent. They are carried on so shamefully that if one of the old Greeks or Romans were to return to those revellers, he would swear by Jupiter the Stone that his own Bacchanalia and Lupercalia were being celebrated. For he would find most of his own rites there, and would see that his former madness and fury were far surpassed. For those men used to observe, every year, not some new ceremonies but the same fixed rites and pomps which they had prescribed for themselves. These people, however, bearing the name of Christ, produce new pomps every year, in every town and village. The Romans, for instance, when they knew the shamefulness of the Bacchic rites, banished them from their city and from all Italy. The Scythians too, a most barbarous people, shrank from them with the greatest horror by the instinct of nature itself. But these men, namely the Catholic Christians, cling to those things with their teeth, they take the greatest delight in them, and with a fury and madness not less than, but perhaps greater than, that of the heathen of old, they carry on with daytime and nighttime revels, games, obscene spectacles, infamous shouting and clamour, monstrous gluttony and drinking, and wanton lusts and debaucheries; so that it seems not men but the Stygian Bacchae, the Furies and Erinyes, roused up from the underworld with their blazing torches, are running about everywhere. Finally they commit under masks and disguises that utterly unnatural wickedness and filthiness, and whatever lewdness or wantonness their unbridled imagination suggests, as if, by hiding their faces from men, they could also deceive God himself and withdraw their detestable actions from his most holy sight. This is surely a sound method for initiating men into every kind of wickedness and wantonness, and for imbuing them with the pestilent opinion that virtue and vice are empty names, and that God is not the inspector and judge of every crime and impurity.

units.la: XVI. Non possum quin profanam illam confuetudinem, & abominabilem impietatem verbis Poëtæ Pontificii Mantuani detester. Sic enim ille & originem festi, & festivitatem ipsam in suis Fastis decantat: Hic memorare libet quoddam grave temporis hujus Crimen: & ipsius subjungere criminis ortum. Roma Lupercales ludos antiquitus isto Mense celebrabat: posita gravitate per urbis Compita cursabant stolidi sine veste Luperci, Et scoricis olidi tractis de tergore capri Pulsabant nuruum palmas: quia verbere tali Pana Deum faciles credebant reddere partus. Ista superstitio, levis hæc insania nostros Transiit in mores. Veteris contagia morbi Haurimus, & quodam simili languore tenemur. Nam juvenes ifiis facit insanire diebus Pan Deus Arcadiæ quondam: totasque per urbes Currere, & acceptis facies abscondere larvis. Est pudor in facie: facies velata pudorem Significat laesum: sciri lascivia non vult,
units.tr: XVI. I cannot refrain from detesting that profane custom and abominable impiety in the words of the Papist poet of Mantua. For he sings of the origin of the feast and of its festivity itself in his Fasti: Here it is fitting to recall a certain grave crime of this season, and to add the origin of the crime itself. Rome once celebrated the Lupercal games in this month: laying aside seriousness, the foolish Luperci ran through the city's crossroads without clothing, and, with thongs drawn from the hide of a stinking goat, they struck the palms of the wives, because they believed that by such a blow Pan, the god, would readily make them fruitful. This superstition, this light madness, passed into our customs. We have drawn in the contagion of an old disease and are held by a similar languor. For Pan, the god of Arcadia, once makes the young men go mad on these days, and to run through the whole town, and to hide their faces with borrowed masks. There is shame in the face; a veiled face signifies wounded modesty; lust does not wish to be known,

units.la: Ora tegit: scelus est pavidum, metuisse videri. Cunctia sub ignotis petulantia vultibus audet, Quæ ablegat gravitas, & quæ proscribit honestas. Per fora, per vicos it personata libido: Et censore carens subit omnia tecta voluptas: Nec nuruum palmas, sed membra recondita pulsat: Pérque domos remanent sædi vestigia capri. Hoc quoque Roma levi cursu gaudebat equorum Tempore: & in Mortis celebrabat Equiria campo: Altera nil melior nuper dementia venit: Sordida produxit vetitos comœdia ludos. Scorta, ambubajas, balatrones & parasitos, Et genus id reliquos trahit in proscenia mensis Improbus: unde trahunt juvenilia pectora pestem Mortiferam: fiúntque ipse sine fronte puellæ. I, pudor, in villas, si non patiuntur eadem Et villæ vomicas: urbs est jam tota lupanar.
units.tr: covers its face. It is a crime to fear being seen. Wantonness dares everything under unknown faces, what seriousness drives away and what honesty banishes. Through the markets, through the streets goes masked lust; and with no censor to restrain it, pleasure enters every house. It does not strike the palms of the wives, but the hidden parts of the body; and through the homes remain the foul traces of the goat. Rome too once rejoiced in the light racing of horses, and celebrated the Equirria in the Field of Mars at the time of the dead. Recently another madness, no better, has come: vile comedy has produced forbidden games. Harlots, dancing-girls, buffoons and parasites, and that whole kind, the shameless one drags onto the stage at the tables; and from there young hearts draw a deadly plague, and they themselves become girls without shame. Go, modesty, to the country villas, if the villas too do not suffer the same sores: the whole city is now a brothel.

units.la: XVII. Similem luxuriæ carnis & impuritati ansam Lex illa Hierarchicorum famosissima, qua Sacerdotibus, aliisque Ordinibus quos vocant, majoribus, promiscuè omnibus, Cœlibatum injungunt, nec non vota cœlibatûs, seu continentiæ à matrimonio, quæ solenniter Religiosi nuncupant; suppeditant. Etenim cælibatum, seu continentiam à matrimonio esse ἴδιον χάρισμα, singulare, seu proprium quibusdam donum, non commune omnium fidelium, nedum hominum Carnalium, quibus mundus scatet, beneficium, ipse S. Paulus 1 Cor. vii. 7. 8. testatur, dicens: Velim omnes homines esse, sicut ego sum. Sed quilibet habet proprium donum à Deo, alius quidem sic, alius autem sic. Dico autem cælibibus & viduis; Bonum est eis, si manserint, ut maneo ego. Quòd si non continent, matrimonium contrahant. Nihil apertius. Optat omnes esse, sicut ipse erat. At ipse talis erat, ut posset continere. Sensus est: Velim omnes continere se, sicut ego me contineo. θέλω, velim, inquit. Ergo sciebat non omnes continere se. Tum causam reddit, quòd non omnibus sint eadem dona; sed quisque proprium donum, alius sic, alius autem sic. Non omnes ergo, fideles etiam, donum continentiæ habent; adeòque singulare illud & proprium quibusdam, non commune omnibus fidelibus, donum est. At quibus hoc deest, ii continere non possunt, adeòque sive lege, sive voto ad cœlibatum adstricti sint, urentur, & in fornicationes pruriunt potius, quàm se continebunt. Apud quos proin tum lex Ecclesiæ, tum vota ab eadem approbata & laudata decumanam ad omne genus impuritatis aperiunt; cùm ad remedium iisdem oppositum, castos thalamos, confugere iidem & lege & voto prohibeantur.
units.tr: XVII. The most notorious law of the hierarchs gives a similar occasion for carnal lust and impurity, the law by which they impose celibacy on priests and on other orders, which they call greater, all alike without distinction, and also the vows of celibacy, or of continence from marriage, which religious men solemnly profess. For that celibacy, or continence from marriage, is a singular gift [ἴδιον χάρισμα], a gift proper to certain people and not common to all the faithful, much less to all carnal men, with whom the world abounds, St. Paul himself testifies in 1 Cor. 7:7, 8, saying: I would that all men were even as I myself am. But every man has his own gift from God, one after this manner, and another after that. But I say to the unmarried and the widows: It is good for them if they abide, even as I do. But if they cannot contain, let them marry. Nothing could be plainer. He wishes all to be as he himself was. But he himself was such that he could contain. The sense is: I would that all contain themselves, as I contain myself. I wish [θέλω], he says, I would. Therefore he knew that not all contain themselves. Then he gives the reason, that not all have the same gifts; but each has his own gift, one this way, another that way. Not all, then, even of the faithful, have the gift of continence; and so that gift is singular and proper to some, not common to all the faithful. But those who lack it cannot contain, and so, whether they are bound to celibacy by law or by vow, they burn and itch for fornication rather than contain themselves. Among such people, therefore, both the law of the Church and the vows approved and praised by the same Church open a broad road to every kind of impurity, since by the same law and vow they are forbidden to take up the opposite remedy, chaste marriage.

units.la: XVIII. Sed & Christi manifestissimum eandem in rem oraculum est. Is enim Matth. xix. 10. 11. discipulis objicientibus: Si tale est negotium hominis cum uxore (ut non posset illa nisi propter fornicationem dimitti) non expedit contrahere matrimonium; respondet: Οὐ πάντες χωροῦσι τὸν λόγον τοῦτον, ἀλλ' οἷς δέδοται. Non omnes capiunt sermonem hunc, sed quibus datum est. Sunt enim Eunuchi, qui ex utero matris nati sunt ita, & sunt Eunuchi qui castrati sunt ab hominibus, & sunt Eunuchi, qui se ipsos castrârunt propter Regnum Cœlorum. Qui potest capere, capiat. Non omnes ergo χωρεῖν capiunt, inquit Christus, συνέχειν ἡ πάγμα τὸ ὕγιες, rei magnitudinem declarans, inquit Chrysostomus. Metaphora ducta est à loco, qui arctior est, quàm ut omnia contineat. Ita Marc. 11. 2. Statim congregati sunt multi, ὥστε μηκέτι χωρεῖν μηδὲ τὰ πρὸς τὴν θύραν, adeò ut non caperent eos ne ea quidem loca, quae erant ad ostium. Sicut ergo qui locus non capit locatum suum, is ne quidem potest capere: sic qui sermonem Christi non capiunt, ne quidem capere possunt. Unde Syrus Interpres convertit per סמך sufficere. לא כל נש סמך לרי Non omnis homo sufficit sibi ad sermonem hunc; vel sermonis hujus capax est. Neque sanè χωρῶν ἢ λόγων capere sermonem hic est sermonem intelligere, uti Maldonatus, aliique interpretantur; repugnante Jansenio, non sine ratione. Nam neque χωρεῖν ea notione ullibi usurpatur; & λόγῳ Hebraeorum more frequenter rem, quae per sermonem significatur, notat. Quid enim difficile erat in sermone discipulorum: Si tale est negotium cum uxore, non expedit homini contrahere matrimonium: ut opus esset gratia Dei, neque aliter sensum assequi quisquam posset? Inprimis cum ipsi discipuli propria & carnali ratiocinatione, atque à seipsis id dixerint, ac proinde conceperint. Non omnes ergo rem hanc, abstinentiam à matrimonio, seu coelibatum, continentiam capiunt, seu ejus capaces sunt; sed, uti Christus clarè explicat, ii demum, οἷς δέδοται quibus datum est, ita ut id omne à δόματι datione, donatione, gratia Dei singulari pendeat; atque destituti hac donatione & gratia vel matrimonium inire debeant, vel praesentissimo ustionum, incontinentiae, impuritatis periculo se exponant. Ipsa denique natura exceptis paucissimis, qui speciali continentiae dono gaudent, severa exactrix est illius tributi, absque quo humanum genus intercideret.
units.tr: XVIII. Christ himself also gives a most manifest oracle on the same matter. When his disciples objected, in Matt. 19:10-11, "If such is the state of a man's case with his wife, that she cannot be dismissed except for fornication, it is not expedient to marry," he replied: "Not all men receive this saying [Οὐ πάντες χωροῦσι τὸν λόγον τοῦτον], but only those to whom it is given [ἀλλ' οἷς δέδοται]. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Let him who can receive it receive it." So not all receive (χωρεῖν) it, says Christ, [συνέχειν ἡ πάγμα τὸ ὕγιες], declaring, as Chrysostom says, the greatness of the matter. The metaphor is taken from a place that is too narrow to hold everything. So in Mark 2:2: "Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no longer room [ὥστε μηκέτι χωρεῖν μηδὲ τὰ πρὸς τὴν θύραν], so much so that they could not even hold the places near the door." Just as a place that cannot hold its occupant cannot even contain him, so those who do not take in Christ's saying cannot even take it in. Hence the Syriac translator renders the word by סמך, "to suffice": lo kol nash samakh lerī, "Not every man suffices for this saying," or is capable of it. Nor does "to receive the saying" here mean "to understand the saying," as Maldonatus and others interpret it, though Jansenius opposes them, not without reason. For χωρεῖν is nowhere used in that sense, and λόγος, after the Hebrew manner, often denotes the thing signified by the word. For what would have been difficult about the disciples' statement, "If such is the case with a wife, it is not expedient for a man to marry," that there would have needed to be a special grace of God before anyone could grasp its sense? Especially since the disciples themselves had said it out of their own fleshly reasoning, and so had conceived it in that way. Therefore not all take up this matter, abstinence from marriage, or celibacy, or continence, or are capable of it; but, as Christ clearly explains, only those "to whom it is given" [οἷς δέδοται], so that the whole of it depends on a special gift (δόμα), a donation, the singular grace of God. Those who lack this gift and grace ought either to enter marriage or expose themselves to the very present danger of burning, incontinence and impurity. Finally, nature itself, with the rare exception of those who enjoy the special gift of continence, is a strict collector of that tribute, without which the human race would perish.

units.la: XIX. Qui coelibatum vel lege, vel voto suscipiunt, ii, ipsorum Hierarchicorum sententia, vel pii & animo mortificati sunt; vel hypocritae, verbis pietatem & castitatem prae se ferentes, reapse pollutam mentem habentes. Utrique per legem & votum certissimo impuritatis periculo se objiciunt. Priores, quia utut inpraesentiarum dono continentiae sibi praediti videantur, vel revera praediti sint, certi tamen non sunt de dono illo durabili & perseverante. Nam qui nunc continere potest per Dei gratiam; ille mox, Deo gratiam illam, quae singularis & per se salutaris non est, subtrahen-
units.tr: XIX. Those who take up celibacy, whether by law or by vow, are, by the judgment of the Hierarchs themselves, either pious and mortified in spirit, or hypocrites who profess piety and chastity in words while in fact having a polluted mind. Both expose themselves by law and vow to the most certain danger of impurity. The former, although for the present they seem, or really are, endowed with the gift of continence, are nonetheless not certain of that lasting and persevering gift. For he who can now restrain himself by the grace of God may soon, when that grace, which is not singular and not saving in itself, is withdrawn

units.la: [Marginal notes at right are very small and cramped; partly illegible, transcribed approximately above.] subtrahente, in tentationes incidere, & iisdem, lege ejus-modi suscepta, & nuncupato voto Deum tentantibus succumbere possunt. Quod forte melius Sacrificuli & Monachi, si conscientiam suam interrogaverint, sentiunt, quam ego verbis exprimere valeam. Annon ergo tales lege & voto impediti, quo minus legitimum medium, matrimonium, capessant, in ustiones impuras, libidines tetras ruunt præcipites, adeóque conscientiæ bonæ naufragium faciunt? Posteriores verò, quos ne pietatis quidem frænum ullum cohibet, lege & voto constrictos, quo minus nubant potius quàm urant & fornicentur, in omne genus impuritatis, vagarùmque libidinum, qua datur porta, suapte indole & inevitabili illa peccati tyrannide, quæ neminem non fidelem & mortificatum sui expertum relinquit, proclives ferri, adeóque porcorum instar in cœno suo volutari necessum est. Lex ergo & votum Cœlibatús in omnibus iis, qui singulari continentiæ dono destituuntur, non occasio duntaxat, sed necessaria impuritatis causa existit.
units.tr: withdrawn, fall into temptations, and, having undertaken such a law and made a vow, may yield to those things that tempt God. Perhaps the little priests and monks feel this better, if they question their own conscience, than I can express in words. Are not such men, hindered by law and vow from taking up the lawful remedy of marriage, plunged headlong into impure burnings and foul lusts, and so suffer shipwreck of a good conscience? As for the latter, whom not even any restraint of piety holds back, bound by law and vow so that they cannot marry rather than burn and commit fornication, they must necessarily, by their own nature and by that inevitable tyranny of sin which leaves no faithful and mortified person free of its experience, be carried headlong into every kind of impurity and wandering lust, wherever an opening is given, and wallow like swine in their own filth. Thus the law and vow of celibacy, in all those who lack the singular gift of continence, is not merely an occasion of impurity but its necessary cause.

units.la: XX. Sed in promptu, inquiunt Hierarchici, sunt remedia, scilicet preces & afflictatio. Precantibus autem, petentibus, pulsantibus omnia promittuntur Matth. vii. 7. xxi. 22. Luc. xi. 9. &c. Et afflictio carnis faces libidinum extinguit. Speciosa equidem oratio, sed parùm efficax. Sed, quæro, remedia illa matrimonio, an fornicationi opponant? Si matrimonio, jam illud cum Tatianis & Encratistis malum esse perhibebunt, quia remedium nullum dicitur nisi mali. Legimus equidem 1. Cor. vii. 5. abstinendum esse ab operibus conjugii, ut vacetur orationi & jejunio. Sed nusquam lectum, vacandum precibus & jejunio, ut abstineatur à matrimonio. Neque etiam adversus matrimonium remedio opus est, quia facile est abstinere à matrimonio. Nam & Manichæi & Priscillianistæ, & Esseni olim, & Ethnici equites Romani apud Dionem Cassium lib. lvi. & Sacerdotes ac Monachi impii, & Turcæ ipsi non pauci facilè matrimonio abstinent. Atque ubicunque terrarum persuasum fuerit, aut non peccari, aut minùs peccari fornicando, quàm matrimonium contrahendo, nunquam hoc genus continentium & à matrimonio temperantium deerit. Sin remedia quærunt fornicationi opposita, nos quoque optima confitemur preces & jejunia; sed his jungimus ab Apostolo quibusvis periculum fornicationis reformidantibus oblatum remedium, ceu morbo ei maximè proprium & naturale, 1. Cor. vii. 2. Propter fornicationem quisque habeat suam uxorem, & quelibet uxor virum proprium. Sed remedia adversus fornicationem quærunt Hierarchici absque matrimonio. Nolunt scortari; atque utinam serió velint: sed non volunt etiam matrimonio uti; imò si optio detur, malint scortari, quàm uti matrimonio. Sic ergo & legem ponunt, ne fas sit Presbyteris nubere; & Religiosorum vota laudant impensè, ac post remedia vestigant, jejunia & preces; hoc est, præposterâ temeritate, & audaciâ intolerandâ, se priùs certissimo periculo exponunt; ac post remedia conquirunt, quibus erui possint. Alto se mari committunt absque velis & remis, imò absque navi; & tum Deum invocant, ut sibi properè succurrat. Quid est Deum tentare, si hoc non est? Priùs oportuit orare, jejunare, & precibus ac jejuniis vires à Deo impetrare. Sed qui in præsens vires à Deo impetrat, in præsens cœlibatum colere, at non ideo vovere perpetuum potest, quia nulla revelatione edocetur unquam, quòd vires continendi, utpote absque quibus salus contingere potest, perpetim duraturæ sint.
units.tr: XX. But, the Hierarchs say, there are remedies at hand, namely prayers and mortification. Everything is promised to those who pray, ask and knock: Matt. 7:7, 21:22; Luke 11:9, etc. And the mortification of the flesh quenches the fires of lust. A fine speech indeed, but of little effect. But I ask: do those remedies oppose marriage or fornication? If marriage, then they will claim that it is an evil, along with the Tatians and Encratites, because a remedy is said to be needed only for evil. We do read in 1 Cor. 7:5 that one must abstain from the duties of marriage in order to give oneself to prayer and fasting. But nowhere is it read that one must give oneself to prayer and fasting in order to abstain from marriage. Nor is any remedy needed against marriage, since it is easy to abstain from marriage. For the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, the Essenes of old, the Roman equites among the heathen in Dio Cassius, book 56, and impure priests and monks, and not a few Turks themselves, abstain from marriage with ease. And wherever in the world it has been persuaded that one sins less by fornicating than by contracting marriage, this kind of continent men who refrain from marriage will never be lacking. But if they seek remedies opposed to fornication, we too confess that prayers and fastings are the best; yet to these we join the remedy that the Apostle offers to all who dread the danger of fornication, as a remedy most proper and natural to that disease: 1 Cor. 7:2, "Because of fornication let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." But the Hierarchs seek remedies against fornication without marriage. They do not want to whore; and would that they seriously wished it. But they do not want to use marriage either; indeed, if the choice were given, they would rather whore than use marriage. Thus they both make a law that it is not lawful for presbyters to marry, and praise the vows of the religious excessively, and afterwards look for remedies, fastings and prayers; that is, with preposterous rashness and intolerable audacity, they first expose themselves to a most certain danger, and afterwards seek for remedies by which they may be rescued. They commit themselves to the deep sea without sails or oars, indeed without a ship; and then they call upon God to come quickly to their aid. What is this if not tempting God? It was necessary first to pray, to fast, and to obtain strength from God by prayers and fastings. But he who obtains strength from God for the present can keep celibacy for the present, but cannot therefore vow it perpetually, since he is never taught by any revelation that the powers of continence, without which salvation may be attained, will last for ever.

units.la: XXI. Nam quod promissiones Dei, quòd petentes exauditurus, pulsantibus aperturus sit, ingeminant, frustra profectò sunt. Nam continentiæ donum non commune omnibus fidelibus, sed particulare & proprium quibusdam sunt. dam charisma esse, supra firmavimus. Atqui hujusmodi quae sunt, non dantur a Deo omnibus: ne quidem precantibus & jejunantibus. Quomodo dona linguarum, cognitionis, prophetiae, sanationum, miraculorum non a quovis fideli, intense licet precante, & authore jejunante impetrantur. Neque rusticus quivis quaesitissimis precibus & jejuniis certo obtinebit, ut Propheta, Rex, praedives evadat. Ineptè ergo promissionibus ejusmodi eorum velatur temeritas, qui, quasi Deum devinctum sibique obstratum tenerent, sibi de eo pollicentur quidvis; atque ea confidentia freti nihil non audent; etiam supra vires suas. Enimverò non alias preces Deus exaudit, quàm eas, quae vera fide funduntur. Fides autem Deo nixa non quid ille possit, attendit, sed quid velit, considerat. Velle autem tum demum certò scit, cùm vel promissiones habet, vel vocationis specialem necessitatem. Utrumque autem hic deest, quia nec Presbyteri officium necessariò continentiam exigit, neque ullus est, qui promissam eam audiverit. Sed neque constat cuiquam, quid de se Divinitus decretum sit; & an velit Deus potiùs opera sua ad propagationem hominum uti. Nunquam ergo fidelis erit oratio, perpetuum coelibatum sine conditione precantium; ac proin neque certa spes exauditionis. Denique fiduciae, quae habenda est, nos in talibus exauditum iri precantes, regula est voluntas Dei arcana; hoc est, tum nos exauditum iri certò, cùm ita postulabimus, ut tamen pendeamus ab ejus decretis, & desideria nostra voluntati ejus subjiciamus; juxta praeceptum Christi, jubentis orare: Fiat voluntas tua. Atqui voluntas haec Dei arcana, licet non raro etiam cum voluntate manifestata, & cum nostra etiam concurrat, non est tamen regula nostrarum actionum, quia nobis incognita, nisi quantum per specialem revelationem, vel eventum manifestatur. Non licet ergo hac fiducia vel legem cœlibatûs accipere, vel eundem vovere.
units.tr: XXI. For as to their insistence that God's promises, that he will hear those who ask and open to those who knock, are true, they are surely in vain. For the gift of continence is not common to all believers, but belongs particularly and peculiarly to some; we have shown above that it is a charisma. But such gifts are not given by God to all, not even to those who pray and fast. Just as the gifts of tongues, knowledge, prophecy, healings and miracles are not obtained by every believer, however earnestly he prays and however much he fasts. Nor will any rustic, with the most sought-after prayers and fastings, certainly obtain that he become a prophet, a king, or a very rich man. Therefore those promises are foolishly used to veil the rashness of those who, as if they held God bound and pledged to themselves, promise themselves whatever they like, and, relying on that confidence, dare everything, even beyond their strength. For God hears no prayers except those poured out in true faith. But faith resting on God does not look at what he is able to do, but considers what he wills. And he knows for certain that he wills something only when he has either promises or a special necessity of calling. But neither of these is present here, since the office of presbyter does not necessarily require continence, and there is no one who has heard it promised. Nor is it established for anyone what God has decreed about him, or whether God would rather use his work for the propagation of mankind. Therefore a prayer for perpetual celibacy, without the condition of the one praying, will never be a faithful prayer; and so there is no certain hope of being heard. Finally, the rule for the trust we ought to have, that in such matters we will be heard, is the hidden will of God: that is, we shall certainly be heard then, when we ask in such a way that we nevertheless depend on his decrees and submit our desires to his will, according to Christ's precept, which bids us pray: "Thy will be done." But this hidden will of God, although it often agrees with his revealed will and with ours, is not nevertheless a rule of our actions, since it is unknown to us, except as far as it is made manifest by special revelation or by the outcome. It is therefore not lawful, on the strength of this confidence, either to take up the law of celibacy or to vow it.

units.la: XXII. Sed Monachorum inprimis & vota, & vita, & ɑ̈γɑ̈γὴ omnis, & iners, quem exercent, cultus ad impuritatem quamvis ducatum præbent. Pone enim (liceat sic cum Theologo Anglo percelebri, Henrico Moro Myst. Iniq. lib. ɥ. cap. 12: 3. argutari) ordinem hominum, eum-que numerosum, qui lautè opiparéque vescantur, edant bibantque ex potissimis, qui otiosam vitam degant, alienisque laboribus vititent, qui nec subtilia, mirèque efascinantia Philosophiæ studia, nobilissimaque speculationis, prosequantur, quibus superfluas corporis vires minuant, Spiritúsque suos exhauriant, nec se ullis penetrantioribus Devotionis angoribus fatigent, sed tumultuario tantùm ac festinatorio modo preculas suas, tanquam externum quoddam officium, obeant, in quibus, si intelligantur, parum fortassis occurrit, quod ita animum assiciat, ut corpus quoquam modo conficiat, aut subdomet; pone, inquam, hos homines, quamvis satis habiles sint ac idonei ad opera virilitatis, voto inviolabili (temerè & impudenter non solùm contra legem Dei, sed & propriæ suæ naturæ & constitutionis corporeæ) facto ad cœlibatum perpetuum damnari, quis naturalis potest esse hujus rei eventus, nisi frequentes fornicationes, aut adulteria, atque Sodomitici? Quamobrem Monachi & Sacerdotes, & quicunque alii, qui huic legi in hujusmodi circumstantiis alligantur, non possunt, nisi per miraculum, quin conentur saltem transgredi, si non crebrò revera Naturæ ac Dei leges transgrediuntur, orbémque Christianum putidissimo fumo ac vapore spurcitiarum suarum implent. Et verisimile est, eos prædam suam facilius reperire posse inter fœminas consimili voto obstrictas, si ipsæ etiam supponerentur naturalis sui ingenii ac temperamenti sponte se obtulisse.
units.tr: XXII. But above all the vows, the way of life, and the whole conduct [ἀγωγή] of the monks, and the idle worship they practise, lead to impurity. Suppose (I may argue thus with the well-known English theologian Henry More, Myst. Iniq. lib. 6, cap. 12: 3.) a large class of men who eat and drink lavishly and well, of the finest food and drink, who live an idle life, shirk the labours of others, and never pursue the subtle and enchanting studies of philosophy or the noblest contemplation, by which they might wear down their excess bodily strength and exhaust their spirits. Suppose they never tire themselves with any deep anxieties of devotion, but perform their prayers in a hurried and careless way, as a kind of outward duty, in which, even if they are understood, there is perhaps little that stirs the mind enough to wear down or subdue the body in any way. Suppose, I say, that these men, though quite able and fit for the works of manhood, are condemned by an inviolable vow to lifelong celibacy, a vow made rashly and shamelessly, not only against the law of God but also against their own nature and bodily constitution. What natural outcome can there be of this, except frequent fornications, adulteries, and sodomy? Therefore monks, priests, and all others who are bound to this law in such circumstances cannot, unless by a miracle, avoid at least attempting to break it, and if they do not often actually break the laws of nature and of God, they fill the Christian world with the most foul smoke and vapour of their filthiness. And it is likely that they could more easily find their prey among women bound by the same vow, if these too were supposed to have offered themselves willingly by their own natural disposition and temperament, or had at last been driven into the monasteries by the tricks and importunate solicitations of others. But let us suppose these women are kept more carefully secluded. Yet the world is wide open enough, and if what is commonly said is true, "She is chaste whom nobody has asked," then surely these men, being so well trained and devoting almost all their time to such arts and schemes, will not find it hard to win their prey. Nor is there any need to devise opportunities, since in some places they are offered to them freely by their religious office, as in the private hearing of auricular confession. So he writes, not merely guiding souls [ψυχαγωγῶν], but truly divining.

units.la: Tom. II. ss obtulisse, aut dolis importunisque aliorum solicitationibus vitæ in Monasteria tandem concessisse. Verùm supponamus, has magis custoditè seclusas esse. Mundus tamen satis latè patens est, & si verum est, quod vulgò dicitur, Casta est, quam nemo rogavit; illis certè cùm tam bene instructi sint, totisque ferè isthiusmodi artibus & machinationibus vacent, haud est difficile prædam consequi. Neque opus est, ut opportunitates excogitentur, cùm in aliquibus partibus, suæ religiosæ functionis ultro ipsis offerantur, ut in auricularis confessionis auditione privata. Hæc ille, non ψυχαγωγῶν[?] nudè, sed verè divinans.
units.tr: Vol. II. ...or had at last been driven into the monasteries by the tricks and importunate solicitations of others. But let us suppose these women are kept more carefully secluded. Yet the world is wide open enough, and if what is commonly said is true, "She is chaste whom nobody has asked," then surely these men, being so well trained and devoting almost all their time to such arts and schemes, will not find it hard to win their prey. Nor is there any need to devise opportunities, since in some places they are offered to them freely by their religious office, as in the private hearing of auricular confession. Thus he writes.

units.la: XXIII. Summum ac inevitabile, quod lege & voto Cœlibatûs constrictis plerisque impendere impuritatis periculum ostendimus, augent non parùm Cœlibatûs immodica, quæ Monachi impuri, non sine matrimonii contumelia, decantare solent encomia. Sic enim apud pessimos quosque externæ professionis typho inflatos, virtus laudatur & alget. In universum ergo Cœlibatum sua natura & intrinseca ratione, non respectu finis, commodi & utilitatis tantùm, matrimonio honestiorem, sanctiorem, excellentiorem esse, tuentur. In iis equidem, quibus datum est se continere, Cœlibatum conjugio ratione συμφέρον, commodi & utilitatis multiplicis præferendum esse Apostolus 1. Cor. vii. toto clarè testatur. Cæterùm sic Hierarchici cœlibatum conjugio præferunt, ut eum prædicent opus sua natura melius, sanctius, honestius conjugio, satisfactorium pro peccatis, meritorium remissionis peccatorum tum propriorum, tum alienorum, uti quidem ex formula absolutionis Monasticæ, Rosario Bernhardini, Theologorum multifariis scriptis cognoscitur. Per cœlibatum supererogari docent. Ipsa opera in cœlibatu facta minima, qualia sunt sedere, stare &c. præferunt operibus maximis in conjugio ex præscripto tabulæ utriusque factis, uti idem Rosarium illud testificatur. Addunt insuper Cœlibatûs encomiastæ, plenísque buccis decantant, votivam, non aliam virginitatem, veram virginitatem esse: ejusdem originem à Novo demum Testamento, Christo & authore & cœlibe eodem arcessendam esse: esse eum opus persectionis Euangelicæ, denique statum cœlestem Angelicum, imò Divinum: Cœlibes esse genuinos Martyres: solum cœlibatum dignum fuisse, unde nasceretur Salvator mundi: Cœlibes eximia & peculiari ratione esse Templa Dei; aliáque ejusmodi non pauca, quæ à vicino quopiam rapsodo corrasa & impotenter satis impudentérque jactata Parthenogam. cap. 4. ad partes vocata hèic vel recensere singula, vel censere supersedemus.
units.tr: XXIII. The great and unavoidable danger of impurity that we have shown to threaten most of those bound by the law and vow of celibacy is greatly increased by the excessive praises of celibacy, which impure monks, not without insult to marriage, are accustomed to sing. For among the worst men, puffed up with the pride of an outward profession, virtue is praised yet remains cold. In general, they maintain that celibacy is, by its own nature and inherent reason, not merely in respect of end, advantage and usefulness, more honourable, holier and more excellent than marriage. Indeed, to those to whom it has been given to contain themselves, the Apostle clearly testifies throughout 1 Cor. 7 that celibacy is to be preferred to marriage in respect of advantage [συμφέρον], convenience and usefulness, which is manifold. But the hierarchs prefer celibacy to marriage in such a way that they proclaim it, by its nature, a work better, holier and more honourable than marriage, satisfactory for sins, and meritorious for the forgiveness of sins, both of one's own and of others. This is known from the formula of monastic absolution, from the Rosary of Bernardino, and from the many writings of the theologians. They teach that through celibacy works of supererogation are performed. They rank the smallest works done in celibacy, such as sitting, standing, and so on, above the greatest works done in marriage under the prescribed rule of both, as that same Rosary attests. The encomiasts of celibacy add further, and sing with puffed cheeks, that the votive virginity, and no other, is true virginity; that its origin must be sought in the New Testament, from Christ himself, its author and celibate; that it is the work of evangelical perfection, and finally a heavenly, angelic, indeed divine state; that the celibates are the genuine martyrs; that only celibacy was worthy to be the birthplace of the Saviour of the world; that celibates are, in an outstanding and special way, the temples of God; and many other things of this kind, which some noisy rhapsodist has gathered and boastfully and rather shamelessly proclaimed in Parthenogam. cap. 4. We pass over here, without listing or judging each of them, as they are not relevant to our purpose.

units.la: XXIV. Atque hæc non possunt non in Matrimonii Divinitus instituti dedecus vergere. Sed graviora etiam sunt probra, quibus Conjugium μισόγαμοι hi, sed haud minùs φιλήδονοι, vix Manichæis, Priscillianistis, Encratitis veteribus clementius proscindunt. Siricius, de cujus tum imperitia Hieronymus Epist. 16. tum superbia Paulinus Epist. j. graviter olim questi sunt, Epist. j. ad Himerium cap. 7. conjugium, ceu carnalem statum, damnavit; ad legem novellam cœlibatûs à se impiè rogatam detorquens verba S. Pauli Rom. viii. 8. Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Vos autem, sic infert, jam non in carne, sed in Spiritu, si tamen Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Alibi Epist. 4. cap. 9. Presbyteris matrimonium prohibet eo scilicet argumento, quòd juxta S. Paulum Tit. 1. 14. coinquinatis & infidelibus nihil mundum sit. Quadere, subjicit, hortor, moneo, rogo, tollatur hoc opprobrium, quod potest jure etiam gentilitas accusare. Idem C. Quia dist. 82. Presbyterorum cum propriis uxoribus commercium obscœnas libidines appellat. Innocentius II.
units.tr: XXIV. These things cannot but redound to the disgrace of marriage, which was instituted by God. Yet even graver are the insults with which these haters of marriage, μισόγαμοι, but no less lovers of pleasure [φιλήδονοι], assail it, hardly more gently than the ancient Manichaeans, Priscillianists and Encratites. Siricius, whose ignorance Jerome Ep. 16. and whose pride Paulinus Ep. 1. once complained of with severity, condemned marriage as a carnal state, Ep. 1. to Himerius, chap. 7. twisting to the new law of celibacy, which he had impiously imposed, the words of St Paul, Rom. 8:8, Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you, he goes on, are no longer in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Elsewhere, Ep. 4, chap. 9, he forbids marriage to elders, on the argument, of course, that according to St Paul, Tit. 1:14, nothing is clean to the defiled and unbelieving. He adds, I exhort, warn and beg that this reproach be removed, which even the Gentiles could justly accuse us of. In the same way, C. Quia dist. 82, he calls the intercourse of elders with their own wives obscene lusts. Innocent II...

units.la: tum continuo monia... (marginal notes, partly illegible) tius II. dist. 28. C. decernimus haud mollius: Cernimus, inquit, ut ii, qui in ordine subdiaconatus & supra uxores duxerint, aut concubinas habuerint, officio atque Ecclesiastico beneficio careant. Cùm enim ipsi Templum, vasa Domini & sacrarium Spiritus S. debeant esse & dici, indignum est (NB) cubilibus & immunditiis deservire. Quid verò multis? Baronius A. 1074. n. 34. petulantibus verbis sic conjugium incessit: Conjugii turpitudine, reti Diaboli tenebantur adstricti clerici conjugati. Bellarminus quoque de Monach. lib. ÿ. 30. pertendit, Religiosos votum continentiæ nubendo violare, non violare fornicando. Et tralatitia, sed Gomorrhæ quàm Christianæ similior vox est, præstare ut cœlibes votivi urantur, fornicentur, adulteria, ac mirica scelera patrent, quàm ut nubant, quæ aliaque similia Parthenog. cap. a. fusius demonstrata hèic ad compendium pono.
units.tr: ...Innocent II, dist. 28, C. decernimus, is no milder: "We decree," he says, "that those who, in the order of subdeacon and above, have taken wives or kept concubines, shall be deprived of office and of ecclesiastical benefice. For since they ought to be and be called the temple, the vessels of the Lord and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, it is unworthy (NB) that they should serve beds and uncleanness." But why say more? Baronius, A. 1074, n. 34, attacked marriage in wanton words: married clergy were held bound in the net of the Devil by the shame of marriage. Bellarmine too, de Monachis, lib. 3, 30, maintains that religious who break their vow of continence by marrying violate it, but not by fornicating. And the commonplace, though it sounds more like Gomorrah than Christendom, is that it is better for votive celibates to burn, fornicate, commit adultery and perform monstrous crimes than to marry. These and similar matters are demonstrated more fully in Parthenog. cap. a.; I here set them down in brief.

units.la: XXV. Cùm ergo sic matrimonium Hierarchici pipulo differant, atque infra cœlibatum contumeliosè deprimant, quin & apud quosvis dono continentiæ sive præditos sive destitutos, voto cœlibatûs perpetui, seu prudente seu imprudente obstrictos fornicationes, adulteria, & horribilia quævis carnalis impuritatis scelera matrimonio potiora ducant, atque eadem ratione unicum post Dei gratiam adversus fornicationes vagasque libidines remedium matrimonium scilicet abipso Deo institutum, & ab Apostolo fornicationi & incontinentiæ oppositum, voti nulla juris vel Divini vel humani legitimi necessitate, nulla pietate nuncupati, prætextu, tot hominum, quos pollere continentiæ dono minimùm illi ignorant, myriadibus eripiant, latam adeò non modò fenestram, sed portam fornicationibus, adulteriis, aliisque nec nominandis quidem flagitiis eosdem aperire conficimus merito: Ut hic quoque illud Bernhardi Serm. 66. in Cantic. valeat: Tolle de Ecclesia clesia honorabile connubium & thorum immaculatum, nonne reples eam concubinariis, incestuosis, seminifluis, mollibus, masculorum concubitoribus, & omni genere immundorum. Quod non minus verum est de parte Ecclesiæ, clero quàm populo.
