Cujus rei addere possumus testem experientiam, ex qua constat, cœlibatûs vota & tam austeram legem pridem degenerâsse in fœdos concubitus passivæ Veneris, ut qui non possunt legitimas uxores, habeant saltem prostitutas mulieres, focarias & concubinas, imò ipsi suum pudorem prostituant.
units.tr: XXV. Since the hierarchs thus differ from marriage so little, and thus contemptuously depress it below celibacy, and since they esteem fornications, adulteries and every horrible crime of carnal impurity above marriage, whether among those who are gifted with the gift of continence or those who lack it, and bound by a perpetual vow of celibacy, whether prudently or imprudently taken, and since they snatch the one remedy against fornications and wandering lusts, after the grace of God, namely marriage, instituted by God himself and set by the Apostle against fornication and incontinence, from myriads of men, who scarcely know that they possess the gift of continence, under the pretext of a vow sworn without any necessity of either divine or lawful human right, and without any piety, we rightly conclude that they open not merely a wide window but a door to fornications, adulteries, and crimes not even to be named. So here too the saying of Bernard, Serm. 66 on the Canticles, holds good: Take away from the Church honourable marriage and the undefiled bed, and does it not fill it with concubinaries, incestuous persons, masturbators, effeminate men, male prostitutes and every kind of unclean person? This is no less true of the part of the Church that is clergy than of the people. To this we may add the witness of experience, from which it is clear that the vows of celibacy and so austere a law have long since degenerated into foul intercourse of passive Venus, so that those who cannot have lawful wives keep at least prostitutes, housekeepers and concubines, and even prostitute their own shame.

units.la: XXVI. Ejusmodi necessitatem per interdictum conjugii usum introduci vidit & agnovit Joh. Gerson de vita Spirit. animæ Lect. iv. Coroll. 14. propos. 3. Cùm enim memorâsset Thomam aliosque dicere, peccare eos, qui à Sacerdotibus fornicariis missam audiunt, subjungit: Inexperti forte erant hi doctores, quàm generale, & quàm radicatum sit hoc malum, & quomodo deteriora flagitia circa uxores aut filias parochianorum, & abominationes horrendæ in aliis provenirent apud multos patrios, rebus stantibus ut stant, si quærerentur per tales censuras arceri. Scandalum certè magnum est apud Parochianos Curati ad concubinam ingressus, sed longè deterius, si erga parochianas suas non servaverit castitatem. Idem Gerson dialogum Naturæ & Sophiæ de Cœlibatu Ecclesiasticorum, quasi castitatem eorum desperans, concludit dicendo, quòd de duobus malis minus est, incontinentes tolerare Sacerdotes, quàm nullos habere. Scilicet vir ille neque malus, neque stupidus, non videbat, nihil necesse esse, ut ad ista extrema aut nullos aut incontinentes Sacerdotes habendi deveniatur. Datur enim medium, sive remedium, nempe ut honestum conjugium cuivis, qui continere nolit aut nequeat, permittatur. Eos verò, quibus castitas ab ipso Spiritu S. commendata sordet, justo Dei judicio ad veras sordes & flagitiosam immunditiem prolabi, nihil mirum est. Albertus Pighius Controv. 15. sub init. hanc ipsam controversiam tractans, Sacerdotii vilitas, ait, contemptus & irreverentia apud populum primùm ex multitudine nimia; deinde ex indignitate & postremò ex vita palam scelerata scandalosaque multorum hujus sacratissimi ordinis mihi pendere videtur. Et post pauca: Hu colophonem addidit, ut diximus, vita publicè scandalosa plurimorum ac palam incontinens, & huic indignitati ac malo fastigium, ac supremam, ut sic dicam, manum imposuit. Dominicus Soto de just. lib. vij. q. 6. a. 1. Fatemur, ait, castitatis votum non esse observatu facile, Sacerdotumque ordinem Ecclesiæ necessarium perquam numerosum esse. Et agnoscimus insuper in privatis ædibus non usque adeò tutò servari posse ejusmodi votum, quàm in Monachorum claustris. Neque verò inficias imus, crebros esse in clero concubinarios & adulteros. Sed hanc in rem longè plura & diserertiora sub finem testimonia producemus. Et vel solus concubinatus Sacerdotum, lupanarium habendorum, & canonum relaxandorum necessitas, de quibus paulò post, passivam illam Cleri impuritatem invictè demonstrat.
units.tr: XXVI. John Gerson saw and acknowledged that this kind of necessity brought in the use of marriage through the prohibition of it. In On the Life of the Spirit of the Soul, Lecture 4, Corollary 14, Proposition 3, after recalling that Thomas and others said that those who hear Mass from fornicating priests sin, he adds: Perhaps these teachers did not know how widespread and deep-rooted this evil is, and how, if things remained as they are and were to be checked only by such censures, worse crimes involving the wives or daughters of parishioners, and horrible abominations, would arise among many people in their homeland. It is certainly a great scandal among the parishioners when a parish priest takes a concubine, but it is far worse if he has not kept chastity towards his own female parishioners. In his dialogue between Nature and Wisdom on the celibacy of the clergy, Gerson also concludes, as if he had given up hope of their chastity, by saying: that of two evils it is less bad to tolerate incontinent priests than to have none at all. Clearly that man, who was neither wicked nor foolish, did not see that there is no need to reach these extremes of having either no priests or incontinent ones. For there is a middle way, or remedy, namely that honourable marriage be permitted to anyone who does not wish or is not able to contain himself. As for those whom the Holy Spirit himself has commended chastity to, yet who despise it, it is no wonder that by the just judgment of God they slip into real filth and shameful uncleanness. Albertus Pighius, treating this very controversy in Controversy 15, near the beginning, says: The worthlessness of the priesthood, the contempt and irreverence it meets with among the people, seem to me to arise first from its excessive numbers, then from the unworthiness of many of its members, and finally from the openly wicked and scandalous lives of many in this most sacred order. And a little later: As I said, a publicly scandalous life, and that of many who are openly incontinent, has put the crown and, as it were, the final touch on this unworthiness and evil. Dominicus Soto, On Justice, Book 7, Question 6, Article 1, says: We admit that the vow of chastity is not easily kept, and that the order of priests, which is necessary to the Church, is very numerous. We acknowledge too that such a vow cannot be kept so safely in private houses as in the cloisters of monks. Nor do we deny that adulterers and concubinaries are frequent among the clergy. But we shall produce far more, and more explicit, testimonies on this point towards the end. Indeed the concubinage of priests alone, and the need to maintain brothels and relax the canons, of which more shortly, clearly demonstrate that passive impurity of the clergy.

units.la: XXVII. De Sacerdotum concubinatu multa equidem dici possent. Id sanè Pontificia doctrina & tyrannide essectum est, ut quàm inter laicos receptus est conjugii usus, tàm frequentes inter clericos sint [?]scortationes, ut videri jam olim potuerit sanctione publica decretum, quemadmodum laici conjugati plurimum sint, ita clericos concubinarios esse oportere. Memorat Sleidanus lib. iij. Hist. vigente Papatu apud Helvetios in nonnullis pagis hunc fuisse morem, quum uxorem quempiam ecclesiæ ministrum reciperent, ut juberent eum habere concubinam, ne pudicitiam alienam tentaret. Is gentis candor erat. Nicolaus Clemangis de corr. Eccl. statu cap. 15. crudè satis: Jam illud, lud, obsecro, quale est, quòd plerisque in diœcesibus, Rectores Parochiarum, ex certo & conducto cum suis Prælatis pretio, passim & publicè concubinas tenent. Idem cap. 20. Quid enim de Capellanis & Canonicis longum me trahere sermonem necesse est, cùm uno verbo dicere liceat, similes Episcoporum pro suo modo canonicos esse. Et post: Adhuc autem ebrios, incontinentissimos, utpote qui passim & inverecundè prolem ex meretrice susceptam, & scorta vice coniugum domi habeant. Johannes Chemnensis Episcopus in Onere Ecclesiæ cap. 23. Sacerdotes, inquit, fornicationibus coinquinantur: maximè Curati scor descunt in concubinatu adeò manifesto, quòd nulla tergiversatione celari possit. Principes & Proceres Imperii, testes omni exceptione majores, inter Gravamina, quibus in Comitiis Norinbergæ A. M. D. XXII. celebratis Germaniam levari flagitabant, hæc quoque Grav. 75. & 91. proposuerunt: Officiales-Clericos religiosósque accepto ab eisdem annuo censu, publicè cum suis concubinis, pellicibus & aliis id genus meretricibus illegitimè cohabitare, liberósque procreare sinunt. Quæ res quantum scandali, periculi, detrimenti animabus & corporibus pariat, non est quod recensetur, cùm nemo id, nisi talpa cæcutiat magis, non videat. Item: In locis plerisque Episcopi & eorum officiales non solùm Sacerdotum tolerant concubinatum, dummodo certa persolvatur pecunia, sed & Sacerdotes continentes, & qui absque concubinis degunt, concubinatûs censum persolvere cogunt, afferentes, Episcopum pecuniæ indigum esse, quâ soluta licere Sacerdotibus, ut vel cœlibes permaneant, vel concubinas alant. Quàm res hæc sit nefanda, nemo non intelligit. In Concilio Tridentino Orator Alberti Bavariæ Ducis Oratione, quæ inter oppuscula Dudithii extat: inter alia dixit: Clerus noster tantùs Ecclesiæ calamitatibus nullo modo neque afficitur, neque affligitur, sed multò magis insolescit, gulæ libidinibúsque indulget. Et post: In proxima visitatione per Bavariam facta, tam frequens concubinatus repertus fuit, ut vix inter centum tres vel quatuor inventi sint, qui aut manifesti concubinarii non fuerint, aut clandestine matrimonia non contraxerint, aut uxores palam non duxerint. Claudius Espencæus in Tit. cap. 1. Turpissimum, inquit, quòd & hos cum concubinis, pellicibus & meretriculis cohabitare, liberósque procreare sinunt, accepto ab eis, atque adeò alicubi à continentibus certo quotannis censu. Habeat, ajunt, si velit. Et quotus enim quisque talis, cùm tales tamen tam multi sint, hodie aliter punitur?
units.tr: XXVII. Much could indeed be said about the concubinage of priests. Papal doctrine and tyranny have brought it about that, just as the use of marriage is accepted among the laity, so fornication is so frequent among the clergy that it could be thought, by public decree, that clergy must have concubines just as laymen are mostly married. Sleidan, Book 3 of his History, records that under the Papacy among the Swiss in some villages it was the custom that, when they received some minister of the Church as husband, they ordered him to keep a concubine, lest he tempt another's chastity. Such was the candour of that people. Nicolas Clamanges, On the Corruption of the State of the Church, chapter 15, puts it rather bluntly: Now, I beg you, what is this, that in most dioceses parish rectors openly keep concubines for a fixed and contracted price agreed with their prelates? The same, chapter 20: Why need I drag out a discourse about chaplains and canons, when in one word it may be said that they are, in their own fashion, like the canons of the bishops? And after: Moreover, they are drunkards and utterly incontinent, since they openly and shamelessly keep at home children born of harlots and whores in place of wives. John, bishop of Chemnitz, in The Burden of the Church, chapter 23: Priests, he says, are defiled by fornication; above all parish priests are stained by concubinage so manifest that it cannot be hidden by any evasion. The princes and nobles of the Empire, witnesses beyond all objection, in the grievances which they demanded be removed from Germany at the Diet held at Nuremberg in 1522, also set forth these points, Grievances 75 and 91: The officials allow clerics and religious, for an annual sum received from them, to live openly and illegitimately with their concubines, mistresses and other such harlots, and to beget children. How much scandal, danger and harm this brings to souls and bodies there is no need to list, since no one can fail to see it unless he is blinder than a mole. Likewise: In most places bishops and their officials not only tolerate the concubinage of priests provided a set sum is paid, but they even compel continent priests, and those who live without concubines, to pay a concubinage tax, claiming that the bishop is in need of money, and that once it is paid priests may remain celibate or keep concubines. Everyone understands how wicked this matter is. At the Council of Trent, the envoy of Duke Albert of Bavaria, in a speech found among the minor works of Dudith, said among other things: Our clergy are in no way touched or afflicted by the calamities of the Church, but grow far more insolent and indulge in gluttony and lust. And after: At the most recent visitation made throughout Bavaria, concubinage was found so common that among a hundred scarcely three or four were found who were not either openly concubinaries, or had not contracted secret marriages, or had not openly taken wives. Claude d'Espence, on Titus, chapter 1: It is most shameful that they are allowed to live with concubines, mistresses and little whores and to beget children, for a fee taken from them, and in some places even from the continent, at a fixed yearly rate. "Let him have them," they say, "if he wishes." And yet how many such men are there today who are punished otherwise, when such men are so very many?

units.la: XXVIII. Quantam verò jam putabimus fornicationi existimationem conciliari, quando libertatis ejus exemplum elucescit in iis, qui castitatis, continentiæ, mortificationis cupiditatum carnis exemplaria exquisitissima, typi ducésque immediati gregis & populi esse debuerant? Quando ergo coùsque corruptio & licentia prorumpit, ut Sancti scilicet unctique Dei viri, permissu legum Summi Sacerdotis sui, concubinas, quæ, cùm uxores non sint, tam prope ad scortorum conditionem accedant, quàm quatuor denarii ad drachmam, in complexu delitiisque habeant, necessum est populum universum incentivo tali seductum ad licentiam similem & majorem etiam ruere præcipitem, cùm eum, qui dux comesque itineris ad Cœlum habetur, Meretriculam audacter adeò in contubernium, itinerisque consortium admittere videt. Religio enim Christiana concubinatum & fornicationem uno eodemque censu habet. Oportet enim quemque maritum esse unius uxoris, concubinæ verò neminem; siquidem id à communi sensu Christianæ pietatis abhorret. Juvenes ergo authenticum adeò fornicationis exemplum intuentes cominus in spirituali illo suo Patre, persona tam sacra scilicet, ut ne Magistratus quidem civilis ministro fas sit manus ei admoliri; qui existimatur idoneus pro populo intercessor apud altare supremum in Sancto Sanctorum; cujus solius labia sic sanctificata putantur, ut soli poculum attrectare, deosculari, exhaurire, abstergere liceat; cujus denique adeò omnipotens halitus est, ut verbis quinque demurmuratis Creatorem humani generis creare possit; quid non audebunt ipsi? Annon cum bello illo adolescente in comœdia dicent: Ego homuncio hoc non faciam. Ego verò illud faciam, ac lubens. Adeò potenter invitabuntur omnes eximio Sacerdotis exemplo, animabuntúrque ad turpitudinem in singulis villis, oppidis, civitatibus cujusvis populi patrandam.
units.tr: XXVIII. But what respect for fornication will we think it gains, when its licence shines forth in those who ought to have been the most exquisite examples of chastity, continence and mortification of the lusts of the flesh, and the immediate types and leaders of the flock and people? When corruption and licence break out to such an extent that holy and anointed men of God, with the permission of the laws of their chief priest, keep in their embrace and pleasure concubines who, since they are not wives, come as near to the status of prostitutes as four pennies come to a drachma, then it is inevitable that the whole people, seduced by such an incentive, will rush headlong into a similar and even greater licence, when they see that he who is considered the leader and companion of the journey to heaven boldly admits a little whore into his household and fellowship on the road. For the Christian religion holds concubinage and fornication to be one and the same thing. For each man ought to be the husband of one wife, and of no concubine, since that is abhorrent to the common sense of Christian piety. Young men, then, seeing such a plain example of fornication in their spiritual father, a person so sacred that not even the civil magistrate may lawfully lay hands on a minister, who is thought fit to intercede for the people at the high altar in the Holy of Holies, whose lips alone are believed to be so sanctified that he alone may touch, kiss, drink from and wipe the cup; whose breath, finally, is so almighty that by murmuring five words he can create the Creator of the human race: what will they not dare themselves? Will they not, with that young fellow in the comedy, say: I, a little man, will not do this. But I will do that, and gladly. So powerfully will all be drawn by the notable example of the priest, and so spurred on to commit the shameful deed in every village, town and city of any people.

units.la: XXIX. Bellarminus de Cleric. lib. j. 21. objicienti, quòd Cœlibatus Clericorum prodigiosas libidines pariat, mundum concubinis, & Ecclesiam scandalis repleat; respondet, falsum esse, quòd cœlibatus ista pariat, sed abusus est, inquit, cœlibatús qui ista parit. Si autem propter abusum res bonæ tollendæ essent, Cœlum & terra etiam tollenda essent. Ineptè dictum, si quid aliud. Abusus enim supponit & includit usum abstractè loquendo, hoc est, rem, de qua agitur, applicari ad praxin, sive opus aliquod. Si rectè applicatur, bonus & legitimus usus est; secus abusus. Quis autem dixerit, cœlibes, dum fornicantur, cœlibatum suum ad praxin & opus transferre? Cœlibatus quidem est status vitæ extra matrimonium; quæ degitur vel continenter; quomodo idem fuerit quod continentia & status continentiæ: vel incontinenter; qualis cœlibatus impurus & prosanus est, Christiano nomine indignus, nec verè propriéque cœlibatus, sed scortationis status appellandus. Qui ergo scortatur, & libidinibus indulget, eo ipso sicut continens, ita cœlebs quoque, secundùm propriam acceptionem appellari & esse definit; adeóqne neque continentia, neque
units.tr: XXIX. Bellarminus, De Cleric. lib. I. cap. 21, answers the objection that clerical celibacy produces monstrous lusts and fills the world with concubines and the Church with scandals, by saying that it is false that celibacy produces these things, but it is the abuse of celibacy that produces them. If, however, good things were to be removed on account of abuse, heaven and earth would have to be removed too. It is badly said, if anything ever was. For, speaking abstractly, abuse presupposes and includes use: that is, the thing in question is applied to practice or some action. If it is applied rightly, it is good and lawful use; otherwise it is abuse. But who would say that celibates, while they fornicate, are carrying their celibacy into practice and action? Celibacy is indeed a state of life outside marriage, and it is lived either continently, in which case it is the same as continence and a state of continence, or incontinently. Such impure and profane celibacy is unworthy of the Christian name, and is not truly and properly celibacy but should be called a state of fornication. Therefore whoever fornicates and indulges his lusts, by that very fact ceases to be called and to be, in the proper sense, continent and likewise celibate. He therefore does not abuse either continence or celibacy, but loses both entirely.

units.la: Tom. II. que cœlibatu abutitur; sed & illam & hunc penitus amittit. Hujus autem prægrandis & enormis peccati inter clericos Pontificios frequentis adeò causa est temerarium continentiæ propositum, seu lex cœlibatûs indifferenter omnibus Ecclesiæ ministrantibus imposita. Causa, inquam, est, quæ removet prohibens. Conjugium enim incontinentiæ & ustionis adæquata, sive, ut Medici loquuntur, appropriata est medicina, per quam fit, ut ardor restinguatur, & legitimè agatur, quod alioquin ageretur vitiosè & nequiter. Prohibet ergo vagas & damnandas libidines. At temerarium continentiæ propositum, & lex universalis cœlibatûs salutarem hanc & Divinitus datam medicinam amovent & secludunt. Si grassante pestilenti lue alexipharmacon in promptu esset, quo adhibito contagium cessaret, & tuti homines præstarentur, alioqui periturî; qui hujusmodi ἀλεξίφαρμακον removeret, is profectò interitus hominum causa esset. Sic planè scortationum & flagitiorum causa est, qui incontinentibus matrimonium interdicit.
units.tr: Tom. II. The cause of this very great and enormous sin, which is common among the Papist clergy, is the rash resolution of continence, or the law of celibacy imposed indiscriminately on all who minister in the Church. The cause, I say, is that which removes what prevents. For marriage is the remedy suited to incontinence and burning, or, as physicians say, the appropriate medicine, through which the ardour is quenched and what would otherwise be done wickedly and vilely is done lawfully. It therefore prevents vagrant and damnable lusts. But the rash resolution of continence and the universal law of celibacy remove and shut out this wholesome medicine, given by God. If, when a deadly plague was raging, there were an antidote at hand by which the contagion would cease and men would be kept safe who otherwise would perish, whoever removed such an antidote [ἀλεξίφαρμακον] would surely be the cause of men's deaths. In just this way, he who forbids marriage to the incontinent is the cause of fornications and shameful deeds.

units.la: XXX. Frustra etiam Hierarchici clamant, neminem à se vel ad vovendum, vel ad suscipiendum cœlibatum cogi.
units.tr: XXX. In vain also do the hierarchs cry out that no one is compelled by them either to vow celibacy or to undertake it.

units.la: Satis enim est, quòd vota, quæ circa res in potestate ventis non positas, impietate & temeritate haud vacant, apud quosvis laudant, approbant, commendant; & singulare continentiæ donum precibus & jejuniis à quovis impetrari posse, pertendunt. Qua ratione miseris laqueos aperte struunt; idque non amore ullo castitatis, sed quæstûs duntaxat & commodi Hierarchiæ suæ, cujus arcanum & palladium quoddam votivum Cœlibatum esse, Parthenog. cap. 6. clarissimè probavimus. Tum neminem patiuntur ordinari nisi hac lege, ut perpetuò contineat; & neminem cogunt? Nimirum, inquiunt, neminem cogimus ad suscipiendos ordines; si quis tamen suscipere ultrò voluerit, hunc cœlibem vivere volumus, jubemus. Inventum scilicet acutissimum! Quasi dicant latrones, neminem se vi spoliare, quia neminem cogant peregrinari; sed eum duntaxat, qui sponte sua peregrinatur, invadant. Imò verò cogunt eos in cœlibatu vivere, qui ordinari & Ecclesiæ inservire volunt: quomodo latrones vere spoliant eos, qui sponte se itineri committunt. Rectè igitur Polydorus coactam castitatem vocat. Quanquam quid fit iis, qui inviti fiunt presbyteri, & seducti illecebris subdolorum verborum continentiam decepti, imprudentes, & non raro poenitudine ducti, voverunt? Hoscine ad continentiam coactos inficiabuntur? An etiam illos, quos jussit Hildebrandus uxores abjicere in Germania, Anglia, Gallia, quas retinuerant, cùm ordinarentur?
units.tr: It is enough that they praise, approve and commend, among anyone at all, vows concerning things not within our power, vows that are not free of impiety and rashness; and they maintain that the singular gift of continence can be obtained from anyone by prayers and fasting. By this reasoning they openly lay snares for the wretched, and they do so not out of any love of chastity but merely for the profit and advantage of their hierarchy, whose secret and palladium, as it were, is votive celibacy, as we have most clearly proved in Parthenog. cap. 6. Then they allow no one to be ordained except on this condition, that he remain continent for ever, and yet they compel no one? Certainly, they say, we compel no one to receive orders; but if anyone is willing to receive them of his own accord, we want and order him to live as a celibate. A most acute invention, indeed! It is as if robbers should say they do not rob anyone by force, because they compel no one to travel, but only attack the one who travels of his own accord. Indeed they compel those who wish to be ordained and serve the Church to live in celibacy, just as robbers truly despoil those who willingly commit themselves to the road. Rightly, then, Polydorus calls it coactam castitatem, compelled chastity. And what of those who become presbyters against their will, and who, seduced by the allurements of deceitful words and deceived about continence, took the vow thoughtlessly and often out of regret? Will they deny that these were compelled to continence? Or those whom Hildebrand ordered to cast off the wives they had kept in Germany, England and France when they were ordained?

units.la: XXXI. Ipsam Hierarchicorum functionem sacram concipiendæ & fovendæ impuritati ansam præbere posse, haud immeritò diximus. Testis ejus rei locuples est secreta, seu auricularis confessio, & ad eandem confessariorum præparatio & instructio, quæ non aliud est, quàm μελέτην ἀσκήσεως studium & exercitatio impudentiæ, quæ tangitur haud dubie 2 Tim. iii. 6. 7. Pudor prohibet scandalosissimas quæstiones, quas apud Toletum, Angelum de Clavasio, Sanchez, Navarrum, Benedictum, Burchardum, Azorium alios Casuistæ Confessariis injungunt. Puduit impudentiæ hujus ipsum Melchiorem Canum, qui Relect. de Pœnit. p. 6. ex summis Confessionum, quæ publicè prostant, non confitendi, sed peccandi rationem & normam didici, fatetur. Planè constat, Casuistarum Confessarios informantium chartas, quæ verecundiæ ac sanctimoniæ plenæ esse debuerant, priscis Elephantidos libellis, & nuperis perditorum Italorum voluminibus obscœniores esse; in quibus, velut in lupanarium scriniis, omnes turpitudines species ac modi, etiam qui nullo apud flagitiosissimos in usu fortasse sunt, exquisitè descripti continentur. Non meo, sed Petri Aurelii, Viri in Romana communione gravissimi, judicio Sanchezii densum, quod de matrimonio inscribitur, opus premam. Opus est, sic ille Vindic. Censur. Facult. Parisi. pag. 517. scribit, non gloriandum, sed pudendum tam immani curiositate, tam invisa in rebus spurcissimis, & infandis, & monstrosis, & Diabolicis perscrutandis sagacitate horrendum, ut mirum sit, pudoris alicujus hominem sine rubore scripsisse, quae quivis modestioris ingenii vix sine rubore legat. Portenta ista sunt, non scripta; animarum insidiae, non mentium subsidia; incentiva libidinum, schola flagitiorum, non honestae disciplinae, non scientiae Christianae instrumenta. Infelix scientia, quae omnes perdere, paucos juvare apta nata est; quae circa sordes & sterquilinia volvenda & revolvenda volutatur, ut ejus doctorem jure cum Scarabaeo conferas, vel cum iis, qui latrinariam facitant, vel qui ejus artis fusissima volumina graphicè conscribenda suscipiunt. Quanquam eò illud tetrius & odiosius est, quia corporum faeces molestiam & turpitudinem breviorem habent; illa animorum purgamenta, illa venereae totius sentinae indagatio, & ante legentium oculos effusio, non foeditatis modò permultùm, sed periculi & perniciei multò amplius vehit, quò animi vel ipsa insufitata & inaudita turpitudinis novitate moveantur. Castigata dein Jesuitarum Granatensium, qui operi huic obscoeniissimo infinita cum laude authoris praefati sunt, dictitantes etiam, neminem superiori Seculo dubias de Matrimonio controversias uberius & limatius, quàm iflum, enodàsse, impudentia, equidem, inquit pag. 518. si de uberrima & subtilissima spurcitiarum omnigenarum ventilatione agitur, nemo unquam eam laudem Thomae Sanchez eripiet; quin omnium primus Sacramentum matrimonii, cum tanta cogitationum sermonisque licentia, imaginatione potiùs quàm judicio duce versavit, quantam ante ipsum Ecclesia ab initio Christiani nominis nec viderat, nec audiverat. Modestiores semper fuerunt Ecclesiastici tractatores, non obliti Apostoli vocem: Fornicatio & omnis immunditia, &c. ne nominetur in vobis. Nec tanti fecerunt ancipitem istam & periculosam conjugalium arcanorum, flagitiorum, piaculorúmque scientiam. Neque tamen querela isthæc & indignatio pauciorum meliorumque ex communione Romana prohibet, quò minùs multi quotidie apud eos ejusdem furfuris libri, maximè à Jesuitis, artis istius turpissimæ & quæstuosissimæ facilè principibus, nulla verecundiæ habita ratione, edantur.
units.tr: XXXI. We have not said without reason that the very sacred function of the hierarchs can give occasion for conceiving and fostering impurity. The witness to this is abundant: the secret or auricular confession, and the preparation and instruction of confessors for it, which is nothing other than a practice and exercise of impudence [μελέτην ἀσκήσεως], undoubtedly alluded to in 2 Tim. 3. 6, 7. Shame forbids the most scandalous questions which Toletus, Angelus de Clavasio, Sanchez, Navarrus, Benedictus, Burchardus, Azorius and the other casuists enjoin on confessors. Melchior Cano himself was ashamed of this impudence; in Relect. de Poenit. p. 6. he confesses that from the manuals of confession that are publicly sold he learned not how to confess but how to sin. It is plain that the casuists' manuals for confessors, which ought to have been full of modesty and holiness, are more obscene than the old books of Elephantis and the recent volumes of the depraved Italians. In these, as in the cabinets of brothels, every kind of turpitude and every mode, even those perhaps not in use among the most shameless, is set out in exquisite detail. I will not press my own judgment but that of Peter Aurelius, a most serious man within the Roman communion, concerning the dense work of Sanchez entitled On Marriage. "The work is," so he writes in Vindic. Censur. Facult. Parisi. pag. 517, "not something to glory in but to be ashamed of, horrifying in its monstrous curiosity and its hateful acuteness in searching out the filthiest, unspeakable, monstrous and diabolical things, so that it is a wonder a man with any shame could write without blushing what a man of more modest talent could scarcely read without blushing. These are monsters, not writings; snares for souls, not aids for minds; incitements to lust, a school of crimes, not instruments of honest discipline or Christian knowledge. Unhappy is the knowledge that is born fit to destroy all and help few, which rolls and re-rolls itself among filth and dung-heaps, so that its teacher may rightly be compared with the beetle, or with those who empty latrines, or with those who undertake to write out in graphic detail the most extensive volumes of that art. Yet this is all the more foul and odious, because the filth of bodies brings a shorter nuisance and turpitude; but those purgings of souls, that investigation of the whole sewer of Venus and its pouring out before the readers' eyes, carry not only much more foulness but far more danger and ruin, since minds are moved even by the unaccustomed and unheard-of novelty of the turpitude." Then the Granadan Jesuits are rebuked, who prefaced this most obscene work with infinite praise of its author, repeatedly saying that no one in the last century unravelled doubtful controversies about marriage more fully and more finely than he did. "Impudence, indeed," he says, "p. 518. If it is a matter of the most copious and subtle airing of every kind of filth, no one will ever snatch that praise from Thomas Sanchez. Indeed, he was the first to deal with the sacrament of marriage with such licence of thought and speech, guided more by imagination than by judgment, as the Church from the beginning of the Christian name had neither seen nor heard." Ecclesiastical writers were always more modest, not forgetting the Apostle's words: "But fornication and all uncleanness, etc., let it not even be named among you." Nor did they value that dangerous, two-edged knowledge of conjugal secrets, crimes and sins. Nor does this complaint and indignation of a few better men within the Roman communion prevent many books of the same dross from being published there every day, especially by the Jesuits, the easy leaders of that most shameful and profitable art, with no regard for shame.

units.la: XXXII. Quales ergo in latrinaria illa, & venerea sententia, uti Aurelius appellat, institutos instructósque Confessarios, in arcanis suis tribunalibus, ubi sententiam isthanc omnem iis movere ac discutere, curioséque à singulis poenitentibus delicta omnia, & eorum circumstantias, quorum nullum scilicet nisi confessum remitti posse praestruunt, requirere, fas est; se gerere putamus? Ibi confitentes contra disertum Apostoli Ephes. v. 3. 4. mandatum, multa inhonesta ac turpia eloqui; praeterita correctáque, & ante plures annos admissa, atque oblivione poenę sepulta flagitia, cogitatione retractare, mente & memoria versare, & quæ penitus obrui ac sepeliri, velut purgamenta decuerat, ea effodere, ac in lucem protrahere, maximo cum dedecore coguntur. Sive enim poenitens verè emendatus, & in spiritualem virum conversus est, necesse est, cum isthac fœditatum suarum recognitione non parum turbari, & pace gaudióque, quo in Christo jam fruebatur, spoliatum angi: sive carnalis adhuc est, uti sunt plurimi, fieri omnino nequit, quin ejus animus polluatur & concupiscentiæ labe, titillatione & prurigine inficiatur. Accedit, quòd confitentes ex ore Confessarii sic, uti vidimus, priùs edoćti & conscientiam scrutantis, multa ignota peccata, multas peccatorum arcanas species discunt, quæ scientia quàm perniciosa sit, omnes vident. Corruptis enim animis vix unquam peccata, & peccatorum imagines impuné monstrantur. Cogita autem, quantum, & quàm pestilens malarum ac impurarum cogitationum ac libidinum agmen in virginum matronarumque simplicium, ac penè innocentium animos invehat, qui eas ex Burchardi vel Sanchezii alicujus canonibus ac disciplina interrogat; quandam exinde pietatis & sanctimoniæ perniciem inducat. Præterea confessio hominum verecundiam deterrit, paulatimque planè consumit. Nam qui semel pudoris primos limites transfilierunt, ii gnaviter impudentes fieri solent; indéque est quòd deprehensis audacia crescit.
units.tr: XXXII. What, then, do we suppose the confessors trained and instructed in that sewer and that venereal doctrine, as Aurelius calls it, are like, in their secret tribunals, where it is lawful for them to stir up and examine all this doctrine, and to inquire carefully from each penitent into all his offences and their circumstances, since they insist that none can be forgiven unless it has been confessed? There the penitents are compelled, against the plain command of the Apostle in Eph. 5. 3, 4, to utter many shameful and filthy things; to call to mind, to turn over in mind and memory, the sins that were corrected and committed many years before and buried in oblivion of punishment; and to dig up and drag into the light, with the greatest disgrace, what ought to have been wholly buried and hidden like refuse. For if the penitent has truly been reformed and has become a spiritual man, he must be greatly disturbed by this recognition of his foulness, and, deprived of the peace and joy which he already enjoyed in Christ, he must be tormented. If he is still carnal, as very many are, it is entirely impossible that his mind should not be polluted and infected with the stain of concupiscence, with titillation and itching. Moreover, the penitents learn from the mouth of the confessor, who first instructs them, as we have seen, and searches their conscience, many unknown sins and secret kinds of sins; and everyone can see how pernicious this knowledge is. For in corrupted minds sins, and the images of sins, are scarcely ever shown with impunity. Consider, too, how much and how pestilential a host of evil and impure thoughts and lusts is carried into the minds of simple virgins and matrons, and almost innocent ones, when they are questioned on the canons and discipline of Burchardus or of some Sanchez; and how this brings about a certain ruin of piety and holiness. Besides, confession drives away men's modesty and gradually wears it away altogether. For those who have once leapt over the first limits of shame usually become bold in impudence, and hence it is that, once detected, their audacity grows.

units.la: XXXIII. Quid verò de confitentibus verba facio? Ipsos Confessarios, quos haud vulgariter esse Sanctos conveniebat, illa impudentiæ exercitatio continua ut plurimùm impurissimos haud dubiè reddit. Ut mirum non sit, quòd inter alia scita sua id scriptis commendare non erubescunt, eum qui prævidet, ex auditu confessionis, aut ex præparatione ad eam, futuram pollutionem, non peccare, etsi live non omittat, unde pollutionem in se secuturam novit.
units.tr: XXXIII. But why should I speak of those who confess? The confessors themselves, who ought to have been remarkably holy, are beyond doubt made very impure by this constant practice of shamelessness. So it is no wonder that among their other doctrines they are not ashamed to commend in their writings this view: that a man who foresees, from hearing a confession or from preparing for it, that a pollution will follow, does not sin, even if he does not omit the thing from which he knows the pollution will follow in himself.

units.la: Ita Azorius Institit. Moral. Tom. y. par. 3. cap. 18. ubi de pollutione voluntaria disputat, definit. Jam suo tempore Alvarus Pelagius de Planctu Eccl. lib. y. art. 14. sic de Confessariis questus est: Sæpe cum Parochianis mulieribus, quæ ad confessionem admittuntur, scelestissimè fornicantur. Neque etiam Erasmus Exomologes. T. 5. pag. 129. dissimulavit, confitentes in eos sæpe Sacerdotes incidere, qui sub prætextu confessionis patrant non referenda, pròque Medicis fiunt aut socii, aut magistri, aut discipuli turpitudinis. Et utinam, inquit, hoc frustra videar monuisse, ac non tam multa passim exempla occurrerent, quæ nec sine dolore recordor, nec sine pudore possum referre. Ex hoc Sacerdotum genere ille fuisse videtur Sanctimonialium præfectus, quem idem Erafmus paulò ante pag. 128. narrabat cuidam Theologo confessum, sese stuprasse ducentas virgines. Quin & mala confessionum in novem classes distributa eodem Exomologeseos opere pag. 128. &c. fusè adeò idem Erafmus explicavit, ut Inquisitores Hispani, propalatorum dedecorum impatientes, integrum locum, sex grandes paginas complectentem, improbè pro consueta audacia resecuerint.
units.tr: So Azorius defines it in Institit. Moral. Tom. y. par. 3. cap. 18., where he discusses voluntary pollution. Already in his own time Alvarus Pelagius complained about confessors in de Planctu Eccl. lib. y. art. 14. in these words: "Often they commit fornication most wickedly with the women of their parishes who are admitted to confession." Nor did Erasmus in Exomologes. T. 5. pag. 129. conceal it: "Penitents often fall into the hands of priests who, under the pretext of confession, commit things that must not be reported, and become either accomplices, or teachers, or pupils of the vileness, as if they were doctors of it. And I wish," he says, "that I seemed to have given this warning in vain, and that so many examples did not present themselves everywhere, which I recall not without grief and cannot relate without shame." From this class of priests seems to have been that prefect of nuns whom Erasmus, a little earlier in pag. 128., reported as having confessed to a certain theologian that he had debauched two hundred virgins. Indeed the same Erasmus, in the same work of Exomologesis at pag. 128. &c., set out at such length the evils of confessions, distributed into nine classes, that the Spanish Inquisitors, unable to bear the open disgraces, shamelessly cut out, with their usual boldness, an entire passage covering six large pages.

units.la: XXXIV. Sed aliunde etiam, cùm Erafmi πυρρηοίαυ Hierarchici oderint nimiùm, probra hæc cognoscere haud arduum est; imprimis ex Casuistarum interioribus scriniis, casus non paucos circa Confessarios pueros, puellas & fœminas pro arcano hoc tribunali ad nefarias libidines solicitantes, enodantium. Diana Panormitanus Resol. Par. j. tract. 4. ubi de Denuntiationibus faciendis ex eodicto Inquisitorum, & in specie ex solicitatione agit, plures casus de solicitantibus Confessariis, Inquisitoribus denuntiandis vel non denuntiandis movens, abundè prodidit, quid in arcanis illis subscelliis geratur. Quærit Resol. xÿ. An Confessarius, qui solicitavit adolescentem in consessione, sit denuntiandus ? Olim quidem se negativam sustinuisse, profitetur Diana cum Aloysio Bariola, Fagundez, Paramo, aliisque, eam videlicet ob rationem, (audite & stupete pii omnes!) quia lex pœnalis non est extendenda, etiamsi militet in alio casu eadem ratio. Sed Pontifices loquebantur adversus Confessarios solicitantes fœminas. Ergo Bulla non erat extendenda adversus solicitantes pueros. Belle profecto & πῳῶς plane. Sed redit tamen in viam confessim. Sed hodie, inquit, ex Constitutione Gregorii XV. cessat omnis dubitatio, quia ibi Pontifex
units.tr: XXXIV. But from elsewhere too it is not difficult to learn these disgraces, since the Hierarchs hate Erasmus' parrhesia too much; above all from the inner chests of the casuists, who resolve not a few cases about confessors who solicit boys, girls and women to wicked lusts in this secret tribunal. Diana of Palermo, in Resol. Par. j. tract. 4., where he treats of making denunciations according to the edict of the Inquisitors, and especially of solicitation, raising many cases about solicitating confessors who are to be denounced or not to the Inquisitors, has amply revealed what goes on in those secret confessionals. He asks in Resol. xÿ.: "Is a confessor who solicited a young man in confession to be denounced?" Diana professes that he once upheld the negative view, together with Aloysius Bariola, Fagundez, Paramo and others, namely for this reason (hear and be astonished, all you pious people!): "because a penal law is not to be extended, even if the same reason applies in another case. But the Pontiffs spoke against confessors who solicit women. Therefore the Bull was not to be extended against those who solicit boys." Truly a fine and altogether plausible argument. But he returns to the right path at once: "But today," he says, "by the Constitution of Gregory XV. all doubt ceases, because there the Pontiff

units.la: {a} Casuistarum casus circa denuntiationes Sacerdotum, qui pueros, puellas, fœminas pro arcano hoc tribunali solicitant, ex Diana Panormitano. Pontifex decernit, etiam folicitantes viros esse denuntiandos. Ergo ante editam Constitutionem Gregorii XV. Confessarius poterat folicitare pueros, sine denuntiatione. Idque inferius Refol. xxv. diserte Diana, nixus Clementis VIII. & Pauli V. contra Confessarios folicitantes foeminas, sine mentione masculorum, Bulla, profitetur. Quid post Gregorium hunc fiat, & an denuntientur illi paederastae ex praescripto Gregorii, eccui certò liquet? Quid videtur vobis, quibus non omnis pudor decoxit? Subjicit dein alios casus, cujusmodi sunt: An Confessarius, qui in Confessionario, vel in alio loco sub praetextu Confessionis, non tamen Confessionis secutae, folicitavit foeminam, sit denuntiandus? An si laicus, vel clericus occultè ponat se in loco Confessionibus deputato, & inter Confessionem foeminae, illam ibi folicitet, sit denuntiandus? An Confessarius, qui ante, vel paulò post Confessionem foeminam folicitavit, sit denuntiandus? An sit denuntiandus Sacerdos, qui non habens facultatem audiendi Confessiones ab Ordinario, folicitat foeminam in Confessione, fingens se habere talem potestatem? An Confessarius, qui in confessione urget poenitentem de prostituenda sibi vel aliis filia, consanguinea, amica &c. sit denuntiandus? Respondet, negativam plerisque Casuistis placuisse ante Constitutionem Gregorii XV. editam. Sed post eam editam affirmativam placere. Quanta ergo ante Gregorium XV. Confessariis pueros & foeminas impunè solicitandi licentia fuit? Post eum castius an cautius solicitatores, seu cynoedi & scortatores Confessarii mercentur, haud inquiro.
units.tr: {a} The casuists' cases about the denunciation of priests who solicit boys, girls and women in this secret tribunal, from Diana of Palermo. "The Pontiff decrees that men who solicit are also to be denounced." Therefore before the Constitution of Gregory XV. was issued, a confessor could solicit boys without denunciation. Diana states this plainly in Resol. xxv., relying on the Bull of Clement VIII. and Paul V. against confessors who solicit women, with no mention of males. What happens after this Gregory, and whether those pederasts are denounced under Gregory's prescription, is certainly not clear to anyone. What do you think, you whom all shame has not abandoned? He then adds other cases, such as these: "Is a confessor who, in the confessional or in another place under the pretext of confession, though not a confession that followed, solicited a woman, to be denounced? Or if a layman or cleric secretly places himself in a place assigned to confessions, and during a woman's confession solicits her there, is he to be denounced? Is a confessor who solicited a woman before or shortly after confession to be denounced? Is a priest to be denounced who, not having faculty from the Ordinary to hear confessions, solicits a woman in confession, pretending to have such power? Is a confessor to be denounced who, in confession, urges the penitent to prostitute to him or to others a daughter, a blood relative, a female friend, etc.?" He answers that the negative view pleased most casuists before the Constitution of Gregory XV. was issued, but that after it was issued the affirmative view pleases. How great, then, was the licence before Gregory XV. for confessors to solicit boys and women with impunity! Whether the solicitors after him, or the sodomites and whoremongering confessors, are dealt with more chastely or more cautiously, I do not inquire.

units.la: XXXV. De Musica voluptuaria amore & studio verba facere supersederem, nisi Spiritus S. inter ea bona, quibus Babylon quandoque privabitur, Apoc. XVIII. 22. Φωνὴ κιθαρῳδῶν, Μουσικῶν, αὐλητῶν καὶ αὐλητῶν citharaedorum, Musicorum, tibicinum & tubicinum vocem numerassbest;
units.tr: XXXV. I would have passed over in silence the love and pursuit of voluptuous music, were it not that the Holy Spirit, among those goods of which Babylon will at some time be deprived, Rev. 18:22, counts the voice of harpers, musicians, pipers and trumpeters: "Φωνὴ κιθαρῳδῶν καὶ μουσικῶν καὶ αὐλητῶν καὶ σαλπιστῶν [The voice of harpers and musicians and pipers and trumpeters]".

units.la: Musicam voluptuariam Babyloni Spiritus Dei tribuit. Eadem Hierarchicorum cultus perstrepu. täffet; atque eâdem operâ tum luctuosissimam pereuntis Babylonis faciem delineâssset, tum Musicam Babylonis non pietati, sed carnali luxuriæ, & ciendis pravis affectibus inservientem obliquè perstrinxisset. Perstrepere autem Hierarchicorum non plateas, conclavia & cubilia duntaxat, sed Templa cumprimis & Basilicas instrumentis Musicis exquisitissimis; atque Jesuitas inprimis operam dare, ut hac suavitate auriúmque, ne dicam, Veneris etiam illecebrâ, homines animales & φιλήδονοι capti seductíque sacra sua ampleċtantur, equidem plus satis constat.
units.tr: The Spirit of God assigns voluptuous music to Babylon. The same music resounds through the worship of the Hierarchs; and by the same work he both depicted the most mournful face of perishing Babylon and obliquely censured the music of Babylon, which serves not piety but carnal luxury and the stirring up of wicked passions. Now it is clear enough that the Hierarchs resound with the most exquisite musical instruments not only in the squares, the chambers and the bedrooms, but above all in the temples and basilicas; and that the Jesuits in particular take pains that men of animal and pleasure-loving disposition, captivated and seduced by this sweetness of the ears, and (I will not say) by the allurement of Venus too, embrace their sacred rites.

units.la: XXXVI. Musicæ utriusque, & vocalis & instrumentalis usus aliquis legitimus in Ecclesia, & extra eam obtinere potest.
units.tr: XXXVI. Some lawful use of music, both vocal and instrumental, can be found in the Church and outside it.

units.la: Neque de hoc controversia est, modò non ex hypocrisi, sed ex corde, non profano more modóque, sed ad audientium canentiúmque ædificationem; denique non voluptatem & oblectamentum, sed ad Dei gloriam eâ utamur. S. Paulus 1. Cor. xiv. 15. Quid est igitur, inquit, orabo Spiritu, sed orabo etiam intelligentiâ: Psallam Spiritu, sed psallam etiam intelligentiâ, ne intelligentia mea alii infructuosa sit. Quam in parænesin primum Hierarchici impingunt, cùm in suis fornicibus (utpote ad spiritualem fornicationem comparatis) hymnos & cantica sua quamvis subinde Sancta & pia, non tam canendo, quàm reboando & mugiendo, plerunque nec in Spiritu, nec intelligentiâ decantant. Non Spiritu, cùm vel sibi ignota, vel sine pio cordis affectu lusciniarum more cantillant. Non intelligentiâ, cùm lingua peregrinâ canentes à populo præsente neutiquam intelliguntur.
units.tr: There is no dispute about this, provided that we use it not out of hypocrisy but from the heart; not in a profane manner or fashion, but for the edification of the hearers and singers; and, in short, not for pleasure and amusement but for the glory of God. St Paul, 1 Cor. 14:15: What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray also with the understanding; I will sing with the spirit, but I will sing also with the understanding, that my understanding may not be unfruitful to others. The Hierarchs first assail this exhortation, since in their vaulted chambers (which are fitted out for spiritual fornication) they sing their hymns and canticles, however holy and pious these may be at times, not so much singing them as bellowing and roaring, and for the most part sing them neither in the Spirit, since they chirp them like nightingales, either not knowing what they sing or without any pious affection of the heart. Nor do they sing with the understanding, since in a foreign tongue their singing is by no means understood by the people present.

units.la: XXXVII. Sed scenicam illam & theatralem Hierarc- hitorum Musicam, ipsorummet saniorum in Papatu Vi- orum Confessione, vitio neutiquam carere, & ad libidi- nes incendere, probemus.
units.tr: XXXVII. But let us prove that the theatrical music of the Hierarchs, which is stage-like and theatrical, is by no means free of fault, and that it kindles lusts, as even the saner men among the Papists in their own Confession admit.

units.la: Erasmus in suis ad 1. Cor. xiv. cap. Annotationibus doctè gravitérque contra eam differens;
units.tr: Erasmus, in his Annotations on 1 Cor. 14, learnedly and gravely disputing against it,
The abuse of music among the same people.

units.la: De scenica & theatrali Musica, vel saniorum lapsi potius quàm culpâ Dei.
units.tr: On stage-like and theatrical music, which the saner men fell into rather than God being at fault.

units.la: rens, Nec his contenti, inquit, operosam quandam & theatricam Musicam in sacras aedes induximus, tumultuosum diversarum vocum garritum, qualem non opinor in Graecorum aut Romanorum theatris unquam auditum fuisse. Omnia tubis, fistulis, lituis ac sambucis perflrepunt: cumque his certant hominum voces. Audiuntur amatoriae foedaeque cantilenae, ad quas scorta mimique saltitant. In sacram aedem, velut in theatrum concurritur, ad delinidendas aures. Et in hunc usum aluntur magnis salariis organorum opifices, puerorum greges, quorum omnis aetas in perdiscendis his consumitur, nihil interim boni rei discentium. Alitur sordidorum, ut plerique sunt, hominum colluvies, & tantis sumptibus oneratur Ecclesia ob rem pestiferam etiam. Quaeso te, ut rationem ineas, quot pauperes de vita periclitantes, poterant ali cantorum salariis? Cur haec nobis sola placent, quae Paulus seu parvulorum infantium parcissimè vult adhiberi, imo quae nullo pacto laturus fuerat? Idem de Lingua pag. 68. querelam similem consignat his verbis: Quid hodie operosius, quàm nostra Musica, tot vocibus multarum avium garritum imitans? Quid diceret Emerepes ille Laconum Ephorus (qui Phrynidis Musici duas è novem cordas incidit bipenni, dicens: Ne corrumpas Musicam) si nunc audiret in Templis eadem organa referre tubas, cornua, lituos, tibias apertas, tibias obscuriores, tibias vacuas, tonitrua, voces hominum & volucrum? Qualis est Musica nostra, talis est cultus, talis victus, talis aedificatio; prisca simplicitas nusquam est, indies augescunt operosae deliciae.
units.tr: says: "Not content with these, we have brought into the sacred buildings a certain elaborate and theatrical music, a tumultuous chatter of diverse voices, such as I think was never heard in the theatres of the Greeks or Romans. Everything resounds with trumpets, pipes, litui and sambucas, and human voices compete with them. Amorous and foul songs are heard, to which harlots and mimes dance. People rush into the sacred building as into a theatre, to tickle the ears. And for this purpose organ-makers are kept at great salaries, and flocks of boys, whose whole age is spent in learning these things, with no good to the things they learn. The filth of base men, as most of them are, is fed, and the Church is burdened with such great expense, and that too for a pestilent thing. I beg you to reckon how many poor people, in danger of their lives, could be fed on the salaries of the singers. Why do these things alone please us, which Paul wished to be used most sparingly, even for little children; indeed, things he would by no means have allowed?" The same man, in his work On the Tongue, page 68, records a similar complaint in these words: "What is more elaborate today than our music, imitating the chattering of many birds? What would that Ephor of the Laconians, Ecprepes (who cut two of the nine strings of the musician Phrynis with an axe, saying: 'Do not corrupt the music'), say if he now heard in the churches these organs reproducing trumpets, horns, litui, open pipes, muffled pipes, hollow pipes, thunders, and the voices of men and birds? Such as our music is, such is our worship, such our way of life, such our building. Nowhere is there ancient simplicity; daily the elaborate delights multiply."

units.la: XXXVIII. Si Erasmus hanc in rem testis, mordaci vero auriculas rodere suetus, atque eandem ob causam Ex- purgatorum spongiam hic passus, displicet, audiatur Guil- helmus Lindanus, Episcopus Ruremondanus, longâ ora- tione
units.tr: XXXVIII. If Erasmus is not enough of a witness in this matter, and since he was used to gnawing at ears with his biting wit, and for that reason has displeased here, the expurgators' sponge notwithstanding, let us hear William Lindanus, Bishop of Roermond, who in a long oration condemns theatrical music in this way:

units.la: Guilhelmi Lindani tione Panopl. lib. iv. 78. sic theatralem Musicam detestans: Lectorum vices explent non Lectores, sicuti & Psalmistarum locum invadunt isti Musici, non tantùm ut de choro ejiciantur dignissimi, cùm propter vitæ improbitatem, quâ passim nimiùm sunt noti, tum propter impudicos amorum atque indignos bellorum modulos sacris Dei laudibus inspersos, sed etiam propter theatricam magis sonorum confusionem, quàm religiosam pietatis ac devotionis moderationem, quam piorum animis passim ignguere noscuntur. Non enim nunc suo cantu Musici auditorum animos tam ad pietatis cultum, cælestiàque excitant desideria, quàm avocant, avertunt & alienant. Scio enim aliquando Divinis me interfuisse laudibus, cùm vel attentissimè auscultarem, ecquid fortè psalleretur; ne unum quidem potuisse intelligere verbum, ita erant omnia syllabarum repetitionibus commixta, vocibus confusa, clamoribus potiùs horridulis, quàm cantus obscurata. Paulò post: Nunc audire est lætissimos Divinæ laudis hymnos tristissimis contaminari Musicorum modulis: contra lugubres Ecclesiæ threnos lætissimo effusos modulamine. Quid? quòd Divinos hymnos non modò theatricis, adeòque bellicis, &, si dicere fas est, Gailardicis contaminant modis, sed venereis quoque conspurcant & amatoriis. Unde illarum magis admiror constantiam Ecclesiarum, quæ ipsum prævidentes Divini cultus abusum, semel Musicam illam choro maluerunt excludere, utri Trajectensis, &, quod audio, Lugdunensis: quàm illarum veneror magnificam, quam ipsi putant & jactant adeò Majestatem, quâ Dei chorum omni phonascorum syntagmate, vocum omnis generis discrimine, imò & tubarum clangore, cornutorum stridore, aliòque strepitu vario, ne quid praetermittere videantur, quod cantici verba semel obscuret, sensumque sepeliat & obruat, sibi præclarè videantur implesse.
units.tr: In his Panoplia, book 4, chapter 78, William Lindanus, detesting theatrical music, says: "Non-readers fill the place of readers, just as those musicians seize the place of the psalmists, not only to be cast out of the choir, most deserving of it, both because of the wickedness of their lives, by which they are everywhere too well known, and because of their shameless love-songs and unworthy war-tunes mixed into the sacred praises of God, but also because of the theatrical confusion of sounds rather than the religious moderation of piety and devotion, which they are known to set on fire everywhere in the minds of the pious. For the musicians now do not with their singing stir the minds of the hearers to the worship of piety and to heavenly longings, but rather call them away, turn them aside and alienate them. For I know that at times I have been present at the divine praises, and though I listened most attentively to see whether anything was sung, I could not make out a single word, so much were all things mixed with the repetition of syllables, confused by voices, obscured by rather harsh shouts than by song." A little later: "Now one hears the most joyful hymns of divine praise polluted by the sorrowful tunes of musicians, and, on the other hand, the mournful laments of the Church poured out in the most joyful melody. What more? They pollute the divine hymns not only with theatrical, and indeed warlike, and, if it is lawful to say so, galliard-like tunes, but also defile them with venereal and amorous ones. Therefore I admire more the steadfastness of those churches which, foreseeing this very abuse of divine worship, once preferred to exclude that music from the choir, as the Church of Utrecht and, as I hear, that of Lyons: how magnificent I think their majesty is, which they themselves think and boast of, by which they seem to have clearly accomplished in the choir of God, with every arrangement of singers, every variety of voices, and indeed with the clangour of trumpets, the screech of horns, and other various noise, lest they seem to omit anything that might obscure the words of the canticle once more, and bury and overwhelm its sense."

units.la: XXXIX. Antiquior & authoritate robustior Lindano Doctor Angelicus Thomas Aquinas in 2. 2. q. 91. art. 2. sic adversus Musicam organicam disputat: Ecclesia non assumit instrumenta Musica, sicut citharas & Psalteria in Divinas laudes, ne videatur judaizare. Aristoteles docuit in 8. libro Politicorum, neque fistulas ad disciplinam esse adducendas, neque aliquod aliud artificiale organum, puta citharam, & si quid tale alterum est; sed quaecunque efficiunt auditores bonos. Hujusmodi enim instrumenta Musica magis animum movent ad delectationem, quàm per ea formetur interius bona anima dispositio. In veteri autem Testamento usus erat talium instrumentorum, tum quia populus erat magis durus & carnalis, unde erat per hujusmodi instrumenta provocandus, sicut & per promissiones terrenas, tum etiam, quia ejusmodi instrumenta corporalia aliquid figurabant spirituale. In quem locum Cajetanus, Notandum, inquit, tempore Thomae Ecclesiam non usam organis. Unde hodie in ejus rei signum Romana Ecclesia coram summo Pontifice ea non utitur.
units.tr: XXXIX. The Angelic Doctor, Thomas Aquinas, older and more weighty in authority than Lindanus, disputes against organ music in this way in 2.2, q. 91, art. 2: "The Church does not take up musical instruments, such as lyres and psalteries, for divine praises, lest it seem to Judaize. Aristotle taught in the eighth book of the Politics that neither pipes nor any other artificial instrument, such as the lyre, nor anything of that sort, is to be brought into discipline, but only those things which make the hearers good. For such musical instruments move the mind more to delight than through them a good disposition of the soul is formed within. In the Old Testament, however, such instruments were in use, both because the people were harder and more carnal, and so had to be stirred by such instruments, as also by earthly promises, and also because such bodily instruments prefigured something spiritual." On this passage Cajetan remarks: "It must be noted that in Thomas's time the Church did not use organs. Hence today, as a sign of this, the Roman Church does not use them in the presence of the supreme Pontiff."

units.la: XL. Sed de cardiacis his, seu irritamentis, occasionibus, imò causis etiam ad impuritatem pellicientibus plus satis. Majus est, quòd Hierarchici de fornicatione, adulterio, aliisque impuritatibus tenuiter nimis sentiunt, eaisque levibus poenis afficiunt. Quoad fornicationem simplicem, non desunt inter Hierarchicos, qui pertendant, haereticum non esse, si quis dicat aut credat, simplicem fornicationem non esse mortale peccatum, quia testimonia S. Scripturae non sunt expressa. Sic enim loquitur Martinus de Magistris, lib. de Temp. q. 2. de Luxuria; ubi etiam videtur velle secundum principia hominis naturalis ac per se & intrinsecè non esse peccatum, ait Lorinus in cap. 15. Act. v. 20. Durandus quoque in 4. Sent. Dist. 33. q. 2. concedit, secundum jus Divinum positivum, nec non humanum esse peccatum grave, seu, uti loquitur, mortale; secundum autem jus naturale, cum debito fine careat, si sit ob delectationem solam, aut si repugnet bono prolis, si ea intendatur, esse itidem malam, non tamen adeo, ut mereatur nomen peccati mortalis: quia lex naturalis nihil dicit, nec nominat mortem æternam, & temporalem propter fornicationem non infligit. Negat etiam Silvester Petra Sancta cap. 3. ss. 9. Scripturam, ne meretrices sint, uspiam prohibuisse; & tam insignis sententiæ authorem Abulensem magnum, sic vocat, in Scriptura Magistrum laudat. Adulterium pro leviori etiam crimine venditavit non gregarius aliquis doctor, sed supremus scilicet Ecclesiæ Pastor Alexander III. qui Extra. de Judic. sic Salertiano Archiepiscopo rescripsit: De adulteriis, & aliis criminibus, quæ sunt minora, potest Episcopus cum clericis post peractam pœnitentiam dispensare. Sed & Thomas Aquinas 2. 2. q. 154. art. 1. negat, adulterium, incestum, stuprum & raptum, metaphysicè loquendo, esse luxuriæ species, quia deformitates, quas addunt, non sunt contra castitatem, sed contra justitiam &c. Sacerdotem vel Regularem fornicando, concubinas fovendo, adulterando, quàm matrimonium contrahendo peccare leviùs, recepta hodie Hierarchicorum doctrina est, dixerit licet S. Paulus 1. Cor. VII. 9. præstare iis, qui continere non possunt, ut nubant, quàm ut urantur, nedum ut strenuè fornicentur & adulterentur. Denique Facultas Theologica Parisiensis A. MDCLXIV. ex libro Amadaei Gaimenii, capita Theologiæ Moralis Jesuiticæ complexo, hanc propositionem excerpsit, & censuræ subjecit: Furtum triginta Regalium, majus peccatum est quàm Sodomia.
units.tr: XL. But enough about these incitements, these occasions, and indeed causes that lure to impurity. It is worse that the Hierarchs think too lightly of fornication, adultery and other impurities, and punish them with slight penalties. As to simple fornication, there are not lacking among the Hierarchs those who contend that it is not heretical if someone says or believes that simple fornication is not a mortal sin, because the testimonies of Holy Scripture are not explicit. For so speaks Martin de Magistris, in his book on the Times, q. 2, on Lust; where he also seems to wish that, according to the principles of natural man, it is not in itself and intrinsically a sin, says Lorinus on chapter 15 of Acts, verse 20. Durandus too, in the 4th Sentences, dist. 33, q. 2, concedes that according to the positive divine law, and also the human, it is a grave sin, or, as he puts it, mortal; but according to natural law, since it lacks its due end if it is for pleasure alone, or if it opposes the good of offspring when that is intended, it is likewise evil, yet not so much that it deserves the name of mortal sin: because the natural law says nothing, nor names eternal death, and does not inflict temporal death for fornication. Silvester Petra Sancta, chapter 3, section 9, also denies that Scripture has anywhere forbidden harlots to exist; and he praises the author of so remarkable an opinion, whom he calls the great Abulensis, a Master in Scripture. Adultery was sold cheaply even for a lesser crime, not by some ordinary teacher but by the supreme Pastor of the Church himself, Alexander III, who in Extra, On Judgments rescripted thus to the Archbishop of Salerno: "Concerning adulteries and other crimes, which are lesser, the bishop may dispense with the clergy after penance has been done." Thomas Aquinas too, 2.2, q. 154, art. 1, denies that adultery, incest, rape and abduction, speaking metaphysically, are species of lust, because the deformities they add are not against chastity but against justice, etc. That it is less sinful for a priest or regular to fornicate, keep concubines, or commit adultery than to contract marriage is today the accepted doctrine of the Hierarchs, although St Paul said (1 Cor. 7:9) that it is better for those who cannot contain to marry than to burn, let alone to fornicate and commit adultery vigorously. Finally, the Theological Faculty of Paris in 1664, from a book of Amadeus Gaimenius which summarised the chapters of Jesuit moral theology, excerpted this proposition and subjected it to censure: "The theft of thirty crowns is a greater sin than sodomy."

units.la: XLI. Monstro, quam homini Christiano similior est, qui ab [illegible, ~8 letters] nefandorum luxuria illla, quæ
units.tr: XLI. What a monster, and how much more like a Christian man is the one who did not shrink from the lust of those unspeakable men, from [illegible] [of] that lust which so greatly tormented the soul of Lot, 2 Pet. 2.7.

units.la: visa tantopere animam Lothi excruciavit, 2 Pet. ii. 7. non abhorruerit. Repertus est tamen, ne quid ad scelerum complementum deesset, haud postremus inter Hierarchicos, ejus encomiastes perditissimus. Extat enim Venetiis editus apud Trajanum Naevum A. M. D. L. liber de laudibus Sodomiae, Italicis versibus, authore Johanne de la Casa, in quo scribit, Sodomiam esse artem singularem, opus bonum, imo Divinum, seque hoc propria experientia compertum habere, & non alia magis Venere delectari. Fuit ille de la Casa, Archiepiscopus Beneventanus, Papalis Camerae Decanus, & Legatus Pontificis a latere ad Serenissimam Rempublicam Venetam. Haec tam foeda, tam horrenda a Carolo Molinaeo Jc. in Oratione habita Tubingae A. MDLIV. obiecta, cum in Apologia Ecclesiae Anglicanae Johannes Juellus, Episcopus Anglus commemorasset, Thomas Hardingus, qui Lovanii Apologiae confutationem suscepit, factum negare ausus non est, sed illud, quantum potuit, elevare conatus, sic ad caput 2. divis. 1. scripsit: Si Johannes Casa, juvenis adhuc & imberbis, priusquam se ad clerum contulerat, adeoque multo prius, quam vel Archiepiscopatu & Legatione Papae fungeretur, amatoria quaedam Poemata Italicis numeris, ad imitationem Petrarchae composuit, (quo genere exercitationis causa, admodum capiuntur, si qui ex Italica juventute ingeniosiores sunt) & defigurato nominatim nemine, nefario facinori assentatorie orationis fuco odium potius ademit, quam laudem attribuit, qua tamen in re peccatum ab eo esse fatemur; & cum eximiis alioqui dotibus animi esset praeditus, ob id ipsum nihilominus adolescentiae erratum, Cardinalitii honore per omnem deinde vitam exclusus est; haec omnia si concedamus, & subducta ratione rite pencитemus, quid hinc Christi Ecclesiae honoris perit & sanctitatis? Nihil equidem, Hardinge. Nam Christi Ecclesia ejusmodi di monstra infernalia ad dignitates Ecclesiasticas pene su- premas non promovet, nunquam scelera talia excusare satagit, vel expressas scelerum laudes emollit, distinguendo scilicet inter laudare & odium adimere. Sed Pontificia, Archiepiscopatu & Legatione Papæ dignos censet, qui ob Sodomiticum scelus & laudatum, & frequenter patratum Cardinalatu excluduntur. Non igitur vera Christi Ecclesia, sed Babylon, abominationum illa mater, in qua Sodoma & Gomorrha hospitium metantur, esse clarissimo hoc indicio cognoscitur. Objici autem poterant alia etiam ejusdem fœtoris carmina, & epigrammata, veluti de Formica, & super Ducem Parmensem, quæ eodem authore cusa, & Sodomiæ lenocinantia, magnus in Italia literator Pontificiæ communionis, pro suo candore, nostris novissime communicavit, quibus magis etiam hominis impietas, & incredibilis devorati pudoris pædor convinci- tur.
units.tr: Yet, lest anything be lacking to the completion of his crimes, a man was found, and no minor one among the Hierarchs, and a most abandoned eulogist of this vice. For there exists a book, printed at Venice by Trajan Naevus in 1550, de laudibus Sodomiae, in Italian verse, by the author Giovanni della Casa, in which he writes that Sodomy is a singular art and a good work, nay a divine one, and that he had found this by his own experience, and that he took no greater delight in any other Venus. That della Casa was Archbishop of Benevento, Dean of the Papal Chamber, and Legate a latere of the Pope to the Most Serene Venetian Republic. Carlo Molinaeus, jurist, objected these foul and horrible things in an oration delivered at Tübingen in 1554. When John Jewel, Bishop of England, had mentioned them in the Apology of the Church of England, Thomas Harding, who undertook a refutation of the Apology at Louvain, did not dare to deny the fact, but tried as hard as he could to lessen it, and wrote thus at chapter 2, division 1: If John della Casa, still a young man and beardless, before he had joined the clergy, and therefore long before he held the archbishopric or the legation of the Pope, composed certain amatory poems in Italian metre in imitation of Petrarch (a kind of exercise to which the more gifted of Italian youth are greatly drawn), and, with no one named, decked a nefarious deed with the flattering colour of speech, he gave it hatred rather than praise; in which matter we confess he sinned; and although he was otherwise endowed with excellent gifts of mind, for that very youthful error he was nevertheless excluded for the rest of his life from the honour of the cardinalate. If we concede all these things, and reckon the account rightly and weigh it, what honour or holiness of the Church of Christ is lost thereby? Nothing at all, Harding. For the Church of Christ does not promote such infernal monsters to almost the highest ecclesiastical dignities, never strives to excuse such crimes, nor softens explicit praises of crimes, by distinguishing, of course, between praising and taking away hatred. But the Papists judge a man worthy of the archbishopric and the legation of the Pope, whom they exclude from the cardinalate on account of a Sodomitical crime both praised and frequently committed. Therefore it is known by this very clear sign that the true Church of Christ is not this, but Babylon, that mother of abominations, in which Sodom and Gomorrah take up their lodging. Other poems and epigrams of the same stench might also be cited, such as On the Ant and Concerning the Duke of Parma, which were published by the same author and which promote Sodomy; a great Italian scholar of the Papal communion, out of his own candour, lately communicated them to us, and by them the impiety of the man and the incredible stench of his shamelessness are shown even more convincingly.

units.la: XLII. Quo loco impuritates istas Hierarchici habeant, ex pœnis & censuris Ecclesiasticis, quibus clericos aliosque scortatores, adulteros, Sodomitas feriendos censent, liquet. Si enim ut cohibeantur crimina, pœnæ infliguntur, quis non videt, pœnis sublatis vel mitigatis, crimina tolli vel mitigari? Scitum enim est illud Æschinis contra Timarchum: Ἐὰν ὦ πολάζῃ τὰς ἁμαρτίας, ἴσως μὴν ἐμὲ.. Ἐὰν δ᾽ ἀφιεῖτε καλοὶ μὴ .. Si-quidem injurios homines puniveritis, leges vobis & bonæ & rateæ erunt. Sin absolveritis, bonæ erunt, ratæ non erunt. Quàm verò levis pœna isthæc erit, si exiguæ aliquot eleemosynæ, preculæ quædam certis vicibus repetitæ, scalarum crucis in foro mercatorio circuitio, jejunum jejunium, atque similia crepundia compensatio idonea pro tam fœdis facinoribus in laico homine, bimestrisque aut trimestris exclusio ab Ecclesia Sacerdoti, quantumvis alligato adulterii, & ἀκυνπόφοτ deprehendebatur?
units.tr: XLII. In what regard the Hierarchs hold these impurities may be clear from the penalties and ecclesiastical censures with which they think clerics and other fornicators, adulterers and Sodomites should be struck. For if penalties are imposed so that crimes may be restrained, who does not see that, with penalties removed or softened, crimes are removed or softened? That saying of Aeschines against Timarchus is apt: If you punish wrongdoers, your laws will be both good and valid; but if you acquit them, they will be good but not valid. [Ἐὰν μὲν πολάζῃ τὰς ἁμαρτίας, ἴσως μὲν ἐμέ.. Ἐὰν δ᾽ ἀφιεῖτε καλοὶ μὴ ..] How light, however, will this penalty be, if a few small alms, certain little prayers repeated at fixed intervals, a circuit of the cross-steps in the marketplace, fasting upon fasting, and similar baubles are offered as a suitable compensation for such foul crimes in a lay man, and exclusion from the Church for two or three months is imposed on a priest, however firmly he is caught in adultery and in the act?

units.la: XLIII. Quorsum obsecro illud Gloffatorem, Qui admisit, Causa 15. q. 6. Minus [?] propter fornicationem, quàm propter aliud crimen, pauci sine eo crimine inveniuntur. Unde laxatio consequi debuit. Non pudet enim [?] Decreti, ad Canonem Presbyter. Dist. 82. [?] nicationis causa hodie nemo est deponendus. Can. Fraternit. tuae, ubi agitur de promotione, nec castitatem in priori conjugio servavera[t]... funĉta liberos ex ancilla suscéperat, sic [?] quamvis multa sunt, quae in hujusmodi casibus canonica jubeat sublimitatis authoritas: [?] sectus nostri temporis, quibus non solum m[?] pora ipsa hominum defecerunt, distinctionem [?] titur manere censuram. Supra quoque A[?] induximus sancientem, quòd Episcopo de[?] que criminibus, quae sunt minora, post p[?] tentiam dispensare liceat.
units.tr: XLIII. Why, I beg you, that gloss on the decree, He who has admitted, Causa 15, q. 6: Minus [?] on account of fornication, than on account of another crime, few are found without that crime. Whence relaxation ought to follow. For it is not shameful [?] of the Decretum, on the canon Presbyter, Dist. 82: no one is today to be deposed on account of fornication. Canon Fraternitatis tuae, where promotion is discussed, nor had he kept chastity in the former marriage [?] had begotten children by a maidservant; thus [?] although there are many things which the canonical authority of higher rank orders in such cases: [?] of our time, when not only the times of men have failed, the distinction [?] remains censure. Above also we have cited the decree that it is lawful for a bishop to dispense, after penance, in those crimes which are lesser.

units.la: XLIV. Olim quidem Sacerdotes & D[?] crimine aliquo, luxuriae inprimis, obstrin[?] rio in perpetuum motos fuisse, exceptis [?] regulam firmantibus, satis constat. Test[?] Epist. Can. 2. can. 3. Concilium Aureliar[?] Johannes II. Papa Epist. 1. ad Caesarium Epist. lib. ij. ep. 26. iv. ep. 16. Nam qu[?] dem lib. vij. Ind. 2. Ep. 54. in contrarium genuina, sed à falsario supposita esse, Mo[?] nistrat. Poenit. lib. iv. 15. fatetur. Atqu[?] fuisse Isidorum Mercatorem, impostorem Wendrokius in Epist. Prov. 6. Not. 2. monstrat; addens ss. 5. ex Spuriis Calix[?]
units.tr: XLIV. It is quite certain that in former times priests and deacons who were bound by some crime, chiefly lust, were moved from office in perpetuity, with exceptions confirming the rule. Witnesses are the Epistles, Canon 2, Canon 3; the Council of Orléans; Pope John II, Epistle 1 to Caesarius; Epistle, book 2, letter 26; book 4, letter 16. For indeed [?] book 7, Indiction 2, Epistle 54, which is said to be contrary, is the genuine work of a forger, as [?] Ministry of Penance, book 4, 15, confesses. And that Isidore Mercator was an impostor, Wendrock shows in the Epistles of Provence, note 2, adding in §5 that from the spurious Epistles of Isidore of Seville the collapse of the ancient discipline towards priests who had fallen came about.

units.la: Isidori Hispalensis Epistolis, antiquæ erga Sacerdotes lapsos disciplinæ collapsionem fluxisse.
units.tr: From the Epistles of Isidore of Seville, the collapse of the ancient discipline towards fallen priests flowed.

units.la: XLV. Quid ergo hic recentiores inprimis Hierarchicorum Casuistæ? Baunius Jesuita Tract. 10. pag. 474, Nulla, inquit, lex aut canon Parochos obligat ad quotidie sacrificandum, imò nec posse dari talem, scripsit cum aliis Possevinus; eò quòd haberet lex ejusmodi peccati mortalis periculum, cui obligatum ad sacrificandum quotidie haud dubiè objiceret, cùm difficile sit & arduum, inter æstus Seculi undâsque fluctuantem aliquando non hærere in vitiorum turpi salo. Hujus verò periculi metum mox demit, rationem offendens, quia possunt Sacerdotes, etiamsi peccata mortalia subinde committant, quotidie tamen sacrificare, ac pronn accepto pretio quotidie sacrificandi obligationem suscipere. Quia, inquit, Sacerdoti juris est omni tempore contritionis exercendæ liberum, potestas quolibet momento temporis redeundi per amorem peccatique odium ad Deum, quo si officio non fungitur, imputet ipse sibi vitium hoc. Atque ut eas removeat difficultates, quibus maximè à celebrando quotidie sacrificio retrahi possent, sic pag. 457. loquitur: Si post habitam eo die copulam carnalem cum fœmina, aut pollutionem voluntariam Sacerdos sit confessus, eine liberum erit sine culpa veniali rei Divinæ incumbere? Negat Villalobos &c. Dissentit Sancius, cujus opinio mihi & tuta, & sequenda videtur in praxi. Quæ verba sic Montaltius Epist. Provinc. 6. excipit: Itáne, sponsore Baunio, tanto contaminatus piaculo Sacerdos ad tremendum altare se sistet? Quanto religiosius antiquis Ecclesiæ canonibus obtemperaret, qui Sacerdotes istiusmodi flagitiis pollutos, sacrificandi munere in perpetuum, vel ad longum certè tempus arcebant, quos à scelere recentes eadem nupera scriptorum vestrorum dogmata propellunt? Idem cum Baunio.
units.tr: XLV. What, then, do the more recent Casuists of the Hierarchs say here, especially?
