Similia de eo Thuanus lib. xxxv ... bemus decem Pontifices, Pium II. Paulum II. Sixtum IV. Innocentium VIII. Alexandrum VI. Julium II. Leonem X. (Clementem VII. ne computem) Paulum III. Pium IV. intra unius Seculi decursum ordine sibi succedentes (ne Successio Papalis, qualis ejusmodi sit, lateat amplius) infamiæ, impuritatis stigmatis non à nostris duntaxat, sed etiam ab aliis authoribus, inustos. Quòd si in camarina ... ter tantummodo commota, aures animum ... plet, concutienda, pergere animus esset, ... nis hujus comperti se offerrent. Sed ex ungue ... quidem, sed divinent alii, quales. Quid vero fiet de ovibus, si sic Pastores lupi sunt?
units.tr: But let this beast be dismissed, or, to speak with Guicciardini, Hist. book 6, this dragon, who infected the whole world with immoderate ambition, pestilential treachery, and examples of horrible cruelty, monstrous lust and unheard-of greed. Let us also dismiss his successor, Pius III, the stage Pope of twenty-six days, and turn to Julius II, nephew of Sixtus IV, whom Guicciardini in book 9 says was a drunkard, brought up on delights and pleasures. He had a daughter, Felix by name, whom the Pope, once made, gave in marriage to Giovanni Giordano Orsini, according to Onuphrius. I pass over what the French objected about violence done by him to noble youths, lest I seem to rely too much on enemies. Julius had as successor the one of whom Jovius writes in book 4 of the Life of Leo: He was not free from infamy, because he joked rather indecently with the courtiers (for they were the noblemen from all over Italy), and with these more tenderly and freely. Excusing the man: But who, even the best prince, has avoided slander in this most slanderous court? And who, on the other hand, consumed by the rot of hateful envy, has so scrutinized the true secrets of the nights? And if by this name illustrious virtue could be besmirched, [Leo] would bear the praise of moderation, more fairly compared with the fame of Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII and Alexander VI. Thus one who has been utterly shameless, and has not yet squandered all shame, can seem honest. Of this man's ... the atheism of Pico of Mirandola, and Sforza's testimonies, Hist. Pap. f. 155, we convict Adrian VI. The German, free of infamy from his German virtue, did not, according to Onuphrius, have any family of his own. Then Clement VII, born of an illegitimate union, Jovius describes in Histories book 3: For, since he loved no one, except those won over by more refined causes, these alone he favoured in particular, so that he raised them to the highest honours, or to a position of stability and wealth without any ... Next to him was Paul III, who had several bastards. He loved Pietro Luigi, to whom he gave Parma and Piacenza, dearly, although he was given over to dreadful lust, and to those reproaching him with this ... the teacher of vices, he did not ... to his son. As if one who professed celibacy and pretended, having condemned intercourse, could beget a son without rubbing the sting of incontinence into the one begotten, and without supplying an example of lust whenever he recalls his own origin! Many horrid things about his debaucheries and unspeakable incests are told in an Italian-written book, excerpted by Sleidanus, Hist. book 21, and cited by Thuanus himself. Yet this is the one who did not hesitate to use as legate Giovanni della Casa, Archbishop of Benevento, whom, as we showed above, composed the poem on the praises of Sodomy. The man who succeeded him, of especially monstrous lust, Julius III, while still a Cardinal, according to Onuphrius, pursued pleasures as if by stealth. Made Pope, now master of all his wishes, having cast aside care of affairs, he indulged too much in merriment and his own inclination. Thuanus says this about the same man in book 6 and book 28: Innocentius Montanus (who, because he looked after the monkey in the household, kept the name Simia even after gaining dignity), was enrolled among the College of Cardinals by Julius III, to the great infamy of the most distinguished order; afterwards he lived a life of even greater infamy, being accused of having killed a father and son, innkeepers, so that he might possess the wife of the one. This youth Innocentius, whom Julius had kept among his favourites when he was legate at Bologna, was reported to have been... Having become Pope, he gave his own cardinal's hat to this Innocentius, readmitted him to his household, and bestowed on him his own surname and insignia. At Rome then there was a rumour, and it was also written about in little books (so Sleidanus records), that Ganymede, though misshapen, was cherished by Jove. But the Pope himself did not conceal this from the other Cardinals, and is said to have mentioned it in jest now and then, how wanton and importunate the youth is. We have given more about him on the authority of Papirius Masson, and indeed of Pallavicini himself, Hist. Pap. f. 176. Finally, Pius IV, who succeeded this Julius, was sharp in words and witticisms, greedy for food and wine, while prone to pleasures, etc. Onuphrius ... is witness. Thuanus says similar things of him in book 35 ... We have ten Popes, Pius II, Paul II, Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII, Alexander VI, Julius II, Leo X (not counting Clement VII), Paul III and Pius IV, succeeding one another in order within the span of one century (so that the papal succession, of what kind it is, may lie hidden no longer), branded with the stigma of infamy and impurity, not only by our writers but also by other authors. But if it were my intention to proceed, and the mind, once stirred by these things, filled the ears ... shaken, these discovered things would present themselves. But from the claw ... indeed, but let others guess what sort. What then will become of the sheep, if the shepherds are such wolves?

units.la: LXII. Sed magna insuper testimonio Hierarchicorum impuritate nubes in proximo ciora ex octo elapsis Seculis excerpere velut quorum, haud pigebit equidem. Seculo ruitque Huldricus Augustanus Episcopus Nicolaum I. adversus Sacerdotum conjugium insurgentem Epistolam, quâ eum ex Scriptura Ecclesiastica sic satis liberè acerbéque ter alia sic ille: Quid Divinæ maledictionis quàm cùm aliqui vel Episcopi videlicet, ita præcipites sunt in libidinem, ut neque ineestus, neque masculorum (probrosissimos amplexus sciant abhorrere) quòd conjugia sibi dicant fœtere, & ab eis non compassione clericos, ut conservos rogent tinere, sed ut servos jubeant ac cogant ad jus imperii, ne dicam consilii tam fatuam addunt suggestionem, ut dicant: Honestum ... occultè implicari, quàm aperte in hominum vultu & conscientia cum una ligari. Quod profectò non dicerent, si ex illo, & in illo essent, qui dicit: Væ vobis, Pharisæi, qui omnia faciunt propter homines. Paulò post: Hic est autem, si diligenter inspiciatur, totius eorum manipulus zizaniæ, totius conventus insaniæ, ut dum clerici licita unius mulieris consortia Pharisaico devicti, quod absit, furore relinquere coguntur, fornicatores & adulteri, & aliarum pravitatum turpissimi ministri cum ipsis efficiantur, qui hanc in Ecclesia Dei hærefin, sicut cæci duces cæcorum machinantur, ut videlicet illud impleatur, quod Psaltes eis, utpote eorum præscius erroris, taliter imprecatur: Obscurentur oculi eorum, ne videant, & dorsum eorum semper incurva. Epistolæ hujus germanitatem Parthenog. cap. xviij. 15. 16. testimoniis Bertholdi seu Bernoldi Append. ad Chron. Herm. Contracti ad A. 1079. Germ. Script. Urstisii p. 349. & Ænexæ Sylvii de moribus Germ. p. 1053. aliisque documentis, ipsiusque Gabr. Vasquezii confessione convicimus, discussis etiam iis, quæ in contrarium Bellarminus obduxit.
units.tr: LXII. But moreover, great clouds of hierarchical impurity, supported by the testimony of the hierarchs themselves, will not trouble me to pick out from the eight centuries just past, as examples. In the ninth century Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg, wrote a letter against Nicholas I, who rose up against the marriage of priests, in which he argues from ecclesiastical Scripture, sufficiently freely and bitterly, and says the following: "What of divine curse, when some, that is bishops, are so headlong into lust that they know neither incest nor (abhorrent) embraces of males, and they call marriages stinking; and they do not ask clerics, as fellow-servants, to restrain themselves out of compassion, but command and compel them as servants by the right of power, not to say of counsel, and they add so foolish a suggestion as to say: 'It is more honourable to be secretly entangled than openly bound to a wife in the face and conscience of men.' They surely would not say this if they were of him, and in him, who says: Woe to you, Pharisees, who do everything for men's sake. A little later: This is, if carefully examined, the whole handful of their tares, the whole assembly of madness, so that while clerics, overcome by Pharisaic fury, are compelled, God forbid, to leave the lawful partnership of one wife, fornicators and adulterers, and the most shameful ministers of other depravities, are made with them, who machinate this heresy in the Church of God, like blind leaders of the blind; so that what the Psalmist, aware of their error, prays against them in such words may be fulfilled: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bend their back always." We prove the genuineness of this letter by the testimonies of Bertold or Bernold, Appendix to the Chronicle of Hermann Contractus, under the year 1079, Urstisius's German Writers p. 349, and Aeneas Silvius on German customs, p. 1053, and by other documents, and by the very confession of Gabriel Vasquez, having also discussed those things which Bellarmine brought forward to the contrary.

units.la: LXIII. Seculi Decimi, fui asperitate ac boni sterilitate ferrei, malique exunda[n]tis deformitate plumbei, uti Baronius ad A. 900. n. 1. appellat, quàm fœda facies fuerit, lippis jam tonsoribusque notum est.
units.tr: LXIII. How foul the face of the Tenth Century was, in its harshness, iron-hard in its barrenness and leaden in the deformity of the evil that overflowed, as Baronius calls it at A.D. 900, n. 1, is already known to men with sore eyes and to barbers.

units.la: Quæ tunc, sic idem Baronius ad A. 912. num. 8. scribit ingenuè, facies sanctæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ? quàm sædissima, quum Romæ dominarentur potentissimæ æquè ac sordidissimæ meretrices? quarum arbitrio mutarentur sedes, darentur episcopi, & quod auditu horrendum & infandum est, intruderentur in sedem Petri earum amasii Pseudo-Pontifices, qui non sunt nisi ad consignanda tempora in catalogo Romanorum Pontificum scripti. Quis enim à scortis hujusmodi intrusos sine lege legitimos posset dicere Pontifices Ro-
units.tr: Baronius, at A.D. 912, n. 8, candidly writes of it: "What face had the holy Roman Church? How most foul it was, when the most powerful and equally most filthy prostitutes ruled at Rome! At their will sees were changed and bishops were given; and, what is horrible and unspeakable to hear, their lovers, false popes, were thrust into the seat of Peter. These are written in the catalogue of Roman pontiffs only to mark the times. For who could say that men intruded without law by such harlots were lawful Roman popes?"

units.la: De Seculo Decimi intrusa Baronii confessio. manos fuisse? Quales non reris dele�including [?] servaret incontaminatam. Quibus auditis Sanctissimus Pontifex, cum Viri Sancti laudavit zelum, tum etiam pro criminum qualitate & quantitate ultor offensi Numinis, poenas dignas opposuit, quas habet ejusdem Pontificis Epistola, ad eundem Petrum reddita, quæ præfixa legitur Gomorrhæo, quæ unà cum pluribus aliis ejusdem auctoris lucubrationibus extat in antiquitus scripto codice Bibliothecæ Sancti Petri in Vaticano, quo sumus usi in his conscribendis. Leonis Epistolam responsoriam idem Baronius recitat, in quo sic ille inter alia: Clerici verò, de quorum vita spurcissima flebiliter pariterque rationabiliter tua prudentia disputavit, verè, & omnino verè ad funiculum hæreditatis ejus non pertinent, de quo ipsi voluptuosis se oblectationibus submovent. Et laudavit sanè librum Leo ob zelum authoris. Sed Alexander II. suppressit paulò post, ita ut hactenus in pulvere Vaticano jacuerit. Prætexit causam Baronius, verborum obscœnitatem: sui tamen oblitus, qui num. 10. contra testatus erat his verbis: Quadripartita vitia carnis, quibus obrueretur Ecclesia, ut decuit, quàm potuit honestè, insinuavit. Si tam honestè, unde nunc tam repentè tanta verborum obscœnitas? Sed si vera tamen est, unde laus Leonis? Aut cur castior Alexander? Aut quæ spes fuit, suppressum iri fœditatem morum, suppressa obscœnitate verborum? Scilicet soliciti sunt magis boni illi viri de comprimendis satyris, quàm de purgandis moribus. Sanè etiam Petrus Damiani literis ad Cardinales Hildebrandum & Stephanum scriptis de Alexandro Gomorrhæum suum supprimente his verbis, quæ in codice Basilicæ S. Petri extant, questus est: Querelam omnipotenti Deo, & vobis, qui estis membra ejus, depono de nostro Domino Papa, qui cor meum tam acerbo mærore confurbat, & grandævi jam senis animam ad amaritudinem provocat. Tulit enim librum nostrum-suisque scriniis infarcivit, munditiæ Sacerdotalis indicium, imò Patris est argumentum. In ipsum verò Alexandrum mordaci invectus, sibi cognita innuit, ne infamiam ipsi allatura sint, ne coactus, querela compellar effluere, quod adhuc silere vix possum ulteriùs occultare.
units.tr: Baronius's admission of the Tenth Century's intrusions. "What sort of ... would you not think ... would keep [it] uncontaminated? When these things were heard, the most holy Pontiff praised the zeal of the holy man, and also, according to the quality and quantity of the crimes, he imposed on the avenger of the offended Deity the punishments that were due. These are contained in that Pontiff's letter, returned to the same Peter, which is prefixed to the Gomorrhian, and which, together with several other writings of the same author, exists in an ancient codex of the Library of St Peter in the Vatican, which we have used in writing these things." Baronius quotes Leo's answering letter, in which he says among other things: "But the clerics, whose most filthy life your prudence has disputed, tearfully and yet reasonably, are truly and altogether not included in the cord of that inheritance, since they withdraw themselves from it by voluptuous pleasures." Leo certainly praised the book for its author's zeal. But Alexander II suppressed it soon after, so that until now it has lain in the dust of the Vatican. Baronius pretends the cause was the obscenity of the words; yet he forgets himself, since at n. 10 he testified to the contrary in these words: "He hinted at the fourfold vices of the flesh, by which the Church was overwhelmed, as becomingly and as decently as he could." If it was so decent, whence now such sudden obscenity of words? But if it is true, whence Leo's praise? Or why was Alexander the more chaste? Or what hope was there that the foulness of morals would be suppressed by suppressing the obscenity of words? Clearly those good men were more concerned with silencing satires than with purifying morals. Peter Damian, too, in letters written to the Cardinals Hildebrand and Stephen, complained of Alexander suppressing his Gomorrhian, in these words, which exist in the codex of the Basilica of St Peter: "I lay my complaint before almighty God and before you, who are his members, about our lord the Pope, who troubles my heart with such bitter grief and provokes to bitterness the soul of an old man now aged. For he has taken away our book and stuffed it into his chests, a token of priestly cleanliness, or rather a proof of a father's." Turning fiercely against Alexander himself, he hints at things known to him, lest they bring infamy upon him: "lest, compelled, I should let slip in a complaint what I can scarcely keep silent and hide any longer."

units.la: LXV. Ex Seculo Duodecimo repræse- ntatis Hierarchicorum plures possem.
units.tr: LXV. From the Twelfth Century I could cite several representations of the hierarchs.

units.la: ero. Bernhardi inprimis Serm. de convers. 20. dignissima memoratu illa sunt: Curr. dines sacros, & reverenda ipsis quoque Sacerdotes suo super ministeria homines apprehendunt sine consideratione. Neque enim signum regni aut illius timent imperii gestare coronam, tyrannia regnat, ambitio imperat, dominatur iniquitas, & luxuria etiam principatur. Hæc forte appareat intra parietes abominationis, Ezechielis prophetiam, parietem fodiat Dei videamus horrendum. Siquidem post adulteria, post incestus, nec ipsæ quidem ignominiosæ passiones, & turpitudinis, nam non fierent, quæ usque adeò non coluerunt. Apostolum hæc scribere, nec nos dicere dicentibus crederetur, quòd humanum verit animum tam abominanda cupido. Num civitates illæ spurcitiæ hujus matres Dei judicio, & incendio sunt delete? Num ullus flamma moram non sustinens, execrationit tollere nationem, quòd ipsius speciale manifesta præcedentia ad judicium? Nam ipsam utpote consciam tantæ confusionis te ignis, sulphur & Spiritus procellarum? locum horribilem solum omne redactum est? Amputatae sunt hydræ capita quinque, sed heu! innumera resurrexerunt. Quis reædificavit urbes flagitii, quis turpitudinis mœnia dilatavit, quis extendit propagines virulentas? Væ, væ, inimicus hominum sulphurei illius incendii reliquias infelices circumquaque dispersit, execrabili illo cinere ecclesiæ corpus aspersit, & ipsorum quoque ministrorum ejus nonnullos sanie fœtidissima spurcissimáque respersit. Heu genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis; quis inter tua illa primordia tam Divina, & spiritualibus affluentem charismatibus Christianæ religionis ortum credere posset, posse talia in te aliquando reperiri? Utinam magus turrim inchoaturi, sedentes computarent: ne forte sumptus non habeant ad perficiendum. Utinam qui continere non valent, perfectionem temeraríe profiteri, aut cœlibatui dare nomina verentur. Sumptuosa quippe turris, & verbum grande, quod non omnes capere possunt. Esset autem sine dubio melius nubere, quam uri, & salvari in humili gradu fidelis populi, quam in cleri sublimitate & deterius vivere, & districtius judicari. Multi enim, non quidem omnes, sed tamen multi, certum est, neque latere queunt præ multitudine, nec præ impudentia quærunt; multi utique libertatem, in qua vocati sunt, in occasionem Carnis dediße videntur, abstinentes remedio nuptiali, & in omne deinceps flagitium effluentes. Vel unum hoc Divi Pontificii testimonium omni exceptione majus ad Hierarchiam Babylonicæ impuritatis convincendam efficax satis est. Sed eodem Seculo etiam Rupertus, Ordinis Benedictini, Abbas Tuitiensis, commentans in Apocalypsin, ubi in mentionem Nicolaitarum incidit, eorum de promiscuo fœminarum usu doctrinam suæ ætatis Clericis lib. viij sic accommodavit: Annon illi doctrinæ victum hoc est, quod ipsi legitimum non volentes habere conju-
units.tr: ... Bernard, above all, in his sermon On conversion 20, has these most worthy of mention: "Why do men seize sacred things, and the priests who are to be revered, upon their own ministries without consideration? For they do not fear to bear the crown as a sign of kingdom or of empire. Tyranny reigns, ambition commands, iniquity dominates, and luxury even holds the principate." Perhaps this appears within the walls of abomination; let us see the horrible thing that Ezekiel prophesied, when he dug through the wall of God. For after adulteries, after incests, not even the shameful passions and filthiness, which they did not so much cultivate, would be believed to have been committed, were the Apostle to write them, nor would we dare to say them. Were those cities not destroyed by the judgment of God and by fire, for their filth? Did no flame, not enduring delay, rise up to root out the nation, because its manifest and special precedence was to judgment? For fire, sulphur and the spirit of storms, as conscious of so great a confusion, reduced that horrible place to a solid whole? The heads of the hydra were cut off, five of them, but alas! countless ones have risen again. Who rebuilt the cities of shame? Who extended the walls of filth? Who spread out its poisonous shoots? Woe, woe! The enemy of men has scattered the unhappy remnants of that sulphurous fire on every side, has sprinkled the body of the Church with that accursed ash, and has spattered some of its very ministers with most foul and filthy matter. Alas, elect race, royal priesthood, holy nation, people of acquisition! Who, amid those most divine beginnings of yours, abounding in spiritual gifts, could believe that the origin of the Christian religion could ever find such things in you? Would that the magician, about to begin a tower, first sat down and counted, lest perhaps they lacked the means to finish it. Would that those who cannot contain themselves rashly professed perfection, or feared to give their names to celibacy. For the tower is costly, and the word is great, which not everyone can grasp. Without doubt it would be better to marry than to burn, and to be saved in the humble rank of the faithful people, than in the height of the clergy to live worse and be judged more strictly. For many, not indeed all, but still many, as is certain, and cannot be hidden for their multitude, nor do they seek to hide for their shamelessness; many, indeed, seem to have turned the liberty to which they were called into an occasion for the flesh, abstaining from the remedy of marriage and pouring themselves out into every disgrace. This one testimony of the divine Pontifical writers, outweighing every exception, is sufficiently effective to convict the hierarchy of Babylonian impurity. But in the same century Rupert, Benedictine monk and Abbot of Tuy, commenting on the Apocalypse, when he came to mention the Nicolaitans, applied their doctrine of the common use of women to the clerics of his own age, in book 8, in this way: "Is it not the case that this doctrine is the fare of those who, not wishing to have a lawful marriage, which is forbidden by ecclesiastical laws, are holy and commanded, because they carry vessels ..."

units.la: lib. viij conjugium, utpote legibus ecclesiasticis interdicta, sancti & mandentur, quia portant vasa ... minus incontinentes sunt? imò deterius ... tantes connubia, quoties volunt, & qui in ... rum licitum dum sic evagantur, nullum conjugii vinculum. Fornicantur autem ... tantur Beelphegor, quicunque exemplo ... vel adulteria audaciores fiunt. Et tunc quod ... fuit, quòd aperuit Dominus os subjugalis (Num. xxiii. 14. Apoc. ii. 14.) & animal hominis redarguit Prophetæ insipientiam, qui hu... dedit: sed & nunc pene illi simile fit, quod beja rectores ecclesiæ clamoribus suis coangustat. Sic clericos matrimonio abstinentes ... nibus sese polluentes, suóque exemplo ... lia scelera invitantes, quin & eos, qui Clericis ... jungunt, at de cætero vagas eidem libidini ... cum Nicolaitis paria facere, merito ille pe...
units.tr: Book 8: "... marriage, as forbidden by ecclesiastical laws, are they less incontinent? Rather, worse ... marry whenever they wish, and those who in ... of it, while they wander thus, have no bond of marriage. They fornicate, however, ... follow Beelphegor, whoever by the example ... or become bolder in adultery. And then what ... was done, that the Lord opened the mouth of the ass (Num. xxiii. 14; Apoc. ii. 14), and the beast rebuked the folly of the prophet, who ... gave; but now also something nearly similar happens, which the rulers of the Church crowd with their outcries. Thus, clerics who abstain from marriage ... pollute themselves, and by their example invite ... other crimes; and indeed those who join clerics ... and henceforth make the wanderers equal in the same lust with the Nicolaitans, rightly that one ..."
LXVI. Nor Is the Tenth Century Lacking Such Examples

units.la: ejusmodi destituitur. Vixit eo Seculo flemus Durandus, Episcopus Mimatensis, ... lum juris, unde ei Speculatoris nomen ... tionale Divinorum officiorum, & Tractatus ... neralis Concilii celebrandi scripsit. In eo ... rubr. 10. hunc in modum verba facit: Cæno, & multis alius Conciliis familiari ... extraneis sit interdicta, nec id tamen ser... multa scandala sequantur, & contra ... populus, videretur utile pro conservatione ... & honoris, quòd mandaretur servari, ... quòd prostibula publica non tenantur ... in Romana curia propè palatium Domini, ... alibi propè domos Prælatorum, & ne ma... Papæ & consimiles aliquid recipiant à meretricibus & lenonibus earundem. En canones de arcendis mulieribus extraneis prorsus extinctos, & jam tum publica prostibula proximè palatium papæ! Quæ Apostolica jam dici debebunt eo jure, quo ea, quæ quoquo modo ad Pontificem spectant, velut Sedem, Cameram, Curiam, Nuntios, Bullas &c. Apostolicas vocare consueverunt. Subjungit rubrica 46. idem: Cùm penè in omnibus Conciliis, & à plerisque Romanis Pontificibus super cohibenda & punienda Clericorum incontinentia, & eorum honestate servanda multa hactenus emanaverint constituta; & nullatenus eorum reformari quiverit correctio morum &c. videretur pensandum, an expediret & posset provideri, quòd in Ecclesia occidentali, quantum ad votum continentiæ, servaretur consuetudo Ecclesiæ Orientalis, quantum ad promovendos, potissimè, cùm tempore Apostolorum consuetudo Ecclesiæ Orientalis servaretur. Eodem Seculo A. MCCLI. Pontifice Innocentio IV. Concilio Lugduni habito, sic ejus & Curiæ nomine Hugo Cardinalis, narrante, uti supra etiam Thesi LVI. attigimus, Matthæo Paris in Henrico III. ad A. 1251. urbi Lugdunensi valedixit: Amici, magnam fecimus, postquam in hanc urbem venimus, utilitatem & eleemosynam: Quando enim primò huc venimus, tria vel quatuor proslibula invenimus. Sed nunc recedentes unum solum relinquimus. Verum ipsum durat continuatum ab Orientali porta civitatis usque ad Occidentalem. Et erat, inquit Paris, verbum offensionis in auribus omnium mulierum, quarum infinita multitudo sermoni assidebat. Hæc autem ironia in ore multorum versabatur, quia Cynicè momordit universos.
units.tr: Such men were not lacking in the tenth century either. In that century lived Durandus, Bishop of Mende, ... law, whence he received the name of Speculator, ... the Rationale of the Divine Offices, and a Treatise ... on the celebration of a general council. In it, under the rubric 10, ... he speaks as follows: "Cæno, and many other councils, ... that prostitutes be forbidden to foreigners, and although this is not carried out, ... many scandals follow, and on the contrary ... the people, it would seem useful, for the preservation ... and honour, that it be ordered to be observed, ... that public prostitutes are not to be kept ... in the Roman curia, near the palace of the Lord, ... elsewhere near the houses of the prelates, and that the Pope and such like receive nothing from the prostitutes and procurers of the same." Here are canons on keeping foreign women away, now utterly extinct, and public brothels already near the Pope's palace! What will henceforth be called Apostolic by that right, by which whatever pertains in any way to the Pontiff, such as the See, the Chamber, the Curia, the Nuncios, the Bulls, etc., they are accustomed to call Apostolic? The same author adds under rubric 46: "Since almost in all councils, and by most Roman Pontiffs, many decrees have hitherto been issued concerning the restraint and punishment of the incontinence of clerics and the keeping of their honour, and since the correction of morals could in no way be reformed, etc., it seems worth weighing whether it would be expedient and possible to provide that in the Western Church, as regards the vow of continence, the custom of the Eastern Church be observed, as regards those to be promoted, especially since in the time of the Apostles the custom of the Eastern Church was observed." In the same century, in the year 1251, under Pope Innocent IV, after the council held at Lyons, Cardinal Hugh, speaking on behalf of himself and the Curia, as we touched on above also in Thesis LVI, bade farewell to the city of Lyons, as Matthew Paris reports in Henry III, under the year 1251: "Friends, since we came into this city we have made a great gain and alms: for when we first came here we found three or four brothels. But now, as we leave, we leave only one. Indeed that one lasts continuously from the eastern gate of the city to the western." And, says Paris, this was a word of offence in the ears of all the women, of whom an infinite multitude sat by the sermon. But this irony was on the lips of many, because it bit everyone in the manner of a Cynic.

units.la: LXVII. In Seculum Decimum quartum Alvarus Pelagius, Sylvensis in Portugallia Episcopus, incidit, & Opus de Planctu Ecclesiæ Avenione in Curia Papæ Johannis hannis
units.tr: LXVII. In the Fourteenth Century Alvarus Pelagius, Bishop of Silves in Portugal, Wrote His Book on the Lament of the Church, Concerning the Curia of Pope John XXII at Avignon

units.la: Tom. II. hannis XXII. perscripsit. In opere isthoc [?] nalium, Episcoporum & Presbyterorum lib. ÿ. art. 27. quartum crimen designat, [?] ter vivant. Enormitatibus se immiscent crapulæ & ebrietati, & incontinentiæ eorum commune) & plerique vitio conti tra sanctam castitatem, quam Domino offendunt continuè etiam publicè: præte DISSIMA quæ in occultis perpetrante reciperent, nec calamus posset exare nam, inquit, continentiam nunquam pro Hispani & Regnicolæ, in quibus Provin jori numero sunt filii laicorum, quàm quod sceleratiùs est, per plurimos annos binæ qualibet die surgunt non præmissa hypocritali cum proposito redeundi, & tare ad terrificam hostiam consecrandam tum, quantum in eis est, Domino cordib sis offerentes. VI. Libentiùs dant jocu ci, quàm pauperi. XIV. Sæpe cum Par bus, quæ ad confessionem admittuntur, nicantur. XXXII. Cùm sint notorii fornicarii, consequens suspensi quantum ad se, & qu & Simoniaci et si occulti, vel aliàs suspen nihilominus celebrant omni die. XLV. serviri in altari, & in Ecclesia per suos XLIX. De bonis Ecclesiæ pascunt conc & filios, & de pecunia Ecclesiæ emunt LIII. Multi Presbyteri, & alii confi maximè in Hispania, Asturia & Gallicia blicè, & aliquoties per publicum instru tunt & jurant quibusdam, maximè nobi nunquam eas dimittere; & dant eis arr clesiæ, & possessionibus Ecclesiæ; & publicè eas ducunt cum consanguineis & amicis & solenni convivio, ac si essent uxores legitimæ. Sed & art. 2. sol. 83. ad verba illa Thren. v. 13. Adolescentibus impunè abusi sunt, sic commentatus idem est: Heu, heu intra Sanctam Ecclesiam
units.tr: Vol. II. John XXII. In this work he marks out the fourth crime ... of the clergy, bishops and presbyters book 5, art. 27., namely that they live ... they plunge themselves into enormities of gluttony and drunkenness, and their incontinence is common, and most of them are given to the vice ... against holy chastity, which they offend continually and also publicly. Besides the ... things which they commit in secret, which no pen could describe, for, he says, they have never been continent. ... Spaniards and natives, in whose provinces the greater number of the children are the sons of laymen, and what is more wicked, for very many years they rise each day to celebrate, without any hypocritical pretence of returning, and ... to the terrible sacrifice to consecrate, offering to the Lord, so far as in them lies, hearts ... VI. They give more willingly to jesters than to the poor. XIV. Often with ... those who are admitted to confession are noted. XXXII. Since they are notorious fornicators, consequently suspended as far as they themselves are concerned, and ... and simoniacs, even if secret, or otherwise suspended, nevertheless they celebrate every day. XLV. They serve at the altar, and in the church through their own ... XLIX. They feed their concubines and sons from the goods of the Church, and they buy with the money of the Church ... LIII. Many presbyters and others, ... especially in Spain, Asturias and Galicia, openly, and sometimes by public instrument, ... they make and swear to certain women, especially noble ones, that they will never dismiss them; and they give them a dowry from the property of the Church, and from the possessions of the Church; and they openly lead them about with their kinsfolk and friends at a solemn feast, as if they were lawful wives. But also in art. 2, sol. 83, on those words of Lamentations 5:13, "They abused the young men with impunity," he comments in the same way: "Alas, alas, within the Holy Church"

units.la: MULTI RELIGIOSI ET CLERICI in suis latebris & conventiculis, & laici jam in plerisque civitatibus, maximè in Italia publicè, quodammodo pu- blicum Gymnasium constituunt & palæstram, in illius fla- gitii abominatione se exercentes, & OPTIMI quique EPHEBORUM in lupanari ponuntur.
units.tr: MANY RELIGIOUS AND CLERICS in their hiding-places and conventicles, and laymen now in most cities, especially in Italy openly, establish in a way a public gymnasium and wrestling-school, exercising themselves in the abomination of that vice, and the BEST of the youths are put into the brothel.

units.la: Quod flagitium, utinam leges; aliàs enim timor Dei eos à tanto malo non revocat, &c. Tantam enim delectationem abominabilem in illo flagitio immundus Spiritus subministrat, ut multò majorem ibi sentiant, quàm in fœtore libidinis mulierum, qui isto morbo laborant, sicut audivi à talibus, hoc non erubescentibus confiteri. Addit versa pagina: In tantum totus mundus, maximè Italia, istius sceleris speciebus obrutus est, quòd remedium non superest, nec prædicationem, nec timoris pœnæ temporalis, nisi ignis de Cœlo sulphureus in ira Dei ad correctionem aliorum, iterum super istos sceleratissimos utraque morte dignissimos, descendat velociter & consumat, sicut consumpsit & exterminavit pessimos Sodomitas. Eodem Seculo Robertus Holkot, Dominicanus, lect. 193. in Sapientiam hanc querelam consignavit: Sacerdotes moderni sunt Angeli incubi per luxuriam. Incubi vel incubones, secundum Isidorum, à Romanis dicuntur Fauni. Sunt etiam, ut creditur, dæmones corpora assumentes, vel sibi jungentes, & sic mulieribus se immiscentes. Et dæmones incubi dicuntur nonnunquam generare gigantes. Ita Sacerdotes per vehementiam voluptatis gignunt communiter pingues, grossos & corpulentos.
units.tr: Would that the laws dealt with this vice; otherwise the fear of God does not call them back from so great an evil, etc. For the unclean spirit supplies such a abominable delight in that vice, that they feel it to be far greater there than in the stench of lust with women, as I have heard from such men, who are not ashamed to confess it. On the next page he adds: "The whole world, and especially Italy, is so overwhelmed by the kinds of this wickedness that no remedy remains, neither preaching nor fear of temporal punishment, unless a sulphurous fire from Heaven, in the wrath of God for the correction of others, descend swiftly upon those most wicked men, most worthy of double death, and consume them, as it consumed and destroyed the most wicked Sodomites." In the same century Robert Holkot, the Dominican, in his lecture 193 on the Book of Wisdom, recorded this complaint: "The present priests are incubus angels through lust. Incubi or incubones, according to Isidore, are called fauns by the Romans. There are also, as is believed, demons who assume bodies or join themselves to them, and so mingle with women. And demons called incubi are sometimes said to beget giants. Thus priests, through the vehemence of pleasure, commonly beget plump, gross and corpulent children."

units.la: Hi possunt dici Sacerdotes Priapi gor.
units.tr: These may be called the priests of Priapus' herd.

units.la: LXVIII. Luculentos inprimis Seculi quintum, Reformationi proximum, testes habet, ex quibus, concubinatum vagásque ... magis tum, quàm unquam invaluisse, ... sub Seculi hujus principium floruit, Johannes Gerson, Cancellarius Parisiensis de vita Spirit. lect. ... quam memorasset Thomam & alios dicentes ... qui à Sacerdotibus fornicariis Missam audire ... Inexpertí forte erant hi doctores, quàm g... radicatum sit hoc malum, & quomodo deterius ... ca uxores aut filias Parochianorum & aliorum ... rendæ in alias provenirent apud multos patres ... tibus ut stant, si quererentur per tales ... Scandalum certè magnum est, apud Parochianos ... concubinam ingressus, sed longè deteriùs ... chianas suas non servent castitatem. Ex Nicolao ... gis, Archidiacono Bajocensi, eodem tempore corrupto Ecclesiæ statu, qui inter opera ... sub titulo, de vitiis Ministrorum Ecclesiæ ... vulgante, nec non Chemensis Episcopi ... est, Onus Ecclesiæ nonnulla superiùs thesauro ... dotum concubinatu & impuritate allegavit ... mangis cap. 16. ff. 3. Sanctimonialium claustra Veneris postibula vocat; addens etiam, ab ipsis Sacerdotes, ut Parochiani pati nisi ... eos ampliùs noluerint, quò uxorem & filias ... pudicitia, quanquam ne sic quidem satis ... cap. 23. sic loquitur: Quid obsecro aliud ... puellarum monasteria, nisi quædam non ... ria, sed Veneris execranda prostibula? ... impudicorum juvenum ad libidines explendas. ut idem hodie sit puellam velare, quod & publicè ad scortandum exponere. Petrus ab Alliaco, Cardinalis Cameracensis, Tract. de Reform. Eccl. inter alia sic consulit: Adhibenda esset correctio circa mores Ecclesiasticorum, qui jam nimis, proh dolor! sunt corrupti irâ, gulâ, luxuriâ, pompâ, prodigalitate, otio & aliis generibus, quod cedit in grave scandalum laicorum. Et maximè obviandum esset illi scandalissimæ consuetudini, seu potius corruptelæ, qua plures hodie non verentur tenere etiam publicè concubinas. Stanislaus Orichovius Ruthenus in supplicatione ad Julium III. Non solum bipedum, inquit, sed etiam quadrupedum nequissimi facti sumus. Multæ enim pecudes nòrunt genus, nòrunt sexum suum. At hæc inter nos confusa multis, adeóque incerta sunt, ut etiam Romæ libellos publicè circumferri videas, quasi quasdam fornicationum isagogas, in quibus, &c. Qui eodem Seculo circa A. MCDXXXV. vixit claruitque Nicolaus Tudescus Siculus, primùm auditor Romæ, dein Abbas Monacensis, tandem Archiepiscopus Panormitanus, quin Cardinalis à Trithemio lucerna juris insignitus, C. Cùm olim de Cler. Conjug. proposita quæstione; Numquid hodie Ecclesia possit statuere, ut Clericus possit contrahere matrimonium, sicut Græci; respondet: Credo quòd sic &c. & non solùm credo, potestatem inesse Ecclesiæ hoc condendi, sed credo pro bono & salute animarum, quòd esset salubre statutum, ut volentes continere & magis mereri, relinquerentur voluntati eorum; non volentes autem continere, possint matrimonium contrahere: quia, experientia docente, cùm hodie non vivant spiritualiter, nec sint mundi, sed maculentur illicito coitu, cum eorum gravissimo peccato, ubi cum propria uxore esset castitas, ut dicitur Cap. Nicæna; unde deberet Ecclesia facere, sicut bonus Medicus, ut si medicina, experientia docente, potiùs officit, quàm prosit, eam tollat. Consentientia plane Polydorus Vergilius de Rer. In didit his verbis: Illud dixerim, tantum a atta castitas illam conjugalem vicerit, u licti crimen majus ordini dedecus, plus m doloris omnibus bonu impresserit, inusferi Sacerdotum libidinis labes. Proinde forp blica Christiana, quàm ex ordinis usu e liquando jus publici matrimonii Sacerdot quod illi sine infamia sanctè potiùs coleren eissimè ejuscemodi naturæ vitio turpific psum etiam visum est Pio II. ante Papatu, cujus varia inter apophtegmata Platina quoque referunt, fuisse causas, cur Sacretur conjugium, sed multò majores esse, Sub aliena proin persona propriam sentenexprompsit, quando res in Concilio Basi rans, cuidam pro Amedæo Sabaudiæ dgendo peroranti hæc verba lib ÿ. in fine t fortasse pejus Sacerdotes quàm plures u multi salvarentur in Sacerdotio conjuga Presbyteratu damnantur. Platina in vita ri impietatem deplorat: Quid futurum no tia nostra eò crevêre, ut vix apud Deum cum nobis reliquerint? Quanta sit avar & eorum maximè, qui rerum potiuntur, dique conquisita, quanta ambitio &c. ne cùm ipsi ita aperte & palam peccent., ac si rant. Unum ex hoc Seculo adhuc addam lum, Tigurinum & Solodurensem Canoempt. & vendit. unius pro 20. pag. 37, au sum quempiam contra clericos concubin collegisse, & in Brixiensi Dioecesi, præsum Attasim, contra clerum publicè præ cos contra suos Curatos concubinarios adeò concitâsse, ut nisi nobiles & ipse Episcopus se interposuissent, clerum ii destructuri fuerint. Agnoscit & detestatur idem Malleolus in sequentibus enormitatem sceleris ex Scriptura & decretis; silendum tamen ajens privato doctori vel clerico per sermones publicos, quia tota (NB) sileat Ecclesia. Alibi de Matrim. p. 40. Non est rarum, inquit, in Diœcesi Constantiensi, & cæteris vicinis mulierum & clericorum cohabitationis concubinatus contubernium.
units.tr: LXVIII. The fifth century, the one nearest the Reformation, provides outstanding witnesses. From them it is clear that concubinage and wandering lusts had taken hold more than ever before. At the beginning of this century, John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, flourished, in his work De vita spirituali, lect. ... Having mentioned Thomas and others who say that ... who hear Mass from fornicating priests ... These teachers were perhaps unaware how deeply rooted this evil was, and how much worse it was becoming, ... the wives or daughters of parishioners and others ... to other places among many fathers ... as they stand, if they were asked through such men ... Certainly it is a great scandal among the parishioners when someone enters a concubine, but much worse when their own ... do not keep chastity. From Nicholas ... de Clamanges, Archdeacon of Bayeux, at the same time when the state of the Church was corrupt, who among his works, under the title On the Vices of the Ministers of the Church ... publishing, and likewise the Bishop of Chartres ... The Burden of the Church, having said some things above in the treasury ... of priests, he cited concubinage and impurity ... in chapter 16, folio 3. He calls the cloisters of nuns brothels of Venus, adding also that by these the priests ... so that the parishioners, unless ... they no longer wished to have them, lest they lose their wives and daughters ... chastity, although even so not sufficiently ... chapter 23, he speaks thus: What, I beg you, else are the convents of girls, unless certain not ... houses, but detestable brothels of Venus? ... of shameless young men to satisfy their lusts. So that today it is the same to veil a girl as to expose her publicly for prostitution. Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, in his Treatise on the Reform of the Church, among other things, advises thus: Correction should be applied to the morals of churchmen, who, alas, are already too much corrupted by anger, gluttony, lust, pomp, prodigality, idleness and other kinds of vice, which results in grave scandal to the laity. And especially should that most scandalous custom, or rather corruption, be opposed, by which many today do not hesitate to keep concubines even openly. Stanislaus Orichovius of Ruthenia, in a supplication to Julius III: We have become the most wicked not only of two-footed but also of four-footed creatures, he says. For many beasts know their kind, know their sex. But among us these things are so confused and uncertain that you may see even at Rome little books publicly circulated, as if they were certain introductions to fornication, in which, etc. In the same century, around the year 1435, lived and flourished Nicholas Tudeschi of Sicily, first an auditor at Rome, then Abbot of Monreale, finally Archbishop of Palermo, and indeed a Cardinal, whom Trithemius honoured with the title Lamp of Law. In his commentary on C. Cum olim de Clericis conjugatis, when the question was put, Can the Church today establish that a cleric may contract marriage, as the Greeks do?, he answers: I believe that it can, etc., and I not only believe that the Church has the power to enact this, but I believe that for the good and the salvation of souls it would be a wholesome statute that those who wish to continue and so merit more should be left to their own will; but those who do not wish to continue should be able to contract marriage. For experience teaches that, since today they do not live spiritually nor are they chaste, but are defiled by illicit intercourse, to their very grave sin, whereas with their own wife there would be chastity, as is said in the chapter Nicaena. Hence the Church ought to act like a good physician, who, when experience teaches that a medicine harms rather than helps, takes it away. Polydore Vergil clearly agrees, in his On Discoverers, where he wrote these words: I would say this, that the impurity of priests has so far outweighed that conjugal chastity, that the crime of illicit union has brought greater dishonour to the order and more sorrow to all good men, and has left a heavier stain. Therefore it would be more useful to the Christian commonwealth, if from the custom of the order the public right of marriage for priests were sometimes dispensed, so that they could live holily without infamy, rather than being most shamefully defiled by this vice of nature. This also seemed right to Pius II before he became pope; Platina too reports among his various sayings that there were reasons why the priesthood should be married, but they were far greater. Under another person's guise he uttered his own opinion, when at the Council of Basel, pleading for a certain man on behalf of Amadeus of Savoy, he spoke these words in the last book: Perhaps priests are damned worse than many, and many are saved in the priesthood, though married. Presbyterate is damned. Platina, in the life of ... deplores the impiety of the times: What will become of us, since our sins have increased so much that they have scarcely left us with God? How great is the avarice, especially of those who hold power, ... how great the ambition, etc., so that since they sin so openly and publicly, as if ... I shall add one more from this century, the Zurich and Solothurn ... Empt. & vend. of one for 20 pages 37, who gathered someone against clergy keeping concubines, and in the diocese of Brescia, presiding over Attasis, roused the clergy publicly against their parish priests who kept concubines to such an extent that, unless the nobles and the bishop himself had intervened, they would have destroyed the clergy. The same Malleolus, in what follows, acknowledges and detests the enormity of the crime, from Scripture and the decrees; yet he says one should be silent, however, that a private teacher or cleric should not preach publicly, because the whole (NB) Church should keep silent. Elsewhere, in On Marriage, p. 40, he says: It is not rare, in the diocese of Constance and other neighbouring places, for concubinage and the living together of women and clerics to be a common arrangement.

units.la: LXIX. In Seculum Decimum Sextum Ecclesiastica Reformatio incidit, quam inter alias causas etiam Cleri cœlibis incontinentia flagitaverat. Et status quidem Romani imperii A. MDXXII. Legato Pontificio Cardinali Campegio centum Gravamina obtulerunt; quorum septuagesimo quinto & nonagesimo primo de cleri impuritate & concubinatu promiscuo querelæ graves consignatæ sunt. Verba ipsa superius thesi xxvij. repræsentavimus. Cùmque circa eadem tempora Argentinæ sacerdotes nonnulli uxores duxissent, & in eos Episcopus animadvertere statuisset, Senatum renitentem expertus ad Campegium eundem, Norinbergæ in Comitiis tum agentem, rem detulit. Aderant è Senatu, qui factum excusarent, monentes inter alia, Sleidano lib. iv. narrante, Ecclesiasticos Argentoratenses magna sui parte turpiter vivere cum meretricibus, quæ domi foveant, magna quidem cum offensione populi, pessimóque exemplo, sed tamen summa cum impunitate, nec eo nomine quenquam adhuc esse multatum ab Episcopo. Regessit Cardinalis: Quòd Sacerdotes mariti fiant, multò esse gravius peccatum, quàm si plurimas domi meretrices alant. Nec enim omnes eâ esse, quâ Johannes Baptista continentiâ: Egregiam scilicet dignámque themate probationem! Antoninus Cornelius Lynnichanus oratione habita coram frequenti clero Coloniæ in Synodo V. Eid. Mart. A.
units.tr: LXIX. In the sixteenth century the ecclesiastical Reformation came about, which, among other causes, had demanded the incontinence of the celibate clergy be corrected. In the year 1522, the states of the Roman Empire presented to the papal legate, Cardinal Campeggio, one hundred grievances; in the seventy-fifth and ninety-first of these, serious complaints about the impurity of the clergy and promiscuous concubinage were recorded. The words themselves I set out above in thesis 27. And when about the same time some priests at Strasbourg had taken wives, and the bishop had resolved to take action against them, finding the Senate resistant, he brought the matter to the same Campeggio, who was then holding a diet at Nuremberg. Some from the Senate were present to excuse the deed, warning among other things, as Sleidan relates in book 4, that the clergy of Strasbourg for the most part live shamefully with prostitutes whom they keep at home, to the great offence of the people and a very bad example, yet with complete impunity, and no one has yet been punished by the bishop for this reason. The Cardinal replied: That priests should become husbands is a far graver sin than if they kept many prostitutes at home. For not all have that continence of John the Baptist! A splendid and worthy proof for the thesis, to be sure! Antoninus Cornelius of Lenningen, in a speech delivered before the numerous clergy at Cologne, in the Synod of 5 Ides of March, 1527, opened his mouth in these words:

Many testimonies of Guillaume Budé, Erasmus, Ferus, Cassander, Wicelius, elsewhere Parthenogam. cap. xiv. 16. etc. as well as the Cardinals of Paul III and Claude d'Espence produced above, I set down in brief.

units.la: LXX. Commemoratu forte haud indignum est, paulò ante Reformationem adeò frequentem fuisse Cleri scortationem, & concubinatum, ut jam in ludum jocúmque abire coeperit. Cujus rei evidens testimonium Celeb. Calixtus de Conjug. Cleric. pag. 437.438. ex libello Heidelbergæ in confinio Seculi decimi quinti & sexti edito affert. Titulus libelli est de fide concubinarum in Sacerdotes, seu Quæstio accessoria causa joci & urbanitatis in Quodlibeto Heidelbergensi determinata à M. Paulo Olear§io Heidelbergensi: in fine scilicet Quodlibetaris disputationis, laxandi animi, jocíque suscitandi causa; uti in adjuncta Cratonis Udenhemii epistola dicitur. Quæstio sic habet: An aures venitilata, a sinine Sacerdoti concubinario imponendæ sint? Sacerdotis vocabulo quomodo in facetiis his utendum sit, sic primò determinat; quòd non loquatur de hoc vocabulo Sacerdos, quod est nomen vel terminus communis generis & tertiæ declinationis; sed de re ipsa per hunc terminum significata, & de viro sacris initiato, sive sit ruralis plebanus, præmissarius aut capellanus, sive urbanus, canonicus aut vicarius. Tum concubinam sic disputator definit: Concubina est vas omnium vitiorum, mulier sine pudore, bestia sine honore, appetens primos recubitus in mensa, primam sedem in Ecclesia, primatum in balneo & chorea, semper pigra, semper plena, rixosa, criminosa, scabiosa, omnibus odiosa, soli Cerbero cara, in fallaciis tam in dictione, quàm extra dictionem optimè instituta. Subjiciuntur diversæ conditiones Sacerdotum concubinariorum, quas ibidem expressas repetere piget. Saltem inde Tom. II. ccc onstat, constat; profligata veteri de extraneis foeminis non admittendis canonum severitate, fornicationes & concubinatum Cleri passim jam pro ludo & deridiculo haberi consuevisse.
units.tr: LXX. It is perhaps not unworthy of mention that shortly before the Reformation the fornication and concubinage of the clergy was so frequent that it began to pass into jest and joking. Clear testimony to this is given by the celebrated Calixtus, On the Marriage of Clerics, pp. 437–438, citing a little book published at Heidelberg at the boundary of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The title of the booklet is On the faith of concubines toward priests, or an incidental question, determined for the sake of fun and wit in the Heidelberg Quodlibet by Master Paul Olearius of Heidelberg: namely at the end of a Quodlibetic disputation, for relaxing the mind and provoking laughter, as is said in the attached letter of Cratonus Udenhemius. The question runs thus: Should ventilated ears of an ass be imposed on a concubinary priest? As to how the word priest is to be used in these jests, the disputant first determines thus: that he does not speak of the word sacerdos, which is a common noun of the third declension, but of the thing itself signified by this term, and of a man initiated into sacred orders, whether he be a rural parish priest, a chantry priest or chaplain, or an urban canon or vicar. Then the disputant defines a concubine thus: A concubine is a vessel of all vices, a woman without shame, a beast without honour, seeking the first place at table, the first seat in church, the first rank in the bath and in the dance; always lazy, always full, quarrelsome, criminal, scabby, hateful to all, dear to Cerberus alone, most excellently trained in deceits, both within speech and outside speech. Various conditions of concubinary priests are then appended, which it is tedious to repeat here. At least from this it is established (Tom. II. ccc) that, with the old severity of the canons against admitting foreign women having been abandoned, fornication and concubinage of the clergy had everywhere come to be regarded as a game and a laughing-stock.

units.la: LXXI. Cùm ergo Hierarchia, quod jam abundè probatum confectúmque dedimus, non tantùm luxuriæ & impuritati carnis ansam multiplicem præbeat, dum videlicet luxuriæ instrumenta avidè nimis conquirit; otium religiosum cum inefficaci cultu & debacchationibus conjunctum sectatur; legem de Sacerdotum Coelibatu figit, & pertinaciter tuetur; votum coelibatûs perpetui laudat & commendat; opportunitatem impuritatis concipiendæ & fovendæ in ipsa functione sacra suppeditat; Musicæ voluptuariæ amore & studio nimio tenetur: sed etiam de fornicatione, adulterio, aliisque impuritatibus tenuiter nimis sentiat, easque levioribus poenis afficiat, & dispensationum indulgentiarumque beneficio poenis exsolvat; contra leges Divinas de incestu dispenset; lupanaria permittat; denique omnis generis libidinibus, quibus gignendis ipsa Hierarchiae constitutio sic lenocinatur; nefariè indulgeat, dum ubique ferè pro casti amoris tœda stupri libido fervet, in Coenobiis passim obscoenæ Veneris spurcitias grassatur, in Praesulum, Summorum etiam, Flaminúmque caeterorum Romanorum vita penè omni non aliud quàm turpissimarum voluptatum illecebræ, stuprorumganeæque cupiditas, cum alienis foeminis adulterii consuetudo, cum cognato sanguine flagitiosi incestus, per omnes obscoenitatum gradus, & cupidinum sceleratarum monstra usurpata Venus regnat; concludere jam proclive est, Hierarchiam illam luxuriâ & impuritate carnis se multis modis polluere, adeóque, caeteris paribus, Babylonem Magnam, Meretricem Magnam, & Matrem fornicationum ac abominationum terrae esse, quo demonstrationis capite ex tw nuwi defungendum nobis fuerat.
units.tr: Since therefore the Hierarchy, as we have already sufficiently proved and established, not only affords manifold occasions for lust and the impurity of the flesh, while it eagerly seeks out the instruments of lust; pursues religious idleness joined with ineffective worship and frenzied excesses; lays down and stubbornly defends the law of priestly celibacy; praises and commends the vow of perpetual celibacy; supplies the opportunity for conceiving and fostering impurity within the sacred function itself; and is held by excessive love and zeal for voluptuous music; but also thinks too lightly of fornication, adultery and other impurities, punishes them with lighter penalties, and releases from penalties by the benefit of dispensations and indulgences; dispenses against the divine laws concerning incest; permits brothels; and finally indulges wickedly in every kind of lust, to which the very constitution of the Hierarchy so pandars, since almost everywhere, in place of the torch of chaste love, the lust of debauchery burns; in monasteries the filth of obscene Venus runs rampant everywhere; and in the life of almost all prelates, even the highest, and of the other Roman priests, there is nothing but the allurements of the most shameful pleasures, the craving for debauchery and whoring, the habit of adultery with other men's wives, and foul incest with close blood kin; Venus reigns, practised through every degree of obscenity and the monstrous forms of wicked desires. It is now easy to conclude that this Hierarchy pollutes itself in many ways with lust and impurity of the flesh, and so, other things being equal, that it is Babylon the Great, the Great Harlot, and the Mother of fornications and abominations of the earth; with this point of demonstration we had to finish off the argument.
DISSERTATION FIFTEEN

units.la: QUA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem esse Babylonem Magnam probatur Decimò, quia se Magicâ impietate gravitèr polluit.
units.tr: IN WHICH it is proved that the Hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church, which rules, is Babylon the Great. Tenthly, because it defiles itself with grave magical impiety.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Babyloni M. Spiritus Dei Magicam impietatem tribuit. II. Voces מבשיף & Φαρμακεία ex Scripturæ usu impietatem Magicam quamvis significant. Definitio impietatis Magicæ. III. Duplex Magia, explicita & implicita distinguitur. IV. Cognoscendæ Magiæ characteres tum generales, tum speciales exponuntur. V. Hierarchia Magicæ impietatis rea Syllogismo apoditico peragitur. Propositionis utriusque membra sigillatim probantur. VI. &c. Idololatria cum impietate Magica individuo nexu conjuncta est. Filesaci de idololatria Magica liber laudatus. Hierarchia proin idololatriæ rea, etiam Magiæ rea peragitur. VII. Magicæ impietatis reus est, quisquis eam extenuat.
units.tr: I. The Spirit of God ascribes magical impiety to Babylon. II. The Hebrew word מבשיף [mekhashshef] and the Greek Φαρμακεία [pharmakeia] signify magical impiety by the usage of Scripture, though. Definition of magical impiety. III. Magic is distinguished as twofold: explicit and implicit. IV. The marks by which magic is to be recognised are set out, both general and special. V. The hierarchy is charged with magical impiety by an apodictic syllogism. Each part of the major premise is proved separately. VI. Etc. Idolatry is bound by an inseparable link to magical impiety. Filesacus's book on magical idolatry is cited. Therefore the hierarchy is guilty of idolatry, and so is also proved guilty of magic. VII. Whoever extenuates magical impiety is guilty of it.

units.la: Extenuant autem Hierarchici, Valentia, Prierias, Navarrus, alii, negantes, superstitionem esse, si quis curiosa à Sathana scisciteur; Victoria, Verracrucius, qui Ensalmatores Hispanos excusant, Cajetanus, figurarum efficaciam afferens;
units.tr: Now the hierarchs extenuate it: Valentia, Prierias, Navarrus and others, who deny that it is superstition if someone asks curious questions of Satan; Victoria and Verracrucius, who excuse the Spanish ensalmadores [charmers]; and Cajetan, who asserts the efficacy of figures.

units.la: VIII. Valesius, incantationis vim in universum tollens.
units.tr: VIII. Valesius, who removes the force of incantation altogether.

units.la: IX. Delrio, Magiam implicitam inter venalia peccata numerans.
units.tr: IX. Delrio, who counts implicit magic among the venial sins.

units.la: X. Hierarchicorum religio omnis magicâ impietate aspersa est. In Papa, ceu Delphico quodam oraculo, divinant omnes.
units.tr: X. All the religion of the hierarchs is tainted with magical impiety. In the Pope, as in some Delphic oracle, they all seek divination.

units.la: XI. Doctrinis daemoniorum Hierarchici attendunt; in cultu Dei rebus & actibus humanis Divinam virtutem sine Dei verbo tribuunt;
units.tr: XI. The hierarchs give heed to the doctrines of demons, and in the worship of God they ascribe divine power to things and human acts without the word of God.

units.la: XII. Sacramentis efficaciam ex opere operato tribuentes, eadem in Φαρμακείαν convertunt.
units.tr: XII. Ascribing efficacy to the sacraments ex opere operato [from the work worked], they turn these same sacraments into pharmakeia.

units.la: XIII. Familiare cum daemoniis & mortuis hominibus commercium, impietate magica non caret. Hierarchici autem familiare commercium colunt cum daemoniis,
units.tr: XIII. Familiar dealings with demons and dead men are not free from magical impiety. The hierarchs, however, cultivate familiar dealings with demons

units.la: XIV. & mortuis hominibus, qui cùm in terram non redeant,
units.tr: XIV. and with dead men. Since these do not return to the earth,

units.la: XV. vel apparere finguntur, vel personati daemones sunt. Unde Hierarchicorum necromantia manifesta efficitur.
units.tr: XV. they are either feigned to appear, or they are demons in disguise. Hence the necromancy of the hierarchs is made plain.
XVI. The frequency of the possessed

units.la: XVII. nec non spectrorum in Papatu, ejusdem cum daemonibus familiaritatis testis est.
units.tr: XVII. and also of apparitions in Papacy is a witness to the same familiarity with demons.

units.la: XVIII. Causa eruitur, ob quam obsessi & spectra in Papatu plurima, apud Euangelicos paucissima comparent.
units.tr: XVIII. The cause is brought out why the possessed and apparitions appear very many in Papacy, but very few among the Evangelicals.

units.la: XIX. Praetextus familiaritatis cum daemonibus, ut eosdem imperio suo exorcistico coërceant, discuti-tur.
units.tr: XIX. The pretext of familiarity with demons, so that they may restrain them by their exorcistic command, is examined.

units.la: XX. Dæmonia veteres fideles unico verbo ejecerunt, sine arte exorcistica. Neque Christus ordinem exorcistarum instituit, sed donum ejiciendi daemonem liberè dispensavit. Expirante eo dono, exorcismi in preces conversi sunt, & catechesis, exorcismi apud veteres nomine venit.
units.tr: XX. The ancient faithful drove out demons by a single word, without exorcistic art. Nor did Christ institute an order of exorcists, but freely bestowed the gift of casting out demons. When that gift ceased, exorcisms were turned into prayers, and catechesis came to be called exorcism among the ancients.

units.la: XXI. Exorcismi Hierarchicorum & exorcismi veterum immane discrimen panditur.
units.tr: XXI. The vast difference between the exorcisms of the hierarchs and those of the ancients is laid open.
XXII., XXIII. The magical impiety of exorcisms is asserted.

units.la: XXIV. Magos inter professos ac notorios, & exorcistas Pontificios affinitas summa demonstratur.
units.tr: XXIV. The close affinity between the Papists' exorcists and the professed and notorious magicians is demonstrated.

units.la: XXV. Impietatem exorcistarum Magicam auget, quòd testimonio Diaboli superstitiones suas commendant. Francisci stigmata Diabolo teste probata sunt.
units.tr: XXV. The magical impiety of the exorcists is increased, because they commend their superstitions by the testimony of the Devil. The stigmata of Francis are proved by the testimony of the Devil.

units.la: XXVI. Exorcismus Maleficiatorum magica impietate laborat totus.
units.tr: XXVI. The exorcism of those bewitched is wholly tainted with magical impiety.

units.la: XXVII. Impietas exorcismi, quo Hierarchi Diabolum ad restituendum chirographum & Eucharistiam cogunt.
units.tr: XXVII. The impiety of the exorcism by which the hierarchs compel the Devil to restore a bond and the Eucharist.

units.la: XXVIII. Exorcismi animalium maleficiis infectorum, lactis, butyri, casei, ovorum, elementorum, tempestatum, tonitruum, nubium impietas summa.
units.tr: XXVIII. The exorcisms of animals infected by witchcraft, of milk, butter, cheese, eggs, the elements, storms, thunder and clouds: their impiety is very great.

units.la: XXIX. Exorcismi animalium noxiorum ab Episcopis pluribus peracti exempla à Malleolo prodita, exhibentur.
units.tr: XXIX. Examples from Malleolus of exorcisms of harmful animals performed by several bishops are set forth.

units.la: XXX. Delrionis adversus Malleolum exorcismos eos commendantem, nec non Suarezii & Gretseri exceptio, ventilatur.
units.tr: XXX. Delrio's defence against Malleolus, who commends such exorcisms, and also the objection of Suarez and Gretser, is discussed.

units.la: XXXI. Inter muliercularum & agricolarum, nec non Episcoporum adjurationes ejusmodi differentiam nullam esse, ostenditur.
units.tr: XXXI. It is shown that there is no difference between the adjurations of such kind used by old women and farm labourers and those of bishops.

units.la: XXXII. Exorcismorum Magicorum impietas nequicquam à Delrione contra Godelmannum defenditur, quoad exorcismorum sive personas, puta obsessos & exorcistas;
units.tr: XXXII. The magical impiety of magical exorcisms is defended in vain by Delrio against Godelmann, as regards the persons of the exorcisms, namely the possessed and the exorcists;

units.la: XXXIII. sive res in iis adhiberi solitas;
units.tr: XXXIII. or the things customarily employed in them;

units.la: XXXIV. ubi asylum rerum & mediorum ab Ecclesia approbatorum vel improbatum tutum neutiquam esse ostenditur;
units.tr: XXXIV. where it is shown that the refuge of things and means approved or disapproved by the Church is by no means safe;

units.la: XXXV. XXXVI. sive quoad verba, seu sacra illa, seu profana sint, seu ad Deum ipsum & Sanctos dirigantur;
units.tr: XXXV., XXXVI. or as regards the words, whether they are sacred or profane, and whether they are addressed to God himself and to the saints;

units.la: XXXVII. ubi formulas exorcizandi superstitiosas in Papatu adhiberi, ipsorum Hierarchicorum confessione evincitur.
units.tr: XXXVII. where it is proved, by the confession of the hierarchs themselves, that superstitious formulas of exorcism are used in Papacy.

units.la: XXXVIII. Seu dirigantur ad daemonem, quò pertinent verba imperantia, in quibus exorcismi prora & puppis collocatur,
units.tr: XXXVIII. Or whether they are addressed to the demon, to which belong the imperative words in which the prow and stern of exorcism are placed;
XXXIX. which are convicted of magical impiety.

units.la: XL. Cavisii Jesuitæ imperare daemonibus non per Christum, sed per Mariam soliti; Cotoni, aliorum daemoni imperantium, ut de controversiis fidei respondeat, vanitas.
units.tr: XL. The Jesuit Cavisius was accustomed to command demons not through Christ but through Mary; the vanity of Coton, who answers questions of the controversies of faith as one commanding demons, and of others.

units.la: XLI. Sive denique quoad intentionem exorcistæ, quam cum Magorum intentione convenire probatur.
units.tr: XLI. Or lastly, as regards the intention of the exorcist, which is proved to agree with the intention of magicians.
XLII. The distinction between lawful and magical blessings is explained.

units.la: XLIII. Benedictionibus Magicis scatet Papatus. Formulæ benedicendi aquam, Sal, Agnos Dei, incensum, sulphur, myrrham, aloë, radices, flores, herbas, campanas, ex Ritualibus Hierarchicorum depromuntur.
units.tr: XLIII. Papacy abounds in magical blessings. Formulas for blessing water, salt, the Agnus Dei, incense, sulphur, myrrh, aloes, roots, flowers, herbs and bells are drawn from the Rituals of the hierarchs.

units.la: XLIV. Benedictiones interposito signo crucis perficiuntur. Verbum, quo creaturas sanctificari S. Paulus 1. Tim. I. Tim. iv. 4. ait, signum illud crucis notare, perperam Bellarminus ex Theophylacto & Chrysostomo contendit.
units.tr: XLIV. Blessings are performed with the interposed sign of the cross. St Paul's word, by which he says creatures are sanctified (1 Tim. 4:4), Bellarmine wrongly contends refers to that sign of the cross, following Theophylact and Chrysostom.

units.la: XLV. Rebus benedictis effectus supernaturales tres, puta delendi peccata venialia, daemonem fugandi, & morbos curandi; Hierarchici deputant.
units.tr: XLV. The hierarchs attribute three supernatural effects to blessed things, namely the blotting out of venial sins, the putting to flight of demons, and the curing of diseases.

units.la: XLVI. Syllogismo probatur, nil distare eos, qui effectus tales rebus benedictis tribuunt, à Magis v. 9. iis, qui nomine Abracadabra chartæ inscripto hemitriteum curare olim conati sunt.
units.tr: XLVI. By a syllogism it is proved that there is no difference between those who ascribe such effects to blessed things and the magicians of Malachi 9 [?], or those who once tried to cure a hemitritaeus with a paper inscribed Abracadabra.

units.la: XLVII. Eosdem contra primum & tertium Decalogi praeceptum peccantes, magiam exercere, & nomen Dei in vanum sumere, probatur ulterius,
units.tr: XLVII. It is further proved that they, sinning against the first and third precepts of the Decalogue, practise magic and take the name of God in vain.
XLVIII. And Bellarmine's objection is refuted.

units.la: XLIX. Baptismi Sacramentum exorcismis Magicis Hierarchici polluunt. Benedictionis salis in Baptismo adhibiti formula, ejusque impietas.
units.tr: XLIX. The hierarchs defile the sacrament of baptism with magical exorcisms. The formula of blessing the salt used in baptism, and its impiety.

units.la: L. Exorcismorum, quibus in eodem Baptismo daemones ex baptizando ejiciuntur, vanitas.
units.tr: L. The vanity of the exorcisms by which, in the same baptism, demons are driven out of the one being baptized.

units.la: LI. Eosdem supplentes post baptismum non solemnem, compellunt daemonem ubi non est, adeoque evocant.
units.tr: LI. Those who supply these exorcisms after a baptism that was not solemn compel a demon where he is not, and so summon him.
LII. The magical impiety of baptismal exorcisms,

units.la: LIII. quae nullum in veteris Ecclesiae Exorcismo in baptismo utentis praxi praesidium habet.
units.tr: LIII. which has no support in the practice of the ancient Church, which used exorcism in baptism.

units.la: LIV. Benedictio olei in baptismo; & vis aquae exorcizatae & chrismate exorcizato conditae tributa conserendi gratiam ex opere operato magiam sapit.
units.tr: LIV. The blessing of oil in baptism, and the attribution to water exorcised and to chrism exorcised of a power of conferring grace ex opere operato, smacks of magic.

units.la: LV. In Eucharistia corpus Christi certorum verborum murmure ex Caelo Hierarchici excantant.
units.tr: LV. In the Eucharist the hierarchs conjure down the body of Christ from heaven by the mumbling of certain words.

units.la: LVI. Excantationem eam Magicis exemplis sagarum, lac vaccarum de manubriis securium extrahentium, Jovis Elicii &c. Gabr. Biel, Caelius Rhodiginus &c. illustrant. LVII. Unctiones in Sacramentis spuriis adhibitæ magicam impietatem spirant. LVIII. Chrismatis exorcismi, effectus & mysteria. LIX. Interveniente eo Sacramentum Confirmationis certâ verborum formulâ administratur, eique effectus spirituales tribuuntur. LX. Papa, nullâ præviâ Divinâ Sacramenti institutione, chrisma in Φαρμακοῖς convertit. LXI. Par ratio est olei infirmorum in extremæ unctionis Sacramento. LXII. Hierarchici amuletis utuntur, LXIII. non sine præsentissima impietate Magica; quod amuletis inscripta contra morbum comitialem, pestilentiam &c. verba, comprobant LXIV. nequicquam Delrione ad Ecclesiæ Catholicæ inveteratum morem provocante. LXV. Idem verbis certis, notis & ignotis, sacris & profanis, quâ talibus; nec non preculis certâ verborum, ad usum ejusmodi nuspiam institutorum formulâ constantibus, singularem efficaciam tribuunt. LXVI. Speciminis loco Oratio seu Responsorium Bonaventuræ ad Antonium de Padua affertur. LXVII. Idem numeris definitis in missa, exorcismis, benedictionibus, preculis efficaciam tribuunt, LXVIII. nec non figuris & characteribus; neque solius crucis, sed etiam literæ ψ & alphabethi Græci; LXIX. Inter Magos verbis, numeris, figuris &c. & Hierarchicos iisdem utentes, differentia ostendi nulla potest. LXX. Idem fortuitis significationem affingunt, qui magiæ character est, LXXI. & magiam per remedia magica depellere conantur, LXXII. remedia vocantes, quæ scelera & morbus ipse sunt. LXXIII. Magos notorios in sinu suo iidem fovent,
units.tr: LVI. They illustrate that incantation with magical examples: the milk of cows drawn by witches, the extraction of milk from the handles of axes, the Jupiter Elicius, etc.; Gabriel Biel, Caelius Rhodiginus, etc. LVII. The anointings used in the spurious sacraments breathe magical impiety. LVIII. The effects and mysteries of the exorcised chrism. LIX. With this intervening, the sacrament of Confirmation is administered by a fixed form of words, and spiritual effects are ascribed to it. LX. The Pope, with no prior divine institution of the sacrament, turns chrism into pharmaka [drugs]. LXI. The same reasoning holds for the oil of the sick in the sacrament of extreme unction. LXII. The hierarchs use amulets, LXIII. not without the most present magical impiety, as the words inscribed on amulets against epilepsy, plague, etc. prove, LXIV. Delrio's appeal in vain to the long-established custom of the Catholic Church. LXV. The same people attribute singular efficacy to certain words, known and unknown, sacred and profane, and likewise to prayers consisting of a fixed form of words, which were nowhere instituted for such use. LXVI. As a specimen, the Oratio or Responsory of Bonaventure to Anthony of Padua is cited. LXVII. The same people attribute efficacy to fixed numbers in the mass, in exorcisms, blessings and prayers, LXVIII. and also to figures and characters, not only the cross but also the letter ψ and the letters of the Greek alphabet. LXIX. No difference can be shown between magicians, with their words, numbers, figures, etc., and the hierarchs using the same things. LXX. The same people assign meaning to chance events, which is the mark of magic, LXXI. and try to drive out magic by magical remedies, LXXII. calling remedies those things which are themselves crimes and the disease. LXXIII. The same people cherish notorious magicians in their own bosom,

units.la: LXXIII. quales inprimis fuère Pontifices Romani, Sylvester II. testibus Cardinale Bennone, Inscriptione in Templo S. Cruce S. Hierusalem, Martino Polono, Authore fasciculi temporum, Platina &c.
units.tr: LXXIII. Of whom the Roman Pontiffs were especially such: Sylvester II, on the testimony of Cardinal Benno, an inscription in the Church of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem, Martin of Poland, author of the Fasciculus temporum, Platina, etc.
LXXIV. Benedict IX.
LXXV. Gregory VII.
LXXVI. Naudé, Baronius and others contending against it in vain.

units.la: LXXVII. Johannes XXI. Felix V. Alexander VI. Paulus III.
units.tr: LXXVII. John XXI. Felix V. Alexander VI. Paul III.

units.la: LXXVIII. ex Clero reliquo innumeri, Delrione, aliisque prodentibus.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Countless others from the rest of the clergy, as Delrio and others report.

units.la: LXXIX. MirTones & Thaumaturgi plurimi, qui, testibus Hierarchicis ipsis, à Diabolo Angeli boni speciem mentito revelationes captârunt.
units.tr: LXXIX. Miracle-mongers and very many wonder-workers who, as the Hierarchs themselves testify, took revelations from the Devil, who feigned the appearance of a good angel.

units.la: LXXX. Quibus etiam nullis hactenus cautionibus, regulisque, per quas apparitiones verae à falsis discerni queant, Hierarchici ipsi prospicere potuerunt.
units.tr: LXXX. Yet the Hierarchs themselves have hitherto been unable to provide any safeguards or rules by which true apparitions can be distinguished from false.
LXXXI. Public teachers of magic and their writings,

units.la: LXXXII. nec non consuetudines notorie Magicas iidem, nullâ Ecclesiæ censurâ notatas, tolerant.
units.tr: LXXXII. and likewise customs notoriously magical, these they tolerate, without any censure from the Church.

units.la: LXXXIII. Quo loco Magicam Impietatem Hierarchici habeant, ex poenis, quas Concilium Lateranense Magis notoriis, religiosis inprimis, levissimas decrevit, colligitur.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The attitude of the Hierarchs towards magical impiety may be gathered here from the penalties which the Lateran Council decreed, very light ones, above all for religious men who were notorious magicians.

units.la: LXXXIV. Impietatem eandem in Papatu incurabilem esse demonstratur, quia Ecclesia actiones, ritus &c. Magicos longa consuetudine receptos à non magicis discernere ausa hactenus non est; & Delrioni id privatim tentanti succenfuit; neque spes ulla est fore, ut aliquando discernat.
units.tr: LXXXIV. It is shown that this same impiety is incurable in Papacy, because the Church has hitherto not dared to distinguish magical actions, rites and so on, long received by custom, from non-magical ones; and it was angry with Delrio when he tried this privately. Nor is there any hope that it will ever make the distinction.

units.la: LXXXV. Romam esse veneficiorum officinam, adeoque Babylonem Magnam, concluditur.
units.tr: LXXXV. It is concluded that Rome is a workshop of poisons, and therefore Babylon the Great.

units.la: Babyloni Magnæ Spiritus Dei Magicam impietatem inter alia maleficia tribuit. Nàm Apoc. xviii. 23. judicii Babylonis decretorii hanc inter plures alias causam perhibet: ὅτι ἐν τῇ Φαρμακείᾳ σου ἐπλανήθησαν πάντα τὰ ἔθνη. Quia in incantatione tuâ omnes gentes seductæ sunt. Planè sicut Esaj. xlvii. 9. judicii adversus Babylonem causa similis his verbis indicatur: Venient tibi duo hæc momento, die uno orbitas & viduitas. Ad quam toti venerunt מרב כשפיך בעצמה חבריך מאד in multitudine præstigiarum tuarum, dum valuerunt incantationes tuæ admodum. Huc etiam Circæum illud abominationum poculum Babyloni Apoc. xvii. 4. tributum pertinet.
units.tr: Among other evils, the Spirit of God ascribes magical impiety to Babylon the Great. For at Rev. 18:23 he gives this as one cause, among several others, of the judgment passed on Babylon: because by your sorcery all nations were led astray [ὅτι ἐν τῇ Φαρμακείᾳ σου ἐπλανήθησαν πάντα τὰ ἔθνη]. Quite similarly, Isa. 47:9 indicates a like cause of judgment against Babylon in these words: These two things shall come upon you in a moment, in one day, bereavement and widowhood; they shall come upon you in full measure [מרב כשפיך בעצמה חבריך מאד], because of the multitude of your sorceries, since your enchantments have been exceedingly powerful. To this also belongs the cup of abominations, the Circean one, given to Babylon at Rev. 17:4.

units.la: II. Vocem מכשף Græci Interpretes passim Φαρμακὸς reddiderunt. Est autem proprié Φάρμακος; veneficus (unde Φαρμακεία, qua voce Spiritus S. hic utitur Hebraicæ כשפים respondente) qui pharmacum venenatum propinat. Cæterum & vox Hebræa כשף proprié nomen generale est, omnes artes Diabolicas respiciens; eorum videlicet, qui habent aut venditant societatem cum impuris spiritibus, per quos vel occulta indicent, vel opera humanis majora, naturam sive immutando, sive, ceu immutatam repræsentando, procurant: & Φαρμακία non quidem vi etymi, sed usûs apud Scriptores Sacros & profanos recepti, non solum veneficium, sed quamvis artem Magicam, quæ sive divinando, sive operando illicita, Diabolo scilicet authore & magistro, exercetur, significat. Sanè etiam Apoc. ix. 21. ubi Babylonica etiam hæc impietas notatur, Φόνων φόνων à Φαρμάκων distinguuntur; cùm tamen in veneficio proprie dicto cædes etiam contineantur.
