Sed de significatu vocis utriusque Hebraicæ & Græcæ alibi de Artibus Mag. Differt. iv. 4. 5. &c. fusiùs ex Hebræis & Græcis authoribus ribus dicta heic repetere nihil attinet. Sufficit ad institutum præsens, quòd φαρμακεία Babyloni attributa quamvis καὶ πνεύματα & impietatem Magicam significat, in eo videlicet consistentem, quòd homines profani & impii, Diaboli, Divinum honorem affectantis & humanum genus sub jugum suum mittere molientis ope, & fœdere seu expresso, seu tacito cum eodem interveniente, mira loquuntur faciúntque, quatenus id Divina justitia & voluntas permittit. Quam Magicæ impietatis definitionem loc. cit. Diff. j. uberius expositimus.
units.tr: II. The Greek interpreters everywhere render the word מכשף by φαρμακός [pharmakos]. Properly, however, it is φάρμακος [pharmakos], a poisoner, who administers a poisonous drug (whence φαρμακεία [pharmakeia], the word the Holy Spirit uses here, corresponding to the Hebrew כשפים [kishshephim]). Moreover, the Hebrew word כשף is properly a general name, embracing all diabolical arts, namely of those who have or offer fellowship with unclean spirits, through whom they either disclose hidden things or bring about works beyond human power, either by altering nature or by presenting it as altered. And φαρμακία [pharmakia], not indeed by the force of its etymology but by the usage received among sacred and profane writers, signifies not only poisoning but also magic art in general, which is practised, whether by divining or by working, in ways that are unlawful, with the devil as its author and teacher. Indeed, at Rev. 9:21, where this Babylonian impiety is also noted, φόνων [phonon] and φαρμάκων [pharmakon] are distinguished, although poisoning properly so called also includes murders. But there is no need to repeat here at length the meaning of each of the Hebrew and Greek words, which we have discussed elsewhere, in our de Artibus Magicis, Dissertation 4, sections 4 and 5 and following, drawing on Hebrew and Greek authors. It is enough for the present purpose that the φαρμακεία [pharmakeia] attributed to Babylon, though it also signifies magical impiety, consists in this: that profane and impious men, by the help of the devil, who seeks divine honour and plans to put the human race under his yoke, and by a covenant, whether express or tacit, entered into with him, say and do marvellous things, so far as divine justice and will permit. We set out this definition of magical impiety more fully in the place cited, Dissertation 1.

units.la: III. Sicut duplex est cum Diabolo pactum, expressum & tacitum: ita duplex Magia, explicita una, altera implicita est. Illa, qua homines profani Diabolo in vota sua voecato & fœderi innexo, mira dicunt faciúntque. Hæc, quâ sine expressa ejusdem invocatione ejusmodi mediis ad rem quampiam vel cognoscendam, vel patrandam utuntur, quæ, vel ipsorum quandoque conscientia judice, nullam in sese rem eam efficiendi vim habent. Qualia sunt, quæ neque ex creationis ordine, neque ex revelatione, vel ratione etiam sana, adeóque neque ex natura, neque ex gratia virtutem sive inhærentem, sive adhærentem habent producendi, significandi, vel obsignandi eos effectus, qui iis tribuuntur. Estque iterum implicita illa duobus modis; priore, cùm Magus sciens prudensque superstitiosis mediis utitur, superstitionis tamen ipsius ignarus, persuasus quippe, virtutem tale quid efficiendi mediis iis vel à natura, vel à gratia inesse. In quo posteriore Magiæ genere periculosissimè equidem Diaboli fraudes regnare, & incautos ac nec opinantes haud raro pervertere solent.
units.tr: III. Just as the pact with the devil is double, express and tacit, so magic is double: one explicit, the other implicit. The first is that by which profane men, calling the devil to their wishes and bound to him by a compact, say and do marvellous things. The second is that by which, without express invocation of him, they use such means to know or to accomplish something, means which, sometimes even in the judgment of their own conscience, have no power in themselves to effect that thing. Such are those means which have, neither from the order of creation, nor from revelation, nor even from sound reason, and so neither from nature nor from grace, any power, inherent or adherent, of producing, signifying or sealing those effects which are ascribed to them. This implicit magic is again twofold. In the first way, a magician knowingly and deliberately uses superstitious means, yet is ignorant that they are superstitious, being persuaded that such means have in them the power to effect such a thing, either from nature or from grace. It is in this latter kind of magic that the frauds of the devil are most dangerously at work, and they are wont to pervert the incautious and the unsuspecting, not infrequently.

units.la: IV. Cognoscendæ cùm omnis, tum implicitæ inprimis illius Magiæ generalis nota est, ut ei operam dare censean-tur, quotquot deserta eâ viâ, quæ verbo Dei rectâque ratione præscripta est, aliâ viâ incedunt, aliisque felicitatis mediis utuntur, adeóque vel scire vel facere gestiunt id, quod naturæ vires revera superat, & nec in verbo Dei revelatur, nec Divinæ promissionem in eodem, certáque & explorata Ἰκμηρία habet; ita ut nulla vel naturæ ordinaria, vel Dei extraordinaria operatio ex fide expectari possit; operationisque omnis vera origo non ad alium quam Diabolum referri possit; licet qui rei illi incumbunt, se cum Sathana commercium ullum habere, vel in vota eundem vocasse unquam, protestentur sciò, persuasique adeo sint, piè licitéque se facere id, cujus vel falsas causas animo concipiunt, vel verasse ignorare ultrò profitentur. Speciales magicæ impietatis ejusdem cognoscendæ notæ & characteres sunt, si opus aliquod vel à fide, nec naturali, nec supernaturali Divina; vel à sola imaginatione in disjuncta; vel à verbis, carminibus, preculis; vel à figuris, characteribus, vel ab amuletis & periaptis, quæ verbis & characteribus constant; vel à sympathiis & antipathiis non naturalibus; vel à numeris, vel à tempore, quà talibus; vel à fortuitis casibus, ceu veris causis suspenditur; vel occultarum rerum cognitio illegitimè tentatur, vel opus productum naturæ vires superat, vel apparet etiam id, quod non est. Ubi vel unum ex indiciis his apparuerit, vel plura etiam concurrerint, antiqui serpentis vestigia patent, atque operatione è dæmonis schola verius, quàm ex naturæ vel gratiæ phrontisterio deducta censebitur merito. Licétque tum Poëtæ verbis præsentissimi periculi indicium facere:
units.tr: IV. The general mark of every kind of magic, and especially of that implicit kind, by which those are judged to practise it who, leaving the way prescribed by the word of God and sound reason, walk another way and use other means of happiness, and so are eager to know or do what truly exceeds the powers of nature, and is neither revealed in the word of God nor has a divine promise in it, nor a certain and tested assurance [ἰκμηρία]. Thus no operation, whether the ordinary operation of nature or an extraordinary operation of God, can be expected from faith, and the true origin of every operation can be referred to no one but the devil. This holds even though those who engage in such things protest that they have no dealings at all with Satan, and never invoked him in their vows, and are so persuaded that they do what is pious and lawful, whose causes they either conceive falsely in their minds or freely profess they do not know. The special marks and signs of this magical impiety, by which it may be recognised, are these: if some work depends on a faith that is neither natural nor divinely supernatural; or on imagination alone, cut off from anything else; or on words, chants, prayers; or on figures, characters, or on amulets and charms made up of words and characters; or on sympathies and antipathies that are not natural; or on numbers, or on time as such; or is made to depend on chance events as if they were true causes; or the knowledge of hidden things is attempted illegitimately; or the work produced exceeds the powers of nature; or even something appears which is not really there. When even one of these indications has appeared, or several have come together, the traces of the ancient serpent are plain, and the operation will rightly be judged to derive from the school of the demon rather than from the thinking-shop of nature or of grace. And then one may use the poet's words to signal the very present danger:

units.la: Callidus, ô pueri, fugite hinc, latet anguis in herba.
units.tr: Cunning one, boys, flee from here: a snake lies hidden in the grass.

units.la: Utramque illam tum generalem, tum specialem & characteristicam cognoscendæ Magicæ impietatis rationem de Artib. Mag. Differt. ÿ. ex professo demonstravimus.
units.tr: We have demonstrated both this general and this special and characteristic way of recognising magical impiety, ex professo, in our de Artibus Magicis, Dissertation v.

units.la: V. Ita præfati propius ad institutum venimus, & Hierarchiam Magicæ impietatis Syllogismo expresso ream peragimus;
units.tr: V. Having said these things by way of preface, we come closer to our purpose and bring the Hierarchy to trial for magical impiety by an express syllogism:

units.la: Ille cœtus impietate Magica graviter se polluit, adeoque, cœteris paribus, Babylon Magna est, qui idololatriam propalam exercet; Magicam impietatem extenuat; religionem universam ejusdem impietatis labe attaminat; cum dæmonibus & mortuis hominibus, ad veritatem ex iis expiscandam, familiare commercium colit; verbum Dei in exorcismis & benedictionibus profanat; Baptismum exorcismis contaminat; in Eucharistia certorum verborum murmure corpus Christi excantat; unctionibus certis, chrismati inprimis in Sacramentis spuriis, effectus tribuit, quos nec à natura, nec à Deo supra naturam operante habent; amuletis benedictis, verbis, figuris & numeris efficaciam tribuit; fortuitis significationem affingit; Magiam per remedia magica depellere conatur; Magos profossos, & scripta consuetudinésque notorie Magicas in sinu suo fovet; Magos levibus pœnis afficit; denique nullam criminis hujus emendationem patitur.
units.tr: That assembly which heavily pollutes itself with magical impiety, and so, other things being equal, is Babylon the Great, is the one which openly practises idolatry; which belittles magical impiety; which taints the whole religion with the stain of that same impiety; which cultivates familiar intercourse with demons and with dead men, to draw truth out of them; which profanes the word of God in exorcisms and blessings; which contaminates baptism with exorcisms; which in the Eucharist enchants the body of Christ by the murmuring of certain words; which ascribes to certain anointings, above all to chrism in spurious sacraments, effects which they have neither from nature nor from God working beyond nature; which attributes efficacy to blessed amulets, words, figures and numbers; which attaches significance to chance events; which tries to drive off magic by magical remedies; which cherishes in its bosom professed magicians, writings and customs notoriously magical; which punishes magicians with light penalties; and which, in short, suffers no amendment of this crime.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans idololatriam propalam exercet; Magicam impietatem extenuat: religionem universam impietatis ejusdem labe attaminat; cum dæmonibus & hominibus mortuis, ad veritatem ex iis expiscandam, familiare commercium colit; Verbum Dei in exorcismis & benedictionibus profanat; Baptismum exorcismis variis contaminat; in Eucharistia certorum verborum murmure corpus Christi excantat; unctionibus certis, chrismati inprimis, in Sacramentis spuriis eos effectus tribuit, quos nec à natura, nec à Deo supra naturam operante habent; amuletis benedictis, verbis, figuris & numeris efficaciam tribuit; fortuitis significationem affingit; Magiam per remedia magica depellere conatur; Magos profossos, & scripta consuetudinésque notorie Magicas in sinu fovet;
units.tr: Moreover, the Hierarchy, that is, the clergy of the Roman Church, openly practises idolatry and softens the guilt of magical impiety. It taints the whole of religion with the stain of that same impiety. It keeps up a familiar commerce with demons and with dead men, to fish the truth out of them. It profanes the Word of God in exorcisms and blessings. It contaminates Baptism with various exorcisms. In the Eucharist it charms the body of Christ with the murmuring of certain words. By certain anointings, especially with chrism, it ascribes to spurious sacraments effects which they have neither from nature nor from God working above nature. It ascribes efficacy to blessed amulets, words, figures and numbers. It attaches significance to chance events. It tries to drive out magic by magical remedies. It cherishes professed magicians, and writings and customs notoriously magical, in its bosom. It punishes magicians with light penalties.

units.la: Magos levibus poenis afficit, denique nullam hujus cri-minis emendationem patitur,
units.tr: It punishes magicians with light penalties, and finally permits no amendment of this crime.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiae Romanae dominans, impietate graviter se polluit, adeoque, caeteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, that is, the clergy of the Roman Church, that dominates, pollutes itself gravely with impiety, and so, other things being equal, Babylon is Great.

units.la: Utriusque propositionis, pluribus quippe membris constantis, probationem solidam ordine & sigillatim molimur.
units.tr: We shall now build a solid proof of each proposition, which consists of several parts, taking them in order and one by one.

units.la: VI. Hierarchiam idololatriae multiplicis jam supra ream peregimus. Omnem porrò idololatriam cum Magica impietate conjunctissimam esse, ipsimet Hierarchici nulli diffitentur; & S. Paulus 1. Cor. x. 20. idololatriam per κοινωνίαν τῶν δαιμονίων, communionem cum daemoniis explicans, docet, & Johannes Filesacus, Parisiensis Theologus, Dissertatione doctissima de Idololatria Magica edita, pluribus liquidò probavit. Jam olim Originem, Magicis artibus patrocinantem, sic Theophilus Alexandrinus Epist. 2. ad Paschal. perstrinxit: Responde ut novae impietatis adsertor, imò aperte audiat: Si non est malum ars Magica, non erit malum etiam idololatria, quae artis Magicae viribus innititur. Quod si malum est idololatria, malum & erit ars Magica, ex qua subsistit idololatria. Tertullianus etiam lib. de Anima Magiam secundam idololatriam appellat. Hinc veteres idololatriae authores Magos eosdem extitisse, constat. Orpheum primum omnium nomina Deorum gentilium invenisse, nativitates & fata exposuisse, & Theologiam istam, Ethnicorum judicio, sinceriùs attigisse, Athenagoras Apolog. j. pro Christianis, & Justinus Martyr Orat. ad gentes confirmant. At Orpheum eundem Magum fuisse, authores plurimi, Plinius inprimis lib. xxx. 1. memorant. Idololatriae Romanae Sacerdos praecipuus fuit Numa Pompilius, institutor ineptarum religionum ideirco à Lactantio dictus. Atqui Magus idem, idololatriam didicit ab Ægeria Nympha, quæ famosa incantatrix, vel potius dæmon succubus ejusdem fuit. Nam cum Diva ea confuciffe[?] illum; Romani scriptores prodidere. Quin & Varro libro de cultu Deorum apud S. Augustinum de Civit. D. lib. vij 33. Numam usum esse generis divinationis, quod hydromantia vocatur; & libros ejus, Magicos scilicet, Senatus Romani authoritate combustos esse, non diffitetur. Ceteris Eleusiniæ, Serapidis, Isidis sacra idololarrica Magiam redoluisse, Varro idem & Apulejus haud dissimulant. Psellus quoque libro de Dæmonibus scribit, putasse Ethnicos, Magiam esse summum apicem Sacerdotii, seu sacrorum, & sacrificandi disciplinæ, ita ut nemo instructus satis Sacerdos sit, quin Magiam non delibasset modò, sed hausisset etiam. Plura eam in rem idem Filesacus, Sorbonicus doctor tradidit. Sed insuper res ipsa illam Magiæ cum idololatria conjunctionem intimam & necessariam loquitur, cum constet plane, in idololatria quavis creaturæ tribui virtutem supernaturalem ad producendos effectus creatis majores, quam vel a natura, vel a Divina revelatione & gratia eam habere, cognoscei nequit, qua in re Magiæ essentia consistit.
units.tr: VI. We have already shown above that the Hierarchy is guilty of manifold idolatry. Moreover, the Hierarchists themselves do not deny that idolatry is most closely joined with magical impiety. St Paul, explaining idolatry as communion with demons [κοινωνίαν τῶν δαιμονίων] in 1 Cor. 10:20, teaches this, and John Filesac, a Parisian theologian, in his most learned dissertation on Magical Idolatry, has proved it clearly at length. Long ago Origen, who defended magical arts, was thus rebuked by Theophilus of Alexandria in his Second Letter on Easter: "Answer, you champion of a new impiety, or rather let him hear plainly: If the magical art is not evil, neither will idolatry be evil, which relies on the powers of the magical art. But if idolatry is evil, the magical art too will be evil, since idolatry subsists by it." Tertullian also, in his book On the Soul, calls magic the second idolatry. Hence it is clear that the same men were both authors of idolatry and magicians. Athenagoras in his First Apology for the Christians and Justin Martyr in his Address to the Gentiles confirm that Orpheus was the first of all to devise the names of the pagan gods, to set out their births and fates, and, by the judgment of the Gentiles, to have touched that theology more purely. That Orpheus was himself a magician, many authors record, Pliny above all, in book 30. The chief priest of Roman idolatry was Numa Pompilius, called by Lactantius the founder of foolish religions. Now the same Numa, a magician, learned idolatry from the nymph Egeria, who was a notorious enchantress, or rather a succubus demon. The Roman writers reported that he held converse with that goddess. Moreover, Varro in his book On the Worship of the Gods, as quoted by St Augustine in City of God 7.33, does not deny that Numa practised a kind of divination called hydromancy, and that his books, evidently magical, were burnt by the authority of the Roman Senate. Varro and Apuleius also do not conceal that magic had been mingled into the other idolatrous rites of Eleusis, Serapis and Isis. Psellus too writes in his book On Demons that the Gentiles thought magic was the highest summit of the priesthood, or of the sacred rites and the discipline of sacrificing, so that no priest was sufficiently trained unless he had not only tasted magic but drunk deeply of it. Filesac, a doctor of the Sorbonne, has handed down more on this point. Yet the thing itself also speaks of this intimate and necessary union of magic with idolatry, since it is plain that in any idolatry a supernatural power is attributed to a creature for producing effects greater than it could have either by nature or by divine revelation and grace; and in this the essence of magic consists.

units.la: VII. Magicam impietatem, quæ, si quia alia, horrenda maximè est, Hierarchici extenuare, atque nescio quibus coloribus sceleris foeditatem gravitatemque ab ea removere, religioni non ducunt. Quod conscientia sceleris hujus anxios cos disturbari, palam argunt. Cum duplex sit Magia, explicita & implicita; utramque subinde Pontificii Doctores à culpæ saltem gravioris reatu liberare conantur, conniveнтibus cæteris, non repugnante saltem Ecclesia. Gregorius de Valentia in 2. 2. tract. 10. cap. 7. dub. 4. referente Maldero, curiosas veritatis interrogationes & communicationes cum Diabolo, adeóque Divinationem, explicitæ Magiæ speciem, superstitionem esse, negat. Syl-
units.tr: VII. The Hierarchists do not scruple to soften magical impiety, which, if any impiety is, is most dreadful, and they somehow strip from it the foulness and gravity of the crime, with I know not what colours. That they are disturbed, anxious in conscience over this crime, they openly betray. Since magic is twofold, explicit and implicit, the Papist teachers from time to time try to free each of them at least from the guilt of the graver fault, the others conniving, and the Church at least not opposing. Gregory of Valencia, in 2.2, tract. 10, ch. 7, dub. 4, as reported by Malderus, denies that curious questions about truth and communications with the Devil, and therefore divination, a species of explicit magic, is superstition. Syl-

units.la: vester Prierias in Summa Sylvestrina sustinet: Non esse peccatum Mortale, si Sacerdos levitate & curiositate duectus, imperet daemoni, ut curiosa dicat, & nihil ad expulsionem facientia. Navarrus Manual. cap. 2. num. 27. 36. definit diserte, Daemones alloqui in surreptitiis ob vanitatem & curiositatem, esse peccatum tantum veniale. Idem contendit, Homines illos perditissimos, qui Salutatores (in Hispania Saludadores dicti, eo quòd vi orationum sanent) vocantur, posse licitè suo munere fungi; quoniam gratia illa gratis data iis conceditur à solo Deo, in utilitatem aliorum. Id ipsum quoque apud Delrionem Disquisit. Mag. lib. j. cap. 3. q. 4. Victoria & Veracrucius affirmant, quibus ipse Delrio calculum suum addit. Cajetanus in 2. 2. quaest. 96. art. 2. figuris vim quandam inesse tuetur, quando eæ sub tali vel tali sidere imaginibus astronomicis hominum artificio imprimuntur. In quam sententiam etiam Thomam contra gent. q. 105. pro se citat; neque eum dissentire, ejus ad locum illum commentator Ferrariensis planè abnuit. Pluribus eandem sententiam Gaffarellus in curiositatibus suis inauditis defendit.
units.tr: vester Prierias in the Summa Silvestrina maintains: It is not a mortal sin if a priest, led by levity and curiosity, commands a demon to tell curious things that have nothing to do with the expulsion. Navarrus in his Manual, ch. 2, nos. 27 and 36, clearly defines that to address demons in secret, out of vanity and curiosity, is only a venial sin. He also maintains that those most desperate men who are called Salutatores (in Spain, Saludadores, because they heal by the power of prayers) may lawfully exercise their office, since that grace, given freely, is granted to them by God alone for the benefit of others. The same thing is affirmed also by Victoria and Veracruz, as reported by Delrio in his Disquisitions on Magic, book 1, ch. 3, q. 4, and Delrio himself adds his own vote. Cajetan, in 2.2, q. 96, art. 2, defends that a certain power lies in figures when they are impressed under such or such a star by the artifice of men, in the form of astronomical images. He cites Thomas Against the Gentiles, q. 105, in support of this opinion, and the Ferrarese commentator on that passage flatly denies that Thomas dissents. Gaffarellus defends the same opinion at length in his Unheard-of Curiosities.

units.la: VIII. Facit huc, quòd Franciscus Valesius Philos. S. cap. 3. incantationis vim in universum tollens, verbis, sive ut causis, sive ut signis curari morbos, incantari angues, ut rumpant, aliàque ejusmodi effici pernegat. Incantationes, inquit, vanæ sunt & superstitiosæ; quaeque de illis narrantur, falsa & maligna. Falsum cantando rumpi angues, falsum quoque eos sibi obthurare aures, ne audiant, quod vel Plinius per derisum narrat, dicens: Non pauci etiam (credunt scilicet) serpentes ipsos incantari, & hunc illis unum esse intellectum, contrahique Magorum cantu. Si quæ verò ejusmodi in sacris & profanis literis occurrunt, cuncta illa ad fabulas morales & apologos referunt, ex quibus non intellectis vulgus existimet, morbos per incantationem fugari, feras & serpentes necari; atque quidam etiam impostores utentes in sua commoda incredulitate vulgi, multa se facere hujusmodi profiteantur. Addit, doctos quosdam Medicos, Trallianum scilicet, Marcellum Empiricum, atque Galenum ipsum, rigidum alioqui Philosophum, ex ignorantia & vana persuasione idololatriæ esse lapsos. Atque postremò credulitatem aliquid facere, ut curari videantur, qui re ipsa tamen non curentur. Eò haud dubiè Valesii sententia, nullâ unquam Ecclesiæ censurâ notata, pertinet, ne similitudo, quæ facta inter Pontificiorum, verbis, uti præ se illi ferunt, sacris dæmones expellentium, morbósque curantium, & facta Magorum, incantationibus suis similia patrantium, intercedit, agnosci possit.
units.tr: VIII. To this point belongs the fact that Francis Valesius, Sacred Philosophy, ch. 3, in general denying the power of incantation, flatly denies that diseases are cured by words, whether as causes or as signs, that snakes are charmed so that they burst, and that other such things are done. Incantations, he says, are vain and superstitious; and what is related about them is false and malicious. That snakes burst by singing is false, and so is the claim that they stop their ears so as not to hear, which even Pliny relates in mockery, saying: "Not a few (of course they believe) that the serpents themselves are charmed, and that this is their one understanding, and that they are drawn in by the song of magicians." If any such things occur in sacred or profane letters, Valesius refers them all to moral fables and parables, from which, not being understood, the common people might think that diseases are driven away by incantation and wild beasts and serpents slain; and that some impostors, taking advantage of the people's incredulity for their own advantage, profess that they do many such things. He adds that certain learned physicians, namely Trallianus, Marcellus Empiricus, and Galen himself, otherwise a stiff philosopher, fell into idolatry from ignorance and vain persuasion. And finally that credulity does something, so that those who in fact are not cured seem to be cured. To this, beyond doubt, Valesius's opinion, never marked by any censure of the Church, tends, so that the resemblance which exists between the sacred words with which the Papists, as they themselves boast, expel demons and heal diseases, and the deeds of magicians who perform similar things by their incantations, may not be recognised.

units.la: IX. A Magia implicita Magicarum artium Marti-nus Delrio Disquisit. Magic. q. 4. omnem ferè peccati labem abstergit. Postquam enim sic eam definivit. Secundum patri taciti genus est, (ex quo Magia implicita oritur) quando quis ignorans utitur Magicis signis, quia nescit esse mala à dæmone instituta; quod illis accidere solet, qui bona fide legere solent libros superstitiosos, putantes, eos esse Philosophorum aut Medicorum probatorum: item qui accipiunt ea ab hominibus, vulgò habitis bonis & fidelibus; eandem mox extenuat his verbis: Hoc in idiotis vel nullum, vel levissimum peccatum est, si duæ conditiones accedant. Prima est, si ignorantia sit probabilis, v. g. eorum, qui hoc scire tenentur, ut Ecclesiæ Pastores, Confessarii, concionatores & doctores: ii ut plurimùm supinâ & crassâ laborant ignorantiâ. Secunda conditio est, ut ignorans ista, sit paratus, quando admonitus fuerit, hujusmodi superstitionem relinquere, quia post agnitionem deficit ignorantia, & oritur contumacia, pro cujus gravitate, delicti magnitudo crescit. Idem lib. iij. p. 2. q. 2. agens de vana observantia, quam Magiam superstitiosam , quâ commodum aliquod speratur ex re, quæ neque fupernaturaliter eò pertinet, neque naturaliter id præstare potest, definit, eandem asferit peccatum esse veniale, quandiu quis ignorat tale pactum cum dæmone, si tamen nec ipse tencatur scire nec fuerit admonitus; vel nullum, veluti cùm quis vel joco duntaxat facit, sine præjudicio vel periculo sui, vel alterius, vel ignorantia vincibili, usus insuper mediis bonis vel indifferentibus.
units.tr: IX. Martin Delrio, Disquisitions on Magic, q. 4, wipes away almost all the stain of sin from implicit magic. For after he has defined it thus: The second kind of tacit magic (from which implicit magic arises) is when someone ignorantly uses magical signs, because he does not know that they were instituted as evil by the demon; which tends to happen to those who in good faith are wont to read superstitious books, thinking they are the works of approved philosophers or physicians; likewise those who receive them from men commonly held to be good and faithful; he soon softens it with these words: In the case of the unlearned this is either no sin or a very slight one, if two conditions are added. The first is that the ignorance be probable, for example in those who are bound to know this, such as ministers, confessors, preachers and teachers: these for the most part labour under a supine and gross ignorance. The second condition is that the one who is ignorant of these things be ready, when he has been admonished, to give up such superstition; because after knowledge ignorance ceases, and obstinacy arises, and the greater the obstinacy, the greater the magnitude of the offence. The same author, in book 3, part 2, q. 2, treating of vain observance, which he defines as superstitious magic, by which some advantage is hoped for from a thing which can neither bring it about supernaturally nor produce it naturally, asserts that this is a venial sin as long as someone is ignorant of such a pact with a demon, if indeed he is neither bound to know it nor has been admonished; or no sin at all, as when someone does it merely in jest, without prejudice or danger to himself or another, or through conquerable ignorance, and besides uses good or indifferent means.

units.la: X. Universa porrò Hierarchicorum religio Magica impietate infecta & contaminata est. Etenim principium ejus est Papæ, ceu Delphici cujusdam oraculi, decretoria vox, à qua eos religionem universam suspendere, non semel jam probavimus. In Papa ergo divinant omnes; ab eo mysteria, sacra, fas omne & nefas arcessunt; & sententiam & vocem ejus, sive demonstratam ex Divina quapiam revelatione, sive non demonstratum examini cujusquam subjacere pernegant. Quam divinationem impiam & verè Magicam esse, eo argumento liquidò constat, quia Papa revelationem rerum occultarum infallibilem promittens, non ex Dei Spiritu, sed aliunde loquitur; saltem se ex Dei Spiritu loqui, non probat; neque probandum sibi incumbere, asserit. Non loqui ex Spiritu Dei, neque Spiritum Dei loqui per ipsum, manifestum est. Etenim Spiritus Dei arguit Joh. xvi. 7. Arguens utitur demonstratione, unde ipsi demonstratio tribuitur, 1. Cor. 11.4. Non enim est Spiritus enthusiasticus. Atqui Spiritus Papæ non arguit demonstrando, adeóque est Spiritus enthusiasmi. Quod Papa non didicit, sed tamen dicit, verum scilicet est, quia errare non potest. Quod Papa non docet, sed præcipit, recipiendum est. Non potest enim fallere. Qui Papæ credunt, non possunt falli, quia is non potest fallere. Papæ obediendum est; non est judicandum de ipso. Non convenit quibusvis fidelibus dijudicare Spiritus. Spiritus bonus est, qui inclinat ad parendum Papæ, quia eo inclinat. Non ergo eo modo arguit, quo Spiritus Dei, atque sic ex Spiritu Dei non loquitur. Et qui eum hâc fiduciâ, quòd ei affixus sit Spiritus Dei ad immunitatem erroris, consulunt, perinde illi agunt, ac si consulerent engastrimuthos & hariolos, eos qui pipiunt & mussitant. A quo graviter sic Spiritus Dei Esaj. viii. 19. 20. dehortatur: Et quomodo dicunt ad vos דרשו אל האבות ואל consulite engaftrimuthos & hariolos? qui pipiunt & mussitant? Annon populus Deum suum consulet? super vivis mortuos? Ad legem & testimonium. Si non dicent secundum verbum hoc quisque, cui non est aurora!
units.tr: X. Moreover, the whole religion of the Hierarchicals is infected and contaminated with magical impiety. Its principle is the Pope's word, like the decisive voice of some Delphic oracle, and as we have already shown more than once, they make their entire religion depend on it. So everyone divines in the Pope; from him they draw mysteries, sacred rites, and all that is lawful and unlawful. They deny that his opinion and voice are subject to the examination of anyone, whether or not it is shown to derive from some divine revelation. That this divination is impious and truly magical is plain from this argument: the Pope, promising infallible revelation of hidden things, speaks not from the Spirit of God but from elsewhere. At least he does not prove that he speaks from the Spirit of God, and he asserts that it is no task of his to prove it. That he does not speak from the Spirit of God, nor the Spirit of God through him, is evident. For the Spirit of God convicts (John 16:7). The one who convicts uses demonstration, and so demonstration is attributed to him (1 Cor. 2:4). For the Spirit is not enthusiastic. But the Pope's spirit does not convict by demonstrating, and so it is a spirit of enthusiasm. What the Pope has not learned but nevertheless says is true, of course, because he cannot err. What the Pope does not teach but commands must be accepted, for he cannot deceive. Those who believe the Pope cannot be deceived, because he cannot deceive. One must obey the Pope; one must not sit in judgment on him. It is not for any faithful person to test the spirits. The spirit is good which inclines one to obey the Pope, because it inclines that way. Therefore it does not convict in the manner of the Spirit of God, and so does not speak from the Spirit of God. Those who consult him in the confidence that the Spirit of God is attached to him for immunity from error act just as if they consulted ventriloquists and soothsayers, those who chirp and mutter. The Spirit of God strongly dissuades from this in Isaiah 8:19, 20: And when they say to you, "Consult the ventriloquists and the soothsayers, who chirp and mutter" [דרשו אל האבות ואל], should not a people consult its God? Should they consult the dead on behalf of the living? To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, there is no dawn for them! ## XI.

units.la: Ipsa quoque religionis Hierarchicorum dogmata non pauca impietatem eandem redolent. Nam S. Paulus 1. Tim. iv. 1. 3. eos, qui vetant nubere, & jubent abstinere cibis à Deo conditis, ut assumantur cum gratiarum actione, ait docere ἀποσχέσθαι, doctrinas dæmoniorum, & eos, qui talibus doctrinis attendunt, πνεύμασιν πλάνοις Spiritibus seductoribus, & doctrinis dæmoniorum attendere monet. Atqui Hierarchici et vetant nubere quosdam, & præcipiunt abstinere à certis cibis. Retinent ergo & tuentur doctrinas dæmoniorum; & Spiritibus seductoribus attendunt; adeóque Magicæ impietati propalam litant. Eodem referimus, quòd in cultu Dei pluribus rebus virtutem quandam Divinam & supernaturalem tribuunt, quam nec à natura, nec à gratia habent; velut scriptis quibusdam humanâ industriâ exaratis Divinam & canonicam authoritatem; justitiæ & operibus humanis virtutem justificandi peccatorem, & promerendi vitam; libero hominis arbitrio ante conversionem & regenerationem hominis facultatem se convertendi ad Deum; attritioni cum absolutione junctæ, & à charitate Dei omni se-iunctæ potestatem peccata remittendi; aliáque ejusmodi innumera, quorum efficacia ex Divina revelatione vel operatione nulla probari potest; arrogant; atque sic יִמ לאלהיו vim suam Deum suum faciunt (Habac. 1. 11.) quòd sine φαρμακείᾳ incantatione quadam fieri nequit.
units.tr: The very doctrines of the Hierarchical religion also smell strongly of the same impiety. For St. Paul, in 1 Timothy 4:1, 3, says that those "who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods created by God, which are to be received with thanksgiving," teach abstinence [ἀποσχέσθαι], doctrines of demons, and he warns that those who attend to such doctrines attend to seducing spirits [πνεύμασιν πλάνοις] and to the doctrines of demons. Now the Hierarchicals both forbid some to marry and command abstinence from certain foods. Therefore they hold and defend doctrines of demons, attend to seducing spirits, and openly sacrifice to magical impiety. We refer to the same category their attribution, in the worship of God, of a certain divine and supernatural power to many things, which they have neither from nature nor from grace. Such are: divine and canonical authority to certain writings composed by human industry; the power of justice and human works to justify a sinner and to merit life; free human will, before the conversion and regeneration of the man, to have the capacity of turning to God; the power of attrition joined with absolution and entirely separated from the love of God to remit sins; and countless other things of this kind, whose efficacy cannot be proved from divine revelation or operation. They arrogate these things, and so make their strength their god [יִמ לאלהיו] (Habakkuk 1:11), which cannot be done without some sorcery [φαρμακείᾳ], that is, incantation.

units.la: XII. Facit huc apprimè Hierarchicorum in opere operato fiducia, qua signis, aliisque rebus efficaciam Divinam inhærentem & insitam tribuunt. Cùm enim Sacramenta, ceu sigilla justitiæ fidei non aliam quàm moralem & objectivam, uti loquuntur, efficaciam habeant, hoc est, vim significandi, commemorandi, certiorandi, &, propter veritatem Dei, bona spiritualia promissa credentibus sistendi; illi contra Concil. Trid. Sess. vij. Can. 8. anathema iis dixerunt, qui statuunt per novæ legis Sacramenta ex opere operato non conferri gratiam. Quæ quidem Concilii verba sic Gropperus interpretatus est, quasi non aliud innuant, quàm quòd Sacramenti veritas non ex Ministri dignitate, sed ex operatione Dei æstimanda sit. Puduit enim Gropperum, pudet alios veri & germani sensûs barbararum vocum, quem Synodus intendit. Revera enim sic Synodus signis Divinam virtutem sive inhærentem, sive ex pacto assistentem tribuit, ut ab eorundem operatione non tantùm Ministri dignitatem, sed etiam accipientis fidem & devotionem excluserit. Ita enim intellexerunt Scholastici ante Synodum; nominatim Albertus in cap. 6. Joh. Petrus de Palude in 4. Sent. dist. 1. q. 1. Ita intellexit ipsa Synodus, cujus Patres inter eas actiones, quibus pietas excitatur, quásque gratiam parere ex opere operantis, hoc est, non ipsius operis, sed ipsius operantis viribus & devotione docebant; & eas, quæ gratiam procurant ex opere operato, hoc est; uti ipsimet, Historico teste, explicárunt, non ex operantis, vel opus recipientis devotione, sed operis ipsius virtute, distinxerunt; & posterioris generis esse Sacramenta Christiana declararunt. Unde peculiari Canone xÿ. Ministri dignitatem ab efficacia Sacramenti Synodus exclusit. Atque eodem Can. vi. anathema dixit negantibus, quòd Sacramenta gratiam, quam significant, contineant. Quo verò modo contineant, Scotistas inter, Thomistas & alios acriter certatum est, quorum certamina Celeb. Forbesius Instruct. lib. ix: 2. fusiùs describit. Sed quocunque modo gratiam contineant, juxta illos continent certè; atque sic continent, ut eandem in utente ex opere operato, etiam non interveniente fide & devotione, exerant. Hoc verò quid aliud est, quàm gratiam Dei, quam Spiritus S. offert, Sacramenta jam præsentem utenti significant & obsignant, atque vera fides apprehendit, in terrestria illa elementa derivare; adeóque φαρμακείας in religionem Christianam introducere, ut sic sacrificuli γαυματουργοί, miraculorum authores patratorésque censeantur. Ita planè Sathanas olim Evæ persuadere conatus, fore, ut vescens arboris vetitæ fructu, vivat & fiat similis Deo, Genef. iii. 4. 5. eandem inducere voluit, ut crederet, Deum per opus isthoc operatum obligari ad dandam vitam beatam & similitudinem suam voluisse; adeóque arborem continere gratiam, & ex opere operato eam conferre, uti de Sacramentis Tridentini loquuntur. Sic Sathanas pro μαγεία sua agit cum Magis & sagis omni tempore. Illis enim se ad opera humanis majora efficienda, certorum verborum, rituum, signorum interventu se obstringit, quorum verborum, rituum, signorum usurpatio reapse & in effectu est Diaboli adoratio, quam à Servatore stipulatus est, cùm ei Regnum pacificum in omnia terræ Regna Matth. iv. 9. promitteret.
units.tr: XII. What bears most directly on this is the Hierarchicals' confidence in the ex opere operato, by which they ascribe a divine efficacy inherent and implanted in signs and other things. For since the sacraments, as seals of the righteousness of faith, have no efficacy other than moral and objective, as they say (that is, the power of signifying, reminding, assuring, and, by the truth of God, presenting the spiritual goods promised to believers), the Council of Trent, on the contrary, pronounced an anathema on those who hold that grace is not conferred by the sacraments of the new law ex opere operato (Sess. 7, Can. 8). Gropper interpreted these words of the Council as if they meant nothing more than that the truth of a sacrament is to be judged not from the dignity of the minister but from the working of God. For Gropper was ashamed, and others are ashamed, of the barbarous words, and of the true and genuine sense which the Synod intended. Indeed the Synod ascribed to signs a divine power, whether inherent or attached by covenant, in such a way that from their operation it excluded not only the dignity of the minister but also the faith and devotion of the recipient. This is how the Scholastics before the Synod understood it, namely Albert on John, chapter 6, and Peter de Palude on the Fourth Book of the Sentences, dist. 1, q. 1. The Synod itself understood it thus, for its Fathers, among the actions by which piety is aroused and which produce grace ex opere operantis, that is, not by the work itself but by the powers and devotion of the one working, taught; and they distinguished those which procure grace ex opere operato, that is, as they themselves explained, as the historian attests, not by the devotion of the one working or of the one receiving the work, but by the virtue of the work itself; and they declared that Christian sacraments belong to the latter kind. Hence in a particular canon (Can. 10) the Synod excluded the dignity of the minister from the efficacy of the sacrament. And in the same Canon 6 it pronounced an anathema on those who deny that the sacraments contain the grace which they signify. But as to how they contain it, there has been sharp dispute between Scotists, Thomists and others, whose quarrels the celebrated Forbes describes more fully in his Instructiones, book 9, part 2. Yet however they contain grace, according to those writers they certainly do contain it, and so contain it that they bring it to effect in the recipient ex opere operato, even without faith and devotion intervening. What else is this than to derive into those earthly elements the grace of God which the Holy Spirit offers, which the sacraments signify and seal to the one who now receives them, and which true faith apprehends; and thus to introduce sorceries into the Christian religion, so that the little priests are regarded as wonder-workers [θαυματουργοί], authors and performers of miracles? Satan plainly tried in the same way to persuade Eve that by eating the fruit of the forbidden tree she would live and become like God (Genesis 3:4, 5), and he wished to induce her to believe that God had by this work performed been bound to give a blessed life and his own likeness; and so that the tree contained grace and conferred it ex opere operato, as they speak of the sacraments of Trent. So Satan acts in this way for his magic with magicians and sorceresses at all times. For he binds himself to them to accomplish works greater than human, through the intervention of certain words, rites and signs; and the use of those words, rites and signs is in fact and effect the worship of the Devil, which he stipulated from the Saviour when he promised him the peaceful kingdom over all the kingdoms of the earth (Matthew 4:9).

units.la: XIII. Cum dæmoniis & mortuis hominibus; ad expi- scanda ex iis arcana, familiaritas, impietatem Magicam vel
units.tr: XIII. Familiarity with demons and dead men, for fishing out secrets from them, either presupposes or produces magical impiety and drags it along behind.

units.la: cum dæmoniis & mortuis (marginal note, illegible) vel suppońit, vel efficit, atque post se trahit. Quid autem Hierarchicorum cum utrisque familiaritate frequentius? Nam commercium cum daemoniis quod attinet, constat fatis, Sacrificulos, artem scilicet exorcisticam, nulla vocatione & ordinatione Divina legitime instructos, nulla miraculorum patrandorum potestate praeditos, adeoque inermes plane exercituros, cum Diabolo commercium subire, colloquia miscere, iisdem mandare multa, comminari, vim intentare, ex dictis & factis ejus methodum & rationem spiritualem curandi instituere, eos adjurationibus constringere, signa ab iis petere, absolutam ab iis obedientiam stipulari, destructionem maleficii imperare; exeuntibus injungere, ut secum socios trahant; adjurare Diabolos superiores, ut inferiores expellant; arcana multa, quae vel ex naturali, vel ex supernaturali revelatione scire non possunt, ex iis scisitari; denique testimonio eorum citato dubias res plures confirmare, qua de re plura inferius prodemus.
units.tr: Familiarity with demons and with the dead either presupposes or produces such impiety and draws it along behind. And what is more common among the Hierarchicals than these two kinds of familiarity? As for dealings with demons, it is well known from the facts that the priests, namely the exorcists, who have not been lawfully instructed by any divine calling or ordination, and who lack any power of performing miracles, and who are therefore plainly unarmed, undertake dealings with the Devil. They hold conversations with him, give him many orders, threaten him, and press their force upon him. From his words and deeds they draw up a method and a spiritual manner of healing. They bind him with adjurations, ask signs from him, demand absolute obedience from him, and command him to destroy witchcraft. They order the departing spirits to take their companions with them; they adjure the superior devils to expel the inferior ones. They question the demons about many secrets which they cannot know either from natural or from supernatural revelation. Finally, they confirm many doubtful matters by citing the demons' testimony. I shall say more about this below.

units.la: XIV. Cum mortuis hominibus eorumque manibus (haud veris equidem, sed a Diabolo confictis) crebro eosdem conversari, & ex iisdem secreta expiscari, notius est, quam ut pluribus asseri debeat. Equidem hominem defunctum non reverti in terram, fides antiquissima fuit Jobi, sic cap.vii. 7. 8. 9. loquentis: Memento quod halitus sit vita mea, non iterum videbit oculus meus bonum. Non lustrabit me oculus ejus, qui videt me. Si tuus oculus ad me sit, non ero. Consumitur nubes & abit. Sic est qui descendit ad inferna; לא יעלו non ascendet. Non redit in posterum domum suam, neque agnoscet eum amplius locus suus. Eodem sensu Hieropsaltes Psal. lxxviii. 39. Recordatus est Deus, quod caro essent, רוח הולך ולא ישוב Spiritus vadens & non revertens; vel, vento similis, qui vadit & non revertitur. Id ipsum Salvator noster in parabola, cujus argumentum est Lazarus & helluo, clarissimè nos docuit. Helluone enim instanter orante, ut dignetur is in paternam domum ex sinu suo Lazarum amandare, qui fratribus suis miserrimæ sortis testis exisseret, non tantum ab Abrahamo id desideriis helluonis negatum, sed addita etiam prægnans ratio est: Habent Mosen & Prophetas. Hos si non audiverint, non persuadebuntur, etiamsi ex mortuis quis resuscitabitur; Luc. xvi. 29. 30. 31. En; Abrahamus Divino Spiritu negat helluoni Lazari defuncti reditum ad viventes: negat allata ratione gravissima, quia Moses & Prophetæ, seu doctrina eorum, non mortui, non recentia mortuorum oracula doctores nostri, monitores nostri irrefragabiles designati sint. Denique Deus disertè prohibuit, ne quisquam mortuos in consilium adhibeat, qui finis est manium apparentium. Deut. xviii. 11. Lex Dei ita sonat: Ne sit inter vos דורש אל המתים quærens à mortuis. Et Esaj. viii. 19. 20. Et quomodo dicent ad vos: Consulite engastrimythos & hariolos &c.? Annon populus Deum suum consulet? בעד החיים אל המתים vivorum causa mortuos? Ad legem & testimonium! q. d. Cùm lex & testimonium extet, num quid populus insuper consulet mortuos de vivis? Hæc aliáque etiam ex antiquitate adversus apparitiones Spirituum Differt, Sel. Tom. j. Diff. vj. producta, & à Delrionis exceptionibus vindicata, prolixius hic repetere nihil attinet.
units.tr: XIV. That they constantly converse with dead men and their ghosts (which are not true, but invented by the Devil), and fish out secrets from them, is too well known to need proof to many. Indeed, that a dead man does not return to the earth was the most ancient belief of Job, who says in chapter 7, verses 7, 8, 9: Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will not see good again. The eye of him who sees me will not look upon me. If your eye is on me, I shall not be. The cloud is consumed and passes away. So is he who goes down to the grave; לא יעלו [lo yaʿaleh] he will not come up. He does not return to his house again, and his place will know him no more. In the same sense the psalmist says in Psalm 78, verse 39: God remembered that they were flesh, רוח הולך ולא ישוב [ruach holekh velo yashuv], a spirit that goes and does not return; or, like the wind, which goes and does not come back. Our Saviour taught this most clearly in the parable whose subject is Lazarus and the rich glutton. When the glutton urgently asked that Lazarus be sent from Abraham's bosom to his father's house, to go and bear witness to his brothers of his wretched lot, Abraham refused this, and not only refused it, but gave a weighty reason: They have Moses and the Prophets. If they do not hear them, neither will they be persuaded, even if someone rise from the dead (Luke 16:29, 30, 31). See: Abraham, by the Divine Spirit, denies to the glutton that the dead Lazarus should return to the living. He denies it for a very serious reason, namely that Moses and the Prophets, that is their doctrine, and not the dead, and not the recent oracles of the dead, are designated as our teachers and our unfailing advisers. Finally, God expressly forbade anyone to consult the dead, which is the purpose of apparitions of the departed. Deut. 18:11. The law of God sounds thus: Let there be none among you who is דורש אל המתים [doresh el ha-metim], inquiring of the dead. And Isaiah 8:19, 20: And when they say to you: Consult the necromancers and the wizards, etc.? Should not a people consult its God? בעד החיים אל המתים [baʿad ha-chayyim el ha-metim], the dead for the sake of the living? To the law and to the testimony! That is to say: since the law and the testimony stand, will the people further consult the dead about the living? These and other arguments from antiquity against apparitions of spirits, Differt, Sel. Tom. j. Diff. vj., were brought forward and defended against the objections of Delrio. There is no need to repeat them at greater length here.

units.la: XV. Hierarchici ergo Spirituum apparitiones fingentes, vel à Diabolo hominum defunctorum schema mentito, delusi, & abiis, quos pro hominibus mortuis reputant, arcana scissitantes, adeóque mortuos consulentes; num quid non apertæ necromantiæ rei sunt? Nam, si fides illis est, Constantiense Concilium apparitionem quandam Decani post obitum suum Episcopo apparentis, & de rebus occultis eum edocentis, comprobavit; atque sic animas defunctas defunctorum apparere, & ex iisdem occulta investigari posse, Conciliari definitione constat, fideïque articulus censetur. Revelationem etiam ejusmodi exempla quàm plurima Gregorius Turonensis retulit, ex quo nonnullas Bellarminus & Becanus collegerunt, licet Baronius ad A. C. 109. num. 49. fateatur ingenuè, parcendum esse simplicitati viri religiosi (Gregorii) qui multa aliter, quàm veritas se habet, æstimans, non calliditatis astu, sed benignitatis & simplicitatis voto, literis commendaverit. Sed nihil apparitionum & revelationum ejusmodi originem infaustam arguit fortius, quàm quòd animæ ex Purgatorio, hoc est, Utopia, reduces, apparentes, & arcana aperientes, non verum & salutarem, sed falsum ferè, culinarem, & verbo Dei repugnantem cultum, Missas, orationes pro defunctis, invocationem Sanctorum, purgatorium, impositurarum clericalium, arcem &c. stabilire conantur. De quo jam olim Cornelius Agrippa de Vanit. Scient. cap. 52. his verbis conquestus est: Nihil unquam solidæ veritatis, aut abditæ scientiæ, quæ veram charitatem, & animarum nostrarum salutem edificarent, ab his animarum apparitionibus revelatum est; sed duntaxat eleemosynæ (pro clero) peregrinationes, orationes (pro mortuis) jejunia (Papistica) & reliqua popularis pietatis opera persuasa sunt.
units.tr: XV. The Hierarchicals, then, who feign apparitions of spirits, either deceived by the Devil who has assumed the shape of dead men, and who question those whom they regard as dead men about secrets, and so consult the dead: are they not guilty of open necromancy? For if they are to be believed, the Council of Constance confirmed an apparition of a dean who, after his death, appeared to a bishop and instructed him about hidden matters. It is established by the decree of that Council, and it is counted as an article of faith, that the souls of the departed appear and that hidden things can be investigated from them. Gregory of Tours recounted very many examples of such revelations, and from him Bellarmine and Becanus gathered some of them, although Baronius, ad A. C. 109, num. 49, frankly admits that one must spare the simplicity of that religious man (Gregory), who, thinking many things otherwise than the truth is, committed them to writing not out of cunning, but out of a wish for kindness and simplicity. But nothing shows the unhappy origin of such apparitions and revelations more strongly than the fact that souls returning from Purgatory, that is, from Utopia, appearing and disclosing secrets, try to establish not a true and wholesome worship, but a false worship that is almost kitchen-like and opposed to the Word of God: Masses, prayers for the dead, invocation of the Saints, Purgatory, clerical impositions, the citadel, and so on. Cornelius Agrippa long ago complained of this in his words, de Vanit. Scient. cap. 52: Nothing of solid truth or hidden knowledge, which might build up true charity and the salvation of our souls, has ever been revealed by these apparitions of souls; but only alms (for the clergy), pilgrimages, prayers (for the dead), fasts (Papistical), and the other works of popular piety have been urged.

units.la: XVI. Atque hæc etiam cum dæmoniis & mortuis familiaritas causa est, quòd in Papatu obsessi & spectra à dæmone tantâ frequentiâ visuntur. Trahitur enim Diabolus dulci eo consortio, & nidulatur promptiùs. De obsessis non tantum experientiam authorem damus, sed exorcisticam etiam artem, quæ passim & ingenti cum studio erga eos sive verè, sive per institutum fraudulenter drama obsessos exercetur; cedente in speciem Sathana, ut superstitionem alat, & majori ac duraturo cum successu grassetur. Ipse Ipse enim, ut Johannis de Hassia, ab ipso Delrione Disquisit. Mag. lib. ij. q. 27. ff. j. repetita aurea verba mea faciam, simulat se captum, ut te capiat: se vinctum, ut te vinciat: se tuo imperio subditum, ut te sibi subdat: à te inclusum, ut contra te finaliter includat: fingit se tua arte vel imagini vel lapidi alligatum, ut funibus peccatorum religatum ad infernum te perducat. Apud nos contra, pura in coetibus nostris Euangelii doctrina sonante, vel rara, vel nulla plane energumenorum copia est. Horret enim Diabolus concilia, in quibus verbum Dei purè praedicatur: & impostores, qui obsessos se fingunt, faciessunt, quia detegi se nôrunt, neque praeter virgindemias & stigmata, aliud operae suae pretium ullum expectare audent.
units.tr: XVI. And this familiarity with demons and the dead is also the reason why, among the Papists, the possessed and phantoms are seen by the demon with such frequency. For the Devil is drawn by that sweet company and nests more readily. Concerning the possessed, we do not merely give experience as the author, but also the art of exorcism, which is practised everywhere and with great zeal upon them, whether they are truly possessed or whether the drama is fraudulently staged by design. Satan yields in appearance, so as to nourish superstition and to spread with greater and lasting success. For he himself, to repeat my golden words, as quoted by Johannes de Hassia from Delrio himself, Disquisit. Mag. lib. ij. q. 27. ff. j.: he pretends to be captured, so that he may capture you; he pretends to be bound, so that he may bind you; he pretends to be subject to your command, so that he may subject you to himself; he lets himself be enclosed by you, so that in the end he may enclose you against yourself; he feigns that he is bound by your art, or to an image or a stone, so that, bound by the cords of your sins, he may lead you down to hell. On our side, by contrast, where the pure doctrine of the Gospel sounds in our assemblies, there is either a very rare or altogether no crowd of demoniacs. For the Devil shudders at assemblies in which the Word of God is preached purely; and the impostors who pretend to be possessed, they cease to act, because they know they would be exposed, and they dare to expect no other reward for their work except scourgings and branding.
XVII.

units.la: Par ratio est spectrorum, quae Papatum ac in eo Hierarchicos, Clericos, Monachos & Moniales potissimum frequentissima exercent & infestant. De Anglia sua sic Jacobus I. Rex, Daemonol. lib. ij. 7. scribit: Hoc nobis in Britannia usu venit, quibus sub Papismi tenebris plura cernebantur spectra, plures genii, quàm quis fando expedire possit: nunc ita rari, ut vix toto Seculo quicquam ejusmodi inaudias. Et mox: Patribus nostris temporum & Papatûs vitio crassè errantibus, familiariter nobiscum versabantur daemones, ignorantiae nostrae nube septi, veluti Lemures aut Manducì infantibus illudentes. Ejusmodi nempe terriculamentis puerilem eorum temporum ridebant inscitiam. Et lib. iij. 2. recitata gentilium persuasione illa, quòd unicuique homini duo haerent vitae individui comites, Δαίμων & καχοδαίμων, genius bonus & genius malus; ille virtutis, hic vitii suasor, subjicit: Diabolus, ut inveteratum illum errorem gentium in imperitorum animis confirmaret, durante Papatûs caecitate, multorum aedes sine maleficio frequentavit, sedulus (uti videbatur) in iis, quæ usus domesticus requirebat, hunc, antiquorum Larem, nostri Brunium appellabant, hominis hirsuti effigie; quo hospites ædes suas credebant fortunatiores. Eò superstitionis devenerat insciitia. Sed & cap. 5. idem Spirituum, quibus Pbariorum nomen erat, quoddam agmen memorans, negat ullam sub Papatu cerebriorem Sathanæ imposituraм fuisse. Quanquam enim, inquit, Diaboli ope futura prædicere etiam tum nefas erat, qui tamen ab his aveeti erant, fortunatissimi probissimique Mortalium habebantur. Sed frequentiam illam in Papatu claustris maximè religiosis, spectrorum denuò experientia, & exorcisticæ artis exercitium luculenter confirmant; cùm apud nos lux verbi Divini pellat Spiritus illos, qui suas res in tenebris libenter expediunt. Accedente clara luce, umbræ & tenebræ evanescunt protinus.
units.tr: The same holds for specters, which chiefly plague and trouble the Papacy, and especially its hierarchs, clergy, monks and nuns, very frequently. King James I of England writes thus about his own country in his Daemonology, book 2, chapter 7: This has happened to us in Britain. Under the darkness of Popery more specters and more spirits were seen than anyone could possibly relate; now they are so rare that one scarcely hears of anything of the kind in a whole century. And soon after: While our fathers, grievously erring through the fault of those times and of the Papacy, lived on familiar terms with demons, shrouded in the cloud of our ignorance, mocking infants like Lemures or Mormos. Indeed, they laughed at the childish ignorance of those times with such terrors. And in book 3, chapter 2, after recounting the heathen belief that each man has two attendant spirits, Daimon and cacodaimon [Δαίμων & καχοδαίμων], a good genius and an evil genius, the one a prompter of virtue, the other of vice, he adds: The devil, in order to confirm that ancient error of the heathen in the minds of the unlearned while Papal blindness lasted, frequented the houses of many without doing any harm, busy (as it seemed) with those things which domestic life required. This spirit our people called Brownie, a hairy figure of a man, the ancient household Lar; by it guests believed their houses were more fortunate. To such a pitch had the ignorance of superstition come. But also in chapter 5, the same author, recalling a certain troop of spirits called Pharisees, denies that any more cunning deception of Satan existed under the Papacy. For although, he says, it was even then wicked to foretell the future by the help of the devil, yet those who were addicted to it were regarded as the most fortunate and upright of mortals. But that frequency among the Papists, especially in the most strict cloisters, is clearly confirmed both by the experience of ghosts and by the practice of the art of exorcism; whereas among us the light of the divine Word drives away those spirits who are glad to carry out their business in darkness. When clear light comes, shadows and darkness vanish at once.
XVIII.

units.la: Sed forte Diabolus Hierarchicorum cœtus frequentius obit & infestat, quia elapsuros sibi metuit: nostros deserit, quia jam sibi mancipatos novit. Sic plane occurrere solent, quibus illam cum Diabolo familiaritatem & necessitudinem objicimus. Et figmento huic quadrat, quod Æneas Sylvius in historia Concilii Basileensis ex vita Benedicti, Monachorum parentis recitat: nempe Benedictum monasterium quoddam virorum Sanctorum visitantem, infinitas dæmonum catervas vidisse, qui cum Sanctis Patribus conflictantes, bona, quæ illi patrabant opera, perturbare conabantur. Mox ad nundinas multis mercibus, multisque contractibus frequentes se conferentem, unicum duntaxat dæmonem, eúmque triste & otiosum in quadam specula constitutum aspexisse, miratúmque, quòd locum Sanctum & orationibus deditum, dæmonibus plenum, locum autem profanum, & perjuriis aliisque delictis occupatum, ab uno tantùm dæmone custoditum offendisset, adjurasse dæmonem, ut sibi causam ejus rei proderet. Respondisse dæmonem, locum Sanctum expugnatione dæmonum indigere; qui autem sua sponte peccarent, his fraude Diabolica opus non esse. Egregium sanè, & Diabolo authore dignum oraculum! Quæro enim, quisquis es, Papista, annon vetustis temporibus idem Gentiles respondere potuissent Christianis interrogantibus, cur oracula illorum, postquam Christo nomen datum est, conticuerint? cur rarę adeò apud Christianos visantur apparitiones? Alia ergo longè veriórque frequentiorum apud illos, rariorum apud nos apparitionum causa est. Delectatur Sathanas suo regno, regníque sui subditis, quos fraudibus suis opportunos, & jam probè circumscriptos novit: nos verò, qui ejus νοημαϚα novimus, dolos & versutiam intelligimus, aversatur. Sicut cùm nocte digitos pedis alicujus reste vis constringere eúmque trahere (uti per jocum solent quandoque iter facientes) si videas, eum, dolum sentire, actutum eo relicto te ad alium, altùm stertentem, & dolum non sentientem confers.
units.tr: But perhaps the devil haunts and troubles the assemblies of the hierarchy more often because he fears they will slip from his grasp, and deserts ours because he knows they are already his. Those who are confronted with that familiarity and intimacy with the devil which we object to usually reply in just this way. And the fiction suits what Aeneas Sylvius recounts in his history of the Council of Basel from the life of Benedict, the father of the monks: namely, that Benedict, visiting a certain monastery of holy men, saw countless troops of demons who, struggling against the holy fathers, tried to disturb the good works they performed. Afterwards, going to a fair full of many goods and many contracts, he saw only one demon, sad and idle, stationed on a lookout. Wondering that a holy place devoted to prayer was full of demons, while a profane place occupied with perjuries and other crimes was guarded by only one demon, he adjured the demon to tell him the reason for this. The demon replied: A holy place needs the assault of demons; but those who sin of their own accord have no need of diabolical trickery. An outstanding, truly devilish oracle! For I ask you, whoever you are, Papist: could not the Gentiles in ancient times have given the same answer to Christians asking why their oracles fell silent after the name of Christ was given? Why are apparitions so rarely seen among Christians? So the cause of the more frequent apparitions among them and the rarer ones among us is quite different and far truer. Satan delights in his kingdom and in its subjects, whom he knows to be suited to his frauds and already thoroughly deceived; but us, who know his devices [νοήματα], who understand his tricks and cunning, he shuns. Just as when at night you try to bind someone's toes with a rope and drag him (as travellers sometimes do for a joke), if you see that he feels the trick, you at once leave him and turn to another, snoring deeply and not feeling the trick.

units.la: XIX. Haud validior, qua familiaritatem illam cum dæmoniis excusare solent, ratio est, quòd sic cum iis conversentur, ut per exorcismos eadem ex hominibus obsessis, aliisque etiam expellant. Non enim sic omni arte sua dæmones expellunt, ut efficere possint, ne frequentissimèconvicente tubernio suo utantur, & expulsus unus cum aliis septem pejoribus vel ad antiquos, vel ad novos etiam lares redeat. Tum exorcismi ipsi, quibus vel ex hominibus obsessis dæmones, vel ex agris & fluminibus infecta aliáque animalia pellere conantur, Magica superstitione neutiquam carent, quod jam nunc demonstrandum nobis est.
units.tr: XIX. Nor is the reason they usually give to excuse that familiarity with demons any stronger: that they associate with them so that by exorcisms they may drive the same spirits out of the possessed and others too. For they do not expel demons by their art in such a way as to prevent them from still using their crowded lodging, and so that one expelled may return with seven worse ones to the old or even new household gods. Moreover, the exorcisms themselves, by which they try to drive demons out of the possessed, or unclean and other animals out of fields and rivers, by no means lack magical superstition, as we must now demonstrate.

units.la: XX. Dæmonia veteres precibus & jejuniis præviis uniconverbo ejecerunt, pro imperio & potestate in Spiritus immundos Divinitus concessa. Fuit illis data potestas calcandi Serpentes & Scorpiones, & supra omnem vim inimici, ut nihil eis nocéret; Luc. x. 19. quod ad miraculosa Dei dona pertinebat. Tales,exorcistas haud equidem Christus & Apostoli, sed vetus Ecclesia nuncupavit; non quòd adjurationis formulâ quâdam dæmonem pellerent; sed quòd pellerent verbo imperante, per potestatem Christi. Neque ad hoc munus ordinari fuerunt, sed sufficiebat iis donum Dei. Unde Clemens Constit. lib. viij. 27. ἐξορκιστὴς, inquit, ὡ χαρισματῶν &c. Exorcista non fit ordinatione. Est enim libera voluntatis præmium, & gratiæ Divinæ per Christum & adventum Spiritus S. Siquidem qui donum accepit sanitatum, per revelationem declaratur à Deo, cùm gratia, quæ in eo est, sit omnibus manifesta. Et primitus quidem si non omnibus, saltem plerisque fidelibus donum ísthoc exercendum videlicet, quoties Dei gloria postuladel; Divinitus indultum est, uti ex Tertulliano de Corona Mil. cap. 2. & ad Scapul. c. 2. & Apolog. cap. 5. Justino Martyre in Apolog. sub finem; Cypriano ad Demetriadem; Eusebio Histor. Eccles. lib. j. cap. 12. 13. Augustino de Civit. D. lib. x. 22. aliisque pluribus liquet; neque ex Pontificiis ipsis Raphaël de la Torre Disput. 5. Maldonatus in Marc. ix. 38. alii dubitant; denique ex nostratibus Justellus Notis ad Tertullianum de Corona Mil. cap. 11. aliíque comprobant. Cessante miraculorum in Ecclesia dono, sic equidem exorcismi in preces piè conversi sunt, ut ipsum tamen Exorcistarum nomen, ἐξορκισταὶ licet, non illico cessaverit, sed deinceps hæserit Catechistis. Ita enim Doctissimus Justellus Not. ad Can. Eccl. Univ. pag. 168. scitè observat, Scholiasten Græcum Harmenopuli in Epitome Canonum sect. j. tit. 9. ἐξορκισμὸς Exorcistas interpretari καταχητὰς Catechetas; & Theodorum Balsamorum in Concil. Laod. can. 26. statuere, quòd eò loci ἐξορκίζειν exorcizare idem sit quod κατηχεῖν catechizare, seu instituere infideles. Quibus addi potest locus difertissimus Cyrilli in Præcatechesi, ubi exorcismi & catecheses promiscuè ponuntur. Festinent, ait, pedes tui ad Catecheses audiendas. Exorcismos studiosè suscipe, etiamsi inspiratus jam sis, & exorcisatus. Salubris enim est tibi res ista. Quod de dæmoniacis intelligi nequit. Sicut enim vigente miraculorum dono, per exorcismos Diabolus pellebatur: ita catechistæ instituentes Catechumenos suos, eosdem ex potestate tenebrarum in Regnum lucis transferebant.
units.tr: XX. The ancients drove out demons by a single word, after prayers and fasting, by the power and authority over unclean spirits given them by God. They were given power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, so that nothing could harm them (Luke 10:19), which pertained to God's miraculous gifts. Such people Christ and the Apostles did not call exorcists, but the ancient Church did; not because they drove out demons by some formula of adjuration, but because they drove them out by a word of command, through the power of Christ. Nor were they ordained to this office; the gift of God was sufficient for them. Hence Clement, in the Constitutions, book 8, chapter 27: exorcist [ἐξορκιστὴς], he says, [ὡ χαρισματῶν] etc. An exorcist is not made by ordination. For it is a reward of free will and of divine grace through Christ and the coming of the Holy Spirit. For he who has received the gift of healings is declared by God through revelation, since the grace that is in him is manifest to all. And at first, if not to all the faithful, then at least to most, this gift of exercising the office, namely whenever the glory of God required it, was granted by God, as is clear from Tertullian, De Corona Militis chapter 2, Ad Scapulam chapter 2, and Apology chapter 5; from Justin Martyr, Apology at the end; from Cyprian, To Demetrianus; from Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History book 1, chapters 12 and 13; from Augustine, City of God book 10, chapter 22, and from many others. Nor do some of the Papists themselves, such as Raphael de la Torre, Disputation 5, or Maldonatus, on Mark 9:38, doubt it; finally, among our own people, Justellus, in his notes to Tertullian, De Corona Militis chapter 11, and others confirm it. When the gift of miracles ceased in the Church, exorcisms were indeed turned into pious prayers, yet the very name of exorcists, ἐξορκισταί though it be, did not cease at once, but afterwards clung to the catechists. For the most learned Justellus, in his notes on the Canons of the Universal Church, p. 168, wisely observes that the Greek scholiast of Harmenopulus, in the Epitome of Canons, section 1, title 9, interprets exorcism [ἐξορκισμὸς] as exorcists [Exorcistas], and catechists [καταχητὰς] as catechetes; and that Theodore Balsamon, on the Council of Laodicea, canon 26, states that there to exorcise [ἐξορκίζειν] is the same as to catechize [κατηχεῖν], that is, to instruct unbelievers. To these may be added the very clear passage of Cyril in his Precatechesis, where exorcisms and catechizings are put side by side without distinction: Let your feet, he says, hasten to hear the catecheses. Undertake the exorcisms eagerly, even if you are already inspired and exorcized. For that thing is wholesome for you. This cannot be understood of the demoniacs. For just as, while the gift of miracles flourished, devils were driven out by exorcisms, so catechists, instructing their catechumens, transferred the same people from the power of darkness into the kingdom of light.

units.la: XXI. Atque huic veterum exorcismo Hierarchicorum exorcismus è diametro oppositus est. Nam primò, Exorcistæ eorum ordinantur, novo & in Ecclesia Christiana veteri prorsus inaudito exemplo, uti vel solum Clementis testimonium à nobis allegatum comprobat. Extat equidem in Concilii Carthaginensis IV. canone VII. ritus & formula exorcistarum ordinandorum, qualis ferme in Pontificiali describitur. Cæterùm & Concilium illud, & Canones spurii sunt, utpote qui in Codice Canonum Africanorum non extant; & primùm à Mercatore, impostore insigni, in orbem Christianum inveđi sunt, quo nomine Mercator ille cum suo hyperaspista Turriano, meritò Blondello vapulat. Secundò, adjuratur ab exorcistis novis dæmon. Olim autem Christus, Apostoli, fideles solo verbo dæmonia ejecerunt, citra adjurationem ullam, quæ apud Exorcistas Judæos equidem recepta erat, Act. xix. 13. apud Christianos non item, quod fusiùs probârunt alii. Tertiò, adjuratur ab Exorcistis novis dæmon, non corporaliter duntaxat obsidens homines, sed etiam spiritualiter; uti exemplum infantum, quos in baptismo exorcizant, fidem facit. Imò adjuratur obsidens quasvis alias creaturas irrationales, elementa, ventos, pluvias, tempestates, fulmina, domos, infesta, aliáque animalia nocentia; denique ubicunque apparet, vel apparere videtur. Quartò, adjurant per Angelos, los, Sanctos, Sacerdotes quoscunque, reliquias, crucem. Christus autem jussit dæmonia ejicere in nomine suo, non alterius cujusquam, Marc. xvi. 17. Quinto, modus exorcizandi apud recentiores non simpliciter in imperio, sed etiam in exprobratione, convitiis, contumeliis, verbis juxta factisque dæmoni illatis; quin etiam contractu, compromisso, ad docenda & præstanda omnia, quæ ad salutem obsessi, aliorumque hominum pertinere putantur. Qui fanè modus nec rationi, nec verbo Dei, nec praxi primitivæ Ecclesiæ consentaneus est. Sextò, exorcizant per media, quæ Magica impietate tota laborant, veluti per Diabolos, ex quibus constituitur princeps, qui alios ejiciat; quod fas esse Mengus in Fuste Dæmon. pag. 21. tuetur; per res inanimatas, thus, panem & salem benedictum, aquam incensam, ramos palmarum, campanas, agnos cereos, lucem, ignem, oleum, suffumigationes &c. trinam exsufflationem in aquam, flagellationem, colaphorum inflictionem; aurium & capillorum vellicationem; figuras, cruces inprimis multiplicatas; verba tum sacra, puta tmemata quædam Scripturæ, liturgiæ, Euangelii inprimis S. Johannis, nomina Dei etiam ignota &c. tum profana, partim acerbè exprobrantia, partim farcasticè dæmonem ridentia, partim examinantia &c.
units.tr: XXI. And the exorcism of the hierarchs is diametrically opposed to this ancient exorcism. For, first, their exorcists are ordained, by a new example utterly unknown to the ancient Christian Church, as even the testimony of Clement quoted by us proves. There does indeed exist, in canon 7 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, the rite and formula for ordaining exorcists, roughly as it is described in the Pontifical. But both that council and those canons are spurious, since they are not found in the Codex of the African Canons; and they were first brought into the Christian world by Mercator, a notorious impostor, for which reason Mercator, together with his hyperaspist Turrianus, is rightly thrashed by Blondel. Second, the devil is adjured by the new exorcists. But Christ, the Apostles and the faithful formerly drove out demons by the word alone, without any adjuration, which indeed was accepted among the Jewish exorcists (Acts 19:13) but not among Christians, as others have shown at length. Third, the devil is adjured by the new exorcists not only when he besieges men bodily but also when he besieges them spiritually; the example of the infants whom they exorcise in baptism bears witness to this. Indeed he is adjured when he besieges any other irrational creatures whatever: elements, winds, rains, storms, lightnings, houses, fields, and other harmful animals; finally, wherever he appears or seems to appear. Fourth, they adjure through angels, saints, priests of whatever kind, relics, and the cross. But Christ ordered demons to be cast out in his name, not in the name of anyone else (Mark 16:17). Fifth, the manner of exorcising among more recent men is not simply by command, but also by reproach, insults, abuse, and words and deeds directed at the demon; indeed even by contract and compromise, to teach and perform all the things which are thought to pertain to the salvation of the possessed and of other men. This manner agrees neither with reason, nor with the Word of God, nor with the practice of the primitive Church. Sixth, they exorcise by means wholly tainted with magical impiety: for instance, through devils, of whom one is set up as prince to expel the others, which Mengus, in Fustis Daemonum, p. 21, defends as lawful; through inanimate things: incense, blessed bread and salt, water mixed with incense, palm branches, bells, wax lambs, light, fire, oil, fumigations, etc.; by blowing three times into water, by flogging, by inflicting blows, by plucking the ears and hair; by figures, above all multiplied crosses; by words, both sacred, that is certain fragments of Scripture, liturgies, above all the Gospel of St John, names of God even unknown, etc., and profane, partly bitterly reproaching, partly mocking the demon with sarcasm, partly interrogating, etc.

units.la: XXII. Hæc omnia Magicam exorcismorum impietatem abundè propalant. Quis enim Magus demum censebitur, si censeri non potest Exorcista, qui omni vocatione Divina destitutus congreditur cum Sathana; atque licet prima fronte severè, comminatorie & cum dignitate agere videatur, tamen, si penitius omnia consideres, ad callidi Serpentis dicta & facta se accommodat, ad quæ verba se contremiscere simulat, ea sæpiùs repetit; causam ingressûs petit, ut à similibus peccatis alii caveant, & eo vitato vel expiato facilius sanetur energumenus, quasi hæc perfido curæ essent; & signum egressionis percontatur, ut constet jam verè liberatum ægrum, perinde ac si fallendi artem dedidicisset: qui ad expellendum eum res, actiones, figuras, verba, numeros adhibet, quibus nec natura, nec revelatio Divina pretium ullum ea in re statuit, vel virtutem ad operandum tale quid contulit: qui Diabolum per creaturas adjurat: qui cum eodem contrahit, ut veritatem vel invitus pandat; atque post contractum eum Sathanam, Pythonem suum examinat, anquirit, quædam etiam curiosa expiscatur, uti Cotonum fecisse cum dæmone Hadrianæ Fraxineæ Thuanus Hist. lib. cxxxii. memorat.
units.tr: XXII. All these things amply reveal the magical impiety of exorcisms. For what sort of magician would be judged such if one cannot be judged an exorcist, who, lacking any divine calling, engages with Satan? Although at first sight he seems to act sternly, threateningly and with dignity, if you consider everything more closely, he adapts himself to the words and deeds of the cunning Serpent. He pretends to tremble at those words and often repeats them. He asks the cause of the entry, so that others may beware of similar sins, and that once the sin is avoided or atoned for, the energumen may be healed more easily, as if these things were of concern to a treacherous spirit. He asks for the sign of departure, so that it may be certain that the sick man is truly freed, just as if the devil had unlearned the art of deceiving. To expel the demon, he uses things, actions, figures, words and numbers, to which neither nature nor divine revelation has assigned any value in this matter, nor given any power for working such an effect. He adjures the devil through creatures. He makes a contract with him, so that the devil, even against his will, may reveal the truth.
