Alexander of Hales, part 4, q. 53, membr. 2, adds to the blasphemy, where he holds it a true opinion, saying that the body of Christ is carried wherever the species are carried, as into the belly of a dog or a pig, or into other unclean places; and Thomas Aquinas, p. 3, q. 80, art. 3, asserts that if a mouse or a dog should eat the consecrated host, the substance of the body of Christ does not cease to be under the species, as long as those species remain, just as also if it were thrown into the mud. I have recited the words of these authors quoted above. To these I add Claude d'Espence, Continuation 3 of the Confession, who reports that he has often heard that descent of Christ from heaven onto the altar from priests and churchmen; yet he is unwilling to excuse them, nor the Sententiarii, Quaestionarii, Rationarii, Manipularii, Scholastici, if they have spoken thus, to whom the advice of Quintilian applies: For a long time one should read only the best, and those who do not mislead a believing reader. So those five little words, and not more nor fewer, Hoc enim est corpus meum, bring low Christ, who sits at the right hand of the throne of Majesty, summoning him again from his heavenly seat and drawing him out, so that he is in great danger of being eaten by dogs, pigs, mice or worms, or of being thrown into the mud. O darkness! O blindness! O utmost magical impiety!

units.la: LVII. Non vera duntaxat Sacramenta Hierarchici Magica impietate polluunt; sed in spuriis etiam & à se confictis unctiones aliáque adhibent quibus effectus, quos nec à natura, nec à Deo suprà naturam operante habent, deputant. In Concilio Meldensi cap. 1. apud Bruchardum lib. iv. 75. & Ivonem par. 1. cap. 268. constitutum asserunt, ut tres ampullæ à Presbytero quintà feriâ in Coenâ Domini afferantur, una ad oleum Catechumenorum , altera ad chrisma, tertia ad oleum infirmorum. Duplex tamen distinguere oleum solent; alterum simplex, quo Catechumeni in pectore & scapulis, & in fronte, antequam abluantur; nec non infirmi & energumeni: alterum balsamo mixtum, & chrismatis nomine insignitum, quo baptizandi in vertice, confirmandi in fronte, & ordinandi etiam unguntur, de quo plura Cafalius de Vet. S. Christ. Ritibus cap. 37. habet. Nos de chrismate, cujus potissimum in Sacramento Confirmationis usus, & oleo, quo in extremæ unctionis Sacramento infirmi ungi solent, pauca dixisse satis habebimus.
units.tr: LVII. The Hierarchs pollute not only the true sacraments with magical impiety, but in spurious and self-invented rites also they use anointings and other things to which they assign effects that they have neither from nature nor from God working above nature. In the Council of Meaux, chap. 1, cited by Burchard, lib. 4, 75, and Ivo, part 1, chap. 268, they lay down that three flasks be brought by the priest on Maundy Thursday, one for the oil of the catechumens, another for the chrism, the third for the oil of the sick. They are accustomed, however, to distinguish two kinds of oil: one plain, with which catechumens are anointed on the chest and shoulders and on the forehead before they are washed, and likewise the sick and the possessed; the other mixed with balsam and marked with the name of chrism, with which those to be baptized are anointed on the crown of the head, the confirmed on the forehead, and the ordained as well. Cabassut, De Vet. S. Christ. Ritibus, chap. 37, has more on this. We shall consider it enough to have said a little about the chrism, whose principal use is in the sacrament of Confirmation, and about the oil with which the sick are usually anointed in the sacrament of extreme unction.

units.la: LVIII. Chrismatis exorcismus in Rituali de Benedictionibus pag. 239. extat talis: Exorcizo te Creatura olei per Deum Patrem, &c. ut fias omnibus, qui ex te ungendi sunt, in adoptionem filiorum Dei per Spiritum S. In Pontificali pag. 177. 179. 180. ter cantatur: Ave Sanctum chrisma. Ave Sanctum oleum. Durandus, Episcopus Mimatensis, Rationalis lib. vj. cap. 78. benedictionem Episcopalem ampullæ, in qua chrisma est, & mysteria ampullæ illius fusè edisserit. Inter alia num. 17. sic ille: Ampulla Christus est, vel ampulla cum chrismate, corpus Domini ex Virgine Maria assumptum cum Divinitate, scilicet Christum vivum esse significat. Ibidem: Fertur ampulla cooperta sindone alba, in sinistro brachio; portantem ampullam præcedit lumen, & antecedunt duo Sacerdotes, unus cum thuribulo, alius cum cruce, & in medio eorum Diaconus, cum libro Euangelii, & super capita eorum fertur umbraculum, seu pallium, & duo antecedunt cantando. In quo facto repræsentatur processio, quam fecerunt, filii Israël; tendentes per desertum ad terram promissionis: quoniam sindon est arca: Ampulla urna: lumen præcedens ampullam, columna ignis, quæ præcedebat populum: Sacerdos cum thuribulo, Aaron cum thuribulo:
units.tr: LVIII. The exorcism of the chrism in the Ritual, De Benedictionibus, p. 239, reads as follows: I exorcise you, creature of oil, by God the Father, etc., that you may become, to all who are to be anointed with you, adoption into the sons of God through the Holy Spirit. In the Pontifical, pp. 177, 179, 180, it is sung three times: Hail, holy chrism. Hail, holy oil. Durandus, Bishop of Mende, Rationale, lib. 6, cap. 78, expounds at length the episcopal blessing of the flask in which the chrism is, and the mysteries of that flask. Among other things, at no. 17, he says: The flask is Christ, or the flask with the chrism signifies the body of the Lord, taken from the Virgin Mary together with the Divinity, that is, signifies that Christ is living. Likewise: The flask is carried covered with a white linen cloth, in the left arm; a light goes before the bearer of the flask, and two priests go before, one with the censer, the other with the cross, and in the middle of them a deacon with the book of the Gospel; and over their heads a canopy or pall is carried, and two go before singing. In this action is represented the procession which the sons of Israel made, travelling through the desert to the promised land: for the linen cloth is the ark, the flask the urn, the light going before the flask the pillar of fire which went before the people, the priest with the censer Aaron with the censer.
Tom. II. mmm

units.la: Sacerdos cum cruce, Josua cum sceptro: Diaconus cum libro Evangelii, Moses cum libro legis: umbraculum est tabernaculum, aut nubes lucidissima, quæ filios Israel obumbravit: qui cantantes præcedunt, lætitiam eorum significant, qui ad terram promissionis transierunt. Nullus mysteriorum finis. Nam num. 19. sic Durandus insistit: Ampulla statim postquam benedicta fuit, ex parte cooperta; & ex parte discooperta, ut allata fuerit, salutatur ab Episcopo & Presbyteris, quia Christus postquam transvit ad altare crucis, id est, ad immolationem, sicut ampulla ad consecrationem Episcopi, aliqua ex parte corpus suum nudum monstravit, ut Thomæ & aliis discipulis, quos voluit esse testes suæ resurrectionis: aliis verò invisibilis fuit. Salutantur autem quinquies ampullæ ab Episcopo, ut de quinque vulneribus gratiarum actio Christo reddatur. Postquam autem ampulla salutata & à ministris altaris, cooperitur, ut à nemine nuda videatur, & cooperta iterum salutatur, quia Christus postquam salutavit, & manifestavit se discipulis suis; quos voluit suos suæque resurrectionis esse testes, ascendit in Cœlum, & invisibilis factus est hominibus. Sanè Episcopus ter HALAT in ampullam: primò, quia sicut halitus ab interioribus & secretis procedit ad publicum, & vocatur Spiritus: sic Episcopus per Spiritum suum demonstrat, Spiritum S. à Patre & Filio procedentem in corpore Domini habitare. Secundò, etiam halat, quia legitur in Evangelio, quòd Dominus insufflavit in discipulos, dicens: Accipite Spiritum S. &c. Hic igitur halitus illam insufflationem significat. Ideò autem ter halat, quia tres personæ sunt.
units.tr: The priest with the cross, Joshua with the sceptre; the deacon with the book of the Gospel, Moses with the book of the law. The canopy is the tabernacle, or the most bright cloud that overshadowed the children of Israel. Those who go before, singing, signify the joy of those who passed over into the promised land. No end to the mysteries. For Durandus, in number 19, insists thus: The ampulla, immediately after it has been blessed, is partly covered and partly uncovered, and as it is carried in it is greeted by the Bishop and the priests, because Christ, after he passed over to the altar of the cross, that is, to the sacrifice, showed his body partly bare, as the ampulla is to the consecration of the Bishop, to Thomas and the other disciples, whom he wished to be witnesses of his resurrection; but to others he was invisible. The ampulla is greeted five times by the Bishop, so that thanks may be rendered to Christ for his five wounds. After the ampulla has been greeted and covered again by the ministers of the altar, so that it may be seen bare by no one, and covered, it is greeted again, because Christ, after he had greeted and revealed himself to his disciples, whom he wished to be witnesses of himself and of his resurrection, ascended into heaven and became invisible to men. Moreover, the Bishop breathes three times [HALAT] into the ampulla: first, because just as breath proceeds from the inward and secret parts into the open, and is called spirit, so the Bishop, through his Spirit, shows that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, dwells in the body of the Lord. Second, he breathes also because it is read in the Gospel that the Lord breathed upon the disciples, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit, etc. This breath therefore signifies that breathing upon them. He breathes three times, moreover, because there are three persons.

units.la: LIX. Tot exorcismis, benedictionibus, mysteriis imprægnatum chrisma, non tantùm certà verborum formulà interveniente, Sacramentum ordinarium Ecclesiæ suæ Hierarchici constituunt, sed virtute etiam & effectibus planè eximiis dotant mactántque. Verba, quibus sacramentum hoc chrismatis confirmando Episcopus (neque enim aliis fas est) administrat, hæc sunt: Consigno te signo crucis, & chrismate salutis, in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus S. His verbis, non aliis administratum Sacramentum, efficaciam habet. Effectus confirmationis seu chrismatis ejusmodi Eugenius decreto in Concilio Florentino ad Armeniorum instructionem edito, prodit: Effectus hujus Sacramenti est, quia in eo datur Spiritus S. ad robur, sicut datus est Apostolis in die Pentecostes, ut videlicet Christianus audacter Christi confiteatur nomen. Ideoque in fronte, ubi verecundiæ sedes est, confirmandus ungitur, ne Christi nomen confiteri erubescat, &c. Similes effectus Bellarminus de Sacr. Confirm. lib. v. cap. 11. pandit his verbis: Gratiam confert gratum facientem, & quidem majorem, quàm ipse Baptismus, in ordine ad roborandum animum adversùs Diaboli impetus; sed minorem in ordine ad remissionem peccatorum, quia non remittit totam pœnam, ut facit gratia Baptismi, quasi non per Baptismum Christum totum induamus. Vocant oleum, chrisma salutis, quasi non Baptismus nos salvet, Usque adeò suum illud chrismatis Sacramentum laudibus suis in tertium Cœlum ferunt, ut bonus Galenus Catech. 120. pag. 366. diserte negaverit, sine unctione hac sua quenquam Christianum effici; literisque mandaverit, Baptismi fructus tantum abesse à consignationis (confirmationem intelligit) perfectione, quantum est inter Virum & infantem discriminis.
units.tr: LIX. The hierarchs, having imbued the chrism with so many exorcisms, blessings and mysteries, establish it as an ordinary sacrament of their Church, not merely with a fixed form of words intervening, but they also endow and load it with quite remarkable power and effects. The words with which the Bishop administers this sacrament of the chrism in confirmation (for it is not lawful for him to use others) are these: I seal you with the sign of the cross and the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The sacrament, administered with these words and no others, has its efficacy. Eugenius, in a decree issued at the Council of Florence for the instruction of the Armenians, sets out the effect of this confirmation or chrism: The effect of this sacrament is that the Holy Spirit is given in it for strength, as he was given to the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, that is, that the Christian may boldly confess the name of Christ. Therefore the one to be confirmed is anointed on the forehead, where the seat of shame is, so that he may not blush to confess the name of Christ, etc. Bellarminus, de Sacr. Confirm. lib. v. cap. 11., sets out similar effects in these words: It confers grace that makes one pleasing to God, and indeed greater than Baptism itself, in order to strengthen the mind against the assaults of the devil; but less in order to the remission of sins, because it does not remit the whole punishment, as the grace of Baptism does, as if we did not put on Christ entire through Baptism. They call it oil, the chrism of salvation, as if Baptism did not save us. So far do they carry their sacrament of the chrism to the third heaven with their praises that the good Galenus, Catech. 120. pag. 366, has plainly denied that any Christian is made without this anointing of theirs; and he has committed to writing that the fruit of Baptism is as far from the perfection of the sealing (he means confirmation) as the difference between a man and an infant.

units.la: LX. Institutum porrò divinitùs esse Chrisma, ut crucis signo, & verborum illorum expressa formulâ interveniente, effectus ejusmodi spirituales & supernaturales præstet, probari, certè hactenus nullo modo potuit. Neque enim chrismatis ejusmodi corporalis, nedum exorcizati
units.tr: LX. That the chrism was instituted by God, so as to produce such spiritual and supernatural effects through the sign of the cross and the express formula of those words, has certainly not been able to be proved in any way up to now. For neither the corporeal chrism of this kind, much less the exorcised one, nor the sign of the cross, with that formula of words added, do the Holy Scriptures mention even in the smallest particle, as either signifying or sealing such spiritual effects, much less conferring them ex opere operato.

units.la: Papa, nulla previa Divina Sacramenti institutione, chrisma in quamvis converti. cizati, & signo, crucis, accedente formulâ illâ verborum, spirituales ejusmodi effectus vel significantis, vel obsignantis, nedum ex opere operato conferentis, S. literæ vel minimo apice meminerunt. Scotus sanè in q.d. 7. q. 1. art. 2. Apostolos sola manuum impositione hoc Sacramentum contulisse, docet. Quin & Alexander Alensis in Summa Theologiæ jussu Innocentii III. scripta, & ab Alexandro IV. diplomate munita, Parte 4. q. 14. membro 1. negat Sacramentum hoc à Christo institutum esse asserítque, quantum ad formam verborum, & materiam elementorum in Concilio demum Meldensi institutum esse, his argumentis inducłus, quia non legitur in Scriptura, quando, vel ubi confirmatio instituta fuerit; & quia nec Christus, nec Apostoli usi sint hác vel materiâ, vel formâ, sed solâ impositione manuum. Unde concludit: Sine præjudicio dicendum, quòd neque Dominus hoc Sacramentum instituit, neque dispensavit, neque Apostoli. Bonaventura ipse quoque hanc Præceptoris sui sententiam sequitur; & cum eodem Jacobus de Vitriaco, Alensis Hist. Occid. cap. 37. paria facit. Ut & Aureolus, Cardinalis Contarenus, alii. Illi porrò, qui à Christo institutum hcc Chrismatis Sacramentum sciscunt, non aliam rationem afferre possunt, quàm quia sic Papa pronuntiet. Sic enim in Manipulo Curatorum Guidonis à monte Rocheni, Antuerpiæ A. MDLV. recusó, sed ducentis ante annis edito; Tract. iij. cap. 2. habetur: Materia Confirmationis est chrisma. In quo quidem chrismate sunt duo, oleum scilicet & balsamum. Et ratio, quare ista duo sunt in materia hujus Sacramenti, est institutio Christi, qui instituit, ista duo esse materiam hujus Sacramenti. Licet enim (NB) non inveniatur in Euangeliis, quòd Christus istud Sacramentum instituerit, tamen Beatus Petrus, qui fuit Vicarius Christi, pastor ac rector universalis Ecclesiæ, ita docuit, ita prædicavit, Christum instituisse. Et licet ista promulgatio non inveniatur in Canonicis, id est, in Epistolis Beati Petri, tamen Dominus Papa habet in decretis Romanæ Ecclesiæ, & potest haberi ex observantia primæva totius Ecclesiæ universalis à tempore Petri usque nunc: quæ quidem observantia præeminet authoritate quicunque, cùm universalis Ecclesia regatur à Spiritu S. & errare non possit. Bella profecto demonstrandi methodus! Christus chrisma instituit, quia sic S. Petrus ejus Vicarius testatur. S. Petrus id testatur, quia Papa id habet in decretis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, & potest haberi ex observantia primæva totius Ecclesiæ universalis, inde à tempore B. Petri. Veteres unctionem quandam adhibuisse in Baptismo, verum est; sed eam ceu à Christo institutam, vel ab Apostolis usurpatam, vel ut Sacramentum à Baptismo distinctum, à solo Episcopo signo crucis, chrismate exorcizato, formulâ verborum præscriptâ, cum promissis chrismati effectis illis supernaturalibus, administrandum, adhibuisse, non Petrus testatur, non Ecclesiæ universalis observantia loquitur, sed solus Papa ille, ἀνδρὶ ἐφα, sine ullis revelationis sibi factæ tabulis, pronuntiat. Ille solus vetus symbolum, sive admonitionis quoddam memoriale, in φαρμακὸν convertit. Nam φαρμακεία incantatio vera est, symbolis Divinitùs non institutis, peculiari ritu nusquam præscripto exorcizatis, accedentibus certis signis & verbis, vim & efficaciam ad producendos effectus supernaturales, ipsius etiam Baptismi effectibus quadantenus potiores, arrogare, quam nec à natura habet, nec à Deo supra naturam operante habere, demonstrari potest.
units.tr: Papa, with no prior divine institution of the sacrament, converts the chrism into whatever. Scotus indeed, in q.d. 7. q. 1. art. 2., teaches that the Apostles conferred this sacrament by the laying on of hands alone. Indeed Alexander of Hales, in his Summa of Theology written at the command of Innocent III and fortified by a diploma of Alexander IV, Part 4, q. 14, member 1, denies that this sacrament was instituted by Christ, and asserts that, as regards the form of words and the matter of the elements, it was instituted only at the Council of Meaux, being led to this by these arguments: because it is not read in Scripture when or where confirmation was instituted; and because neither Christ nor the Apostles used this matter or this form, but only the laying on of hands. Whence he concludes: Without prejudice it must be said that neither the Lord instituted this sacrament, nor dispensed it, nor did the Apostles. Bonaventura himself also follows this opinion of his teacher, and Jacobus de Vitriaco, in his Historia Occidentalis cap. 37, agrees with him. So too Aureolus, Cardinal Contarenus, and others. Those, moreover, who lay it down that this sacrament of the chrism was instituted by Christ cannot give any other reason than that the Pope so pronounces. For in the Manipulus Curatorum of Guido of Monte Rochen, printed at Antwerp in 1555 but published two hundred years earlier, Tract. iij. cap. 2., it is stated: The matter of Confirmation is the chrism. In this chrism there are two things, namely oil and balsam. And the reason why these two are in the matter of this sacrament is the institution of Christ, who instituted these two to be the matter of this sacrament. For although (NB) it is not found in the Gospels that Christ instituted this sacrament, nevertheless Blessed Peter, who was the Vicar of Christ, the universal pastor and ruler of the Church, so taught and so preached that Christ instituted it. And although this promulgation is not found in the canonical writings, that is, in the Epistles of Blessed Peter, nevertheless the Lord Pope has it in the decrees of the Roman Church, and it can be had from the primitive observance of the whole universal Church from the time of Peter until now; which observance certainly carries authority, since the universal Church is ruled by the Holy Spirit and cannot err. What a fine method of proof! Christ instituted the chrism, because St Peter his Vicar so testifies. St Peter so testifies, because the Pope has it in the decrees of the Roman Church, and it can be had from the primitive observance of the whole universal Church, from the time of Blessed Peter. That the ancients used some anointing in Baptism is true; but that they used it as instituted by Christ, or employed by the Apostles, or as a sacrament distinct from Baptism, to be administered only by the Bishop, with the sign of the cross, exorcised chrism, and a prescribed formula of words, with those supernatural effects promised to the chrism, is not attested by Peter, nor does the observance of the universal Church speak to it; but that one Pope alone pronounces it [ἀνδρὶ ἐφα], without any tablets of revelation made to him. He alone has turned an old symbol, or a certain memorial reminder, into a charm [φαρμακὸν]. For sorcery [φαρμακεία] is true incantation: the attributing to symbols not instituted by God, exorcised with a peculiar rite nowhere prescribed, and with certain signs and words added, a power and efficacy for producing supernatural effects, in some respects greater even than the effects of Baptism itself, which can be shown to belong neither to nature nor to a God who works above nature.

units.la: LXI. Haud dispar ratio est Olei infirmorum, quo Extremæ Unctionis Sacramentum administrari solet. Ubi à Sacerdote ægrotum inungente, verba illa proferuntur: Per istam sanctam unctionem, & suam piissimam misericordiam... am indulgeat tibi dominus, quicquid deliquisti per visum &c. Atque unctioni illi splendidissima quæcunque præmittuntur, Spiritus S. inprimis unctio interna & gratia, qua delicta, si quæ supersint, expientur, ægroti anima alleviatur & confirmetur, magnáque in unCto Divinæ misericordiæ fiducia excitetur, ad sublevandum infirmum, quò morbi incommoda ac labores leviùs ferat, & tentationibus dæmonis, calcaneo insidiantis, facilius resistat, & sanitatem corporis interdum, ubi saluti animæ expedierit, consequatur. Ita Tridentini Patres Seß. xiv. cap. 2. Tale Sacramentum à Christo institutum esse, Synodus jactat, non probat, nec probavit quisquam hactenus. Nam unctio tum illa, qua Christus usus legitur Marc. vi. 13. tum illa, quæ Jac. v. 14. præcipitur, miraculosa tota, ad morborum corporis curationem absolutè tota refertur. Illa autem, qua Hierarchici utuntur, & ordinaria est, administraturque ab iis, qui dono miraculorum nullo pollent; & ad diversos planè fines effectusque dirigitur. Utrumque in Concilii Tridentini Anatome & Funere solidè demonstravimus. Cùm ergò oleum, quo infirmes Hierarchici inungunt, vires, quas eidem illi tribuunt, non habeat vel à creatione, vel à Divina ordinatione, verbique ejus institutione; à φαρμακεία seu incantatione, adeóque Magia saltem implicita eas possideat necesse est. Taceo alia superstitionis manifestæ circa moribundos & mortuos genera; veluti frequentes aquæ lustralis aspersiones; crucis in pectus atque frontem descriptionem; imaginis Christi, Mariæ & Sanctuli cujuspiam repræsentationem & adorationem. Defuncti jam manui in pectore recumbenti crux imponitur, aut saltem manus loco crucis in crucis modum decussatim componitur; & aquâ benedicta ei ritè aspergitur, quæ scilicet vim eximiam ad Diabolum à cadavere abigendum habeat. Quæ singula, aliáque haud dissimilia sic comparata sunt, ut Sacrificuli suis incantationibus homines ad tumulum usque persequi videri possint.
units.tr: LXI. The reasoning is not unlike for the Oil of the sick, with which the Sacrament of Extreme Unction is usually administered. There the priest anointing the sick person pronounces these words: Through this holy unction and his most pious mercy... may the Lord forgive you whatever you have sinned by sight, etc. And to that anointing are prefixed the most splendid things whatever: above all, the inward anointing and grace of the Holy Spirit, by which sins, if any remain, are expiated, the soul of the sick person is relieved and strengthened, and a great confidence in the divine mercy is roused in the one anointed, to lift up the sick person, so that he may bear the discomforts and labours of the illness more lightly, and resist more easily the temptations of the demon who lies in wait at the heel, and obtain health of body at times, where it has been expedient for the health of the soul. Thus the Fathers of Trent, Sess. xiv. cap. 2. The Synod boasts that such a sacrament was instituted by Christ, but does not prove it, and no one has proved it up to now. For that anointing which Christ is read to have used (Mark 6:13), and that which is commanded in James 5:14, were wholly miraculous and referred absolutely entirely to the healing of bodily diseases. But the anointing which the hierarchs use is ordinary, and is administered by men who possess no gift of miracles, and is directed to quite different ends and effects. We have solidly demonstrated both in our Anatome and in our Funus of the Council of Trent. Since therefore the oil with which the hierarchs anoint the sick does not have the powers they ascribe to it, either from creation or from divine ordinance and the institution of his word, it necessarily possesses them from sorcery or incantation [φαρμακεία], and so at least from implicit magic. I pass over other kinds of manifest superstition about the dying and the dead: such as the frequent sprinklings of lustral water, the tracing of the cross on the breast and forehead, the representation and adoration of the image of Christ, of Mary and of some saint. A cross is placed on the hand of the dead man lying on his breast, or at least the hands are laid crosswise in the manner of a cross instead of the cross; and holy water is duly sprinkled on him, which of course is supposed to have an excellent power for driving the devil away from the corpse. These particulars, and others not very unlike them, are so arranged that the little priests may seem to pursue men with their incantations even to the tomb.

units.la: LXII. Amuletorum, quæ verborum, characterum, figurarum certarum conformatione constant, & efficaciam suam ex verbis, figuris, fide, imaginatione mutuantur, usus Magicus haud dubiè est.
units.tr: LXII. Amulets, which consist of words, letters and certain figures arranged in a fixed form, and which borrow their efficacy from the words, figures, faith and imagination, are undoubtedly a magical practice.

units.la: Hanc tamen superstitionem per amuleta de collo suspensa mira præstandi, Pontificiis Pontificius ipse, Remigius Lotharingus, lib. de ligaturis impingere non dubitavit, & impegit merito. Quid enim apud eos reliquiarum, cerearum Agni Dei effigierum, crucium, dictorum quorundam S. Scripturæ, Evangelii inprimis S. Johannis, Psalmorum Davidis, chartis vel pergamenis inscriptorum usitatius est? Cùmque reliquiarum gestationem etiam Ciruelus Darocensis, quem ipse Delrio lib. 1. cap. 4. q. 4. elogio insignis Doctoris Theologi exornat, improbàsset, parùm cautè eum locutum esse, Delrio loc. cit. queritur, ubi etiam conclusionem hanc ponit: Quando in ipsis verbis, modo scriptionis, crucium numero, figura, vel similibus spes non ponitur, pium & sanctum est, reverentiæ causa Sanctorum reliquias, cereas Agni Dei effigies, Evangelium S. Johannis, Psalmum Davidis, & similia S. Scripturæ testimonia secum gestare collo appensa. Sic ergò piè sanctèque fecerint, quotquot amuletis ejusmodi de collo suspensis sibi faustissima quæque promiserint, dummodo spem suam non in ligaturis, sed in Deo collocaverint. Quo fuco omnis simplicium & credulorum Magia implicita tegi, & pietatis etiam sanctitatisque speciem induere potest. Quòd si fragmenta ejusmodi Scripturæ de collo suspensa vim ejusmodi habent mira, fiduciâ modò in Deo collocatâ, efficiendi, quid non S. Scripturæ codex integer circumgestatus efficiet? Atqui non Scripturæ Syllabæ collo appensæ, sed syllabarum sensus cordi inscriptus, & per Spiritum S. implantatus, verâque ràque fide receptus, procurandæ æternæ salutis, non mirabilium ejusmodi efficiendorum promissionem habet. Quo argumento S. Chrysostomus homil. 43. in Matth. 23· stultidos mystas, verbi Divini lacinias quasdam collo alligantes, graviter pulsat.
units.tr: Yet the Papist himself, Remigius of Lorraine, did not hesitate to charge the Papists with this superstition of working wonders through amulets hung round the neck, in his book on ligatures, and he charged them rightly. For what is more common among them than relics, wax images of the Lamb of God, crosses, and certain sayings of Holy Scripture, especially the Gospel of St John and the Psalms of David, written on paper or parchment? When Ciruelo of Daroca rejected the carrying of relics, Delrio, who himself adorns him with the praise of a distinguished Doctor of Theology in book 1, chapter 4, question 4, complains in loc. cit. that he had spoken rather carelessly. In the same place Delrio sets forth this conclusion: When no hope is placed in the words themselves, in the manner of writing, in the number of crosses, in the figure or in similar things, it is a pious and holy thing, out of reverence, to carry around the neck the relics of the saints, wax images of the Lamb of God, the Gospel of St John, the Psalm of David and similar testimonies of Holy Scripture. So those who hang such amulets round their necks and promise themselves every blessing from them act piously and holily, provided they place their hope not in the ligatures but in God. Under this cover all the magic of simple and credulous people can be concealed, and can even take on the appearance of piety and holiness. But if fragments of Scripture hung round the neck have such wonderful power, provided only that trust is placed in God, what will not a whole codex of Scripture carried about achieve? Yet the syllables of Scripture hung on the neck do not promise the procuring of eternal salvation; that comes from the sense of the syllables inscribed on the heart, implanted by the Holy Spirit and received with true faith, not from any promise of such wonders. With this argument Chrysostom, in Homily 43 on Matthew 23, sharply attacks the foolish mystics who tie scraps of the divine Word round their necks.

units.la: LXIII. Quid judicaret nunc Chrysostomus, si modernos mystas, Catholico supercilio turgentes, amuleta ejusmodi commendantes, & singularem iis virtutem tribuentes cerneret? Quid si amuleta gestantes videret v. g. contra morbum comitialem, quibus talis verborum formula insculpta reperitur: Sancte Johannes Baptista, Sancte Johannes Evangelista, Sancte Johannes Chrysostome, juva seu subleva hunc miserum brevi momento, quæ ipsa quoque verba, morbo eo correptis, in aures insusurrari solent.
units.tr: LXIII. What would Chrysostom judge now, if he saw modern mystics, swelling with Catholic pride, commending amulets of this kind and attributing a singular power to them? What if he saw people wearing amulets against epilepsy, for example, on which this formula of words is engraved: Holy John the Baptist, holy John the Evangelist, holy John Chrysostom, help or raise up this wretched man in a moment, words which are usually whispered into the ears of those seized by that disease?

units.la: Amuleta contra maniam, morbos oculorum, pestem, arma, plagas & quæcunque mala, in Papatu frequentissima, recensere heic nihil attinet. Unum memorare ex innumeris libet. Marchinus Tract. de Peste Probl. 33. horrendum amuletum contra pestem, constans characteribus annulo inclusis, A. MDCXXX. per Italiam universam vulgatum, ab omnibus ferè Christi fidelibus, nec non à viris, inquit ille, religiosis, Monialibus ac Prælatis velut salutare antidotum cœlitùs revelatum, applicatum (sinistro scilicet brachio) & à sapientissimis Theologis approbatum, prodit. Constat 25. characteribus, qui per cabalam dictam Notaricon integram sententiam, aut plures conjunctas designant. Additur præcatiuncula ad Christum, & verba Zachariæ (sic habet amuletum) quæ sic incipiunt: Maledicti, Excommunicati, blasphemi dæmones in virtute verborum istorum, Messias, Emmanuel, Sabaoth, Athanajos, Hyschisos, Eleyson, Tetragrammaton, vos constringimus, vos privamus, vos expellimus, ex ista civitate, & ex hominibus ejus, & præcipimus vobis, ut non audeatis per pestem nocere corporibus habitantium in ea. Ite, ite maledicti in stagnum ignis. Idem Marchinus pag. 47. memorat & commendat novum Exorcismum A. MDCXXX. à Cardinale & Archiepiscopo Mediolanensi Friderico Borromæo inventum, qui sic sonat: J. N. †. R. J. Qui verbum caro factum est, &c. conterat omnem potestatem inimicorum nostrorum visibilium & invisibilium: Ille ab hac domo & habitantibus in ea expellat omnem Diaboli nequitiam &c. ipsamque purificet, benedicat & sanctificet. Ecce crucem † Christi. Fugite partes adversæ. Vicit leo de tribu Juda, radix David. Hagios † Otheos † Hagios † Ischyrios † Hagios Athanatos † Eleyson Hymos † Kyrie Eleyson, Christe Eleyson, Kyrie Eleyson. Conjuro, exorcizo vos Spiritus malignos per Patrem, Filium &c. Invitus equidem ἐξ ἐτέρα hæc repeto, nec repetenda putarem, nisi Babylonis pudenda detegenda femel suscepissem.
units.tr: There is no point in listing here the amulets against madness, eye diseases, plague, weapons, wounds and all evils, which are very common in Papacy. I will mention one out of countless. Marchinus, in his Treatise on the Plague, Problem 33, makes known a horrible amulet against the plague, consisting of characters enclosed in a ring, which was spread throughout the whole of Italy in the year 1630. He says it was applied by almost all the faithful of Christ, and also by men who are, he says, religious, by nuns and prelates, as a salutary antidote revealed from heaven (on the left arm, of course), and approved by the most learned Theologians. It consists of 25 characters, which by the so-called cabala of Notaricon designate a whole sentence or several sentences joined together. A short prayer to Christ is added, and the words of Zechariah (so the amulet has it), which begin thus: Cursed, excommunicated, blaspheming demons, in the power of these words, Messiah, Emmanuel, Sabaoth, Athanajos, Hyschisos, Eleyson, Tetragrammaton, we bind you, we deprive you, we expel you from this city and from its people, and we command you that you not dare to harm the bodies of those who dwell in it by plague. Go, go, cursed ones, into the lake of fire. The same Marchinus, p. 47, mentions and commends a new exorcism, devised in the year 1630 by Cardinal and Archbishop of Milan Frederick Borromeo, which runs thus: J. N. † R. J. He who was made flesh from the Word, etc., crush all the power of our enemies, visible and invisible. Let him drive out of this house and its inhabitants all the wickedness of the Devil, etc., and let him purify, bless and sanctify it. Behold the cross † of Christ. Flee, adverse powers. The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered. Hagios † Otheos † Hagios † Ischyrios † Hagios Athanatos † Eleyson Hymos † Kyrie Eleyson, Christe Eleyson, Kyrie Eleyson. I conjure and exorcise you, unclean spirits, by the Father, the Son, etc. I repeat these things reluctantly, from elsewhere [ἐξ ἐτέρας], and I would not have thought them worth repeating, had I not undertaken once to uncover the shameful things of Babylon.

units.la: LXIV. Provocat Delrio, amuleta defensurus, loc. cit.
units.tr: LXIV. Delrio appeals, in defending amulets, to loc. cit.

units.la: ad Ecclesiæ Catholicæ inveteratum & salutarem morem, nec non sententiam D. Thomæ, Navarri, Sylvestri, Malldonati & aliorum. Qui vero alii illi sunt? Certè non Christus, non Apostoli, non Sancti ex cana & veneranda antiquitate Patres, uti vel solius Chrysostomi laudatum suprà testimonium luculentum comprobat. Inveteratus ille, sed parùm salutaris mos effœminato Seculo Undecimo cunabula sua debet; de quo sic inter alia Fasciculus Temporum Venetiis A. MCCCCLXXX. editus, loquitur: Tempus effœminatum incepit circa annos Domini mille: in quo fides Christiana valdè cœpit deficere & declinare à pristina virilitate, uti patet ex Prophetia S. Hildegardis, & in multis regionibus Christianitatis nec Sacramenta, nec Ecclesiastici ritus servabantur. Auguriis & maleficiis intendebant. Sed de origine consuetudinis illius quicquid fiat, amuleta Pontificia quæcunque, cereæ inprimis imagines Agni Dei, Magiam manifestè sapiunt, tum quia certo verborum & crucium numero eorum benedictio peragitur, à quo discedere religio iis est: tum quia eorum usus omnis contra naturæ ac Divinæ institutionis ordinem, ad usum tum naturalem curandi morbos, & ab iisdem præservandi, aliáque mala averruncandi; tum supernaturalem & spiritualem, dæmonum videlicet depulsionem & salutem æternam refertur.
units.tr: to the ancient and salutary custom of the Catholic Church, and also the opinion of St Thomas, Navarrus, Silvester, Medina and others. But who, then, are these others? Certainly not Christ, not the Apostles, not the Fathers of the hoary and venerable antiquity; the clear testimony of Chrysostom alone, cited above, proves this. That ancient but hardly salutary custom owes its cradle to the effeminate eleventh century. Of this the Fasciculus Temporum, published at Venice in 1480, speaks among other things as follows: The effeminate age began about the year of the Lord one thousand, in which the Christian faith began greatly to fail and to decline from its former manliness, as is clear from the prophecy of St Hildegard; and in many regions of Christendom neither the sacraments nor the ecclesiastical rites were observed. They gave themselves to augury and sorcery. But whatever the origin of that custom, all the Papist amulets, above all the wax images of the Lamb of God, plainly smack of magic, both because their blessing is performed by a fixed number of words and crosses, from which they think it impious to depart, and because all their use is referred, contrary to the order of nature and of divine institution, both to the natural use of curing diseases and guarding against them and warding off other evils, and to the supernatural and spiritual use, namely the driving out of demons and eternal salvation.

units.la: LXV. Quantum Hierarchici verbis certis, notis & ignotis seu barbaris, sacris & profanis, in preculis etiam suis incognitâ haud raro linguâ fusis, tribuant, satis ex iis, quæ de exorcismis & benedictionibus eorum, supra diximus, constat. Et precularum quidem ejusmodi ac medicamentorum etiam per verba certa strenuum olim hyperaspisten se gessit is, quem supra citavimus, Felix Malleolus, scripto de exorcismis libro, ubi varias curandi morbos hominum & animalium formulas præivit, cumulatis etiam argumentis pluribus, quibus fas piúmque esse, formulis ejusmodi uti, acriter contendit. Cum iis sic Delrio confligit, ut verba & preculas eas demum rejiciat, quæ ab Ecclesia approbatæ non sunt. Vana, sic etiam lib. vj. Anaceph. Monit. 5. scribit, est prolatio verborum, quæ non est ex usu Ecclesiæ Catholicæ recepta. Quam exceptionem, quæ Hierarchicorum hoc in argumento Achilles est, non semel jam diluimus. Fidem modò faciant Hierarchici, Episcopo cuiquam, vel Papæ, vel Concilio à Papa probato, Divinitùs concessam esse facultatem approbandi, adhibendíque certam verborum, quæ à Deo profecta, & in destinatum ab iis usum instituta esse, ratione solida nulla demonstrari potest, formulam, qua pronuntiata vera fide miracula, & opera maxima tum corporalia, tum spiritualia expectari possint; adeóque ex peccato non peccatum ; superstitione & magia religionem ac pietatem efficiendi.
units.tr: LXV. How much the Hierarchy attributes to certain words, known and unknown, or barbarous, sacred and profane, even in their prayers, which are often poured out in a language nobody understands, is clear enough from what we have said above about their exorcisms and blessings. Felix Malleolus, whom we cited above, was a vigorous champion of such prayers and of such remedies by fixed words; in his book on exorcisms he set out various formulas for curing the diseases of men and animals, and he vigorously contended, with many additional arguments, that it is right and pious to use such formulas. Delrio contends with them in such a way that he finally rejects only those words and prayers which have not been approved by the Church. The utterance of words is vain, he writes in book 6 of the Anacephalaeosis, Monitor 5, if it is not received in the practice of the Catholic Church. We have already more than once refuted this exception, which is the Achilles of the Hierarchy in this matter. Let the Hierarchy first prove that some bishop, or the Pope, or a council approved by the Pope, has been granted by God the power of approving and using a fixed form of words, which can be shown by solid reasoning to have come from God and to have been instituted by them for the use they intend, a formula by whose utterance, with true faith, miracles and very great works, both bodily and spiritual, may be expected. Otherwise, from sin they make no sin, and by superstition and magic they make religion and piety.

units.la: LXVI. Ut hanc Hierarchicorum in approbandis formulis verè Magicis audaciam & impietatem amplius apricemur, lubet vel unicam Orationem, quæ ex certis verbis, eorúmque complexione pondus & efficaciam habet, ab Ecclesia Catholica approbatam scilicet, & cùm ab aliis, tum à Capucinis maximè, in quorum manibus illa hæret, usurpari ad recuperandas res perditas, aliáque mira patranda, solitam, ex tenebris suis, quibus certè infernalibus dignissima est, in lucem proferre. Est hæc Oratio sive Responsorium Bonaventuræ ad Antonium de Padua, cujus copiam nonnemo, qui superstitioni addictus adhuc παρρησία eadem patraverat, non ita pridem fecit. Sic autem Oratio sonat: Si quæris miracula, mors, error, calamitas, Dæmon, lepra fugiunt, ægri surgunt sani: Cedunt mare, vincula, membra, résque perditas Petunt & accipiunt juvenes & cani. Pereunt pericula, cessat & necessitas: narrent Hi, qui sentiunt, dicant Paduani. Cedunt mare, vincula membra, résque perditas Petunt, & accipiunt juvenes & cani. Gloria Patri, & Filio, & Spiritui Sancto, Cedunt mare, vincula, membra, résque perditas Petunt, & accipiunt juvenes & cani. Ora pro nobis, Beate Antoni, Ut digni efficiamur promissionibus Christi. Oremus:
units.tr: LXVI. To lay open more fully this truly magical audacity and impiety of the Hierarchy in approving formulas, let us bring into the light, out of its darkness, which is certainly most worthy of hell, a single prayer which has weight and efficacy from fixed words and their combination, approved by the Catholic Church, and used not only by others but chiefly by the Capuchins, in whose hands it sticks, for recovering lost things and performing other wonders. It is the Prayer or Responsory of Bonaventure to Anthony of Padua, a copy of which someone who, being addicted to superstition, had carried out the same things with boldness [παρρησία], did not long ago publish. The prayer runs thus: If you seek miracles: death, error, calamity, the Demon, leprosy flee; the sick rise up healthy. The sea yields, chains and limbs yield, and lost things are sought and received by the young and the old. Dangers perish, necessity ceases; let those who feel it tell, let the Paduans say. The sea yields, chains and limbs yield, and lost things are sought and received by the young and the old. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. The sea yields, chains and limbs yield, and lost things are sought and received by the young and the old. Pray for us, blessed Anthony, that we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Let us pray:

units.la: Ecclesiam tuam, Deus, Beati Antonii Confessoris tui deprecatio votiva lætificet, ut spiritualibus semper muniatur auxiliis, & gaudiis perfrui mereatur æternis, per Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen. Deinde dicuntur expansis pansis manibus quinque Pater noster & Ave Maria. In eundem finem aliquando etiam leguntur missæ votivæ de Antonio de Padua. Quam causam dicent, quin carmen isthoc & similia, certa verborum formula, certo eorundem numero illigata, & mirifica quædam, humanisque viribus majora, quæ nec verborum illorum natura, nec per verba talia Deus uspiam promisit, promittentia, & subinde etiam præstantia, pro verissimis incantationibus jure meritoque habeantur.
units.tr: May your Church, O God, be gladdened by the votive prayer of your confessor Blessed Anthony, so that it may always be protected by spiritual aids and be deemed worthy to enjoy eternal joys, through Christ our Lord, Amen. Then five Our Fathers and Hail Marys are said with the hands spread out. To the same end, votive Masses of Anthony of Padua are sometimes also read. What reason will they give why this verse and similar things, bound together by a fixed form of words and a fixed number of the same, and certain marvellous powers beyond human strength, which neither the nature of those words nor God anywhere promised through such words, yet which promise and even afterwards perform, should not rightly and deservedly be held to be most true incantations?

units.la: LXVII. Numerorum virtutem & efficaciam per se nullam esse; & si qua iis accidit, ex pacto expresso, vel tacito cum dæmone accidere, Differt. de Characteribus Magiæ, probavimus. Certos autem numeros Hierarchici in Missa, Exorcismis, Benedictionibus, preculis suis exigunt, & sine iis efficaciam & virtutem Missæ, Exorcismorum, benedictionum, precularum constare negant. Atque efficaciam illam numerorum spisso volumine de mysteriis numerorum asserere conatus est Bongus, pallians Magiam eo argumento, quòd numeris utantur mysticis & sacris. Quasi vel ulli numeri sic per se mystici & sacri sint, ut propter mysterium ejusmodi singulari virtute polleant: vel similia numerorum mysteria & sanctimoniam non ipsi etiam circulatores, Magi, Cabalistæ impietati suæ prætexant. Quando ergo eos Hierarchici refellere tentant, quo colore suam causam à Magorum causa discernent? Añon jure Magi reponent;
units.tr: LXVII. We have shown in the Dissertation on the Characters of Magic that the power and efficacy of numbers are in themselves nothing, and that if any efficacy befalls them, it happens through an express or tacit pact with the devil. The Hierarchics, however, demand certain numbers in their Mass, exorcisms, blessings and prayers, and deny that the efficacy and power of the Mass, of exorcisms, of blessings and of prayers can stand without them. Bongus, in his thick volume On the Mysteries of Numbers, has tried to assert that efficacy of numbers, cloaking magic with the argument that they use mystical and sacred numbers. As if any numbers are so mystical and sacred in themselves that they are powerful with a singular virtue on account of such a mystery; or as if the same mysteries and sanctity of numbers were not pleaded by the very charlatans, magicians and Cabalists in defence of their impiety. When, therefore, the Hierarchics try to refute them, by what colour will they distinguish their cause from the cause of the magicians? Will not the magicians rightly reply?
The tale is told of you, with only the name changed?

units.la: Quo denique argumento à superstitione liberabunt observationem definiti & certi numeri dierum in peregrinationibus; ut videlicet tribus diebus Sabbathi visitetur hic vel ille locus; bibatur ex calice consecrato aqua, ab Augustino Wichmans in Sabbatho Mariano defensam? Quid mysterii vel efficaciæ habet numerus Novenarius, qui apud plures usu obtinere nunc incipit? quod vel sola Novena Antonii de Padua, à Celeb. Conringio solidè discussa, docet.
units.tr: Finally, by what argument will they free from superstition the observance of a fixed and certain number of days in pilgrimages, namely that this or that place should be visited on three Sabbath days, or that holy water be drunk from a consecrated chalice, a practice defended by Augustine Wichmans in his Marian Sabbath? What mystery or efficacy does the number nine have, which is now beginning to obtain in use among many? This alone, the Novena of Anthony of Padua, solidly discussed by the celebrated Conring, teaches.

units.la: LXVIII. Idem de figuris & characteribus, quibus efficaciam tribuentes Cajetanum, Thomam, Gaffarellum supra thesivÿ. vidimus; judicium est: eadem praetextus vanitas, quòd non aliis, quàm sacris figuris & characteribus utantur. Et Teletus quidem instruct. Sacerd. lib. iv. 14. aperte omnes figuras, excepta cruce, adhibitas, superstitionem & magiam implicare, pronuntiat; atque sic Papatum universum ἀλλαχῶς ἀχ ... in superstitionis & magiæ lutum praecipitat. Nam Graecum ⍤ & characteres Alphabethi Graeci, quo in consecrationibus suis Hierarchici utuntur, non sunt utique figura crucis. Sed & crucis immissæ figura non magis sacra & mystica est, quàm crucis commissæ, aut cujuscunque alterius figurae, veluti circuli, trianguli, pentaculi, hexagoni. Denique etiam Magiæ crimine apud Hierarchicos infames Trithemius, Cornelius Agrippa, Petrus de Albano, alii in suis incantamentis, conjurationibus & operationibus Magicis crucem adhibere consueverunt. Neque profectò in usu verborum, numerorum, characterum, amuletorum ulla essentialis differentia praedictos inter Magos & Hierarchicos constitui poterit, nisi pertendere hi velint, sua omnia habere Divinum mandatum & promissionem, atque sibi nudè id asserentibus, nulla certè idonea ratione probantibus simpliciter & bona fide credendum; illis contra Magiæ authoribus de suis Theurgicis eadem jactantibus, & contra Magiam omnem pactámque cum Diabolo vehementer protestantibus fidem prorsùs negandam esse, hoc est, duos cùm faciunt idem, non esse idem.
units.tr: LXVIII. The same judgement applies to figures and characters, to which we have seen above, in the thesis, that Cajetan, Thomas and Gaffarel attribute efficacy: the same pretext of vanity is at work, because they use no figures and characters other than sacred ones. Teletus, in Instruction of Priests, book 4, chapter 14, plainly declares that all figures, except the cross, when employed, involve superstition and magic; and so he hurls the whole Papacy [ἀλλαχῶς ἀχ ...; "in other ways ..."] into the mire of superstition and magic. For the Greek [symbol] and the characters of the Greek alphabet, which the Hierarchics use in their consecrations, are certainly not the figure of a cross. But the figure of a cross placed upright is no more sacred and mystical than a cross placed crosswise, or any other figure, such as a circle, a triangle, a pentacle or a hexagon. Finally, Trithemius, Cornelius Agrippa and Peter of Albano, who are notorious among the Hierarchics for the crime of magic, and others, have customarily used the cross in their incantations, conjurations and magical operations. Indeed, no essential difference in the use of words, numbers, characters and amulets can be set up between the aforesaid magicians and the Hierarchics, unless these men wish to maintain that all their own things have a divine command and promise, and that what they assert without any sound reason is to be believed simply and in good faith; while the authors of magic, boasting of the same things about their theurgies and vehemently protesting against all magic and any pact with the devil, are to be denied all trust. That is, when they do the same things, they say that two are not the same.

units.la: LXIX. Ubi enim, sodes, ut pleraque illa constringam, Scriptura, ubi Patrum consensus, ubi Conciliorum decisiones infinitum illud discrimen statuunt inter benedictiones dictiones fumigiorum, & exorcismum ignis, cui superponuntur fumigia, ceremonias, res, verba sacra, preces, litanias eò pertinentes ad arcendum Diabolum, & omnia phantasmata, ac nocumenta ejus; item ad constringendum Diabolum,ut hoc vel illud faciat aut dicat,juxta tenorem Magiæ apud CorneliumAgrippam lib.de occulta Philosoph. sect. de ceremoniis Mag. & Petrum de Albano lib. de Elementis Magicis: & inter adjurationes dæmonum, benedictiones fumigiorum, exorcismos ignis, incensationes per eosdem, aut similes ceremonias, preces, litanias, ad eosdem effectus, ex præscripto Ritualium & librorum Exorcisticorum? Ubi eadem discrimen statuunt inter amuleta sacra in Papatu usitata & probata, thus, Psalmos, panem & sal benedictum, ramos palmarum, pulsus campanæ, initium Euangelii S. Johannis &c- quæ Delrio lib. 1. cap. 4. & iij.p. 2. q. 4.. & lib vj. 2. defendit: & inter signa ac pentacula Cornelii Agrippæ; nec non inter figuras & situs insufflatione in aquam observandos, item characteres ignotos Græcos in dedicatione Templi scribendos; & inter certas figuras, situum, positionumque differentias ac modos, item peregrinos characteres Magorum, quæ omnia uno ore Summistæ & Theologi eorum, exceptâ figurâ crucis, condemnant? Non ovum ovo similius est; & chimærica sunt, quæcunque ad separandas causas obduci solent, discrimina. In ipso Concilio Tridentino non defuisse, qui abusum Scripturæ in incantationibus tollendum censerent, repugnantibus aliis, & usum formularum receptarum pium, licitum, religiosum esse, contendentibus, S. Polanus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. y. fusius commemorat.
units.tr: LXIX. For where, I pray, to bind up most of those points, do Scripture, the consensus of the Fathers, or the decisions of Councils set up that infinite distinction between blessings of fumigations and the exorcism of fire over which the fumigations are placed; between the ceremonies, things, sacred words, prayers and litanies directed to ward off the devil and all his phantasms and harms; likewise to bind the devil so that he does or says this or that, according to the tenor of magic in Cornelius Agrippa, book On Occult Philosophy, section on the ceremonies of magic, and Peter of Albano, book On Magical Elements; and between the adjurations of demons, blessings of fumigations, exorcisms of fire, incensings by the same, or similar ceremonies, prayers and litanies to the same effects, according to the prescription of the Rituals and the exorcistic books? Where do they set up the same distinction between the sacred amulets used and approved in Papacy, incense, Psalms, blessed bread and salt, palm branches, the ringing of bells, the opening of the Gospel of St John, etc., which Delrio defends in book 1, chapter 4, and part 3, question 4, and book 6, 2; and between the signs and pentacles of Cornelius Agrippa; nor between the figures and postures to be observed in breathing upon water, likewise the unknown Greek characters to be written at the dedication of a temple; and between certain differences and modes of figures, postures and positions, likewise the foreign characters of the magicians, all of which their Summists and Theologians, with one voice, condemn, except the figure of the cross? One egg is not more like another; and all the distinctions that are usually brought forward to separate the causes are chimerical. That among the Council of Trent itself there were not lacking those who judged that the abuse of Scripture in incantations ought to be removed, while others objected and contended that the use of the received formulas was pious, lawful and religious, Polanus recounts at greater length in his History of the Council of Trent, book 5.

units.la: LXX. Fortuitis significationem affingere, inter Magiæ characteres de charact. Mag. ß. LXXXIX. retulimus merito.
units.tr: LXX. We have rightly counted the attribution of significance to chance events among the characters of magic (De charact. Mag. §89).

units.la: Si quam enim ominandi vim insitam illa habent, vel naturalis illa, vel supernaturalis Divina, vel Magica erit. Naturalem nullam inesse, ominatores ipsi fatentur, qui à casu talia dependere, & rationem inclusam effectus habere nullam agnoscunt. At nec supernaturalis illa est, cùm nec à providentia Dei ordinaria illa proficiscatur, & extraordinariæ in iis vestigium nullum appareat. Magica ergò & superstitiosa omnis est. Et tamen Cajetanus Cardinalis fortuitis & ominationibus favet. Sic enim ille in Summ. v. superstitio scribit: Potest homo absque omni præsagio cavere prudentes ab imminentibus, dubitando, ne præsens accursus sit signum futuri ex communi utriusque causa cœlesti, vel etiam Divina providentia; ut si quis cadens corporaliter timeat aliquem casum in statu, vel honore &c. Propterea tamen non desistat operibus prudenter agendis, sed cautiùs vigilet. Potest enim esse, ut iste casus sit effectus causæ futuri casus, & propterea significet illum. De qua sententia meriròé verba illa Ciceronis de Divinat, usurpem: Nonne hoc si suscipimus, & pedis offensio nobis, & abruptio corrigiæ, & sternutamenta observanda erunt. Sanè hoc ipsum gentiles καλοῦντες contendebant, quamvis scilicet pedum offensionem Divinam iram portendere, & casum quemvis effectum esse causæ futuri casus, fierique posse, ut illum significet. Quis verò casibus fortuitis ejusmodi significationem indidit?
units.tr: For if these omens have any inherent power, it must be natural, supernatural divine, or magical. Omen-takers themselves admit there is no natural power in them, since they hold that such things depend on chance and have no intrinsic cause of the effect. Nor is it supernatural, since it does not come from God's ordinary providence, and no trace of extraordinary action appears in them. So all of it is magical and superstitious. Yet Cardinal Cajetan favours chance events and omens. In his in Summa, s.v. superstitio he writes: A man may, without any omen, guard against prudent dangers by doubting whether a present mishap is a sign of a future one, from the common cause of both in heaven or even in divine providence; for example, if someone who has fallen physically fears some misfortune in his state or honour. Yet he should not therefore give up doing what must be done prudently, but should watch more carefully. For it may be that this mishap is the effect of a cause of a future misfortune, and so signifies it. On this opinion I may fairly borrow the words of Cicero, De divinatione: If we admit this, then a stumble of the foot, a broken shoelace and sneezes will also have to be observed. Indeed the Gentiles, calling [καλοῦντες], argued exactly this, namely that a stumble of the foot foretold divine wrath, and that any mishap is the effect of the cause of a future mishap and can signify it. But who gave such a signifying power to chance mishaps?

units.la: LXXI. Quid quòd Magiam per remedia illicita depellere Hierarchici conantur? Ita enim Delrio lib. vj. 3. remedia quædam adversus Magiam Ecclesiastica, morbo ipso laborantia, hoc est, Magica impietate tincta ipsa, adversus Godelmannum tuetur acriter. Bufæus quoque in Panario, seu Arte medica, variis animi morbis opposita, remedia adversus veneficia colligens, inter alia numerat Missæ incruentum sacrificium, oleum infirmorum per Episcopum benedictum, Exorcismum Ecclesiasticum, Aquam benedictam tum baptismalem, tum lustralem; Agnos
units.tr: LXXI. What of the fact that the hierarchs try to drive out magic by unlawful remedies? Thus Delrio, in book vj. 3, stoutly defends certain ecclesiastical remedies against magic, which are themselves infected with the disease, that is, tainted by magical impiety, against Godelmann. Bufaeus too, in his Panarium, or medical art, which collects remedies against various diseases of the mind, lists among remedies against poisonings: the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass, oil for the sick blessed by the bishop, ecclesiastical exorcism, holy water both baptismal and lustral, the Lambs

units.la: magica depellere conantur gnos Dei solenni ritu certis temporibus à Summo Pontifice benedictos; Reliquias Sanctorum; Amuleta sacra collo appensa, veluti Symbolum Apostolicum, initium Euangelii Johannis, Psalmi alicujus particulam, Effigies cereas Agni Dei, campanarum benedictarum pulsum; Maleficiis illatam vim, ut signa maleficii, ipsúmque maleficium tollant. Quod postremum remedium, destructionem scilicet signorum maleficii per maleficos ipsos id facere compulsos, olim quidem, fatente Delrione, à Johanne Hessel de Lovanio, Wilhelmo Eftio &c. improbatum merito, hodie in Papatu communiter receptum est, & ab eodem Delrione, necnon Raphaële de la Torre, Binsfelsio, ac inprimis Maldero, non Christi, vel Apostolorum, sed Scoti, qui lib. iv. dist. 34. asserit, superstitiosum esse, si quis dicat, non esse maleficium superstitione depellendum, authoritate defendit. Diaboli sane opera haud unquam Diabolum ejici, Christus ipse Matth. xii. 26. 27. profitetur. Illi tamen ejiciunt, daemonem compellentes, ut maleficia solvat; & quandoque etiam daemonem potentiorem congentes exorcismis suis, ut impotentiores expellat.
units.tr: of God, blessed with solemn rite at certain times by the Supreme Pontiff; relics of the saints; sacred amulets hung round the neck, such as the Apostles' Creed, the opening of John's Gospel, a fragment of some psalm, wax images of the Lamb of God, the ringing of blessed bells; force done by sorcery, so that they remove the signs of sorcery and sorcery itself. This last remedy, namely the destruction of the signs of sorcery by the sorcerers themselves compelled to do it, was once rightly disapproved by Johannes Hessel of Louvain, Wilhelm Estius and others, as Delrio admits; today it is commonly accepted in Papacy, and it is defended by Delrio himself, as well as by Raphael de la Torre, Binsfeld, and above all Maldero, on the authority not of Christ or the Apostles but of Scotus, who in book iv, dist. 34 asserts that it is superstitious to say that sorcery must not be driven out by superstition. Yet Christ himself, in Matt. 12:26-27, declares that Satan's works never drive out Satan. Still they drive him out, compelling the devil to undo the sorcery; and sometimes, by their exorcisms, they summon a more powerful demon to expel a weaker one.
LXXII.

units.la: Olim quidem Galba, exprobrante apud Tacitum Hist. j. 37: 5. Othone, remedia vocabat, quae alii scelera. Ita Bufaeo, Delrioni, Romanis remedia adversus maleficia audiunt, quae ab iisdem usurpata scelera potius, ac ipse Magiae morbus appellanda fuerant. Id vero de singulis jam probatum, de universis uno efficacissimo argumento demonstramus, quod videlicet per remedia ejusmodi verbis, characteribus, ritibus, rebus, quae in singulis iis praescribuntur, vis & operatio talis adscribabatur, qualem nec à natura, per sanam rationem, nec à Deo & institutione ac promissione qualicunque Divina, per revelationem omni exceptione majorem, habere cognoscuntur, qui generalis Magiae character est.
units.tr: Once Galba, when Otho reproached him in Tacitus (Hist. j. 37: 5.), called remedies what others call crimes. So the remedies against sorcery that Bufaeus, Delrio and the Romanists speak of ought rather to be called the crimes that they themselves commit, and the very disease of magic. This we have already proved for individual cases; for all of them we demonstrate by one very strong argument: namely that by such remedies a power and operation are attributed to words, characters, rites and things prescribed in each of them, of a kind which we know neither nature (by sound reason) nor God (by any divine institution and promise, revealed beyond all exception) has given them. That is the general character of magic.

units.la: remedia vo-canari, quae scelera & morbus ipse sunt.
units.tr: ... to be called remedies, which are crimes and the disease itself.

units.la: LXXIII. Accedit his omnibus grave profectò illud, quod Hierarchici Magos notorios & professos, & scripta Magica notoria in sinu suo fovent. Cujus rei nunc fidem paucis faciamus. Quo tempore primùm auguria, maleficia, incantationes in Ecclesiam irrepserint, jam suprà ex Authore Fasciculi temporum conjectavimus; Seculo scilicet Undecimo effœminato illo. Præfuit illis temporibus Sedi Romanæ Sylvester II. Magus haud incelebris, quod Scriptorum Pontificiorum authoritate mihi confirmandum est.
units.tr: LXXIII. To all this is added something truly grave: the hierarchs harbour in their bosom notorious and professed magicians and notorious magical writings. Let us now make this clear in a few words. At what time augury, sorcery and incantations first crept into the Church we have already conjectured from the author of the Fasciculus temporum: namely the effeminate eleventh century. At that time Sylvester II, a magician of no small fame, presided over the Roman See. This must be confirmed by the authority of Pontifical writers.

units.la: LXXIV. Qui à Sylvestri hujus, cui ante Papatum Gerberto nomen erat, temporibus proximè abfuit, & non easdem adversùs ipsum, quas adversùs Hildebrandum, causas odii habuit, Cardinalis Benno in vita Hildebrandi, sic scribit: Gerbertus paulò post completum millenarium ascendens de abysso permissionis Divinæ, quatuor annis sedit, mutato nomine dictus Sylvester secundus. Et per quæ multos decepit, per eadem dæmonum responsa decep-tus, morte improvisa, Dei judicio est interceptus. Neque id Benno solus, Hierarchicis invisus satis, prodidit, sed magna cum ipso Historicorum turba firmavit. Wer-nerus Rollfink, Author Fasciculi temporum, Sylvester inquit, factus est Papa, auxilio Diaboli, cui homagium fecit, ut cuncta ei ad votum succederent. Romæ in I emplo S. Crucis in Hierusalem, ad dextram ingredientibus basilicam Subterraneam S. Helenæ, ejusmodi, Laurentio Schradero Monum. Ital. lib. ÿ. narrante, Inscriptio, à Bernhardino Carvajola Cardinale posita visitur: Anno Domini MIII. tempore Othonis iij. Sylvester Papa ÿ. qui fuerat antea ejusdem Othonis præceptor, non satis ritè forsitan Papatum adeptus, à SPIRITU prænomitus, qua die Hierusalem accederet, se fore moriturum; nesciens fortè, hoc sacellum esse Hierusalem secundum, sui Tom. II. 000 · Pontifi-
units.tr: LXXIV. Cardinal Benno, who lived quite close to the times of this Sylvester, who before his papacy was called Gerbert, and who had reasons for hatred against him different from those against Hildebrand, writes in his life of Hildebrand as follows: Gerbert, rising a little after the millennium completed from the abyss of divine permission, sat for four years under the name Sylvester II. And by the same means by which he deceived many, deceived by the demons' answers, he was cut off by God's judgement in an unforeseen death. Nor did Benno alone, who was hostile enough to the hierarchs, report this, but with him a great crowd of historians confirmed it. Werner Rolevinck, author of the Fasciculus temporum, says: Sylvester became pope with the help of the Devil, to whom he did homage, so that everything would turn out as he wished. In Rome, in the Church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, on the right as one enters the underground basilica of St. Helena, there is seen an inscription of this kind, as Laurentius Schrader narrates in Monumenta Italiae, book v, set up by Cardinal Bernardino Carvajal: In the year of the Lord 1003, in the time of Otho III, Sylvester II, who had earlier been Otho's own tutor, having perhaps not quite rightly obtained the papacy, was forewarned by the SPIRIT that on the day he came to Jerusalem he would die; not knowing perhaps that this chapel is the second Jerusalem, in the fifth year of his pontificate, on the appointed day celebrating the divine rite, died that very day.

units.la: Magos notorios profitentur: scripta magica notoria in sinu suo fovent.
units.tr: They profess notorious magicians; they harbour notorious magical writings in their bosom.

units.la: Pontificatus anno quinto, statuta die rem hic Divinam faciens, ipsa die moritur. A spiritu, inquit, praemonitus, non illo quidem Sancto, sed ejusmodi, quoniam Pythias suas afflavit Apollo Loxias. Sic enim, quemadmodum dignum suis meritis exitum invenerit Sylvester, inter alios narrat Benno: Responsum a suo daemone acceperat, se non moriturum, nisi prius in Hierusalem Missa ab eo celebrata. Hac ambage, hac nominis aequivocatione delusus, dum civitatem Hierusalem sibi praedictam credit; Roma in Ecclesia, quae vocatur Hierusalem, Missam faciens in die stationis, ibidem miserabili & horrida morte praeventus, inter ipsas mortis angustias supplicat, manus & linguam sibi abscindi, per quas sacrificando daemonibus, Deum inhonoravit. Addit Martinus Polonus, qui Archiepiscopus Consentinus, & Innocentii IV. Poenitentiarius fuit, Chron. lib. iv. pag. 348. eum in Lateranensi Ecclesia sepultum esse; & tamen ex tumultu ossium, quam ex sudore, vel humectatione ipsius sepulchri, deinceps moriturí Papae praesagium colligi solitum; idque in eodem sepulchro literis esse exaratum, quo ostento, num significaverit Deus, misericordiam consecutum esse Sylvestrum (uti affirmat ille;) an Diabolus potius significaverit, cum Pontificibus successoribus eandem necessitudinem sibi esse, quae cum Sylvestro fuit, uti Roberto Barno in vita Sylvestri hujus visum, quaerant alii. Ego cum Platina in Papae hujus vita dico: Verumne hoc sit, an secus, Pontifices viderint, ad quos pertinet. Tantum quae ex Alberico Monacho trium fontium, in Magno Chronico Belgico, a Joh. Pistorio edito, recitantur; hic subjicio: In dextero latere Ecclesiae Lateranensis prope altare Sanctorum, Vincentii & Anastasii Martyrum, sepultus jacet Gerbertus Archiepiscopus, qui Papa effectus, Sylvester appellatus fuit. Quod autem tumba ejus quasi guttas lachrymarum emittat, quando Papa, aut magnus Cardinalis moriturus, satis probatum est, & satis vulgatum. Dicitur etiam, quicunque tumbam ejus visitaverit, & Dominicam orationem dixerit, quoties hoc fecerit, indulgentiam obtinere aliquot dierum à summis Pontificibus constitutam. Platina, Gerbertus, inquit, ambitione & Diabolica dominandi cupiditate impulsus, largitione primò quidem Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem, inde Ravennatem adeptus, Pontificatum postremò, majore conatu adjuvante Diabolo consecutus est; hac tamen lege, ut post mortem totius illius esset, cujus fraudibus tantam dignitatem adeptus erat. Nicolaus Lyranus ad 2. Machab. cap. xiv. per Alchimum, qui Demetrio coronam auream, & palmam obtulit, ut per hoc summum Sacerdotium obtineret, scribit, significari ambitiosum in tantum, ut Diabolo faciat sacrificium, ut per hoc promoveatur ad dignitatem; sicut, inquit, refert Guillermus in Chronico de quodam, nomine Gerbertus, qui per hoc ascendit ad Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem, & postea ad Ravennensem, & post ad statum Papalem. Sed & apud Æneam Sylvium in Commentariis de gestis Concilii Basileensis legimus: Nec nos fugit, Marcellinum jussu Cæsareo idolis thurificâsse, alium verò, quod majus & horribilius est, Diabolica fraude Romanum Pontificatum confexendisse. Nauclerus, cui res Pontificias narranti, magnam fidem Pontificii substringere solent, in Chronico, ipso Surio Carthusiano obstetricante, edito, rem totam ita narrat, ut extra dubitationis aleam eandem ponat. Interim, inquit, ipse Magica tam studiosè sectatus, ut illorum regulis omnem vitæ rationem moderaretur, quem ea lege Diabolus adjutum devinxit, ut post mortem suus esset. Et dum daemonem sunm consulit, quandiu in humanis futurus esset, ille ambiguo, ut solet, responso, diuquidem, si Hierusalem non attigeris. Accidit igitur, &c. Subjicit: Hic inter claros scientiâ literarum sua æta-te connumeratus esset, si suam scientiam arte Diabolica non fœdâsset. Addi plures alii ejus rei testes, Vincentius Bellovacensis, Galfridus, Malmesburiensis, Antonius Archiepiscopus, Henricus Erphordiensis, Carthusianus, Stella, alii possent; hoc etiam inter alia commemorantes, Sylvestrum artem Magicam hausisse ex libro, quem Hispali suffuratus erat, Diabolo inde homagium præstitisse, & caput æneum, per quod dæmon consultus respondisset, in conclavi habuisse.
units.tr: "Forewarned," he says, "by a spirit, not indeed the holy one but such a one as Apollo Loxias inspired into his Pythias." Thus, among others, Benno narrates how Sylvester found an end worthy of his deeds: he had received an answer from his demon that he would not die unless first he had celebrated Mass in Jerusalem. Deceived by this ambiguity, by this play on the name, he believed the city of Jerusalem was meant; celebrating Mass in Rome, in the church called Jerusalem, on the day of the station, he was overtaken there by a miserable and horrible death, and in the very pangs of death he begged that the hands and tongue, by which he had dishonoured God by sacrificing to demons, be cut off. Martinus Polonus, who was archbishop of Cosenza and penitentiary of Innocent IV, adds (Chron. book iv, p. 348) that he was buried in the Lateran church; and yet that from the rattling of the bones, rather than from sweat or moisture of the tomb, a foreboding of the pope who was to die later was usually gathered, and that this was written in letters on the same tomb. Whether God signified by this portent that Sylvester had obtained mercy (as that author affirms), or whether the Devil rather signified that the successors of the Pontiffs would have the same fate as Sylvester had, as Robert Barnes in the life of this Sylvester thought fit to ask, others may inquire. I, with Platina in the life of this pope, say: whether this is true or not, the Pontiffs must judge, to whom it belongs. Only the following, which is recited from Alberic the monk of Trois-Fontaines in the Great Belgian Chronicle published by Johannes Pistorius, I add here: In the right side of the Lateran church, near the altar of Saints Vincent and Anastasius, the martyrs, lies buried Gerbert, archbishop, who became pope and was called Sylvester. That his tomb emits drops of tears, as if weeping, when a pope or great cardinal is about to die, has been sufficiently proved and is widely known. It is also said that whoever visits his tomb and says the Lord's Prayer obtains, each time he does so, an indulgence of some days established by the supreme pontiffs. Platina: Gerbert, impelled by ambition and the diabolical desire to rule, first obtained by bribery the archbishopric of Reims, then that of Ravenna, and finally, with greater effort and the Devil's help, reached the papacy; yet on this condition, that after death it would belong to him whose frauds had won him so great a dignity. Nicholas of Lyra, on 2 Maccabees, chapter 14, writes that the man who offered Demetrius a golden crown and palm, so as to obtain the high priesthood through this (Alcimus), signifies a man so ambitious that he sacrifices to the Devil in order to be advanced to dignity; as, he says, William reports in his Chronicle about a certain man named Gerbert, who by this means rose to the archbishopric of Reims, afterwards to Ravenna, and afterwards to the papal state. But also in Aeneas Sylvius, in the Commentaries on the acts of the Council of Basel, we read: Nor are we unaware that Marcellinus, by Caesar's command, offered incense to idols, and that another, which is greater and more horrible, by diabolical fraud purchased the Roman pontificate. Naucler, whom the Papists usually rely on greatly when he narrates Pontifical affairs, in his Chronicle, published with Surius the Carthusian acting as midwife, relates the whole matter in such a way as to put it beyond the reach of doubt. Meanwhile, he says, he himself pursued magic so eagerly that he governed the whole course of his life by its rules; and the Devil bound him, on this condition, that he would help him, that after death he would be his. And while he consulted his demon how long he would live among men, the demon, as usual, gave an ambiguous answer: long indeed, if you do not reach Jerusalem. It therefore happened, etc. He adds: Here he would have been counted among the famous for learning in his age, if he had not defiled his learning by diabolical art. Several other witnesses to this matter could be added: Vincent of Beauvais, Geoffrey of Malmesbury, Antoninus the archbishop, Henry of Erfurt, the Carthusian, Stella, and others; among other things they also record that Sylvester drew his magic art from a book he had stolen at Seville, that he did homage to the Devil, and that he kept in his chamber a bronze head through which the consulted demon gave answers.

units.la: LXXV. Sylvestrum haud longo adeo intervallo excepit Benedictus IX. Theophylactus antedictus. De eo idem, qui supra, Cardinalis Benno in vita Hildebrandi: Sacris dæmoniorum fuit deditus, & montibus mulieres post se currere fecit, quas magicis artibus ad sui amorem coëgerat. Testantur hoc libelli inventi in domo ejus, postquam vitam malè finierat. Is, dum ad Ecclesiam rediret de Sylvarum secretis, ubique secum habens prædictum Laurentium Principem maleficiorum, cum eo etiam publicè de Mathesi disputabat, & de complice & discipulo suo Papa securus, gaudebat etiam publicè in conventu Episcoporum & Cardinalium & Senatorum auguria sua magnificare. Denique, inquit, à Diabolo in sylvis fuit suffocatus, Archipresbyter in exilium missus, Laurentius in fugam coactus. De conditione ejus post mortem narratio apud Petrum Damiani in Epist. 5. ad Fratres Eremi ex relatione Humberti Episcopi de Sylva candida, cap. 3. Bibliotheca Patrum tomo iij. planè monstrum extat, quam, utpote monstrum hoc hominis belle depingentem, attexemus. Vaclus, inquit, quidam dum iter ageret, accidit ut juxta molendinum equo insidens pertransiret: Ecce repente monstrum immane conspexit: quo viso subitus eum terror invasit, & stupefactus intremuit. Videbatur autem monstrum illud in aures mures aselli caudámque desinere, cætera ursus erat. Cúmque viator ad hoc portentum territus obrigescéret, fugámque præcipitem formidolosus iniret; informe prodigium humanæ vocis verba formavit. Noli, inquit, ô Vir, expavescere, hominem me olim fuisse sicut & ipse nunc es, proculdubio crede. Sed quia bestialiter vixi, post finem vitæ bestiæ præferre speciem merui. Porrò cùm ille perquireret, quis fuisset; Ego, ait ille, solo nomine Benedictus fui, qui nuper Apostolicæ Sedis apicem indignus obtinui. Inquisitus autem, quid jam retributionis haberet: Nunc, inquit, usque ad diem judicii per dumosa atque squalentia, per sulphurea loca & fœtorem exhalantia; atque incendiis conflagrata rapior atque pertrahor. Post extremum verò judicium corpus meum simul & animam irremediabilis cruciatus, & gehennalis barathri me irrevocabilis olla deglutiet, ita ut nulla mihi recuperationis spes inposterum restet. Post hæc verò & ejusmodi verba disparuit. Visionem eandem pro certa etiam Author Fasciculi Temporum, Platina, Onuphrius, aliíque venditant.
units.tr: LXXV. Sylvester was succeeded, after no long interval, by Benedict IX, the Theophylact mentioned above. Concerning him, the same Cardinal Benno as above, in the life of Hildebrand: He was given over to demonic rites, and he made women run after him over the mountains, whom he had forced into love of himself by magic arts. Books found in his house after he had ended his life badly bear witness to this. As he returned to the Church from the secrets of the woods, always keeping with him the aforesaid Laurentius, prince of wicked arts, he even disputed publicly with him about mathematics, and, secure in his accomplice and pupil the Pope, he rejoiced to magnify his augury publicly before the assembly of bishops, cardinals and senators. Finally, he says, he was suffocated by the Devil in the woods, the archpriest was sent into exile, and Laurentius was driven to flight. Concerning his condition after death, there is an account in Peter Damian, Epist. 5 to the Brothers of the Hermitage, from the report of Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, chap. 3, Bibliotheca Patrum vol. iii. which is plainly a monster; since it depicts this man's monstrous form well, I shall append it. A certain Vaclus, he says, while travelling, happened to ride past a mill on horseback. Suddenly he saw a huge monster; at the sight sudden terror seized him, and he trembled, stupefied. That monster seemed to end in the ears, mouse and tail of a donkey; the rest of it was a bear.
