When the traveller, terrified at this portent, stood transfixed and fled headlong in dread, the shapeless prodigy formed words with a human voice. "Do not be afraid, O man," it said, "believe for certain that I was once a man, just as you now are. But because I lived like a beast, after the end of my life I earned the shape of a beast." When he asked who it was, it replied: "I was Benedict in name alone, who lately and unworthily obtained the summit of the Apostolic See." When asked what retribution he now had, he said: "Until the day of judgment I am snatched and dragged through brambly and squalid places, through sulphurous places exhaling stench, and scorched by fires. But after the final judgment my body and soul together will be swallowed up by the irremediable torment of the vessel of hell and the gehennal abyss, so that no hope of recovery remains for me henceforth." After these words and such speech it vanished. The same vision is vouched for as certain also by the author of the Fasciculus Temporum, Platina, Onuphrius and others.

units.la: LXXVI. Qui haud diu post Romanam Cathedram insedit, furialis ille mundi incendiarius, Gregorius VII. Hildebrandus dictus, Diabolicarum artium studiis à prædecessoribus suis imbutus, malorum corvorum pessimum ovum, quoties vellet, (sic de eo Benno scribit) manicas suas discutiebat, & in modum scintillarum ignis dissiliebat, & iis miraculis oculos simplicium velut signo Sanctitatis ludificabat. Et quia Diabolus per Paganos Christum publicè persequi non poterat, per falsum Monachum sub habitu Monastico, sub specie religionis, nomen Christi fraudulenter subvertere disponebat. Hiccine, quærit haud immeritò Celeb. Ufferius Armachanus, ignis ille erat, quem Christus venit missurus in terram (Luc. xii. 49.) an ille potiùs, quem Bestia Apocalyptica Apoc. xiii. 13. 14. factura erat ra erat descendere è Cœlo in terram in conspectu hominum? Certè ut Spiritus S. de Bestia hac agens, quæ seducit incolas terræ propter signa, quæ datum est ei ut faciat, abigne Eliæ sermonem mutuari voluit: ita Paulus Bernriedensis in vita Gregorii VII. pag. 20.22. varia Hildebrandi portenta per ignem edicta commemorans, Eliæ cum identidem assimilat. Neque tamen unus Benno Magicam Gregorii impietatem prodidit; sed Episcopi insuper triginta, A. MLXXX. Brixinæ Noricæ ex Italia, Gallia & Germania convenerunt, teste Trithemio in Chronico Hirsaugiensi, eundem accusârunt, quòd per artem Magicam , necromanticam, & Dæmonum suffragio, sedem Apostolicam invaserit; quin & cum, Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. v. narrante, ut falsum Monachum , Magum , Divinaculum , somniorum prodigiorumque conjectorem condemnârunt. Similia Marianus Scotus lib. iij. A. 1081. & Otho Frisingensis Episcopus lib. 1. de rebus gestis Friderici cap. 1. docent. Quin & ipsa decreti conclusio conceptis verbis extat à Conrado à Liechtenau, Abbate Urspergensi, & post eum à Carolo Sigonio de Regno Ital. lib. ix. A. 1080. nec non Onuphrio Panvinio in vita Gregorii VII. his verbis consignata: Divinationem ac somniorum cultorem, manifestum necromanticum, Pythonico spiritu laborantem, & iccirco à vera fide exorbitantem, judicamus canonicè deponendum & expellendum: & nisi ab ipsa Sede, hîs auditis, descenderit, in perpetuum condemnandum. Talis cùm fuerit Gregorius, mirum non est, dæmoniacam ab eodem doctrinam, conjugia casta clerí prohibentem, stabilitam esse. LXXVII. Quæ cùm ita sint, atrociter criminatur famen Gabriel Naudæus, Parisinus, qui Apologiæ suæ pro necromanticis his Pontificibus cap. 19. scribere non erubuit, mendaciis, calumniis & malitiæ hæreticorum famam istam acceptam referri debere. An tales fuêre, quos laudavimus clericos plerosque, in communione Papæ mortuos, & quorum plerorumque fide ipsimet Hierarchici in aliis nituntur? Nisi forte hæreticus est, quisquis adversùs Papam testimonium verum enuntiat. Et quo argumento Authorum illorum narrationem suspectam reddere nititur ille? Omnes ejus colores & præfractæ inficiationes similimæ sunt iis; quibus idem Agrippam, Chicum, Petrum de Apono, Anselmum, Parmensem, Mich. Scotum, Trithemium, Jamblichum, Porphyrium, Zoroastrum, infames & notorios Magos plerosque, purgare non dubitavit. De paradoxis ejusmodi apologiis idem forte serendum judicium est, quod de laudibus Neronis à Cardano,& ipsius Diaboli à Brunone quodam Italo Witenbergii decantata: Neque minor audacia est Baronii, qui ad A. 1080. ff. 20. decretum illud Brixiense ab Urspergensi Abbate, additis de Gregorii necromantia ex Bennone convitiis, 'interpolatum fingit; quasi videlicet aut solus Brixiensis Synodi sententiam aperuisset ille Abbas; aut apud nos Cardinalis Baronii antiquior esse deberet, quàm Cardinalis Bennonis authoritas; aut denique Benno ille in aperta luce, & tot hominum spirantium adhuc conscientia impunè ausus fuisset obtrudere figmenta ejusmodi, quæ à quovis deprehendi & accusari potuissent; deprehensa autem & accusata à nemine sunt.
units.tr: LXXVI. Not long after, he who sat in the Roman chair was that frenzied incendiary of the world, Gregory VII, called Hildebrand, imbued by his predecessors with the study of diabolical arts, the worst egg of evil ravens. As often as he wished (so Benno writes of him) he shook off his cuffs, and leapt out like sparks of fire, and with such miracles he deluded the eyes of simple people as a sign of holiness. And since the Devil could not openly persecute Christ through the pagans, he arranged to subvert the name of Christ fraudulently through a false monk in monastic habit, under the appearance of religion. Is this, asks the learned Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, not without reason, that fire which Christ came to send on the earth (Luke 12:49), or rather the one which the Apocalyptic Beast (Rev. 13:13-14) was going to make come down from heaven to earth in the sight of men? Certainly, as the Holy Spirit, speaking of this Beast, who deceives the inhabitants of the earth by the signs which it was given to do, wished to borrow the language of Elijah's fire, so Paul of Bernried, in the life of Gregory VII, pp. 20-22, recounting the various portents of Hildebrand accomplished by fire, repeatedly compares him to Elijah. Yet Benno alone did not reveal Gregory's magical impiety. Moreover, thirty bishops gathered at Brixen in Noricum in the year 1080, from Italy, Gaul and Germany, as Trithemius witnesses in the Chronicle of Hirsau, and accused the same man that, through magic art, necromancy and the aid of demons, he had invaded the Apostolic See. Indeed, as Aventinus relates in the Annals of Bavaria, book 5, they condemned him as a false monk, a magician, a soothsayer, and an interpreter of dreams and portents. Marianus Scotus, book 3, year 1081, and Otto, bishop of Freising, book 1 of the Deeds of Frederick, chap. 1, teach similar things. Indeed the very conclusion of the decree stands in express words, recorded by Conrad of Liechtenau, abbot of Ursperg, and after him by Carlo Sigonio, On the Kingdom of Italy, book 9, year 1080, and likewise by Onuphrius Panvinius in the life of Gregory VII, in these words: We judge that the diviner and observer of dreams, a manifest necromancer, afflicted with a Pythonic spirit, and therefore straying from the true faith, is to be canonically deposed and expelled; and unless he descends from the See itself, having heard these charges, he is to be condemned forever. Since Gregory was such a man, it is no wonder that the demonic doctrine forbidding the chaste marriage of the clergy was established by him. LXXVII. These things being so, Gabriel Naudé of Paris bitterly accuses Gregory, and in his Apology for these necromantic Pontiffs, chap. 19, he did not blush to write that this reputation must be ascribed to the lies, calumnies and malice of heretics. Were they such as those many clergy we have cited, who died in communion with the Pope, and on whose faith the hierarchs themselves in other matters rely? Unless perhaps whoever bears true witness against the Pope is a heretic. And by what argument does he try to make the narrative of those authors suspect? All his colours and stubborn denials are very like those by which the same man did not hesitate to purge Agrippa, Cecco of Ascoli, Peter of Abano, Anselm of Parma, Michael Scot, Trithemius, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Zoroaster, and most of them infamous and notorious magicians. For apologies of this paradoxical kind, perhaps the same judgment must be passed as on the praises of Nero sung by Cardano, and of the Devil himself sung at Wittenberg by a certain Italian, Bruno. Baronius's audacity is no less, who at the year 1080, par. 20, pretends that the Brixen decree was interpolated by the abbot of Ursperg, with the abuse about Gregory's necromancy taken from Benno added; as if that abbot alone had revealed the sentence of the Synod of Brixen; or as if, in our view, Cardinal Baronius ought to be more ancient than the authority of Cardinal Benno; or finally, as if that Benno, in broad daylight and with the knowledge of so many people still living, had dared with impunity to foist on us figments of this kind, which anyone could have detected and accused. Yet they were detected and accused by no one.

units.la: LXXVIII. Possent alii etiam summi Pontifices criminis hujus suspecti vel manifesti etiam produci. Ita enim Johannem xxi. astrologiæ superstitiosæ confisum, longam sibi vitam promisisse, fato spem non implente, ex Stella & Valerio, Delrio lib. iv. cap. 3. q. 2. refert. Felicem V. in Basileensi Concilio Papam factum, constat ab Antipapæ Eugenii complicibus accusatum palàm, quòd sortilegos & veneficos inde ab adolescentia consulere sueverit. Alexandrum quoque Sextum Cardinalibus nonnullis propinato veneno mortem intentasse, at sibi eandem accersivisse, testes idonei, Guictiardinus, Bembus, Onuphrius retulêre. Paulum iii. Divinationem astrologicam judiciariam palàm adamasse, exercuisse, & per eam cuncta negotia sua direxisse, ejus denique mystam, Lucam Gauricum, in sinu suo fovisse, & Episcopatu Civitatensi donasse, Thuanus Histor. lib. iv. testis est.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Other supreme Pontiffs too could be brought forward as suspected or manifestly guilty of this crime. Thus John XXI, trusting in superstitious astrology, promised himself a long life, which fate did not fulfil, as Delrio reports from Stella and Valerius, book 4, chap. 3, q. 2. That Felix V, made Pope at the Council of Basel, was openly accused by the accomplices of the Antipope Eugenius of consulting sorcerers and poisoners from boyhood, is established. Alexander VI, too, attempted death by poison against some cardinals, but drew it upon himself, as trustworthy witnesses Guicciardini, Bembo and Onuphrius have reported. Paul III openly loved and practised judicial astrological divination, and directed all his affairs by it; finally he fostered in his bosom his initiate Luca Gaurico and gave him the bishopric of Civitate, as Thuanus, History book 4, bears witness.

units.la: LXXIX. Unumquodque amare & producere sibi simile, regula est, qua Baronius passim delectatur. Si ergo Pontifices ipsi, Hierarchiae Capita, Magicae impietati litarunt, quid de Cardinalibus, Episcopis, Sacerdotibus & reliquo clero, quos illi creârunt, foverunt, censendum? Auguriis, repetam Authoris fasciculi de Undecimo seculo verba, & maleficiis intendebant, & erat Sacerdos sicut populus. Martinus Delrio Disquisit. lib. ij q. 3. alibique ex sacro ordine criminis hujus reos memorat Johanne Teutonicum, Canonicum Halberstadiensem: Monachum illum, qui in gratiam Ducis Aureliani incantabat Regem Carolum, de quo Mejerus in Annalibus Flandriae: Palumbum Presbyterum Necromanticum, Romae quondam potentem, cujus D. Antonius in historia meminit; Dominicanos Bernae exustos; Felicem Malleolum, qui Magicas adjurationes & formulas aperte defendit: Paulum Jovium & Comitem Mirandulanum, amniomantiae & astrologiae judiciariae deditos: Ægidium Canonicum Lusitanum. Nihil dicam de Magdalena Crucia Cordubensi, Abbatissa Mariae de visitatione, Abbate Brandolino, à Paulo v. ex carcere liberato: Demetrio Spartano, qui Romae sub Hadriano vi. ad pestilentiam averruncandam, ferocem taurum publicè & impunè per magica incantamenta cicuravit & sacrificavit, Jovio Histor. lib. xxi. teste: Monacho, magni cujusdam Principis mago; qui, Bodino narrante, puerum decennem nem oem ad usum Magicum capite truncavit; Cotono, Hermolao Barbaro, Aquilegiensi Patriarcha, ex dæmone sensum vocis Aristotelicæ entelecheja expiscato; uti Baptista Monlorius lib. de Entelech. tradidit: Presbyterorillo, qui, teste Botereo Comment. lib. xv. coetui Magotum a sacris erat, & sacra sacerrima, uti Historicus loquitur, ibi faciebat, lemures larvasque Orci exciebat: Presbytero Massilensi Gaufredo, cujus historiam peculiari volumine Michael Monachus descripsit; aliisque pluribus, quorum plerisque impune fuit.
units.tr: LXXIX. It is a rule, in which Baronius delights everywhere, that each thing loves and produces what is like itself. If therefore the Pontiffs themselves, the heads of the hierarchy, sacrificed to magical impiety, what is to be judged of the cardinals, bishops, priests and the rest of the clergy whom they created and fostered? They devoted themselves to augury and to evil arts, and the priest was like the people, I repeat the words of the author of the Fasciculus on the eleventh century. Martin Delrio, Disquisitions book 2, q. 3, and elsewhere, mentions guilty men from the sacred order of this crime: John Teutonicus, canon of Halberstadt; that monk who, to please the Duke of Orleans, enchanted King Charles, concerning whom Meyer in the Annals of Flanders; Palumbus, a priest and necromancer, once powerful at Rome, whom St Antoninus mentions in his history; the Dominicans burned at Bern; Felix Malleolus, who openly defended magical adjurations and formulas; Paulus Jovius and the Count of Mirandola, given over to amniomancy and judicial astrology; Egidius, a Portuguese canon. I say nothing of Magdalena Crucia of Cordoba, abbess of the Visitation of Mary, nor of Abbot Brandolino, freed from prison by Paul V; of Demetrius the Spartan, who at Rome under Hadrian VI publicly and with impunity tamed and sacrificed a fierce bull by magic incantations to avert a plague, as Jovius witnesses in History book 21; of a monk, magician to a certain great prince, who, as Bodin relates, beheaded a ten-year-old boy for magical use; of Cotonus, and of Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarch of Aquileia, who fished out from a demon the sense of the Aristotelian word entelechy [ἐντελέχεια], as Baptista Monlorius has handed down in his book on entelechy; of a little priest who, as Botero witnesses in his Commentaries, book 15, was among the company of magicians and performed there the most sacred rites, as the historian puts it, and raised the lemures and larvae of Orcus; of the priest Gaufredus of Marseilles, whose history Michael the Monk described in a separate volume; and of many others, most of whom went unpunished.

units.la: Diaboli discipulos esse miriones & Thaumaturgos omnes, qui vana curiositate Deum tentantes, revelationes ab eodem personato licet expetunt, Delrio lib. iv. & 1. q. 3. sect. 1. aliique nulli diffitentur. Talis tamen qui apparitionibus & revelationibus Diaboli, se in Angelum lucis transformantis, velut Divinis, decepti sunt, in Papatu innumeros extitisse, ipsi etiam Hierarchici non dissimulant. Cornelium à Lapide Comment. ad 2. Cor. xj. 15. audiamus: Sathanas, inquit ille, veritatem, justitiam & pietatem præ se fert, & promittit hominibus, quorum vel oculis visibiliter apparet, vel phantasiæ se suaque consilia insinuat, offendit; imprimit, &c. Multi Eremitæ ab eo decepti sunt. In vitis Patrum multa & luculuosa hujus rei exempla extant; uti inter alia Hieronimi & Monachi, qui Diabolus persuasit, ut se in puteum præcipitem daret, &c. Paulo post: Valentem Monachum decepit dæmon, credhò ei apparens quasi Angelus. Tandem dæmon apparuit, fingens se esse Christum. Egressus est, & pro Christo Diabolum adoravit. Qui miser Monachus Theologiæ Jesuiticæ apicem attigisse videtur, apud Vasquesium in 3. parte 4. q. 25. disp. 98. cap. 1. statuentis scilicet, speciem crucifixi, aut radium, sub quo delitescit dæmon, secure adorari posse. Aliud exemplum B. Jordanis, Prædicatorum
units.tr: The Devil's disciples are all wonder-workers and miracle-makers who, tempting God through vain curiosity, seek revelations from that masked deceiver. Delrio lib. iv. & 1. q. 3. sect. 1. and others admit this without hesitation. Yet the Papists' own hierarchs do not conceal that countless people in the Papacy have been deceived by apparitions and revelations of the Devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light, as if they were divine. Let us hear Cornelius à Lapide on 2 Cor. 11:15 Comment. ad 2. Cor. xj. 15.: Satan," he says, "puts on a show of truth, justice and piety, and offers himself and his counsels to men, either appearing visibly before their eyes or insinuating himself into their imagination; he presses upon them, etc. Many hermits have been deceived by him. In the Lives of the Fathers there are many striking examples of this, such as the one in which the Devil persuaded Jerome's monk to throw himself headlong into a well, etc. A little later: the demon deceived the monk Valens, appearing to him as if he were an angel. At last the demon appeared, pretending to be Christ. He went out and worshipped the Devil as Christ." That unhappy monk seems to have reached the summit of Jesuit theology, as in Vasquez on the third part, question 25, disputation 98, chapter 1, where he lays down that the image of the crucified, or a ray under which the demon lies hidden, may be adored safely. Another example is that of Blessed Jordan, Master General of the Preachers

units.la: miriones & Thaumaturgi, qui, miri, ... (marginal notes, partly illegible) rum Magistri Generalis, Diaboli boni Angeli specie apparentis consilio & magisterio usi, idem Delrio lib. iv. cap. 1. q. 3. ff. 5. ex Leandro Alberto describit. Ita Simon Monachus Trevirensis à Diabolo ad celebrandam Missam se moveri, ad altare perduci, & ab eodem alba indui passus est. Primæ quoque plantationis Præmonstratensium Monachos, ac inter illos Abbatem Simonem S. Nicolai, Diaboli ductum & inspirationem secutos, omnes à Diabolo factos esse Pseudoprophetas, Delrio prodidit. Similia plurima Metaphraltes, Cæsarius, Cantipratensis, Discipulus, Lipomannus, Surius, Sanctorum vitas & res gestas commemorantes, tradidere.
units.tr: Wonder-workers and miracle-workers, who, wonderful... (marginal notes, partly illegible)... of the Master General, having followed the counsel and teaching of the Devil, who appeared in the shape of a good angel: Delrio describes this from Leandro Alberti, lib. iv. cap. 1. q. 3. ff. 5. In the same way Simon, a monk of Trier, allowed himself to be moved by the Devil to celebrate Mass, was led to the altar by him, and was clothed in a white vestment by him. Delrio also reports that the first monks of the Premonstratensian plantation, and among them Abbot Simon of St Nicholas, followed the Devil's guidance and inspiration, and were all made false prophets by the Devil. Metaphrastes, Caesarius, Cantipratensis, Discipulus, Lipomannus and Surius, recalling the lives and deeds of the saints, have handed down many similar accounts.
LXXXI.

units.la: Tamque frequens hæc in tenebris Papatus deceptio fuit, religiosarum maximè, ut Gerson Parisiensis, Thyræus, Vicentius Ferreria, Turrecremata, Henricus de Firmaria, Ægidius, Carlerius, Picus, Ribadeneira, alii, à Delrione lib. iv. cap. 1. q. 3. laudati, necesse habuerint peculiares cautelas ad explorandos spiritus, in eorundem usum conscribere. Post tot tamen cautelas, regulas & disceptationes scriptas, arduam esse hujus quæstionis pertractationem, propter quotidianas etiam spiritualium personarum illusiones, idem Delrio loc. cit. fatetur. Alibi lib. v. q. 26. ff. 3. Delrio de notis apparitionum discernendarum sic scribit: Hæc, ne notis ab illis traditis indubitanter assentiar, memoratur: sed in primis, quia totam hanc spirituum discretionem, quod illi non diffitentur, ex Divina potissimum revelatione dependere arbitror. Propterea tutius & præstabilius judico cum B. Augustino, meam hic ignorantiam fateri, & discipulum me præstare, quàm præcipiti temeritate aliquid definire, vel agere præceptorem. Res enim hæc altior est, quàm ut à me possit attingi, & abstrusior, quàm ut eruere; & profundior, quàm ut vadare queam. Judicent ergò æqui & prudentes arbitri omnes, quàm certum Magiæ periculum omnes, qui apparitionibus & revelationibus attendunt, destituti Ariadnæo Divinas à Diabolicis distinguendi filo, subeant: quàm certam Magiam committant ferè omnes.
units.tr: This deception was so common in the darkness of the Papacy, especially among religious persons, that Gerson of Paris, Thyraeus, Vincentius Ferreria, Torquemada, Henry of Firmaria, Giles, Carlerius, Pico, Ribadeneira and others, praised by Delrio, book 4, chapter 1, question 3, found it necessary to write down special safeguards for testing the spirits, for the use of the same persons. Yet after so many written safeguards, rules and disputations, Delrio himself, loc. cit., confesses that the treatment of this question is difficult, on account of the daily illusions even of spiritual persons. Elsewhere, book 5, question 26, section 3, Delrio writes thus about the marks by which apparitions are to be distinguished: Lest I assent without doubt to the marks handed down by them, this must be recorded: but chiefly because I think that the whole discernment of spirits, as they themselves do not deny, depends above all on divine revelation. Therefore I judge it safer and better, with Blessed Augustine, to confess my ignorance here and to be a disciple rather than, with reckless rashness, to define something or act as a teacher. For this matter is too lofty for me to attain, too abstruse for me to unravel, and too deep for me to wade through. Let all fair and prudent judges therefore consider how certain is the danger of magic for all who attend to apparitions and revelations, lacking Ariadne's thread to distinguish the divine from the diabolical; how almost all of them are sure to commit true magic.

units.la: LXXXII. Majùs & detestabiliùs est, quòd in Papatu non defuerunt, qui Magiam publicè docerent, eámque editis libris notorie Magicis defenderent. Salmanticæ enim in Hispania scholas Magicas diu satis habitas, & primùm Caroli V. Imperatoris jussu clausas esse, satis constat, & pluribus Tholosanus Syntagm. lib. xxxiv. cap. 21. ff. iv. prodidit. Legulejos, Medicos, Philosophos, Cornelium Agrippam, Petrum de Albano, seu Apono, Picatricem Hispanum, Anselmum Parmensem alios præterea. Theologos memoro, Trithemium, qui in sua Steganographia & libro de septem intelligentiis Coloniæ apud Birkmannū A. MDLXVII. excusò, nefariam hanc artem, sub Magiæ naturalis nomine, summopere, & quidem piè ac Theologicè (sic loquitur ille) commendat, altùm stertentibus Inquisitoribus, Censoribus, Curialibus cum suo Papa, sub quolibet aliàs lapide scorpium venari solitis: Albertum Magnum, mira de virtutibus lapidum ad futura prænoscenda philosophantem: Petrum de Aliaco Cardinalem & Episcopum Cameracensem, qui Arithmantiæ indulgens, scripto vigintiloquio de Astrologiæ cum Theologia & historia concordantia, aliisque Dialogis eodem pertinentibus, non erubuit defendere, Dilavium Noëticum & ortum Christi, aliáque summa prodigia & miracula sideralis scientiæ peritia ex astris prænosci potuisse: Marinum Mersennum, Minoritam Parisiensem, Philosophum & Theologum magni nominis, quem Jacobus Gaffarellus magno spiritu Diabolicam Magiam scriptis suis docere, & librum Thomæ Campanellæ de Magia magnam partem exscriptum ptum in suos in Genesin Commentarios transtulisse queritur: Gaffarellum ipsum, Sacerdotem Gallum, cujus Inaudita Curiositates passim male audiunt, Georgium Venetum Minoritam, cujus Problemata, Sacra Magorum redolere sacra, ipse Magiae insimulatus Mersennus contendit: Basilium Monachum, Benedictinum, qui publico Scripto opuatriam defendit: Navarrum & Victoriam, qui Ensalmatores Hispanos apertos Magos defendunt, vel saltem excusant: Paulum Ritium, qui Coelorum animationem & Cabalisticam suam Arithmantiam per decem enumerationes tradens, Magiae principia non parum promovet Commentariis suis ad librum R. Joseph Castiliensis, qui Porta lucis dicitur; alios.
units.tr: 82. Greater and more detestable is this: that in the Papacy there were not lacking men who taught magic publicly and defended it in books openly devoted to magic. It is quite well established that at Salamanca in Spain there were magical schools which were long tolerated, and were first closed by the order of the Emperor Charles V, and the Tholosan has reported this in many places in his Syntagma, book 34, chapter 21, section 4. I mention the Legulejos, physicians, philosophers, Cornelius Agrippa, Peter of Abano or Apono, the Spanish Picatrix, Anselm of Parma, and others besides. I mention theologians: Trithemius, who in his Steganographia and his book de septem intelligentiis, published at Cologne by Birkmann in 1567, commends this nefarious art, under the name of natural magic, very highly, and indeed piously and theologically (so he speaks), while the Inquisitors, censors and courtiers with their Pope, who are otherwise accustomed to hunt scorpions under every stone, snore loudly; Albertus Magnus, philosophising marvellously about the powers of stones for foreknowing future things; Peter of Ailly, Cardinal and Bishop of Cambrai, who, indulging in arithmancy, in a long-winded written work on the agreement of astrology with theology and history, and in other dialogues pertaining to the same subject, did not blush to defend that the Flood of Noah and the birth of Christ, and other great prodigies and miracles, could be foreknown from the stars by skill in sidereal science; Marin Mersenne, a Minorite of Paris, a philosopher and theologian of great name, whom Jacques Gaffarel, with great spirit, accuses of teaching diabolical magic in his writings, and whom he complains has transferred into his commentaries on Genesis a large part of Thomas Campanella's book de Magia; Gaffarel himself, a French priest, whose Unheard-of Curiosities are everywhere ill received; Georgius Venetus, a Minorite, whose Problems, sacred things smelling of the sacred rites of the Magi, Mersenne, who himself was accused of magic, insists upon; Basil, a Benedictine monk, who defended the Patriarch in a public writing; Navarrus and Victoria, who defend, or at least excuse, the Spanish charmers as open magicians; Paulus Ritius, who, setting out the animation of the heavens and his Cabalistic arithmancy through ten enumerations, promotes the principles of magic not a little in his commentaries on the book of R. Joseph of Castile, which is called Gate of Light; and others.

units.la: LXXXIII. Affines huic scriptorum Magicorum tolerantiae sunt consuetudines Magicae, quas itidem Papatus tolerat.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Customs akin to this toleration of magical writers are likewise tolerated by the Papacy.

units.la: Sic enim in Gallia & Italia venales publice prostare daemones paredros, vasculis, speculis, phialis, annulis alligatos & inclusos, non tantum experientia testatur, sed etiam Crespetus fatetur. Imo licite vendi posse, Pontificius Poeta Ronsardus pertendit. Ensalmatores, seu incantatores publicos Hispani tolerant, & uti modo diximus, nonnulli defendunt. Annulum contra contractionem, nervorum ex Carlino in parasceve crucifixo oblato, similesque superstitiosas observantias simul tolerari, simul excusari, Cajetanus in Summula his verbis indicat: Videntur simplici corde similia credentes & facientes ex devotione excusandi &c. licet nesciant aliam reddere rationem, quare has conditiones, quae vanae sunt, observent, nisi quia sic acceperunt a majoribus. Difficile est enim confutare, quod Seniorum traditione & authoritate firmatum vulgares acceperunt. Tralatitium etiam in Papatu est, Toleto de Instr. Sac. lib. iv. 16. teste, in die ascensionis, & D. Iohannis ante Solis ortum herbas decerpere, Nemo tamen id faciens ad Mallei Inquisitores rapitur. Gerson Tract. de erroribus circa artem Magicam, sibi per occupationem objicit: Nonne, inquiunt, Magi scilicet; talia frequenter fiunt, aut tolerantur ab Ecclesia in peregrinationibus certis, in cultu imaginum, in cereis, aut ceris, aquis benedictis, exorcismis? Nonne dicitur quotidie, si novem diebus perdurat in Ecclesia, si aqua illa perfundatur, aut tali se imagini voveat, aut tale quid faciat, ipse mox sanabitur? Respondet Gerson: Fateor, abnegare non possumus, multa inter Christianos simplices sub specie religionis introducta esse, quorum sanctior est omissio. Similes consuetudines, formulas, ceremonias, actiones, ne dicam, opiniones periculosas multorum Canonistarum, Legistarum, Theologorum, puta Aureoli, Brianfoni, Remigii, Angeli de Clavasio, Levini Crucii, Malleoli &c. innumeras Delrio in Disquisitionibus suis detexit. Quibus unum hoc addo, quod Jesuita à Lapide ex Rescio de sectis refert, hoc seculo esse sectam Diabolistarum, qui gloriantur, se esse sortiarios, & Diaboli charactere insignitos; quem, ubi vino incaluere, nudata carne ostendere non vereantur. Auditum est, inquit, ex ipsorum consessione, quòd numerus eorum usque ad sexaginta millia in Galliis excreverit. LXXXIV. Quo loco numeróque peccata habeantur, ex eorundem poenis maximè liquet. Spiritus igitur S. universas καθολικὰς Magicas Deo supra modum invisas esse, ea ratione testatus est, quòd non tantùm eas severissimè interdixit, sed etiam dictatis poenis capitalibus coërcuit Exod. xxii. 18. ubi sic sancit: מכשפה לא תחיה Præstigiatricem non sines vivere. Quam legem Dei poenalem peculiari de poenis & Magorum diatriba explicatam dedimus. Quid verò hic Hictarchici? Quo foco crimen isthoc atrocissimum, omnium scelerum aliorum sentinam habeant, produnt ea ratione, Quo loco: Magicam Impietatem Hierarchici habeant, ex poenis, quas Concilium Lateranense Magi notorii, religiosi in primis, levissimas decrevit, colligitur ratione, quòd leves eidem confesso etiam pœnas decer Sicenim Decretum in Concilio Lateranensi Sess. 9. cusum sonat: Clerici, qui inventi fuerint culpabiles in fortilegiis, per invocationem dæmonum, incantationibus ac divinationibus, superstitionibus, arbitrio Superiorum infamiâ notentur. Si verò non desiterint, deponantur, atque in Monasterium ad tempus arbitrio Superiorum præfiniendum detrudantur, beneficiisque & officiis Ecclesiasticis priventur. An mitior pœna dictari poterat, & quidem Magiæ etiam explicitæ, cum aperta invocatione dæmonis conjunctæ? Nam Clericorum quidem infamia, superiorum inprimis arbitrio definita, intra septa paucorum, quos plerosque parium vel majorum scelerum conscientia torquet, conclusa, ad populum ipsum non penetrat, nullamque adeò, vel exiguam pœnæ vim habet. Hominum proin ejusmodi exanguem & ferream frontem infamiæ punctis nequicquam profecto convulneraveris, cùm ipsi notas suas rideant. Depositio verò, & ab officiis ac beneficiis Ecclesiasticis, quæ indebita sunt, gratisque collata, remotio, & in Monasterium inclusio, inprimis si arbitrio superiorum ad tempus duntaxat præfiniatur, cum perseverante impietate illa nullum planè commensum habet. Ludibria proin hæc veriùs, quàm pœnæ tanto sceleri debitæ, censeri possunt. Præterea quæstio haud immeritò movetur, cur in Bulla de Cœna Domini memoratis levioribus multò criminibus, hodie quidem omittatur Magia, quæ olim in eadem expressa apparuit? Interdicto Bulla illa subjicit quosvis libertatis seu immunitatis Ecclesiasticæ pupillam leviter attrectantes, Cardinalis cujuspiam familiarem offendentes, ad Concilium futurum provocantes, denique leve quid committentes, quod potestatis Pontificis apices eminùs tangere videri possit. At Divinæ Majestatis horribiliter offensæ rei Magi alto silentio prætereuntur.
units.tr: For in France and Italy, demons bound and shut up in little vessels, mirrors, phials and rings are openly offered for sale, as not only experience attests but Crespetus also admits. That they may even be sold lawfully, the Papist poet Ronsard maintains. The Spanish tolerate public charmers or enchanters, and, as we have just said, some defend them. That a ring against cramps, made from the nerves of a Carlino crucifix offered on Good Friday, and similar superstitious observances are at once tolerated and excused, Cajetan indicates in his Summula in these words: They seem, believing and doing similar things with a simple heart, to be excused out of devotion, etc., although they do not know how to give any other reason why they observe these conditions, which are vain, except that they have received them thus from their elders. For it is difficult to refute what ordinary people have received, confirmed by the tradition and authority of their seniors. It is also traditional in the Papacy, as Toledo testifies in de Instr. Sac. lib. iv. 16., to pluck herbs on Ascension Day and on the day of St John before sunrise; yet nobody who does so is dragged before the Malleus inquisitors. Gerson, in his tract de erroribus circa artem Magicam, objects to himself by way of an objection: Surely, they say, Magi (that is): such things frequently happen, or are tolerated by the Church, on certain pilgrimages, in the worship of images, in candles or wax, holy water, exorcisms? Is it not said every day that if someone persists for nine days in the Church, if he is sprinkled with that water, or vows himself to such an image, or does something of the sort, he will soon be healed? Gerson replies: I admit, we cannot deny that many things have been introduced among simple Christians under the appearance of religion, of which the more holy course is to leave them out. Innumerable similar customs, formulas, ceremonies, actions, not to mention dangerous opinions, of many canonists, jurists and theologians, such as Aureolus, Brianfoni, Remigius, Angelus de Clavasio, Levinus Crucius, Malleolus, etc., Delrio has uncovered in his Disquisitions. To these I add this one thing, which the Jesuit à Lapide reports from Rescius de sectis: that in this century there is a sect of Diabolists, who boast that they are sorcerers and marked with the character of the Devil, whom, when they have grown warm with wine, they do not hesitate to show with their flesh bared. It has been heard, he says, from their own confession, that their number has grown to sixty thousand in the Gauls. LXXXIV. How grave these sins are held to be, and how they are counted, is especially clear from the penalties imposed for them. The Holy Spirit therefore testified that all magical arts are exceedingly hateful to God, for the reason that he not only forbade them most severely but also restrained them with capital penalties (Exod. 22:18), where he thus decrees: מכשפה לא תחיה [You shall not let a sorceress live]. We have explained this penal law of God in a separate dissertation de poenis & Magorum. But what do the hierarchs here? By what reasoning do they show that this most atrocious crime, the sink of all other sins, is held by them as the greatest impiety of magic? It is gathered from the penalties which the Lateran Council decreed for notorious magicians, especially religious ones, which were the lightest: that even for a confessed offence the penalties were light. For the decree of the Lateran Council, Session 9, sounds thus: Clerics who are found guilty of sorcery, through the invocation of demons, incantations and divinations, superstitions, shall be marked with infamy at the discretion of their superiors. But if they do not desist, they shall be deposed, and thrust into a monastery for a period to be fixed at the discretion of their superiors, and deprived of benefices and ecclesiastical offices. Could a milder penalty be laid down, and that for magic which is explicit and joined with an open invocation of a demon? For the infamy of clerics, defined chiefly at the discretion of superiors, is enclosed within the walls of a few men, whom for the most part the consciousness of equal or greater crimes torments, and it does not penetrate to the people themselves, and so has little or no force as a penalty. Indeed, you will certainly pierce the bloodless and iron brow of such men in vain with the marks of infamy, since they laugh at their own brands. Deposition, and removal from ecclesiastical offices and benefices, which are undue and conferred gratuitously, and enclosure in a monastery, especially if it is fixed for a period only at the discretion of superiors, has no proper proportion to that persisting impiety. These things can therefore be regarded as mockeries rather than penalties owed to so great a crime. Moreover, it is not unreasonably asked why magic, which once appeared expressly in the Bull of the Lord's Supper, is today omitted there, although the Bull lists far lighter crimes: those who lightly touch the ward of ecclesiastical liberty or immunity, who offend a familiar of some cardinal, who appeal to a future council, and finally those who commit some slight thing which may seem to touch from afar the authority of the Pontiff. But the guilty of magic, who have grievously offended the Divine Majesty, are passed over in deep silence.

units.la: LXXXV. Denique impietetis Magicæ in Papatu abo- minationem auget, quòd ἀψεύστῳ illa est, adeóque emendationem patitur omnino nullam. Quod vel uno argumento, à Delrionis fato petito planè constat. Quot quantæque superstitiones in Papatu etiamnum grassentur: quot fovendis aut incrustandis iis scripta edita sint, & edantur continuè, luculenter, si quisquam alius, Delrio docuit. Ille Augiæ hoc stabulum ingressus, expurgare pro viribus conatus licet minimè tamen à Papatu labem abstersit, vel abstergere etiam potuit. Tentavit tamen nonnihil, & movit camarinam, sed quo operæ pretio? Eo videlicet, ut Romæ, inter Antesignanos sacræ istius militiæ de libro ejus per Inquisitores condemnando agi jam coeperit; ipsique adeò necessitas Apologiam ad Congregationem Generalem Inquisitorum consignandi impositta fuerit. Quæ cùm ita sint, jure meritóque omnia illa, quæ passim & impunè in Ecclesia Romana, antiqua & perpetua consuetudine, quam optimam juris interpretem Bellarminus de Cler. lib. 1. c. 2. dixit, recepta sunt; nec non, quæ à privatis, tacito Ecclesiæ consensu, scripta, dicta, facta sunt, quicquid Delrio vel Malderus aliquis, χῆς ἢ πεόχῆς natus, contra mussitaverit; non vitio & abusui cuipiam graffanti, sed ipsi Ecclesiæ Hierarchicæ imputabimus tantisper, dum Ecclesiæ sententiâ & censoriâ virgulâ impii illi abusus non notati, & Delrionis aliorúmque correctiones & censuræ non absolutæ approbataeque fuerint. Quomodo ipse quoque Delrio, postquam diu satis cum suis conflixit, tandem communi artificio Romanensium hoc circulo se munivit, ut historiam suam his verbis clauderet: In quo quæcunque scripsi, ea cunctæ Sanctæ Apostolicæ & Catholicæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ judicio, & piorum Theologorum censuræ subjicio: si quid ignaro elapsum, quod Ecclesiæ minùs probetur, improbo, damno, & pro non scripto haberi volo.
units.tr: LXXXV. Finally, the abomination of magical impiety in the Papacy is increased by the fact that it is infallible [ἀψεύστῳ], and therefore suffers no correction at all. This is plainly established by a single argument, drawn from the fate of Delrio. How many and how great superstitions are still flourishing in the Papacy, how many writings have been published, and are continually being published, to foster or to plaster over them, Delrio has taught clearly, if anyone has. Entering this Augean stable, he tried with all his strength to clean it out, yet he did not wipe away the stain from the Papacy, nor could he have done so. He did attempt something and stirred the pot, but to what good purpose? Namely, that at Rome, among the leaders of that sacred militia, the condemnation of his book by the Inquisitors has already begun to be debated, and he himself was indeed compelled to submit an Apology to the General Congregation of the Inquisitors. Since these things are so, we shall rightly and justly impute all those things which are received everywhere and with impunity in the Roman Church by ancient and perpetual custom, which Bellarmine, de Cler. lib. 1. c. 2., called the best interpreter of law; and likewise whatever has been written, said, or done by private persons with the tacit consent of the Church, whatever Delrio or some Malderus, of no particular stripe [χῆς ἢ πεόχῆς], has muttered against it: we will impute these not to some vice and abuse spreading among people, but to the hierarchical Church itself, for as long as those impious abuses have not been noted by the sentence and the censorial rod of the Church, and the corrections and censures of Delrio and others have not been finally approved. Thus Delrio himself, after he had struggled long enough with his own people, at last fortified himself with that common device of the Romanists, to close his history with these words: In which whatever I have written, I submit to the judgment of the whole Holy, Apostolic and Catholic Roman Church, and to the censure of pious theologians; if anything has slipped from me in ignorance which the Church may less approve, I disapprove it, condemn it, and wish it to be held as unwritten.

units.la: Hoc verò scutum æquè etiam infiniti in Papatu authores, qui scriptis, exorcismis, actionibus suis magica, & superstitiosa multa admiscuerunt, & hodiéque admiscent, adversùs Delrionem aliosque censores suos prætendunt. Utris verò, cùm ex æquo boni Romano-Catholici habeantur, credemus, ut sensum tandem Ecclesiæ Romanæ percipiamus? Imò cùm spes nulla sit, Ecclesiam decretis suis pia ab impiis, licita ab illicitis discreturam unquam, διαίρεσιν ποιῶν, incurabile & deploratum esse hoc in Papatu malum, ultrò consequitur.
units.tr: This same shield is held up against Delrio and his other censors by the countless authors in the Papacy who have mingled magical and superstitious matters with their writings, exorcisms and actions, and who still do so today. But which of these, since both are regarded alike as good Roman Catholics, shall we believe, so that we may at last perceive the mind of the Roman Church? Indeed, since there is no hope that the Church will ever distinguish by its decrees the pious from the impious, the lawful from the unlawful, making a distinction [διαίρεσιν ποιῶν], it follows of its own accord that this evil in the Papacy is incurable and desperate.

units.la: LXXXVI. Ex iis, quæ hactenus studiosè collegimus,
units.tr: LXXXVI. From those things which we have hitherto diligently gathered together,

units.la: nemo, nisi qui in meridie cæcutit, non videt, verisimum esse, quod Doctiss. Theologus Anglus, Thomas Brightmannus, Comment. in Apoc. ix. 21. paucis multa complexus dixit, Romam esse veneficiorum officinam; neque, minùs pro vero Celeb. Paræum Comment. ad j. cit. dixisse: Veneficia & artes Magicas omnes nouæ Papatui debemus? Adeóque ut isthoc etiam demonstrationis caput claudam, Hierarchiam Romanam esse purpuratam illam Meretricem Babylonicam, quam inter alias etiam Magicæ impietatis nota Spiritus S. compunxit.
units.tr: no one, unless he is blind at midday, fails to see that what the very learned English theologian Thomas Brightman said in his Commentary on Revelation 9:21 is true, summing up much in few words: that Rome is a workshop of poisonings (veneficiorum officinam). Nor is it less true, as the renowned Paraeus said in his commentary on the same passage, that we owe all poisonings and all magical arts to the new Papacy. And so, to close this part of the demonstration as well, I say that the Roman hierarchy is that purple-clad Babylonian harlot, whom the Holy Spirit marked, among other tokens, with the stamp of magical impiety.
DISSERTATION SIXTEEN,

units.la: QVA Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem esse Babylonem Magnam probatur Undecimò, quia avaritiâ & nundinatione spirituali sese immaniter polluit.
units.tr: In which it is proved that the Hierarchy, or the clergy of the Roman Church that dominates, is the Great Babylon, eleventhly because it defiles itself monstrously by avarice and spiritual trafficking.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Falsorum doctorum inter alias nota est, quòd per avaritiam fictis sermonibus homines nundinantur.
units.tr: I. Among other marks of false teachers is this, that through avarice they trade in men by means of feigned sermons.

units.la: II. Nundinationem similem Spiritus S. Babyloni tribuit.
units.tr: II. The Holy Spirit ascribes a similar trafficking to Babylon.

units.la: III. quæ nonnam secundùm literam earum mercium, quæ Babyloni tribuuntur, quàm secundùm allegoriam explicari debet.
units.tr: III. The merchandise ascribed to Babylon must be explained not so much according to the letter as according to allegory.

units.la: IV. Nundinationem tamen eandem & secundùm literam & allegoricè explicatam in Hierarchia reperiri, generali Syllogismo demonstratur, cujus quoad utramque propositionem singula membra explanantur.
units.tr: IV. That the same trafficking, explained both literally and allegorically, is found in the Hierarchy, is demonstrated by a general syllogism, whose individual members are explained with regard to each premise.

units.la: V. Merces Babyloni tributæ, Hierarchiæ secundùm literam conveniunt, & per varias gentes Romæ obnoxias eodem importantur.
units.tr: V. The merchandise ascribed to Babylon agrees literally with the Hierarchy, and is imported under the same heading by the various nations subject to Rome.

units.la: VI. Easdem secundùm literam in externo Hierarchicorum cultu conspicuas, & ad tabernaculi Mosaici imitationem, in cultum externum introductas esse, probatur.
units.tr: VI. It is proved that the same goods, literally visible in the external worship of the hierarchs, were introduced into external worship in imitation of the Mosaic tabernacle.

units.la: VII. Adeò ut Spiritum S. tabernam institoriam mercium, quas in externo cultu Hierarchici usurpant, & Jesuitæ novi Bezaleeles strenuè adornant, ob oculos posuisse, sit longè clarissimum.
units.tr: VII. So that it is most clear that the Holy Spirit set before our eyes the trading-booth of merchandise which the hierarchs use in external worship, and which the Jesuits, the new Bezalels, diligently furnish.

units.la: VIII. In Missa inprimis merces illæ Babylonicæ secundùm literam inveniuntur.
units.tr: VIII. Above all, those Babylonian wares are literally found in the Mass.

units.la: IX. Ex personato & theatrali externo comptu, qualem Hierarchici habent, optimè Ecclesia Christi à Babylonica distinguitur.
units.tr: IX. The Church of Christ is very well distinguished from the Babylonian by the masked and theatrical outward adornment that the hierarchs have.

units.la: X. Nundinatio Babylonica Hierarchicis magis etiam convenit secundùm allegoriam, juxta quam merces Babylonis corporales emblema sunt spiritualium, quæ in commercio habentur.
units.tr: X. The Babylonian trafficking agrees even more with the hierarchs according to allegory, according to which the corporeal wares of Babylon are an emblem of the spiritual things that are held in commerce.

units.la: XI. Habet ergò Hierarchia suos Mercatores, qui sunt Magnates terræ, quorum supremus est Papa, quem ut hac impietate eximiant perasiti ejus, Simoniam committere posse, negant.
units.tr: XI. The Hierarchy therefore has its merchants, who are the magnates of the earth, the chief of whom is the Pope, whom his parasites, to exempt him from this impiety, deny is able to commit simony.
XII. The falsity of that dogma is shown;

units.la: XIII. & verbis Friderici II. Imp. exaggeratur.
units.tr: XIII. and it is intensified by the words of the Emperor Frederick II.

units.la: XIV. Moralis Jesuitarum Theologia falsam Simoniæ definitionem excogitavit, ut Clerum crimine facilius liberet.
units.tr: XIV. Jesuit moral theology has devised a false definition of simony, so as more easily to free the clergy from the crime.

units.la: XV. Mercatores Magnates terræ sunt inprimis Cardinales, quorum nonnulli etiam Regio sanguine creti sunt.
units.tr: XV. The magnates of the earth who are merchants are above all the cardinals, some of whom are also born of royal blood.

units.la: XVI. Archiepiscopi nundinationum suarum industriâ, ex humili sorte ad dignitatem tantam quandoque provecti. Ipsi etiam Reges nonnulli, Hierarchiæ hac in re inservientes.
units.tr: XVI. Archbishops, by the industry of their trafficking, have sometimes been raised from a humble lot to such dignity. Even some kings themselves have served the Hierarchy in this matter.

units.la: XVII. Naucleri Babylonis Episcopi; Nautæ Canonici, Regulares, Seculares, Jesuitæ inprimis.
units.tr: XVII. The shipmasters of Babylon are the bishops; the sailors are the canons, the regulars, the secular clergy, and above all the Jesuits.

units.la: XVIII. Hamiß unci, quibus opes totius orbis Hierarchici ad se pertrahunt, innumerabiles sunt. Præcipui ex Erasmo compendio proponuntur.
units.tr: XVIII. The hooks, by which they draw to themselves the wealth of the whole hierarchical world, are innumerable. The principal ones are set out from Erasmus's compendium.

units.la: XIX. Hierarchia nundinationem suam ex cogitatis falsis dogmatis, quibus merces suas exponit, exercet.
units.tr: XIX. The Hierarchy carries on its trafficking by means of the false doctrines it has devised, by which it puts forward its wares.

units.la: XX. Ejus religio propria tota quæstui inservit,
units.tr: XX. Its own religion is wholly devoted to gain,

units.la: XXI. quod inductione dogmatum Hierarchiæ propriorum, per quæ fictitias suas merces extrudit, probatur,
units.tr: XXI. which is proved by the introduction of the doctrines peculiar to the Hierarchy, through which it foists off its fictitious wares,

units.la: XXII. veluti Missæ, quæ Hierarchiæ anima est,
units.tr: XXII. such as the Mass, which is the soul of the Hierarchy,

units.la: XXIII. quam ad quæstum inde occipiendum plane comparatam esse, ostenditur.
units.tr: XXIII. which is shown to have been wholly fitted for drawing profit from it.

units.la: XXIV. Quæstui eandem actu haberi, ex applicatione ejusdem ad universos & singulos;
units.tr: XXIV. That the same is in fact held for gain is shown from its application to all and to each;
XXV. according to the rules of the old and newer canons;
XXVI. it is solidly proved.

units.la: XXVII. Missa etiam civilis in Papatu nundinationis,
units.tr: XXVII. The civil Mass also is held in Papacy as the basis of trafficking,

units.la: XXVIII. nec non incolumitatis & jurium Imperiorum, Regnorum, Provinciarum, Urbium &c. fundamentum habetur.
units.tr: XXVIII. and of the safety and rights of empires, kingdoms, provinces, cities, etc.

units.la: XXIX. XXX. Cultus externus Divorum, imaginum, reliquiarum totus ad quæstum inde faciendum comparatus est.
units.tr: XXIX. XXX. The external cult of the saints, images and relics is wholly fitted for making profit from it.

units.la: XXXI. Actu quæstui eundem subservire ex apotheosi Sanctorum;
units.tr: XXXI. That it actually serves the same purpose is shown from the apotheosis of the saints;

units.la: XXXII. Festis eorundem, & peregrinationibus ad imagines & memorias eorum, Lauretana inprimis;
units.tr: XXXII. from their feast days and pilgrimages to their images and memorials, especially Loreto;
XXXIII. it is proved by the extortion of the old stationarii.

units.la: XXXIV. Orationes vicariæ Monachorum inprimis pro viventibus, & defunctis in Purgatorio, nundinationi spirituali ancillantur.
units.tr: XXXIV. The vicarious prayers of monks, especially for the living and for the dead in Purgatory, serve this spiritual trafficking.

units.la: XXXV. Monachatus ad exercendam eam aptus natus est.
units.tr: XXXV. Monasticism was born fit for carrying it on.

units.la: XXXVI. Actu etiam quæstuariam per Monachatum exerceri, ex Monachorum, Jesuitarum inprimis statu, ostenditur.
units.tr: XXXVI. That it is also actually carried on as a money-making business through monasticism is shown from the condition of the monks, especially the Jesuits.

units.la: XXXVII. Ditescendi artes a Jesuitis usitatae ex Petro Aurelio, Sorbonico doctore, & Petro Deza, explicantur.
units.tr: XXXVII. The arts of getting rich used by the Jesuits are explained from Petrus Aurelius, doctor of the Sorbonne, and Petrus Deza.

units.la: XXXVIII. Monachorum mendicantium, quibus Terminarius nomen, impudens nundinatio.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The shameless trafficking of the mendicant friars, who are called Terminarii.

units.la: XXXIX. Dominicanorum & Franciscanorum de divitiis & paupertate, Christo inprimis paupere, certamen; & Monachatus arcana, eundem vaframentum Babylonicum esse, propalant.
units.tr: XXXIX. The contest of the Dominicans and Franciscans about riches and poverty, with Christ above all poor, and the secrets of monasticism, reveal that this is the same Babylonian trick.

units.la: XL. Purgatorii fides nundiationi promovendae idonea inprimis est.
units.tr: XL. The belief in Purgatory is especially suited to promoting trafficking.
XLI. Its defenders, relying on flimsy protections,

units.la: XLII. produnt, genuinam ejus causam esse auri sacerrimam famem,
units.tr: XLII. reveal that its genuine cause is the most accursed hunger for gold,

units.la: XLIII. quod ex Bernhardino, Concilio Tridentino, Graecorum consensu, Episcopi Chemensis suffragio, probatur:
units.tr: XLIII. as is proved from Bernardine, the Council of Trent, the consent of the Greeks, and the suffrage of the Bishop of Chemnitz:

units.la: XLIV. Progressus ad abusum clavium, in Sacramento Poenitentiae;
units.tr: XLIV. The progress to the abuse of the keys in the Sacrament of Penance;

units.la: XLV. In quo Sacerdos judex sedens pro tribunali, & absolutionem promittens facile miseros ad impendenda sua omnia pellicit.
units.tr: XLV. in which the priest, sitting as judge on his tribunal and promising absolution, easily entices wretched people to spend all their goods.

units.la: XLVI. Poenitentiae inmultas pecuniarias Burchardi tempore converti coeptae sunt.
units.tr: XLVI. In the time of Burchard, penances began to be converted into large monetary fines.

units.la: XLVII. Nundinatio Poenitentiaria ex Taxis inprimis Cancellariae & Poenitentiaria, demonstratur.
units.tr: XLVII. Penitential trafficking is demonstrated from the tariffs above all of the Chancery and the Penitentiary.

units.la: XLVIII. In quibus etiam Judaeis numerata pecunia facultas blasphemandi Christum conceditur.
units.tr: XLVIII. Among these, permission to blaspheme Christ is granted even to the Jews for money counted out.

units.la: XLIX. Papa sibi casus certos, in quibus Sacerdotes absolvere nequeunt, reservavit,
units.tr: XLIX. The Pope reserved to himself certain cases in which priests cannot absolve,

units.la: L. ad stabiliendam scilicet tyrannidem, augendumque quaestum.
units.tr: L. namely to establish tyranny and to increase profit.

units.la: LI. Imperii R.de pœnitentia in aucupium pecuniæ conversa querela.
units.tr: LI. Complaint of the Imperial Diet that repentance has been turned into a snare for money.

units.la: LII. Papa extra Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum summam sibi potestatem absolvendi vendicat; prætextu thesauri meritorum Christi & Sanctorum abundantium possessi, & per indulgentias concessas applicandi.
units.tr: LII. The Pope claims for himself, outside the Sacrament of Penance, supreme power of absolving, on the pretext of possessing the abundant treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints, and of applying it through the indulgences granted.
LIII. The origin and progress of indulgences.
LIV. The old formulas of indulgences.

units.la: LV. Per Scholasticorum de indulgentiis disputationes, nundinationi fenestra aperta est; & pecuniæ pro iis datæ ut spirituales, non ut corporales considerentur sunt. Questiorum impudentia Concilii Viennensis decreto reprimitur; mox tamen Pontificum falsa interpretatione enervato.
units.tr: LV. Through the disputations of the Schoolmen about indulgences, a window was opened for trafficking; and the sums paid for them were regarded as spiritual rather than material. The shamelessness of the questors was checked by a decree of the Council of Vienne; yet soon it was weakened by the false interpretation of the Popes.

units.la: LVI. Plenam dispensandi easdem potestatem sibi Pontifices reservant, & easdem distinguunt, atque ad mortuos etiam, saltem per modum suffragii extendunt.
units.tr: LVI. The Popes reserve to themselves the full power of dispensing indulgences, and they distinguish them, and extend them even to the dead, at least by way of suffrage.

units.la: LVII. Indulgentiarum nundinæ sunt Jubilæa, auri sacra fame à Bonifacio VIII. primùm instituta,
units.tr: LVII. The markets of indulgences are the Jubilees, first instituted by Boniface VIII from a sacred hunger for gold,

units.la: LVIII. & à successoribus continuata, ac ad breviorem temporis terminum contracta.
units.tr: LVIII. and continued by his successors, and shortened to a briefer span of time.

units.la: LIX. Jis qui Jubilæi tempore Romam adire non possunt, Papa Legatis missis, & facultate certis Collegiis, Ecclesiis &c. data, aliisque modis lucrosis prospexit.
units.tr: LIX. For those who cannot go to Rome at the time of the Jubilee, the Pope provided, by sending legates and by granting the faculty to certain colleges, churches, etc., and by other profitable means.

units.la: LX. Indulgentiæ in articulo mortis concessæ, carissimo pretio emptæ; nec sine novis imposturis, & disputatione de articulo mortis vero & præsumpto.
units.tr: LX. Indulgences granted at the point of death were bought at a very dear price; nor were they without new impostures and disputes about whether the article of death was real or presumed.

units.la: LXI. Indulgentiis inserviverunt tum confessionalia, magno pretio redempta,
units.tr: LXI. Confessionals bought back at a great price served the indulgences,

units.la: LXII. tum stationes, Romanæ inprimis, quarum multiplicatio mirè nundinationem auxit.
units.tr: LXII. as did the stations, especially the Roman ones, whose multiplication greatly increased the trafficking.

units.la: LXIII. Stationum omnium indulgentiæ tantum innumerum excreverunt, ut iis nec vitæ præsentis, nec purgatorii tempus sufficiat. Unde intricatae quaestorum disputationes exortae, & à nonnullis Geometrica proportio in subsidium vocata est.
units.tr: LXIII. The indulgences of all the stations grew so innumerable that neither the time of the present life nor of Purgatory suffices for them. Hence intricate disputations of the questors arose, and some called in a geometrical proportion to their aid.

units.la: LXIV. Stationum indulgentiae absentibus pro pecunia per quaestores vendi incipiunt.
units.tr: LXIV. The indulgences of the stations begin to be sold for money to absent persons through questors.

units.la: LXV. Fabula putidissima de plenaria indulgentia sine pecunia in Ecclesia S. Mariae de Angelis apud Assisium per Franciscum à Christo impetrata, indulgentiariae illorum temporum nundinationis testis est.
units.tr: LXV. The most putrid fable of a plenary indulgence without money in the Church of St Mary of the Angels at Assisi, obtained from Christ by Francis, is a witness to the indulgence-trafficking of those times.

units.la: LXVI. Nundinationi eidem optimi quinque contradixerunt, inprimis Wilhelmus Durandus, Schola Parisiensis, Wesselus Groningensis, Joh. Vesalienfis, &c.
units.tr: LXVI. Five excellent men opposed this same trafficking, above all William Durand of the Paris school, Wessel of Groningen, John of Wesel, etc.

units.la: LXVII. donec Deus collybisticas illas mensas Leone X. authore impudentissimè exercitas in Germania per Lutherum;
units.tr: LXVII. until God, through Luther, exposed and overthrew those money-changers' tables, shamelessly run in Germany under Leo X as their author;

units.la: LXVIII. in Helvetia per Zwingelium detexit evertitque.
units.tr: LXVIII. and in Helvetia through Zwingli.
LXIX. The simony of Leo X is demonstrated.

units.la: LXX. LXXI. LXXII. & nequicquam à Pallavicino desensa.
units.tr: LXX. LXXI. LXXII. and in vain defended by Pallavicino.

units.la: LXXIII. Statuum Imperii Gravamina adversus indulgentiarum nundinationem.
units.tr: LXXIII. The grievances of the Estates of the Empire against the trafficking in indulgences.

units.la: LXXIV. LXXV. Tridentinum de indulgentiis decretum eidem finem non imposuisse, ex verbis, declaratione ejusdem, & praxi ostenditur.
units.tr: LXXIV. LXXV. It is shown from the words, the declaration of the same, and the practice, that the Tridentine decree on indulgences did not put an end to it.

units.la: LXXVI. Sciopii clamoribus, quòd indulgentias Papa hodie nullas vendat, occurritur.
units.tr: LXXVI. The clamours of Sciopius, that the Pope today sells no indulgences, are answered.

units.la: LXXVII. Transitur ad Sacramentum Ordinis, in quo abusuum Oceanum Veronensis Episcopus notavit.
units.tr: LXXVII. We pass to the Sacrament of Orders, in which the Bishop of Verona noted an ocean of abuses.

units.la: LXXVIII. Origo & progressus nundinationis circa collationem ipsam ordinum.
units.tr: LXXVIII. The origin and progress of the trafficking concerning the very conferral of the orders.

units.la: LXXIX. LXXX. De ea in Concilio Tridentino exorta disceptatio eum finem habuit, ut ex decreto ejusdem tum praeterita circa eandem nundinatio solidè convincatur, tum in futurum parùm Simoniæ illi præcautem esse, colligatur.
units.tr: LXXIX. LXXX. The dispute that arose about this at the Council of Trent had the outcome that, from its decree, both the past trafficking about it is solidly convicted, and it is inferred that little precaution against that simony is taken for the future.

units.la: LXXXI. Major longè in collatione beneficiorum à collatione ordinum separata, Simonia in Papatu grassatur, quæ verbis Espencæi & M. A. de Dominis generaliter perstringitur.
units.tr: LXXXI. Simony rages far more widely in the Papacy in the conferral of benefices than in the conferral of orders, and it is condemned in general terms in the words of Espencaeus and M. A. de Dominis.

units.la: LXXXII. Basis nundinationis illius est, quòd Papa se supremum beneficiorum Dominum profitetur.
units.tr: LXXXII. The basis of this trafficking is that the Pope professes himself the supreme lord of benefices.

units.la: LXXXIII. Controversia ab eodem Imperatoribus de investituris mota.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The controversy raised by the same Pope against the Emperors concerning investitures.
LXXXIV. The papal trafficking in benefices through expectatives,
LXXXV. through reservations of vacant benefices,
LXXXVI. through the introduced pluralities of benefices,

units.la: LXXXVII. de quarum abominatione gravissimè Gerson & Duarenus questi sunt,
units.tr: LXXXVII. at whose abomination Gerson and Duaren complained most bitterly.
LXXXVIII. through commendams,
LXXXIX. through unions of benefices,

units.la: XC. per Permutationes, Devolutiones eorundem, Pensiones, quarum fœditatem ipsi quandoque Canonistæ detestantur.
units.tr: XC. through exchanges, devolutions of the same, pensions, whose foulness the Canonists themselves sometimes detest.

units.la: XCI. Simoniacarum harum technarum successus demonstratur tum in Cardinalium,
units.tr: XCI. The success of these simoniacal devices is shown both in the elevation of Cardinals

units.la: XCII. tum in Curiæ Romanæ ministrorum, & Papæ adulatorum ac clientum exaltatione, in Anglia maximè;
units.tr: XCII. and in the advancement of the ministers of the Roman Curia and of the flatterers and clients of the Pope, especially in England;

units.la: XCIII. Germania de Curtisanis, Romanis nebulonibus quiritante,
units.tr: XCIII. Germany complains of the Curtisans, the Roman scoundrels;
XCIV. Helvetia, France.

units.la: XCV. XCVI. XCVII. XCVIII. Eadem Beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum nundinatio porrò demonstratur ex Annatis apertissimè Simoniacis;
units.tr: XCV. XCVI. XCVII. XCVIII. The same trafficking in ecclesiastical benefices is further shown by the annates, which are most openly simoniacal;
XCIX. by the most unjust exaction for the pallium of archbishops,
C. by the pretence of a divine right to tithes.

units.la: CI. Tributis gravissimus Clero à Pontifice impositis, veluti Decima quinta, Decima, Quinta, Tertia, Medietate, &c.
units.tr: CI. by the most grievous taxes laid upon the clergy by the Pontiff, such as the fifteenth, the tenth, the fifth, the third, the half, etc.

units.la: CII. aliisque expilationibus beneficiorum Ecclesiæ & Cleri multifariis.
units.tr: CII. and by the manifold other plunderings of the benefices of the Church and clergy.

units.la: CIII. In regimine Ecclesiæ Hierarchia nundinatur leges tum Divinas, matrimoniales inprimis, per dispensationes circa easdem, in matrimonius vetitis contrahendis,
units.tr: CIII. In the government of the Church the hierarchy trades in the laws, both divine and especially matrimonial, through dispensations concerning them, in permitting marriages that are forbidden,

units.la: CIV. & contractus pro libitu Papæ dissolvendis;
units.tr: CIV. and in dissolving contracts at the Pope's pleasure;
CV. as well as in the relaxation of oaths;
CVI. and of vows, especially monastic ones;

units.la: CVII. cui Denarius S. Petri, nobile Papæ tributum, originem debet,
units.tr: CVII. to which the Peter's Pence, the noble tribute of the Pope, owes its origin;

units.la: CVIII. quin & lenoniam, quam pro pecunia Papa indulget.
units.tr: CVIII. indeed also the licence to sin for money, which the Pope grants.

units.la: CIX. Tum humanas & Ecclesiasticas, quas lucri ex dispensatione earundem captandi gratia multiplicavit idem; ad quas inprimis leges compositionum sic dictæ referendæ sunt.
units.tr: CIX. Also the human and ecclesiastical laws which the same man has multiplied for the sake of seeking profit from dispensing them; to these especially the so-called laws of composition are to be referred.

units.la: CX. Dispensationum illarum pretia Taxa Pœnitentiaria definivit.
units.tr: CX. The Penitentiary Taxa fixed the prices of those dispensations.
CXI. These circulate most widely,

units.la: CXII. & in foro etiam conscientiæ tutæ pronuntiantur.
units.tr: CXII. and are declared safe even in the court of conscience.

units.la: CXIII. In eodem Ecclesiæ regimine Hierarchia nundinatur judicia, seu causas ad tribunal Romanum per acceptas ab omnibus terris appellationes sevocatas, de qua re querelæ Urspergensis; ipsius Imperii Romani.
units.tr: CXIII. In the same government of the Church the hierarchy trades in judgments, that is, in causes drawn to the Roman tribunal by appeals received from all lands; of this matter the complaints of Urspergensis,
CXIV. of Bernard of Clairvaux,

units.la: CXV. & Johannis Gropperi in Concilio Tridentino motæ, & à Job. Baptista Castello nequicquam repulsæ panduntur.
units.tr: CXV. and of John Gropper, raised at the Council of Trent and vainly rejected by Giovanni Battista Castelli, are set out.

units.la: CXVI. Pertinent eodem causæ matrimoniales, quas Sacramenti prætextu, ad forum suum Hierarchia pertraxit.
units.tr: CXVI. To the same heading belong the matrimonial cases, which the hierarchy has drawn to its own forum under the pretext of the sacrament.

units.la: CXVII. CXVIII. Nundinationes Hierarchicæ operum pietatis & charitatis ex quæstuis eleemosynarum;
units.tr: CXVII. CXVIII. The hierarchical trafficking in works of piety and charity from the profits of almsgiving;
CXIX. in the hunting for wills,
CXX. in the usurious lending of the pious pawnshops (Monti di pietà);
CXXI. is proved by the tricks of donations.
CXXII. The trafficking in blessings and consecrations is described.

units.la: CXXIII. ad quam etiam corporum & cadaverum nundinatio, per quæstum ex sepultura occæptum, refertur.
units.tr: CXXIII. To this also is referred the trafficking in bodies and corpses, through the gain begun from burial.

units.la: CXXIV. In jurisdictione Papali, universa animarum fœda nundinatio exercetur.
units.tr: CXXIV. In papal jurisdiction the whole foul trade in souls is carried on.

units.la: CXXV. ad quam animarum in seminariis Romanis cauponatio jure refertur.
units.tr: CXXV. To this the peddling of souls in the Roman seminaries is rightly referred.

units.la: CXXVI. Nundinationi Hierarchicorum inserviunt tum leges & canones Ecclesiæ, quibus eadem sic firmatur, ut justitiæ speciem accipiat;
units.tr: CXXVI. The laws and canons of the Church also serve the trafficking of the hierarchs, by which it is so confirmed that it takes on the appearance of justice;
CXXVII. the liberties of the Church being hidden under a veil.

units.la: CXXVIII. Tum censuræ Ecclesiasticæ, quibus nundinationi illi resistentes, feriuntur,
units.tr: CXXVIII. Then there are the ecclesiastical censures, with which those resisting that trafficking are struck,

units.la: CXXIX. & quæ quandoque grandi pecuniæ summâ remittuntur;
units.tr: CXXIX. and which are sometimes remitted for a large sum of money;

units.la: CXXX. quin etiam Sacramento fidelitatis, quo Episcopos Papa sibi obnoxios fecit, corroborantur.
units.tr: CXXX. indeed they are even strengthened by the oath of fealty, by which the Pope has bound the bishops to himself.
CXXXI. Finally, there are the many workshops and shops,

units.la: CXXXII. quas inter Romæ Pœnitentiaria & Dataria eminent. In Dataria cuduntur Bullae, quarum vanitas ostenditur.
units.tr: CXXXII. among which at Rome the Penitentiary and the Datary stand out. In the Datary the Bulls are minted, and their emptiness is shown.

units.la: CXXXIII. Bonifacii VIII. pro Bullarum necessitate ra‐ tiunculae discutiuntur.
units.tr: CXXXIII. The petty arguments of Boniface VIII for the necessity of the Bulls are examined.
CXXXIV. The Apostolic Chamber is the Pope's treasury.

units.la: CXXXV. Nundinationis Romanensium fructus sunt divitiae Cleri, & expilationes Regnorum.
units.tr: CXXXV. The fruits of the Roman trafficking are the riches of the clergy and the plundering of kingdoms.

units.la: CXXXVI. Romam gentilem insatiabilis divitiarum cupiditas per didit.
units.tr: CXXXVI. An insatiable lust for riches destroyed pagan Rome.

units.la: CXXXVII. Eadem Romam quoque Christianam pessum‐ dedit,
units.tr: CXXXVII. The same lust also ruined Christian Rome,

units.la: CXXXVIII. quae eò vecordia processit, ut divitias ve‐ rae Ecclesiae notam faceret.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. which proceeded to such madness that it made riches a mark of the true Church.

units.la: CXXXIX. Roma artibus suis Germaniam, Galliam, Angliam, Hispaniam, alidque Regna & Nationes hor‐ rendum in modum expilavit.
units.tr: CXXXIX. By its arts Rome has plundered Germany, France, England, Spain, and other kingdoms and nations in a horrible manner.

units.la: CXL. Johannis xxy. opulentia à Paulo Langio meritò sugillata.
units.tr: CXL. The opulence of John XXV was rightly rebuked by Paul Lang.

units.la: CXLI. Thomae Aquinatis ad Innocentium III. divitias suas jactantem, apophtegma.
units.tr: CXLI. The saying of Thomas Aquinas to Innocent III, boasting of his riches.

units.la: CXLII. Erarii Papalis subindè languescentis causae.
units.tr: CXLII. The causes of the Papal treasury's occasional decline.

units.la: CXLIII. Objectio Hierarchicorum, ab Ecclesiae Roma‐ nae necessitatibus, & sumptuum faciendorum magnitu‐ dine petita, discutitur.
units.tr: CXLIII. The objection of the hierarchs, drawn from the needs of the Roman Church and the magnitude of the expenses to be met, is examined.

units.la: CXLIV. Nundinatio Hierarchicorum testimoniis dome‐ sticis, convincitur.
units.tr: CXLIV. The trafficking of the hierarchs is refuted by domestic testimonies.

units.la: CXLV. Testes inducuntur ex Seculo Decimo, Otho III. Imperator, & Magister ejus Gerbertus.
units.tr: CXLV. Witnesses are brought forward from the tenth century: Emperor Otto III and his teacher Gerbert.

units.la: CXLVI. Ex Undecimo Leo ix. Papa, Petrus Damia‐ ni Cardinalis, Jao Carnotensis;
units.tr: CXLVI. From the eleventh: Pope Leo IX, Peter Damian the Cardinal, John of Chartres;
CXLVII. Bernard of Corbie.

units.la: CXLVIII. Ex Seculo Duodecimo Fridericus I. Imp.
units.tr: CXLVIII. From the twelfth century: Emperor Frederick I.

units.la: CXLIX. CL. Bernhardus Claraevallensis. CLI. Thomas Cantuariensis, Johannes Sarisberiensis, Petrus Blesensis. CLII. Ex seculo Decimo-tertio Richardus Angliæ, & Alphonsus Arragoniæ Reges. CLIII. Stephanus Tornacensis, Guilhelmus Durandus Mimatensis, Petrus Thullensis, & Eberhardus Salisburgensis Episcopi. CLIV. Ex Seculo Decimo-quarto Ludovicus Bavarus Imp. CLV. Alvarus Pelagius. CLVI. Franciscus Petrarcha, Marsilius Patavinus & Albericus Roxiatus. CLVII. Ex Seculo Decimo-quinto Regum Galliæ Sanctiæ Pragmatica: Ecclesiæ Græcæ. CLVIII. Æneas Sylvius, Cardinalis Cusanus. CLIX. Nicolaus Clemangis. CLX. Laurentius Valla, Baptista Mantuanus. CLXI. Ex Seculo Decimo-sexto Imperator Maximilianus I. Hadrianus VI. Cardinales Pauli III. CLXII. Franciscus Duarenus; Dominicus Soto, Jason, Budaeus, Erasmus, Espencaeus, Sansovinus. CLXIII. Nundinationem Hierarchicorum morbum incurabilem esse, ex historia Concilii Basileensis, CLXIV. & Tridentini, demonstratur. CLXV. Argumentum concluditur.
units.tr: CXLIX. CL. Bernard of Clairvaux. CLI. Thomas of Canterbury, John of Salisbury, Peter of Blois. CLII. From the thirteenth century: the kings Richard of England and Alfonso of Aragon. CLIII. The bishops Stephen of Tournai, Guillaume Durand of Mende, Peter of Toulouse, and Eberhard of Salzburg. CLIV. From the fourteenth century: Emperor Louis of Bavaria. CLV. Alvarus Pelagius. CLVI. Francis Petrarch, Marsilius of Padua, and Albericus of Rosciate. CLVII. From the fifteenth century: the Pragmatic Sanction of the kings of France; the Greek Church. CLVIII. Aeneas Sylvius, Cardinal Cusanus. CLIX. Nicolas Clemanges. CLX. Lorenzo Valla, Baptista Mantuanus. CLXI. From the sixteenth century: Emperor Maximilian I, Adrian VI, the Cardinals of Paul III. CLXII. Francis Duaren; Dominic Soto, Jason, Budé, Erasmus, Espencaeus, Sansovino. CLXIII. That the trafficking of the hierarchs is an incurable disease is shown from the history of the Council of Basel, CLXIV. and of Trent. CLXV. The argument is concluded.

units.la: I. Lalsos doctores, perditas quandoque hæreses in Ecclesiam invecturos, & in consortium erroris perditionisque complures, per quos via veritatis blasphemabitur, tracturos, hac interalias nota Spiritus S. 2. Pet. II. 2 distinguit: ... Per avaritiam fictis sermonibus vos quæstui habebunt, vel negotiabuntur. Ficti illi sermones μύθοι fabulæ sunt, sermones & doctrinæ artificiosè ad hoc comparatæ, ut qui eos proferunt, hominibus placeant, eos sibi devinciant, & in potestatem suam redigant; quo ex iis pro lubitu lucrum emolumentúmque terrenum accipiant.
units.tr: I. The false teachers who will at times bring destructive heresies into the Church, and draw many into the fellowship of error and perdition, through whom the way of truth will be blasphemed, the Holy Spirit distinguishes by this mark among others, 2 Pet. II. 2: "Through covetousness they will exploit you with feigned words" [ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ]. Those feigned words are fables [μύθοι], words and teachings artfully devised so that those who utter them may please men, bind them to themselves, and bring them under their power, so that they may take from them at will gain and earthly profit.

units.la: II. Ejusmodi ἐμπορίαν negotiationem, nundinationem etiam Babyloni M. Spiritus Dei tribuit Apoc. xviii. n. 12. ubi mentio est ἐμπορων mercatorum, qui v. 23. Μεγιστᾶνες Magnates terræ vocantur; nec non γένος mercimonii, puta auri, argenti, lapidis pretiosi, margaritæ, byssi, purpuræ, serici, coccini, ligni odorati, vasis eburnei, omnis vasis ex ligno pretiosissimo, & ære, & ferro, & marmore, & cinnamomi, & odoramentorum, & myri, & thuris, & vini, & olei, & similaginis, & tritici, & jumentorum, & ovium, & equorum, & rhedarum, & corporum, & animarum hominum &c. Neque tantùm Mercatorum ejusmodi, sed etiam v. 17. Gubernatores, turbæ in navibus, nautæ, & ex mari quæstum facientium mentio est.
units.tr: II. The Spirit of God also ascribes such trading [ἐμπορίαν], traffic, to Babylon, Apoc. xviii. 12, where mention is made of merchants [ἐμπόρων], who in verse 23 are called the magnates of the earth [Μεγιστᾶνες]; and also of the kind of merchandise [γένος], namely gold, silver, precious stone, pearl, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, scented wood, ivory vessels, every vessel of most precious wood, and of bronze, and of iron, and of marble, and of cinnamon, and of spices, and of myrrh, and of frankincense, and of wine, and of oil, and of fine flour, and of wheat, and of beasts of burden, and of sheep, and of horses, and of chariots, and of the bodies, and of the souls of men, etc. And mention is made not only of such merchants, but also, in verse 17, of the governors, the crowds in the ships, the sailors, and those who make their gain from the sea.

units.la: III. Possunt hæc secundùm literam intelligi, siquidem in Babylone, cèu Regno terreno, spirituali nomine fucato licet, hoc agitur, ut rebus talibus homines affluant; & ut potestas sit illas vendendi aliis. Quia tamen destructa Babylone merces hasce nemo ampliùs emere v.11. dicitur, adeóque ex Babyloni propriæ vendicantur, cùm merces hæ secundùm literam acceptæ communes sint gentibus, tum ante Babylonem existentes, tum eâ deletâ superstites futuræ in commercio hominum; potius est, ut primariò non secundùm literam, sed ἀλληγορικῶς isthæc explicentur.
units.tr: III. These things can be understood according to the letter, since in Babylon, as an earthly kingdom, though under the disguised name of the spiritual, this is done: that men may flow in abundance of such things, and that there may be power to sell them to others. Yet since, Babylon having been destroyed, no one is said to buy these wares any more (v. 11), and so they are claimed from Babylon's own domain, and since these wares, taken according to the letter, are common to the nations, both those existing before Babylon and those which will remain in human commerce after it has been destroyed, it is rather the case that these things are to be explained primarily not according to the letter but allegorically [ἀλληγορικῶς].

units.la: Sic aurum, principalis Babylonis merx, est emblema Dei, Spiritus S. Verbi Dei: argentum puritatis naturæ humanæ Christi; lapis pretiosus & margaritæ S. Petri & Apostolorum: byssus iustitiæ Sanctorum: purpura passionum Christi: sericum novæ obedientiæ & sanctitatis fidelium: coccinum passionum Sanctorum: lignum odoratum hominum natorum in horto Dei, præditorum spiritu vitæ & fragrantia sive bonorum operum,sive doctrina: vasa ex ebore, ligno pretioso, ære, ferro, marmore omnium eorum, qui in Ecclesia usum aliquem habent, sive docendo, sive muniendo, protegendo: cinnamomum doni sanationis: suffimenta orationum Sanctorum pro se vel aliis: unguentum charismatis virtutum illustrium: Thus oblationis pro peccatis: vinum verbi Dei omnia recreantis: oleum consolationis: similago doctrinæ de perfectione Christiana: triticum doctrinæ de Christianæ pietatis initiis: jumenta homines portantia, & in arvis laborantia eorum, qui ministrant: Oves eorum, qui pascuntur, subsunt: Equi populorum, regnorum, principum: quadrigæ eorum, quæ Regibus, principibus vehendis inserviunt: corpora poenarum corporalium: animæ spirituum, qui vel occiduntur, vel redimuntur.
