units.tr: Thus gold, the principal merchandise of Babylon, is the emblem of God, of the Holy Spirit, and of the Word of God; silver of the purity of Christ's human nature; precious stone and pearls of St. Peter and the Apostles; fine linen of the righteousness of the saints; purple of the sufferings of Christ; silk of the new obedience and holiness of the faithful; scarlet of the sufferings of the saints; scented wood of men born in the garden of God, endowed with the spirit of life and the fragrance either of good works or of doctrine; vessels of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron, marble of all those who have some use in the Church, whether by teaching, fortifying, or protecting; cinnamon of the gift of healing; incense of the prayers of the saints for themselves or others; ointment of the charisms of illustrious virtues; frankincense of the offering for sins; wine of the Word of God, which refreshes all things; oil of consolation; fine flour of the doctrine of Christian perfection; wheat of the doctrine of the beginnings of Christian piety; beasts of burden, men who carry burdens and labour in the fields for those who minister; sheep are those who are fed and are subject; horses of peoples, kingdoms, and princes; chariots of those who serve to carry kings and princes; bodies of bodily punishments; souls of spirits who are either slain or redeemed.

units.la: IV. Atque hi Babylonii mercatores hæ Babyloniæ mercès sunt, quas, quisquis non plane oscitanter consideravenit, in Ecclesiæ Romanæ Hierarchia nullo negotio reperiet; sive secundùm literam, sive allegoricè explicentur. Id verò Syllogismo sequenti probatum clarissimè dabimus: Ille cœtus avaritia & nundinatione spirituali se immaniter polluit, adeoque cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est, in quo merces illæ Babyloni tributæ reperiuntur tum ad literam, in cultu externo & Missa inprimis: tum secundùm allegoriam, juxta quam habet magnos mercatores, gubernatores, naucleros, & nautas, & lucri causa Christum, falsa dogmata confinxit, atque sic in Missa Deum, remissionem peccatorum: in cultu reliquo externo Sanctorum, Imaginum & reliquiarum invocatarum opem & intercessionem apud Deum, nec non viventium, Monachorum inprimis, pro viventibus & defunctis in fictitio Purgatorio laborantibus vicarias orationes, oblationes, suffragia & supererogationis merita in Sacramento Poenitentiæ, & extra illud in applicatione Thesauri meritorum Christi & Sanctorum abundantium per indulgentiarum dispensationem inprimis, claves Regni Cœlorum: in Sacramento Ordinis collationem tum Ordinum, adeoque ipsum Spiritum S. tum beneficiorum: in regimine Ecclesiæ tum leges & Divinas & humanas, tum judicia & censuras ecclesiasticas: in communione externa Ecclesiæ opera pietatis & charitatis: in Sanctificatione externa benedictiones & consecrationes rerum: denique in jurisdictione universa animas hominum in commercio habet, suamque illam nundinationem legibus, censuriisque firmat, & in publicis officinis impune exercet, neque, reclamantibus licet optimis quibusque, ea inre emendationem petitur.
units.tr: IV. And these Babylonian merchants and Babylonian wares are what anyone who has not considered the matter with careless yawning will find without any difficulty in the hierarchy of the Roman Church, whether they are explained literally or allegorically. We shall prove this most clearly by the following syllogism: That assembly defiles itself monstrously with greed and spiritual trafficking; and therefore, other things being equal, it is Babylon the Great, in which those wares are found that are sold to Babylon, both literally, in the external worship and above all in the Mass; and allegorically, according to which it has great merchants, governors, shipmasters and sailors, and for the sake of gain has invented false doctrines, so that in the Mass they have God and the remission of sins for sale; in the rest of the external worship, the help and intercession of the saints, images and invoked relics with God, and also of the living, especially monks, who offer vicarious prayers, oblations, suffrages and works of supererogation for the living and the dead who are suffering in an imaginary Purgatory; in the Sacrament of Penance, and outside it in applying the treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints, which abounds, chiefly through the dispensing of indulgences, the keys of the kingdom of heaven; in the Sacrament of Orders, the conferring of orders, and thus of the Holy Spirit himself, and of benefices; in the governing of the Church, both divine and human laws, and judgments and ecclesiastical censures; in the external communion of the Church, works of piety and charity; in external sanctification, blessings and consecrations of things; and finally, in its whole jurisdiction it holds the souls of men in commerce, and it confirms that trafficking by laws and censures, and carries it on with impunity in public workshops; and although all the best men protest, no amendment is sought in this matter.

units.la: Atqui in Hierarchia, seu Clero Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem merces Babylonis tributa reperiuntur tum ad literam, in cultu externo & Missa inprimis: tum secundùm allegoriam, juxta quam illa habet magnos Mercatores, gubernatores, naucleros & nautas, & lucri causa falsa dogmata confinxit, atque sic in Missa Deum, Christum, remissionem peccatorum: in cultu reliquo externo Sanctorum, Imaginum & reliquiarum invocatarum opem & intercessionem apud Deum, nec non viventium, Monachorum inprimis, pro viventibus & defunctis in fictitio Purgatorio laborantibus vicarias orationes, oblationes, suffragia & supererogationis merita: in Sacramento Poenitentiæ & extra illud in applicatione thesauri meritorum Christi & Sanctorum abundantium, per indulgentiarum dispensationem inprimis, claves Regni Cœlorum: in Sacramento Ordinis collationem tum Ordinum, adeo-que que ipsum Spiritum S. tum beneficiorum: in regimine Ecclesiæ tum leges & Divinas & humanas, tum judicia & censuras ecclesiasticas: in communione externa Ecclesiæ opera pietatis & charitatis: in Sanctificatione externa benedictiones & consecrationes rerum: denique in jurisdictione universa, animas hominum in commercio habet; suamque illam nundinationem legibus & censuris firmat, & in publicis officinis impune exercet; neque, reclamantibus licet optimis quibusque, ea in re emendationem patitur.
units.tr: But in the Hierarchy, or clergy, of the Roman Church, which dominates, the wares of Babylon are found, both literally, in the external worship and above all in the Mass; and allegorically, according to which it has great merchants, governors, shipmasters and sailors, and for the sake of gain has invented false doctrines, so that in the Mass they have God, Christ and the remission of sins for sale; in the rest of the external worship, the help and intercession of the saints, images and invoked relics with God, and also of the living, especially monks, who offer vicarious prayers, oblations, suffrages and works of supererogation for the living and the dead who are suffering in an imaginary Purgatory; in the Sacrament of Penance, and outside it in applying the treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints, which abounds, chiefly through the dispensing of indulgences, the keys of the kingdom of heaven; in the Sacrament of Orders, the conferring of orders, and thus of the Holy Spirit himself, and of benefices; in the governing of the Church, both divine and human laws, and judgments and ecclesiastical censures; in the external communion of the Church, works of piety and charity; in external sanctification, blessings and consecrations of things; and finally, in its whole jurisdiction it holds the souls of men in commerce, and it confirms that trafficking by laws and censures, and carries it on with impunity in public workshops; and, although all the best men protest, it suffers no amendment in this matter.

units.la: Ergo Hierarchia, seu Clerus Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominans avaritia & nundinatione spirituali sese immaniter polluit, adeoque, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the Hierarchy, or the dominant clergy of the Roman Church, defiles itself monstrously with greed and spiritual trafficking, and so, other things being equal, it is Babylon the Great.

units.la: Propositionem utramque, pluribus quippe membris constantem, ἀτὰ μέρῳ demonstrabimus.
units.tr: We shall demonstrate both propositions, which consist of several parts, part by part [κατὰ μέρος].

units.la: V. Ibi, cæteris paribus, esse Babylonem Magnam, ubi merces eidem nundinanti tributæ, ad literam etiam conspicuæ sunt, dubitationem habere nullam potest. In Hierarchia autem Romana conspicuas esse, quis inficias iverit? Ubi enim terrarum rerum earum copia major & abundantior est? Sicut olim gentes diversæ talibus Tyrum, nobilissimum emporium occuparunt, Ezech. xxvii. sic plane populi omnes in Roma & Hierarchia mercibus hisditanda & dotanda, certare videntur. Aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos &c. ex ultimis Indiis Hispani per Oceanum advehentes, universam Europam iisdem beant; atque omnes Europæ populi tandem ea Romæ tantum non exonerant, iisque Hierarchiam mactant. Cinnamomum, suffitum, unguentum, thus & vinum Itali ipsi per internum mare ex Græcia, Cilicia, Arabia, Ægypto, Africa afportant, earumque rerum copiam toti fere Europæ faciunt; cùm insuper eorum tellus deliciarum genus omne feracissima sit. Similam & triticum Sicilia & Sardinia, horrea & penariæ cellæ Italiæ : jumenta Germania : oves Anglia: equos ac rhedas Gallia: corpora Helvetia : animas populi omnes, superstitionibus imbuendas suppeditant. Atque iidem populi merces hasce Romam serentes, eidem Romæ veƚigales fuerunt, vel etiamnum sunt. Sed hoc parùm forte videbitur, quia horum æstimatio & negotiatio non ex una Roma pendet. Nisi forte sublato tam avido emptore multò viliora illa erunt, quod ipsum etiam post Reformationem contigisse videmus, profanis etiam Mercatoribus dolentibus, tam copiosæ negotiationis, & ditescendi occasionem sibi interceptam esse, quam in his ipsis rebus sub florente olim Papatu habuerunt.
units.tr: V. That, other things being equal, that is Babylon the Great where the wares are sold to the one trafficking in them, and are also visible in the literal sense, admits of no doubt. But who could deny that they are visible in the Roman Hierarchy? For where on earth is there a greater and more abundant supply of such things? Just as once different nations occupied Tyre, the most noble market, with such goods (Ezek. 27), so all peoples seem to vie with one another in Rome and the Hierarchy to be laden and enriched with these wares. Spaniards, bringing gold, silver, precious stones, etc. from the farthest Indies across the ocean, enrich the whole of Europe with them; and all the peoples of Europe at last nearly unload them at Rome, and thereby fatten the Hierarchy. Cinnamon, incense, ointment, frankincense and wine the Italians themselves bring over the inland sea from Greece, Cilicia, Arabia, Egypt and Africa, and supply nearly all of Europe with that abundance of goods, since their own land is most fertile in every kind of delight. Semolina and wheat come from Sicily and Sardinia, the granaries and storerooms of Italy; beasts of burden from Germany; sheep from England; horses and carriages from France; bodies from Switzerland; souls all the peoples supply, to be steeped in superstitions. And these same peoples, bringing these wares to Rome, were, or still are, tributaries to that same Rome. But this will perhaps seem a small matter, because the valuation and trade in these things does not depend on Rome alone. Unless perhaps, with such a greedy buyer removed, those things would be much cheaper; which we see happened even after the Reformation, when even secular merchants complained that the opportunity of such a copious trade and of getting rich, which they had once had in these very things under the flourishing Papacy, had been cut off from them.

units.la: VI. Majùs illud est, quòd merces illas ad literam etiam in externo Hierarchiæ cultu, Missa inprimis, ejusque instrumentis, clarissimè omnium cernere est. Olim quidem pleraque illa, quæ hic inter merces Babylonis Spiritus S. refert, in Tabernaculo à Mose, Deo mandante, extructo comparuerunt, uti ex Exod. xxv. & xxxv. colligi potest; exceptis forte ψυχαῖς animabus hominum, quale mercium genus non solùm apud Mosen non habetur, sed toti ante hac mundo, cœloque & inferno incognitum fuit; soli tabernæ Babylonis & Hierarchiæ proprium. Porrò S. Johannes, dum nos sic ad Tabernaculi veteris apparatum deducit, Babylonis Magnæ κατοικία nobis considerandam proponit, qua veteris Sacerdotii operosam supelleƚilem, à Deo ipso jam reprobatam, ab Apostolis abrogatam, & cum veteri Synagoga sepultam, in Ecclesiæ Catholicæ simplicissimum cultum proprio usu reduxit, & per eandem hinc doƚrinam de Christo obscuravit, illinc peculium ejus supra modum aggravavit, ut sic non Christo solummodo, sed etiam Mosi contrariam ostenderet, qui per hæc olim involucra Christi, tum adhuc venturi, mysterium typicè adumbraverat.
units.tr: VI. What is greater is that these wares are seen most clearly of all, literally, even in the external worship of the Hierarchy, above all in the Mass and its instruments. Indeed, many of those things which the Holy Spirit here lists among the wares of Babylon once appeared in the Tabernacle built by Moses at God's command, as can be gathered from Exodus 25 and 35; perhaps with the exception of souls [ψυχαῖς], a kind of merchandise which is not only not found in Moses but was unknown to the whole world, heaven and hell until now; it belongs solely to the shop of Babylon and the Hierarchy. Moreover, St John, while leading us in this way to the furnishings of the old Tabernacle, sets before us the dwelling-place [κατοικία] of Great Babylon to be considered, in which he has brought back into the simplest worship of the Catholic Church, for its own use, the laborious equipment of the old priesthood, already rejected by God himself, abrogated by the Apostles, and buried with the old Synagogue; and from there, on one side, he has obscured the doctrine of Christ through the same, and on the other has burdened its peculiar people beyond measure. Thus he shows that it is contrary not only to Christ but also to Moses, who once through these veils foreshadowed in types the mystery of Christ, still to come.

units.la: VII. Mirum planè, si non erubescant Hierarchici mangenes & propolæ, quoties in Inventarium illud tabernæ Babylonicæ, proprium mercium suarum indicem, inciducent. Ejus quidem apparatus commodè duas in classes distribuitur, in instrumenta nimirum idololatriæ, cultúsque idololatrici, per quæ is exercetur & exornatur, nec non instrumenta avaritiæ, luxûs, fastûs, quem sub eodem tam in Sacrificulatûs officio, quàm in victu & amictu exercent. Ibi, si uspiam alibi, merces argenti, lapidis pretiosi, margaritarum, byssi, purpuræ, serici, cocci, omne lignum thyinum, omne vas eburneum, omne vas ex ligno pretiosissimo, ære, ferro, marmore; cinnamomum, suffitum, unguentum (seu chrisma) thus, vinum, oleum, similam, triticum, jumenta, oves, equos, rhedas, mancipia; notissimæ, usitatissimæ, vulgatissimæ sunt. An, Jesuitæ, novi Bezaleeles, in his ipsis mercibus denuò interpolandis, exornandáque hâc Tabernâ nescio quod novum artificium nobis ostentantes, sic frontem perfricuistis, ut, inspectâ Babylonicâ hâc mercium tabernâ, vestras in cultu & sacrarum personarum vestrarum usu omni, spirituali negotatione subjectas non recognoscatis merces, & erubescatis toti? Nisi forte in vobis illud Germanorum impletur adagium: Quando Diabolus meretricem creavit, unà frontem meretriciam creavit. Sed quicquid etiam vos dissimuletis, vel talpa Tiresia cæcior videbit in cultu vestro obvias hasce merces: Aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, margaritas, byssum, purpuram, aut coccum in Missali idolo, Papa, Cardinalibus, aliisque Magnatibus Babylonicis eorúmque Ministris exornandis: lignum thyinum in Templorum testudinibus adornandis sculpendisque idolis: thura, suffimenta in imaginibus colendis: lignum, æs, ferrum, marmor, in imaginibus iisdem, aliisque utensilibus sacris fabricandis: cinnamomum, odoresque aromaticos similes & unguenta in sacris unctionibus conficiendis: similam & triticum in Numine Panaceo producendo: vinum in calice aurato, quod solus Sacrificulus conficiens pitissat: jumenta, puta vituli, ovesque seu agni Dei, & sacra vellera: equi, rhedæ, corpora, rhedas bijugas, quadrijugas, sejugas, id est, equos binos, quaternos, senosve habentes, & pedisequos utrinque ad latera rhedæ currentes, qui Σωμαῖοι corpora hic vocantur; non eo solum sensu, quo vox ea servos, mancipia significat, quales certe etiam pedisequi ii sunt; sed eo etiam, quòd hi servuli nudi, id est, sine pallio penuláve, currere solent; quales equi, rhedæ, corpora in Papæ, Cardinalium, Episcoporum, Magnatum omnium cavalcadis, equitationibus, vecturis, adeoque ipsarum Ecclesiasticarum Dignitatum nundinationibus maximè conspicui sunt: denique animæ, quas in Purgatorio detineri, atque inde pretio auri, argenti, lapidum pretiosorum, byssi &c. redimi posse, Babylonii mercatores illi nugantur.
units.tr: VII. It is truly astonishing if the Hierarchical hucksters and hawkers do not blush whenever they come upon that inventory of the Babylonian shop, the index of their own wares. Its equipment is conveniently divided into two classes: namely, the instruments of idolatry and of idolatrous worship, by which it is carried on and adorned; and also the instruments of greed, luxury and pride, which they practise under the same guise both in the priestly office and in their food and clothing. There, if anywhere else, silver, precious stone, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, every thyine wood, every vessel of ivory, every vessel of most precious wood, bronze, iron, marble; cinnamon, incense, ointment (or chrism), frankincense, wine, oil, semolina, wheat, beasts of burden, sheep, horses, carriages, slaves, are well known, most customary and most common. Are you, Jesuits, new Bezalels, so shameless, in re-working these very wares and adorning this shop with some new artifice you display to us, that, looking at this Babylonian shop of wares, you do not recognize in your own worship and in the whole use of your sacred persons the wares subjected to spiritual trade, and are not wholly ashamed? Unless perhaps the German proverb is fulfilled in you: When the Devil created a harlot, he created a harlot's brow with her. But whatever you may dissemble, even a mole blinder than Tiresias will see these wares present in your worship: Gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, or scarlet to adorn the idol of the Mass, the Pope, the Cardinals and the other Babylonian magnates and their ministers; thyine wood to adorn the vaulted ceilings of the temples and to carve the idols; frankincense and incense for worshipping images; wood, bronze, iron, marble for making those same images and other sacred utensils; cinnamon and similar aromatic spices and ointments for preparing the sacred anointings; semolina and wheat for producing the panacean deity; wine in the golden chalice, which the priest alone drinks while consecrating; beasts of burden, namely calves and sheep or lambs of God, and sacred fleeces; horses, carriages, bodies: two-horse, four-horse and six-horse carriages, that is, carriages with two, four or six horses, and attendants running on both sides of the carriage, who here are called bodies [Σωμαῖοι]; not only in that sense in which the word means slaves, chattels, which these attendants certainly are, but also because these little servants are wont to run naked, that is, without cloak or cape; and such horses, carriages, bodies are especially conspicuous in the cavalcades, rides and journeys of the Pope, the Cardinals, the bishops and all the magnates, and indeed in the very trafficking of the ecclesiastical dignities themselves. Finally, souls, which those Babylonian merchants babble are detained in Purgatory and can be redeemed from there for the price of gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, etc.

units.la: VIII. Jam olim, ut hoc unum addam, Antichristo, Rege se exaltanti, & supra omne Numen se efferenti, (quem Babylonis emblemate Apocalypsis depingit) phrygionicum ejusmodi mangonium Daniel cap. xi. 38. tribuit his verbis: Deum מעוזים Mauzim (arcium, Basilicarum) loco Dei majorum suorum colet: Deum, quem non agnoverunt majores ejus, colet כהב ובכסף באבן יקרה בחמדות auro, & argento, & lapide pretioso, & desiderabilibus, seu pretiosis quibusque. Utitur autem Daniel generali voce חמדות desiderabilium, seu pretiosorum, quam in speciem suas S. Johannes diducit. Quis verò mangonium isthoc Numini inprimis Panaceo, Deo, seu idolo illi Mauzim, Basilicarum, in Missa, unicè inservire, non videt? Ibi enim hierothecæ
units.tr: VIII. Long ago, to add just this one thing, Daniel (chap. 11, verse 38) assigned this kind of Phrygian merchandise to Antichrist, the king who exalts himself and raises himself above every deity (whom the Apocalypse portrays under the emblem of Babylon), in these words: He shall worship the god Mauzim [מעוזים] (of fortresses, that is, of basilicas) in place of the god of his fathers; the god whom his fathers did not know, he shall worship [בזהב ובכסף באבן יקרה בחמדות] with gold, and with silver, and with precious stone, and with desirable things, or with costly things of every kind. Daniel uses the general word [חמדות] for desirable things, or precious things, which St John spreads out into particulars. Who does not see that this merchandise serves especially that all-healing deity, or that idol Mauzim of the basilicas, in the Mass? For there the reliquaries

units.la: In Missa inprimis mercet illa Babylonica secundum literam intelligitur. hierothecæ illæ, seu Monstrantiæ, quibus novellum illud Numen includitur, altaria, vasa sacra, vestes, sacrificulorum, reliquáque sacri dramatis illius instrumenta auro, argento, lapidibus pretiosis, reliquisque pretiosis à S. Johanne ordine recensitis plerisque sic nitent & splendescunt, ut frustrà alibi illa conjunctiora & fulgentiora requiras. Repertas esse, & reperiri adhuc novimus Monstrantias, auro, argento, lapidibus pretiosis intertextas, tanto pretio, ut non unius tonnæ auri pretium superent.
units.tr: In the Mass, above all, that Babylonian merchandise is to be understood literally. Those reliquaries, or monstrances, in which that newfangled deity is enclosed, along with the altars, sacred vessels, the vestments of the little priests, and the other instruments of that sacred drama, gleam and shine so much with gold, silver, precious stones and the other costly things listed in order by St John, for the most part, that you will look in vain elsewhere for things more splendid and dazzling. We know that monstrances have been found, and are still found, interwoven with gold, silver and precious stones, at a price that exceeds the value of a single ton of gold.

units.la: IX. Certum equidem est, nullam in terris religionem, extare, quæ majore faštu, majore apparatu, gravioribusque sumptibus exerceatur, quàm Romana. Sicut contra nulla in orbe religio castiori & simpliciori hac in parte cultu instituta est, quæ à meretricio hoc fuco magis abhorret, quàm Christiana. Ut in hoc personato & theatrali comptu oppositio Christum inter & Romanam Hierarchiam valdè conspicua sit. Et in his ipsis phaleris non minima pars glisci t efficacium irritamentorum idolomaniæ, quibus nimirum imperita plebs facilè capitur. Cujus rei vel ipsimet Jesuitæ testes esse possunt, qui, ceu novi & exotici phrygiones ornatui huic præcipuè studént, quia ejus ad imperitos pelliciendos vim præcipuam hactenùs experti sunt. Quantum porrò mercium illarum pretium sit, vel hinc æstimare licet, quòd Papa, si quando in periculum præsens Papatus adduceretur, neque defendi aliter posset, beneficio unius alicujus Provinciæ vasorum Templariorum, si ea conflari aut distrahi jubeat, aliquot annorum bellum alere posset.
units.tr: IX. It is certainly true that there is no religion on earth practised with greater pomp, greater display and heavier expense than the Roman. Conversely, no religion in the world has been instituted with a purer and simpler worship in this respect, one that abhors this harlot's paint more than the Christian. So in this masked and theatrical finery the opposition between Christ and the Roman Hierarchy is very conspicuous. And in these very trappings no small part consists of the efficacious incentives to idolatry, by which the untaught common people are easily captured. The Jesuits themselves can bear witness to this, for they, like new and exotic Phrygians, devote their chief zeal to this adornment, because they have so far found its main power in drawing in the unlearned. How great the price of those wares is may be gauged even from this: if the present Papacy were ever brought into danger and could not otherwise be defended, the Pope, by means of the vessels of a single province of the Templars, if he ordered them melted down or sold, could sustain a war for several years.

units.la: X. Sic Babylonicæ merces Hierarchiæ quadrant. Sed magis etiam quadrant secundùm allegoriam, juxta quam merces hæ corporales emblema sunt mercium spiritualium, quas Hierarchici in commercio habent. Neque absonum videri potest, utrumque Spi-
units.tr: X. Thus the Babylonian wares suit the Hierarchy. But they suit even better according to the allegory, by which these bodily wares are emblems of the spiritual wares that the hierarchs have in their trade. Nor can it seem absurd that the Holy Spirit intended both senses, namely, to show in Babylon those wares both as bodily goods and as signs and images of the spiritual things subject to this trade, in the sense we have set out above.

units.la: ritum S. intendisse, demonstrare videlicet in Babylone merces illas tum ut corporales, tum ut signa & imagines rerum spiritualium, nundinationi huic subjectarum, eo sensu, quem supra expressimus. Pertendo igitur, Hierarchiam pridem vanum exposuisse, & adhuc dum exponere aurum, Deum ipsum, Christum, Spiritum S. cjusque gratiam & peccatorum remissionem: argentum, puritatem & justitiam meriti Christi: lapidem pretiosum & margaritas, Sanctos, Divos, eorum factitias fictitiasque imagines & reliquias: byssum, merita & justitiam Sanctorum: purpuram, passiones superabundantes Christi: sericum, opera fidelium: coccinum, passiones Sanctorum: lignum odoratum, Sanctos, quos ob merita eorum in Divorum numerum refert, quo illos invocare, & omnem ex iis voluptatem percipere liceat: vasa ex ebore, ligno pretiosó, marmore, &c. tutelam principum, sapientiam doctorum, patientiam monachorum: cinnamomum, dona fanationis apud reliquias Sanctorum: suffitus, orationes Sanctorum, etiam pro mortuis: utguentum, spirituales gratias multiplices: thus, oblationes pro peccatis: vinum, verbum Dei, prout à Papa proponitur, recreans scilicet & vivificans animam: similaginem, Numen Panaceum: triticum, beneficia & bona Ecclesiæ: jumenta, Clerum Ecclesiæ, qui venditur Episcopis: Equos, rhedas, populos, Regna, principatus, quos vectigales Papa habet: animas, hominum conscientias, quas superstitione imbutas Papa quæstui habet. Sive ergò corporales hæ merces spiritualium illarum symbola sint (quod negari temere nequit, quia apprimè congruunt, & tum symbola ipsa, tum res illæ significatæ in Hierarchica illa ἐμπορία utramque paginam faciunt) sive res saltem significatæ Hierarchiæ conveniunt, manifestum erit, illam avaritia & nundinatione Spirituali, quam Babyloni Spiritus S. tribuit, immaniter sepolluere.
units.tr: I therefore contend that the Hierarchy has long been setting out, and still sets out, as gold God himself, Christ, the Holy Spirit and his grace and the forgiveness of sins; as silver, the purity and righteousness of Christ's merit; as precious stone and pearls, the saints, the divine ones, and their fabricated and fictitious images and relics; as fine linen, the merits and righteousness of the saints; as purple, the superabundant sufferings of Christ; as silk, the works of the faithful; as scarlet, the sufferings of the saints; as fragrant wood, the saints whom, on account of their merits, it counts among the number of the divine, so that it may be permitted to invoke them and to derive every pleasure from them; as vessels of ivory, of precious wood, of marble, etc., the protection of princes, the wisdom of teachers, the patience of monks; as cinnamon, the gifts of healing at the relics of the saints; as incense, the prayers of the saints, even for the dead; as ointment, manifold spiritual graces; as frankincense, offerings for sins; as wine, the Word of God as the Pope puts it forward, that is, refreshing and giving life to the soul; as fine flour, the all-healing deity; as wheat, the benefices and goods of the Church; as beasts of burden, the clergy of the Church, who are sold to bishops; as horses and chariots, peoples, kingdoms and principalities, which the Pope holds as tributaries; as souls, the consciences of men, which the Pope holds for profit, steeped in superstition. So whether these bodily wares are symbols of those spiritual things (which cannot rashly be denied, since they fit together very well, and both the symbols and the things they signify make the two pages agree in that Hierarchical trade [ἐμπορία]), or at least the things signified suit the Hierarchy, it will be plain that it has foully polluted itself with that avarice and spiritual trading which the Holy Spirit attributes to Babylon.

units.la: XI. Ante omnia Hierarchia habet suos ἀμπρες τῆς γῆς Mercatores terræ, qui sunt μεγισῶνες τῆς γῆς Magnates terræ. Eorum supremus Papa, maximus Cananæus licet (juxta carmen illud Poëtæ de Alexandro M.
units.tr: XI. Above all, the Hierarchy has its merchants of the earth [ἔμποροι τῆς γῆς], who are the magnates of the earth [μεγιστᾶνες τῆς γῆς]. Their chief is the Pope, though he is the greatest Canaanite (according to that verse of the poet about Alexander the Great,

units.la: Vendit Alexander claves, altaria, Christum; Venderejure potest, emerat illeprius.
units.tr: Alexander sells the keys, the altars, Christ; he could sell them by right, for he bought them before.

units.la: quod de Pontificibus plerisque omnibus jure cantaveris) à quo proin universa illa mercatura dirigitur, & ad quem, ceu centrum, omnis nundinationis fructus confluit; non tamen Mercator, sed Rex Regum est, habens Regnum in Reges terræ. Quæ etiam causa est, cur cum ceu supremum videlicet Regem & Dominum, nunquam in mercatura sua peccare, vel Simoniæ crimen committere posse, assentatores illi, quibus Papæ oletum amaricinum olet, pertendunt.
units.tr: which you may rightly sing of most of the Pontiffs), from whom all that trade is directed, and to whom, as to a centre, the fruit of all the trading flows together. Yet he is not a merchant but the King of kings, having a kingdom over the kings of the earth. This is also the reason why those flatterers, to whom the Pope's fragrant oil smells sweet, maintain that, as supreme King and Lord, he can never sin in his trade or commit the crime of simony.

units.la: Refert enim P. Jovius Histor. lib. iv. Laurentium Puccium Cardinalem dicere solitum: Nullum lucrum quacunque etiam ex re, Papæ illicitum esse. Quod Senecæ verbis Epist. 95. efferre potuisset Pontifici Romano, nihil turpe esse, cujus placet pretium. Quòd Papa in Simoniacis non illaquetur, nec committat Simoniam vendendo beneficia, Felinus, multíque alii ab ipso citati, nec non Jacobatius, tuentur. Sic Jurisconsultus magnæ famæ Bartolus in l. Barbotius 2. Colum. ff. de offic. Prætoris decernit: Papa non dicitur committere Simoniam, si confert beneficia vel dignitates, acceptâ pecunid. Ecquare? Pulchellam accipe, sed sine ratione, rationem: Quia Papatus, inquit, est Apostolatus, & aut sanctum facit, aut sanctum recipit. Quod est notandum, sic ex ordine JCtorum alius, Jodocus Dumhauderius in Praxi criminali cap. 61. num. 67. &c. contra rabidè latrantes adversus sedem Apostolicam, quibus non est licitum os opponere in Cœlum: sed LICITUM est Pontifici ut mutet quadrata rotundis. Scilicet sacrilegia minuta, & minutorum tantùm hominum punienda: magna aut magnorum in triumphis ferenda sunt?
units.tr: For P. Jovius, in his Histor. lib. iv., reports that Cardinal Lorenzo Puccio used to say: No gain, from whatever source, is unlawful for the Pope. He could have applied to the Roman Pontiff Seneca's words in Epist. 95.: nothing is shameful whose price is pleasing. That the Pope is not ensnared in simony, and does not commit simony by selling benefices, is maintained by Felinus and many others cited by him, as well as by Jacobatius. Thus the jurist Bartolus, of great fame, in in l. Barbotius 2 Colum. ff. de offic. Prætoris, decides: The Pope is not said to commit simony if he confers benefices or dignities, having received money. Why? Here is a pretty reason, though without sense: Because the Papacy, he says, is an apostolate, and either makes a thing holy or receives one already holy. This is to be noted, since another of the jurists, Jodocus Dumhauderius, in his Praxi criminali cap. 61. num. 67. &c., against those who bark furiously at the Apostolic See, to whom it is not permitted to open their mouth against heaven, says: but it is LAWFUL for the Pontiff to change squares into circles. Evidently petty sacrileges are to be punished, and only those of petty men; great ones are to be borne in triumph, or those of great men?

units.la: XII. Sed ô vocem nonnisi eorum hominum, qui virtutem ipsam exscindere concupiscunt! Quod virtutis excidium tantò certiùs hæc doctrina secum trahit, cùm vitia sua Pontifices sanctitatis opinione commendata, non solùm ipsi concipiant, sed etiam in civitatem suam sacram infundant: neque solùm obsint, quòd ipsi corrumpuntur, sed etiam quòd corrumpunt: plúsque exemplo quàm peccato nocent; facientes, ut unius culpa ab omnibus peccetur, more gentis illius, cujus cùm Rex aliqua corporis parte debilitatus est, domestici omnes sponte sua eandem partê debilitant; quòd turpe existiment, Regè claudo, non & omnes amicos claudicare. Quia enim mores & vitia summi Antistitis imitari, genus obsequii judicatur, abjicient omnes pietatem, ne ipsi scelus exprobrare videantur, si piè vivant. Et sanè, si Avaritia sacra, quam Simoniâ appellant, in Papa vitii nomen amittit, quid obstat, quò minùs cæterorum quoque scelerum quantumvis enormium virus, quod habent insitum, facilè Pontificia sanctitas exugat, & absorbeat: imò bonitatis quoque lumen iis de suo lumine fœnaret? Ex quo illud denique consequens est, ut quantò plus scelerum in Sanctam & Sanctificam illam Sedem confluxerit, tantò sanctiorem eam reddi, cunctis, mirificá illà, sanctum è non sancto faciendi facultate, in boni naturam conversis. Huc descendunt ii, quibus omnia Pontificum honesta atque inhonesta laudare mos est; & tam altè illa magnæ Virtutis comes adulatio in illam Papalis Sanctitatis arcem sese penetravit, tam peritis in hac arte magistris instructam, qui vel sacris Herculis operari queant.
units.tr: XII. But oh, what a voice, coming only from men who desire to root out virtue itself! This doctrine drags the ruin of virtue along all the more surely, since the Pontiffs, commended by the reputation of holiness, not only conceive their vices but pour them into their holy city. They do harm not only by being corrupted but also by corrupting, and they hurt more by example than by sin, causing the fault of one to be committed by all. It is like that nation whose king, weakened in some part of his body, sees all his household weaken the same part of their own accord, thinking it shameful that, with the king lame, not all his friends should limp. For since imitating the morals and vices of the highest prelate is judged a kind of obsequiousness, everyone will cast off piety, lest they seem to reproach themselves with crime if they live piously. And indeed, if sacred avarice, which they call simony, loses the name of vice in the Pope, what stands in the way of Papal holiness easily sucking out and absorbing the poison of all the other crimes, however enormous, which it has inborn? Nay, would it not even lend them light from its own light to dress their goodness? From this it finally follows that the more crimes flow into that Holy and Sanctifying See, the holier it is made, by that wonderful power of making the holy out of the unholy, all things being turned into the nature of good. To this point descend those who make a custom of praising all the honourable and dishonourable deeds of the Pontiffs; and flattery, the companion of great Virtue, has so deeply penetrated into that citadel of Papal Holiness, instructed by masters so skilled in this art that they could work even the sacred labours of Hercules.

units.la: XIII. Adeò scilicet res Romana à moribus antiquis declinavit, ut homo ille (liceat Friderici II: Imperatoris apud Aventi-
units.tr: XIII. So far, indeed, has the Roman affair departed from ancient morals that that man (let me borrow the words of Frederick II, Emperor, as cited by Aventinus,

units.la: { } Verba Friderici II, Imp. Aventinum lib. vÿ. verba, ad Othonem Bavariæ Ducem scripta, mea facere) qui dicitur Papa, divitiis nimium auctus, maximo pietatis Christianæ detrimento, omnia sibi licere, more tyrannorum pessimorum, putet : rationem actuum nemini, quasi sit Deus, reddere velit: id quod soli Deo convenit, usurpet: SE PECCARE NON POSSE, credi sibi impudentissimè, simulque imperiosè postulet: fraudes, dolos, commenta, fucum taceri jubeat. Proin illa tantoperè jactata Pontificis ἀναμαρτησία quàm vel hac in re decipiat, & quàm illa sacra Cleri avaritia sit ἀναλήψη, liquebit magis, ubi eum, quem is adhibet, opes acquirendi modum (de impendendi enim ratione jam supra plusscula diximus) deinceps explicaverimus.
units.tr: (the words of Frederick II, Emperor, cited by Aventinus in book 5, written to Otto, Duke of Bavaria, which I make my own) who is called the Pope, grown too rich, to the great detriment of Christian piety, thinks that everything is permitted to him, like the worst tyrants; he will render an account of his acts to no one, as if he were God; he claims for himself what belongs to God alone; he demands, most shamelessly and at the same time imperiously, that it be believed that he cannot sin; he orders frauds, deceits, inventions and trickery to be kept silent. Therefore how far that much-vaunted sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησία] of the Pontiff deceives him in this matter, and how that sacred avarice of the clergy is a taking up [ἀναλήψη], will become clearer when we have explained the method of acquiring wealth which he employs (for we have already said a good deal above about the method of spending it).

units.la: XIV. Omittere hac occasione non possum commemorare impudentiam Theologiæ Moralis Jesuitarum, qui Simoniam Cleri notoriam palliaturi, ejusmodi Simoniæ definitionem commenti sunt, ut eâ in consilium adhibitâ, universa ferè cleri impia nundinatio defendi valeat. Nam inter arcana Theologiæ Casuisticæ & Moralis Jesuitarum haud postremum est, Ars mutandi virtutum & vitiorum definitiones, quæ arte, quam subtiliter admodum exercent, nullo negotio peccata quævis purgant. Ita ergò Simonia iis non amplius est ablatio rei spiritualis pro temporali, quemodo jam olim Thomas Aquinas absolutè docuit, spirituale pro temporali dari sine Simonia non posse, cum propter temporale datur. Sic enim Ecclesiæ Romanæ Simoniam nimis in propatulo futuram omnium, iis subuoluit. Nova igitur definitione lenocinandum sceleri putárunt. Dupliciter, ita Greg. de Valentia Tom. iij. d. 6. q. 16. p. 3. p. 204. 2. scribit, potest quis conferre spirituale propter temporale principaliter, & tanquam propter finem. Uno modo, si temporale æstimet pluris, quàm ipsum spirituale; & tunc omninò committit talis Simoniam. Altero modo potest quis conferre spirituale propter temporale sim- pliciter, tanquam propter finem, ita ut temporale apud eum non sit finis ipsius rei spiritualis; quasi temporale pluris ab eo quàm spirituale æstimetur: sed tantummodò voluntatis, sive applicationis animi ad actum conferendi spirituale: & hoc non est Simonia. Et infra: Cùm petitur temporale pro spirituali, non tanquam pretium debitum ex justitia, sed tanquam finis applicationis animi ad conferendum spirituale, minimè erit Simonia, etiamsi principaliter intendatur & expectetur. Valentiæ subscribit Tannerus, quamvis fateatur, Thomam verbis, quæ supra citavimus, huic sententiæ adversari. Hac via universam Ecclesiæ Romanæ Simoniam subtiliter illi scelerum doctores purgárunt, expiárúntque. Quis enim tam perditus est, qui rem spiritualem pro temporali, vel temporalem pro spirituali offerens, profiteri velit, se majoris rem temporalem, quàm spritualem æstimare, vel non malit pecuniam potiùs tanquam conferendæ rei spiritualis invitamentum & illicem offerre vel accipere, quàm tanquam rei spiritualis pretium? Nemo sic à Deo desertus est, ut hoc recusset. Et de interiori æstimatione sic nundinantium, quis, præter Deum, idoneus judex erit? Sed hæc παρέργα ἐᾶσον.
units.tr: XIV. On this occasion I cannot omit to mention the shamelessness of the Jesuits' moral theology, who, intending to cover up the notorious simony of the clergy, have devised such a definition of simony that, once it is applied, almost the whole impious trafficking of the clergy can be defended. For among the secrets of the casuistic and moral theology of the Jesuits is no small art of changing the definitions of virtues and vices, by which, with the subtlety they practise it, they cleanse any sins with no trouble at all. So for them simony is no longer the exchange of a spiritual thing for a temporal one, as Thomas Aquinas long ago taught outright: a spiritual thing cannot be given without simony in exchange for a temporal thing, when it is given on account of the temporal. For in this way simony would be too plainly visible to all, and it would overthrow the Roman Church's position. They therefore thought the crime needed to be dressed up with a new definition. In two ways, so Gregory of Valentia writes (vol. 3, disp. 6, q. 16, p. 3, p. 204, sec. 2), can one confer a spiritual thing on account of a temporal one, principally and as for an end. In one way, if one values the temporal more than the spiritual itself; and then such a person certainly commits simony. In the other way one can confer a spiritual thing on account of a temporal thing simply, as for an end, so that the temporal is not the end of the spiritual thing itself; as if the temporal were valued by him more than the spiritual; but only as the will, or the application of the mind, to the act of conferring the spiritual thing: and this is not simony. And further on: When a temporal thing is sought in return for a spiritual thing, not as a price owed in justice, but as the end of the application of the mind to conferring the spiritual thing, it will by no means be simony, even if it is principally intended and expected. Tanner agrees with Valentia, although he admits that Thomas's words, which we cited above, oppose this opinion. In this way those teachers of crime have subtly cleansed and expiated the whole simony of the Roman Church. For who is so lost that, offering a spiritual thing for a temporal one, or a temporal thing for a spiritual one, would want to profess that he values the temporal thing above the spiritual, or would not rather prefer to offer or accept money as an inducement and enticement to conferring the spiritual thing, rather than as the price of the spiritual thing? No one is so forsaken by God that he refuses this. And who, besides God, will be a fit judge of the inner valuation of such traders? But let these side matters be set aside [παρέργα ἐᾶσον].

units.la: XV. Mercatores Babylonis, ut ad eos redeam, non quivis sordidi cerdones, institores, ex fœce populi, sed μεγιστᾶνες τῆς γῆς Magnates terræ sunt Apoc. xviii. 23. Nam qui docere ac regere debebant Ecclesiam Christóque lucrari animas, ii se converterunt ad quæstum & mercedem injustificæ, quàm diligebat Balearicus: & mediante quæstu se fecerunt Dominos terræ, sive per terram intelligamus, territoria, sive stylo Prophetico, Ecclesiam. Ita Cant. viii. 11. accusantur custodes vineæ Domini, quòd pro fructu vineæ quisque illorum domum retulerit mille argenteos. Cui non statim Hierarchici Proceres, magnifici Cardinales, Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, qui nundinationes animarum maxima cum industria exercent, & ex commercio gloriâ Magnatum Procerúmque terræ florent, mentem subeant? Cardinales inprimis Regibus pridem æquiparati, Electoribus & Principibus prælati. Ita Thomas Wolsejus Cardinalis Anglus crebro sermone dicere non erubuit: Ego & Rex meus. Hoc Cardinalitium supercilium est. Quidni verò tam superbè se jactent, cùm viderint pridem, maximos quosque Principes hanc suam Regiæ æmulam dignitatem ambire, neque minùs impetrata ea gloriari, quàm præcipuo Majestatis ornamento? Nam Regia stirpe satos dignitatem eam affectâsse, satis constat. Apud Anglos Cardinalis Polus Regali prosapia ortus est: apud Gallos Borbonius Regio sanguine cretus; & Lotharingus frater Ducis Guisii: apud Germanos Albertus Austriacus, Rodolphi Imperatoris frater. Magnates Terræ salutaveris magis, si consessum Magnificorum Dominorum Romæ oculis usurpaveris. Ibi enim si Princeps quispiam Serenissimus compareat, quem Papa honoris gratia in cœtu Cardinalium admittere velit, quem ei locum assignabit? Nempe, ante ultimum Cardinalem Diaconum, at si frequens & plenus senatus fuerit, ipse Princeps post sexaginta octo purpuratos sedeat penultimus, uti A. MDXCIII. Principi Bavariæ Maximiliano contigit. Hic ille fastus intolerabilis est, Romanæ Curiæ congruens tamen, ubi vel Imperatores pedes Summi Pontificis osculantur. Quidni ergo qui Pontifici à consiliis sunt reliquos Principes dignitate superent? Sed de Cardinalium, Magnatum terræ, & in Emporio Romano Mercatorum summatum fastu plura in Historia Papatûs diximus.
units.tr: XV. The merchants of Babylon, to return to them, are not just any filthy butchers or hawkers from the dregs of the people, but the magnates of the earth [μεγιστᾶνες τῆς γῆς], Rev. 18:23. For those who ought to teach and govern the Church and gain souls for Christ have turned to profit and to unjust gain, which Balaam loved; and by means of this gain they have made themselves lords of the earth, whether by earth we understand territories, or, in prophetic style, the Church. Thus in Song 8:11 the keepers of the vineyard of the Lord are accused, because each of them brought home a thousand pieces of silver for the fruit of the vineyard. Does not the thought of the hierarchical nobles, the magnificent cardinals, archbishops and bishops, who carry on the trafficking in souls with the greatest diligence, and who flourish from this trade with the glory of the magnates and nobles of the earth, come to mind at once? Above all the cardinals, long ago made equal to kings and placed above electors and princes. Thus the English cardinal Thomas Wolsey was not ashamed to say often in conversation: I and my King. This is the cardinalitial arrogance. And why should they not boast so proudly, when they have seen for some time that the greatest princes seek this dignity, which rivals a royal one, and that, having obtained it, they glory in it no less than in the chief ornament of majesty? For it is well known that men born of royal stock have aspired to this dignity. Among the English, Cardinal Pole was born of royal lineage; among the French, Bourbon was born of royal blood, and the Lorrainer, brother of the Duke of Guise; among the Germans, Albert of Austria, brother of Emperor Rudolph. You would greet the magnates of the earth more readily if you took in with your eyes the assembly of the magnificent lords at Rome. For there, if some most serene prince appears whom the Pope wishes to admit to the company of cardinals as a mark of honour, what place will he assign him? Surely, before the last cardinal deacon; but if the senate is full and crowded, the prince himself will sit second to last, after sixty-eight purple-clad men, as happened to Maximilian, Prince of Bavaria, in 1593. This is an intolerable pride, yet fitting for the Roman Curia, where even emperors kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff. Why, then, should those who are the Pope's counsellors not surpass the other princes in dignity? But we have said more about the pride of the cardinals, the magnates of the earth, and the chief merchants in the Roman marketplace, in our History of the Papacy.

units.la: XVI. Neque soli Cardinales, sed alii etiam Hierarchiæ Præsules, Archiepiscopi inprimis, in Mercatorum
units.tr: XVI. Nor are cardinals alone among the magnates of the earth, but other prelates of the hierarchy, above all archbishops, are also counted among the merchants

units.la: Magnatum terræ censu sunt. Nam & hi tanquam purpuratæ Babylonis negotiatores, emptores, venditores ; ex mercaturâ sua ditati supra modum, denique Principes terræ facti sunt. Sic Augustinus, Monachus, forsan domi nullius numeri, quòd Britannos sub jugum Romanum misisset, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis constitutus est. Venefridus Anglus, mutato nomine, Bonifacius, hac via Moguntinus Archiepiscopus, simúlque Præfectus Ecclesiæ Coloniensis evasit. Alanus Anglus, transfuga, fidem patriam Principem Pontifici prodens, hac mercaturâ meruit, ut esset in Proceribus terræ, rubri insuper galeri dignitatem mercatus. Quis omnes enumeret, qui hac eadem ratione sibi aditum ad summas dignitates struxerunt? Et quis insicias iverit Archiepiscopos, quæstuosissimam hanc artem exercentes, Principes, Proceres, Magnates terræ, Regnorum, Dioecefeon & Provinciarum Primates esse, & haberi? Imò ne frigeret hæc negotiatio, quos lucrum & commoda non movebant, eos callida meretrix honore & gloria inflammatum ivit. Ita Rex Hispaniarum Catholicus, Galliarum, Christianissimus, Helvetii, Defensores Ecclesiæ, duobus majoribus vexillis, nec non pileo & gladio, redhostimenti gratia donati, audiunt. Nemini enim deest liberale aliquod præmium, quò fruƈtuosam negotiationem studiosiùs colat.
units.tr: of the magnates of the earth. For these too, as the purple-clad merchants, buyers and sellers of Babylon, enriched beyond measure by their trade, have at last become princes of the earth. Thus Augustine, a monk, perhaps of no standing at home, because he had sent the Britons under the Roman yoke, was made archbishop of Canterbury. Winfrid, an Englishman who changed his name to Boniface, by this route became archbishop of Mainz, and at the same time prefect of the Church of Cologne. Alan, an Englishman and a deserter, who betrayed his native faith and prince to the Pope, earned by this trade a place among the nobles of the earth, and moreover bought the dignity of the red hat. Who could list all those who by the same method built themselves a way to the highest dignities? And who would deny that archbishops, practising this most profitable art, are and are regarded as princes, nobles and magnates of the earth, and primates of kingdoms, dioceses and provinces? Indeed, lest this business grow cold, that shrewd harlot has inflamed with honour and glory those whom profit and advantage did not move. Thus the King of Spain is heard as Catholic, the King of France as Most Christian, and the Swiss as Defenders of the Church, being rewarded with two greater banners, as well as a cap and a sword, as a thank-you. For no one lacks some generous prize with which to cultivate the fruitful trade more eagerly.

units.la: XVII. Mercatoribus illis, Magnatibus terræ, accedunt in famoso hoc Emporio Gubernatores, & omnis in maribus turba & nautæ, mare isthoc exercentes. Esto Mare mundus. Naves Ecclesiæ particulares per mundum dispersæ. Naucleri seu Gubernatores qui alii erunt, quàm Episcopi, dioecefion rectores, quibus Archimandritæ, Generales Ordinum, Abbates, quorum nonnulli Principes S. R. Imperii, salutari gestiunt? Nautæ denique Canonici Clerici, Monachi regulares, qui omnes in mari hoc rem faciunt, & ceu circumforanei institores magnorum Mercatorum & Gubernatorum merces per tabernas distrahunt. Quos inter Jesuitæ facilè reliquis palmam præripiunt, qui gnaviter incumbunt remis, & omnibus viribus hoc mare pulsant; absque quibus si fuisset, jam pridem navicula piscatoris ad scopulos allisa, pessum ivisset. Quanquam illi dum Scyllam remigando vitare student, in Charybdin incidunt, & fœditatem Meretricis hujus, quam disputando tegere student, magis in propatulo collocant.
units.tr: XVII. To those merchants, the magnates of the earth, are added in this notorious marketplace the governors and all the crowd and sailors upon the seas, who ply this sea. Let the sea be the world. The particular churches are ships scattered throughout the world. Who else will be the shipmasters or governors than the bishops, the rulers of dioceses, whom the archimandrites, generals of orders, and abbots, some of whom are princes of the Holy Roman Empire, long to greet? Finally, the sailors are canons, clerics and regular monks, who all do business on this sea and, like peddlers, sell the wares of the great merchants and governors through the shops. Among them the Jesuits easily snatch the palm from the rest; they bend vigorously to the oars and beat this sea with all their strength; without them the little fisherman's boat, dashed on the rocks, would long ago have gone to the bottom. Yet while they strive by rowing to avoid Scylla, they fall into Charybdis, and by disputing they set the foulness of this harlot, which they strive to cover, more openly in view.

units.la: XVIII. Hi sunt Mercatores, Magnates terræ, Gubernatores, Naucleri, & Nautæ spirituales Babylonis. Quòd, si scire jam quis aveat, quibus hamis, quibus tandem uncis opes Europæas in suum illud fœdum prædarum receptaculum attraxerint, atque etiamnum attrahant, næ idem ille volet
units.tr: XVIII. These are the merchants, the great men of the earth, the governors, the shipmasters, and the spiritual sailors of Babylon. If anyone now wishes to know with what hooks, and finally with what grappling irons, they have drawn, and are still drawing, the wealth of Europe into that foul storehouse of plunder, he will want to hear the following.

units.la: Nosse, quot Jonii veniant ad littora fluctus. Est enim eorum tanta varietas, ut nominibus tantùm comprehendendis vix Calepini volumen sufficiat. Fas mihi esto Desiderii Erasmi, cui ingenia Babylonicorum mercatorum notissima fuerunt, verbis præfari, & multa paucis constringere, deinceps certo ordine digerenda. Sic autem ille in Adagiorum Chiliad. 1. cent. 9. pag. 196. sub Adagio A mortuo tributum exigere, mercaturam Hierarchicorum strictim depingit: Quanquam fœdum est Christianos Principes in hisce rebus inhumaniores videri, quàm ulli fuerunt ethnici tyranni, tamen aliquanto minus execrandum hoc, quàm quod apud sacerdotes quoque, quibus oportebat omnem pecuniam esse vilissimam, & quorum erat, suas doteis gratis acceptas, gratis item communicare, nihil non venale est, nihil immune. Quas non tragœdias movent pro suis illis decimis, quàm odiosè divexant miseram plebeculam? Non datur baptismus, hoc est, non licet fieri Christianum, nisi numeres, atque his præclaris auspiciis foreis ingrederis Ecclesiæ. Non comprobant matrimonium, nisi numeres: non audiunt pœnitentium commissa, nisi sperent præmium. Sacrificant conducti. Non psallunt gratis, non imponunt manum gratis. Vix procul mota manu benedicunt, nisi dederis. Non consecrant saxum aut calicem, nisi data mercede. Quin & illud verè Pontificium munus docendi populum, quæstu vitiatum est. Denique non impertiunt corpus Christi, nisi numeres. Ut ne dicam interim quanta messis colligatur, ex litibus, ex dispensationibus, sic enim vocant, ex condonationibus, quas vulgus appellat indulgentias, è conferendis Sacerdotiis, confirmandis Episcopis & Abbatibus. Sed quid apud istos gratuitum est, apud quos emitur & sepultura, etiam in alieno solo? Apud ethnicos miseræ plebi stabat commune sepulchrum: erat ubi gratis, quos velles, sepelires. Apud Christianos nec mortuis terra aperiri licet, nisi à Sacerdote tantum spatii conduxeris, & pro pretii modo dabitur locus amplus & magnificus. Si plurimùm numeraveris, in templo proximè summum altare licebit putrescere: sin parcè dederis, inter plebejos sub dio complueris. Turpe, si pretium acciperent oblatum: nunc jus suum vocant, & dictu mirum, quanta exigant improbitate. Barbarus ille & gentilis Hebron, offert Abrahæ ignoto hospiti gratuitum sepulchri munus, & vix adduci precibus potest, ut oblatam accipiat pecuniam, & Sacerdotes sepulturæ jus vendimus in alieno? vel potiùs quod publicum est, id ceu privatum ære locamus. Atque hujusmodi messem nemo metit avidiùs, quàm hi, qui nihil serunt populo, sed toti fibi vivunt, aut certè Principi. Alii cantionem illam nobis occinunt: Dignus est operarius mercede, perinde, quasi nihil interfit inter Episcopum, & conductum militem aut fossorem. Serviles operæ præmio pensantur. Principum & Sacerdotum munus sublimius est, quàm ut mercede sit æstimandum. Hactenus Erasmus, cujus vel solius testimonium, perpetuâ experientiâ confirmatum, & piorum omnium querelis comprobatum, abundè Hierarchicorum Babylonicam nundinationem convincit. Cui suffragatur Baptistæ Mantuani de Romanæ Curiæ quotidiana consuetudine notissimum, verissimúmque carmen: Venalia nobis Templa, Sacerdotes, Altaria, Sacra, Coronæ, Ignis, thura, preces, Cælum est venale Deúsque.
units.tr: To know how many waves come to the Ionian shores. Their variety is so great that a volume like Calepinus's would scarcely suffice to list their names alone. Let me be allowed, with the words of Desiderius Erasmus, who knew the habits of the Babylonian merchants very well, to introduce the subject, to compress much into few words, and then to arrange the points in a fixed order. In his Adagiorum Chiliad. 1. cent. 9. pag. 196, under the adage "To exact tribute from the dead," he sketches the trade of the Hierarchy in brief: Although it is a disgrace that Christian princes should appear more inhuman in these matters than any heathen tyrant ever was, yet this is somewhat less detestable than what happens among the priests as well, who ought to regard all money as worthless, and who are bound to share freely the gifts they received freely; yet nothing among them is not for sale, nothing is exempt. What tragedies do they stir up over their tithes, how cruelly do they harass the poor common folk! Baptism is not given, that is, you may not become a Christian, unless you pay, and with such splendid auspices you enter the doors of the Church. They do not confirm a marriage unless you pay; they do not hear the sins of penitents unless they hope for a reward. They celebrate Mass for hire. They do not sing without payment, they do not lay on hands without payment. They hardly bless with a hand lifted from afar unless you have given something. They do not consecrate a stone or a chalice unless a fee is paid. Indeed, even that truly Papal duty of teaching the people has been spoiled by profit. Finally, they do not give the body of Christ unless you pay. To say nothing yet of how great a harvest is gathered from lawsuits, from dispensations (for so they call them), from the remissions that the common people call indulgences, and from the conferring of benefices and the confirming of bishops and abbots. But what is free among them, when even burial is bought, even in another's ground? Among the heathens a common tomb stood ready for the wretched common folk; there you could bury whomever you wished for nothing. Among Christians not even the earth may be opened for the dead, unless you have hired so much space from the priest, and a wide and splendid place will be given according to the price. If you have paid a great deal, the dead may rot in the church, close to the high altar; if you have given sparingly, they will be thrown in among the common people under the open sky. It would be shameful if they took a price that was offered; now they call it their right, and, strange to say, they demand it with such shamelessness. That barbarous and heathen Hebron offers Abraham, a stranger, a free gift of a burial place, and can hardly be persuaded to accept the money offered; and shall we priests sell the right of burial in another's ground? Or rather, we let out for money what is public as though it were private. And no one reaps this harvest more eagerly than those who sow nothing for the people, but live wholly for themselves, or at least for the prince. Others sing us that song: "The labourer is worthy of his hire," as if there were no difference between a bishop and a hired soldier or a gravedigger. Servile labours are paid by wages; the office of princes and priests is too lofty to be valued in wages. Thus far Erasmus, whose testimony alone, confirmed by constant experience and borne out by the complaints of all the pious, amply convicts the Babylonian trafficking of the Hierarchy. To this agrees the most famous and most true verse of Baptista Mantuanus about the daily custom of the Roman Curia: "Temples, priests, altars, sacred things, crowns, fire, incense, prayers are for sale to us; heaven is for sale, and God too."

units.la: XIX. Sed ex dogmatibus Hierarchiæ ad faciendum lucrum fictis factisque ejusdem merces Babylonicæ, universaque spiritualis ὑμνεῖα optimè cognoscitur. Hanc enim præcipuam fraudem fraufa est, quod sui quæstús causa fictas suscitavit sententias, quas ψευδεῖς λόγους fictos & affabre factos sermones S. Petrus appellat; eaque in rerum periorum temporum simplicitate mirificè ad commodum suum abusa est, cùm securà esset de facilitate credentium.
units.tr: XIX. But the merchandise of Babylon, and the whole spiritual ὑμνεῖα, is best recognised from the dogmas and deeds of the Hierarchy, which were invented to make profit. For its chief fraud is this: for the sake of its gain it raised up invented opinions, which St Peter calls [ψευδεῖς λόγους] feigned words, fabricated and skilfully made speeches; and in the simplicity of the less enlightened times it abused them wonderfully to its own advantage, since it was confident of the credulity of believers.

units.la: Nam simplices ac religiosi illi homines, semel acri illo thyrso percussi, quò magis talia credebant, eò etiam plura fingebantur: pro eo ac fieri amat, cùm creduntur (sic sapienter Cicero de Divinat. lib. ii. loquitur) facilius, tum singunter impunius: ac minimis etiam rebus prava religio Deos inserit. Quis autem vir pius probúsque probet hoc institutum sacrificulorum ac votum, si in id mentes hominum capiant, ut quæstum ex alieno errore facilem, velut ex concessæ artis usu exerceant, sive, ut cum S. Petro loquar, in avaritia fictis verbis de hominibus negotientur?
units.tr: For those simple and religious men, once struck by that sharp thyrsus, the more they believed such things, the more were further things invented, as is the way: when they are believed (so wisely Cicero speaks in De Divinatione book 2) they are more easily, and then they are invented with less risk; and a perverse religion inserts gods even into the smallest matters. But what upright and pious man would approve this practice and vow of the little priests, if men's minds were set on this: to carry on gain from another's error as easy profit, as if from the use of a licensed trade, or, to speak with St Peter, to trade on men in covetousness with feigned words?

units.la: Cùm enim, Thucydide lib. iv. in orat. Brasidæ judice, habeatur ἀιοχιον, ἀπάτη ἐυπεμῖ ἀλεσπελήσαι, ἡ βία ἐμφανὲς, turpius fraude speciosa, quàm vi aperta sibi aliquid vindicare: ac Cicerone Offic. lib. i. arbitro, totius injustitiæ nulla capitalior sit, quàm eorum, qui tum, cùm maximè fallunt, id tamen agunt, ut viri boni, pii, religiosi, sancti, ʃti, esse videantur: profecto eos, quibus quaestui sunt capti superstitione animi, esse quàm injustissimos, avarissimos oportet.
units.tr: For since, in the judgement of Thucydides (book 4, in the speech of Brasidas), it is held shameful to be taken by a seemingly fair deception [ἀισχρὸν ... ἀπάτῃ εὐπρεπεῖ ἁλίσκεσθαι] rather than to claim something for oneself by open force; and since, in Cicero's judgement (Offices book 1), there is no more serious injustice than that of those who, while deceiving most, nevertheless manage to appear good, pious, religious, and holy; surely those whose gain is made from captive minds through superstition must be the most unjust and the most greedy of men.

units.la: XX. Hoc ergò mihi onus impositum video demonstrandi, ipsam Hierarchicorum religionem propriam ad quaestum superstitionibus ab avaris hominibus interpolatam, ac veluti dilutam fuisse;
units.tr: XX. I see, then, that the burden laid upon me is to demonstrate that the very religion of the Hierarchy, its own, has been interpolated and, as it were, diluted with superstitions, by greedy men, for the sake of profit.

units.la: Rem nulli obscuram, nostrae nec vocis egentem, Nam quia, S. Augustino lib. de utilit. credendi, docente, Haereticus est, qui alicujus temporalis commodi, & maximè gloriae principatúsque sui gratia falsas ac novas opiniones vel gignit vel sequitur; concinente S. Hieronymo in Jerem. cap. iy. quòd nulla haeresis nisi propter gulam ventremque constituatur, ut seducat cùm alios fraudibus opportunos, tum mulierculas oneratas peccatis, semper discentes, & nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes; de quibus verè dicatur: Qui devorant populum meum velut escam panis; & quos Christus notat devorantes domos viduarum: Cúmque praeterea Avarus omnis idololatra, ipsáque avaritia sit idololatria, Ephes. v. 5. Col. iii. 5. quicunque haereseos & idololatriae convincuntur, non possunt non quaestuosarum superstitionum invectarum arcessi. Nos autem Hierarchiam Haereseos & idololatriae supra manifeste convicimus.
units.tr: A matter obscure to no one, nor in need of our voice. For, as St Augustine teaches in his book On the Profit of Believing, a heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and above all for the sake of glory and his own leadership, either generates or follows false and new opinions; and as St Jerome agrees, in his commentary on Jeremiah chapter 4, that no heresy is established except for the sake of the belly and the stomach, so that it may seduce both those who are open to deceit and women burdened with sins, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth; of whom it may truly be said: who devour my people as they eat bread; and whom Christ marks as devouring the houses of widows. And since, besides, every covetous man is an idolater, and covetousness itself is idolatry (Eph. 5.5; Col. 3.5), whoever are convicted of heresy and idolatry cannot but be drawn from superstitions introduced for gain. We, however, have above plainly convicted the Hierarchy of heresy and idolatry.

units.la: XXI. Verùm insuper res ipsa loquitur. Nam ἀνεμίαι ἀλόξω seu principalia Hierarchiae dogmata, planè adamussim quaestuosissimae nundinationis facta & fidta sunt. Sic enim in Missa aurum, argentum, purpuram, hoc est, Deum, Christum, remissionem peccatorum: in Cultu Sanctorum, imaginum, reliquiarum lapidem pretiosum, margaritas, thus, hoc est, Divos Coelites, & eorum intercessionem ac merita: in Orationibus & oblationibus pro viventibus, & mortuis in purgatorio suffitum, thus, &c. hoc est preces & officia Ecclesiæ, Monachorum inprimis votis ad talia officia obstrictorum: in abusu clavium, obtinente tum in Sacramento Pœnitentiæ, tum extra illud in applicatione thesauri Ecclesiæ per indulgentias, aurum &c. byssum, purpuram, coccinum, hoc est, claves Regni cœlorum, remissionem peccatorum, & vitam æternam: in Sacramento Ordinis itidem aurum, argentum, tritieum, hoc est, Spiritum S. ejus dona & beneficia Ecclesiæ: in regimine Ecclesiæ leges per dispensationem in iisdem: in operibus charitatis &c. eleemosynas: in benedictionibus & consecrationibus unguentum, seu gratias Dei spirituales, ipsámque sepulturam: in universa jurisdictione Papali jumenta, rhedas, equos, animas, hoc est, corpora & animas subjectorum omnium in commercio suo habet. Sunt autem hæ fictitiæ merces, quas meretrix illa, carbones pro thesauris, hoc est, res nihili vilissimáfque omnium pro pecuniis, aliisque rebus, quas quantivis homines mundani faciunt, vendens, extrudere perfricta fronte satagit. Neque enim qui finguntur in Missa, cultu Sanctorum, orationibus pro viventibus & mortuis, purgatorio, Sacramento Pœnitentiæ, indulgentiis, Ordine &c. præsentes adsunt, vel præstantur Deus, Christus, Spiritus S. remissio & purgatio peccatorum, gratia Dei salutifera; sed præsentes adesse, præstarique à Quæstoribus & Trapezitis Hierarchicis, quæstûs occupandi gratia, finguntur.
units.tr: XXI. Moreover, the matter itself speaks. For the principal dogmas of the Hierarchy, [ἀνεμίαι ἀλόξω], were made and feigned exactly in the manner of the most profitable trade. Thus in the Mass gold, silver, and purple, that is, God, Christ, and the remission of sins; in the cult of the saints, of images, and of relics, precious stones, pearls, and incense, that is, the heavenly gods and their intercession and merits; in the prayers and offerings for the living and the dead in purgatory, incense and so on, that is, the prayers and services of the Church, especially of the monks bound by vows to such services; in the abuse of the keys, which holds sway both in the Sacrament of Penance and outside it, in the application of the treasury of the Church through indulgences: gold, fine linen, purple, scarlet, that is, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the remission of sins, and eternal life; in the Sacrament of Orders, likewise gold, silver, wheat, that is, the Holy Spirit, his gifts, and the benefits of the Church; in the government of the Church, laws through dispensations in the same matters; in the works of charity, alms; in blessings and consecrations, ointment, or the spiritual graces of God, and burial itself; in the whole Papal jurisdiction, beasts of burden, carriages, horses, souls, that is, the bodies and souls of all subjects, it keeps in its trade. These are the feigned wares which that harlot, selling charcoal for treasures, that is, worthless things, the cheapest of all, in exchange for money and other things which worldly men make, sets out with brazen face. For those things which are feigned in the Mass, in the cult of the saints, in prayers for the living and the dead, in purgatory, in the Sacrament of Penance, in indulgences, in Orders and so on, are not really present, nor is God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, the remission and cleansing of sins, or the saving grace of God actually supplied; rather, it is feigned that they are present and supplied by the Hierarchical quaestors and money-changers, for the sake of seizing profit.

units.la: XXII. Hierarchiæ anima Missa est. In ea enim sub larvis accidentium spumæ Deus ipse, Christus, atque is sacrificatus Deo ad expiationem peccatorum tum viventium tum mortuorum, promittitur; qua re nihil majùs, præstabilùs nihil promitti poterat. Ejus usus sub Papatu ad omnes actus extenditur, in quibus Papa secundùm duplicem jurisdictionem suam invenit, quod agat. Per Missam enim non solùm Templa, altaria, imagines, &c. confecrantur, sed regna per eandem eriguntur, incuntur, comitia celebrantur, statuta sanciuntur, dignitates conferuntur, imperia auspicatò traduntur, privilegia confirmantur, nuptiæ benedicuntur &c. Omnesdenique Creaturæ papales Missæ interventu creantur, & ab eadem vitam & spiritum accipiunt.
units.tr: XXII. The soul of the hierarchy is the Mass. For in it, under the masks of the accidents of the bread, God himself, Christ, and he who was sacrificed to God for the expiation of sins, both of the living and of the dead, are promised. Nothing greater and nothing more advantageous could be promised. Under the Papacy its use is extended to every act in which the Pope, according to his twofold jurisdiction, finds something he may do. For through the Mass not only temples, altars, images, etc. are consecrated, but kingdoms are set up and entered upon, assemblies are held, statutes are enacted, dignities are conferred, empires are auspiciously handed over, privileges are confirmed, marriages are blessed, etc. In short, all papal creatures are created by the intervention of the Mass, and receive life and spirit from it.

units.la: XXIII. Dogma hoc, quod verbo Dei & religioni Christianæ universæ adversari, alibi comprobavimus, ad quæstum occipiendum planè comparatum est.
units.tr: XXIII. This dogma, which we have shown elsewhere to be opposed to the word of God and to the whole Christian religion, is wholly designed for the acquisition of gain.

units.la: Etenim sacrificulo cuivis tribuitur immensa illa & verè Θαυμαστὴ potestas, pronuntiatis quinque vocibus, & Divino veluti carmine Θεὸν ἐκ μηχανῆς Deum Christum ipsum ex machina Cœli devocandi, ut ibi spirituali ratione sub accidentibus panis præsto sit, & maxima quæque efficiat. Hoc præterquam quòd Sacerdoti Divinam exi-stimationem conciliat, insuper etiam apud homines superstitione captos persuasionem, commendante virtutem Missæ eodem, gignit, quòd sacrificium hoc valeat pro vivis & mortuis, pro sanis & ægris; hominibus & bestiis, quòd per illud animæ liberentur e purgatorio, homines præservemur à pestilentia, quòd medeatur pecoribus, febres depellat, dentium dolorem prævertat, bona perdita recuperet, oculorum lippitudinem curet, victoriam adversùs inimicos procuret, conjugia salutaria efficiat. Aliáque ejusmodi Missæ ἀποτελέσματα, iidem plenis buccis decantant. Cùm ergò tam eximia potestate instructus sacrificulus creditur, si constiterit, cum prece vel pretio adduci posse, ut pro re nata facultatem illam suam applicet, quis non ei se totum, quis non facultates suas æquo animo eidem impenderit? Unde manifestum est, in Sacerdotis potestate planè esse, an hac ratione ungi ditari queant velit?
units.tr: For to any little priest is attributed that immense and truly wondrous [Θαυμαστὴ] power: by pronouncing five words and, as it were by a divine charm, summoning down from heaven God, Christ himself, "God from the machine" [Θεὸν ἐκ μηχανῆς], so that he is present there spiritually under the accidents of bread and effects all manner of things. This, besides winning the priest divine esteem, also produces in men held captive by superstition the persuasion, which commends the power of the Mass to them, that this sacrifice avails for the living and the dead, for the healthy and the sick, for men and beasts: that through it souls are freed from purgatory, men are preserved from plague, cattle are healed, fevers are driven away, toothache is prevented, lost goods are recovered, inflammation of the eyes is cured, victory over enemies is procured, and marriages are made salutary. The same people sing out with full cheeks other such effects [ἀποτελέσματα] of the Mass. Since, therefore, the little priest is believed to be endowed with such outstanding power, if it is established that he can be induced by prayer or by price to apply that power of his as the occasion requires, who would not devote himself wholly to him, who would not spend his means on him with a willing mind? Whence it is clear that it lies entirely in the priest's power whether he wishes to be anointed and enriched in this way.

units.la: XXIV. Velle autem, res ipsa, applicatio scilicet sacrificii hujus, clamat. Nam applicatur illud vel toti Ecclesiæ, siæ, vel singulis fidelibus, unde publicarum & privatarum Missarum discrimen incessit. Et privatæ quidem fere infinitæ sunt. Celebrantur enim pro divitibus, pro pauperibus, pro navigantibus, militantibus, peregrinantibus, ægrotantibus, negotiantibus, nubentibus, res perditas quærentibus, criminis patrati suspicione laborantibus, urbibus aut munitionibus sacrandis, sterilibus, gravidis, parturientibus, medicinâ utentibus, belligerantibus, fœdus ineuntibus, veneficio locisi; denique ut numero dicam, pro vivis, & defunctis quibusvis, quibus prodesse Missam ex opere Sacerdotis operato, hoc est, uti Albertus M. in cap. vj. Joh. explicat, perfectione externi operis sine motu interno, absentibus, nihil agentibus, dormientibus, de Missa non cogitantibus, sed alia omnia agentibus, illi sciscunt. Si Missa est de S. Gregorio, animas è purgatorio liberat; Si de S. Rocho, à peste; Si de S. Antonio, pecoribus medetur; de S. Sigismundo, febrim pellit; de S. Antonio Paduano, amissa recuperat; de S. Apolonia, dentium dolores sedat; de S. Lucia oculos sanat &c.
units.tr: XXIV. That he does wish it, the thing itself cries out: namely, the application of this sacrifice. For it is applied either to the whole Church or to individual faithful, and from this arose the distinction between public and private Masses. Private Masses are almost infinite in number. For they are celebrated for the rich, for the poor, for sailors, soldiers, travellers, the sick, merchants, newly married couples, those seeking lost things, those labouring under suspicion of a committed crime, for the consecration of cities or fortifications, for the barren, the pregnant, women in labour, those using medicine, those going to war, those entering a covenant, those bewitched. In short, to say it in a word, they are celebrated for the living and the dead of any kind, to whom the Mass profits by the work of the priest performed (ex opere operato), that is, as Albertus Magnus explains in in cap. vj. Joh., by perfectione externi operis sine motu interno: the absent, those doing nothing, those sleeping, those not thinking of the Mass but doing all other things. They decree this. If the Mass is of St Gregory, it frees souls from purgatory; if of St Roch, from plague; if of St Anthony, it heals cattle; of St Sigismund, it drives away fever; of St Anthony of Padua, it recovers lost things; of St Apollonia, it calms toothaches; of St Lucy, it cures the eyes, etc.

units.la: XXV. In universum autem obtinet regula, quam Emmanuel Sa, Aphorism. in verbo Missa, §. 43. his verbis consignavit: Missa illis plus prodest, pro quibus particulariter offertur. Quòd si pro multis offertur, non tantum singulis prodesse, ac si pro illis offerretur, docent Sylvester, Navarrus, Soto, Toletus, Suarezius, Scotus. Idque Cardinalis Toletus de Instructione Sacerd. lib. v. 8. declarat hoc exemplo: Sicut, si ego jejunem pro quatuor, minus prodest ad satisfactionem singulis, quàm uni prodesset, si pro uno tantum jejunàssem. Quis non arcanum subolfacit? Si pro duobus tantundem valeret una Missa, quantum pro uno: pro tribus etiam, quatuor, decem, centum, tantundem valeret. Si ergò pro centum laborantibus ex æquo una Missa pecuniæ pretio redempta, valeret,
units.tr: XXV. In general, the following rule holds, which Emmanuel Sa set down in these words in his Aphorisms, under the word Missa, §. 43: A Mass benefits most those for whom it is offered in particular. But if it is offered for many, it does not benefit each of them as much as if it were offered for each one alone; Sylvester, Navarrus, Soto, Toletus, Suarez and Scotus teach this. Cardinal Toletus, On the Instruction of Priests, book 5, ch. 8, illustrates this with an example: Just as, if I fast for four people, it benefits each of them less toward satisfaction than it would have benefited one person if I had fasted for that one alone. Who does not smell a secret here? If one Mass were worth as much for two people as for one, it would be worth as much for three, four, ten, or a hundred. So if one Mass, bought for money, were worth equally for a hundred sufferers,

units.la: Tom. II. ret, conclamatum esset de quæstu sacrificulorum, atque lentis maxillis comedendum longè pluribus esset.
