Idem, qui suprà Emmanuel Sa, s. 44. scribit: Illud certum est, Sacerdotem, si uni debeat unam Missam, & alteri alteram, non satisfacere, si unam dicat pro utroque simul: Idem Doctores, qui suprà. Addit tamen: Duas eleemosynas pro una Missa accipi posse, docet Soto. Eleemosynam vocat quæstum pro Missa. Toletus vocat pitantiam, hoc est, contributionem. Sic enim Instruct. Sacerd. lib. ȳ. 8. loquitur: Soto tenet, quòd pauper potest saltem duas pitantias recipere pro una Missa ad sustentationem. Idem Toletus eodem libro cap. 6. negat Missam per modum satisfactionis & justitiæ conferre; nisi, sic excipit, mortui, dum vixerunt, ad missas sibi celebrandas pecunias erogârunt. Tunc enim per modum satisfactionis & justitiæ conferunt. Pecuniam ergò erogantibus Deus ipse constituitur debitor, ut Missæ pro iis obitæ satisfactionis & justitiæ rationem habeant, atque sic demum remissionem peccatorum promereantur. Hinc adeò Missæ cariori vel viliori pretio venduntur, prout in ejus celebratione ornamenta sumptuosiora, vel minùs sumptuosa adhibentur. Sunt enim Missæ aureæ, sunt stannæ, sunt cupreæ, sunt lignæ, sunt summæ, sunt medioxumæ, sunt infimæ. Accedit regula inter trapeziticas haud postrema, quam idem Emanuel Sa in verbo Missa, his verbis prodidit: Cui datur certa summa pecuniæ pro Missis à se dicendis, potest alios pro pretio minore conducere, qui adjuvent, & reliquum sibi retinere. Sic Sacerdos quispiam altioris subsellii adhibito servientium famelicorum sacerdotum ministerio, non contemnendum quæstum ex Missa facere potest, licet ipse raro vel nunquam missificet.
units.tr: Tom. II. it would be cried out against as a trade of the little sacrificers, and it would have to be swallowed by far more people with slow jaws. The same Emmanuel Sa, cited above, §. 44, writes: It is certain that a priest who owes one Mass to one person and another to a second does not satisfy his debt if he says one Mass for both at once. The same teachers as above. He adds, however: Soto teaches that two alms may be received for one Mass. He calls the payment for a Mass an alms. Toletus calls it pitantia, that is, a contribution. For so he speaks in the Instruction of Priests, book 5, ch. 8: Soto holds that a poor man may receive at least two pitantias for one Mass, for his support. The same Toletus, in the same book, ch. 6, denies that a Mass is applied by way of satisfaction and justice, except, as he makes exception, when the dead, while they were alive, paid out money for Masses to be said for them. For then they apply it by way of satisfaction and justice. Therefore God himself is made the debtor to those who pay out money, so that the Masses offered for them may count as satisfaction and justice, and so at last they may earn the forgiveness of sins. Hence Masses are sold at a higher or lower price, according as costlier or cheaper ornaments are used in their celebration. For there are golden Masses, tin Masses, copper Masses, wooden Masses, highest Masses, middling Masses, and lowest Masses. To this is added a rule, not the least among the money-changers' rules, which the same Emmanuel Sa gave under the word Missa in these words: One who is given a fixed sum of money for Masses to be said by himself may hire others at a lower price to help him, and keep the rest for himself. So a certain priest, by using the service of starving priests who serve under him, can make no small profit from Masses, even though he himself rarely or never says Mass.

units.la: XXVI. Iam ergò fœda missantium nundinatio in propatulo omnium est. Si enim sordidum illi quæstum missando præcipuè non intendunt, cur privatas quæstuosas, quàm publicas non quæstuosas Missas, frequentiores: imò has cum illis comparatas ferè nullas habent? Cur privatas Missas, communicantibus orbatas, tanquam unicè salutares infatiabiliter commendant, publicas non item? Cur publicis Missis tantundem efficaciæ pro singulis, quàm privatis pro singulis, non tribuunt? An enim sanguinis Christi sacrificium publicè & sine pretio applicatum, minorem efficaciam habet, quàm applicatum seorsim, & numerato pretio? Si, quod Gabriel Biel Lect. 26. sustinet, non solus Deus, sed etiam Sacerdos offerens Sacrificium in persona Ecclesiæ potest ejus fructum & virtutem alicui, vel aliquibus specialiter applicare, & sacerdotis est virtutem Sacrificii & oblationis determinare, ut illis, vel illis indigentibus præmium reddendum pro hujusmodi Ecclesiæ sacrificio conferatur, cur igitur Sacerdos non determinat, ut vel Missa publica eandem erga singulos virtutem exerat, quam privata erga singulos exerit: vel privata pro pluribus celebrata eandem virtutem singulis communicet: vel una Missa, seu Christus, cujus victima infiniti pretii est, semel oblatus, idem præstet, atque Missa frequentata, seu Christus identidem oblatus? Manifestum est, solam Reginam pecuniam totam hanc differentiam invexisse. Sed & rationem Missifici reddant velim, quare divitis, qui largius pretium contulit, vel conscientiâ scelerum pressus, & suppliciorum post hanc vitam gravi metu anxius, altare exstrui curavit, vel proventus Sacerdoti pro se Missanti liberaliter legavit, anima ad sui redemtionem pluribus Missis indigeat, pauperis contra, sive piè ille, sive impiè vixit, qui æra, quæ Sacerdoti largiatur, nulla habet, anima, longè paucioribus, fortè unâ, & quandoque nullâ? vel hujus animam ob solum pecuniæ defectum, diuturniora & pertinaciora tormenta pati sinant: vel unâ, imò quandóque nullâ Missâ, eas æquè ac divitum animas redimant? Illud Sacrificulorum animum barbarum, crudelissimúmque, hoc sordidissimè avarum arguit. Cùm dives moritur, vix ullum in Templo altare non occupatur à missificibus ad redemptionem animæ ejus, non in exequiis duntaxat, sed etiam trigesimâ septimâ, uti appellant, & feriis anniversariis, quandiu Pactoli fluvius stagnat. Hinc adeò præbendæ pinguescere, proventus Altarium, Sacellorum, Templorum, incrementa capere, denique Papa bonorum Ecclesiasticorum administer præbendas & proventus emungendi, & irrigua illa Pactoli fluenta ad Romanam Datariam, atque inde ad Cameram Apostolicam derivandi occasione oblata strenuè uti. Atque querelam hac de re suam jam pridem Alvarus Pelagius de Planctu Ecclesiæ lib. ij. art. 5. consignavit his verbis: Tot hodiè dicuntur Missæ quasi QUÆSTUARIÆ, vel consuetudinariæ, & ad complacentiam, vel ad scelera cooperienda, vel propriam justificationem, quòd apud populum vel Clerum Sacrosanctum corpus Domini jam vilescit. Dixerat paulò antè: Nostra Ecclesia est plena & superplena altaribus, missis & sacrificiis. Sed cum hoc plena in sacrificantibus, homicidiis, sacrilegiis, & immunditiis, & SIMONIIS, & aliis sceleribus. Unum addo insignem, & imò immanem mercaturam Missalem vel inde etiam agnosci, quòd in Gallia Sacerdotes non suos duntaxat ex fundis reditus locant, sed etiam illud, quod vocant Les dedans de l'Eglise, hoc est, quicquid ex oblationibus, quæ fiunt intra septa Templorum, corradunt, publicè licitatum addicunt. An fœdior rerum sacrarum nundinatio excogitari potest? XXVII. Quid quòd Missa etiam civilis in Papatu nundinationis fundamentum constituitur, ut ad χάραγμα seu characterem illum, quo signatus potestatem accipit emendi& vendendi, quæ lex Antichristi est Apoc. xiii. 16. 17. præprimis referri debeat. Unde celeberrimæ nundinæ Missæ nomine pridem venerunt. Quam in rem aliquid B. Rhenanus Præf· ad Liturgiam Chrysostomi dixit his verbis: Missæ publicæ tanta populi religione, & tam frequenti conventu fiebant solennibus duntaxat diebus, ut in Francorum legibus, quæ ipsi capitula vocitabant, & aliis scriptoribus præcedentium seculorum, quorum præfinitum terminum nominare opus est, ad Missam Johannis vel Andreæ, vel candelarum Missam, aut inter duas D. Mariæ Missas, Assumptionem & Nativitatem intelligentes, aliquid faciendum intelligunt. Quemadmodum autem ad publicam Missam tanta populi vis undique confluebat, ita solebant & mercatores publico peracto sacro, res venales proponere, ex opportunitate frequentiæ popularis quæstum captantes. Unde factum est, ut à Gallis & Germanis Missæ vocabulum nundinis ac mercatui tribuatur. Vocant enim Missam Lugdunensem, Francofordiensem, Antverpiensem &c. ubi merces solenni negotiatorum conventu distrahuntur. Proinde non est mirandum, cur Calixtus Pontifex Romanus prohibuerit, ne Abbas publicas Missas cantet, & Gregorius, ne Episcopi, vel Clerici in Monasterio idem facere tentent, ne videlicet, ut idem ad Castorium scribit, in Dei servorum recessibus, & eorum receptaculis ulla popularis præbeatur occasio conventús. Siquidem promiscua hominum multitudo, viri, mulieres, adolescentes, & puellæ sacram etiam communionem si quibus collibuisset, una cum sacerdote percipiebant. Quàm verò jus mercaturæ, cum jure missandi arcto nexu conjunctum fuerit, maximè ex interdictis illis perspicere licuit, per quæ olim R. Pontifices Missæ usum & cultum in Regno, Provincia, Ducatu, vel Urbe, dicto eorum minùs obedientes, suspendere solebant, qua calamitate in nocte illa temporum nihil calamitosius, tristius nihil judicabatur, sol enim & luna illis nigrescere videbatur, si vel uno die Missa carere cogerentur: Ideoque Pontifices hoc ceu fulmine, & maxime penetrabili telo hostes suos terrere, & vires eorum frangere consueverunt. Id quod, Resp. Veneta sub Julio II. non sine damno suo experta est. Qui idem deinceps telum in Ludovicum XII. direxerat, Lugdunensibus minitatus, se, si pergant Regi suo contra Ecclesiam opitulari, Missam, qua hactenus antecessorum suorum indultu fruerentur, iis ereptam, Avinionensibus collaturum. Sub Missa autem celeberrimas nundinas intellexit, quarum videlicet jus super Missae idolo fundatum erat. Quod si tum Gallia Jesuitas concionatores & turbatores habuisset, res plane ex sententia Papae successisset, & Lugdunensis Missa colonias suas haud dubie migrasset.
units.tr: XXVI. So the shameful trafficking of those who say Masses is now plain to all. If they do not chiefly aim at sordid gain by saying Masses, why do they have far more private Masses, which bring in money, than public Masses, which do not; indeed, why do they hardly have any public Masses by comparison? Why do they tirelessly commend private Masses, which are without communicants, as the only truly saving ones, but not public Masses? Why do they not grant that public Masses have as much efficacy for each individual as private Masses have for each individual? Does the sacrifice of Christ's blood, applied publicly and without payment, have less efficacy than when it is applied separately for a set price? If, as Gabriel Biel maintains in Lect. 26, the priest offering the sacrifice in the person of the Church can apply its fruit and power specially to someone or some people, and it is for the priest to determine the power of the sacrifice and oblation, so that it is given as a reward for such a sacrifice of the Church to those or those in need, why then does the priest not determine that either a public Mass exerts the same power on each individual as a private Mass exerts on each individual; or that a private Mass celebrated for many imparts the same power to each individual; or that one Mass, or Christ, whose victim is of infinite worth, offered once, does the same thing as a Mass repeated often, or Christ offered again and again? It is clear that money alone has introduced this whole difference. But I would like the Mass-monger to explain also why the soul of a rich man, who has paid a larger sum, or who, oppressed by the awareness of his sins and anxious with the heavy fear of punishment after this life, has had an altar built, or has generously left income to a priest to say Mass for him, needs many Masses for its redemption, while the soul of a poor man, whether he lived piously or impiously, who has no money to give the priest, needs far fewer, perhaps one, and sometimes none; or why they allow the soul of the poor man, for lack of money alone, to suffer longer and more stubborn torments, while they redeem the souls of the rich, and those of the poor equally, with one Mass, or sometimes with none at all. The first practice betrays the barbarous and most cruel spirit of these little priests; the second betrays the most sordid avarice. When a rich man dies, scarcely any altar in the Temple is left unoccupied by Mass-sayers for the redemption of his soul, not only at the funeral, but also on the thirty-seventh day, as they call it, and on the anniversary days, for as long as the river Pactolus flows. Hence prebends grow fat, the revenues of altars, chapels and temples increase, and finally the Pope, the steward of ecclesiastical goods, eagerly uses the opportunity offered to squeeze out prebends and revenues and to channel those rich streams of Pactolus to the Roman Datary, and from there to the Apostolic Chamber. And Alvarus Pelagius long ago recorded his complaint on this matter in de Planctu Ecclesiæ lib. ij. art. 5. in these words: So many Masses are today said as QUESTUARY, or customary, and for pleasing, or for covering up crimes, or for one's own justification, that the most holy body of the Lord is already held cheap among the people and the clergy. He had said a little before: Our Church is full and more than full of altars, Masses and sacrifices. But it is full also of sacrilege, homicide, uncleanness, SIMONY and other crimes. I add one more notable and even monstrous Mass-trade, recognised from this: in France the priests not only let out the income from their own estates, but also sell at public auction what they call Les dedans de l'Eglise, that is, whatever they collect from the offerings made within the walls of the temples. Can a more shameful trafficking in sacred things be imagined? XXVII. Moreover, even the civil Mass is made the foundation of trade in Papacy, so that it should be referred above all to that character [χάραγμα], or mark, by which the one who is marked receives the power to buy and sell, which is the law of Antichrist, Rev. 13:16, 17. Hence the most famous fairs have long been named after the Mass. On this matter B. Rhenanus said something in his Preface to the Liturgy of Chrysostom in these words: Public Masses were celebrated with such reverence of the people and such a frequent gathering only on solemn days, that in the laws of the Franks, which they called capitularies, and in other writers of earlier centuries, whose fixed term it is necessary to name, they understand that something is to be done at the Mass of John or Andrew, or the Mass of the candles, or between the two Masses of the Blessed Mary, the Assumption and the Nativity. Just as a great crowd of people flocked from everywhere to the public Mass, so merchants too, once the sacred rite was finished, used to put their goods up for sale, seizing gain from the opportunity of the popular gathering. Hence it came about that the Gauls and Germans gave the word Mass to fairs and trade. For they call the Mass of Lyon, of Frankfurt, of Antwerp, and so on, where goods are sold at a solemn gathering of traders. Therefore it is no wonder that Pope Callixtus forbade abbots to sing public Masses, and that Gregory forbade bishops or clerics to attempt the same in a monastery, lest, as he writes to Castorius, any popular occasion for a gathering should be given in the retreats of God's servants and their shelters. For a mixed multitude of men, women, young men and girls used to receive even the sacred communion, if they wished, together with the priest. How closely the right of trade was bound up with the right of saying Mass can best be seen from those interdicts by which the Roman Pontiffs used to suspend the use and worship of Mass in a kingdom, province, duchy or city whose people were less obedient to their word. In that dark age nothing was judged more calamitous or sadder than this calamity; for the sun and moon seemed to grow dark for them if they were forced to go without Mass even for one day. So the Pontiffs were accustomed to terrify their enemies with this as with a thunderbolt, and a most penetrating weapon, and to break their strength. The Venetian Republic experienced this to its cost under Julius II. The same Pope afterwards aimed this weapon at Louis XII, threatening the people of Lyon that, if they continued to help their King against the Church, he would take away from them the Mass which they had enjoyed until then by the indulgence of his predecessors and bestow it on the people of Avignon. By Mass he meant the most famous fairs, whose right was founded, that is, upon the idol of the Mass. And if France had then had Jesuit preachers and troublemakers, the matter would have turned out entirely according to the Pope's wishes, and the Mass of Lyon would undoubtedly have migrated to its colonies.

units.la: XXVIII. Accedit & hoc non postremum, quod non tantum Imperiorum, Regnorum, Provinciarum, Urbium, & potentissimarum familiarum jura, immunitates, privilegia, honor, stemmata, adeoque incolumitas ipsa, sed etiam Ecclesiae Collegiatae, quas vocant, & Templorum Cathedralium Basilicae cum censibus, reditibus, & privilegiis suis, nec non diversarum religionum diversi ordines cum suis regulis, coenobiis, approbationibus & indulgentiis: denique Clerus omnis & Sacerdotium universum cum omnibus suis plus quam Regalibus divitiis, cum Missali hoc idolo adeo arte colligata sunt, ut nemo hoc vel uno digitulo tangere possit, vel potuerit unquam, quin haec omnia una convellere, atque sic totum orbem turbare videretur.
units.tr: XXVIII. Add to this, and this is no small matter, that not only the rights, immunities, privileges, honours, pedigrees of empires, kingdoms, provinces, cities and most powerful families, and indeed their very safety, but also the so-called collegiate churches and the basilicas of cathedral temples, with their revenues, incomes and privileges, as well as the various orders of various religious bodies with their rules, monasteries, approvals and indulgences; finally, the whole clergy and the entire priesthood with all their riches, more than royal, are so closely bound together with this Mass-idol that no one can touch it even with a little finger, or ever could, without seeming to overthrow all of these at once and so throw the whole world into turmoil.

units.la: XXIX. Sic fuit Missalis Hierarchicorum nundinatio: Cui proxima est, quam in cultu externo circa Sanctos, eorumque imagines & reliquias exercent. Ibi enim sanctorum
units.tr: XXIX. Such was the Mass-trading of the hierarchs. Next to it is the trade they carry on in external worship of the saints, and their images and relics. For there these new publicans put up for public sale the fictitious merits of the saints

units.la: rum nım fictitia merita, & meritis innixa suffragia intercessionésque ad impetranda beneficia corporalia & spiritualia, publico quæstui novi hi publicani exponunt. Neque enim hic etiam consilia eorum tam altè abscondita sunt, quin quivis, etiam sine emissitiis oculis dispicere possint, dummodò ne data operâ cœcutiant. Et sanè nisi cultui huic Divorum, imaginum & reliquiarum eorum crassè idololatrico temporalis emolumenti mysterium subesset ejusmodi, quale olim etiam cultu idololatrico Belis, Babylloniorum Sacerdotum impia machinatione, subfuisse, in Epistola Jeremiæ v. 28. &c. narratur, mirum profecto esset, à Christianis Sacerdotibus cultum istiusmodi retinere, qui Dei verbo tam manifestè repugnat, primo & secundo Decalogi præcepto è diametro adversatur; & immane adeò scandalum piis & sobriis Christianis, ipsisque denique infidelibus Judæis & Turcis objicit.
units.tr: of the saints, and the intercessions and suffrages founded on merits for obtaining bodily and spiritual benefits. Nor are their schemes here so deeply hidden that anyone, even without piercing eyes, cannot see through them, unless they deliberately make themselves blind. And indeed, if this worship of the saints, their images and relics did not conceal a mystery of temporal gain, of the crudely idolatrous kind, like that which, as is related in the Epistle of Jeremiah 5:28 and following, once lay behind the idolatrous worship of Bel, through the impious contrivance of the priests of Babylon, it would truly be a marvel that Christian priests retain a worship of this kind, which so plainly contradicts God's word, is diametrically opposed to the first and second commandments of the Decalogue, and offers such an enormous scandal to pious and sober Christians, and finally even to the unbelieving Jews and Turks.

units.la: XXX. Sanctorum invocatio cum imaginum & reli- quiarum earundem cultu conjunctissima est.
units.tr: XXX. The invocation of the saints is most closely bound up with the worship of their images and relics.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem cultus ille universus suâ naturâ ad quæstum faciendum comparatus sit, nullo negotio cognoscere poterit, quisquis secum reputaverit, statuam hujus vel illius Sancti, puta B. Virginis Mariæ, S. Petri Janitoris Cœli, S. Jacobi, Sebastiani, Rochi, aliorumque quorumvis scitè adeò & decorè exornatorum, & satis vivis coloribus depictorum, aptam natam esse movere & irritare populum ad fornicationem spiritualem suâptè naturâ, cum verbo Dei non dirigitur & lenocinantium contra ductorum suorum consilio & exemplo seducitur, proclivem, ut non solùm ora sua in orationes resolvat, sed etiam manus sportis & oblationibus muniat, anxio scilicet jam metu imbutum, ne Sanctulum suum vacuâ manu adeuntes, minùs propitium ad faciendá desiderata experiatur. Inprimis si potentior accedat illecebra, & arte quadam idolorum quæstores efficiant, ut imago nunc frontem caperare, nunc suavius arridere, pro donorum tenuitate vel amplitudine videatur; vel statuarum cultores, suspensis in omnium conspectu donationibus, & donantium religiosorum, liberaliúmque clientum nominibus publice consignatis, ad æmulationem provocent. Neque levior ad liberalitatem exercendam stimulus erit, si quæstores iidem publicam fidem fecerint, quod hic vel ille Sanctus eximiam virtutem, hæc vel illa miracula patrandi, huic vel illi morbo medendi, his, aliisque angustiis & calamitatibus succurrendi habeat, magnáque insuper indulgentiarum vi, ab earundem diributore Papa dotatus sit. Quàm hæc aliáque potenter in animos superstitione imbutos influant, ut vota in morbis, periculis, calamitatibus huic vel illi Sancto & Patrono nuncupent, & ad Sanctorum Templa vel Sacella, eorum imagines & reliquias, peregrinationes religiosas promtè instituant? Ubi introducti ad visibilem quasi Sancti illius præsentiam, non poterunt præ pudore, quin ob beneficia ab eo jam præstita vel præstanda, pro facultatum suarum ratione, pretium offerant, certa spe freti, fore ut par vel majus pretio mercimonium reportent.
units.tr: Anyone who reflects on it will easily see how this whole cult is by its nature designed for profit. A statue of this or that saint, say the Blessed Virgin Mary, St Peter the Doorkeeper of Heaven, St James, Sebastian, Roch, or any other saint elegantly adorned and painted in lively colours, is naturally apt to move and stir the people to spiritual fornication. Not guided by the Word of God, they are seduced by the counsel and example of their pimps and leaders, and so they are inclined not only to turn their lips to prayers but also to arm their hands with baskets and offerings, already imbued with anxious fear that, approaching their little saint empty-handed, they will find him less willing to grant their desires. This is especially so if a stronger enticement is added, when by some art the sellers of idols make the image now seem to frown and now to smile more sweetly, according to the meagreness or abundance of the gifts. Or the devotees of the statues, with gifts hung up in full view and the names of pious and generous clients publicly recorded, provoke emulation. The spur to open-handed giving will be no weaker if the same sellers vouch publicly that this or that saint has remarkable power to work this or that miracle, to heal this or that disease, and to relieve these or other distresses and calamities, and moreover that he has been endowed by the Pope, the distributor of indulgences, with a great power of indulgences. How powerfully these and other things flow into minds steeped in superstition, so that they make vows to this or that saint and patron in sickness, dangers and calamities, and readily undertake pilgrimages to the temples or shrines of the saints, to their images and relics! Once brought into the quasi-visible presence of that saint, they cannot, for shame, refrain from offering a price, according to their means, for the benefits already conferred or still to be conferred, trusting with firm hope that they will obtain a bargain of equal or greater value.

units.la: XXXI. Manifestum hinc est, cultum Sanctorum, imaginum & reliquiarum eorum ad mangonum seu mercatorum horum Babylonicorum incudem formatu exactum, que esse. Sed & opportunitate illa mercandi ab aliquot jam seculis iidem utuntur strenuè, & Sanctorum illo cultu defunguntur ad insaniam usque, majore profecto lucro νεωκόρων ædituorum Clericorum, quàm pietatis. Etenim primò, ipsa Apotheosis, seu Canonizatio Sanctorum, quid aliud est, quàm ars χρυσοποιητική, qua Sancti creantur non sine Regiis Regum & Principum muneribus, Papæ, Bileami hic viam insistenti, oblatis, ne non per auream scalam thronum suum Sancti conscendere cogantur. Nisi enim
units.tr: XXXI. It is clear from this that the cult of the saints, of their images and of their relics, has been fashioned to the exact pattern of the anvil of these Babylonian merchants and dealers. And these men have long since used this opportunity for trade vigorously, and they drain the saints' cult to the point of madness, the sacristans [νεωκόρων] and clerics gaining far more profit than piety. For, first, the very apotheosis, or canonization, of saints is nothing other than the art of alchemy [χρυσοποιητική], by which saints are created not without gifts offered to the Pope, who here follows the way of Balaam, by kings and princes, lest they be forced to climb to their throne by a golden ladder. For unless

units.la: Sanctis illis primùm essent propitii cultores suieorum sanctitas intra privatos lateret lares, laterémque lavaret, qui pecuniâ non numeratâ suum in album referri candidatum suum peteret. Exemplnm in Apotheosi Francisci Salesii Historia Papatús ff. cclxxiv. repræsentavit. Neque ipsi hoc Jesuitæ dissimulabunt, memores, non sine ingentibus impensis suis, novos suos Apostolos Beatitudinis & Sanctitatis suæ gradum conscendisse. Quidni autem isthoc ἐκθεώσεως seu Deificandi artificium magno constet, cùm ii, qui sic creantur Divi, & quorum ipsa ossa, vestes, supellectilia canonizantur, regnorum, nationum, provinciarum, urbium, arcium, collegiorum, sodalitatum, communitatum, opificiorum, religionum, ordinum, Episcopatuum, studiorum, facultatum, commerciorum, meretricum, militiæ, terra nascentium, aurifodinarum, illustrium familiarum, ipsorúmque animalium Patroni, Disque Tutelares constituantur, adeóque ad Divinam authoritatem evehantur?
units.tr: those saints first had devoted worshippers, their sanctity would lie hidden within private household shrines and would be washing bricks to no purpose, since whoever wished to have his candidate entered in the roll would have to pay out ready money. The Historia Papatus, p. 274, gives an example in the apotheosis of Francis de Sales. Nor will the Jesuits themselves deny it, mindful that their new apostles climbed to the rank of His Beatitude and Holiness not without enormous expense of their own. Why should this art of apotheosis, or deification, not be a great expense, when those who are thus made divine, whose very bones, clothes and furnishings are canonized, are appointed patrons and protectors of kingdoms, nations, provinces, cities, citadels, colleges, fraternities, communities, trades, religious orders, bishoprics, schools, faculties, commerce, prostitutes, soldiers, lands, gold mines, illustrious families, and even animals, and are thus raised to divine authority?

units.la: XXXII. Neque Canonizatio duntaxat, sed Canoni- zati etiam Divi, eorum imagines & reliquiæ ingenti lu- cro mactantur.
units.tr: XXXII. Not only canonization, but also the canonized saints themselves, and their images and relics, are sacrificed for great gain.

units.la: Nihil dicam de festis Sanctorum, quorum nullum non est destinatum nundinis: nihil de exactionibus, cùm forte per Dioecesin Episcopi alicujus nova efferetur Sancti celebritas, ad quam passim fit concursus. Tum enim (sic Germani in Gravamine suo LII. conqueruntur) Episcopi aut Prælati eò loci oblationum omnium tertiam, aut certè quartam partem sibi vendicare præsumunt. Dicam pauca de religiosis ad loca Divorum imaginibus & reliquiis inclyta peregrinationibus. Sunt autem eæ secundariæ penè innumeræ: primariæ, Busæo distribuente, quatuor, Hierosolymitana, Romana, Compostellensis & Lauretena. Scopus omnium unus idémque est, beatis quibusdam, & ad compendium quæstúmque affabrè confictis
units.tr: I will say nothing of the feasts of the saints, for there is not one of them that is not appointed to a fair. I will say nothing of the exactions, when perhaps a new celebration of some saint is put forward throughout the diocese of a bishop, to which people flock from everywhere. For then (as the Germans complain in their Gravamen LII) the bishops or prelates presume to claim for themselves a third, or at least a quarter, of all the offerings made on the spot. I will say a few words about the religious pilgrimages to places famous for the images and relics of the divine saints. These are almost countless, though Busaeus lists four principal ones: Jerusalem, Rome, Compostela and Loreto. The aim of all of them is the same: to fleece people captured by that superstition with certain blessed trifles, cleverly fashioned for profit, and to lie in wait diligently for their purses.

units.la: nugis,homines superstitione illa captos, emungere, eorúmque loculis gnaviter insidiari. Excellit hodie Lauretana, fabulosæ transportatæ Nazaretho per aëra Cameræ Deiparæ innixa,quæ quantum assertoribus suis profuerit,ex eo perspicitur, quòd non tantùm Curio Lauretanus, nomine Teremanus author narrationis, luculentum culinæ suæ focum inde instruxit: verùm etiam ex pago, vix unum ante sacrificulum alente, frequens oppidum, cinctum mœnibus & propugnaculis munitissimis effectum est, ubi Canonici & Capellani plurimi habitant, & deliciis luxúque diffluunt. Quin usque adeò simul existimatio & commoditas loci crevit, ut Cardinales inter se de præfectura loci gladiari soleant. Turselinus ipse Jesuita quinque hac de fabula perscriptis libris, hoc unum fere agit, ut quàm tenuibus à principiis Lauretanum cum oppido Templum, quantis auctibus accreverit, exponat: & invidendas, stupendas, superbas opes explicet hac ærufcatione comparatas, & in illam humilem pauperculámque Mariam collatas. Quæ benigna Diva non ita tamen rerum suarum tenax est, quin eas cum aliis quoque communicet. Nam & fama certa constat, & ex Turselini locis aliquot haud obscurè colligitur, Papam non raro solere Lauretanos illos thesauros excutere; & sumtá sibi parte superfluâ, relinquere reliquas, quarum ostentatione Diva munificentiam aliorum provocet. Nam etiam Eleusina, uti proverbium habet, servat, quod ostendat. Constat planè, Papam ex isto Europæ spoliario, fœdóque prædonum receptaculo, quotannis ad centena millia nummorum aureorum collegisse, quanquam illi reditus admodùm accisi & imminuti fuerint, ab eo tempore, quo {grc}μαχυπιδια{/grc} nimiáque credulitas in orbis Europæi parte meliore desiit, & animadverti coeptum est, sacrificulos non vero Zelo domûs Dei, sed utilitatis suæ, turpis lucri, viscerationúmque suarum ratione ductos, commentis ejusmodi fidem adstruere. Sufficiat, Lauretanam peregrinationem solam produxisse in exemplum reliquarum, quarum nulla abjecta adeo & vilis est, quin sacerdotibus Divi cujuspiam, imaginis, vel reliquiarum ejus custodibus, qui merces hasce licitatum addicunt, opes non contemnendas conciliet. Et idolorum illorum vestibula sciunt omnes non magis peregrinis trita, quam mercatoribus quisquilias vendentibus. Ubicunque enim ejusmodi fana, & fanis inclusa Numina adeuntur, ibi tabernæ etiam institoriæ, ibi collybisticæ trapezitarum mensæ iisdem individuo nexu cohærentes, & extremâ impudentiâ exercitæ, palam prostant, & sacerrimam illam cauponationem apertissimè produnt.
units.tr: Loreto is the chief one today, with its fabulous chamber of the Mother of God, said to have been carried through the air from Nazareth. How much this has benefited its champions is evident from the fact that not only did the Loreto curate, Teremanus by name, the author of the narrative, build a splendid hearth for his kitchen from it, but also a little village, which hardly fed one priest before, has become a busy town, enclosed by walls and very strongly fortified, where many canons and chaplains live and wallow in luxury and pleasures. Indeed, the reputation and convenience of the place have so grown that cardinals are wont to fight with one another over the governorship of it. Turselinus himself, the Jesuit, in five books on this story, mainly sets out to show how the Loreto temple, together with the town, grew from such slender beginnings to such increases, and to explain the enviable, astonishing, proud wealth gathered by this bronze-trading and heaped upon that humble and poor Mary. Yet this kindly goddess is not so tight-fisted with her possessions that she does not share them with others too. For it is well established by report, and is quite clearly gathered from several passages of Turselinus, that the Pope has often been accustomed to shake out those Loreto treasures, and, taking the superfluous part for himself, to leave the rest, by whose display the goddess might provoke the generosity of others. For even Eleusis, as the proverb says, keeps what it shows. It is plain that the Pope has collected some hundreds of thousands of gold coins yearly from this Europe-wide plunder and foul receptacle of robbers, although those revenues have been much reduced and diminished since the time when [μαχυπιδια] and excessive credulity ceased in the better part of the European world, and men began to notice that the sacristans, moved not by zeal for God's house but by their own advantage, base gain and the care of their bellies, were confirming faith in such fictions. It is enough that the Loreto pilgrimage alone has been brought forward as an example of the rest, none of which is so abject and cheap that it fails to win considerable riches for the priests of some saint, of his image, or of the keepers of his relics, who bring these wares to auction and sell them to the highest bidder. And everyone knows that the porches of those idols are as worn by pilgrims as they are by merchants selling trifles. For wherever such temples are visited, and the deities enclosed in them, there too shops and money-changers' tables, joined in indissoluble union with them and carried on with the utmost shamelessness, openly flourish and betray that most sacred huckstering.

units.la: XXXIII. Quàm impudenter Babylonii hi mercatores Stationarii Divorum cultum jam olim etiam cauponati sint, uno ad- huc specimine pandam.
units.tr: XXXIII. How shamelessly these Babylonian merchants, the Stationarii, long ago turned the worship of the saints into a trade: I will show this from one example.

units.la: Erat superioribus seculis genus quoddam sacrorum quæstorum, quos Stationarios, quippe stationes seu Ecclesias certis Divis dedicatas obeuntes, & inde orbem circumeuntes, cultorésque Divorum istorum quæsitantes, appellavère. De his inter gravamina centum statuum Imperii Pontificiorum & Potestantium A. MDXXIII. collecta, septimum sic sonat: Est & aliud indulgentiis vendendis addictum hominum genus, quod Stationarios vulgò vocant. Hi rusticorum plerunque abutuntur simplicitate, dum omnes vicos, villas, pagos, angiportus, omniaque peragrant castella & oppidula, prædicantes sancti cujuspiam Valentini puta, Huperti, Cornelii, Anastasiive sanctimoniam: ac quantum ad rem familiarem conducat, si quot annis hunc vel illum munusculo aliquo, quod eis, Stationariis scilicet in commodum cedat, demulceas. Inscribentésque dehinc simplices sub sancti alicujus nomen ac tutelam, promittentéque, ut hoc aut altero genere morborum vacaturus sit, qui eis annuum censum penderet. Quæ omnia ad hoc excogitata sunt, ut simplices illi ad vivum exugantur. Nam primùm hoc negotium à S. Antonio cæptum, in innumera morborum genera dehinc assuevit diduci: ita ut vix supersit nunc morbus aliquis, cui Stationarii non & peculiarem Sanctum, tanquam tabernæ, vel negotiationi præposuerit. Procefsitque eo usque ejus mali serpigo, ut pauperum ac simplicium illorum Quæstuarii & Stationarii Prædicatores, sanguinem vorent & medullam. Dúmque illi unà cum liberis suis necessariis spoliantur, in deliciis & luxu plus quàm Sybaritico Stationarii degunt. Hactenus illi. In Gallia quoque veteratorias illas artes exercuisse Antonianos, aliófque, testisest magnus Galliæ Jurisconsultus Rivallius, cujus hæc in Histor. Juris, verba sunt: Hodie quidem hujus legis (xii. nempe tabularum) reliquiæ extant. Nam cùm es & pecuniam, tum fructus & alia pro alimentis Divorum Antonii & Francisci Sacerdotes, aliique id genus homines cogunt, & domos exhauriunt. Sed Christi ratione his omnibus Christiani libenter bona largiuntur &c.
units.tr: In earlier centuries there was a kind of sacred fundraiser, whom they called Stationarii, because they visited stations, that is, churches dedicated to certain saints, and from there went round the world seeking out the worshippers of those saints. Among the grievances of the hundred estates of the Papist and Protestant Empire collected in 1523, the seventh runs as follows: There is another class of men devoted to selling indulgences, whom they commonly call Stationarii. They mostly take advantage of the simplicity of country folk, going through every village, farm, district, alley, and every castle and small town, proclaiming the holiness of some saint, say Valentine, Hubert, Cornelius, or Anastasius, and how much it profits one's household if each year one soothes this or that saint with some little gift that goes to the Stationarii. Then they enrol the simple folk under the name and protection of some saint, promising that they will be free from this or that kind of illness, in return for an annual tax. All these things have been devised so that those simple folk are drained to the quick. For this business, begun first by St Anthony, has since spread into countless kinds of illness, so that scarcely any illness is left for which the Stationarii have not appointed a particular saint, as if he were a shop or a trade. And the ulcer of this evil has advanced so far that the questers and Stationarii preachers devour the blood and marrow of the poor and simple. While those folk are stripped together with their necessary children, the Stationarii live in delights and luxury more than Sybarite. So far that document. That the Antonines and others practised those crafty arts in France too is attested by the great French jurist Rivallius, whose words in his History of Law are: Today indeed remnants of this law (namely of the Twelve Tables) survive. For priests of St Anthony and St Francis, and other men of that kind, extract money, fruits and other things as alimony, and drain houses dry. But by Christ's reasoning Christians gladly give all these goods etc.

units.la: XXXIV. Proxima pecuniarum aucupia sunt Orationes vicarie, tum pro viventibus, tum pro defunctis in purgatorio laborantibus.
units.tr: XXXIV. The next means of catching money are vicarious prayers, both for the living and for the dead who suffer in purgatory.

units.la: Neque enim tot religiosorum ordines, ipsúmque Purgatorii commentum vicariis Monachorum pro viventibus, & Clericorum omnium pro mortuis orationibus meritisque superstructæ, alium certiorem finem habent, quàm ut populi pecuniæ & facultates ad religiosum Clerum, & à Clero ad Culinæ Romanæ voraginem inexplebilem migrent.
units.tr: Indeed, so many orders of religious, and the very fiction of purgatory, built on the vicarious prayers and merits of monks for the living and of all clergy for the dead, have no other surer end than that the money and wealth of the people should flow to the religious clergy, and from the clergy into the insatiable whirlpool of the Roman kitchen.

units.la: XXXV. Monachatus speciosa equidem professio est.
units.tr: XXXV. Monasticism is indeed a showy profession.

units.la: Euangelica enim perfectio, orationes pro reliquo populo, mundo interea, uti loquuntur illi, inserviente, & vice populi fundendæ, efficaciam suam à meritis & supererogationis operibus acquisituræ, aliæque ejusmodi ad populum phaleræ prætexuntur. Si tamen penitius introspicias, vix aliud est, quàm Babylonicum vaframentum, uti Disfert. viij. ff. 1. th. lvii. &c. fidem abundè fecimus, demonstrantes fusius, exceptis paucis bonis viris, quos sic superstitio dementavit, ut animarum suarum, & alienarum saluti ita consuli posse perperam confidant: plerósque alia omnia, quàm religionis curam, Monachos facere. Quemadmodum verò institutum ordinum, avaritiæ & nundinationi inserviat, nullo negotio cognoscitur. Dum enim hac persuasione populus, qui curis hujus seculi securè implicari & distringi amat, occupatur, Monachos, mundo in universum renunciantes, & per vota irrevocabilia pietatis eximiæ & austeræ vitæ obstrictos, multúmque ea ratione apud Deum promerentes, hoc unum fere agere, ut tum pro se quisque Deo favorabilis esse contendat, tum vice reliqui populi fungatur, orando, psallendo, jejunando, aliáque religiosæ pietatis opera, obeundo: ingens pietatis hujus vicariæ hostimentū iis se debere merito agnoscet, & profitebitur ultrò. Quomodo S. Paulus alio licet planè animo & scopo de Macedonibus & Achivis dixit Rom. xv. 27. Si (pauperes) spiritualia sua communicaverunt gentibus, debent & (hæ) in carnalibus illis ministrare. Sed & ii, qui religiosam illam pietatem sectari sive suâ sponte, sive sic à parentibus avaris, sic liberos suos nonnullos immolantibus, ut cæteri splendidiore in mundo fortuna fruantur, inducti, gestiunt, persuasi videlicet, se in ordinibus aureolas promerituros, & sibi aliisque ἀσχήσι suâ Deum propitium redditurosi, promtè illi terrestres facultates suas universas, quas in potestate sua habent, eásque quandoque amplissimas Deo devovebunt, & ex temporalibus spirituales facient, eásque sic ordini, quem jam jam subituri sunt, legabunt. Sic planè occasio dabitur immen-sas fas divitias illo fictitiæ pietatis hamo in nassam illam Monasticam pertrahendi, & partem ejus non modicam pro lubitu Papæ in Romanam Culinam infundendi.
units.tr: For evangelical perfection, prayers for the rest of the people, while the world, as they put it, is served in the meantime, and prayers to be poured out in place of the people, obtaining their efficacy from merits and works of supererogation, and other such decorations, are put forward to the people. Yet if you look more closely, it is hardly anything other than a Babylonian trick, as we have amply shown in Dissertation 8, ff. 1, th. 57 etc., demonstrating at length that, apart from a few good men whom superstition so maddened that they foolishly trust their own souls and those of others can be cared for in this way, most monks make everything else their concern rather than the care of religion. But how the institution of the orders serves greed and trade is known without difficulty. For while the people, who love to be carelessly caught up and distracted by the cares of this age, are occupied by this persuasion, the monks, renouncing the world altogether and bound by irrevocable vows of extraordinary piety and austere life, and by this means earning much before God, do almost nothing except this: each strives to be favourable to God for himself, and at the same time acts in place of the rest of the people, praying, chanting, fasting and performing other works of religious piety. Such a person will rightly recognise, and will freely profess, that he owes a great debt of gratitude to this vicarious piety. Just as St Paul, though with a quite different mind and aim, said of the Macedonians and Achaians in Rom. 15.27: If (the poor) have shared their spiritual things with the Gentiles, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things. But also those who, either of their own accord or persuaded by greedy parents who sacrifice some of their children so that the rest may enjoy more splendid fortune in the world, eagerly embrace that religious piety, convinced, namely, that they will earn golden crowns in the orders, and will render God propitious to themselves and to others by their ascetic exercises [ἀσκήσει], readily dedicate to God all their earthly goods which are in their power, and these often very large, and will make spiritual things out of temporal ones, and so bequeath them to the order which they are about to enter. In this way an opportunity will plainly be given to draw immense and unjust riches into that monastic net with the bait of feigned piety, and to pour a considerable part of it into the Roman kitchen at the Pope's pleasure.

units.la: XXXVI. Neque occasione adeò commoda, & ad comparandas divitias, atque exiis alendum luxum propitia non uti strenuè Monachos, affirmabit, quisquis Simonias illorum artes, quæstuariam omnem & divitias inde conflatas incredibiles non plane ignorat. De fui temporis Monachis nonnullis S. Hieronymus ad Nepotianum sic conqueritur: Nonnulli sunt ditiores Monachi, quàm fuerant Seculares & Clerici, qui possident opes sub Christo paupere, quas sub locuplete & fallace Diabolo non habuerant; at suspiret Ecclesia eos divites, quos mundus tenuit antè mendicos. Quid diceret ille, si hodie viveret, & magnifica ædificia, ingentes reditus, sumptus immensos, verbo, omnem maximæ partis Monachorum luxum videret? Si tertiam bonorum Italiæ v. g. partem à Monachis, malis belluis, pigris ventribus, occupari cerneret? Si Jesuitarum collegia ingrederetur, si leges eorum perlegens animadverteret, mirè his pauperibus (nam Mendicantium Ordinibus cos Pius V. adscripsit) curæ cordíque esse, ut benè habitent, ægri juxtà sanique delicatè habeantur, commodè sint vestiti, benè loti, ita ut magna ístarum regularum parsProvinicialium acPræfectorum instructioni impendatur, ut quæcunque ad reditus sucs conservandos augendósque fieri poterunt, diligenter curent præsecti refectorii, similésque ministri; omnia nitida, tersa & abundanter parata habeant; denique curent enixè, ne qua re ulla indigeant. Neque divites pauperratem voventes, quamcunque præ se devotionem ferant, aliud agunt, quàm ut incertiora stabiliant, dum privata bona relinquentes, communionem divitiis affluentem ingrediantur. Quòd si quidam mendicantes fiunt, præterquam quòd hodie ferè omnes reditibus fruuntur, ita illi se componunt, ut quandiu ignis purgatorius non extinguitur, ollam perpetuò ebullientem habeant.
units.tr: XXXVI. Nor will anyone who does not thoroughly ignore the simony of their arts, their whole business of questing, and the incredible riches gathered from it, deny that monks have very diligently used an occasion so convenient, and so favourable for acquiring riches and feeding luxury from them. St Jerome complains of some monks of his own time in his letter To Nepotian in this way: There are some monks richer than they were when they were laymen and clergy, who possess wealth under poor Christ which they did not have under the rich and deceitful Devil; yet let the Church sigh that they are rich, whom the world once held as beggars. What would he say if he lived today and saw the splendid buildings, the huge revenues, the immense expenses, in a word, the luxury of the greater part of the monks? If he saw that a third part of the goods of Italy, for example, is held by monks, those evil beasts, lazy bellies? If he entered the Jesuit colleges, and reading through their rules noticed how wonderfully these poor men (for Pius V assigned them to the mendicant orders) are cared for, that they are housed well, that the sick and healthy alike are treated delicately, that they are clothed suitably and bathed well, so that a large part of those rules is spent on the instruction of the provincials and prefects, and that the prefects of the refectory and similar officers diligently take care to preserve and increase their revenues by every means, keeping everything bright, clean and abundantly supplied, and strenuously see to it that they lack nothing. Rich men who vow poverty, whatever devotion they display, are doing nothing else than making uncertain things secure, while, leaving private goods behind, they enter a community flowing with riches. And if some of them become mendicants, besides the fact that almost all of them today enjoy revenues, they so arrange matters that, as long as the purgatorial fire is not extinguished, they have a pot always boiling.

units.la: XXXVII. Omittere non possum querelam Sorbonici Doctoris, Petri Aurelii adversus Jesuitarum nefarias ditescendi artes motam, Monasticæ cauponationis argumentum evidentissimum. Is nempe libro, cui Spongiæ Jesuitarum titulum fecit pag. 307. testatur, totius orbis fidem & diuturnam rerum experientiam indignissimam ostentationem Jesuitarum respuere, quòd à terrenis opibus sint alienissimi. Exi-stimare contra, sicut religiosorum omnium ditissimos, ita ditescendi cupidissimos & scientissimos, homines iniquissimos, qui non solùm divitiarum, sed etiam paupertatis præ cæteris omnibus possessionem ad se trahunt. Longum est, sic pag. 308. pergit, commemorare quos fructuum proventus in civitatibus decerpere, & quam suprà ullius operarii, quantumvis in temporalem, ut ajunt, mercedem intenti, votum, carnalia metere solent, ubi spiritualia seminaverunt. Quod beneficia Ecclesiastica, quibus nulla manifestiora laborum in Ecclesia stipendia sunt, eorum possessionibus inserta referam? tot Abbatias nobiles, tot optimos Prioratus etiam parochiales, undique totâ Gallia longè latèque captârunt. In civitate Rhotomagensi tres Prioratus amplissimos, invidiosos, urbis mœnibus circumquaque objacentes occupârunt, sermonis hominum & publicæ famæ securi. Hinc est, sic pag. 311. prosequitur, ut omnes quæstuum nôrint vias, & una eorum domus professa Lutetiæ, privatarum largitionum tantum ad se contrahere dicatur, quantum cæteræ omnes Regularium domus, quæ in ea urbe frequentissimæ sunt, non colligant, ut religiosos etiam instituti severioris, testificantes audivimus &c. Cohibent denique & comprimunt publicæ offensionis metu multò majorem opum copiam, multò majorem animorum sublimia spirantium elationem, quàm quantum cum omnium admiratione patefaciunt. Quid templum illud Antverpiense, toto Belgio, aliisque regionibus famosum, marmore Italico, Genuá per utraque maria delato, exædificatum, commemorem. Subjicit pag. 313. idem: Quid rursus enumerem non jam spiritualia, sed prorsùs temporalia eorum mercimonia plurimis in locis instituta, unde naves in oras Indicas, & variorum regiones destinârunt? An qui ne hoc quidem commercii genus sibi inconcessum putant, ii sunt, quorum statui à terreno quæstu, & lucrorum temporalium cupiditate, & quidem peculiaribus votis recessisse debeat existimari, cùm eum nec à mercatoria nauticaque fortuna, quà nihil terrenius, terrenisque compendiis deditius, abhorrere, sed cum ea bellè consentire ipsimet judicaverint? Paulò post: Illi quidem fœminæ similimos se exhibent, qua (Prov. 30.) comedit, & tergens os suum dicit: Non operatâ sum iniquitatem. Illi populo, qui exsatiatam cupidinum suarum ingluviem (Jerem. 8.) procaciter ingerebat: quid feci? Illi hominum societati, qui excolabant culicem unum, camelum autem glutiebant. (Matth. 23.) Tales nempe sunt Jesuitæ, qualis ille, qui Impiger extremos currit mercator ad Indos.
units.tr: XXXVII. I cannot omit the complaint raised by the Sorbonne doctor Pierre Auriol against the nefarious arts of the Jesuits for getting rich, a very clear proof of monastic trading. In his book, which he titled The Sponge of the Jesuits, p. 307, he testifies that the whole world's faith and long experience reject the most shameful display of the Jesuits, since they are most alien to earthly wealth. On the contrary, he judges that they, like all religious, are most eager to get rich, the most knowing in it, and the most unjust men, who draw to themselves not only riches but also the possession of poverty above all others. "It would be long," he continues on p. 308, "to recount what harvests of revenue they pluck from the cities, and what carnal things they usually reap, where they have sown spiritual things, more than any labourer, however intent on temporal wages, as they say, would vow. Why should I mention the ecclesiastical benefices, than which there are no clearer wages for labour in the Church, inserted into their possessions? They have seized so many noble abbeys and so many excellent priories, even parochial ones, from all over France, far and wide. In the city of Rouen they have occupied three very large, envied priories lying all around the city walls, unconcerned about men's talk and public reputation." Hence, he goes on on p. 311, they all know the ways of gain, and their one professed house in Paris is said to draw to itself as much private largesse as all the other houses of the regulars, which are very numerous in that city, do not collect; we have heard this from religious of stricter rule too, who testify to it, etc. Finally, for fear of public offence, they hold back and suppress a far greater abundance of wealth, and a far greater elation of spirits breathing high things, than they reveal to the admiration of all. Why should I mention that temple at Antwerp, famous throughout Belgium and other regions, built of Italian marble carried by sea from Genoa?" The same author adds on p. 313: "Why should I further enumerate not spiritual but entirely temporal merchandise of theirs, established in very many places, from which they have sent ships to the shores of the Indies and the regions of various peoples? Or are those who do not think even this kind of trade forbidden to them, those whose state ought to be thought to have withdrawn from earthly gain and the greed for temporal profits, and indeed by special vows, when they themselves have judged that it agrees well with it, and that it does not shrink from mercantile and nautical fortune, than which nothing is more earthly, and nothing more devoted to earthly profit?" A little later: "They show themselves most like that woman (Prov. 30) who eats, and wiping her mouth says: I have done no wickedness. They are like that people who bitterly kept saying to the glutted greed of their desires (Jer. 8): What have I done? They are like that society of men who strained out a gnat but swallowed a camel (Matth. 23)." Such indeed are the Jesuits, like that merchant who, eager, runs to the furthest Indians.

units.la: En Jesuitas Monachos mercatores Babylonios, vivis coloribus à Sorbonico Doctore depictos! Quibus si addatur testimonium Petri Dezæ, qui Oratione de Ignatii Beatificat. pag. 52. miraculum & velut digitum Dei interpretatur, quòd Jesuitæ hoc tempore adeò perverso & avaro ubi-rint & possint abundè quicquid velint, extorquere. Illudque Jesuitarum miraculum (nam aliis miraculis illi destituuntur, cum eo confert, quod Deus operatus est cum Ægyptiis in favorem populi sui, cùm Judæis mutuò dederunt, quicquid petierunt; quod totum Deus ipsos voluerit auferre; ferre; quomodo ait Jesuitas totum auferre, quicquid petunt; quod argumento sit, eos Deo curæ esse, & ab eo tenerrimo affectu diligi; nihil ad cognoscendam eorundem domesticis testibus inexplebilem avaritiam, & nundinationem Babylonicam desiderabimus.
units.tr: Here are the Jesuits, monks and Babylonian merchants, painted in lively colours by a doctor of the Sorbonne! To this add the testimony of Pierre de Dez, who in his Oratione de Ignatii Beatificat. pag. 52. interprets the miracle as the finger of God, because the Jesuits at this perverse and greedy time can and do extort abundantly whatever they wish. He compares this Jesuit miracle (for they have no other miracles) with what God did among the Egyptians for the sake of his people, when they lent the Jews whatever they asked for: all of which God wished to take away from them; to bear; as he says, the Jesuits take away everything they ask for; which is a sign that they are cared for by God and loved by him with the tenderest affection. For information about the insatiable avarice and Babylonian trading of these men, we need no more than the testimony of their own household members.

units.la: XXXVIII. Pertinent huc Terminarii veteres, Monachi mendicantes, de quibus ejusmodi querelam Principes Imperii in Gravaminibus centum, Grav. viÿ. consignarunt: Nec minùs & in hoc à Religiosis gravantur profani, maximè pauperes, quibus res est angusta domi: nempè quòd mendicitas ordinum mendicantium nihil in rure, neque in Urbe finit non peragratum, dum à terminis, quos pervagantur Terminarii dicuntur. Quas quidem pervagationes contra ordinis eorum statuta, neque etiam ad necessitatem, per avaritiam (NB) insatiabilem adinvenerunt. Ita enim fit, ut cùm in oppidulo aliquando non admodùm celebri, sed perexiguo, duo, tria, aut eo amplius illorum sint conventicula, in quæ omne, quicquid eleemosynæ undique disquiri potest, confertur, dum tamen interim morbo aut senio confecti cives vel incolæ, qui per ætatem ex laboribus & sudoribus suis unà cum uxoribus & liberis honestè vixerant, egeant, ac famâ & inediâ perire necesse habeant.
units.tr: XXXVIII. To this belong the old Terminarii, the mendicant monks, about whom the princes of the Empire recorded such a complaint in the Gravamina centum, Grav. viÿ.: Nor are the profane, especially the poor whose household is in straitened circumstances, burdened less by the religious in this respect: namely, that the begging of the mendicant orders leaves nothing in the countryside or in the city unexplored, since they are called Terminarians from the districts which they roam. Indeed they devised these wanderings contrary to the statutes of their order, and not even out of necessity, but out of insatiable avarice (NB). For it happens that, where there are two, three, or more of their convents in some small town, not very populous, all the alms that can be sought from every side are gathered into them, while meanwhile citizens or residents who, through their age, had lived honestly by their labours and sweat together with their wives and children, fall ill or grow old, lack necessities, and must perish from hunger and want.
XXXIX.

units.la: Haud fortè de nihilo est, quòd Johanne XXIII. Pontifice, Monachos inter Dominicanos & Franciscanos de divitiis & paupertate certamen acerrimum exarsit, Pontifice eodem pro divitiarum assertoribus, Dominicanis, adversùs Franciscanos, paupertatis hyperaspistas, pronuntiante, paupertatem palam irridente, & Christum divitem, in cruce ipsa non nudum, nec spineâ coronâ caput redimitum, sed ornatum in capite coronâ aureâ & Regia, indutum verò togâ purpureâ, usque ad talos demissâ, & limbis aureis præextextatâ, protervè effingente.
units.tr: It is perhaps not without reason that, under Pope John XXIII, a very bitter quarrel over wealth and poverty flared up among the monks, between the Dominicans and the Franciscans. The Pope himself was on the side of the defenders of wealth, the Dominicans, and pronounced against the Franciscans, the champions of poverty; he openly mocked poverty and shamelessly portrayed Christ as rich: not naked on the cross, nor with his head wreathed in a crown of thorns, but with a golden royal crown on his head, clothed in a purple toga reaching down to his ankles and fringed with gold borders.

units.la: Dominicanorum & Franciscanorum de divitiis; norum de divitiis & paupertate; Christo primis pauperes certamen; Monachatus arcana, eum demvafra; mentum BaHistoriam fufiùs Hist. Pap. ff. 129. narravimus. In certamine sthoc Dominicani eorumque suffragator, Papa Johannes XXIII. levàsse velum, &, quod res est, apud Monachos ingenuè professi: Francıscani ὑπηρέτικοι tegendis Monachatûs arcanis studuisse paulò inixiùs mihi videntur. Arcana isthæc Monachatûs post Tridentinum etiam Concilium cordatiores quídam Galli, teste Suave libr. viij. pag. 740. referàrunt, asserentes aperтè, in principiò Romanam curiam satagere, ut prætextu voti paupertatis, Monachi existimationem acquirant; quasi nullam rem temporalem intueantur, sed omnia charitatis causa faciant in populi servitutem: post, existimatione parta, curiam cum ipsis de voto dispensare, unde facilè ditescant: cúmque bene opulenta facta sunt Monasteria, demendari in comendam, & id omne denique in curiam influere.
units.tr: I have related the history of the dispute between the Dominicans and Franciscans over wealth and poverty more fully in Hist. Pap. 129. In that dispute the Dominicans and their supporter, Pope John XXIII, lifted the veil, and, as is the case, openly and frankly admitted among the monks the secrets of monasticism. The Franciscans, eager servants [ὑπηρέτικοι], seem to me to have taken more pains to conceal the secrets of monasticism. After the Council of Trent, some rather sensible Frenchmen, as Suave reports in libr. viij. pag. 740., also disclosed these secrets, plainly asserting: At first the Roman curia takes care that monks gain a reputation under the pretext of a vow of poverty, as though they regarded no temporal thing but did everything for charity's sake, in the enslavement of the people. Afterwards, once their reputation is established, the curia dispenses them from the vow with themselves, whereby they grow rich easily; and when the monasteries have become quite wealthy, they are handed over in commendam, and all of it at last flows into the curia.

units.la: XL. Orationes vicariæ, oblationes & suffragia pro defunctis iis conducere feruntur, qui in purgatorio laborant. Ex Purgatorio igitur omnis illa orationum, suffragiorum, oblationum, atque aliorum etiam ejusmodi operum plurium existimatio pendet. Esse autem Purgatorii fidem planè ad quæstum faciendum comparatum, dubitari nequit. Si enim fidelium animæ post mortem rectà ignem purgatorium subire, & in eo tormenta & cruciatus infernalibus planè æquipollentes, non unam horam, diem, mensem, annum, sed quandóque centum, mille, plurésque annos sustinere, adeóque horribilem & ineffabilem in modum ustulari tenentur: si cruciatus & tormenta illa orationibus, oblationibus, suffragiis vicariis, indulgentiis mitigari vel contrahi: si denique orationes, oblationes, suffragia vicaria indulgentiæ tum liberalibus viventium adhuc collationibus, piis quinetiam legatis in usum Monasteriorum, Ecclesiarum, orantium, offerentium, suffragantium, indulgentium: tum consanguineorum & amicorum defunctı similibus pecuniarum dispendiis redimi & impetrari possunt: quotusquisque est paulò salutis animæ suæ studiosior, qui non promtissimè Monachis, Sacrificulis, Papæ facultates suas, saltem quibus carere commodè potest, erogare, eosdémque quàm unctissimos reddere velit? Quantum enim opum suarum non profunderet libens damnatus vivicomburii, cujus cruciatus vix dimidiam horæ quadrantem durant, si profusione illa vivicomburium redimi posse cognosceret? Vel igitur homines in Papatu morientes Purgatorium ore quidem profitentur, at corde abnegant, & næniam illam, non ignari quippe doli, intùs suaviter rident: vel, quid de anima sua post mortem fiat, pensi nil habent: vel parati sunt sævissimos, quos sibi imminere credunt cruciatus, facultatum suarum quantarumvis impendio redimere.
units.tr: XL. Vicarious prayers, offerings and suffrages for the dead are said to benefit those who suffer in purgatory. Therefore the whole esteem in which such prayers, suffrages, offerings and many other works of this kind are held depends on Purgatory. That the belief in Purgatory is wholly designed to make money there can be no doubt. For if the souls of the faithful after death are held to undergo the fire of purgatory directly, and to endure in it torments and sufferings wholly equal to those of hell, lasting not an hour, a day, a month or a year, but sometimes a hundred, a thousand or more years, and to be burned in a horrible and unspeakable manner; if those torments and sufferings can be softened or shortened by prayers, offerings, vicarious suffrages and indulgences; and finally, if prayers, offerings, vicarious suffrages and indulgences can be bought and obtained, both by the living through their liberal donations and by pious bequests for the use of monasteries, churches, those praying, offering, interceding and granting indulgences, and by the relatives and friends of the dead through similar expenditures of money: who is at all more concerned for the health of his soul, and would not most readily be willing to give his wealth, at least what he can conveniently spare, to monks, priests and the Pope, and to make them as rich as possible? For how much of his wealth would a condemned man, whose burning lasts scarcely a quarter of an hour, not gladly pour out, if he knew that by such lavish spending he could redeem himself from the fire? So either men dying in Papacy profess Purgatory with their mouths but deny it in their hearts, and inwardly laugh pleasantly at that old wives' tale, being not unaware of the deceit; or they care nothing for what becomes of their soul after death; or they are ready to redeem, at whatever cost of their possessions, the most cruel torments which they believe hang over them.

units.la: XLI. Neque tantùm suapte indole Purgatorium ad faciendum quæstum sic comparatum est: sed reapse etiam Babylonicæ huic mercaturæ totum ancillatur, & impoturarum clericalium arx unica est. Deum testamur & conscientiam ipsius Cleri, cui morbus aliquis animi mentem non ademit. Nam cùm S. Augustino contra literas Petiliani judice, illud demum quod de sacris voluminibus sumitur, firmum & solidum sit, ipsi, qui in Clero ingenui adhuc sunt, ultrò fatentur, Purgatorium ad Scripturam ferri, non inde referri, neque veteris Ecclesiæ certa de eo haberi testimonia, quia serò admodùm illud Ecclesiæ innotuisse. Ita Petrus Soto lect. j. de Purg. Cæsar Bullengerus, Peresius Ajata, Johannes Episcopus Rofensis inprimis, qui art. 13. & 18. contra Lutherum scribit, diligentissimos inquisitores hactenùs latuisse Scripturam aliquam Purgatorium probantem: & serò admodùm illud Ecclesiæ innotuisse. Quæ causa est, quòd Jesuita Cottonus Sathana ipso doctore & indice loci alicujus Scripturæ uti voluit. Et tam clara, manifestáque passim in Scripturis testimonia occurrunt, ut allegoricis, tropicis, obscuris, dubiis illis, quæ alii Scripturas ad concupiscentiæ suæ lenocinium trahentes, in subsidium vocant, lucem addant, & verò purgatorii ignem penitùs extinguant. Cùm ergò in Scriptura Canonica nihil præsidii purgatorium habeat, architectis ejus eò descendere necessum fuit, ut vel suffragatores appellarent homines gentiles, Poëtas, Philosophos, quos hæreticorum esse Patriarchas, Tertullianus olim dixit: vel apocrypha commenta nonnulla jactarent, quæ juxta Hieronymum, eadem facilitate contemnimus, qua illi probant; præsertim à Divinis literis non modò diversa, sed iis etiam adversa: vel Origenicum Purgatorium, in quinta generali Synodo publicè ab Ecclesia Græca damnatum, aliáque Patrum, alias præcipua fundamenta, quæ hodie Purgatorio præstrui solent, destruentium, dicta dubitabunda, ambigua, quædam etiam ψυ-δσπ/γεφα in subsidium advocent: vel, quod ii, qui extremam Purgatorio manum admoverunt, de omnibus reliquis desperantes, tentárunt, eorum testimonio firmarent, qui se non, ut isti sceptici disputatores apud Ciceronem pro Archia, opinari, sed scire; non audivisse, sed vidisse; non interfuisse modò Purgatorio, sed cruciatus illos suos ipso corpore sustinuisse dixerunt; & , quod apud Senecam de Tranquill. animi cap. 14. Caninius olim se factúrum promiserat, post mortem circumierunt amicos, indicárúntque, quem explorâssent animarũ statum, opémque adeò supplices orárunt. Extat authentica, imò aurea Legenda, quam Lombardicam appellant, Jacobi de Voragine, Archiepiscopi Genuensis: extat speculum exemplorum: extant revelationes Brigittæ, & hujusmodi commatis alii plures authores, talibus spestrorum purgatoriorum apparitionibus, revelationibúsque scatentes, in id unicè comparatis, ut & in purgatorio commodiùs agere, & citiùs eo carcere liberari nobis persuadeant eos,qui pinguiorimunere Sacerdotes Ditis ostiarios demulserint. Quantum verò visionibus ejusmodi revelationibusque tribuendum sit, alibi Dissert. Tomo ÿ. Diß. vj: fusiùs ostendimus, & jam olim D. Chrysostomus in Matth. cap. 8. homil. 29. demonstravit, conceptis verbis asserens, orationem illam clamantium: Anima talis ego sum; à fraude & deceptione Diabolica manare. Etsi, mea quidem opinione, sœpiùs hic humanæ, quàm Diabolicæ fraudes intervenerunt, ut nimirum Sacerdotes suffragia sua pro defunctis efficere vendibiliora & eò carius extrudere possint. Scilicet
units.tr: XLI. Nor is Purgatory arranged for making money merely by its own nature: in fact it also wholly serves this Babylonian trade, and it is the sole citadel of clerical impostures. We call God and the conscience of the clergy itself to witness, for no mental disease has taken away their mind. For since, as judge, Augustine says against the letters of Petilian that only that which is taken from the sacred books is firm and solid, those in the clergy who are still honest themselves freely admit that Purgatory is not derived from Scripture, nor is it brought from it, and that there are no certain testimonies to it from the old Church, because it became known to the Church very late. So Pedro de Soto, lect. j. de Purg.; Cesare Baronio... Peresius Ajata; and above all John, Bishop of Rochester, who in art. 13. & 18. writes against Luther, that the most diligent investigators have hitherto failed to find any Scripture proving Purgatory, and it became known to the Church very late. This is why the Jesuit Cotton wished to use a passage of Scripture with Satan himself as teacher and judge. And there are so many clear and manifest testimonies scattered through the Scriptures, that allegorical, tropical, obscure and doubtful passages, which others drag in to aid, bringing Scripture to the flattery of their own lust and calling them in for help, would add light to them, and would indeed utterly extinguish the fire of purgatory. Since therefore Purgatory has no support in the canonical Scripture, its architects had to descend there, so that they either appealed for support to gentile men, poets and philosophers, whom Tertullian once called the patriarchs of heretics; or they bragged of certain apocryphal fictions, which, according to Jerome, we despise with the same ease with which they approve them, especially those that differ from, and are even opposed to, the divine letters; or they call in, as aid, the Origenist Purgatory, publicly condemned by the Greek Church in the Fifth General Council, and other sayings of the Fathers that overturn the other main foundations usually laid for Purgatory, sayings that are doubtful, ambiguous, and even [pseudepigraphal] writings; or, since they despaired of all the rest, they tried to confirm it by the testimony of those who did not, as those sceptical disputants in Cicero's Pro Archia put it, think but know; who did not hear but saw; who said they were not merely present at Purgatory but had endured those torments in their own body; and what Caninius once promised in Seneca's De tranquillitate animi, cap. 14, that after death he would go round to his friends, point out the state of souls which he had explored, and so pray suppliantly for help. There is an authentic, indeed golden, Legenda which they call Lombardica, by Jacobus de Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa; there is a mirror of examples; there are the revelations of Bridget, and many other authors of this kind, teeming with such apparitions and revelations of ghosts from purgatory, all made solely to persuade us that they will act more comfortably in purgatory and be released from that prison more quickly, those who have soothed the doorkeepers of Dis, the priests, with a rather fat gift. How much credit such visions and revelations deserve, we have shown more fully elsewhere in Dissert. Tomo ÿ. Diß. vj:; and long ago St Chrysostom already demonstrated it in Matth. cap. 8. homil. 29., asserting in plain words that that saying of those crying out: I am such a soul, comes from diabolical fraud and deception. Yet in my opinion, human frauds have more often intervened here than diabolical ones, namely so that priests may make their suffrages for the dead more saleable and push them at a higher price. Certainly
when there are rewards for falsehood
No witness should have his testimony believed as sound;

units.la: Si enim spectrorum è purgatorio visiones illi memorarent, apud quos nullum mendacio pretium est, possent fortasse fidem alicui facere. Atqui fuit apud illos testes, & est etiamnum apud successores eorum pretium insanum grande.
units.tr: For if the witnesses who report visions of spirits from purgatory were people for whom lying brings no reward, they might perhaps win some credit. But there were such witnesses, and even now their successors earn an enormous reward for it.
XLII.

units.la: Cùm ergò ipsi Purgatorii hyperaspistæ ficulneis adeò fictisque nitantur præsidiis; atque præterea commentum isthoc jam dudum à nostris nænia soricina consusius redditum sit, quis dubitat, quin assertores ejus ipsi impostoras suas, & veram, unicam, genuinámque causam ejus asserti, sacerrimum quæstum interiùs agnoscant, licet dicere non adeò ventri & culinæ suæ infensi, mussent. Cur enim Clerici quidem aperirent tam utilem sibi fabulam? Quin potiùs, liceat Macrobii Saturnal. lib. v. 17. verbis rem præsentem effari, conniventfabulæ, & intra conscientiam veri fidem prementes, malunt pro vero celebrari, quod pectoribus humanis fingentium calliditas infudit: stultam in tot caveis prædam tacitis intra se cachinnis ipsi persequuntur. Quòd ergò quondam Marcus Cato apud
units.tr: Since, then, the defenders of Purgatory lean on such fig-leaf and fictitious supports, and since this fable has long since been refuted by our people as a mouse's lullaby, who doubts that its advocates themselves know inwardly that their deceptions and the one true, genuine cause of this assertion is the most sacred business? They may not dare to say so, since they are not entirely hostile to their bellies and kitchens, but they keep quiet. For why would the clergy openly reveal so useful a fable? Rather, to borrow Macrobius's words (Saturn. 5.17), let me state the matter as it is: they connive at the fable, and, suppressing the truth within their conscience, prefer that what the cunning of its inventors has poured into human hearts be celebrated as true. They themselves pursue the foolish prey in so many cages with silent laughter inside. Therefore, as Marcus Cato once among

units.la: prodant, ge-nuinam ejus causam esse auri facerni-mam fa-men, Ciceronem de Divinat. lib.j. mirari se ajebat, quòd non rideret aruspex, aruspicem cùm vidisset; idem de Clericorum illorum ουνωπκ͡ο͡ν haud incommodè pronuntiari potest, tot fraudium, quibus miseram illi plebem circumscribunt, sibi mutuò conscìorum, ut mirum omninò sit, si quis alteri obvius, quasi quoddam exemplar intueatur sui, non extemplò rideat effusissimè.
units.tr: the others declared, that the genuine cause of it is the accursed hunger for gold, Cicero (De Divin. 1) says he marvelled that a soothsayer did not laugh when he saw another soothsayer. The same can fairly be said of those clergy and their complicity [συνωπικὸν]: so many frauds, by which they cheat the wretched common people, are shared among themselves that it would be surprising if anyone meeting another, as if looking at a sort of image of himself, did not burst out laughing at once.

units.la: XLIII. Quæstui haberi totam hanc de Purgatorio doctrinam, res ipsa loquitur, & affluentes inde Sacerdotum Regales opes, qui non aliis magis viscerationibus cibum sibi posterisque æternum dapinaverunt. Produnt quinetiam subinde, uti veritas quandoque vi erumpere solet, æruscatores ipsi, ex quorum genere Bernhardinus in Rosario, VALDE UTILE EST, inquit, HABERE DEVOTOS HÆREDES, qui multas scilicet, & sumptuosas suffragiorum sacerdotalium nundinationes exerceant. Et quis neget, valdè utile hoc esse, si non animabus defunctorum, at certè Sacrificis,
units.tr: XLIII. That this whole doctrine of Purgatory is a source of profit, the thing itself speaks, and so do the royal riches of the priests that flow from it, who have feasted themselves and their descendants for ever on nothing else more than on these entrails. Even the hawkers themselves sometimes reveal it, as truth is wont to break out by force now and then. Among them is Bernardinus in the Rosarium: IT IS VERY USEFUL, he says, TO HAVE PIOUS HEIRS, who, of course, carry on the many and costly trade in priestly intercessions. And who would deny that this is very useful, if not for the souls of the dead, then certainly for the sacrificers,

units.la: Qui Curias simulant, & Bacchanalia vivunt; Si non ad purgatorii refrigerandum ignem, saltem ad hoc, ut in istorum culinis —— assiduo luceat igne focus.
units.tr: who pretend to be sober and live in Bacchic revels; if not to cool the fire of purgatory, then at least so that in their kitchens the hearth may shine with constant fire.

units.la: Sed & Concilii Tridentini Patres Seff. xxv. de Purgatorio inter alia Episcopis præcipiunt, ut ea, quæ in materia hac de Purgatorio ad curiositatem quandam aut superstitionem spectant, vel (NB) turpe lucrum sapiunt, tanquam scandala & fidelium offendicula prohibeant. Multa ergò ante Concilium in Ecclesia obtinuisse, quæ turpe lucrum saperent, agnoscunt: & prohibent solæ verborum pompæ, cùm lucrum esse Purgatorii animam nulli forte ignoaverint. Subjiciunt iidem Concilii Patres: Curent Episcopi, ut fidelium vivorum suffragia Missarum scilicet sacrificia, orationes, eleemosynæ (hoc nomine iis lucrosæ collationes veniunt) aliaque pietatis pera, quæ à fidelibus pro aliis defunctis fieri consueverunt, secundum Ecclesiæ instituta piè & devotè fiant; & quæ pro illis ex testatorum fundationibus, vel alia ratione debentur, non perfunctoriè, sed à sacerdotibus & Ecclesiæ Ministris, & aliys, qui hoc præstare tenentur, diligenter & accuratè persolvantur. Et mercaturam genuinam, contractum videlicet ementes inter vendentésque, & persolventes qui debitum, seu obligationem persolvendi, ob datas scilicet eleemosynas, fundationes, aliasque ejusmodi rationes inducit. Si tamen rem rectè putaveris, malæ fidei contractus hic est, quia ἀνθρακες ὁ Ἡσαυρὸς πίφυκε carbones pro thesauro dantur, ut est in Proverbio. Carbones autem? imò NIHIL, quia nullæ in Purgatorio sunt animæ, adeóque nihil orationes, suffragia, Missarum sacrificia, quæ pro fundationibus & eleemosynis persolvi dicuntur, iis prosunt. Sic ærugatores illi ne illam quidem solertiam Diomedis in permutando munere imitantur,
units.tr: But also the Fathers of the Council of Trent, in Session 25 on Purgatory, order among other things that bishops should forbid those matters in this doctrine of Purgatory that tend to some curiosity or superstition, or (NB) smack of shameful gain, as scandals and stumbling-blocks to the faithful. So they acknowledge that much had prevailed in the Church before the Council which smacked of shameful gain; and it is only the pomp of words that forbids it, since they were perhaps not unaware that the souls in Purgatory were a source of profit.
