The same Fathers of the Council add: Bishops shall take care that the intercessions of the living faithful, namely the sacrifices of the Masses, prayers, alms (by this name the profitable contributions are meant) and other works of piety, which the faithful are accustomed to perform for other deceased persons, be carried out piously and devoutly according to the institutions of the Church; and that what is owed to them from the foundations of testators, or in some other way, be paid not perfunctorily, but diligently and accurately by the priests, the ministers of the Church, and others who are bound to perform this. Here they introduce a genuine trade: a contract between buyers and sellers, and those who pay the debt, that is, an obligation to pay, arising from alms, foundations and other such grounds. Yet if you judge the matter rightly, this is a contract of bad faith, since coals are given for treasure [ἀνθρακες ὁ Ἡσαυρὸς πίφυκε], as the proverb says. But coals? Nay, NOTHING, since there are no souls in Purgatory, and so nothing is of use to them: not the prayers, not the intercessions, not the sacrifices of the Masses, which are said to be paid for foundations and alms. So these hucksters do not even imitate the cleverness of Diomedes in exchanging gifts,

units.la: χρύσεα donanti, χάλκεα qui dederat; sed hanc potius illudentium jocantiúmque paræmiam sequuntur: λαβὲ μηδὲν· ἐκ κέρατι καλῶς. Cape NIHIL & serva bene. Nisi forsan ALIQUID alicui vidcantur chartæ & plumbum, applicandarum indulgentiarum instrumenta: quibus est equidem ab igne purgatorio magnoperè metuendum, ne & ipsa redigantur in NIHILUM, eó quòd Diaboli tam calentes dicuntur habere manus, ut & membranæ comburantur, & plumbum colliquescat inter eas priùs, quàm legendo percurrerint. Hinc adeò est, quòd jam olim Græci, ut refert Cardinalis Aureolus in 4. d. 21. art. j. pag. 151. d Latinos graviter accusárunt, quòd Purgatorium propter lucrum invenerint. Denique Episcopi Salisburgensis, & Chemnensis Suffraganeus, libro, cui Onus Ecclesiæ titulum fecit Landshutæ in Bavaria A. MDXXIV. impresso, de quæstoribus his queritur, quòd suis prædicationibus decipiant simplices, & aurum subtili, vel fallaci potiùs ingenio ab eis extorqueant, de purgatorio mendaciter extrahendo animas, quæ Dei judicio reservatæ sunt. Nam si domum vendere malè materiatam, ruinosam, pestilentem, & hæc tamen emptorem vitia celare, Cicero de Offic. libr. iij. 3. judicavit, esse hominis non aperti, non simplicis, non ingenui, non justi, non viri boni, versuti potiùs, obscuri, astuti, fallacis, malitiosi, callidi, veteratoris, vafri: quinimò Plato in Hipparcho verè sceleratos & impios esse dixit eos, qui sciunt, nullius esse pretii ea, ex quibus lucrantur, & tamen ex impudentia lucrum amplecti audent: quid de iis statuendum putamus, qui, non dicam è re vitiosa, sed planè NULLA tantum lucri capiunt? Et si, uti Cicero idem loc. cit. loquitur, vituperandi sunt, qui reticuerunt rem, quam vendunt, aut vitiosam, aut nullam esse; quid de iis existimandum est, qui orationis vanitatem insuper adhibuerunt? Quod cùm ab omnibus aliis circa Purgatorii mercatum occupatis: tum præcipuè, præconibus indulgentiarum factitatum esse constat, miro verborum lenocinio, promissionum illicio merces suas extrudere solitis.
units.tr: gold for bronze [χρύσεα donanti, χάλκεα qui dederat, i.e. Iliad 6.236 in the Latin version]; rather they follow this proverb of mockers and jesters: Take nothing and keep it well [λαβὲ μηδὲν· ἐκ κέρατι καλῶς]. Unless perhaps the paper and lead, the instruments of applying indulgences, seem to them to be something of value to someone. Of course, they have much to fear from the fire of purgatory, lest these too be reduced to NOTHING, since the devils are said to have such hot hands that the parchment burns and the lead melts between them before they have read through them. Hence it is that long ago the Greeks, as Cardinal Aureolus reports (in 4 d. 21 art. 1, p. 151 d), sharply accused the Latins that they had invented Purgatory for the sake of profit. Finally, the Bishop of Salzburg and the suffragan of Chiemsee, in a book he entitled Onus Ecclesiae, printed at Landshut in Bavaria in 1524, complains about these questors, that by their preaching they deceive simple people and extract gold from them by a subtle or rather deceitful cleverness, falsely promising to draw souls out of purgatory, souls that are reserved for God's judgement. For if Cicero (De Off. 3) judged that to sell a house badly built, ruinous, unhealthy, and yet to hide its defects from the buyer, was the act of a man who is not open, not simple, not frank, not just, not good, but rather crafty, shady, sly, deceitful, malicious, cunning, a sharper, a trickster; and Plato (in the Hipparchus) said that those are truly wicked and impious who know that the things from which they profit are worth nothing, and yet from impudence dare to embrace the profit: what shall we think should be decided about those who make no profit not merely from a faulty thing, but from something that is plainly NOTHING? And if, as Cicero says in the same place, those are to be blamed who have kept silent that the thing they sell is faulty or worth nothing; what must be thought of those who have added the vanity of rhetoric besides? This is established to have been done not only by all others who occupy themselves with the trade in Purgatory, but especially by the heralds of indulgences, who are accustomed to push their wares with wonderful wheedling of words and enticing promises.

units.la: XLIV. Est & aliud mercaturæ Babylonicæ genus in usu, seu potiùs nefario abusu clavium, seu absolutionis, quæ gemina statuitur. Altera enim locum habet in Sacramento Pænitentiæ, quo absolutio, seu remissio peccatorum contritis, confitentibus & satisfacientibus saltem pro pœna temporali promittitur: altera, extra Sacramentum Pænitentiæ, cùm Papa pro nutu & arbitrio suo peccata remittit. Utramque ad quæstum faciendum aptam natam esse, & quæstui inservire, paucis demonstrabimus.
units.tr: XLIV. There is also another kind of Babylonian trade in use, or rather a wicked abuse of the keys, or absolution, which is set up in two forms. For one has its place in the Sacrament of Penance, in which absolution, or remission of sins, is promised to those who are contrite, confess, and make satisfaction at least for the temporal punishment; the other, outside the Sacrament of Penance, is when the Pope remits sins at his own nod and pleasure. We will show in a few words that both are suited to making profit, and serve profit.
XLV.

units.la: XLV. Ac priorem quod attinet, satis constat, Sacrificulo cuivis potestatem eximiam esse sedendi pro tribunali, confessiones peccatorum audiendi, peccata judiciali authoritate remittendi, vel retinendi, & pro poena temporali peccatis debita idoneas satisfactiones praescribendi. Quis non hic, ut Clemente & benigno judice, confessionem æquo animo audiente, peccata ἐπιμέλειαν dijudicante, ab iisdem absolvente, & satisfactionem pro reliqua poena temporali tolerabilem praescribente utatur, libens pretium aliquod penstet, si penstato pretio tali judice uti possit? Inprimis si persuasio animum confitentis & poenitentis occupaverit, absque tali confessione & absolutione Sacerdotis nemini in foro Divino peccata remitti posse, vel ad Regnum Cœlorum viam patere? Accedit, quòd inter species satisfactionum Sacramentalium (nam ab his spontaneæ distinguuntur) quas Sacerdos præscribere jure suo potest, non tantùm poenæ corporales, sed etiam pecuniariæ numerentur. Irrogat ergò Sacerdos pro lubitu suo multas pecuniarias sub titulo eleemosynæ. Nam quæ dantur Monachis aqualiculo distentis, & ipsi Papæ, eleemosynæ appellantur, neque, uti eleemosynæ solent, sponte, sed ex imperio persolvuntur. His ergò artibus venerandi illi Patres populum emungunt argento, & in corpora fortunasque laicorum, ne Regibus quidem exceptis, imperium exercent. Atque adeò frequens & luculentus est hic ex confessione & absolutione administrata Sacerdotum quæstus, ut Jesuitæ perfectionem suam supra reliquos ordines, inter alia in eo etiam collocare soleant, quòd consessiones gratis audiant. Sed callidi scilicet trapezitæ illi hoc agunt, ut pecunias in loco negligant, quod interdum maximum lucrum est. Nam sic neglecta exiguà pecuniâ, lucrantur illi animos, quos ubi semel in potestatem suam redegerunt, opportunos deinceps ad subeunda imperia longè graviora, faciendúmque ex iis quæstum non vulgarem, sed Jesuitis dignum, habent.
units.tr: XLV. As for the former, it is well established that every priest has a remarkable power to sit on the tribunal, hear confessions of sins, remit or retain sins by judicial authority, and prescribe suitable satisfactions for the temporal punishment due to sins. Who would not gladly pay some price to use such a judge, one who listens to confession with an even mind, weighs the sins with care [ἐπιμέλειαν], absolves from them, and prescribes a tolerable satisfaction for the rest of the temporal punishment, if he could use such a judge for a price? Above all, if the conviction has taken hold of the penitent's mind that without such confession and absolution by a priest no one can have sins remitted in the divine forum, or have a way open to the kingdom of heaven? Add to this that among the kinds of sacramental satisfactions (for these are distinguished from spontaneous ones), which a priest may prescribe by his right, not only bodily punishments but also pecuniary ones are counted. The priest therefore imposes pecuniary fines at his pleasure under the title of alms. For what is given to monks with bellies distended, and even to the Pope himself, is called alms, yet it is not paid voluntarily, as alms usually are, but by command. By these arts those venerable Fathers drain the people of silver and exercise authority over the bodies and fortunes of laymen, not even excepting kings. And this gain from the administration of confession and absolution by priests is so frequent and conspicuous that the Jesuits are wont to place their perfection above the other orders, among other things, in this, that they hear confessions free of charge. But those crafty money-changers do this, that they neglect money on the spot, which is sometimes the greatest profit. For by neglecting a small sum in this way, they win over souls, which once they have brought under their power, they keep ready for submitting to far heavier commands, and from these they make a gain that is not ordinary but worthy of Jesuits.

units.la: XLVI. Quia pœnæ temporales, jejunia, peregrinationes, flagellationes, nudipedalia, χαμευνίαι, aliáque ejusmodi pœnalia opera, in foro pœnitentiæ à Sacerdote pœnitentibus præscripta, & per aliquot annorum spatium extracta, uti quidem illa à Burchardo lib. xix. & Gratiano passim describuntur, molesta & exercita nimis visa sunt, placuit Sacerdotibus eadem pro lubitu & circumstantiarum ratione in pecuniarias multas convertere. Sic enim in Decreto Burchardi lib. xix. 19. legere est: Si quis forte non potuerit jejunare, & habuerit, unde possit redimere, si dives fuerit, pro septem hebdomadibus det solidos viginti. Si non habuerit, unde totidem dare possit, det solidos decem. Si autem multum pauper fuerit, det solidos tres. Addit, pecunias inde redactas vel redimendis captivis, vel altari, vel servis Dei (Sacrificulis) vel in usum eleemosynarum Ecclesiæ scilicet conferendarum impendi debere. Concilium Lateranense ultimum Sess. ix. sic definit: Laicus blasphemans, si nobilis fuerit, pœnâ 25. ducatorum multetur, & pro secunda vice quinquaginta fabricæ Basilicæ Principis Apostolorum de urbe applicandis. Emmanuel Sa Aphorismis in verbo Episcopus: Potest, inquit, Episcopus laicos cohibere à peccatis per pœnam pecuniariam vel exilii. Baronius ad A. 1055. ff. 9. Cardinalis Petri Damiani isthæc verba allegat: Non ignoras, quia cùm à pœnitentibus terras, possessiones agrorum videlicet accipimus, juxta mensuram muneris, eis de quantitate pœnitentiæ relaxamus. Sicut scriptum est: Divitiæ hominis, redemtio ejus Prov xiv. 8. Rem acu tetigit Cardinalis, insignis scilicet Scripturæ interpres, quasi sapiens ibi egisset de redemptione remissionis peccatorum apud Deum, à qua pauper excluderetur. Subjicit Baronius: Quibus bus plane ostendit Damianus, bona Ecclesiastica ejusmodi fieri solita, redemptione au&ta crevisse. Sic est, Cardinales vos, bona Ecclesiastica redemptione hac creverunt, in immensum creverunt; & claves Petri feliciter referárunt pridem cistas, abditósque thesauros populi, ut rapinæ vehementer paterent promtius.
units.tr: XLVI. Because temporal punishments (fasting, pilgrimages, flagellations, going barefoot, sleeping on the ground [χαμευνίαι], and other such penal works), which the priest in the forum of penance prescribed to penitents and drew out over some years, as Burchard in book xix and Gratian describe them throughout, seemed too burdensome and wearisome, the priests resolved to convert these, according to their pleasure and the circumstances, into pecuniary fines. Thus in Burchard's Decree, book xix, chapter 19, one may read: If anyone perhaps cannot fast, and has the means to redeem it, let him, if he is rich, give twenty shillings for seven weeks. If he has not the means to give that much, let him give ten shillings. But if he is very poor, let him give three shillings. He adds that the money thus raised must be spent either on ransoming captives, on the altar, on the servants of God (the priests), or on the uses of the alms of the Church. The last Lateran Council, session ix, defines thus: A layman who blasphemes, if he is noble, shall be fined twenty-five ducats, and for a second offence fifty, to be applied to the building of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the city. Emmanuel Sa, in his Aphorisms under the word Bishop: A bishop, he says, can restrain laymen from sins by a pecuniary penalty or by exile. Baronius, on the year 1055, section 9, cites the words of Cardinal Peter Damian: You are not unaware that when we receive lands and possessions of fields from penitents, we relax part of the penance according to the measure of the gift. As it is written: The riches of a man are his redemption, Prov. xiv. 8. The Cardinal hit the mark, being a distinguished interpreter of Scripture, as if he had there been wise about the redemption of the forgiveness of sins before God, from which the poor man would be excluded. Baronius adds: By these things Damian plainly shows that church goods of this kind, which were customarily made, grew by the increase of redemption. Yes indeed, you cardinals: church goods have grown by this redemption, grown immensely; and the keys of Peter have happily unlocked the chests and hidden treasures of the people long ago, so that they lay more readily open to plunder.

units.la: XLVII. Hæc equidem jam Seculo undecimo acta sunt:
units.tr: XLVII. These things were indeed already done in the eleventh century:

units.la: Sed vergente Papatu Lutetiæ A. M. D. xx. apud Tossanum Denis prodiit infaustus ille, Lucina obstetricante, partus, Taxa Cancellariæ Apostolicæ, ipso tenore verorum, utque sono Babylonicam mercaturam & nundinationem clamans, à Datario quodam, seu Cancellariæ Publicano, Pontificia authoritate cusa, & quibuslibet flagitiosis Neratiis opportunissima. Nullum enim tam tetrum aut horrendum scelus cogitari potest, cujus venia parari non potuerit, aut absolutio ac dispensatio non impetrari, dummodò pecunia ad eam rem pro ratione Taxæ necessaria interveniret. Prodiit quoque (uti quidem non una, sed plures taxæ reperiuntur passim in tractatibus Od. juris, præsertim in volumine sexto, editione veteri A. M. D. xxxiii.) Imperii Procerum jussu altera Taxa Sacra Pœnitentiaria dicta, cujus compendium supra Differt. xiv. s. 49. repræsentavimus, quod hunc etiam in locum studiosus lector sevocabit. Ibidem s. 48. Claudii Espencæi gravissimam de Taxæ Cancellariæ Apostolicæ nundinatione querelam consignatis verbis expressam recitavimus. In eadem sub rubrica de causis matrimonialibus, disertis verbis scribit: Nota diligenter, quòd hujusmodi gratias & dispensationes non conceduntur pauperibus, quia non habent, & ideò non possunt consolari. Extat in ea quoque peculiare caput de absolutionibus, in quo sic legere est: Absolutio pro eo, qui in Ecclesia cognovit mulierem, & alia mala commisit, gros. 6. Absolutio pro eo, qui defloravit virginem, grof. 6. Absolutio pro perjuro, grof. 6. Absolutio pro eo, qui revelavit confessione n alterius, grof. 7. Absolutio pro eo, qui falsificavit literas Apostolicas, grof. 16. vel 18. Absolutio pro eo, qui interfecit patrem, matrem, &c. grof. 5. Exiguum videri poterat, & leve nimis grossorum pretium. Coeterum, sub finem mirè taxa augetur, & grossi in ducatos permutantur. Sed &pag. 32. diplomatis mentio est, cui Confessionale nomen impositum, quo Papa permittit, ut in extremo vitæ discrimine positus, Confessarium pro lubitu deligat, qui potestatem habeat perfectam ci omnium peccatorum remissionem impertiendi. Additur tamen, non cuivis, sed summis duntaxat Principibus, neque ita facilè hoc concedi. Cùm igitur hæc illorum mercatura, juxtà Taxas illas, aliásque etiam (sunt enim multiplices illæ & prolixæ) in omnibus Regnis, totiúsque orbis Christiani Provinciis agitata fuerit, promtum est hinc perspicere, quàm uberes, nullo queterminati numero proventus, ex istius Babylonicæ negotiationis deliciis Romana Curia percepit.
units.tr: But as the Papacy was declining, at Paris in 1520, at the press of Denis Tossanus, that ill-omened offspring was published, with Lucina assisting at the birth: the Taxa Cancellariae Apostolicae, which by its very tenor, and as it were by its sound, proclaims Babylonian merchandise and haggling. It was coined under papal authority by a certain datary, or tax-collector of the Chancery, and is most convenient for any flagitious Neros. For no crime so foul or horrible can be imagined whose pardon could not be obtained, or whose absolution and dispensation could not be procured, provided the money required for the business according to the rate of the Tax was forthcoming. There also appeared, by command of the princes of the Empire, another so-called Sacred Penitentiary Tax, though not only one but several taxes are found scattered through the treatises on law, especially in the sixth volume, the old edition of 1533. A summary of it we presented above, Differt. xiv, s. 49, and the studious reader will also consult it here. In the same place, s. 48, we quoted the very grave complaint of Claude d'Espence about the trafficking in the Taxa of the Apostolic Chancery, expressed in set words. In the same work, under the heading on matrimonial causes, he writes in plain words: Note carefully that such graces and dispensations are not granted to the poor, because they do not have them, and therefore cannot be comforted. In it there is also a special chapter on absolutions, in which one may read: Absolution for one who has known a woman in the church and committed other evils, 6 grossi. Absolution for one who has deflowered a virgin, 6 grossi. Absolution for a perjurer, 6 grossi. Absolution for one who has revealed another's confession, 7 grossi. Absolution for one who has forged apostolic letters, 16 or 18 grossi. Absolution for one who has killed his father, mother, etc., 5 grossi. The price in grossi might seem small and too slight. Moreover, near the end the tax is greatly increased, and the grossi are exchanged for ducats. But on page 32 there is also mention of a document given the name Confessionale, by which the Pope permits one placed in extreme danger of life to choose a confessor at will, who has full power to impart to him the remission of all his sins. It is added, however, that this is granted not to anyone but only to the highest princes, and not so easily. Since, therefore, this their trade, according to those taxes and others as well (for they are many and lengthy), has been carried on in all the kingdoms and provinces of the whole Christian world, it is easy to see from this how rich the revenues the Roman Curia drew from the delights of this Babylonian business were, with no fixed limit.

units.la: XLVIII. In Taxa Poenitentiaria, ut hoc obiter aspergam, sub rubrica de Hebræis hæc legere est: Ut Hebræus possit habere Synagogam in domo propria, taxatur tur. 30. duc. 7. Cart. 6. Pro licentia erigendi de novo publicam Synagogam, taxa est tur. 60. duc. 15. Eò ergò res justo Dei judicio devenit in Regno illo Babylonico, ut si Judæi Domino Papæ numerent pecuniam in Sacra Taxa proscriptam & expressam, ilicò ad blasphemias suas in Jesum Nazarenum impunè effundendas, Synagogæ illis ædificandæ permittantur; qui contra in Jesum hunc Nazarenum omnem suam spem, fiduciam, justitiæ summam, & æternæ salutis anchoram, ita defigunt, ut solo ipsius merito in æternum salvari cupiant, hi Papæ & Cardinalium lium Collegio tanti admissi sceleris rei habeantur, ut eos ferro flammáque necandos, & rebus humanis eximendos esse clamitent. Agite Jesuitæ, Purpuratæ Meretricis lenones, pulcherrimum hoc facinus excusate, palliate, singite, pingite, fucate, colorate: & pudenda hæc Babylonici scorti tam fœdè prominentia, quibus tandem potestis cinctoriis contegite. Excusare, palliare, fingere, pingere, fucare, colorare, contegere satis poteritis nunquam. In aperto impietas est.
units.tr: XLVIII. In the Penitentiary Tax, to add this in passing, under the heading concerning Hebrews, one reads the following: For a Hebrew to have a synagogue in his own house, the charge is 30 tur., 7 duc., 6 cart. For a licence to erect a new public synagogue, the charge is 60 tur., 15 duc. By the just judgment of God, things have therefore come to such a pass in that Babylonian kingdom that if the Jews count out money prescribed and expressed in the Sacred Tax to the Lord Pope, they are at once permitted to have synagogues built for them, in which to pour out their blasphemies against Jesus of Nazareth with impunity. Yet those who place all their hope, trust, the sum of their righteousness, and the anchor of eternal salvation in this Jesus of Nazareth, so that they desire to be saved for ever by his merit alone, are considered by these Popes and the College of Cardinals guilty of so great a crime that they cry out that such people should be put to death with sword and fire and removed from human affairs. Come on, Jesuits, pimps of the Purple Harlot: excuse, cloak, feign, paint, dye, and colour this most beautiful deed; and cover, with whatever girdles you can, these shameful parts of the Babylonian whore that stick out so foully. You will never be able to excuse, cloak, feign, paint, dye, colour, or cover them enough. Impiety is in the open.

units.la: XLIX. Ne tamen vel Sacerdotes quivis, vel Episcopi etiam nimium sibi in impertienda absolutione indulgerent, & quæstum omnem soli devorarent, visum est Papæ, refervare casus quosdam à Sacerdotibus ad Superiores, & ab his (certos quidem & definitos) Romam ad suum pœnitentiæ sacræ tribunal sevocandos, ubi absolutio ex arbitrio Papæ solius expediatur. Extat super casuum horum Reservatione Decretum Clementis VIII. die 26. May, A. MDXCIII. Romæ solenni Bulla publicatum, ab omnibus Regularium Superioribus observandum; quo Superioribus reserventur undecim casus, veluti 1. Veneficia, incantationes & fortilegia. 2. Apostasia à religione, sive habitu dimisso, sive detento, quando eò pervenerit, ut extra sepla Monasterii, seu Conventûs fiat egressio. 3. Nocturna & furtiva à Monasterio sive conventu egressio, etiam non animo apostolandi facta. 4. Proprietas contra votum paupertatis, quæ sit peccatum mortale. 5. Juramentum falsum in judicio Regulari, seu legitimo. 6. Procuratio, consilium seu auxilium ad abortum faciendum post animatum fœtum, etiam effectu non secuto. 7. Falsificatio manûs aut sigilli Officialium Monasterii, aut Conventûs. 8. Furtum de rebus Monasterii seu Conventûs, in ea quantitate, quæ sit peccatum mortale. 9. Lapsus carnis voluntarius, opere consummatus. 10. Occisio aut vulneratio, seu gravis percussio cujuscunque persona. Jone. xi. Malitiosum impedimentum, aut retardatio, aut apertio literarum à Superioribus ad inferiores, & ab inferioribus ad Superiores. Hi quidem sunt casus confitentium Regularium reservati. Alii casus sunt confitentium non Regularium. Sunt etiam casus soli Papæ reservati, ipsorum Episcoporum potestatem supergressi, qui in Bulla de Cœna Domini recensentur; ubi etiam habetur forma excommunicationis, cujus fulmina Papa anniversariis diebus Jovis, Pascha præcedentibus, delinquentes circa casus illos, jacta ex sublimi ardente face, ferit. Frustrà ibi homicidia, adulteria, incestus, veneficia, à quibus singuli Episcopi absolvere possunt, requiras. Longè graviora Papæ scilicet, pro Suprematu & temporali elatione, ceu pupilla oculi sui, soliciti exi&imatione, crimina sunt, quæ illi reservare solent, puta eorum, qui ad futurum Concilium appellare audent: qui piraticam exercent proximè territorium Papæ, inde à monte Argentario Terracinam usque: qui Apostolicas literas falsant; qui hæreticis arma suppeditant: qui commeatum Aulæ Pontificis afferentes, morantur: qui Prælatum quempiam occidunt: qui decimas à Clero exigunt: qui jura Ecclesiæ violant, Reges imprimis, Cancellarii & Parlamenta: qui receptioni Concilii Tridentini adversantur: qui Romipetas impediunt, aut læduntur. Hæc scilicet atrocia & inexpiabilia illa crimina sunt, quæ de facto Papæ anathemata incurrunt, neque nisi à Papa absolvi, & anathematis nexu exui possunt.
units.tr: XLIX. Lest any priests, or even bishops, should be too free in granting absolution and devour all the profit for themselves, the Pope thought fit to reserve certain cases from priests to superiors, and from the superiors (certain and defined ones) to be sent to Rome, to his tribunal of sacred repentance, where absolution is dispensed at the Pope's sole discretion. There is a decree of Clement VIII on the reservation of these cases, dated 26 May 1593, published at Rome by solemn bull and to be observed by all regular superiors. By it eleven cases are reserved to superiors, such as: (1) Witchcraft, incantations and fortune-telling. (2) Apostasy from religion, whether the habit is laid aside or kept, when it comes about that someone leaves beyond the walls of the monastery or convent. (3) Nocturnal and furtive departure from the monastery or convent, even if done without intent to preach abroad. (4) Ownership of property against the vow of poverty, which is a mortal sin. (5) A false oath in a regular or lawful court. (6) Procuring, counsel or help for an abortion after the foetus has been animated, even if the effect does not follow. (7) Forgery of the hand or seal of the officials of a monastery or convent. (8) Theft of goods of a monastery or convent, in an amount that is a mortal sin. (9) Voluntary carnal lapse, carried through in deed. (10) Killing or wounding, or grievous assault upon any person. Jone. xi. (11) Malicious hindrance, delay or opening of letters from superiors to inferiors and from inferiors to superiors. These are the reserved cases of confessing regulars. There are other cases of confessing non-regulars. There are also cases reserved to the Pope alone, which exceed the power of the bishops themselves, and are listed in the Bull In Coena Domini; there too is the form of excommunication, whose thunderbolts the Pope hurls, on the Thursdays of the anniversary before Easter, at offenders against those cases, flinging a burning torch from on high. In vain will you look there for murders, adulteries, incests and poisonings, from which individual bishops can absolve. Far graver crimes, clearly, are those the Pope is accustomed to reserve, for the sake of his supremacy and temporal exaltation, which he guards anxiously as the apple of his eye: those who dare to appeal to a future council; who carry on piracy close to the Pope's territory, from Monte Argentario as far as Terracina; who forge apostolic letters; who supply arms to heretics; who, bringing provisions to the Pope's court, delay them; who kill some prelate; who exact tithes from the clergy; who violate the rights of the Church, especially kings, chancellors and parliaments; who oppose the reception of the Council of Trent; who hinder or injure pilgrims to Rome. These, surely, are the atrocious and inexpiable crimes which, by the Pope's own act, incur anathemas, and which can be absolved only by the Pope and freed from the bond of anathema.

units.la: L. Quò verò hæc aurigentur, obscurum non est. Olim quidem enormia crimina contra Dei, non Papæ legem admissa, quibus excommunicationis censuræ annexa est, referebantur ad Episcopos, ut de ipsorum consilio, certa publicæ pœnitentiæ ratio, reis ad ipsorum emendationem, & Ecclesiæ ædificationem imponeretur. Innocentii constitutio cap. Omnis utriusque dicit: Si Confessarius opus habuerit, ut in enormi aliquo crimine se majores & doctiores consulat, ut illud absque ulla expressione persona caute requirat. Inde postea emerserunt Casus Reservati puriori antiquitati, uti ipsi in Concilio Tridentino Colonienses & Lovanienses Theologi pertenderunt, prorsus incogniti, in quibus verbum Dei peccatorum poenitentum per nullum ministrum, quantumvis legitime vocatum, in foro Divino, absolvere possit, nisi id faciat Episcopus, vel Romanus Pontifex, utpote in quo solo plenitudo potestatis remittendi peccata resideat, quique pro arbitrio suo vel ipse remittere, vel remittendi potestatem aliis inferioribus delegare possit. Unde Concilium Tridentinum Seff. xiv. cap. 7. asserit, nullius momenti absolutionem esse, quam Sacerdos in eum profert, in quem ordinariam, aut subdelegatam non habet jurisdictionem. Magnopere vero ad Christiani populi disciplinam pertinere visum est, inquit, ut atrociora quaedam & graviora crimina, non a quibusvis, sed a summis duntaxat Sacerdotibus absolventur. Unde merito Pontifices Maximi pro summa potestate sibi in Ecclesia universa tradita, causas aliquas criminum graviores suo potuerunt peculiari judicio reservare. Quasi scilicet verbum Dei non possit remittere peccata, nisi ubi, in quantum, & quibus in casibus ipsi potestas ex scrinio pectoris Papalis derivata assistat, vel ejus vis & potentia pro differentia eorum, a quibus administratur, variet; ita ut per quosdam tantum parva peccata, hoc est ea, quae contra legem Divinam militant, per Papam vero quaevis, inprimis maxima, scilicet ea, quae contra legem ejus, culinariam praecipue, militant, remitti possint. Quod verbi Divini potestas, & Christi ipsius authoritas non praestat, Papae potestas & authoritas praestat. Satis apparet, id omne a Babyloniis mercatoribus, ad stabiliendam tyrannidem, alendum, conservandum, & augendum Regni Papalis quæstum excogitatum esse, quod vel sola casuum re‐servatorum ex Bulla Cœnæ Domini supra repetitorum na‐ tiva indoles, & Romanæ in casibus hisce licitationes, ma‐ nifestè arguunt. De qua re Imperii Romani status A. M D XXII. graviter sic questi sunt, inter gravamina cen‐ tum, tertio: Papalis sanctitas, & cæteri Episcopi casus aliquot suæ tantum absolutioni reliquos fecerunt &c. ut inde nummorum aliquid eis accrescat. Quod ex eo conji‐ cere licet, quòd in casibus etiam quantumvis pro tempore honestis, aut necessariis, nunquam tamen, nisi numeretur aliquid, dispensant. At si nihil attuleris, indispensatus perpetuò maneas oportet.
units.tr: L. But where all this is leading is not obscure. Formerly, enormous crimes committed against the law of God, not of the Pope, to which excommunication was attached, were referred to the bishops, so that, on their advice, a fixed form of public penance might be imposed on the guilty for their amendment and the building up of the Church. The constitution of Innocent, chapter Omnis utriusque, says: If the confessor needs to consult his elders and betters about some enormous crime, let him inquire about it carefully and without any mention of the person. Afterwards there emerged the reserved cases, wholly unknown to purer antiquity, as the Louvain and Cologne theologians themselves argued at the Council of Trent. In these cases the word of God cannot absolve penitent sinners in the divine forum through any minister, however lawfully called, unless it is done by the bishop or the Roman Pontiff, since the fullness of the power of remitting sins resides in him alone, and he may at his discretion either remit them himself or delegate the power of remitting them to inferiors. Hence the Council of Trent, Sess. xiv. chap. 7, asserts that the absolution which a priest pronounces on one over whom he has no ordinary or subdelegated jurisdiction is of no account. It has been thought of great importance to the discipline of the Christian people, it says, that certain more atrocious and grave crimes should be absolved not by just any priests, but only by the chief priests. Hence the supreme Pontiffs, by the great power committed to them over the whole Church, could rightly reserve some graver crimes to their own special judgement. As if, forsooth, the word of God could not remit sins except where, to the extent, in the cases and by the power which is derived from the coffers of the Papal breast, it stands by; or as if its force and power varied according to the difference of those by whom it is administered, so that by some only small sins, that is, those which militate against the divine law, can be remitted, but by the Pope any sins whatever, above all the greatest, namely those which militate against his law, especially the culinary law, can be remitted. What the power of the divine Word and the authority of Christ himself do not supply, the power and authority of the Pope supply. It is plain enough that all this was devised by the Babylonian merchants to establish their tyranny and to feed, preserve and increase the gain of the Papal kingdom; the native character of the reserved cases repeated above from the Bull In Coena Domini, and the Roman auctions of these cases, clearly prove it. On this matter the estates of the Roman Empire, in the year 1522, complained gravely, among their hundred grievances, in the third: The Papal holiness and the other bishops have left some cases to their own absolution alone, so that something accrues to them in money. This may be conjectured from the fact that they never dispense in cases, however honourable or necessary for the time being, unless something is paid. But if you bring nothing, you must remain unabsolved for ever.

units.la: LI. Cùm ergò sic Hierarchici refipiscentiam primò in pœnas pœnitentiales, in argenteas, aureáspue fodinas per‐ mutaverint, haud immeritò statibus Imperii Romani tum Pontificii, tum Protestantes iidem inter gravamina sua ad‐ versus Romanam Curiam colleƈta, isthoc etiam numero I.XVII.retulerunt.Rubrica est: Quemadmodum plus pecu‐ niæ quàm pœnitentiæ peccatoribus imponunt. Textus sequi‐ tur: Patrum Canonibus sancitum est, spiritualibus ac ma‐ nifestis peccatis spiritualem pœnitentiam seu satisfactionem imponendam esse, ut sic non pecuniæ lucrum, sed potiùs animarum salus quæri intelligatur. At Ecclesiastici ju‐ dices & Officiales perperàm animadversis Canonibus, di‐ stam spiritualem pœnitentiam in tantum exasperant, ag‐ gravant, & augent, ut laici priusquam eam satisfactio‐ nem acceptare velint, pecuniâ magis sibi ab ipsis immuni‐ tatem comparent. Quare laici multùm premuntur, Ec‐ clesiastici contra multùm ditantur, utpote qui in suum pri‐ vatum commodum & partis, agunt munus & judicis: quod tamen omnibus juribus dissonum est.
units.tr: LI. Since, therefore, the hierarchs have turned repentance first into penitential penalties, and then into silver and gold mines, the estates of the Roman Empire, both Papists and Protestants, rightly listed this among their grievances against the Roman Curia, under number 117. The heading is: How they impose more money than penance on sinners. The text follows: It is decreed by the canons of the Fathers that a spiritual penance or satisfaction is to be imposed for spiritual and manifest sins, so that it may be understood that the aim is the salvation of souls and not the profit of money. But ecclesiastical judges and officials, wrongly interpreting the canons, so exaggerate, aggravate and increase the prescribed spiritual penance that laymen, before they are willing to accept that satisfaction, procure immunity for themselves from them with money. Hence laymen are heavily burdened, while the clergy are greatly enriched, since they discharge the office of judge for their own private advantage and that of their party; and this is nonetheless at odds with all rights.

units.la: LII. Sic fuit abusus Clavium, seu Absolutionis Hie‐rarchicorum in Sacramento Pœnitentiæ. Gravior est abus‐ sus Clavium seu Absolutionis alterius, qua extra Sacramentum Pœnitentiæ Papa, Hierarchicorum caput, pro plenitudine potestatis à peccatis absolvit, & per merita aliena ex Ecclesiæ fictitio thesauro, liberè applicata, indulgentias dispensat, quibus, quando & qua lege vult. Pecuniæ autem pro indulgentia expendendæ lege maximè vult. Et potestas quidem hæc Papæ à Doctore Angelico, Thoma Aquinate, sic Opusc. xxi. 10. describitur: Cùm Summus Pontifex sit caput in corpore mystico omnium fidelium Christi, & à capite sit omnis motus & sensus in corpore vero, sic etiam in proposito. Propter quod oportet discere, in Summo Pontifice esse plenitudinem omnium gratiarum, quia ipse solus confert plenam indulgentiam omnium peccatorum. Ut competat sibi, quod de primo Principe Domino dicimus, quia de plenitudine ejus nos omnes accipimus. Hæc licet nihil à blasphemia absint, exprimunt tamen sententiam Hierarchiæ, juxta quam Papa tum in Sacramento Pœnitentiæ Sacerdotibus & Episcopis potestatem remittendi peccata delegat: tum eadem extra Sacramentum pro lubitu utitur. Innixus enim passionibus meritisque Christi & Sanctorum superabundantibus, quas ille pro ejusdem potestatis suæ plenitudine, & singulari frugalitate illa, qua nihil ex hesternis fragmentis perire patitur, in Ecclesiæ thesaurum, conjungendas scilicet cum auro & argento Papæ, ut horum contactu & ipsæ in aurum & argentum transsubstantientur, & ab eodem ceu radicali horrei hujus custode conservandas, importat pro lubitu suo auxiliares manus porrigentibus indulgentias plenissimas, pleniores, plenas, quibus peccata, & peccatorum pœnæ, etiam illæ, quæ à Sacerdotibus in Pœnitentiæ foro jam impositæ sunt, remittantur, dispensat. Neque tantum à pœnis & peccatis, sed ab ipsa etiam obligatione faciendi fructus pœnitentia dignos, indulgentiæ relaxant,
units.tr: LII. Thus there was the abuse of the keys, or of the absolution of the hierarchs, in the Sacrament of Penance. Graver is the abuse of the other key, or absolution, by which the Pope, head of the hierarchs, outside the Sacrament of Penance, absolves from sins by the fullness of his power, and from the fictitious treasury of the Church, freely applying the merits of others, dispenses indulgences, when, how and under what law he wishes. He lays down the law especially about the money to be spent on an indulgence. This power of the Pope is described thus by the Angelic Doctor, Thomas Aquinas, in Opusc. xxi. 10: Since the Supreme Pontiff is the head in the mystical body of all the faithful of Christ, and all motion and sense in the body comes from the head, so also in the present case. Wherefore one must learn that in the Supreme Pontiff there is the fullness of all graces, because he alone confers the full indulgence of all sins, so that what we say of the first Prince, the Lord, applies to him: for we all receive from his fullness. Although these statements are not free from blasphemy, they express the opinion of the Hierarchy, according to which the Pope, on the one hand, delegates to priests and bishops in the Sacrament of Penance the power of remitting sins, and on the other, outside the Sacrament, uses the same power at his pleasure. For, relying on the sufferings and superabundant merits of Christ and the Saints, which he, by virtue of the fullness of that same power and by that singular thrift, which allows nothing to perish of yesterday's leftovers, brings into the treasury of the Church, to be joined, that is, with the Pope's gold and silver, so that by their contact they may themselves be transubstantiated into gold and silver, and be preserved by him as the root custodian of this storehouse, he dispenses, at his pleasure, the fullest, fuller and full indulgences to those who stretch out helping hands, by which sins and the penalties of sins, even those already imposed by priests in the forum of penance, are remitted. And indulgences relax not only penalties and sins, but also the very obligation of producing fruits worthy of repentance.

units.la: Tom. II. aaaa BellarmiBellarmino ipso eò impudentiæ provecto, ut de Pœnit. lib. j. 13. apertè assereret, indulgentias facere, ut propænis, quæ nobis per indulgentiam condonantur, non tenemur præcepto illo de faciendis dignis pœnitentiæ fructibus, utque non teneamur Domino, quem superbia, cupiditate, atque illicita delectatione offendimus, humilitate, largitione, compunctione & afflictione voluntaria satisfacere. Siccine pretio necessitas veræ pœnitentiæ agendæ eximi potest?
units.tr: Vol. II. aaaa Bellarmine himself advanced so far in impudence that in De Poenit. book 1, chapter 13, he openly asserted that indulgences have this effect, that for the punishments which are remitted to us through an indulgence we are not bound by that precept of bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance, and that we are not bound to make satisfaction to the Lord, whom we offend by pride, greed and unlawful delight, by humility, almsgiving, contrition and voluntary affliction. Can the necessity of true repentance really be removed for a price?

units.la: LIII. Satisfactionum Pœnitentialium in pecuniarias mulctas Seculo circiter undecimo, Burchardi tempore ortas esse, suprà ostendimus. Indulgentiarum verò nulla in Burchardi vel Gratiani scriptis mentio occurrit. Paulò ante Seculum decimum tertium exortæ sunt. Scribit Astexanus in Summa sua, quòd pœnitens, si sentiat satisfactionem sibi injunctam nimis esse gravem, aut ad servandum periculosam, posset ad eundem suum confessorem, vel alium recurrere, & petere vel commutationem, vel relaxationem seu indulgentiam injunctæ satisfactionis: & sacerdotem habere potestatem vel commutandi, vel etiam relaxandi satisfactionem prius injunctam. Hæc de Sacerdotum seu confessorum indulgentiis in foro Pœnitentiali ex multis Canonistis probat Bernhardinus. Postea disputari cœptum est, à quonam remissiones tales fieri possint, à proprio sacerdote, æquali an superiore? Postremò ad solos Episcopos & Archiepiscopos relaxatio illa translata est. Tandem de plenariis Papæ indulgentiis disputari magnificè cœptum est. Cùmque primùm Astexano teste, relaxationes illæ factæ sint ad petitionem pœnitentium, si imbecillitatem suam ad sustinendas satisfactiones satis probàssent, postea ad corrogationes eleemosynarum, dedicationes Templorum, peregrinationes, & tandem ad tinnitum munerum in genere cœperunt variæ indulgentiæ concedi. LIV. In
units.tr: LIII. We have shown above that penitential satisfactions were turned into money fines around the eleventh century, in the time of Burchard. But no mention of indulgences occurs in the writings of Burchard or Gratian. They arose a little before the thirteenth century. Astexanus writes in his Summa that if a penitent feels that the satisfaction imposed on him is too heavy, or dangerous to perform, he may have recourse to the same confessor or to another and ask either a commutation or a relaxation, or indulgence, of the imposed satisfaction, and that the priest has the power either to commute or even to relax the satisfaction previously imposed. Bernhardinus proves these things about the indulgences of priests or confessors in the penitential forum from many Canonists. Afterwards it began to be disputed by whom such remissions could be granted: by the proper priest, by an equal, or by a superior? Finally that relaxation was transferred to bishops and archbishops alone. At last the plenary indulgences of the Pope began to be discussed in grand terms. And although at first, according to the testimony of Astexanus, such relaxations were granted at the request of penitents who had sufficiently proved their weakness in bearing the satisfactions, afterwards various indulgences began to be granted for the collecting of alms, the dedication of churches, pilgrimages, and finally for the jingle of money in general. LIV. In

units.la: LIV. In Decretalibus Gregorii IX. lib. v. tit. 38. Capitulo Cùm ex ea, ponitur forma literarum, à Sede Romana quæstoribus illis eleemosynarum (sic diserte vocantur,) dari solitarum ejusmodi: Quia scriptum est, qui parcè seminat, parcè & metet, qui verò seminant in benedictionibus, de benedictionibus metent vitam æternam.
units.tr: LIV. In the Decretals of Gregory IX, book 5, title 38, the chapter Cum ex ea gives the form of letters, of the kind usually given from the Roman See to those collectors of alms (so they are expressly called): Because it is written, he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and those who sow in blessings will reap eternal life from blessings.

units.la: Cùm igitur ad sustentationem fratrum & egenorum ad hospitale confluentium propriæ non suppetant facultates, universitatem vestram monemus, atque in remissionem vobis injungimus peccatorum, ut de bonis vobis à Deo collatis, eis erogetis, ut per subventionem vestram ipsorum inopiæ consulatur, & vos per hæc bona & alia, ad æterna possitis gaudia pervenire. En indulgentiam non petitam, sed ultrò oblatam: & oblatam occasione inopiæ facultatum: & sub conditione erogandi bona à Deo collata, ne dubitari posset, primario intentum quæstum, contractumque Do ut des, exercitum fuisse. Eodem titulo Alexander III. loquitur de remissionibus, quæ fiebant in dedicationibus Ecclesiarum, aut conferentibus aliquid ad ædificationem pontium. Mox A. MCCXV. in Lateranensi Concilio ejusmodi constitutio prodiit: Quia per indiscretas & superfluas indulgentias, quas quidem Ecclesiarum Prælati facere non verentur, & claves Ecclesiæ contemnuntur, & pœnitentialis satisfactio enervatur: decernimus, ut, cùm dedicatur Basilica, non extendatur indulgentia ultra annum, ac deinde in anniversario dedicationis tempore 40. dies de injunctis pœnitentiis indulta remissio non excedat. Hunc quoque dierum numerum indulgentiarum literis præcipimus moderari &c. Post A. MCCXLIV. Innocentius IV. uti habetur in Sexto Decret. lib. v. tit. 10. pro fabrica Ecclesiæ Rhemensis permisit concedere indulgentias vel unius anni, vel 40. dierum.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the means of the brothers and of the poor who flock to the hospital are not sufficient from their own resources, we admonish your community and enjoin on you, for the remission of your sins, that you distribute to them from the goods conferred on you by God, so that their poverty may be relieved by your help, and that through these and other goods you may attain to the joys of eternity. Here is an indulgence not sought but offered unasked: offered on the occasion of the poverty of resources, and on condition that the goods conferred by God be given away, so that it could not be doubted that the primary aim was gain, and that a contract of do ut des was being carried on. In the same title Alexander III speaks of the remissions which were made at the dedication of churches, or for those contributing something towards the building of bridges. Soon after, in the year 1215, a constitution of this kind came out at the Lateran Council: Because through indiscreet and superfluous indulgences, which the prelates of the churches do not hesitate to grant, the keys of the Church are despised and penitential satisfaction is weakened, we decree that, when a basilica is dedicated, the indulgence shall not extend beyond a year, and that the remission of enjoined penances granted on the anniversary of the dedication shall not exceed forty days. We likewise order this number of days to be restrained by letters of indulgence, etc. After the year 1244, Innocent IV, as is found in the Sixth Book of Decretals, book 5, title 10, permitted indulgences of either one year or forty days to be granted for the building of the church of Reims.

units.la: LV. Hoc argumentum deinceps scholasticis disceptationibus exercitum, eóque perductum est, ut eorundem operâ nundinationibus indulgentiarum non tam fenestræ, quàm decumanæ portæ aperirentur, afferentibus plerisque, principaliter dari indulgentias, si quis manus adjutrices porrexerit (hac phrasi Sixtus IV. in bulla, quæ Extravag. com. lib. v. tit. 9. extat) ad hospitalia, ad Basilicas & similia, si modò temporalia, quæ exponuntur, ordinentur ad spiritualia. Sic enim Simoniam non committi. Sic planè pecuniæ pro remissione peccatorum exactæ & datæ, juxta institores Romanos, non ut corporales, sed ut spirituales considerantur, adeóque Simoniæ admittendæ metus nullus est. Nam indulgentiæ fiunt; sic Augustinus de Ancona, de potestate Papæ quæst. 30. art. 3. loquitur; ad relevandam indigentiam Ecclesiæ. Unde non solam voluntatem, sed actum dantis requiri, subjicit: Indulgentia, inquiens, Ecclesiæ non revelatur per solam voluntatem dandi, sed per datum. Proin divitis conditionem hic meliorem esse, quàm pauperis idem infert. Accesserunt indulgentiarum quæstores, qui suis artificiis mirè negotiationem illam promoverunt, atque eò impudentiæ progressi sunt, ut A. MCCCXI. in Viennensi Concilio, cui Clemens V. præfuit, nonnihil reprimi debuerint, peculiari edita constitutione contra quæstores indulgentiarum, quæ in Clementinarum libro quinto tit. 9. extat. Ibi inter alia habetur, quæstores illos eleemosynarum in suis prædicationibus proponere abusus, ut simplices decipiant, & aurum subtili, vel fallaci potiùs ingenio ab illis extorqueant, quod in animarum periculum & scandalum plurimorum cedat. Abusus recitantur sequentes, quòd non sine temeritate, audacia & deceptione multiplici animarum, indulgentias populo motu suo proprio de facto concedant, super votis dispensent, à perjuriis, homicidiis & peccatis catis aliis sibi confitentes absolvant, male ablata incerta (data sibi aliqua pecuniæ quantitate) remittant, tertiam aut quartam partem de pœnitentiis injunctis relaxent, animas tres vel plures parentum vel amicorum illorum, qui eleemosynas ei conferunt de purgatorio (ut afferunt mendaciter) extrahant, & ad gaudia Paradisi perducant, benefactoribus locorum, quorum quæstores exstiterunt remissionem plenariam peccatorum indulgeant, & aliqui ex ipsis eos à pœna & à culpa absolvant. Decretum Concilii adversus quæstores illos ejusmodi cusum est: Nos abusus hujusmodi, per quos censura vilescit Ecclesiastica, & clavium Ecclesiæ authoritas ducitur in contemptum, omnimodè aboleri volentes, per quoscunque quæstores fieri vel attentari de cætero districtius inhibemus: Omnia & singula privilegia, si qua super præmissis, vel eorum aliquo, sive aliquibus locis, ordinibus vel personis quæstorum hujusmodi quomodocunque concessa (ne ipsorum prætextu sit eis materia ulterius præsumendi) authoritate Apostolica, quantum ad præmissa penitus revocamus. Quæstores autem, qui deinceps in præmissis, vel aliquo præmissorum deliquerint &c. sic per locorum Episcopos puniri volumus (nullo prorsus Quæstoribus privilegio in hac parte suffragante) quòd à suis temerariis abusibus, qui (NB.) UBIQUE (ut communis habet assertio) NIMIUM EXCREVERUNT, pœnæ formidine propensius compescantur. Videbantur sic abusus illi indulgentiarum per Clementinam illam satis taxari, damnari & aboleri. Cœterùm Pontifices mox ipso facto decreti hujus interpretationem ediderunt, quòd videlicet abusus illi sint damnabiles & abolendi, si fiant à quæstoribus hospitalium, si verò à Pontificibus ipsis exerceantur jubentúrque, opus maximè pium esse.
units.tr: LV. This question was then exercised in scholastic disputations and was carried so far that, by their labour, not merely windows but the great gates were opened for the trading in indulgences, most of them asserting that indulgences are granted principally if someone has stretched out helping hands (this phrase is used by Sixtus IV in the bull which is found in the Extravagantes communes, book 5, title 9) to hospitals, basilicas and similar things, provided only that the temporal goods which are expended are directed to spiritual ends. For in this way simony is not committed. And so, according to the Roman hawkers, money exacted and given for the remission of sins is considered not as bodily but as spiritual, and therefore there is no fear of admitting simony. For indulgences are made; so Augustinus de Ancona speaks in De potestate Papae, question 30, article 3, for relieving the need of the Church. From this he adds that not only the will of the giver but the act of giving is required: An indulgence of the Church, he says, is not revealed by the mere will to give, but by the gift itself. Hence he infers that the condition of the rich man here is better than that of the poor man. There came the indulgence-sellers, who by their tricks greatly promoted that trade, and advanced so far in impudence that in the year 1311, at the Council of Vienne, over which Clement V presided, they had to be somewhat restrained, a special constitution being issued against the sellers of indulgences, which is found in the Clementines, book 5, title 9. There, among other things, it is stated that those sellers of alms, in their sermons, put forward abuses so that they may deceive the simple and extort gold from them by a subtle or rather a deceitful cleverness, which turns to the peril of souls and the scandal of many. The following abuses are recited: that without rashness, audacity and manifold deception of souls, they grant indulgences to the people on their own initiative, dispense from vows, absolve from perjuries, homicides and other sins confessed to them, remit ill-gotten goods of uncertain owners (for some sum of money given to them), relax a third or a fourth part of enjoined penances, extract from purgatory (as they falsely claim) the souls of three or more parents or friends of those who give alms to them and lead them to the joys of Paradise, grant a plenary remission of sins to the benefactors of the places of which they are the sellers, and some of them absolve them from punishment and from guilt. The decree of the Council against those sellers was issued in this form: Wishing utterly to abolish abuses of this kind, through which ecclesiastical censure is cheapened and the authority of the keys of the Church is brought into contempt, we strictly forbid that they be committed or attempted by any sellers in future. All and single privileges, if any have been granted in any way concerning the aforesaid matters, or any of them, to any places, orders or persons of such sellers, (lest under their pretext they have any further matter for presuming) we entirely revoke by Apostolic authority, so far as concerns the aforesaid matters. Moreover, those sellers who henceforth offend in the aforesaid matters, or any of them, etc., we wish to be punished thus by the bishops of the places (no privilege of the sellers at all supporting them in this respect), so that from their rash abuses, which (note) EVERYWHERE (as the common assertion holds) HAVE GROWN EXCESSIVELY, they may be more readily restrained by fear of punishment. Those abuses of indulgences seemed to have been sufficiently censured, condemned and abolished by that Clementine. Yet the Popes at once, by the very fact, issued an interpretation of this decree, namely that those abuses are indeed to be condemned and abolished if they are practised by sellers for hospitals, but if they are exercised by the Popes themselves and are commanded, they are a most pious work.

units.la: LVI. Sic ergò deinceps Pontifices aliis quæstoribus
units.tr: LVI. Thus from then on the Pontiffs dealt with other quaestors
The full gran-

units.la: indulgentiarum concessionem simpliciter prohibuerunt; Episcopis verò, vel Archiepiscopis indulgentias duntaxat partiales & limitatas, anni puta, vel 40. dierum concesserunt: sibi verò ex plenitudine potestatis plenarias indulgentias omnium peccatorum ad tempus longissimum, nullisque nisi papalibus arbitrii finibus limitatum, refervárunt, sic tamen ut jus illud indulgentias illas conferendi & applicandi committere possint, cui voluerint, & laicis. Placuit autem discrimen indulgentias inter plenas & plenissimas. Ita Petrus de Palude indulgentiam plenam vocari ait, respectu remissionis poenae mortalium & venialium, & plenissimam dici respectu non solùm poenae, sed etiam culpae venialium; quia, inquit, indulgentia habet rationem cujusdam absolutionis. Alii mediast, pleniores addiderunt. Ut ergo Pontifices opinionem vulgi de indulgentiis alerent, confirmarentque, cùm antea in literis indulgentiarum usi fuissent hac forma, remitti vel totum, vel partem de injunctis poenitentiis: aut, fieri remissionem vel totalem vel partialem poenae temporalis pro peccatis debitae, sicut Innocentii III. Bulla sonat: recentiores hac generalitate usi sunt: Plenam, pleniorem, plenissimam omnium peccatorum veniam Cajo Sejo concedimus & indulgemus. Neque viventibus duntaxat, sed etiam mortuis indulgentias dare consueverunt. In Taxa Cancellariae Apostolicae pag. 41. pretium à consanguineis superstitibus pro mortuis expendendum, sic definitur: Pro mortuo excommunicato, pro quo supplicant consanguinei, litura absolutionis venit duc. 1. Carl. 9. pro muliere, quae se suspendit, sive pro viro, ut possit Ecclesiae tradi censurae duc. 1. Carl. 9. Toletus quoque de Instruct. Sacerd. lib. 1. 7. sic definit: potest excommunicatione contracta in vita absolvi post mortem. Testes ejus rei sunt crebrae adeò indulgentiae, mortuis concessae, faceræ quinetiam aræ, Romæ inprimis, privilegiis solenniter munitæ, ut toties liberetur anima, quoties in iis lituntur: Navarrus Commentario de Jubilæo & indulg. concedit, indulgentias ad mortuos in Purgatorio laborantes extendi posse, negat tamen, cuiquam Papa inferiori, hoc est, alii quàm Papæ fas esse ad mortuos extendere. An verò extendi ad mortuos possint per modum authoritatis judicialis, an suffragii, deprecationis, vel intercessionis, certant Doctores, & adhuc sub judice lis est. Per modum suffragii duntaxat mortuis prodesse, Bonaventura, Richardus, Cajetanus, Cordubus, alii affirmant, metuentes, ne aliàs studium pro redimendis Missis, & orationibus in usum mortuorum frigesceret. Sed hanc sententiam Valentia incautam, nullo modo audiendam, appellat: Bellarminus probabilem, sed contrariam magis piam vocat. Parùm tamen refert quo modo mortuis prosint (nam indulgentiæ quidem per modum deprecationis collatæ, nil minùs quàm indulgentiæ sunt) dummodò quod adagio nefas putatur, ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν φορτλογεῖν à mortuo tributum exigere. Papæ fas integrúmque putetur.
units.tr: ting of indulgences they simply forbade. To bishops or archbishops they granted only partial and limited indulgences, of a year or forty days, say. For themselves, however, they reserved from the fullness of their power plenary indulgences for all sins, for the longest period, limited by no bounds except papal discretion. Yet they arranged that this right of granting and applying those indulgences could be committed to whomever they wished, even to laymen. They also chose to distinguish between full and fuller indulgences. Thus Peter of Palude says that an indulgence is called full with respect to the remission of the penalty for mortal and venial sins, and fullest with respect not only to the penalty but also to the guilt of venial sins, "because," he says, "an indulgence has the character of a kind of absolution." Others added fuller as a middle grade. So that the Pontiffs might nourish and confirm the common people's opinion of indulgences, they had previously used in their letters of indulgence this form: that either the whole or part of the imposed penances be remitted, or that there be a remission, either total or partial, of the temporal penalty owed for sins, as the bull of Innocent III has it. More recent letters used this general phrase: We grant and indulge full, fuller and fullest pardon of all sins to Gaius Seius. They were accustomed to give indulgences not only to the living but also to the dead. In the Taxa of the Apostolic Chancery, p. 41, the price to be paid by surviving relatives on behalf of the dead is fixed thus: for an excommunicated dead person, for whom relatives plead, the erasure of absolution costs 1 ducat 9 carlini; for a woman who hanged herself, or for a man, so that he may be handed over to the Church's censure, 1 ducat 9 carlini. Toletus also defines it thus: a excommunication incurred in life can be absolved after death. Witnesses to this are the many indulgences granted to the dead, and even altars, especially at Rome, solemnly fortified with privileges, so that a soul is freed as often as masses are said at them. Navarrus, in his commentary On the Jubilee and Indulgences, concedes that indulgences can be extended to the dead suffering in Purgatory, but he denies that any Pope inferior to the Pope, that is, anyone other than the Pope, may lawfully extend them to the dead. Whether they can be extended to the dead by way of judicial authority, or of suffrage, entreaty, or intercession, the doctors dispute, and the question is still before the court. Bonaventure, Richard, Cajetan, Cordubus and others affirm that indulgences benefit the dead only by way of suffrage, fearing that otherwise zeal for buying Masses and prayers for the dead would cool. Valentia calls this opinion rash and not to be heard on any account; Bellarmine calls it probable, but calls the contrary opinion more pious. Yet it matters little how they benefit the dead (for indulgences granted by way of entreaty are in no way indulgences), provided that what is proverbially thought impious, to exact tribute from the dead [ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν φορτλογεῖν], is thought lawful and right for the Pope.
LVII. The panegyrics and fairs of indulgences are the Jubilees

units.la: sunt. Anno nempe MCCC. cùm Jubilæum verè Christianum, quod unico Christi merito afflictas conscientias confidere docet, fatali hominum superstitione obsolevit, Bonifacius VIII. tempus idoneum nactus, hunc novum & solennem indulgentiarum mercatum in ejus locum substituendum putans, bullato edicto Christianos invitavit Romam ad Basilicam S. Petri & Pauli, obsequentibus non solùm plena & pleniore, sed etiam plenissima peccatorum omnium remissione promissa. Quid potissimùm ille spectaverit, ex vita & moribus ejus æstimandum est. Præclarè enim alicubi Cicero omnibus in rebus, quæ graviores majoréfque sunt, quid quisque voluerit, cogitârit, admiserit, non ex crimine, sed ex moribus ejus, qui arguitur, ponderandum esse, monet. Anne ergò hic Papa, ut nomine, ita re quoque fuit Bonifacius? Imò omnium hominum, quos sol vidit, pessimus & flagitiosissimus fuit, procella Ecclesiæ, turbo & tempestas Reipublicæ Christianæ, idemque gurges profundissimus & insatiabilis, aurum undiquaque conquisitum plus quàm dici potest sitiens. Hoc enim præclaro scilicet testimonio à Sabellico, Nauclero, Platina, aliis mactatur. Ex mera igitur auri fame, omnium malorum radice, ingeniosus Bonifacius novum aucupium isthoc excogitavit, & hominibus superstitione occæcatis, purgatoriisque terriculamentis dementatis obtrusit.
units.tr: For in the year 1300, when the truly Christian Jubilee, which teaches that troubled consciences should trust in the sole merit of Christ, had fallen into disuse through the fatal superstition of men, Boniface VIII, seizing a suitable time and thinking to substitute this new and solemn trade in indulgences in its place, invited Christians by a bulled edict to Rome, to the Basilica of St Peter and St Paul, with the promise of full, fuller, and even fullest remission of all sins to those who obeyed. What he chiefly aimed at must be judged from his life and character. For Cicero wisely observes somewhere that in all matters which are weightier and more important, what a man willed, intended, or allowed must be weighed not by the charge but by the character of the one accused. Was this Pope then a Boniface in deed as in name? Nay, he was the worst and most shameless of all men the sun has seen, the storm of the Church, the whirlwind and tempest of the Christian commonwealth, and at the same time a most deep and insatiable whirlpool, thirsting for gold gathered from every quarter more than can be told. For this is the notable testimony by which Sabellicus, Naucler, Platina and others condemn him. Out of pure hunger for gold, the root of all evils, the ingenious Boniface therefore devised this new fowling-net and foisted it on men blinded by superstition and driven mad by fears of Purgatory.

units.la: LVIII. Ingeniosa res quæstura est. Lucri enim odor bonus ex re qualibet est, &
units.tr: LVIII. The quaestorship is a clever business. For the smell of gain is good from any source, and

units.la: Crescit amor nummi, quantum pecunia crescit.
units.tr: Love of money grows as money grows.

units.la: Sic planè Romani Pontifices subindè alia & nova excogitaverunt pecuniarum aucupia, ut indulgentiarum quæstum, cujus jam suavitate mirè afficiebantur, retinerent, & confirmarent. Quæ igitur Bonifacio jubilæi centesimo quoque anno instituendi, eadem sequentibus Papis ejusdem ad brevius temporis spatium contrahendi causa fuit. Quid enim Clementem VI. ut hanc festivitatem centesimo quoque anno secundùm Bonifacium celebrandam, ad quinquagesimum reduceret induxit? Auri sacra fames, & offertoriorum ex indulgentiis amplissimorum magna spes, qua sic elatus & dementatus est, ut in Bulla sua Angelis Paradisi mandaret, ut animas morientium in itinere à Purgatorio penitùs absolutas, in Paradisi gloriam introduceret. Neque intra hanc sanctionem res stetit. Nam quæstûs dulcedine allectus Urbanus VI. Jubilæum ad trigesimum tertium quemque annum, prætextu similis ætatis Christi, reducere conatus est. Sed cum fato ille prævoccuparetur, pro eo quæstum hunc accepit Bonifacius IX, reclamante in fraudibus tam manifestis conscientia, quod de eo testatur Platina, scribens, quòd aliquoties is constituerit profusinem plenariarum indulgentiarum revocare, sed ob agnatos locupletandos coactus fuerit ad aucupium illud maximè compendiarium reverti. Hic ergò quæstor callidissimus, Cranzio Metropol. lib. xj. 10. teste, gratias & indulgentias fecit inauditas: & quàm facilè dedit, tam revocavit leviter, fabulas excitans in orbe Christiano, quòd auro expleri non posset. Adeò impudenter ab eo venditas esse indulgentias, Platina testatur, ut evilucerit clavium & literarum Apostolicarum authoritas. De eodem sic Theodoricus à Nyem, consiliarius ejus scribit: Aliquando (quæstores ejus) in uno Regno seu in una Provincia hujusmodi venditionibus ultrà centum millia florenorum reportárunt, quia omnia peccata, etiam sine pœnitentia confitentibus relaxárunt, super quibuslibet irregularitatibus dispensando interventu pecuniæ. Sed en Sacram Piscatoris hujus Romani sagenam! Non contentus enim Jubilæi hujus proventu Bonifacius post paucos exactos annos, nimirum A. MCCCC. alterum Jubilæum, quod Pontifici nulli contigit, celebravit. Denique ad quintum & vicesimum annum nundinas hasce Sixtus IV. restrinxit, auri sacra fame & φιλαργυρία concitus; tam avarus quippe, & impurus, ut ædificato lupanari publico, ex meretricio etiam quæstu plurimùm emolumenti ærario suo accumulaverit. Atque intra hanc Jubilæi ordinarii definitionem res stetit stabitque, donec novum Papam aliquem libido mutandi incesset. Neque enim unquam prætextus desuerunt. Quidni enim argutulus quispiam, Nepotibus suis velificaturus eo prætextu, quòd apud Judæos veteres annus quisque septimus שמיטה remissionis annus fuerit, concludere poterit, apud Christianos æquè convenire, ut annus quisque septimus sit annus remissionis peccatorum, adeóque Jubilæus? Hoc unum scilicet reflat.
units.tr: Thus the Roman Pontiffs from time to time devised other new schemes for raising money, so that they might keep and secure the profit from indulgences, the sweetness of which they had come to enjoy greatly. Boniface's reason for instituting the Jubilee every hundredth year was the same that led later Popes to shorten the interval. What led Clement VI to reduce this festival, which by Boniface's decree was to be kept every hundredth year, to every fiftieth year? The sacred hunger for gold and the great hope of large offerings from indulgences so elated and maddened him that in his bull he ordered the Angels of Paradise to lead into the glory of Paradise the souls of the dying who, on their journey, had been wholly released from Purgatory. Nor did the matter stop at this decree. For Urban VI, enticed by the sweetness of gain, tried to bring the Jubilee back to every thirty-third year, on the pretext of the same age as Christ. But since he was forestalled by death, Boniface IX took up this profit; his conscience, which Platina bears witness to in writing, protested at such manifest frauds: "that he had several times resolved to revoke the flood of plenary indulgences, but, to enrich his kinsmen, was compelled to return to that most profitable trade." This most cunning quaestor, according to the witness of Cranzius in Metropolis, book 11, chapter 10, granted unheard-of graces and indulgences; and as easily as he gave them, so lightly he revoked them, stirring up fables throughout the Christian world that his gold could never be filled. Platina testifies that indulgences were sold by him so shamelessly that the authority of the keys and of the apostolic letters grew dim. Theodoric of Niem, his counsellor, writes about the same man thus: Sometimes (his quaestors) brought back more than a hundred thousand florins from such sales in a single kingdom or province, because they remitted all sins even to those confessing without repentance, and dispensed from any irregularities by the intervention of money. But behold the sacred net of this Roman fisherman! For Boniface, not content with the proceeds of this Jubilee, celebrated after a few years, namely in 1400, another Jubilee, which had fallen to no other Pope. Finally Sixtus IV restricted these fairs to every twenty-fifth year, roused by the sacred hunger for gold and by philargyria [φιλαργυρία]; he was so greedy and impure that, having built a public brothel, he piled up a great deal of profit for his treasury even from the wages of prostitution. And within this definition of the ordinary Jubilee the matter has stood and will stand, until the desire for change seizes some new Pope. For pretexts never fail. Why could some subtle fellow, aiming to favour his nephews by this pretext, that among the ancient Jews every seventh year was a year of remission [שמיטה], not conclude that among Christians it is equally fitting that every seventh year should be a year of remission of sins, and so a Jubilee? This one thing, surely, remains.

units.la: LIX. Non omnibus tamen datum fuit, vel datur etiamnum adire Romam. Ne ergò non adeuntes ἀσύμβολοι abirent, & ab expilationibus ejusmodi immunes essent, bonum factum Papæ visum, vel negotiationem istam per alios exercere, vel facultatem exercendi cum certis limitationibus aliis vendere. Legatos enim suos per varias misit provincias, assignatis certis legationis terminis, cum plenitudine potestatis concedendi Papæ nomine plenarias indulgentias adinstar Jubilæi. Sed & certis Ecclesiis, Collegiis, Monasteriis, Capitulis, Conventibus, Hospitalibus, Confraternitatibus, Universitatibus privilegia & facultatem concedendi indulgentias plenarias, certis cum limitationibus vendidit. Sed poterant sic prostantibus passim indulgentiis Romæ Jubilæi nundinationes frigescere. Ut ergò incommodum hoc Pontifices averterent, imminentibus Jubilæis venditas prius facultates & concessiones suspenderunt post jubilæum usque, vel ad beneplacitum, sæpius etiam posteriores Pontifices indulgentiarum privilegia à prædecessoribus vendita, revocárunt, ut de novo cariore pretio redimerentur. Quòd à moderno etiam Pontifice Innocentio XI. factitatum fama fert. Alexander verò VI. Polydoro Vergilio teste, ut spurios suos locupletaret A. MD. stationes Jubilæi non in Romanæ Ecclesiæ Basilicis duntaxat, sed in longinquis etiam Provinciis ubique gentium vicatimferè constituit, ut & absentes datâ pecuniâ plenarias Jubilæi indulgentias mercari possent.
units.tr: LIX. Yet not everyone has been, or is even now, able to go to Rome. So that those who did not go might not depart empty-handed [ἀσύμβολοι] and might be spared such plunderings, the Pope thought it good either to carry on this trade through others, or to sell to others the power of carrying it on under certain restrictions. For he sent his legates through various provinces, assigned to them definite bounds of their legation, and gave them full power to grant plenary indulgences in the Pope's name, like the Jubilee. He also sold to certain churches, colleges, monasteries, chapters, convents, hospitals, confraternities and universities the privilege and faculty of granting plenary indulgences, under certain restrictions. But while indulgences were being hawked everywhere, the Jubilee trade at Rome might have grown cold. So to avert this inconvenience, the Pontiffs, when a Jubilee was approaching, suspended the faculties and grants sold earlier, until after the Jubilee, or until their pleasure; and later Popes often revoked the indulgence privileges sold by their predecessors, so that they might be bought again at a new and dearer price. Report says that the present Pope, Innocent XI, has also done this. Alexander VI, according to the testimony of Polydore Vergil, in order to enrich his bastard children in the year 1500, set up Jubilee stations not only in the basilicas of the Roman Church but also in distant provinces, village by village almost everywhere in the world, so that even absent people might buy plenary Jubilee indulgences for money.

units.la: LX. Haud postremum pecuniarum aucupium fuit de indulgentiis plenariis in articulo mortis conferendis. Nam in vita quidem mercatus plenariam indulgentiam, poterat tamen relabi, & nova peccata peccare, novúmque adeò reatum contrahere. Ut igitur à poenis Purgatorii animam prorsus metu vacuam redderent, confinxerunt nundinationem indulgentiarum in articulo mortis conferendarum, ut acceptis pro illis pecuniis, anima defuncti ilicò superas ad auras evaderet. Hæ indulgentiæ omnium carissimo pretio distrahi sueverunt; Eugenio IV. Pontifice maximè, circa A. MCCCCXL, licet ante ipsum etiam Gerson earum meminerit. Cœterùm & hoc aucupium varias impofturas peperit, ut eò luculentior quæstus esset. Cœptum enim est disputari de articulo vero & præsumto. Si enim quis moriturus præsumeretur, & convalesceret, indulgentiæ concessæ gratiam expirâsse, novâsque adeò indulgentias redimendas esse, placuit. Eugenius verò IV. acceptâ pecuniâ hanc declarationem addidit, valere illam indulgentiam in articulo mortis vero, non præsumpto, & non expirare etiamsi antea recitata fuisset. Cùmque in repentinis casibus sæpè Sacerdos vel Clericus in promtu non sit, denuò pretium numerandum fuit, ut valeret etiamsi laicus indulti formam pronuntiaret. Cùmque primùm in bullis talibus addita fuerit hæc exceptio: Concedo tibi plenariam indulgentiam omnium peccatorum, præter ea, quæ ex confidentia hujus indulti commiffisti; novo contractu opus fuit, ut illa clausula vel omitteretur, vel expungeretur. Demùm magno studio disceptatum est, tanquam pro focis, si non pro aris, an illi, cui in articulo mortis indulgentia talis collata fuit, post mortem exequiis & suffragiis opus sit. Ne igitur propter ejusmodi indulgentias Sacerdotum exequias curantium culinæ algerent, illis etiam indulgentiis variæ additæ limitationes sunt de peccatis oblivione præteritis, cùm tamen indulgentiæ de peccatis talibus non loquantur, sed de contritis & confessis, nec non de peccatis venialibus, ad quæ se contritio non extendit. Sic una indulgentia in fœcunda negotiatione ista, non alteram, sed ter geminam semper
units.tr: LX. Not the least of the money-catching schemes was the granting of plenary indulgences to be conferred at the point of death. A person who had bought a plenary indulgence while still alive could nonetheless fall back and commit new sins, and so incur fresh guilt. So that they might free the soul entirely from the pains of Purgatory, they devised a trade in indulgences to be conferred at the point of death, so that once money had been received for them, the soul of the deceased would at once rise up into the upper air. These indulgences were usually sold at the dearest price, especially under Pope Eugenius IV, around the year 1440, although Gerson too mentions them even before his time. But this trickery also gave rise to various impostures, so that the profit would be the richer. For it began to be disputed whether the death was true or merely presumed. If someone was presumed to be dying and then recovered, it was decided that the grace of the indulgence granted had lapsed, and that new indulgences therefore had to be bought. Eugenius IV, however, after receiving money, added this declaration: the indulgence was valid in a true, not a presumed, article of death, and did not lapse even if it had been read out earlier. And since in sudden cases a priest or cleric is often not at hand, the price had to be paid again, so that the indulgence would be valid even if a layman pronounced the form of the grant. And since this exception was first added in such bulls, "I grant you a plenary indulgence of all sins, except those which you have committed in reliance on this indulgence," a new contract was needed so that this clause was either omitted or struck out. Finally, it was debated with great zeal, as if for hearths if not for altars, whether the person to whom such an indulgence had been granted at the point of death still needed funeral rites and intercessions after death. So that the kitchens of the priests who looked after funerals would not grow cold because of such indulgences, limitations were added to those indulgences concerning sins that had been forgotten, although the indulgences do not speak of such sins but of those that are contrite and confessed, and also of venial sins, to which contrition does not extend. Thus one indulgence in this fruitful trade did not bring forth another, but always three times its double.

units.la: bbbb 2 peperit. Et tam multiplex forma fuit impofturarum illarum, ut non ab alio, quàm à Curtisano quopiam in ossicina illa nundinationum probè exercitato, accuratè explicari valeat. Tot videlicet artibus, tot calidis callidisque inventionibus opus fuit, ut quæstus ille pinguis satis, & ex desiderio inexplebili negotiantium proveniret.
units.tr: And the forms of these impostures were so many and varied that they could be accurately explained by no one but some courtier well trained in that workshop of trading. So many arts and such clever, cunning inventions were needed for that profit to be large enough, and to arise from the insatiable desire of the dealers.

units.la: LXI. Indulgentiis Confessionalia & stationes ac stationarii inserviverunt. Non sufficiebat efficaciæ erroris intdulgentias vendere illo tempore & in locis illis, ubi & quando publicè prostabant ad remissionem peccatorum præteritorum, sed ad futuros etiam casus, pro peccatis adhuc committendis emebantur, & vendebantur.
