Ergò pro numerata pecunia vendebantur Bullæ, ut cùm quis inposterum crimen aliquod perpetràssèt, potestatem haberet eligendi, quem vellet, confessorem, qui & ipse vigore Bullæ coëmptæ haberet potestatem sibi hac in parte commissam, ut vel in certis, vel in quibuscunque casibus posset confitentem absolvere, & plenariam ipsi indulgentiam conferre, vel semel in vita, vel bis in anno, vel toties, quoties, prout cariùs quis Bullas licitatus fuerat. Hæc diplomata Confessionalium nomine veniebant, diversa ab indulgentiis hactenùs, quòd indulgentiarum valor, & mensura à Pontifice, plenam vel plenissimam peccatorum veniam concedente, & modò contractiùs, modò latiùs fimbrias suas expandente, nec reservatos casus eodem semper numero exprimente, determinari suevit: Confessionalium verò candidati ipsi petitionis suæ modum & rationem præscripserunt, & signato, quantum sibi satis exiftimârunt catalogo Papæ obtulerunt; nec peccatorum liberam tantùm confessionem aut remissionem, sed etiam, ut peccatum in foro saltem Romano, peccatum esse desineret, effecerunt. Confessionalium ejusmodi di diplomata aliquot Celeb. Hottingerus, Hist. Eccles. Tomo VII. pag. 113. 114. &c. repræsentat.
units.tr: LXI. The Confessionalia, the stationes and the stationarii served the indulgences. It was not enough for the sale of indulgences in that age and in those places, where and when they were publicly offered for the remission of past sins, to be effective in deceiving; they were also bought and sold for future cases, for sins not yet committed. So for money paid, bulls were sold, so that when someone afterwards committed some crime, he would have the power of choosing whatever confessor he wished, and that confessor, by virtue of the bull he had bought, would himself have the power committed to him in this matter, so as to absolve the penitent in certain cases or in any cases whatever, and to confer on him a plenary indulgence, once in his life, or twice a year, or as often as he wished, according to how dearly each bull had been bid for. These documents went under the name of Confessionalia, and differed from indulgences hitherto in this respect: the value and measure of an indulgence was usually determined by the Pope, who granted full or fullest pardon of sins, and who spread its fringes now more narrowly, now more widely, and did not always state the same number of reserved cases. But the candidates for Confessionalia themselves prescribed the manner and terms of their request, and offered the Pope a list marked out as far as they thought sufficient; and they brought it about not only that the free confession or remission of sins was granted, but also that a sin would cease to be a sin, at least in the Roman forum. Several such Confessionalia documents are presented by the much-celebrated Hottinger, Hist. Eccles. Tomo VII. pag. 113. 114. &c.

units.la: LXII. Apud veteres mentio est Stationum, quæ iis fuerunt statæ feriæ, quibus populus in certis templis conveniebat ad auditum verbi, communionem mysteriorum, & preces. Stationum nomine venerunt, quia stantes die inprimis Dominico, & toto tempore inde à Pascha ad Pentecosten, quo in memoriam resurrectionis Christi non geniculabantur, verbum audire, & preces fundere consueverunt. A militia, uti apud Rigaltium ad Tertull. in lib. ý. ad ux. cap. 4. loquitur Rhenanus, tractum & usurpatum hoc vocabulum ut alia multa, hæsit in usu Christianorum. Faciebant stationem milites, certo loco præsidium agitantes. Unde & stationarii dicti Christiani nunc in hac Basilica, nunc in alia convenientes, nonnunquam apud Martyria, hoc est, Martyrum sepulchra, Deum stantes precabantur. Stationis vocabulum in hoc sensu non ignotum urbi Romanæ &c. Apud Gregorium M. extant Homiliæ ad populum in stationibus illis habitæ. Sed indulgentiarum mentio; ne levissima quidem est. Procedente tempore, cùm exercitia illa penè obsolevissent, & maneret tantùm opus operatum visitationum Ecclesiarum illarum in quibus olim verbum Dei audire & precari mos erat, visitantibus promissæ sunt indulgentiæ, ut promtiùs invitati in Ecclesiis seu stationibus illis comparerent. Bonifacius VIII. privilegium hoc dedit Basilicæ Petri & Pauli; Clemens VI. Ecclesiæ Lateranensi; Sixtus IV. Ecclesiæ Mariæ majoris. Primùm autem jubilæorum tantùm tempore in Ecclesiis illis indulgentiæ vendebantur. Post feliciter succedente negotiatione, additæ sunt aliæ etiam urbis Ecclesiæ, & numerus indulgentiarum singulis fermè diebus in infinitum auctus est, uti id ex tabula stationum urbis Romæ, ex innumeris, quæ ibi sunt, principalium septem, Lateranensis, Vaticanæ, ad S. Paulum, S. Mariam majorem, S. Laurentium, S. Sebastianum, & S. Crucem majori privilegio privilegiatarum, nec non minus principalium nonnullarum, Cl. Chemnitus Exam. Concil. Trid. pag. 738. &c. demonstravit. Nos quoque supra Differt. xiv. 50. ex eadem tabula unius Ecclesiæ Lateranensis indulgentias, speciminis gratia narravimus.
units.tr: LXII. Among the ancients there is mention of Stations, which were fixed holy days on which the people gathered in certain churches to hear the Word, to take part in the mysteries, and to pray. They were called Stations because, above all on the Lord's day and during the whole time from Easter to Pentecost, when they did not kneel in memory of Christ's resurrection, standing, they used to hear the Word and pour out prayers. Rhenanus, speaking of Tertullian in lib. ý. ad ux. cap. 4. as found in Rigaltius, says that this word, taken and used from the military, like many others, stuck in the usage of Christians. Soldiers made a station, keeping guard in a certain place. Hence Christians were also called station-keepers, gathering now in this basilica, now in another, and sometimes at the martyria, that is, the tombs of the martyrs, praying to God standing. The word station in this sense is not unknown to the city of Rome, etc. Homilies to the people delivered at those stations survive from Gregory the Great. But there is not even the slightest mention of indulgences. As time went on, when those exercises had nearly fallen into disuse, and only the mere work done of visiting those churches remained, where once it had been the custom to hear the Word of God and pray, indulgences were promised to visitors, so that people would more readily come to those churches or stations when invited. Boniface VIII gave this privilege to the basilicas of Peter and Paul; Clement VI to the Church of the Lateran; Sixtus IV to the Church of St Mary Major. At first indulgences were sold in those churches only in the time of jubilees. Afterwards, as the trade succeeded happily, other churches of the city were added, and the number of indulgences was increased almost every day to an infinite extent, as Chemnitz has shown, Exam. Concil. Trid. pag. 738. &c., from the table of the stations of the city of Rome, from the innumerable which are there, of the seven principal churches, Lateran, Vatican, St Paul's, St Mary Major, St Lawrence, St Sebastian, and the Holy Cross, privileged with greater privilege, and also of some less principal ones. I too, above in Differt. xiv. 50., have related from the same table the indulgences of the Lateran church alone, by way of example.

units.la: LXIII. Omnium & singularum urbis Romanæ stationum indulgentias numerârunt Quæstores Hospitalis Spiritus S. quod Romæ est, summámque earum ad decies centena millia annorum, & plus quàm quadraginta duas plenarias indulgentias redegerunt, præter animarum illarum, quæ ex Purgatorio liberantur, indulgentias. Quibus indulgentiis quomodo vel hujus vitæ, vel purgatorii tempus sufficiat, ipsi viderint. Nisi forte illis placet confugere ad usitatum illud: Superabundans cautela non nocet; vel illud Francisci Maironis recipitur, superfluas indulgentias ad augmentum gratiæ & gloriæ converti; vel denique taxantur indulgentiæ juxta proportionem non arithmeticam, sed geometricam, de qua disputatum video ab Adriano Florentino. Is enim objicienti: Si per primam eleemosynam, quam quis dat fabricæ consequitur remissionem tertiæ partis pœnæ totius debitæ: pari ratione per secundam consequeretur remissionem alterius tertiæ, & per tertiam eleemosynam relaxationem novissimæ tertiæ & reliquæ: & sic per tres parvos denarios consequeretur remissionem totius pœnæ: ut pro tunc decedens posset sine purgatorio volare ad Cœlum; satisfacere conatur ex Glossatore Gratiani in caput, Tempus, quæst. 2. C. 13. ubi sic ille: Dico quòd si prima eleemosyna tollit centesimam pœnæ: secunda eleemosyna etiam tantam tollit pœnam, sed non tantam in quantitate, sed tantam in proportione, & sic semper aliquid remanet de pœna. Subiicit Adrianus: Et sic solvo illud, quod objicitur de indulgentiis: quod si propter oblationem unius denarii tollitur quarta pars peccatorum mortalium & venialium, per oblationem secundi denarii tollitur tantum in proportione, non tantum in quantitate, & semper aliquid remanet, licet (NB) omne argentum effunderetur. Satis acutè! Et neget quis, indulgentiarum hujusmodi nundinationi utilissimam esse Geometriam! Profectò sic nunquam adeò multiplicari poterit indulgentia, & cum indulgentia eleemosyna; nunquam ejus fructus in millenos annos promitti poterit, quin aliquod saltem minutissimum Purgatorio superst. Nam quaternis eleemosynis non, ut illi putant, consumetur tota pœna: sed de ducentis quinquaginta sex partibus duntaxat centum septuaginta quinque: atque ita purgatorio supererunt una & octoginta ne extinguatur, & sic nihil frigidius, ut vulgus loquitur, Purgatorii culina fiat. Sed nunquam, dent veniam viri subtilissimi, passurus videtur Euclides, nedum S. Paulus eandem esse rationem unius denarii ad quadrantem, quæ est ad quadrantem dodrantis, & deinceps; utpote qui docuit, esse duplam, & deinceps. Neque hæc subtilitas locum habere potest in indulgentiis, quarum mensura sumitur à tempore, vel si quis non unam, duas aut tres eleemosynas succesivè largiatur, sed simul semelque, vel si indulgentias plenarias accipiat; ubi una eleemosyna si abstulit peccata omnia, nihil residuum faciet, unde proportionalis fiat diminutio. Manifestum igitur est, nil nisi fraudes hic grassari, & vel cornicum oculos configi.
units.tr: LXIII. The indulgences of all and each of the stations of the city of Rome were counted up by the Quaestors of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, which is at Rome, and they reckoned their sum at a hundred thousand times ten thousand years, and more than forty-two plenary indulgences, apart from the indulgences by which souls are freed from Purgatory. As to how these indulgences are enough for the time of this life or of purgatory, they themselves will see. Unless perhaps they choose to take refuge in that common saying, Superabundant caution does no harm; or the saying of Francis Maron is accepted, that superfluous indulgences are turned to the increase of grace and glory; or finally the indulgences are assessed by a proportion not arithmetical but geometrical, which I see discussed by Adrian of Florence. For when someone objects to him: If by the first alms which a man gives to the fabric he obtains the remission of a third part of the whole penalty due, by the same reasoning by a second he would obtain the remission of another third, and by a third alms the relaxation of the last third and the rest; and so by three small pennies he would obtain the remission of the whole penalty, so that at his death he could fly to heaven without purgatory; he tries to satisfy the objection from the Glossator of Gratian in caput, Tempus, quaest. 2. C. 13., where he says: I say that if the first alms removes a hundredth of the penalty, the second alms also removes as much penalty, but not as much in quantity, as much in proportion, and so something always remains of the penalty. Adrian adds: And so I resolve that which is objected about indulgences: that if on account of the offering of one penny a quarter of mortal and venial sins is removed, by the offering of a second penny as much is removed in proportion, not in quantity, and something always remains, even if (NB) all the silver were poured out. Very sharply indeed! And let anyone deny that geometry is most useful for the trade in such indulgences! Certainly an indulgence can never be multiplied in this way, nor can its fruit ever be promised for a thousand years together with alms, without some least little part still surviving for Purgatory. For by four alms, as they think, the whole penalty is not consumed, but only one hundred and seventy-five out of two hundred and fifty-six parts; and so there will remain for Purgatory eighty-one parts, lest it be extinguished, and thus the kitchen of Purgatory will become, as the common people say, nothing colder. But Euclid never, let the most subtle men pardon me, seems to have admitted that the ratio of one penny to a quarter is the same as that of a quarter to a three-quarters, and so on; for he taught that it is double, and so on. Nor can this subtlety have a place in indulgences, whose measure is taken from time; or if someone gives not one, two or three alms in succession, but all at once together, or if he receives plenary indulgences; where one alms, if it has removed all sins, will leave nothing over from which a proportional diminution could be made. It is therefore evident that nothing but frauds are rampant here, and that one may even blind the eyes of crows.

units.la: LXIV. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, cùm stationum illarum indulgentias non amplius Romani & Itali curarent, alias gentes longius dissitas ad suscipiendas ad illas Ecclesias & urbis stationes invitandas Pontifices putârunt. Atque primùm illi incredibili numero confluxerunt. Sed deferv[?]escente mox eorum Zelo, & peregrinis rarius adventantibus, aliud aucupium excogitatum est, ut indulgentiæ illarum stationum absentibus pro pecunia in omnibus terris per legatos seu quæstores venderentur. Hæc nundinatio, cujus formam supra descripsimus, adeò frequens & impudens fuit, ut oppidatim, vicatim, templatim, oftiatim ab emissis illis à Papa quæstoribus indulgentiæ sint adscriptæ; ut, fi quis hunc vel illum locum viiitaverit, fi Missam audiverit, ante imaginem candelam accenderit, tot Patres nostros, Avéque Marias dixerit, inprimis verò manus adjutrices porrexerit, tot ille dierum, annorum ab hoc vel illo Pontifice indulgentiis concessis potiatur. Ut vel uno specimine exhibito fidem faciam, Biturigibus in Templo Cathedrali D. Stephani, ad altare Cardinalis, lapidi antiquo inscriptum ejusmodi carmen, Babylonicæ negotiationis luculentum testimonium, repertum, & à Vecheldio, Reip. Lubecensis Consule descriptum; Clarissimóque Chemnitio exhibitum est: Hic des devote, Cœlestibus associa te Mentes ægrotæ per munera sunt tibi lotæ. Ergò venitote gentes à sede remotæ, Qui datis, estote certi de divite dote. Te precor, accelera, spargas hic, dum potes ærâ. Et sic revera securè Cœlica spera. O si tu scires, quantum data prosit ibi res, Tu juxta vires donares, quod dare quires. Te miser à pœna, dum tempus habes, aliena, Ut tibi sit pœnæ venia, sit aperta crumena: Consors Cœlestis fabricæ, qui porrigit, est is, Ex hoc sum testis, vos hic mundare potestis. Crede mihi, Crede Cœli donaberis ædè, Nam pro mercede, Christo dices, mihi cede. Hic datur exponi paradisus venditioni, Currant ergò boni, rapientes culmina throniVis retinere forum, mihi pendas pauca obolorumPro summa quorum reserabitur aula polorum. Hic si large des, in Cœlo fit tua sedes.Qui serit hic parcè, parcè comprendit in arce. Cur tardas, tantum nummi des aliquantum, Pro solo nummo, gaudebis in æthere summo.
units.tr: LXIV. But whatever the reason, when the Romans and Italians no longer cared about the indulgences of those station churches, the Popes thought that people from more distant nations should be invited to visit those churches and the stations of the city. At first they came in incredible numbers. But as their zeal soon cooled and pilgrims arrived less often, another means of catching money was devised: the indulgences of those stations were sold for money in all lands, to people who were absent, through legates or quaestors. This trade, whose form I described above, became so frequent and shameless that indulgences were assigned by the quaestors sent out by the Pope to towns, villages, churches and doorways. So if someone visited this or that place, heard Mass, lit a candle before an image, said so many Our Fathers and Hail Marys, and above all stretched out helping hands, he would gain so many days and years of indulgence granted by this or that Pope. To make the point with a single example: at Bourges, in the cathedral church of St Stephen, beside the altar of the Cardinal, an ancient stone was found bearing an inscription in verse, a clear testimony to Babylonian trade. Vechelius, Consul of the Republic of Lübeck, copied it, and the distinguished Chemnitz displayed it. It reads: Here give devoutly and join yourself to the heavenly ones; sick minds are washed clean for you by these gifts. So come, you nations far removed from the seat. You who give, be sure of a rich dowry. I beg you, hurry, scatter money here while you can, and so you may truly hope securely for heaven. Oh, if you knew how much the thing given profits there, you would give according to your means whatever you are able to give. Wretched man, while you have time, redeem yourself from punishment by another's, so that pardon may be yours for your penalty, and let your purse be open. Partner in the heavenly building, whoever gives, he is a witness: by this you can cleanse yourselves here. Believe me, believe, you will be given a house in heaven, for as a reward you will say to Christ, "Yield to me." Here paradise is put up for sale; so let the good hurry, snatching at the heights of the throne. If you wish to keep the market, pay me a few halfpennies, for the sum of which the hall of the heavens will be unlocked. If you give generously here, your seat will be in heaven. He who sows sparingly reaps sparingly in the citadel. Why do you delay? Give just a little money, and for the one coin you will rejoice in the highest air.

units.la: LXV. Horribilem illam in nocte illorum temporum Babylonicæ nundinationis faciem prodit fabula illa putidissima & blasphema, de plenaria indulgentia absque pecunia in Ecclesia S. Mariæ de Angelis apud Assisium à S. Francisco impetrata, quam in Rosario suo Bernhardinus de Bustis describere, & posteritati mandare haud erubuit. Referam Bernhardini verbis: Cum, inquit ille, apud Assisium per Franciscus apud illum locum in Cella sua oraret, apparuit ei Angelus, dicens, ut iret ad Ecclesiam, quoniam Christus & Beata Virgo cum Angelis eum expectaret. Christus autem dixit: Francisce, postula quid circa salutem animarum, qui datus es in lucem gentium. Franciscus dixit: Supplico, ut digneris facere hanc gratiam generi humano, concedere scilicet omnibus & singulis venientibus ad locum illum, veniam & indulgentiam omnium peccatorum suorum universaliter & generaliter. Et supplico beatæ Virgini, advocatæ humani generis, ut pro hac petitione impetranda me adjuvare digneris, &c. Christus vero respondit dicens: Satis grande est, quod petiisti, sed majoribus dignus es, frater Francisce. Admitto igitur supplicationem tuam: sed volo ut vadas ad meum vicarium, cui dedi potestatem ligandi & solvendi in Cœlo & terra, & petas ab eo ex parte mea dictam indulgentiam. Franciscus manè se contulit ad Papam Honorium, & petiit, ut ad honorem Virginis Mariæ dignaretur in ipsa
units.tr: LXV. That foul and blasphemous story reveals the horrible face of the Babylonian trade in those times: the story of a plenary indulgence, without money, obtained by St Francis in the church of St Mary of the Angels at Assisi. Bernardino de Busti was not ashamed to describe it in his Rosary and hand it down to posterity. I will give Bernardino's words: When, he says, Francis was praying in his cell at that place near Assisi, an angel appeared to him, telling him to go to the church, since Christ and the Blessed Virgin with the angels were waiting for him. Christ then said: Francis, ask what concerns the salvation of souls, you who were given as a light to the nations. Francis said: I beg that you deign to grant this favour to the human race, namely to give to all and each who come to that place pardon and indulgence for all their sins, universally and generally. And I beseech the Blessed Virgin, advocate of the human race, that you deign to help me to obtain this petition, etc. Christ replied, saying: What you have asked is great enough, but you are worthy of greater things, brother Francis. I therefore accept your supplication, but I want you to go to my vicar, to whom I have given the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and ask him on my behalf for that indulgence. In the morning Francis went to Pope Honorius and asked that, to the honour of the Virgin Mary, he would deign to set in that very church of the Portiuncula a plenary indulgence without offerings.

units.la: Tom. II. cccc ipsa Ecclesia Portiunculæ ponere indulgentiam plenariam sine oblationibus. Papa respondit, se non posse hoc facere, ut qui vult indulgentiam, eam non mereatur ponendo manus adjutrices. Interrogavit autem Franciscum Pontifex, quot annos vellet ibi poni de indulgentia. Qui respondit, se non velle annos, sed animas, ut quicunque dictam Ecclesiam intrarent contriti & confessi, plenam peccatorum omnium suorum à culpa & à pœna, quæ peccata commisissent à die Baptismi usque ad diem & horam introitus in Ecclesiam: Addens quòd non ex se hoc peteret, sed ex parte Christi, qui eum miserat. Tunc Papa annuit, & quod postulaverat concessit. Egrediente autem Francisco, Papa dixit: Ubi habes Bullam? At ille respondit: Nullum de hac re volo instrumentum, sed sit B. Virgo charta, Notarius seu plumbator, Christus, Angeli, testes, sigilla, stigmata Francisci. Postmodum ad petitionem Cardinalium Papæ indulgentiam illam ad unam diem naturalem singulis annis in perpetuum extendi declaravit, prima scilicet die Augusti, à primis vesperis, usque ad vesperas secundæ diei. Hæc & plura ille fabularum & blasphemiarum hamaxarius Bernhardinus. Quid videtur, Mercatores Babylonii? Si vera sunt, quæ vera esse creditis, efficacia erroris actí transversi, ut libentes mendacio credatis, Papa, ne ipso Christo mandante, æquo animo fert indulgentias dari gratis non ementibus, non merentibus ponendo manus adjutrices.
units.tr: Vol. II, p. 400. The Pope replied that he could not do this, since whoever wants an indulgence should not obtain it without putting in helping hands. The Pontiff then asked Francis how many years of indulgence he wished to have placed there. He replied that he did not wish years but souls: that whoever entered the said church, contrite and confessed, should have full pardon of all their sins, both of guilt and of punishment, which they had committed from the day of their baptism to the day and hour of their entering the church. He added that he did not ask this on his own account but on behalf of Christ, who had sent him. Then the Pope nodded assent and granted what he had asked. As Francis was going out, the Pope said: Where do you have the bull? But he answered: I want no document in this matter; let the Blessed Virgin be the paper, Christ the notary or sealer, the angels the witnesses, the seals the stigmata of Francis. Afterwards, at the request of the Cardinals, the Pope declared that this indulgence should be extended in perpetuity to one natural day each year, namely the first day of August, from the first vespers until the vespers of the second day. These and more such fables and blasphemies are told by that hack Bernardino. What do you think, Babylonian merchants? If the things are true, which you believe to be true, then the effect of the twisted error is that you willingly believe a lie: the Pope, even at the command of Christ himself, calmly bears that indulgences should be given freely to those who neither buy nor earn them by putting in helping hands.

units.la: LXVI. Hinc adeò viri pii & cordati nundinationi huic per Emulgentias (ita non immeritò non nemo insignit) contradixerunt. Lateranensis & Viennensis Concilii decreta supra adduximus. Wilhelmus Durandus Speculator insignitus, consilio de celebrando Concilio, jussu Clementis V. scripto, sic parte iii. tit. 15. de Indulgentiis scriscribit : Cum in universali Ecclesia quæstores indulgentiarum multos errores disseminent, multósque seducant simplices, & multas abusiones procurent, & vitam gerant enormiter dissolutam &c. potestásque Clavium contemnitur, cum pro uno obolo, vel nihilo indulgentia conceditur, nec proficiat provisio Concilii Lateranensis, unde populi contemnunt pœnitentias à Confessoribus impositas adimplere &c. videretur super hoc de competenti remedio providendum, & insuper ut cessarent quæstus cursorum & nuntiorum Romanæ Curiæ. Notæ sunt querelæ Waldensium, Wiclefi, Ruthenorum, Hussi, Hieronymi Pragensis, Bohemorum, qui impudentes nundinatores in carcerem compegerunt, totius Scholæ Parisiensis, quæ Clementi VI. contradixit, &c, Aventino teste, Indulgentiarias ejus Bullas, solenniter adhibitis tubis & campanis, damnavit. Wesselus Groningensis, qui ob suas contra indulgentias disputationes dictus est Magister contradictionis, Monachorum sui temporis opinionem recitat, quòd indulgentiæ sint piæ fraudes, & dolus non malus, quo plebs officioso errore ad pietatem trahatur. Quam eandem etiam opinionem Thomas Aquinas Supplem. p. iii. q. 25. art. 3. narrat. Taceo Johannem Vesaliensem & Savanarolam, qui suam, quæ indulgentias esse veram deceptionem piorum ad Cleri quæstum comparatam declamárunt aperte, igne piárunt. Tandem A. MDX. tota Natio Germanica inter Gravamina sua Imp. Maximiliano I. oblata, loco decimo, retulit, quòd indulgentiæ novæ, cum revocatione aut suspensione veterum (laicis contra Clerum murmurantibus) ad corradendas pecunias concedantur.
units.tr: LXVI. Hence pious and sensible men opposed this trade, which some not unfittingly call by the name of "milkings" (Emulgentias). We have already cited the decrees of the Councils of Lateran and Vienne. William Durandus, called the Speculator, in his memorandum on holding a Council, written at the command of Clement V, writes thus in part iii, title 15, on indulgences: Since in the universal Church the sellers of indulgences spread many errors, lead many simple people astray, bring about many abuses, and lead a shamefully dissolute life, etc., and the power of the Keys is despised, since an indulgence is granted for one small coin or for nothing, and the provision of the Council of Lateran does not help, so that the people despise the penances imposed by confessors and do not perform them, etc., it would seem that a suitable remedy should be provided for this, and also that the profits of the couriers and messengers of the Roman Curia should cease. The complaints of the Waldensians, of Wycliffe, of the Ruthenians, of Hus, of Jerome of Prague, and of the Bohemians are well known; they threw the shameless sellers into prison. The whole school of Paris, which opposed Clement VI, solemnly condemned his indulgence bulls with trumpets and bells, as Aventinus testifies. Wessel of Groningen, who for his disputations against indulgences was called the Master of Contradiction, recounts the opinion of the monks of his time, that indulgences are pious frauds, and a not-wicked deceit, by which the common people are drawn to piety through a dutiful error. Thomas Aquinas also reports this same opinion in Supplement, part iii, question 25, article 3. I say nothing of John of Wesel and Savonarola, who openly declared that indulgences were a true deception of the pious, devised for the profit of the clergy, and who were burned for it. Finally, in 1510, the whole German nation, in its grievances presented to the Emperor Maximilian I, listed in tenth place that new indulgences are granted, with the revocation or suspension of the old, to gather money (the laity murmuring against the clergy).

units.la: LXVII. Sed surdis illi, aliique plures, fabulam Cecinerunt. Venter enim, bestia pessima, aures non habet. Crescebat indies magis nundinationis indulgentiarum im-
units.tr: LXVII. But those men, and many others, sang their song to deaf ears. For the belly, the worst of beasts, has no ears. The shamelessness of the indulgence trade grew daily greater,

units.la: pudentia, ut quò tandem progrederetur ampliùs, haud inveniret, nec ubi consisteret haberet. Leo Papa decimus, cui successus nundinationis praeteritae, Alexandri VI. inprimis salivam movit, cùm Jubilaeum novum operiri provectior aetas, & lucri flagrantior cupido (auri enim sitientissimum fuisse, accedente Romanorum avaritia, Florentinorum cupiditate, Langius ejus vnyχov Monachus Cittizensis Chron. ad A. 1513. testatur) eum non sineret, novo exemplo A.MDXV.& deinceps, impulsore, uti putabatur, Cardinale quatuor Sanctorum, missis per omnia Regna quaestoribus, eandem gratiam, quae in Jubilaeo Romam venientibus concedi solet, extra Jubilaei terminum pro numerata pecunia, positis publicè in Ecclesiis aerariis, seu mensis collybisticis, venalem obtulit. Praetextus erat bellum Turcicum, & apud Germanos structura Templi S. Petri à Julio II. inchoata; sed praetextus sanè, non res, uti Hist. Pap. §. CLII. ostendimus, & paulò post ostendemus fusiùs. Ut impostura illa procederet ordine, & cum authoritate in Germania cumprimis exerceretur, Archiepiscopo Moguntino, Germaniae Primati, id negotii dedit, qui ea conditione illud suscepit, ut pars praedae Romano Pontifici, pars sibi ad solvendum pallium cederet. Usus ille est sordidi hujus ministerii satellite, nebulone insigni, Johanne Tezelio, Dominicano, quem paulò ante Imp. Maximilianus in adulterio deprehensum Oeniponte sacco ad submersionem adjudicaverat, liberatum intercessione Ducis Friderici. Cùmque ordini militari in Livonia ex indulgentiis amplissimum quaestum confecisset, visus ille Moguntino ad saltandam hanc fabulam maximè idoneus fuit, qui Commissarius Apostolicus, & haereticae pravitatis Inquisitor à Papa crearetur, quò inquisitoriis artibus opprimere contradicentes posset. Sic ille tam pro suggestu impudentissimis praeconiis, & orationibus artificiosè compositis, tum sparso libello quem Summariam Instructionem appellavit, indulgentiarum merces per Germaniam venales exposuit. Quibus ille artibus passim Germanos suam pro illorum salute animam, si cistæ modò pecunias imponerent, oppignorans emunxerit, donec collybisticæ ejus mensæ à Luthero eversæ sunt, C. Chemnitius Exam.Concil.Trid. p. 744. aliique fusiùs exposuêre. Orationis pro suggestu summam liceat attexere. En, sic Babylonius Stentor declamavit, Cœlum undique jam apertum est, si nunc non intres, quando unquam intrabis? O insensatos & crassi cordis homines, bestiis propè similes, qui non percipitis tantam effusionem gratiarum! En tot potestis redimere animas! O duri, duri, negligentes! Duodecim denariis patrem extrahere potes, & tam ingratus parenti in tantis pœnis non succurris? Ego sanè in extremo judicio excusatus sum. Vos videritis. Dico tibi, si unam solam tunicam haberes, hanc quoque exuendam & distrahendam judico, ut tantas gratias obtineres. Amplificationes addebat, Si quis literas indulgentiarum redimeret, ejus animam securam esse de salute sua. Animas in Purgatorio existentes, pro quibus indulgentiæ redimantur, statim ubi conjectus in cistam nummus tinniret, in Cœlum evolare. Tantas esse illas gratias, ut nullum sit adeò magnum peccatum, etiamsi per impossibile matrem Dei violâsset, quin per indulgentias solvi posset. Liberum per indulgentias istas fieri hominem ab omni culpa & pœna. Esse enim gratias istas donum illud Dei inæstimabile, quo homo reconcilietur Deo, & omnes pœnæ Purgatorii delentur. Nec necessariam esse contritionem his, qui vel animas, vel confessionalia redimerent. Finis Concionis fuit: Impone, impone, impone. Et ne verbis duntaxat distento gutture declamatis, sed exemplo etiam moverent quæstores, primi ad cistam in omnium conspectu procedebant splendido geftu, & astantes imponentibus arridebant, omittentibus indignabantur.
units.tr: so that it could not find any further point to which to advance, nor a place where it could stand. Pope Leo X, whom the success of the earlier trade under Alexander VI especially stirred to greed, since the new Jubilee was awaited by an older age and a more burning desire for gain (for, as the Cittizensis monk Langius, anonymous [ἀνωνύμου] in his Chronicle for the year 1513 testifies, the Romans were greedy and the Florentines covetous, and so he was very thirsty for gold) would not allow it to wait. In the year 1515 and after, by a new example, and at the urging, as was thought, of the Cardinal of the Four Saints, he sent quaestors through all kingdoms, and offered for sale, for money paid, the same grace that is usually granted to those coming to Rome at the Jubilee, outside the term of the Jubilee. Chests for money were set up publicly in the churches, or tables for the counting of coins. The pretext was the Turkish war, and among the Germans the building of the Church of St. Peter, begun by Julius II; but it was surely a pretext, not the real reason, as we have shown in the History of the Popes, §152, and as we shall show more fully shortly. So that this deception might proceed in an orderly way and be carried out with authority, especially in Germany, he gave the business to the Archbishop of Mainz, primate of Germany, who undertook it on the condition that part of the spoil would go to the Roman Pontiff and part to himself, to pay for his pallium. He used for this sordid ministry an attendant, a notorious rascal, John Tetzel, a Dominican, whom the Emperor Maximilian, shortly before, had caught in adultery at Innsbruck and had condemned to be drowned in a sack, but who was freed through the intercession of Duke Frederick. Since he had made a very large profit from indulgences for the Order of Knights in Livonia, he seemed to the Mainz archbishop the most suitable man to dance this farce, and he was made Apostolic Commissary and Inquisitor of heretical depravity by the Pope, so that he could suppress by inquisitorial arts those who contradicted. Thus he displayed the wares of indulgences for sale throughout Germany, both with the most shameless boasts from the pulpit and with artfully composed speeches, and by a leaflet he scattered, which he called the Summary Instruction. By these arts he everywhere drained the Germans, pledging their souls for their salvation if only they would put money in the chest, until his counting-tables were overturned by Luther; C. Chemnitz in Examination of the Council of Trent, p. 744, and others have explained this more fully. It may be permitted to add the substance of his speech from the pulpit. "Behold, thus the Babylonian Stentor declaimed: Heaven is now open on every side; if you do not enter now, when will you ever enter? O foolish men of dull heart, almost like beasts, who do not perceive so great an outpouring of graces! Behold, for so little you can redeem so many souls! O hard, hard, careless people! For twelve pence you can draw your father out, and will you not help a parent so ungrateful in such great torments? I, at least, will be excused at the last judgment. See to it yourselves. I tell you, if you had only one tunic, I judge that you should strip it off and sell it, to obtain such great graces." He added amplifications: "If anyone should buy letters of indulgence, his soul would be secure of its salvation. The souls in Purgatory for whom indulgences are bought fly straight up to Heaven as soon as the coin rings in the chest. These graces are so great that there is no sin so grave, even if one had, by impossibility, violated the Mother of God, that cannot be paid off by indulgences. Through these indulgences a man is made free from all guilt and punishment. For these graces are that inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to God and all the pains of Purgatory are wiped away. Nor is contrition necessary for those who redeem either souls or confessionals." The end of the sermon was: "Pay, pay, pay." And so that the quaestors might move people not only by words declaimed with throat stretched wide, but also by example, they were the first to come up to the chest in full view of all, with a splendid gesture, and they smiled on those who paid, and showed indignation toward those who did not.

units.la: LXVIII. Similium in Helvetia Baccharum fuit Bernhardinus Samson, Mediolanensis, Franciscanus Monachus, qui ab eodem Leone Papa Commissarius Apostolicæ sedis ad eos missus, brevi suo indulgentiarum mercimonio tam feliciter Helvetios circumscripsit, ut cistas argento & argenteis vasis refertas in Italiam deportari curaverit.
units.tr: LXVIII. Of a similar sort in Switzerland was the Bacchanal Bernhardin Samson of Milan, a Franciscan friar, whom Pope Leo sent to them as Commissary of the Apostolic See. With his brief and his trade in indulgences he deceived the Swiss so successfully that he had chests full of silver and silver vessels carried off to Italy.

units.la: Cùm Tugii magno emturientium confluxu is turbaretur: Ne quæso, inquiebat ille, vobis mutuò ita molesti estote. Illis primus pateat aditus, qui pecunias ferunt. De cæteris post viderimus. Bernæ duobus ursis (nummi hoc genus erat, ab impresso urso) pauperioribus, cæteris majore longè pretio, coronato, ampliore etiam merces suas addixit. Bernâ digressurus, populo campanæ signo in Templum majus convocato, triplicem Papæ gratiam promulgavit. Primò enim, ex superabundanti Christi & Sanctorum omnium thesauro, cunctis præsentibus, qui flexis genubus peccata confiterentur, Orationem Dominicam, & Ave Maria ter recitarent, omnium peccatorum à culpa & pœna remissionem indulsit, & ei integritati, quam in Baptismo habuissent, eosdem restituit. Secundò, ex Purgatorii flammis animam quam vellent liberandi facultatem concessit iis, qui quotidiè Templum majus ter orantes circumirent. Tertiò, postquam singuli genubus flexis quinquies tum Orationem Dominicam, tum Salutationem Angelicam in defunctorum subsidium recitàssent, elata voce exclamavit: Ab eo momento omnes Bernensium defunctos, ubicunque excessissent simul liberatos tam ab inferorum, quàm Purgatorii cruciatibus, in Cœlum transferri. Sed & memoratu dignifsimum est Confessionale, quod idem ille agyrta authoritate Leonis X. Bernæ Antonio Spilmanno tredecim florenorum Rhenensium pretio venditum, à Cel. Hottingero Hist. Eccles. Tom. VII. pag. 165 ——— 171. αὐτὸς ἐξέ insertum, indulgentiarum mercaturæ lernam & sententiam prodit. Badæ Missa, & cœteris pro defunctis officiis peractis, in cœmiterium quotidie magna cum pompa excurrere solitus clamavit: Ecce volant! Bremogardi Decanum Bullingerum Simoniæ huic obnitentem, & mercesces exponere vetantem, Samsonius anathemate perculit, obnuntians eo expeditum non iri, nisi numeratis aureis trecentis. Tiguri cum appulisset Mercator, Huldricum Zwinglium, authoritate Hugonis, Episcopi Constantiensis nequitiæ suæ gravissimæ adversantem expertus, Italiam cum rapinis suis repetiit, & Helvetiis posthac rectius animabus suis consulendi uberrimam ansam reliquit.
units.tr: When he was causing a stir at Zug, where a large crowd of buyers had gathered, he said: Please, do not be so troublesome to one another. Let the way be open first to those who bring money. We shall see to the rest afterwards. At Bern he sold his wares to the poorer buyers for two bears (a coin so called from the bear stamped on it), and to the others for a much higher price, the crowned coin, and even took larger sums from them. About to leave Bern, he called the people to the greater church by the sound of the bell and announced the Pope's threefold grace. First, from the overflowing treasury of Christ and all the saints, he granted to all who were present, kneeling and confessing their sins, and who recited the Lord's Prayer and the Hail Mary three times, the remission of all sins, both of guilt and of punishment, and restored them to that state of innocence which they had possessed at baptism. Second, he granted to those who went round the greater church praying three times every day the power to free from the flames of Purgatory whatever soul they wished. Third, after each had knelt and recited the Lord's Prayer and the Angelic Salutation five times for the relief of the dead, he cried out in a loud voice: From this moment all the dead of Bern, wherever they have died, are at once freed from the torments both of hell and of Purgatory and are carried into Heaven. It is also worth recalling the Confession-form which the same charlatan, by the authority of Leo X, sold at Bern to Anton Spilmann for thirteen Rhenish florins. Hottinger in his Church History, vol. VII, pp. 165–171 has published it, and it shows the whole pit and method of the indulgence trade, inserted αὐτὸς ἐξέ. At Baden, when the Mass and the other offices for the dead had been performed, he would regularly go out to the cemetery every day with great ceremony and cry: Behold, they fly! Samson struck with anathema Dean Bullinger of Bremgarten, who opposed this simony and forbade the sale of his wares, declaring that no one would be absolved unless three hundred gold coins were counted out. When the merchant arrived at Zurich, he found Huldrych Zwingli opposing his wickedness with the authority of Hugo, Bishop of Constance. He then returned to Italy with his plunder, and he left the Swiss a very rich occasion of looking after their souls more wisely from then on.

units.la: LXIX. Parum equidem refert quem in finem sic Leo Papa indulgentias suas promercales fecerit, an ex pecuniis inde redactis, quod quæstores in diplomatis suis præferebant, fabricam Basilicæ D. Petri à Julio cœptam adfinem perducere paraverit; an, quod plus verisimilitudinis habet, & authoribus hac in re fide dignis, Guicciardino, Papæ illius Ministro, & Paulo Jovio, Episcopo Nucerino, proditum, & à Paulo Langio Cittizensi Monacho insinuatum est, Saxoniæ, & totius ejus tractus Germaniæ, qui Saxoniam & Mare interjacet, Magdalenæ sororis, Francisco Cibo, Innocentii VIII. Pontificis spurio connubio junctæ, dono dederit, non tam sorori gratificaturus, quàm hostimentum aliquod redditurus familiæ Ciborum, cujus sumtibus Genuæ Florentia extorris sustentatus fuerat. Sufficit ad convincendum spiritualis nundinationis flagitium, quòd sic indulgentias per quæstores emissos, pecuniarum præsentaneo pretio vendidit, & tesseras illas suas propositus, non modò, uti Budæus de Asse Asse eas describit, veniales, sed etiam venales, impunitatem scelerum, & solutionem sacrarum legum sordida benignitate largientes, capturam supra fidem modumque quaestuosissimam propositit, de qua non immeritò Legatus ille Venetus Michaël Surianus apud Folietam lib. I. de S. foedere, & Thuanum lib. xlvij. dixit, nullum esse opulentius toto terrarum Orbe Veltigal Pontificis calamo, cujus simplex ductus quantumvis ingentem pecuniae vim momento pariat; & festivè nescio quis alius Juris Canonici Doctor, Curiam Romanam multò solertiore μεταμορφωσι, quàm è Paracelsi schola discipulos, plumbum in aurum convertere, pronuntiavit, quia scilicet Romanenses illa sua arte immensùm aucti, nitidi & splendidi incedant, hi verò squalore inediáque contabescant.
units.tr: LXIX. It makes little difference, to be sure, for what end Pope Leo made his indulgences so saleable in this way. Whether, from the money thus raised, as the sellers declared in their documents, he planned to bring to completion the building of the Basilica of St Peter, begun by Julius, or whether (what is more probable, and which is reported by authors worthy of trust in this matter, Guicciardini, the minister of that Pope, and Paolo Giovio, Bishop of Nocera, and which was hinted at by Paul Lang, a Cistercian monk of Citizen) he gave Saxony and the whole stretch of Germany lying between Saxony and the sea as a gift to Francesco Cibo, the son of Innocent VIII by an irregular union, who had married his sister Maddalena. He would not so much be doing a favour to his sister as making some return to the family of the Cibos, at whose expense he had been supported at Genoa after his exile from Florence. It is enough to prove the disgrace of this spiritual trafficking that he sold indulgences in this way through the sellers he had sent out, for ready money, and that he offered those tickets of his, not only, as Budé describes them in his book De Asse, saleable, but also for sale, bestowing impunity for crimes and the dissolution of sacred laws with a sordid generosity, and proposing a profit beyond belief and beyond measure. Of this the Venetian envoy Michele Suriano rightly said, as reported by Foglietta in book I of On the Holy League, and by de Thou in book 47, that there is no richer tax in the whole world than the Pope's pen, whose simple stroke can produce a sum of money however enormous in a moment. And some Doctor of Canon Law, wittily (I know not who), declared that the Roman Curia, by a far more skilful transmutation than the disciples of the school of Paracelsus, turns lead into gold, since its members, greatly enriched by that art, go about sleek and splendid, while the others waste away in squalor and hunger.

units.la: LXX. Neque Papalis hujus nundinationis idonea defensio est, quam Sfortia Pallavicinus Cardinalis Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. I. cap. 2. ff. 8. meditatus est. Objicientium enim, quòd sic Papa Caelestes thesauros pretio venales fecerit, adeòque criminis Simoniae se alligaverit, respondet, accusationi huic facilè occurri, si animo recolamus, pecuniam esse necessarium instrumentum ad obtinendum, quicquid est in aliorum hominum potestate, sive id opes sint ab illis possessae, sive illorum labores & opificia. Quocirca, inquit ille, cùm fieri non posset, ut Vaticana Basilica extrueretur, absque subsidiis multorum millium hominum, & absque multorum etiam millium sudoribus; perinde erat, impertiri indulgentias & privilegia cuicunque partem aliquam illius Basilicae aedificanti, atque eadem concedere tribuenti pecuniam idoneam ad caementorum partem aliquam comparandam, & aliquibus operis mercedem persolvendam. Caeterum, quis ignoret, hominem nihil habere, & nihil esse nisi terram? Deus autem hac terra contentus pro ea nobis solvit, non quanti ea est, sed quanti à nobis æstimatur. Idcirco Regem illum hortatus est Daniel, ut eleemosynis peccata sua redimeret, Sacrilegus quidem est, qui Cœli thesauros argento commutat in propria lucra converso, non qui eos spondet uti premium oblatæ Deo pecuniæ, & ad ejusdem cultum expensæ. Enim verò si opus hujusmodi æternum Divinæ amicitiæ, claraque Dei visionis incrementum mereri potest, quidni mereri possit condemnationem alicujus pœnæ certo tempore post mortem luendæ, & alicujus Ecclesiasticæ legis laxationem, modò id ritè & ordine fiat? Hactenùs ille.
units.tr: LXX. Nor is the defence of this Papal trafficking sound, which Cardinal Sforza Pallavicino devised in his History of the Council of Trent, book I, ch. 2, p. 8. For to those objecting that the Pope in this way made the heavenly treasures saleable for money, and so bound himself to the crime of simony, he replies that this accusation is easily met if we bear in mind that money is the necessary instrument for obtaining whatever lies in the power of other men, whether it be wealth possessed by them or their labours and workmanship. Therefore, he says, since the Basilica of the Vatican could not be built without the help of many thousands of men and without the sweat of many thousands more, it made no difference whether indulgences and privileges were granted to anyone who contributed to the building of part of that Basilica, and whether they were given to one who supplied money suitable for buying a part of the stone, and for paying the wages of some of the workmen. Moreover, who does not know that man has nothing and is nothing but earth? God, however, being content with this earth, pays us for it, not what it is worth, but what we value it at. For this reason Daniel urged that king to redeem his sins by almsgiving. He is indeed a sacrilegious man who exchanges the treasures of heaven for silver, turning them into his own profit, but not he who promises them as the reward of money offered to God and spent on his worship. Indeed, if a work of this kind can merit eternal friendship with God and an increase in the clear vision of God, why should it not be able to merit the remission of some penalty to be paid at a set time after death, and some relaxation of an ecclesiastical law, provided that this is done rightly and in order? Thus far he.
LXXI.

units.la: In defensione ea probamus, quòd Pallavicinus Pontificem in hac negotiatione non æquè, ut alii mangones solent, à culpa eximere tentat, & culpam omnem in quæstores derivare non conatur. Noverat enim, hanc esse campanam sine pistillo. Si enim maximè nullo Pontifice authore quæsturam sic Romani nebulones exercuissent, (exercuerunt autem conscii, volentibus, lucrum captantibus,) quem tamen Papam nobis demonstrabunt, qui quæsturas & impostauras illas Italicas in re tanti momenti severitate disciplinæ castigaverit? Hic siluère leges, atque semel fixæ, citò refixæ sunt. In cœteris defensio Pallavicini titubat, & ipsi Simoni-Mago purgando idonea est. Nam & ipsi æquè ac purpuratis nostris facilè subduxit, pecuniam esse necessariam instrumentum ad obtinendum quicquid in aliorum hominum potestate est. Sicut ergo Pontifices pro pecunia, necessario adeò instrumento ad obtinendum id, quod in aliena potestate est, remissionem peccatorum vendunt, ita Simon pro pecunia Spiritum S. & ejus dona vendere instituerat. Neque fucus publicæ Ecclesiæ utilitatis & privati quæstûs labem illam à Pontificibus abstergit, tum quia Leonem Papam fabricam Basilicæ falsò prætendi‑ se ostendimus : tum quia quæstus ex re spirituali , sive ad unum , sive ad plures , ipsámque adeò communitatem, redundet , criminis Simoniæ speciem non mutat ; imò impietatem eam auget potiùs, eò quòd quæstus ille Ecclesiæ impensus eandem polluit & profanat, neque magis, quàm meretricia olim merces in Sanctuarium Domini inferri potest : tum quia sicut Ecclesia indigere potest Basilica vel Templo, sic privatus domo vel tugurio: tum quia non ea magnificè adeò extruendæ Basilicæ necessitas incubuit, ut ex sudore & sanguine pauperum, peccatisque hominum ære redemtis provehenda , turpitérque adeò per Quirinales istos prædones Christianorum simplicitati illudendum fuerit. Neque, quicquid Pallavicinus spirituali seu Babylonica sua politica machinetur , peccata auro vel argento corruptibili, sed solo pretioso sanguine Agni immaculati Christi piantur., & redimuntur 1 Petr. 1. 18, 19. Neque Nebucadnezar pecuniis suis peccata redimere, sed justitiâ ea abrumpere, hoc est, peccata cum justitia commutare jussus est. Quòd si necessitas fidelium operam & collationem flagitâssent, non illa turpi illa rerum spiritualium, quæ in commercio esse nequeunt, nundinatione provocari, sed liberali prece solicitari, vel Papali imperio, cui omnia subesse sciscunt illi, extorqueri debuisset. Denique sive spiritualia, ut prœmium pecuniæ Deo oblatæ , sive ut merces rependantur , rependuntur certè , & rependuntur ex pacto , quod obligationem inducit. Imò propriè non rependuntur ut prœmium, sed offeruntur sub conditione pecuniæ & manûs adjutricis. Hoc ergò si Simoniacum non est, quid Simoniacum verè sit, velim Pallavicinus nos edoceat. Nam ξϋϱιαις Jesuitarum de Simonia Νῖξας, quibus Babyloni suæ lenocinari solent, non soli nos aspernamur validè , sed ipsa etiam non ita pridem Facultas Theologica Parisiensis, ex Amedei Guimenii opere extraßas damnavit his verbis: Hæ Propositiones (quas inter etiam hanc refulit: Non est Simonia, pacto expresso se obligare ad aliquid temporale pro spirituali ex gratitudine conferendum) falsæ sunt, & Simoniam contra jus Divinum apertissimè approbantes, atque alias à Facultate damnatæ.
units.tr: In this defence we note that Pallavicini does not try, as other hucksters usually do, to free the Pope from blame in this business as well, nor does he try to shift all the blame onto the quaestors. For he knew that this is a bell without a clapper. Even if the Roman scoundrels had carried on this questing without any Pope as its author (and they did carry it on, knowingly and willingly, grasping for gain), which Pope will they show us who punished those Italian quests and impostures with the severity of discipline in a matter of such weight? Here the laws fell silent, and once fixed they were quickly unfixed. In other respects Pallavicini's defence wavers, and it is well suited to clearing Simon Magus himself. For he has slyly argued, just as our purple-clad men do, that money is a necessary instrument for obtaining whatever is in the power of other men. So just as the Popes, for money, which is the necessary instrument for obtaining what lies in another's power, sell the forgiveness of sins, so Simon had resolved to sell the Holy Spirit and his gifts for money. Nor does the cloak of the public utility of the Church wipe that stain from the Popes, both because we have shown that Pope Leo falsely pretended the building of the Basilica, and because gain from a spiritual thing, whether it flows to one person or to many, or indeed to the whole community, does not change the kind of crime that is simony; rather it increases the impiety, since the gain spent on the Church pollutes and profanes it, just as the wages of a prostitute could never be brought into the Sanctuary of the Lord. Again, just as the Church may need a Basilica or Temple, so a private person may need a house or a hut. Moreover, there was no such pressing need to build the Basilica on so magnificent a scale that it had to be pushed forward with the sweat and blood of the poor and with men's sins redeemed by money, and shamefully mocked upon the simplicity of Christians by those Roman robbers. Nor, whatever Pallavicini may contrive by his spiritual or Babylonian politics, are sins expiated and redeemed with corruptible gold or silver, but only with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Christ (1 Pet. 1:18, 19). Nor was Nebuchadnezzar ordered to redeem his sins with his money, but to break them off by righteousness, that is, to exchange sins for righteousness (Dan. 4:24). But if the needs of the faithful had called for work and contributions, they should have been sought not by that shameful bargaining over spiritual things, which cannot be the subject of commerce, but by a generous prayer, or extorted by the Papal command, to which they claim all things are subject. Finally, whether spiritual things are repaid as the price of money given to God, or as wages, they are certainly repaid, and repaid by a pact, which creates an obligation. Indeed they are not properly repaid as a price, but offered on condition of money and of a helping hand. If this, then, is not simoniacal, I would like Pallavicini to teach us what simony truly is. For the Jesuits' subtleties [ξϋϱιαις] about simony, and their Nixas [Νῖξας], with which they are wont to pander to their Babylon, are not only rejected by us in no uncertain terms; the Theological Faculty of Paris, not long ago, condemned them too, drawn from the work of Amedeus Guimenius, in these words: These propositions (among which this one also shines out: It is not simony to bind oneself by an express pact to confer something temporal for something spiritual out of gratitude) are false, and clearly approve simony against divine law, and have been condemned elsewhere by the Faculty.

units.la: LXXII. Dicit Pallavicinus: Deum pro terra, hoc est, pecunia, vel rebus terrestribus, nobis solvere non quanti ea est, sed quanti à nobis æstimatur. Plus ergò solvet illi, qui majoris æstimat terram, quàm qui minoris; hoc est, plus avaro, fiduciam in pecuniis collocanti, mundo abutenti, quàm ei, qui αὐτάρκης est, forte sua contentus, & propter Christum omnia pro stercoribus habens, mundo præsente utitur, non abutitur. Sed præterea, annon vera Simonia est, ubi intervenit æstimatio pecuniæ, ceu rei terrestris & temporalis, & solutio rei spiritualis? ubi emtio, venditio? Tametsi enim indulgentiariis vendendi vocabulum displicet, nihil tamen aliud intelligunt per causas justas, sine quibus indulgentiæ nullius sunt fructûs. De quibus causis vehementer inter se litigant. Alii enim volunt, ut indulgentiis sint proportionales (hoc est, stylo Pallavicini, ut tantum solvatur spirituale, quanti æstimatur terra, seu temporale) alii proportionales esse debere negant. Prior opinio obtinet apud gregales Pallavicini Jesuitas, qui statuunt, nullius valoris esse, si magna concedatur pro parva causa, id est, uti Bellarminus & ipse Jesuita de Indulg. lib. j. cap. 12. loquitur, si pro sestertio, vel alio parvi momenti pretio daretur indulgentia pro decem annis: nisi forte hæc Emulgentia universo cuipiam populo data sit, ut ex universa multitudine pretium pontificali dono dignum colligi queat. Nam (ita Josephus Angles, ex Ordine Minorum Episcopus Hispanus nus Quaest. de indulg. in 4. sent. art. 2. dissic. 5. in concl. loquitur) conceditur toti Hispaniae, & omnibus Regnis invictissimi nostri Regis Philippi pro INGENTI THESAURO qui explicatione diplomatis ad expugnandos Turcas aggregatur: & cum tantus thesaurus non posset ab uno offerri, hac de causa omnibus, qui partem illius THESAURI SOLVERINT conceditur. Quemadmodum esset sufficiens causa si Rex centum mille ducatos Romano Pontifici offerret, ut illas indulgentias omnibus Regnis Hispaniae conferret, etiamsi Rex postea a singulis civibus partem istius summae EXEGERIT. Id est, posse Reges magno pretio, ac merci proportionato, Bullam a Papa emere, eamque postea minutatim inter ementes distrahere. Ibi scilicet SOLVERE, EXIGERE, Romana hodierna lingua significat eleemosynas dare non emere.
units.tr: LXXII. Pallavicini says: God does not pay us for earth, that is, for money or earthly things, at what it is worth, but at what we value it. Therefore he will pay more to the one who values earth more highly than to the one who values it less; that is, more to the miser, who places his trust in money and abuses the world, than to the one who is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης], content with what he has, and, for Christ's sake, counting all things as dung, uses the present world and does not abuse it. But further, is this not true simony, where there intervenes an estimate of money, as of an earthly and temporal thing, and the payment of a spiritual thing? Where is the buying and selling? For although the word to sell displeases the indulgence-mongers, they nevertheless understand nothing else by just causes, without which indulgences are of no benefit. About these causes they quarrel fiercely among themselves. Some want indulgences to be proportionate (that is, in Pallavicini's style, that the spiritual thing paid should be as much as the earthly or temporal thing is valued); others deny that they ought to be proportionate. The former opinion prevails among Pallavicini's fellow Jesuits, who hold that an indulgence is worth nothing if a great thing is granted for a small cause; that is, as Bellarmine, himself a Jesuit, speaks in On Indulgences, book 1, chapter 12, if an indulgence for ten years were given for a sestertius or some other trifling price, unless perhaps this Emulgence were given to a whole people, so that from the whole multitude a sum worthy of a papal gift might be gathered. For (so speaks Josephus Angles, the Spanish bishop of the Order of Minors, in Questions on Indulgences, on the fourth book of the Sentences, article 2, dispute 5, in the conclusion): It is granted to all Spain, and to all the kingdoms of our most invincible King Philip, in return for an IMMENSE TREASURE which is added to the explanation of the bull for the overthrow of the Turks; and since so great a treasure could not be offered by one man, for this reason it is granted to all who have paid part of that TREASURE. It would be a sufficient cause if the King offered the Roman Pontiff a hundred thousand ducats, so that he might confer those indulgences on all the kingdoms of Spain, even if the King afterwards EXACTED part of that sum from individual citizens. That is, kings may buy a bull from the Pope at a great price, proportionate to the merchandise, and afterwards sell it off piecemeal to the buyers. There, of course, in today's Roman tongue, to pay and to exact mean to give alms, not to buy.

units.la: Nos vero, quibus tam acutis esse datum non est, existimamus, dare pro indulgentiis ingentem thesaurum, vel summam, & eam postea a singulis exigere, esse ἀγοράζειν ἐν πωλεῖν emere & vendere, quod Bestiae characterem habentibus tribuitur Apoc. xiij. 17. Quamvis mercium harum institores aliter loquantur. Qui ipsi tamen apud Augustinum de Ancona Quaest. 30. ad tertium statuunt, solam voluntatem dandi aliquid temporale, in paupere, qui actu dare non potest, non sufficere ad indulgentiam, etsi sufficiat ad vitam aeternam. Ratio est, quia indulgentiae fiunt ad relevandam indigentiam Ecclesiae, sed indigentia Ecclesiae non relevatur per solam voluntatem dandi, sed per DATUM. Sic in indulgentiarum collatione locum habet; Do, ut des. Unde est, quod quantum ad remissionem poenae, quae acquiritur per indulgentiam, in tali casu non est inconveniens, quod dives sit melioris conditionis, quam pauper. Nec obstat, quod DARE est corporale, velle autem dare est spirituale: Ergo deberet magis dari induldulgentia pro voluntate dandi, quàm pro dato. Quia corporale, in quantum est pœnale & SOLUTORIUM pœnæ, vel COMMUTABILE in pœnam. Unde est ibi commutatio pœnæ majoris in minorem. Et ideò indulgentia, quæ est quædam relaxatio pœnæ, magis fit pro ipso DATO, quam pro voluntate dandi. Hactenus de Ancona. Hinc etiam sequitur, pro ratione donationis majoris vel minoris intendi vel remitti indulgentias. Nam si duo æquè divites largiantur, unus decem, alius viginti, pro indulgentia quadraginta dierum, ille qui viginti largitus est, etsi quantum ad exactionem non recipiat plures dies, quantum ad intensionem tamen valebunt, ac si duplo satisfecisset. Ita idem, qui supra, Josephus Angles in 4. Sent. q. de indulg. diff. 6. definit. Quis non hic genuinam negotiationem, mercaturam, cauponationem, qua peccata scilicet pecuniæ pretio redimi putantur, utraque manu palpat?
units.tr: We, however, to whom it has not been granted to be so sharp, judge that to give an immense treasure, or a sum, for indulgences, and afterwards to exact it from individuals, is to buy and to sell [ἀγοράζειν καὶ πωλεῖν], which is ascribed to those bearing the mark of the Beast (Rev. 13:17). Although the agents of these wares speak otherwise. Yet they themselves, in Augustine of Ancona, Question 30, to the third point, hold that the mere will to give something temporal, in a poor man who cannot give in act, does not suffice for an indulgence, though it suffices for eternal life. The reason is that indulgences are made to relieve the need of the Church, but the need of the Church is not relieved by the mere will to give, but by the GIFT. Thus in the conferring of indulgences there holds: I give, that you may give. Hence it is that as regards the remission of the penalty which is obtained through an indulgence, in such a case it is no inconvenience that the rich man is in a better condition than the poor one. Nor does it stand in the way that to GIVE is bodily, but to be willing to give is spiritual: therefore an indulgence ought rather to be given for the gift than for the will to give. Because the bodily thing, insofar as it is penal and the PAYMENT of the penalty, or COMMUTABLE into a penalty, there is here a commutation of a greater penalty into a lesser. And therefore an indulgence, which is a certain relaxation of the penalty, is granted rather for the GIFT itself than for the will to give. So far Ancona. From this it also follows that indulgences are increased or diminished according to the measure of a greater or lesser donation. For if two equally rich men give, one ten, the other twenty, for an indulgence of forty days, he who gave twenty, although as regards the number of days exacted he does not receive more, yet as regards intensity will be as valuable as if he had satisfied twice over. So Josephus Angles, mentioned above, defines it in On the Fourth Book of the Sentences, question on indulgences, distinction 6. Who would not here clap both hands on the genuine trade, the merchandising and the hawking, by which sins are supposed to be redeemed for a price in money?

units.la: LXXIII. Sed larvam Pallavicino, aliisque indulgentiarum Papalium hyperaspistis detrahamus querela gravissima statuum Imperii Romani tum Pontificiorum, tum Protestantium, quam illi inter centum gravamina, tertio, quarto, quinto, sexto, sub rubrica De Oneribus papalium indulgentiarum, in sinum Cæsareæ Majestatis depositerunt his verbis:
units.tr: LXXIII. But let us strip the mask from Pallavicino and the other champions of papal indulgences, by the most serious complaint of the estates of the Roman Empire, both Papists and Protestants, which they lodged in the bosom of his Caesarean Majesty among the hundred grievances, third, fourth, fifth and sixth, under the heading On the Burdens of the papal indulgences, in these words:

units.la: III. Illud importabile jam olim increbuit Romanarum indulgentiarum onus, quando (NB) sub persona pietatis, cùm aut Basilicas Romanas instruere, aut profectionem in Turcam parare pollicitifunt Romani Pontifices, omnem à simplicibus nimiúmque credulis Germanis exuxerunt pecuniarum medullam. Et, quod longè majorus est faciendum, per has impostu-ras, ac eorum conductitios præcones & prædicatores, profligata est Germana Christianorum pietas, dum, qui extrudere volebant venales suas bullas, laudes suas mercibus accinebant, miras & inauditas condo-
units.tr: III. That burden of Roman indulgences has long since grown intolerable, when (NB) under the guise of piety, the Roman Pontiffs promised either to furnish the Roman basilicas or to prepare an expedition against the Turk, and drained the very marrow of money from the simple and overly credulous Germans. And, what is far more to be lamented, through these deceptions and their hired heralds and preachers, the German piety of Christians has been ruined, since those who wished to push off their venal bulls sang the praises of their wares, and promised marvellous and unheard-of condo-

units.la: Statuum Imperii. Gravamina adversus indulgentias. Gravamina nationis. condonari per emptitias has condonationes, nedum noxas praeteritas aut futuras viventium, sed & defunctorum vitâ, existentium in Purgatorio (quod vocant cantores illi indulgentiarum) igni, modò numeretur aliquid, modò tinniat dextera. Atque his mercium nundinationibus simul & spoliata est ære Germania, & Christi pietas extincta: quando quilibet pro pretii, quod in has merces expenderat, modo, peccandi impunitatem sibi pollicebatur. Hinc stupra, incestus, adulteria, perjuria, homicidia, furta, rapinae, faenora, ac tota malorum lerna semel originem sibi traxerant. Quod enim malorum amplius jam horrebunt Mortales, quando sibi peccandi licentiam ac impunitatem, nedum in vita, sed & post obitum, ære licet immodico comparari posse à nundinationibus illis indulgentiariis, semel persuasum habent? maximè Germani, quibus per hos vera pietatis fucos, sub religionis persona, nihil persuaderi difficile est, ut ingenio plane ad pietatem credulo est Germania. IV. Et licet indulgentiae hae non semel in hoc ad Germanos missae sint, quasi ex corrasa earum venditione, pecuniâ fideles contra barbaros essent tutandi, ac defendendi, eventu tamen compertum habent Germani, pecuniam hanc non in rem fidei, aut alioqui Reip. Christianae necessariam, sed in propinquorum luxum, ac sublevandam familiam ipsorum esse versam, quo uno bina haec nata sunt perquàm maxima incommoda, quòd & offendicula sunt nata, & quòd nunc Germani, toties sentientes lusam fidem, cum vere jam res postulat, ut contra Turcas instituatur expeditio bellica, nullis rationibus se persuaderi patiuntur, ut credant, quod res ipsa fere notorium facit, ita scilicet instare cervicibus nostris crudeles Turcas, suspicantes semper, prioribus simile quidpiam agi. Quae una ratio est, ut tam aegre contra Turcas manus jungant. Quantorum ergò malorum, & in rebus temporalibus, ac Christi fidelium conscientiis, causa fuerint Romanæ indulgentiæ, Sanctitas Apostolica pro sublimitate captùs sui, exigua opera, vel inde, si non ex re ulla alia, conjectura consequi poterint: V. Præterea Papalis sanctitas, cæterique Episcopi casus aliquos suæ absolutioni reliquos fecerunt &c. (Gravamen hoc supra ff. xtviij. recitavimus.) VI. Verùm, si quis habeat, unde numeret, jam nedum præsentes indulgentur harum constitutionum transgressiones, sed & in futurum impunè, ut eas ipsas transgredi liceat, indulto permittitur. Quo fit, ut ansam accipiant ii, cum quibus ita dispensatum est, pejerandi, homicidia, adulteria, & similia flagitia perpetrandi, quando quilibet ex Sacerdotum vulgo absolutionem emtitiam virtute indulti, his impartiri potest. Quæ malorum seges tota, ex habendi libidine, aurique sacra fame, qua nunc Ecclesiasticorum non nulli miserè excruciantur, originem ducit. Hactenùs Imperii Magnates, testes de illa suorum temporum indulgentiaria nundinatione omni exceptione majores, utpote qui ipsimet præsentis mali vim experti sunt, & de quorum corio Romanæ harpyæ petulanter adeò luserunt.
units.tr: Grievances of the Estates of the Empire against the indulgences; grievances of the nation. Remissions are granted through these purchased pardons, not only for the past or future sins of the living but also for the dead, who exist in Purgatory (which those indulgence-singers call) by fire, as soon as something is counted out, as soon as the coin rings. And by these market-dealings Germany was both stripped of its money and Christian piety was extinguished, since each person, for whatever price he had spent on these wares, promised himself impunity for sinning. Hence fornication, incest, adultery, perjury, murder, theft, robbery, usury, and the whole Lerna of evils had at once taken their origin. For what evils will mortals henceforth shrink from, once they have been persuaded that a license to sin and impunity can be bought, not only for this life but also after death, at whatever immoderate price, from those indulgence-markets? Especially the Germans, to whom, through these counterfeits of true piety under the name of religion, nothing is hard to persuade, since Germany is by nature wholly credulous toward piety. IV. Although these indulgences were not sent to the Germans only once, on the pretext that money raised from their sale would be used to defend the faithful against the barbarians, the Germans have learned by experience that this money was not spent on the matter of faith or otherwise on the necessities of the Christian commonwealth, but was diverted to the luxury of relatives and to the advancement of their own households. From this single source two very great evils have arisen: stumbling-blocks have been created, and now the Germans, having so often perceived their faith to have been mocked, will not allow themselves to be persuaded by any reasons, when the situation truly requires a military expedition against the Turks. They believe what the matter itself almost makes notorious, namely that cruel Turks are thus threatening our necks, always suspecting that something similar is being done as before. This is the one reason why they join hands so reluctantly against the Turks. How many evils, both in temporal affairs and in the consciences of Christ's faithful, the Roman indulgences have caused, the Apostolic Holiness may, according to the measure of its understanding, infer with little effort, if not from anything else, at least from this: V. Moreover, the Papal holiness and the other bishops have reserved certain cases to their own absolution, etc. (We have recited this grievance above, at fol. 48.) VI. But if anyone has the means to pay, then not only are present transgressions of these constitutions pardoned, but by an indult it is also permitted, with impunity in future, to transgress them themselves. Hence those with whom this has been so arranged receive occasion for perjury, murder, adultery and similar crimes, since any one of the common priests may, by virtue of the indult, impart a purchased absolution to them. This whole crop of evils springs from the lust for possession and the sacred hunger for gold, by which some of the clergy are now miserably tormented. Thus far the magnates of the Empire, witnesses beyond all exception to that indulgence-trading of their times, since they have themselves experienced the force of the present evil, and from whose hides the Roman harpies have so wantonly played.
LXXIV. With these most just complaints, and with the theologians

units.la: subactissimorum Huldrici Zwinglii & Martini Lutheri ῥήσεως res eò perducta est, ut Supremus Indulgentiarius Papa diu licet, ursi adinstar palo alligandi, restitans, actus fuerit argumentum isthoc Concilio Tridentino subjicere. Congregatio igitur Tridenti die 22. Nov. A. MDLXIII. instituta ad partes illud vocavit; sed timidè prosecto, supensóque gradu, neque concordantibus initio calculis. Erant, qui scopulum illum præternavigandum, & tractationem de indulgentiis penitùs omittendam censerent. Alii hæreticorum, uti vocabant, metu omitti haud posse, pertendere. Quinquecclesiensis Episcopus, pudendum fore Synodo arguit, si argumentum adeò necessarium condonari per emptitias has condonationes, nedum noxas praeteritas aut futuras viventium, sed & defunctorum vitâ, existentium in Purgatorio (quod vocant cantores illi indulgentiarum) igni, modo numeretur aliquid, modo tinniat dextera. Atque his mercium nundinationibus simul & spoliata est ære Germania, & Christi pietas extincta: quando quilibet pro pretii, quod in has merces expenderat, modo, peccandi impunitatem sibi pollicebatur. Hinc supra, incestus, adulteria, perjuria, homicidia, furta, rapinae, faenora, ac tota malorum lerna semel originem sibi traxerant.
units.tr: most thoroughly trained, Huldrych Zwingli and Martin Luther, by their writings, the matter was brought to such a pass that the Supreme Indulgence-monger, the Pope, though for a long time resisting like a bear tied to a stake, was compelled to submit this question to the Council of Trent. The congregation instituted at Trent on 22 November 1563 therefore called it onto the agenda; but indeed timidly, with a hesitant step, and with the votes not agreeing at the start. Some thought that this rock should be sailed past and the treatment of indulgences wholly omitted. Others insisted that, for fear of what they called the heretics, it could not be omitted. The Bishop of Quinque Ecclesiae argued that it would be a disgrace to the Synod if so necessary a subject were passed over. Remissions are granted through these purchased pardons, not only for the past or future sins of the living but also for the dead, who exist in Purgatory (which those indulgence-singers call) by fire, as soon as something is counted out, as soon as the coin rings. And by these market-dealings Germany was both stripped of its money and Christian piety was extinguished, since each person, for whatever price he had spent on these wares, promised himself impunity for sinning. Hence fornication, incest, adultery, perjury, murder, theft, robbery, usury, and the whole Lerna of evils had at once taken their origin.

units.la: Quod enim malorum amplius jam horrebunt Mortales, quando sibi peccandi licentiam ac impunitatem, nedum in vita, sed & post obitum, ære licet immodico comparari posse à nundinationibus illis indulgentiariis, semel persuasum habent? maximè Germani, quibus per hos verae pietatis fucos, sub religionis persona, nihil persuaderi difficile est, ut ingenio plane ad pietatem credulo est Germania. IV. Et licet indulgentiae hae non semel in hoc ad Germanos missae sint, quasi ex corrasa earum venditione, pecuniâ fideles contra barbaros essent tutandi, ac defendendi, eventu tamen compertum habent Germani, pecuniam hanc non in rem fidei, aut alioqui Reip. Christianae necessariam, sed in propinquorum luxum, ac sublevandam familiam ipsorum esse versam, quo uno bina haec nata sunt perquàm maxima incommoda, quòd & offendicula sunt nata, & quòd nunc Germani, toties sentientes lusam fidem, cum vere jam res postulat, ut contra Turcas instituatur expeditio bellica, nullis rationibus se persuaderi patiuntur, ut credant, quod res ipsa fere notorium facit, ita scilicet infiare cervicibus nostris crudeles Turcas, suspicantes semper, prioribus simile quidpiam agi. Quae una ratio est, ut tam aegre contra Turcas manus jungant. Quantorum ergò malorum, & in rebus temporalibus, ac Christi fidelium conscienscientiis, causa fuerint Romanæ indulgentiæ, Sanctitas Apostolica pro sublimitate captús sui, exigua opera, vel inde, si non ex re ulla alia, conjectura consequi poterint. V. Præterea Papalis sanctitas, cæterique Episcopi casus aliquos suæ absolutioni reliquos fecerunt &c. (Gravamen hoc supra ff. xtviij. recitavimus.) VI. Verùm, si quis habeat, unde numeret, jam nedum præsentes indulgentur harum constitutionum transgressiones, sed & in futurum impunè, ut eas ipsas transgredi liceat, indulto permittitur. Quo fit, ut ansam accipiant ii, cum quibus ita dispensatum est, pejerandi, homicidia, adulteria, & similia flagitia perpetrandi, quando quilibet ex Sacerdotum vulgo absolutionem emtitiam virtute indulti, his impartiri poterit. Quæ malorum seges tota, ex habendi libidine, aurique sacra fame, qua nunc Ecclesiasticorum non nulli miserè excruciantur, originem ducit. Hactenùs Imperii Magnates, testes de illa suorum temporum indulgentiaria nundinatione omni exceptione majores, utpote qui ipsimet præsentis mali vim experti sunt, & de quorum corio Romanæ harpyæ petulanter adeò luserunt.
units.tr: For what will mortals now shudder at more of evils, once they have been persuaded that the license and impunity for sinning can be bought, not only in this life but also after death, for however exorbitant a price, from those indulgence markets? Especially the Germans, to whom it is easy to persuade anything through these counterfeits of true piety under the name of religion, since Germany is by nature wholly credulous toward piety. IV. And although these indulgences have been sent to the Germans more than once on this pretext, namely that the faithful would be protected and defended against the barbarians with money gathered from their sale, the Germans have nonetheless learned by experience that this money was not turned to the needs of the faith or of the Christian commonwealth, but to the luxury of relatives and the support of their households. From this one thing two very great inconveniences have arisen: stumbling blocks have been created, and now the Germans, having so often felt their faith mocked, refuse to be persuaded by any reasons, even when the situation truly demands that a military expedition be undertaken against the Turks. They will not believe what the matter itself makes almost notorious, namely that the cruel Turks are so threatening our necks, always suspecting that something similar is being done as before. This is the one reason why they join hands so reluctantly against the Turks. How many evils, both in temporal affairs and in the consciences of Christ's faithful, the Roman indulgences have been the cause of, the Apostolic See, given the height of its understanding, may infer with little effort, if from nothing else, at least from this. V. Moreover, the Papal holiness and the other bishops have reserved certain cases to their own absolution, etc. (We recited this grievance above at page 48.) VI.
