But if anyone has the means to pay, not only are the present transgressions of these constitutions indulged, but also, so that they may be transgressed with impunity in the future, permission is granted by indulgence. As a result, those with whom it has been so dispensed receive an occasion for perjuring themselves, committing murders, adulteries and similar crimes, since any one of the common priests can impart to them a purchased absolution by virtue of the indulgence. This whole crop of evils arises from the desire for possession and from the sacred hunger for gold, by which some of the clergy now miserably suffer. Thus far the Magnates of the Empire, witnesses of that indulgence-trading of their times beyond all exception, since they themselves have experienced the force of the present evil, and from whose hides the Roman harpies have so wantonly played.

units.la: LXXIV. Querelis hisce justissimis, & Theologorum subactissimorum Huldrici Zwinglii & Martini Lutheri ⁊υσμῶ res eò perducta est, ut Supremus Indulgentiarius Papa diu licet, ursi adinstar palo alligandi, restitans, coactus fuerit argumentum isthoc Concilio Tridentino subjicere. Congregatio igitur Tridenti die 22. Nov. A. MDLXIII. instituta ad partes illud vocavit; sed timidè profectò, suspensóque gradu, neque concordantibus initiò calculis. Erant, qui scopulum illum præternavigandum, & tractationem de indulgentiis penitus omittendam censerent. Alii hæreticorum, uti vocabant, metu omitti haud posse, pertendere. Quinquecclesiensis Episcopus, pudendum fore Synodo arguit, si argumentum adeò necessarium
units.tr: LXXIV. By these most just complaints, and by the most skilled theologians Huldrich Zwingli and Martin Luther, stirred up [ἐρεθισμῷ], the matter was brought to such a point that the Supreme Indulgence-seller, the Pope, though for a long time resisting like a bear tied to a stake, was forced to submit this question to the Council of Trent. The Congregation accordingly instituted at Trent on 22 November 1563 took it up, but timidly indeed, with a hesitant step, and with the votes not agreeing at first. Some thought that this rock should be sailed past and the treatment of indulgences wholly omitted. Others insisted that it could not be omitted, from fear of what they called the heretics. The Bishop of Pécs argued that it would be a shameful thing for the Synod if it were to handle so necessary a matter

units.la: Tridentinum de indulgentiis decretum eidem finem non imposuit, ex verbis, declaratione ejusdem, & praxi ostendit. rium molli brachio attingeret. Itum tandem in sententiam Episcopi Molinensis, sic Patres admonentis? Si de indulgentiis tractationem instituere vellent, eum in modum, quo de Justificatione tractatum esset, causis omnibus consideratis, & quaestionibus excussis, rem fore longam admodum & difficilem, multumque temporis desideraturam. Neque enim caput illud satis dilucide explicari posse, nisi prius illud constitutum sit, an sint absolutiones, an vero compensationes & suffragia: & utrum poenas tantum a Confessore impositas remittant, an quascunque debitas. Idem an thesaurus, qui fundamento loco substernitur, ex solis Christi meritis constet, an vero opus sit insuper meritis Sanctorum: an dari possint sine ulla accipientis opera: an ad mortuos se etiam extendant & alia non minoris difficultatis. Verum ad haec determinanda, Ecclesia earum concedendarum potestatem habere (temperque eas concessisse; quodque valde utiles sint, eas digne percipientibus, tanta disputatione opus non esse. Nam authoritatem eas concedendi in S. literis haberi: usum continuatum ex traditione Apostolica, & Conciliorum authoritate, totiusque materiae dilucidam cognitionem ex concordi doctrina Scholasticorum. Hisce de rebus condi posse decretum, nullus difficultatibus obnoxium. Haec sententia, narrante sic S. Polano Hist. C.T. lib. VIJ. p. 722. magno coronae assensu accepta est, confectumque decretum his verbis Sess. xxv. conceptum: Cum potestas conferendi indulgentias a Christo Ecclesiae concessa sit, atque hujusmodi potestate Divinitus sibi tradita, antiquissimus etiam temporibus illa usa fuerit; SS. Synodus Indulgentiarum usum, Christiano populo maxime salutarem, & S. Conciliorum authoritate probatum, in Ecclesia retinendum esse docet, & praecipit, coque anathemate damnat, qui aut inutiles esse asseruerunt, vel eas concedendi potestatem in Ecclesia esse negant. In his tamen concedendis, moderationem, juxta veterem probatamque in Ecclesia consuetudinem, adhiberi cupit, ne nimia facilitate Ecclesiastica disciplina enervetur. Abusus vero qui in his irrepserunt, & quorum occasione insigne hoc indulgentiarum nomen ab haereticis blasphematur, emendatos & correctos cupiens, praesenti decreto generaliter statuit, pravos quaestus omnes pro his consequendis, unde plurima in Christiano populo abusuum causa fluxit, omnino abolendos esse. Caeteros vero, qui ex superstitione, ignorantia, irreverentia, aut aliunde quomodocunque provenerunt, cum ob multiplices locorum & Provinciarum, apud quos hi committuntur, corruptelas, commodè nequeant specialiter prohiberi, mandat omnibus Episcopis, ut diligenter quisque hujusmodi abusus Ecclesiae suae colligat, eósque in prima Provinciali Synodo referat, ut aliorum quoque Episcoporum sententia cogniti, statim ad Summum Romanum Pontificem referantur, cujus authoritate & prudentia, quod universali Ecclesiae expedit, statuatur, ut ita sanctarum indulgentiarum munus piè, sanctè & incorruptè omnibus fidelibus dispensetur. Sic omisso sagaciore scrutinio, arbitrio Papae, qui ipse, ceu Summus in Ecclesia indulgentiarum Foenerator & Institor, & à quo Simoniam committi non posse, ejus parasiti pertendunt, acri censura feriendus fuerat, Venerandi Patres, egregii scilicet Ecclesiae Reformatores, totum isthoc indulgentiarum thema subjiciunt, & pravos quaestus omnes abolendos esse statuunt. Nam quaestus certè hactenus à Papa exercitos pravos non reputárunt. Proin nec similes à sequentibus Pontificibus exercendi in pravorum quaestuum censum referri poterunt. Constat ergo satis nihil omninò à Concilio immutatum, & quaestum indulgentiarum non abolitum, sed hoc unum definitum esse, quaestum licet ex indulgentiis factum, pravum tamen quaestum non esse, si probante Papa exerceatur. Quod ergò pretium pro indulgentiis dandum posthàc erat? Eleemosynæ & charitatis subsidia, definiente eadem Synodo Seff. xxj. cap. 9. quæ colligendi facultatem ordinarius nulla prorsus accepta mercede dedit; ut tandem, inquiunt Patres, hos Ecclesiæ thesauros non ad quæstum, sed ad pietatem exerceri, omnes verè intelligant. Tandem ergò intelligere debemus, quod nemo hactenus intelligere potuit. En mirabilis Babylonicæ meretricio nominum fuco imponentis specimen insigne! Non caștius sed cautiùs forte deinceps mercati sunt. Unde de quæstoribus indulgentiarum querelas in Gallia Synodi Rhotomagensis A. MDLXXXI. Aquensis A. MDLXXXV. & Turonensis A. MDLXXXIII. graves, à Bochello Decret. Eccl. Gall. lib. v. consignatas, moverunt.
units.tr: The Tridentine decree on indulgences did not put an end to the matter, as is shown from its words, its declaration and its practice, and so it would handle it with a gentle arm? Then at last they went along with the opinion of the Bishop of Molina, who admonished the Fathers thus: If they wished to institute a treatment of indulgences in the manner in which justification had been treated, with all causes considered and questions examined, the matter would be very long and difficult and would need much time. For that chapter could not be explained clearly enough unless it were first settled whether there are absolutions, or rather compensations and suffrages; and whether they remit only the penances imposed by the confessor or any debts whatever. Likewise whether the treasury laid as the foundation consists of Christ's merits alone, or whether the merits of the saints are needed besides; whether they can be given without any work of the recipient; whether they extend also to the dead; and other questions of no less difficulty. But for settling these things, the Church has the power of granting them, and has granted them at times; and since they are very useful to those who receive them worthily, no great dispute is needed. For authority to grant them is found in Holy Scripture; continuous use derives from apostolic tradition and the authority of the Councils; and a clear knowledge of the whole matter comes from the agreed doctrine of the Schoolmen. A decree on these matters could be framed that is open to no difficulties. This opinion, as S. Polanus narrates in Hist. C.T. lib. VII. p. 722., was received with great applause, and the decree was drawn up in these words, Sess. xxv.: Since the power of conferring indulgences has been granted to the Church by Christ, and since the Church has used this power, given to it by God, from the most ancient times, the holy Synod teaches and commands that the use of indulgences, most salutary to the Christian people and approved by the authority of the holy Councils, is to be retained in the Church, and condemns with anathema those who assert that they are useless or deny that the Church has the power of granting them. In granting these, however, it wishes moderation to be used, according to the old and approved custom of the Church, lest church discipline be weakened by excessive ease. But desiring that the abuses which have crept into these, and on whose occasion this famous name of indulgences is blasphemed by the heretics, be amended and corrected, it decrees generally by the present decree that all base gains sought for obtaining them, from which very many causes of abuse flowed among the Christian people, are to be utterly abolished. The other abuses, however, which arose from superstition, ignorance, irreverence, or from elsewhere in any way, since they cannot conveniently be specifically prohibited because of the manifold corruptions of the places and provinces where they are committed, it orders all bishops to collect diligently the abuses of this kind in their own churches and report them at the first provincial synod, so that, having been learned also by the opinion of the other bishops, they may be referred at once to the Roman Pontiff, by whose authority and prudence what is expedient for the universal Church may be decided, so that the office of the holy indulgences may be dispensed piously, holily and incorruptly to all the faithful. Thus, passing over a sharper scrutiny and leaving the matter to the judgement of the Pope, the Pope himself being (as his parasites maintain, and by whom simony cannot be committed) the Supreme Usurer and Hawker of indulgences in the Church, who ought to have been struck with a sharp censure, the Venerable Fathers, to wit the distinguished Reformers of the Church, submit this whole theme of indulgences and decree that all base gains are to be abolished. For they certainly did not regard as base the gains hitherto made by the Pope. Therefore neither can similar gains exercised by later Popes be counted among base gains. It is therefore quite clear that nothing at all was changed by the Council, and that the gain from indulgences was not abolished, but this only was defined: that gain made from indulgences is not base gain, provided it is exercised with the Pope's approval. What price, then, was henceforth to be paid for indulgences? Alms and aids of charity, as the same Synod defined in Sess. xxi. cap. 9., which the ordinary granted the power of collecting without any reward at all; so that at last, say the Fathers, all truly understand that these treasures of the Church are used not for gain but for piety. So at last we ought to understand what no one has hitherto been able to understand. Behold a wonderful remarkable specimen of the Babylonian harlot deceiving with the paint of names! Perhaps they afterwards traded not more chastely, but more cautiously. Hence the grave complaints about the quaestors of indulgences in France, from the Synods of Rouen in 1581, Aix in 1585 and Tours in 1583, were raised, and were recorded by Bochellus in Decret. Eccl. Gall. lib. v.
LXXV.

units.la: Et sanè quæstuariās indulgentias denuò Pius V. concessit, atque earundem revocatio paulatim variis limitationibus, quas venter ingenii, uti vulgò ajunt, largitor dictavit, elusa est. Ita enim Augustinus Barbosa Collect. in Concil. Trid. pag. 151. de privilegiis mendicantium: Privilegia, inquit, mendicantium, non prohibentur petere eleemosynas; per hoc decretum Concilii non sunt abrogata, quia in eo tantùm abolentur quæstores, qui prædicant, vel publicant indulgentias concessas his, qui manus adjutrices porrexerint piis locis, pro quibus petunt eleemosynam: non verò in mendicantibus pro sua sustentatione QUÆSTUANTIBUS, juxta quoddam decretum Pii V. revocantis similes indulgentiarum quæstuarias porrigentibus manus adjutrices piis locis. Sed & Cardinales ad Seff. xxi. cap. 9. declarârunt, per decreti illius (quo loco citato, non aliis, quàm ordinariis facultas datur publicandi indulgentias &c.) posteriorem partem non posse ordinarios prohibere, quò minùs Religiosi indulgentias, sibi olim à Summo Pontifice concessas publicent, nullo etiam verbo cum eis facto: at indulgentias, inquiunt, sibi ipsis denuò concessas absque ordinarii licentia publicare non possunt. Idem qui supra Barbosa Remiff. ad loc. cit. Geroldum inducit; asserentem, quòd in sacra Cardinalium congregatione decisum sit, dari posse licentiam petendi eleemosynas (hoc est, pecunias, aliaque pro indulgentiis) cum his circumstantiis. 1. ut sint personæ bonæ existimationis. 2. ne sint participes eleemosynarum. 3. ne habeant ullo modo nomen quæstoris. 4. Nullas indulgentias divulgent, nec concionentur. 5. Ne sua privilegia, aut sacras reliquias circumferant. 6. Ne imprecationibus aut minis eleemosynas exprimant, aut extorqueant, nec campanas, aliaque instrumenta deferant. 7. Ne quicquam debitum aut usitatum petant. 8. Ne ullo artificio commemorandæ orationis alicujus Sancti, aut alio perverso more utantur. 9 Sed simpliciter ac modestè eleemosynas petant, easque in pii loci utilitatem transportent. Hæc præteritam nundinationem vivis coloribus depingunt, & quæstuariæ substantiam non abolent. Et Hieronymus Rodericus Compend. quæst. regul. resol. 59. scribit, pro ordine Sanctissimæ Trinitatis redemptionis captivorum extare duas concessiones, Benedicti XII. quibus conceditur quæstus eleemosynarum dicto ordini pro redemtione captivorum. Et plures indulgentias etiam post Concilium à Pio IV. Clemente VIII. Clemente X. probatas modernum Papam Innocentium XI. inducere coactum esse, Hist. Pap. s. 323. ostendimus. Atque id bono animo factum nos interpretabamur. Qui verò Papales artes penitius pernoruntz, asseverant, modernum Papam, Mercatorem maximum, veteres indulgentias abolevisse, ut novis concessis, majorem quæstum faceret. Sic hydræ capite uno resecto, alia æquè nocentia subnascuntur. Et quàm segniter quæstui huic suo dulcissimo Hierarchici renunciârint, vel solæ quæstiones Casuisticæ, quas circa indulgentias Je-suitæ, & inter eos Diana Panormitanus Tom.j. Tract. ii. de Bulla cruciatæ, nec non, Tom.ÿ. Tract. i2. de Indulg. & Jubilæo, maximè movent, cognoscere est.
units.tr: Indeed, Pius V granted profit-making indulgences again, and their revocation was gradually evaded through various limitations, which, as people commonly say, the belly, the giver of wit, dictated. Thus Augustinus Barbosa, in Collect. in Concil. Trid., p. 151, on the privileges of the mendicants: The privileges of the mendicants, he says, do not forbid them to seek alms; they are not abrogated by this decree of the Council, because it abolishes only those quaestors who preach or publish indulgences granted to those who extend helping hands to pious places for which they seek alms; it does not abolish mendicants who seek for their own support, making a trade of it, in accordance with a certain decree of Pius V revoking similar profit-making indulgences granted to those who extend helping hands to pious places. But the Cardinals too, at Session 21, chapter 9, declared that by that decree (in which, as cited, only ordinaries are given the power of publishing indulgences, etc.) the latter part cannot prevent ordinaries from keeping Religious from publishing indulgences once granted to them by the Supreme Pontiff, even without any word spoken to them; but indulgences, they say, granted to them again, cannot be published without the licence of the ordinary. Barbosa, in his Remiff. ad loc. cit., cites the same Gerold, who asserts that it was decided in the sacred congregation of Cardinals that a licence to seek alms (that is, money and other things for indulgences) may be given under these conditions: (1) that they be persons of good repute; (2) that they not share in the alms; (3) that they in no way bear the name of quaestor; (4) that they publish no indulgences and do not preach; (5) that they do not carry about their own privileges or sacred relics; (6) that they do not extort or wring alms by curses or threats, nor carry bells or other instruments; (7) that they demand nothing owed or customary; (8) that they use no trick of reciting the prayer of some Saint or other perverse practice; (9) but that they ask for alms simply and modestly, and carry them over to the benefit of the pious place. These provisions paint the former trade in lively colours, and do not abolish the substance of quaestuary indulgence. Hieronymus Rodericus, in Compend. quaest. regul. resol. 59, writes that for the Order of the Most Holy Trinity of the redemption of captives there exist two grants of Benedict XII, by which the collecting of alms is granted to the said order for the redemption of captives. And we have shown, in Hist. Pap., s. 323, that the present Pope Innocent XI was compelled to bring in several indulgences, approved even after the Council by Pius IV, Clement VIII and Clement X. We used to interpret this as done in good faith. But those who know the Papal arts more thoroughly assert that the present Pope, the greatest merchant, has abolished the old indulgences so that by granting new ones he might make more profit. Thus when one head of the hydra is cut off, others equally harmful sprout up. And how sluggishly the Hierarchs have renounced this most sweet trade of theirs can be learned from the casuistical questions alone, which the Jesuits, and among them Diana of Palermo, raise especially about indulgences, in Tom. I, Tract. ii, de Bulla cruciatae, and also in Tom. V, Tract. 12, de Indulg. & Jubilaeo.

units.la: LXXVI. Clamet proin boëtque, quantum voluerit, fœdus Alastor Sciopius in Apologetico suo Hunnio opposito Cap. ii. mendacium crassum esse indulgentias pro pecunia vendi à Pontifice. Nihil clamor, nihil boatus ille proficit. Si hodiè Papa post detectas, & in apricum productas pudendas fraudes, detractâmque persona non aperto foro ampliùs eas vendere audet, an nec olim vendidisse aperto foro, verè meretricia fronte, consequitur? Sed ipse se sorex suo indicio prodidit. Nam capite proximè superiore ipsemet duo dixerat. Primò, expeditiones causarum (quas inter sunt quoque indulgentiæ ex operibus supererogationis collectæ) à Pontifice quidem sine pecunia impetrari posse, literas verò sive bullas indulgentiales non nisi solutâ pecuniâ dari. Secundò, literas illas indulgentiarias esse necessarias, si velis pacem conscientiæ afferre. Certò enim constare debere, quòd Papa dispensaverit. Indulgentiæ ergò absque bullis indulgentialibus pacem conscientiæ afferre non possunt, adeóque nihil prosunt. Sed indulgentiales illæ bullæ non dantur absque pecunia. Ergò indulgentiæ ex operibus supererogationis, collectæ ut pacem conscientiæ afferre possint, pecuniâ redimendæ sunt. Idem Sciopius cap. 9. scribit, dispensationem seu beneficium, seu quidvis denique (adeóque etiam indulgentias) sub scripto à Pontifice non concedi, nisi æstimatio cancellariæ soluta sit. Quin ex Bellarmino etiam probat, à Papa indulgentias petentibus pecunias & eleemosynas JUBERI, INJUNGI & IMPERARI. Egregias eleemosynas, quæ jubentur, injunguntur, imperantur: Capti sunt Sophistæ. Rem solvant.
units.tr: LXXVI. Let Alastor Sciopius, then, shout and bluster as much as he likes in his Apologeticus against Hunnius, chapter 2, that it is a gross lie that the Pope sells indulgences for money. That clamour and bluster achieve nothing. If today the Pope, after his shameful frauds have been detected and brought into the open, and his reputation destroyed, dares no longer sell them in the open forum, does it follow that he did not once sell them openly, with a truly harlot's brazenness? But the mouse has betrayed himself by his own evidence. For in the chapter immediately before, he himself had said two things. First, that dispatches of causes (among which are also indulgences collected from works of supererogation) can indeed be obtained from the Pope without money, but the letters or indulgential bulls cannot be given except for money paid. Second, those indulgential letters are necessary if you wish to bring peace of conscience. For it must be certain that the Pope has granted a dispensation. Therefore indulgences without indulgential bulls cannot bring peace of conscience, and so are of no benefit. But those indulgential bulls are not given without money. Therefore indulgences from works of supererogation, collected so that they may bring peace of conscience, must be bought back with money. The same Sciopius, in chapter 9, writes that a dispensation, whether a benefice or indeed anything at all (and so also indulgences), is not granted in writing by the Pope unless the chancery's fee has been paid. Indeed, he also proves from Bellarmine that those who seek indulgences from the Pope are ordered, enjoined and commanded to give money and alms. Splendid alms, which are ordered, enjoined and commanded! The Sophists are caught. Let them pay up.
LXXVII.

units.la: LXXVII. Sed missis tandem obsoletis & rancidis illis indulgentiarum mercibus, ordo nos ad Sacramentum Ordinis provehit. De eo Sacramento fictitio, ejusque abusibus cùm agere Tridentini instituissent, Veronensis Episcopus, Papæ Nuntius, ingenuè professus est, ubique esse abusum aliquem, qui emendationem postulet, sed in hoc Sacramento esse abusuum Oceanum; uti S. Polanus Hist. C. T. lib. iv. p. 327. prodidit. Oceanum hunc cùm emetiri instituti nostri cancelli prohibeant, litora saltem legere conabimur.
units.tr: LXXVII. But with those obsolete and rancid wares of indulgences finally set aside, the order of our discussion now brings us to the Sacrament of Orders. When the Tridentine fathers undertook to treat of this fictitious sacrament and its abuses, the Bishop of Verona, the Pope's Nuncio, frankly admitted that there is some abuse everywhere that calls for correction, but in this sacrament there is an ocean of abuse, as Polanus reports in Hist. C. T. lib. iv. p. 327. Since the limits of our plan forbid us to measure this ocean, we will at least try to survey its shores.

units.la: LXXVIII. Cùm in Christianæ religionis cunabulis abundaret charitas, populus Christianus, qui à Christi ministris spiritualia occipiebat, non modò iisdem τὰ βίω-λικά, seu ad victum & amictum necessaria, juxta ipsius Christi præceptum à S. Paulo 1 Cor. ix. 1. &c. explicatum, suppeditavit alacriter, sed etiam copiosè adeò ex facultatibus suis in medium contulit, ut etiam pauperibus inde prospici posset. Neque tamen ullius mentem cogitatio ea subivit, quòd temporale illud quod dabatur, pretium sit doni spiritualis. Sustentationem deberi iis, qui Ecclesiæ ministerio unicè vacantes, alia ratione victum & amictum sibi acquirere non poterant, piè rectéque judicârunt. Postquam verò temporale, quod in communi asservabatur, in partes dividi, & reditus certus, appellatione Beneficii, titulis applicari cœpit, cùm hucusque non esset distincta ordinatio à collatione tituli, ac proin etiam beneficii titulo annexi, sed unà darentur, acciperentúrque, tum demùm placuit Ordinatoribus propter emolumenta, Ordinatis ex Ordinatione proventura, præter spirituale etiam temporale aliquid dari, cujus intuitu in remunerationem temporale quid fumi posset. Is ergò qui beneficii compos fieri voluit, voluntati conferentis beneficium morem ultrò gessit. Inde incessit aperta negotiatio, quæ in orientali Ecclesia nullis ferè canonibus ac censuris emen& shy;dari unquam potuit, utcunque præpotens Dei manus, emolumentorum magna parte à Saracenis intercepta, non parùm eandem inhibuerit, & imminuerit. In occidentali Ecclesia, bonis nequicquam indignantibus & intercedentibus, eodem negotio alibi minùs, alibi magis obtinuit ad annum usque salutis millesimum, quo distinctione Ordinationem inter & beneficii collationem introducta, ordinatio quidem gratis dari ad tempus aliquod consuevit. Sed non diu liberalitas illa duravit, Episcopi enim spreta ordinatione, tanquam abjecta & infructosa, ad solam beneficii collationem, ex qua emolumentum perceperunt, & temporalia attenti, ordinationum administrationem Titularibus Episcopis, qui Ecclesiastica sua munera obirent demandárunt. Hi verò, quòd reditus nullos possiderent, necesse habebant à functionibus, quas obibant, victum parare: iisque vicissim, quos ad ordines admittebant, ordinantibus aliquid conferre tenebantur, primùm eleemosynæ sive oblationis nomine, post, honoratiore titulo, donationis, ac demùm, ne cùm debitum esset, omitteretur, mercedis, non quæ Episcopo ordinanti, sed famulis ejus, aut tabellioni, aut aliis inter ordinandum ministrantibus cederet.
units.tr: LXXVIII. When charity abounded in the cradle of the Christian religion, the Christian people, who received spiritual things from the ministers of Christ, not only generously supplied them with temporal things [τὰ βιωτικά], that is, the necessities of food and clothing, according to Christ's own command as S. Paul explains it in 1 Cor. 9 and following, but also gave so abundantly from their resources that the poor could be provided for from them as well. Yet no one's mind was troubled by the thought that the temporal gift given was the price of a spiritual gift. They rightly and piously judged that support was owed to those who devoted themselves wholly to the ministry of the Church and could not otherwise obtain food and clothing for themselves. But when the temporal goods held in common began to be divided into portions, and fixed revenues began to be attached to titles under the name of benefice, then, since ordination had until then not been distinguished from the conferring of a title, or of a benefice attached to the title, but both were given and received together, the ordainers at last decided that, over and above the spiritual gift, something temporal should also be given to those ordained, in return for the income that would come to them from their ordination; and in view of this a temporal reward could be taken. So the man who wished to become possessed of a benefice courted the will of the one conferring it. From this an open trafficking arose, which in the Eastern Church could scarcely ever be checked by any canons or censures; although the powerful hand of God, with a large part of the revenues intercepted by the Saracens, greatly restrained and diminished it. In the Western Church, though good men protested and interceded in vain, the same business prevailed to a lesser or greater degree in different places until the year of salvation 1000, when, with a distinction introduced between ordination and the conferring of a benefice, ordination was customarily given free of charge for some time. But that generosity did not last long. For the bishops, disdaining ordination as something cheap and unprofitable, attended only to the conferring of benefices, from which they drew income, and, intent on temporal things, entrusted the administration of ordinations to titular bishops, who performed their ecclesiastical duties. These men, since they possessed no revenues, were obliged to earn their living from the functions they performed; and in turn those whom they admitted to the orders were bound to give something to the ordainers: first under the name of alms or oblation, then under a more honourable title, of donation, and finally, so that what was owed should not be omitted, of fee, which went not to the ordaining bishop but to his servants, or to the notary, or to others who assisted at the ordination.

units.la: LXXIX. Hæc res in Concilio Tridentino in controversiam adducta est, Patribus in partes scissis. Alii enim illud, quod hactenùs usu receptum erat, ceu sacrilegum ac Simoniacum damnárunt merito, citatis eam in rem Gehazi, Prophetæ Eliæ famuli, & Simonis Magi exemplis, nec non rigido Christi præcepto: Gratis accepistis, gratis date; multisque S. Patrum contra peccatum illud testimoniis. Sanè etiam Æneas Sylvius, postea Papa, Pius II. dictus, Epist. 66. ad Johannem Peregatum quæstus est; ipsam impositionem manuum & dona Spiritus S. vendi pecuniis. Et Erasmum eadem de re quiritantem supra vidimus. Addebant Episcopi illi, nomina donationis & eleemosynæ speciosa quidem esse, sed inanes tantùm obtentus, quibus effectus repugnet. Propter ordinem enim acceptum dari, absque quo nihil daretur. Si eleemosynæ nomine darentur, cur non alia occasione, aut alio tempore? Ordines verò nulla omninò re interveniente conferendos esse. Quinimò Episcopum contumeliam interpretaturum, si quis profiteatur eleemosynæ nomine se quidquam ei conferre. Concludebant illi, absoluto decreto statuendum esse, ne quicquam ordinanti vel ejus ministris, etiam ultrò, seu eleemosynæ nomine detur. Contra Episcopi titulo tenus tales & tenuiores nitebantur. Sicut enim, inquiebant illi, sacrilegus censeatur merito, qui ordines vendiderit: ita, qui eleemosynam à Christo tantoperè commendatam sustulerit, charitatem eum evertere, & Ecclesiam deformare. Eandem rationem in ordinibus militare, quæ in confessionibus, communionibus, Missis, Sepulturis aliisque functionibus ecclesiasticis obtinet. In his si ultrò dari aliquid & accipi potest, cur non etiam in illis? A quingentis jam annis constare, quòd divites ministeria Ecclesiæ non obeant. Si ergò pauperioribus nihil accipere liceat, brevi ministerium Ecclesiæ interiturum. Si reprehensione vacat, propter pallia, à Papa Metropolitanis data, etiam millia aliquot aureorum dependere, cur Episcopis vitio verti, si ab iis, qui ordine inferiores sunt, grati animi testificationem acceperint? Etiam in Pontificali proditum esse, in ordinationibus, cùm in peragenda re Divina ad oblationes venitur, cereos, nempe res Seculares, Episcopo ordinanti ab ordinato afferri: quibus tamen vel quantitas, vel apparatus, pretium & æstimationem possit addere. Non ergò, inquiebant illi, adeò odiosum est, quòd in miserellis Episco-pis pis reprehenditur : neque meretur, ut cum ejus or dini infamia, alii laudem sibi reformatorum arrogent, veriùs Pharisæorum imitatores, dum festucas observant, ipsi culicem excolantes. Addebant alii ab Innocentio III. in Concilio generali non solùm probari consuetudinem dandi & accipiendi quidpiam pro administratione Sacramentorum, sed præcipi etiam Episcopis, ut censuris & poenis Ecclesiasticis adigant ad eam laudabilem (sic enim vocari) consuetudinem observandam. Opponebat se illis Dionysius Græcus, Episcopus Milopotamensis, pertendens, Ecclesiæ planè honorificum & conducibile futurum, si Sacramenta mero charitatis studio ministrarentur. Sustentationi Episcoporum & Sacerdotum abundè provisum esse assignatis decimis. Clerum enim, etsi decimam partem populi non constituat, tam grandem portionem accipere, ac præter alia bona, quæ duplo plura possidet. Quòd si contendant, pauperes esse Episcopos, id non arguere Ecclesiæ egestatem, sed opes ejusdem non æquis portionibus divisas. Justa enim & legitima instituta distributione, fore, unde omnibus abundè sufficiat, sic ut operam suam liberè communicare debeant absque alio hostimento, quàm eo, quod ultrà debitum jam acceperint. Addebat, reformationem extendi ad ea etiam debere, quæ ordinationem antecedunt. Absurdum enim esse, ut Clericus licentiam procurandi sibi ordinatoris postulans, literas dimissoriales à Cancellariis Episcopatuum magno licitetur, aut facultatem sui extra præscriptum tempus ordinandi Romæ magno pretio comparet: horum verò reformatione neglecta de solis Episcopis ordinatoribus emendandis cura suscipiatur. Hactenùs conflictus ille partium in Concilio colluctantium, quem S. Polanus Hist. C.T. lib. vj. p. 446. 447. 448. narrat.
units.tr: LXXIX. This matter was brought into controversy at the Council of Trent, the Fathers being split into parties. Some rightly condemned what had hitherto been customary as sacrilegious and Simoniacal, citing for this purpose the examples of Gehazi, the servant of the prophet Elisha, and of Simon Magus, as well as Christ's strict command, Freely you have received, freely give; and many testimonies of the Fathers against that sin. Indeed Aeneas Sylvius, later Pope Pius II, complained in his Epistle 66 to John Peregatus that the very laying on of hands and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are sold for money. And we have seen above that Erasmus too lamented the same matter. Those bishops added that the names donation and alms were indeed specious, but were mere pretexts, whose effect contradicted them: for something was given on account of the order received, without which nothing would be given. If it were given under the name of alms, why not on some other occasion or at some other time? Orders, however, ought to be conferred with no consideration of anything at all. Indeed, the bishop would take it as an insult if anyone declared that he was giving him something under the name of alms. They concluded that a settled decree must be made that nothing should be given to the ordainer or his ministers, even voluntarily, or under the name of alms. The other side, the bishops, fought on the mere level of the title, and in a more modest way. For just as one who sells orders is rightly judged sacrilegious, they said, so one who removes alms, which Christ so highly commended, overturns charity and disfigures the Church. The same principle applies to orders as to confessions, communions, Masses, burials and other ecclesiastical functions. If something may be given and received voluntarily in these, why not in orders too? For nearly five hundred years it has been established that the rich do not perform the ministries of the Church. So if it were not permitted to receive anything from the poorer, the ministry of the Church would soon perish. If no blame attaches to the sums of several thousand gold pieces paid for the palliums that the Pope gives to metropolitans, why should bishops be censured if they receive a token of grateful feeling from those who are lower in rank? It is also recorded in the Pontifical that in ordinations, when in the course of the Divine service the offerings are brought forward, the ordained man brings candles, that is, secular things, to the ordaining bishop; to these, however, quantity or display can add value and estimation. Therefore, they said, it is not so hateful that it is censured in the poor bishops; nor does it deserve that others should claim praise for themselves as reformers, at the cost of the infamy of that order, truer imitators of the Pharisees, who while they watch for motes, strain out the gnat themselves. Others added that by Innocent III in the General Council not only was the custom of giving and receiving something for the administration of the sacraments approved, but bishops were also commanded to compel, by ecclesiastical censures and penalties, the observance of that praiseworthy (for so it was called) custom. Against them stood Dionysius the Greek, Bishop of Milopotamos, maintaining that it would be entirely honourable and advantageous to the Church if the sacraments were administered from pure zeal for charity. He held that provision had been abundantly made for the support of bishops and priests by the assigned tithes. For the clergy, though they do not make up a tenth part of the people, receive so large a portion, and besides other goods which they possess, twice as much. And if they should contend that the bishops are poor, that does not prove the poverty of the Church, but that its wealth is not divided into equal portions. For with a just and lawful arrangement of distribution there would be enough for all, so that they could freely share their labour without any other payment than what they had already received beyond what was owed. He added that the reform ought also to extend to the matters that precede ordination. For it was absurd that a cleric, asking permission from his ordainer to procure orders, should be bought from the chancelleries of the bishoprics for a large price, or that the power to be ordained outside the prescribed time should be bought at Rome for a great sum; yet while these were neglected, care was taken to correct only the bishops who ordain. So far that conflict of the parties struggling in the Council, which S. Polanus narrates in his History of the Council of Trent, book 6, pp. 446, 447, 448.

units.la: LXXX. Decretum verò Sess. xxj. de Reformat. cap.
units.tr: LXXX. But the decree of Session 21, On Reformation, chapter 1, was framed in these words:

units.la: cap. j. hæc in verba factum est: Quoniam ab Ecclesiastico ordine omnis avaritiæ suspicio abesse debet; nihil pro collatione quorumcunque ordinum, etiam clericalis tonsuræ, nec pro literis dimissoriis aut testimonialibus, nec pro sigillo, nec alia quacunque de causa, etiam sponte oblatum, Episcopi & alii ordinum collatores, aut eorum ministri quovis prætextu accipiant. Notarii verò in iis tantùm locis, in quibus non viget laudabilis consuetudo nihil accipiendi, pro singulis literis dimissoriis, aut testimonialibus decimam tantùm unius aurei partem accipere possint &c. Contrarias taxas, ac statuta & consuetudines, etiam immemorabiles quorumcunque locorum, quæ potiùs abusus & corruptelæ, Simoniacæ pravitati faveнтes, nuncupari possunt, penitùs cassando & interdicendo, & qui secus fecerint, tam dantes, quàm accipientes, ultrà Divinam ultionem, pœnas in jure inflictas ipso facto incurrant. Ex hoc decreto Papatus ad Tridentinum usque Concilium avaritiæ & Simoniacæ pravitatis reus nullo negotio peragitur. In eo enim avaritiæ & Simoniacæ pravitatis notâ inuruntur, quotquot non gratis, sed pretio, etiam sponte oblato ordinant, vel pro literis dimissoriis, testimonialibus, sigillo vel alia quacunque causa aliquid accipiunt. Cassantur quoque & interdicuntur taxæ statuta, consuetudines etiam immemorabiles, quorumcunque locorum, quæ potiùs abusus & corruptelæ Simoniacæ pravitati favéntes nuncupari possint. Erant ergò eò usque taxæ, erant statuta (nam suprà ipsum Pontificale, & Innocentii III. in Concilio Lateranensi constitutionem ab Episcopis illis, qui ordinationes pro pretio propugnabant, allegatam vidimus) erant consuetudines immemorabiles Simoniacæ pravitati favéntes, ipsomet Concilio indice, à quo sic candidè detectus est Simoniacæ pravitatis Spiritum S. & ejusdem dona nundinantis, sacer morbus, qui hactenus Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ corpus integrum, Papalibus etiam statutis confirmatus, corripuerat. Sed an in futurum satis Simoniæ circa ordinationes Concilium cavit? Haud equidem ita visum in ipso Concilio est Alberto Duimio, Episcopo Veglensi, aperte professo, se decretum illud habere pro imperfecto, nisi una statuatur, Romæ quoque abstinendum à pecuniis exigendis propter dispensationes, sine ordinum indebito tempore, ætate immatura absque venia & examine Ordinarii sumendorum, sive irregularitatum, aliorumque impedimentorum Canonicorum: quandoquidem in his ingentes sumtus fieri soleant. Sic Romanos, Episcopos pauperibus eleemosynam, quæ iis ordinantibus dari consueverit, subducentes, rutam decimare, aurum verò & argentum sufurari. Cùmque talia Romæ determinanda esse Legati regererent, Veglensis respondit, se, cùm carnisprivii ultimo tempore Romæ esset, de eadem re in ædibus Cardinalis Perusini multis Cardinalibus & Præsulibus Romanis coram conquestum, respônsum tulisse, in Concilio hæc esse proponenda. Nunc cùm videat contra fieri, & à Synodo ad Pontificem se rejici, decrevisse se perpes silentium, & emendationis curam Deo relinquere.
units.tr: chapter 1. Since all suspicion of avarice ought to be absent from the ecclesiastical order, the bishops and other collators of orders, or their ministers, shall accept nothing, on any pretext, for conferring any orders, even the clerical tonsure, nor for letters dimissory or testimonial, nor for a seal, nor for any other cause, even if it is offered of its own accord. Notaries, however, may receive, only in those places where the praiseworthy custom of taking nothing does not prevail, a tenth part of one gold coin for each letter dimissory or testimonial, and so on. Contrary taxes, statutes and customs, even immemorial ones of any places, which may rather be called abuses and corruptions favouring Simoniacal depravity, are entirely quashed and forbidden, and those who act otherwise, both givers and receivers, beyond the divine vengeance, incur ipso facto the penalties laid down in law. By this decree the Papacy, up to the Council of Trent, is convicted without difficulty of avarice and Simoniacal depravity. For in it those are branded with the mark of avarice and Simoniacal depravity who ordain not freely but for a price, even one offered of its own accord, or who receive anything for letters dimissory, testimonial letters, a seal, or any other cause. Likewise taxes, statutes, customs, even immemorial ones of any places, which may rather be called abuses and corruptions favouring Simoniacal depravity, are quashed and forbidden. Up to that point, then, there were taxes, there were statutes (for above we have seen the Pontifical itself, and the constitution of Innocent III in the Lateran Council, cited by those bishops who defended paid ordinations), there were immemorial customs favouring Simoniacal depravity, as the Council itself indicates, by which the holy sickness of Simoniacal depravity, which trades in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, was so candidly detected. This sickness had hitherto seized the whole body of the Papal Church, confirmed even by Papal statutes. But did the Council take sufficient care against simony in ordinations for the future? Certainly this did not seem so in the Council itself to Albert Duimius, Bishop of Veglia, who openly declared that he regarded that decree as imperfect unless it also laid down that at Rome too they should abstain from exacting money for dispensations concerning the unlawful time of ordinations, the immature age of those to be ordained, absence of pardon and examination by the ordinary, or irregularities and other canonical impediments; since in these matters huge expenses are usually incurred. Thus the Romans, by withholding from bishops the alms which were customarily given to the poor when they ordained, tithe the rue, but purloin the gold and silver. When the legates reported that such matters were to be settled at Rome, Veglia replied that when he was at Rome in the last part of the carnival season, he had complained of the same thing in the house of Cardinal Perusinus before many cardinals and Roman prelates, and had received the answer that these things were to be proposed in the Council. Now, since he sees the opposite being done, and that he is being referred from the Synod to the Pontiff, he has decided to keep perpetual silence and to leave the care of amendment to God.

units.la: LXXXI. Fuit Simonia in collatione Ordinum. Sed longè major, foedior, & incurabilis illa est, quæ in collatione beneficiorum, à collatione Ordinum separata, impunè grassatur, exigua ipse abusus tollendi (inquit S. Polanus loc. cit. pag. 446.) quoad Christus ipse alia vice mularium mensas evertat, & flagello nundinatores istos è templo ejiciat. Claudius Espencæus in Epist. ad Tit. cap. 3. paucis verbis multas Simoniæ illius species comprehendit: Jam, inquit, ut omittam Annatas, quocunque colore & prætextu emungantur, in Basileensi Concilio Sess. 21. de Simonia damnatas, qua subtilitate ab αἰχρο-κερδία αἰ̈δία excusari possunt, quæ vocantur Exspectativæ gratiæ, reservationes in pectore, beneficiorum primo currenti collationes, plurium curionatuum ad unum sacellum, vel canonicatum, aut simplex alioqui beneficium, unio, seu unitio, ne scilicet objet pluralitas, mandata, præventiones, popinæ, minuta, seu communia servitia, regressus omnium fructuum, pensionis loco retentiones, & infinita id genus, primùm quidem Ecclesiæ tandiu inaudita, nec à redivivis Petro & Paulo intelligenda. Eadem ratione M.A. de Dominis probè peritus Romanarum nundinationum, de Rep. Eccl. lib. ix. 9: 48. artes, quibus Romæ Ecclesiastica pecunia ex tota penè Christi Ecclesia emungitur, exugitur, hauritur, absorbetur, innumerabiles esse ait. Huc spectant, inquit, Bullæ, annatæ, propriæ decimæ, quindennia, compositiones, dispensationes, absolutiones, indulgentiarum perpetuæ concessiones, vocationum implicati modi, resignationes, permutationes, subrogationes, accessus, regressus, coadjutoriæ, commissiones extra tempora, si inevidentem significavit gratiæ, Privilegia, licentiæ, aliáque innumerabilia mihi etiam ignota. Nos ex innumerabilibus illis, quibus Papa, beneficia Ecclesiastica & Sacerdotalia cauponatur, rationibus paucas, speciminis ergò, depromemus.
units.tr: LXXXI. There was simony in the conferring of orders. But that simony is far greater, fouler and incurable which, separated from the conferring of orders, rages with impunity in the conferring of benefices; it is hard to remove even the small abuses (says Polanus, loc. cit., p. 446), although Christ himself once overturned the tables of the money-changers and drove those traders out of the temple with a whip. Claudius Espencaeus, in his Epistle to Titus, chapter 3, sums up in a few words the many species of that simony: Now, to pass over annates, however they are extorted, under whatever colour and pretext, condemned in the Council of Basel, Session 21, on simony, by what subtlety can those things be excused from avaricious shamelessness which are called expectative graces, reservations in petto, collations of the first benefice falling vacant, the conferring of several curacies on one chapel or canonry, or on some other simple benefice, union or unification, lest plurality should be an objection, mandates, prevention, popinae, minuta or common services, the retention of all fruits as a substitute for a pension, and an endless number of such things, first of all hitherto unheard of in the Church, and not to be understood even by Peter and Paul risen again. In the same way M. A. de Dominis, well versed in Roman trading, On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 9, 48, says that the arts by which Church money is squeezed, drawn off, drained and absorbed from almost the whole Church of Christ at Rome are innumerable. To this belong, he says, bulls, annates, proper tithes, quindennia, compositions, dispensations, absolutions, perpetual grants of indulgences, intricate modes of calling, resignations, exchanges, substitutions, accessions, regresses, coadjutorships, commissions outside the proper times, privileges of grace, licences, and other innumerable things unknown even to me. From those countless methods by which the Pope hawks ecclesiastical and priestly benefices, we shall draw out a few, by way of sample.

units.la: LXXXII. Basis nundinationis hujus Papalis est, quòd Pontifex non Episcopatuum modò, sed etiam quorumcunque beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, in quacunque Christiana Dioecesi existentium, pro suæ voluntatis arbitrio supremam sibi collaturam & Dominium, invitis etiam & renitentibus Episcopis, arrogat. De ejus suprà Episcopatûs Episcopos ὑπερόχῃ, actum à nobis suprà est. De potestate in beneficia eorundem, paucis etiam heic agamus. Primus omnium Clemens III. seu IV. apertè pronuntiavit, Romanos Pontifices de jure esse plenarios omnium
units.tr: LXXXII. The basis of this Papal trading is that the Pontiff claims for himself supreme collation and dominion, at his own discretion, not only over the bishoprics but also over any ecclesiastical benefices existing in any Christian diocese, even against the will and resistance of the bishops. We have already spoken above of his superiority [ὑπερόχῃ] over the bishops of the bishoprics. Let us here also say a few words about his power over their benefices. Clement III or IV was the first of all to declare openly that the Roman Pontiffs are by right the full
The basis of this trading is:

units.la: quòd Papa se supremum beneficiorum Dominum profitetur. omnium beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum collatores. Verba ejus: licet de præb. & dignit. in 6. sunt: Licet Ecclesiarum, personatuum, dignitatum, aliorúmque beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum plenaria dispositio ad Romanum notscatur Pontificem pertinere, ita quòd non solùm ipsa cùm vacant, potest de jure conferre, verùm etiam jus in ipsis tribuere vacaturis: collationem tamen, &c. Secuti Bonifacius VIII. c. si Papa de Priv. in 6. & Clemens V. Clement. Si duobus. Ut tit.pend. eandem sibi potestatem disertis verbis vendicant. Quam potestatem non Divino, sed Canonico jure iis competere, Gerson lib. de vit. spirit. lest. 3. ait: cùm tamen canones his Pontificibus vetustiores solos Episcopos quosque in sua dioecesi veros & legitimos beneficiorum collatores faciant. Monstrum ergò hoc primi duo illi Clementes & Bonifacius VIII. pepererunt, & potestatem, quam iis nec Christus, nec Apostoli, nec Ecclesia unquam tradidit non pretio abstulerunt, sed vi rapuerunt.
units.tr: that the Pope professes himself the supreme lord of benefices, the collator of all ecclesiastical benefices. His words are these: Although the full disposal of churches, personages, dignities and other ecclesiastical benefices is said by right to belong to the Roman Pontiff, so that he can not only confer them when they fall vacant, but also grant a right in them to those who will become vacant; nevertheless the collation, and so on. Following him, Boniface VIII, chapter "si Papa", On Privileges, in the Sixth book, and Clement V, Clementines, "Si duobus", On pending matters, claim the same power for themselves in plain words. Gerson, On the Spiritual Life, lesson 3, says that this power belongs to them not by divine but by canon law, since the older canons make only the bishops, each in his own diocese, the true and lawful collators of benefices. This monster, therefore, those two first Clements and Boniface VIII brought forth, and the power which neither Christ, nor the Apostles, nor the Church ever gave them, they did not take by price but seized by force.

units.la: LXXXIII. Nihil dicam de gravi controversia illa, quam Gregorius VII. aliique Pontifices Principibus moverunt circa investituras, quas, Ecclesiâ bonis temporalibus, imò etiam Regalibus, jurisdictionibus & feudis secularibus ditatâ, peculiares quasdam sibi merito reservârunt; quas tamen ad sola temporalia illi extenderunt, nunquam sacri ministerii ipsius collationem tentantes vel ambientes, contenti ad summum consensu in electum, & approbatione ejusdem. Vera enim & propria beneficii ecclesiastici collatio est, cùm quis ad sacrum ministerium applicatur, cui necessaria vitæ subsidia consequenter ex bonis Ecclesiæ decernuntur, quam Principes non affectârunt. Sed Papæ post Gregorium VII. ab omni prorsus cura temporalium etiam, & in Regalio jure Vasallagii Principes amovere, eaque diris modis spoliare conati sunt, ut fe supremos & absolutos rerum temporalium Dominos efficerent; aspersa repugnantibus Simoniacæ labis hæresi, quâ ipsimet toti incøcti erant, quia spiritualium prætextu rerum merè temporalium dominium impiè affectârunt.
units.tr: LXXXIII. I will say nothing of that grave controversy which Gregory VII and other Popes raised with princes concerning investitures, which they rightly reserved for themselves in certain special ways, since the Church was enriched with temporal goods, indeed even with royal rights, jurisdictions and secular fiefs. Yet they extended these claims only to temporal matters, never attempting or seeking the conferral of the sacred ministry itself, content at most with the consent to the person elected and approval of him. For the true and proper collation of an ecclesiastical benefice occurs when someone is assigned to the sacred ministry, to whom the necessary means of life are consequently assigned from the goods of the Church; this the princes did not aim at. But after Gregory VII the Popes tried entirely to remove princes from every care of temporal affairs, even in the regalian right of vassalage, and to strip them of these by dreadful means, so that they might make themselves supreme and absolute lords of temporal things. They fastened on their opponents the heresy of the Simoniacal stain, by which they themselves were wholly infected, because under the pretext of spiritual things they impiously sought dominion over merely temporal things.

units.la: LXXXIV. Accidit etiam, ut certis occasionibus clerici à suis, in quibus primùm ordinati erant ecclesiis, vel recedentes vel expulsi, Romanam Ecclesiam, tanquam toto Orbe celeberrimam, adirent, & ejus intercessione vel Episcopis propriis reconciliarentur. Quibus facilè Pontifices annuerunt. Ita Gregorius M. lib.iy. Ind. 12. ep.14. Felicem quendam Diaconum Episcopo Syracusano: alii alios commendárunt. Commendationi mox juncta sunt imperia: Demùm præceptum & imperium merum & ordinarium de providendo in vacaturis: quæ fuerunt gratiæ Exspectativarum, per quas Papa, aliique, munera nondum vacantia exspectanda, quibus placuit, etiam infantibus & pueris in longa arundine equitantibus, non tamen sine interveniente pretio, assignárunt. Quæ infamis Curiæ Romanæ mercatura erat, quando, uti Cardinalis Cusanus de Concord. Cath. lib. ÿ. 40. queritur, propter eas omnis sudor parentum per filios ad Curiam deferebatur. Neque tamen sic Pontifices se gesserunt collatores, sed precatores, non tamen sine præcepto. Namque
units.tr: LXXXIV. It also happened that, on certain occasions, clerics who had either withdrawn or been expelled from the churches in which they were first ordained went to the Roman Church, as the most famous in the whole world, and were reconciled through its intercession either to their own bishops. The Popes readily agreed to this. Thus Gregory the Great, book 4, indiction 12, letter 14, to the bishop of Syracuse on behalf of a certain deacon named Felix; others recommended others. Commendation was soon joined with commands. At last there arose a precept and an absolute and ordinary command about providing for vacancies, which were the graces of expectatives, by which the Pope and others assigned, to whomever they pleased, offices not yet vacant to be awaited, even to infants and boys riding on a long cane, yet not without a price intervening. This was the infamous trade of the Roman Curia, when, as Cardinal Cusanus complains in On Catholic Concord, book 3, 40, because of them all the sweat of parents was carried to the Curia through their sons. Yet the Popes did not conduct themselves as collators in this way, but as petitioners, though not without a command. For
It is a request, the violent face of a Pope commanding.

units.la: Collatores manebant ordinarii, sed non sine præjudicio & gravamine, donec à precibus, commendationibus, præceptis ad vim apertam deventum est, datis executoribus, qui ordinarios repugnantes cogerent, vel ipsi conferrent. Maximas deinceps Exspectativæ gratiæ in Ecclesia turbas dederunt, adeò ut Concilium Basileense Seff. 31. necesse habuerit statuere, ut Pontifex eas deinceps gratias Exspectativas, aut Nominationes, nullo modo, nullave ex ex causa concedat, cùm ipse præ cæteris, ne sit occasio tantorum Ecclesiæ malorum, abstinere debeat. Hoc decretum Pragmatica in Gallia sanctio confirmavit, totiusque Ecclesiæ clamor tandem effecit, ut in Concilio Tridentino Sess. xxiv. cap. 19. Exspectativæ è medio tollerentur. Cesserunt sic gratiæ Exspectativæ, sed nomine tenus. Nam earum locum subiverunt Coadjutoriæ fine causa cum futura successione, quæ ipsissimæ Exspectativæ sunt.
units.tr: The ordinary collators remained, but not without prejudice and burden. Then, from requests, recommendations and commands, they came to open force, with executors appointed who would compel the resisting ordinaries or confer the benefices themselves. Expectative graces afterwards caused the greatest disturbances in the Church, so much so that the Council of Basel (Sess. 31.) found it necessary to decree that the Pope should not thereafter grant expectative graces or nominations in any way or for any cause, since he himself, above all others, ought to abstain, so that there be no occasion for such great evils to the Church. The Pragmatic Sanction in France confirmed this decree, and the outcry of the whole Church at last brought it about that at the Council of Trent (Sess. xxiv. cap. 19) expectatives were abolished. Expectative graces thus ceased, but only in name. For their place was taken by Coadjutorships without cause, with future succession, which are the very same thing as expectatives.
LXXXV. Reservations are closely akin to expectatives

units.la: beneficiorum vacantium, quæ unà cum illis, uti Gomesius Tract. de Grat. Expect. n. 7. scribit, ceperunt in Palatio Romano audiri, & earum materia foveri, quod expertum sit, habere illam in se lac, lanam, pelles, & carnes, id est, abundantiam temporalem, & ubi causidici Romani perceperunt plus lucri ex illa quæri, quàm ex qualibet alia, studium longè majus in ea posuerunt addiscenda, quàm in materia de pœnitentia & similibus. Primus Innocentius III. nepotem quendam subdiaconi cujuspiam sui apud sedem Apostolicam defuncti, de patrui sui præbenda in Ecclesia Cremonensi, facta libera collatione, providit. Inde Clemens III. alias IV. præmissa declaratione supremæ suæ in beneficia potestatis, prætextúque usus, quòd sedis Apostolicæ sit providere, ne ullis Ecclesiis idonei Pastores desint, primam beneficiorum generalem reservationem fecit, qua, uti C. licet Ecclesiarum de præb. & dign. in 6. habetur, decrevit, ut beneficia omnia in Curia vacantia, ad liberam Papæ collationem pertinerent. Quam reservationem post Bonifacius VIII. innovavit, & extra Curiam ad loca propinqua extendit: Johannes XXII. ampliavit, & ad omnia beneficia, quæ vacarent ex pluralitate non omissa, extendit, & fructus sede vacante collectos Camerae Apostolicae consecravit. Benedictus XII. omnibus curialium beneficiis Sedi Apostolicæ reservatis, probavit, donec regulæ Cancellariæ 1.2. 3-8. tantas reservationes fecerunt, ut præter indigitatas illas generales ad collationem Papæ paulatim reductæ sint Cathedrales omnes, ac Monasteria, & omnia beneficia Cardinalium & eorum familiarium, collectorum, & subcollectorum, cubiculariorum, cursorum, ac generalissimè, quæcunque alia beneficia ubique terrarum octo anni mensibus vacant, vel ex gratia concessa alternatio Episcopis, ut ad summum sex certis mensibus vacantia ab ipsis conferantur, si ipsi sint illorum locorum ordinarii collatores & resideant. Præterea, quæcunque conferuntur ab ordinariis, non servatâ formâ Concilii Tridentini ad sedem trahuntur Apostolicam, ut ab eo conferantur. Pius etiam IV. reservavit omnia beneficia vacantia ex collatione Simoniaca: Pius V. omnia beneficia propter crimen hæreseos vacantia: Gregorius XIII. beneficia quæ dantur personis propter genus, vel suspicionem hæresis, prohibitis. Sicut autem Exspectativas, ita etiam Reservationes Concilium Basileense Sess. 23. & 31. compescere statuit, statuens Reservationes etiam particulares, quæcunque fuerint beneficiorum vacaturorum, tam per Romanos Pontifices, quàm per Legatos Sedis Apostolicæ, de cætero nullæ sint ipso facto. Indulget tamen Pontifici, ut unum beneficium reservare possit, ubi decem sunt; & duo, ubi sunt quinquaginta. Basileense Concilium secuta Ecclesia Gallicana, habito conventu generali Bituricensi, Clero & populo omni consentiente, ipsoque Rege subscribente, Pragmatica Sanctione A. MCCCCXXXVIII. confirmata, Reservationes, ex quibus à Regno Galliæ ingens pecuniæ vis quotannis Romam defluxit, sustulit, frustrà Pio II. Sixto IV. & Julio IV. annitentibus, ut sanctio illa aboleatur; donec Leo X. opportunitatem nactus cum Francisco I. Concordata inivit, quibus magna licet Sanctionis illius parte mutata, Exspectativæ tamen & Reservationes generales, tribus illis exceptis, quæ sunt in corpore juris, uti statuta Basileensia præceperant, & Pragmatica sanctio continebat, in Regno eo sublatæ sunt. Quod verò sic Regno Galliæ concessit, cur reliquis Ecclesiis, quas captivas adhuc retinet, non æquè concedat, ipse viderit, inprimis cum concordato illo haud obscurè fateri coactus sit, collationem beneficiorum ad se jure non pertinere. Alias enim haud dubiè jus sibi integrum mordicùs, facto licet concessìo, retinuisset.
units.tr: of vacant benefices. Together with these, as Gomesius writes (Tract. de Grat. Expect. n. 7.), they began to be heard of in the Roman palace, and their subject matter to be cherished, because it has been found to contain milk, wool, skins and flesh, that is, temporal abundance. And when the Roman lawyers saw that more profit was to be gained from them than from any other matter, they applied themselves to learning it with far greater zeal than to the matter of repentance and the like. Innocent III was the first who, by a free collation, provided a certain nephew of a subdeacon of his, who had died at the Apostolic See, to his uncle's prebend in the Church of Cremona. Then Clement III (alias IV), after declaring his supreme power over benefices, and under the pretext of the custom that it belongs to the Apostolic See to provide that no churches lack suitable ministers, made the first general reservation of benefices. By it, as is contained in C. licet Ecclesiarum de præb. & dign. in 6., he decreed that all benefices falling vacant in the Curia should belong to the free collation of the Pope. Boniface VIII afterwards renewed this reservation and extended it to places nearby outside the Curia. John XXII enlarged it and extended it to all benefices that fell vacant through a pluralism not given up, and he consecrated to the Apostolic Chamber the fruits collected while the see was vacant. Benedict XII approved the reservation of all benefices of the curial officials to the Apostolic See, until the rules of the Chancery (1.2. 3-8.) made so many reservations that, besides those general ones already indicated, there were gradually brought back to the Pope's collation all cathedrals and monasteries, and all benefices of the Cardinals and their household, of the collectors and sub-collectors, of the chamberlains, couriers, and, most generally, whatever other benefices anywhere in the world fall vacant in the eight months of the year, or, by a granted alternation, the benefices that fall vacant in six fixed months are conferred by the bishops themselves, if they are the ordinary collators of those places and reside there. Moreover, whatever is conferred by the ordinaries without observing the form of the Council of Trent is drawn to the Apostolic See, to be conferred by it. Pius IV reserved all benefices falling vacant through simoniacal collation; Pius V all benefices vacant on account of the crime of heresy; Gregory XIII prohibited benefices given to persons on account of birth or suspicion of heresy. But just as the Council of Basel (Sess. 23. & 31.) decided to curb expectatives, so it also curbed reservations, decreeing that reservations, even particular ones, of whatever benefices are to fall vacant, whether made by the Roman Pontiffs or by the Legates of the Apostolic See, shall from now on be null by the very fact. Nevertheless, it allowed the Pope to reserve one benefice where there are ten, and two where there are fifty. Following the Council of Basel, the Gallican Church, after a general assembly at Bourges, with the whole clergy and people consenting and the King himself subscribing, confirmed by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1438, abolished the reservations, by which a huge sum of money flowed every year from the kingdom of France to Rome. Pius II, Sixtus IV and Julius II strove in vain to have that sanction annulled, until Leo X, finding an opportunity, entered into the Concordats with Francis I. By these, although a large part of that sanction was altered, the expectatives and general reservations were nevertheless abolished in that kingdom, except for those three which are in the body of the law, as the Basel statutes had prescribed and the Pragmatic Sanction contained. Why he should not grant the same to the other churches, which he still holds captive, that he himself must judge, especially since by that concordat he was compelled to admit fairly plainly that the collation of benefices does not belong to him by right. Otherwise, no doubt, he would have stubbornly kept his whole right, even though he had made the concession.

units.la: LXXXVI. Tot reservationibus contra omne jus Divinum & humanum usurpatis non contenta Romana Curia, Pluralitates etiam & Uniones beneficiorum introduxit. Satis equidem, ut paulò altius rem repetamus, constat, initio Ecclesiæ bona Ecclesiastica spectâsse ad omnes, & ex communi massa sumtum, quantum ad victum & amictum pauperum ac ministrorum Ecclesiæ sufficeret. Dein unica illa massa in quatuor partes distributa est, quarum infima pauperibus cessit. Quæ massæ unius separatio, dissectio, appropriatio, & beneficiorum institutio seculo inprimis duodecimo cum maxima disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ relaxatione, obtinuit. Mox exclusò ab Ecclesia populo, & solo clero illud sibi nomen vendicante, & usufructus, & dominium cessit in paucos, quod prius erat omnium, & quæ prius à cura spirituali ministeria vocabantur, & sæcularia inprimis spectare, & beneficia nominari coeperunt. Vigentibus tamen adhuc antiquis canonibus, quibus non licebat unum in duos titulos ordinari, nemo unus nisi unicum beneficium obtinere poterat. Attritis deinceps per varias bellorum calamitates bonis ecclesiasticis, ut ad ministrorum victum ægrè sufficerent, factum est, ut beneficium conferretur in cum, qui jam aliud obtinebat, dummodò utrique Ecclesiæ satis prospiceret, necessitate urgente, idqúe non tam in gratiam Ministri, quàm Ecclesiæ, Ministro proprio destitutæ. Hoc deinceps colore itum est ad plura beneficia, etiam non postulante necessitate uni conferendo, tandémque positâ pedetentim larvâ, puditum non est in gratiam Ministri, seu Sacerdotis facere, quod antè fiebat bono Ecclesiæ, adhibita tamen ad sucum populo faciendum, tum distinctione inter beneficia incompatibilia, quæ residentiam postulabant, & compatibilia, quæ eam non postulabant, quæ & seorsim, & simul cum aliis retineri poterant: tum glossa illa Canonistarum, plura uni beneficia deferenda non esse, nisi quando unum Ministro alendo non sufficit. Quantum autem satis esset uni, longo pede metiri soliti, non personam, sed qualitatem personæ, consanguineorum familiam, equos, famulos, statum &c. respexerunt. Neque credibile est, quàm larga manu Episcopo portionem suam assignárint Pontifices, ut dignitatem & pompam suam sa-tis tueri possent. Cardinalibus verò, quos Regibus Curia Romana æquiparat, nullus apparatus aut reditus nimius videbatur, nisi qui Regium superaret. Consuetudine, quæ tyrannus est, sic invalescente, Pontifices Romani sibi solis reservárunt potestatem dispensandi de bonis incompatibilibus, & cœteris etiam, ut plura duobus beneficiis, unus obtinere posset. Cùmque nimiùm abusus illi in Ecclesia jam grassarentur, Pontifices, Innocentius III. in Concilio Lateranensi, Gregorius X. Bonifacius VIII. Clemens V. Johannes XXII. ipsúmque Concilium Tridentinum Sess. vÿ. cap. 4. & xxiv. cap. 17. eos coërcuerunt; sed verborum potiùs forma, quàm vi ulla. Omnes enim prohibitiones hæ per Romanas dispensationes, & repagulum clausulæ illius, Non obstantibus, quas Tridentini Patres, Præsulibus nonnullis adnitentibus licet, abolere non potuerunt, nec non per restrictiones ationes ipsis Præsulibus relictas elusæ, irritæque redditæ sunt.
units.tr: LXXXVI. Not content with so many reservations usurped against all divine and human law, the Roman Curia also introduced pluralities and unions of benefices. To go back a little further in the matter, it is certainly established that at the beginning of the Church the ecclesiastical goods belonged to all, and that from a common fund was taken as much as sufficed for the food and clothing of the poor and of the ministers of the Church. Then that single fund was divided into four parts, the lowest of which went to the poor. This separation, division, appropriation of the single fund, and the institution of benefices took hold especially in the twelfth century, together with a very great relaxation of church discipline. Soon the people were shut out of the Church, and the clergy alone claimed that name for themselves, and both the usufruct and the ownership passed to a few what had previously belonged to all. Those things which had earlier been called ministries from spiritual care, and which chiefly concerned secular matters, began to be called benefices. Yet while the ancient canons were still in force, by which it was not lawful for one man to be ordained to two titles, no one could hold more than one benefice. Afterwards, as the ecclesiastical goods were worn down by the various calamities of war, so that they scarcely sufficed for the food of ministers, it came about that a benefice was conferred on one who already held another, provided that both churches were adequately provided for, when necessity pressed, and this not so much for the sake of the minister as of the Church, which lacked its own minister. Under this colour they went on to confer several benefices on one man, even when necessity did not demand it. At last, the mask being gradually laid aside, they were not ashamed to do for the sake of the minister or priest what had earlier been done for the good of the Church. Yet to deceive the people they employed a distinction between incompatible benefices, which required residence, and compatible ones, which did not require it and could be held both separately and together with others; and that gloss of the canonists, that several benefices should not be conferred on one man, unless one is not enough to support the minister. But as to how much would suffice for one man, which they were accustomed to measure with a long foot, they regarded not the person but the quality of the person: his family of relatives, horses, servants, rank, and so on. Nor is it credible with what a generous hand the Popes assigned a bishop his portion, so that he could sufficiently maintain his dignity and pomp. But for Cardinals, whom the Roman Curia equates with kings, no equipage or income seemed excessive unless it surpassed that of a king. Custom, which is a tyrant, thus gaining strength, the Roman Popes reserved to themselves alone the power of dispensing concerning incompatible benefices, and the others as well, so that one man might hold more than two benefices. And when those abuses were already running riot in the Church, the Popes Innocent III at the Lateran Council, Gregory X, Boniface VIII, Clement V, John XXII, and the Council of Trent itself (Sess. vÿ. cap. 4. & xxiv. cap. 17.) restrained them, but by the form of words rather than by any force. For all these prohibitions were evaded through Roman dispensations and that barrier of the clause Non obstantibus (notwithstanding), which the Fathers of Trent, although some bishops urged them, could not abolish; and they were also rendered vain and void through restrictions left to the bishops themselves.

units.la: - LXXXVII. Operæ pretium fuerit de hac per pluralitatem, vel nundinationem beneficiorum, in Ecclesiam introducta ἀπεξία & abominatione, querelas Gerfonis & Francisci Duareni audire. Et Gerson quidem tract. de defect. num. 49. sic scribit: Iterum ad quid expedit, aut quid utilitatis Ecclesiæ confert, tam magnifica Principum gloria, & tam superba Prælatorum & Cardinalium pompa, ut quasi se homines esse nescire faciant? Et quæ utique abominatio, quòd unus tenet ducenta, alter trecenta beneficia Ecclesiastica? Nonne inde cultus Divinus diminuitur, Ecclesiæ depauperantur, valentibus Viris & Doctoribus privantur, fidelibus mala exempla dantur? Et post num. 51. Quid est, inquit, quòd hodie unus, utinam mediocriter doctus, tenet quatuor, quinque, sex vel octo beneficia Ecclesiastica, quorum uno non est dignus, quibus octo sustentari possent, doctrinis, orationibus, & Divinis laudibus insistentes? Attendite, an potius hodiè equi, canes, aves, & superflua Ecclesiasticorum familia patrimonium Ecclesiæ comedere debeant, quàm pauperes Christi? & quàm ad Divini cultus ampliationem, & pro infidelium conversione, aut in hujusmodi pietatis operibus, modis congruis expendendum sit? In sermone coram Alexandro III. habito idem Gerson sic exclamavit: Videas alios novem ordinibus non contentos, non enim novenis beneficiis saturantur, tandiu novos hiatus pandere, quandiu vivunt; conjungere domum ad domum, agrum agro copulare, quasi in medio terræ soli habitarent; ipsum verò Propheticum. (Esai. iv. 5.) pro fabula contemnere. Videmus fere omnes summis importunitatibus in leges irruere, dum nunc petunt gratiam obtinendorum simul incompatibilium, nunc nunc in absentia posse fructus colligere, nunc ante omnes dignitate consequi, nunc ad sacros ordines non compelli, & mille alia rectis legibus vetita. Franciscus Duarenus de S. Minist. Eccl. & Benef. lib. viij. 4. sic abusum eundem detestatur: In gratiam personarum magis quàm Ecclesiæ beneficia coacervare, quamvis & genere & doctrina alios antecellant, pessimi res exempli, & antiquis canonibus omninò contraria est. Itaque gratiam horum canonum à solo Pontifice Romano, cujus voluntas pro ratione habetur, fieri posse, de mul. de Præb. & dign. constitutum est. Atque ita Canones prima specie pugnantes invicem conciliari posse videntur, quamvis alii aliter nodum dissolvant &c. Hinc fit, ut captatores beneficiorum Romam certatim cursitent, prætextu literaturæ, aut nobilitatis, veniam à Pontifice impetraturi (quæ nemini, quamlibet indigno nebulóni, modò is numeret, denegari consuevit.) Quâ ex re tanta Ecclesiæ deformatio exorta est, & propè dixerim, μανίᾳ, ut nulla vis humani ingenii ad eam dignitatem exprimendam sufficiat. Prodigiosa sanè res est in Ecclesia hæc beneficiorum cumulatio, quæ sine delectu passim recipitur: nec minùs mihi monstrosi videntur, qui tot personas in Ecclesia sustinent, quàm Briareus ille, qui centum manus habuit, at est in fabulis; aut Gerson, quem trinum fuisse corporum perhibent.
units.tr: LXXXVII. It will be worth our while to hear the complaints of Gerson and Francis Duaren about this aversion [ἀπεξία] and abomination introduced into the Church by the pluralityj or wholesale trafficking of benefices. Gerson, in tract. de defect. num. 49., writes as follows: Again, what good is it, or what benefit does it bring to the Church, that there should be such magnificent glory of princes and such proud display of prelates and cardinals, so that men seem to forget that they are men? And what abomination it is that one man holds two hundred ecclesiastical benefices and another three hundred! Does not divine worship thereby decline, do not the churches grow poor, are capable men and teachers deprived of their posts, and bad examples given to the faithful? And after num. 51: What is it, he says, that today one man, would that he were moderately learned, holds four, five, six or eight ecclesiastical benefices, of which he is not worthy of one, when eight could support men devoted to teaching, prayer and divine praises? Consider whether today horses, dogs, birds and the superfluous household of the clergy ought to eat up the patrimony of the Church rather than the poor of Christ; and how it ought to be spent, by suitable means, on the enlargement of divine worship, on the conversion of unbelievers, or on works of this kind of piety.* In a sermon delivered before Alexander III, the same Gerson cried out thus: You may see others, not content with nine orders, since they are not satisfied with nine benefices, opening new gaps as long as they live, joining house to house and field to field, as if they dwelt alone in the middle of the earth; and they despise the very prophetic saying (Isai. 4.5) as a fable. We see almost everyone rushing into the laws with the greatest importunity: now they seek the grace of holding incompatible posts at once, now they seek to collect the revenues while absent, now they seek to obtain precedence over all in dignity, now they seek not to be compelled to holy orders, and a thousand other things forbidden by the sound laws. Francis Duaren, in de S. Minist. Eccl. & Benef. lib. viij. 4., denounces the same abuse in this way: To heap up benefices for the favour of persons rather than for the good of the Church, although they surpass others in birth and learning, is a most wicked example and wholly contrary to the ancient canons. Therefore it has been established that the favour of these canons can be granted only by the Roman Pontiff, whose will is taken as the rule. And so the canons, which seem at first sight to conflict with one another, can seem to be reconciled, although others loosen the knot in other ways, etc. Hence it comes about that those who hunt after benefices rush eagerly to Rome, under the pretext of learning or nobility, intending to obtain a dispensation from the Pontiff (which is usually refused to no one, however unworthy a scoundrel he may be, provided he pays the price). From this matter such a great deformation of the Church has arisen, and I would almost say madness [μανίᾳ], that no power of human wit is sufficient to express it. Truly this accumulation of benefices in the Church, which is received everywhere without any discrimination, is a monstrous thing; and those who sustain so many persons in the Church seem to me no less monstrous than that Briareus who had a hundred hands, which is in the fables, or than Gerson, whom they report to have been three-bodied.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Ad pluralitatem hanc beneficiorum paliandam via facta est Commendis, novo Babylonicarum technarum generi. Olim quidem bello, pestilentia, aut alia causa sic per regionem aliquam grassante, ut in Ministri vitâ functi locum alius statim eligi non posset, is, penes quem regimen erat Ecclesiasticæ administrationis, vacantem Ecclesiam homini idoneo commendabat, ut præter Ecclesiæ propriæ curam vacantem etiam administraret, donec de proprio ei ministro prospiceretur.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. A way has been opened to cover up this plurality of benefices by commendams, a new kind of Babylonian contrivance. Formerly, when war, pestilence or some other cause raged through a region in such a way that a minister who had died could not at once be replaced, the one who held the government of the ecclesiastical administration commended the vacant church to a suitable man, so that he might administer it, in addition to the care of his own church, until a minister of its own could be provided for it.

units.la: Qui tamen men non aliam in Ecclesiæ facultates potestatem exercebant, quàm ut eas ritè gubernaret & conservaret. Procedente tempore commendatarii necessitatem vel honestatem prætexentes, fructus occupárunt, utque diutiùs iis fruerentur, varia impedimenta, quominùs Ecclesiæ aliter prospiceretur, objectárunt. Cui malo ut iretur obviam, sancitum est, ne commoda ultrà sex mensfes durarent. Pontificibus verò visum ex plenitudine potestatis, multò longiori tempore ejusmodi Ecclesias commendare, tandémque eò deventum, ut commendatio ad finem usque vitæ duraret, & ut præter impensas necessarias emolumentis omnibus utendi, fruendi, facultas esset.
