Sic, quod necessitas & usus introduxit, cùm à prima institutione degenerâsset, corruptis temporibus ad pluralitatem prohibitam honesto aliquo velamine obtegendam adhibitum est; cùm ei, qui beneficio fruebatur, aliud beneficium, aut plura etiam commendarentur, servato tenore legis, ne uni personæ, nisi unicum beneficium conferretur, sed legis mente neglecta, cùm commendatarius ad vitam usque ab eo, qui cum titulo possidebat, solo nomine, non re differret. Et in immenso illo beneficiorum commendatorum numero adeò fœdè turpitérque ab officii tramite exorbitatum est, ut A. MDXXXV. ipso Reformationis tempore, Clemens VII. non erubuerit Hippolyto Medicæo Cardinali, Nepoti suo, omnia per totum orbem beneficia Regularia & Secularia, dignitates & rectoratus, simplicia & curata vacantia, commendare spatio sex mensium, ab eo die, quo in possessionem eorum mittendus esset, computandorum, cum plena potestate de fructibus omnium arbitratu suo disponendi, eòsque in usum suum liberrimè convertendi. De eo iterum Franciscum Duarenum audiamus, sic de S. Eccl. Min. & Beneficib. v. 8. quiritantem: Nam quibus per Canones non licet praefici Ecclesiis aut Monasteriis, moribus comparatum est, ut eisdem Ecclesiae vel Monasteria in perpetuum, & quandiu vivunt, commendentur. Atque ita concipitur formula huius commendationis in diplomatibus Pontificiis, ut libera non solum dispensatio rerum, sed etiam consumtio atque dissipatio ipsis permissa intelligatur. Et sane mirum est, homines ingeniosos, qui fucum hunc commenti sunt, tantae corruptelae non alium colorem quaesivisse, ne tam aperte despici canones, & palam ludibrio haberi viderentur: quasi vero consilium eorum non cuivis notum, perspectumque sit, qui hac arte & impostura corruptelam omnium, quae unquam in Ecclesiam irrepserunt, maximam tueri & adumbrare conantur, qui verbis decoris obvolvunt vitium. Haec ille.
units.tr: Yet those who were so commended did not exercise any power over the church's goods other than to govern and preserve them properly. As time went on, the commendatories, pretending necessity or propriety, seized the revenues, and, so that they might enjoy them longer, they raised various obstacles to the church being otherwise provided for. To meet this evil, it was enacted that commendations should not last longer than six months. But the Pontiffs, by the fullness of their power, judged it right to commend such churches for a much longer time, and at last it came to this: that the commendation lasted until the end of a man's life, and that, apart from the necessary expenses, he had the power of using and enjoying all the revenues. Thus what necessity and custom had introduced, once it had degenerated from its first institution, was, as the times grew corrupt, employed under some honest veil to cover up the forbidden plurality: although another benefice, or even several, was commended to the one who already enjoyed a benefice, the letter of the law being kept, that no single person should be given more than one benefice, but the mind of the law being neglected, since the commendatory differed from the one who held the benefice by title for life only in name, not in fact. And in that immense number of commended benefices things went so foully and shamefully off the path of duty that in MDXXXV, in the very time of the Reformation, Clement VII did not blush to commend to his nephew, Cardinal Hippolytus de' Medici, all the regular and secular benefices, dignities and rectorships, simple and cure-bearing, that were vacant throughout the whole world, for a period of six months, to be counted from the day on which he was to be put into possession of them, with full power to dispose of the fruits of all of them at his own discretion, and to convert them most freely to his own use. Let us hear Francis Duaren complaining about this again, in de S. Eccl. Min. & Beneficib. v. 8.: For it has become the custom that those who by the canons may not be set over churches or monasteries are commended to those same churches or monasteries in perpetuity, or as long as they live. And the formula of this commendation in the papal documents is so framed that it is understood to permit not only the free disposal of the goods but also their consumption and squandering. And indeed it is remarkable that clever men who devised this pretence did not seek some other colour for so great a corruption, lest the canons should seem so openly despised and made a laughing-stock; as if their purpose were not known and clearly seen by everyone, since by this art and imposture they try to protect and shade over the greatest corruption that has ever crept into the Church, covering the vice with words of decency. So he;

units.la: LXXXIX. Eidem beneficiorum pluralitati, fuco quodam tegendae, inventa earundem Unio est.
units.tr: LXXXIX. The union of benefices, which is a kind of paint to conceal the same plurality of benefices, was also devised.

units.la: Haec quoque antiquitus bono fine usurpata est, uti quidem ex Concilio Toletano XVI. 10. q. 3. cap. Unio liquet, ubi decretum est, ut Ecclesia, quae usque ad decem mancipia habuerit, supra se sacerdotem habeat: quae vero minus decem, alii conjungantur Ecclesiae. Inprimis ejus usus tum erat, quando Ecclesia aliqua vel eversa, vel obventionibus suis privata, quod erat reliquum, ad vicinum beneficium una cum onere transferebatur, ut ex duobus unicum conflaretur. Coeterum, Curialium industria factum est, ut cessante ejusmodi necessitate, plura in unum beneficia conjungerentur; cujus collatione pluralitas tegi poterat, si forte in gratiam Cardinalis, aut viri cujuspiam illustris triginta vel quadraginta beneficia, etiam in diversis orbis Christiani locis sita unirentur. Quia tamen incommodum, & Curiae ac Cancellariae ipsi noxium visum est, sic beneficia imminui, & uni factam gratiam cum multis succedentibus gratiam illam nec meritis, nec pofcen-
units.tr: This too was once put to a good use, as is clear from the Council of Toledo, 10 q. 3, cap. Unio, where it was decreed that a church which had as many as ten dependants should have a priest over it, but those with fewer than ten should be joined to other churches. At first its use was chiefly when a church had either been destroyed or stripped of its revenues, and what remained was transferred, together with its burden, to a neighbouring benefice, so that two were made into one. Afterwards, however, through the cleverness of the Curialists, it came about that, once such necessity had ceased, several benefices were joined together. By this conferral plurality could be concealed, if, for example, for the favour of a Cardinal or some illustrious man, thirty or forty benefices, even those situated in different parts of the Christian world, were united. But since this seemed inconvenient and harmful to the Curia and to the Chancery itself, that benefices should be diminished in this way, and that the favour shown to one man should, together with that favour, be passed on to many successors who deserved neither merit nor asked for it, a remedy was found against this evil, by the subtle and crafty ingenuity of uniting into one body as many benefices as the Pope thought fitting. And this was to last only as long as the life of the person to whom it was conferred; at his death the union was to be dissolved by the fact itself, and the benefices were understood to be restored to their former state.

units.la: per Unionem beneficiorum. scentibus, communicari; huic malo obviam irum est subtili & arguta folertia uniendi in unum corpus, quot beneficia Papæ æquum videretur; idque durante solummodò ejus, in quem conferebatur, vita, cujus obitu Unio illa ipso facto soluta, & beneficia in pristinum statum restituta intelligerentur. Hac inventionum via, argutiis Simoniacis aditus patefactus est, collato in speciem unico beneficio, sed quod reapse plura, & quandoque innumera secum traheret, quo, quicunque gauderet, verba S. Polani Hist. C. T. lib. y. p. 225. refero, poterat ad eundem modum peccata sua confiteri, quo is, qui sacerdoti fassus, se furto abstulisse frænum equi, reticuit interim, fræno huic alligatum fuisse caballum.
units.tr: (by the union of benefices.) By this way of inventing, a path was opened to Simoniacal tricks: a single benefice was conferred in appearance, but in fact it carried several with it, and sometimes innumerable ones, so that whoever enjoyed it (I cite the words of S. Polanus, Hist. C. T. lib. 7, p. 225) could confess his sins in the same way as the man who, having told the priest that he had stolen a bridle from a horse, kept quiet meanwhile that the horse was tied to this bridle.

units.la: XC. Taceo Permutationes beneficiorum, quàs omnes Ordinariis surreptas, Romana Curia ad se pertraxit; nec non Devolutiones collationis beneficiorum. Veluti si conferatur beneficium nondum legitimam ætatem habenti, si indigno, si electio, vel collatio ultrà tres, vel in minoribus beneficiis ultrà sex menses differatur. His enim casibus devolvitur collatio ad superiorem, & tandem ad Papam. Taceo denique Pensiones maximas, quas Papa vel Episcopi Cardinalibus, Curialibus, amicis, propinquis, absque ullo merito, ministerio, onere, sive spirituali sive temporali, solo favore erga personam, & prætextu falso meritorum, quæ nulla sunt, vel inopiæ, vel infirmæ valetudinis largiuntur. Quas quidem iniquissimas esse, ipsimet Canonistæ, aliàs pronuntiantes, quòd Papa, cùm sit D. Dominus omnium beneficiorum, assignare possit pensiones, cuicunque placuerit, etiam sine causa, fateri quandoque cogantur. Gygas enim, aliique apud eum Datores de Pens. q. 96. asserunt, earum artem esse contra regularem juris dispositionem, cùm ex illis detur scissio in beneficiis. Nihil etenim, inquiunt, est pensio aliud, quàm certa portio ex beneficio separata ad tempus; & imponere pensionem beneficio, est illi servitutem injungere: & pensio est plaga fœtida ex percussione nervi ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ similitudinarie inflicta. Et: Pensionis inflictio est odiosa, quia est contra charitatem. Nam qui non servit altari, non debet de altari vivere. Et sub titulo privilegiorum pensionis numerat Paulus de Roma ibidem absurda turpissima. Primum est, inquit, quòd pensio est beneficium sine obligatione Ecclesiastici Ordinis. Secundò, quòd in pensione gratia in debitum reputatur, contra illud Pauli; quia nimirum Papa & Cardinales hujusmodi pensionibus suis Curialibus servitutis sibi præstitæ stipendia debita solvunt, & mercedes, & miser beneficiarius, quod ex gratia & eleemosyna solvere solet, cogitur ex debito solvere. Tertiò, quia Pensionarius fructus beneficii sine labore manducat, contra sententiam Apostoli. Quartò, quia Pensionarius frangit justitiæ æqualitatem. Honores etenim & commoda dividi debent secundum qualitates laborum. Quintò, quia pensio est præmium sine opere, quia qui non servit altari, inde vivere non debet, nec præmium consequi; & Bovi trituranti os alligatur. Sextò, quòd pensio sit seges sine vomere & aratro, & messis sine semine, quia Pensionarius metit, ubi non seminavit. Septimò, quia pensio est merces sine custodia, ad quam Pastor de jure tenetur. Octavò, quia est beneficium, sine onere, & est medulla tritici, & adeps frumenti, butyrum de armento, lac de ovibus, meracissimus sanguis, mel de petra, oleum de saxo durissimo, videlicet de Patrimonio Christi. Hæc illi, simul flantes, veritatem vel invito pectore propalantes; simul sorbentes, vomitum scilicet illum suum, quo Papæ, ceu supremo omnium beneficiorum Domino, liberóque collatori, assentati priùs fuerant.
units.tr: XC. I pass over the exchanges of benefices, which the Roman Curia drew to itself, having snatched them from all the ordinaries, and likewise the devolutions of the conferral of benefices: for example, if a benefice is conferred on someone who has not yet reached the lawful age, or on an unworthy person, or if the election or the conferral is postponed beyond three months, or beyond six months in the case of minor benefices. In these cases the conferral devolves to the superior, and finally to the Pope. Lastly I pass over the very large pensions which the Pope or the bishops grant to Cardinals, Curialists, friends and relatives, without any merit, ministry or burden, whether spiritual or temporal, from favour towards the person alone, and under the false pretext of merits, which do not exist, or of poverty or ill health. Indeed the canonists themselves, who elsewhere declare that the Pope, since he is the lord of all benefices, can assign pensions to whomever he pleases, even without cause, are sometimes forced to admit that these are most unjust. For Gygas and the other Datarii with him (de Pens. q. 96) assert that this art is contrary to the regular disposition of the law, since by means of pensions a splitting of benefices is brought about. For a pension, they say, is nothing other than a fixed portion separated from a benefice for a time; and to impose a pension on a benefice is to impose servitude on it; and a pension is a foul wound, inflicted as it were by a blow to the nerve of ecclesiastical discipline. And: the imposition of a pension is hateful, because it is contrary to charity. For he who does not serve the altar ought not to live from the altar. And under the heading of the privileges of pensions Paulus de Roma enumerates, in the same place, most absurd and shameful points: The first, he says, is that a pension is a benefice without any obligation of the ecclesiastical order. Second, that in a pension grace is reckoned as a debt, contrary to what Paul says; for the Pope and the Cardinals pay to their Curialists, by means of such pensions, wages and rewards owed for the service rendered to them, and the wretched beneficiary is compelled to pay as a debt what he is accustomed to pay out of grace and alms. Third, because the pensioner eats the fruits of the benefice without labour, contrary to the saying of the Apostle. Fourth, because the pensioner breaks the equality of justice; for honours and advantages ought to be divided according to the quality of the labours. Fifth, because a pension is a reward without work, since he who does not serve the altar ought not to live from it nor receive a reward; and it is like tying up the mouth of the ox that treads out the corn. Sixth, that a pension is a crop without the plough and the ploughshare, and a harvest without seed, because the pensioner reaps where he has not sowed. Seventh, because a pension is a wage without watching, for which the minister is bound by law. Eighth, because it is a benefice without burden, and it is the marrow of wheat, the fat of corn, butter from the herd, milk from the sheep, the purest blood, honey from the rock, oil from the hardest stone, that is, from the patrimony of Christ. These are their words: blowing hard at the same time, and declaring the truth, though against their will; and at the same time swallowing up that vomit of theirs, with which they had earlier flattered the Pope, as the supreme lord and free conferrer of all benefices.

units.la: XCI. Quemadmodùm verò Simoniacæ hæ Reservationum, pluralitatem beneficiorum, commendarum, provisionum, unionum, pensionum &c. technæ Hierarchicis, Papæ inprimis ad extollendum in immensum Cardinalium suorum statum, amplificandámque Ministrorum, Clientum, Nepotum fortunam, denique locupletandum ærarium succesirint, longo equidem sermone exponere possemus. Dicemus pauca, primò de Cardinalibus. Illi primò meri Ecclesiæ Romanæ Diaconi, paulatim eò surrexerunt, ut ex iis sex essent Episcopi, reliqui Presbyteri aut Diaconi, pro arbitrio Papæ nunc plures, nunc pauciores. Ad annum tamen usque millesimum ducentesimum plerunque Ecclesiis suis aderant, & munus suum locúmque retinuerant, & quamdiu veteres canones viguerunt, quòd unicus homo non nisi uno sacerdotio potiri possit, nemo simul Cardinalis Presbyter urbis Romæ, simul Episcopus alterius Ecclesiæ esse poterat. Sed conculcato à Pontifice Imperatore, & sede sua maximum in terris fastigium evecta, Cardinalium simul ab eo exaltatam esse mirificè Majestatem, suprà, & in Historia Papatûs ostendimus. Id tamen fieri, nisi Simoniacis stratagematis non poterat. Amplissimos ergò Dicœcesium & Provinciarum maximarum Præsules delegit, Eboracensem puta, & Cantuariensem, Angliæ; Rhemensem, & Rhodum, Galliæ; Toletanum, Hispaniæ; Lisbonensem, Portugalliæ; Mediolanensem, Ravennatem, Venetum, Italiæ; Moguntinum, Trevirensem, Colonien-sem, Germaniæ; Pragensem, Bohemiæ; Cracovien-sem, Poloniæ; Strigoniensem, Hungariæ; itemque cœteros eximos per universam Christianam Rempublicam Antistites; qui ipsi Presbyteri Cardinales, Cardinalésque Diaconi fieri possent. Neque ita eos solebat instituere, ut Episcopatu suo cederent quò alii in eorum loca subrogati, munere illo defungerentur, & ipsi curæ Gar-
units.tr: XCI. Indeed, how these Simoniacal arts, the reservations, plurality of benefices, commendams, provisions, unions, pensions &c., served the hierarchs, chiefly the Pope, to raise immensely the state of his Cardinals, to enlarge the fortunes of his ministers, clients and nephews, and finally to enrich the treasury, we could explain at great length. We shall say a few things, first about the Cardinals. At first they were simply deacons of the Roman Church; gradually they rose so that some of them were bishops, and the rest priests or deacons, now more, now fewer, at the Pope's pleasure. Yet down to about the year 1200 they were for the most part present in their own churches, and kept their office and place; and as long as the ancient canons were in force, that one man cannot hold more than one priesthood, no one could at the same time be a Cardinal priest of the city of Rome and bishop of another church. But once the Pope had trampled on the Emperor and had raised his see to the greatest height on earth, we have shown above, and in the History of the Papacy, that the majesty of the Cardinals was exalted by him in a remarkable way. This, however, could not be done except by Simoniacal stratagems. So he chose out the most eminent prelates of the largest dioceses and provinces: for example, York and Canterbury in England; Reims and Rhodez in France; Toledo in Spain; Lisbon in Portugal; Milan, Ravenna and Venice in Italy; Mainz, Trier and Cologne in Germany; Prague in Bohemia; Kraków in Poland; Esztergom in Hungary; and likewise the other outstanding bishops throughout the whole Christian commonwealth, who might themselves become Cardinal priests and Cardinal deacons. Nor did he usually appoint them in such a way that they gave up their bishoprics so that others might be substituted in their places and discharge that office, while they themselves watched over the care of the Cardinal priesthood and deaconship at Rome. Rather, in order to protect their dignity better and to strengthen the papacy, he allowed them to hold both the episcopal and the cardinalitial honour together.

units.la: Cardinalis Presbyterii & Diaconatûs Romæ invigilarent, sed ut dignitatem suam melius tuerentur, & Papatum corroborarent, permisit, ut utroque, tum Episcopatu, tum Cardinalitio honore potirentur. Ubi ne canonem supra citatum infringere videretur Papa, decrevit, ut Episcopatu fruentes licet, non appellarentur Episcopi, sed Episcopus; si Cardinalis Diaconus eligeretur, electus Episcopus, si Cardinalis Presbyter, Administrator perpetuus sui Episcopatûs diceretur. Quomodo Thomas Wolseus, Archiepiscopus Eboracensis, Cardinalis Presbyter urbis Romanæ creatus, non amplius Archiepiscopus, sed Cardinalis Wolseus, Presbyter tituli S. Ceciliæ, & perpetuus Administrator Archiepiscopatûs Eboracensis: & Æneas Sylvius, Senensis Episcopus, ordinatus Cardinalis Diaconus, non amplius Episcopus, sed Cardinalis Sylvius, Diaconus S. Eustachii, & electus Episcopus Senensis, dici debuerunt. Quanquam pudore non nihil adhuc vetante, parcius perfugio eo usi sunt ad Clementis V. tempora usque. Is enim aditu jam patefacto audaciùs progressus est, cúmque seculi Pontifices, qui in Gallia, ut ille prius, commorati sunt, & sedem Romanam Avinione collocabant, in morem & exemplum hoc perduxerunt, adeò ut nullus deinceps ferè Cardinalis crearetur, quin Episcopatum vel in titulum, vel in commendam, vel in perpetuam administrationem haberet. His artibus multas illi Ecclesias orbárunt Episcopis, ut Romanam Ecclesiam, verbo tenus, Presbyteris & Diaconis, re autem vera Romanam Curiam opulentis & potentibus Cardinalibus ornarent. Cœterùm, cùm in hanc se salebram Pontifices conjecissent, ut sic necesse haberent providere, ne Ecclesiis idonei Pastores desint, reservárunt beneficia Ecclesiastica, quoties & quæ demumcunque vellent, eaque rapta conferendi potestate, invaserunt, ut his etiam Cardinalibus dinadinalium suorum dignitatem tutarentur. Sic plane Clemens V. novis creatis Cardinalibus, sibi beneficia Angliae vacantia, & proxime vacatura, Episcopatibus tantum & Abbatiis exceptis, reservavit, ad duorum millium marcarum summam, iisque providebat, ut duobus Cardinalibus pastoribus suis fruerentur. Id vero cum impediret Eduardus III. provisionibus ejusmodi, quae alienis distributae sunt, Ecclesiam simul & Remp. exhauriri sentiens, Clemens apud Walsingam Hist. Angl. in Eduardo III. rescripsit, aequum esse, ut creatis nuper a se Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalibus, ipsis ille secundum status sui decentiam provideret; & hoc praestitisse se quidem in elargiendis beneficiis aut vacantibus, aut vacaturis, in Anglia usque ad certam summam, duobus ex Cardinalibus, reliquis vero in aliis Regnis & partibus Christianitatis, in quibus omnibus consimilem gratiam novis Cardinalibus fecerit, nec in iis ullam rebellionem, praeter istam Angliae, audierit. Duodecim tum Cardinales Clemens legerat, ex quibus duos beneficiis duobus millibus marcarum valentibus (valor hodie tribus partibus auctior,) mactavit; adeo ut duo illi probabili conjectura centum beneficiis locupletari potuerint, priusquam annuam suam duarum millium marcarum pensionem assequerentur. Sicut autem duobus illis, ita caeteris quoque aliunde Papa providit. Ad proportionem ergo hanc si universam multitudinem, si dimidiam, si quartam partem Cardinalium revocemus, quos Clemens ejusque successores inde ab annis plus trecentis creârunt, subductis rationibus, in myriadas numerus parochiarum illarum crescet, quas illi desertas, tanquam greges Pastoribus orbatos, reliquerunt, ut Carnalium modo suorum statum nitidum satis unctumque redderent. Vix tamen haec pars est abominandae illius desolationis, quam in locis sanctis illi reposuerunt. Quasi enim tot Ecclesiarum
units.tr: Here, lest the Pope seem to break the canon cited above, he decreed that those who enjoyed the episcopate should not be called bishops, but bishop: if a Cardinal deacon was chosen, he was to be called elect bishop; if a Cardinal priest, perpetual administrator of his bishopric. Thus Thomas Wolsey, Archbishop of York, created Cardinal priest of the city of Rome, was no longer to be called archbishop, but Cardinal Wolsey, priest of the title of St Cecilia, and perpetual administrator of the archbishopric of York; and Aeneas Sylvius, Bishop of Siena, ordained Cardinal deacon, was no longer to be called bishop, but Cardinal Sylvius, deacon of St Eustace, and elect bishop of Siena. Although shame still forbade this a little, they used this refuge more sparingly down to the time of Clement V. For he, the door having now been opened, advanced more boldly; and the Pontiffs of that age, who stayed in France as he had done before, and placed the Roman see at Avignon, brought this into custom and example, so that from then on almost no Cardinal was created who did not hold a bishopric either in title, or in commendam, or in perpetual administration. By these arts they deprived many churches of their bishops, so that they might adorn the Roman Church, in word, with priests and deacons, but in fact the Roman Curia with powerful and wealthy Cardinals. However, since the Pontiffs had thrown themselves into this difficulty, they were obliged to provide so that churches should not lack suitable ministers; and so they reserved ecclesiastical benefices, whenever and whatever they wished, and seized the power of conferring them by plunder, so that they might also protect the dignity of their Cardinal nephews by these means. Thus clearly Clement V, when he created new Cardinals, reserved for them the English benefices that were vacant, and those about to become vacant, with the exception only of bishoprics and abbacies, up to the sum of two thousand marks, and provided them to those Cardinals so that two of them might enjoy their pastorates. When Edward III hindered provisions of this kind, which were distributed to foreigners, feeling that the Church and the commonwealth were being drained, Clement wrote back, as reported by Walsingham (Hist. Angl. in Eduardo III.): it is fair that he should provide for the Cardinals of the Roman Church recently created by him, according to the decency of their rank; and that he had indeed granted this in bestowing benefices, whether vacant or about to become vacant, in England up to a certain sum, for two of the Cardinals, and in the other kingdoms and parts of Christendom, in all of which he had done a similar favour for the new Cardinals, and had heard of no rebellion in them, except that one in England. Clement had then chosen twelve Cardinals, and of these he enriched two with benefices worth two thousand marks (a value now three parts greater); so that those two could, by probable conjecture, have been enriched with a hundred benefices before they received their annual pension of two thousand marks. But just as he provided for those two, so the Pope provided for the others too, from other sources. If we therefore reckon in this proportion the whole number, or half, or a quarter of the Cardinals whom Clement and his successors have created over more than three hundred years, the number of parishes, when the calculations are made, will rise to myriads, which they left desolate, like flocks bereft of shepherds, so that they might make the state of their Carnals sleek and well anointed. Yet this part of that abominable desolation which they set up in holy places is hardly the greatest. For as if the revenues of so many churches were too slender to suffice for the priests and deacons of the Roman Curia, they went on from the plurality of benefices to a plurality of bishoprics, and under the name of commendation, two, as Onuphrius on episcopal titles…

units.la: Ecclesiarum: the catchword "clesiarum" is printed at the foot right. clesiarum commoda tenuiora essent, quàm ut Presbyteris & Diaconis Romanæ Curiæ sufficerent, à beneficiorum pluralitate ad Episcopatuum pluralitatem perrexerunt, & commendandi nomine, duos, uti Onuphrius de Episcopalibus titulis & Diaconis scribit, uni Cardinali Episcopatus commiserunt, etiam tres, quandoque quatuor, quinque, sex. Sic Guicciardino Hist. Ital. lib. vj. memorante, Cardinalis Hippolitus, ille scilicet, qui fratrem suum Julium, ambobus erutis luminibus excœcavit, eò quòd puella quam adamabat, in eum magis, quàm in se amorem inclinâssset, cùm esset Diaconus S. Luciæ Romæ, & Archipresbyter S. Petri, Episcopatum Mediolanensem, & Ferrariensem simul possedit. Ex sex istis Archiepiscopatibus tres, Mediolanensis, Capuanus, & Strigoniensis singuli à se aliquot centenis milliaribus distiti: tres reliqui viciniores sibi adjacent. Si ergò Pontifices sex dioeceses Provinciasque tantis locorum intervallis disjunctas acceperunt, eásque Episcopis & Archiepiscopis orbârunt, ut unius Cardinalis Diaconi pompam eveherent, ad quam eos vastitatem & solitudinem dioeceses & provincias propinquiores, quæ commodiùs conjungi poterant, ipsas adduxisse putabimus, ut reliquos, eósque majoris dignitatis, puta Cardinales Presbyteros & Episcopos amplificarent?
units.tr: Ecclesiarum: the catchword "clesiarum" is printed at the foot right. Since the revenues of the churches were too slender to suffice for the presbyters and deacons of the Roman Curia, they moved from pluralities of benefices to pluralities of bishoprics. Under the name of commendam they committed bishoprics to one cardinal, two at a time, as Onuphrius writes in de Episcopalibus titulis & Diaconis, and sometimes three, four, five or even six. So Guicciardini relates in Hist. Ital. lib. vj. that Cardinal Hippolytus, the one who blinded his brother Giulio by gouging out both his eyes, because a girl he loved had inclined her affection towards Hippolytus rather than towards Giulio, held the archbishopric of Milan and the archbishopric of Ferrara at the same time, while he was deacon of St Lucy in Rome and archpriest of St Peter's. Of these six archbishoprics, three (Milan, Capua and Strigonium) were each several hundred miles distant from the others, and the remaining three lie closer to one another. If, then, the Popes took six dioceses and provinces separated by such great distances, and stripped them of their bishops and archbishops so that the pomp of a single cardinal deacon might be raised up, shall we suppose that they brought the nearer dioceses and provinces, which could more conveniently have been joined together, to such desolation and solitude, in order to enrich the rest, namely the cardinal presbyters and bishops, who were of greater dignity?

units.la: XCII. Cœterùm, Pontificum tribunal alii etiam canes lambebant, affines, nepotes, officiarii, famuli, clientuli, vassalli, assectæ, omníque Caterva Curiæ, qui non ex micis à Cardinalium mensis cadentibus alebantur, sed ipsi quoque & videri, & genialiter vivere gestiebant, quorum tanta multitudo fuit, quanta locustarum illarum, quæ totius Ægypti terræ superficiem operuerunt. Atque hi etiam Pastores Ecclesiarum, non qui eas pascerent, sed qui degluberent, facti sunt iisdem artibus Papalium reservationum, commendarum, provisionum, unionum, aliisque ejusmodi Ægyptiacis præstigiis. Documentum ejus rei tradit Matthæus Paris in Henrico III. Angliæ Rege, quo regnante, Pontifex unico mandato suo emisso, Episcopo Cantuariensi, Licolniensi & Sarisburiensi præcepit, ut trecentis Romanis in primis beneficiis vacantibus providerent, omni beneficiorum collatione iis interdicta, donec trecentis illis competenter provisum fuerit. Quinimò à Romanorum & Italorum, qui in Ecclesiasticas Angliæ possessiones invecti sunt, Gregorio IX. & Innocentio IV, maximè Pontificibus, adeò paucorum annorum spatio aucta est multitudo, ut cùm eorum omnium per universam Angliam jussu Regis rationes collectæ essent, summa reditum eorum inventa sit quotannis sexaginta millia marcarum; quam summam reditus annuus totius Regni Angliæ non attingebat. Quam rerum perturbationem, cùm magnoperè Rex aversaretur, nec tamen ei metu Papæ resistere auderent, Magnates & Populares Regni missa ad Innocentium IV. & Synodum Generalem Lugdunensem Epistolà, post querelam de infinito Italicorum numero, qui ditabantur in Anglia gregibus, qui neque pascebant, neque cognoscebant, neque curabant oves, sed fructus tantùm percipiebant, extra Regnum asportantes: de annuis reditibus Italorum in Anglia, qui summam sexaginta millium marcarum, & amplius confecerunt, aliis perceptionibus diversis exceptis, quas metebant, ubi sementem non percipiebant: de spe illa, quam de gravaminum istorum remedio aliquo post Innocentii creationem conceperunt, cùm jam tamen opprimantur multis modis à Legato Pontificis, qui majore potestate, quàm unquam habuit Legatus, nuper Angliam ingressus, excedens excedit; quædam beneficia jam vacantia, trigintamarcas, vel amplius annuatim valentia personis Italicis confert; quædam decedentibus prioribus, aliis
units.tr: XCII. Moreover, other dogs also licked the Pontiffs' table: relatives, nephews, officials, servants, hangers-on, vassals, dependants and the whole rabble of the Curia. These did not live on the crumbs falling from the cardinals' tables; they too longed both to be seen and to live in luxury. Their multitude was as great as that of the locusts which covered the surface of the whole land of Egypt. These also became pastors of the churches, not to feed them but to devour them, by the same arts of papal reservations, commendams, provisions, unions and other such Egyptian tricks. Matthew Paris, in the reign of Henry III, King of England, gives evidence of this. In that reign the Pontiff, by a single mandate, ordered the bishops of Canterbury, Lincoln and Salisbury to provide for three hundred Romans in the first benefices that fell vacant, all collation of benefices being forbidden to them until those three hundred had been suitably provided for. Indeed, under Gregory IX and especially Innocent IV, the number of Romans and Italians who had been brought into the ecclesiastical possessions of England grew so much in a few years that, when an account of all of them was gathered throughout England by the king's order, their annual revenues were found to amount to sixty thousand marks, a sum which the whole annual revenue of the kingdom of England did not reach. The king deeply resented this disorder, yet they did not dare to resist the Pope. So the magnates and commons of the kingdom sent a letter to Innocent IV and the General Council of Lyons. In it they complained of the infinite number of Italians who were enriched in England with flocks that they neither fed, nor knew, nor cared for, but only took the fruits, carrying them out of the kingdom; of the annual revenues of the Italians in England, which amounted to sixty thousand marks and more, apart from other receipts which they reaped where they had not sown; of the hope they had conceived of some remedy for these grievances after Innocent's election, although they were still oppressed in many ways by the Legate of the Pontiff, who, having greater power than any legate ever had, recently entered England and, exceeding his authority, goes on exceeding it; he confers on Italian persons benefices already vacant and worth thirty marks or more a year; when earlier holders die, he grants them to others

units.la: . aliis Italicis suppositis concedit; quædam cum ea vacare, contigerit, Italicis nititur assignare; immoderatas insuper a viris religiosis pensiones extorquet; & contradicentes & resistentes excommunicationis & interdicti sententiis passim supponit; post hanc inquam, querelam, Papæ supplicant humiliter, ut ad filios suos manum misericordiæ vellet extendere, & eos ab illis oneribus gravaminum & oppressionum, quæ tum Deo, tum hominibus erant detestabiles, relevare. Nuntii, per quos Epistola mittebatur, illam præsente Pontifice, generali Synodo obtulerunt, questi simul oretenus de adjectione quadam Papalibus bullis inserta, quæ dicta est (Non obstante) cujus, inquiebant illi, vi omnes illes leges & instituta Ecclesiæ perrupit, ut his conatibus suis prodesset. Quicquid enim scripto Bullæ videbatur officere, id amovere solitus est ista sua machina: (Non obstante) Ita Synodus Lateranensis sub Alexandro III. decrevit, ut non nisi uno beneficio unus potiatur, neque quisquam ullum possideret, nisi qui per se ipsum curam ejus valeat exercere. Emittit contra Bullas suas Pontifex, velut apud eundem Paris in Henrico III. A. 1231. ut quinque Romanis, nato Rumfredi, & nato talis, & talis, in singulis Ecclesiis provisum sit, unicuique eorum in reditu centum librarum, Non obstante lege. Dolebat non parum Innocentio Papæ, quod querela isthac Angli tanta Papatum ad vivum resecarent. Optima tamen pollicitus, varia Anglis ex Synodo illa privilegia remisit, ut Patroni beneficiorum Ecclesiæ deinceps liberè designarent, & Episcopi reciperent personas idoneas, quæ velint & possint in beneficiis utiliter deservire: ut Camerae suae clericus (Legatus is erat) non nisi duodecim pluribus, sine Patronorum consensu provideret; si Angli studiosos, honestos & gratos se exhibere vellent (præsertim Nobilium & Magnatum filii) se paratum esse provisionis Ecclesiasticæ dexteram liberaliter aperire, ac etiam cum illis, quos velut nobiliores esse noverit, super beneficiorum pluralitate honorificè dispensare; denique ne Italicus Italico immediatè succederet, quod impetratum est propter fraudes eorum, qui mortuo beneficiato alium properè & furtim substituebant. Et his quidem liberaliter promissis, Anglis ora sublinenda putavit. Nam post discessum Synodi, Papa ad solitas artes suas rediit, & (verba sunt Paris ad A. 1246.) Omnia hæc & alia per hoc repagulum (Non obstante) infirmavit. Imò graviora velut ex facili tolerantibus impositum, lateresque, indurati Pharaonis instar, multiplicavit, adeò ut cùm sex aut septem post annos rursùs inquiri cœptum esset in lateres, ab Anglicis Israëlitis Italico Pharaoni fabricatos, summa redituum illorum, quæ priùs sexaginta millia marcarum confecerat, ad plus quàm septuaginta millia marcarum ascenderet.
units.tr: . He grants to other Italian substitutes; when a benefice happens to fall vacant, he strives to assign it to Italians; he also extorts immoderate pensions from religious men; and he everywhere imposes sentences of excommunication and interdict on those who contradict or resist him. After this complaint, I say, they humbly beseech the Pope to extend the hand of mercy to his sons and to relieve them of those burdens of grievances and oppressions, which were detestable both to God and to men. The messengers who carried the letter presented it to the General Council in the Pope's presence, and at the same time complained orally of a clause inserted into the papal bulls, called (Notwithstanding) which, they said, by its force breaks through all the laws and institutions of the Church, so that it may serve these efforts of his. For whatever in the wording of a bull seemed to hinder him, this machine of his was accustomed to remove: (Notwithstanding). So the Lateran Council under Alexander III decreed that no one should hold more than one benefice, and that no one should possess any benefice unless he could exercise its care in person. The Pope issued his bulls against this, as Paris reports under Henry III, in the year 1231, that provision be made in individual churches for five Romans, the son of Rumfred, the son of such-and-such, and so on, each with an income of one hundred pounds, Notwithstanding the law. Innocent the Pope was not a little distressed that these English complaints cut so deeply into the Papacy's living flesh. Yet, promising the best, he remitted to the English various privileges from that Council: that patrons of benefices should henceforth freely nominate, and bishops should admit suitable persons who are willing and able to serve the benefices usefully; that the clerk of his Chamber (for that was the legate) should not provide to more than twelve benefices without the patrons' consent; that, if the English should show themselves zealous, upright and pleasing (especially the sons of nobles and magnates), he was prepared to open generously the hand of ecclesiastical provision, and also to dispense honourably with those whom he knew to be of higher rank regarding the plurality of benefices; finally, that an Italian should not succeed immediately to an Italian, which was obtained because of the frauds of those who, when a beneficed man died, quickly and furtively substituted another. Having made these generous promises, he thought the English had been given something to wipe their mouths on. For after the Council broke up, the Pope returned to his usual arts, and (in Paris's words under 1246) annulled all these and other things by this barrier (Notwithstanding). Indeed, he imposed heavier burdens on those who had tolerated the earlier ones too easily, and, like the hardened Pharaoh, multiplied their bricks, so that when, six or seven years later, an inquiry into the bricks, which the English Israelites had made for the Italian Pharaoh, was begun again, the sum of those revenues, which had earlier amounted to sixty thousand marks, rose to more than seventy thousand marks.
XCIII.

units.la: Quòd si importuna hujus abominandæ mundinationis libido in una illa natione tam prodigiosa extitit, quàm tandem fuisse in universis totius reliquæ Christianæ ditionis census censebimus? Certò etiam Germani in Gravaminibus suis sæpiùs citatis, gravissimas eandem in rem querelas consignârunt. Paucas adducere haud pigebit.
units.tr: If the unseemly lust of this abominable trade was so monstrous in that one nation, what shall we suppose the revenues of the whole rest of the Christian realm to have been? The Germans, certainly, in their oft-cited Gravamina, recorded very grave complaints on this very matter. I will not hesitate to adduce a few.

units.la: Sub rubrica, Quo pacto sub prætextu familiaritatis Papalis curiæ multorum beneficiorum per Curtisanos impugnetur collatio &c. Sic Grav. xvj. & xviij. queruntur: Nec minùs & illud suetum hucusque fuit, ut quorundam magni pensi beneficiorum, sub nomine officialium vel familiarium Papæ & Curiæ Papalis, per idiotas, & alioqui inhabiles personas sit impugnata collatio: ac per illos conatum tentatùmque, si quomodo fieri posset, ut beneficia hæc in commendas seu provisiones (ita enim ipsi vocant,) verterentur, ac censibus annuis obnoxia reddere queant: hinc hinc prætendentes regressus, reservationes, pensiones, ac plura alia incompatibilia sibi in bis competere. Quibus technis ac dolis malis beneficia illa penitus exuguntur, enervantur, attenuanturque, cum perpetuo Romanæ Curiæ pensionibus annuis serviunt; fitque ut Germanorum, utcunque habilium, nemo unquam ad hæc aspirare possit.
units.tr: Under the heading, How, under the pretext of familiarity with the Papal court, the conferring of many benefices is attacked by the Curtisans, etc. the Gravamina xvi and xviii complain thus: Nor, moreover, has it hitherto been less customary that the conferring of certain benefices of great value be assailed, in the name of officials or familiars of the Pope and of the Papal Court, by unskilled and otherwise unfit persons; and that they have attempted and tried, if somehow it could be done, to turn these benefices into commendams or provisions (for so they call them) and make them liable to annual charges; hence pretending rights of regress, reservations, pensions, and many other incompatibles belonging to them. By these crafty tricks and wicked frauds those benefices are utterly stripped, enfeebled and wasted, since they are continually subject to annual pensions to the Roman Curia; and so none of the Germans, however able, can ever aspire to them.

units.la: XVIII. Item obviam veniunt & tum Germanis non ferenda a Curtisanis onera. Ita enim per Germaniam subtili ingenio beneficia venantur, ut conentur viris presbyteris, ætate & integritate vitæ spectabilibus, qui beneficia sua, absque omni controversia, justo titulo & bona fide multos jam annos quietè possederant, in longæva possessione negotium facere, possessionem interturbare, ad Romanam Curiam perfunaliter ut compareant in jus vocare, ac mille aliis artibus, ita eos adigere, ut transactiones quantumvis iniquas, inire necessum habeant, modò supremos hos annos quietè agere velint. Cogantur enim hoc, quo dictum est, modo, a Curtisanis ad pensiones annuas, reservata & id genus alias præstationes. Atque hoc agunt Curtisani nebulones, non propria authoritate, sed Romanorum suorum statutorum ac regularum, quas vocant, Cancellariæ. Quæ constitutiones omnes quotidie pro libidine Curtisanorum figuntur ac refiguntur, cum derogatur prioribus non admodum, ut videbatur, æquis, & ferunt iniquiores. Quare nedum senio confectis beneficiorum possessoribus, harum decipularum utque fraudum rudibus, sed & beneficiorum collatoribus imponunt, mille instructi dolis Curtisani. Nam etsi possidens beneficium presbyter cum Curtisano litigatore fictitio non transfigat, tamen ita litem sibi facit præstigiator ille Curtisanus, ut si pendente effecta hac controversia, moriatur beneficii litigiosi possessor, quod debinc continuò litem faciens, neglecto collatoris ordinario jure, in possessionem ejus beneficiimittatur. XIX. Item quæcunque dignitates seu beneficia pinguia, utpote Præpositura, Decanatus, Cantoratus, ac cætera officia, Canonicatus Ecclesiæ curatæ, & beneficia simplicia, quæ sub mense ordinario extramœnia Romana vacare incipiant, quorum antehac ad jus ordinarium patronatus Ecclesiasticorum & laicorum spectabat collatio & electio, tunc excogitatur à Romana sede juris patronatus ab ordinariis collatoribus abalienatio, maximè si possessores pristini beneficiorum aut officiorum, dignitatumve talium familiares vel officiales Papæ aut Cardinalium fuerint. Paulò post, sub rubrica de Ecclesiasticis beneficiis, curatis, & non curatis in genere, Grav. xxj. sic quiritari Germaniæ status Pontificii etiam, pergunt: Necminus & illud in Romana Curia hucusque observatum est, ut gratiæ & reservationes pectorales, mentales, generales & speciales regressus, accessus, incorporationes, uniones & concordata, uti suis vocant excogitatis nominibus, ob pecuniæ & privati lucri amorem super beneficiis ac prælaturis, præsertim per Germaniam Curtisanis à sede Romana concederentur. Neque hoc contentus fuit habendi sceleratus amor, quin & ea ipsa beneficia ac prælaturæ prædictæ, societatibus mercatorum potentum ære cum onere census mediocris, sed ita, ut deinde latius venderentur, concedantur. Qua subtili practica atque techna factum est, quod plurima, aut certè pinguium beneficiorum magna, si non maxima portio ex Germanorum manu Romam est translata: quæ beneficia hinc idiotis inidoneis, ac inhonestis etiam personis non raro sunt collata: & quidem nec Germanis, sed barbaris, qui Germanam linguam nec loquantur, neque intelligant: ut inauditum dictu hoc inde fit consecutum, quod ovibus Christi præfecti sunt Pastores, quorum etsi vocem oves forte audierint, non intelligant. Verum gravius etiam inde oritur Germanis onus, quòd cùm beneficia hæc & Parochiales Ecclesias ipsi propria persona neque possidere, neque gubernare possunt (quod tamen Pastoris officium inprimis sibi postulabát,) nimirum ut subditis parochialibus & integritate ac innocentiâ morum egregium de se præberent Exemplum, ut oves suas tanquam oves Christi, doctrinâ solidâ, sincerâ pascerent, eorum neutrum per pastores illus subditizios curatur. Primùm enim ipsi, qui beneficia hæc Ecclesiastica à mercatoribus quo prædictum est, assequuntur modo, quia propria persona ad possidenda ea sunt minùs idonei: ideò hæc eadem aliis æquè, aut longè etiam, quàm sint, ad onus hoc inhabilioribus pro annuo censu locant, non secùs atque census ac reditus annui ex agris locantur, & emuntur, ut is demùm habeatur emptor idoneus, qui pluris mercem licitaverit. Ita planè pro pretii quantitate elocantur nunc per Curtisanos Ecclesiastica beneficia. Deinceps quibus nexibus Archiepiscopi & Episcopi à suis Capitulis ob beneficiorum collationem sint adstricti Grav. xxÿ. & xxiÿ. exponunt; & de Prælaturarum commendis & incorporationibus Grav. xxiv. gravissimè queruntur.
units.tr: Gravamen xviii. Likewise, the Curtisans impose burdens which the Germans cannot bear. For they hunt benefices through Germany with such cunning that they try to cause trouble, in their long-enjoyed possession, for presbyters of age and integrity of life, who for many years had quietly held their benefices with no dispute, by just title and in good faith; they disturb their possession, and by summoning them to appear before the Roman Curia in person, and by a thousand other arts, they force them to enter into transactions however unfair, provided only they wish to live quietly in their last years. For they are compelled, in the manner described, by the Curtisans, to pay annual pensions, reservations and other such payments. And the Curtisan scoundrels do this not on their own authority, but by their Roman statutes and so-called rules of the Chancery. All these constitutions are drawn up and redrawn daily at the whim of the Curtisans, as earlier ones, which were not very fair, as it seemed, are repealed and replaced by more unfair ones. Therefore, the Curtisans, equipped with a thousand tricks, impose these snares and frauds not only on benefice-holders worn out with age and unversed in such deceits, but also on the conferrers of benefices. For even if a presbyter holding a benefit does not come to terms with a fictitious Curtisan litigant, that trickster Curtisan so contrives a lawsuit against him that, if while the dispute is pending the holder of the disputed benefice dies, the Curtisan, continuing the litigation without regard to the ordinary right of the conferrer, is put into possession of it. [4a] Gravamen xix. Likewise, whatever dignities or rich benefices, such as provostships, deaneries, precentorships and other offices, canonries of a parish church, and simple benefices, which begin to fall vacant outside the ordinary Roman see, and whose conferring and election formerly belonged by ordinary right of patronage to ecclesiastics and laymen, are then contrived by the Roman see to be alienated from the ordinary conferrers of the right of patronage, especially if the former holders of such benefices, offices or dignities were familiars or officials of the Pope or of the Cardinals. Shortly afterwards, under the heading concerning ecclesiastical benefices, curate and non-curate, in general, Gravamen xxi, the estates of Germany, still complaining in the Papist manner, go on thus: Nor less has this also been hitherto observed in the Roman Curia, that graces and reservations, pectoral, mental, general and special regresses, accesses, incorporations, unions and concordats, as they call them by invented names, were granted to the Curtisans by the Roman see over benefices and prelacies, especially throughout Germany, out of love of money and private gain. Nor was this wicked greed of possessing content with it, but those same benefices and aforesaid prelacies are granted to societies of powerful merchants for money, with a charge of moderate rent, but so that they may then be sold more widely. By this subtle practice and trick it has come about that very many, or at least a great, if not the greatest, part of the rich benefices has been transferred from German hands to Rome; and those benefices have not seldom been conferred on unskilled and even dishonourable persons, and indeed not on Germans but on barbarians who neither speak nor understand the German tongue. Thence has followed the unheard-of thing to be said: shepherds have been set over Christ's sheep, whose voice the sheep may perhaps have heard, but do not understand. Yet an even graver burden arises for the Germans from this, that since they cannot themselves in person hold or govern these benefices and parish churches (which nevertheless the office of pastor especially requires of them, namely, that they should give to their parishioners an outstanding example of integrity and innocence of life, and that they should feed their sheep, as sheep of Christ, with solid and sincere doctrine), neither of these is provided for by those subject shepherds. For first, those who obtain these ecclesiastical benefices from the merchants in the manner described are less suited, because they are not present in person to hold them; therefore these same benefices are let out for an annual rent to others equally, or even much more, unfit for this burden, just as fields are let and bought for an annual rent, so that he is finally considered a suitable buyer who has bid the higher price for the commodity. Thus, plainly, ecclesiastical benefices are now let out by the Curtisans according to the amount of the price. [4b] Next, the Gravamina xxiii and xxiv explain the bonds by which archbishops and bishops are bound to their chapters on account of the conferring of benefices; and Gravamen xxiv complains most gravely about the commendams and incorporations of prelacies.

units.la: XCIV. Exemplo Statuum Germaniæ novem quoque Helvetiæ Cantonum & Valesiorum legati A. MDXXV. Lucernæ reformationis articulos condere ausi, temporum suorum calamitatem diserte Sacerdotum iniquitati & avaritiæ imputant, nundinationes fœdas prohibent, & Curtisanis, quos Romanos etiam nebulones vocant, pessulum obdere conantur. In Gallia quid actum sit, Pragmatica Sanctio, nundinationum Papalium circa beneficia Ecclesiæ testis irrefragabilis, luculenter demonstravit. Quam ergò prodigiosam abominationem, in universis Christianæ ditionis locis extitisse putabimus? Et si ante quadringentos penè annos in flore Pontificatûs, cùm ejus adhuc vix Helvetii, Gallia. connexi & confirmati essent artus, eòusque Pontifices, uti suprà ex Matthæo Paris vidimus, provecti sunt, quid posteà aulos esse cogitabimus: Si unico artificio, vel parte ejus potiùs aliqua ad Italos suos locupletandos applicata, tantis opibus, copiisque Curiam & statum suum ditârunt, quid de eadem machina credi poterit, admota ad cujusque regionis incolas, quosque in patria sua ornandos?
units.tr: XCIV. Following the example of the estates of Germany, the envoys of the nine cantons of Switzerland and of the Valais, in the year 1525, at Lucerne, dared to draw up articles of reform, and expressly ascribe the calamity of their times to the iniquity and avarice of the priests; they forbid shameful trafficking and try to bar the door against the Curtisans, whom they also call Romans and scoundrels. What was done in France, the Pragmatic Sanction, an irrefutable witness of the Papal trafficking in ecclesiastical benefices, has clearly shown. What monstrous abomination, then, shall we think existed in all the places of the Christian realm? And if, nearly four hundred years ago, in the flower of the Papacy, when the joints of the Swiss and of Gaul were scarcely yet connected and confirmed, the Popes advanced so far, as we saw above from Matthew Paris, what shall we imagine afterwards? If by a single contrivance, or rather by some part of it applied to enriching their Italians, they have enriched the Curia and their state with such great wealth and resources, what can be believed of the same machine, when it is brought to bear on the inhabitants of each region, to be stripped of their goods in their own country?

units.la: XCV. Inter Babylonicæ beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum nundinationis species haud postrema, adeóque silentio haud prætereunda est Annatarum, seu vacantiarum reditus ex reservatione fructuum anni, quo Sacerdos defunctus est, sic insignitus. Eas primùm Johannem XXII. indixisse, sunt qui putent. Sed Bonifacio IX. Paparum Suetonius inventum acceptum refert. Et quamvis ista exactio & cupido auri immensa, obtentum habebat, quasi subsidium adversùs Turcam pararetur: longè tamen aliter esse, res docuit, non sine crebris & magnis offensionibus, ut etiam in Gravaminibus Imperii Maximilianus Cæsar hoc Alexandro VI. exprobrandum judicaverit, quòd proventus illos, hac potissimùm de causa concessos olim, in eum usum non contribueret. In Concilio quidem Basileensi Sess. 21. decretum erat, ut abrogaretur Simoniaca hæc exactio; & missi ad Papam Eugenium IV. Concilii nomine legati, sic, uti in Concilii appendice refertur, lamentati sunt: Quamvis autem B. P. ista annata introducta fuerint ex causa passagii terræ Sanctæ, nunc autem cessante causa, cessare poterit & effectus. Non cessavit tamen. Quin potiùs ex constitutione Leonis X. uti apud Hieronymum Gygantem in tract. de pensionibus q. 26. n: 2. habetur, præter Episcopatus & Prælaturas, alia etiam minora beneficia, quæ electiva dicuntur, quorum reditus annui 24. imò 10. ducatos non excedunt, singula pensiones certas Camerae Pontificiæ persolvere jussa sunt. Inde inere-
units.tr: XCV. Among the forms of the Babylonian trafficking in ecclesiastical benefices, not the least, and therefore not to be passed over in silence, is that of the annates, or the revenue of vacancies, arising from the reservation of the fruits of the year in which the priest died, so called. Some think that John XXII first imposed them. But Suetonius of the Popes attributes the invention to Boniface IX. And although this exaction and immense greed for gold had the pretext that it was being prepared as an aid against the Turk, the matter has shown that the reality was far otherwise, not without frequent and great offences; so that Maximilian Caesar, even in the Gravamina of the Empire, judged that this was to be charged against Alexander VI, that he did not apply those revenues, originally granted chiefly for this reason, to that use. In the Council of Basel, Session 21, it was indeed decreed that this simoniacal exaction be abolished; and the envoys sent to Pope Eugene IV in the name of the Council lamented, as is related in the appendix to the Council: Although, most holy Father, these annates were introduced on account of the passage to the Holy Land, now that the cause has ceased, the effect too may cease. Yet it did not cease. Indeed, rather, by a constitution of Leo X, as is found in Hieronymus Gygas, in his tract on pensions, question 26, number 2, besides bishoprics and prelacies, other lesser benefices also, which are called elective, whose annual revenues do not exceed 24, or even 10, ducats, were ordered each to pay certain pensions to the Papal Chamber. Hence, if you consider the breadth of the Papal realm, it is incredible to say how great a quantity of gold flowed back into the Roman Curia.

units.la: q. 26. n: 2. incredibile dictu est, si Regni Papalis amplitudinem cogites, quanta vis auri ad Romanam Curiam redundaverit.
units.tr: q. 26. n: 2. It is hard to believe, if you consider the extent of the Papal realm, how much gold flowed into the Roman Curia.

units.la: XCVI. Solent equidem feudatarii, certa quædam officia dominis feudi præstare, tum ut honorem iis debitum deferant, tum ut se iis obnoxios fateantur. Et in venditione feudi solet fructus aliquis ad dominum feudi pervenire, sive hic fructus sit quinta pars pretii venditionis, sive quidpiam aliud, pro varietate municipalium consuetudinum. Eadem ergò jura olim Imperatores & Reges habebant in possessiones & bona immobilia Episcoporum, non minùs quàm laicorum, idque merito, quia proventus & fundi Episcoporum ex Principum liberalitate ad clerum pervenerunt, qui ad memoriam conservandam collati beneficii sibi jus collationis & patronatûs reservabant, & munusculum aliquod ab Episcopo aut Abbate pro admissione in possessionem bonorum à sua liberalitate provenientium admittebant. Hæc jura Papa, qui fundos & possessiones clero nullas dedit, Principibus & fundatoribus erepta ad se transtulit, & sic Episcopatus ac Abbatias feuda esse à sede Romana sola dependentia, pro plenitudine suæ potestatis voluit, jussit. Atque hoc obtentu ab Episcopis & Abbatibus priorem annum proventus sui; aut si clementius transfigere velit, dimidium proventus annui exigit.
units.tr: XCVI. Vassals are indeed accustomed to render certain services to the lords of their fief, both to show them the honour owed and to acknowledge their dependence. And on the sale of a fief some fee usually passes to the lord of the fief, whether it is a fifth part of the sale price or something else, according to the varying local customs. Emperors and kings therefore once held the same rights over the estates and immovable goods of bishops as over those of laymen, and rightly so, since the revenues and lands of the bishops came to the clergy from the generosity of princes. To preserve the memory of the benefice conferred, these princes reserved for themselves the right of conferring it and of patronage, and the clergy admitted that a small gift be made by the bishop or abbot when he was admitted to possession of goods that came from the princes' generosity. The Pope, who gave the clergy no lands or estates, took these rights away from princes and founders and transferred them to himself. By his fullness of power he wished and ordered that bishoprics and abbeys be fiefs depending on the Roman See alone. On this pretext he exacts from bishops and abbots the first year's income; or, if he wishes to be more merciful, he takes half of the annual income.

units.la: XCVII. Non tantùm injustas, sed apertè etiam Simoniacas esse has Annatarum exactiones, res ipsa loquitur. Quid enim Simonia aliud est, quàm traditio potestatis, seu gratiæ spiritualis, sub pacto expresso pecuniæ, & pro pecunia, aut quocunque pretio: quæ est propriè venditio? Qui verò potestatem spiritualem Ecclesiam pascendi tradit, sub pacto ejusmodi annatarum expresso, is potestatem & gratiam spiritualem pro pecunia vel pretio vendit. Agnovit id ipsum Gerson, de pot. Eccles. consid.8. ubi ministrorum institutionem Papæ merito auferendam docet, maximè dum recipit annatas, quoniam ex hoc, capula, quandiu perseveraverit, oriétur inevitabiliter leprosa pestis Simoniæ, inficiens sua contagione nedum caput, sed penè singula Ecclesiæ membra.
units.tr: XCVII. The thing itself speaks: these exactions of annates are not only unjust but openly Simoniacal. For what is simony other than the handing over of a power, or of spiritual grace, under an express agreement for money, and in exchange for money or any price, which is properly a sale? Whoever hands over the spiritual power of feeding the Church under such an express agreement for annates sells spiritual power and grace for money or price. Gerson acknowledged this himself, de pot. Eccles. consid. 8, where he teaches that the Pope rightly loses the appointment of ministers, especially while he receives annates, since from this a leprous plague of simony will inevitably arise, as long as it lasts, infecting with its contagion not only the head but almost every member of the Church.

units.la: XCVIII. Neque verò ictum hunc exibunt Papæ gnathones, si regesserint, eum non vendere ipsum officium sacrum, seu potestatem spiritualem regendi animas, sed pro solo beneficio, hoc est, pro jure illo accipiendi reditus temporales, quod temporale & non spirituale, neque sacrum est, accipere pecuniam. Æquum enim esse, ut Papa, ceu primus Prælatus, super omnes Ecclesias vigilans, de proventibus illis etiam participet, ita ut ne venditio quidem ulla sit, sed sola quædam fructuum sibi applicatorum anticipata collectio; aut si venditio est, Papa fructus suos, hoc est, sibi jam debitos & applicatos vendat nuper provisò, qui solutâ pecuniâ suos faciet fructus primi anni, quos alioquin non sibi, sed Papæ colligere tenebatur. Non sic profectò Simoniæ labem à Papa abstergunt. Non dicam, Romam hodie tenere, docere, & factis ipsis judiciisque comprobare, quod reditus beneficiorum, qui habent adnexam rem spiritualem, fiant etiam sacri, & naturam rei spiritualis induant. Hoc si verum esset, κρησφύγετον plané evanesceret, quia juxta Romana axiomata vendere spiritualia, vel temporalia, quæ spiritualitatem aliquam contrahunt, manifesta Simonia est. Sed missò hoc figmento, quo tamen se ipsos Hierarchici jugulant, aliud solidius oppono, quòd annatarum exactiones ex pacto & conventione expressa fiant in ipsa sacri officii collatione, ita ut sacrum officium non possit haberi, nisi prævia pecuniæ solutione, quod annatæ Curiæ debitæ nomine Curia palliare conatur. Separetur tur ergò temporale à Spirituali, & tunc Simoniæ periculum cessabit. Ita vendere aquam baptismalem à baptismo separatam, ad potandum vel alium usum, Simonia non est. At vendere in ipso actu Baptismi, & nolle aquam illam uti ad baptizandum, nisi prius ex pacto & conventione baptizandus solvat pecuniam, potentissima Simonia erit. Ego enim, qui baptismum cupio, aquam à te baptizatore peto, non ad aliud, nisi ut cum aqua simul baptismum suscipiam; & dices tu sine Simonia: Solve mihi pecuniam pro aqua, & tum te baptizabo, nisi solveris non baptizabo? Hoc planè in annatis fit. Quærit aliquis Episcopatum à Papa collatore: Papa collator dicit: solve pecuniam pro redditibus Episcopatui annexis; soluta pecuniâ tradam Episcopatum, neque tradam prius quàm solveris. An ovum ovo simílius? Denique sicut omnes consentiunt, Soto de Just. & jure lib. ix. q. 5. art. 1. docente, esse Simoniam vendere calicem sanctificatum, accepto peculiari pretio propter annexam illam consecrationem: ita necesse est omninò dicant, Simoniam esse vendere peculiari pretio proventus Episcopatûs, non quia sunt proventus temporales, sed quia iis Episcopatus adjunctus est. Hoc fit sub annatarum velamine, ubi pretium Papa accipit ad hoc, ut cum proventibus simul Episcopatum largiatur. Alioquin, inquit, si non solveris pecuniam, non dabo Episcopatum, non dicit, non dabo proventus. Si ergò Papa hic Simoniacus esse & audire non vult, det prius Episcopatum, postea dicat: Non do tibi jus ad redditus percipiendos, nisi solveris pecuniam. Ita Simoniacus non erit, erit tamen injustus, quia nullo jure partem proventuum Ecclesiæ affectat, quorum ille, ne minimam quidem particulam Ecclesiæ prius contulit. Cæterùm, nunquam tamen sic Papa dicet, gnarus quippe, quàm primùm quis Ecclesiastico officio applicatur, statim ei Euangelico jure sustentationem de beri.
units.tr: XCVIII. Nor will the Pope's flatterers escape this blow if they reply that he does not sell the sacred office itself, or the spiritual power of ruling souls, but only the benefice, that is, the right to receive temporal revenues; that receiving money for what is temporal, and not spiritual or sacred, is no simony. For they say it is fair that the Pope, as first prelate watching over all churches, should also share in those revenues, so that there is not even any sale, but only a kind of advance collection of fruits assigned to him. Or if it is a sale, the Pope sells his own fruits, that is, fruits already owed and assigned to him, to a newly provided man, who by paying the money makes his own the first year's fruits, which otherwise he would have been bound to collect not for himself but for the Pope. These arguments certainly do not wipe the stain of simony from the Pope. I will not say that Rome today holds, teaches, and confirms by its very deeds and judgments that the revenues of benefices which have something spiritual attached become sacred too and take on the nature of a spiritual thing. If that were true, the [κρησφύγετον] refuge would plainly vanish, since by Roman axioms to sell spiritual things, or temporal things that acquire some spirituality, is manifest simony. But setting aside this fiction, by which the hierarchs cut their own throats, I oppose another and sounder argument: the annate exactions are made by express pact and agreement at the very conferring of the sacred office, so that the sacred office cannot be had unless the money is paid first. The Curia tries to disguise this under the name of the annates owed to it. Let the temporal therefore be separated from the spiritual, and then the danger of simony will cease. Thus to sell baptismal water apart from baptism, for drinking or some other use, is not simony. But to sell it in the very act of baptism, and to refuse to use that water for baptizing unless the one to be baptized first pays money by agreement, will be most powerful simony. For I, who desire baptism, ask you the baptizer for water, not for any other purpose than that I may receive baptism together with the water; and will you say, without simony: "Pay me money for the water, and then I will baptize you; unless you pay, I will not baptize you"? This is exactly what happens with annates. Someone seeks a bishopric from the Pope who confers it. The Pope says: "Pay the money for the revenues attached to the bishopric; once the money is paid I will hand over the bishopric, and I will not hand it over before you pay." Is one egg more like another? Finally, as all agree, since Soto teaches de Just. & jure lib. ix. q. 5. art. 1. that it is simony to sell a consecrated chalice for a special price because of that consecration attached to it, so they must altogether say that it is simony to sell the revenues of a bishopric for a special price, not because they are temporal revenues, but because the bishopric is attached to them. This is done under the cover of annates, where the Pope takes the price so that he may bestow the bishopric together with the revenues. Otherwise, he says, if you do not pay the money, I will not give the bishopric; he does not say, I will not give the revenues. So if the Pope here does not want to be called simoniacal, let him first give the bishopric, and afterwards say: "I do not give you the right to receive the revenues unless you pay the money." Thus he will not be simoniacal, but he will still be unjust, because by no right does he claim a share of the Church's revenues, of which he has not first contributed even the smallest part to the Church. Moreover, the Pope will never say this, being well aware that as soon as anyone is devoted to an ecclesiastical office, by evangelical right his maintenance is owed to him.

units.la: XCIX. Annatis cohærent Pallia è lana linóque consecta, quam nec operosam, nec sanè pretiosam mercem Archiepiscopi maxima vi pecuniæ à Pontifice redimere coguntur. Conficitur Pallium illud hoc ferè modo. Monachi & Moniales S. Agnetis, quæ Romæ est, quotannis duos agnos albos imponunt altari, quando in Missa canitur Agnus Dei. Hi Agni inde elati tondentur, & ex eorum lana texuntur palliola alba, lata digitos tres, in pectus & in dorsum propendula ad longitudinem palmi. Limbo assuuntur laminæ plumbeæ, quarum extremus orbiculus serico nigro tegitur. Hæc pallia imponuntur feretro Petri & Pauli. Designatus Archiepiscopus accedit, petens instanter, instantius & instantissimè sibi dari hoc Pallium : Optimi Archiepiscopatus, qualis est Toletanus in Hispania, Moguntinus & Coloniensis in Germania, aliique etiam in Papæ fiscum sexaginta, vel septuaginta millia ducatorum, aut amplius etiam, inferunt. Libro S. Ceremoniarum primo Sect. x. 8. hæc habentur: Componitur cum subdiaconis tenentibus pallia, qui accipiunt secundùm valorem & taxam Ecclesiæ, aliquando plus, aliquando minùs pro centenario. Tanti venit linum Papæ, & tanta unius indulsii charitas est: Ut non immeritò Jacobus, Archiepiscopus Moguntinus, jam fere moriens dixerit: Se de morte sua non adeò dolere, quàm ob id, quòd subditi sui pauperes iterum pro Pallio gravem exactionem dare cogerentur. Neque enim licet antecessoris pallio uti, sed quisque illud sibi Romæ comparare tenetur. Deinde qui forte vel permutatione, vel quavis alia ratione fit alterius Ecclesiæ Metropolita, licet anteà paraverit illud, necesse tamen habet, ut iterum emat. Vel igitur incredibilis est pallii toties emti & redemti sanctitas. ξitas: vel certè auri Episcopalis fames prodigiosè sacra. Prærer pallia hæc insuper præsenti pecunia redimere oportet Bullam Principalem, Bullam commissionis, Bullam absolutionis, Bullam ad Capitulum, Bullam ad Clerum, Bullam ad populum, Bullam ad Vasallos, Bullam ad Archiepiscopum, Bullam ad Regem (vide quàm Bullis omnia bulliant!) solvendúmque Consistorialibus pro munere consecrationis, pro munere benedictionis.
units.tr: XCIX. Connected with annates are the palls woven of wool and linen. Archbishops are forced to buy this from the Pope at great cost, though it is neither a laborious nor a truly precious commodity. The pall is made in roughly this way. The monks and nuns of St Agnes, which is at Rome, each year place two white lambs on the altar when the Agnus Dei is sung at Mass. The lambs, lifted from there, are shorn, and from their wool white palls are woven, three fingers wide, hanging down on the breast and back to the length of a palm. Leaden plates are attached to the border, the outermost little disc of which is covered with black silk. These palls are placed on the shrine of Peter and Paul. The designated archbishop comes forward, asking urgently, more urgently, and most urgently that this pall be given to him. The best archbishoprics, such as Toledo in Spain, Mainz and Cologne in Germany, and others too, bring to the papal treasury sixty or seventy thousand ducats, or even more. In the first book of the Sacred Ceremonies, Sect. x. 8., these things are found: He bargains with the subdeacons holding the palls, who receive according to the value and tax of the Church, sometimes more, sometimes less, per hundred. So much does linen cost the Pope, and so great is the charity of one indulgence: that Jacob, Archbishop of Mainz, nearly dying, rightly said that he did not grieve so much at his death as because his poor subjects would again be forced to pay a heavy exaction for the pall. For it is not permitted to use a predecessor's pall; each man is bound to buy his own at Rome. Then, if by exchange or some other means someone becomes metropolitan of another church, although he had previously bought one, he must nevertheless buy again. Either the holiness of a pall bought and redeemed so many times is incredible, or certainly the episcopal hunger for gold is prodigiously holy. Besides these palls, one must also redeem for ready money the Principal Bull, the Bull of commission, the Bull of absolution, the Bull to the chapter, the Bull to the clergy, the Bull to the people, the Bull to the vassals, the Bull to the archbishop, the Bull to the king (see how everything bubbles with bulls!), and pay the consistorial officials for the service of consecration and for the service of blessing.

units.la: C. De exactione Decimarum suprà Erasmum sic quiritantem vidimus: Quas non tragœdias movent pro suis il-lis decimis, quàm odiosè divexant miseram plebeculam?
units.tr: C. On the exaction of tithes, we have seen above how Erasmus complains: What tragedies they stir up over those tithes of theirs, and how odiously they harass the wretched common folk!

units.la: Nulli equidem improbamus, si consentientibus summis Potestatibus & Populo, Ecclesiæ Ministris ex decimis necessaria & honesta sustentatio decernatur. Nam si sub V. T. iniquum non fuit, ut Levitis altari inservientibus, ex decimis vitæ subsidia cederent: neque sub N. T. injustitiæ labem Christianus populus contrahet, si Ecclesiæ Ministris ex iisdem sustentationem procuraverit. Cœterùm, Hierarchici avaritiam suam produnt, quòd sacerdotibus suis non populorum liberalitate & applicatione libera, sed juris Divini inviolabili necessitate decimas universas vindicant; perindè ac si sacrilegium populus Christianus admitteret, sicubi decimas vel abundantes, vel universas, in alios usus convertit, vel liberas relinquit, ac de cætero Ecclesiæ Ministris alibi de sustentatione necessaria prospicit. Qua enim ratione necessaria, legem Mosaicam de decimis Levitis pendendis, perpetuam, immutabilem illi statuant, non liquet mihi hactenùs. Inprimis cùm ipse Bellarminus de Cler. cap. 26. fateatur, Deum sibi decimas à Judæis exigisse titulo Regio, quia erat illius gentis Rex specialis. Tum etiam motofa illa & solicita nimis decimarum exactio, eundem clericalis avaritiæ spiritum redolet.
units.tr: We certainly do not disapprove if, with the consent of the highest powers and the people, a necessary and honourable maintenance for the ministers of the Church is decreed from tithes. For if under the Old Testament it was not unjust that the Levites, who served at the altar, should receive their living from tithes, neither will the Christian people contract the stain of injustice under the New Testament if it provides for the ministers of the Church from the same source. But the Hierarchy betrays its avarice in that it claims all tithes for its priests not by the free liberality and assignment of the people but by the inviolable necessity of divine law, just as if the Christian people would commit sacrilege wherever it turns tithes, whether abundant or entire, to other uses, or leaves them free, and provides elsewhere for the necessary maintenance of the ministers of the Church. For I have not yet seen clearly on what ground they declare the Mosaic law on paying tithes to the Levites to be necessary, perpetual and unchangeable. Above all, since Bellarmine himself confesses, On the Clergy, chap. 26, that God exacted tithes from the Jews under a royal title, because he was that people's special King. Then too, that restless and overly anxious exaction of tithes smells of the same spirit of clerical avarice.

units.la: Dixit enim jam olim Hieronymus Epist. 2. merito: Nunquam petentes, raro accipiamus rogati. Nam melius est non habere, quod tribuam, quàm imprudenter petere quod recondam. Et Augustinus in Psalm. 146. Facite, inquit laicis, vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis. Non tacet ipse, audite vocem ejus. Nemo enim à vobis potest exigere, nisi forte exactione opus est, ut qui vobis in Euangelio serviunt, petant à vobis, si ad hoc ventum fuerit, ut petant, videte, ne quod vos à Deo petiistis, frustrà petatis. Ergò estote exactores vestri, ne aliquid illi, qui in Euangelio serviunt, vobis non dicam petere cogantur. Nam forte nec coacti petent, sed ne libenter vos arguant. Unde scriptum est: Beatus, qui intelligit super egenum & pauperem.
units.tr: For long ago Jerome rightly said, in Epistle 2: Let us accept rarely when we are asked, never when we ask. For it is better not to have what I might give than to ask imprudently for what I would lay up. And Augustine, on Psalm 146: Make for yourselves, he says to the laity, friends out of the mammon of unrighteousness. He is not silent himself; hear his voice. For no one can demand anything from you, unless perhaps there is need of exaction, so that those who serve you in the Gospel should ask from you, if it has come to this, that they ask; see that you do not ask in vain what you have asked of God. Therefore be your own exactors, lest those who serve you in the Gospel be compelled to ask anything of you, I will not say. For perhaps they will not even ask when compelled, but so that they do not reproach you gladly. Hence it is written: Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy.

units.la: CI. Sed Pontifices inprimis beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum indefessam nundinationem suam in eo etiam exercuerunt, & exercent adhuc, quòd Ecclesiarum & Ecclesiasticorum possessiones non tantum onerârunt pensionibus, tributis & subsidiis, sed ab illis etiam praetextu belli gerendi contra Caesares vel Turcam, decimas quintas, decimas, quintas, tertias, medietates bonorum suorum exegerunt. Longum esset ex historiarum monumentis nundinationem hanc condigna ratione repraesentare. De Innocentio III. Caesarius in Dialogis refert, cum Cistertiensi Ordini praecepisse, ut quadragesimam partem mobilium suorum in bellum sacrum contribueret, & ordini privilegia sua objicienti, comminatum esse, quòd possessiones ejus Principum Secularium praedae exponere velit. Itaque Monachos in angustias redactos ad D. Mariam confugisse, ejusque opem implorâsse, quae exorata apparuerit Regnerio Monacho, jusseritque eum Innocentio renunciare, omnem se ei potestatem adempturam, nisi à coepti desisterit. Pontificem apparitioni fidem habentem à coepta exactione destitisse, & ordinis privilegia confirmasse. Sic Caesarius, quem penes fides esto. Tentavit etiam aliquid Honorius III. qui, Matthæo Paris ad A. 1226. narrante, Othonem Legatum in Galliam & Angliam misit, rogaturum Episcopos, dignarentur pii liberi matris inopiam sublevare, quandoquidem rapacitate & iniquitate Romanæ Curiæ ærarium Pontificis exhaustum sit. Sublevari autem ærarium posse, si ei concederent percipere ab omnibus Ecclesiis Cathedralibus duas præbendas, unam de portione Episcopi, alteram de capitulo, & similiter de Cœnobiis, ubi divisæ erant portiones Abbatis & Conventus, à Conventibus quantum pertineret ad unum Monachum æquali facta distributione bonorum Conventus, ita ut inter Monachos Pontifex Romanus computaretur, & ab Abbate tantundem. Sed desiderio Papæ, intercedente Angliæ Rege, factum satis non est. Fortunatior Gregorius IX. apud eundem Paris ad A. 1229. suscepto in Fridericum Imperatorem gravi odio, decimas non Ecclesiasticis duntaxat, sed laicis etiam imperavit, laicis non audientibus dicto, audire Ecclesiastici Angli inprimis à Rege suo non protecti, censurarum interitarum metu compulsi sunt.
