Idem Gregorius post etiam Paris ad A. 1240. referente, ab Ecclesiasticis quartam bonorum partem exegit. Et in Gallia jam grandem pecuniarum vim Nuntius ejus corrogaverat, sed, Rege prohibente, auferre non poterat, donec cum Friderico Imperatore in gratiam rediisset. Innocentius IV. apud eundem Paris ad A. 1246. 1247. 1254. idem subsidium à Clericis Anglis exigit, sed non impetravit. Vigesimam dein imperavit & collegit. Cumque post tertiam bonorum partem repetiisset, repulsam passus est. Mox tributum Clerorindixit, tallagii nomine, sed ei Rex iterum interceslit. Ne vero soli Angliæ gravis esse videretur, misit quatuor Cardinales Legatos per Italiam, Hispaniam, Norwegiam, Germaniam, aliasque
units.tr: CI. But the Pontiffs, above all, have also carried on, and still carry on, their tireless trade in ecclesiastical benefices in this respect: they have not only burdened the possessions of the Churches and of churchmen with pensions, taxes and subsidies, but have also demanded from them, under the pretext of waging war against the Caesars or the Turk, fifteenths, tenths, fifths, thirds, and halves of their goods. It would be long to portray this trade, worthily, from the records of histories. Concerning Innocent III, Caesarius reports in his Dialogues that he ordered the Cistercian Order to contribute the fortieth part of its movable goods to the holy war, and when the Order objected its privileges, he threatened that he would expose its possessions to the plunder of secular princes. So the monks, reduced to straits, fled to the Blessed Virgin Mary and implored her aid; she, having been entreated, appeared to the monk Regner and ordered him to announce to Innocent that she would take away all his power unless he desisted from his undertaking. The Pontiff, believing the apparition, desisted from the exaction he had begun and confirmed the privileges of the Order. So Caesarius, whose word may be trusted. Honorius III also attempted something; as Matthew Paris in the year 1226 relates, he sent Otto as legate into France and England, to ask the bishops whether they would deign to relieve the poverty of the pious free mother, since the Pontiff's treasury had been drained by the rapacity and iniquity of the Roman Curia. The treasury could be relieved, he said, if they would concede that he receive from all the cathedral churches two prebends, one from the bishop's portion and the other from the chapter, and likewise from the monasteries, where the portions of the abbot and the convent were divided, from the convent as much as would fall to one monk, by an equal distribution of the goods of the convent, so that the Roman Pontiff would be counted among the monks, and receive as much from the abbot. But, though the Pope desired it, and the King of England interceded, nothing sufficient was done. Gregory IX was more fortunate: as Paris again records in the year 1229, having conceived a serious hatred against the Emperor Frederick, he imposed tithes not only on the clergy but also on the laity; the laity did not obey, but the English clergy, not protected above all by their own King, were compelled by fear of the threatened censures to obey. The same Gregory, as Paris reports in the year 1240, afterwards exacted a fourth part of the goods from the clergy. And in France his legate had already collected a great sum of money, but, the King forbidding it, he could not carry it off, until he had returned to favour with the Emperor Frederick. Innocent IV, as the same Paris reports in the years 1246, 1247, 1254, demanded the same subsidy from the English clergy, but did not obtain it. Then he imposed and collected a twentieth. And when he had afterwards demanded a third part of the goods, he met with a rebuff. Soon he imposed a tax on the clergy, under the name of tallage, but the King again interposed. Lest it seem to be a burden on England alone, he sent four cardinal legates through Italy, Spain, Norway, Germany and other

units.la: Tom. II. quam petentes, raro accipiamus rogati. Nam melius est non habere, quod tribuam, quàm imprudenter petere quod recondam. Et Augustinus in Psalm. 146. Facite, inquit laicis, vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis. Non tacet ipse, audite vocem ejus. Nemo enim à vobis potest exigere, nisi forte exactione opus est, ut qui vobis in Euangelio serviunt, petant à vobis, si ad hoc ventum fuerit, ut petant, videte, ne quod vos à Deo petiistis, frustrà petatis. Ergò estote exactores vestri, ne aliquid illi, qui in Euangelio serviunt, vobis non dicam petere cogantur. Nam forte nec coacti petent, sed ne libenter vos arguant. Unde scriptum est: Beatus, qui intelligit super egenum & pauperem.
units.tr: Tom. II. We who ask seldom receive when we are asked. For it is better not to have what I might give than to ask imprudently for what I would keep back. And Augustine, on Psalm 146, says to the laity, "Make for yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness." He is not silent himself; hear his voice. For no one can demand this of you, unless perhaps there is need of exaction, that those who serve you in the Gospel should ask something of you. If it has come to this, that they must ask, see that you do not ask in vain what you have asked of God. Therefore be your own exactors, lest those who serve you in the Gospel be compelled to ask anything of you, I will not say. For perhaps they will not even ask under compulsion, but so as not to rebuke you willingly. Hence it is written: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor.

units.la: CI. Sed Pontifices inprimis beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum indesessam nundinationem suam in eo etiam exercuerunt, & exercent adhuc, quòd Ecclesiarum & Ecclesiasticorum possessiones non tantum onerárunt pensionibus, tributis & subsidiis, sed ab illis etiam praetextu belli gerendi contra Caesares vel Turcam, decimas quintas, decimas, quintas, tertias, medietates bonorum suorum exegerunt.
units.tr: CI. But the Pontiffs, above all, have also carried on, and still carry on, their unwearied trade in ecclesiastical benefices in this respect: they have not only burdened the possessions of the Churches and of churchmen with pensions, taxes and subsidies, but have also demanded from them, under the pretext of waging war against the Caesars or the Turk, fifteenths, tenths, fifths, thirds, and halves of their goods.

units.la: Longum esset ex historiarum monumentis nundinationem hanc condigna ratione repraesentare. De Innocentio III. Caesarius in Dialogis refert, cum Cistertiensi Ordini praecepisse, ut quadragesimam partem mobilium suorum in bellum sacrum contribuerent, & ordini privilegia sua objicienti, comminatum esse, quòd possessiones ejus Principum Secularium praedae exponere velit. Itaque Monachos in angustias redactos ad D. Mariam confugisse, ejusque opem implorâsse, quae exorata apparuerit Regnerio Monacho, jusserítque cum Innocentio renunciare, omnem se ei potestatem adempturam, nisi à coeptis desisterit. Pontificem apparitioni fidem habentem à coepta exactione desistisse, & ordinis privilegia confirmâsse. Sic Caesarius, quem penes fides esto. Tentavit etiam aliquid Honorius III. qui, Matthæo Paris ad A. 1226. narrante, Othonem Legatum in Galliam & Angliam misit, rogaturum Episcopos, dignarentur pii liberi matris inopiam sublevare, quandoquidem rapacitate & iniquitate Romanæ Curiæ ærarium Pontificis exhaustum sit. Sublevari autem ærarium posse, si ei concederent percipere ab omnibus Ecclesiis Cathedralibus duas præbendas, unam de portione Episcopi, alteram de capitulo, & similiter de Cœnobiis, ubi divisæ erant portiones Abbatis & Conventús, à Conventibus quantum pertineret ad unum Monachum æquali facta distributione bonorum Conventús, ita ut inter Monachos Pontifex Romanus computaretur, & ab Abbate tantundem. Sed desiderio Papæ, intercedente Angliæ Rege, factum satis non est. Fortunatior Gregorius IX. apud eundem Paris ad A. 1229. suscepto in Fridericum Imperatorem gravi odio, decimas non Ecclesiasticis duntaxat, sed laicis etiam imperavit, laicis non audientibus dicto, audire Ecclesiastici Angli inprimis à Rege suo non protecti, censurarum intentarum metu compulsi sunt. Idem Gregorius post etiam Paris ad A. 1240. referente, ab Ecclesiasticis quartam bonorum partem exegit. Et in Gallia jam grandem pecuniarum vim Nuntius ejus corrogaverat, sed, Rege prohibente, auferre non poterat, donec cum Friderico Imperatore in gratiam rediisset. Innocentius IV. apud eundem Paris ad A. 1246. 1247. 1254. idem subsidium à Clericis Anglis exigit, sed non impetravit. Vigesimam dein imperavit & collegit. Cùmque post tertiam bonorum partem repetiisset, repulsam passus est. Mox tributum Cleroindixit, tallagii nomine, sed ei Rex iterum intercessit. Ne vero soli Angliæ gravis esse videretur, misit quatuor Cardinales Legatos per Italiam, Hispaniam, Norwegiam, Germaniam, aliåsque regioregiones, ut pecuniam colligerent. Denique sic de eodem Pontifice Paris loquitur: Plures ille thesauros congessit, & plus Ecclesiam universalem depauperavit, quàm omnes praedecessores à tempore Papatus primitivi, licet per tales effusiones pecuniae, Ecclesia non suscipepat incrementum, imò potiùs infaustum detrimentum incurreret. Clemens IV. decimas indixit in redemtionem terrae sanctae. Honorius IV. omnium proventuum Cleri partem quar-tam indixit per quatuor annos. Clementi V. Germani Praesules in Concilio Salisburgensi I. decimas duorum un-norum, deductis expensis necessariis, concesserunt. Et jam Bonifacius VIII. lege lata, quae Cap. und. de Decimis in Extravag. com. extat, amplissimè expresserat, qui ab iis immunes sint, & quas ob causas praestari debeant. Exempla plura referre piget, cum & plurima à Michaële Rouffelio Hist. Jurisd. Pont. lib. v. cap. 2. ff. 11. memorata fusiùs extent, & hodiéque exactiones ejusmodi frequentari soleant, Pontifice in suam, vel Regum ab eo emendicantium gratiam, Cleri proventus, ministerio Ecclesiae primitùs dicatos, inclementer invadente, & ad alienos usus, privatúmque quaestum suum traducente. Nam in solius Papae potestate nundinatio haec est. Unde Gregorius X. in Lugdunensi Concilio sanxit, ut nisi volente & jubente Papa, vel Regibus indictionem super Ecclesiasticis bonis tentare, vel Ecclesiasticis quicquam con-ferre, nefas esset.
units.tr: It would be long to portray this trade, worthily, from the records of histories. Concerning Innocent III, Caesarius reports in his Dialogues that he ordered the Cistercian Order to contribute the fortieth part of its movable goods to the holy war, and when the Order objected its privileges, he threatened that he would expose its possessions to the plunder of secular princes. So the monks, reduced to straits, fled to the Blessed Virgin Mary and implored her aid; she, having been entreated, appeared to the monk Regner and ordered him to announce to Innocent that she would take away all his power unless he desisted from his undertakings. The Pontiff, believing the apparition, desisted from the exaction he had begun and confirmed the privileges of the Order. So Caesarius, whose word may be trusted. Honorius III also attempted something; as Matthew Paris in the year 1226 relates, he sent Otto as legate into France and England, to ask the bishops whether they would deign to relieve the poverty of the pious free mother, since the Pontiff's treasury had been drained by the rapacity and iniquity of the Roman Curia. The treasury could be relieved, he said, if they would concede that he receive from all the cathedral churches two prebends, one from the bishop's portion and the other from the chapter, and likewise from the monasteries, where the portions of the abbot and the convent were divided, from the convent as much as would fall to one monk, by an equal distribution of the goods of the convent, so that the Roman Pontiff would be counted among the monks, and receive as much from the abbot. But, though the Pope desired it, and the King of England interceded, nothing sufficient was done. Gregory IX was more fortunate: as Paris records in the year 1229, having conceived a serious hatred against the Emperor Frederick, he imposed tithes not only on the clergy but also on the laity; the laity did not obey, but the English clergy, not protected above all by their own King, were compelled by fear of the threatened censures to obey. The same Gregory, as Paris reports in the year 1240, afterwards exacted a fourth part of the goods from the clergy. And in France his legate had already collected a great sum of money, but, the King forbidding it, he could not carry it off, until he had returned to favour with the Emperor Frederick. Innocent IV, as the same Paris reports in the years 1246, 1247, 1254, demanded the same subsidy from the English clergy, but did not obtain it. Then he imposed and collected a twentieth. And when he had afterwards demanded a third part of the goods, he met with a rebuff. Soon he imposed a tax on the clergy, under the name of tallage, but the King again interposed. Lest it seem to be a burden on England alone, he sent four cardinal legates through Italy, Spain, Norway, Germany and other regions, to collect money. Finally, Paris speaks thus of the same Pontiff: He amassed more treasures, and impoverished the universal Church more, than all his predecessors since the time of the primitive Papacy, although through such outpourings of money the Church did not gain increase but rather suffered unlucky loss. Clement IV imposed tithes for the redemption of the Holy Land. Honorius IV imposed a fourth part of all the revenues of the clergy for four years. To Clement V the German prelates at the Council of Salzburg granted tithes of two years' income, after deducting necessary expenses. And already Boniface VIII, by a law passed, which stands as Cap. und. on Tithes in the Extravagantes communes, had set out most fully who are immune from them and for what causes they ought to be paid. It irks me to recount more examples, since very many have been related at greater length by Michael Rouffelius, Hist. Jurisd. Pont. book 5, chap. 2, p. 11, and such exactions are still commonly practised today, when the Pontiff, for his own favour or that of the Kings who beg from him, cruelly invades the revenues of the clergy, which were first dedicated to the ministry of the Church, and diverts them to alien uses and to his own private gain. For this trade lies in the power of the Pope alone. Hence Gregory X, in the Council of Lyons, decreed that it was wrong to attempt any levy on ecclesiastical goods, or to contribute anything to the clergy, unless the Pope willed and commanded it, or the Kings.

units.la: CII. Quid dicam de multis aliis Hierarchicorum te-chnis, & beneficia Ecclesiastica devorandi artibus, quid de universa administratione Papali, in qua plenitudinem potestatis sibi vendicárunt, atque hanc à se venditatam potestatem gnaviter exercuerunt? Quibus demùm verbis eloquar praedas, rapinásque coeteras, quas ex Ecclesia Christi, Pontifices, praetextu ordinationis & administrationis bonorum Ecclesiæ, quæ illi ut injusti, sed prudentes dispensatores à Domino ad privatum quæstum sevocârunt ; ceperunt? Veluti cùm abrogârunt nonnullorum ritè electorum electiones, aliis verò, qui jure legi non potuerunt, concesserunt, ut loca per postulationes occuparent: mutârunt traduxerúntque tum ipsos ab una sede ad aliam per translationes, tum dioceses ipsorum per divisiones: circa fructus malè perceptos, compositionem cum Camera Apostolica instituerunt, qua compositione, ceu reti magno Camera magnos pisces capit & exquamat, argenteas ex eis squamas & aureas deponens, sibíque capiens, atque sic in rapinæ & furti manifesti partem veniens: fabricârunt nova animalia, Prædicantes Fraterculos, sive atratos fratres Dominicanos, & Minoritas, Franciscanos, Fratres mendicantes, dictos Speculatores Papæ, iisque prædicandi potestatem, Ecclesiarum interim reditus ad se pertrahentes, permiserunt: pueris, spuriis, fatuis animarum curam permiserunt: Homicidis, adulteris, Simoniacis, ut beneficia sua retinere possent, concesserunt: non residentiæ indulserunt, ut non residentibus, Ecclesiæ bona abligurientibus necesse non esset greges suos invisere, iisque invigilare: beneficia expilârunt ad Abbatias per approbationes ditandas, ut ipsi posteà in fructibus Abbatiarum grandius spicilegium facerent: Prælatis & Prælaturas affectantibus imperârunt, ut cum ipsis componant non tantùm pro palliis, uti suprà vidimus, sed etiam pro baculis pastoralibus, pro mitris, pro annulis, pro schedulis signandis, ac ut eorum quoque servis transigant, pro scriptione, pro lectione, pro subscriptione, pro approbatione, pro collatione cum exemplari, pro relatione in acta, pro taxatione, pro receptione, pro asseveratione, pro traditione, atque etiam pro funiculo & plumbo, quibus Bullæ Papales ligari &
units.tr: CII. What shall I say of the many other tricks of the hierarchs and their arts of devouring ecclesiastical benefices? What of the whole Papal administration, in which they claimed for themselves the fullness of power and vigorously exercised the power they had thus sold to themselves? In what words shall I at last describe the other plunder and robbery that the Popes took from the Church of Christ under the pretext of ordering and administering the goods of the Church? The Lord had entrusted these goods to them as unjust but prudent stewards, and they diverted them to private gain. For example, when they annulled the lawful elections of some and granted to others, who could not be legitimately elected, the right to seize places by postulation; when they moved men from one see to another by translations and carved up their dioceses by divisions; when, concerning badly acquired fruits, they set up a composition with the Apostolic Chamber, by which composition the Chamber, like a great net, catches great fish and scales them, laying aside their silver and golden scales and taking them for itself, and so comes to share in rapine and manifest theft; when they fabricated new creatures, the Preaching Little Brothers, or black-robed Dominican brothers, and the Minorites, the Franciscans, mendicant friars called the Pope's Speculators, and granted them the power of preaching while drawing the revenues of the churches to themselves; when they entrusted the care of souls to boys, bastards and fools; when they granted to murderers, adulterers and simoniacs the right to keep their benefices; when they indulged non-residence, so that non-resident men devouring the goods of the Church would not need to visit their flocks or watch over them; when they plundered benefices to enrich abbacies by approbationes, so that afterwards they could make a richer gleaning from the revenues of the abbacies; when they ordered prelates who aspired to prelacies to come to terms with them not only for palls, as we have seen above, but also for pastoral staves, for mitres, for rings, for the signing of schedules, and that they should settle with their servants too, for writing, for reading, for subscription, for approval, for collation with the copy, for entry in the records, for taxation, for receipt, for attestation, for delivery, and even for the cord and lead with which Papal bulls were wont to be tied and sealed.

units.la: obsignari sueverunt: novos excogitârunt officiarios, imò armenta nova, catervásque officiariorum Cancellariæ suæ, hoc consilio, ut illis loca ista venundarent, quibus multis aureorum millibus venditis, exegerunt hi à miseris clientibus, Romam propter gratiam aut justitiam itantibus, ut pecunias illis annumerarent, auctis maximum in modum bullarum suarum pretiis & impensis: exercitus illos Registrariorum suorum, Notariorum, Protonotariorum, Dictatorum, Scribarum, Abbreviatorum, Datariorum, Refcribendariorum, Rationalium, Sollicitatorum, Plumbatorum, Speculatorum, Regentium, Viatorum, Ceremoniarum Clericorum, Clericorum cubiculi, Clericorum Camerae, aliàque extra numerum mancipia, pretio sanguinis Servorum Christi aluerunt: annuum statúmque imperárunt vectigal ex primitiis, decimis Sacerdotum, Abbatum, Episcoporum, & Cardinalium defunctorum fortuis, in quas ut executores invaserunt, & cùm illis testamenta faciendi licentiam concesserint (quà à Pontifice non obtentâ, bona eorum, juxta Pauli III. constitutionem velut intestatorum Camerae Apostolicæ cederent) sibi ipsis tamen partem aliquam reservárunt, velut à Cardinale præter quingentos illos ducatos quo pretio annulum suum quisque mercatur, omnes gemmas ejus capellares, ornamenta vasáque tam aurea, quàm argentea, cruces, candelabra, imagines, aliáque ejusmodi spolia (quo etiam diserto nomine in jure Papali veniunt, & quæ sui juris esse Pontifices decretis sanxerunt; quo fretus Gregorius XI. Joachimo Cureo in Annalibus Silesiæ, ad A. 1375. narrante, Capitulum Uratislaviense sibi triginta millia aureorum pro reliquis ab Episcopo Pretiflao bonis numerare coëgit; & Julius II. Bembo Hist. Ven. lib. x. referente, ex thesauris quorundam Sacerdotum Romæ defunctorum se ditavit. Tot denique tendiculis hamisque ad mortalium ubique terrarum bona in arculas suas conrogan-da, piscati sunt, & piscantur adhuc pro viribus suis; ut Aulicus Romanus Theodoricus à Niem in Nemor. Unionis Tract. 6. cap. 37. asserat, Cameram Pontificis maris assimilatam esse, in quod intrant omnia flumina, & non inundat.
units.tr: They devised new officials, indeed new herds and troops of officials of their Chancery, with this aim, that these posts should be sold; and having sold them for many thousands of gold pieces, they exacted money from the wretched clients who journeyed to Rome for favour or justice, so that they would pay it out to them, the prices and expenses of their bulls being raised to a great degree. These armies of their Registrars, Notaries, Protonotaries, Dictators, Scribes, Abbreviators, Datars, Rescript-writers, Accountants, Solicitors, Leaden-seal keepers, Spies, Regents, Messengers, Clerks of Ceremonies, Chamber clerks, Clerks of the Camera, and other slaves beyond number, they fed with the price of the blood of the servants of Christ. They imposed a fixed annual tax on the first-fruits and tithes, and on the chance goods of deceased priests, abbots, bishops and cardinals, into which they intruded as executors. And although they had granted these men permission to make wills (and if no such permission was obtained from the Pope, their goods, according to the constitution of Paul III, would fall to the Apostolic Chamber as those of the intestate), they still reserved some part for themselves. Thus, from a cardinal, besides those five hundred ducats which each man pays for the price of his ring, they took all his chapel jewels, ornaments and vessels, both gold and silver, crosses, candlesticks, images, and other such spoils. These are expressly included in Papal law, and the Popes decreed by their decrees that they were their own right. Relying on this, Gregory XI, as Joachim Cureus relates in the Annals of Silesia at the year 1375, compelled the Chapter of Breslau to pay them thirty thousand gold pieces for the goods left by Bishop Preslaus. And Julius II, as Bembo reports in Hist. Ven. book x., enriched himself from the treasures of certain priests who died in Rome. In short, they have fished, and still fish as best they can, with so many nets and hooks, to gather the goods of mortals into their little coffers everywhere on earth. As the Roman courtier Theodoric of Niem asserts in De Nemore Unionis, tract. 6, chap. 37, the Papal Chamber is like the sea, into which all rivers flow, yet it does not overflow.
CIII.

units.la: Venimus ad Regimen Ecclesiæ. Cùm igitur Ecclesiam ab hominibus regi ex præscripto legum, & judiciorum ministerio constet, Hierachici tum leges ipsas per dispensationem earum, tum judicia per causarum Ecclesiasticarum ad tribunal Romanum sevocationem quæstui habent. Leges vel divinæ vel humanæ sunt. In utrisque Papam Papaliter dispensandi jus sibi arrogare, suprà manifestum fecimus. Nunc non sine quæstu dispensare, circa manifestum similiter faciamus. Legibus strictis Deus Levit. xviii. & xx. matrimonia intrà quoslibet affinitatis & consanguinitatis gradus prohibuit, & contracta in iisdem abominationum nomine detestatus est. Sed eò tandem Papalium dispensationum, vel crudelium dissipationum potiùs Divini & humani juris (sic olim Bernhardus ad Eugenium, & post illum Gerson insigniverunt) licentia progressa est, ut nulli ferè gradui, dum dulcis lucelli facula alluceret, pepercerit. Ita Gusmanno Assidonensi Duci indultum est, ut duabus successivè sororibus: Duci Burgundiæ, ut avunculi sui Comitis Nivernensis viduæ: Emmanuelì Portugalliæ Regi, ut duabus sororibus, quarum prima nepotis ejus defuncti uxor fuerat, ac tertio conjugio nepti, harum uxorum gratiam faciente Alexandro VI. Ferdinando Regi Neapolitano, ut Johannis, avi sui filiæ, Alphonsi Patris ex alia matre sororì: Henrico VIII. Angliæ Regi, ut fratris sui viduæ, Catharinæ Austriacæ Philippo II. Hispaniæ Regi, ut nepti suæ: Petro Portugalliæ nuper Regenti, nunc Regi, ut Alphonsi fratris viventis uxori nuberet. Alia exempla superius produximus. In Taxa Poenitentiaria, titulo de causis Matrimonialibus sic legere est: In primo gradu affinitatis dispensatur in foro conscientiæ tantùm, & taxa est turon. 30. duc. 7. Carol. 6. In Concilio quidem Tridentino Seff. xxj. Decret. Reformat. cap. 5. hunc in modum sancitum est: In contrahendis matrimoniis intra gradus prohibitos, vel nullam omninò dandam esse dispensationem, vel rarò: idque ex causa & gratis. In secundo gradu nunquam dispensandum, nisi inter magnos Principes, & ob publicam causam. Dispensationes ergò ejusmodi probantur, sed raræ, judicio Papæ definiendæ, ex causa, Papæ ejusque Regno utili; & gratis, seu gratitudinem suam Papæ testantibus. Sic enim fert usus & praxis Papæ, quæ, utpote infallibilis, legis interpres est. Alioquin etiam facta dictis non suppetunt. Et jam olim Alvarus Pelagius de Planctu Eccl. lib. ij. art. 10. adversùs frivolas explicationes Prælatorum, qui Sacramenta vendunt, eorundem fraudes sic detexit: Sed dicunt isti ficti Prælati: Sacramenta non vendimus. Sed dicendum est, etsi ipsa Sacramenta invendibilia non vendunt, contra sacros canones, vendunt vocem, sigillum & calamum. Et canoni fraudem faciunt, de persona ad personam, quia quicquid accipit Notarius pro literis ordinatorum, vel totum, vel quasi totum tollit Episcopus. Et art. 5. iis applicat dictum Jeremiæ: Principes sunt socii furum, id est, inquit, Notariorum suorum, & tenentium sua sigilla, cum quibus participant lucra Simoniaca. CIV. Jam & in matrimoniis contractis, sine sontica, Divino jure expressa causa dirimendis, eadem Papalium dispensationum licentia obtinet. Jam olim enim, sic Suavis Hist. C. T. lib. j. pag. 61. scribit, Pontifices Romani dispensationibus matrimonialibus, repudiorúmque sententiis tam {&} conus. tam negatis, quàm concessis, magnam olim rebus suis accessionem fecerunt, nomine Vicarii Christi tanquam umbrā obtegentes eos Principes, quibus erat commodum per incestum aliquod connubium, aut matrimonio uno diremto ut aliud contraherent, ditionibus novam aliquam adjungere, aut diversorum petitorum jura extinguere: idque firmā cum ipsis amicitiā stabilitā, eorūmque potentiā ad autoritatem illam tuendam advocatā, absque qua foret, uti actiones ipsorum, quippe illegitimæ, damnarentur palām & impedirentur: neque ipsis duntaxat Principibus, sed & omnibus eorum liberis ad natalium suorum legitimationem defendendam accitis. Exempla haud pauca nundinationis illius per dispensata divortia Michaël Rousselius Hist. Jurisd. Pontif. lib. j. cap. 5. s. 9. recitat. Memorabilis certè vox est Bernhardi, qui comperto, quòd Rodolphus Virimanduorum Comes, uxorem suam repudiāsset, ut Petronillam Alienoræ Reginæ propinquam duceret, obtenta etiam dispensatione Cameræ Apostolicæ, in hæc verba erupit: Quomodo, quos Ecclesia conjunxit, disjunxit Camera? Sed & Alexandrum VI. acceptis triginta mille ducatis Ludovici XII. & conjugis sola deformitate exosæ, Ludovici XI. filiæ matrimonium distraxisse, & Episcopum Sittensem unà cum bulla dispensationis misisse, cum hoc secretiore mandato, ne bullam, nisi acceptis pecuniis & obligato adversùs Romandiolæ Vicarios auxilio, promeret, Franc. Gucciardinus testis est. Denique dispensationes Papales circa gradus matrimoniales prohibitos, & divortia, Regni Papalis haud postremum nervum fuisse semper, atque etiamnum esse, temporum Papatûs experientia dubitare non finit. Quod legum Divinarum quæstui habitarum irrefragabile argumentum est.
units.tr: We come to the government of the Church. Since the Church is governed by men through the prescription of laws and through the ministry of judgments, the hierarchs make a profit both from the laws themselves, through their dispensation, and from the judgments, through the summoning of ecclesiastical cases to the Roman tribunal. Laws are either divine or human. We have already shown above that the Pope claims for himself the right to dispense in both, in a papal manner. Now let us similarly show that he dispenses not without profit. By strict laws, God in Leviticus 18 and 20 forbade marriages within any degree of affinity and consanguinity, and detested those contracted within them under the name of abominations. But the licence of Papal dispensations, or rather of cruel dissipations of divine and human law (as Bernard long ago to Eugenius, and after him Gerson, named them), has advanced so far that it has spared almost no degree, as long as the little torch of sweet gain was shining. Thus it was granted to Guzmán, Duke of Medina Sidonia, to marry two sisters in succession; to the Duke of Burgundy, to marry the widow of his uncle, the Count of Nevers; to Emmanuel, King of Portugal, to marry two sisters, the first of whom had been the wife of his deceased nephew, and the third marriage to a niece, Alexander VI granting these wives as a favour; to Ferdinand, King of Naples, to marry the sister of his father Alfonso by another mother, the daughter of his grandfather John; to Henry VIII, King of England, to marry the widow of his brother, Catherine of Austria; to Philip II, King of Spain, to marry his niece; to Peter, formerly Regent and now King of Portugal, to marry the wife of his living brother Alfonso. We have brought forward other examples above. In the Penitentiary Taxes, under the title concerning matrimonial causes, one may read as follows: In the first degree of affinity, a dispensation is granted only in the court of conscience, and the tax is thirty Tours pounds, seven ducats, Charles VI. In the Council of Trent, Session 24, Decree of Reform, chapter 5, it was enacted in this manner: In contracting marriages within the forbidden degrees, either no dispensation at all is to be given, or rarely; and that for a cause and gratis. In the second degree, dispensation is never to be given, except between great princes and for a public cause. Such dispensations are therefore approved, but to be granted rarely, at the judgment of the Pope, for a cause useful to the Pope and his kingdom, and gratis, that is, with the recipients bearing witness to their gratitude to the Pope. For this is what the custom and practice of the Pope require, and the Pope, being infallible, is the interpreter of the law. Otherwise, things done contrary to these rules have no support. And long ago Alvarus Pelagius, in De Planctu Ecclesiae, book 2, art. 10, against the frivolous explanations of prelates who sell sacraments, exposed their frauds in this way: But those false prelates say: we do not sell sacraments. But it must be said that, even if they do not sell the sacraments themselves, which cannot be sold, they sell, contrary to the sacred canons, the voice, the seal and the pen. And they defraud the canon from person to person, because whatever the notary receives for the letters of ordinations, the bishop takes all or nearly all of it. And in art. 5 he applies to them the saying of Jeremiah: the princes are companions of thieves, that is, he says, of their notaries, and of those who hold their seals, with whom they share the Simoniacal gains. CIV. Also in marriages contracted without any sin, and dissolved for a cause expressed by divine law, the same licence of Papal dispensations prevails. For long ago, as Suavis writes in Hist. Council of Trent, book 1, page 61, the Roman Pontiffs, by their matrimonial dispensations and their sentences of divorce, both those refused and those granted, long ago greatly increased their possessions. Under the name of Vicar of Christ they covered, like a shadow, those princes for whom it was advantageous, through some incestuous union, or by dissolving one marriage, to contract another, to add some new dominion to their lands, or to extinguish the rights of various claimants. And this was done with a firm friendship established with them, and with their power summoned to defend that authority; without which their actions, being illegitimate, would have been openly condemned and hindered. And this was done not only for the princes themselves, but also for all their children, summoned to defend the legitimation of their birth. Michael Rousselius, in Hist. Jurisd. Pontif. book 1, chap. 5, sect. 9, recites no few examples of this trade in divorces obtained by dispensation. Bernard's words are certainly memorable. When he learned that Rodolph, Count of the Vermandois, had put away his wife so that he might marry Petronilla, a kinswoman of Queen Aliénor, and had even obtained a dispensation from the Apostolic Chamber, he burst out in these words: How is it that the Chamber has separated those whom the Church joined together? Francesco Guicciardini is also a witness that Alexander VI, having received thirty thousand ducats from Louis XII, dissolved the marriage of Louis's daughter, a woman hated for her deformity alone, and sent the Bishop of Sion together with the bull of dispensation, with this more secret mandate: not to issue the bull unless the money had been received and an obligation made for help against the Vicars of Romagna. Finally, the experience of the Papal times does not permit us to doubt that Papal dispensations concerning the forbidden matrimonial degrees and divorces have always been, and still are, no small sinew of the Papal kingdom. This is an irrefutable proof of divine laws turned into a source of profit.

units.la: CV. Leges Divinæ juramentorum & votorum legitimè præstitorum & nuncupatorum religionem sacrosanctam esse
units.tr: CV. The divine laws command that oaths and vows lawfully made and sworn are to be regarded as a sacred obligation.

units.la: effejubent. Hanc quoque religionem dispensationibus suis identidem violare Papas, supra apertæ veritati dedimus. Violat autem etiam in juramentis summorum Principum, ut partibus commodisque suis eos obstringat, quæ sacrosanctarum rerum scelesta nundinatio est. E multis exemplis unicum proferam illud, quo Clemens VIII. Francisocum I. Galliæ Regem juramenti Madriti Carolo V. præstiti nexu exsolvit, ut Galliæ Regem in suas adversus Imperatorem partes pertraheret. Quoties vero in Gallia, Anglia, alibique Papa sola stabiliendæ tyrannidis suæ libidine nefaria, subditis Imperiorum frangendi juramenti fidelitatis, quo superioribus suis devincti erant, gratiam fecit?
units.tr: Earlier we showed from plain truth that the Popes repeatedly violate this sacred obligation by their dispensations. They also violate it in the oaths of the greatest princes, binding them to the Pope's own parties and advantages, which is a wicked trafficking in holy things. Of many examples I will cite only one, in which Clement VIII released Francis I, King of France, from the bond of the oath he had sworn to Charles V at Madrid, so that he might draw the King of France into the Pope's own side against the Emperor. And how often in France, England and elsewhere has the Pope, out of nothing but the wicked lust of establishing his own tyranny, granted subjects release from breaking the oath of allegiance by which they were bound to their superiors?

units.la: CVI. Votorum quæ legitimè nuncupata Hierarchici
units.tr: CVI. Of vows lawfully made

units.la: credunt, ab eodem Papa, prout commoda ejus ferebant, refciforum exempla non minus obvia sunt, è quorum numero nonnulla idem Rouffelius loco cit. cap. 5. ff. 1. recitat. Quoties enim Papa votorum peregrinationis, castitatis, obedientiæ, Monachorum, Monialium, Fraterculorum, religionem pecuniæ remisit? Sic Benedictus IX. Baronio ad A. 1041. narrante, Polonis concessit, ut Casimirum, Monachum Benedictinum è clausTRO eductum, sibi Regem crearent, hac tamen lege, ut Polonorum Regnum ad regiones in signum accepti beneficii B. Petro & successoribus de quolibet capite nobilium usualem nummum annis singulis persolverent. Thomas equidem Aquinas 2. 2. q. 88. art. 11. tenet, illicitam & nullam esse dispensationem à Pontifice indultam, qua Monachus voto continentiæ, quod essentialiter religionis statui inhæret, solvatur; licet, inquit, nonnulli Juristæ contrarium dicant, eo prætextu, quod inde (NBr) utilitas publica (Papalis scilicet Regni,) procuratur. Inter Juristas illos sunt præter alios Covarruvias de Testam. cap. 2. Jacobus Almain
units.tr: They believed, from the same Pope, as their advantage required, that release from such vows was granted. Examples of this are no less common, and Rouffelius, loc. cit. cap. 5, ff. 1, recounts some of them. For how often has a Pope remitted the vows of pilgrimage, chastity, and obedience, or the religious obligations of monks, nuns, and friars, in return for money? Thus Benedict IX, as Baronius relates under the year 1041, allowed the Poles to make Casimir, a Benedictine monk taken out of the cloister, their king for himself, on this condition: that the Polish kingdom should pay to St Peter and his successors, in token of the benefit received, a customary coin each year from every head of a noble household. Thomas Aquinas indeed holds (2.2, q. 88, art. 11) that a dispensation granted by the Pontiff, by which a monk is released from the vow of continence, which is essential to the state of religion, is unlawful and void, although, he says, some jurists say the opposite, on the pretext that public utility (namely that of the Papal realm) is thereby promoted. Among those jurists are, besides others, Covarruvias, de Testam. cap. 2, and James Almain.

units.la: {y} Votorum main tract. de pot. Eccl. & laica cap. 13. 14. Tomoj. Gersonis, ubi arrestum Curiæ Parisiensis, hujusmodi Dispensationem Papalem, rejecta appellatione ab abusu improbans, refertur: aliique. Recte tamen Thomas eidem illi Jurisconsultorum objectioni ab utilitate publica petitæ, respondet, periculis rerum humanarum obviandum esse per res humanas, non autem per hoc, quòd res divinæ convertantur in usum humanum, dicente lege in Levitico: Quod semel sanctificatum est Domino, non potest in alios usus commutari. Extant etiam exempla relaxationis voti cruce signatorum. Matthæus Paris ad ann. 1240. Eisdem temporibus, inquit, inceperunt ipsi Prædicatores fratres, & Minores, & alii viri liberati præcipuè Theologi, cruce signatos absolvere à voto suo accepta tamen pecunia, quanta sufficere videbatur unicuique ad viaticum ultrà marinum. Et factum est in populo scandalum cum schismate, absurdum enim videbatur simplicibus, quòd diversis muscipulis Romana Curia moliretur populum substantia sua privare, nil petens nisi aurum & argentum.
units.tr: {y} Almain, tract. de pot. Eccl. & laica cap. 13, 14; Tomo j. Gersonis, where a decree of the Parisian Court is cited, which rejects such a Papal dispensation by appeal against abuse; and others. Nevertheless Thomas answers this objection of the jurists, drawn from public utility, rightly: dangers of human affairs must be met by human means, not by turning divine things to human use, since the law in Leviticus says: What has once been sanctified to the Lord cannot be changed to other uses. There are also examples of the release of those who had taken the cross from their vow. Matthew Paris, under the year 1240, writes: At the same time, the friars Preachers themselves, and the Minorites, and other men, chiefly theologians, began to absolve those signed with the cross from their vow, provided they accepted money, as much as seemed enough for each one's journey beyond the sea. And a scandal arose among the people, with schism; for it seemed absurd to simple folk that the Roman Curia was contriving, with various traps, to strip the people of their wealth, asking for nothing but gold and silver.

units.la: CVII. Dispensationi simili originem debet Denarius S. Petri, nobile tributum, quod Latialis ille flamen Anglis, aliisque ceu nexu mancipióque propriis, aut duro Marte subactis, in singula hominum capita pro recognitione imposuit. De tributo hoc sic Hovedenus Annalium parte posteriore in legibus Guilhelmi senioris: Omnis qui habuerit triginta denariatos vivæ pecuniæ in domo sua de proprio suo, Anglorum lege dabit denarium S. Petri, & lege Danorum dimidiam marcam. In Chronico Johannis Brontom inter leges Kanuti Regis hæc xii. recensetur. Et Romfet (sic appellabatur, alias etiam Rome-Scot, & Peterpence) id est, Romæ censu, quem Beato Petro singulis annis reddendum, ad laudem & gloriam Dei Regis nostri larga benignitas semper instituit, in festo S. Petri reddareddatur, qui supra tenuerit, reddat Episcopo denarium illum, & xxx. denarios addat, & Regi det xxx. Quo verò jure tributum isthoc Papa exegit? Recitat de Anglis idem Hovedenus, primum Ethel Wolphum gratitudinis signum perpetuum hoc decrevisse Papæ Leoni IV. eò quod votum Monachatûs, quo jam obstringebatur, sibi remisisset, ut Angliæ Rex fieri posset. Sic ergò muliebri superstitione totam Angliam Papæ tributariam fecit, decimámque Regni sui partem concessit, ut ex qualibet domo quotannis nummus argenteus pensitaretur. Ex libera rerum suarum dispensatione sic fecisse Regem, Sciopius, clitellarium Papæ mancipium, objicit. Scilicet si libere agit, & dispensat is, quem cogit superstitiosum alienæ gratiæ aucupium. Superstitionis enim fascino vis infertur voluntati, nec ordine eligitur quod opinio præconcepta imperat.
units.tr: CVII. A similar dispensation gave rise to the Denarius of St Peter, the noble tribute, which that Latin priest imposed on the English and other peoples bound to him as if by a chain and by ownership, or subdued by harsh war, as a payment for each head of a household. Concerning this tribute, Hoveden says thus in the later part of his Annals, under the laws of William the Elder: Every man who has thirty pence of living money in his house, from his own property, shall pay the Denarius of St Peter by the law of the English, and half a mark by the law of the Danes. In the Chronicle of John of Brompton, among the laws of King Canute, these twelve are listed: And Romfeoh (as it was called, otherwise also Rome-scot or Peter's pence), that is, the Roman tax, which is to be paid to blessed Peter every year, our king's generous kindness has always ordained, to the praise and glory of God, that it be paid on St Peter's feast. Whoever has held more than this shall pay that penny to the bishop, and add thirty pence, and give thirty to the king. But by what right did this Pope exact the tribute? The same Hoveden records, concerning the English, that first Ethelwulf decreed this perpetual token of gratitude to Pope Leo IV, because the Pope had released him from the vow of monastic life by which he was already bound, so that he might become King of England. Thus, by womanish superstition, he made the whole of England tributary to the Pope, and granted a tenth part of his kingdom, so that a silver coin should be paid from every household each year. Sciopius, the Pope's pack-saddle slave, objects that the king acted in this way from a free disposal of his own property. Clearly, a man acts and disposes freely only when he is not compelled by superstitious courting of another's favour. For force is done to the will by the spell of superstition, and what a preconceived opinion commands is not chosen in due order.

units.la: CVIII. Quid quòd Papa pecuniâ numerata lenoniam permisit, hoc est, facultatem in lupanaribus impunè scortandi, numerato sibi pretio, concessit, adeoque à lege divina castitatis solenniter dispensavit? Qua re quid sœdius, sordidius quid excogitari potest? Eam in rem non pauca Dissert. xv. ff. 52 — 58. diximus. Addo illud Gobelini Ætat. vj. cap. 90. ubi sic ille: Papa Bononiæ residens rigorem, quo Bononiensibus priùs dominabatur, non laxans, maximam pecuniarum summam ex gabellis civitatis etiam per eum augmentatis recepit per singulos menses, ita ut etiam meretrices de statu suo circa slorenos trecentos solvere viderentur in mense, quòd, uti in Statuum Imperii Gravamine LXXVI. habetur, clericos, religiossque & seculares accepto ab eisdem annuo censu, publicè cum suis concubinis, aliisque id genus meretricibus illegitimè cohabitare, liberòsque procreare sinunt, quòdque, uti Gravamine sequente exponitur, officiales, absente quin & lenoniam, quam pro pecunia Papa indulget, sente altera Conjuge, belli, votorum, vel alia quapiam causa pacta numeratáque priùs mercede satis magna, cum alia vicitare persona indulget, sub tolerantiæ nomine: Inunc, & Vespasiano suum illud objice: Odor lucri bonus, è re qualibet! Et manet hodieque infame illud tributum, mediaque Roma erectum lupanar, ut ne desit, unde exigatur. Imò ut ne desit, unde Roma Mater fornicationum agnoscatur.
units.tr: CVIII. What of the fact that the Pope, for numbered money, permitted prostitution, that is, granted, for a price paid to himself, the liberty to fornicate with impunity in brothels, and so solemnly dispensed from the divine law of chastity? What can be devised more foul or more sordid than this? On this matter we have said not a few things in our Dissertation 15, folios 52–58. I add that passage of Gobelinus, Age 6, chapter 90, where he writes: The Pope, residing at Bologna, not relaxing the rigour with which he had formerly ruled the Bolognese, received each month a very large sum of money from the city's taxes, which he had also increased, so that even prostitutes seemed to pay about three hundred florins a month from their earnings. For he allowed clerics, religious and laymen, having received an annual rent from them, to live openly with their concubines and other women of that kind, and to beget children; and, as is set out in the next Grievance, his officials indulge, for money paid in advance and a large enough fee, the practice of living with another woman while the lawful spouse is absent, under the name of tolerance, for reasons of war, of vows, or some other cause. Now, object to him also that saying of Vespasian: The smell of profit is good, from whatever source! And that infamous tax remains to this day, and a brothel was set up in the middle of Rome, lest there be any lack of a source from which to collect it. Indeed, lest there be any lack, Rome is recognised as the Mother of fornications.

units.la: CIX. Haud verecundior est à legibus humanis, & constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis, quas amplificare placuit, ut iis velut laqueis quibusdam alites irretirentur, pecuniosa dispensatio.
units.tr: CIX. No less shameless is the dispensation for money from human laws and ecclesiastical constitutions, which men have chosen to multiply, so that birds of passage might be ensnared in them as in a kind of nets.

units.la: De qua Status Imperii jam olim Gravamine primo, sub titulo, de Dispensationibus æ re redemtis, ejusmodi querelam consignarunt: Inter reliqua onera, vel illud maximè postremo loco est collocandum, quòd constitutionibus humanis multa prohibentur, imperantur item multa, quæ nullo Divino præcepto vel interdicta sunt vel imperata. Quod genus sunt matrimoniorum tam innumera excogitata obstacula, ex affinitatis, publicæ honestatis cognatione spirituali, legalique, & consanguinitatis, tam multis gradibus, originem trahentia. Ciborum item usus interdictus, quos Deus tamen ad hominis necessitatem creavit, ac cum gratiarum actione promiscuè sumendos Apostolus docuit. Hæ nimirum, atque his similes complures humanæ constitutiones eò usque ligant homines, donec pecuniâ sibi harum legum gratiam à statuentibus impetrant, ut ita pecunia faciat divitibus licitum, quod tenuibus gratis sit prohibitum. Illicitisque his legum ac constitutionum humanarum retiaculis non modò magna nummorum copia à Germanis expiscata, è Germania & trans Alpes lata: sed & maxima inter æquè Christianos orta iniquitas, plura offendicula, simultates, dum omnes hisce laqueis vident se illaqueari, non ob aliud, nisi quòd spinas Euangelicas (ita enim Christus divitias non semel appellat) non possideant. Gravamine secundo querelam de Tempore interdicto, sic iidem ingeminant: Pari modo agitur etiam cum celebrandis nuptiarum solennibus, à Dominica septuagesima, qua cantatur in Ecclesia: Circumdederunt me &c. sub quadragesima usque initium, quo tempore ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ Primoribus undique nuptias celebrari interdictum est: cùm tamen interim & ab Ecclesiasticis, & à Secularibus, passim sine discrimine genialiter vivatur. Sed ita demùm interdictum illud procedit, si gratis hoc facere quis intendat. Quod si nummi spes refulserit, jam quod primùm erat prohibitum, impunè ac liberè facere licet. Est enim & hoc grave Germanorum crumenis retiaculum, quo extrahuntur nummi. Nec minus interim gravamen, quòd pauperis & divitis longè diversa in relaxandis his constitutionibus sit conditio. Pertinent huc leges compositionum uti vocant, quibus Pontifex Datario suo facultatem concessit, transfigendi cum eo, qui dispensationem petit, ut certam pecuniæ summam pro ea pensitet. Eas abolere voluisse Pontifices nonnulli feruntur; Hadrianus VI. Paulus IV. qui Onuphrio in vita ejus teste, Datarium severè admonuit, ne pro impetrandarum quarumlibet rerum quæ concessione parùm digna viderentur, compositionibus aliquas pecunias acciperet, cùm sibi persuasisset, multas pecuniarum summas eo munere contra jus cogi. Cùmque plures eam in rem deliberationes instituisset, quærens, an hæ solutiones pecuniarum, quæ compositionum nomine veniunt, legitimæ essent, auditis omnium sententiis, affirmantes corripuisse dicitur. Erat nempè ex numero Delegatorum Pauli III. Cardinalis, Caspari Cantareni nomine, qui à Paulo III. in consilium Ecclesiæ Reformandæ missi, decreverant, in usu clavium, seu Ecclesiastica functione nihil pecuniâ geri debere. Sed deinceps placuit distinctio inter compositiones, quæ fiunt ob gratias concessas in foro fori, veluti cùm quis dispensaretur ad plura beneficia, vel super defectu natalium, residentia, consanguinitate, voto, thoro conjugali, & similibus: & quæ in foro conscientiæ. Ob priores deberi compositionem visum est, non ob posteriores, quia hic nihil adjudicetur à judice, nihil canonizari, uti loquuntur, permittatur, sed anima duntaxat ad salutem dirigatur, atque ad hoc literæ forum fori concernentes, & ad probationem producendæ non requirantur, cùm in foro conscientiæ solo afferentis dicto stetur. Ita Gamesius ad regul. de non judic. juxta fori suppl. q. 14. & Rebuffus ad tit. de dispens. super defectu nat. num. 96. Hinc esse iidem asserunt, quòd juxta veterem inde à Benedicto XII. receptum stylum in Sacra Pœnitentiaria, quando gratia in foro Conscientiæ petitur, absolutio confessori committatur in literis laniatis, & nullis testibus adhibitis. Distinctionem verò hanc meritò vellicat ipse Rouffelius Hist. Jurisd. Pontif. lib. j. cap. 6. ff. 12. eo videlicet argumento, quòd Apostolis generali sermone præceptum sit, ut gratis darent, quia gratis acceperant: ac dici etiam posset, hujusmodi compositiones viam sternere tot dispensationibus per fas & nefas. Unde jam diu dissipationes appellatæ fuerint. Ecquid non enim, inquit,
units.tr: Of this, the Estates of the Empire, long ago, in their first Grievance under the heading Of dispensations redeemed with money, recorded such a complaint: Among the other burdens, this must be placed last of all: that by human constitutions many things are forbidden, and likewise many things are commanded which have been neither forbidden nor commanded by any divine precept. Of this kind are the countless obstacles devised for marriages, arising from affinity, public decency, spiritual and legal kinship, and kinship within so many degrees. Likewise the use of foods is forbidden, which God nevertheless created for man's necessity, and which the Apostle taught must be taken with thanksgiving and without distinction. These and many similar human constitutions bind men so far, until they obtain by money from the lawgivers favour in these laws, so that money makes lawful for the rich what is forbidden to the poor. And by these unlawful nets of laws and human constitutions, not only has a great quantity of money been fished out of the Germans and carried out of Germany and across the Alps, but also the greatest injustice has arisen among those equally Christian, many stumbling-blocks and enmities, while all see themselves ensnared by these nooses, for no other reason than that they do not possess the Gospel thorns (for Christ more than once calls riches by that name). In the second Grievance, under the heading Of forbidden time, they repeat the complaint in these words: In the same way, it is also the case with the celebration of marriage solemnities: from the Sunday of Septuagesima, when in the Church is sung, "The cords of death compassed me," until the Quadragesima, during which time it is forbidden by the chief men of the Roman Church to celebrate marriages everywhere; while meanwhile both clergy and laymen live together in marriage here and there without distinction. But that prohibition holds only if someone intends to do this without payment. If the hope of money glimmers, then what was first forbidden may be done freely and with impunity. For this too is a grave net for the purses of the Germans, by which money is drawn out. No less a grievance is the very different condition of the poor man and the rich man in the relaxation of these constitutions. To this belong the rules called compositions, by which the Pontiff granted his Datary the power of settling with the one who seeks a dispensation, that he should pay a certain sum of money for it. Some report that the Popes wished to abolish these: Hadrian VI and Paul IV, who, as Onuphrius attests in his life, sharply admonished the Datary not to take any sums of money by way of compositions for obtaining any favours which seemed scarcely worthy of being granted, since he had persuaded himself that large sums of money were extorted by this office contrary to law. And when he had held several deliberations on this matter, asking whether these payments of money, which come under the name of compositions, were lawful, and after hearing everyone's opinion, he is said to have rebuked those who affirmed it. For he was one of the Delegates of Pope Paul III, the Cardinal named Caspar Contarini, who, sent by Paul III into the council for reforming the Church, had decreed that in the use of the keys, or in ecclesiastical function, nothing should be done for money. But afterwards a distinction was accepted between compositions made for favours granted in the outer forum, as when someone was dispensed for several benefices, or concerning defect of birth, residence, consanguinity, vow, conjugal bed and the like, and those made in the forum of conscience. It was thought that a composition was owed for the former, not for the latter, because in the latter nothing is adjudged by a judge, nothing is canonised, as they say, is permitted, but the soul alone is directed to salvation; and for this purpose letters concerning the outer forum are not required, nor are they to be produced as proof, since in the forum of conscience the word of the one making the claim alone is relied upon. So Gamesius, on the rule de non judicando, juxta fori supplementum, question 14, and Rebuffus, on the title de dispensationibus super defectu natalium, number 96. Hence, they assert, according to the old practice received from Benedict XII in the Sacred Penitentiary, when a favour is sought in the forum of conscience, absolution is committed to the confessor in torn letters, with no witnesses present. But this distinction is rightly censured by Rouffelius himself, History of Papal Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 6, folio 12, on the argument that it was commanded to the Apostles in general terms that they should give freely, because they had received freely; and it could also be said that such compositions pave the way for so many dispensations by right and wrong. Whence for a long time they have been called dissipations. For what, he says, does not the sacred hunger for gold compel mortal hearts to do?
Accursed hunger for gold, to what do you not drive mortal hearts?

units.la: Unde non mirum, si hujusmodi dispensationes ignotæ fuerint in Curia Romana per plura Secula, cùm venalitas ibi locum non haberet. Hactenus ille.
units.tr: Hence it is no wonder that dispensations of this kind were unknown in the Roman Curia for many centuries, since venality had no place there. So far he.

units.la: CX. Dispensationum ejusmodi pretia extra compositiones cum Datario Taxa pœnitentiaria definire non omittit. Ita enim sub titulo de Causis matrimonialibus inter alia finivit,
units.tr: CX. The prices of such dispensations, apart from compositions, the penitentiary taxes do not fail to fix together with the Datary. Thus under the title concerning matrimonial causes, among other things, it has laid down as follows:

units.la: Ita enim sub titulo de Causis matrimonialibus inter alia finivit. alia legere est: Pro contractu quarti gradus taxa est turon. 7. duc. 1. Carol. 6. Si qui gradus hujus impedimentum scientes carnaliter commixti sunt, taxantur turon. 16. duc. 4. pro legitimatione prolis suscipiende indicta gravidæ specialis taxa est turon. 9. duc. 1. Carol. 10. Qui ignorantes, hoc impedimentum carnaliter copulati sunt, turon. 9. duc. 1. Carol. 10. Qui ignoranter contraxerunt, & scienter consummârunt, pendunt turon. 7. duc. 1. Carol. 6. De contractu matrimonio in tertio gradu consanguinitatis vel affinitatis, taxa est turon. 14. Du- cat 3. Carol. 4. Et præterea componendum semper est cum Datario. In secundo consanguinitatis vel affinitatis gradu dispensatur tantum per Signoriam Papæ, aut sede vacante per Summum Pœnitentiarium, & taxa est turon. 50. duc. 12. Carol. 6. Divortium simplex taxatur turon. 7. duc. 1. Carol. 6. Qui contraxerunt in cognatione spirituali, taxantur turon. 17. duc. 3. Carol. 9. Si cognatio hujusmodi fuerit duplex, taxa est tur. 30. duc. 7. Carol. 2. In compaternitate dispensatur tantum per Signoriam Papæ, vel sede vacante, per Signoriam Pœnitentiarii Summi, & taxa est turon. 50. duc. 12. Carol. 3. Si quis mortem conjugi suæ machinatus est, effectu non consecuto, nec side alteri data, dispensatur, ut mortua conjuge cum altera contrahat, & taxatur turon. 9. duc. 2. Carol. 9. Cum eo qui vovit perpetuam castitatem, dispensatur in foro Conscientiæ tantum, & taxa est turon. 16. duc. 3. Carol. 6. Cum eo, qui vovit, quod religionem intrare velit, non tamen solenniter, dispensatur, ut contrahat matrimonium in foro Conscientiæ tantum, & ta- xa est turon. 15. duc. 4. &c. Dispensationibus ejusmodi ab aliis etiam quàm matrimonialibus legibus, plena taxa est. Pauca adscripsimus, ut ex simbria vestimentum cognoscatur.
units.tr: Among other things it lays down, under the title concerning matrimonial causes, as follows. Other items may be read: For a contract in the fourth degree the tax is turon. 7, duc. 1, Carol. 6. Those who, knowing of the impediment of this degree, have had carnal intercourse are assessed at turon. 16, duc. 4. For the legitimation of offspring to be received, a special tax is imposed on a pregnant woman: turon. 9, duc. 1, Carol. 10. Those who, being ignorant of this impediment, have been carnally joined: turon. 9, duc. 1, Carol. 10. Those who contracted in ignorance and consummated knowingly pay turon. 7, duc. 1, Carol. 6. For a marriage contract in the third degree of consanguinity or affinity, the tax is turon. 14, ducats 3, Carol. 4. And besides, one must always compound with the Datary. In the second degree of consanguinity or affinity, dispensation is granted only by the Signory of the Pope, or, when the see is vacant, by the Chief Penitentiary, and the tax is turon. 50, duc. 12, Carol. 6. A simple divorce is taxed at turon. 7, duc. 1, Carol. 6. Those who contracted in spiritual kinship are taxed at turon. 17, duc. 3, Carol. 9. If such kinship is double, the tax is tur. 30, duc. 7, Carol. 2. In co-parenthood, dispensation is granted only by the Signory of the Pope, or, when the see is vacant, by the Signory of the Chief Penitentiary, and the tax is turon. 50, duc. 12, Carol. 3. If anyone has plotted the death of his spouse, without the effect following and without a promise given to another, dispensation is granted so that, once the spouse is dead, he may marry another; the tax is turon. 9, duc. 2, Carol. 9. With one who has vowed perpetual chastity, dispensation is granted in the forum of conscience only, and the tax is turon. 16, duc. 3, Carol. 6. With one who has vowed that he wishes to enter a religious order, but not solemnly, dispensation is granted that he may contract marriage in the forum of conscience only, and the tax is turon. 15, duc. 4, etc. Dispensations of this kind from laws other than matrimonial ones carry the full tax. We have added only a few, so that the garment may be known from its fringe.

units.la: CXI. Tam enim latè se hæc dispensationum nundinatio extendit, quàm latè ipsæ leges, canones, statuta Ecclefiastica se porrigunt. Nam qui legem, Canonem, statutum tulit Papa, idem ab iisdem dispensandi jus absolutum ad se pertinere pertendit. Quis autem legum Papalium Oceanum & abyssum penetraverit? Et dispensationes à legibus humanis eas demùm probandas esse veteres statuerunt, quas necessitas & communis utilitas exigit. Rectè Abbas Vindocinensis Opusc. 5. Qui, inquit, absque necessitate dispensat, non rectè dicitur Christi Vica-rius, sed Dux est cæcorum, ipse cæcus. Bernhardus lib. iij. de consid. in ferm. coram Alex. in die Ascens. in eundem sensum: Ubi, inquit, necessitas urget, excusabilis dispensatio est, ubi utilitas provocat, laudabilis dispensatio est; utilitas dico communis, non propria. Nam cùm nihil horum est, non plane fidelis dispensatio, sed fru-delis est dispensatio. Papam verò ad promiscuam dispensationem non aliud, quàm rabida pecuniæ orexis stimulat. Nam quæ necessitas fuit, ejusdem Rousselii verbis quærere liceat, ut quis dispensaretur ad plura beneficia, incompatibilia etiam beneficia, incompatibilia etiam curam animarum habentia, sicque unus affiueret, alter esuriret, ac uno verbo, illud os apertum prodiret, quod jam versum est in derisionem? ut cum Simoniaco, irregulari dispensaretur, & tot aliis casibus, in quibus nulla versatur Ecclesiæ necessitas, nulla utilitas publica: sed (NB.) sola nundinantis opes Ecclesiasticas, quas pauperibus, quibus debentur, ereptas privatis cupiditatibus absorbeat? Definitum tamen pridem est à pluribus apud Sanchez de Matrim. Tomo III. lib. viij. disp. 17. num. 11. valere dispensationem, cùm Papa in propriis legibus sine causa dispensat. Idem apud P. de Marca de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. lib. iij. 15. 1. asserunt; Glossa, BarBartolus, Innocentius IV. Panormitanus, Felinus, alii quàm plurimi, eo argumento, quia leges omnes à Pontificis nutu pendeant. Atque hinc maximè liquet, quàm universalis & penè infinita sit illa dispensationum fœda nundinatio, vel potiùs bonorum Ecclesiæ & Seculi fraudulenta depraedatio.
units.tr: CXI. For this trade in dispensations extends as widely as the ecclesiastical laws, canons and statutes themselves reach. For the Pope who issued a law, canon or statute claims that the absolute right to dispense from the same belongs to himself. But who has penetrated the ocean and abyss of papal laws? The ancients also laid down that dispensations from human laws are to be approved only where necessity and the common good require them. Rightly the Abbot of Vendôme says: Opusc. 5. He who dispenses without necessity is not rightly called the vicar of Christ, but is a leader of the blind, himself blind. Bernard, to the same effect, in lib. iij. de consid., in a sermon before Alexander on Ascension Day: Where necessity presses, dispensation is excusable; where utility calls for it, dispensation is praiseworthy; I mean common utility, not private. For when none of these is present, the dispensation is not faithful but fraudulent. But that the Pope should dispense promiscuously is prompted by nothing but the raging greed for money. For, to ask in the words of the same Rousselius: what necessity was there that someone be dispensed to hold several benefices, even incompatible benefices, even benefices with the cure of souls, so that one man should be full while another starves, and, in a word, that open mouth should come forth which has already been turned into a mockery? That a simoniac should be dispensed as irregular, and in so many other cases in which there is no necessity of the Church and no public utility, but (NB.) only the wealth of the Church, which the trader swallows up, having been snatched from the poor to whom it is owed, for private desires? Yet it has long been established by many, as in Sánchez, de Matrim. Tomo III. lib. viij. disp. 17. num. 11., that a dispensation is valid when the Pope dispenses without cause from his own laws. They assert the same in P. de Marca, de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. lib. iij. 15. 1.; the Gloss, Bartolus, Innocent IV, Panormitanus, Felinus and very many others, on the ground that all laws depend on the nod of the Pontiff. And from this it is most clearly evident how universal and almost infinite that foul trade in dispensations is, or rather how fraudulent a plundering of the goods of the Church and the world it is.

units.la: CXII. Ne quid ad securitatem hujus dispensationum nundinationis desiderari posset, quæri inter Theologos coepta est; An qui dispensationem obtinuit illegitimam, id est, sine causa, tutus sit in foro conscientiæ? Unde quaque enim nundinationem suam tutam & expeditam esse Babylonii Mercatores cupiunt. Quæstionem disceptavit Augustinus Morla Emporii part. 1. tit. 1. q. 2. n. 14. ubi affirmantes Theologos plures affert. Unde sententia affirmans, quippe plurium virorum prudentum judicio innixa, juxta Casuisticæ recentioris definitionem, probabilis conscientiæ satisfaciet. Quasi videlicet Deus, qui clavium, & ligandi solvendique potestatem dedit, hunc in finem dederit, ut quod injustum est, ea sola potestate fieret justum, starétque pro ratione voluntas. Unde toto Cœlo aberrant, inquit idem Rousselius, qui satis sibi putant etiam apud Deum, si dispensationes quomodocunque furentur. Unusquisque enim peribit in sua, quae crassa est, ignorantia: & si caecus caecum duxerit, ambo in foveam cadent. CXIII. Non solas leges, sed judicia etiam Ecclesiæ per causarum Ecclesiasticarum ad tribunal Romanum revocationem nundinari Hierarchia suevit. Ubi abomnibus terris Pontifices appellationes acceperunt, ut possent ipsi interim in perturbatis aquis piscari, per mille milliaria homines per citationes ad consistorium suum traxerunt; pacem disciplinámque Ecclesiæ disturbárunt miss legatis à latere, commissis causis suis delegatis, munitis adversùs legum authoritatem privilegio suo nocentibus, & inferioribus à superiorum imperio solutis. De hac causarum & litium fevocatione sic Abbas Urfpergenfis in Philippo Imperatore: Vix remansit aliquis Episcopatus, sive dignitas Ecclesiastica, vel etiam Parochialis Ecclesia, quæ non fieret litigiosa, & Romam deduceretur ipsa causa, sed non vacua manu. Gaude Mater nostra Roma, quoniam aperiuntur cataractæ thesaurorum in terra, ut ad te confluant rivi, & aggeres nummorum in magna copia. Lætare super iniquitate filiorum hominum, quoniam in recompensationem tantorum malorum datur tibi pretium. Jucundare super adjutrice tibi discordia: quia erupit de puteo infernalis abyssi, ut accumulentur tibi multa pecuniarum præmia. Habes, quod semper sitisti: decanta canticum: quia per malitiam hominum, non per tuam religionem orbem vicisti. Ad te trahit homines, non ipsorum devotio aut pura conscientia, sed scelerum multiplicium perpetratio, & litium decisio pretio comparata. De eadem causarum fevocatione sic Germaniæ status Gravamine VII. & VIII. titulo præscripto: Quàm iniquè causæ profanæ in prima instantia ad Romanum tribunal judiciarium trahantur, quiritantur: IX. Cùm nedum juris ratio, sed & re ipsa series postulet, ut distincti sint jurisdictionum limites, & ut quilibet ordinarius sit suis finibus contentus, alterúmque in sua jurisdictione non disturbet: minimè tamen Pontifices Romani pro tempore existentes, æquitatem hanc communem confiderârunt, sed neglecta hac, ad petitionem personarum Ecclesiasticarum laicos non rarò in causis etiam prophanis, puta hæreditatum, aut pignorum, & in prima quidem instantia, coram se Romam citari, ac in jus vocari fecerunt. Quæ res nedum ita (ut prædictum est) in jus vocatis, sed & totius Romani Imperii ordinibus cedit in jacturam, perniciem, contemptum,
units.tr: CXII. Lest anything be lacking to the security of this trade in dispensations, the theologians began to ask: whether one who has obtained an illegitimate dispensation, that is, without cause, is safe in the forum of conscience? For the Babylonian merchants desire that their trade, wherever it is carried on, be safe and unhindered. Augustinus Morla, in Emporii part. 1. tit. 1. q. 2. n. 14., debated this question, where he cites several theologians who affirm it. Hence the opinion that affirms it, resting on the judgment of many prudent men, will satisfy a probable conscience, according to the definition of recent casuistry. As if God, who gave the power of the keys to bind and loose, had given it for this purpose, that what is unjust should become just by that power alone, and that the will should stand in place of reason. Hence they are wholly astray, says the same Rousselius, who think it enough for themselves even before God if they somehow steal dispensations. For each will perish in his own ignorance, which is gross; and if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit. CXIII. The hierarchy has been accustomed to trade not only in laws but also in the judgments of the Church, through the revocation of ecclesiastical causes to the Roman tribunal. From every land the Pontiffs received appeals, so that they themselves might fish in troubled waters meanwhile; from a thousand miles away they dragged men by citations to their consistory; they disturbed the peace and discipline of the Church by sending legates a latere, by committing their causes to delegates, by fortifying themselves against the authority of the laws with a privilege that protected wrongdoers, and by freeing inferiors from the rule of their superiors. Concerning this revocation of causes and lawsuits, the Abbot of Ursperg writes thus, under the Emperor Philip: Hardly any bishopric, or ecclesiastical dignity, or even parish church remained that did not become a matter of litigation, and the case itself was carried to Rome, but not with empty hands. Rejoice, our Mother Rome, since the floodgates of the treasures of the earth are opened, so that streams and heaps of money in great abundance flow together to you. Rejoice over the iniquity of the sons of men, since as a recompense for such great evils a price is given to you. Be glad over discord, your helper: for it has burst forth from the pit of the infernal abyss, so that many rewards of money may be heaped upon you. You have what you have always thirsted for: sing a song, for by the malice of men, not by your religion, you have conquered the world. Men are drawn to you not by their devotion or pure conscience, but by the commission of manifold crimes and by the settling of lawsuits bought at a price. Concerning the same revocation of causes, the grievance VII and VIII of the German estates, under the title already given, complains: How unjustly profane causes are drawn in the first instance before the Roman judicial tribunal, they complain: IX. Since not only the reason of law but the very course of things requires that the limits of jurisdictions be distinct, and that each ordinary be content with his own bounds and not disturb another in his jurisdiction, the Roman Pontiffs in office have by no means respected this common equity, but, neglecting it, at the petition of ecclesiastical persons, have often had laymen summoned and cited before themselves at Rome, even in profane causes, for instance of inheritances or pledges, and indeed in the first instance. This matter results not only in loss, ruin, contempt and dishonour and diminution of jurisdiction for those so cited into court, as has been said, but also for all the estates of the Roman Empire.

units.la: Tom. II. ac jurisdictionis dehonestationem diminutionemque. X. Item cum Romæ quispiam etiam laicus, interposito juramento, asserit, asserit, se non sperare justitiam apud judicem competentem in Germania, protinus ad tale juramentum admittitur, ac citatio ei contra partem adversam decernitur. Sicque processus à judice ordinario ex Germania Romam, nec judice interpellato, nec parte adversa monita protrahitur inde juramenti prætextu nec fori declinatio, nec ulla admittitur probatio, etiamsi plane doceri posset, authorem illum perjerâsse. Quæ res si altius radices ageret, nec principuo resisteretur, omnes tandem causæ ad Romanæ Curiæ tribunal devolverentur, ordinariique universi sua privarentur jurisdictione &c. Infra Grav. lxx. & lxxj. idem querelam instituunt, quòd judices Ecclesiastici causas promiscuas, quæ eorum civili etiam magistratu in jus deduci possunt, sibi solus vendicare conentur: quodque causæ profanæ sub prætextu denegatæ executionis, ad Ecclesiasticum consistorium trahantur.
units.tr: Tom. II. the dishonouring and diminution of jurisdiction. X. Likewise, when someone, even a layman, at Rome, having interposed an oath, asserts that he does not hope for justice before a competent judge in Germany, he is at once admitted to such an oath, and a summons against the opposing party is decreed for him. And so the process is dragged from the ordinary judge in Germany to Rome, without the judge being appealed to and without the opposing party being warned. Under the pretext of the oath, neither a declining of the court nor any proof is admitted, even if it could plainly be shown that the author had perjured himself. If this matter took deeper root, and were not resisted by the prince, all causes would in the end be transferred to the tribunal of the Roman Curia, and all ordinary judges would be deprived of their jurisdiction, etc. Below, Grav. lxx. and lxxj. the same complaint is raised: that ecclesiastical judges try to claim for themselves alone mixed causes, which can also be brought before their civil magistrate; and that profane causes are drawn to the ecclesiastical consistory under the pretext of denied execution.

units.la: CXIV. Ante Status hosce pridem Bernhardus de Consideratione ad Eugenium scripta lib iij. Pontifici illi appellationes iniquas gravissimè exprobravit: Quousque, sic ille inter alia, dormitas? Quousque non evigilat consideratio tua ad tantam appellationum confusionem, atque abusionem? Non locus, non modus, non tempus, non causa discernitur, aut persona. Præsumuntur leviter passim plerùnque & nequiter. Volentes maligari, nonne hu potissimum terreri solebant? Nunc terrori ipsi ex his magis fiunt, atque id bonis. Antidotum versum in venenum, non mutatio dextrae Excelsi hæc. Appellantur boni à malis, ut non faciant bona, & superseedent à voce tonitrui tui formidantes. Denique appellantur Episcopi, ne illicita audeant matrimonia solvere vel prohibere. Appellantur, ne rapinæ, ne furta, ne sacrilegia, & quæ ejusmodi sunt; punire ullatenus vel cohibere præsumant. Appellantur, ne indignas & infames personas à sacris officiis beneficiisque repellere, seu amovere queant. Quod tu invenis remedium morbo huic, ne quod repertum ad remedium fuit, reperiatur ad mortem? Zelatus est Dominus domum orationis factam speluncam latronum. Tu ejus minister dissimulas miserorum refugium datum arma iniquitati. Videas prerepi passim partes oppressorum, & prorumpere ad appellandum non tam gravatos, quàm gravare volentes. Quid hoc mysteris? Tuum est considerare, non meum commentari istud. Et cur, inquis, male appellati non veniunt, ostensuri suam innocentiam, malitiam convicturi? Dico quod dicere ad hoc solent: Nolumus vexari frustrà. In curia esse, qui proclivius faveant appellantibus, foveant appellationes. Cessuris Romæ domi sedere satius. Fateor me non omninò decredere bis. Quem das mihi in tam crebris appellationibus, quæ hodie fiunt, qui pro expensis itineris vel summum restituerit illi, quem forte appellaverit? Mirum verò, si ita omnes & appellantes justi, & appellati rei vestro examine inventi sunt. Diligite, inquit, justitiam, qui judicatis terram. Parùm est justitiam tenere, nisi & diligas: Qui tenent, tenent: qui diligunt zelantur. Amator justitiæ inquirit justitiam, & prosequitur eam. Porrò omnem injustitiam persequitur. Nihil tibi & illis, qui appellationes venationes putant. Pudes alogiò quod apud Ethnicos vertitur in parabolam: Duos novimus servos pingues. Ut mitius loquar, plus facetiæ hîc, quàm justitiæ. Hactenùs Bernhardus, cujùs verbis facerrimum illum Romanæ Curiæ morbum, quo jam olim causas, & earundem appellationes mundinari suevit, prodere è reduxi.
units.tr: CXIV. Before these Estates, Bernhard in his On Consideration, written to Eugenius, book iii, most severely reproached that Pontiff for unjust appeals: "How long, he says among other things, will you sleep? How long will your consideration not awake to such a great confusion and abuse of appeals? No place, no manner, no time, no cause or person is distinguished. Appeals are presumed lightly everywhere, and for the most part wickedly. Were not those who wish to do evil especially wont to be terrified by these? Now they become a terror to the good, and this from the very things. The antidote is turned into poison; this is not the change of the right hand of the Most High. The good are appealed against by the bad, so that they may not do good, and they hold back, fearing the voice of your thunder. Finally, bishops are appealed against, so that they may not dare to dissolve or forbid unlawful marriages. They are appealed against, so that they may not presume in any way to punish or restrain robberies, thefts, sacrileges, and such like. They are appealed against, so that they cannot repel or remove unworthy and infamous persons from sacred offices and benefices. What remedy do you find for this disease, lest what was found as a remedy be found to be death? The Lord was zealous, and made the house of prayer a den of robbers. You, his minister, dissemble, giving the refuge of the wretched as arms to iniquity. You see the parts of the oppressed snatched away on every side, and people bursting out to appeal, not so much burdened as wishing to burden. What is this mystery? It is for you to consider; it is not mine to comment on that. And why, you say, do those wrongly appealed against not come, to show their innocence and convict the malice? I say what they usually say to this: we do not want to be harassed in vain. There are men at the Curia who more readily favour appellants and foster appeals. It is better to sit at home than to go to Rome to lose. I confess I do not altogether believe these things. Who do you give me, among so many appeals made today, who would restore to the man he perhaps appealed against even the expenses of the journey, or at least...?
