It would be remarkable indeed if all appellants were found just and all those appealed against guilty by your examination. Love, he says, justice, you who judge the earth. It is not enough to hold justice unless you also love it: those who hold, hold; those who love are zealous. A lover of justice seeks justice and pursues it, and moreover pursues all injustice. Have nothing to do with those who think appeals are hunting. You are ashamed of what among the pagans is turned into a parable: 'We know two fat slaves.' To speak more gently, there is more wit here than justice." Thus far Bernhard, whose words I have brought forward to reveal that most filthy disease of the Roman Curia, by which causes and their appeals have long been wont to be traded like merchandise.

units.la: CXV. Detectus idem ille morbus in Concilio Tridentino, eique quæsita remedia sunt. Ea occasione Johannes
units.tr: CXV. This same disease was detected at the Council of Trent, and remedies were sought for it. On that occasion John

units.la: Groppèrus , Coloniensis Theologus , in ipso Concilio appellationum abusus graviter perstrinxit. Summa orationis huc redit , inauditum fuisse appellationis nomen, quandiu fidei Christianæ feruor duravit, ac demùm defervescente in judicibus charitate, & dato affectibus loco, eas in Ecclesiam irrepsisse, ad sublevandos primùm afflictos. Appellatum esse primitùs non ad unum aliquem, puta Episcopum , sed ad congregationem universam. Post, sublatis Synodis visum esse Episcopis , more secularium judicum, forum & officiales instituere. Neque in hoc vestigio malum pedem fixisse, sed ad abusus majores , quàm in foro seculari gradum struxisse. Illic enim provocationem non fieri , nisi ad judicem immediatè superiorem, neque à causa interlocutoria. Contra in judiciis Ecclesiasticis & appellari à singulis actis judicis, unde causarum immensitas nascatur & immediatè ad supremum, unde sequatur, ut extra territorium, magno cum sumtuum impendio, & aliorum intolerabilium malorum mole, proficiscendi necessitas. Sic omnem prorsùs populi corrumpi disciplinam, cum maximo populi onere, sumptu, offendiculo. Abusibus verò his occurri posse idem ajebat, si vetetur, ne appellaturi intermedios judices præterveĉti, ad supremum uno saltu provocent, & ne ab articulis, aut decretis interlocutoriis provocatio fiat, decernatúrque ut restituantur Synodi, & Officiales profligentur. Hìc tamen Gropperi sermo Legato Pontificio, iisque, qui Pontificem sustentabant, gravis accidit, qui ruiturum brevi Papatum arguebant, si appellationes ad Pontificem restringantur, vel interdicantur penitùs. Subornatus ergò ab iis Johannes Baptista Castellus Bononiensis in sequente congregatione, Synodalium judiciorum incommoda exaggeravit, nec non officialium instituendorum, & appellationum ad Pontificem necessitatem demonstrare sustinuit. Sed ab utraque & Gropperi & Castelli sententia Præsules Itali discedentes, mediam calcárunt viam, decreveruntque tandem, ut provocatio ad Pontificem maneret, sed à sententia non interlocutoria, verùm definitiva judicum, ad Metropolitanam tanquam Sedis Apostolicæ delegatum, & in causis non civilibus, sed criminalibus: uti Seff. xiij. Decreto, Reform. cap. 2. habetur.
units.tr: Gropper, a theologian of Cologne, in the Council itself severely censured the abuses of appeal. The sum of his speech comes to this: the name of appeal was unheard of as long as the fervour of the Christian faith lasted; when charity cooled in judges and affections took its place, appeals crept into the Church, at first to relieve the afflicted. At first an appeal was made not to one single person, say a bishop, but to the whole congregation. Afterwards, when synods were abolished, it seemed good to the bishops, in the manner of secular judges, to institute a forum and officials. Nor did evil set its foot only in this track, but built a step to greater abuses than in the secular forum. For there an appeal is not made except to the immediately superior judge, and not from an interlocutory matter. On the contrary, in ecclesiastical judgments appeal is made from every act of the judge, whence arises the immensity of causes, and immediately to the supreme judge, whence follows the necessity of travelling outside the territory, with great expense and a heap of other intolerable evils. Thus all discipline of the people is utterly corrupted, to the greatest burden, expense and stumbling block of the people. He said these abuses could be met if it were forbidden that those appealing, passing over the intermediate judges, should appeal to the supreme judge in one leap, and if appeal were not made from articles or interlocutory decrees, and if it were decreed that synods be restored and officials abolished. Yet Gropper's speech fell heavily on the papal legate and on those who upheld the Pope, who argued that the papacy would soon collapse if appeals to the Pope were restricted or entirely forbidden. Therefore John Baptist Castellus of Bologna, suborned by them, in the following congregation enlarged on the inconveniences of synodal judgments, and undertook to demonstrate the necessity of instituting officials and of appeals to the Pope. But the Italian prelates, departing from both the opinion of Gropper and that of Castellus, trod a middle way and at last decreed that appeal to the Pope should remain, but from a definitive sentence of the judges, not an interlocutory one, to the metropolitan as delegate of the Apostolic See, and in causes not civil but criminal: as is found in Session 13, Decree on Reform, chapter 2.

units.la: CXVI. Pertinent huc etiam matrimoniorum causæ amplissimæ, quas fictitio Sacramenti prætextu, ad forum suum Hierarchici pertraxerunt; haud postrema Babyloniacæ nundinationis pars. Conjugium sanè, licet ex accidenti,& quoad repræsentationem sit res sacra,suâ tamen naturâ contractus merè civilis est. Ejus proin causæ, ad civile non Ecclesiasticum forum, æquè ac Civiles omnes, referendæ sunt. Hinc adeò tot de matrimonio leges à Magistratu politico conditæ: tot de causis matrimonialibus judicia ab eodem exercita sunt. Id sola lectio Codicis Theodosiani, Justiniani & Novellarum, in quibus de Matrimonio innumeræ leges occurrunt, abundè demonstrat. Inter Cassiodori formulas supersunt memoriæ verborum, quibus usi sunt Reges Gothorum, cùm de gradibus prohibitis dispensarent. Et Concilium Milevitanum in quæstione de causa divortii lege Imperiali opus esse, sancivit. Plures ejusmodi civiles de Matrimonio leges M. Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. lib. vj. cap. 6. 20. 21. &c. prodidit. Paulatim verò ad causas ejusmodi dijudicandas Clerus partim per Commissionem, partim per Principum ac Magistratuum negligentiam, aditum sibi struxit, non ignarus, quantum inde commodi, & præsentis lucri non tam ad aras, quàm ad focos suos redundet. Hinc adeò matrimonii confirmationem & cohibitionem, dissolutionem, impedimenta, tempora, aliáque merè civilia sui arbitrii, beneficiùque tota fecit. Nundinationis illius Specimen Germaniæ Status Grav. lxix. sub titulo: Quomodo Ecclesiastici Judices illicitum ex jactatis matrimoniorum causis petant interesse ; his verbis indicarunt: Deinceps cum inter virum atque fœminam, de pangendis matrimonialibus sacris illis fœderibus, negotium quod inter eos fere agebatur, eòusque processit quod ab alterutra partium matrimonii contractus, ex pactionibus illis, ratus persectúsque prætendatur: at inficietur altera, datúmque est ab altera alteri personæ vestium, aut alioqui mundi mulieris quippiam, tanquam arrhabonis loco ad servandum ac custodiendum: accidatque deinde, ut asserti contractus, matrimonii scilicet, contemplatione, contrahentes ad Ecclesiasticum perveniant tribunal, ac ibidem, per sententiam in diversum ire jubeantur, separenturque: tum judex ille Ecclesiasticus iniquè hoc sibi in hac causa prætendit interesse, nimirum, ut omne, quicquid hinc inde arrhabonis vice traditum sit, sibi cedat, tanquam commissum. Id quod nedum contra omnia jura, sed & æquitatem ac honestatem ipsam procul dubio est. Sed universa illa nundinatio ex Taxæ pretiis supra Thes. ex, expositis, cognoscitur rectius.
units.tr: CXVI. Also belonging here are the very large causes of marriages, which under the fictitious pretext of a sacrament they have drawn to their own hierarchical forum; no small part of the Babylonian trade. Marriage, indeed, although it is a sacred thing by accident and as to its representation, is nevertheless by its own nature a purely civil contract. Therefore its causes are to be referred to the civil, not the ecclesiastical, forum, just like all civil causes. Hence so many laws about marriage have been enacted by the political magistrate, and so many judgments about matrimonial causes have been exercised by the same. The mere reading of the Codes of Theodosius and Justinian and the Novels, in which innumerable laws on marriage occur, abundantly demonstrates this. Among the formulas of Cassiodorus survive the words of memory which the kings of the Goths used when they dispensed from prohibited degrees. And the Council of Milevis, in the question about the cause of divorce, sanctioned that an imperial law was needed. M. Antonius de Dominis, On the Ecclesiastical Republic, book vi, chapters 6, 20, 21, etc., has set out many such civil laws about marriage. But gradually the clergy, partly through commission and partly through the negligence of princes and magistrates, built an approach for itself to judge such causes, not unaware of how much advantage and present gain accrues thence, not so much to their altars as to their hearths. Hence it made the confirmation and restraint, dissolution, impediments, times, and other merely civil matters of marriage entirely subject to its own discretion and profit. The Estates of Germany, in Gravamen 69, under the title How ecclesiastical judges seek to intrude illicitly into the disputed causes of marriages, indicated a specimen of that trade in these words: "Thereafter, when between a man and a woman, concerning the pledging of those sacred matrimonial covenants, the business that was being carried on between them has gone so far that the contract of marriage is claimed by one of the parties to have been made and completed from those agreements, but the other denies it, and a garment or some other clean thing of the woman has been given by one to the other person as a pledge for keeping and guarding; and then it happens that, on account of the alleged contract, namely of marriage, the contracting parties come before the ecclesiastical tribunal, and there by sentence are ordered to go their separate ways and are separated: then that ecclesiastical judge unjustly claims for himself an interest in this cause, namely that whatever has been handed over on either side in place of a pledge should fall to him as committed. This is without doubt not only against all law, but against equity and honesty itself." But that whole trade is better known from the prices set out in the Taxa above, Thes. ex.

units.la: CXVII. Ad opera pietatis & charitatis, eorúmqu- e
units.tr: CXVII. We now come to the works of piety and charity, and to the huckstering of them.

units.la: cauponationem accedimus. Nam & illa in rem quæstuariam converta esse, satis constat, adeò ut quæstorum Eleemosynariorum nomen jam olim satis innotuerit, eorum videlicet, qui ex eleemosynis in pia opera collatis, quæstum captárunt. Cujus impietatis occasionem paucis pandemus. Visum est antiquitus pium consultúmque in gratiam peregrinorum, pauperum, pupillorum Xenodochia, Nosotrophia, & Orphanotrophia, aliáque id genus opera pia instituere. Cumque ad id non aliunde, quàm ex Elemosynis fidelium facultates suppeterent, pii quidam boníque viri eleemosynas domatim colligendi provinciam sibi sumserunt; atque ut facilius aditus pateret, fidésque major dictis esset, Episcoporum literis συνεληλυθότες sese communiverunt. Alii etiam metuentes, ne Episcopi remoram objicerent, ab ipso Pontifice facultatem unà cum literis commendatitiis impetrarunt, idque eò proclivius, quòd pars emolumenti propter diplomatis expeditionem Romanæ Curiæ cederet. Hæc institutio confestim immanem in abusum degeneravit. Nam à pecuniis corrogatis minima pars in opus institutum impensa est, & ii ipsi, quibus quæstuariam exercendi facultas concessa est, in locum suum viles atque infames æruscatores quosdam substituerunt, quibus cum eleemosynarum commoda partiebantur, aut certè iisdem quæstum omnem pretio locabant. Denique sordidum hoc hominum genus, ut quæstum uberiorem facerent, mille artibus impiisque fraudibus populo illudere, insolenti habitu amicti, ignes, aquas, tintinnabula, crepitacula circumgestare, terroris superstitionisque in plebejorum animis concitandæ gratia, miracula ficta narrare, indulgentias prædicare, & stipem dare recusantibus, dirissima quæque imprecari. Atque hæc illi, Deo hominibúsque invisi, Apostolicis scilicet freti privilegiis & facultatibus, impunè perpetrárunt.
units.tr: For it is well established that these too have been turned into a source of profit, so much so that the name of collectors of alms (quaestores eleemosynariorum) has long been notorious, namely of those who made gain from alms contributed to pious works. We shall briefly lay open the occasion of this impiety. In ancient times it seemed a pious and prudent course to establish, for the relief of travellers, the poor and orphans, xenodochia, nosotrophia, orphanotrophia, and other pious works of that kind. Since the funds for this could come from nowhere but the alms of the faithful, certain pious and good men took upon themselves the task of collecting alms from house to house. And so that access might be easier and their word carry more weight, they bound themselves together [συνεληλυθότες] by letters from the bishops. Others, fearing that the bishops would put obstacles in their way, obtained permission from the Pontiff himself, along with letters of recommendation; and they did so all the more readily because part of the profit would go to the Roman Curia for the expedition of the diploma. This institution at once degenerated into an monstrous abuse. For only a very small part of the money gathered was spent on the work for which it was intended; and those to whom the licence to collect had been granted set up in their place certain cheap and infamous brass-hawkers, with whom they shared the proceeds of the alms, or else they let out the whole business to them for a fee. Finally, this filthy class of men, to make their takings greater, mocked the people with a thousand arts and impious frauds: dressed in showy garb, they carried about fire, water, bells and rattles, told made-up miracles to stir terror and superstition in the minds of the common folk, preached indulgences, and called down the most dreadful curses on those who refused to give. And these men, hateful to God and to humankind, did all this with impunity, relying of course on apostolic privileges and powers.

units.la: CXVIII. De sacrilegis hisce Eleemosynarum quæsto- ribus in Concilio Tridentino instituta quæstio est.
units.tr: CXVIII. The question of these sacrilegious collectors of alms was raised at the Council of Trent.

units.la: Non paucis eos diris omnibus devoventibus, eò res perducta est, ut quæstorum illorum nomen & usum penitus abolendum esse omnes fcaruerint. Decretum confectum est, quod Seff xxj de Reform. cap. 9. ejusmodi recitatur: Cùm multa à diversis antea Conciliis, tam Lateranensi ac Lugdunensi, quàm Viennensi adversus pravos Eleemosynarum Quæstorum abusus remedia tunc adhibita, posterioribus temporibus reddita fuerint inutilia, potiúsque eorum malitia ita quotidie magno fidelium omnium scandalo & querela rela excrescere deprehendatur, ut de eorum emendatione nulla spes amplius relicta videatur: statuit, ut posthac in quibuscunque religionis Christianæ locis eorum nomen atque usus penitus aboleatur: nec ad officium hujusmodi exercendum ullatenus admittantur: non obstantibus privilegiis, Ecclesiis, Monasteriis, piis locis, & quibusve, cuiuscunque gradus, status & dignitatis, personis, concessis, aut consuetudinibus etiam immemorabilibus. En sœdissimæ hujus nundinationis non tantùm consuetudines immemorabiles, sed etiam privilegia à Pontifice Ecclesiis, Monasteriis, piis locis, & quibusve, cuiuscunque gradus, status, dignitatis, personis concessa! Ne in solos cerdones, & alienæ libidinis mancipia culpa æruscationis hujus detorqueatur. Cœterùm, decreti illius, quo & nomen & usus quæstorum illorum aboletur, infirmitatem subsecutæ declarationes demonstrant. Nomine & in speciem etiam usu abolito, res ipsa non ilicò abolita est. Nam facultas quærendi Eleemosynam, inquiunt Cardinales declaratores decreti, Hospitalibus conceditur à sede Apostolica, si in eis realiter hospitalitas exerceatur: quinimo conceditur nonnunquam aliis etiam nonnullis religionis mendicantibus. Iidem declarant, Sedem Apostolicam rationabili ex causa concedere alicui pro loco, ut possit Eleemosynam quærere; atque tum ordinario scribere per hæc verba: Has Eleemosynas, quæ in tua Civitate & Diocesi, pro usu dicti Hospitalis dabuntur, permittas, dummodo personæ, quæ eas colligent, honestæ vitæ, & spectatæ religionis, & tuo judicio approbatæ sint, miniméque participes datarum Eleemosynarum, & Quæstorum nomen nullo modo gerant, sed simpliciter Eleemosynarum collectores dicantur: quique non publicent ullas indulgentias, nec concionentur, nec circumferant sua privilegia, nec reliquias, nec minis aut imprecationibus inducant fideles ad Eleemofynam: non campanellam, alidque instrumenta quædam insignia ferant, non petant Eleemosynam tanquam debitum aut solitum, neque ulla arte (etiam prætextu dicendi orationes S. Antonii, aut alterius Sancti, vel aliter) extorqueant pecuniam, sed simpliciter, permodestè, & cum omni dexteritate petendo Eleemosynam recipiant tantùm, quod sibi liberaliter offertur &c. Hinc ergò quales illi quæstores privilegiati ante Concilium Tridentinum fuerint; & quòd post Concilium cautiùs iis, si non castiùs mercandum sit, abundè liquet. Nam ne nunc quidem, in Italia saltem, desinere improbitatem illam Antonianorum Sodalium & quæstorum, narrant constanter, qui terras illas cum cura perlustrárunt. Neque id ab Hermanno Conringio Animadvers. in Novenam Anton. objectum diluere antagonista ejus Dionysius Werlensis Capucinus potuit.
units.tr: When almost everyone was denouncing them with every kind of curse, matters came to the point that all men of zeal agreed the name and practice of those collectors should be utterly abolished. A decree was drawn up, which is quoted in the following form: Sess. XXI, de Reform. cap. 9. Since many remedies that were applied against the wicked abuses of the collectors of alms by various earlier councils, both the Lateran and Lyons and Vienne, have in later times proved useless, and since their malice is found to grow daily to such a degree, to the great scandal and complaint of all the faithful, that no hope of their amendment seems to remain, it decrees that henceforth, in every place of the Christian religion, their name and practice be utterly abolished, and that they be in no way admitted to the exercise of this office, notwithstanding privileges granted to churches, monasteries, pious places, and to whatever persons of any rank, status or dignity, or customs even immemorial. Here we have a most foul huckstering, in which not only immemorial customs but also privileges granted by the Pontiff to churches, monasteries, pious places, and to whatever persons of any rank, status or dignity, are at issue! Nor should the blame for this brass-hawking be laid on tradesmen and the hirelings of others' lust alone. Moreover, the declarations that followed the decree, by which both the name and the practice of those collectors were abolished, show how weak it was. Even with the name abolished, and the practice abolished in appearance, the thing itself was not abolished at once. For, as the Cardinals who issued the declarations of the decree say, the faculty of seeking alms is granted by the Apostolic See to hospitals, if hospitality is really practised in them; indeed it is sometimes granted to some other mendicant religious orders as well. The same declarations state that the Apostolic See, for a reasonable cause, grants to someone for a place the power to seek alms, and then writes to the ordinary in these words: You may permit these alms, which will be given in your city and diocese for the use of the said hospital, provided that the persons who collect them are of honest life, of respected religion, and approved by your judgment, and that they are in no way sharers in the alms given, nor bear the name of collectors of alms, but are simply called collectors of alms; and that they publish no indulgences, nor preach, nor carry about their privileges, nor relics, nor move the faithful to give alms by threats or curses; that they carry no little bell or other conspicuous instruments, nor ask for alms as a debt or customary due, nor extort money by any art (even under the pretext of reciting the prayers of St Anthony, or of some other saint, or otherwise), but simply receive, asking very modestly and with all dexterity, only what is freely offered to them, and so on. Hence it is quite clear what sort of privileged collectors those were before the Council of Trent, and that after the Council they must be dealt with more cautiously, if not more chastely, for trade to go on. For even now, at least in Italy, the shamelessness of those Antonian brothers and collectors does not cease, as all who have carefully travelled those lands consistently report. Nor was Dionysius of Werl, the Capuchin, able to answer this charge made by Hermann Conring in his Animadversiones in Novenam Antonianam, although his opponent tried.

units.la: CXIX. Referri huc possunt aucupia non postrema ex testamentis, seu pìis legatis morientium.
units.tr: CXIX. These snares may also be listed here, and they are no small ones: the bequests of dying people, that is, their pious legacies in wills.

units.la: De Ecclesiasticorum testamentis suprà diximus. Jam olim verò etiam de testamentis, & hæreditatibus laicorum cognitionem Ecclesiastica sibi jurisdictio vendicavit, admonitique in confessione sunt ægri, ut coram Curiæ Episcopalis Notario testamentum conderent. Sic autem exceptum signabatur sigillo Ecclesiastico, & ad clericum officii testamentorum Curiæ Episcopalis transmittebatur, uti variis Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Synodis compertum esse Bochellus lib. iij. Decret. tit. 22. cap. 4, 5, 6. tradit. Qui excepturus erat testamentum, in mandatis habebat, admoneret testatorem, ut saluti animæ suæ per pia legata, seu pecunias aut fundos pro eleemosynis faciendis, aut Divinis officiis celebrandis legatos consuleret. Inde constitutus est procurator testamentorum, excommunicati quin etiam, qui nollent publicationes testamentorum in Curia Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: We have spoken above about the wills of clergy. But long ago the ecclesiastical jurisdiction also claimed for itself the cognizance of the wills and inheritances of laymen. Sick people were urged in confession to make their wills before the notary of the episcopal court. The will was then recorded, sealed with the ecclesiastical seal, and sent to the clerk of the testamentary office of the episcopal court, as Bochellus lib. iij. Decret. tit. 22. cap. 4, 5, 6. reports from the various synods of the Gallican Church. The man who was to take down the will had instructions to advise the testator to provide for the good of his soul by pious legacies, that is, by money or lands bequeathed for almsgiving or for the celebration of divine offices. From this there was appointed a procurator of wills, and there were even people excommunicated who refused to have their wills published in the ecclesiastical court.

units.la: Tom. II. nnnn stica fieri, & si executores intra annum muneri suo non satisfecissent, id omne ad Episcopos ordinarios remittendum fuit, à quibus executor vel hæres prehensione mobilium & immobilium cogi poterat. Denique testamenta à Tabellionibus Secularibus excepta, rata non fuisse, nisi ab officialibus prius approbata essent, P. Coniērus queritur. In Anglia Episcopos rationes testamentorum exegisse, & jusjurandum hæredibus vel executoribus, se impleturos, quæ morientes constituissent, imposuisse, atque inde vectigal ex bonis æstimatis percepisse, Polydorus Vergilius lib. xxvij. scribit. Quin & jure Scotici testator inter hæredes suos Ecclesiam scribere debuisse, ex Reg. Majest. lib. ij. 36. liquet. Testis quoque Bodinus de Rep. lib. v. 2. est, avorum suorum memoria in Gallia honore sepulturæ caruisse, qui testamento nihil curionibus aut Collegiis Ecclesiasticis legasset. Cùm verò, inquit idem, inopinato casu quisquam occubuisset, Sacrificulus Pontificis jussu, mortuo testamentum condere, & quæ vellet Ecclesiæ arbitratu suo, quasi testator, legare solebat, quem morem, tametsi inveteraverat, sustulit Curia Parisiorum. Idem in Anglia factum, atque ibi mortuum insepultum jacuisse, donec Sacerdos defuncto testamentum condidisset, Matthæus Paris in Richardo I. aliique testantur. Et in Hispania tertiam partem bonorum intestatorum Ecclesiæ cessisse, memorant.
units.tr: ...ecclesiastical courts, and if the executors had not discharged their office within a year, the whole matter was to be referred to the ordinary bishops, by whose seizure of movable and immovable goods the executor or heir could be compelled. Finally, Pierre Coignet complains that wills drawn up by secular notaries were not valid unless they had first been approved by the officials. Polydore Vergil lib. xxvij. writes that in England the bishops demanded accounts of wills, imposed an oath on heirs or executors that they would carry out what the dying had appointed, and so drew a levy from the goods that had been valued. Indeed, by the law of Scotland, as Reg. Majest. lib. ij. 36. makes plain, a testator was bound to name the Church among his heirs. Bodin also testifies, de Rep. lib. v. 2., that in the memory of his grandfathers in France a man who had left nothing in his will to the parish priests or the ecclesiastical colleges was denied the honour of burial. "When, however," he says, "someone died by an unexpected accident, the sacristan, at the bidding of the Pontiff, used to draw up the will for the dead man and bequeath to the Church, as if he were the testator, whatever he pleased at his own discretion. This custom, though it had grown old, was abolished by the Parliament of Paris." Matthew Paris in Richardo I. and others record that the same thing happened in England, where the dead man lay unburied until a priest had drawn up his will. They also report that in Spain a third part of the goods of those who died intestate fell to the Church.

units.la: CXX. Nescio an de Montibus Pietatis heic commemorandum nonnihil etiam sit. Nam & ibi pietatem quæstui haberi constat. Sanè Perrus Gregorius Tholosanus de Republ. lib. xiij. cap. 16. ff 10. proventus, seu reditus, qui accipiuntur ex montibus illis, qui cum authoritate Summorum Pontificum, maximè Leonis X. (qui in constitutione sua decima, juxta ordinem à Laurentio Cherubino constitutum, declaravit, ita demùm dictos montes pietatis esse licitos, si nihil ab his ultra necessarias impensas recipiatur, & si detur pro impensis & indemnitate moderatè, excommunicatis etiam iis, qui contrarium prædicârint, & illicitos esse dixerint, inter bonorum Ecclesiasticorum abusus refert.) Erectioni vel permissioni montium ejusmodi causam dedisse necessitatem conquirendæ pecuniæ ad negotia exîstimata conducibilia, quæ sine præsente pecunia expediri non possunt, ait Tholosanus. Et forte initio sublevandæ egestati pauperum inservierunt. Sed procedente tempore ipsi Pontifices æris indigentes ad montes illos confugerunt, & pauperibus destinata, in usum suum converterunt. Irrepserunt postea, inquit idem, multa, quæ occasionem malè iis abutendi forsan dedisse pluribus non immeritò videntur. Monet etiam Pontifices, provideant accuratè, ne pauperes, quorum gratia isti montes præcipuè introducti dicuntur, mutuumque datum est, reditibus istis, fœnore non dico aut usuris locedantur, nèvè occasio fœnerandi hoc speciosò nomine pietatis tegatur, contra Christi præceptum expressum: Mutuum dantes, nihil inde sperantes. Deinceps quindecim ejusmodi montes diversis nominibus à Pontificibus Romanis, indultis variis privilegiis & juribus, institutos recensét. Sic Clemens VII. erecto monte, fidei dicto, ad conquirendas pecunias, quibus alma urbs Roma defenderetur, oppignoratis omnibus Sedis & Camerae Apostolicæ bonis, & decem pro centum promissis, etiam religiosos ad pecunias in eo collocandas invitavit, cum hoc inter alia privilegio, ut de collocatis disponere posset, aliàs disponere prohibitus, disponere etiam in favorem illegitimorum absque superiorum licentia, atque etiam mulieres impudicè viventes, teneantur bonorum Monasterio convertitarum; cùm tamen alia constitutione idem Papa statuisset, mulierum impudicè viventium quintam bono-rum rum partem eidem Monasterio applicari debere, mulierúmque earum dispositiones & testamenta nullius esse momenti. Quæ omnia dura satis & parùm pia ipsi Tholosano visa sunt: atque illud inprimis, quòd Pontifices alios etiam montes Romæ erexerint, velut montem farinæ & anonymos, in quibus otiosi & epicurei viventes Romæ quidem victum habent ex reditibus sine labore, vacantes voluptatibus. Quod certè, inquit ille, detestabile est. Ubi enim quis infimæ fortis corradere potest sive justè, sive injustè alicunde pecunias, ad montes illos confugit, & reditus sibi comparat, ut reliquum vitæ tempus sine labore instar brutorum animantium transigat. Non dicam etiam, scorta plurima ex pietate montium splendere & ornari. Non dicam fructus beneficiorum ex provinciis & egentibus pauperibus & clericis locorum, eo forsan impunè transferri, & posteà in illegitimos juxta privilegium expendi.
units.tr: CXX. I do not know whether something should be said here also about the Monts-de-Piété, for it is clear that piety too was made a source of gain there. Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, de Republ. lib. xiij. cap. 16. ff 10., counts among the abuses of ecclesiastical goods the revenues that are taken from those banks which were established with the authority of the supreme Pontiffs, above all of Leo X. (who, in his tenth constitution, following the order laid down by Laurentius Cherubinus, declared that such banks of piety are lawful only if nothing more is taken from them than the necessary expenses, and if these are paid moderately and as indemnity; he also excommunicated those who taught the contrary and called such banks unlawful). Tholosanus says that the need to raise money for business matters, which cannot be carried through without ready cash, gave the occasion for setting up or permitting such banks. And perhaps at first they served to relieve the poverty of the needy. But as time went on, the Pontiffs themselves, short of money, had recourse to these banks and turned to their own use what had been destined for the poor. "Afterwards," he says, "many things crept in which, not undeservedly, seem to have given many people an opportunity to abuse them." He also warns the Pontiffs to take care that the poor, for whose sake these banks are said to have been chiefly introduced, and to whom a loan has been made, should not have these revenues let out at interest, nor should the opportunity for lending at interest be concealed under this specious name of piety, against the express precept of Christ: Lending, expecting nothing again. Next he lists fifteen such banks set up by the Roman Pontiffs under various names, with various privileges and rights granted to them. Thus Clement VII, having set up a bank called of faith, to raise money with which the nurturing city of Rome might be defended, with all the goods of the See and the Apostolic Chamber pledged and ten per cent promised, invited even religious persons to place their money in it. Among other privileges, he allowed them to dispose of what had been placed there, though otherwise forbidden to dispose of it, to dispose of it in favour of illegitimate children without the licence of their superiors, and women who live unchastely were to be kept in the convent of converted women from its goods. Yet by another constitution the same Pope had decreed that a fifth part of the goods of women who live unchastely should go to the same convent, and that the dispositions and wills of such women should be of no effect. All these things seemed to Tholosanus harsh enough and not very pious; and above all this, that the Pontiffs had also set up other banks at Rome, such as the bank of flour and the anonymous banks, in which idle and epicurean people living in Rome have their food from the revenues without labour, given over to pleasures. This is certainly detestable, he says. For when a man of the lowest rank can scrape together money from somewhere, whether justly or unjustly, he has recourse to those banks and secures an income for himself, so that he may spend the rest of his life without labour, like brute beasts. I will not even say that many prostitutes shine and are adorned by the piety of the banks. I will not say that the revenues of benefices are perhaps transferred from the provinces, and from the needy poor and clergy of the places, with impunity, and afterwards spent on illegitimate persons under cover of the privilege.

units.la: CXXI. Taceo fictitiæ pietatis & charitatis munera, ex quæstuosissima falsorum Chirographorum officina petitas Donationes, puta Constantini M. Ludovici Pii, & Othonis M. quas post alios Hist. Papatus Ss. lxiv. obiter perstrinximus. Multùm certè grani paleas illas Ecclesiæ attulisse, vetus de Constantini Palea proverbium habet. Non pauci equidem in medio Papatu illas, Constantinianam inprimis, quæ mundum immundum Papæ ἀλφ ψυλάκῳ adjudicavit, rejecerunt, atque næxia soricina confossiorem reddiderunt; atque inter eos etiam Aeneas Sylvius, post Papa creatus in Dialogis suis, Cardinalis Cusanus, Accursius, Georgius Merula, de Vice-comitibus, Petrarcha, Baptista Egnatius, Valla, ac nuper etiam Baronius, qui Donationem Constantinianam à Græcis confictam, ut Romanæ Ecclesiæ Principatum ab Imperatore, non à Christo constitutam probarent, confinxit ipse. Sed commentum Baronianum Johannes Morinus, & post hunc, Petrus de Marca; de Concord. Sacerd. & Imper. lib. ij. cap. 12. toto confixit; plurimis conjecturis argumentisque comprobans uterque, authorem figmenti esse Johannem Diaconum, cognomento Digitorum. De quo dubitare haut finit Diploma Othonis III. editum ab Anonymo, id est, Marquardo Frehero, in quo haec verba: Haec enim sunt commenta ab illis ipsis (Pontificibus) inventa, quibus Johanes Diaconus, cognomento Digitorum, mutuis praeceptum aureis literis scripsit, sub titulo Magni Constantini, longa mendacii tempora finxit. Haec sunt etiam commenta, quibus dicunt quendam Carolum S. Petro nostra publica tribuisse. Sed eam in rem plura erudite satis idem Petrus de Marca dixit. Et de inauspicati foetus parente, quicquid fiat, illud satis constat, sicut ficta quoque arguere solent, ita etiam putidissima isthaec Donationum figmenta, Imperatoriae charitatis fuco tecta, Papae in mundana, quibus magis ille quam Divinis rebus delectatur, potestatem in immensum extulisse & ampliasse.
units.tr: CXXI. I say nothing of the gifts of feigned piety and charity, the Donations, namely those of Constantine the Great, Louis the Pious and Otto the Great, which, after others, I touched on in passing in the Hist. Papatus Ss. lxiv. There is an old proverb about the chaff of Constantine, that it brought much chaff into the Church with the grain. Indeed, in the midst of the Papacy, not a few rejected those documents, above all the Constantinian one, which awarded the unclean world to the Pope's [ἀλφ ψυλάκῳ], and by gnawing at them made the cloth of the mice more full of holes. Among these were Aeneas Sylvius, who was afterwards made Pope, in his Dialogues, Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, Accursius, Giorgio Merula, de' Visconti, Petrarch, Battista Egnazio, Valla, and lately even Baronius, who himself invented the fiction in order to prove that the Constantinian Donation was made up by the Greeks and that the Roman Church's principality came from the Emperor, not from Christ. But John Morin, and after him Pierre de Marca, de Concord. Sacerd. & Imper. lib. ij. cap. 12., wholly demolished Baronius's fabrication, both proving by many conjectures and arguments that its author was John the Deacon, surnamed Digitorum. The diploma of Otto III, published by an anonymous writer, that is, by Marquard Freher, does not allow us to doubt this, and it contains these words: "For these are the fabrications devised by those very Pontiffs, for which John the Deacon, surnamed Digitorum, wrote a precept in golden letters under the title of Constantine the Great, and invented a long period of lies. These are also the fabrications by which they say that a certain Charles gave our public domains to St Peter." Pierre de Marca has said more on this point, and learnedly enough. As for the parent of this ill-omened offspring, whatever happens, this much is certain: just as forgeries usually show their nature, so these utterly foul fictions of Donations, covered with the rouge of imperial charity, have raised and enlarged the Pope's power to an immense extent in worldly matters, in which he takes more delight than in divine ones.

units.la: CXXII. Haud postrema benedictionum & consecrationum Ecclesiae nundinatio subit. Jam olim in C. ad Apostolicam 42. de Simonia hanc querelam relatam legimus: Ad Apostolicam audientiam frequenti relatione pervenit, quod quidam clerici pro exequiis mortuorum & benedictionibus nubentium, & similibus pecuniam exigunt & extorquent; & si forte eorum cupiditatibus non fuerit satisfactum, impedimenta fictitia fraudulenter opponunt. E contra vero quidam laici laudabilem consuetudinem erga sanctam Ecclesiam pia devotione fidelium introductam, ex fermento haeretica pravitatis nituntur infringere, sub praetextu Canonicae pietatis. Quapropter super his pravas exactiones fieri prohibemus, & pias consuetudines praecipimus observari, statuentes, ut libera conserantur Ecclesiastica Sacramenta, sed per Episcopum, loci veritate cognita, compescantur, qui malitiosè nitantur laudabilem consuetudinem immutare. Cœterùm, nemini obscurum est, quanta, non obstante ejusmodi prohibitione, mercatura exercita sit, quando pro oleo Catechumenorum, pro sputo Sacerdotis, pro oleo Chrismatis, pro oleo extremæ Unctionis, pro consecratione Altarium, Templorum, Altarium linteaminum, tabularum, Cereorum, imaginum, ovorum, herbarum &c. certum pretium exigi consuevit: Agni quoque Dei & Rosæ à Papa recens electo consecratæ ad eos destinatæ sunt, quos ampla possidere Imperia, Regna, principatus, adeóque mercedi reddendæ præ cæteris idoneos Papa nullus ignoravit. De impensis immodicis in Ecclesiarum consecrationes insumtis, non pauci quæsti sunt. Benedictus VIII. rogatus ab Henrico Imperatore ut Templum, quod Bambergæ struxerat, in Cathedralem consecraret Ecclesiam, ea lege annuit postulatis, ut quotannis ea Ecclesia Romano Pontifici, census loco, numeraret centum argenti marcas, cum equo albo ac phalerato. Sic Centuriatores Magdenburgenses Cent. xj. cap. 10. referunt. De iisdem Templorum consecrationibus sic Status Imperii Grav. xlviij, & xlix. queruntur: Cùm Ecclesias ac Templa, prætenuia quidem Deo dicant sacrántque nonnulli suffraganeorum, subditos, utcunque per se egestate laborantes, superfluis miniméque necessariis sumptibus onerant. Neque hoc contenti, quin munera quoque, & illa quidem immodica à miserâ plebecula exigant. xlix. Item cùm laici Ecclesiis altaris donant ornamenta, nec non casulas & similia, ac in honorem Dei pecunias suas expendunt, nihilominus tamen suffraganei exigunt, ut talia, priusquam ad altaris conferantur usum, consecrentur, pro qua demum consecratione munera ac dona petuntur innumera.
units.tr: CXXII. Nor is the trade in blessings and consecrations of the Church the least. Long ago we read this complaint recorded in C. ad Apostolicam 42. de Simonia: "It has come to the hearing of the Apostolic See by frequent report that certain clergy extort and exact money for funerals, for the blessing of brides and grooms, and for similar things; and if their greed is not satisfied, they fraudulently raise false impediments." On the other hand, certain laymen strive to break the praiseworthy custom, introduced into the holy Church by the pious devotion of the faithful, with the leaven of heretical perversity, under the pretext of canonical piety. "Therefore we forbid wrongful exactions to be made in these matters, and we command that the pious customs be observed, decreeing that the ecclesiastical sacraments be conferred freely, but that those who maliciously strive to change the praiseworthy custom be restrained by the bishop, once the truth of the matter has been known." Moreover, it is obscure to no one how great a trade has been carried on, despite such a prohibition, when a fixed price has customarily been exacted for the oil of the catechumens, for the priest's spittle, for the oil of chrism, for the oil of extreme unction, for the consecration of altars, temples, altar-linens, tablets, candles, images, eggs, herbs, and so on. The Lamb of God and the Rose, consecrated by the newly elected Pope, have also been sent to those who possess wide empires, kingdoms and principalities, and no Pope has been unaware that such persons were the most suitable to repay the favour. Not a few have complained of the excessive expenses incurred on the consecration of churches. When Emperor Henry asked Benedict VIII to consecrate as a cathedral the church he had built at Bamberg, Benedict agreed to the request on this condition, that every year that church should pay to the Roman Pontiff, in place of a tax, a hundred marks of silver together with a white harnessed horse. So the Magdeburg Centuriators report, Cent. xj. cap. 10. The estates of the Empire complain in these terms about the same consecrations of churches, Grav. xlviij, & xlix.: "Since some of the suffragan bishops consecrate and dedicate churches and temples to God, though they are very poor, they burden their subjects, who labour in poverty themselves, with superfluous and by no means necessary expenses. Not content with this, they also exact gifts from the wretched common people, and those gifts excessive. xlix. Likewise, when laymen give the church altar ornaments, as well as chasubles and the like, and spend their own money in honour of God, the suffragans nevertheless require that such things be consecrated before they are put to use at the altar, and for that consecration countless gifts and presents are demanded."
CXXIII. Re-

units.la: CXXIII. Referenda huc inprimis est Σεμάτων Corporum, seu Cadaverum illa nundinatio, quam circa illorum sepulturam in consecratis locis, consecrationis videlicet jure, Hierarchici exercent. Nam & sepulturam ære redimendam esse, quis ignorat? Pridem Innocentius III. C. ad Apostol. de Sim. Pravas equidem exactiones pro exequiis prohibens, pias tamen consuetudines præcepit observari, tali præcepto fideles obligans, ut in funeribus mortuorum, Ecclesiasticos ducentes funus, debita mercede recognoscant. A qua proin Innocentii constitutione hoc genus expiscandi in exequiis pecuniæ manasse, Franciscus Duarenus de Minist. Eccl. & Benef. lib. vj. 6. asserit. Efpencæus in Epist. ad Tit. cap. j. conquestus est, Sacramentorum multis in locis gratuitam minus esse ministrationem, in aliquibus adeo venalem, ut etiam CUM SEPULTURA pauperibus denegata sit. Et Proceres Imperii Grav. l. Cœmiteria nonnunquam superflue & minus necessario consecrari, non sine gravibus laicorum impensis: quin & campanas baptizari à solis suffraganeis, eo nomine mercedem stipulantibus, quam illi munusculum vocare solent, adeo ut aliquando in parvis etiam villis centum floreni in tali absumantur & expendantur baptizatione, deplorant. Idem Grav. lxxxix. Sepulturæ jus quibusdam mortuorum cadaveribus magno ære redimendum esse conquiruntur. Papalibus, inquiunt, statutum est canonibus, ut his duntaxat publici juris Ecclesiastica denegetur sepultura, quos manifestis & plane notoriis, mortalibus, ut vocant, peccatis, ex communi hac mortalium forte, absque Dominici corporis sanguinisve participatione, migrasse compertum sit. Verum Ecclesiastici, non animadversis talibus Pontificum decretis, forte fortuna aquis suffocatos, gladio, ruina, vel incendio occisos, jugulatos, atque vita casu functos, etiamsi non pateat peccatis mortalibus obnoxii decesserint, nec ne, in Ecclefiasticam tumulare sepulturam non permittunt, quousque tam iniquo fato mortuorum uxores, liberi, amicive ab ipsis cœmiterium non modico ære redemerint.
units.tr: CXXIII. Here, above all, belongs the trade in bodies, or corpses (σωμάτων), which the hierarchs carry on over their burial in consecrated places, by the right of consecration. For who does not know that burial too must be bought with money? Innocent III, in the chapter ad Apostolicam on simony, forbade the wicked exactions made for funerals, yet ordered that the pious custom be kept, obliging the faithful by this precept to pay the ministers of the Church, who conduct the funeral, their due fee. Francis Duaren, in De Ministeriis Ecclesiasticis et Beneficiis book 6, chapter 6, asserts that from this constitution of Innocent the practice of fishing for money at funerals arose. Espencaeus, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, complained that in many places the administration of the sacraments is less free of charge, and in some so much for sale that even burial is denied to the poor unless they pay. The nobles of the Empire, in the Gravamina, lament that cemeteries are sometimes consecrated superfluously and without real need, not without heavy expense to the laity; and that bells are baptized only by the suffragans, who demand a fee for it, which they usually call a little gift, so that sometimes even in small villages a hundred florins are spent and laid out on such a baptism. The same Gravamina, number 89, complain that the right of burial is to be bought at a great price for certain corpses. "By the Papal canons," they say, "it is laid down that ecclesiastical burial is denied only to those who are known to have departed, by that common mortal fate which they call mortal sin, in manifest and plainly notorious sin, without partaking of the Lord's body and blood. But the churchmen, not heeding such decrees of the Pontiffs, do not permit burial in consecrated ground for those who by chance have been drowned, killed by the sword, a falling building or fire, slain or who have died by accident, even when it is not clear whether they died subject to mortal sins or not, until the wives, children or friends of these unfortunate dead have bought the cemetery at no small price."

units.la: CXXIV. Denique & ψυχῶν ᾿Αnimarum nundinatio, toti antehac mundo, Cœlóque & inferno ignota, Hierarchiæ notissima est. Nam & animas pestiferis illis dogmatis plane ad nundinationem, uti vidimus, comparatis, imbutas, turpissimè nundinatur, adeóque sub prætextu etiam mysterii quo animata, ceu aureo quodam hamo piscandis insidias struit, uti supra Dissert. viii. ostendimus, latè dominatur: & in universa jurisdictione sua quæstui habet, dando potestatem eas occidendi, ex purgatorio liberandi, in eo retinendi, denique eas gehennæ addicendi, vel in Cœlum mittendi. Hæc potestas solvendi & ligandi est. Constat, Papas etiam Angelis mandàsse, ut animas pro Regno Papali in prœliis occisorum rectà in Paradisum deferrent. Quibus potestas illa venditur, illis animæ hominum venduntur. Hinc Basilicæ, Templa, Altaria, Missæ, monasteria, claustra, legata, anniversaria, peregrinationes, cerei, & quicquid est lucrosi in Papatu operis, originem habet. Omnia hæc pro redemtione animarum ex inferno vel purgatorio facta sunt. Accedit potestas præcipiendi, prohibendi ἀωπκεχλοξικῶς, & conscientias immediatè obligandi ad servanda religiosè omnia, quæ Papali illi avaritiæ Regno stabiliendo conducere videntur. Hanc animarum nundinationem horribilem ante quingentos ferè annos Virgo Germana Elisabetha, Prophetico Spiritu afflata, (cujus scripta Lutetiæ cum Præfatione Fabri impressa sunt,) notavit, & deploravit his verbis, quibus Hierarchiam alloquitur: Dico vobis, quòd iniquitates terræ, quas absconditis PROPTER AURUM ET ARGENTUM, ascendant coramme, sicut fumus de igne. Numquid non animæ plus plus quàm aurum & argentum, quas suffocatis in ignem æternum propter avaritiam vestram? Iccirco accusat vos religio vestra coram me. Ecce enim fœtere fecistis sanctificationem meam in conspectu populi, & versa est in abominationem mihi. Occupástis principatum Sanctorum meorum, & nescivi. Quid mihi & vobis, exasperatores manfuetudinis meæ? Unde ascendistis turbare ovile meum, & aggravare cor meum super filios meos, quos genui in amaritudine animæ meæ, in die laboris & angustiarum mearum? Fuit virgo isthæc, ne de ejus authoritate litem nobis Hierarchici, vel Sciopius aliquis, eorum parasitus, quærere ausus, Lutherana an Catholica fuerit? moveant, Moabitica, hoc est, ex eorum numero, quorum mentionem facit Daniel cap. xi. 41. qui אב מאם à patre, seu teneris pietatem didicerunt à parentibus, neque se Antichristi corruptelis seduci siverunt, interdum etiam intrepidè adversus Babylonicam impietatem testimonium dixerunt: quorum grandiorem numerum inferius producemus.
units.tr: CXXIV. Finally, the trade in souls (ψυχῶν), unknown to the whole world, to heaven and to hell until now, is very well known to the hierarchy. For they shamefully trade in souls, which, as we have seen, have been imbued with those pestilential dogmas made entirely for trade, and under the pretext of the mystery by which they are animated, they lay snares for them like a golden hook for fishing, as we showed above in Dissertation 8, and they rule widely. In their whole jurisdiction they make a profit, by giving power to kill souls, to free them from purgatory, to hold them there, and finally to consign them to hell or send them to heaven. This is the power of loosing and binding. It is well established that the Popes even commanded the angels to carry the souls of men slain in battle for the Papal kingdom straight into Paradise. To whomever that power is sold, to them the souls of men are sold. From this come the basilicas, temples, altars, masses, monasteries, cloisters, legacies, anniversaries, pilgrimages, candles, and whatever profitable work there is in the Papacy. All these things have been done for the redemption of souls from hell or purgatory. To this is added the power of commanding and forbidding authoritatively (ἀωπκεχλοξικῶς), and of binding consciences directly to keep devoutly all those things which seem to serve that Papal avarice in establishing its kingdom. This horrible trade in souls, almost five hundred years ago, the Germanic virgin Elizabeth, inspired by the prophetic Spirit (whose writings were printed at Paris with a preface by Faber), noticed and lamented in these words, with which she addresses the hierarchy: I tell you that the iniquities of the land, which you hide FOR GOLD AND SILVER, rise before me like smoke from a fire. Do not the souls, more and more than gold and silver, which you suffocate in eternal fire because of your avarice? Therefore your religion accuses you before me. For behold, you have made my sanctification stink in the sight of the people, and it has been turned into abomination to me. You have seized the principate of my Saints, and I did not know it. What have I to do with you, you who provoke my gentleness? Why have you come up to trouble my fold and to weigh down my heart upon my sons, whom I begot in the bitterness of my soul, in the day of my labour and my distress? This virgin was (lest the hierarchs, or some Sciopius, their parasite, dare to raise a quarrel about her authority, asking whether she was Lutheran or Catholic) of the Moabitic kind, that is, of that number whom Daniel mentions in chapter 11, verse 41, who learned piety from father [אב מאם] and mother, and did not allow themselves to be seduced by the corruptions of Antichrist, and sometimes bore fearless witness against Babylonian impiety. We shall bring forward a larger number of them below.

units.la: CXXV. Neque hic præterire etiam possum apertam illam animarum nundinationem, qua Hierarchici animas emunt, ut emtæ lucrum deinceps majus afferant. Sic enim Papa Gregorius XIII. passim Collegia, seu Seminaria haud exiguo sumtu instituit, in quibus scilicet à Jesuitis, novis Nebucadnezaris Asphenazis, educarentur formarentúrque novi ex Germania, Anglia, Græcia &c. conducitii non tam haruspices, quorum apud Romanos olim famosa Collegia, seu Seminaria fuerunt, quàm Cyclopes Euangelicorum carnes mox laceraturi, seu mavis gigantei Atlantes, Cœlum Pontificium humeris suis, ne rueret, sustentaturi. Nam Alano Apol. pro Semin. cap. 2. referente, Pontifex ille pecuniam grandem expendit immutando Xenodochium Anglicum Romæ in Collegium,
units.tr: CXXV. Nor can I pass over here that open trade in souls, by which the hierarchs buy souls, so that once bought they may bring them greater profit. Thus Pope Gregory XIII everywhere founded colleges or seminaries at no small expense, in which, namely, new men from Germany, England, Greece and so on were to be educated and formed by the Jesuits, the new Ashpenaz of Nebuchadnezzar, hired not so much as soothsayers, whose famous colleges or seminaries once existed among the Romans, but as Cyclopes who would soon tear the flesh of the Evangelicals, or, if you prefer, as giant Atlases who would hold up the Papal heaven on their shoulders lest it fall. For, as Allen reports in his Apology for the Seminaries, chapter 2, that Pontiff spent a large sum of money in converting the English hospice at Rome into a college,

units.la: Tom. II. censibúsque augendo, ac Rhemense etiam Collegium fovendo menstrua elcemosyna; sed eum sciticet in finem, quem Martinus Navarrus Consil. lib. iij. de Regul. cons. 1. his verbis evulgavit: Romæ in Collegio Anglorum est statutum, & constitutio Papalis, ut quicunque illud ingredi voluerit, teneatur jurare, se post tot annos pro defensione fidei catholicæ in Anglium professurum, illámque ibi publicè & privatè prædicaturum. Mera hæc animarum nundinatio est. Cui gemella illa est, qua hodiè pecuniá emuntur animæ pauperum, & ad amplectenda Hierarchicorum mysteria auctorantur.
units.tr: vol. II, and in increasing its revenues and fostering the Rheims college with a monthly alms; but clearly to the end which Martin Navarrus made known in these words, Consilia book 3, De Regulis Consiliorum 1: At Rome in the College of the English it is established and Papally ordained that whoever wishes to enter it shall be bound to swear that, after so many years, he will profess in England for the defence of the Catholic faith, and there publicly and privately preach it. This is pure trade in souls. Twin to it is that other trade, by which today the souls of the poor are bought with money and enlisted to embrace the mysteries of the hierarchy.

units.la: CXXVI. Nundinationi illi, cujus species juxta filum Apocalypseos, & dogmatum ad quæstum comparatorum, haëtenùs pertexuimus, fovendæ & confervandæ leges, censuræ Ecclesiasticæ, & officinæ publicæ strenuè inserviunt, canones Ecclesiæ, quibus eadem sic firmantur, ut justitia speciem accipiat;
units.tr: CXXVI. To that trade, whose forms, along the thread of the Apocalypse and of the dogmas made for profit, we have traced up to now, the laws, ecclesiastical censures and public workshops serve vigorously to foster and preserve it; the canons of the Church, by which these things are so confirmed that they take on the appearance of justice;

units.la: runt. Etenim, ut de legibus dicamus, si patrassent, & solum patrassent ista flagitia quà homines (uti quidem vix ullam Papæ alicujus electionem Simoniæ crimine vacare Hist. Pap. s. cclxj. & cclxÿ. ostendimus,) non quà Pontifices ista commisse viderentur, & subesset spes quædam, uno sublato tyranno, proximum rectiùs gubernacula Ecclesiæ tractaturum. Sed facinorafua legibus illi confirmârunt, effeceruntque ut leges illæ pro Canonibus & regulis Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ acciperentur. Hinc adeò frequentatæ illæ Decretales, Clementinæ, Extravagantes, & verè quidem extra modum vagantes, Constitutiones Apostolicæ, & irregulares illæ, ut ita dicam, Regulæ Apostolicæ Cancellariæ, Taxæque publica authoritate introductæ, & sancitæ. Quarum omnium spectatus finis & usus adeò crassus, adeò palpabilis est, ut Budæus, Jurisconsultus doctissimus, Gallorum Regis Secretarius, gravem querimoniam instituens, de magna Pontificum & Cleri iniquitate ac avaritia, culpam ejus omnem in leges eorum & jurisdictio{ctd} stionem conferat. Pontificiam, sic ille de Asse lib. v. scribit, jurisdictionem sic degenerdsse cernimus ex caritate prisca, ut ubi æqui bonique sinus solebat esse, ibi litium officina capturarumque improbiorum nunc esse videatur. Inde illa formularum aucupia, & rituum Pontificiorum cautiones, ad circumscribendam familiam Domini concinnatæ. Inde multarum compendia Præsulibus enata. Indidem sacrilegæ nundinæ earum rerum, quæ in commercio humano sine piaculo esse non possunt. Mitto tesseras non modò veniales, sed etiam venales, impunitatem scelerum, & solutionem sacrarum legum, sordida benignitate largientes. Itaque sacrosanctos Canones melioribus annis factos ut iis velut regulis vita Clericorum dirigeretur, jam in amusses plumbeas evasisse, quis non videt? Quales olim fuisse canones Lesbiæ structuræ tradit Aristoteles. Nam ut Canones plumbei & molles non structuram operum tenore æquabili dirigunt, sed ex structorum commodo & libidine flexiles, structuræ accommodantur: sic Canones Pontificii ex usu flexibiles, plumbei & cerei facti sunt, ut jam diu instituta majorum & sanctiones Pontificiæ non moribus regendis usui esse, sed (propemodum dixerim) argentariæ factitandæ auctoritatem accommodare videantur. Scribserat hæc Budæus A. MDXIV. triennio ante quam Lutherus quicquam contra Pontificis indulgentias attentaret. Adeò perspicuè leges Pontificum ad sua commoda non Ecclesiæ, ipsis prudentioribus Pontificiis judicibus vergere videbantur.
units.tr: ...they do so. For, to speak of the laws: if they had committed those crimes, and only those, as men (for we have shown in the History of the Popes, sections 261 and 262, that hardly any Pope's election was free of the crime of simony), and not as Pontiffs, who appeared to have committed them, and if some hope had remained that, once one tyrant was removed, the next would steer the helm of the Church more rightly. But their crimes they confirmed by those laws, and brought it about that those laws were taken as canons and rules of ecclesiastical discipline. Hence those much used Decretals, Clementines, Extravagants, and truly wandering beyond all measure, the Apostolic Constitutions, and those irregular, so to speak, Rules of the Apostolic Chancery and Taxes, introduced and sanctioned by public authority. The purpose and use of all of these is so gross and so palpable that Budaeus, the most learned jurist, Secretary to the King of the French, lodging a grave complaint about the great iniquity and avarice of the Pontiffs and the Clergy, confers all their guilt upon their laws and jurisdiction. "We see," he writes thus in On the As, book 5, "the Papal jurisdiction so degenerated from its ancient charity that where there used to be a haven of justice and goodness, there now seems to be a workshop of lawsuits and a snare for the more wicked. Hence those hunts for formulas, and the Papal cautions of rites, contrived to circumvent the household of the Lord. Hence the shortcuts to money devised for the Prelates. Hence the sacrilegious markets in those things which in human commerce cannot be without sin. I say nothing of the tokens, not only cheap but even for sale, which they bestow with a dirty kindness, as impunity for crimes and release from the sacred laws. So who does not see that the sacrosanct canons, made in better years so that the life of the clergy might be directed by them as by rules, have now turned into leaden rules? Such, Aristotle tells us, were the canons of the Lesbian building. For as leaden and pliant canons do not guide the construction of works with an even line, but bend according to the convenience and whim of the builders and adapt themselves to the structure, so the Papal canons, bending according to use, have become leaden and waxen, so that now the long-established institutions of our ancestors and the Papal sanctions seem to serve not to govern morals but (I might almost say) to furnish authority for the business of money-making." Budaeus wrote this in the year 1514, three years before Luther undertook anything against the Papal indulgences. So clearly did the laws of the Pontiffs seem to lean towards their own advantage and not the Church's, even to the more prudent Papist judges themselves.

units.la: CXXVII. Atque pro his suis legibus, Ecclesiæ libertatem (sic nundinationem illam legibus munitam appellare placuit) munientibus, πνξ ... pugnis, quod ajunt, & calcibus propugnant. Neque maximis etiam Imperatoribus & Regibus, si qui libertatem illorum, quibus scilicet se à jugo Principum secularium, & legitimarum potestatum liberârunt, & in earundem dominos transmutârunt, pupillam attrectare videntur, parcunt. Novissimè documentum ejus rei in certamine Innocentii XI. cum Rege Galliæ de jure Regaliæ quod ceu Coronæ suæ innexum hic vindicaverat, de quo fusius Hist. Pap. ß. cxlj. &c. actum à nobis est, vidimus.
units.tr: CXXVII. Yet to defend these laws, which they call the liberty of the Church (for so they like to describe that fair-trade protected by law), they fight, as the saying goes, with fists and kicks. Nor do they spare even the greatest Emperors and Kings, if any of these seem to touch that ward of theirs, namely the liberty by which the Church has freed itself from the yoke of secular princes and lawful powers and made those same powers its subjects. Most recently we saw proof of this in the dispute of Innocent XI with the King of France over the right of regale, which he claimed as bound to his own crown. We have treated this at greater length in the Hist. Pap. ß. cxlj. and elsewhere.

units.la: CXXVIII. Cùm verò frustrà sint leges, quæ legislatorum vim ad puniendos transgressores conjunctam nullam habent, accesserunt ad eas Censuræ Ecclesiasticæ, quibus ceu violentiæ instrumentis Hierarchici usi sunt, quò sic omnium votorum suorum avarissimorum compotes facilius redderentur.
units.tr: CXXVIII. But since laws are futile when those who make them have no power attached to punish transgressors, the Ecclesiastical Censures were added to them. The hierarchs used these as instruments of violence, so that they might more easily gain possession of all their most greedy desires.

units.la: Si quis igitur sive Patronus, sive Episcopus, sive Archiepiscopus, curam gregum suorum Romanis Pastoribus, seu potiùs lupis tradere recusaret: si quis flagitiosam nundinationem, & auctionem impiam Papalium dispensationum, absolutionum, indulgentiarum reprehenderet: si quis ea ipsis vectigalia pendere renueret, quæ per Legatos suos, mercatores, collectores, nuntios, speculatores & viatores exigebant: statim pro hominis & delicti conditione in ipsum censura emissa est vel suspensionis ab officii sui administratione, vel interdictionis ab usu omni Ecclesiasticæ functionis, vel excommunicationis ex societate fidelium, vel citationis, ut se Romæ sisteret, ibidem correptionis supplicium subiturus, vel denuntiationis pro hæretico, si obstinatus persisteret, Seculari brachio tradendus, ut ignibus tanquam hæreticus cremaretur. Quod in eam consuetudinem venit, ut usitatè Auditori Cameræ Papalis authoritas data sit excommunicandi, aliásque censuras stringendi, si lupæ Romanæ, quæ pendunt vectigalia, ut ipsis scortis esse liceat, aliique sanctorum redituum mancipes ad diem non dissolvant. Quid quòd quotannis in Bulla Cœnæ Domini omnes, etiamsi Imperialis, Regali, Ducali &c. dignitate præfulgeant, qui statuta, ordinationes, constitutiones Pragmaticas, seu quævis alia decreta in genere, vel in specie, ex quavis causa & quovis quæsito colore, ac prætextu cujusvis consuetudinis aut privilegii, vel quomodo libet fecerint, & publicaverint, vel factis & ordinatis usi fuerint, unde libertas Ecclesiastica tollitur, seu in aliquo lædITur, vel deprimitur, aut quovis modo restringitur, diro excommunicationis fulmine percellun-tur?
units.tr: If anyone, whether patron, bishop or archbishop, refused to hand over the care of his flock to the Roman shepherds, or rather wolves; if anyone denounced the shameful trade and impious auction of papal dispensations, absolutions and indulgences; if anyone refused to pay those taxes which their legates, merchants, collectors, messengers, spies and travelling agents demanded, then at once, according to the man's standing and the nature of his offence, a censure was launched against him: either suspension from the administration of his office, or interdict from every exercise of ecclesiastical function, or excommunication from the fellowship of the faithful, or citation to appear in Rome, there to undergo punishment for his correction, or denunciation as a heretic, so that if he persisted obstinately he would be handed over to the secular arm to be burned at the stake as a heretic. It has become the custom that the Auditor of the Papal Chamber is ordinarily given authority to excommunicate and to impose other censures if the Roman she-wolves who pay the taxes (so that they may have leave to keep their whores) and other dealers in the holy revenues do not pay up on the day. Why, every year in the Bull of the Lord's Supper, all who, though they shine with imperial, royal, ducal or any other dignity, have made or published statutes, ordinances, pragmatic constitutions, or any other decrees whatever, in general or in particular, for whatever cause and under whatever pretext, whether of custom or privilege, or in any other way, or have used such acts and ordinances once made, by which ecclesiastical liberty is removed, or harmed in any respect, or lowered, or restricted in any way, are struck by the dreadful thunderbolt of excommunication?

units.la: CXXIX. Non tantùm terrorem censuræ Papales restitantibus incusserunt, sed novo etiam rem faciendi compendio ansam dederunt. Nam qui excommunicat, vel suspendit, vel interdicit, idem à pœna hac absolvere potest. Papa autem absolvit quandoque grandi ære soluto: Exemplum eadem Anglia suppeditat. Nam A. MCCXIII. Innocentius, Johannem Angliæ Regem excommunicavit, & universis in remissionem peccatorum injunxit, ut ad Angliam accedentes eum è Regni solio deponerent, aliúmque substituerent. Ut pacem Rex obtineret (persuasit autem ei Pandulphus, nisi confugerit sub alas Papæ, amissurum omnia) resignavit Papæ Coronam Angliæ, & ei (verba sunt Westmonasteriensis) fecit homagium, & fecit de liberrima religione ancillam, ut Princeps Provinciarum fieret sub tributo. Fuit autem tributum ejusmodi, ut Rex & hæredes darent singulis annis Ecclesiæ Romanæ mille marcas sterlingorum, scilicet pro Regno Angliæ septingentas marcas, & pro Regno Hiberniæ trecentas. Atque hoc expilatiuncula nomine venit.
units.tr: CXXIX. Not only did the papal censures strike terror into those who resisted, but they also gave occasion for a new shortcut in doing business. For whoever excommunicates, suspends or interdicts can also absolve from that penalty. The Pope, however, absolves sometimes when a large sum of money has been paid. England supplies an example of this. In the year 1213 Innocent excommunicated John, King of England, and enjoined on all, for the remission of their sins, that those who came to England should depose him from the throne of the kingdom and set another in his place. To secure peace the King (Pandulf persuaded him that otherwise he would lose everything unless he took refuge under the wings of the Pope) surrendered the crown of England to the Pope, and did homage to him (these are the words of the Westminster writer), and made the most free religion his handmaid, so that he might become prince of the provinces under tribute. The tribute was of this kind: that the King and his heirs should give each year to the Roman Church a thousand sterling marks, namely seven hundred marks for the kingdom of England and three hundred for the kingdom of Ireland. And this is what comes under the name of expilatiuncula (a little pillage).

units.la: CXXX. Sicut autem censuras suas adversùs civiles potestates Pontifices dilatàrunt, ut inde lucrarentur aliquid: sic contra Ecclesiasticos Antistites easdem firmârunt Sacramento fidelitatis, quo Præsules ad defendendum Papatum & Regalia S. Petri obligárunt, intexentes pariter authoritatem, qua ipsis solis, & prætereà nemini Episcopos deponere liceat. Si ergò gravarentur Episcopi Pontificum voluntati obsequi, & ejusdem imperata cuncta, quæ sub Sacramento obedientiæ injungerentur, facere, at possessiones tamen dignitatésque suas, etiam libertatem, denique vitam ipsam, si in Pontificis ditione fuerint, amittendi metu, Domino suo addictissimè servire didicerunt. Sic omnia repagula mercandi impunè & impudentissimè (uti raro verecundus Mercator pinguescit) adeóque furaciffima illa sua sacrorum nundinatione civitates, Regna domosque omnes depeculandi avaritissima illa Meretrix perrupit, ut non tantùm jam ei fas sit sic cauponari per leges, quæ factis justitiam conciliare solent, sed cunctis etiam legibus his, pœnarum propositarum metu, obsequentibus uterentur.
units.tr: CXXX. Just as the Pontiffs extended their censures against the civil powers, so that they might gain something from them, so against the ecclesiastical prelates they strengthened the same censures by the oath of fidelity, by which they bound the bishops to defend the Papacy and the Regalia of St Peter, and at the same time they inserted the authority by which bishops may be deposed by them alone and by no one else. Thus, if bishops were burdened by having to obey the will of the Pontiffs and to do everything he commanded and enjoined under the oath of obedience, yet, fearing the loss of their possessions and dignities, and even of liberty and finally life itself if they were within the Pontiff's power, they learned to serve their lord most devotedly. So that greedy harlot broke down every barrier to trading with impunity and with the greatest shamelessness (for an honest merchant seldom grows fat), and with that most thievish trade in sacred things she plundered all cities, kingdoms and houses with the greatest avarice. The result is that not only is it now lawful for her to hawk her wares in this way under laws which usually procure justice for deeds, but she even makes all such laws obedient to her, under fear of the penalties proposed.

units.la: CXXXI. Neque etiam Babylonica hæc rerum sacrarum nundinatio Officinis & Tabernis suis, in quibus uniuersæ hæ artes excogitantur quotidiè & exercentur sine ullo pudore, deffituitur. Tales Romæ sunt Consistorium, Dataria, Cancellaria, Curiæ Libellorum, Signaturæ gratiæ & justitiæ, Pœnitentiaria, Rota, aliæque congregationes plures, in quibus ne minimum quidem responsum editur sine pretio, ut in iis vetus illud apud Nazianzenum Orat. 1. in Jul. quòd Phœbus sine ære oraculum nullum reddat, quàm maximè impleatur. In Officinis hisce videre est agmina mangonum, veluti Clericos de Camera, Auditores Camerae, Rotæ, veculos Bullistas, Notarios, Protonotarios, Dictatores, Scribas, Abbreviatores, Refcribendarios, Referendarios, Rationales, Solicitatores, Plumbatores, horret animus & calamus Nundinationis instrumenta omnia referre.
units.tr: CXXXI. Nor does this Babylonian trade in sacred things lack its workshops and shops, in which all these arts are devised and practised daily without any shame. Such are, at Rome, the Consistory, the Datary, the Chancery, the Court of Petitions, the Signatures of Grace and of Justice, the Penitentiary, the Rota, and many other congregations, in which not even the smallest answer is given without a price, so that that old saying in Nazianzen (Orat. 1. in Jul.) that Phoebus gives no oracle without money is most fully fulfilled. In these workshops one may see whole troops of hucksters: the Clerks of the Chamber, Auditors of the Chamber, of the Rota, the carriers of bulls, the bullers, notaries, protonotaries, dictators, scribes, abbreviators, rescript-writers, referendaries, accountants, solicitors, leaden-sealers. My mind shrinks, and my pen with it, from listing all the instruments of this trade.

units.la: CXXXII. Præcipua ex his sunt Officinæ Pœnitentiaria & Dataria. De Pœnitentiaria ex Taxa sæpè citata proclive judicatu est. Ibi enim peccata contra leges Divinas & humanas Papales in innumeras in casibus Reservatis inprimis, æɌe redimuntur. In Datariam, ceu nassam quandam Romani Piscatoris, influunt pecuniæ redactæ ex Annatis, Præventionibus, Resignationibus in favorem Commendatiombus, Dispensationibus ætatis, Privilegiationibus, legitimationibus, Concessionibus, Expectativis, Devolutionibus, Beneficiis, Vacaturis, Exemtionibus non visitandi, vel per procuratorem visitandi, Concordatorum transfactionibus, Beneficiorum permutationibus, Tolerantuis, & quæ alia exactionibus illicitis nomina Sacri isti Publicani invenerunt. Ibi cuduntur Bullæ, quibus Curiam Romanam artificiosiore & solertiore μετεμψυχωσις, quàm quæ discipulis è Paracelsi schola recepta est, plumbum in aurum convertere, jam pridem pii doctique viri, justo equidem sarcasmo, dicere nulli dubitarunt: significantes, eos, quibus per bullas beneficia conferuntur, tot impensis nihil aliud Romæ consequi, nisi chartas, plumbum & funiculum, cùm nihil aliud iis Roma pro tanto auro & argento dare possit. Nam ipsa beneficia ab ordinariis tandem ordinaria eorum potestate eis conferantur: præsertim ubi Bullæ sunt in forma Dignum. In gratiosis verò Curia dat, quod non habet, & collatio vera ac legitima ad ordinarios spectat, non ad alios. Sed & generalis regula bonis omnibus ecclesiasticis necessariò annexa est, ut nemo Ecclesiasticus ex iis plus habeat, quàm necessitas ipsius cum magna sobrietate postulet, & pro solis laboribus in opere Ecclesiastico suscept is. Si quid plus accipiat aliquis, merum latrocinium ac sacrilegium reputatur merito. Neque negari potest, insana illa Bullarum pretia, esse bona Ecclesiarum, pretia peccatorum, & patrimonia pauperum.
units.tr: CXXXII. The chief of these are the workshops of the Penitentiary and the Datary. As to the Penitentiary, it is easy to judge from the Taxa often cited. For there sins against the divine and human laws of the Papacy are bought off in countless cases, especially in the reserved cases, for money. Into the Datary, like a net of some Roman fisherman, flow the sums raised from annates, preventions, resignations in favour of commendams, dispensations for age, privileges, legitimations, concessions, expectatives, devolutions, benefices, vacancies, exemptions from visitation or from visitation by proxy, transactions of concordats, exchanges of benefices, toleration, and whatever other names these sacred publicans have invented for illicit exactions. There are minted the bulls by which, with a more skilful and cunning metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις] than the one taught to the disciples of Paracelsus' school, the Roman Curia turns lead into gold. Pious and learned men have long since not hesitated to say so, and with a just sarcasm, pointing out that those to whom benefices are conferred by bulls gain nothing at Rome for so much gold and silver except paper, lead and a cord, since Rome can give them nothing else for so much gold and silver. For the benefices themselves are in the end conferred by the ordinaries, by their ordinary power, especially where the bulls are in the form Dignum. But in the matter of favours the Curia gives what it does not have, whereas true and lawful collation belongs to the ordinaries, not to others. Moreover there is a general rule necessarily attached to all ecclesiastical goods, that no ecclesiastic should have from them more than his need, with great sobriety, requires, and only in payment for the labours he has undertaken in ecclesiastical work. If anyone receives more, it is rightly regarded as pure robbery and sacrilege. Nor can it be denied that those mad prices of the bulls are the goods of the churches, the prices of sins, and the patrimony of the poor.

units.la: CXXXIII. Bullarum necessitatem pluribus sic Boni- facius
units.tr: CXXXIII. How Boniface VIII further enlarges on the necessity of bulls

units.la: facius VIII. Extrav. Injunctæ de elic. in com. amplificat: Sanè quàm periculosum existat, quòd aliquis in ossi-cio, dignitate vel gradu fore se asserat, & pro tali etiam habeatur, nisi priùs ipse quod asserit, legitimis ostenderit documentis, tam ex civilibus, quàm ex canonicis institutis colligitur evidenter. Asserenti namque cum mandatis Principis se venisse, credendum non est, nisi hoc scripto probaverit; nec similiter creditur se asserenti Legatum. Nunquam enim Apostolicæ sedi moris fuit, absque signatis apicibus undecunque legationem suscipere. Sed nec dicenti se delegatum ejusdem Sedis creditur, vel intenditur, nisi de mandato Apostolico fide doceat oculata. Similiter Clerici ad alienam Diœcesin sine suorum ordinariorum literis venientes, nec in suis recipiantur ordinibus, nec ad superiores ascendunt. Clerici quoque & Monachi, qui de suis Civitatibus ad alienam urbem proficiscuntur, nisi muniti veniant suorum literis prælatorum, non sunt Clerici vel Monachi reputandi &c. Præsenti itaque perpetuò valitura constitutione sancimus &c. statimque decernit, ne quis promotus in Curia ad suas ecclesias accedere, & proventus accipere ausit, absque literis illius Sedis, promotionem, confirmationem, & consecrationem suam continentibus; sub pœnis suspensionis à perceptione suorum beneficiorum. Quam Constitutionem post uterque Julius & Pius IV. innovârunt, & majori cum rigore ampliârunt. Cœterùm, incommoda & pericula illa sic à Pontificibus illis exaggerata nulla omninò essent, si collationes iis relinquerentur, quorum propriæ sunt. Omnia ergò illa Romanæ Curiæ, & insatiabili ejus avaritiæ accepta referenda sunt. Si tamen pericula ejusmodi extimescenda essent, facilè iis per literas breves & simplices, aut gratis, uti olim fiebat, aut æqua pro labore scriptorum mercede, concedendas occurri posset. Quàm verò male ageretur cum Legatis, Nuntiis, Procuratoribus, Commissariis, Delegatis Papæ, nec non Clericis, Sacerdotibus & Monachis, si suas illi commissiones, & hi suas dimissorias & testimoniales literas tanto pretio, quanto Bullæ solent, redimere necessum haberent? Et olim quidem simplicissimas fuisse literas, nulloque ære redimendas M. A. de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. lib. ix. 9. 52. &c. ex Decreto Gregorii M. ejusque Registro, quo earum formulæ nonnullæ continentur, probat. Etiam Innocentius III. simpliciores longè confici curavit, & Antonioparte iij tit. 19. cap. j. teste, modum exactionibus statuere decrevit, cogitans, qualiter illam venalitatem posset à Curia Romana extirpare. Unde statim fecit edictum, ut nullus Officialium Curiæ suæ quicquam ab aliquo exigeret, præter solos scriptores & bullatores, quibus etiam certum modum præfixit, distinctè præcipiens, ut singuli suum officium gratis impenderent. Fecit præterea Ostiarios à notariorum Camerâ amoveri, ut liber ad eos pateret accessus. Erat autem intra Lateranense palatium mensa, supra quam ponebantur vasa aurea & argentea, multiusque thesaurus, quam ille solertissimus Pontisex fecit illicò de toto palatio amoveri.
