Nunc verò longissimo tractatu bullæ circumscribuntur, plenæ tricis, plenæ tot conditionibus & particulis cum modis vacationis, cum expressione valoris, cum absolutionibus ad effectum, cum tot Non obstantibus, aliisque. Et quò plures cautelæ etiam non petitæ à proviso ponuntur, eo plus conferendum pecuniæ est. Quin ex ipsis cautelis, vel maximè lites suscitantur, ut si leve quid in Bullis claudicet, alteri statim impetrationem præparet: ex quo novæ Bullæ in eadem vacatione cum integro novo pretio expediuntur. Ac insuper lites ex nova Curiæ lucra suppeditant, aut saltem novo soluto pretio perindè valere; & cum nova compositione impetrantur. O Bullas verè bullas, & spumam, quæ nil nisi venventum & inanem tumorem continet, pro quo ipso tamen tanta vis auri & argenti colligitur: Illudunt denique Datarii hi mundo Bullas suas solenniter claudentes his verbis: Datum Romæ, à quo Dato Dataria nomen habet. Rectius longè clauderent his verbis: Venditum Romæ.
units.tr: Boniface VIII, in the Extravagant Injunctae, de electione in communi, enlarges on this: "How dangerous it is that someone should claim to hold an office, dignity or rank, and be regarded as holding it, unless he first shows by lawful documents what he asserts, is plainly gathered from both civil and canonical institutions. For a man who claims to have come with a prince's commission is not to be believed unless he proves it by this writing; nor likewise is a man who claims to be a legate believed. For it was never the custom of the Apostolic See to receive a legation from anywhere without sealed letters. Nor is a man who says he is a delegate of the same See believed or attended to, unless he proves by his own eyes that he has an Apostolic mandate. Likewise, clerics who come into another diocese without letters from their own ordinaries are not received into their orders, nor are they advanced to higher ones. Clerics and monks too, who travel from their own cities to another city, are not to be reckoned clerics or monks unless they come provided with letters from their own prelates, etc. Therefore we decree by this constitution, which shall remain in force forever, etc." He at once decrees that no one promoted in the Curia may dare to go to his churches and take the revenues without letters of that See containing his promotion, confirmation and consecration, under penalty of suspension from the receipt of his benefices. Both Julius and Pius IV afterwards renewed this constitution and extended it with greater rigour. Yet these inconveniences and dangers, so exaggerated by those Pontiffs, would be nothing at all if the appointments were left to those to whom they properly belong. All of this must therefore be credited to the Roman Curia and its insatiable avarice. If such dangers were nonetheless to be feared, they could easily be met by granting these things by short and simple letters, either free of charge, as was once done, or for a fair fee for the work of the scribes. But how badly would it go with the legates, nuncios, procurators, commissaries and delegates of the Pope, and also with clerics, priests and monks, if they had to buy back their commissions, and these men their dimissory and testimonial letters, at the price that bulls usually cost? That the letters were once very simple and were not bought back for any money, M. A. de Dominis proves in de Republica Ecclesiastica, book 9, sections 9 and 52 etc., from a decree of Gregory the Great and his Register, in which several of their formulas are contained. Innocent III too took care that they were made much simpler, and, as Antoninus witnesses (part 3, title 19, chapter 1), he decided to set a limit to the exactions, thinking how he might be able to root out that venality from the Roman Curia. Hence he at once issued an edict that none of the officials of his Curia should demand anything from anyone, except from the scribes and the bullers only, for whom he also fixed a set rate, expressly ordering that each should perform his office free of charge. He further had the doorkeepers removed from the chamber of the notaries, so that free access would lie open to them. Within the Lateran palace there was a table on which gold and silver vessels and a great treasure were set; that most shrewd Pontiff immediately had it all removed from the palace. But now bulls are hemmed in by the longest of treatises, full of snares, full of so many conditions and clauses, with modes of vacancy, with the expression of value, with absolutions to take effect, with so many Non obstantibus, and so on. And the more numerous the safeguards, even those not requested, that are placed in the proviso, the more money must be paid. Indeed, lawsuits are stirred up chiefly by these very safeguards, so that if something in the bulls limps slightly, the request is at once prepared for another person; from this new bulls are dispatched in the same vacancy at a full new price. Moreover, the lawsuits supply the Curia with new profits, or at least it is said that after a new fee has been paid they hold good in the same way, and they are obtained with a new composition. O truly bulls, and froth, which contains nothing but something to be sold and empty swelling, yet for which so much gold and silver is collected! Finally these Datary officials mock the world by solemnly closing their bulls with these words: Datum Romae, from which word the Dataria takes its name. They would close them far more rightly with these words: Venditum Romae: sold at Rome.

units.la: CXXXIV. Quicquid porrò in Pœnitentiaria, Datariá, aliisque Officinis & argentariis, auri argentique conficitur, illud omne denique in Apostolicam Cameram, Papæ Bursam, & ærarium proprium, & prædarum omnium commune receptaculum infertur, demtis tamen iis, quæ officinarum illarum Ministri, ceu Sacri Publicani & Sectores, officia & tributa magno subindè pretio redimentes, decerpunt. Quorum tamen vicem pecuniæ ex æstimationibus & venditionibus officiorum illorum subeunt. Hanc Cameram Innocentii VIII. Regularum Scholiastes Petuniarum Matrem appellat. Eandem Theodoricus à Nyem Tract. VI. cap. 36. cum mari sic comparat: Camera Apostolica assimilatur mari, in quod intrant omnia flumina, & non exundat. Sic enim in isiam portantur ex diversis mundi partibus auri pondo millia, attamen non impletur; in qua est generatio, quæ pro dentibus gladios immutat, ut comedat inopes de terra, & pauperes ex hominibus: in qua sunt multæ sanguisugæ dicentes. Affer, Offer. Cujus quidem Cameræ officiales gentes Cameræ nuncupantur. Bene quidem. Gentes enim sunt barbaræ nationes, habentes ritus extraneos à moribus hominum. Ojustissimè gentes, rectè cum infernalibus furiis, seu Harpyiis & Tantalo, sortem sitibundæ posituræ, qui nunquam satiantur.
units.tr: CXXXIV. Whatever is further produced in the Penitentiary, the Dataria and the other offices and money-changers' counters of gold and silver, all of it is finally carried into the Apostolic Chamber, the Pope's purse, his own treasury and the common receptacle of all plunder, except for what the ministers of those offices, as sacred publicans and tax-farmers, pick off, redeeming offices and taxes at a high price from time to time. Yet in return for those offices they pay a sum of money from the valuations and sales of the offices. The commentator on the Rules calls this Chamber the Mother of Pennies in the time of Innocent VIII. Theodoric of Niem, Tract 6, chapter 36, compares it with the sea in this way: "The Apostolic Chamber is likened to the sea, into which all rivers enter and it does not overflow. For thus thousands of pounds of gold are carried into it from different parts of the world, yet it is never filled; in it is a breed which changes swords for teeth, so that it may devour the poor of the earth and the needy of mankind; in it are many bloodsuckers who say: Bring, Offer. The officials of this Chamber are rightly called the Gentiles of the Chamber. For gentiles are barbarous nations, having rites foreign to the customs of men. Most justly are they called gentiles, and rightly are they to share the lot, with the infernal furies, or the Harpies and Tantalus, of the thirsty, who are never sated."

units.la: CXXXV. Hactenùs nundinationis Hierarchicorum genera potiora, eorúmque hamos, retia, uncos, tabernas denique prosecuti sumus. Restat ut eandem ex fructibus inde pullulantibus, divitiis nimirum Curiæ Romanæ, Cle- ririque universi, & exterorum Regnorum expilatione, nec non domesticis testimoniis comprobemus.
units.tr: CXXXV. Hitherto we have pursued the more important kinds of hierarchical trafficking, and their hooks, nets, barbs and finally their shops. It remains to prove the same from the fruits that spring from it, namely the riches of the Roman Curia, the plundering of the whole clergy and of foreign kingdoms, and also from domestic testimonies.

units.la: CXXXVI. Fuit quondam tempus cùm Româ nulla unquam Respublica major, nec sanctior, nec bonis exemplis ditior esse prædicaretur. Hæc ut Imperii, sic virtutum omnium Lar ac domicilium audiebat. Postquam verò, Sallustii Catilin. cap. 10. & 12. verbis uti liceat, divitiæ honori esse cœpère, hebescere virtus, paupertas probro haberi, innocentia pro malevolentia duci cœpit. Igitur ex divitiis luxuria, atque avaritia cum superbia invasère. Unde civitas immutata, imperium ex justissimo atque optimo crudele intolerandúmque factum; & inter alia flagitia cumprimis, quam dixi, Avaritia, bellua illa fera, immanis, intoleranda, Divina cum humanis permiscens invaluit; adeò quidem, ut juxta Juvenalis illud,
units.tr: CXXXVI. There was once a time when no commonwealth was proclaimed to be greater, holier, or richer in good examples than Rome. It was heard as the hearth and home of the empire and of all virtues. But after, to use Sallust's words (Catiline, chapters 10 and 12), riches began to be an honour, virtue grew dull, poverty began to be counted a reproach, and innocence began to be taken for malevolence. Thus luxury and avarice, together with pride, invaded from riches. Hence the state was changed, and the empire, from the most just and best, became cruel and intolerable; and among the other crimes, above all that avarice I have named, that wild, monstrous, intolerable beast, mixing divine things with human, grew strong. So much so that, according to Juvenal's line,
"All things at Rome"
"have their price"

units.la: imò ipsa urbs venalis, & maturè peritura diceretur, si emtorem invenerit. Ad tantam implendam ingluviem ipsa fibi vel Roma, vel Italia non sufficiebat, verùm externæ opus indigebat, ac nisi Provinciarum Copiæ (sic, Tacito A. 111. 54. narrante ad Romanos Tiberius) & dominis, & servitiis, & agris subvenerint, nostra nos nostraque villæ minimè tuebuntur. Notúmque illud apud Justinum lib. xxxvii. 6. Mithridatis: Ut conditores Romæ lupæ uberibus altos, sic omnem illum populum luporum animos, inexplebiles sanguinis atque Imperii, divitiarúmque avidos ac jejunos habere.
units.tr: indeed the city itself was said to be for sale and soon doomed to perish, if it found a buyer. Rome itself or Italy did not suffice to fill such a gluttony; rather, external resources were needed, and unless the wealth of the provinces (as Tacitus, Annals 3.54, relates Tiberius saying to the Romans) "comes to help with masters, slaves and fields, our villas and what is ours will by no means protect us." And that well-known saying of Mithridates in Justin, book 37, chapter 6: "As the founders of Rome were suckled by a she-wolf's udders, so that whole people has the minds of wolves, insatiable for blood and empire, and greedy and hungry for riches."

units.la: CXXXVII. Hæc de vetere gentili Roma dicta, Christianæ ex ámussim quadrant. Nam & hæc initio, salutari doctrinæ Christianæ femine consita, si non erat prisca illa major, erat tamen melior: si non cultior, at sanctior. Quàm primùm verò illa à Christo prædicta infelicia lollia, ac cumprimis divitiarum spinæ agrum Dominicum infe‑ stare cœperunt, pristinæ fidei virtutisque puritatem cor‑ruperunt; unà cum superciliosa sacrorum hominum am‑ bitione, & regnandi dira cupidine, insatiabilis avaritia sic invaluit, ut sitim illam nec Tagus, nec Hermus, nec Pa‑ ƈtolus, nec postremò, si sit aureus, totus explere posset Oceanus, atque, quod Alphonsum Regem Arragonum pronuntiāsse Panormitanus lib. j, dist. & facŧ. Alph. A‑ popht. 8. retulit: Harpyæ non jam amplius infulas, ut Poëtæ existimárunt, incolere, sed ex Insulis migrâsse in Curiam Romanam, ibique sedem fixisse, viderentur. E reti illo piscatorio Petrino verriculum sibi, Regnorum flo‑ rentissimorum opibus deglutiendis, quàm assabrè Papæ concinnauerint, vel inde constare potest, quòd non so‑lùm ipsam Romam urbem, Caput rerum, unde in omnia regimen, propriam Imperatoriæ fortunæ sedem, non pau‑ cas item alias Imperii provincias ac urbes, Aquila deplu‑ mata, fallaciter occupárunt: Verùm etiam Europæ cœ‑ teræ partem multò maximam veƈtigalem sibi redditam Laverniones isti ἀλιων ἅρπαγικωτροι, felibus rapaciores, diripuerunt expilárúntque deglutiendo potiûs, ac minu‑ tatim dilaniando, quàm tondendo, quas suas videri vole‑ bant, oviculas: ut non magis facetè quàm verè Monachus nonnemo apud Johannem Andreæ, Juris Canonici inter‑ pretem, Romam fundatam à prædonibus adhuc sapere sua primordia; & S. Brigida, Papam decem Dei præcepta in unum commutavisse, DA PECUNIAM, dixisse videan‑tur.
units.tr: CXXXVII. What has been said of ancient pagan Rome fits Christian Rome exactly. For this too, planted at the beginning by the seed of the saving Christian doctrine, if it was not as great as that ancient one, was nevertheless better; if not more cultivated, yet more holy. But as soon as those unhappy tares foretold by Christ, and above all the thorns of riches, began to infest the Lord's field, they corrupted the purity of the former faith and virtue. Together with the haughty ambition of holy men and the dire lust for ruling, insatiable avarice grew so strong that neither the Tagus, nor the Hermus, nor the Pactolus, nor finally the whole ocean, even if it were golden, could satisfy that thirst. As Panormitanus reports (book 1, dist. and fact. Alphonsus, Apophthegms, 8), King Alphonso of Aragon declared that the Harpies no longer seemed to inhabit islands, as the poets thought, but to have migrated from the islands to the Roman Curia and fixed their seat there. How skilfully the Popes have fashioned for themselves, from that Petrine fishing net, a dragnet to swallow the wealth of the most flourishing kingdoms, can be gathered from this alone: they fraudulently seized not only the city of Rome itself, the head of all things, whence all rule comes, the proper seat of imperial fortune, and not a few other provinces and cities of the empire, stripping the eagle of its feathers; but they also tore apart and plundered by devouring, and by tearing to pieces bit by bit, rather than by shearing, the far greater part of the rest of Europe, made tributary to themselves; these Lavernians, [αἰλούρων ἁρπαγικώτεροι] more rapacious than cats, wished the sheep they called their own to be shorn thus. So a certain monk, quoted by Johannes Andreae, the interpreter of canon law, said, not more wittily than truly, that Rome, founded by robbers, still savours of its beginnings; and St Bridget seems to have said that the Pope had turned the ten commandments into one: GIVE MONEY.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Eò vecordiæ Hierarchici processerunt, ut divitias veræ-religionis notam esse, non mussarent, sed palam edicerent. De Johannis XXII. definitiva pro iis, qui Christum divitem fuisse jaƈtárunt, sententia, & pau‑ pertatis contemtu, supra diximus. Nuper etiam Sylvester Petrasanēto, Lojolæ pullus, apud Molinæum Hyperaspi. p. 9. ex paupertate Hugonotarum, vanam & prorsus nullam esse eorum religionem arguit, nullam reputans esse religionem, ubi nummorum copia non suppetit. Qui etiam suum illud verè Babylonicum ex αυρεο aureo Johannis Euangelistæ tanquam Asiæ Episcopi, aliisque etiam sutilissimis argumentis astruere conatus est, quem Molinæus loc. cit. & post eum Andreas Rivetus Jef. Vapul. cap. 4. pro merito depexum dederunt. Quid vero multis? Felicitatem temporalem, quæ sine divitiarum abundantia nulla est, in censu notarum veræ & Catholicæ, Babylonicæ dixisset rectius, Ecclesiæ, ipse Bellarminus Cardinalis, habens Rhinocerotis nasum, dixit.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. The hierarchs have gone so far in their madness that they no longer hush up the claim that riches are the mark of true religion but openly proclaim it. We have already said above what John XXII pronounced, in his definitive sentence, against those who claimed that Christ was rich, and on the contempt of poverty. Recently, too, Sylvester Petrasanctus, the young pup of Loyola, in Molinaeus, Hyperaspi. p. 9., argues from the poverty of the Huguenots that their religion is empty and utterly nothing, holding that there is no religion where a plentiful supply of money is lacking. He also tried to establish his truly Babylonian claim from the gold [χρυσίῳ] of John the Evangelist, as bishop of Asia, and by other very subtle arguments, which Molinaeus, loc. cit., and after him Andreas Rivetus, Jef. Vapul. cap. 4., rightly combed over. But why say more? Cardinal Bellarmine himself, with the nose of a rhinoceros, said that temporal happiness, which exists only with an abundance of riches, should be counted among the marks of the true and Catholic Church, or, more correctly, of the Babylonian Church.

units.la: CXXXIX. Sed voraginem hanc insatiabilem Hierarchicorum propius ex Imperiorum & Regnorum expilationibus intueri licet. In omnes enim terras Venator ille in Sennaar, & Architectus Babelis, suam extendit nassam. Germania certè, Romani Imperii nomine insignis, pro innata probitate crimen ac dolum à Papis compositum altius non scrutata, se diutissimè expilandam præbuit, donec sub onere suo gemens, ad sensum aliquem doloris & impatientiæ excitata est. Quamobrem expilationes istas sacras inter Imperii Gravamina, uti non semel jam vidimus, relata sunt. Eâsque primus Germanus Poëta Conradus Celtes, indignanti hoc carmine perstrinxit:
units.tr: CXXXIX. But one can see this insatiable whirlpool of the hierarchs more closely in the plundering of empires and kingdoms. That hunter in Shinar, the architect of Babel, spreads his net into every land. Germany, certainly, distinguished by the name of the Roman Empire, on account of its innate honesty did not look closely into the crime and deceit contrived by the Papists, and it allowed itself to be plundered for a very long time, until, groaning under its burden, it was roused to some sense of pain and impatience. Therefore these sacred plunderings are listed among the Grievances of the Empire, as we have already seen more than once. And the first German poet, Conrad Celtes, lashed them in this indignant poem:

units.la: Quicquid in extremis habuit Germania terris, Et mediis quicquid continet illa pagus, Exhaustum est: totum Latias migravit in arces, Expleat ut luxus, impia Roma tuos.
units.tr: Whatever Germany had in its farthest lands, and whatever that country holds in its midst, has been drained dry; all has migrated to the Latin citadels, so that impious Rome may satisfy your luxury.

units.la: Aliorum optimorum virorum adversus hæc βλασφημίας querulas voces infra referam. Quantum prædarum ex Galliæ Regno quotannis corrasum, & in sacram illam Piscatoris Romani sagenam illapsum sit, vix computari potest.
units.tr: I will set out below the complaints of other excellent men against these blasphemies. How much plunder has been scraped together each year from the kingdom of France and poured into that sacred net of the Roman Fisherman can scarcely be computed.

units.la: Roma attributus fuit Germaniam; Galliam, Anglian, Hispaniam; aliaque regna et Nationes tributum exactum pilavit. test. Curia suprema Parisiensis defensione pro libertate Ecclesiæ Gallicæ adversus Romanam aulam Regi Ludovico XI. exhibita, Artic. 72. 73. &c. commemorat, quòd Pontifice Pio II. viginti Archiepiscopatus & Episcopatus vacantes, Annatarum titulo, centum & viginti millia coronatorum; neque minùs Abbatiæ sexaginta vacantes, & Prioratus, Decanatus, Præposituræ itidem vacantes centum millia coronatorum; denique Parochiæ & filiales universæ viginti quinque millia coronatorum, in Romanum ærarium derivaverint. Atque adeò tum exaćtiones Papales Regnum illud exhausisse, ut æred tantùm, & minutior moneta incolis relinqueretur, aurea omnis Romam exportaretur, iidem artic. 71. queruntur. Cui consentaneum est, quòd Archiepiscopi Magdenburgensis Legatus in Sylva Locorum Communium prodidit, Lugdunensem Archiepiscopum in Basileensi Concilio edixisse, quòd Martini V. tempore novem milliones auri ex Gallia Romam commearint, non computatis immensis sumptibus, quos Clerici Romam frequenter euntes, redeuntesque, ibidem, & in itineribus consumserint. Subjicit autem hæc verba: Judi-cet moratus, quanta vorago hæc. Sed & Bodinus de Rep. lib. v. cap. 2. scribit: cùm Caroli IX. Regis jussu census in Gallia bonorum Ecclesiasticorum ageretur, quater millies Sestertium, hoc est, duodecim milliones reditus annui in censum relata esse extra pecuniam & gratuitas oblationes, & gravia auro templorum dona, idque parcè ac tenuiter, neex vero censu periculum aut invidia crearetur Pontificio ordini, qui ipse, Lanovii calculo hodiè in reditibus annuis ad auri tonnas centum triginta tres, & ultra possidet. Idem qui suprà Bodinus loc. cit. sibi ab Alemannò, rerum publicarum prætore narratum scribit, duos ferè trientes agri Gallici ad sacrum ordinem possessione vel dominio pertinere. Hoc sibi incredibile visum ait, tametsi non ignoraret, quatuor suprà centum in Gallia esse Episcopos, duodecim Archiepiscopos, quingentos & quadraginta octo Abbates, curionum viginti septem millia & quadringentos, si modò singulis urbibus & pagis singuli curiones tribuantur: extra minores Archimandritas, & cœnobia tenuium Monachorum vicatim mendicantium. Ac multò majores in Gallia opes Ecclesiæ futuras fuisse addit, nisi Johannes XXII. Nicolai Papæ decretum antiquassět, quo quidem licebat mendicantium ordinibus prædia possidere, quæ usu & fructu ad se pertinerent, nexu verò & mancupio ad Papam. De Anglia, quam Casaubono Præfat. ad Exercit. in Annal. Baronii referente, hortum deliciarum Papæ, & inexhaustum puteum fuisse venustè Innocentius IV. & ipse Papa dixit, suprà vidimus. Sanè per eandem tanta cum auri famè rapinas exercuère legati à Latere, qui cum Demade ad Provincias, tanquam ad aueam messem proficisci fuerunt, ut de illorum uno Othone à Gregorio IX. missò, Petrus Casiodorus Epistola ad Anglos A. MCCCII. scripta, perhibuerit, ipsum postquam toto triennio detestandis artibus pecuniam undiquaque corrasisset, tandem cùm discederet, non tantùm pecuniæ in toto hoc Regno reliquisse, quantum ipse partim jam miserat Romam, partim abiens auferebat, Varo Quintilio non absimilis, qui apud Vellejum Paterculum lib ij. dicitur Syriam, cui præfuerat, pauper divitem ingressus, dives pauperem reliquisse. Possent plurima veterum Angliæ Historicorum testimonia commemorari, qui superioribus seculis sæpè factum quaeruntur, ut propter innumerabilem Papārum rapacitatem fides in eo Regno ferè deficeret. De Hispania Sebastianus Munsterus Cosmographr. sol. 69. retulit, quòd in ea ex Archiepiscopatibus & Episcopatibus quotannis ultra novem auri tonnas Quirinales illos prædones conficere fuesuêverint. Ut ne quid interim de Regnis, Nationibus, Provinciis aliis ingenti numero: ne de plus quàm ter mille Episcopatibus, quos in orbe Papali reperiri Cardinalis Jacobatius Tract. de Concilio lib. v. art. 7. col. 7. testatur, ex quorum palliis, mitris, Annatis, Reservationibus, aliisque cauponandi generibus suprà expositis, innumerabilem haud dubiè auri summam ille conficit, dicam.
units.tr: Rome was assigned tribute from Germany; from France, England, Spain and other kingdoms and nations it squeezed out the tribute exacted. The supreme Parisian court, in its defence of the liberty of the Gallican Church against the Roman court, presented to King Louis XI (Articles 72, 73, etc.), records that under Pope Pius II, twenty vacant archbishoprics and bishoprics yielded 120,000 crowns under the title of annates; likewise sixty vacant abbacies, and priories, deaneries and provostships, 100,000 crowns; and finally all parishes and their filial churches diverted 25,000 crowns into the Roman treasury. And so, the same articles, artic. 71., complain that papal exactions had so drained that kingdom that only copper and small coin were left to its inhabitants, while all the gold was exported to Rome. In line with this is what the legate of the Archbishop of Magdeburg reported in the Sylva Locorum Communium: that the Archbishop of Lyon declared at the Council of Basel that in the time of Martin V nine million gold [crowns] had gone from France to Rome, not counting the immense expenses which clergy, going to and returning from Rome frequently, spent there and on the journeys. He adds these words: Let the one who has dwelt there judge what a whirlpool this is. But Bodin also writes, de Rep. lib. v. cap. 2., that when by the order of King Charles IX a census was taken of the ecclesiastical goods in France, the revenues entered in the census amounted to four million sesterces, that is, twelve million of annual income, apart from money, free offerings and heavy gifts of gold to the temples; and this was reckoned sparingly and meagrely, lest danger or envy be stirred up against the priestly order, which, by the reckoning of Lanovius, today possesses in annual revenues one hundred and thirty-three tons of gold and more. The same Bodin, loc. cit., writes that he was told by a German, a magistrate of public affairs, that nearly two thirds of French land belonged to the sacred order, by possession or ownership. He says this seemed incredible to him, although he knew that in France there are more than four hundred bishops, twelve archbishops, five hundred and forty-eight abbots and 27,400 parish priests, if indeed single parish priests are assigned to each town and village, not counting the lesser archimandrites and the monasteries of poor monks begging from village to village. He adds that the wealth of the Church in France would have been far greater still, had John XXII not annulled the decree of Pope Nicholas, by which the mendicant orders were allowed to hold estates which belonged to them in use and usufruct, but in bond and mortgage to the Pope. As for England, which, as Casaubon reports in his Præfat. ad Exercit. in Annal. Baronii, the pleasure garden and inexhaustible well of the Pope, Innocent IV himself wittily called it, as we saw above. Certainly, legates a latere plundered through the same country with such hunger for gold; they set out with Demades into the provinces as to a rich harvest. Peter Cassiodorus, in his letter to the English written in 1302, reports of one of them, Otto, sent by Gregory IX, that after he had for a whole three years gathered money from everywhere by detestable arts, when at last he was leaving, he left in the whole kingdom not as much money as he had partly already sent to Rome and partly carried away with him as he departed. He was not unlike Varus Quintilius, who, according to Velleius Paterculus, lib ij., entering Syria, which he had governed, as a poor man into a rich province, left it as a rich man in a poor one. Many testimonies of the old English historians could be cited, who complain that in earlier centuries it often happened, on account of the countless rapacity of the Popes, that faith in that kingdom nearly failed. Concerning Spain, Sebastian Münster, in his Cosmography, p. 69, reported that there those Quirinal robbers were accustomed to extract from the archbishoprics and bishoprics more than nine tons of gold each year. Meanwhile I say nothing of the other kingdoms, nations and provinces in great number, nor of the more than three thousand bishoprics which Cardinal Jacobatius, Tract. de Concilio lib. v. art. 7. col. 7., attests are found in the Papal world, from whose palls, mitres, annates, reservations and other kinds of huckstering, set out above, he surely makes up an innumerable sum of gold.

units.la: CXL. Mirum ergò non est, Romanos Pontifices plus quàm Regalibus opibus abundantes, ipsis Imperatoribus & Regibus aliquando de divitiarum gloria controversiam movere potuisse. Ex plurimis unum repræsentare libet Johannem XXII. illum paupertatis hostem longè infensissimum, de quo sic Palmerius in Chronol. ad A. 1334. scribit: Johannes Pontifex ætatis suæ anno nonagesimo, pridie Nonas Decembris Avinione moritur: relinquens in thesauris suis ingentem vim auri atque argenti: cujus retta comparatio fuit aurearum drachmarum quindecim millionum, hoc est, millies quindecim millia: quod scripsisse arduum quippe videtur. Nec legitur alias temporibus Ecclesia Romana fuisse locupletior. Quæ postrema verba de eodem cùm usurpasset Antoninus, tale Paulus Langius, Monachus Tzizicensis in Chronico de iis judicium tulit: Non legitur aliis temporibus Ecclesia Romana fuisse locupletior, inquit Antoninus, quod quidem est certissimum. Neque enim tam dives erat temporibus Apostolorum, dum videlicet B. Petrus eandem rexerat Ecclesiam, qui velut verus paupertatis Christi Zelator petenti eleemosynam, respondit: Argentum & aurum non est mihi, quod autem habeo, hoc tribuo. Habuit quippe alium thesaurum, virtutum scilicet & gratiarum, quem & egenti communicavit: Papa inops auro virtute locuples, pauper in arca, dives in conscientia. Ditior denique procul dubio hoc tempore fuit, quàm olim Sixti Papæ & Martyris ævo, qui per B. Laurentium thesauros Ecclesiæ distribuit pauperibus. Opulentior denique, quàm fuit Gregorii I. Beatissimis temporibus, qui aliquot pauperum millia quotidiè alebat. Quorum solicitudinem pastoralem, gubernationem & vitam si ipse Papa Johannes fuisset imitatus, tantam auri copiam minimè post se relinquere quivisset: securior atque Beatior, Misericordiæ videlicet, ac bonorum operum fructu comitatus ex hoc seculo migravisset. Allegat tandem Canonem illum: Aurum habet Ecclesia, non ut conservet, sed ut pauperibus eroget, non dicit, inquit ille, scortis aut histrionibus.
units.tr: CXL. It is therefore no wonder that the Roman pontiffs, abounding in more than royal wealth, could sometimes have a controversy over the glory of riches with the emperors and kings themselves. It is worth setting out one example from many: John XXII, that most bitter enemy of poverty, of whom Palmerius in Chronol. ad A. 1334. writes thus: Pope John died at Avignon in the ninetieth year of his age, on the day before the Nones of December, leaving in his treasuries a huge quantity of gold and silver, whose sound estimate was fifteen million gold drachmas, that is, fifteen thousand thousand, which seems hard even to write down. Nor is it read that at any other time the Roman Church was richer. When Antoninus had used these last words about the same man, Paulus Langius, a monk of Zizka (Tzizicensis), passed this judgement on them in his Chronicle: "It is not read that at any other time the Roman Church was richer," says Antoninus, which is quite certain. For it was not so rich in the time of the Apostles, when St Peter ruled that same Church, who, as a true zealot of Christ's poverty, answered the one asking for alms: "Silver and gold I have not; what I have, that I give." He indeed had another treasure, namely of virtues and graces, which he also shared with the needy: a Pope poor in gold, rich in virtue, poor in his chest, rich in conscience. Richer, beyond doubt, is this time than in the age of Sixtus the Pope and Martyr, who through St Laurence distributed the treasures of the Church to the poor. Richer, finally, than in the most blessed times of Gregory I, who fed some thousands of poor every day. If Pope John himself had imitated their pastoral care, government and life, he could not have left behind so great a store of gold; he would have departed from this age more secure and blessed, accompanied by the fruit of mercy and good works. Finally he cites that canon: "The Church has gold, not to keep, but to dispense to the poor; it does not say, as he puts it, to harlots or actors."

units.la: CXLI. Illud quoque ἀξιομνημόνευτον, quòd Cornelius à Lapide Comment. in Act. cap. iv. se apud plures fide dignos authores legisse scribit, quòd Innocentius III. apud Thomam Aquinatem, quo præsente magna signati auri summa appendebatur, jactans, non amplius habere Ecclesiam causam quiritandi cum S. Petro, Aurum & argentum non habeo, hoc ab eodem Aquinate responso exceptus fit; verissimum id esse, sed Ecclesiæ tamen hoc deesse, quòd cum S. Petro itidem dicere claudo cuipiam mendicanti non posset: Surge & ambula. Neque proin mirum, doluisse Sixto IV. qui post Paulum II. ærarium invenit inane repertis, teste Onuphrio, tantum quinque aureorum millibus. Cordatè! Nam longè locupletius, credo, traditum Lino, Clementique. Sed mutata erant tempora.
units.tr: CXLI. Also worth remembering [ἀξιομνημόνευτον] is what Cornelius à Lapide writes in Commentary on Acts, ch. iv., that he has read in several trustworthy authors: when Innocent III, with a great sum of minted gold being weighed out in the presence of Thomas Aquinas, boasted that the Church no longer had any reason to complain to St Peter, Silver and gold have I none, Aquinas took up the reply that this was most true, but that the Church lacked the ability to say to a lame beggar, as St Peter did, Rise up and walk. Nor is it surprising, then, that Sixtus IV grieved, who after Paul II found the treasury empty, with only five thousand gold pieces discovered, according to Onuphrius. Wisely! For far richer, I believe, was what had been handed down by Linus and Clement. But times had changed.

units.la: CXLII. Audiuntur tamen, ne quid dissimulemus, querelæ, quòd Pontifices morientes plerumque ærarium minùs grave, & millionibus onustum, successoribus relinquant. Nam & modernus Papa Innocentius XI. Mercatorum maximus, & purpura, quam gestat, voracior, clavum Papalis Imperii excipiens, querelam similem movisse dicitur, cujus jam ingluviem non opes terrarum, nedum spospolia tot Cardinalium vacationibus detracta explere posse videntur. Coeterùm, causæ languescentis ærarii tres reddi solent. Prima est, Lutheri peccatum geminum, ausi Papæ coronam, & Monachorum ventrem, qui ipsorum Deus est, juxta celebre illud Erasmi, attingere. Cujus peccati duplicis ea vis fuit, ut non tantùm plurimæ Civitates, Provinciæ, Regna nihil amplius in istam voraginem conferrent, sed etiam Babyloniis Mercatoribus cautiùs verecundiúsque cum obnoxiis adhuc Italis, Gallis, Hispanis, aliisque, ne & ipsi fœnum admorderent, deinceps mercandum, imò quæstus etiam ex peccatis populorum & beneficiis Ecclesiæ antehac liberalissimè percep-tus, non tantùm multùm imminutus, sed etiam cum populorum illorum Regibus & Principibus, ut propitiis iis uterentur, partiendus fuerit. Mansit nihilominus in Italia & Hispania maximus proventus minimè contemnendus, ex Annatis imprimis, decimis, dispensationibus, spoliis, belli contra Turcas, vel hæreticos gerendi prætextibus, & indulgentiis, quarum tractandarum facultas à Papa integris Monasteriis concedi solet hunc in finem, ut abundans pinguedo inde in Romanam culinam, quoties lubitum est per tributorum, decimarum, quintarum, dimidietatum &c. exactionem derivetur: aliis denique subtilium exactionum generibus. Quam in rem multa Nobilis. Eduinus Santis scripto accuratissimo de Statu Religionis in Europa cap. 29. perdoctè edisseruit. Secunda est, Pontificiæ Sedis suprà Imperatorum Regúmque fastigium eminentis magnificentia, & Secularis ille typhus, quo sub mysteriorum & religionis fuco ad præstringendos populorum oculos, ut in fide & obsequio retineantur faciliùs, utitur. Quanti verò id constare Papæ putamus? Aulæ splendorem, & tot Legatorum, Nuntiorum, Corycæorum, Parasitorum dignitatem statúmque & effrœnem, quo se saginant, luxum ut sustineat, immensa facultatum vi opus habet, quibus nisi Croesus Crassúsque aliquis par esse nequit. Tertia denique est, immodica profusio amplissimarum opum in liberos, spurios, Nepotes, Consanguineos Pontificum, qui plerúmque senes electi brevem in Cathedra moram prospicientes, singuli fere necessariis suis ex Ecclesiæ bonis ditandis dotandisque gnaviter incumbunt. De quo Nepotismi studio Hist. Pap. ß. cclxx. &c. plura diximus.
units.tr: CXLII. Yet, lest we conceal anything, complaints are heard that Popes, when dying, usually leave to their successors a treasury less weighty than burdened with millions. For the present Pope, Innocent XI, the greatest of merchants, more voracious than the purple he wears, taking up the helm of the Papal empire, is said to have made a similar complaint, whose gluttony the riches of the lands, let alone the spoils drawn from the vacancies of so many Cardinals, seem unable to satisfy. Moreover, the causes of the languishing treasury are usually given as three. (1) The first is Luther's twofold sin, in daring to touch the Pope's crown and the monks' belly, which is their god, according to Erasmus' famous saying. The force of this twofold sin was such that not only very many cities, provinces and kingdoms contributed nothing more to that abyss, but the Babylonian merchants also, more cautiously and shamefacedly, with the Italians, French, Spanish and others still liable, lest they too bite the hay, ceased trading thereafter. Indeed the profit once most liberally drawn from the sins of peoples and the benefits of the Church was not only greatly reduced but had to be shared with the kings and princes of those peoples, so as to keep them favourable. Nevertheless a very large revenue, by no means to be despised, remained in Italy and Spain, chiefly from annates, tithes, dispensations, spoils, the pretexts of waging war against the Turks or heretics, and indulgences, whose management the Pope usually grants to whole monasteries for this purpose, so that abundant fat may flow thence into the Roman kitchen whenever it pleases, through the exaction of tributes, tithes, fifths, halves and so on, and finally by other kinds of subtle exactions. On this matter the nobleman Edwin Sandys has expounded most learnedly in his most accurate writing on the state of religion in Europe, chapter 29. (2) The second is the magnificence of the Pontifical See, raised above the height of emperors and kings, and that worldly pride which it uses under a veneer of mysteries and religion, to dazzle the eyes of the people so that they may be more easily kept in faith and obedience. But how much do we think this costs the Pope? The splendour of the court and the dignity of so many legates, nuncios, flatterers and parasites, and the unbridled luxury with which they gorge themselves, require an immense store of wealth, to match which none but some Croesus or Crassus would suffice. (3) The third finally is the immoderate lavishing of very great resources on the children, bastards, nephews and kinsmen of the Popes, who, mostly elected when old and looking ahead to a brief stay in the Chair, each busily devote themselves to enriching and endowing their own from the goods of the Church. On this zeal for nepotism History of the Popes, §§ 270 etc. has said more.

units.la: CXLIII. Frustrà ergò Hierarchici Avaritiam & tot Simoniaca Stratagemata sua sumtuum faciendorum magnitudine & gravitate, & Ecclesiæ Romanæ necessitatibus exaggeratis, defendere satagunt.
units.tr: CXLIII. In vain, therefore, do the Hierarchs try to defend their avarice and so many simoniacal stratagems by exaggerating the magnitude and weight of the expenses to be made and the necessities of the Roman Church.

units.la: Sic enim Ecclesiæ Romanæ necessitates Johannes XXII. Extravag. Cum nonnulla I. in com. de Præbend. Summi Pontificis & Cardinalium sustentationem Eugenius IV. Concil. Basil. in Resp. ad collationem Joh. de Brachenstein obtendunt.
units.tr: For thus John XXII, Extravagant Cum nonnulla I, on Prebends, puts forward the needs of the Roman Church, and Eugenius IV, Council of Basel, in reply to the proposal of John of Brachenstein, puts forward the maintenance of the Supreme Pontiff and the Cardinals.

units.la: Cardinalis Toletus de Instruct. Sac. cap. 89. sic scribit: Dico non esse murmurandum contra Papam, quòd exigit pro his (absolutionibus & dispensationibus) pecunias: non per modum pretii. Nam ista ad sustentationem dantur, qua multa indiget tanta in Ecclesia dignitas. Atqui etiam fur pro suis necessitatibus furatur, ut habeat, unde genialiter vivat, & se suámque familiam splendidè alat, ornet, ditet. An propterea furtum licitum & honestum erit? At quæ sunt illæ necessitates? ad concinnanda ne luminaria? Ad clerum Ecclesiæ utilem & necessarium, pauperésve alendos? His verò faciendis sumtibus Ecclesia Romana sibi sufficit, neque opus habet retia sua aliò mittere. Ad pompam verò temporalis Principatus bona Christi, Ecclesiæ & pauperum insumi & abliguriri non debent. Sed & sustentatio Papæ, si, uti decet, frugaliter vivat, & pompas hujus sæculi abdicet, cleróque suo con-
units.tr: Cardinal Toletus, On the Instruction of Priests, ch. 89, writes thus: I say that one should not murmur against the Pope because he demands money for these (absolutions and dispensations): not as a price. For these are given for the support which so great a dignity in the Church requires. And yet even a thief steals for his own needs, so that he may have something to live on pleasantly and may feed, adorn and enrich his household splendidly. Will theft therefore become lawful and honourable? But what are those needs? To make up lamps? For the clergy of the Church, useful and necessary, or for feeding the poor? For these expenses the Roman Church is sufficient to itself and has no need to send its nets elsewhere. But the goods of Christ, of the Church and of the poor ought not to be spent and squandered on the pomp of a temporal principality. But if the Pope, as is fitting, lives frugally and renounces the pomps of this age, then his maintenance too, together with his clergy,

units.la: Hierarchi-corum, ab Ecclesia Romana necessitatibus, sumptuum faciendorum magnitudine petita, discontentus sit, paucis contenta esse poterit, ut nil necesse sit in peregrinas possessiones involare. Denique impensæ Papæ si ordinariæ sunt, habet ille Patrimonium, quod vocant, Petri, sin extraordinariæ, veluti si à Patrimonio suo disturbaretur, quò minùs eo uti liberè possit, tunc (ita habet Arrestum Curiæ Parlamenti Parisiensis in formam edicti sub Carolo VI. d. 11. Sept. MCCCCLXVI. relatum, & à Bochello Decret. Eccl. Gallic. lib. iv. 5. recitatum) cæteras monere debuit Ecclesias, excitare, adhortari & requirere de subsidio charitativo, quòd ei Ecclesiæ Romanæ annuì posset & deberet, cum tamen consilio, moderamine & justa causa, absque prejudicio, culpa non precedente, durante necessitate, ac de consensu & benignitate Principum, Patronorum & aliorum Prælatorum, & non cum gravamine assiduo & indistincto cæterarum Ecclesiarum. Petrus de Alliaco, Cardinalis Cameracensis in libello de Reformatione Ecclesiæ, postquam ex Huberto Monacho notâsset, causam dispositivam schismatis Græcorum inter alias unam fuisse propter gravamina Romanæ Ecclesiæ in exactionibus, &c. De primo, ait, Gravamine, & contra hanc magnitudinem & multitudinem exactionum providendum esset tripliciter. Primò, per diminutionem pomposorum Statuum, & excessivarum expensarum, ut sic Romana Ecclesia minùs esset onerosa subjectis, & ut etiam esset exemplum humilitatis, & forma virtutis instar Christi, cujus ista vicariatum, & à quo primatus honorem tenet, qui ait: Discite à me, quia mitis sum & humilis corde. Secundò, per diminutionem & arctationem hujusmodi exactionum, sic scilicet, quod certa summa rationabilis determinaretur & limitaretur pro moderato statu Papæ & Cardinalium subjectis Ecclesiæ imponenda &c. ultrà quam summam nova exactio non posset imponi sine authoritate & consensu generalis Concilii. Tertiò, per diminutionem numeri Cardinalium, ita quòd non effet tantus & tam onerosus numerus ipsorum, sicut hastenus fuit: nec Romanæ Ecclesiæ dici posset: Multiplicâsti gentem, & non magnificâsti lætitiam. Pluribus etiam objectionem illam Michaël Rousselius ipse Histor. Jurisd. Pontif. lib. v. cap. 4. n. 29. 30. &c. diluit, ostendens, veteres Pontifices Gregorium M. inprimis, ab ejusmodi exactionibus abhorrentes, ex solo reditu patrimoniali satis habuisse, quo & se suòsque alerent, & necessitatibus omnibus consulerent, Templa multa ædificarent, reficerent, denique erga pauperes liberalitatem maximam exercerent.
units.tr: Hierarchs', sought from the necessities of the Roman Church and the magnitude of the expenses to be made, being discontented, he will be able to be content with little, so that there is no need to fly off to foreign possessions. Finally, if the Pope's expenses are ordinary, he has what they call the Patrimony of Peter; if extraordinary, as if he were disturbed in his patrimony so that he could not freely use it, then (so the Arrest of the Parliament of Paris has it, set out in the form of an edict under Charles VI on 11 September 1466, and recited by Bochellus in Decrees of the Gallican Church, book iv, 5) it ought to admonish, rouse, exhort and request the other churches for a charitable subsidy, which they could and should grant to the Roman Church, yet with counsel, moderation and just cause, without prejudice, no prior fault, while the necessity lasts, and with the consent and goodwill of princes, patrons and other prelates, and not with a continual and indiscriminate burden on the other churches. Peter of Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, in his libel On the Reform of the Church, after noting from the monk Hubert that the efficient cause of the Greek schism was, among others, the grievances of the Roman Church in exactions, etc., says: On the first grievance, and against this magnitude and multitude of exactions, provision should be made in three ways. First, by diminishing the pompous state and excessive expenses, so that the Roman Church would be less burdensome to its subjects, and would also be an example of humility and a form of virtue like Christ, whose vicar it is and from whom it holds the honour of primacy, who said: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart. Second, by diminishing and restraining exactions of this kind, namely that a certain reasonable sum be determined and limited to be imposed on the subjects of the Church for the moderate state of the Pope and Cardinals, etc.; beyond that sum no new exaction could be imposed without the authority and consent of a general Council. Third, by diminishing the number of Cardinals, so that their number would not be so great and so burdensome as hitherto, nor could it be said of the Roman Church: Thou hast multiplied the nation and not increased the joy. Michael Rousselius himself, in History of Papal Jurisdiction, book v, ch. 4, nn. 29, 30 etc., refutes that objection at length too, showing that the ancient Popes, Gregory the Great above all, abhorring such exactions, were content with the revenue of the patrimony alone, by which they supported themselves and their own and met all necessities, built and repaired many temples, and finally exercised the greatest liberality towards the poor.

units.la: CXLIV. Restat Hierarchicorum Avaritiam & Nun- dinationem testibus domesticis, & è sinu eorum petitis, convincamus.
units.tr: CXLIV. We shall now convict the avarice and trafficking of the hierarchs by witnesses from their own household, drawn from their own bosom.

units.la: Non paucos equidem hastenus citavimus. Et allegare penè innumera possemus. Sed paucis, quia in longum nimis hæc tractatio provesta jam est, contenti erimus, productis ex septem retrò seculis Auctoribus gravissimis, Imperatoribus, Regibus, Purpuratis, Theologis, Jurisconsultis, Vatibus, ne quas possemus altiùs querelas scrutemur.
units.tr: We have indeed cited not a few so far, and we could cite almost countless more. But we will be content with a few, since this treatment has already run on too long. We bring forward authors of the greatest weight from the seven centuries past, emperors, kings, princes, theologians, jurists and poets, so that we need not search out complaints from further back.

units.la: CXLV. Ex Decimo Seculo prodeat primus Imperator Otho III. qui quales Romæ Pontifices observaverit, sic Elest. Sylv. 2. in fine Epist. Gerberti pandit: Romanam, matrem esse testamur: sed incuria & inscientia Pontificum suæ claritatis titulos obfuscâsse.
units.tr: CXLV. From the tenth century let the first emperor come forward, Otto III, who, setting out what kind of Popes he saw at Rome, says in the closing part of the letter of the elected Sylvester II (Gerbert): "We testify that the Roman Church is our mother; but through the carelessness and ignorance of the Popes she has obscured the titles of her glory."

units.la: Nam non solùm quæ extra urbem esse videantur, vendiderunt, & quibusdam colluviis à lare S. Petri alienaverunt; sed quod absque dolore non dicimus, si quid in hac nostra urbe Regia habuerunt, ut majore licentia evagarentur omnibus, judicante pecunia, in commune dederunt: & S. PETRUM & S. PAULUM, ipsa quoque ALTARIA SPOLIAVERUNT. Confusis verò Papaticis legibus, & jam abjecta Ecclesia Romana in tantum quidem Pontifices creverunt, ut maximam partem Imperii nostri Apostolatui suo conjungerent. Jam non quaerentes, quae & quanta suis culpis perdiderunt, non curantes, quanta ex voluntaria varietate effuderunt, sed sua propria, utpote ab illis ipsis dilapidata dimittentes, quasi culpam suam in Imperium nostrum retorquentes, ad aliena, id est, nostra & nostri Imperii maximè migraverunt. Ejusdem Imperatoris, Magister Gerbertus apud Baronium ad A. 992. n. 20. sic loquitur: Roma nunc temporis venalis exposita, ad nummorum quantitatem judicia trutinat.
units.tr: For they have not only sold what seem to lie outside the city and alienated them to certain rabble from the hearth of St Peter; but, which we cannot say without grief, whatever they had in this our royal city they have given over to common use, letting money be the judge, so that they might roam about with greater licence for everyone. They have even despoiled St Peter and St Paul, and the altars themselves. But with the Papal laws confused, and the Roman Church now cast down, the Popes have grown so great that they have joined the greater part of our Empire to their apostolate. Now, not asking what and how much they lost through their own faults, not caring how much they poured out through voluntary change, but dismissing their own property as squandered by themselves, and as if turning their fault back upon our Empire, they have migrated above all to what is alien, that is, to ours and our Empire's. Gerbert, the teacher of the same Emperor, speaks thus in Baronius, ad A. 992, n. 20: "Rome, put up for sale at this time, weighs judgments by the quantity of coins."

units.la: CXLVI. Seculo Undecimo Leo IX. ipse Papa Epist. 9.
units.tr: CXLVI. In the eleventh century Pope Leo IX himself, Epistle 9,

units.la: sic de Praedecessoribus suis queritur: Et quia abundante iniquitate, & frigescente charitate, S. Romana Ecclesia Catholica & Apostolica sedes nimis diu obsessa fuit mercenariis & non Pastoribus, à quibus sua, non quae sunt Jesu Christi quaerentibus devastata jacebant mirabiliter hactenus, Divinum consilium voluit meam humilitatem suscipere tantae cathedrae pondus &c. Petrus Damiani Cardinalis Episcopus Ostiensis, cùm ferre Ecclesiae Romanae perditos mores amplius non posset, Cardinalitia dignitate & Episcopatu abdicato, ad suam cellam rediit, ubi uberrimos de Ecclesiae Romanae moribus, & avaritia inprimis quaestus fudit. Inter alia Epist. 7. sic scribit: Heu Sedes Apostolica, Urbis olim gloria; Nunc proh dolor! efficeris Officina Simonis Magi; Terunt incudem mallei. Nummi sunt Tartarei. Justo Dei judicio fit ista conditio, ut quisquis Apostolicam sedem semel comparat, redimere non desinat, donec male pereat. Idem apud Baronium ad A. 1061. num. 47. hujusmodi ad Alexandrum II. Epigramma misit: Sedis Apostolicae qui vult retinere vigorem, Aequa libret rigidè pondera justitiae. Juris enim pariles nescit respicere lances, Quem favor inflectit, spes vel avara trahit. Muneribus plena qui laxat ora crumenæ, Justitiæ vacuam perdit inops animam. Cœli Romæ feras tenet, & regit orbis habenas. His si plura velit, Tartara sola petit.
units.tr: complains thus of his predecessors: "And because iniquity abounds and charity grows cold, the holy Roman Church, the Catholic and Apostolic See, has been besieged for too long by mercenaries and not by shepherds, who sought their own things and not those of Jesus Christ, and it has lain wonderfully devastated until now. The divine counsel has willed that my humility should take up the weight of so great a chair," and so on. Peter Damian, Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, when he could no longer bear the corrupt morals of the Roman Church, gave up his cardinalate and bishopric and returned to his cell, where he poured out most copious accounts of the morals of the Roman Church, and above all of its avarice in gain. Among other things, in Epistle 7, he writes thus: "Alas, Apostolic See, once the glory of the City, now, alas! you have become the workshop of Simon Magus. They wear out the anvil with the hammer. The coins are of Tartarus. By the just judgment of God this is the condition: whoever once acquires the Apostolic See does not cease to buy it back, until he perishes wickedly." The same man, in Baronius, ad A. 1061, n. 47, sent such an epigram to Alexander II: "Whoever wishes to keep the vigour of the Apostolic See must weigh the scales of justice evenly and rigidly. For he does not know how to regard equal pans of the law whom favour bends or greedy hope draws. Whoever loosens the mouth of his purse, full of gifts, a pauper, loses his soul, emptied of justice. At Rome he holds the wild beasts of heaven and rules the reins of the world. If he wishes more of this, he seeks only Tartarus."

units.la: Eodem Seculo Ivo Carnotensis floruit. Is passim Romanæ Ecclesiæ avaritiam perstringit. Ex Epist. 133. sequentia ejus verba depromere libet. Infusurrárat, inquit, aliquis in aures Legatorum Romanorum, Ivonem in Ecclesia Carnotensi permittere labem Simoniacam dominari. Hac de re à Legatis monitus, negat ipse, & potius gloriatur, se multas malas consuetudines in Ecclesia sua inventas, & toto pene Regno radicatas avulsisse. Si quæ autem sunt adhuc, quæ pro consuetudine antiqua publicè exigunt Decanus & Cantor, & alii Ministri ab iis, qui Canonici fiunt, me contradicente & persequente, Ecclesiæ Romanæ consuetudine se defendunt, in qua dicunt cubicularios & ministros Sacri Palatii multa exigere à consecratis Episcopis vel Abbatibus, quæ oblationis, vel benedictionis nomine palliantur, cùm nec calamus, nec charta gratis ibi, ut ajunt, habeatur. Et hoc quasi lapide conterunt frontem meam, cùm non habeam, quod respondeam, nisi Evangelicum illud: Quod dicunt, servate & facite, secundùm eorum opera nolite facere. Si autem hanc (NB) pestem radicitùs evellere non valeo, non tantùm invaletudini meæ hoc imputandum est, quia ad hoc ab origine nascentis Ecclesiæ Romana Ecclesia laboravit, nec à gremio etiam suo tales sua quærentes penitùs prævaluit eliminare, nec in diebus malis regnare desinat cupiditas, donec finito mundi termino regnum accipiat charitas. μάλα ἰμφαλικῶς sic avaritiæ Romanæ incurabilem pestem ille depinxit.
units.tr: Ivo of Chartres flourished in the same century. He everywhere censures the avarice of the Roman Church. From his Epistle 133 it pleases us to bring forth the following words: "Someone, he says, had whispered into the ears of the Roman Legates that Ivo was allowing simoniacal stain to hold sway in the Church of Chartres. Warned about this by the Legates, he denies it himself, and rather boasts that he has torn up many bad customs found in his church and rooted throughout almost the whole kingdom. But if there are still some which the Dean, the Cantor and other ministers publicly exact from those who become canons, under the old custom, while I object and pursue them, they defend themselves by the custom of the Roman Church, in which, they say, chamberlains and ministers of the Sacred Palace exact many things from consecrated bishops or abbots, which are disguised under the name of offering or blessing, since neither pen nor paper is there, as they say, had for nothing. And with this they batter my forehead as with a stone, since I have nothing to answer except that Gospel saying: What they say, keep and do; according to their works, do not do. But if I cannot tear up this (NB) plague by the roots, this must not be imputed only to my weakness, since the Roman Church has laboured at this from the origin of the nascent Church, nor has she been able utterly to eliminate from her own bosom such men seeking their own; nor does desire cease to reign in evil days, until, the end of the world's term being reached, charity receives the kingdom." Very pointedly [μάλα ἐμφαλικῶς] he thus depicted the incurable plague of Roman avarice.

units.la: CXLVII. In Seculum idem undecimum incidit Bern- har-
units.tr: CXLVII. In the same eleventh century falls Bern-

units.la: hardus, non Clarevallensis ille Abbas, sed Monachus Benedictinus Corbejensis, Vir, Trithemii in scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, elogio, in Divinis Scripturis nobiliter doctus, in saecularibus literis peritissimus. Ille Planctum Ecclesiae carmine conscripsit, statumque sui temporis Clericalem & Simoniacam impietatem vivis coloribus depinxit. Cum non ubique obvius liber sit, ex eo integrum carmen, quo Romanos Simones, Curtisanos, Mercatores, Pilatos non Praelatos &c. egregie venustéque depexos dedit, adscribere non pigrabor, ut quam foeda jam tum Ecclesiae Romanae facies fuerit, Monacho haud incelebri indice patescat. Sic autem ille cecinit: Collationes gratia | Religio tam sacrum: Pertractaturus aliqua | Qui purè propter Dominum, De statu clericali: | Religionis habitum Narrabo de insania | Portare videatur. Quae regnat in Ecclesia | Sed permulti nunc proh dolor, Processu criminali. | Conversi quidè non ad cor, Ubique nunc religio | Sed magis ad pulmonem: Recedit à vestigio | Ut vivant commodiùs, Sanctorum Praecessorum: | Et bibant gloriosiùs, Mundanis est mundanior, | Intrant religionem. Et vanis multò vanior: | Non sic vos impii, non sic, Ubilibet locorum. | Sed tanquà pulvis estis hic, Non est in ea sanitas, | Qui rapitur de terra. Sed vanitatum vanitas, | Si vivitis neutraliter, Et omnia neglecta. | Torquebimini poenaliter, Permixta saecularibus, | Sub Inferorum ferra. Et foeminis & maribus | Indigni Deo Domino, Omnino fit despecta. | Despecti quoque saeculo, A maximis ad minimum, | Peribitis in Guerra: Vix habet unum filium | Vos omnes esse, timeo, De Presbyterorum numero Damnabili revera. Omnes ad Clericalia Recurrunt, ut per talia, Quæ sua sunt, acquirant: Messiam non inveniunt, Nec invenire cupiunt Spontaneè delirant. De Christi patrimonio, Sub pompis & præconio Viventes, intumescunt: Intenti voluptatibus, Et mundi vanitatibus, De cappis erubescunt. Non solum noto Monachos, Sed etiam Canonicos, Et fictas Moniales: Quæ propter Jesu minimè, Videntur esse filiæ, Et filii spirituales: Sed magis, ut divitiis Fruantur, & deliciis, Et cæteris cupitis. Quæ replicare nequeo, Nec volo, neque debeo De istis hypocritis. A quibus multa patitur Confunditur, & quatitur Navicula marina, In qua dormit jã Dominus, Quem suscitat discipulus Et postulat divina. Es Clericis & laicis, In mundo constituti: Impellitur manicula Iam tanta sunt pericula,
units.tr: hardus, not that Abbot of Clairvaux but a Benedictine monk of Corbie, a man whom Trithemius, in his list of Ecclesiastical Writers, praises as nobly learned in the Divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular letters. He wrote a Lament for the Church in verse, and painted in vivid colours the clerical and simoniacal impiety of his own time. Since the book is not found everywhere, I will not hesitate to copy out the whole poem, in which he finely and charmingly depicts the Roman Simons, courtiers, merchants and Pilates, who are not prelates, so that the foul face the Roman Church already wore in that age may be made plain by a monk not without reputation. He sang thus: Benefices bestowed by favour | Religion so sacred: I am about to treat some matters | Which purely for the Lord's sake, concerning the clerical state: | I will tell of the madness of wearing the habit of religion, which reigns in the Church. | But very many now, alas, in criminal proceedings. Now religion is everywhere | Converted indeed, not to the heart, but rather to the belly: it departs from the footsteps | so that they may live more comfortably, of the holy predecessors: and drink more splendidly, it is more worldly than the world, they enter religion, and far more vain than vanities. | Not so, you impious men, not so, wherever you are in places. But you are here as dust, there is no health in it, which is snatched from the earth; but vanity of vanities, if you live neutrally and all things are neglected. You will be tormented with punishment, mixed with worldly things, under the iron of the underworld. And with women and men unworthy of God the Lord, it is wholly despised. Despised also by the age, from the greatest to the least, you will perish in war: scarcely has one son of you all been, I fear, truly of the number of the damnable elders. All run to clerical offices, so that by such means they may acquire what is their own: they do not find the Messiah, nor do they desire to find him; they rave of their own accord. From the patrimony of Christ, living under pomp and proclamation, they swell up: intent on pleasures and the vanities of the world, they blush at the cowls. I note not only monks, but also canons and feigned nuns: who for Jesus' sake by no means seem to be daughters and spiritual sons: but rather that they may enjoy riches and delights, and other desired things. Which I cannot recount, nor do I wish, nor ought I, concerning these hypocrites. By whom the little sea-boat suffers much, is confounded and shaken, in which the Lord already sleeps, whom the disciple wakes and asks for divine aid. From clerics and laymen established in the world: Impellitur manicula now the dangers are so great,
That there is scarcely hope of salvation.

units.la: Vix tamen surgit aliquis, Et rogat Dominum pro iisPericulis, instanter: Ne navis Sanctæ fideiMergatur ab hypocrisi,Quæ regnat abundanter.
units.tr: Yet scarcely does someone rise up, and asks the Lord for them in the perils, urgently: that the ship of holy faith be not sunk by hypocrisy, which reigns abundantly.

units.la: In cunctis terræ finibus, In ventis & turbinibusInnumeris, tam dirè:Quod nisi Deus faciatDe speciali gratia, Timendum est perire.
units.tr: In all the lands of the earth, amid winds and whirlwinds innumerable, so dreadfully: that unless God does it by special grace, we must fear to perish.

units.la: In die propinquissimoZizania cum tritico, Et è controverso quidem: Nam Satan est in foribus, Et in mille coloribus, Ad destruendam fidem, Quam Christus suo sanguineConstruxit in examineCruentæ passionis: Dum perfidos damnaverat, Et credulos salvaveratIn propriis personis.
units.tr: On the very near day the tares with the wheat, and indeed on the opposite side: for Satan is at the doors, and in a thousand colours, to destroy the faith which Christ by his blood built in the trial of his bloody passion, while he condemned the faithless and saved the believing in their own persons.

units.la: Quid amplius edisseram, Si vera loqui debeam; De vita Clericorum: Prælati sedent hodie
units.tr: What more shall I set forth, if I ought to speak the truth, concerning the life of the clergy: the Prelates sit today
Woe to the world now because of scandals, Vol. II.

units.la: In opulenta requie,De sorte miserorum. Vivendo supervacuè:Qui charitatem maximèDeberent exercere, Pra cateris fidelibusIn omnibus hominibus: Virtutes exhibere. Cum bonus exemplaribusTam fœminis, quàm maribus: Viam salutis dare: Non alta quidem sapere: Non fremere, non rapere: Non aliquem truffareHæc essent meritoria, Servorum Dei gloria, Fidelium tutela: Per quæ manerêt Principes, Et Christiani simplicesIn fidei sequela. Sed ubi possunt hæc discerni? Cùm nec priores nec moderniPro Deo famulentur: Imò pro temporalibusOmnes ceu SpiritualibusInsistere videntur. Majores cum minoribusIndocti cum doctoribusEt cæteri de clero, Non habent rectam speciem, Nec curant Cœli pretium,
units.tr: In opulent rest, concerning the lot of the wretched. Living to no purpose: who ought most of all to exercise charity before the other faithful among all men: to display virtues. Since good examples both to women and to men: to give the way of salvation: not indeed to think high things: not to rage, not to rob: not to deceive anyone. These would be meritorious, the glory of God's servants, the protection of the faithful: by which princes would remain, and simple Christians in the following of the faith. But where can these be discerned? For neither the former nor the moderns serve God: but for temporal things all, as if for spiritual things, seem to labour. The greater with the lesser, the unlearned with the teachers, and the rest of the clergy, do not have the right appearance, nor do they care for the price of heaven,

units.la: De Christo Deo vero, Sub cujus umbra latitant, Et sua bona dissipantIn pompa seculari: Sunt PILATI non PRÆLATI, Plus quàm Tyranni depravati: In virtutibus ignari.
units.tr: Concerning Christ the true God, under whose shade they hide, and squander their goods in worldly pomp: they are Pilates, not Prelates, more depraved than tyrants: ignorant in virtues.
Through whom also the flock of the faithful
Is treated to ruin,
The Messiah permitting:
The corrupt together perish,
And they have become abominable
The devil persuading.
There is none who does good,
There is none who loves God,
Made useless.
They look to gifts,
They do not thirst for justice,
Enticed by delights.
They do not live as Christians,
Neither justly nor humanely,
In the present age:
So that great fortresses,
And more benefices
They may possess, intent upon them.
Their spirit truly
Is empty and void,
For the service of God:
From these all gravity

units.la: Egreditur, & ruit pravi-tas. In seculo passatum. Emergit insolentia, Recedit conscientia, Communiter à Clero: Quæ, qualis, quanta furia Committitur in Curia? De Curtisanis quæro. Nam illi sciunt practicam De Simone trussaticam, Scripturas & Calendas: Quas ille mille artifex, Diabolus, eorum rex Invenit exercendas: Ut pauperes abjiciant, Et divites alliciant, In modis & in formis.. Quid aliud per atria, Quàm patens idolatria, Et Clericus enormis. Non psallitur Davidicè, Sed prorsùs hypocriticè, De beneficiatis: Qui qualiter & quomodo Servire solent Domino, Jam dicebatur satis. Nunc de eorum vestibus, Et moribus & gestibus, Ad modicum tractabo: In quibus fatualiter, Et merè laicaliter Incedunt, increpabo. Canonici cum cæteris Collegiatis sociis, Mundaniter imbuti, In varis & sérico Vestiti vadunt Jericho, Mollissimis induti. Ne quid eorum corpora Sustineant vel aspera Tenerrimos offendant: De preciosis pellibus Subtilibus & mollibusCamisias emendant. Ut placeant hominibusNituntur suis crinibusIncedere politis: Coronas in capitibusFerunt, de pilis mitibus, Et rebus exquisitis. Sic imitantur Dominum,Qui pro salute hominumEst spinis coronatus: Sic serviunt altissimoQui non pepercit Filio,Dum stetit immolatus. In cruce nudis genibus, Et manibus & pedibusEt dextra perforatus. Sic deridetur Dominus, A Servo nihilominusIn via prosperatus. Præbendas habet quatuor, Et est Ecclesiæ pastor, Vel potius mercator: Si forte chorum visitat, Non propter Jesum ibi stat,
units.tr: Departs, and wickedness collapses. In the past age. Insolence arises, conscience recedes, commonly among the clergy: what, what kind of frenzy, how great, is committed in the Curia? I ask about the Courtiers. For they know the practical art of Simon's trickery, the Scriptures and the Calendars, which that thousand-skilled artisan, the devil, their king, has invented for them to exercise: so that they may cast down the poor and entice the rich, in ways and forms. What else through the courts, than open idolatry, and an outrageous clergy? They do not sing the psalms in David's manner, but altogether hypocritically, the beneficed: concerning how and in what manner they are wont to serve the Lord, enough has already been said. Now concerning their garments, and their manners and gestures, I shall treat briefly: in which, foolishly and purely like laymen, they walk, I shall rebuke. Canons with the other collegiate companions, worldly imbued, clothed in various and silken garments, go to Jericho, dressed in the softest things. Lest their bodies suffer anything harsh, or offend their tender parts: from precious furs, subtle and soft, they mend their shirts. That they may please men, they strive with their hair styled and arranged to walk: they wear crowns on their heads, of gentle furs, and of exquisite things. Thus they imitate the Lord, who for the salvation of men was crowned with thorns: thus they serve the Most High, who did not spare his Son, while he stood sacrificed. On the cross with bare knees, and with hands and feet, and pierced on the right. Thus the Lord is mocked, by a servant nonetheless, prospering on the way. He has four prebends, and is a minister of the Church, or rather a merchant: if perchance he visits the choir, he does not stand there for Jesus' sake,

units.la: Collegiorum jocus, Præsentiæ spectator. Mox habitâ præsentiâ, Cum magna vehementia Recurrit ad mundana: Sequentibus consociis, In seculi negotiis Multiplicat profana. Cum longis, amplis manicis, Et actibus tyrannicis, Incedit equitando: Persequitur Desficos, Subsannat scientificos, In malis gloriando &c.
units.tr: The jest of the colleges, a spectator of attendance. Soon, attendance having been recorded, with great vehemence he runs back to worldly things: his companions following, in the affairs of the age he multiplies profane things. With long, wide sleeves, and tyrannical acts, he walks riding: he persecutes the Desficos, mocks the learned, glorying in evils, etc.

units.la: CXLVIII. Inter Seculi Duodecimi testes primas Fridericus I. Imperator, Barbarossa dictus, obtineat. Ejus vitam Radevicus, Frisingensis Ecclesiæ Canonicus descripsit. Sic autem lib. j. cap. 10. de illo habet:
units.tr: CXLVIII. Among the witnesses of the twelfth century the first place is held by the Emperor Frederick I, called Barbarossa. Radevicus, a Canon of the Church of Freising, described his life. He says of him thus in book 1, chapter 10:

units.la: Fridericus sanè Imperator dolet, quòd Legati Hadriani IV. ad se venerint, quasi de Mammona iniquitatis inflati, de altitudine superbiæ, de fastu arrogantiæ, de execrabili tumidi cordis elatione. Et postea sic Imperator loquitur: Quia multa paria literarum apud eos reperta sunt, & Schedulæ sigillatæ, ad arbitrium eorum adhuc scribenda, quibus, sicut (NB.) hactenùs consuetudinis eorum fuit, per singulas Ecclesias Teutonici Regni conceptum iniquitatis suæ virus respergere, altaria denudare, vasa domus Dei asportare, cruces excoriare nitebantur, ne ultrà procedendi facultas eis daretur, eadem quâ venerant via, ad urbem eos redire fecimus. In responsione ad objecta Pontificis idem Fridericus apud eundem cap. 16. inter alia sic loquitur: Introitum & exitum Italiæ nec clausimus edicto, nec claudere aliquo modo volumus peregrinantibus, vel pro suis necessitatibus rationabiliter cum testimonio Episcoporum & Prælatorum suorum Romanam sedem adeuntibus: sed illis abusionibus, quibus omnes Ecclesiæ Regni nostri gravatæ & attenuatæ sunt, & omnes penè claustrales disciplinæ emortuæ & sepultæ, obviare intendimus. In capite orbis Deus per Im. Imperium exaltavit Ecclesiam: In capite orbis Ecclesia non per Deum, ut credimus, nunc demolitur Imperium.
units.tr: Emperor Frederick indeed grieves that the legates of Hadrian IV came to him, as if puffed up with the mammon of iniquity, with the height of pride, with the haughtiness of arrogance, with the detestable elation of a swollen heart. And afterwards the Emperor speaks thus: Because many pairs of letters were found among them, and sealed schedules, still to be written at their pleasure, by which, as (NB.) has hitherto been their custom, they strove to sprinkle the poison of their iniquity through each church of the Teutonic kingdom, to strip the altars, to carry off the vessels of the house of God, to tear down the crosses, we caused them to return to the city by the same way by which they had come, so that they might not be given the opportunity of proceeding further. In his reply to the objections of the Pontiff, the same Frederick, in the same chapter 16, speaks among other things thus: We have neither closed the entry and exit of Italy by edict, nor in any way wish to close it to pilgrims, or to those who, for their necessities, reasonably come to the Roman see with the testimony of their Bishops and Prelates: but we intend to oppose those abuses by which all the churches of our kingdom are burdened and weakened, and almost all the monastic disciplines are dead and buried. In the head of the world God through the Imperium exalted the Church: in the head of the world the Church, not through God, as we believe, now tears down the Empire.

units.la: CXLIX. Eodem Sæculo vitam traduxit Bernhardus, Clarevallensis Abbas, qui mirè passim & magna cum ꝑnoiᵴ Romanæ Curiæ avaritiam perstrinxit. De appellationibus querelam ejus suprà descripsimus. Epistola 42. reprehendens nimiam Prælatorum ambitionem cum avaritia conjunctam, beneficium Ecclesiasticum beneficio copulare conantium, sic inter alia loquitur: Hujus rei gratia non pigritantur crebrò terere limina Apostolorum, inventuri & ibi, quod magis dolendum est, qui suæ faveant improbæ voluntati: non quòd valdè Romani curent, quo fine res terminetur, sed quia valdè diligunt munera, sequuntur retributiones. Unde nuda loquor, nec retego verenda, sed inverecunda confuto. Utinam privatim & in cameris hæc fierent: utinam foli viderimus & audierimus: utinam nec loquentibus crederetur: utinam nobis reliquerint moderni Noæ, unde à nobis possent aliquatenus operiri. Nunc verò cernente orbe mundi fabulam, foli tacebimus? Caput meum undique conquassatum est, & ego sanguine circumquaque ebulliente putaverim esse tegendum? Quicquid apposuero, cruentabitur, & major erit confusio voluisse celare, cum celari nequiverit. Idem Epist. 237. ad Eugenium Papam, reformationis Curiæ Romanæ cupidissimus, sic exclamat: Quis mihi det antequam moriar, videre Ecclesiam Dei, sicut in diebus antiquis, quando Apostoli laxabant retia in capturam, non in capturam auri & argenti, sed in capturam animarum? quàm cupio illius te hæreditare vocem, cujus adeptus es sedem. Pecunia, inquit, tua tecum sit in perditionem. O vox tonitrui, O vox magnificentiæ & virtutis, ad cujus terrorem confundantur & convertantur retrorsum omnes, qui oderunt Sion. Alibi Confid. lib. j. cap. 10. 11. plane Divino Spiritu, & vera libertate religiosa non semel hanc Romanæ avaritiæ pestem pulsat. Si Christi discipulus es, sic Eugenium alloquitur, ignescat Zelus tuus, exurgat authoritas tua adversus impudentiam hanc & generalem pestem. Iuuere magistrum sic facientem. Ergo & tu fac similiter. Erubescant vultum tuum istiusmodi negotiatores, si fieri potest, si non, timeant, & tu flagellum tenes. Timeant nummularii nec fidant in nummis, sed diffidant, abscindant ea tuum à te scientes effundere, quàm accipere parationem. Sugillat potissimùm causidicos & procuratores litium beneficialium anfractus quærentes, ut inde emolumenta capiant, an rapiant, & miseros litigantes exugant, exoptátque, ut Papa remedium adhibeat, & paucas causas judicandas ipse sumat, vel committat, eâsque graviores tantùm, & summariè ac succinctè. Atqui nulla in toto orbe tribunalia sunt, quæ longioribus tricis litigantes infelices involvant, quàm Sacra Romana; unde tota Curia, & ipse Papa lucrum opimum percipit. Officia enim plurima Notariorum, Curiorum & similium officialium prostant. Et quæ multiplicantur officia, hoc pluris à Papa venduntur. Frustrà proin Bernhardus in votis habuit, ut litium anfractus à Papa præcidantur; quarum occasione Curia Papalis auctior locupletiórque evasit. Eodem libro, Pauci, inquit, ad os Legislatoris: ad MANUS omnes respiciunt. Non immeritò tamen omne Papale negotium illæ (manus) agunt. Quale est, quòd de spoliis emuntur Ecclesiarum, qui dicunt tibi: Euge, euge! Pauperum vita in plateis divitum seminatur: Argentum micat in luto, accurritur undique, tollit illud non pauperior, sed fortior, ac qui forte citiùs præcurrit. At te tamen mos iste, vel potius mors ista non venit. Utinam in te desinat! Inter hæc tu Pastor incedis, multo & pretioso circumdatus ornatu. Si auderem dicere, dæmonum magis quàm ovium pascua, hæc scilicet sic faciitabat Petrus, sic Paulus ludebat. Curia tua recipere magis bonos, quàm facere consuevit. Sed & de Consid. lib. ij. 1. causam non conversarum Australium nationum idem in avaritiam Cleri conjicit. Et forsitan, inquit, audivissemus bonos eorum fructus, nisi præ auro Hispaniæ salus populi viluisset. Tuum est, sic ille ad Papam, & plagæ huic remedium providere &c. Quomodo & Ecclesiam Catholicam totam hoc virus infecit? Nam dum & in ipsa quoque quæ nostra sunt, quærimus, sit ut invicem invidentes &c.
units.tr: CXLIX. In the same century Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, departed this life. He rebuked the avarice of the Roman Curia everywhere, remarkably and with great frankness [παρρησία]. We have described his complaint about appeals above. In Epistle 42, rebuking the excessive ambition of prelates joined with avarice, of those who try to join one ecclesiastical benefice to another, he speaks among other things thus: For the sake of this matter they are not slow to wear out the thresholds of the Apostles, finding there (what is more to be lamented) men who favour their wicked will. Not that the Romans care much how the matter is ended, but because they greatly love gifts and pursue rewards. So I speak plainly, and do not uncover what should be covered, but I refute the shameless. Would that these things were done privately and in chambers; would that we alone saw and heard them; would that they were not believed even of those who speak; would that the modern Noahs had left us something by which they might in some measure be covered by us. But now, with the world looking on at the spectacle, shall we alone be silent? My head is shaken on every side, and with blood boiling up all around, should I think it ought to be covered? Whatever I put on it will be stained, and the confusion will be greater for having wished to conceal what could not be concealed. Likewise, in Epistle 237 to Pope Eugenius, the most eager for reform of the Roman Curia, he exclaims thus: Who will give me, before I die, to see the Church of God as in the days of old, when the Apostles let down their nets for a catch, not a catch of gold and silver, but a catch of souls? How I long to make you heir to that voice whose seat you have obtained. Your money, he says, go with you to perdition. O voice of thunder, O voice of majesty and power, at whose terror all who hate Sion are confounded and turned backward. Elsewhere, Consid. book 1, ch. 10, 11, clearly by the Divine Spirit and true religious freedom, he strikes at this pest of Roman avarice more than once. If you are a disciple of Christ, he addresses Eugenius, let your zeal burn, let your authority rise up against this impudence and this general pest.
