They imitated the Master in doing so; so you too do likewise. Let such merchants blush before your face, if it can be; if not, let them fear, and you hold the scourge. Let the money-changers fear, and not trust in their coins, but distrust them, cutting off those things which you know it is better to pour out than to receive. He chiefly lashes the advocates and procurators of benefice suits, who seek out the windings of lawsuits in order to take profits, or rather to plunder, and drain wretched litigants dry. He desires that the Pope apply a remedy, and that he himself take up, or commit, only a few cases to be judged, and only the weightier ones, and these summarily and briefly. Yet there is no tribunal in the whole world that entangles unhappy litigants in longer snares than the Sacred Roman one; from this the whole Curia, and the Pope himself, draws rich profit. For very many offices of notaries, clerks and similar officials are put up for sale, and the more offices are multiplied, the more they are sold for by the Pope. In vain, therefore, did Bernard hope that the windings of lawsuits would be cut off by the Pope; on the occasion of these the Papal Curia grew larger and richer. In the same book, Few, he says, at the mouth of the Lawgiver; all look to the HANDS. Not undeservedly, however, do those hands (manus) carry out all Papal business. What sort of thing is it that they buy from the spoils of the Churches, who say to you: Well done, well done! The life of the poor is sown in the streets of the rich; silver gleams in the mud; everyone runs to it, and it is taken up not by the poorer but by the stronger, or by whoever happens to run faster. But that custom, or rather that death, does not come to you. Would that it might cease in you! Among these things you walk as a Shepherd, surrounded with much precious ornament. If I dared say it, these are the pastures of demons rather than of sheep. Peter was not doing this, Paul was not playing like this. Your Curia has been accustomed to receive the good rather than to make them. But also, from Consid. book 2, ch. 1, he attributes to the avarice of the clergy the failure to convert the Southern nations. And perhaps, he says, we would have heard of good fruits from them, unless the welfare of the people had been cheapened for the sake of Spanish gold. It is yours, he says to the Pope, to provide a remedy for this wound, etc. How has this poison infected the whole Catholic Church too? For while we seek in those things which are ours as well, it comes about that, envying one another, etc.

units.la: CL. Nihil præter rem facturi sumus, si tralatitiam illam objectionem, quòd multa hic ministri Papæ designant, quorum culpam Papa ipse præstare non debeat, ejusdem Bernhardi verbis dissolverimus. Sic autem ille ad Eugenium: Veniamus ad collaterales & coadjutores tuos: hi seduli tibi, hi intimi. Quamobrem si boni sunt, tibi potissimum sunt: Si mali æquè plus tibi. Ne te dixeris sanum, dolentem latera: hoc est, ne te dixeris bonum, malis innitentem. Aut si bonus sis, bonitas tui solius, quem fructum afferre potest? Quid, inquam, emolumenti affert Ecclesiis Dei tua unius hominis justitia, ubi sententia prævalet affectorum aliter? Sed nec tuta tibi bonitas obsessa malis, non magis quàm sanitas vicino serpente: nec est, quo te subducas malo intestino. Et è regione bonum domesticum eò amplius, quò sæpius juvat. Sed sive levent, sive gravent, cui rectius imputandum quàm tibi, qui aut tales elegisti, aut admisisti. Potestatem non habent, nisi quam tu eis aut tribueris, aut permiseris.
units.tr: CL. We shall do nothing beside the point if we dissolve, by the very words of this Bernard, that commonplace objection, that many things done here are done by the ministers of the Pope, whose fault the Pope himself ought not to answer for. He writes thus to Eugenius: Let us come to your collaterals and helpers: these are zealous for you, these are your intimates. Therefore if they are good, they are chiefly yours; if they are bad, they are equally more yours. Do not call yourself healthy while your sides ache; that is, do not call yourself good while leaning on bad men. Or if you are good, what fruit can the goodness of you alone bring? What, I say, profit does your one man's justice bring to the Churches of God, where the sentence of the affected men prevails otherwise? But your goodness is not safe, besieged by evils, any more than health is safe with a serpent nearby; nor is there anywhere to withdraw yourself from the inner evil. And the good at home, the more often it helps, the more it is from the region of... But whether they relieve or burden, to whom is it more rightly imputed than to you, who either chose such men or admitted them? They have no power except what you have given them or permitted.

units.la: CLI. Eodem Seculo Duodecimo Thomas Cantuariensis sic apud Baronium ad A. 1167. de Ecclesia Romana queritur: Ego dolendo dico rem dolendam nimis. Capta est urbs inclyta, quæ jam totum ferè subegerat orbem, sub-
units.tr: CLI. In the same twelfth century Thomas of Canterbury complains thus about the Roman Church, as cited in Baronius at the year 1167: I say with grief a thing too grievous to grieve over. The famous city has been taken, which had already almost subdued the whole world, sub-

units.la: Thomas Cantuariensis, Iohannes Saresberiensis, Petrus Blesensis. subversa humanæ gratiæ cupiditate; & quæ gladio perire non poterat, occidentali veneno infecta succumbit. Prob dolor ipsius occasu fit undique dispendium libertatis Ecclesiæ compendio temporalium. Itur in ipsius ruinam per anfractus divitiarum. Prostituta est (NB) ut fornicaria, quæ multorum libidini patet in platea. Fornicantur cum ea quilibet potentum. Idem apud eundem Baronium ad ᴗA. 1168. nuntium quendam Regis sic loquentem inducit, & probat: Dicit etiam (nuntius) quòd si Dominus Papa decederet, faceret nos deleri de libro vitæ: jactitans Curiam Romanam ita venalem esse, ut intervenientibus muneribus, quicquid velit, impetrare possit. Qui eadem ætate floruit, Johannes Sarisberiensis, eidem Thomæ à Secretis, multa in Epistolis, & Policratico de Romanæ Curiæ avaritia notavit. Romanos, sic Epist. 222. scribit, amicis verba dare, jam nemo miratur, quia percelebre est, & innotuit universis, quòd apud eos, quantum quisque nummorum habet in arca, tantum habet & fidei & plerunque obliquata mente legum & canonum, qui munere potior est, potentior est jure. Si ergò ibi duplicitas reperitur, nihil accidit inopinatum, cùm frequens sit, ut Divina lex dispendium patiatur, ubi dispensandi necessitatem fingit avaritia: Etiam illud Epist. 232. habet: Cardinalium nomen viluit apud Francos, eò quòd Balaamitæ, quatenus licuit inventi sunt, & digni, qui cum suis ᴗMadianitis corruant gladio Mosis. Vivificant enim animas, quæ non vivunt, & ᴗMoabitarum captantes munera, populum Dei maledicto & infamia conantur involvere. Paulò post: De suis moribus alios metientes, nec Deo, nec hominibus habent fidem, ubi dolosi spes refulserit nummi. Voces publicas, quæ de Papa & Romana Ecclesia circumferebantur, eo tempore, fideliter idem Sarisberiensis, in Policratico seu de Nugis Curialium editis libris, lib. vj. 24. his verbis describit: Romana Ecclesia, quæ mater omnium Ecclesiarum est, se non tam matrem aliis exhibet, quàm novercam. Sedent in ea Scribæ & Pharisæi, portantes onera importabilia in humeris hominum, quæ digitis non contingunt. Dominantur in Clero nec forma fiunt gregi, qui recto calle pergit ad vitam; pretiosam suppellectilem congerunt, auro & argento onerant mensas, sibi etiam ab avaritia nimis parci. Nam pauper aut nullus, aut rarus admittitur, quem interdum non tam Christus, quàm vana gloria introducit. Concutiunt Ecclesias, lites excitant, collidunt clerum & populum, laboribus & miseriis afflictorum nequaquam compatiuntur. Justitiam non tam veritati, quàm pretio reddunt: omnia nàmque cum pretio hodiè, sed nec cras aliquid sine pretio obtinebis, &c. Sed & ipse Romanus Pontifex omnibus gravis &ferè intolerabilis est. Præterea omnes arguuntur, quòd ruentibus & collabentibus Ecclesiis, quas Patrum constuxit devotio, altaribus quoque incultis palatia exstruit, & ipse non modò purpuratus, sed deauratus incedit. Palatia splendent Sacerdotum, & in manibus eorum Christi sordidatur Ecclesia. Provinciarum diripiunt spolia, ac si thesauros Cræsi studeant reparare, &c. Paulò post Papam sic alloquitur: Omnes applaudunt tibi, Pater omnium vocaris & Dominus: & capiti tuo infunditur omne oleum peccatoris. Si ergò Pater es, quare à filiis munera & retributiones exspectas? Si Dominus, quare Romanis tuis timorem non incutis, & temeritate repressa, eos ad fidem non revocas? At urbem vis Ecclesiæ tuis muneribus conservare. Numquid eam sic Silvester muneribus acquisivit? In invio Pater es, & non in via. Eisdem est conservanda muneribus, quibus est acquisita. Quod gratis accepistis, gratis date. Justitia Regina virtutum est, & erubescit quovis pretio permutari. Si gratiosa futura est, Tom. II. ssss sit gratuita, nequaquam prostituatur ad pretium, quæ corrumpi non potest. Integra est, & semper incorrupta. Dum premis alios, & tu graviùs opprimeris. Quid ad hæc Hadrianus Pontifex? Risit, & apologo illo, quo apud Livium lib. ij. usus est Menenius Agrippa, ventris comedentis in otio, & aliorum membrorum laborantium, objecta elusit. Tale est, inquit, frater, si rectè attendas in corpore Reipublicæ, ubi licet plurimum appetat Magistratus, non tam sibi, quàm aliis coacervet. Si enim exinanitus fuerit, nihil est quod membris valeat impartiri. Nam stomachi in corpore & Principis in Republica idem officium est. Egregiè sanè, O Archislamen Babylonie! Quid verò Reipublicæ seculari cum bonis Ecclesiæ? Ea, quæ emungitis, bona sunt Christi Ministrorum, Ecclesiarum Sanctarum & Christi pauperum, neque ad temporalem Rempublicam sustentandam converti possunt. Si Princeps es secularis, habes principatûs tui emolumenta ordinaria, vectigalia, taxas, siscum &c. Bonis verò Ecclesiasticis ne temporalia tua tegito, sed in Ecclesiasticos ea usus converti cura. Et quid si venter tam magnus extendatur, & se tantoperè ingurgitet, ut saginato abundè proprio corpore tantum acceperit, quantum centum aut mille alia corpora ali possent, & tamen ex hac nimia unius repletione illa plura proprio priventur alimento? Annon venter hic dignus erit, qui disrumpatur, atque projectus in ignem, in cinerem redigatur, si cibo sibi & suo corpori soli sufficienti & adæquato acquiscere gravetur? Optimè enim Gerson de Pot. Eccl. cap. 12. dicit, Summum Pontificem cum Collegio suo ita præsidere bonis Ecclesiasticis, ut de eis satum habere sufficientem & decentem oporteat. Sed non ita, ut caput gravidum reliqua membra obruat mole sua, neque velit usurpare contra naturam singularis membri omnia officia membrorum. Extenuantur profectò EcEcclesiæ omnes, & ad solitudinem rediguntur, ministri earum & pauperes fame pereunt, ut Papa modò cum suis Curialibus abundet, omne genus deliciis affluat, & in mundo latissimè dominetur. Non possum quin ejusdem Sarisberiensis verba, quibus amplius ille avaritiam & technas Caussidicorum Romanensium depingit, ex Policrat. lib. v. cap. 10. adducam. Qui corruptior, inquit, moribus, & corrumpentior muneribus, apud ipsos beatior est. Si Principum manus evaseris, grandis tibi restat via, arcta & ardua, antequam tortores extremos fugias, fudandum est tibi: Ecce instrumenta tua conficit Cassus, si eum salutare licuerit, pro magno reputa: Si Schedulam non attuleris, frustrà accedes: Si autem attuleris, inutilis est, nec acquiescet, ut manus nobili vitio membranæ degeneret.
units.tr: Thomas of Canterbury, John of Salisbury, Peter of Blois. Her faith in human grace having been overthrown, and she who could not perish by the sword succumbs, infected with Western poison. Indeed, by her fall there is everywhere a loss of the Church's liberty, for the sake of temporal gain. Men press on to her ruin through the winding paths of riches. She has been prostituted (NB) like a harlot, who lies open to the lust of many in the public square. Every one of the powerful fornicates with her. In the same Baronius, under the year 1168, he introduces and proves the words of a certain messenger of the King: The messenger also says that if the Lord Pope were to die, he would have us blotted out of the book of life, boasting that the Roman Curia is so venal that, with gifts intervening, it can obtain whatever it wishes. John of Salisbury, who flourished in the same age and was secretary to the same Thomas, noted much about the avarice of the Roman Curia in his Letters and in the Policraticus. Nobody is now surprised, he writes in Letter 222, that the Romans deceive their friends with words, because it is very well known and has become common knowledge that among them each man has as much faith and as much (his mind often twisted from the laws and canons) as he has coins in his chest; and he who is more powerful in gifts is more powerful in right. If therefore duplicity is found there, nothing has happened unexpectedly, since it is frequent that Divine law suffers loss where avarice feigns the need for dispensation. He also has this in Letter 232: The name of the Cardinals has become cheap among the Franks, because they have been found, so far as it was permitted, to be Balaamites, and worthy to fall with their Midianites by the sword of Moses. For they make alive souls that are not alive, and, seeking the gifts of the Moabites, they try to entangle the people of God in curse and infamy. A little later: Measuring others by their own morals, they have faith neither in God nor in men, where the hope of deceitful money has shone forth. The public rumours that were spread at that time about the Pope and the Roman Church, the same Salisbury describes faithfully in the books of the Policraticus, or On the Trifles of Courtiers, Book 6, chapter 24, in these words: The Roman Church, which is the mother of all churches, shows herself less a mother to others than a stepmother. Scribes and Pharisees sit in her, carrying burdens unbearable on the shoulders of men, which they do not touch with their fingers. They lord it over the clergy and are not made a pattern to the flock, which walks by the straight path to life. They heap up costly furniture, load their tables with gold and silver, and are themselves too sparing with avarice. For a poor man is admitted either not at all or rarely, and sometimes he is introduced not so much by Christ as by vainglory. They shake the churches, stir up quarrels, crush clergy and people, and feel no compassion for the labours and miseries of the afflicted. They render justice not so much for truth as for a price; for nowadays everything is obtained for a price, and you will get nothing tomorrow without a price, etc. But the Roman Pontiff himself is burdensome and almost intolerable to all. Moreover, all are accused that, while the churches fall and collapse which the devotion of the Fathers built, he builds palaces, and the altars lie neglected; and he himself walks about not only purple-clad but gilded. The palaces of the priests shine, and in their hands the Church of Christ is defiled. They tear away the spoils of the provinces, as if they were eager to restore the treasures of Croesus, etc. A little later he addresses the Pope thus: All applaud you; you are called Father and Lord of all; and all the oil of the sinner is poured upon your head. If then you are a Father, why do you expect gifts and rewards from your sons? If you are a Lord, why do you not strike fear into your Romans, and, having curbed their rashness, call them back to faith? But you wish to preserve the city of the Church by your gifts. Did Sylvester acquire it thus by gifts? You are a Father in the unseen, and not in the way. It must be preserved by the same gifts by which it was acquired. What you have received freely, give freely. Justice is the queen of virtues, and she blushes to be exchanged for any price. If she is going to be bought with favour, let her be free; let her not be prostituted for a price, she who cannot be corrupted. She is whole and always incorrupt. While you oppress others, you yourself are oppressed more heavily. What did Pope Hadrian say to these things? He laughed, and he met the complaints with that fable by which Menenius Agrippa, in Livy, Book 2, had the belly, eating in idleness, and the other limbs labouring. It is like this, brother, he said, if you rightly consider the body of the Commonwealth, where, although the magistrate seems to heap up a great deal, he heaps it not so much for himself as for others. For if he is emptied, there is nothing he can impart to the limbs. For the stomach in the body and the Prince in the Commonwealth have the same office. Splendidly indeed, O Archislamen of Babylon! But what has the secular commonwealth to do with the goods of the Church? Those things you are squeezing out are the goods of Christ's ministers, of holy churches and of Christ's poor, and they cannot be turned to sustaining the temporal commonwealth. If you are a secular prince, you have the ordinary emoluments of your principality: tolls, taxes, the treasury, etc. But do not cover your temporal affairs with the goods of the Church; rather take care that those goods be turned to the use of ecclesiastics. And what if a belly is stretched so great, and gorges itself so much, that, having sufficiently fed its own body, it has taken as much as a hundred or a thousand other bodies could be fed with, and yet by this excessive filling of one, the many others are deprived of their proper nourishment? Will not this belly deserve to be burst, and, cast into the fire, be reduced to ash, if it is burdened with being content with food sufficient and adequate for itself and its own body alone? For Gerson, On the Power of the Church, chapter 12, rightly says: The supreme Pontiff with his College ought so to preside over the ecclesiastical goods that he has a sufficient and decent provision from them. But not so that the head, heavy with its weight, crushes the other members, nor wishes to usurp against nature all the offices of the single member. Indeed all the Churches are emaciated and reduced to desolation, their ministers and poor perish of hunger, so that the Pope alone, with his Curials, may abound, flow with every kind of delight, and rule most widely in the world. I cannot refrain from adducing, from Policraticus, Book 5, chapter 10, the words of the same Salisbury, with which he more fully depicts the avarice and the tricks of the Roman advocates. The one more corrupt in morals, he says, and more corruptible by gifts, is the happier among them. If you have escaped the hands of the Princes, a great, narrow and steep road still remains for you, and you must sweat before you flee the last tormentors. Behold, Cassus makes out your papers; count it great if it is allowed you to greet him. If you have not brought a schedule, you will approach in vain; but if you have brought one, it is useless, and he will not give way, so that his hand may be degraded by the noble vice of parchment.

units.la: Quid multa? Suam necesse est comparari, cum nec opera nec calamus, aut sepiolæ, aut nigræ loliginis succus tibi conflet inemtus. Sed & ipsas syllabas & apices, nisi eum tibi propitium feceris, sic distorquebit, tot tibi verborum ponet tendiculas, ut pro pace bellum, pro quiete litigium amici instrumento videatur inscribere. Si cingulum forte tibi venustius fererit, si inciforium aptius, si quid in minuta suppellectile decentius, rebus ejus connumera, nisi tibi perire velis operam & impensam. Aut enim pretibus extorquebitur, aut eas liberalitate prævenies. Tandem pileum qualecunque sit, asportabit amicus in memoriam tui.
units.tr: What more? It is necessary to buy his favour, since neither work nor pen, nor cuttlefish ink, nor the juice of black squid, will be brought together for you without cost. But he will twist even the syllables and the accents for you, unless you have made him favourable to you; he will set so many snares of words for you that he seems to write war for peace and litigation for the quiet of a friend. If by chance a more elegant belt suits you, or a more fitting knife, or anything more becoming among your small furniture, number it among his things, unless you wish to lose your labour and expense. For either it will be extorted by prayers, or you will forestall them by generosity. In the end, whatever kind of cap it is, your friend will carry it away as a memento of you.

units.la: Jam à Cosso digredieris. Sed tibi ignis purgatorius imminet, superest vejemo, quem multâ solicitabis instantiâ, & magno artificio, gestu, precum & munerum, ut te clauso labello respiciat. Tunc de singulis verbis in Concilium itur, deliberationi præscibit tempus, & apices singuli ponuntur in flatera. Nisi eum præmulseris occurret tibi non fideliter rei gestæ concepta series, aut stylus oberit, aut à publica forma Notarii vel scriniarii divertens benignitas, aut negligentia juris aut aliquis semper nodus pecunia vindice indigebit. Ut verò minimum lœdat, longa expectatione torqueberis, dum differtur, quod negari non potest. Experto crede. In manus eorum millies incidi. Fuit nempe Episcopus, cujus negotia fuerunt Ecclesiastica, & in Curia Romana sæpius tractata. Pergit deinceps in eodem avaritiæ argumento, eámque pluribus excogitans, sic inter alia loquitur: Quid est, quòd apud Curiales omnia queror esse venalia, cùm ea etiam, quæ non sunt, rerum scilicet privationes, venalitio constet esse obnoxias? Non opus, non sermo gratuitus est: non tacetur nisi ad pretium. Silentium, namque res venalis est &c. Hoc autem à maximu pertransit ad minimos, qui mulcentur obsequiis, & refociantur muneribus sibi fieri injuriam suspicantur &c. Inclementiam Cerberi omnes abhorrent. Ego me credo vidisse Cerberos ostiario duriores. Apud inferos tamen Cerberus unus est. Quot sunt diverticula curialium, tot cerberi sunt. Atrienses quoque cerberos sustinebus, totámque familiam, quæ semper aut mordet, aut latrat, &c. Alibi lib. viij. 17. ironicè sic scribit: Quis ergo credat, quòd Patres Ecclesiæ judices orbis, & ut ita dicam, clarissima lumina mundi, diligant munera, sequantur retributiones, Provincias concutiant, ut executiant loculos, exinanient alienos, ut solident suos, verbis prædicent pauperta-tem, & criminibus ad divitias properent, bonorum spiritualium damnent commercia, ut cum eis duntaxat intalibus contrahere liceat, id agentes, ut omnibus sint terrori, amentur à nullo &c. Denique & Petrus Blesensis, ejusdem temporis scriptor passim in Epistolis suis Romanensium avaritiam diris proscindit. Illud noveritis, sic Epist. 39. scribit, quia Romana Curia me more suo multipliciter debitis obligavit, sed si semel evasero per Dei gratiam, non recidam in charybdim. Et Epist. 42. Nuntii vestri (Re(Regis Angliæ) inquit, à Romana Curia redierunt exonerati quidem argento, onerati plumbo, non multùm indumentis aut vectionibus honorati.
units.tr: Now you will depart from Cassus. But purgatory fire hangs over you; there remains the doorkeeper, whom you will entreat with much insistence and great skill, by gesture, prayers and gifts, so that he may look upon you with closed lips. Then the matter goes before the Council, time is prescribed for deliberation, and each word is placed in the scales. Unless you have first softened him up, the sequence of the business as you have conceived it will not meet you faithfully; either the style will hinder you, or the kindness that turns aside from the public form of the notary or the clerk, or the negligence of the law, or some knot will always need the avenger money. And so that he may do you the least harm, you will be tormented by long waiting, while what cannot be denied is put off. Trust one who has experienced it; I fell into their hands a thousand times. He was, to be sure, a Bishop, whose business was ecclesiastical and was often handled in the Roman Curia. He goes on in the same argument of avarice, thinking it out at greater length, and among other things he speaks thus: Why is it that I complain that everything is venal among the Curials, since even those things which are not, namely privations of things, are known to be liable to sale? Nothing is done gratuitously, no word is free: silence is not kept except for a price. For silence is a venal thing, etc. But this passes from the greatest to the least, who are soothed by services and refreshed by gifts, and who suspect that an injury is done them, etc. All abhor the cruelty of Cerberus. I think I have seen Cerberuses harsher than the doorkeeper. Yet in Hell there is only one Cerberus. As many as are the lodgings of the Curials, so many Cerberuses there are. You also endure Cerberuses in the halls, and the whole household, which always either bites or barks, etc. Elsewhere, Book 8, chapter 17, he writes ironically thus: Who then would believe that the Fathers of the Church, the judges of the world, and, so to speak, the most brilliant lights of the world, love gifts, pursue rewards, shake the provinces that they may empty purses, strip others that they may fill their own, preach poverty in words and hasten to riches by crimes, condemn the traffic in spiritual goods so that it may be lawful to deal with them only in such things, taking care that they be a terror to all and loved by none, etc.? Finally, Peter of Blois, a writer of the same time, everywhere in his Letters tears to pieces with dire words the avarice of the Romans. Know this, he writes in Letter 39, that the Roman Curia, in its usual way, has bound me by many debts; but if by God's grace I once escape, I will not fall back into Charybdis. And Letter 42: Your messengers (of the King of England), he says, have returned from the Roman Curia, indeed loaded down with silver, burdened with lead, and not much honoured with garments or conveyances.

units.la: CLII. Seculo Decimo-Tertio duo primùm Reges testimonium deponent. Prior est Richardus Angliæ Rex, qui in orientem ad sacrum bellum profecturus, Elienfem Episcopum ad Regni sui custodiam reliquit, Apostolicae legatione firmare laboravit, idque Romæ obtinuit, sed non sine pretio. Audi Regem ipsum apud Rogerium in Annal. 1290. Cardinali Oftienfi id, aliásque avaritiæ turpitudines exprobrantem: Quòd septingentas marcas debuerint habere pro consecratione Episcopi Cenomanensis, & mille ac quingentas marcas pro legatione Elienfis Episcopi, & pecuniam magnam, ne deponeretur Burdegalensis, qui à Clericis suis accusabatur in crimine. Posterior, Alphonsus Aragoniæ Rex est, quem de Harpyis ex insulis in Romanam Curiam digressis suprà lamentantem vidimus.. Id J Cti, Panormitanus lib. de dictis & factis Alphonsi, & Gomesius in Præf. regul. de valore benefic. tanquam scitum quoddam apophtegma laudant. De advocatis tamen Curiæ Romanæ Alphonsum locutum esse, Sciopius regerit, quasi non catulæ dominas imitari soleant. Et tamen Alphonsus de Romana Curia universa aperte locutus est.
units.tr: CLII. In the thirteenth century, two kings first gave testimony. The first was Richard, King of England. About to set out for the holy war in the East, he left the Bishop of Ely to guard his kingdom and worked to secure this through an apostolic legation. He obtained it at Rome, but not without payment. Hear the king himself, as Roger reports in his Annals for 1290, rebuking the Cardinal of Ostia for this and other shameful acts of greed: "They ought to have had seven hundred marks for the consecration of the Bishop of Le Mans, and fifteen hundred marks for the legation of the Bishop of Ely, and a large sum of money so that the Bishop of Bordeaux would not be deposed, who was accused of a crime by his own clergy." The second was Alphonsus, King of Aragon, whom we saw above lamenting the Harpies that had flown from the islands into the Roman Curia. Panormitanus, in his book on the sayings and deeds of Alphonsus, and Gomesius, in the preface to his rules on the value of benefices, praise this as a witty saying. Sciopius objects that Alphonsus was speaking of the advocates of the Roman Curia, as if lapdogs did not usually imitate their masters. Yet Alphonsus plainly spoke about the whole Roman Curia.

units.la: CLIII. Neque eadem ætate Ecclesiasticorum etiam nullæ querelæ 'auditæ sunt. Etenim Stephanus Episcopus Tornacensis adhuc Abbas in Monasterio S. Genevæ, instaurationem Ecclesiæ illius molitus, Romanam Ecclesiam Epist. 165. haud obscurè sic pungit: Parietes reficere incepimus, comparata jam lignorum macerie, quæ & superpotnatur innovatis parietibus, & tecto plumbeo supponatur. Sub quodam mendicantes rogamus & petimus, ut aliquid de benevola & benefica liberalitate vestra mittatis nobis, quo plumbum emamus, non Romanum, sed Anglicum: quo- niam Anglico plumbo teguntur Ecclesiæ, nudantur Romano. Guilhelmus Durandus, Episcopus Mimatensis, eodem tempore de modo celebrandi Concilii generalis tractatum scripsit, Parisiis A. 1545. excusum. Ibi Parte .v. tit. 26. agnoscit, hæresin Simoniæ maximè corrumpere Ecclesiam universalem, & universos populos. Et provisa remedia jam pro nihilo reputari. Et cùm in Curia Romana publicè contrarium fiat, ac si non esset peccatum committere Simoniam, vel si dare & accipere post, non esset sicut dare & accipere ante. Ex quo provenit, sicut Gregorius Francorum Regibus scribit, quòd fides deperit. Eam Simoniam dixerat paulò ante maximè exerceri in Curia Romana, in qua cœtus D. Cardinalium vult habere unà cum Domino Papa, certam portionem à Prælatis, qui promoventur ibidem. Infrà tit. 41. conqueritur, quòd Romana Ecclesia causas electionum multis viis & remediis ad se trahit, & Ecclesiæ remanent longis temporibus viduatæ &c. propter appellationes inanes & frivolas deductas ad Romanam Curiam, ubi lites efficiuntur quodammodo immortales. Probus Tullensis Episcopus, qui A. 1280. vixit & floruit, Aventino Annal. lib. vj. recitante, his acerrimis verbis Avaritiam, aliáque Romanæ Curiæ scelera perstringit: Quousque Collegæ charissimi, Romulei illi vulturei patientia, ne dicam stultitia nostra abutentur? quousque eorum flagitia, avaritiam, superbiam, luxum, tolerabimus? Non cessabit hoc genus Archisÿnagon pessimum, nisi omnes ad egestatem & servitutem durissimam redegerit. Discordiâ nostrâ hoccè malum crevit, discordiâ nostrâ nebulones illi tuti sunt. Denique Everhardus Salisburgensis Episcopus, eodem Aventino, eodémque libro referente, sic coram Imperii Panegyri de Romanorum avaritia oravit. Flamines illi Babylonii foli regnare cupiunt, parem ferre non possunt: non desistent, donec omnia pedibus suis conculcárint, atque in Templo Dei sedeant, extollantúr que supra omne id quod colitur. FAMES OPUM, sitis bonorum INEXPLEBILIS est. Quò plura avido concesserit, eò plura appetit.
units.tr: CLIII. Nor in the same age were complaints from churchmen lacking. Stephen, Bishop of Tournai, then still abbot of the monastery of St Geneviève, undertook the restoration of that church, and in Epist. 165 he stings the Roman Church quite openly: "We have begun to rebuild the walls; the timber is now bought, to be placed over the renewed walls and under a lead roof. We beg and ask you, as beggars, to send us something from your kindly and generous liberality," so that we may buy lead, not Roman but English, "since the churches are roofed with English lead and stripped of Roman." William Durand, Bishop of Mende, wrote at the same time a treatise on how a general council should be held, printed at Paris in 1545. There, Part 5, title 26, he acknowledges "that the heresy of simony above all corrupts the universal Church and all peoples. And the remedies provided are now regarded as nothing. And since in the Roman Curia the contrary is done openly, as if it were not a sin to commit simony, or as if giving and receiving afterwards were not the same as giving and receiving beforehand. From this arises, as Gregory writes to the kings of the Franks, that faith perishes." He had said shortly before that simony is practised especially "in the Roman Curia, in which the college of the lord cardinals wishes to have, together with the lord Pope, a certain share from the prelates who are promoted there." Further on, title 41, he complains "that the Roman Church draws the causes of elections to itself by many ways and means, and churches remain widowed for long periods... because of empty and frivolous appeals brought to the Roman Curia, where lawsuits become in a way immortal." Probus, Bishop of Toul, who lived and flourished in 1280, as Aventinus recites in Annals, book 6, attacks avarice and the other crimes of the Roman Curia in these very bitter words: "How long, dearest colleagues, will those Romulean vultures abuse our patience, not to say our folly? How long shall we tolerate their shameful acts, their avarice, pride and luxury? This most wicked kind of archisynagogue [ἀρχισυνάγωγος] will not cease until it has reduced everyone to poverty and the harshest slavery. This evil has grown through our discord; through our discord those scoundrels are safe." Finally, Everhard, Bishop of Salzburg, as Aventinus reports in the same book, spoke thus before the Imperial assembly about the avarice of the Romans: "Those Babylonian flamens want to reign alone and cannot bear an equal. They will not stop until they have trampled everything under their feet, and sit in the temple of God, and raise themselves above everything that is worshipped. The hunger for wealth, the thirst for goods, is insatiable. The more is granted to the greedy man, the more he craves."

units.la: CLIV. Ad Seculum Decimum-quartum festinantes, principem ea ætate testem citamus Gloriosissimum Imperatorem, Ludovicum Bavarum, qui in Edicto Imperiali sic inter alia pronuntiavit: Jam egregii illi Pastores opibus & splendore à majoribus nostris auƈti, pacem ferre nequeunt, Cæsarem Italiá, Romá, Christum terris extrusêre, illi Cœlum quidem permittunt, inferos atque terras sibi asseruère. Aviditate potentiæ, PECUNIÆ ima summus misçet, OMNIA VENALIA, DEUM ET INFEROS habet &c. In alio Edicto sic idem queritur. Homines sceleratissimi, crudelissimis manibus, IMMANI AVARITIA, nocentissimi, & iidem superbissimi, itidem luxu effœminati, atque ambitione perditi, quibus fides, decus, pietas, postremò vitia, virtutes, HONESTA ATQUE INHONESTA OMNIA QUÆSTUI sunt, arcem Reipublicæ Christianæ occupant, tumultum ex tumultu, bellum ex bello ferunt. Caput factionis, Jacobus ille de Baburca, qui se Papam Johannem XXII. nominat, ingentem vim pecuniæ, quam undique à Christiana plebe fraudulenter corrasit, adversus Sanctos Dei, Imperio Christiano devotos expendit. Ab hoste Pontificis, ob confirmationem sibi denegatam, profecta hæc testimonia Scipius caussatur. Scilicet hostes Papæ, adeóque intestabiles omnes sunt, qui eum non adorant. Sed si vel maximè Papa ille Ludovico Imperium, quod unanimi Principum Germaniæ suffragio obtinuit, neque Papali ulla confirmatione indiguit, confirmásseт, an hic propterea pro sua magnanimitate illa, quæ tum temporis jam lippis & tonsoribus bus nota erant, Romanæ Ecclesiæ ulcera atque σκύβαλα reticuissLet?
units.tr: CLIV. Hastening to the fourteenth century, we cite as witness a prince of that age, the most glorious Emperor Louis of Bavaria, who in an Imperial edict pronounced among other things: "Those distinguished shepherds, now enlarged by the wealth and splendour that our forefathers gave them, cannot bear peace. They have driven Caesar out of Italy and Rome, and Christ out of the lands. They allow heaven to others, but claim hell and earth for themselves. Through the desire for power and the basest greed for money, ALL THINGS ARE FOR SALE; THEY HAVE GOD AND HELL" etc. In another edict the same man complains thus: "The most wicked men, with the cruellest hands, with monstrous greed, most harmful and at the same time most proud, likewise made effeminate by luxury and ruined by ambition, for whom faith, honour, piety, and in short vices and virtues, honourable and dishonourable alike, are all matters of profit, occupy the citadel of the Christian commonwealth, bringing tumult upon tumult and war upon war. The head of the faction, that Jacques of Cahors who calls himself Pope John XXII, spends the huge sum of money which he has fraudulently scraped together from the Christian common people on all sides, against the saints of God who are devoted to the Christian Empire." Scioppius complains that these testimonies came from an enemy of the Pope, because the Pope had denied him confirmation. Of course, all enemies of the Pope, and therefore all who do not adore him, are unreliable. But if that Pope had confirmed Louis's Empire, which he had obtained by the unanimous vote of the princes of Germany and which needed no papal confirmation, would he, out of that magnanimity, have kept silent about the ulcers and dregs [σκύβαλα] of the Roman Church, which at that time were already known even to bleary-eyed men and barbers?

units.la: CLV. Memoratu digna cumprimis sunt, quæ Alvarus Pelagius, Sylvensis in Portugallia Episcopus, ejusdem Seculi Scriptor eximius, libro de Planctu Ecclesiæ, de Romanensi Avaritia & Simonia posteritati reliquit. Inter alia lib. ÿ. art. 15. Nepotismum vivis coloribus depingit iis verbis, quæ Hist. Pap. ff. cclxxÿ. fusius repræsentavimus. Idem lib. j. art. 67. inter alia multa, sic Ecclesiæ Romanæ avaritiam perstringit: In bonis temporalibus dilatata, spiritu minorata, & in terrenis voluit dilatari, non contenta terminis suis etiam temporalibus legitimis, quos habebat, sed etiam insuper invasit terminos alienos. O sponsa mea, quis te excæcavit, ut nuditatem meam non aspiceres! & eam nuditate tua non cooperires? Verè pulvis terræ te occœcavit, humor crassus telluris pupillam oculi tui obtenebravit. Auro, & argento & gemmis, & diversis coloribus me cooperuisti, sed decepta fuisti, & illaqueavit te Synagoga aurea, cui successisti authoritate: quæ templum suum & templi vasa deaurabat, & aurum quærebat, & possessionem in terra, sed carnalis erat, & cæca & rudis, & prona idololatrare, & carnalibus sacrificiis dedita, ne flueret. Quàm longè jam diu viæ tuæ à viis meis fuerunt! In ligno, & à ligno regnavi, meum Imperium dilatavi. Et tu sæmitus contrariis laboribus meos cassâsti, possessione me filiorum tuorum & meorum pro majori parte privâsti, & fidem meam & tuam quasi ad nihilum reduxisti, & in fabulam ac derisum eam apud exteros conduxisti, & apud laicos propter malum exindè datum, scandalum posuisti, dicentes: Ubi est Deus clericorum sic viventium?
units.tr: CLV. Especially worth recording are the things Alvarus Pelagius, Bishop of Silves in Portugal, an outstanding writer of the same century, left to posterity in his book On the Lament of the Church, concerning Roman avarice and simony. Among other things, in book 5, art. 15, he portrays nepotism in vivid colours, in words which we have presented at greater length in Hist. Pap. ff. cclxxÿ. The same author, in book 1, art. 67, among many other things, censures the avarice of the Roman Church in this way: "Extended in temporal goods, diminished in spirit, she wished to spread into earthly things, not content with her own lawful temporal boundaries, but also invading the boundaries of others. O my bride, who has blinded you, so that you did not see my nakedness and did not cover it with your own? Truly the dust of the earth has blinded you, and thick moisture of the soil has darkened the pupil of your eye. You covered me with gold, silver, gems and various colours, but you were deceived, and the golden synagogue has ensnared you, to whose authority you succeeded. It gilded its temple and the vessels of the temple, and sought gold and possessions on earth; but it was carnal, blind and crude, prone to idolatry, and given over to carnal sacrifices, so that it might not slip away. How long have your ways been far from my ways! I reigned by and from the wood, and I enlarged my empire. But you, by contrary labours, have wasted my labours, deprived me of possession of my sons and yours for the greater part, and have reduced my faith and yours almost to nothing; you have made it a fable and a laughing-stock among outsiders, and you have set a stumbling-block before the laity because of the evil given by it, saying: 'Where is the God of clerics who live like this?'"

units.la: CLVI. Addam ex eodem Seculo quatuor verè inclyta nomina, Francifcum Petrarcham, Marsilium Paravinum Albericum Roxiatum, & Johannem Vitoduranum. Petrarcha passim in Epistolis sine titulo libera candidáque de Synagoga potiùs Babylonica, quàm Ecclesia Romana judicia profert, quæ alibi differtiora referam. Satis hic erit, quæ inter alia calamitates urbis Romæ deplorans Epist. 15. profert, verba exhibuisse. Vides, inquit, populum non modò Christi adversarium, sed quod est gravius, sub Christi vexillo, Christo rebellantem, militantem Sathanæ, & Christi sanguine tumidum atque lascivientem populum, cui non modò proprie convenire dixeris Evangelicum illud atque Propheticum: Populus hic me labiis honorat, cor autem eorum longè est à me: Sed illud etiam Judæ Iscariotis, qui Dominum suum prodens & exosculans ajebat, Ave Rabbi: & Judæorum, qui indutum purpurâ, coronatum spinis, percutientes & conspuentes illusione amarissima, flexis poplitibus adorabant & salutabant: Ave Rex Judæorum. Quid enim? quid, oro, aliud assiduè geritur hos inter Christi hostes, & nostri temporis Pharisæos? Nonne etenim Christum ipsum, cujus nomen die ac nocte altissimis laudibus attollunt, quem purpurâ atque auro vestiunt, quem salutant & adorant, eundem in terra EMUNT, VENDUNT, NUNDINANTUR eundem, quasi velatis oculis non visurum, & impiarum opum vepribus coronant, & impurissimi oris sputis conquinant, & vipereis sibilis insectantur, & venenatorum ictuum cuspide feriunt, & quantum in eis est, illusum, nudum, inopem, flagellatum, iterum atque iterum in Calvariam trahunt, ac nefariis assensibus cruci rursus affigunt. Et O pudor! O dolor! O indignitas! Talium hodie Roma est. Alibi sic Hierarchicorum Simoniam describit: Auro tristis Janitor mollitur, Auro Cœlum panditur, quid multis? AURO CHRISTUS VENDITUR. Jam & Marsilius Patavinus in Defensore Pacis cap. 24. Romanam Curiam Domum negotiationis aperte insignit, subjiciens: Quid aliud Romæ, quàm Simoniacorum undique concursus? Præmiserat hæc verba: Quoniam Simonia, quamvis post factum expleatur, amplissima est, quod eadem potestate reddituss & proventus beneficiorum omnium, & ubique, quo primum anno vacantia fuerint, sibi reservat, secundum hunc modum sibi congregans omnes mundi thesauros, & eisdem omnia Regna spolians, atque Provincias, in quibus distribui debent ministris Euangelicis, & personis miserabilibus, aut in Reipublicæ, de qua sumuntur subsidium oportet converti, quoniam ad hoc statuta & ordinata fuerunt. Albericus quoque Roxiatus JCtus celebris, qui A. MCCCXL. claruit, in Dictionario Juris Civilis & Canonici, verbo Roma, hos ætate sua tritos versus memorat:
units.tr: CLVI. I will add from the same century four truly illustrious names: Francis Petrarch, Marsilius of Padua, Alberic of Rosate, and John of Winterthur. Petrarch, throughout his letters without a title, offers free and candid judgments of the Babylonian synagogue rather than of the Roman Church, which I shall report more fully elsewhere. It will be enough here to give the words he sets out, lamenting among other calamities of the city of Rome, in Epist. 15: "You see," he says, "a people not only hostile to Christ but, what is worse, rebelling against Christ under Christ's own banner, a people serving Satan, swollen and wanton with the blood of Christ, of whom you may say not only that Gospel and prophetic saying, 'This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me,' but also that of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed and kissed his Lord, saying, 'Hail, Rabbi'; and of the Jews who, clothing him in purple, crowning him with thorns, striking and spitting on him in most bitter mockery, bent their knees and adored and saluted him, 'Hail, King of the Jews.' For what, I ask, else is constantly done among these enemies of Christ and the Pharisees of our time? Do they not indeed buy, sell and trade in Christ himself, whose name they extol day and night with the highest praises, whom they clothe in purple and gold, whom they greet and adore, and whom they crown with the thorns of impious riches, defile with the spittle of most impure mouths, pursue with viperous hisses, and strike with the point of poisoned blows; and, as far as in them lies, they drag him again and again, mocked, naked, poor and scourged, to Calvary, and nail him again to the cross with wicked assent? And O shame! O grief! O indignity! Such is Rome today."* Elsewhere he describes the simony of the hierarchs thus: "By gold the sad doorkeeper is softened; by gold heaven is opened. Why say more? By gold Christ is sold." Marsilius of Padua too, in Defensor Pacis ch. 24, plainly marks the Roman Curia as a house of trade, adding: "What else is Rome than a gathering of simoniacs from every side?" He had prefaced these words with: "Since simony, although it is completed after the deed, is very great, because by the same power he reserves to himself the revenues of all benefices, everywhere, in the first year in which they fall vacant, thus gathering to himself all the treasures of the world, and despoiling all kingdoms and provinces, from which they ought to be distributed to evangelical ministers and wretched persons, or turned to the aid of the commonwealth from which they are taken, since they were established and ordained for this." Alberic of Rosate, a celebrated jurist who flourished in 1340, in his Dictionary of Civil and Canon Law, under the word Roma, records these verses, worn common in his own time:

units.la: Curia Romana non quærit ovem sine lana.
units.tr: The Roman Curia does not seek a sheep without its wool.
And

units.la: Roma manus rodit, non dantes spernit & odit.
units.tr: Rome gnaws at the hand; it scorns and hates those who do not give.
Likewise:

units.la: Si caput à capio, vel dixeris à capiendo
units.tr: If caput is derived from capio, or you say it comes from capiendo (taking),

units.la: Tunc est ipsa Caput: omnia namque capit.
units.tr: then it is itself the head, for it takes everything.
If by declining I take caput, you take it for capiendum,
it has loosened its nets, nets far too wide.

units.la: Denique Johannes Vitoduranus ad A. 1344. sic exclamat: O Deus quanta avaritia, idolorum servitus Ecclesiam fœdavit & deformavit! Quando S. Petrus, cæterique Apostoli, & eorum Successores, Martyres, Doctores, Ecclesiæ militantis fundamenta ponentes, credidissent, vel credere potuissent in nostris temporibus statum Ecclesiæ quandoque inclytum & gloriosum, fore ex pestifera radice avaritiæ taliter deturpandum? Impletum est verbum Jeremiæ: A majori ad minimum omnes student avaritiæ. Plura ex eodem Celeb. Hott. Anal. p. 43. &c. affert.
units.tr: Finally, John of Winterthur, under the year 1344, cries out thus: O God, what greed! The servitude to idols has defiled and disfigured the Church! When Saint Peter and the other Apostles, and their successors, Martyrs and Teachers, laying the foundations of the militant Church, had believed, or could have believed, that in our times the state of the Church, once renowned and glorious, would be so disfigured by the pestilent root of avarice? The word of Jeremiah is fulfilled: from the greatest to the least, all pursue avarice. Much more from the same, the celebrated Hottinger Anal. p. 43 etc. brings forward.
CLVII. Sc.

units.la: CLVII. Seculum Decimum quintum excipit. Eo celebratum Concilium Basileense, Seff. 21. Annatas ante & post illud tempus Romæ receptas damnâsse, suprà vidimus. Eodem Seculo in Gallia Carolo VII. Rege ejus, & A. MCCCCXXXIX. promulgata Pragmatica Sanctio, Pontificiæ circa Annatas, Exspectativas, similésque expilandæ Galliæ artes Simoniæ fibulam imposuit. Eam Sanctionem cùm instante Pio II. abolere Ludovicus XI. Caroli filius cogitâsset, Senatus Curiæ Parisiensis supremus intercessit, Regiqué inter alia demonstravit: Nisi sanctio Patris valeret, quotannis è Galliis Romam elatum iri decies centeno millia aureorum. Cùmque Rex nihilominus Papæ assensurus videretur, Procurator Regius, & Schola Parisina magnis animis obstitit, & à Papa ad Concilium provocavit. Dein Ludovicus XII. graves hoc nomine inimicitias exercuit cum Julio II. donec Franciscus I. in prædæ partem cum Papa veniens, cum Leone X. certis conditionibus Bononiæ transegit, & Sanctioni Concordata succenturiavit. Accedit hisce publicum Ecclesiæ Græcæ testimonium. Testis enim est Johannes Mandavilla lib. j. cap. 7. Illos Johanni xxii sub jugum suum eos mittere molienti, laconicè sic respondisse: Potentiam tuam summam erga subditos tuos firmiter credimus: Superbiam tuam summam tolerare non possumus: Avaritiam tuam satiare non valemus. Diabolus tecum, quid Dominus nobiscum.
units.tr: CLVII. The fifteenth century follows. At that time the Council of Basel, Session 21, condemned the annates received at Rome before and after that period, as we have seen above. In the same century, in France, under King Charles VII, in the year 1439 the Pragmatic Sanction was promulgated, which put a clasp of simony on the Papal arts of plundering France through annates, expectative benefices and similar devices. When Louis XI, son of Charles, had thought of abolishing that Sanction at the urging of Pius II, the Supreme Senate of the Parisian Court interceded, and among other things showed the King: Unless the Father's sanction stood, every year ten times a hundred thousand gold crowns would be carried from France to Rome. And when the King nevertheless seemed about to assent to the Pope, the King's Procurator and the Parisian School resisted with great spirit and appealed from the Pope to a Council. Afterwards Louis XII waged serious enmities on this account with Julius II, until Francis I, coming to a share of the spoils with the Pope, concluded terms with Leo X at Bologna under certain conditions, and added the Concordat as a supplement to the Sanction. To these is added the public testimony of the Greek Church. For John Mandeville book 1, chapter 7 is a witness that when John XXII tried to bring them under his yoke, they answered briefly thus: We firmly believe in your great power over your subjects; your great pride we cannot tolerate; your great avarice we cannot satisfy. The devil be with you, the Lord be with us.

units.la: CLVIII. Qui eadem ætate spiritum traxit, Æneas Sylvius, nondum Papali typho corruptus, Epist. 66. scripsit: Nihil est quod absque argento Romana Curia dedat. Ipsa manuum impositio, & Spiritus S. dona venduntur: nec peccatorum venia nisi nummatis impenditur. Cardinalis quoque Cusanus de Concord. Cathol. lib. j. 40. ubi Curiæ Romanæ Reformationem exoptat: Et quia, inquit, passim promotiones ad fortunam in curia fiunt, illuc confluunt omnes à teneris annis ibi agentes, & exspectantes ditari, ac postponunt studia & religionum exercitia: deserunt aurum & argentum, & reportant chartas.
units.tr: CLVIII. Breathing the spirit of the same age, Aeneas Sylvius, not yet corrupted by Papal pride, wrote Epist. 66: There is nothing the Roman Curia gives without silver. The very laying on of hands and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are sold; nor is the pardon of sins granted except for money. The Cardinal Cusanus also, On the Catholic Concord, book 1, 40, where he longs for a reformation of the Roman Curia, says: And because promotions to fortune are made everywhere in the Curia, all those who from their earliest years serve there and hope to grow rich flock thither, and they put aside studies and the exercises of religion; they abandon gold and silver, and bring back documents.

units.la: CLIX. Ex Nicolao Clemangis, Parisiensi doctore, & Archidiacono Bajocensi, qui eodem Seculo librum de corrupto Ecclesiæ statu, aliaque scripsit, eam in rem plura afferri possent. Afferam pauca. Inter alia de Papa hæc habet: Qui emolumentis Romani Episcopatus, Petrique patrimonio super Regna queque amplissima non contentus, in aliena ovilia lana & lacte copiosa incurrit, omnisque Præsulatuum & Ecclesiarum vacantium, quocunque per orbem terrarum Christiana religio tenetur, jura & collationes sibi tribuit, & legitimas electiones Pastorum suis reservationibus, provisionibus & advocationibus irritas fecit: & Ecclesias annua, biennali, triennali, quandoque quadriennali fructuum exactione; decimis, angariis, procurationibus, Prælatorum spoliis, & infinitis aliis oneribus oppressit, & collectores ad hæc omnia exigenda per omnes provincias instituit, non sine horribili abusu suspensionum interdictionum & anathematum, si quis solvere recusabat. Et eam negotiationem per Curiæ suæ lites & Cancellariæ regulas exercuit, ut domus Dei facta sit SPELUNCA LATRONUM. Et Cardinales suos, tanquam sui Pompatus socios, ex sortis infimæ clericatu in elationem evexit, ut Reges ipsos æquiparare contendant: & per dispensationes suas locupletavit ipsos, ut officia, beneficiaque nonnunquam duo vel tria, decem vel viginti, sed centena & ducentena, & interdum usque ad quadraginta, vel quinquaginta aut amplius, eaque non parva, vel tenuia, sed omnium pinguissima, & optima possideant. Replevit Ecclesiam mutis canibus, & malis bestiis per usurpationes, exemtiones, compositiones, Simoniam, prostitutionem, & fornicationem cum Principibus terræ commissam, ut tueatur superbiam, libidinem, luxúmque Regificum statūs sui mundani, quem ultra Reges & Imperatores extulit. Inter ejusdem opera extant rythmi, quibus Papæ & Curiæ Simoniam graphicè ille depingit. Curiam Papalem confert cum Freto Siculo. Dicit, Eam sorbere aurum, imò totum mundum devorare instar Scyllæ & Charybdis, ita ut vix fit possibile, homines ab ea sibi servare vel obulum. Addit, Romæ venalia esse jura: plus dantem melius allegare: Ibi Nummum loqui, & Leges tacere. Apud Papam non esse locum nisi danti. Papam derivari à papando, quia omnium opes devorat. Hortatur turgida marsupia, Romam modò veniant, ibi enim esse Medicos qui ea purgare sciant. Qui eodem Seculo vixit, Felix Malleolus nostras Recapitul. Jubil. p. 62. sic suorum, Nicolai inprimis V. temporum Simoniam depingit: Nunc facie ad faciem experienter videmus, quod in Curialibus & Officialibus post majorem, & usque ad minimum nunquam visus est execrabilioris exorbitationis, direptionis, deceptionis, circumventionis, derogationis, exactionis, corrasionis, & omnis, si audemus dicere, Simoniacæ pravitatis, adinventionis novæ, & renovationis antiquæ, continuationis usus & exercitatio continua, quàm pro nunc, & tempore Pontificis moderni (Nicolai) & interim pauperum nullus est adjutor. Dixerat paulò suprà, sub Bonifacio IX. Simoniam, cæteráque omnia vitia præ frequentatione non ampliùs fuisse palliata.
units.tr: CLIX. From Nicholas of Clamanges, Parisian teacher and Archdeacon of Bayeux, who in the same century wrote a book on the corrupt state of the Church, and other works, many things could be cited on this subject. I will cite a few. Among other things he says of the Pope: He, not content with the revenues of the Roman bishopric and the patrimony of Peter over the most extensive kingdoms, runs into other folds rich in wool and milk, and claims for himself the rights and collations of all prelacies and vacant churches wherever in the world the Christian religion is held, and by his reservations, provisions and advowsons has made lawful elections of ministers void. He has oppressed the churches by annual, biennial, triennial, and sometimes quadrennial exactions of revenues, by tithes, forced services, procurations, the spoils of prelates, and countless other burdens, and he has appointed collectors to exact all these in every province, not without the horrible abuse of suspensions, interdicts and anathemas against whoever refused to pay. And he has carried on this business through the lawsuits of his Curia and the rules of his Chancery, so that the house of God has become a DEN OF ROBBERS. And he has raised his Cardinals, as companions of his pomp, from the lowest rank of the clergy to such pride that they strive to equal kings themselves; and by his dispensations he has enriched them so that they hold offices and benefices, sometimes two or three, ten or twenty, but hundreds and two hundreds, and sometimes up to forty or fifty or more, and these not small or slight, but the fattest and best of all. He has filled the Church with dumb dogs and evil beasts through usurpations, exemptions, compositions, simony, prostitution and fornication committed with the princes of the earth, so that he may maintain the pride, lust and royal luxury of his worldly state, which he has raised above kings and emperors. Among his works there survive verses in which he graphically depicts the simony of the Pope and the Curia. He compares the Papal Curia with the Strait of Sicily. He says that it swallows gold, indeed devours the whole world like Scylla and Charybdis, so that it is scarcely possible for men to keep even a farthing for themselves from it. He adds that rights are for sale at Rome: whoever gives more is better pleaded for. There money speaks and laws are silent. With the Pope there is no place except for the giver. The Pope is derived from papando, because he devours the wealth of all. He urges swollen purses: let them come to Rome now, for there are doctors there who know how to purge them. Also living in the same century, Felix Malleolus in our Recapitulation of the Jubilee, p. 62, depicts the simony of his own times, especially under Nicholas V, thus: Now we see face to face, from experience, that among Curial officials, from the greatest down to the least, there was never seen such execrable excess, plundering, deception, circumvention, detraction, extortion, scraping, and every kind of simoniacal wickedness (if we dare to say so), new inventions and renewal of old ones, continuous practice and continual exercise, as now, in the time of the present Pontiff (Nicholas), and meanwhile there is no helper of the poor. A little above he had said that under Boniface IX simony and all other vices were no longer disguised, because of their frequent practice.

units.la: CLX. Laurentius Valla, Romanus Senator, & Alphonsi Aragonum Regis ac ipsius Papæ Secretarius, qui mendacissimam Constantini M Donationem solidissimè refutavit, sic inter cætera Romanæ Curiæ statum deplorat:
units.tr: CLX. Laurentius Valla, a Roman senator, and secretary both to Alfonso, King of Aragon, and to the Pope himself, who most solidly refuted the most mendacious Donation of Constantine the Great, thus deplores, among other things, the state of the Roman Curia:

units.la: Melius Summus Pontifex ab augendo AUGUSTUS, diceretur, nisi quod dum temporalia auget, spiritualia minuit. Papa & alienas sibi opes, & suas exsorbet, ut Achilles in Agamemnone ἀηµεξίρ@ βασιλεύς. Dico, & exclamo (neque enim timebo homines, Deo fretus) neminem mea aetate in Summo Pontificatu fuisse, ut fidelem dispensatorem & prudentem, qui tantum abest, ut walked dederit familiae Dei cibum & escam panis. Papa & ipse bella pacatis populis infert, & inter civitates Principesque discordias serit. Papa & alienas sibi opes, & suas exsorbet. Jungam ex eo Seculo unum Baptistam Mantuanum, sic Romanae Curiae in Alphonso lib. iij. statum depingentem:
units.tr: The Supreme Pontiff would more fittingly be called Augustus, from augendo (increasing), were it not that while he increases temporal things he diminishes spiritual ones. The Pope both devours others' wealth and his own, like Achilles' Agamemnon, a people-devouring king [δημοβόρος βασιλεύς]. I say, and I cry out (for I shall not fear men, trusting in God), that in my age there has been no one in the Supreme Pontificate who was a faithful and prudent steward, who is so far from having given the household of God food and the nourishment of bread. The Pope himself wages wars on peaceful peoples, and sows discord among cities and princes. The Pope both devours others' wealth and his own. I will add from the same century one passage by Baptista Mantuanus, depicting the state of the Roman Curia in his Alphonsus, book 3:

units.la: Petrique domus polluta fluente Marcescit luxu. Nulla hic arcana revelo. Non ignota loquor, liceat vulgata referre: Sic urbes populique ferunt, ea fama per omnem Jam vetus, Europam mores extirpat honestos. Sanctus ager scurris, venerabilis ara Cynaedis Servit, honorandae Divam, Ganymedibus aedes. Quid miremur opes, recidivaque surgere tecta? Thuris adorati globulos & cinnama vendit Mollis Arabs, Tyrii vestes: venalia nobis Templa, Sacerdotes, altaria sacra, coronae, Ignis, thura, preces, Caelum est venale Deusque.
units.tr: The house of Peter, polluted, withers in a flowing luxury. I reveal no hidden secrets here. I speak of things not unknown; let me repeat what is commonly said. So say cities and peoples; that report, already old, runs through all Europe and uproots honest morals. The holy field serves the buffoons, the venerable altar serves the catamites, the temples of the goddess serve the Ganymedes. Why should we wonder at the wealth and the roofs rising again after collapse? The soft Arab sells the little balls of incense that are worshipped, and cinnamon, and the Tyrian robes: for sale to us are temples, priests, sacred altars, crowns, fire, incense, prayers; heaven is for sale, and God.

units.la: Plura ex eodem ipse Espencaeus in cap. j. ad Tit. excerpsit.
units.tr: Ipse Espencaeus excerpted many more from the same author on chapter 1 of Titus.

units.la: CLXI. Ex Seculo Decimo-sexto ad testimonium diceendum prodeant Imperatores, Principes, Papa, Cardi- nales.
units.tr: CLXI. Let emperors, princes, the Pope and cardinals of the sixteenth century come forward to give testimony.

units.la: Gravamina Imperii crebrò à nobis allegata, Imperatore Maximiliano I. & Principibus Imperii Pontificiis adhuc authoribus composita, & post à Principibus Pontificiis & Protestantibus, Norimbergae Papae Legato exhibita, Imperatoris & Principum de Romanorum nundinationum extrema impudentia reconditum sensum clarissimè patefaciunt. Idem verò Maximilianus Cæsar, cùm à Legato Pontificis Cardinale Cajetano A. MDXVIII. urgereStur ad sumtus in bellum Turcicum conferendos, Ecclesiasticorúmque per Germaniam decimas eidem devovendas, respondit: Vix posse sperari, ut ab ordine sacerdotum illud impetretur. Nam Curiæ Romanæ variis ac subinde novis artificiis illorum facultates atque jura vehementer impediri: populum verò, si quid imperetur, clamare, totes jam hoc nomine datam esse pecuniam, & demirari, quomodo profusa sit, quoque census ille pervenerit è solis Annatis per Germaniam collectus? Inter Hadriani VI. Papæ laudes Onuphrius hoc retulit, quòd reservas, accessus, regressus, coadjutorias, & id genus alia Romani aucupii nescio inquit, quo nomine appellata retia, quæ facilitate Leonis supra modum propagata erant, ex parte sustulerit, præsertim quòd ea via plurimi probrosi ineptique ad optima Sacerdotia obreperent, qui pecuniam haberent, qua nihil non parare est, maximè Romæ, ubi probi literatique, qui eam non haberent, ab eis excluderentur. Fassus idem est per Nuntium suum ad Comitia Imperialia A. MDXXII. missum, in Sede Sancta aliquot jam annis multa abominanda fuisse, abusus in spiritualibus, excessus in mandatis, omnia denique in perversum mutata, addens, Prælatos ac Sacerdotes maximè indigere reformatione, quomodo Salvator curaturus infirmam civitatem Hierusalem prius Templum ingressus sit, ut Sacerdotum peccata (ementium inprimis & vendentium) primò castigaret. Facit huc consilium Cardinalium & Præsulum à Paulo III. delegatorum de emendanda Ecclesia, eidem Papæ exhibitum, & à nobis in Hist. Pap. ff. clxvij. clxviij. commemoratum. Ibi abusus Curiæ plurimos, inprimis circa ordinationem Clericorum, collationem beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum, maximè mè Curatorum, expectativas, reservationes beneficio‑ rum, absentiam Clericorum ab Ecclesiis suis, gratias & dispensationes &c. ad incudem revocatos cernere est.
units.tr: The grievances of the Empire, which we have often cited, drawn up under the Emperor Maximilian I and the Papist princes of the Empire, and afterwards presented at Nuremberg by the Papist princes and the Protestants to the Pope's legate, lay bare most clearly the hidden meaning of the Romans' shameless trading. Emperor Maximilian himself, when in 1518 the Pope's legate, Cardinal Cajetan, pressed him to raise money for the war against the Turks and to assign to the Pope the tithes of the clergy throughout Germany, replied: It can hardly be hoped that this will be obtained from the order of priests. For the Roman Curia, by its various and ever new devices, greatly hinders their revenues and rights. As for the people, if anything is demanded of them, they cry out that money has already been given under this name so many times, and they wonder how it has been spent, and what became of that great sum collected from the annates alone throughout Germany? In praise of Pope Hadrian VI, Onuphrius reported this: that he removed in part the reservations, rights of access and recall, coadjutorships, and other snares of that sort of Roman fowling, I know not by what name they are called, which had spread beyond measure under the easy-going Leo, especially because by this route many disgraceful and incompetent men slipped into the best priesthoods, men who had money, with which everything can be obtained, above all at Rome, where upright and learned men who lacked it were shut out. The same Hadrian confessed through his nuncio sent to the Imperial Diet in 1522 that for some years many abominable things had existed in the Holy See, abuses in spiritual matters, excesses in commissions, and, in short, everything turned to the perverse, adding that prelates and priests above all needed reform, just as the Saviour, about to heal the sick city of Jerusalem, first entered the Temple, so that he might first punish the sins of the priests (especially of those who buy and sell). To this belongs the counsel of the cardinals and prelates appointed by Paul III for the amendment of the Church, presented to that same Pope and mentioned by us in the History of the Papacy, pp. 167–168. There one may see that the many abuses of the Curia are called back to the anvil, especially concerning the ordination of clergy, the conferring of ecclesiastical benefices, above all of parish cures, expectatives, reservations of benefices, the absence of clergy from their churches, graces and dispensations, and so on.

units.la: CLXII. Langii Citizensis, Erasmi, Budæi, aliorum que ex eadem ætate testimonia superius laudata repetere nihil attinet.
units.tr: CLXII. There is no need to repeat the testimonies of Langius Citizensis, Erasmus, Budaeus and the others of the same age that were cited above.

units.la: Ex Francisco Duareno nonnulla jam quoque allegavimus. Idem vero de S. Eccles. & Benefic. lib. v. 8. sic scribit: Ex aula Pontificis Romani proficis‑ cuntur diplomata, quibus mandat ac præcipit beneficia quibuslibet conferre. Convenit tamen inter omnes, quot‑ quot sunt, juris Pontificii enarratores, hanc beneficiorum distribuendorum rationem apud veteres in usu non fuisse. Avaritia etenim aulæ Pontificiæ post aliquot Secula hoc novum pecuniæ aucupium adinvenit, quod nunquam veteribus in mentem venerat. Res ipsa loquitur, & nos quoti‑diè satis docet experientia, quantum hæc lues pestisque noceat Ecclesiæ. Supra lib. j. cap. 6. sic idem scripserat: Quis est adeò imperitus rerum, ut Romanæ Curiæ artes non nôrit, & quantum ea hirudo Gallici exsorbeat sangui‑ nis quotidiè non intelligat? Dicam, quod à Viris peri‑tissimis, ac diu in Republ. versatis non semel accepi, quan‑ quam incredibile videtur, quotannis variorum diploma‑ tum à Pontifice obtentorum nomine, ad septingenta, aut eo amplius aureorum millia Romam hinc exportari solere, quæ ita illic velut capta vinctâque detineantur & custodi‑ antur, ut nullo unquam postliminio ad nos redeant. Quid multa? In proverbium abiit jam pridem Romana permu‑ tatio, plumbi videlicet cum auro. Tot artium Romanarum turpitudinem etiam Dominicus Soto, homo Pontifi‑ ciæ potestati addictissimus, vidit, & de Just. & Jure lib. ix. q. 4. art. 4. sic modestè perstrinxit: Congrueus fuit Dei præceptum, ut Decimarum decimam summo Sacerdoti penderent. Qua utique ratione summus Pontifex, justa iningruente necessitate decimam decimarum à Clero exigere valet. Imò verò utinam universalis, eaque perpetua toti Clero imponeretur: si tamen illa ratione omnis alia occluderetur in perpetuum via & modus alia commentandi jura, aliásque excogitandi artes sustentandi Apostolicam sedem, quibus Ecclesiasticæ leges non possunt non periculosissimè arctari. Jason Magnus, JCtus celebris in L. qui Romæ s. Sejan 16. ff. de verbo oblig. Sic Imperatorem & Papam contendit: Imperator tanquam Aquilas prædam suam partitur, nec curat in omnibus epulis os suum apponere, tanquam sit insatiabilis. Secus est in Papa, qui quasi totum continet. Ex Claudio Espencæo multa satis hanc in rem suprà excerpsimus. Longum nimis foret huc fevocare gravissimas ejus de Romanensium αἰχμοπρὰ querelas, quas Com. in Tit. cap. j. subtitulo Turpilucri confignavit. Annon, sic querelam suam auspicatur, αἰχμοπρὰ-sία est clarissima, quòd tam multa positivo tantùm jure præcepta vel prohibita, eousque ligant homines, donec pecunia sibi harum constitutionum gratiam impetrent? Ita ut Regina rerum pecunia divitibus licitum faciat, quod pauperibus illicitum est, quia divitias, hoc est, spinas non habent. Hæc enim sic demum procedunt, si gratis ea facere quis intendat. Quòd si dolosi spes refulserit nummi, jam quod priùs erat interdictum liberè fit ac impunè. Tum diversa est in his relaxandis divitis atque pauperis conditio. Vix enim quicquam prohibetur, quàm ut ne quis gratis controveniat, & quod vetatur numeratâ statim pecuniâ dispensatur, quasi nullum sit peccatum majus, quàm nummis carere. Ut quidam apud Horatium serm. 2. s. 3. Credidit ingens Pauperiem vitium. Et quod alter lib. 3. elog. 7. Nunc sit barbaries grandis habere nihil. Late deinceps hoc argumentum ita persequitur, ut vix in Romanensium insatiabili Avaritia & Simonia describenda ardori suo satisfacere possit. Denique Franciscus Sansovinus Venetus, describens Romanae Curiae administrationem primum in Consistorio, deinde in Poenitentiaria, tum in Curiis libellorum, altera gratiae, altera Justitiae; postea in Cancellaria, & postremò in Camera, tantundem perstringit, quantum à nobis dictum est de importuna Pontificum libidine, in officiariorum ordinatione, tractatione causarum, bonorum Ecclesiae administratione, censurarum abusu, & legum Ecclesiae sanctione. Etiam hoc addit amplius, quo manifestè docetur, quàm degenerent Papae ab Episcopali statu ad Regium, esse certum videlicet, Praesulem constitutum, quem Vicarium Romanum appellant, cui earum rerum omnium intra Romanae Diœceseos fines curam mandârunt, quae ad quemque in sua Diœcesi Episcopum spectant, & quae similiter ad ipsos in sua pertinent, quâ propriè sunt Episcopi Romani.
units.tr: I have already cited some passages from Franciscus Duaren. He writes thus in de S. Eccles. & Benefic. lib. v. 8.: Letters that order and command the conferring of benefices on whomever they please go out from the court of the Roman Pontiff. Yet all the expounders of Pontifical law agree that this method of distributing benefices was not in use among the ancients. The greed of the Papal court, after some centuries, devised this new hunting for money, which had never occurred to the ancients. The thing itself speaks, and daily experience teaches us well enough how much this plague and pestilence harms the Church. Earlier, in lib. j. cap. 6., the same author had written: Who is so ignorant of affairs that he does not know the arts of the Roman Curia, and does not understand daily how much that leech drains the blood of France? I will say what I have heard more than once from very skilled men who have been long engaged in public affairs. Though it seems incredible, it is said that every year, in the name of various documents obtained from the Pope, some seven hundred thousand gold pieces or more are customarily carried from here to Rome. There they are held and guarded, as if captured and bound, so that they never return to us by any right of recovery. What more? The Roman exchange, lead for gold, passed into a proverb long ago. Dominicus Soto, a man most devoted to the Pontifical power, also saw the baseness of so many Roman arts, and touched on it with restraint in de Just. & Jure lib. ix. q. 4. art. 4.: It was fitting that God's command should have tithes of tithes paid to the high priest. By this reasoning the supreme Pontiff may certainly exact a tithe of tithes from the clergy when pressing necessity comes on. Indeed, I wish a universal tithe, and a perpetual one, were imposed on the whole clergy: provided that, by that reasoning, every other way were shut off for ever, and every other method of devising rights and every other art of sustaining the Apostolic See were closed, arts by which the ecclesiastical laws cannot help being most dangerously constrained. Jason Magnus, the famous jurist, in in L. qui Romæ s. Sejan 16. ff. de verbo oblig., argues thus about the Emperor and the Pope: The Emperor divides his prey like an eagle, and does not trouble to put his mouth to every feast, as though he were insatiable. It is otherwise with the Pope, who, as it were, holds everything. From Claudius Espencaeus I have already excerpted quite enough on this matter above. It would be far too long to recall here his very grave complaints about the Romanists' venality [αἰχμοπρασία], which he set down in Com. in Tit. cap. j. under the subheading Turpilucri. Is it not most clear venality, as he begins his complaint, that so many things, commanded or forbidden by positive law alone, bind men until they win the favour of these constitutions with money? So that money, the queen of things, makes lawful for the rich what is unlawful for the poor, because the rich have no thorns, that is, no obstacles. For these rules operate only if someone intends to do them for nothing. But if the hope of dishonest money shines forth, then what was forbidden before is done freely and with impunity. Then the condition of the rich and the poor differs in this relaxing of the rules. For hardly anything is forbidden except that no one should act against them for nothing; and what is forbidden is dispensed at once for counted money, as though there were no greater sin than lacking money. Like the man in Horace who "thought that great poverty was a vice", and as another says, "Now it is a great barbarism to have nothing." Afterwards he pursues this theme so far that he can hardly satisfy his zeal in describing the insatiable avarice and simony of the Romanists. Finally, Franciscus Sansovinus of Venice, describing the administration of the Roman Curia, first in the Consistorio, then in the Poenitentiaria, then in Curiis libellorum, one gratiae, the other Justitiae; afterwards in the Cancellaria, and lastly in the Camera, touches on the same points as we have said about the unseemly lust of the Popes in the appointment of officials, the handling of cases, the administration of Church property, the abuse of censures, and the sanctioning of Church laws. He adds also something more, which plainly shows how far the Popes degenerate from the episcopal state to the royal: It is certain that a prelate has been appointed whom they call the Roman Vicar, to whom they have entrusted the care, within the bounds of the Roman diocese, of all those matters which belong to each bishop in his own diocese, and which likewise belong to them in their own, since they are properly Roman bishops.

units.la: CLXIII. Fundus calamitatis est, quòd nullam Hierarchia Simoniacae hujus pravitatis emendationem hactenus passa est, vel patietur unquam, donec Christus è machina coeli Babylonicum ejus Emporium destruet. Nullius enim mortalis, sed solius Christi judicio hic se subesse, pertendit. Id quod disertis verbis ex hypobolimaeo Anacleto suo Juris Canonici Consulti C. 2. q. 6. cap. 15. probare conantur. Ibi enim Anacletus sic Epist. 2. ad Episcopos Italiae scribens inducitur: Accusatio quoque eorum, super quae nos consulere voluistis, non nisi ab idoneis & probatissimis viris, qui & suspicionibus & sceleribus carent, fieri debet: quia Dominus sacri sui corporis tractatores à vilibus reprobis, ac non idoneis personis infamari noluit, nec ca-lumniari permisit: sed ipse proprio flagello peccantes Sacerdotes è Templo ejecit, unde liquet, quòd Summi Sacer-dodotes, id est, Episcopi à Deo sunt judicandi, non ab humanis aut pravæ vitæ hominibus lacerandi, sed potiùs ab omnibus fidelibus portandi: ipso Domino Exemplum dante, quando per semet ipsum, & non per alium vendentes & ementes ejecit de Templo. Et paulò post: Nullus enim, ut reor, invenitur inter nos, qui velit suum servum ab alio, quàm à se judicari. Quod si præsumptum fuerit, aut multa ipse indignatione irascitur, aut potiùs ultionem quaerit super eum. Et infra: Unde & Dominus per Prophetam inquit: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Sic solus Christus idoneus ille & probatissimus Vir est, qui Hierarchicorum illorum collybistarum mensas evertere possit. Atque ita rem habere, argumento est, quod ipsorum Conciliorum, quae hactenus mensas illas eversura videbantur, contentionem nullo fere negotio Papa sufflaminavit. Olim quidem dum adhuc moribus sanctior, & doctrinâ purior esset Ecclesia, si quando Romani Episcopi (sic Augustinus epist. 162. scribit) non boni judices fuisse putarentur, restabat adhuc plenarium universæ Ecclesiæ Concilium, ubi etiam cum ipsis judicibus causa posset agitari, ut, si male judicare convicti essent, eorum sententiæ solverentur. Ast deinceps, quando religio, ad superstitionem, & more Cleri ad nimiam ambitionem ac avaritiam incubuerunt, Concilium appellare causa remedii licuit nemini, nisi ei, qui piorum coetu moveri, quod & Bulla Cœnæ Domini obnuntiat, & Archiduci Sigismundo, & ejus Oratori Heimburgensi accidit: aut etiam laqueo vitam finire; quod Andream Carnorum Archiepiscopum, procurante Sixto IV. Pontifice, passum fuisse eandem ob causam scribunt; vellet. Atque id etiam aliquot nonnisi ad inanem speciem indictis Conciliis clarè patuit. Nam in Concilio Basileensi Cæsaris ac Principum expectationem frustrati Hierarchici, talia vel consimilia decrevere: Clericus curcurtam vestem non gerat : laxas manicas in tunica non habeat : Cardinalis supra 30. beneficia Ecclesiastica non possideat : concubinam Clericus aperte ne foveat : crines ac barbam minimùm semel in mense tondeat. Atque haec anilia deliramenta Ecclesiae Reformationem appellare ausi sunt. Ubi verò ejusdem Synodi Patres id meditantes conantesque, ut graviora quædam reformarent, plenitudinem Pontificiæ potestatis arctioribus limitibus concludebant, amputando maximam partem Reservationum ejus, omnesque expectativas gratias, & compositiones : contrahendo etiam citationes, dispensationes, appellationes, numerúmque & possessionesCardinalium; inprimis definiendo, Papam teneri Synodo obedire: Onuphrius in Rom. Pontif. & Card. hinc pronuntiat, illos sub praetextu reformandi Remp. Christianam, pleraque Romanae Ecclesiae privilegia, & ea, quae magis necessaria, omninò tollere & antiquare studuisse. Concilium igitur, Papa tergiversante, & suum illud Non obstante opponente, irritum cecidit.
