Sic planè Sigismundus Imperator populis undequaque conquerentibus spem fecerat, curaturum se in Concilio Constantiensi, ut de reformanda Ecclesia cogitaretur: nec omisit Concilii Patres eo nomine serió solicitare, eò impensiùs, quòd capite nondum constituto (novi enim Papæ electio tum suscipienda erat) de eo in ordinem redigendo Concilium & majore cum authoritate, & minore cum contradictione statuere possit. Concilii igitur Praefes, Cardinalis Hostiensis, quaedam decreta legit, de quibus Concilium sententiam ferre rogatur, ut à Papa futuro ante Concilii solutionem publicarentur: atque inter ea etiam numerum, qualitatem, notionem Cardinalium: Reservationes, Annatas, Expectativas gratias & collationes, Regulas Cancellariae & Parlamentarias, Indulgentias, Decimas, &c. quae nihilominus omnia post electio-
units.tr: CLXIII. The root of the calamity is that the hierarchy has never yet suffered, and will never suffer, any correction of this simoniacal wickedness, until Christ from heaven's machine destroys their Babylonian marketplace. For they maintain that the Hierarchy is subject to the judgment of no mortal, but of Christ alone. The canonists try to prove this in plain words from their supposititious Anacletus, in C. 2. q. 6. cap. 15. For there Anacletus is introduced writing thus in Epist. 2. to the bishops of Italy: An accusation about the matters on which you wished us to give counsel must be brought only by fit and most approved men, who are free from suspicion and crimes. For the Lord did not wish the handlers of his sacred body to be defamed by base, reprobate and unfit persons, nor did he permit them to be slandered. Rather, he himself drove the sinning priests from the Temple with his own scourge. From this it is clear that the chief priests, that is, the bishops, are to be judged by God, not torn to pieces by men or men of wicked life, but rather borne up by all the faithful, the Lord himself giving the example, when he himself, and not through another, drove the sellers and buyers from the Temple. And a little later: For I think there is no one among us who would wish his servant to be judged by another than himself. But if this is presumed, he is either angered with great indignation, or rather seeks vengeance upon him. And below: Whence also the Lord says through the Prophet: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Thus Christ alone is that fit and most approved Man who can overturn the tables of those hierarchical money-changers. That this is so is shown by the fact that the Pope, almost without effort, has checked the struggle of the very Councils which seemed until now likely to overturn those tables. Indeed, in former times, while the Church was still holier in morals and purer in doctrine, if at any time the Roman bishops (so Augustine writes in epist. 162.) were thought not to be good judges, there still remained a full council of the whole Church, where the cause could be argued even before the judges themselves, so that, if they were convicted of judging badly, their sentences might be annulled. But afterwards, when religion had sunk into superstition and the clergy, by their manner of life, had given themselves to excessive ambition and avarice, no one was permitted to appeal to a Council as a remedy, except one who wished to be moved by the assembly of the pious. This happened also in the Bull of the Lord's Supper, and to Archduke Sigismund and his Heidelberg envoy; or else to end one's life by a noose. They write that Andrew, Archbishop of Carnorum, suffered this for the same cause, at the instigation of Pope Sixtus IV. This has also been plainly shown by several Councils that were held only for an empty show. For in the Council of Basel, the hierarchs, having frustrated the expectation of the Emperor and the princes, decreed such things or things like them: Let a cleric not wear a short garment; let him not have loose sleeves in his tunic; let a cardinal not possess more than thirty ecclesiastical benefices; let a cleric not openly keep a concubine; let him shave his hair and beard at least once a month. And these silly fancies they dared to call the Reformation of the Church. But where the Fathers of the same Synod, meaning and attempting to reform certain weightier matters, confined the fullness of Pontifical power within narrower limits, cutting away the greater part of its Reservations, and all the expectative graces and compositions, and also curtailing citations, dispensations, appeals, and the number and possessions of the Cardinals; and above all by defining that the Pope is bound to obey the Synod: Onuphrius, in his work on the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals, declares from this that under the pretext of reforming the Christian commonwealth, they sought to abolish and annul altogether most of the privileges of the Roman Church, and those which were more necessary. Therefore the Council, with the Pope evading and opposing his usual Notwithstanding, fell void. Likewise the Emperor Sigismund, when peoples everywhere complained, had given hope that he would see to it at the Council of Constance that the reform of the Church should be considered. Nor did he neglect to press the Fathers of the Council seriously on that account, all the more earnestly because the head was not yet settled (for the election of a new Pope was then to be undertaken), and the Council could decide on setting that in order with greater authority and less contradiction. So the President of the Council, the Cardinal of Ostia, read out certain decrees, on which the Council was asked to pass judgment, so that they might be published by the future Pope before the Council was dissolved. Among them were the number, the quality, and the definition of Cardinals; Reservations, Annates, expectative graces and collations, the Rules of the Chancery and of the Parliament, Indulgences, Tithes, etc. Nevertheless all these were rejected, to be settled after the election of the Pope. Doubtless this was because it vexed them that the little word which Sigismund let slip troubled them: when some said that the reform should begin with the Minorites, he answered, "No, with the Majorites," pointing at the Pope and the Cardinals. So, the Pope having been elected, all reform was broken off, and by the Pope's command it was announced…

units.la: ctio. stionem Papæ terminanda rejiciuntur: haud dubiè, quia angebat eos, quod Sigismundo excidebat, verbulum, qui dicentibus, Reformationem inchoandam esse à Minoritis, respondit; Imò à Majoritis; Papam & Cardinales innuens. Pontifice ergò electo omnis reformatio abrupta, & ex mandato Papæ pronuntiatum est: Domini, ite in pace; quibus verbis dimittebantur, sublato inquit Platina in Martino V. omnium consensu, maximè verò Imperatoris: quo rogante, ut saltem pauxillum in Germania moræ facerent, necessitatem Romam redeundi obtendit Papa, quòd Sanctorum Capellæ per absentiam suam collaberentur. Regreditur igitur Pontifex in Italiam, ovans haud dubiè, quòd solertiâ suâ formidabilem hunc Reformationis scopulum evasisset.
units.tr: ...tion. These matters were set aside to be settled only after the election of the Pope, no doubt because a little word that slipped from Sigismund troubled them. When some said the reform must be begun by the Minorites, he replied, Rather by the Majorites, hinting at the Pope and the cardinals. Once the Pope was elected, all reform was broken off, and by the Pope's command it was announced, Lords, go in peace. By these words, says Platina in his life of Martin V, they were dismissed, the business having been dropped, with the consent of all, and above all of the Emperor, at whose request that they might at least stay a little longer in Germany, the Pope pleaded the necessity of returning to Rome, because the chapels of the saints were collapsing in his absence. The Pontiff therefore returned to Italy, undoubtedly exulting that by his shrewdness he had escaped this dangerous rock of reformation.

units.la: CLXIV. De Reformatione nundinationum in Tri- dentino Concilio suscepta, frivola illa, ludicra, hypocri- tica, desultoria, & in unius soliusque Papæ arbitrio po- sito, in Anatome Concilii Tridentini passim multa dixi- mus.
units.tr: CLXIV. On the reform of simony undertaken at the Council of Trent, a frivolous, playful, hypocritical, evasive affair, placed entirely at the discretion of one man, the Pope. In my Anatome Concilii Tridentini I have said many things about it here and there.

units.la: Omnium penè malorum radicem in Papa & Curia Romana, & utriusque tyrannide, avaritia, luxu, ambitione fixam vix attingere, certè tollere Patres illi ausi non sunt. Si qua salutaria decreta, Pontificémque Curiámque obliquè ferientia, cudi visa sunt, iis nervos succidit omnes tum secutum Sess. xxv. cap. 21. decretum, ut in omnibus morum Reformatione & Ecclesiastica disciplina decretis salva semper Sedis Apostolicæ authoritas & sit, & esse intelligatur: tum jus interpretandi & declarandi singula Concilii decreta, quod, Synodo indulgente, sibi Papa reservavit. Quæ duo efficere posse, ut omnia Papæ & Curiæ noxia decreta in nihilum recidant, & sensim sine sensu in antiquum cuncta statum redigantur, Pontifici de confirmando Concilio anxio Cardinalis Amulius & Episcopus Vestanus suggesserant. Multorum abusuum, nun-didinationum multarum fontem non-residentiam, & Episcoporum mediatam institutionem, quàm mala fide abrogaverint, tractaverintque, fusè satis ostendimus. Ista Tridentini Concilii Reformatio, sic Julius Clemens Scotus, Monachus Servita Italus, Not. Censor. pag. 93. loquitur, effecit, ut nunc non ea pecuniarum summa in urbem Romam deveheretur, quae prius ac Pontificii reditus ipsimet inde imminuti. An vero haec imminutio compensata deinde fuerit auctus ordinarius, seu confusus alim contributionibus, pro quibus nihil statutum, aut non servatus quibusdam Tridentinis legibus, quae ipsum Pontificem nullatenus obstringunt, ut aperte declararunt Tridentini Patres aut novis officiis in curia constitutis, aut alunde norunt illi, qui illis colligendis praefecti sunt. Sed & Claudius Espencæus, Theologus Sorbonicus gravissimus, Comment. in Ep. ad Tit. cap. j. Reformationis à Tridentinis suscepta vanitatem solidissimè demonstrat, & demonstrationem suam his verbis pag. m. 480. 481. claudit: Tam diuturnorum motuum non alia causa major, quàm quòd tot annis nihil immutatur, nihil renovatur, & omnis reformandi spes inde abrupta, species ablata, quod reliquum Ecclesiæ corpus reformatum velint, qui tam multis annorum centenariis urbem, in qua merum atque mixtum habent imperium, deformatissimam adhuc reliquerunt. Quid enim vel excusare, vel excogitare verum aut verisimile possunt, quibus non vel Rex, vel Cæsar non populus, non clerus, non generalis Synodus, non denique tota Ecclesia dicere potest, Cur ita facis? quid, inquam, prætexere possunt, quod eis sibi suisque reformandis moram vel remoram tamdiu fecerit? Et ubi tamen sub sole major malorum omnium licentia, clamor, impunitas, ne dicam infamia & impudentia? talis sane ac tanta, ut nemo credat, nisi qui viderit, neget nemo, nisi qui non viderit.
units.tr: Those Fathers did not dare to touch, much less to remove, the root of almost all evils, which lies in the Pope and the Roman Curia and in the tyranny of both, their greed, luxury and ambition. If any salutary decrees seemed to be hammered out that strike at the Pope and the Curia indirectly, all their sinews were cut by the decree that followed, Sess. xxv. cap. 21., that in all decrees on the reformation of morals and ecclesiastical discipline the authority of the Apostolic See always remain, and be understood to remain, intact; and by the right to interpret and declare each decree of the Council, which the Pope reserved to himself with the Synod's indulgence. Cardinal Amulius and the Bishop of Vestan, anxious about the Pope's confirming the Council, had suggested that these two measures could bring it about that all the harmful decrees of the Pope and Curia come to nothing, and that everything be gradually and imperceptibly led back to the old state. We have shown at sufficient length how they abrogated, and with bad faith treated, non-residence and the mediated institution of bishops, the source of many abuses and of many simonies. This reform of the Council of Trent, thus speaks Julius Clemens Scotus, an Italian Servite monk, Not. Censor. pag. 93., has brought it about that now the sum of money that used to be carried to the city of Rome is no longer carried there, and the Pope's own revenues have been diminished. Whether this diminution was afterwards compensated by an increase in the ordinary income, or by confused contributions from elsewhere, for which nothing was laid down, or some Tridentine laws, which in no way bind the Pope himself, were not observed, as the Tridentine Fathers clearly declared, either by new offices established in the Curia, or they know from elsewhere, those who have been set in charge of collecting them. But also Claudius Espencaeus, a most weighty Sorbonne theologian, Comment. in Ep. ad Tit. cap. j., most solidly demonstrates the vanity of the reformation undertaken at Trent, and closes his demonstration with these words, pag. m. 480. 481.: No greater cause of such long-lasting disturbances can be found than that for so many years nothing is changed, nothing renewed, and every hope of reform is cut off, its appearance taken away, since they wish the rest of the body of the Church to be reformed while they have left the city, in which they hold pure and mixed rule, so utterly deformed for so many centuries. For what can they excuse or invent that is true or plausible, to whom neither the King, nor Caesar, nor the people, nor the clergy, nor a general Synod, nor finally the whole Church can say, Why do you do so? What, I say, can they put forward as the reason why the reform of themselves and their own people has been delayed or held back so long? And where under the sun is there greater licence for all evils, clamour, impunity, not to mention infamy and impudence? Such indeed and so great, that no one will believe it unless he has seen it, and no one will deny it unless he has not seen it.

units.la: CLXV. Hæc cùm ita se habeant, universæ Hierarchiæ, ejus Principi supremo, Papæ, inprimis jure dicemus, quod Jehova ipse Regi Jehudæ Jehojakimo dixit Esai. XXII. 17. אין עינו ולבו כי אם אל בצעו Non sunt oculi tui & cor tuum intenti nisi ad avaritiam. Neque amplius vel Simonis Petri, sed potiùs Magi successor, vel Caput, sed potiùs Venter Ecclesiæ Papa salutabitur, juxta apologum Menenii Agrippæ apud Livium Annal. lib. ij. quem, uti suprà vidimus, ipse Hadrianus IV. Papa cum Johanne Sarisberiense colloquens, sibi applicavit. Denique hac non postrema nota, ut argumentum hucusque solidè demonstratum concludam, Hierarchiam, utpote Avaritia & spirituali nundinatione nefariè pollutam, Babylonicæ impietatis ream justissimè nos peregisse, planè meritóque confidimus.
units.tr: CLXV. Since these things stand so, we shall say with full right to the whole Hierarchy and its supreme head, the Pope, what Jehovah himself said to King Jehoiakim of Judah, Isaiah 22:17: Thine eyes and thy heart are set on nothing but gain [אין עינו ולבו כי אם אל בצעו]. Nor shall the Pope be greeted any longer as the successor of Peter, but rather of Magus, nor as the Head of the Church, but rather as its Belly, according to the fable of Menenius Agrippa in Livy, Annals, book 2, which, as we saw above, Pope Hadrian IV himself applied to himself when conversing with John of Salisbury. Finally, as a not least mark by which to conclude the argument so far solidly demonstrated, we confidently and plainly trust that we have most justly brought the Hierarchy, as one foully polluted by avarice and spiritual simony, to trial as guilty of Babylonian impiety.
DISSERTATION SEVENTEEN
IN WHICH

units.la: Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiæ Romanæ dominantem, Babylonem Magnam esse, probatur Duodecimò, quia ob impietatem suam severum Dei judicium provocans, illud aliquatenus jam subivit, & finale illud ac decretorium porrò subitura est.
units.tr: That the Hierarchy, or the Clergy of the Roman Church which dominates, is Babylon the Great, is proved in the twelfth place, because by its impiety it has provoked the severe judgment of God, has already in some measure undergone it, and is going to undergo that final and decisive judgment.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Babylonis M. postremus actus, isque tragicus, est judicium Dei, quo illa perdi debuit, quod duplici casu, primo & finali, seu peremptorio absolvitur.
units.tr: I. The last act of Babylon the Great, and a tragic one, is the judgment of God by which she must be destroyed; it is completed in a twofold stroke, the first and the final, or decisive, one.

units.la: II. In Hierarchiam judicium illud competere, tum illud demonstrat, quòd peccata Hierarchiæ & Babylonis congruunt: tum Syllogismo probatur ulterius.
units.tr: II. That this judgment applies to the Hierarchy is shown, first, by the fact that the sins of the Hierarchy and of Babylon agree; and then it is further proved by a syllogism.

units.la: III. Judicium seu casus Babylonis prior cum illuminatione illa, quà terra gloriâ Dei collustrari debuit adeóque Euangelii præconio amplissimo, conjunctissimus esse debuit.
units.tr: III. The first judgment or fall of Babylon ought to have been most closely joined with that enlightenment by which the earth was to be lit up with the glory of God, and so with the very wide proclamation of the Gospel.

units.la: IV. Generalitas vaticinii, quòd terra gloriâ Dei collustrari debeat, explicatur.
units.tr: IV. The generality of the prophecy, that the earth ought to be lit up with the glory of God, is explained.

units.la: V. Splendor illê ex oppositis præcedentibus tenebris cognoscitur.
units.tr: V. That splendour is recognised from the darkness that preceded it, which was its opposite.

units.la: VI. Tenebræ Papatûs Reformationi præviæ describuntur tum in universum:
units.tr: VI. The darkness of the Papacy that preceded the Reformation is described, first in general:

units.la: VII. tum in specie, quoad ejusdem fidem & religionis dogmata:
units.tr: VII. then in particular, as regards its faith and the doctrines of its religion:
VIII. as regards its ceremonies:

units.la: IX. quoad cultum externum, idololatria, superstitione multiplici & magica impietate fœdatum:
units.tr: IX. as regards its external worship, which is defiled by idolatry, manifold superstition and magical impiety:

units.la: X. tum quoad gubernationem, & Ecclesiam ac Politiam universam Papali tyrannide oppressam:
units.tr: X. then as regards its government, and the whole Church and polity oppressed by papal tyranny:

units.la: XI. tum quoad media Religionis cognoscendæ; cujusmodi sunt inprimis Verbum Dei, cujus penè extincti loco, legendæ, fabulæ, scripta Aristotelis, &c. pro suggestu tractari fuerunt.
units.tr: XI. then as regards the means of knowing religion; of which the chief is the Word of God, which, nearly extinguished, was replaced by legends, fables, the writings of Aristotle, and so on, which were handled from the pulpit.

units.la: XII. Linguæ, Originales maximè, Latina etiam, quarum ignorantia, atque sic barbarie extrema Clerus ferè omnis laboravit.
units.tr: XII. The languages, especially the original ones, and Latin too, whose ignorance, and so the utmost barbarism, afflicted nearly the whole clergy.

units.la: XIII. Philosophiæ sobriæ usus, cujus locum futilis & sterilis Sophisticè subivit:
units.tr: XIII. The sober use of philosophy, whose place was taken by a trifling and barren sophistry:

units.la: XIV. quæ cum rebus sacris commixta Theologiam Scholasticam, optimis quibusque fœtentem, & Verbi Divini Majestati è diametro oppositam peperit:
units.tr: XIV. which, mixed with sacred matters, produced a Scholastic theology, stinking of the worst things and diametrically opposed to the majesty of the Divine Word.

units.la: XV. quomodo etiam Juri Cæsareo Canonicum oppositum, atque hoc supra illud exaltatum est.
units.tr: XV. In the same way, the canon law was set against the civil law of the emperors, and this was exalted above that.

units.la: XVI. Tenebras hasce Papatûs cœlestis lucis scintillæ quædam, Testes Veritatis, publicæ corruptioni resistentes, interfuerunt.
units.tr: XVI. Some sparks of heavenly light, witnesses of the truth, resisting the public corruption, were present amid these darknesses of the Papacy.

units.la: XVII. Splendor ille, quo terra illustranda fuit, phosphoros suos habuit; puta tum linguarum Orientalium studium quoddam Viennensis Concilii decreto commendatum: unde editio Bibliorum Complutensis profecta est.
units.tr: XVII. That splendour by which the earth was to be illuminated had its own bearers of light; namely, a certain study of the Oriental languages, commended by a decree of the Council of Vienne, from which the Complutensian edition of the Bibles came forth.

units.la: XVIII. Tum Academiarum & Scholarum instaurationem, literarúmque adeo & literatorum florem.
units.tr: XVIII. Then the restoration of the academies and schools, and so the flowering of letters and of learned men.

units.la: XIX. Tum inservientem utrique Typographiam, qua Babylonis casum maturari debuisse, ostenditur.
units.tr: XIX. Then it is shown that printing, which served both, ought to have hastened the fall of Babylon.

units.la: XX. Reformationis prodromus hisce acciderunt desideria ejusdem testatissima:
units.tr: XX. Among the forerunners of the Reformation were these most evident longings for it:

units.la: XXI. neque quoad mores duntaxat, sed etiam fidem ipsam, uti ex Gersone & Ænea Sylvio ostenditur
units.tr: XXI. not only as regards morals alone, but also faith itself, as is shown from Gerson and Aeneas Sylvius.

units.la: XXII. nec non bona omina & præsagia, Visionésque Babylonis mox ruituræ
units.tr: XXII. as well as good omens and presages, and visions of Babylon about to fall soon.

units.la: XXIII. Quas tandem ipsa cœlestis illuminatio, terram præconio Euangelii seu justitiæ solius Christi, ceu causse salutis unicæ, collustrans, excepit.
units.tr: XXIII. These at last were received by that heavenly illumination which lit up the earth with the proclamation of the Gospel, that is, of the righteousness of Christ alone, as the sole cause of salvation.

units.la: XXIV. Præconium illud Euangelii cum judicio Babylonis conjunctissimum fuisse probatur.
units.tr: XXIV. It is proved that this proclamation of the Gospel was most closely joined with the judgment of Babylon.

units.la: XXV. Illuminatio illa terræ, seu Reformatio, tenebris Papatûs è diametro opposita fuit, quod ex restituto dogmatis fidei, ceremoniis, cultu externo, regimine Ecclesiæ, religionis cognoscendæ mediis, Verbo Dei inprimis, asseritur.
units.tr: XXV. That illumination of the earth, or Reformation, was diametrically opposed to the darkness of the Papacy, which is asserted from the restored doctrine of the faith, the ceremonies, external worship, the government of the Church, and the means of knowing religion, above all the Word of God.

units.la: XXVI. Facies inde Papatus inverti, & retrò sublabi tota cœpit.
units.tr: XXVI. From then on the face of the Papacy began to be overturned and to collapse backwards entirely.

units.la: XXVII. Hierarchiæ quoque potestas pluribus in Occidente Regnis atque Provinciis corruit.
units.tr: XXVII. The power of the Hierarchy also fell in many kingdoms and provinces of the West.

units.la: XXVIII. Neque tamen Papa priore hoc casu regnum suum universum amisit, sed sceleton quoddam retinuit. Unde Babylon Papalis Domicilium dæmonum, & custodia omnis spiritus immundi, & avis invisæ evasit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Yet in this first fall the Pope did not lose his whole kingdom, but kept a certain skeleton of it. Hence Papal Babylon became a dwelling of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a hold of every hateful bird.

units.la: XXIX. Duo genera hominum in Papatu post ejus casum priorem residua:
units.tr: XXIX. Two kinds of men remained in the Papacy after its first fall:

units.la: XXX. quorum alterum dæmoniorum, impurorum spiritum & exosarum avium indolem refert.
units.tr: XXX. of which one resembles demons, unclean spirits and the nature of hateful birds.

units.la: XXXI. In Papatu spiritus immundi, similes ranis, grassantur.
units.tr: XXXI. In the Papacy unclean spirits, like frogs, swarm about.

units.la: XXXII. In eodem regnant doctrinæ dæmoniorum, de quibus S. Paulus 1 Tim. iv. 1, 2, 3. &c. vaticinatus est, quod ex characteribus doctrinarum illarum à S. Paulo expressis ostenditur.
units.tr: XXXII. In the same place reign the doctrines of demons, concerning which St Paul prophesied, 1 Tim. iv. 1, 2, 3, etc., as is shown from the marks of those doctrines expressed by St Paul.
XXXIII. The Apostle in the same place condemns celibacy;

units.la: XXXIV. nec non ciborum certorum in jejunio interdictum Pontificium directè impetit.
units.tr: XXXIV. and also the Papal prohibition of certain foods in fasting he attacks directly.

units.la: XXXV. Ex characteribus iisdem ad liquidum perducitur, Papatum dæmoniacarum doctrinarum corpus integrum in sinu suo fovere.
units.tr: XXXV. From the same marks it is brought clearly to light that the Papacy cherishes in its bosom the whole body of demonic doctrines.

units.la: XXXVI. Cujusmodi sit Papalis Ecclesia, etiam ex definitione Ecclesiæ à Bellarmino prodita,
units.tr: XXXVI. What sort of Church the Papal Church is, is also gathered from the definition of the Church given by Bellarmine,

units.la: XXXVII. nec non novis Tridentini Concilii creaturis colligitur.
units.tr: XXXVII. and also from the new creatures of the Council of Trent.

units.la: XXXVIII. Papatum post Reformationem custodiam immundorum spirituum, & avium impurarum exosarumque factum esse, ex claustris religiosorum ostenditur.
units.tr: XXXVIII. That the Papacy after the Reformation became a prison of unclean spirits and of unclean and hateful birds is shown from the cloisters of the religious orders.

units.la: XXXIX. Jesuitas præ cæteris aves impuras & exosas esse, cum ex aliis, tum ex Theologia eorum casuistica, nec non Censura ejusdem in Facultate Parisiensi adornata, in qua permultis ejus Propositionibus dæmoniacarum doctrinarum stigma inuritur; demonstratur.
units.tr: XXXIX. That the Jesuits above all others are unclean and hateful birds is demonstrated, both from other sources and from their casuistic theology, and also from the censure of it drawn up by the Faculty of Paris, in which the stigma of demonic doctrines is branded upon very many of their propositions.

units.la: XL. Vaticinium de immundis avibus Babylone relictis, ex historia Concilii Romani, cui feralis bubo præfuit, illustratur.
units.tr: XL. The prophecy about the unclean birds left in Babylon is illustrated from the history of the Roman Council, over which a deadly owl presided.

units.la: XLI. Vox alia ex Cœlo audita, exitum ex Babylone mandans, patefacit, futurum, ut janua exeundi quandoque aperiatur.
units.tr: XLI. Another voice heard from heaven, commanding departure from Babylon, reveals that it will come to pass that the door of leaving will at some time be opened.

units.la: XLII. Impletum id in Pacificationibus Religiosis ostenditur.
units.tr: XLII. That this has been fulfilled is shown in the religious peace settlements.

units.la: XLIII. Exitum ex Babylone commendant Viri pii & docti, fermentum Pontificium magis magisque expurgantes, & Syncretismo resistentes.
units.tr: XLIII. Pious and learned men urge the departure from Babylon, purging the Papal leaven more and more, and resisting syncretism.

units.la: XLIV. Regum, qui Babylonem oderunt, desolârunt, & carnibus privârunt historia.
units.tr: XLIV. History tells of kings who have made Babylon desolate and stripped her of her flesh.

units.la: XLV. Ipse quoque Imperator, & Reges Hispaniæ, Galliæ, Hungariæ &c. licet amorem Papatûs præ se ferant, Hierarchiam odisse, desolare & carnibus privare pridem cœperunt:
units.tr: XLV. The Emperor himself too, and the kings of Spain, France, Hungary, etc., although they display their love for the Papacy, have for some time begun to hate the Hierarchy, to make it desolate and to strip it of its flesh.
XLVI. And there is hope that they will bring their hatred to completion.

units.la: XLVII. Exitum ex Hierarchica Babylone multùm Concilii Tridentini anathema promoverunt.
units.tr: XLVII. The anathemas of the Council of Trent have greatly promoted departure from the Hierarchical Babylon.

units.la: XLVIII. Separatos à Papatu Schismatis reos non esse cùm aliis argumentis;
units.tr: XLVIII. That those separated from the Papacy are not guilty of schism is asserted with other arguments;

units.la: XLIX. tum ex historia ipsa separationis asseritur.
units.tr: XLIX. and also from the history of the separation itself.

units.la: L. Concilii cujuspiam reformaturi expectatio irrita fuit, & erit semper.
units.tr: L. The expectation of some council that would reform the Church has been vain, and always will be.
LI. All the arguments opposed to the Reformation are set down.

units.la: LII. Vox cælestis vindictam de Babylone sumere, eámque cruciare imperat.
units.tr: LII. A heavenly voice commands that vengeance be taken on Babylon and that she be tormented.

units.la: LIII. Cruciatum Hierarchia exquisitum per scripta & præconia, quibus impietas ejus denudata est, & denudatur quotidie, experta est, & experitur adhuc.
units.tr: LIII. The Hierarchy has experienced, and still experiences, exquisite torment through the writings and proclamations by which its impiety has been, and is every day, laid bare.

units.la: LIV. Falsò Lipsius, aliique studia oppugnantium Papatum ab afrorum positu arcessunt, quem Cælesti inspirationi Spiritus S. ipse tribuit.
units.tr: LIV. Lipsius and others wrongly derive the zeal of those who attack the Papacy from the position of the Africans, which he himself attributes to the heavenly inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: LV. Causa cruciandæ Babylonis ejusmodi insolens ejusdem jactantia, quòd sedeat Regina &c. perhibetur:
units.tr: LV. The cause for tormenting Babylon is said to be her unusual boasting, that she sits as queen, etc.:

units.la: LVI. cujus occasio est ingratitudo populi Babylone exeuntis:
units.tr: LVI. the occasion of which is the ingratitude of the people who came out of Babylon:

units.la: LVII. quæ ipsi Babyloni vires colligendi & insolescendi ansam suppeditavit, & suppeditat adhuc:
units.tr: LVII. which has given, and still gives, Babylon herself the means of gathering strength and an occasion for growing insolent:

units.la: LVIII. quod ex Prophetia Esaiæ de Tyro illustratur.
units.tr: LVIII. which is illustrated from the prophecy of Isaiah about Tyre.
LIX. Thus far God's progress against the Hierarchy

units.la: judicio, finale & decretorium eidem imminere ostendi-
units.tr: has shown that the final and decisive judgment is impending over it, and it is demon-
strated.

units.la: LX. Plagæ novissimæ Babyloni imminentes explicatæ.
units.tr: LX. The last plagues impending over Babylon are explained.

units.la: LXI. Celeritas excidii ejus ab Angelo adumbrata.
units.tr: LXI. The speed of her destruction is foreshadowed by the Angel.

units.la: LXII. Tempus finalis excidii hujus approximans, licet,
units.tr: LXII. The time of this approaching final destruction, although
it can scarcely be defined exactly.

units.la: LXIII. Pontificiorum nonnullorum de imminente Romæ
units.tr: LXIII. Testimonies of some Papists about the impending ruin of Rome are produced.
(continuation)

units.la: LXIV. Ejus potentia & prosperitas præsens judicium
units.tr: LXIV. Her present power and prosperity will not be able to check the divine judgment.
It will not be able to check the divine purpose.

units.la: LXV. Gemina orbis conversio improvisa, à Gentilismo
units.tr: LXV. A twofold conversion of the world, unforeseen: one from Gentilism to Christianity

units.la: ad Christianismum una; à Papismo ad renovationem
units.tr: and the other from Papism to the renewal of Christianity.

units.la: Christianismi altera, fidem de secuturo Babylonis ex-
units.tr: (continuation)
(continuation)

units.la: LXVI. Neque illud obstat, quòd Romæ timendus hostis
units.tr: LXVI. Nor does it stand in the way that no enemy to be feared at Rome appears.
(continuation)

units.la: LXVII. Regum, Mercatorum & Nautarum super Ba-
units.tr: LXVII. The lament of kings, merchants and sailors over the destruction of Babylon.
(continuation)

units.la: LXVIII. Ex quo colligitur, Babylonis excidium cum
units.tr: LXVIII. From this it is gathered that the destruction of Babylon will not be joined with the end of the world.
(continuation)

units.la: LXIX. Locus S. Pauli 2 Thess. ÿ. 8. explicatus.
units.tr: LXIX. The passage of St Paul, 2 Thess. 2:8, is explained.

units.la: LXX. Nec non locus alter Apoc. xix. 19, 20. sententiæ eidem obstare visus.
units.tr: LXX. Another passage, Rev. 19:19, 20, is also seen to stand in the way of this opinion.
LXXI. The lament of kings, merchants and sailors
is set against the shout of the angel, of heaven, of the apostles and prophets calling to rejoicing.
(continuation)

units.la: LXXII. Cœlum, Apostoli & Prophetæ ad jubila invi-
units.tr: LXXII. Who are the heavens, the apostles and the prophets invited to rejoicing?
invited to rejoicing: who are they?

units.la: LXXIII. Eorundem hymnus, seu Hallelujah, ob delec-
units.tr: LXXIII. Their hymn, or Hallelujah, sung on account of the delightful Babylon.
...thus sung concerning Babylon.
LXXIV. Conclusion of the argument and of the work.

units.la: I. Superest postremus Babylonis Magnæ actus, verè tragicus is & horribilis, judicium Divinum, quod ob scortationem cum Regibus & incolis terræ fœdissimam omnium, superbiam, tyrannidem, blasphemias, impuritatem, veneficia & nundinationes spirituales, provocavit, & post impletam iniquitatis mensuram destinato à Deo tempore subitura fuit. Per gradus illud processurum, duplicique casu, quorum prior incipiens vitam & Spiritum, sed afflictissimum illi relinquet: posterior, finalis ille & peremtorius subitò, in solidum, magnáque cum χαρᾷ auferet, absolutum iri, ex filo Prophetiæ S. Johannis de Babylone M. jam suprà Dissert. iij. s. 41–47. pluribus demonstravimus. Atque ut ibi paulò fusiùs dicta, heic contractiora repetam, Babylonis M. casus prior in eo collocatur, quòd post Angelum è Cœlo descendentem, magnáque potestate prædictum, gloriâ suâ totam terram illustrantem, sic Babylon cadere debuit, ut separatis ab eadem fidelibus, & Regibus eandem denudantibus, desolantibus & carnes ejus devorantibus, fieret habitaculum dæmonum & custodia omnis spiritus immundi, avisque immundæ & odiosæ: quódque per continuatam demonstrationem Veritatis ejusdem insolenter licet se jactantis, authoritas, Regnum & felicitas quotidiè magis infringi, debilitari & labefactari, ipsáque talionis lege, duplicatis etiam pœnis multari debuit, donec, ad tempus cessantibus licet ejus fatis, iisque continuata impietate provocatis, ad finale suum exitium approximet. Posterior verò, idémque finalis, cum συνολέθρια ejus conjunctus, in eo consistet, quòd una die, Deo omnipotentiam suam exerente, & impetu eandem prosternente, venient ejus plagæ, mors, luctus, fames & combustio, ita ut in mundo amplius non inveniatur. Hæc ex Apoc.xvii. 1.16. I. 16. XVIII. I. 2. &c. eruta, dedita operâ superius jam explicavimus.
units.tr: I. There remains the last act of Babylon the Great, truly tragic and dreadful: the divine judgment, which she has provoked by her fornication with the kings and the inhabitants of the earth, the most foul of all, by her pride, tyranny, blasphemies, impurity, sorceries and spiritual merchandising. After the measure of her iniquity has been filled, it is to befall her at the time appointed by God. It will proceed by steps and by a double fall. The first, beginning, will leave her life and spirit, but in the most afflicted state. The second, final and sudden, will remove her altogether and completely, with great joy [χαρᾷ], and she will be made an end of. We have shown this at more length above, in Dissertation III, sections 41 to 47, from the thread of the prophecy of St John concerning Babylon the Great. To repeat in brief what was said there more fully: the first fall of Babylon the Great is placed in this, that after an angel comes down from heaven, endowed with great power and lighting the whole earth with his glory, Babylon must fall in such a way that, with the faithful separated from her, and with the kings stripping her bare, laying her waste and devouring her flesh, she becomes a dwelling of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit, and a hold of every unclean and hateful bird. And it must be that, through the continued demonstration of the truth, which she boastfully though insolently claims for herself, her authority, kingdom and prosperity are more and more broken, weakened and shaken, and that she must be punished by the law of retaliation, even with doubled penalties, until, although for a time her fates are at rest, and though provoked by her continued impiety, she draws near to her final destruction. The second, which is the final fall, together with her utter ruin [συνολέθρια], will consist in this: that on one day, when God exerts his omnipotence and overthrows her with force, her plagues will come, death, mourning, famine and burning, so that she is no more found in the world. We have already explained these things in their place above, drawn from Rev. 17:1–16; 1:16; 18:1–2 and following.

units.la: II. Penè superfluum videri potest, ostendere, quemadmodum Divina isthæc judicia Hierarchiam jam appetierint, atque appetitura amplius sint, donec circumacto faextorum ejusdem orbe, novissimum sibi exitium, & Sanctorum omnium jubila maturabit. Cum enim Hierarchiam mensuram implevisse, & implere adhuc omnium abominationum, quas in Babylone M. Spiritus S. notavit, hactenus firmissimè & φθαλμοφανῶς demonstraverimus: ipsa Dei justitia, & impietatis ejusdem vindicatio similis neminem pium cordatúmque dubitare patitur, quin judicium Divinum Babyloni M. denuntiatum, Hierarchiam, abominationum Babylonis convictam, corripere debuerit. Ne tamen lectoris expectationem in postremo isthoc actu destituamus, demonstrandum in præsentiarum suscipimus, Hierarchiam judicium Divinitus Babyloni intentatum, aliquatenus jam subivisse, & porrò subituram esse. Syllogismus talis esto:
units.tr: That assembly which has to some extent already undergone, and will further undergo, the judgement of God declared against Babylon; other things being equal, Babylon the Great is that assembly, which, after the earth was illuminated by the glory of God, by all-kinds of wisdom and by evangelical truth, and after those very kings, who had earlier given their power to the Beast, were persuaded by heavenly truth and recognised that Babylon the Great is what she is, laid her waste, stripped her and deprived her of her flesh; and after the other saints too, with the Reformation instituted and the abominations of Babylon repudiated, deserted her, either leaving her of their own accord or driven out by anathema; and which, after this separation, on account of its demonic doctrines, concerning faith as well as morals, vigorously defended, and its teachers of darkness, active and hateful to many, is, like the dwelling of demons, the prison of every unclean spirit and of every unclean and hateful bird, on account of its impurity, cruelty and rapacity; which the saints torment with continual and vehement demonstration of the truth; and which finally, with the boast of its secure power and infallibility, will hasten its own dreadful and final destruction.

units.la: Ille cœtus judicium Dei Babyloni Divinitus denuntiatum, aliquatenus jam subivit atque porrò subiturus est, adeòque cæteris paribus. Babylon Magna est, quem post terram gloriâ Dei, omnigenâ Sapientiâ & Evangelicâ veritate illustratam, & Reges illi ipsi, qui prius Bestiæ potestatem suam dederant, à Cœlesti veritate perfuasi, agnitum, quòd Babylon Magna sit desolarunt, nudarunt, carnibus privarunt; ipsique etiam Sancti reliqui Reformatione instituta, & Babylonicis abominationibus repudiatis, sive sponte ab ea exeuntes, sive anathematis expulsi deseruerunt: qui post separationem ishanc ob doctrinas dæmoniacas, fidem juxta atque mores concernentes, acriter defensas, doctores tenebrarum strenuos & invisos pluribus, impuritatem, crudelitas litatem & rapacitatem similis est domicilio daemoniorum, custodiae spiritus immundi, avis immundae & invisae omnis: quem Sancti demonstratione veritatis continua & vehemente cruciant: quique denique securâ potestatis & infallibilitatis suae jactantiâ horrendum sibi & finale excidium maturabit.
units.tr: That assembly has already in some measure undergone the judgment divinely announced against Babylon, and will yet undergo it further, and so, other things being equal, Babylon is the Great. She, after the earth has been illumined by the glory of God, by all-embracing wisdom and by evangelical truth, and after those very kings who had earlier given their power to the beast have been persuaded by heavenly truth and have recognised that Babylon is the Great, have laid her waste, stripped her bare and deprived her of her flesh; and after the remaining saints themselves, once the Reformation was instituted and the Babylonish abominations rejected, have forsaken her, either departing from her of their own accord or driven out by anathema; and after that separation, on account of the demonic doctrines, concerning faith as well as morals, which she has fiercely defended, and her many hardy and hateful teachers of darkness, her impurity, cruelty and rapacity, she is like a dwelling of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a hold of every unclean and hateful bird. The saints torment her with a continual and vehement demonstration of the truth; and she, finally, with her boast of secure power and infallibility, will hasten her own dreadful and final destruction.

units.la: Atqui Hierarchiam, seu Clerum Ecclesiae R. dominantem, post terram gloriâ Dei, omnigenâ sapientiâ & veritate Euangelica illustratam, & Reges illi ipsi, qui priùs Bestiae potestatem suam dederant, à Caelesti veritate persuasi, agnitam, quòd Babylon Magna sit, desolârunt, nudárunt, caribus privárunt; ipsique etiam Sancti reliqui, reformatione institura, & Babylonis abominationibus repudiatis, sive sponte ab ea excuntes, sive anathematis expulsi deseruerunt; isque post separationem isthanc ob doctrinas daemoniacas, fidem juxta atque mores concernentes, acriter defensas, doctores tenebrarum strenuos & invisos pluribus, impuritatem, crudelitatem & rapacitatem similis est domicilio daemoniorum, custodiae spiritus immundi, avis immundae & invisae omnis: à Sanctis demonstratione veritatis continua & vehemente cruciatur: denique securâ potestatis & infallibilitatis suae jactantiâ horrendum sibi & finale excidium maturabit.
units.tr: But the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, after the earth has been illumined by the glory of God, by all-embracing wisdom and by evangelical truth, and after those very kings who had earlier given their power to the beast have been persuaded by heavenly truth and have recognised that Babylon is the Great, have laid her waste, stripped her bare and deprived her of her flesh; and after the remaining saints themselves, once the Reformation was instituted and the Babylonish abominations rejected, have forsaken her, either departing from her of their own accord or driven out by anathema; and after that separation, on account of the demonic doctrines, concerning faith as well as morals, which they have fiercely defended, and their many hardy and hateful teachers of darkness, their impurity, cruelty and rapacity, she is like a dwelling of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a hold of every unclean and hateful bird. She is tormented by the saints with a continual and vehement demonstration of the truth; and finally, with her boast of secure power and infallibility, she will hasten her own dreadful and final destruction.

units.la: Ergò Hierarchia seu Clerus Ecclesiae Romanae dominans judicium Dei Babyloni Divinitûs denuntiatum, aliquatenus jam subivit, atque porrò subitura est, adeòque, cæteris paribus, Babylon Magna est.
units.tr: Therefore the hierarchy, or the ruling clergy of the Roman Church, has in some measure already undergone the judgment divinely announced against Babylon, and is yet to undergo it further; and so, other things being equal, Babylon is the Great.

units.la: Propositio harmoniae Propheticam inter de Babylonis Magnae judicio praedictionem, & eventus commemoratos: Assumtio experientiae innititur. Utrique Prophetiam cum eventu ἀπὸ μέρους comparantes, ampliorem lucem fœnerabimur.
units.tr: The proposition rests on the harmony between the prophecy of the judgment of Babylon the Great and the events recalled; the assumption rests on experience. By comparing the prophecy with the event in part (ἀπὸ μέρους), we shall gain a fuller light.

units.la: III. S. Johannes judicium Babylonis M. repræsentaturus vidisse se testatur Angelum de Cœlo descendentem, qui habebat potestatem magnam, & à cujus gloria terra illustrata est. Apoc. xviii. 1. Sive Angelus ille Christus est, efficacem Spiritus sui illuminantis gratiam ex Cœlo in terram demittens, & veritatis cœlitùs patefactæ gloriâ mundum colluströns: sive Spiritus S. propter jus Christi efficax in multorum hominum cordibus, atque id efficiens, ut luce veritatis & Sapientiæ Divinæ atque humanæ omnia collustrentur: sive organa utriusque, Viri Dei & Heroës, gloriæ ejusdem spargendæ & propagandæ intenti, sunt: illud certè constat, judicium Babylonis Magnæ conjunctissimum esse cum illuminatione illa terræ, qua illa gloriâ Dei, omnigenâque adeò Sapientiâ, ea maximè, quæ revelationi Divinæ explicandæ ancillantur, & Veritatis Euangelicæ notitia, qua Babylonis ipsius scortatio, & impietatis detegi debuit, colluströbitur. Convenitque haud dubiè, quod Angelus volans in medio Cœli, habens Euangelium æternum, ad annuntiandum habitantibus in terra, & omni genti, & tribui & linguæ, & populo, dicésque voce magna: Timete Deum, & date ei gloriam, quia venit hora judicii ejus: & adorate eum, qui fecit Cœlum & terram & mare & fontes aquarum, Apoc. xiv. 6. 7. inducitur. Quo Euangelii æterni prædconio audito, alius Angelus secutus est, dicens: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon, Civitas illa magna, v. 8. Unde satis liquet per æterni Euangelii prædconium, tanquam Babylonici excidii causam, Babylonis casum promoveri maturarique debuisse.
units.tr: III. St John testifies that, to portray the judgment of Great Babylon, he saw an angel coming down from heaven, who had great power and by whose glory the earth was illuminated (Apoc. 18:1). Whether that angel is Christ, sending down from heaven the effective grace of his illuminating Spirit and brightening the world with the glory of truth revealed from above; or the Holy Spirit, acting by the right of Christ in the hearts of many people and causing all things to be lit up by the light of truth and of divine and human wisdom; or whether he represents the instruments of both, men of God and heroes intent on spreading and propagating that same glory: this much is certain, that the judgment of Great Babylon is closely bound up with that illumination of the earth, by which the glory of God and every kind of wisdom, especially those disciplines that serve the explanation of divine revelation, and the knowledge of evangelical truth, by which the whistoring of Babylon itself and its impiety ought to be exposed, are brightened. And there is no doubt that it fits that the angel is introduced "flying in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach to those who dwell on the earth, and to every nation and tribe and tongue and people, saying with a loud voice: Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and the fountains of waters" (Apoc. 14:6, 7). When this proclamation of the everlasting gospel had been heard, another angel followed, saying: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, that great city" (v. 8). Whence it is sufficiently clear that by the proclamation of the everlasting gospel, as the cause of Babylon's overthrow, the fall of Babylon ought to be advanced and hastened.

units.la: IV. Neque illud emphasi caret, quòd de illuminatione terræ per Angelum, Propheta tam generaliter loquitur: Καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐφωτίσθη ἐκ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ· Et terra illustrata est à gloria ejus. Sub hac enim generalitate Spiritus S. comprehendere universum illum splendorem voluit, quo res hu-manæ ma-
units.tr: IV. Nor is it without emphasis that the prophet speaks so generally of the illumination of the earth by the angel: "Καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐφωτίσθη ἐκ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ" [And the earth was illuminated by his glory]. For under this generality the Holy Spirit meant to comprehend that whole splendour by which human affairs were illuminated, in every kind of discipline, science and art.

units.la: Tom. II. yyyy manæ superiori Seculo etiam extra religionis Reformationem, in omni disciplinarum, scientiarum & artium genere illustratæ sunt, dum illæ etiam Linguæ in communem usum revocatæ sunt, quæ sub adventum Christi in carnem, in potissima orbis parte publicè obtinuerunt ; in quibus etiam traditum, & ad posteritatis instructionem transmissum est, quicquid Dei providentia Beatissimo isti Seculo, ad omnis Divinæ & humanæ scientiæ cognitionem, uberrimè contulit. Hunc splendorum verè Divinum cùm prædicâssét merito, summisque laudibus tulisset Wigandus, Oratione de bonis & malis Germaniæ, habitâ, Laurentius Surius donorum à Spiritu S. in superiori tempore liberaliter adeò effusorum iniquus æstimator, Comment. Rerum in orbe gestarum ad A. 1566. albis eum dentibus derisit. Sed nota scilicet novercalis illius judicii causa est. Urebat locustam illam, quòd hic splendor, qui toti Mortalium generi tam gratus & jucundus extitit, soli Babyloni, Matri suæ tam funestus & calamitosus acciderit, ut ejus marisca, quæ eousque tam feliciter latuerant, ita in apricum producta sint, ut nulla amplius cerussa se fucari aut obduci patiantur.
units.tr: Tom. II. yyyy human affairs were illuminated in the last century, even outside the Reformation of religion, in every kind of discipline, science and art, while those languages also were restored to common use which, at the coming of Christ in the flesh, had held public sway in the chief part of the world; in which also was handed down, and transmitted for the instruction of posterity, whatever the providence of God most abundantly contributed to that most blessed age for the knowledge of every divine and human science. When Wigand had rightly proclaimed this truly divine splendour and praised it with the highest commendations in his oration on the good and bad things of Germany, Laurentius Surius, an unfair judge of the gifts that the Holy Spirit had so generously poured out in earlier times, mocked him with white teeth in his Commentary on the Events of the World for the Year 1566. But the reason for that stepmotherly judgment is well known. That locust was burning because this splendour, which had proved so welcome and pleasing to the whole human race, had fallen so calamitously and fatally on Babylon alone, its mother, so that her cankers, which had hitherto lain hidden so happily, have been brought out into the open so that they no longer allow themselves to be disguised or covered with white lead.

units.la: V. Lucem splendorémque orientem tenebræ præcedunt. Et utræque oppositæ cognoscuntur penitius. Pari ratione ex tenebris Papatùs splendorem illum, quo tenebra subitò colluttata est, præcedentibus, ipsum splendorem illum cognoscemus rectius. Age igitur, tenebras Papatûs Reformationi prævias, paucis pandamus. Licet enim ex iis, quæ hactenùs de Hierarchia Babylonica diximus, ignorari nequeant, juvabit tamen easdem tum in universum: tum seorsim, prout illæ fidem, ceremonias, cultum externum & gubernationem Ecclesiæ, mediáque ipsa religionis conservandæ obscurârunt, suppressérintque penitùs, compendiaria narratione, eáque magnam partem non tam meis, quàm Gravissimi Theologi, Friderici Spanhemii P. efficacissimis verbis, dignis planè, quæ ex Geneva ejus restituta, cujus pauci forte copiam habent, huc sevocentur, contexta perstringere.
units.tr: V. Darkness goes before the rising light and dawn, and each of two opposites is known more fully by its contrast. In the same way, if we first see the darkness of the Papacy that came before the Reformation, we will recognise more accurately that very light by which the darkness was suddenly shaken off. Let us therefore briefly set out the darkness of the Papacy that preceded the Reformation. What we have said so far about the Babylonian hierarchy may suffice to make it known, but it will be helpful to touch on that darkness in a concise narrative, both in general and in particular, insofar as it obscured and entirely suppressed the faith, ceremonies, external worship and government of the Church and the very means of preserving religion. We will do this largely in the very effective words of the most weighty theologian, Friedrich Spanheim, which are truly worthy to be set down here, woven together from his Geneva Restored, of which perhaps few have a copy.

units.la: VI. Crassæ utique erant tenebræ Ægyptiacæ, quæ palpari etiam poterant: Opacæ erant illæ Cimmeriorum veterum, nullo Sole, lucis strictura nullâ collustratæ specus. Neque tamen illæ comparari possunt cum spissa illa & profunda nocte, qua, Hierarchia universa connitente, totum Ecclesiæ Christianæ Cœlum velut obductum horrebat. Ex quo enim illa mysterio iniquitatis operari, ipséque Supremus Hierarcha se supra omne illud, quod Numen vocatur, efferre, & in Templo Dei sedem suam figere coepit: mox apostasia universalis incessere, religio superstitione, Divinum verbum humanis commentis, cultus idolomaniâ, conscientia fictis terroribus, orbis denique Christianus horrenda tyrannide occupari & pessundari. Tanta inde rei Christianæ vastitas & strages passim secuta est, ut ignoraret penè orbis se Christianum esse, esse aliquod Dei verbum, Religionem ad Deum & conscientiam pertinere. Illud manibus populi excussum, & sub modio abstrusum: hæc ad digitorum articulos, labiorum murmura, Sacrificulorum mugitus, Monachorum crepitacula, claustrales tonsuras, Anachoretarum cilicia, laciniarum, pestinum, crepidarum venerationem, indulgentiarum nundinationes, spectrorum, lemurum & fatuorum ignium aliáque id genus fascina, dementandæ plebi idonea, redacta est. Hic in universum Ecclesiæ ante exortum Euangelii splendorem status fuit.
units.tr: VI. The Egyptian darkness was indeed thick, so thick that it could even be felt. The caves of the ancient Cimmerians were murky, with no sun and no ray of light to brighten them. Yet those cannot be compared with the dense and deep night in which, with the whole hierarchy straining, the whole heaven of the Christian Church lay as if covered over and shuddering. For from the time when the mystery of iniquity began to work, and the Supreme Hierarch began to raise himself above everything called God and to set up his seat in the temple of God, at once a universal apostasy swept in: religion was corrupted by superstition, the divine Word by human inventions, worship by idolatry, conscience by feigned terrors; and at last the Christian world was seized and ruined by a horrible tyranny. From this followed such a devastation and slaughter of the Christian cause everywhere that the world hardly knew it was Christian, that there was some Word of God, or that religion pertains to God and to conscience. That Word was shaken from the hands of the people and hidden under a bushel, and religion was reduced to finger-counting, murmured lip-prayers, the bellowing of little priests, the rattling of monks, cloister tonsures, the hair shirts of anchorites, and the veneration of rags, relics and sandals, the trading of indulgences, and such charms as ghosts, lemures and will-o'-the-wisps, fit for stupefying the common people. Such was the general state of the Church before the rising of the splendour of the Gospel.

units.la: VII. Quæ fides in Ecclesia invaluerit, ex dogmatibus receptis liquet. Hæc verò universa penè non ad amussim verbi Divini, sed ad compendium cleri exacta: illa suppressa, quæ Deum, illa publicata, & veris ac saluta-ri-
units.tr: VII. What faith prevailed in the Church is clear from the doctrines that were accepted. And these were almost all framed not according to the rule of the divine Word, but to the profit of the clergy: those doctrines that set forth God were suppressed, and those that were published and

units.la: Note: marginal notes in the right margin read "Tenebræ Pa-stûsRefor-mationi praevia describuntur tum in uni-versum", "tum in spe-cie, quod ejusdem si-dem & reli-gionis dog-mata:" (partially legible). ribus dogmatibus substituta sunt, quæ hominem homini commendarent, imò quæ hominem supra Deum nefaria, sed utili fraudum architectis impietate efferrent. Hinc Christi Salvatoris officia & beneficia obliterata: gratia Dei velut in triumpho ducta: corruptio hominis, statu puræ naturæ commendato, dissimulata, vel abnegata etiam: salutis gratuitæ canalis occlusus: humani arbitrii idolum erectum: meritorum fiducia inculcata: intercessionum, satisfactionum alienarum & supererogationum cauponatio introducta, pergula excitata, & institoria, in Ecclesia exercita, licitationique à sacris publicanis Sacra & profana, uti abundè demonstravimus, omnia subjecta sunt. Non conscientiis afflictis quæsita pax, sed animis miserorum excussa, fictisque terroribus perculsi animi, obnoxii redditi sunt imposturis, atque id denique addictum pretio terreno est, quod pretium nec habet, nec habere potest. Ne dicam profligata sic pietate & reverentia nominis Dei, meras eásque multiplices blasphemias Papatus, universam ferè fidem contaminâsse: quod de Hierarchia supra quoque probavimus.
units.tr: Note: marginal notes in the right margin read "The darkness that preceded the Reformation is described, first in general," "and then in particular, namely the doctrines of its faith and religion" (partially legible). were put in place of true and salutary doctrines, which commended man to man, indeed which raised man above God by an impiety that was wicked but useful to the architects of frauds. Hence the offices and benefits of Christ the Saviour were obliterated; the grace of God was, as it were, led in triumph; the corruption of man was concealed, or even denied, while a state of pure nature was commended; the channel of free salvation was blocked; the idol of human free will was erected; trust in merits was impressed; a trade in intercessions, satisfactions of others and works of supererogation was introduced, a booth was set up, and a shop was run in the Church; and, as we have amply demonstrated, all things sacred and profane were subjected to auction by sacred publicans. Peace was sought not for afflicted consciences but was beaten out of wretched souls, and minds struck by feigned terrors were made liable to impostures; and finally that was delivered over to earthly price which has no price and cannot have one. Not to mention that, with piety and reverence for the name of God thus cast down, the Papacy's mere and manifold blasphemies have contaminated almost the whole of the faith, as we also proved above concerning the hierarchy.

units.la: VIII. In Ceremonias Papatus superstitio, seu, Epiphanii verbo utar, ἰθελοπεζαπολατρεια mera invasit, candidámque Ecclesiæ primitivæ faciem indignè deturpavit. Quicquid ergò in ceremoniis Judaicis splendidum, puta traditiones, consecrationes, unctiones, benedictiones, purificationes Templi, Pontificatûs & Sacerdotii magnificentia, ac innumera alia; Quicquid in gentilitia superstitione floridum, puta pigmenta & figmenta imaginum, incensatio, cerei, derafio verticum Sacerdotum, Februalia, festa &c. Quicquid in Muhamedica impietate nitidum, veluti Alcorani lingua, Turcis incognita, demurmuratio, lectionis ejusdem promiscuæ prohibitio, religionis violenta propagatio, peregrinationes religiosæ, Monachatûs, jejuniorum fictitia sanctitas; Quicquid in veterum hæreticorum quisquiliis coruscum; Quicquid denique in occupandis, demulcendis hominum oculis, auribus, animis potens, illud omne prudenti in speciem, & ad Judæorum simul ac Gentilium conversionem accommodo, sed infelici tamen consilio Ecclesiasticas in sanctiones infartum, & à Romano Pontifice, ceu vulture Romulejo, magnâ cum veritatis & pietatis jactura interceptum est. Et quod liberum primò erat, id sensim in necessitatem, & post in rationes meriti & expensi coram tribunali Divino abiit.
units.tr: VIII. Into the ceremonies of the Papacy crept a pure superstition, or, to use Epiphanius's word, will-worship [ἐθελοπεζαπολατρεία], and it has shamefully disfigured the bright face of the primitive Church. Whatever is splendid in the Jewish ceremonies, such as the traditions, consecrations, anointings, blessings, purifications of the Temple, the magnificence of the high priesthood and priesthood, and countless other things; whatever is showy in pagan superstition, such as the painting and modelling of images, incense, candles, the shaving of the crowns of priests, the Februalia, festivals and so on; whatever is polished in Muhammadan impiety, such as the muttering of the Qur'an, a language unknown to the Turks, the prohibition of promiscuous reading of the same, the violent spread of religion, religious pilgrimages, monkery, and the feigned sanctity of fasts; whatever glitters in the rubbish of the ancient heretics; and finally whatever is powerful in seizing and soothing men's eyes, ears and minds: all this was, with a prudent appearance and adapted to the conversion of Jews and Gentiles alike, but with an unhappy plan, stuffed into ecclesiastical decrees, and was seized by the Roman Pontiff, like a Romulean vulture, with great loss of truth and piety. And what was at first free gradually became a necessity, and afterwards passed into a reckoning of merit and debit before the divine tribunal.

units.la: IX. Sic ergò Cultus, etiam externus non solùm Ceremoniarum istarum ἀμίξων coagmentatione & μυστηρίας fœdè collutulatus, sed idololatriæ etiam multifariæ, quin Magicæ etiam impietatis pestè correptus corruptúsque est. Pro Christo beata Virgo: pro Deo tutelarium Numinum plaustra, gentili apotheosi postliminio introducta: cadaveribus, ossibus, cineribus, ligno, lapidi tributum, quod Dei solius erat; & illa omnia in societatem fiduciæ, spei, adorationis, cultûs religiosi soli Deo debiti, communi omnium praxi, si non communibus & conspirantibus Doctorum placitis calculisque vocata sunt. Deum inter & B. Virginem provinciæ in diribitorio Romano distributæ; illi rigor justitiæ, huic clementia Diva assignata est: Francisci stigmata, Christi stigmatibus exaquata: Lauretana, Compostellensia, Romana, Montisferratensia & alia id genus fana ac idola, mendacibus præstigiarum & prodigiorum centonibus in summo veneratio-nis fastigio locata, ad quæ ex remotissimis locis excurrere, pars felicitatis, & devotionis supremus apex habebatur. In angustiis, calamitatibus etiam publicis, morbis, pestilentia non amplius ad Deum itum, sed ad legatos & optiones, quibus Pontificum arbitrio & consultis talia commissa ; quorum egregiâ scilicet providentiâ non Regnis tantùm, provinciis, civitatibus, sed & morbis, opificiis, brutis sua præstituta Numina, ad quæ promta accessio, neglecta Dei ipsius accessione, promittebatur. Febri correptis Petronella, morbo comitiali Valentinus, ophtalmiæ Ottilia, odontalgiæ Apollonia, thoracis angustiis Blasius, calculo Liberius, podagræ Wolphgangus, pestilentiæ Sebastianus & Rochus, curatores & averrunci destinati sunt. Pictores Lucam, agricolæ Medardum, rustici Urbanum, vinitores Chilianum, piscatores Christophorum, nautæ Nicolaum, venatores Eustachium, equites Georgium, Carminarii Blasium, Sartores Lucium, fabri Eligium, textores Severum, moli- nores Arnoldum, figuli Guarum, alii alios artis suæ antesignanos & vexillarios venerabantur. Bobus Pelagius, equis & vaccis Eulogius, ovibus Wendelinus, anseribus Gallus, canibus Hundbertus, porcis Antonius, muribus Nicasius, alii aliis & capitibus & curis Romanæ curiæ instituto addicti sunt. Deus interim solio suo excussus, & cum Jove Homerico in Æthiopiam convivatum relegatus est. Tales scilicet Deastros patronos habere, venerari, eorum delubris, idolis, iconibus oscula figere, vota nuncupare, anathemata suspendere, primas inter curas pietatis erat. Francisci cuculllo vestiri, claustrali disciplína macerari, hæc verò recta in Cœlum via, & aureolæ promerendæ indubius callis habebatur. Reliquiarum quinetiam exoletis pudendisque mercibus, adeò simplicitati populi illusum est, ut non illa duntaxat, quæ specie aliqua obtrudi poterant, sed ea etiam, quæ ad mera ludibria comparata erant, obtruderentur. Non solùm Mariæ pesten, Elifabethæ peplus, Eliæ zona, Judæ laqueus, Johannis crepidæ, & alia id genus crepundia; sed etiam Michaëlis Archangeli pugio, Gabrielis pennæ, Josephi serram reciprocantis, vel idem retorquentis spiritus, Nicodemi scilicet chirotheca exceptus, diducto sipario, velut in scena ostendebantur: ut complura alia omittam, quibus projecti & prostituti pudoris homines plebis Christianæ stoliditati illuserunt miserè. Multorum denique, qui nunquam dias luminis hujus auras salutârunt, reliquiæ auro gemmisque variegatæ, cultuíque expositæ sunt: multi Sanctorum Geryones & Briarei redditi, quibus capita, ora, brachia, pectora complura affixta sunt; fucatæque ejusmodi merces protrusæ innumeræ sunt. Nihil de Magica impietate dicam, qua universum cultum externum aspersum & incestatum fuisse, & hodie- que esse, supra demonstravimus.
units.tr: IX. Thus worship, even external worship, was not only foully smeared with the unmixable joining of these ceremonies and mysteries [μυστηρίας], but was also seized and corrupted by a plague of manifold idolatry, and even of magical impiety. In place of Christ the blessed Virgin was put; in place of God the wagons of guardian deities, introduced by the pagan apotheosis as a return; to cadavers, bones, ashes, wood and stone was given what belonged to God alone; and all these things were called into fellowship of trust, hope, adoration and religious worship due to God alone, by the common practice of all, if not by the shared and agreeing opinions and votes of the teachers. Between God and the blessed Virgin, provinces were distributed as in the Roman dispensary: to God was assigned the rigour of justice, to the Virgin the mercy of the goddess. The stigmata of Francis were made equal to the stigmata of Christ. The shrines and idols of Loreto, Compostela, Rome, Montserrat and others of that kind, placed at the summit of veneration by patchwork of lying tricks and prodigies, were regarded as the chief part of happiness and devotion, and people ran to them from the most distant places. In straits, in public calamities, diseases and plague, men no longer went to God, but to the envoys and officials to whom such matters had been committed at the will and discretion of the Pontiffs; by whose excellent foresight not only kingdoms, provinces and cities, but also diseases, trades and beasts were assigned their own appointed deities, to whom ready access was promised, while access to God himself was neglected. For those seized by fever, Petronella was appointed as healer and averter; for epilepsy, Valentinus; for eye disease, Ottilia; for toothache, Apollonia; for tightness of the chest, Blasius; for stone, Liberius; for gout, Wolfgang; for plague, Sebastian and Roch. Painters venerated Luke, farmers Medard, labourers Urban, vintners Kilian, fishermen Christopher, sailors Nicholas, hunters Eustace, knights George, carders Blasius, tailors Lucius, smiths Eligius, weavers Severus, millers Arnold, potters Guarus; each venerated others as the forerunners and standard-bearers of his art. Pelagius was given to oxen, Eulogius to horses and cows, Wendelin to sheep, Gall to geese, Hundbert to dogs, Anthony to pigs, Nicasius to mice; and others were assigned by the custom of the Roman curia to other diseases and cares. Meanwhile God was thrown from his throne and, like the Homeric Jove, banished to a feast among the Ethiopians. To have such patrons of deities, to venerate them, to press kisses on their shrines, idols and images, to make vows, and to hang up offerings, was counted the first concern of piety. To be clothed in the cowl of Francis, to be worn down by cloistered discipline, was regarded as the straight road to heaven and the sure path to earning a crown of glory. Moreover, with obsolete and shameful wares of relics, the common people were so mocked in their simplicity that not only those things which could be palmed off with some plausibility were foisted on them, but even those made purely for ridicule. Not only the veil of Mary, the robe of Elizabeth, the girdle of Elijah, the noose of Judas, the sandals of John, and other trinkets of that kind; but also the dagger of the Archangel Michael, the wings of Gabriel, the saw of Joseph, or the spirit that turns it back and forth, and the glove of Nicodemus were shown as on a stage with the curtain drawn back. I will omit many other items with which shameless and abandoned men miserably mocked the stupidity of the Christian people. Finally, the relics of many who never breathed the air of this light were displayed, decked with gold and gems, for veneration; many were made into monsters like Geryon and Briareus, with several heads, faces, arms and breasts attached; and countless such wares were pushed forward. I will say nothing of the magical impiety by which, as we have shown above, the whole external worship was spattered and defiled, and still is today.

units.la: X. Gubernationem inprimis dominatio invasit & intoleranda tyrannis, quæ Thologiæ Romanensis erat acropolis & Helena illa, cui uni & falsitate in dogmatis, & superstitione in ceremoniis, & idololatria ac Magia in cultu externo novæ Babylonis architecti litárunt. Sic ergò Christo Petrum, Petro vicarium caput ferè Italicum substitutum est; & Homo ille peccati, Babylonius Rex supremus, populi universi libertatem, Episcoporum mitras, Principum, Regum, Cæsarum sceptra, diademata, coronas, ipsum denique verbum Dei, Christum, adeóque quicquid in Cœlo & terra venerabile est, libidini dominationis suæ subjecit. Atque occupato semel sublimi illo fastigio, pro arbitrio suo religionem Christianam corrupit, cultum voluntarium constituit, conscientias constrinxit, gratias distribuit, Cœlos clausit, inferos aperuit, Imperatorum, Regum, Principum jura, sceptra, capita rexit, totum orbem obnoxium, vectigalem sibi, & prodigiosa Episcopi Urbis in Orbis Monarcham metamorphosi, ex Christiano Romanum reddidit; denique non secus ac callidus ille Europæ bajulus, orbem è litore inalti flimum pelagus nihil sentientem deduxit, donec ex flamine Latiali inglorio factus
units.tr: X. Government was above all seized by domination and intolerable tyranny. This was the citadel of Roman theology and that Helen alone, for whose sake the architects of the new Babylon offered their sacrifices of falsehood in doctrine, superstition in ceremonies, and idolatry and magic in external worship. Thus Peter was substituted for Christ, and an almost Italian head, Peter's vicar, was substituted for Peter. That man of sin, the supreme Babylonian king, subjected to his lust for domination the freedom of the whole people, the mitres of bishops, the sceptres, diadems and crowns of princes, kings and emperors, the very Word of God, Christ himself, and so whatever is venerable in heaven and earth. Once he had seized that lofty summit, he corrupted the Christian religion as he pleased, established voluntary worship, bound consciences, distributed graces, shut the heavens and opened the depths. He ruled the rights, sceptres and heads of emperors, kings and princes, and made the whole world subject and tributary to himself. By the monstrous metamorphosis of the bishop of the city into the monarch of the world, he made the Christian into the Roman. Finally, like that crafty ferryman of Europe, he led the world away from the shore into the deep sea, where it felt nothing, until from an inglorious Latian priest of Phoebus he became (Anius-like)

units.la: Rex Anius, Rex idem hominum Phœbique Sacerdos, caput Cœlo efferret, imperiúmque adeò sibi, non ulla quidem quod mireris, vi, sed sola fama & opinione hominum constans, vindicaret. Sic demùm Sedis Romanæ Præsules, postquam se fortunæ & flagrantissimæ imperandi libidini permisère, naturam & officium suum dedidicêre, & per licita atque illicita fœdati, Divina & humana inter dominationis flagitia, & servitutis instrumenta habuêre. Hæc & à Spiritu S. prædicta varie, & experiundo cognita in historia Papatûs, atque hoc ipso Opere procedente, sic demonstravimus, ut ea non nisi præfractus, & tantorum decorum sibi ipse conscius, inficias ire posset.
units.tr: King Anius, king of men and priest of Phoebus alike, raised his head to heaven and claimed for himself an empire, not indeed one to be wondered at for its force, but one resting only on the fame and opinion of men. So at last the prelates of the Roman See, after they had surrendered themselves to fortune and to the most burning lust for command, unlearned their own nature and duty. Defiled by lawful and unlawful means, they made divine and human things into instruments of their domineering crimes and of servitude. These things, foretold variously by the Holy Spirit and known through experience in the history of the Papacy, we have demonstrated in this very work as it proceeds, in such a way that no one, unless stubborn and conscious to himself of such great offences, could deny them.

units.la: XI. Jam & media ipsa religionis verae cognoscendæ & conservandæ suppressa sunt, ut facilius obscurata & tantum non deleta religione salutifera, Christianæ plebi Romanensia placita, & placitorum eorum supremus apex, αὐτοκράτωρ dictatoria potestate, imperari obtrudique possent. Sicut ergò nocturni grassatores lucem extinguere solent: sic Romani Pontifices lucem verbi Divini, quod solum regenerationis incorruptibile semen est, extinguere penitus curæ habuerunt. Hinc adeò pericula ex lectione Scripturæ emergentia exaggerari, conscientiis scrupuli super ejusdem lectione anxiè injici, Dominici, Franciscii, Veronicæ acta inculcari, Legendæ aureæ dictæ, cùm ferreæ essent, febrilibus & anilibus deliriis confui, farciri, & publicè prælegi. Historia Euangelica in theatrales operas, saeratissima passionis Dominicæ memoria in scenicos actus converså, & risu, quem vocant Pascbali, quo luctus Quadragesimali jejunio contractus, abstergi sueyit, terminata est. Si quandoque S. Biblia attingerentur, statim illa sacra sementis laciniosis & spinosis Seraphicorum Doctorum, Lombardi, Comestoris, Thomæ, Scoti, Bonaventuræ, Durandi, Occami, aliorúmque id genus hominum, verborum barbarie, & rerum inutilium otiosa subtilitate certantium, commentationibus & interpretationibus, velut in herba strangulabatur. Certè Philippus Melanchton, Vir candidissimus, testis est, diebus Dominicis variis in locis, pro thematibus Dominicalibus, inde à Caroli M. ætate in cathedris Ecclesiasticas introductis, Ethica Aristotelis publicè populo prælecta, & à se Tubingæ in agro Wirtenbergico audita esse. Tiguri quoque, & alibi passim, ex Thoma & Scoto conciones habitæ sunt. Et jactatum à multis est, tametsi S. literæ intercidissent, ex Platonis, Aristotelis, Senecæ, Plutarchi, aliorúmque id genus scriptorum monumentis, viam ad salutem satis superque erui posse. Eò tandem res Christiana, temporum illorum calamitate, redacta est, ut Abbas quidam Neuhusianus, in contermino Vangionibus coenobio, diserte professus fuerit, ni Lutherus grassanti superstitioni se opposuisset, futurum fuisse, ut Monachi homines jumentorum instar præsepibus alligarent, & fœnum comesse docerent. Adeo nulla unquam potestas sua potentia ad impotentiam superbiùs isto hominum genere usa fuit.
units.tr: XI. Now the very means of knowing and preserving the true religion have also been suppressed, so that, with saving religion obscured and almost destroyed, the doctrines of the Romanists and their supreme summit, the self-ruler with dictatorial power, could be imposed and forced upon the Christian people more easily. Just as nocturnal robbers are accustomed to extinguish the light, so the Roman Pontiffs took care to extinguish utterly the light of the divine Word, which alone is the incorruptible seed of regeneration. Hence the dangers arising from reading Scripture were exaggerated, scruples were anxiously cast into consciences concerning its reading, and the deeds of Dominic, Francis and Veronica were pressed upon them. The so-called Golden Legends, which were in fact iron, were stitched together, stuffed with feverish and old-wives' ravings, and publicly read aloud. The Gospel history was turned into theatrical shows, and the most sacred memory of the Lord's passion was turned into scenic acts, and the end was a laughter they call Paschale, by which they were accustomed to wipe away the grief contracted in the Lenten fast. Whenever the Holy Bible was touched upon, at once that holy seed was choked in the bud, as it were, by the tangled and thorny commentaries and interpretations of the seraphic doctors, Lombard, Comestor, Thomas, Scotus, Bonaventure, Durandus, Ockham, and others of that kind, who vied with one another in barbarous words and idle subtlety about useless things. Certainly Philip Melanchthon, a most upright man, is a witness that on various Sunday themes, in various places, from the time of Charlemagne when such things were introduced into the ecclesiastical chairs, Aristotle's Ethics was publicly read to the people, and that he himself heard it at Tübingen in the Württemberg country. At Zurich too, and elsewhere everywhere, sermons were delivered from Thomas and Scotus. And it has been boasted by many that, even if the sacred letters had perished, a way to salvation could be drawn sufficiently and more than sufficiently from the monuments of Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch and other writers of that kind. To such a point the Christian cause had been reduced by the calamity of those times that a certain abbot of Neuhausen, in the monastery bordering on the Vangiones, openly professed that unless Luther had opposed himself to the raging superstition, it would have come about that the monks, like beasts of burden, would tie men to their mangers and teach them to eat hay. So no power ever used its might for impotence more arrogantly than this class of men.

units.la: XII. Verbi Divini rectè intelligendi adminicula sunt bonæ literæ, Linguæ, Originales inprimis, & artes liberales, earúmque usus sobrius. Harum etiam studia præfocata sunt, contra barbaries introducta, & stupor omni arte promotus est. Authores Scholastici, sic Melchior Canus ipse Loc. Comm. pag. 59. queritur, quadringentis integris annis solam editionem Latinam retinuerunt, quippe Linguæ Græcæ & Hebraicæ nullam habuerunt peritiam. Udalricus Zasius in funere Cæs. Maximil. p. 8. fatetur, barbariem ducentis & amplius annis fœda tyrannide invasisse, & omnia oppressisse. Claudius Espencæus Comment. in Tit. 3. testatur, eam inter Clericos grafsatam esse linguarum originalium ignorantiam & barbariem, ut in Latinis authoribus Græcè nosse suspectum fuerit, Hebraicè propè hæreticum. In explicandis proin vocibus Hebraicis, quàm turpitur se dederint Magistri illi nostri, multis equidem ostendi posset.
