Vel ex uno Guilhelmo Durando, at quanto Doctore illo ! vocem Hebraicam Alleluja in Rationali Div. offic. sol. 58. explicante, conjecturam capiamus. Est Alleluja, sic ille, Hebraicum nomen : vocabulum signidem significans potiùs, quàm exprimens ineffabile gaudium ab hac vita peregrinum &c. Cujus verbi expositio secundùm Innocentium III. ex ÿ. Psalmo habetur, cui cùm Alleluja præmittatur, in titulo, statim Psal. exponendo titulum, incipit, Laudate pueri Dominum. Unde secundùm eum Halleluja interpretatur, Laudate pueri Dominum. Augustinus verò sic exponit: Al, id est, salvum: le, id est, me: lu, id est, fac: jah, id est, Domine. Hieronymus sic: Alle, id est, cantate: lu, id est, laudem: ja, id est, ad Dominum. Gregorius sic: Alle, Pater, lu Filius, ja, Spiritus S. Vel: Alle, id est, lux, lu, id est, vita, ja, id est, salus. Magister Petrus Antisiodorensis sic: Al, id est, Altissimus: le, id est, levatus in cruce: lu, id est, lugebant Apostoli: jah, id est, jam surrexit. Petrus Manducator dicit super Apocalypsin, & Augustinus in glossa Psalterii, quòd alla verbum est imperativi modi, & sonat allelu, id est, laudate, ja, id est, universalem, vel ja, invisibilem, scilicet, Deum &c. Neque melioribus fatis gavisam esse Hellada, idem Durandus documentum præbet, quando eodem Divinorum officiorum libro, vocem Græcam ἁμαλοῦ, derivat à ςω, quod est, cum, & βόλ@ sententia: quòd (symbolum nempe Apostolicum) compositum fuit ex diversis verbis Apostolorum: sicut pueri in festivis convenientes, offerre solent bolos, id est frusta carnium & panis, quæ in unum collecta, symbolum vocantur, id est, collectio minutiarum. Sic Glossator decretorum Papalium Dist. 15. Apocryphum ab ἀπὸ de & κρύπτω secretum, derivat. Cornicum quoque oculos confixit Monachus ille, qui vocem Græcam Ἀπακάλυψις ab ἀπὸ re, & clipsón, velo deduxit. Satis nugarum. Notum omnibus est celebre temporum illorum apophtegma, quod Accursio authori refertur acceptum: Græca sunt, legi non possunt. Neque Latinæ Linguæ studium apud Vœjovis Latini clientes tutum satis erat. Terrebat eos exemplum Hieronymi, cujus lumbos κατ' ὀναρ dæmon dedolavit, quòd Ciceroni addictior esset. De quo sic Erasmus ad Epist. Hieron. de custodienda Virg. ad Eustachium scribit: Hæc est illa fabula, quam memoriter etiam tenent omnes ii, qui ne verbum quidem unquam legerunt in scriptis Hieronymianis. Vapulavit, inquiunt, Hieronymus, quòd Ciceronem legerit. Ac mira quadam religione sic ab omnibus bonis abstinent literis, ut nec attingant, ne forte impudenter incidant in aliquod verbum Ciceronis, & cum Hieronymo vapulent: & tum sibi videntur Apostolis proximi, si quàm spurcissimè loquantur. Hinc Vatinianum in literas & literatós odium æstuavit. Francisçum Petrarcham, scriptorem doctissimum, palam Magum appellárunt, eò quòd Virgilium legisset, uti in vita ejus Andreas Schraderus testatur. Hinc tot calumniarum imbres, convitiorum plaustra, imprecationum fulmina, quibus à Monachis, sanctæ inscitiæ suæ (sic appellabant) tenacissimis, Erasmus Roterodamus impetitus & obrutus fuit. Ipsos Pontifices RoRomanos multos adeò illiteratos fuisse, ut etiam Grammaticam ignorárint, Alphonsus de Castro adv. hær. lib. j. cap. 4. queritur. Plerorumque omnium animos ineptum illud, sed ætate ea haud indignum Johannis Dullardi axioma: Quantò eris melior Grammaticus, tantò pejor Theologus, occupavit.
units.tr: XII. The aids to understanding the divine Word rightly are good letters, languages, above all the original tongues, and the liberal arts, used with sobriety. The study of these too was stifled, barbarism was introduced in opposition, and stupidity was promoted in every art. The Scholastic authors, as Melchior Cano himself complains in his Loci Communes, p. 59, for four hundred whole years retained only the Latin edition, since they had no skill at all in Greek and Hebrew. Ulrich Zasius, in his Funeral of Emperor Maximilian, p. 8, confesses that barbarism had invaded for more than two hundred years with a foul tyranny and had oppressed everything. Claude d'Espence, in his Commentary on Titus 3, testifies that ignorance of the original languages and barbarism had spread among the clergy, so that to know Greek in Latin authors was considered suspicious, and to know Hebrew was almost heretical. In explaining Hebrew words, how shamefully those masters of ours went about it could be shown at length. Let us gauge it from one man alone, William Durandus, and what a doctor he was! When he explains the Hebrew word Alleluia in his Rationale of the Divine Offices, fol. 58, he says: Alleluia is a Hebrew name, a word signifying rather than expressing the ineffable joy that is a stranger to this life, etc. The explanation of this word, according to Innocent III, is found in Psalm 9, where since Alleluia is put before it in the title, straightaway, in expounding the title, the psalm begins, Praise the Lord, children. Hence, according to him, Halleluia is interpreted as Praise the Lord, children. Augustine, however, explains it thus: Al, that is, save; le, that is, me; lu, that is, make; jah, that is, Lord. Jerome thus: Alle, that is, sing; lu, that is, praise; ja, that is, to the Lord. Gregory thus: Alle, Father; lu, Son; ja, Holy Spirit. Or: Alle, that is, light; lu, that is, life; ja, that is, salvation. Master Peter of Auxerre thus: Al, that is, Most High; le, that is, lifted up on the cross; lu, that is, the Apostles mourned; jah, that is, now he has risen. Peter Manducator says on the Apocalypse, and Augustine in the gloss on the Psalter, that alla is a word of the imperative mood and sounds like allelu, that is, praise; ja, that is, the universal, or ja, the invisible, namely God, etc. That Hellas also did not rejoice in a better lot, the same Durandus gives proof when, in the same book of the divine offices, he derives the Greek word ἁμαλοῦ [σύμβολον] from σύν [with] and βόλος [throw], the sense being that the creed (namely the Apostles' Creed) was composed from various words of the Apostles, just as children who gather at festivals are accustomed to bring bolos, that is, scraps of meat and bread, which, collected together, are called a symbol, that is, a collection of small pieces. So the glossator of the Papal decretals, Dist. 15, derives apocryphum from ἀπό [from] and κρύπτω [hide], meaning secret. That monk also put out the eyes of crows who derived the Greek word Ἀποκάλυψις from ἀπό [from] and καλύπτω [cover]. Enough of trifles. It is well known to everyone that the famous saying of those times, which is reported as received from the author Accursius, is: Greek things cannot be read. Nor was the study of Latin safe enough among the clients of the Latin Vejovis. The example of Jerome terrified them, whose loins a demon thrashed in a dream because he was too devoted to Cicero. Erasmus writes about this in his note on Jerome's letter On Keeping Virginity, to Eustochium: This is that story which all those remember word for word who have never read a single word in the writings of Jerome. Jerome, they say, was beaten because he read Cicero. And with a strange kind of piety they so abstain from all good letters that they do not even touch them, lest they should happen shamelessly to fall upon some word of Cicero and be beaten with Jerome; and then they seem to themselves close to the Apostles if they speak as filthily as possible. Hence a hatred of letters and literary men boiled up in Vatinius. They openly called Francesco Petrarch, a most learned writer, a magician, because he had read Virgil, as Andreas Schrader testifies in his life. Hence came so many showers of slander, wagonloads of insults, and thunderbolts of curses, by which Erasmus of Rotterdam was attacked and overwhelmed by the monks, most tenacious of their holy ignorance (as they called it). Alphonsus de Castro, in Against Heresies, book 1, chapter 4, complains that many of the Roman Pontiffs were so unlettered that they did not even know grammar. That foolish saying of John Dullard, which in that age was not unworthy, took hold of the minds of almost all: The better a grammarian you are, the worse a theologian you will be.

units.la: XIII. Sed & Philosophiæ sobriæ, Theologiæ ancillantis usus omnis in illa temporum nocte exoleverat. Aristotelis philosophemata se sectari, præferebant ferè omnes. Quibus Ludovicus Vives de causis corrupt. art. lib. j. sic merito insultat: Quid dicitis, Aristotelem disputando vos victuros? Ne juretis ipsi, ego id pro vobis dejerabo, & quidem perfanctè. Nam quas artes vos modò exomniáftis, quas nugas, & quidem ex illius, ut putatis dogmatibus, ipse, si revivisceret, non intelligeret, ac ne suos quidem libros, uti vos explicatis. In Dialecticis cavillationibus omne ævum consumi consuêsse, etiam Æneas Sylvius Epist. 165. sic queritur: Maximum autem hujus (Viennensis) Gymnasii vitium est, quòd nimis diutinam operam in Dialectica, nimiúmque temporis in re non magni fructús terunt. Qui Magisterii artium titulo decorantur, hac una in arte maximè examinantur; quibus omne studium in elenchis est, vanisque cavillationibus, solidi haud quicquam. Juvabit etiam Bullingerum nostrum, Divinarum juxta atque humanarum artium peritissimum, sic de Philosophiæ studio in Scholis Pontificiorum recepto quiritantem audire. Et ut nonnihil, sic ille, hujus negotii attingam, nonne Academiæ, quas hodie Universitates vocant, corruptissimæ sint? Quid enim in his audias aliud, quàm Genus, Species, Differentia, Proprium, Accidens, Individuum, Subsistentia, tia, Quantitas, Propositio, Sorites currit, & Plato disputat? Nullus interim simplicium vocum prædicabilium, Prædicamentorum aut Propositionum, aut ullarum præceptionum dialecticarum demonstratur usus. Hinc quoque sine fructu disputatur ab adolescentibus, an definitio generis sit bona: quæ tamen quæstio nonnihil conferret ad definitionum naturam rectè cognoscendam, si methodo agerent disputatores. Stultiores & ineptiores sunt illæ quæstiones, utrum omne animal fuerit in arca Noë? An Logica sit de primis, an secundis intentionibus? Quomodo differant hæ propositiones: Romæ venditur piper, & piper venditur Romæ? An vera Propositio: Nullus & Nemo mordent se in sacco? An homo mortuus possit celebrare Missam? An consequentia bona, annon bona: Tu differs ab Ente: Ergò tu non differs ab Ente? Utrum bona sit consequentia: Deus est: Ergò baculus stat in angulo? Utrum omne impossibile sit concedendum? Prælegitur Petrus Hispanus, infelix & jejunus Dialectices Magister. Prælegitur Porphyrii isagoge elegans quidem, sed malè reddita & expositä. Prælegitur denique Aristotelis organon nobilissimi hac in re artificis: sed, si rediret Aristoteles, non agnosceret illam, qua utuntur, versionem tam affabrè exornatam hujuscemodi flosculis: Quoniam, quandoquidem igitur, &c. Utuntur interpretibus sive expositoribus putidissimis, Tartareto, Bricoto, Scoto & Capulatis quibusdam ter quaterque ineptissimis. His fraudantur, frustrantur & seducuntur optima ingenia. Nam nullus vel ex præceptoribus, vel ex discipulis genuinam authoris optimi mentem ex talibus commentatoribus assequitur. Et quod majori cum detrimento studiorum conjunctum est, novator vator protinus dicitur, quisquis studia juvare, & sin‑ ceriores Aristotelis expositores, Themistium, Alex‑andrum, Boëtium, Argyropylum, Stapulensem, ac hujus ordinis alios eruditos viros proferre in me‑dium cupit.
units.tr: XIII. But the whole practice of sober philosophy, serving as handmaid to theology, had also withered away in that night of the times. Almost everyone professed to follow the philosophical teachings of Aristotle. Ludovicus Vives rightly mocks them for this in On the Causes of the Corruption of the Arts, book 1: What do you say? That you will win by disputing with Aristotle? Do not swear to it yourselves; I will swear it for you, and most solemnly too. For the arts you have now invented, and the trifles, which you think come from his doctrines, he himself, if he came back to life, would not understand, nor even his own books as you explain them. Æneas Sylvius also complains in Epistle 165 that the whole age was spent on dialectical quibbling: The greatest fault of this (Vienna) gymnasium is that they waste too long a time on dialectic, and too much time on a thing of no great profit. Those who are adorned with the title of Master of Arts are examined most of all in this one art; all their zeal is for refutations and empty cavilling, and there is nothing solid in it. It will also be pleasing to hear our Bullinger, most skilled in divine and human arts, complaining thus about the study of philosophy as received in the schools of the Papists: And to touch somewhat on this matter: are not the academies, which today they call universities, most corrupt? For what else do you hear in them but Genus, Species, Difference, Property, Accident, Individual, Subsistence, Quantity, Proposition, the Sorites runs, and Plato disputes? Meanwhile no use of simple predicables, categories, propositions, or any dialectical precepts is shown. Hence also young men dispute without profit whether the definition of a genus is good; yet this question would contribute something to knowing the nature of definitions correctly, if the disputants proceeded by method. Stupider and more foolish are those questions: whether every animal was in Noah's ark? Whether logic is about first or second intentions? How do these propositions differ: "Pepper is sold in Rome" and "Pepper is sold in Rome"? Is this proposition true: "No one and nobody bites himself in a sack"? Can a dead man celebrate Mass? Is this consequence good or not good: "You differ from being; therefore you do not differ from being"? Is this consequence good: "God is; therefore a stick stands in the corner"? Must every impossibility be conceded? Peter of Spain is read, an unhappy and dry master of dialectic. Porphyry's Isagoge is read, elegant indeed but badly rendered and explained. Finally Aristotle's Organon is read, by that most noble craftsman in this matter; but if Aristotle returned, he would not recognise the version they use, so elaborately decked out with such flowers: "Since, therefore, etc." They use the most filthy interpreters or expositors, Tartaretus, Bricot, Scotus, and certain Capulati, three and four times most foolish. By these the best minds are cheated, frustrated and led astray. For neither teacher nor pupil grasps the genuine mind of the best author from such commentators. And, what is joined with greater loss to studies, whoever wishes to help the studies and bring forward the purer expositors of Aristotle, Themistius, Alexander, Boethius, Argyropylus, Stapulensis, and other learned men of this sort, is at once called an innovator.

units.la: XIV. Talis igitur, bella scilicet Philosophia, cum rebus sacris commixta, Theologiam tandem Scholasti‑cam Scripturae Sacrae oppositam conflavit, & in arce Ecclesiae collocavit. Trithemius Abbas Spanheimensis in Petro Abaelardo Dialectico, qui circa A. MCL. vixit, haec verba habet: Ex hoc tempore Philosophia secula‑ris sacram Theologiam sua curiositate inutili fraudare coepit. Et Nicolaus Beroaldus, Sorbonicus doctor Catal. test. lib. xvj. sic queritur: Sophisticis nugis arcanae coelestesque literae jam diu nimium depravatae sunt & obrutae. Non enim studiorum ingenia exacuunt istae captiunculae & tricae spinosae, sed mentis succum omnem exhauriunt. Cornelius Musfius, Episcopus Bitontinus, Comment. ad Rom. 6. gravem etiam his verbis querelam consignavit: Divinae Scripturae olim quanto damno omnium negligebantur? Vigebat spinosa & molesta nescio quae Theologia, de instantibus, relationibus, quidd​itatibus, formalitatibus: itemque haec omnia Syllogismis arctè contortis, & humanis duntaxat argutiis, quae procul dubio qua authoritate recipiuntur, ea & refelli possunt, pertractabantur. Is sublimis Theologus habebatur, qui majora portenta pro suis traditiunculis effingere sciret; pretiisque pars erat gloriola inanis, non intelligi grandia illa verba, quae altosupercilio inter mulierculas de sacris literis philosophantes trutinabant. Juraverant universi verbi Divini duces in verba Magistrorum. Hinc sexcentae sectae, Thomistae, Scotistæ, Occamistæ, Bacconistæ, Albertistæ, Ægidiani, Alexandrini, ô scelus! Posthabebantur Euangelia, Epistolæ, Christiana Philosophia delitescebat, à paucissimis tractabatur, sed frigidè, ne dicam infincerè. Cornelius Agrippa de Vanit. Scient. cap. 97. eandem Theologiam ait à Parisiensi Sorbona mixtione quadam ex Divinis eloquiis & philosophicis rationibus, tanquam ex Centaurorum genere biformem disciplinam conflatam, & paulatim in sophismata delapsam esse, dum recentiores isti Theosophistæ ac verbi Dei Cauponatores, qui nonnisi emto titulo Theologi sunt, ex tam sublimi facultate logomachiam effecerint. Sed & Melchior Canus Loc. Theolog. lib. viij. 1. disertè sic scribit: Efficitur, quod ego magno cum assensu omnium dicere me video, miseram esse Scholæ doctrinam, quæ se titulo Magisterii defendat: miseram etiam, quæ detracta Scripturæ Sacræ authoritate, syllogismis contortis de rebus Divinis philosophatur. Et lib. ix. 1. id egisse Diabolum scribit, quod sine lachrymis dicere non possit, ut, quo tempore adversus ingruentes hæreses in Germania oportebat Scholæ Theologos optimus esse armis instructos, nihil prorsus haberent, nisi arundines longas, levia puerorum arma. Sic est, Cane; nisi quòd canina facundia hæresin insignis, Cœlestem doctrinam, non ex Centauris illis Agrippæ, sed ex Scripturæ, cui contortis Syllogismis authoritatem Scholæ vestræ Doctores detraxisse ingenuè profitebare, penetralibus haustam. Neque proin nulla causa est, cur eruditi Apocalypseos Interpretes, Theologiam hancce portendi astruerent ab Angelo primo, phialam suam in terram effundente: unde ἐλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρὸν, ulcus malum & malignum in homines habentes signaturam bestiæ & imaginem ejus adorantes,
units.tr: XIV. Such, then, was philosophy, plainly mixed with sacred things, which at last fused Scholastic theology, opposed to Holy Scripture, and set it up in the citadel of the Church. Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, in his account of Peter Abelard, the dialectician, who lived around 1150, has these words: From this time secular philosophy began to defraud sacred theology by its useless curiosity. And Nicolaus Beroaldus, doctor of the Sorbonne, in Catalogue of Witnesses, book 16, complains thus: The hidden and heavenly letters have long since been far too corrupted and overwhelmed by sophistical trifles. For these little captious tricks and thorny snares do not sharpen the wits of students, but drain every bit of the juice of the mind. Cornelius Musfius, Bishop of Bitonto, in his Commentary on Romans 6, has also recorded a serious complaint in these words: How much loss did all men once suffer from neglecting Divine Scripture? There flourished a thorny and troublesome theology, I know not what, about instants, relations, quiddities, formalities; and all these things were handled with tightly twisted syllogisms and merely human subtleties, which undoubtedly could be refuted by the same authority by which they are received. He was considered a sublime theologian who knew how to fashion great monsters out of his little traditions; and it was part of the empty glory of the price that those grand words, which they weighed with lofty brows among the women who philosophised about Sacred Letters, were not understood. All the leaders of the Divine Word had sworn to the words of the Masters. Hence come six hundred sects: Thomists, Scotists, Occamists, Baconists, Albertists, Aegidians, Alexandrists, O the crime! The Gospels and Epistles were set aside, Christian philosophy lay hidden, was handled by very few, and that coldly, not to say insincerely. Cornelius Agrippa, in On the Vanity of the Sciences, chapter 97, says that this same theology was by a certain mixture of Divine oracles and philosophical reasons, from the Parisian Sorbonne, fused like a two-formed discipline from the race of Centaurs, and gradually fallen into sophisms, while those recent Theosophists and hucksters of the Word of God, who are theologians only by bought title, have made a war of words out of so lofty a faculty. And Melchior Cano in Loci Theologici, book 8, part 1, writes plainly: It comes about, as I see I am saying with the great assent of all, that the doctrine of the School, which defends itself by the title of Mastership, is wretched; wretched too is that which, with the authority of Holy Scripture removed, philosophises about divine things with twisted syllogisms. And in book 9, part 1, he writes that the Devil did what he cannot speak of without tears, so that, at a time when against the assaults of heresies in Germany the theologians of the School ought to have been best armed, they had nothing at all but long reeds, the light weapons of boys. So it is, Cano; except that by canine eloquence you have stamped the heresy, while you confessed ingenuously that you had taken the heavenly doctrine not from those Centaurs of Agrippa, but from the inner sanctuary of Scripture, whose authority your School's Doctors had dragged down with twisted syllogisms. Nor, therefore, is there no reason why learned interpreters of the Apocalypse assert that this theology is portended by the first angel pouring out his vial on the earth, whence an evil and malignant sore [ἕλκος κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν], a malignant and wicked ulcer on men who bear the mark of the beast and worship its image,

units.la: Apoc. xvi. 2. Sicut nempe ulcus non statim cutim dividit, sed unionis speciem relinquit, dum intus caro fatiscit, inflammatur & putrefit; unde scabies, pruritus, erosio oritur: ita Theologia haec, & ex ea enata innumera dissidia, quæstiones ἀνιῤῥαύλει, disputandi vitiligo, dissensio hæreditaria Thomistarum, Scotistarum, &c. in Regno Pontificio, unionis quamvis speciem præferente, ulceris instar fuit, quod scabiem & intestinam rupturam effecit, multumque adeò promovendo iniquitatis mysterio inservivit. Neque adeò immeritò Theologiam hanc Nicolaus Clemanges cum fructibus lacus Asphaltitis, qui foris speciem pulchram habeant, sed intus fumum ac cinerem, comparavit. Et quid sunt αἱ βάθη καὶ ζαπνά, Profunditates illæ Sathanæ, Apoc. ii. 24. si Scholastica illæ profunditates, Doctores profundos protrudentes non sunt? Sed Theologiæ hujus famosæ Helenæ, & Meretriculæ Babylone dignæ, quam Diabolicam artem litigandi Calvinus Comment. in 1. Tim. j. definivit, & cum caverna Caci ac Trojano equo scitè Antonius Sadaël comparavit; errores varios, cujusmodi sunt, quòd falsis & heterogeneis principiis innititur: quòd de rebus Theologicis gravissimis utramque in partem topicè, sceptice & Academicè disceptat: quò veritatem non illustrat, sed argutis sophismatis, & terminorum obscurissimorum prodigiis involvit: quòd tota in quæstionibus curiosis, vanis & futilibus occupatur: quòd denique perpetuis sententiarum divortiis, litibus & pugnis scatet; Dissert. de Theologia Scholastica, fusius prosecuti fumus.
units.tr: Apoc. xvi. 2. For just as an ulcer does not at once split the skin, but leaves a semblance of smoothness while the flesh within rots, inflames and putrefies, whence scab, itch and erosion arise: so this theology, and the countless disputes born of it, the questions [ἀνιῤῥαύλει], the leprosy of disputation, the hereditary quarrel of Thomists, Scotists, and so on, in the Papal kingdom, though presenting a semblance of unity, was like an ulcer, which produced scab and internal rupture, and so served greatly to advance the mystery of iniquity. Nor, indeed, without reason did Nicolaus Clemangis compare this theology to the fruits of the Dead Sea, which outwardly have a fair appearance, but inside are smoke and ashes. And what are the depths and Satan's profundities [αἱ βάθη καὶ ζαπνά, Profunditates illæ Sathanæ], Rev. 2:24, if not those Scholastic profundities, thrusting forth profound Doctors? But of this famous Helen and harlot worthy of Babylon, whom Calvin in Commentary on 1 Timothy, chapter 1, defined as the diabolical art of wrangling, and whom Antonius Sadael aptly compared to the cave of Cacus and the Trojan horse, we have pursued the various errors more fully in our Dissertation on Scholastic Theology: that she rests on false and heterogeneous principles; that she disputes topically, sceptically and academically, on both sides, the gravest theological matters; that she does not illuminate the truth but wraps it in subtle sophisms and the monstrosities of most obscure terms; that she is wholly occupied with curious, vain and trifling questions; and finally that she abounds in perpetual divergences of opinion, quarrels and fights.

units.la: XV. Sicut autem juris Divini Majestatem Theologiæ talis præsidio lacessere & oppugnare: sic humani, Cæsarei puta, Majestatem alteram oppositio Canonico jujure convellere placuit. Id quoque Hist. Pap. ß. xcv. xcvj. demonstrat; ubi etiam diserti pro Papali omnipotentia textus allegantur. Et constat, juxta Canonistas, quos sequuntur, aut sequi debent Jurisconsulti sub Papatu, uti quidem Chassaneus part. x. confid. 17. fusius astruere conatur, Jus Canonicum multis parasangis civili antecellere; atque sicubi pugnant, illo, non hoc standum esse.
units.tr: XV. Just as they have chosen to assail the majesty of divine law with such a bulwark of theology, so the opponents have chosen to overthrow the other majesty, the human (namely Caesarean) majesty, with canon law. Hist. Pap. ß. xcv. xcvj. also demonstrates this, where explicit texts are cited for papal omnipotence. It is agreed, according to the canonists whom the jurists under the Papacy follow or ought to follow, that canon law far surpasses civil law by many parasangs, as Chassaneus tries to show at length in part. x. confid. 17. Wherever they conflict, the canon law, not the civil law, must be followed.

units.la: XVI. Sic fuerunt tenebrae, quae Coelum Pontificium ante splendorem Divinitus exortum, non tam obduxerunt, quàm obtuerunt. Scintillas tamen coelestis lucis, seu stellulas quasdam intermicantes fulsisse, nulli equidem diffitemur. Cùm enim cum externo illo Ecclesiae adeò obtenebratae Occidentalis maximè, Corpore, vera Christi Ecclesia, in captivitate hac Babylonica gemens fluctuánsque, & velut in deserto palabunda, commixta fuerit: neque adeò penitùs verbum Dei & palmarii fidei articuli, in Symbolo Apostolico comprehensi, obliterari & deleri potuerint, quò minùs lux nonnulla reliquiis salvandis affulgeret: Deus è medio quoque Sacrorum Antistitum, Episcoporum & Cleri totius ordine, Coelesti Virgula tactos, Viros nonnullos pios, eruditos, Divinae veritatis scrutandae, asserendae & propagandae studio mirificè flagrantes excivit, qui Pontificis tyrannidi, injustitiae, idololatriae, erroribus palam praedicando, scribendo, attestando, disputando, carceres & exilia sustinendo, martyria quoque subeundo, se constanter opponerent: quorum nonnulli etiam à Pontificum secretis, domestici, familiares, auriti & oculati testes extiterunt; quorum tria inprimis, inde à Bonifacii VIII. Papatu ad Leonis usque X. tempora; adeóque Decimumtertium, quartum & quintum Secula feracissima fuerunt.
units.tr: XVI. So there were the shadows, which did not so much cloud over the Papal heaven before the light divinely arose as they dimmed it. Nobody, however, denies that sparks of heavenly light, or certain little stars flickering here and there, did shine. For although the true Church of Christ, groaning and tossed about in this Babylonian captivity, was mingled with the external body of the Church, especially the Western Church, which was so darkened, and wandered like a fugitive in the desert, nevertheless the Word of God and the chief articles of faith contained in the Apostles' Creed could not be wholly erased and destroyed, so that some light did not shine on the remnants to be saved. God also summoned out of the midst of the order of the sacred prelates, bishops and the whole clergy, some pious and learned men, touched by a heavenly rod, who burned wonderfully with zeal to search out, assert and spread divine truth. These men set themselves firmly against the tyranny, injustice, idolatry and errors of the Pope, by preaching openly, writing, bearing witness, disputing, enduring prisons and exile, and even undergoing martyrdom. Some of them were also privy to the Popes' secrets, as household servants, intimates, and ears and eyes witnesses. Of these, three flourished especially, from the Papacy of Boniface VIII to the times of Leo X; and so the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth centuries were most fruitful.

units.la: Tenebrae hasce Papatus caelestis lucis fulgentis quaedam Testes Veritatis, publicae corruptioni resistentes, inter fluctuantes runt. Quorum strenuissimorum Christi athletarum nomina, dicta, scripta & facta utcunque in Historia Papatûs ex Catalogis Testium Veritatis, aliisque monumentis prodita, percensere hujus loci non est. Neque singulares duntaxat personæ apostasiam Papalis Ecclesiæ accusárunt, detexerunt, oppugnárunt: verùm integri etiam & populosi cœtus non in Orientali duntaxat, sed Occidentali etiam Ecclesia; Waldenses cumprimis aliíque, qui in Gallia, Belgio, Germania, Anglia, Bohemia, aliisque in locis segreges cœtus instituerunt, atque in iis Romanensis Ecclesiæ apostasiæ pleno gutture, & μέχρι αἵματ@-, ad sanguinem usque, reclamárunt: quorum reliquiæ tristes hoc ipso tempore à novis Cyclopibus dirissima quæque perpessæ, adeò ut denuò in iis impletam esse Prophetiam Esajæ lvii. 5. Qui mastatis pueros in vallibus, sub fastigiis petrarum, dicatur merító; cœlestémque adeò Nemesin ad vindictam, de iis, qui terram corruperunt, propediem exigendam inclamantes, testimonium suum ad finem perducere videntur.
units.tr: Amid these darknesses of the Papacy there were certain witnesses of the truth, shining with the heavenly light, who resisted public corruption and were tossed about. It is not the place here to list the names, sayings, writings and deeds of these most vigorous athletes of Christ, which have been handed down in some way in the history of the Papacy, in the Catalogues of the Witnesses of the Truth, and in other records. Not only individual persons accused, exposed and assailed the apostasy of the Papal Church, but also entire and numerous congregations, not only in the Eastern but also in the Western Church: above all the Waldenses and others, who established separate congregations in France, Belgium, Germany, England, Bohemia and other places, and in them protested with full voice against the apostasy of the Roman Church, μέχρι αἵματος [even unto blood]. Their sad remnants, at this very time, have suffered the most dreadful things at the hands of the new Cyclopes, so that the prophecy of Isaiah 57:5 seems to be fulfilled again in them: "who slay the children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks." Rightly so; and they seem to bring their testimony to its end, crying out for a heavenly vengeance, soon to be exacted, on those who have corrupted the earth.

units.la: XVII. Splendori porrò illi, quo terra collustranda fuit, promovendo, tria potissimùm propitiâ Dei providentiâ, remedia, ceu prodromos phosphorúmque paulatim ex thalamo suo prodituri Solis adhibuit; puta Versionem Bibliorum, Scholarum & studiorum instauratione qualemcunque, & artem Typographicam.
units.tr: XVII. Furthermore, to promote that brightness by which the earth was to be illumined, God in his gracious providence applied three chief remedies, as forerunners and as lights that would gradually come forth from his chamber like the sun: namely, the translation of the Bible, some restoration of schools and studies, and the art of printing.

units.la: Cùm enim Romani Pontifices supra annos ducentos, incredibili sanguinis Christiani jactura, pro Palæstina recuperanda, infelicia bella gessissent, & recuperatam amisissent iterum, tandem in celebri Galliæ Synodo Viennensi, circa A. D. MCCCXII. sancitum fuerat, ut linguæ Orientalibus populis vernaculæ, puta Hebrœa, Syria-
units.tr: For when the Roman Pontiffs, for more than two hundred years, at an incredible loss of Christian blood, had waged unhappy wars to recover Palestine, and had lost it again once recovered, it was finally decreed at the famous Council of Vienne in Gaul, around A.D. MCCCXII, that the languages vernacular to the Eastern peoples, namely Hebrew, Syriac,

units.la: Splendor illi, quo terra illustranda fuit, phosphoros suos habuit; puta tum linguarum Orientalium studium quoddam Viennensis Concilii decreto commendatum: unde editio Biblia-orum Complutensis profecta est. riaca , Chaldaica , Arabica & Græca in publicis Scholis docerentur : útque Sacra Biblia in eàdem linguas converterentur , quò Saraceni infideles , qui nulla hactenùs bellorum cruentissimorum vi subigi poterant, lectione sacrarum literarum ad viam salutis revocati , Christo postliminio lucrifierent. Quod decretum tardos licet & exiguos habuit successus , habuit tamen nonnullos. Nam Franciscus Ximenius, Archiepiscopus Toletanus in Hispania, Academiæ Complutensis fundator, circa A. D. mdxv. Sacra Biblia, sex tomis incredibili sumtu ediderat; vetus quidem Testamentum textu Hebraico , Paraphrasi item Chaldaïca, totidémque versionibus Latinis : Novum verò Græco , & translatione Latina. Atque opus isthoc à Leone X. magnificis privilegiis communitum, universóque orbi Christiano commendatum fuerat, veluti κειμήλιον sacratissimum, & oraculum cœlitùs delapsum. Qua occasione exoptatissima factum est , ut textus Bibliorum Sacrosanctus, jam pridem Monachorum & Sacrificulorum torpore , pulvere sitúque coopertus , in apertam lucem revocaretur ; & mox hoc ipso gladio spirituali , Viris doctis in manus porrecto , vulnera Pontificio corpori lethalia infligerentur. Nam eo ipso tempore , quo Versio ista Bibliorum Complutensis Hispanica in lucem prodiit, Cœlestis mox Splendor ille terram perfundere cœpit.
units.tr: That brightness by which the earth was to be illumined had its phosphors: namely, a certain study of the Eastern languages, commended by the decree of the Council of Vienne, from which the Complutensian edition of the Bibles proceeded. Chaldean, Arabic and Greek were to be taught in the public schools, and the Holy Bible was to be translated into these same languages, so that the unbelieving Saracens, who had hitherto been unable to be subdued by any force of the bloodiest wars, might be called back to the way of salvation by reading the sacred letters and be won back to Christ by right of return. This decree had slow and meagre results, but it did have some. For Francis Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo in Spain, founder of the University of Alcalá, had published the Holy Bibles in six volumes at incredible expense around A.D. MDXV: the Old Testament in the Hebrew text, likewise with the Chaldean paraphrase and as many Latin versions, and the New Testament in Greek with a Latin translation. This work was furnished with magnificent privileges by Leo X and commended to the whole Christian world, as a most sacred treasure and an oracle fallen from heaven. On this occasion it came about, most desirably, that the sacred text of the Bible, long covered over with the torpor, dust and squalor of monks and sacrificing priests, was brought back into the open light; and soon, with this very spiritual sword put into the hands of learned men, deadly wounds were inflicted on the Papal body. For at the very time when this Spanish Complutensian version of the Bible came out into the light, that heavenly brightness began to flood the earth.
XVIII.

units.la: Sed & inclytæ Academiæ & Scholæ in præcipuis Europæ Regnis , puta Germania , Gallia , Anglia , Hispania , Italia , Bohemia apertæ & constitutæ sunt ; in quibus Monachali barbarie profligata , literæ & artes liberales pristino suo nitori atque puritati restitutæ ; ingenia doctorum mirifico studio atque ardore revocarentur ; et florem re.
units.tr: But the famous academies and schools were also opened and founded in the chief kingdoms of Europe, namely Germany, France, England, Spain, Italy and Bohemia. There, once Monkish barbarism had been put to flight, letters and the liberal arts were restored to their former brightness and purity, and the minds of scholars were recalled with wonderful zeal and ardour, and the flower [of learning] ...

units.la: aaaaa 2 re sacras literas legendi, scrutandi, veritatem Divinam cognoscendi, eandem à scoriis & fraudibus humanis separandi, impostura denique Papales detegendi oppugnandique accensa fuerunt. Commodúmque etiam, uti in Hist. Pap. ss. cxliy. narravimus, capta Constantinopoli, & exilio perpetuo bonis literis in Oriente indicto, Turcarum metu Romam se contulerunt Viri undequaque doctissimi, quos Nicolaus V. Papa, literarum juxta atque literatorum, rara Pontificum indole, amantissimus, perhumaniter excepit, & liberaliter sustentavit. Sicut igitur olim Moses in aula Ægyptiaca educatus est, qui postea filios Israëlis ex Ægypto eduxit, ipsámque Ægyptiacam aulam pessundedit: ita in ipsa quoque Antichristi hujus aula bonae literae promotae sunt, quarum deinceps auxilio, Antichristus orbi revelari, & in multorum cordibus jugulari debuit. Atque huic Pontifici acceptum referimus, quicquid deinceps splendoris Latinae & Graecae literae in Italia primum, postea etiam in Germania, acceperunt. Sic, ringentibus licet, & sacra omnia commoventibus Monachis, aliisque φιλέβαςέβαρoις, Græcas juxta atque Hebraicas literas Germaniae Capnio seu Reuchlinus; Syriacas & Arabicas Thefeus & Widmanstadius; Philosophiam saniorem Agricola, Valla, alii, intulerunt: omnem denique eruditionis Oceanum Picus Mirandulanus, Erasmus inprimis Roterodamus, Lud. Vives, Budæus, Stephani, alii, exhauserunt. Quorum vestigiis laudabilibus ii ipsi, quorum opera & ministerio Deus lucem Euangelii sparsit, Zwinglius, Lutherus, Theodorus Bibliander, Pellicanus, Melanchton, alii, instituerunt sedulò; quos proin ob literarum etiam bonarum, & elegantiorum linguarum inprimis exactiorem notitiam, insulsissimi mi Monachi, Cœli Pontificii Atlantes, hæreseos crimine arcessere nulli dubitârunt.
units.tr: ...to read the sacred letters, to search them, to know the divine truth, to separate it from human dross and frauds, and finally to expose and assail the papal impostures, were all kindled. And it was opportune, as we related in Hist. Pap. ss. cxliv., that when Constantinople was captured, and a perpetual exile was decreed against good letters in the East, learned men from every quarter fled to Rome for fear of the Turks. Nicholas V, a Pope most fond of letters and of learned men, with the rare character of the popes, welcomed them most courteously and supported them generously. So just as Moses was once brought up in the Egyptian court, and afterwards led the sons of Israel out of Egypt and overthrew that Egyptian court itself, so in the very court of this Antichrist good letters were advanced, by whose help Antichrist was to be revealed to the world and slain in the hearts of many. And to this Pope we attribute whatever splendour Latin and Greek letters afterwards received, first in Italy and then also in Germany. Thus, though the monks laughed and stirred up everything sacred, and the other impious [philosebastoi], Capnio, or Reuchlin, introduced Greek and Hebrew letters into Germany; Thesaeus and Widmanstadt introduced Syriac and Arabic; Agricola, Valla and others introduced a saner philosophy; and finally Pico of Mirandola, above all Erasmus of Rotterdam, Ludovicus Vives, Budaeus, the Stephani and others drained the whole ocean of learning. In the footsteps of these praiseworthy men, those very men through whose work and ministry God spread the light of the Gospel, Zwingli, Luther, Theodore Bibliander, Pellicanus, Melanchthon and others, zealously followed; and these men, on account of their more exact knowledge of good letters and especially of the more elegant languages, the most foolish monks, the Atlases of the papal heaven, did not hesitate to call to account on the charge of heresy.

units.la: XIX. Utrisque & versionibus S. Scripturæ, & literarum humaniorum notitiæ propagandæ, Splendori inprimis Euangelii diffundendo mirificè Typographia, media Seculi Decimi-quinti ætate inventa, beneficium Divinum nunquam satis laudatum, inservivit. Nam ars isthæc nobilissima mox Babylonicæ Meretricis pudenda detexit, & Cœlestem verbi Divini lucem longè latéque, nequicquam resistentibus, imò vento occlamitantibus Papæ mancipiis, sparsit, etiamnum spargit, & spargere nunquam desinet. Dignissimum profectò memoratu est, quòd Antichristum, adeóque etiam Babylonem Magnam, ejusdem emblema, per linum perdendum Sibylla Erythræa non semel Romam, Christi nomen professam, Babylonis nomine insigniens, prædixit. Verba ejus sunt:
units.tr: XIX. The divine benefit, never sufficiently praised, of printing, discovered in the middle of the fifteenth century, served wonderfully to spread both the versions of Holy Scripture and the knowledge of humane letters, and above all to spread the splendour of the Gospel. For this most noble art soon exposed the shame of the Babylonian harlot, and it spread, and still spreads, and will never cease to spread, the heavenly light of the divine Word far and wide, though the servants of the Pope resisted in vain, or rather shouted against it in the wind. It is certainly most worthy of mention that the Erythraean Sibyl, more than once, foretold Antichrist, and therefore also Babylon the Great, the emblem of the same, by means of the flax that was to destroy him, labelling Rome, which professed the name of Christ, with the name of Babylon. Her words are:

units.la: Αἴλιν@ ἐκπὶς κακρὸς, ἓπ λίν@ αὐτὴν ἐλάπτ.
units.tr: Αἴλιν@ ἐκπὶς κακρὸς, ἓπ λίν@ αὐτὴν ἐλάπτ.

units.la: Miserum inde tempus, quia linum perdet eum.
units.tr: Then comes a wretched time, for a thread will be his undoing.

units.la: En modum atque instrumentum, quo perimi oportebat immanem hostem, idque ex fatis atque prædictionibus Sibyllinis. Linum, sic fatidica mulier, perdet eum: non utique ex lino pharmacum aliquod, quo poto aut comesto pestis illa emoriatur. Nam Divinâ potentiâ seu Spiritu oris Christi & Cœlestibus armis expugnari debuit. Quid verò, inquias, ad pugnam hanc, victoriam & triumphum Christi adversùs Antichristum linum, gramen fragile, adferet? Scilicet materia, in qua scriptitatur vel excuditur quidvis, ex lineo panno minutatim conciso in aquis, & glutine densato fit: quam chartam lineam, abusione veteris nominis, papyrum appellant. Ex ea fiunt epistolæ, quas Apostolos etiam
units.tr: Here is the means and the instrument by which that monstrous enemy had to be destroyed, and this comes from the Sibylline fates and predictions: "The linen, so the prophetess says, will destroy him." It does not mean that some drug made from linen would kill that plague when drunk or eaten. For he had to be overcome by divine power, or the Spirit of the mouth of Christ, and by heavenly arms. But, you may say, what does linen, a fragile grass, contribute to this battle, this victory and triumph of Christ against Antichrist? Clearly, the material on which anything is written or printed is made from linen cloth cut into small pieces, soaked in water and thickened with glue. People call this linen paper, by an abuse of the old name, papyrus. From it letters are made, which the Apostles also…

units.la: {y} debuisse, offenditur. vocant : ex ea codicilli , ex ea codices de rebus Divinis & humanis. Nec quisquam ignorat, libros authorum suorum accipere nomina ; ut qui librum Mosis legit, dicatur Mosen legere ; qui libros Pauli recitari audit, Paulum audiat. Libri ergò Prophetarum & Apostolorum scripti , &c , quod præstantius multò est , impressi, hac notione Prophetæ & Apostoli sunt, ex lino quadam παλιγγενεσία & regeneratione Divina procreati. Hæ legiones præliari validissimè contra Babylonem : hæc tormenta, gladii , sarissæ , lanceæ, lethales ei plagas inferre debuerunt. His velis & rudentibus naviculæ Petri orthodoxæ & Apostolicæ moveri, ut piraticam triremem in mari supero & infero vagantem effugerent: his verriculis & sagenis capi Leviathan : his retibus feræ immanes , quæ agrum Domini , Ecclesias & Politias legitimas infestant , capi debuerunt. Hæc invicta potentia est Principis nostri Jesu Christi , dominantis in medio inimicorum suorum : qui cùm nutu omnia peragere posset, operum tamen suorum socios & συνεργὸς homines adhibet, eos ad prælia Domini animat & instruit; eligendo sic res infirmas, quas mundus vilipendit : quibus alta , firma , præpotentia , inexpugnabiliáque Mortalium judicio , & molitiones Sathanæ evertit. Factúmque adeò est , ut qui in mundo supremam sibi dignitatem arrogabant, tonantes fulminantésque, ut Salmoneus iste, aut Sapores Persarum tyrannus , linum tamen isthoc perinde ut lymphatici aquas metuerint; & quia metuerunt, cane pejùs & angue oderint , libros minimè malos ferro & igni persecuti fuerint ; quos abolere non potuerunt , corruperint , legi prohibuerint, expurgárint ; id unicè & flagrantissimè voventes , ut typographicas officinas vel in suam potestatem redigant , vel penitùs abolcant leant omnes: quod vel solum Tridentini Concilii de librorum publicatione decretum, Sessioni IV. insertum comprobat.
units.tr: ...ought to have used, one may take offence; they call them letters. From it come notebooks, and from it books on divine and human matters. Nor is anyone unaware that books take the names of their authors: whoever reads the book of Moses is said to read Moses, and whoever hears the letters of Paul read is said to hear Paul. The books of the Prophets and Apostles, written and, what is far more excellent, printed, are therefore in this sense the Prophets and Apostles, produced from linen by a certain rebirth [παλιγγενεσία] and divine regeneration. These are the legions that must fight most powerfully against Babylon; these are the weapons, swords, spears and lances that must deal her deadly blows. With these sails and ropes the orthodox and apostolic little boat of Peter is moved, so that it may escape the pirate galley wandering over the upper and lower seas; with these dragnets and nets Leviathan is to be caught, and the savage beasts that harass the Lord's field, the Churches and the lawful commonwealths, must be taken. This is the invincible power of our Prince Jesus Christ, who reigns in the midst of his enemies: although he could accomplish all things by a nod, he nonetheless employs men as the co-workers [συνεργὸς] of his works, rouses and trains them for the Lord's battles, choosing thus the weak things that the world despises, by which he overturns what is high, firm, all-powerful and, by the judgment of mortals, impregnable, and the schemes of Satan. And so it has come about that those who in the world arrogated to themselves supreme dignity, thundering and hurling lightning like that Salmoneus, or like Sapor, tyrant of the Persians, have nevertheless feared this linen just as madmen fear water; and because they feared it, they have hated it worse than dog or snake, and have persecuted by sword and fire books that were in no way evil; those they could not abolish they have corrupted, forbidden to be read, and purged. They vow this one thing, and most ardently: either to bring the printing houses wholly into their own power, or to abolish them entirely. This alone is confirmed by the decree of the Council of Trent on the publication of books, inserted in Session IV.

units.la: XX. Prodromis hisce secuturi mox Splendoris ipsius, accesserunt vota enixissima bonorum omnium, quibus ex meliore luto praecordia Deus finxit. Inter eos enim nemo non Reformationem Ecclesiæ adeo corruptæ in votis flagrantissimis habuit: quorum cogitationes exhibentur Psal. iv. 7. Multi dicunt: Quis nos faciet videre bonum? Sua quisque ætate successuram eam, spe bona praecepit. Johannes Vitoduranus Barvota noster ad ⁊A. 1348. haec notavit: In his temporibus apud homines diversi generis, imò cuncti generis multos valdè apertissimè vulgabantur, Imperatorem Fridericum II. hujus nominis ad Reformandum statum omninò depravatum Ecclesiæ esse venturum in robore maximi Potentatus. Adjiciunt quoque homines praedicta sentientes, quòd necesse sit eum venire, si in mille partes secatus esset, imò si in pulverem per combustionem redactus foret, eò quòd divinitùs sit decretum, ita debere fieri, quod immutari impossibile est. Extant adhuc lucubrationes eorum, qui publicis scriptis & necessitatem Reformationis demonstrárunt, & modum ejusdem praescripserunt; veluti Dominici Brixiensis Episcopi libellus ad Pium II. titulo, Reformatio Curiæ Romanæ, scriptus: Jacobi de Guitrade liber de Septem statibus Ecclesiæ in ⁊Apocalypsi, ejúsque Reformatione: Petri Numagen Trevirensis, Gesta ⁊Archiepiscopi Craynensis in facto indictionis Concilii, à Celeb. Hottingero Histor. Eccl. Tomo IV. pag. 355. &c. ex Manuscripto edita: Nicolai Clemangis de Corrupto Ecclesiæ statu querela, liber à Cl. Lydio publici juris factus,
units.tr: XX. Following these forerunners of the coming Splendour itself, there came the most fervent prayers of all good men, for whom God fashioned hearts from better clay. Among them indeed none failed to have the Reformation of the so-corrupted Church among their most ardent wishes. Their thoughts are set forth in Ps. 4:7: "Many say, Who will show us good?" Each one in his own age hopefully predicted that it would come. Our Barvota, Johannes Vitoduranus, noted these things at the year 1348: "In these times it was openly and widely spread among people of various kinds, indeed of every kind, that the Emperor Frederick II of that name would come, in the strength of the greatest potentate, to reform the Church's utterly depraved state. Those who think these things add that he must come even if he were cut into a thousand parts, indeed even if he were reduced to powder by burning, because it has been decreed by God that it must be so, and this cannot be changed." Their writings still survive, those who by public writings demonstrated the need for Reformation and prescribed its method: the little book of Dominic, Bishop of Brescia, addressed to Pius II and entitled Reformation of the Roman Curia; the book of Jacob of Gütrade, On the Seven States of the Church in the Apocalypse, and its Reformation; Peter Numagen of Trier, Acts of the Archbishop of Cranenburg in the matter of the calling of the Council, published from a manuscript by the celebrated Hottinger, Church History vol. IV, p. 355, etc.; Nicholas Clémangis' Complaint on the Corrupt State of the Church, a book made public by the learned Lydius,

units.la: Reformatio nis prodromis hisce accesserunt; de fideria ejusdem statis ētus, notisque illustratus, cujus capite 31. demonstrat, quòd status Ecclesiæ Papalis propter superbiam tendat ad ruinam; & cap. 32. quòd Ecclesia priùs humilianda, quàm erigenda sit: Petri de Aliaco, Cardinalis Cameracensis tractatus de Reformatione Ecclesiæ, sex considerationibus absolutus: ubi non morum duntaxat Cleri & populi, sed etiam consuetudinum ecclesiasticarum, superstitionum, Scholarum, Theologiæ cumprimis Scholasticæ & linguarum καταψηφίζειν vehementer urget: Andreæ de Petra, Archiepiscopi Coloffensis, Eugenii IV. in Concilio Basileensi Oratoris, de Reformatione Ecclesiæ oratio, qua ob Cleri corruptionem, mystici Templi structuram gravissimum lapsum atque ruinam minari præsagivit; ipso Bzovio ad A. 1432. narrante: Epistola Christi nomine ad Concilium Constantiense, secundo ejus anno scripta, quæ in Bibliotheca S. Andreæ Brunsuigæ reperitur, qua Reformationem à Papa, aliisque summi ordinis inchoandam esse, asseritur: Colloquium Petrum inter & Paulum institutum, passimque in Bibliothecis obvium; quo paucos metu tyrannidis Papæ errores Antichristi perstringere sustinere, queritur: Johannis Gerfonis scripta complura, Constantiensis Concilii tempore vulgata, quibus Reformationis Ecclesiæ necessitatem ursit, modumque aphorismis & propositionibus pluribus comprehensis præfinivit. Cujus inprimis articuli sedecim, etiam Catalogo testium veritatis lib. ix. p. 831. non expresso authoris, qui forte scriptorem Catalogi illius latuit, nomine, inserti sunt, Ecclesiæ Romanæ fœdam faciem, reformationis indigam, vivis coloribus depingit. Taceo Durandum Mimatensem, Sigismundum Imperatorem, Concilium Constantiense & Basileense, Langium Citizentizenfem, Chemenfem Episcopum, Hadrianum VI. Ordines Imperii & Cantones IX. Helvetiæ, Prælatos Pauli IV. jussu Consilium de reformanda Ecclesia meditatos, ipsos Tridentini Concilii Patres, quos Reformationis necessitatem agnoscentes Histor. Papatûs s. 123. 140. 141. 156 — 173. induximus.
units.tr: These forerunners of the Reformation were joined by the work on the same state, edited and illustrated with notes, whose chapter 31 demonstrates that the state of the Papal Church tends to ruin on account of pride, and chapter 32 that the Church must be humbled before it is raised up; the treatise of Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, on the Reformation of the Church, completed in six considerations, in which he presses vigorously not only the morals of the clergy and people, but also the ecclesiastical customs, superstitions, schools, and especially scholastic theology and the condemnation of languages; the oration of Andrew of Pietra, Archbishop of Colossi, orator of Eugenius IV at the Council of Basel, on the Reformation of the Church, in which, on account of the corruption of the clergy, he foretold that the structure of the mystical Temple threatened a most grievous fall and ruin, as Baronius relates under the year 1432; a letter written in the name of Christ to the Council of Constance in its second year, which is found in the library of St Andrew at Brunswick, asserting that the Reformation must be begun by the Pope and the other men of the highest rank; the Colloquy instituted between Peter and Paul, found everywhere in libraries, in which he complains that few dare, for fear of the tyranny of the Pope, to expose the errors of Antichrist; the many writings of John Gerson, published at the time of the Council of Constance, in which he urged the necessity of the Reformation of the Church and prescribed its manner in aphorisms and many propositions. Of these, especially the sixteen articles, inserted without the name of the author, who perhaps was hidden as the writer of that Catalogue, in the Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth, book 9, p. 831, paint in vivid colours the foul face of the Roman Church, in need of reformation. I pass over Durand of Mende, the Emperor Sigismund, the Councils of Constance and Basel, Lang of Cieza, the Bishop of Chemnitz, Adrian VI, the Orders of the Empire and the nine Cantons of Helvetia, the Prelates who at the command of Paul IV meditated a council on reforming the Church, and the very Fathers of the Council of Trent, who, acknowledging the necessity of Reformation, I have cited in Hist. Papatûs pp. 123, 140, 141, 156–173.

units.la: XXI. Ne verò de morum duntaxat reformatione folicitos fuisse hosce ἐχθρολίκες putemus, en inter Gersonis regulas, Constantiensi Concilio oblatas, has etiam: 1. S. Scriptura est fidei regula, contra quam bene intellectam, non est admittenda authoritas, nec ratio hominis cujuscunque, nec aliqua consuetudo, nec consti-tutio, nec observatio valet, si contra S. Scripturam militare convincatur. 2. S. Scriptura dum consideratur in aliqua sui parte, vel propositione, non est tenenda in solis terminis illius propositionis, aut in illo sensu, quem illa propositio per se & nudè considerata facit; sed conferenda & concordanda est per comparationem ad alios S. Scripturæ passus. 3. S. Scriptura potest & debet in suis partibus, & partialibus assertionibus reverenter, & humiliter, & diligenter expositionem recipere, concordando passum cum passu, & unum per alterum judicando. 4. S. Scriptura in expositione partium requisivit homines præditos ingenio, exercitatos studio. Nervum tetigit Gerson, & fidei principium, Scripturam à nullius authoritate suspendendam, restitui pertendit. Vel ex his laciniis de reliqua textura judicare licet. Quin & Papam ipsum Euangelicæ traditioni contradicentem, coërcendum, & Concilio subjiciendum esse, Æneas Sylvius sic Epistola ad Colonienses scripta pertendit: Homini Christiano, qui verè Christianus dici vult, nullam rem magis cordi es-
units.tr: XXI. Lest we think these wolf-haters were concerned only with the reform of morals, look at these rules of Gerson, which were presented to the Council of Constance, among them the following: 1. Scripture is the rule of faith, against which, once rightly understood, no authority, no human reasoning, no custom, no constitution, and no observance is to be admitted or holds force, if it is shown to conflict with Scripture. 2. When Scripture is considered in some part or proposition of it, it is not to be held to the bare terms of that proposition, or to the sense that the proposition yields when taken alone and by itself; it must be compared and reconciled with the other passages of Scripture. 3. Scripture can and must, in its parts and in its particular assertions, receive exposition reverently, humbly, and diligently, by matching passage with passage and judging one thing by another. 4. In expounding the parts of Scripture, Scripture requires men gifted in intellect and trained in study. Gerson touched the sinew, and he insisted that the principle of faith, that Scripture must depend on no one's authority, be restored. From these scraps one may judge the rest of the fabric. Indeed, Aeneas Sylvius, in his letter written to the Colognese, maintains that the Pope himself, if he contradicts the evangelical tradition, must be restrained and made subject to the Council, in these words: For a Christian man, who wishes to be called truly Christian, nothing should be closer to his heart than to take care that the purity of the faith handed down to him by his forefathers is kept spotless by all.

units.la: Tom. II. se convenit, quàm ut fidei sibi per majores traditæ puritatem servari, ab omnibus immaculatam studeat. Et quippe, si quando adversùs Euangelicas traditiones aliquid astruitur, surgendum populariter est, & ad commune restinguendum incendium afferre aquam omnes tenemur. Nec timendum est, ut inimici aut invisi fiamus, verum dicentes. Resistendum est quibuscunque in faciem, sive Paulus, sive Petrus sit, qui ad veritatem non ambulat Euangelii. Quam rem fecisse per hos dies Universitatem vestram, gaudio in hoc Concilio Basileensi gaudemus omnes. Allatus nempè ad nos est tractatulus vester, quo imperitiam, vel, veriùs dicam, temeritatem illorum arguitis, qui & subjectum Concilio Romanum Pontificem, & supremi judicii tribunal in Ecclesia esse diffitentur, quos sic vivacibus rationibus, & Scripturarum veritatibus & rationibus premitis & retunditis, ut nec tanquam lubrici angues se evolvere, nec in aliquo cavillari aut sibilare queant. Hanc mentem si Papa factus Æneas retinuisset, & poculo aureo hausto inebriari se passus non esset, poterat optimos quosque votorum suorum damnare. Sed non inde salutem Ecclesiæ affulgere Deus voluit, unde maxima corruptio ejusdem originem traxit.
units.tr: It is also fitting that, whenever anything is asserted against the evangelical traditions, the people should rise up, and that we all are bound to bring water to put out the common fire. Nor should we fear becoming enemies or objects of hatred by speaking the truth. We must resist to the face whoever does not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, whether he be Paul or Peter. We all rejoice at the Council of Basel that your University has done this in recent days. For your little treatise has reached us, in which you refute the ignorance, or, to speak more truthfully, the rashness, of those who deny that the Roman Pontiff is subject to the Council and that there is a tribunal of supreme judgment in the Church. You press and beat them down with such lively arguments and truths of Scripture and reason that they can neither wriggle away like slippery snakes nor hiss or quibble about anything. If Aeneas, once made Pope, had kept this mind, and had not allowed himself to be made drunk by drinking from the golden cup, he could have condemned all the best of his own wishes. But God did not will that salvation should shine forth to the Church from the very source from which her greatest corruption arose.

units.la: XXII. Sed neque bona omina, & secuturæ mox Reformationis calusque Antichristi prædictiones deerant; quas haud paucas Johannes Wolphius, diligentissimus memorabilium & reconditarum rerum collector, Catalogi Testium veritatis, & Rhonæus in idea Reformationis consignârunt. Mitto Johanem Huffum, qui constantissimus Martyr jamjam cremandus, cygneum ejusmodi vaticinium emisit: Huffum (anserem non Bohemis modò ea vox notat, sed & Hebræis ac Arabibus vox ꝑꝓ) crecrematis hodie: (die 6. Jul. MCCCCXV.) Post centum annos cygnus veniet, quem cremare non poteritis Hiltenus quoque, Ifenacenfis Franciscanus, annum Reformationis prædixit, cujus se vidisse vaticinium ἀντιγραφοι Melanchton alicubi testatur. Extat epistola Farelli ad Pellicanum A. MDLVI. scripta his verbis: Pius senex, Jacobus Faber, quem tu nosti, ante annos plus minus quadraginta, me manu apprehensum ita alloquebatur: Guilhelme, oportet orbem immutari, & tu videbis, dicebat. Ego tum charus eram seni, & perrexit mihi esse pater. Sed nihil erat nisi superstitio, in qua seni adnitebar accedere aliquantum. Nam æquare vix poterat quisquam, tantum abest, ut vinceret. Sane stupesco, quando cogito insanam tanti Viri superstitionem, qui vel floribus jubebat Marianum idolum, dum unâ soli murmuremus preces Marianas ad idolum, ornari. In Missa omnes vincebat. Tandem aliquid lucis cœpit intueri. Sed quanta caligo adhuc restabat? Demùm coactus Gallid Argentoratum descendit: ubi Virum commonefeci eorum, quæ olim prædixerat, & jam tempus instare dicebam. Quod & pius Senex fatebatur, meque hortabatur, pergerem in annuntiatione Euangelii. Prophetiam civis cujusdam Erfurdiensis A. MCCCXLI. scriptam, ex Lubecensi Bibliotheca Pomeranus eruit, quæ sic sonat: Cum numerabitur annus millesimus quingentesimus decimus-octavus, res maximi momenti in his oris continget, quæ suis viribus nixa, potestatem habebit super omnia, tamque potens erit, ut vim nullam ipsa passura sit. Superabit enim potentiam omnem, & qui vim ei opponere cogitabit, vim patietur ipse. Posset huc etiam referri Visio, quam Fratri Nicolao Helvetio Subsylvano, paulò ante Reformationem factam, filius ejus Carolo Bovillo tradi­dit, atque hic recta ad Nicolaum Horium, Archiepi& shy;scopum Rhemensem, qui eam publicè primus celebra& shy;vit, misit. Vidit is splendenti & pellucido circulo in& shy;clusum caput Papale, redimitum trifido diademate, cujus fastigio orbiculus cum cruce fuerat impositus; sicut is Imperatoribus haftenus præferri consuevit. Caput ipsum mediam circuli aream occupabat. Facies ru& shy;bicunda erat, vultus atrox & valdè minax: frons cor­rugata, trucésque & micantes oculi excandescentis spe­ciem præ se ferebant: mentum barbâ valdè hirsutâ, & in tres cirros discretâ, vestiebat, sed canitiei situ squa­lidâ: superiùs labium itidem mystace prominente fero­ciebat. Porrò in faciem ex circi circumferentia tres acuti gladiorum mucrones tendebant, quorum unus ex imo circi progrediens perrupta barba os papale petebat; reliqui duo ab utroque latere oculos fodicabant. Con& shy;tra hos ex ipso capite alii totidem tendebant, duo nem­pe ex naribus versùs utrúmque circuli latus cúspides demittebant, tertius ex caperata fronte sursùm per diã­dematis longitudinem versùs orbiculum tiaræ impofi& shy;tum vergebat. Visionem hanc μυστικῶς Theologus fagacissimus, Conradus Graserus, in Plaga Regia. pag. 218. &c. explicavit, & futuro Papæ casui & excidio in phialarum septem effusione, aliisque vaticiniis Divi­no Spiritu prædicto, clarissimè aptavit. Alios plures, splendorem Euangelii insecuturum prænuntiantes, pu& shy;to Nicolaum Cusanum, Johannem Lichtenbergium, Joachimum Abbatem, Hildegardem, Brigittam, An& shy;dream Prolem &c. ad compendium pono.
units.tr: XXII. Yet there were not lacking good omens and predictions that the reform was soon to follow and that the downfall of Antichrist was at hand. John Wolf, the most diligent collector of memorable and recondite matters, in his Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth, and Rhoneus in his Idea of the Reformation, recorded not a few of them. I pass over John Hus, the most steadfast martyr, who, just about to be burned, uttered this prophecy like a swan's song: You are burning the goose (the word for goose means not only "Huss" in Bohemian, but also in Hebrew and Arabic) today (on 6 July 1415). After a hundred years a swan will come, whom you will not be able to burn. Hiltenus also, the Franciscan of Ifenach, foretold the year of the Reformation; Melanchthon testifies somewhere that he had seen the prophecy in copies [ἀντιγραφοι]. There is a letter of Farel to Pellicanus, written in 1556, in these words: The pious old man, Jacques Lefèvre, whom you know, took me by the hand about forty years ago and spoke to me thus: "William, the world must be changed, and you will see it," he said. I was dear to the old man then, and he went on being a father to me. But it was nothing but superstition, in which I struggled to come somewhat closer to the old man. For hardly anyone could equal him, let alone surpass him. Indeed I am amazed when I think of the insane superstition of so great a man, who ordered even the Marian idol to be adorned with flowers, while we alone murmured Marian prayers to the idol. In the Mass he surpassed everyone. At last he began to see some light. But how much darkness still remained? At length, compelled by the Gallic... he came down to Strasbourg, where I reminded the man of what he had once predicted, and said that the time was at hand. The pious old man admitted this too, and urged me to press on with the proclamation of the Gospel. A prophecy written by a certain citizen of Erfurt in 1341 was brought to light by the Pomeranian from the library at Lübeck, and it runs thus: When the year one thousand five hundred and eighteen is counted, a matter of the greatest moment will happen in these parts, which, resting on its own strength, will have power over all things, and will be so powerful that it will itself suffer no violence. For it will overcome all power, and whoever plans to oppose it will himself suffer violence. A vision could also be cited here, which the son of Nicholas Helvetius of Subsylvania, shortly before the Reformation, handed on to Charles Bovillus, who sent it straight to Nicholas Horius, Archbishop of Reims, who was the first to make it publicly known. He saw a Papal head enclosed in a shining and transparent circle, crowned with a three-cleft diadem, on the summit of which a little orb with a cross had been placed, as is customary for emperors to be shown. The head itself occupied the middle of the circle's area. The face was ruddy, the expression fierce and very threatening; the brow was wrinkled, and the eyes, grim and glittering, showed the look of kindled anger; the chin was clothed with a very bushy beard divided into three locks, but squalid in its grey-haired state; the upper lip likewise projected with a prominent moustache. Moreover, from the circumference of the circle three sharp points of swords stretched towards the face, one of which, coming from the bottom of the circle, pierced through the beard and aimed at the papal mouth; the other two stabbed the eyes from either side. Against these, from the head itself, as many others extended: two, namely, sent points from the nostrils towards each side of the circle, and a third from the wrinkled brow ran upward along the length of the diadem towards the little orb placed on the tiara. The most acute theologian Conrad Graser explained this vision mystically [μυστικῶς], in his Plaga Regia, p. 218 and following, and applied it most clearly to the future fall and ruin of the Pope, to the pouring out of the seven vials, and to other prophecies foretold by the Divine Spirit. I pass over many others who foretold that the splendour of the Gospel would follow, such as Nicholas of Cusa, John Lichtenberger, Joachim the Abbot, Hildegard, Bridget, Andreas Proles, and so on; I put them aside for brevity.

units.la: XXIII. Neque præsagia ejusmodi eventus fefellit. Post tot enim prodromos, phosphoros, desideria bono& shy;rum rum & omina, ipse Cœlestis Veritatis Sol subitò ex thalamo suo eluctatus, gloriâ suâ terram illustravit, atque mox terra, juxta vaticinium Esai. xi. 9. plena facta est in cognitione Domini, sicut mare aquis tegitur. Hoc ve- ròtum effectum est, quando Leone X. ad Romanæ Ecclesiæ gubernacula sedente, ejusdémque nutu indulgentiarum nundinatione, principio fidei de Jesu Christi Salvatoris unici gratia, è diametro opposita, per institores ejusdem in orbem terrarum emissos impudentissimè exercita, & ad impietatis fastigium summum producta, Deus Spiritu suo Heroës induit, ut legę justitiæ Christi, quæ est Lex fidei in Christum, cujus solius merito & justitiâ consummatissimâ, peccata credentibus remittuntur, plenissimáque adeò venia indulgetur, ex Dei infallibili verbo, semotis traditionibus, Papalibus Bullis, omnique authoritate alia, illustrata, nusquam non sermo de ea esset, atque integra Regna, Provinciæ, Civitates ei adstipulari cogerentur. Qui verò hanc Legem justitiæ Christi, seu viam justitiæ novit, is novit Dominum, Jerem. xxxi. 33, 34. De qua justitiæ via manifestanda, sic loquitur, Esaias cap. xxxv. 8. Via sanctitatis ita in aperto futura est, ut & stulti non errent.
units.tr: XXIII. Nor did such presages deceive as to the outcome. For after so many forerunners, harbingers, longings for good things, and omens, the very Sun of Heavenly Truth burst forth suddenly from his bridal chamber, lit up the earth with his glory, and soon the earth, according to the prophecy of Isaiah 11:9, was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the sea is covered with waters. This truly came to pass when Leo X sat at the helm of the Roman Church, and at his nod the trafficking in indulgences, by which the principle of faith in the grace of Jesus Christ the sole Saviour, diametrically opposed to it, was most shamelessly practised through his agents sent throughout the world and carried to the highest peak of impiety, God clothed heroes with his Spirit, so that the law of the justice of Christ, which is the Law of faith in Christ, by whose merit alone and most perfect righteousness sins are forgiven to believers, and the fullest pardon is granted, according to the infallible Word of God, with traditions set aside, Papal Bulls and every other authority set aside, was made clear, so that the word about it was everywhere, and whole kingdoms, provinces, and cities were compelled to agree with it. But whoever knows this Law of justice of Christ, or the way of justice, knows the Lord, Jer. 31:33, 34. Concerning the manifestation of this way of justice, Isaiah speaks thus, chap. 35:8: The way of holiness will be so open that even fools will not go astray.

units.la: XXIV. Revelatio illa Legis justitiæ multùm ad judicium Babylonis faciebat haud dubiè, quia per eam non tantùm denudari illa, desolari, compertumque fieri cœpit, quòd non sit Ecclesia Christi, & quòd Jezabel non sit Prophetissa, sed Meretrix & Babylon, utpote deficiens à Lege justitiæ Christi, & aliud amoris fiduciæque suæ objectum, aliud salutis præsidium, amplexa: sed etiam per eam factum est, ut quorum cordibus Deus Legem hanc inscripsit, apud eam manere non potuerint, quia Babylon Legem illam justitiæ reapse blasphemavit, eámque profitentes hostili odio persecuta est; ita enim plané evenit. Postquam enim Viri Dei, Zwinglius, Lutherus, aliique doctrinam de justificatione per solam Christi justitiam, non per ulla hominis opera, indulgentiarum nundinationi, ex Dei verbo strenuè opposuerunt, & Euangelium ex eodem sincerè, clarè, efficacitérque prædicârunt, atque in Regiam illam salutis viam plurimos induxerunt, præconio huic Romanus Præsul se <bl>ποντιφικα</bl> oppositum, & sementem in herba suffocare conatus, omnes vineas pluteósque suos admovit, ut Præcones Euangelii strenuos illos & indefessos fulminibus suis afflatos è medio tolleret. Machinatio illa reluctantis Papæ exacuit Euangelicorum Pastorum studia, ut non tantùm ipsius authoritatem & potestatem, adeóque pupillam ejus validissimè, magnóque cum successu oppugnare inciperent, sed etiam ad alia maximi momenti dogmata deflecterent, reformationémque indies perfectiorem redderent. Quare casus Babylonis plurimùm promotus fuit, contumacia & inobedientia errantium indies crescente, ut hon tam per stultitiam, quàm per rebellionem veritati resisterent, atque ita Babylon ipsa ad judicium suum maturesceret.
units.tr: XXIV. That revelation of the law of righteousness contributed greatly, without doubt, to the judgment of Babylon. Through it, not only did that church begin to be stripped bare, deserted, and shown up, so that it became clear that it is not the Church of Christ, and that Jezebel is not a prophetess but a harlot and Babylon, since she had fallen away from the law of Christ's righteousness and embraced another object for her love and trust and another refuge for salvation. It also came about through it that those in whose hearts God had written this law could not remain under her authority, because Babylon really did blaspheme that law of righteousness and persecuted with hostile hatred those who professed it. And so it truly happened. When the men of God, Zwingli, Luther and others, vigorously opposed from God's Word the doctrine of justification by Christ's righteousness alone and not by any human works, against the peddling of indulgences, and preached the Gospel from the same Word sincerely, clearly and effectively, and led very many into that royal way of salvation, the Roman Prelate, set against this proclamation as Pontiff [ποντιφικα], tried to suffocate the seed while it was still in the blade. He brought up all his vines and siege-engines, so that he might remove from the midst those vigorous and tireless heralds of the Gospel, whom he wanted to strike with his thunderbolts. That scheming of the reluctant Pope sharpened the zeal of the evangelical ministers, so that they began to attack his authority and power, and indeed his very apple of the eye, most forcefully and with great success, and also turned their attention to other doctrines of the greatest importance, making the Reformation more perfect day by day. Hence the fall of Babylon was greatly advanced, while the obstinacy and disobedience of the erring grew day by day, so that they resisted the truth not so much through foolishness as through rebellion, and in this way Babylon herself ripened toward her judgment.

units.la: XXV. Illuminatio illa terræ, tenebris, quibus Pa- patum totum involutum fuisse suprà ostendimus, con- traria omnia habuit.
units.tr: XXV. That illumination of the earth, opposite to the darkness in which we have shown above that the whole Papacy was wrapped, had all things contrary to it.

units.la: Nam, ut paucis res maximas complectar, fidei dogmata ad verbi Divini amussim exacta tota, pristinum nitorem suum receperunt. Scripturæ eminentissima authoritas, sepositá & spretá omni authoritate alia, in arce collocata est: corruptio hominis ex eadem ostensa: liberi arbitrii idolum confractum: gratiæ divinæ non partes duntaxat sive primæ, sive secundæ tributæ sunt, sed universa salus, conversio, fidedes, denique quicquid in homine boni auspicatíque est, in solidum relatum acceptum est: Christo Salvatori officia & beneficia sua illibata restituta, & ab eorum societate Angeli hominésque exclusi: Justitiæ merito, satisfactioni & δικαιώματα ejus in verbo & sacramentis oblato, à Deo peccatori per solam gratiam imputato, veráque fide recepto, uni soliique, exclusa omni dignitate humanæ operationis, nedum pretio rerum terrestrium, cui hactenùs Dei gratia addici suevit, meritum omne, justitia omnis, remissio peccatorum, vita æterna, transscripta: denique universa, quæ ad fidem & charitatem pertinent, ad Lydium solium Scripturæ, demonstrato ejusdem ex Scriptura sensu, lapidem exacta sunt. In Ceremoniis cuncta simplicitati institutionis Christi & praxeos Apostolorum, nec non ordini & decoro conformata, & sacramenta ex Dei verbo pristinæ suæ simplicitati, atque iis, quibus à Christo sacrata sunt, usibus restituta: quæ ad ἐντολίαι pertinent, pauca, innocua, sine necessitatis & singularis mysterii opinione, solius ordinis & decori præscriptione, vel retenta vel recepta sunt. In Cultu externo, invocatio, adoratio, veneratio solius Supremi Numinis, & infinitæ Majestatis probata: Creaturarum in universum omnium religiosa veneratio omnis profligata: fuci illi cultûs duliæ, hyperduliæ; directi, obliqui, majoris, minoris, transfitivi, intransfitivi abstersi sunt. In Gubernatione Ecclesiæ, omnis Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, Tros Rutulusve suant, in temporalibus & spiritualibus dominatio, elatio, ἀλλοτριοπαθεια omnis severè interdicta, & pro Dominis, ne dicam, tyrannis conscientiis ipsis dominantibus. Pastores legitimi, gregem soli Christo, non sibi & concupiscen-
units.tr: For, to sum up very great matters in a few words: the dogmas of faith, all brought into line with the measure of the Divine Word, have recovered their former lustre. The most eminent authority of Scripture, with every other authority set aside and scorned, has been placed on the citadel. The corruption of man has been shown from it; the idol of free will has been broken. The parts of divine grace, whether first or second, are not merely assigned to it, but the whole of salvation, conversion, faith, and finally whatever is good and auspicious in man, is referred and credited entirely to grace. The offices and benefits of Christ the Savior have been restored to him unimpaired, and angels and men have been excluded from sharing them. The merit of his righteousness, his satisfaction and his δικαιώματα [righteous acts], offered in the Word and sacraments, imputed by God to the sinner through grace alone and received by true faith, have been transferred wholly to him alone, with every dignity of human action excluded, and far less any price of earthly things, to which the grace of God has hitherto been wont to be sold: all merit, all righteousness, the remission of sins, eternal life. Finally, everything that pertains to faith and love has been brought to the Lydian touchstone of Scripture, the sense of Scripture being demonstrated from Scripture itself. In Ceremonies, everything has been conformed to the simplicity of Christ's institution and the practice of the Apostles, and also to order and decorum; the sacraments have been restored from the Word of God to their former simplicity and to those uses for which Christ consecrated them. Whatever pertains to the ἐντολίαι [ordinances] has been either retained or received, few in number and harmless, without the opinion of necessity or of a special mystery, prescribed only for order and decorum. In the External worship, the invocation, adoration and veneration of the Supreme Deity alone, and of infinite Majesty, have been approved; the whole religious veneration of creatures in general has been put to rout; those counterfeit forms of worship, dulia and hyperdulia, direct and indirect, greater and lesser, transitive and intransitive, have been wiped away. In the Government of the Church, every domination, pride and ἀλλοτριοπαθεια [lording it over others] of the ministers of the Church, whether "Trojan or Rutulian," in temporal and spiritual matters, has been severely forbidden, and men are not to be lords, not to say tyrants, over consciences themselves.
