units.la: Item, dicit idem, quod frater simplex, vel quilibet homo cum salute potest sequi in consiliis quamcunque opinionem voluerit; dummodo alicujus magni Doctoris opinionem sequatur, sic ille & merito. Nam unicum gravem Doctorem constituere opinionem extrinsecè probabilem, docent quatuor super viginti Doctores.
units.tr: Likewise the same author says that a simple brother, or any man whatever, may safely follow in his counsels whatever opinion he likes, provided he follows the opinion of some great teacher; and so he does rightly. For twenty-four teachers teach that a single grave teacher makes an opinion externally probable.

units.la: P. 27. prop. 1. Quamvis opinio sit falsa, potest quilibet tutâ conscientiâ illam practicè sequi, propter authoritatem docentis, judicare probabilem & juxta illam operari: quæ doctrina ferè communis est inter Doctores.
units.tr: Page 27, proposition 1. Although an opinion is false, anyone may with a safe conscience follow it in practice, judging it probable on the authority of the one who teaches it, and act according to it; this doctrine is almost common among teachers.

units.la: P. 28. n. 2. Imò quæ si el consultante pideque le aconseje conforme à la opinion mas favorable, pecca en no hazerlo assi.
units.tr: Page 28, number 2. Indeed, if the one consulting asks and begs that he be advised according to the more favourable opinion, the one consulted sins in not doing so.

units.la: Imò si is, qui sibi consulti vult, postulat, ut sibi consulatur secundùm opinionem omnium faventissimam, peccatis qui consulitur (licet ejusmodi opinionem judicet improbabilem) si morem consultantis cupiditati non gerit.
units.tr: Indeed, if the one who wishes to be advised demands that he be advised according to the most favourable of all opinions, the one consulted sins, even if he judges such an opinion improbable, if he does not indulge the desire of the one consulting.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina harum propositionum falsa est, temeraria, innumeris novitatibus & corruptelis viam aperiens, & conscientiæ regulas evertens.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine of these propositions is false, rash, opens the way to countless novelties and corruptions, and overturns the rules of conscience.

units.la: P. 191. n. 4. Puto omnia esse hodiè melius examinata, & hanc ob rem, in omni materia, & præcipuè morali, libentius juniores, quàm antiquiores lego & sequor.
units.tr: P. 191. n. 4. I think everything is examined better today, and for this reason, in every subject, and especially in moral matters, I read and follow the younger writers more willingly than the older ones.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, temeraria in moribus periculosa, sanctis Patribus & antiquis Doctoribus contumeliosa.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false, rash, dangerous in morals, and insulting to the holy Fathers and the ancient Doctors.

units.la: De CHARITATE. p. 66. n. 3. Et illam amplectuntur non ignobiles Magistri; atque Doctores, quando defendunt præceptum charitatis, per se tantùm obligare in articulo mortis.
units.tr: On CHARITY. p. 66. n. 3. Some not undistinguished Masters and Doctors also embrace this view, when they defend that the precept of charity binds by itself only at the point of death.

units.la: P. 68. n. 8. Præceptum affirmativum amoris Dei & proximi, non esse speciale, sed generale; cui per aliorum præceptorum adimpletionem satisfit.
units.tr: P. 68. n. 8. The affirmative precept of love for God and neighbour is not a special precept but a general one, which is satisfied by the fulfilment of other precepts.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc doctrina falsa est, erronea, impia, & primo ac maximo Legis Euangelicæ mandato contraria. De CORRECTIONE FRATERNA. p. 74. n. 6. Probatur multipliciter, quòd ille ordo procedendi Euangelicus neminem obliget, ut præceptum communiter accipitur à Theologis, pro lege obligante ad mortale peccatum, ejus transgressores.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine is false, erroneous, impious, and contrary to the first and greatest command of the Gospel law. On FRATERNAL CORRECTION. p. 74. n. 6. It is proved in many ways that this Gospel order of procedure binds no one, if a precept is understood in the sense the theologians commonly give it, as a law binding under pain of mortal sin on those who transgress it.

units.la: Frustrà excipiuntur tot casus & conditiones ab illo Tom. II. præcepto Euangelico, quia non datur tale præceptum; cùm secundùm naturale præceptum charitatis correctio fraterna debeat regulari, &c. tertio loco ostendetur id, quod gravius est, præceptum illud perniciosum fore, nedum inutile: præcepta verò Christi esse verè utilia testatur ipse Dominus, Esaiæ 48. Ego Dominus docens utilia.
units.tr: It is vainly objected that so many cases and conditions are attached to that Tom. II. Gospel precept, because no such precept exists; since, according to the natural precept of charity, fraternal correction ought to be regulated, and so on. In the third place it will be shown that what is more serious is that this precept would be not only useless but pernicious; yet the Lord himself testifies that the precepts of Christ are truly profitable: Isaiah 48. "I am the Lord, teaching what is profitable."

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina his propositionibus con- tenta, falsa est, & temeraria, Sanctis Patribus co- ntraria, & quatenùs dicit fore perniciosum præceptum, si quod foret in Euangelio Matthæi, cap. 18. bl- asphema. De MISSA ET COMMUNIONE. p. 127. n. 3.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine contained in these propositions is false and rash, contrary to the holy Fathers, and, insofar as it says that a precept would be pernicious if it were in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 18, blasphemous. On the MASS AND COMMUNION. p. 127. n. 3.

units.la: Dico tradentem stipendium taxatum (sacerdoti Missam celebranti) retenta sibi parte minori, aut etiam majori, non peccare mortaliter, nec teneri ad restitutionem &c. Quia nulli infertur damnum, neque injuria, sed solùm fit contra simplicem prohibitionem, quod non potest esse nisi peccatum veniale.
units.tr: I say that a person who hands over a fixed stipend to a priest celebrating Mass, keeping back a smaller or even a larger part of it, does not sin mortally, nor is he bound to restitution, and so on. For no one is harmed or wronged; there is only a breach of a simple prohibition, which can only be a venial sin.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio jacet, falsa est & scandalosa, favet turpi lucro avaritiæ & inju- stitiæ.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition lies, is false and scandalous, favours shameful gain, avarice and injustice.

units.la: P. 236. prop. 4. Non datur præceptum sub lethali obligans, ad recipiendam Eucharistiam in articulo mortis.
units.tr: P. 236. prop. 4. There is no precept binding under mortal sin to receive the Eucharist at the point of death.

units.la: P. 237. n. 3. Addunt alii, nullum dari præceptum Divinum Communionis, sed tantùm Ecclesiasticum, ac inde, seclusò Ecclesiæ præcepto, non peccaturum, qui in tota vita non communicaret.
units.tr: P. 237. n. 3. Others add that there is no divine precept of Communion, but only an ecclesiastical one; and so, with the Church's precept set aside, a person who did not communicate in his whole life would not sin.
CENSURE. The doctrine of these propositions is false

units.la: sa est, scandalosa, & respectivè verbo Dei scripto & non scripto contraria.
units.tr: and scandalous, and, in its bearing, contrary to the written and unwritten Word of God.
On SIMONY. p. 113. n. 2.

units.la: Non esse contra justitiam beneficia Ecclesiastica non conferre gratis, quia collator conferens illa beneficia Ecclesiastica, pecuniâ interveniente, non exigit illam pro collatione beneficii, sed veluti pro emolumento temporali, quod tibi conferre non tenebatur; tum quia dum exclusis aliis, te præfert conferendo tibi Beneficium, affectum ad te determinat, & se privat potestate alteri gratificandi, quod est magno pretio æstimabile. Hæc ille, qui à fortiori tenetur idem dicere in nostro casu, cùm eadem prorsùs militet ratio.
units.tr: It is not against justice to refrain from conferring ecclesiastical benefices freely, because a patron who confers such benefices, with money passing, does not demand it as the price of the benefice, but as a temporal advantage which he was not bound to confer on you; and also because, while he prefers you to others by conferring a benefice on you, he determines his affection towards you and deprives himself of the power of favouring another, which is worth a great price. So he says; and one who is bound, a fortiori, to say the same in our case, since exactly the same reasoning applies.

units.la: P 149. Non est Simonia pacto expresso se obligare ad aliquid temporale pro spirituali ex gratitudine conferendum.
units.tr: p. 149. It is not simony to bind oneself by an express agreement to confer something temporal in return for something spiritual, out of gratitude.

units.la: P. 150. n. 2. Ex pacto velle, non est vendere spiritualia; quia pactum non mutat materiam actuum.
units.tr: p. 150. n. 2. To wish something by agreement is not to sell spiritual things, because an agreement does not change the matter of the acts.

units.la: P. 152. n. 6. Non est Simonia donare aliquid temporale, vel ante vel post, ei qui exhibet aliquid spirituale, etiam, cum intentione quod donatarius moveatur ad dandum spirituale ex gratitudine. Et Inferius, si quis mutuum daret non ut pretium Beneficii Ecclesiastici, sed, ut hac ratione provocet amicitiam collatoris, aut ut gratiam præstet, quam non vult præstare, nisi alter statim gratificetur conferendo Beneficium, probabile est nec usuram, nec Simoniam fore.
units.tr: p. 152. n. 6. It is not simony to give something temporal, either before or after, to one who provides something spiritual, even if the intention is that the recipient be moved to give the spiritual thing out of gratitude. And below, if someone were to lend money not as the price of an ecclesiastical benefice, but so that by this means he might win the friendship of the patron, or might grant a favour he does not wish to grant unless the other immediately repays him by conferring a benefice, it is probable that this is neither usury nor simony.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæ propositiones falsæ sunt, & Si- moniam contra jus divinum apertissimè approbantes, at- que alias à Facultate damnatæ.
units.tr: CENSURE. These propositions are false, and openly approve simony against divine law, and have been condemned by the Faculty on other grounds.

units.la: P. 154. n. 5. Electores ad Majoratum vel Cathedram posse
units.tr: P. 154. n. 5. Electors may take a price for a majorship or a chair, so that they choose one person rather than another,

units.la: ffff 2 posse pretium accipere ; ut unum præ alio eligant ; eò quòd ejusmodi prælatio , cùm huic determinatæ personæ non sit debita , & aliundè sit ei valdè utilis , pretio æstimabilis est.
units.tr: because such a preference, since it is not owed to that particular person and is otherwise very useful to him, is worth a price.

units.la: P. 155. prop. 3. Qui Electores pecunià corrumpit , ut eum in Generalem , Provincialem , Priorem , vel Guardianum eligant, non subjacet pœnis contra Simoniacos latis.
units.tr: p. 155. prop. 3. A person who bribes electors to choose him as General, Provincial, Prior, or Guardian is not subject to the penalties laid down against simoniacs.

units.la: CENSURÆ. Hæ duæ propositiones , ut jacent , sunt falsæ , temerariæ , juri Canonico contrariæ , & respectivè turpe lucrum ac Simoniam in Ecclesiam invehentes.
units.tr: CENSURES. These two propositions, as they stand, are false, rash, contrary to the canon law, and, in their bearing, introduce shameful gain and simony into the Church.

units.la: De USURA. p. 158. prop. 1. Mutuanti licitum est aliquid ultra fortem exigere , ratione periculi, cui in ea recuperanda exponitur.
units.tr: On USURY. p. 158, prop. 1. It is lawful for a lender to demand something beyond the principal by way of compensation for the risk to which he exposes himself in recovering it.

units.la: P. eadem n. 1. Quamvis enim usura sit , si quis recipit aliquid ultra fortem, ratione mutui : non est usura, si recipit ratione periculi tantùm , ut pretium periculi. Et inferiùs.
units.tr: Same page, n. 1. For although it is usury if someone receives anything beyond the principal by reason of a loan, it is not usury if he receives it only by reason of risk, as the price of the risk. And further on.

units.la: Nullus potest esse itafecurus, quin possit aliquod intervenire periculum, vel saltem aliqua difficultas, vel labor in re habenda.
units.tr: No one can be so secure that some danger, or at least some difficulty or labour in obtaining the thing, may not intervene.

units.la: P. 160. n. 7. Licitum etiam esse mutuanti , aliquid ultra fortem exigere , si se obliget ad non repetendam fortem, usque ad certum terminum.
units.tr: P. 160, n. 7. It is also lawful for a lender to demand something beyond the principal if he binds himself not to demand the principal until a certain date.

units.la: P. 161. n. 10. Et si mutuans dicat , non mutuabo, nisi ultra fortem loco interesse , aliquid certum solvas , quòd hoc non sit de se illicitum , apparet ex dictis.
units.tr: P. 161, n. 10. And that, if the lender says, "I will not lend unless you pay me something certain beyond the principal in place of interest," this is not in itself unlawful, appears from what has been said.

units.la: P. 163. prop. 2. Licitum est mercatori credito vendere merces pretio rigoroso v. g. 100. & statim nume. meratâ pecuniâ eas emere 8o. quod est pretium infimum.
units.tr: P. 163, prop. 2. It is lawful for a merchant to sell goods on credit at a strict price, for example 100, and at once, with the money counted out, to buy them back for 80, which is the lowest price.

units.la: Nec etiam ad rem facit, si quis vendat ex necessitate, vel non necessitate oppressus, quia necessitas non mutat rei pretium.
units.tr: Nor does it matter whether someone sells from necessity or under the pressure of not being in need, because necessity does not change the price of a thing.

units.la: Posse aliquem emere rem vilius ab illo qui vendit, necessitate compulsus, quia ex modo vendendi minuitur pretium rei, & merces efficiuntur ultroneæ.
units.tr: One may buy a thing more cheaply from the one who sells it when he is compelled by necessity, because by the manner of selling the price of the thing is lowered and the goods are offered freely.

units.la: Vilescit res non solum pro tertia, sed etiam pro dimidia parte, quando quis illam vendere necessitate compellitur.
units.tr: A thing becomes cheaper not only by a third but even by a half, when someone is compelled by necessity to sell it.

units.la: Si contractui Societatis superaddantur contractus assecurationis capitalis & venditionis lucri incerti pro lucro certo, ex vi horum licitum est exigere lucrum certum, salva sorte.
units.tr: If to a partnership contract there are added a contract of insurance of the capital and a sale of uncertain profit for a certain profit, then by virtue of these it is lawful to demand the certain profit, the principal being safe.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina harum propositionum salsa est, scandalosa, inducens ad usuras committendas; variasque aperit artes: eas palliandi; justitiam, ac charitatem violandi, & à Sacra Facultate jam damnata.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine of these propositions is false, scandalous, leads men to commit usury, and opens up various arts for disguising it, for violating justice and charity; and it has already been condemned by the Sacred Faculty.

units.la: De FURTO. p. 172. prop. 4. Licitum est Tabernariis vinum aquâ miscere, & agricolis triticum paleis, & communi pretio vendere, dummodò deteriora non reddantur eis, quæ communiter venduntur.
units.tr: On THEFT. p. 172, prop. 4. It is lawful for tavern-keepers to mix wine with water, and for farmers to mix wheat with chaff, and to sell at the common price, provided that the goods are not made worse than those commonly sold.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, bonæ fi- dei, & publicæ justitiæ contraria.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false and contrary to good faith and public justice.

units.la: p. 218. n. 3. Eum qui rem furtivam à Latrone accepisset, sciens esse furtivam, non teneri ad ejus, seu frufructuum restitutionem, etiamsi illis factus sit locupletior, dummodo fur non reddatur impotens ex illa donatione ad restituendum vero domino, & res ab illo accepta sit unico usu consumtibilis, & materia mutui, qualis est pecunia, pannus, vinum &c.
units.tr: P. 218, n. 3. A man who has received stolen goods from a robber, knowing them to be stolen, is not bound to restore them or their fruits, even if he has become richer by them, provided that the thief is not thereby made unable to restore them to the true owner, and that the thing received is consumable by a single use and is the matter of a loan, such as money, cloth, wine, etc.

units.la: Utrum ille, qui pecuniam accepit mutuò, ut redimeret se à latronibus, teneatur restituere? Cujus prima ratio difficultandi, pro parte negativa, est; Quia tempore necessitatis omnia sunt communia &c. Cùm ergò ille, qui in latrones incidit, fuerit in maxima necessitate constitutus, utpote in periculo mortis existens, videtur quòd factum sit sibi commune aliquid, quod erat alterius, & ita non teneatur ei restituere, qui mutuavit, ac si esset proprium ejus, &c. Ergò cùm non possit per amicos à mortis periculo ab extrinseco imminenti se liberare, fient ei omnia communia.
units.tr: Whether he who received money as a loan in order to ransom himself from robbers is bound to repay it? The first reason for doubt, on the negative side, is this: because in a time of necessity all things are common, etc. Since, therefore, the one who fell into the hands of robbers was placed in the greatest necessity, as one existing in danger of death, it seems that something which belonged to another has become common to him, and so he is not bound to repay the lender, just as if it were his own, etc. Therefore, since he cannot free himself from the danger of death threatening him from outside through friends, all things will become common to him.

units.la: Non solùm in extremâ, sed in gravi etiam necessitate licitum esse furari: v. gr. quando est periculum amittendi honorem, & homini valdè inhonestum esset mendicare, dummodò aliter non possit sibi succurrere, & habeat animum restituendi cùm possit.
units.tr: Not only in extreme but even in grave necessity it is lawful to steal; for example, when there is danger of losing one's honour, and it would be very dishonourable for a man to beg, provided he cannot otherwise help himself and has the intention of restoring when he is able.

units.la: CENSURA. Haec doctrina falsa est, & teme-raria, Reipublicæ perniciosa, furibus ac furtorum consciis, favens, & abutitur author doctrinâ san- ctî Thomæ.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine is false and rash, pernicious to the commonwealth, favours thieves and accomplices in thefts, and the author abuses the doctrine of St. Thomas.

units.la: De JUDICIBUS, p. 113. prop. 11. Quandò litigantes pro se habent opiniones æquè probabiles, potest judex pecuniam accipere pro ferenda sententia in favorem unius, præ alio.
units.tr: On JUDGES, p. 113, prop. 11. When litigants have opinions equally probable in their favour, a judge may accept money for pronouncing a sentence in favour of one rather than the other.

units.la: N. 1. Quia non accipitur pretium pro sententia, tanquam merces functionis, sed quasi compensatio pro commodo alteri parti collato, & pro illa electione, quæ est pretio æstimabilis.
units.tr: N. 1. Because money is not received for the sentence as the wage of an office, but as a compensation for a benefit conferred on the other party, and for that choice, which is worth a price.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc doctrina falsa est, tem- eraria, scandalosa, Legum & æquitatis eversiva.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine is false, rash, scandalous, and subversive of laws and of equity.

units.la: De MENDACIO. p. iii. n. 1. Falsare non est, nec peccatum mortale, amissæ scripturæ de hæreditate, aut nobilitate, aliam similem efficere. Nulli enim fit injuria.
units.tr: On LYING. p. iii, n. 1. To falsify is not even a mortal sin, when one makes another similar document in place of a lost writing about an inheritance or nobility. For no one is wronged.

units.la: P. 112. n. 3. Nota modò, quòd si quis privatam aliquam scripturam, aut syngraphaм, aut apocham, quâ constaret se certæ quantitati pecuniæ mutuò acceptæ satisfecisse, falsificaret; quia aliam legitimam à conditore confectam amisisset; nec alio modo probare posset solutionem, non damnarem peccati mortalis, quia falsificationes hæ privatarum videlicet scripturarum, non sunt ita Reipub. perniciosæ.
units.tr: P. 112, n. 3. Note only this: if someone were to falsify some private writing, or a bond, or a receipt, by which it would appear that he had repaid a certain sum of money lent to him, because he had lost the legitimate one drawn up by the creditor, and could not otherwise prove the payment, I would not condemn him of mortal sin, because such falsifications of private writings are not so pernicious to the commonwealth.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc doctrina falsa est, scandalosa & Reipub. perniciosa.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine is false, scandalous, and pernicious to the commonwealth.

units.la: De HORIS CANONICIS. p. 117. n. 6. Eum, qui non potest solus recitare, non teneri admittere socium, etiam ultrò se offerentem. Quia recitare cum socio est favor unicuique concessus, & nemo tenetur uti favoribus invitus.
units.tr: On the Canonical Hours. p. 117, n. 6. One who cannot recite alone is not bound to admit a companion, even one who offers himself unasked, because reciting with a companion is a favour granted to everyone, and no one is bound to use a favour against his will.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio, falsa est, & in contemtum officii Ecclesiastici temerè, & inepte excogitata, atque à debita ejusdem recitatione abducens.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false, rashly and foolishly devised against the due office of the Church, and it leads people away from its proper recitation.

units.la: De JUSTIS TRIBUTIS. p. 34. prop. 2. Subditi possunt justa tributa non solvere.
units.tr: On Just Taxes. p. 34, prop. 2. Subjects may refuse to pay just taxes.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, verbo Dei contraria, & seditiosa.
units.tr: This proposition is false, contrary to the Word of God, and seditious.

units.la: De JEJUNIO. p. 133. prop. 1. Qui habent privilegium edendi ova, & lacticinia in Quadragesimâ, possunt edere lardum & sagimen.
units.tr: On Fasting. p. 133, prop. 1. Those who have the privilege of eating eggs and milk foods in Lent may eat bacon and lard.

units.la: P. 134. n. 3. Pueri non obligantur usque ad duodecimum annum (abstinere à carnibus & ovis, tempore quadragesimali) quando aliis tenentur Ecclesiæ legibus.
units.tr: P. 134, n. 3. Children are not bound to abstain from meat and eggs in Lent until their twelfth year, when they are bound by the other laws of the Church.

units.la: P. 135. n, 2. Materia collationis olim soli fructus erant, nunc autem sumat quilibet quod vult: nihil refert, dummodo parvitas apud pios recepta non excedatur.
units.tr: P. 135, n. 2. The matter of the collation was once only fruit, but now anyone may take what he likes. It makes no difference, provided the small amount approved among the pious is not exceeded.

units.la: P. 136. n. 3. Deducitur secundò sine violatione jejunii, servatâ debitâ quantitate, fumi posse ova, lacticinia, &c. in vespertinâ refectiunculâ, quando licitè comeduntur in die jejunii. (Et Inferiùs,) Possunt & nimium studentes & capite debiles, qui malè cœnati non dormiunt; aliquantulò in hoc largiores esse, quibus usque ad paris ovorum esum concedebat, neque nobis videtur in hoc largus, cùm sciamus jejunium cum illis omnibus servari posse, quæ ejus essentiæ neque saluti repugnent.
units.tr: P. 136, n. 3. It is deduced, secondly, that without violating the fast, provided the due quantity is kept, eggs, milk foods, etc. may be taken at the evening light meal, when they may lawfully be eaten on a fast day. (And below,) Those who study excessively and are weak in the head, and who do not sleep when they have dined poorly, may be somewhat more liberal in this. He allowed them to eat up to a pair of eggs, and this does not seem to us liberal, since we know the fast can be kept with all those things that do not oppose its essence or health.

units.la: P. 142. prop. 6. Si quis voluntate absoluta vellet in die jejunii sæpius comedere, semper tamen parùm cibi sumendo, peccaret mortaliter, secùs si voluntate conditionatâ, in quâ conditione interveniret, quòd omnes sumtiones essent veniales.
units.tr: P. 142, prop. 6. If someone, with an unconditional intention, wished to eat often on a fast day, always taking only a little food, he would sin mortally; but not so if he acted with a conditional intention, the condition being that all the takings were venial.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina harum propositionum falsa est, scandalosa & leges Ecclesiæ de jejunio infrin- gens.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine of these propositions is false, scandalous, and infringes the Church's laws on fasting.

units.la: De POENITENTIA. p. 210. prop. 15. Prælatus, qui ex Confessione Sacramentali subditi peccata cognoscit; potest, hujus notitiæ virtute, ab officio ad nutum tum amovibili eum amovere.
units.tr: On Penance. p. 210, prop. 15. A prelate who learns of a subject's sins from sacramental confession may, by virtue of this knowledge, remove him from an office that is removable at will.

units.la: P. 21. n. 8. Si poenitens absque necessitate manifestavit in confessione complicem sui peccati, non tenetur confessor complicis peccatum occultare sub sigillo consessionis; & sic pro bono communi est manifestandum; sicut & alia secreta naturalia, dum tamen non explicetur poenitens.
units.tr: P. 21, n. 8. If a penitent, without necessity, has revealed in confession an accomplice in his sin, the confessor is not bound to conceal the accomplice's sin under the seal of confession; and so it is to be revealed for the common good, as with other natural secrets, provided the penitent is not named.
CENSURE.

units.la: Prima harum propositionum absolutè, & secunda, ut jacet; falsæ sunt, scandalosæ, contrariæ sigillo Confessionis, & à Sacramento Pœnitentiæ avertunt.
units.tr: The first of these propositions, absolutely taken, and the second as it stands, are false, scandalous, contrary to the seal of confession, and turn people away from the Sacrament of Penance.

units.la: P. 203. prop. 10. Defloratio Virginis sponte consentientis, etiam sub patria potestate, malitiam tantum simplicis fornicationis continet, & per consequens circumstantiam virginitatis in confessione explicare non est necesse.
units.tr: P. 203, prop. 10. The deflowering of a virgin who willingly consents, even under paternal power, contains only the malice of simple fornication, and consequently it is not necessary to explain the circumstance of virginity in confession.
CENSURE.

units.la: Hæc propositio falsa est, & favet raptoribus, Patriæ potestati injuriosa, & contraria integritati confessionis.
units.tr: This proposition is false, favours ravishers, is injurious to paternal power, and contrary to the integrity of confession.

units.la: P. 208. prop. 13. Qui habuit copulam cum soluta, satisfacit confessionis præcepto, dicens (commisi cum soluta grave peccatum contra castitatem) non explicando copulam.
units.tr: P. 208, prop. 13. One who has had intercourse with an unmarried woman satisfies the precept of confession by saying "I committed a grave sin against chastity with an unmarried woman," without explaining the intercourse.
CENSURE.

units.la: Hæc propositio falsa est, & erronea, Conciliis & Traditioni contraria.
units.tr: This proposition is false and erroneous, contrary to the Councils and to Tradition.

units.la: P. 216. n. 4. Si ipse confessarius petat quantitatem (furti) ipsum posse dicere, non teneor ad hoc confitendum.
units.tr: P. 216, n. 4. If the confessor himself asks for the amount (of the theft), I may say it, but I am not bound to confess this.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, sinceritati & humilitati confessionis, fini Sacramenti adversa, atque authoritati Sacerdotis detrahens.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false, adverse to the sincerity and humility of confession and to the end of the Sacrament, and it detracts from the authority of the priest.

units.la: P. 225. n. 21. Non posse absolvi qui nullum signum dederit, quo videatur actualiter petere confessionem. Sentis quidem probabilissimè. Tibi enim Viri Doctissimi consentiunt. Et tamen te peccaturum esse mortaliter, si non mutes dictamen, affero, cùm moribundo omnibus sensibus destituto, qui nullo signo externo consessionem petit, non occurris.
units.tr: P. 225, n. 21. One cannot be absolved who has given no sign by which he appears actually to seek confession. You think this most probable, and indeed the most learned men agree with you. Yet I point out that you would sin mortally if you did not change your judgment, since you take no account of a dying man, deprived of all his senses, who seeks confession by no external sign.

units.la: P. 224. n. 13. Quod si forte ita actualiter peccando, subitò destituatur sensibus, ut non possit humanitus loquendo atteri; respondeo, tunc non esse præsumendum attritum; atque adeò nec absolvendum docent, communiter: sed ego sub prædicta conditione vix illum regulariter sine absolutione dimitterem; quia rarissimè evenit, ut tam citò sensibus quis, dum actu peccat, destituatur; ita ut vicinus morti, non velit suæ saluti consulere per aliquam attritionem. Sic ille; & ego, cùm è suggestu tractatum de Pœnitentia discipulis dictavi anno 1645. &c.
units.tr: P. 224, n. 13. But if perhaps, while actually sinning in this way, he is suddenly deprived of his senses so that he cannot be reached by human speech, I answer that attrition is not then to be presumed, and so neither is absolution to be given, as is commonly taught. But I, under the aforesaid condition, would scarcely ever dismiss him without absolution, because it very rarely happens that someone, while actually sinning, is so quickly deprived of his senses that, being near death, he does not wish to provide for his salvation by some attrition. Thus he; and I, when I dictated a treatise on Penance to my disciples from the pulpit in 1645, etc.

units.la: P. 226. n. 23. Militant etiam pro hac sententia Doctores alii, afferentes agoniam Catholici esse probabile signum, tum contritionis, tum voluntatis confitendi: nam ita frequenter contingit inter Catholicos.
units.tr: P. 226, n. 23. Other doctors also support this opinion, asserting that the agony of a Catholic is a probable sign both of contrition and of the will to confess, for this so often happens among Catholics.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina his tribus propositionibus contenta, falsa est, temeraria, scandalosa, & Sacramento Pœnitentiæ injuriosa.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine contained in these three propositions is false, rash, scandalous, and injurious to the Sacrament of Penance.

units.la: P. 221. n. 1. Talis infirmus, qui amisit loquelam vel usum rationis, si bene vivebat, ut bonus & fidelis, & frequentabat Confessionem, quamvis non petierit Sacramenta, quia ex insperato talia acciderunt, debet præsupponi contritus, & faciente aliquo Confessionem generalem pro eo, sicut fit in populo, Sacerdos faciat absolutionem ab omni sententia & peccato.
units.tr: P. 221, n. 1. Such a sick man, who has lost speech or the use of reason, if he lived well as a good and faithful man and frequented confession, although he has not asked for the sacraments, because such things happened unexpectedly, is to be presumed contrite; and, with some general confession made on his behalf, as is done for the people, the priest should give absolution from every sentence and sin.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina hujus propositionis uni- versim & absolutè sumta, est in praxi periculosa.
units.tr: CENSURE. The doctrine of this proposition, taken universally and absolutely, is dangerous in practice.

units.la: P. 233. n. 5. Hanc opinionem benignam fateor, sed nescio, an benignior ea, quæ non solum dubitanti, sed certissimè etiam sibi conscio de culpa lethali, concedit licitum esse, missa Confessione, Eucharistiam sumere, etiam præsente idoneo Confessario, si sperauur idoneior, cui devotius & securius confiteatur.
units.tr: P. 233, n. 5. I admit this opinion is mild, but I do not know whether it is milder than the view that allows a person not only in doubt but who is fully aware of mortal guilt to receive the Eucharist, after confession has been omitted, even with a suitable confessor present, provided a more suitable confessor can be hoped for, to whom he may confess more devoutly and safely.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, & contraria Concilio Tridentino.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false and contrary to the Council of Trent.

units.la: P. 277. n. 17. Imò, addunt alii, non solùm cum, qui bona fide putat se habere dolorem, cùm revera non habeat; sed etiam qui scienter, absque ullo prorsùs dolore accedit, judicans, bona fide non esse necessarium, confessionem validam & non iterandam efficere. Et paulò inferiùs. Et secundùm aliquos, licèt cognoscat, se peccare lethaliter, accedendo scienter sine dolore sufficienti, dum de tali defectu doloris simul cum aliis peccatis se accusat. Et inferiùs. Quod de accedente etiam absque ullo prorsus dolore tenet.
units.tr: P. 277, n. 17. Indeed, others add, not only the one who in good faith thinks he has contrition when in fact he does not, but also the one who knowingly approaches without any sorrow at all, judging that in good faith it is not necessary, and that the confession is valid and need not be repeated. And a little lower. And according to some, even if he knows that he sins mortally by approaching knowingly without sufficient sorrow, provided that he accuses himself of this lack of sorrow along with his other sins. And lower. This is held of the one who approaches even without any sorrow whatever.

units.la: P. 277. n. 18. Sacramentum in non ponente obicem, suum semper habet effectum. Et saltem illum qui confitetur cum aliqua displicentia & dolore, sed tamen scienter, sine proposito vitandi lethalia, efficere confessionem validam & non iterandam.
units.tr: P. 277, n. 18. A sacrament, when it places no obstacle, always has its effect. And at least it makes the confession valid and not to be repeated for the one who confesses with some displeasure and sorrow, yet knowingly, without the purpose of avoiding mortal sins.

units.la: P. 278. n. 19. Ex his inquam, doctrinis, potest argui. Contritio est materia proxima poenitentiae; peccata vero materia remota; sed confessio valida est deficiente revera contritione: ergo & deficientibus peccatis: potuit ergo beatissima Virgo, licet nec contritionem habuerit, nec ullum vel levissimum peccatum commiserit. D. Johanni confiteri.
units.tr: P. 278, n. 19. From these doctrines, I say, the following can be argued. Contrition is the proximate matter of penance; sins, however, are the remote matter; but a confession is valid even when contrition is in fact lacking: therefore also when sins are lacking. Thus the most blessed Virgin could confess to St John, although she had neither contrition nor committed any sin, however slight.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina haec prout ab authore intenditur & infertur, falsa est, temeraria, erronea, & contraria Conciliis & Traditioni, ac sacramentum Poenitentiae prorsus evacuans.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine, as the author intends and infers it, is false, rash, erroneous, and contrary to the Councils and to Tradition, and it utterly empties the sacrament of Penance.

units.la: P. 216. n. 3. Post Concilium Tridentinum potest Parochus sacerdotem simplicem, non approbatum ab ordinario, exponere ad audiendas suorum Parochianorum Confessiones.
units.tr: P. 216, n. 3. After the Council of Trent, a parish priest may appoint a simple priest, not approved by the ordinary, to hear the confessions of his parishioners.

units.la: CENSURA. Haec propositio falsa est, & contra- ria Concilio Tridentino. De SUMMO PONTIFICE. pag. 177. n. 4.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false and contrary to the Council of Trent. On the SUPREME PONTIFF. p. 177, n. 4.

units.la: Ideo etiam ad fidem pertinet inhaerere determinationi Summi Pontificis in his quae sunt fidei, etiam in his quae spectant bonos mores, quia in hujusmodi etiam Ecclesia errare non potest, & consequenter nec Caput ejus &c.
units.tr: Therefore it also belongs to faith to adhere to the determination of the Supreme Pontiff in matters of faith, even in those which concern good morals, because in such matters too the Church cannot err, and consequently neither can its Head, etc.

units.la: P. 50. n. 2. De Fide esse, non posse Pontificem errare, &c. Ita ut approbet tanquam consentaneum Euangelicae perfectioni, quod consentaneum non sit. Et inferius. p. 61. n. eod. Tam certa est conclusio, ut oppositum non dubitem esse haereticum.
units.tr: P. 50, n. 2. That it is a matter of faith that the Pontiff cannot err, etc. So that he approves as consonant with evangelical perfection what is not consonant with it. And below. P. 61, n. ibid. The conclusion is so certain that I do not doubt the contrary to be heretical.

units.la: CENSURA. Doctrina his propositionibus conten- ta & illata, falsa est & temeraria, Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ libertatibus contraria, Universitatibus, Theologicis Facultatibus, ac orthodoxis Doctoribus contume- liosa.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine, contained and advanced in these propositions, is false and rash, contrary to the liberties of the Gallican Church, and insulting to the universities, the theological faculties, and orthodox teachers.

units.la: De CENSURIS. p. 283. prop. 5. Qui Clericum occidit veneno in cibo vel in potu, non incurrit excommunicationem.
units.tr: On CENSURES. p. 283, proposition 5. He who kills a cleric by poison in food or drink does not incur excommunication.

units.la: P. 284. n. 1. Item, excommunicatio Canonis posita occidenti Clericum, ajunt quidam, non incurritur, illum veneno occidendo nisi per vim illum interficeret, probant ex eo, quòd Lex dicat: Si quis manus violentas &c. Sed non occidit, nisi per vim cogat venenum sumere: ergò.
units.tr: P. 284, n. 1. Likewise, some say that the excommunication of the Canon, laid down against one who kills a cleric, is not incurred when one kills him by poison, unless he kills him by force; they prove this from the fact that the law says: "If anyone lays violent hands" etc. But he does not kill, unless by force he compels him to take the poison: therefore...

units.la: N. 2. Si verò excommunicatio lata esset contra committentes homicidium, & quis alteri propinato veneno, ante ejus mortem respiisceret, non incurrere excommunicationem.
units.tr: N. 2. But if the excommunication were pronounced against those who commit homicide, and someone who had given another poison to drink repented before the other's death, he would not incur excommunication.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc doctrina falsa est, temeraria, Canonibus & censuris Ecclesiæ illudens.
units.tr: CENSURE. This doctrine is false, rash, and mocks the Canons and the censures of the Church.

units.la: De VOTO. p. 244. prop. 2. Religiosus professus, qui judicio sibi probabili, crederet sibi factam à Deo revelationem de dispensatione ad contrahendum matrimonium, posset licitè contrahere.
units.tr: On VOW. p. 244, proposition 2. A professed religious who, by a judgment probable to himself, believed that a revelation had been made to him by God concerning a dispensation to contract marriage, could lawfully contract it.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, votorum & disciplinæ regularis destructiva, sacrilegiis & apostasiæ viam aperiens.
units.tr: CENSURE. This proposition is false, destructive of vows and of regular discipline, and opens the way to sacrileges and apostasy.

units.la: De IMPURITATE. p. 25. prop. 12. Furtum triginta regalium, majus peccatum est, quàm Sodomia.
units.tr: On IMPURITY. p. 25, proposition 12. The theft of thirty royals is a greater sin than sodomy.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc propositio falsa est, & piis ac castis auribus horrorem injiciens.
units.tr: CENSURA. This proposition is false, and it strikes horror into pious and chaste ears.

units.la: P. 91. n. 4. Licet locare domos meretricibus ; non intentione, ut peccent, sed ut ibi inhabitent.
units.tr: P. 91. n. 4. It is lawful to let houses to prostitutes; not with the intention that they sin, but that they may live there.

units.la: Posse servos deferre literas, quibus vocantur ad peccandum, & eos verbis à sua domina prælatis vocare; dum tamen neque eos ad malum incitent, sed solùm simpliciter proponant verba Dominæ suæ. Et paulò post.
units.tr: It is lawful for servants to carry letters by which they are summoned to sin, and to call them with the words dictated by their mistress, provided that they do not incite them to evil but merely set out the words of their mistress simply. And a little after.

units.la: Si ergò hæc licent, quare non & apponere pecuniam in loco patenti, & uxori consulere, ut consanguineam visitet? nam etsi conjuncta sint peccato, tamen secundùm se & suapte natura non sunt peccata, & consequenter, propter bonum finem scjungi poterunt à peccato.
units.tr: If therefore these things are lawful, why not also to place money in a visible spot, and to advise one's wife to visit her kinswoman? For even if these things are joined to sin, nevertheless in themselves and by their own nature they are not sins, and consequently, for a good end, they can be separated from sin.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæc doctrina falsa est, & scandalosa, perniciosa Reipublicæ, novis & futilibus inventis ad turpia inducens.
units.tr: CENSURA. This doctrine is false and scandalous, harmful to the commonwealth, leading to shameful acts by means of new and frivolous inventions.

units.la: P. 8. prop. 4. Pollutio pag. 11. prop. 6. Inter sponsos p. 13. prop. 7. Sentienti p. 14. prop. 8. A sanguine. p. 204. n. 3. Quare. p. 251. prop. 5. In Conjugatis p. 252. prop. 6. Conjugati, p. 253. prop. 7. Conjugatus p. 257. prop. 8. Si conjugatus p. 259. n. 4. Addunt p. 260. n. 5. Si ergò. p. 261. prop. 10. Si conjugatus. ibid. n. 2. Addit. p. 262. n. 4. Dicit p. 264. n. 3. Videatur p. 266. n. 2. De adstricto.
units.tr: P. 8. prop. 4. Pollution. p. 11. prop. 6. Between betrothed persons, p. 13. prop. 7. To one feeling it, p. 14. prop. 8. From blood. p. 204. n. 3. Why. p. 251. prop. 5. Among the married, p. 252. prop. 6. Married persons, p. 253. prop. 7. A married man, p. 257. prop. 8. If a married man, p. 259. n. 4. They add, p. 260. n. 5. If therefore. p. 261. prop. 10. If a married man. ibid. n. 2. He adds. p. 262. n. 4. He says. p. 264. n. 3. See p. 266. n. 2. On the bound.

units.la: CENSURA. Hæ propositiones (quas Sacra Facultas verbis tantum initialibus designandas de industria judicavit, ut modestiæ & pudoris castarum aurium ac mentium consuleret,) sunt turpes, scandalosæ, propudio-
units.tr: CENSURE. These propositions (which the Sacred Faculty deliberately decided should be indicated only by their initial words, so as to spare the modesty and decency of chaste ears and minds) are base, scandalous, shameless-

units.la: pudiosæ, nefandæ, piarum aurium offensivæ, atque ab Ecclesia & ab omni hominum memoriâ prorsus abolendæ.
units.tr: shameless, unspeakable, offensive to pious ears, and to be utterly abolished by the Church and blotted from all human memory.

units.la: Declarat autem Sacra Facultas, etsi plura ex prædicto libello selegerit damnaveritque, multa nihilominùs superesse, quæ quia ut veritati, morum integritati, castitati ac publicæ honestati adversantur, sic & justâ possent sigillatim censuræ notâ configi; à qua tamen hujus authoris sordibus attonita abstinuit; Ad quas Theologos non decet inaniter esse curiosos, qui nec propter libidinis malum nuptias condemnare; nec propter nuptiarum bonum, libidinem laudare debent. Quamobrem non intendit Sacra Facultas ea probare, quæ velut intacta reliquit, quinimò totum hoc putidum opusculum damnat, ac reprobat, dignúmque judicat quòd æternæ oblivionis silentio sepeliatur. Sanxit etiam Facultas diem dicendum esse Doctoribus, qui ejusdem libelli approbationi subscripserunt, uti coram eadem Facultate compareant ad primam diem mensis Martii proximi, rationem reddituri dictæ approbationis. Ac si comparere neglexerint, dicto die elapso, ex hoc ipso atque impræsentiarum donec præsenti mandato iisdem significando satisfecerint, omnibus Facultatis juribus privat ac privatos declarat, eandémque censuram in Comitiis generalibus relectam & confirmatam, quàm primùm prelo committi atque evulgari jussit. Datum in Sorbona, die tertiâ, mensis Februarii. 1665.
units.tr: The Sacred Faculty declares, however, that although it has selected and condemned many propositions from the said little book, many others nonetheless remain, which, because they are opposed to truth, to the integrity of morals, to chastity and to public decency, could justly be branded individually with the mark of censure. Yet, appalled at the filth of this author, it has refrained from doing so. Theologians ought not to be idly curious about such matters: they should neither condemn marriage on account of the evil of lust, nor praise lust on account of the good of marriage. Wherefore the Faculty does not intend to approve those things which it has left untouched; rather, it condemns and rejects this whole foul little work, and judges it worthy to be buried in the silence of eternal oblivion. The Faculty has also decreed that a day be appointed for the doctors who subscribed to the approval of the same little book to appear before the same Faculty on the first day of next March, to give an account of that approval. If they neglect to appear, the said day having passed, then from that very fact, and for the present until they have satisfied this present mandate by notifying them of it, it deprives them of all the rights of the Faculty and declares them deprived, and it has ordered this same censure, read and confirmed in the general assembly, to be committed to the press and published as soon as possible. Given at the Sorbonne, on the third day of February, 1665.

units.la: Demandato D. D. Decani & Magistrorum dictæ Facultatis Sacræ Theologiæ Parisiensis.
units.tr: By command of the Dean and Doctors of the said Sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris.
PH. BOVVOT, Chief Apparitor.

units.la: XL. Hactenus Censura, impuras illas, infaustas; & Deo hominibusque invisas, atque in Romanæ Ecclesiæ communione haud postremo loco nidulantes Aves ex nativis plumis suis exacte referens. Haud denique <bl>ἀπεσταλμένος</bl> fuerit, vaticinium illud de immundis avibus in spirituali illa Babylone nidificantibus, etiam ad literam impletum, ex Concilii Romani historia comprobare.
units.tr: XL. Thus far the Censure, exactly describing those filthy, ill-omened birds, hateful to God and men, which nest no small part in the communion of the Roman Church. Finally, it may not be out of place, sent [ἀπεσταλμένος] as it were from God, to confirm from the history of the Roman Council that the prophecy about the unclean birds nesting in that spiritual Babylon has also been fulfilled to the letter.

units.la: Johannes XXIV. prius Balthasar Cossa dictus. Ille (liceat hominem Gobelini Personæ, Bilefeldensis quondam Decani, verbis, quæ in Cosmodromio ejus extant, describere) Pauperum oppressor, justitiæ persecutor, Iniquorum columna, Simoniacorum stator, Carnis cultor, Vitiorum fax, peregrinus à virtutibus, Infamiæ speculum, & omnium malitiarum profundus adinventor, adeò & in tantùm scandalizans Ecclesiam Christi, ut inter Christi fideles vitam & mores, ejus cognoscentes, vulgariter dicatur Diabolus incarnatus. (En Dæmonium!) hic inquam, narrante historiam Nicolao Clemangis Archidiacono Bajocensi, in Epistolis, statim atque electus est Papa, Sigismundum Hungariæ Regem, Cæsareâ Coronâ impertiturus, Romæ Synodum celebravit. In Synodi illius prima sessione, post Missam de Spiritu S. cùm ipse Johannes in sublimiore cathedra præsideret, mox aderat bubo (exosa[?]scilicet & immunda avis) qui supra Templi trabem horrifica sua voce, injectis in Papam oculis, ipsum monstrifico modo salutavit. Astantes autem cùm vehementer ostentum mirarentur, non pauci submissa voce dicebant. En Spiritus S. adest, quem tam ardenter invocabant, ut illis expectatum ferat auxilium. Ceteri se mutuò, & Papam aspicientes, risum non continebant. Papa ipse rubore suffusus sudore, atque intra semet ipsum æstuare. Tandémque non inveniens, qua ratione confusioni illi suæ consuleret, soluto Concilio surgens discèssit. Secuta est altera sessio, in qua similia rursùs, sed majori cum veretundia passus est. Nec bubo aut clamoribus abigi, aut fustibus terreri poterat. Occisus tandem turbare desiit. Conciliúmque ipsum sine fructu solutum est. Atque tales ex hoc portento spirituales columbas Ecclesiam illam longo tempore rexisse, à multis palàm assertum esse, idem Clemangis confirmat.
units.tr: John XXIII, formerly called Baldassare Cossa. He (let me describe the man in the words of Gobelinus Person, once Dean of Bielefeld, which are found in his Cosmodromium) was an oppressor of the poor, a persecutor of justice, a pillar of the wicked, a promoter of simony, a worshipper of the flesh, a torch of vices, a stranger to virtues, a mirror of infamy, and a deep inventor of every wickedness, so greatly and so far scandalizing the Church of Christ that among the faithful of Christ, those who know his life and morals commonly call him the Devil incarnate. (Behold the Devil!) This man, I say, as Nicolas Clemangis, archdeacon of Bayeux, relates in his Letters, as soon as he was elected Pope, celebrated a Synod at Rome, intending to bestow the imperial crown on Sigismund, King of Hungary. In the first session of that Synod, after the Mass of the Holy Spirit, while John himself presided in the higher chair, an owl (a hateful and unclean bird, surely) immediately appeared, and perched on a beam of the temple, and with its dreadful voice, fixing its eyes on the Pope, greeted him in a monstrous manner. The bystanders, greatly wondering at the portent, said in lowered voices, not a few of them: Behold, the Holy Spirit is present, whom they invoked so ardently, that He might bring them the help they awaited. The others, looking at one another and at the Pope, could not restrain their laughter. The Pope himself was suffused with red, sweating, and seething within himself. At last, not finding by what means he might remedy that confusion, he rose, the Council was dissolved, and he departed. A second session followed, in which he suffered similar things again, but with greater shame. Nor could the owl be driven away by shouts, or frightened by clubs. At last, when killed, it ceased to disturb. And the Council itself was dissolved without fruit. That the Church was ruled for a long time by such spiritual doves, many openly asserted, as the same Clemangis confirms.
XLI. But let us continue the thread of the prophecy.

units.la: Postquam cecidit Babylon & dæmoniorum facta domicilium est, S. Johannes aliam vocem seu hortationem ἀὸεαρελον, non expresso edentis nomine, audivit, dicentem: Exi te ex ea, populę mi, ne communicetis cum peccatis ejus, & ne accipiatis de plagis ejus. Apoc. xviii. 4. Non confundendum id esse cum annuntiatione casùs Babylonis, sive quòd jam cadere cœperit, satis apparet. Non potest igitur intelligi tantùm præceptum vel adhortatio ad fugiendam communionem peccatorum Babylonis, sed vox quasi ex cœlo audita, ut egrediantur Babylone; quæ vox illa ipsa est, quæ hîc & alibi in Sacro Codice scripta est. Ex qua intelligitur, futurum tempus, ut post Babylonis casum jam cœptum aperiatur janua, liberque ex Babylone, velut inferni portis, exitus detur. Cùm igitur peccata Babylonis extant, & ejusdem plagæ imminent, & libertas exeundi datur, & locus, in quem confugiant, qui piè vivere velint, ubi id liceat, patet; tum verò quasi de Cœlo auditur hæc vox: Exite ex ea, populi mi, quid cunctamini? Aperuit januam is, qui clavim Davidis habet, quo aperiente claudit nemo, Apoc. ii. 7. Ita cùm
units.tr: After Babylon had fallen and become a dwelling of demons, St. John heard another voice or exhortation, not naming the speaker, saying: Come out of her, my people, that you do not share in her sins and that you do not receive of her plagues. Rev. 18:4. That this is not to be confused with the announcement of Babylon's fall, even if it has already begun to fall, is quite clear. Therefore it cannot be understood as merely a command or exhortation to flee communion in the sins of Babylon, but as a voice heard as if from heaven, that they should go out of Babylon; this is the very voice which is written here and elsewhere in the Sacred Book. From it we understand that there would be a time, after the fall of Babylon has begun, when the gate is opened and a free exit is given out of Babylon, as out of the gates of hell. Since therefore the sins of Babylon still exist, and her plagues hang over her, and the freedom to depart is given, and a place where those who wish to live piously may flee, where this is permitted, it is plain; then indeed this voice is heard as if from heaven: Come out of her, my people; why do you delay? He has opened the door who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, Rev. 3:7. So when

units.la: Tom. II. Cyrus promulgavit edictum, licere omnibus, qui essent de populo Dei, in patriam reverti, tantundem id fuit, ac si ex cœlo audiretur vox Prophetæ: Fugite ex Babylone, Esai. xlviii. 20. Jer. li. 6. 45. sic cùm auditum est: Pax, Pax propinquo & longinquo, Esai. lvii. 19. tum audita est vox & cœleusma cœleste: Exite ex ea, populi mi.
units.tr: Vol. II. Cyrus issued the edict that all who were of the people of God might return to their homeland, it was just as if the voice of the Prophet were heard from heaven: Flee out of Babylon, Isa. 48:20; Jer. 51:6, 45. So when it was heard: Peace, peace to him who is near and to him who is far, Isa. 57:19, then the voice and heavenly proclamation was heard: Come out of her, my people.

units.la: XLII. Cùm primùm cœlestis ille Splendor terram, uti vidimus collustravit, atque sic Papatus cadere cœpit, magna hominum, Regnorum, Provinciarum, Civitatum pars à Papatu abhorruit, Missam abolevit, Idololatriam sustulit, Papæ authoritatem sprevit, denique religionem ad S. Scripturæ amussim exactam, reformare alacriter cœpit.
units.tr: XLII. As soon as that heavenly Splendor illuminated the earth, as we have seen, and Papacy began to fall, a great part of men, kingdoms, provinces and cities turned away from Papacy, abolished the Mass, removed idolatry, scorned the authority of the Pope, and at last began eagerly to reform religion, brought into exact conformity with the standard of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Sed piis conatibus restitit Papa, nec ulla pietatis, vel studii veritatis, sola commodorum suorum ratione ductus. Neque defuerunt etiam passim, qui pro ejus focis strenuè pugnarent, stylum pilumque stringerent; adeò ut passim etiam armis decerneretur. Nondum ergò hinc inde tutum fuerat Babylonem deserere, & cœlestis luminis ductum sequi. Paulatim tamen Deum Ecclesiæ dedisse locum in diversis Civitatibus, Regnis, Terris, ubi ei fidem profiteri, pietatémque exercere tutò liceret, in propatulo est. Maximè autem tum Ecclesia ex Babylone vocata est, quando Lege Imperii, seu Pace Imperiali A. MDL. II. Augustæ fancita, & A. MDLV. Passavii constituta, Principum & Civitatum, quæ Euangelio nomen dederant, vel deinceps datura erant, infestatio vel persecutio ob causam religionis prohibita est. Quod ipsum antehac etiam A. MDXXXI. in Helvetia, Pace Provinciali pacta, contigerat. Idem in Dania, Suecia, Anglia, Scotia, Gallia, Hungaria, Bohemia, Belgio Fœderato factum.
units.tr: But the Pope resisted these pious efforts, moved by no piety or zeal for truth, but solely by regard for his own advantages. Nor were there lacking everywhere those who fought vigorously for his hearths, wielding pen and spear, so that everywhere the matter was even decided by arms. Therefore, it was not yet safe on either side to desert Babylon and follow the guidance of heavenly light. Nevertheless, it is evident that God gradually gave the Church a place in various cities, kingdoms and lands, where it was safe to profess faith in Him and exercise piety. The Church was called out of Babylon most of all when, by the Law of the Empire, or the Imperial Peace, sanctioned at Augsburg in 1555 and established at Passau in 1552, the persecution or harassment of princes and cities which had given their name to the Gospel, or were about to do so, was forbidden for reasons of religion. This had already happened earlier, in 1531, in Switzerland, by the Provincial Peace agreed there. The same occurred in Denmark, Sweden, England, Scotland, France, Hungary, Bohemia, and the United Netherlands.

units.la: Omnibus hisce in locis Ecclesia libertatem religionis, Dei immenso beneficio, nacta, sicut Babylon reliqua domicilium dæmoniorum; ita ipsa hospitium fidelium, sive indigenarum, sive advenarum, Babylone, aperta veluti janua, exeuntium evasit. Tum ergo passim cœlestis illa vox percrebuit: Exite ex ea, populE mi, dato scilicet tuto loco, ubi sine periculo cuivis vera loqui & recta facere liceret; & conscientia magno teste cuique suggerente, non esse tentandum Deum, neque diligendum locum, in quo semper tentetur, & ad communionem mali ipse illiciatur.
units.tr: In all these places the Church, having obtained freedom of religion by the immense benefit of God, became, just as the rest of Babylon became a dwelling of demons, a refuge of the faithful, whether natives or foreigners, opening like a door to those coming out of Babylon. Then therefore that heavenly voice spread on all sides: Come out of her, my people, that is, since a safe place was given where anyone could speak the truth and do right without danger; and as conscience, a great witness, suggests to each person, that God must not be tested, nor should a place be loved in which one is always tempted and drawn into communion with evil.

units.la: XLIII. Sed & impleta eadem vox est, hodieque impletur in ore multorum, qui disputárunt disputántque adhuc vel de reliquiis fermenti Romani, vel de reconciliatione cum Papatu. Sic enim & in Germania alibi{a} que Reformati Augustanos: & in Anglia Presbyteriani Episcopales, ad abjiciendas Romani fermenti reliquias, adeóque plenissimè reformandam Ecclesiam, Babylonémque deserendam penitus, strenuè cohortantur. Ac majore etiam contentione vox illa cœlestis; Exite ex ea, populE mi, ingeminata est, & ingeminatur adhuc adversus eos, qui Papatum incrustare, Babylonem cum Sione, Belialem cum Christo conciliare, adeóque ἀμι-κτα μιγνύμ nunquam non tentárunt: cujusmodi jam olim fuêre Erasmus, Cassander, Wicelius, Modrevius, Milleterius, Grotius, alii, Syncretistarum nomine famosi, quibus se Lutherus, Calvinus, alii; ac non ita pridem Josephus Hallus & Andreas Rivetus, cœlestem illam vocem pleno gutture declamantes, masculè oppofuerunt.
units.tr: XLIII. But this same voice has been fulfilled, and is fulfilled even today, on the lips of many who have disputed, and still dispute, either about the remnants of Roman leaven or about reconciliation with Papacy. Thus in Germany and elsewhere the Reformed exhort the Augsburg Confessors, and in England the Presbyterians exhort the Episcopalians, vigorously, to cast off the remnants of Roman leaven, and thus to reform the Church fully and to desert Babylon completely. And that heavenly voice, Come out of her, my people, has been repeated with even greater vehemence, and is still repeated against those who have tried, and always try, to plaster over Papacy, to reconcile Babylon with Zion and Belial with Christ, and thus to mix things that cannot be mixed [ἄμικτα μιγνύναι]. Such men were long ago Erasmus, Cassander, Wicelius, Modrevius, Milletier, Grotius and others, notorious under the name of Syncretists, against whom Luther, Calvin and others set themselves; and not so long ago Joseph Hall and Andreas Rivet, declaring that heavenly voice with full throat, opposed them manfully.

units.la: XLIV. Pertinet huc, quòd Apocalypsis cap. xvii. 16. dicit: Reges & Principes cornua Bestiæ, Babylonem odiunt, deserent.
units.tr: XLIV. To this belongs what Revelation 17:16 says: the kings and princes, the horns of the Beast, will hate Babylon, forsake her,

units.la: nem odio prosecuturos , desolatam nudámque reddituros , ejus carnes comesturos, edmque denique igni crematuros. Illud quoque judicium post exitum ex Papatu fidelium impleri coepit, impletúrque quotidie. Nam juxtà eandem Prophetiam, ex iis, qui potestatem suam, ut Reges, unam horam acceperunt cum Bestia, potentiam & potestatem suam Bestiæ & per eam Meretrici tradiderunt, & cum Agno συμφωνήν ἀρετή, pro Papa ejúsque παμβασιλεία belligerati sunt, eo ipso tempore, quo Leo X. Papa, Lutherum damnavit; quos Diss. viij. s. 2. th. 23. nominatim recensuimus; nonnulli, puta Reges Angliæ, Scotiæ, Hiberniæ, Daniæ, Sueciæ, unà cum parte haud exigua Germaniæ, Helvetiæ, Hispaniæ, cui priùs Foederati Belgii Ordines serviverunt, ab Agno, Domino Dominorum & Rege regum, atque iis, qui cum ipso fuerunt, vocatis, electis & fidelibus, victi sunt; hoc est, demonstratam ex Dei verbo veritatem, per ὁμολογίαν τῆς πίστεως illi receperunt, & in Regnis ac Provinciis publica authoritate introduxerunt. Ita enim, ut superius dicta repetam, in Suecia, in locum Sigismundi persecutoris, qui Rex Poloniæ factus erat, Carolus patruus ipsius Rex factus est, doctrinæ Euangelicæ addictus. In Dania & Norwegia, Christiano, Fridericus I. & ipse Euangelicæ confessioni addictus, successit. Anglia post Eduardum VI. & Johannem Grajam, Elisabetham faventem nacta est. In Scotia Mariæ exauctoratæ, Jacobus VI. Euangelicam religionem professus, successit. Hi ergò Meretricem agnitam odio habuerunt, desertam subductis aquis, hoc est populis sibi subditis, desolárunt, nudárunt & devoratis ejus carnibus, eidem funestum carnisprivium indixerunt. Quod factum esse tum publicis blicis confessionibus scriptisque, Meretrici huic habitum suum meretricium detrahendo; tum Papæ obsequium omne suum populorumque suorum negando; tum eidem Archiepiscopatus, Episcopatus, Abbatias, Canonicatus, Beneficia, Annatas, Denarios, Decimas, omnia denique culinæ Papalis & luxuriæ, quibus haftenus fraudulenter violenterque raptis, cuticulam unêta illa cohors curaverat, instrumenta subducendo; vectigalia resecando; Romanasque nundinationes in regionibus suis in universum prohibendo; res ipsa loquitur: sic autem bona illa, quatenus rapinæ rationem non habuêre, Meretrici huic subtraxerunt, ut eadem in legitimum Ecclesiæ vel Reipublicæ usum converterint. Neque profecto clarius dici, vel distertius cogitari quicquam potest.
units.tr: and [will] pursue her with hatred, make her desolate and naked, eat her flesh, and finally burn her with fire. This judgment also began to be fulfilled after the departure of the faithful from Papacy, and it is fulfilled every day. For according to the same prophecy, those who received power as kings for one hour with the Beast gave their power and authority to the Beast and through it to the Harlot, and they have made war with the Lamb [in consent with the Lamb, συμφωνήν], fighting for the Pope and his universal kingship [παμβασιλεία], at the very time when Pope Leo X condemned Luther. We listed them by name in Diss. viii, s. 2, th. 23: some, namely the kings of England, Scotland, Ireland, Denmark, Sweden, together with a not small part of Germany, Switzerland, and Spain (to which the Estates of the Dutch Netherlands had earlier been subject), have been conquered by the Lamb, Lord of lords and King of kings, and by those who are with him, called, chosen and faithful. That is, having been shown the truth from God's Word, they received it through the confession of the faith [ὁμολογίαν τῆς πίστεως] and introduced it into their kingdoms and provinces by public authority. For so, to repeat what was said above: in Sweden, in place of Sigismund the persecutor, who had become King of Poland, Charles, his uncle, became king, devoted to the Evangelical doctrine. In Denmark and Norway, Frederick I, himself also devoted to the Evangelical confession, succeeded Christian. England, after Edward VI and John Grey, received Elizabeth, who favored the cause. In Scotland, after Mary was deposed, James VI, who professed the Evangelical religion, succeeded. These therefore have hated the Harlot once recognized, have left her, drawn off the waters, that is, their subjects, made her desolate, stripped her naked, and, having eaten her flesh, have proclaimed a deadly fast upon her. That this has been done is shown by public confessions and writings, by stripping this Harlot of her harlot's dress; by denying the Pope all obedience from themselves and their peoples; by taking from him archbishoprics, bishoprics, abbeys, canonries, benefices, annates, pennies, tithes, and finally all the instruments of the Papal kitchen and luxury, which that crew had until then fraudulently and violently seized and had carefully cultivated; by cutting off revenues; and by forbidding Roman markets in their lands altogether. The thing speaks for itself. And so they withdrew those goods from this Harlot, insofar as they had not been taken by plunder, and converted them to the lawful use of the Church or the Commonwealth. Certainly nothing could be said more clearly or thought more plainly.

units.la: XLV. Sed & coeteri Reges plerique post prædicationem Euangelii inducti sunt, non quidem ut veritatem haftenus amarent, tamen Meretricem subinde odio Hispania, (utcunque illud, externæ Papæ communioni adhæren-do, occultare satagunt) ut haberent, desolarent, imò carnes ejus devorarent. Ita enim ipsam Urbem Romam Carolus V. per Carolum Borbonium A. MDXXV cepit, captam non leviter concussit, & Papam juxta atque Cardinales ipsos extremo ludibrio exposuit. Ipse quoque, & secuti ad modernum usque Imperatores, coronam suam à Papa excipere, vel Romæ pedes ejus præsentes osculari neglexerunt: quod certè cùm amoris indicium haberi nequeat, secreti odii argumentum haberi debet. Accedit, quòd non tantùm Ferdinandus I. Imperiali pace fancita, Protestantibus per universam Germaniam pacem securitatémque procuravit, adeóque odium Hierarchiæ, desolationem & triste illud carnisprivium remisit: sed etiam Ferdinandus III. fancita solenniter pace Monalterienfi, frustrà uti Hist. Pap.s. cclviij. narravimus, protestante & ringente Innonocentii X. Nuntio, Fabio Chusio, cum Protestantibus Imperii solenne pastum inivit, cujus vi Germaniæ Principibus bona Episcoporum occupare, Dioceses in terrenos dominatus convertere; Episcopos, Capitula, Monasteria, Abbatias, &c. extinguere sas integrúmque fuit. Annon sic carnes Meretricis devoratæ sunt? Neque enim Reges Meretricis carnes comedentes Cannibales antropophagi ex Brasilia esse debuerunt. Hispaniæ quoque Rex Catholicus, non solùm Belgicis Provinciis solenni pacto libertatem utrámque civilem & religiosam concessit; sed etiam Romanæ Curiæ libertates Regni, velut in patronatibus Regiis, cœterísque laicis; beneficiorum patrimonialium à reservationibus, præventionibus, expectativis, Romanis, nec non beneficiorum quorumvis, vel pensionum exteris, veluti Curtisanis Romanis, non conferendarum immunitate; nominationes Regias; jura Regia in bona temporalia Ecclesiasticorum delinquentium; aliáque ejusmodi invadenti, non semel fibulam imposuit: quin & Papales Bullas, ne Regis & Regni jura delibare possint, Regiorum judicum examini subjicere solet: quod nundinationis Papalis præsentissimum fræœnum est. Venetos quoque cum Paulo V. pro suis circa bona immobilia à Clero non possidenda, jurisdictionémque in Ecclesiasticos, depugnantes; magna cum Papæ ipsius, cujus fulmina bruta jam esse, ex contentione illa omnibus innotuit; nec non Jesuitarum, pupillæ oculorum Papæ, ignominia, strenuè depugnantes victores discessisse, Papámque ipsum foro cedere coactum, Histor. Pap. s. ccxx. §. cccx. narravimus. In Gallia, Hungaria, Polonia, Bohemia, Religiosa Libertas Protestantibus concessa, non parùm etiam Babylonem denudavit, desolavit, carnibúsque suis privavit. Nihil dicam de nundinationibus Papæ post Reformationem in Regnis ac Provinciis ei adhærentibus, multis modis infraćtis prohibitisque: nihil de libertatibus Regnorum, Galliæ inprimis, novissimè à Rousselio in Historia Jurisdictionis Pontificiæ fusè admodùm dedućtis, & à Petro de Marca, Parisiensi Archiepiscopo, libris de Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii editis, propugnatis: nihil denique de novissimis Definitionibus Regni & Cleri Gallicani, quibus Papæ in temporalibus potestas omnis, & in Spiritualibus dominatio ac infallibilitas, Papatûs anima, penitûs, uti in Historia etiam Papatûs §. cccxlÿ. commemoravimus, sic concussa & convulsa est, ut jure meritóque asseveretur, Papæ nomen & authoritatem, quæ in ejusdem ἀπιϱοϛ elatione, dominatione ἀνωτάℓῥ̀νψ & infallibilitate etiam extra Concilium consistit, per Galliam omnem jam extinćtam abolitámque jacere.
units.tr: XLV. But also most of the other kings, after the preaching of the Gospel, have been led, not indeed to love the truth so far, yet from time to time to hate the Harlot (however much Spain strives to conceal this, while adhering to communion with the foreign Pope), so as to hold her, make her desolate, and indeed devour her flesh. For thus Charles V, through Charles of Bourbon, in 1527 took the city of Rome itself, shook it violently when captured, and exposed the Pope, just as much as the Cardinals themselves, to extreme mockery. Also he himself and the emperors who followed, down to the present, have neglected to receive their crown from the Pope or to kiss his feet when in Rome; which, since it cannot be taken as a sign of love, must be taken as evidence of a hidden hatred. Add to this that Ferdinand I, when the Imperial peace was ratified, not only procured peace and security for the Protestants throughout Germany, and so remitted the hatred of the Hierarchy, the desolation, and that sad fast from flesh; but also Ferdinand III, when the peace of Münster had been solemnly ratified (as we related in Hist. Pap. s. 258, in vain), with the Nuncio of Innocent X, Fabio Chigi, protesting and resisting, entered a solemn pact with the Protestants of the Empire, by virtue of which it was lawful and whole for the princes of Germany to occupy the goods of the bishops, to turn the dioceses into temporal dominions, and to extinguish bishops, chapters, monasteries, abbeys, and so on. Were not her flesh devoured in this way? For kings eating the Harlot's flesh need not be cannibal man-eaters from Brazil. The Catholic King of Spain, too, not only granted both civil and religious liberty to the Belgian Provinces by solemn pact, but has also more than once imposed a bridle upon the liberties of the Roman Curia that invade the kingdom: such as the royal patronages, and the other lay rights; the immunity from reservations, prevention, and expectatives of Rome for patrimonial benefices, and the non-conferring of any benefices or pensions upon foreigners, such as Roman courtiers; royal nominations; royal rights over the temporal goods of delinquent ecclesiastics; and other such things. Indeed, he usually subjects Papal bulls to the examination of royal judges, so that they cannot touch the rights of the King and kingdom: which is the most present bridle of the Papal market. Also the Venetians, when they fought with Paul V over their not possessing immovable goods held by the Clergy, and over jurisdiction against ecclesiastics, departed as victors, with great scandal to the Pope himself, whose thunderbolts, now known to be empty, became known to all from that contest; and also the Jesuits, the apple of the Pope's eye, to their disgrace, bravely fighting, and forcing the Pope himself to give way in the court, as we related in Histor. Pap. s. 220, §. 310. In France, Hungary, Poland, and Bohemia, religious liberty granted to the Protestants has no little stripped Babylon bare, made her desolate, and deprived her of her flesh. I say nothing about the Pope's markets in the kingdoms and provinces that adhere to him after the Reformation, which have been forbidden and restrained in many ways; nothing about the liberties of the kingdoms, of France above all, set out very fully most recently by Rousselius in his History of Papal Jurisdiction, and defended by Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, in his books on the Concord of Priesthood and Empire; nothing, finally, about the most recent Definitions of the Gallican Kingdom and Clergy, by which all the Pope's power in temporal matters, and his domination and infallibility in spiritual matters, the soul of Papacy, as we have also recalled in the History of Papacy §. 341, has been so shaken and convulsed, down to its core, that it is rightly and deservedly asserted that the name and authority of the Pope, which in his supreme [ἀπειρος] lofty exaltation, domination, supreme [ἀνωτάτω] authority, and infallibility even apart from a Council, lies extinguished and abolished throughout all France.

units.la: XLVI. Ex Regum igitur Occidentalium Christianorum, de quibus Prophetia loquitur, numero, non pauci Papatum hostili odio prosecuti desolárunt, nudárunt, carnibus privárunt in solidum: reliqui id ipsum aggressi, præcisa vel circumcisa saltem Curiæ Meretricia mercede sua, subdućtísque ejus obedientiæ populis nonnullis suis, nondum planè perfecerunt. Spes tamen est, perfećturos quandoque, dummodò tanto Divinæ gloriæ zelo ducantur, quantam suorum commodorum rationem habent. Æquissimum enim est, ut cùm jura sua adversùs Papas, Prælatos & Clerum universum, armis & minis strenuè defendant, majorem longè Dei & Christi rationem habeant, neque Dei verbum profanari, & Christi meritum conculcari semper sinant: ne indicio tali se prodant, quòd à semetipsis loquantur, adeóque Dei verbo & Spiritu instructi nondum sint. Hunc enim indagandæ & cognoscendæ veritatis Canonem, Christus ipse ostendit Joh. vii. 18. dicens: Qui à semetipso loquitur, gloriam suam quærit. Quiverò quærit gloriam ejus, qui misit eum, is verax est, & injustitia caret,
units.tr: XLVI. Thus from the number of the Western Christian kings, of whom the Prophecy speaks, not a few have pursued Papacy with hostile hatred, made her desolate, stripped her naked, and deprived her wholly of her flesh. The rest, having undertaken the same, have not yet fully accomplished it: they have cut off or at least trimmed back the Harlot Curia's wages, and have withdrawn some of their peoples from her obedience, but not yet altogether. Yet there is hope that they will bring it to completion at some time, provided they are led by as great a zeal for divine glory as they have regard for their own advantages. For it is most just that, since they defend their rights vigorously with arms and threats against the Popes, the prelates, and the whole Clergy, they should have far greater regard for God and Christ, and not allow the Word of God to be profaned and the merit of Christ always to be trampled underfoot; lest by such a sign they betray that they speak from themselves, and so are not yet instructed by God's Word and Spirit. For Christ himself shows this canon for searching out and knowing the truth, John 7:18, saying: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory. But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, he is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him.

units.la: XLVII. Ad exeundum ex Babylone, eámque magis magisque desolandam, nudandámque, acerrimum stimulum populo Dei fulmina Concilii Tridentini, nullo legitimo judicio contra veritatem vibrata, addiderunt. Effecerunt enim ea, ut qui veritatem nôssent, & anathemata illa audirent, in Babylonica Civitate hærere amplius non possent. Quin & ea ipsa anathemata Babylonem se ipsa deteriorem reddiderunt, quia errores suos decretis firmârunt, conscientiis obtruserunt, ceu Idola quædam adoranda, ab omnibus sub æternæ mortis pœna erexerunt, denique id, quantum in anathematizantibus est, effecerunt, ut nemo amplius in ea communione veritatis amans & studiosus reperiatur. Per anathemata illa, qui in eadem communione habitant, se quasi sepeliverunt, & mortuos inter collocárunt, uti Ezechiel cap. xxxix. 11. loquitur.
units.tr: XLVII. To drive the people out of Babylon, and to make her more and more desolate and naked, the thunderbolts of the Council of Trent, hurled without any lawful judgment against the truth, have added the sharpest goad. For they have brought it about that those who knew the truth, and heard those anathemas, could no longer remain in the Babylonian city. Moreover, those very anathemas have made Babylon worse than she was, because they confirmed her errors by decrees, forced them upon consciences, and set them up, like certain idols to be adored, under pain of eternal death for all; finally, insofar as it lies with those who anathematize, they have brought it about that no one who loves and studies the truth any longer remains in that communion. By those anathemas, those who dwell in that same communion have as it were buried themselves and placed themselves among the dead, as Ezekiel speaks, chapter 39:11.

units.la: XLVIII. Frustrà ergò sic exeuntibus Babylone, & separatis, schismatis reatum objiciunt. Nam Babylone omninò, Deo ipso ex Cœlo instante, & vehementer urgente, exeuntem fuit. Romam autem Babylonem esse, exeuntes iis ipsis, quæ hoc libro paulò accuratiùs deduximus, argumentis compertum habuerunt. Neque enim separatio vel divisio, sed causa separationis injusta, & Dei verbo contraria, schisma facit. Abitus vero noster laudabilis fuit, talis videlicet, qualis Abrahami è Chaldæa, & Apostolorum è Judæa fuit. Sed insuper non tam exivimus, quàm Leonis Papæ, & Tridentini Concilii anathematis, expulsi fuimus; atque sic expulsi, nisi in merum Atheismum prolabi voluissemus, de cultu Publico, eoque Legitimo prospicere nobis debuimus. Neque adeo Ecclesiâ exivimus, sed ad veram Ecclesiam à Christo & Apostolis institutam, veteremque adeò Apostolicam & Romanam, regressi sumus. Non nos denique Ecclesiam deseruimus, sed in nobis Ecclesia Papatum deseruit.
units.tr: XLVIII. It is therefore in vain that they charge us with schism for leaving Babylon and separating ourselves from it. For we left Babylon entirely at God's own command, since he himself urged us from heaven with great insistence. And our adversaries have themselves found, from the arguments which we have set out somewhat more fully in this book, that Rome is Babylon. Separation or division does not make a schism; an unjust cause of separation, one contrary to the Word of God, does. Our departure was praiseworthy, of the same kind as Abraham's departure from Chaldea and the Apostles' from Judea. Moreover, we were not so much departing as being expelled by the anathemas of Pope Leo and the Council of Trent. And having been expelled in this way, unless we wished to slip into sheer atheism, we had to provide for ourselves a public and therefore lawful worship. Nor, indeed, did we leave the Church. Rather, we returned to the true Church instituted by Christ and the Apostles, and indeed to the ancient Apostolic and Roman Church. Finally, we did not desert the Church; it was the Papacy that deserted the Church, in us.
