units.la: XLIX. Sed nostros non fuisse schismatis authores, ex ipsa historia clarius longè est, quàm imber, cùm pluit. Cùm enim Tezelius aliique in Germania, Simonius in Helvetia, indulgentias prædicâssent, & væ-num expositissent, nihil non Lutherus & Zwinglius cauponatieni huic adversantes, pro piis Christianis & sanis cordatisque Theologiæ Doctoribus fecerunt. Publicè quippe cauponationem illam reprehenderunt, & ex Scripturis refutârunt. Tam enim fœda illa fuit, ut honestiores Pontificios hodiéque ejus pudeat. Ipsum Concilium Tridentinum, indulgentiarum illam nundinationem, verbis saltem, uti supra ostendimus, prohibens, haud obscurè id confirmat. Illene ergò schisma facit, qui fratres falsum prædicantes & malum facientes, reprehendit: an qui falsum prædicat, sordium causa malúmque facit? Is verò fuit Leo X. Papa, de quo id scriptores omni exceptione majores testatum fecisse, alibi ostendimus. Neque id Laurentius Surius ipse, qui omnem historiam suam purgando Papatui Tom. II. iiiii concontexuit, dissimulare potuit, scribens: Fortassis importunos quosdam indulgentiarum praedicatores turpis quaestus causa pro concione temere multa dixisse. Culpam tamen à Pontifice abstergere nixus, fatetur nihilominus, Lutherum plerisque Viris gravibus & eruditis non pessimo zelo moveri visum esse, planéque nihil spectare aliud, quàm Ecclesiae reformationem; cujus quidem, inquit, deformes abusus non parùm malè habebant omnes bonos. Haec in Commentariis ejus ad A. 1517. p. 93. legere est. Narrat deinceps, Lutherum provocasse ad Papam, sed post ab eo palàm defecisse, & jus Canonicum combussisse, quod ipsius inconstantiae imputat. Sed omittit homo ex dolis consutus, Bullam Leonis in Lutherum prius emissam, cujus capita praecipua Sleidanus Lib. II. commemorat. Summa Bullae est, quòd Papa damnat Lutheri sententias; vetat sub poena gravissima, ne quis ita sentiat: Lutheri libros incendi jubet: damnat inprimis, quòd à Papa ad Concilium provocaverit contra Pii II. & Julii II. decretum, quo decretum sit, ut qui sic provocant, poenam haereticis constitutam subeant. Post Bullam emissam, Lutheri libri incensi sunt. Omittit etiam Surius mala fide, quae Hadrianus VI. ad Principes Imperii, Norinbergae congregatos, A. MDXXII. scripsit, ubi inter alia vetat Lutherum admitti ad defensionem eorum, quae de fide & Sacramentis scripsit; simúlque per os Cheregati, cui ita in mandatis dederat, fatetur, aliquot jam annis in sancta fede multa abominanda fuisse, abusus in spiritualibus, excessus in mandatis, & omnia denique perversum mutata, nec mirum, si aegritudo à capite in membra, à summis Pontificibus in alios inferiores Praelatos descenderit.
units.tr: XLIX. But that our side were not the authors of the schism is clearer from history itself than rain when it falls. For when Tetzel and others in Germany, and Simon in Helvetia, had preached indulgences and put them up for sale, Luther and Zwingli, opposing this peddling in every way, did what pious Christians and sound, judicious doctors of theology ought to do. They publicly rebuked that huckstering and refuted it from the Scriptures. It was indeed so disgraceful that even the more honourable Papists are ashamed of it today. The Council of Trent itself, which at least in words forbade that trafficking in indulgences, as we have shown above, clearly confirms this. So who makes a schism: the one who rebukes brethren who preach falsely and do evil, or the one who preaches falsely and does evil for the sake of filthy gain? The latter was Pope Leo X, of whom we have shown elsewhere that writers beyond all exception have testified this. Nor could Laurentius Surius himself, who wove together his whole history in purging it for the Papacy, dissimulate this, when he wrote: Perhaps some importunate preachers of indulgences, for the sake of shameful gain, rashly said many things from the pulpit. Yet, labouring to wipe the blame from the Pontiff, he nevertheless admits that Luther seemed to most grave and learned men to be moved by no bad zeal, and to aim at nothing else than the reformation of the Church; whose deformed abuses, he says, grieved all good men not a little. This can be read in his Commentaries for the year 1517, p. 93. He goes on to relate that Luther appealed to the Pope, but afterwards openly abandoned him and burned the canon law, which he imputes to Luther's inconstancy. But this man, stitched together from deceptions, omits the Bull of Leo issued earlier against Luther, whose principal heads Sleidanus records Book II. The sum of the Bull is that the Pope condemns Luther's opinions; forbids anyone under the heaviest penalty to think thus; orders Luther's books to be burned; and especially condemns that he appealed from the Pope to a council, against the decree of Pius II and Julius II, by which it was decreed that those who so appeal are to undergo the penalty established for heretics. After the Bull was issued, Luther's books were burned. Surius also dishonestly omits what Hadrian VI wrote in 1522 to the princes of the Empire gathered at Nuremberg, where, among other things, he forbids Luther to be admitted to defend what he wrote about faith and the sacraments; and, through Chieregati, to whom he had given such instructions, he confesses that for some years many abominable things had been in the holy see: abuses in spiritual matters, excesses in commands, and, in short, everything turned upside down; nor is it surprising if the sickness has descended from the head to the members, from the supreme Pontiffs to the other inferior prelates.

units.la: PolliPollliceberis, sic Hadrianus ad Cheregetum Nuntium, nos omnem operam adhibituros, ut primùm Curia hæc UNDE FORTE OMNE HOC MALUM PROCESSIT, reformetur, ut sicut inde corruptio in omnes inferiores emanavit, ita etiam ab eadem sanitas & reformatio omnium emanet. Consentiebant verba hæc cum sententia Concilii Constantiensis & Basileensis, præ se ferentium, quòd Ecclesia in Capite, Papa, & membris reformanda sit. Liquet adeò post Papalem damnationem Lutheri omnes, qui quicquam quod is docuisset, profiterentur, & non in omnibus se ad nutum Papæ componerent, pœnis hæreseos subjectos esse; atque insuper Concilium Constantiense anathema dixisse omnibus, qui Romanenses reprehenderent: inprimis traditiones Scripturæ æquâsse, Romanam Ecclesiam Ecclesiarum Magistram definivisse, & Concilium ipsum Papæ subjecisse. Quinam igitur schismatis authores argui possunt? Illine, qui apertos & confessos abusus, scandala, mendacia, consentientibus bonis omnibus reprehenderunt, & se opponentibus adversariis, eòsque vexantibus, confisi sunt, se Papæ causam suam approbare posse, existimantes, illum, officii sui memorem, manifestis rationibus locum datur-um, atque ita acturum, uti vero Ecclesiæ Episcopo, non fidei Domino conveniebat; quique, Papa officium negligente, & anathemate suo veritati præjudicante, ad Concilium liberum, nullisque juramentis Papæ obnoxium provocârunt, spe bona freti, fore, ut in tali Concilio non dicta & opiniones hominum, sed Scriptura pro regula fidei admittratur, ex qua sola demonstranda sint omnia, declaretúrque, quoúsque Ecclesiæ per demonstrationem Scripturarum pervenerint, deniique que error ex eadem arguatur, sive is apud plures sive pauciores essent? An potius Papa, ejusque complices, qui indulgentiarum nundinationem instituerunt, nihil emendarunt, reprehendi noluerunt, provocationem à Papa ad Concilium hæresin dixerunt, veras, saltem tolerabiles doctrinas damnârunt, dissidentes quosvis anathematizârunt & persecuti sunt, traditiones incertas Scripturæ æquârunt, Interpretationes Papales genuino ejusdem sensui ex ipsa Scriptura demonstrato, prætulerunt, Papam supra judicii aleam constituerunt, Romanam Ecclesiam Magistram Ecclesiarum omnium fecerunt, atque in his omnibus sic obstinatè pergunt, ut nihil apud se in doctrina emendandum, quin & ad salutem necessarium esse, nihil eorum; quæ Papa dictat improbare, aperte profiteantur? Adeò certè si schismatis authores & rei sunt, ut cum iis pii in æternum jungi nequeant, donec Papales bullæ & Tridentinum Concilium aboleantur, atque Papali idolo profligato, Scripturæ in arce collocentur.
units.tr: You will promise, so Hadrian wrote to the nuncio Chieregati, that we shall apply every effort so that, first, this Curia, WHENCE PERHAPS ALL THIS EVIL PROCEEDED, be reformed, so that just as corruption has spread from it to all inferiors, so soundness and reformation may likewise flow from it to all. These words agreed with the judgement of the Councils of Constance and Basel, which declared that the Church is to be reformed in its Head, the Pope, and in its members. It is therefore clear that after the Papal condemnation of Luther, all who professed anything that he had taught, and did not conform themselves in all things to the nod of the Pope, were subject to the penalties of heresy. Moreover, the Council of Constance pronounced anathema on all who rebuked the Roman teachers: those who placed the traditions on a level with Scripture, who defined the Roman Church to be the Teacher of Churches, and who subjected the Council itself to the Pope. Who, then, can be argued to be the authors of the schism? Is it they who rebuked the open and confessed abuses, scandals and lies, with the agreement of all good men, and who, trusting that they could win the Pope's approval for their cause, when opposed and harassed by adversaries, thought that he, mindful of his office, would give place to manifest reasons and act as a true Bishop of the Church should, not as a Lord of faith; and who, when the Pope neglected his duty and prejudiced the truth by his anathema, appealed to a free council, bound by no oaths to the Pope, hoping in good faith that in such a council not the sayings and opinions of men but Scripture would be admitted as the rule of faith, by which alone all things are to be demonstrated, and by which it would be declared how far the Churches had got through the demonstration of the Scriptures, and finally by which error would be refuted, whether it was held by many or by few? Or rather is it the Pope and his accomplices, who set up the huckstering of indulgences, corrected nothing, would not allow themselves to be rebuked, called the appeal from the Pope to a council heresy, condemned true, or at least tolerable, doctrines, anathematized and persecuted all dissenters, placed uncertain traditions on a level with Scripture, preferred Papal interpretations to the genuine sense of the same Scripture as demonstrated from Scripture itself, placed the Pope beyond the chance of judgement, made the Roman Church the Teacher of all Churches, and persist so obstinately in all these things that they openly profess that nothing among them in doctrine needs correcting, nay, that nothing that the Pope dictates is to be disapproved, and that it is necessary for salvation? Thus, assuredly, if the authors and guilty parties of the schism are these, the pious cannot be joined with them for ever, until the Papal bulls and the Council of Trent are abolished, and the Papal idol is overthrown and the Scriptures are placed in the citadel.

units.la: L. Plurimos præclaros, in ipsius Romanæ communionis gremio Viros, ipsáque Concilia nonnulla, Constantiense & Basileense, à pluribus retrò Seculis, Reformationem in Capite & membris non solùm desiderâsse, sed vehementer etiam flagitâsse, non semel vidimus. Frustrà desiderârunt, exspectârunt. Concilium enim Tridentinum nihil tale præstitisse, quin potius in fide hæreses fundamentales, in cultu idololatriam, in regimine tyrannidem, statumimâsse, Sole meridiano clarius est. Neque aliarsalutaris Reformatio expectari potuit. Papa enim Concilia omnia haud secus quàm ursus palum, cui alligandus est, reformidat: neque ullum aliud institueré ex eo tempore ausus est, vel audebit deinceps. Si quæ tamen Concilia institueret, vana illa forent, fructúque destituerentur omni; quia à Papæ, cujus hodiè in jure & facto infallibilitas propugnatur, nutu & oraculis suspenderentur tota, atque sic illa instituerentur, ne Tridentinis anathematis, quæ Papa sine infallibilitatis & potestatis suæ jactura refigere non potest, quàm minimam derogarent. Sic Babylon planè ἀθεράπευτος incurabilis deseri omninò à nobis debuit, si salvos nos cuperemus. Sustulimus theriacam ad dolorem ejus, si fortè sanetur. Curavimus Babel, & non est curata. Jerem. li. 9. Quibus malis immedicabilibus illud demùm accedit, quòd nullus turpi huic in Babylone mansioni, color prætendi potuerit, detecta jam agnitáque ejus turpitudine. Cum qua proin in eadem sede morari, nedum longiorem consuetudinem colere, quid aliud fuisset, quàm Christo ipsi se opponere, & Deo bellum indicere? Sicut ergò Israëlitæ Babylone relicta, altare Dei & templum restaurabant; ita à nobis valere, & res suas sibi habere jussa Spirituali hac Babylone, externo etiam opere verus veri Dei cultus instaurandus fuit.
units.tr: L. We have seen, more than once, that many distinguished men within the very bosom of the Roman communion, and some councils, namely Constance and Basel, for many centuries past, not only longed for a reformation in the Head and the members but also earnestly demanded it. They longed and waited in vain. For that the Council of Trent accomplished nothing of the kind, but rather established fundamental heresies in faith, idolatry in worship, and tyranny in government, is clearer than the noonday sun. Nor could any other salutary reformation be expected. For the Pope dreads all councils no less than a bear dreads the stake to which it is tied; and he has not dared, since that time, to convene any other, nor will he dare in future. Yet if he were to convene any councils, they would be empty and wholly without fruit, since they would depend entirely on the nod and the oracles of the Pope, whose infallibility is now defended both in law and in fact; and so they would be convened in such a way that they would not derogate in the least from the Tridentine anathemas, which the Pope cannot retract without loss of his infallibility and power. Thus Babylon, incurable [ἀθεράπευτος], had to be wholly abandoned by us, if we wished to be safe. We have applied a remedy to her pain, if perhaps she might be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed. Jer. 51.9. To these incurable evils there is finally added this: no pretext of colour can be offered for remaining in that shameful dwelling in Babylon, now that its filthiness has been detected and acknowledged. To remain in that seat, let alone to keep up a longer habit of it, what else would it be than to set oneself against Christ himself and declare war on God? Therefore, just as the Israelites, having left Babylon, restored the altar and the temple of God, so we had to bid farewell to this spiritual Babylon and restore the true worship of the true God, in outward work as well.

units.la: LI. Jam ergò Reformationi, seu separationi nostræ Hierarchici mille maculas, si velint, inurant, vocationis, successionis, aliósque ejusmodi defectus, secessionem à matre, à corpore, à trunco, novitatem, aliáque uti solent, plurima caussentur. Pigmenta hæc sunt meretricia, quæ apud eos, quibus Babylonis fœditas innotuit, flocci penduntur, merito Babylone exire, peccata & plagas ejus vitare, non aliud, cœlesti oraculo severè jussi sumus. Roma Babylon est. Nos Româ exivimus, Hierarchiam Romanam valere jussimus, Babylonem illam purgavimus; ejus peccata plagásque exhorruimus. Divino ergò mandato religiosè obsecuti, Meretricis illius criminationes, convitia, fucos universos adeò validè altéque spernimus, ut haud postremam felicitatis nostræ partem in eo collocemus, quòd ingens modò murus nos inter & Babylonem interest.
units.tr: LI. So if they want, the hierarchs may brand our Reformation, or separation, with a thousand stains: defects of calling and succession and the like, and they may charge us with secession from the mother, the body, the trunk, and novelty, and with the many other accusations they usually bring. These are harlot's cosmetics, which are held in no esteem by those who have come to know Babylon's foulness. We have been solemnly commanded by the heavenly oracle to go out of Babylon and to avoid her sins and plagues. Rome is Babylon. We have gone out of Rome, bidden farewell to the Roman Hierarchy, and cleansed that Babylon; we have shuddered at her sins and plagues. Having therefore obeyed the divine command with devotion, we so thoroughly and deeply despise that harlot's accusations, insults and all her pretences that we count it no small part of our happiness that a high wall now stands between us and Babylon.

units.la: LII. Tantùm verò abest, ut Hierarchicorum illa concepta indignatio, odia, insultus, convitia movere separatos quicquam potuerint, ut ipsi potiùs non satis habuerint sic à Babylone illa secedere, sed facta etiam in eam impressione acriter hactenùs eam impugnaverint, memores veterum, quas ab eadem perpessi sunt, injuriarum. Impulit eos, impellitque adhuc acerrima illa, & planè militaris ex Cœlo concio, quæ sic exeuntes exhortatur: Reddite illi (Babyloni) quemadmodum & ipsa reddidit vobis, & reduplicate ei secundùm opera ejus. In poculo, quod infudit, ei duplum. Quantum glorificavit se ipsam & luxuriavit, tantum date ei cruciatum & luctum. Apoc. xviii. 6. 7. Babylon sanctos dolore gravissimo, per suas abominationes affecit. Vox ergò ex Cœlo imperat exeuntibus, ne & ipsi Babyloni parcant, blandiantur, vel eam excusent; sed vicissim potiùs ei dolorem revelatione & publicatione turpitudinis & abominationum ejus, demonstratione veritatis, sanctâque conversatione inurant; atque sic inurant, ut duplum illi reddere, utroque ordine Ecclesiastico & Politico Babylonis fundamenta strenuè subruente, atque sic exercitam ab ea hypocrisin & tyrannidem largissimè rependente, contendant. Glorificavit se impotenter Babylon, & luxuriavit supra modum: Vicissim ei eadem mensura βασιλεύς ... cruciatum & luctum rependere, Cœlestis vox jubet. Planè sicut Apoc. xi. 10. de Testibus Jesu contra Bestialitas locutus fuerat, quòd cruciaverint, probè vexaverint incolas terræ, retegendo nimirum turpitudinem, & arguendo fraudes ac mendacia Bestiæ.
units.tr: LII. But that indignation, hatred, assaults and insults which the hierarchs have conceived have been so far from moving the separated churches at all that they have not been content merely to withdraw from Babylon in this way. Having made an impression upon her, they have fought hard against her to this day, mindful of the injuries they suffered from her long ago. That most fierce and truly military sermon from heaven drove them on, and still drives them, urging those who come out in this way: Render to her (Babylon) as she also rendered to you, and double to her double according to her works. In the cup which she has mixed, mix to her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning. Rev. 18:6, 7. Babylon has afflicted the saints with the gravest grief through her abominations. The voice from heaven therefore commands those who go out not to spare Babylon, nor to flatter her or make excuses for her; rather, in turn, they are to brand her with grief by revealing and publishing her foulness and abominations, by demonstrating the truth, and by holy conduct. They are to brand her in such a way that they strive to repay her double, vigorously undermining the foundations of Babylon in both her ecclesiastical and her political orders, and so repaying with the fullest measure the hypocrisy and tyranny she has practised. Babylon has glorified herself without restraint and lived in luxury beyond measure; the heavenly voice bids that she be repaid in turn with the same measure, [βασανισμόν] torment and mourning. Just as in Rev. 11:10 he had spoken of the Witnesses of Jesus against the beast, that they tormented and sorely vexed the inhabitants of the earth, namely by exposing the foulness and by refuting the frauds and lies of the beast.

units.la: LIII. Vindiƈtam hanc cœlesti imperio exeuntibus injunƈtam Hierarchia, ad insaniam & furorem ejus, hu- cúsque experta est.
units.tr: LIII. The Hierarchy has so far experienced to its madness and fury the vengeance enjoined by the heavenly command upon those who go out.

units.la: Certárunt enim ad hunc usque diem sanƈto zelo ingenia doƈtissimorum, & in S. Literis versatissimorum in depingenda & coram universo orbe confundenda Meretrice, ejúsque in fide hæresibus perditissimis, in cultu idolomania & scortatione tum spiritual tum corporali, in regimine tyrannide crudeli. Papam esse Anti-Christum, hominem perditionis, Pseudoprophetam, Exlegem illum: Hierarchiam esse Babylonem, Matrem Scortationum & abominationum, Bestiam illam bicornem, in Apocalypsi figuratam: in eandem quadrare vaticinium S. Pauli de apostasia novissimorum temporum: Concilii Tridentini anathemata non hæreses, sed veritatem Cœlestem, Christum, ejus justitiam, Euangelium feriisse & proscripsisse; aliáque ejusmodi non nudè illi asseruerunt, sed demonstrárunt fortissimè, solidissimè, irrefragabiliter: sophismata, quibus veritatem opprimere vel obscurare Romanæ Thaidis alumni ingeniis astutissimis præditi, Jesuitæ inprimis, Babylonici hujus Cœli Atlantes, laborárunt haƈtenùs, sic discusserunt, ut nunquam non à bello victores discesserint, & adversariis, tam gloriosis scilicet militibus, pudorem, βασιλικὸν, cruciatum, reconditum dolorem & luƈtum reliquerint: adeò ut, quod de tyrannis nonnemo præstantissimus sapientiæ apud Tacitum ɩA. vj. 6, 7. firmavit, si recludantur videlicet eorum mentes, posse aspici laniatus & ictus; quando, ut corpora verberibus, ita sævitia, libidine, malis consultis animus dilaceretur; de Sophistis illis, veritatem hactenùs cauteriata cum conscientia oppugnantibus, dici merito possit. Nota omnibus sunt בלחמות יהוה Bella Domini, feliciter adeò ore & calamo bellata, quibus jam dudum eò promotum est, ut Romæ promachi, Jesuitæ cum primis, abjectâ hastâ, omnia alia agere, & vi aperta Euangelium extinguere potiùs duxerint. Sic planè lino abolendum esse Anti-Christum, etiam suprà Sibyllam Erythræam vaticinantem, vidimus.
units.tr: For to this day the minds of the most learned men, most versed in the Holy Scriptures, have contended with holy zeal in portraying the harlot and exposing her before the whole world: in her most pernicious heresies of faith, in her idolatrous worship and fornication both spiritual and bodily, and in her cruel tyranny of government. They have not merely asserted, but have most strongly, solidly and irrefutably demonstrated, that the Pope is Antichrist, the man of sin, the false prophet, that lawless one; that the Hierarchy is Babylon, the Mother of fornications and abominations, that two-horned beast figured in the Apocalypse; that St Paul's prophecy of the apostasy of the last times fits it; and that the anathemas of the Council of Trent strike at and proscribe not heresies but heavenly truth, Christ, his righteousness and the Gospel. They have also laboured to dispel the sophisms by which the pupils of the Roman Thais, the Jesuits above all, those Atlases of this Babylonish heaven, endowed with the most cunning wits, have tried to oppress or obscure the truth. They have so routed these that they never left the battle other than as victors, and they left their opponents, glorious soldiers forsooth, with shame, [βασιλικόν] torment, hidden pain and mourning. So that what a certain most distinguished man of wisdom affirmed concerning tyrants in Tacitus, Hist. 6.6, 7, namely that if their minds were laid open, one could see their wounds and blows, since, as bodies are torn by lashes, so the mind is torn by cruelty, lust and evil counsels, may rightly be said of those sophists who, with a cauterised conscience, have hitherto opposed the truth. The Wars of the Lord [בלחמות יהוה] are known to all, waged so happily by voice and pen that it has long since come about that the Roman champions, the Jesuits above all, have thrown away their spears, preferred to do everything else, and to extinguish the Gospel by open force. Thus we have plainly seen that Antichrist is to be destroyed without the sword, even as the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied.

units.la: LIV. Ausus equidem est post Gauricum in Nativitate Lutheri, & Cardanum, Justus Lipsius adv. Dialogistam pag. 44. pro Politica sua sapientia impetum illum, quo hactenùs præstantissima ingenia ad Romanæ impietatis oppugnationem feruntur, ab aliquo maligno astrorum positu arcessere. Et univesam illam Papatùs oppugnationem non aliud esse, quàm fatalem ingeniorum scabiem, & præsentis ævi curiositatem, ibidem decernit. Sed aliud longè vox ἐκ ξ ἱερῆς ex Cœlo ipso à Johanne audita portendit, jubens Babylonem βασιλίζειν cruciare, & pro abominationibus ejus sic duplum ei reddere; innuens, gratum potiùs hoc tempore Dei Optimi Maximi cultum hunc esse, quin ipsius Spiritus S. instinctum, cui omnes obedire oportet, qui ex lectione, meditatione, aut auditu verbi Dei ejus aliquem stimulum acceperunt. Adeò ut hoc tandem locum habeat illud Jeremiæ quo alias se in istis calamitosis certaminibus mutuò exhortantur: Maledictus, qui secerit opus Domini fraudulenter. Jerem. XLVIII. 10. Sicut ergò Deus in cor Regum dedit, ut Meretricem odio ōdio habendo, denudando &c. voluntatem ejus faciant. Apoc.xvii. 16. Sic Deus, non astrorum positus aliquis, vel ingeniorum scabies, Viris Dei inspiravit, & inspirabit deinceps, ut Babyloni, denudando ejus turpitudinem & abominationes, cruciatum lustúmque infligere nunquam desinant.
units.tr: LIV. Indeed, after Gauricus in his Nativity of Luther, and Cardanus, Justus Lipsius in his Against the Dialogist, p. 44, has dared, in the interests of his political wisdom, to trace back to some malign arrangement of the stars that impulse by which the most outstanding minds have hitherto been driven to attack Roman impiety. And he decides in the same place that the whole assault on the papacy is nothing but a fated itch of wits and a curiosity of the present age. But the voice that John heard from heaven itself, [ἐκ τῆς ἱερῆς] from the holy place, portends something quite different, bidding Babylon be tormented [βασανίζειν] and that double be repaid to her for her abominations. It signifies that this worship of God, the Best and Greatest, is rather pleasing at this time, and is indeed the prompting of the Holy Spirit himself, to whom all must obey who have received any goad from the reading, meditation or hearing of God's Word. So that at last that saying of Jeremiah applies, by which they urge one another in these calamitous conflicts: Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord fraudulently. Jer. 48:10. Just as God put it into the hearts of kings to hate the harlot, to make her desolate and naked, etc., and to do his will (Rev. 17:16), so God, and not some arrangement of the stars or itch of wits, has inspired, and will continue to inspire, the men of God never to cease from inflicting torment and mourning on Babylon, stripping her bare of her foulness and abominations.

units.la: LV. Ecquænam verò causa fuit vindiƈtam illam tan-to ardore adversus Babylonem injungendi? Babylonisequidem abominationes universæ, quas in lucem protrahi Deus voluit: præ cœteris autem Babylonis, jamlapsæ & detectæ licet, procax gloriatio, in corde suosic sibi applaudentis: Καθηµαι βασίλισσα, ἡ χήρα οὐκ εἰ-µὶ, ἡ πένθος ἐ µη, ἰδω. Sedeo Regina, vidua non ero, & luctum non videbo. Apoc xviii. 7. Si quicquam in hoc de Babylone Magna vaticinio notatum dignum est, hæc certè verba sunt, propter evidentissimam præteritorum & præsentium temporum experientiam, ubi jaƈtantiæ de æterna & invićta Ecclesiæ Romanæ perduratione & dominatione nec finis, nec modus est. Perspicua enim & propriissima est mimesis verborum, quibus Romani Pontifices, eorúmque Gnathones gloriari consueverunt. Sedet in cathedra Pontifex. Gloriatur Roma, se Dominam & Reginam Ecclesiarum & Regnorum omnium. In cujus rei symbolum Ecclesiam Romanam depingunt REGINAM, sedentem in throno diademate Regio coronatam, Codicem Decretalium cum imposita infula Papali tenentem dextrâ, claves duas decussatas sinistrâ, pedibus Lutherum & Calvinum cum suis Bibliis proculcantem, uti ex Stapletoni Relectione Princip. Antuerpiæ A. MDXCVI. edita liquet. Sed & Viduam nunquam se fore Roma jaƈtat, quæ ut Matrem Ecclesiarum, sic Sponsam Christi, quam nun-
units.tr: LV. But what was the cause for enjoining that vengeance against Babylon with such ardour? Certainly all Babylon's abominations, which God willed to be brought to light; but above all, the bold boasting of Babylon, though she has already fallen and been exposed, which she applauds in her heart: Κάθηµαι βασίλισσα, ἡ χήρα οὐκ εἰµὶ, καὶ πένθος οὐ μὴ ἴδω. [Κάθημαι βασίλισσα καὶ χήρα οὐκ εἰμί, καὶ πένθος οὐ μὴ ἴδω.] I sit a queen, I am no widow, and I shall never see mourning. Rev. 18:7. If anything in this great prophecy about Babylon is worth noting, these words certainly are, on account of the most evident experience of past and present times, when there is neither end nor limit to the boasting about the eternal and unconquered endurance and dominion of the Roman Church. For the mimicry of the words by which the Roman Pontiffs and their flatterers have been accustomed to glory is clear and most exact. She sits in the chair, the Pontiff. Rome glories that she is the Queen and Mistress of all the Churches and Kingdoms. As a symbol of this they depict the Roman Church as a QUEEN, seated on a throne crowned with a royal diadem, holding in her right hand the Code of Decretals with the papal mitre placed upon it, and in her left two crossed keys, trampling underfoot Luther and Calvin with their Bibles; as is clear from Stapleton's Relectio Principiorum, published at Antwerp in 1596. But Rome also boasts that she will never be a Widow; she bears herself as the Mother of the Churches, and so as the Bride of Christ, whom the Bridegroom Christ could never forsake, and she denies that she can ever err, be defiled or fall, because she has the Holy Spirit as her paranymph and perpetual guardian of her chastity.

units.la: Tom. II. kkkkk quam Christus Sponsus deserat, se fert, & errare, inquinari, labi unquam posse, negat, eò quòd Spiritum S. paranymphum & perpetuum pudicitiæ suæ custodem habeat. Denique luctum nullum unquam se visuram, sibi Roma blanditur, cui sic acclamare Gnathones solent. Hæc est Ecclesia ædificata super petram, adversùs quam portæ inferni non prævalebunt: Hæc PETRI navicula, quæ ventis jactari, quassari, premi, fluctibus mergi non potest. Quò etiam Bellarminianæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Catholicæ notæ, prosperitas defensorum, & infelicitas hostium Romæ, pertinent. En quàm exactè Cathedrali huic Reginæ Babylonica illa jactantia quadrat! Sed jactantiæ ejusdem, etiam post casum priorem, occasio dissimulanda non est.
units.tr: Vol. II. kkkkk Finally, Rome flatters herself that she will never see mourning, and the flatterers are accustomed to cry out to her thus: This is the Church built upon the rock, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail; this is the little ship of Peter, which cannot be tossed by the winds, shaken, pressed down, or sunk by the waves. To this also pertain the prosperity of the defenders of Bellarmine's Roman Church, the mark of Catholicity, and the misfortune of Rome's enemies. See how exactly that Babylonian boasting fits this enthroned Queen! But the occasion for this same boasting, even after the earlier fall, must not be passed over in silence.

units.la: LVI. Etenim Prophetia de iis, qui liberationis ex Babylone participes facti sunt, testatur apertè, quòd ingens Dei beneficium, haud perinde grato plerique animo exceperint recoluerintque; neque planè, ita se gesserint, uti dignum erat ea gratia, auxilio & potenti brachio, sapienti gubernatione Dei, libertate & verbo, quod quotidiè audiverunt. Multis enim hujus gratiæ Divinæ consortibus, quæ Apoc. iii. 1. 2. 3. & 15. 16. &c. extant, dicta videri possunt. Neque tamen Prophetiis opus est, cùm res ipsa locuples nimis ejus rei testis existat. Licet enim nunquam defuerint, vel desint verè fideles, sancto gloriæ Divinæ zelo flagrantes, & digno Euangelio tramite incedentes; constat nihilominus, alios etiam ad exitiales hæreses præcipites deviâsse: alios, qui communem causam agere debuerunt, lites de rebus exigui momenti ἀσεβεῖς agitâsse: alios in sententiis, ad principia, dogmata & fermentum Pontificium relabi coepisse: alios à fratribus sine sontica cau-sa fa sese seperâsse & erroribus detestandis fores patefecisse: Scripturæ studium, piúmque solius verbi Divini discendi docendique studium, apud plures refrixisse: circa Ecclesiæ Regimen exortas controversias hinc inde Ecclesiam distraxisse: Doctores accensis litibus, de rebus subindè frivolis, odio, invidiâ, aliisque carnalibus affectibus fræenum laxâsse: non eos passim cerni fructus, qui populo Dei conveniant: denique in plerisque neglecto Dei Regno, ejúsque justitia, rerum hujus seculi studia fervere.
units.tr: LVI. For the prophecy plainly testifies that those who shared in the liberation from Babylon received this great benefit of God without a truly grateful mind, and did not conduct themselves as befitted such grace, the help and mighty arm, the wise governance of God, the liberty and the Word they heard every day. Many of the things said to the partners in this divine grace, in Rev. iii. 1, 2, 3, and 15, 16, etc., may seem to apply here. Yet there is no need of prophecies, since the matter itself is a rich enough witness. For although there have never been lacking, and are not lacking now, truly faithful people, burning with holy zeal for the glory of God and walking the path worthy of the Gospel, it is nonetheless plain that others have also rushed headlong into destructive heresies; that others, who ought to have made common cause, have waged quarrels over matters of slight importance [ἀσεβεῖς]; that others have begun to slide back into Papist opinions, principles, doctrines and leaven; that others have separated themselves from their brethren without any just cause and thrown open the doors to detestable errors; that the zeal for Scripture, and the pious zeal for learning and teaching the Divine Word alone, has cooled among many; that controversies arising over the government of the Church have torn the Church apart on every side; that teachers, with quarrels kindled over sometimes trivial matters, have let loose the reins of hatred, envy and other carnal passions; that the fruits which befit the people of God are not seen everywhere; and finally, that in most the Kingdom of God and its righteousness being neglected, zeal for the affairs of this age runs hot.

units.la: LVII. Hæc, inquam, & similia Babyloni, Divino judicio iterum ab Ecclesia incipiente, vires suas colligendi gendi, & insolescendi ansam suppeditárunt hactenùs, atque hodie magis quàm unquam suppeditant. Diu enim est, ex quo bellis gestis ferocissimis, aliisque rationibus, per reliqua illa sua cornua Ecclesias amplif- simas in Austria, Stiria, Carinthia, Bohemia, Silesia, Moravia, Palatinatu Superiore, alibíque sub suum iterum jugum Papa misit. Nostrâ verò, atque eâ recentissimâ memoriâ, quot in Gallia, Pedemontio, Ecclesiæ florentissimæ feralibus edictis perversæ sunt? Quanto in miseriarum caucaso fideles diri ssima quæque in desertis, carceribus, triremibus patientes hærent? Quot animarum myriades, persecutionum, quibus pares ætas nulla vidit, gravitati tolerandæ impares, ad inferni portas usque descenderunt, atque intra eas constituti gemunt, clausisque undique januis, exitum nullum reperiunt? Nihil de Ecclesiis à Babylone diu equidem separatis, in Anglia, Scotia, Hungaria, Transylvania, ac nunc demùm in præceps adductis, cum Babylone ancipite eventu luctantibus, dicam.
units.tr: LVII. These things, I say, and things like them, gave Babylon, with God's judgment beginning again from the Church, the occasion to gather its strength and grow insolent, until now, and today more than ever they supply it. For it is long since, by fierce wars and other means, that through those remaining horns of hers the Pope sent the most ample Churches in Austria, Styria, Carinthia, Bohemia, Silesia, Moravia, Upper Palatinate and elsewhere back under his yoke. And what Churches, in our own and most recent memory, have been overturned in France and Piedmont by deadly edicts, once most flourishing? In what abyss of miseries do the faithful lie, enduring the most dreadful things in deserts, prisons and galleys? How many myriads of souls, bearing persecutions such as no age has seen, unequal to the weight of enduring them, have gone down even to the gates of hell, and lie there groaning, with every door shut and finding no way out? I say nothing of the Churches long since separated from Babylon, in England, Scotland, Hungary and Transylvania, and now at last thrown into crisis, struggling with Babylon in doubtful outcome.

units.la: LVIII. Adcò Babyloni evenit, quod Tyro mysticæ
units.tr: LVIII. Thus it has come to pass with Babylon, what happened to Tyre, the mystical

units.la: (alteri simillimóque Hierarchiæ emblemati) quæ (Esai. xxiii. 15, 16, &c.) per septuaginta annos relicta & contempta rediit ad שירית ונור Carmen suum meretricium, hoc est, lætitiam & gloriationem de victoriis suis in nomine non Dei veri, quale carmen Tyri recitat Ezechiel cap. xxvi. 2. Dixit Tyrus super Hierusalem, Euge, fracta est, valvæ populorum, revoluta est ad me, implebor, vastata est. Cum quo Babylonis epinicion: Sedeo Regina & vidua non ero, & luctum non videbo; congruit. Haud difficilis est septuaginta annorum illorum computatio. Nam inde ab anno MDLII. quo Augustæ Pax Imperialis Religiosa sancita est, ad A. MDCXXII. septuaginta anni lapsi sunt. Circa posterius tempus, Bohemia & Palatinatu subactis, Jesuitæ Pragenses & Heidelbergenses Academiam occupárunt, & Papa Gregorius XV. Ignatium Lojolam, aliósque ejusdem ordinis canonizavit: quæ apotheosis magna ubique festivitate celebrata est; simulque iis, aliisque idolis de victoriis Cæsaris & subactis Protestantibus gratiæ actæ sunt. Addit Prophetia v. 16. epiphonema, seu adhortationem sarcasticam: Accipe citharam, perambula civitatem נשכחרה ונור Meretrix oblivioni tradita, seu exoleta הטיב נן Stude benè modulari, multiplica carmen, ut tui sit recordatio. Convenit, quòd Jesuitæ cæterique Doctores Pontificii scriptis & præconiis suis veritatem exosam reddere, & falsitatem incrustare satagerunt, Romanenses quoque artibus & fallaciis suis homines reddere securos conati sunt: denique universi ob victorias suas incredibilem lætitiam testati, Ecclesiæ insolenter insultárunt, & super malis ejus exultárunt. Post etiam Tyrus (v. 17.) reversa est לאתנור ad quæstum suum, & fcortata est cum cum omnibus Regnis terræ in superficie terræ. Testis ejus rei est Germania Sacra Restaurata Caraffæ Legati Papæ. Ipsa quoque experientia docuit, docetque hodie, plurimos ubique cum Romanis fornicatos esse, & adhuc fornicari. Denique concinunt Prophetiæ omnes, primam reformationem, seu statum Ecclesiæ Reformatæ insignem ad tempus catastrophen & eclipsin passuram, per Anti-Christum vehementer interturbatum & res Ecclesiæ denuò ad eas angustias redactum iri, ut dissipata populi Sancti manu (Dan. xii. 7.) de Ecclesia victa & oppressa, hostes ubique ferè terrarum triumphaturi sint.
units.tr: (the other and very similar emblem of the Hierarchy), which (Isa. xxiii. 15, 16, etc.), left and despised for seventy years, returned to its harlot's song, שירית ונור [shirit ve-nur], that is, to joy and boasting over its victories in the name of no true God. Ezekiel, chap. xxvi. 2, recites this song of Tyre: Tyre said against Jerusalem, Aha, she is broken, the gates of the peoples are turned to me; I shall be filled, she is laid waste. With this agrees Babylon's song of triumph: I sit a queen, and I shall not be a widow, and I shall not see mourning. The computation of those seventy years is not difficult. For from the year 1552, when the Religious Peace of Augsburg was ratified, to 1622, seventy years had passed. About the later time, when Bohemia and the Palatinate had been subdued, the Jesuits of Prague and Heidelberg occupied the Academy, and Pope Gregory XV canonized Ignatius Loyola and others of the same order. This apotheosis was celebrated everywhere with great festivity, and at the same time thanks were given to these and other idols for the victories of the Emperor and the subdued Protestants. Verse 16 of the prophecy adds an epiphonema, or sarcastic exhortation: Take a harp, go about the city, נשכחרה ונור [nishkachah zonah], a harlot forgotten, or worn out, הטיב נן [hetev nen], study to sing well, multiply the song, that you may be remembered. It agrees that the Jesuits and the other Papist teachers have, by their writings and their boasts, laboured to make the truth hateful and to plaster over falsehood, and the Romanists also have tried, by their arts and deceits, to make men secure; finally, all of them, testifying their incredible joy at their victories, have insolently insulted the Church and exulted over her misfortunes. Afterwards, too, Tyre (v. 17) returned לאתנור [le-ethnunah], to her hire, and played the harlot with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth. A witness to this is the Germania Sacra Restaurata of the Papal Legate Caraffa. Experience itself has taught, and teaches today, that very many everywhere have fornicated with the Romanists, and still do. Finally, all the prophecies agree that the first Reformation, or the notable state of the Reformed Church, will for a time suffer catastrophe and eclipse, will be violently disturbed by the Antichrist, and the affairs of the Church will be reduced again to such straits that, the power of the holy people being scattered (Dan. xii. 7), and the Church conquered and oppressed, the enemies will triumph almost everywhere on earth.

units.la: LIX. Hactenùs ergò progressum est Dei adversùs Babylonem judicium: atque ea hodiè tempora vivimus, quibus Hierarchia non tam suis viribus vel causæ suæ bonitate, quàm nostris peccatis, nostra illa passiva in gratitudine nixa, recepto passim; in speciem saltem, amplitudinis suæ fastigio, suum illud Meretricium carmen: Sedeo Regina, Vidua non ero, luctum non videbo, adeóque Romanæ Ecclesiæ magnificentiam, amplitudinem, durationem perpetuam, infallibilitatem, victoriam, pleno gutture decantat: & decantabit porrò, donec Deum pœniteat super servos, & jactantiam hanc fastúmque Meretricis subitaneo & improviso excidio contundat. Quia enim sic se glorificavit, & ante victoriam insolenter adeò triumphum cecinit, adeóque periculorum suorum secura, cessantia fata provocavit, idcirco, sic Prophetia definit, in uno die venient plagæ ejus; mors & luctus & fames, & igne comburetur. Apoc. xviii. 8. Hæc illa decretoria dies est, quæ Babyloni adhuc imminet; & quæ tam certò, definito à Deo tempore, Hierarchiæ superveniet, quàm verè Hucusque progressi Dei adversus Hierarchiam judicium, finale decretum eidem imminere ostenditur. verè reliqua de Babylone prædicta, usque ad excidium illud finale, omnia in Hierarchia exitum nacta sunt. Qui enim tot de Babylone prædictiones in eventu jam repræsentavit, is fidem dictorum suorum in postremo illo actu neutiquam destituet. Ille enim annuntiat ab exordio novissimum, & ab initio ea, quæ nondum facta sunt, dicens: Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam. Esai. XLVI. 10.
units.tr: LIX. Thus far, then, God's judgment against Babylon has proceeded. And we live in those times in which the Hierarchy, resting less on its own strength or the goodness of its cause than on our sins and that passive ingratitude of ours, has in appearance at least reached the height of its greatness, and everywhere sings with full throat its harlot's song: I sit a queen, I shall not be a widow, I shall not see mourning, and so proclaims the magnificence, the amplitude, the perpetual duration, the infallibility, the victory of the Roman Church; and it will go on singing, until God repents concerning his servants, and crushes this boasting and pride of the harlot with a sudden and unforeseen destruction. For since she glorified herself, and so insolently sang triumph before the victory, and being thus secure in her dangers provoked fates that do not cease, therefore, so the prophecy concludes, in one day her plagues shall come: death and mourning and famine, and she shall be burned with fire. Rev. xviii. 8. This is the decisive day which still hangs over Babylon; and it will come upon the Hierarchy at a time fixed by God as surely as it is shown that God's judgment against the Hierarchy, up to now, has come forward, and that the final decree hangs over it. For as truly as all the other things foretold concerning Babylon, up to that final catastrophe, have already found their outcome in the Hierarchy, so he who has already presented so many predictions about Babylon in their fulfilment will by no means fail the faith of his words in that last act. For he declares the end from the beginning, and from the start the things not yet done, saying: My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure. Isa. xlvi. 10.

units.la: LX. Plagæ Babyloni imminentes, & uno die superventuræ erunt, λιμὸς, λοιμὸς, Λιμὸς & κατάκαυ-σις; Mors, luctus, fames & combustio. Totis enim quadrigis super eam irruent. Occidentur mœchi & filii ejus, ut utrósque Babylon, tanquam vidua & orba lugeat. Incesset fames, ut consolationem non inveniat, voluptate, quam in hoc Seculo ex lasciviæ suæ abundantia percepit, sublata. Denique comburetur igni; sive hic παντελῶς totius politiæ Babylonicæ; sive cum eadem Romæ etiam urbis conflagratio significatur, quod eventus, Prophetiarum optimus interpres, docebit. Singulæ porrò hæ plagæ singulis Hierarchiæ sceleribus respondebunt. Fortunam sibi perpetuam Roma promisit, & bacchari interim, inebriari, & conservos suos verberare non cessans, subitanea morte fortunam abrumpet. Voluptatibus tripudiisque exultavit; ideò luctu opprimetur. Luxuriæ insatiabili cum cupiditate indulsit. Idcircò fame necabitur. Pios martyres, ceu hæreticos, flammis exussit. Ergò ipsa quoque flammis exuretur. Hoc illud Babylonicum ἀντιμισθὸς erit, quòd justissimus mundi judex jam decretum ei meritissimum supplicium infliget.
units.tr: LX. The plagues hanging over Babylon, and to come upon her in one day, will be λιμὸς, λοιμὸς, Λιμὸς & κατάκαυσις [limos, loimos, limos and katakausis]: death, mourning, famine and burning. For they will rush upon her with all their chariots. Her adulterers and her sons will be slain, so that Babylon mourns both, as a widow and a childless woman. Famine will come on, so that she finds no consolation, the pleasure which she has received in this age from the abundance of her lust being taken away. Finally she will be burned with fire, whether this signifies the total παντελῶς [pantelōs] destruction of the Babylonian polity, or whether the conflagration of the city of Rome is also meant, which the outcome, the best interpreter of prophecies, will teach. Moreover, each of these plagues will answer to each of the crimes of the Hierarchy. Rome has promised herself perpetual fortune, and, while not ceasing meanwhile to revel, to get drunk, and to beat her fellow servants, she will cut short her fortune by a sudden death. She has exulted in pleasures and revelries; therefore she will be overwhelmed with mourning. She has indulged her insatiable lust for luxury; therefore she will be destroyed by famine. She has burned the pious martyrs with flames as if they were heretics; therefore she herself will also be burned with flames. This will be that Babylonian ἀντιμισθὸς [antimisthos], that the most just judge of the world will inflict on her the punishment she has rightly deserved.

units.la: LXI. Celeritatem abolitionis Babylonis hujus Magnæ, novus Angelus, qui v. 21. introducitur, signo gnæ, novus Angelus, qui v. 21. introducitur, signo subsublati magni lapidis, impetu in mare projecti, adumbrat. Sustulit enim unus Angelus robustus lapidem, ut molarem magnum, & conjecit in mare, dicens: Sic impetu conjicietur illa Magna Civitas , & non invenietur amplius, ἰσχυρὸς, Robustus Angelus vocatur propter symbolum, quod robur plus quàm humanum requirebat. Lapidem enim quasi molarem, eúmque ingentem, quem vix decem Viri robusti loco moverent, ipse plumæ instar levissimæ in profundum mare cum impetu projecit. Sic plane Roma, Babylon Magna lapide molari longè immobilior visa, ἐν ἐρμηνεία, cum repentino impetu præcipitabitur; & sicut lapis molaris in mare cum impetu projectus, sic ibidem sepelitur, ut inde extrahi nulla vi possit: Sic Roma igne, contrario elemento devorata, restaurari amplius nullo modo poterit, sed in æternis tenebris suis sepulta jacebit.
units.tr: LXI. The swiftness of the overthrow of this Great Babylon is foreshadowed by the sign of the lifting up of the great stone, which the new Angel introduced at verse 21 casts into the sea with force: "Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: With such violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more." He is called the "Mighty" Angel [ἰσχυρὸς] because of the symbol, which required strength more than human. For he lifted a stone like a millstone, and a huge one, which ten strong men could scarcely move, and hurled it with force into the depths of the sea, as if it were a feather. So plainly Rome, Great Babylon, which seemed far more immovable than a millstone, will be cast down with sudden force, as the interpretation shows [ἐν ἐρμηνεία]. And just as a millstone thrown with force into the sea is buried there so that no force can draw it out again, so Rome, devoured by fire, the contrary element, will in no way be restored again, but will lie buried in its eternal darkness.

units.la: LXII. Propènè instet, an procul absit, finalis hujus excidii dies, quo Babylon, hoc est, Politia integra Babylonicæ Hierarchiæ delebitur, adeóque juxta fatidicas illas Friderici II. Imperatoris pientissimi & fortissimi voces:
units.tr: LXII. Whether the final day of this destruction is near or still far off, the day on which Babylon, that is, the whole polity of the Babylonish Hierarchy, will be destroyed, and so according to those prophetic words of the most pious and most brave Emperor Frederick II:

units.la: Roma diu titubans longis erroribus acta, Corruet & mundi desinet esse Caput;
units.tr: Rome, long tottering and driven by long errors, will fall, and will cease to be the head of the world;

units.la: LXIII. Res nobis est cum Hierarchicis: Illi Romæ perpetuam felicitatem & stabilitatem promittunt, & scævum quid ei annuntiantes ridentes vehementer, vel pessimè etiam mulctant. Neque tamen è sinu eorum testes nobis desunt, qui malè Romæ ominati sunt. Friderici Imperatoris augurium supra narravimus. Quid Ludovicus XII. Galliarum Rex, animo suo volutaverit, cùm in moneta verba hæc excudi curavit: PERDAM BABYLONEM, item: PERDAM BABYLONIS NOMEN; nemini obscurum esse potest. Et jam olim Hieronymus Savanorola vaticinatus est, Gallos venturos, ac universam Italiam, Romam cumprimis vastaturos. Sed & Guilhelmus Durantus, Episcopus Mimatensis, in libro de modo celebrandi Concilii Generalis A. MDXLV. Parisiis edito, scribere non dubitavit: Proverbium vulgare est, qui vult totum, perdit totum. Ecclesia autem Romana sibi vendicat universa (93. Dist. Diaconi sunt) unde timendum est, quòd universa perdat. In alio etiam Scholæ Parisiensis libro de periculis Ecclesiæ A. MCCCLXXXIX. conscripto, verba Dan. v. 25. Meneh, Meneh, Thekel, Upharsin; hoc est: Numeravit Deus Regnum tuum: appensus es in statera, divisum est Regnum tuum &c. Romanæ Ecclesiæ applicavit. Sed & Joachimus Abbas Petrum senescentem rursus cingendum in famosis vaticiniis suis prædixit. Idem in cap. iv. Jerem. scribere non dubitavit: Aquila grandis & magnarum alarum, scilicet Imperator Alemanniæ percutiet Ecclesiam, ut unde aliquando protecta fuerat, inde flagelletur, & sic desituta subsidiis direptioni pateat viatorum. Pertinet eodem visio Fratris Nicolai Helvetii, quam supra recitavimus. Ribera comm. ad Apoc. xiv. & xvij. & quotquot cum eo Ecclesiam Romanam sub finem mundi ad Ethnicismum relapsuram Babylonem esse, in Apocalypsi præfiguratam, sentiunt, ingenuè fatentur, Romam, hanc urbem fornicariam, in fine mundi: VASTANDAM ET EVERTENDAM esse. Sic juxta Veterum Prophetiam apud Valerium Probum, literis hisce R. R. R. F. F. F. consignatam REGNUM ROMÆ RUET, FERRO, FAME, FLAMMA. Imò Viegas in cap. xviii. Apoc. asserit, Decem Reges Imperium Romanum eversuros, primùm ab ipsa Romana urbe bellum auspicaturos esse, eíque primùm excidium & vastitatem illaturos: Addit Ribera, Romam ùsque adeò vastandam, miserrimóque incendio delendam, ut in desertum & solitudinem sit evasura, atque habitatio bestiarum & dæmoniorum futura. Denique Henricus Vechietus Florentinus lib. vij. Chronol. CM. cui significationem novissimorum titulum fecit, cap. 26. & 27. argutè admodùm & subtiliter de excidio Romæ disseruit, quem tamen calculus in eo, quòd ab A. MDCXXI. præcisè intra centum viginti sex annos Romam destruendam exiítimaverit, falsurus sit nec ne, tempus docebit. Ratio certè calculi non apparet. Neque refert, quòd, qui Riberam sequuntur, excidium ísthoc non Christiana, sed denuò Ethnicæ futuræ Romæ impendere, pertendunt. Nam qualis hodiè Roma est, Christiana nominetenus, reapse nihil ab Ethnica distat. Et satis est ab authoribus iis excidium Romæ novissimæ, ceu prædictum in Apocalypsi, propugnari acriter.
units.tr: LXIII. We have to do with the Hierarchical men. They promise Rome perpetual happiness and stability, and laughing heartily at anyone who announces some ill omen to her, they punish him very severely, or even most cruelly. Nor are witnesses lacking to us from their own bosom who have augured ill for Rome. We have related above the augury of Emperor Frederick. What King Louis XII of France had in mind when he had these words struck on his coinage, PERDAM BABYLONEM, and again PERDAM BABYLONIS NOMEN [I will destroy Babylon; I will destroy the name of Babylon], can be obscure to no one. And long ago Girolamo Savonarola prophesied that "the Gauls would come and would lay waste all Italy, and Rome above all." But also Guillaume Durand, Bishop of Mende, in his book On the Manner of Celebrating a General Council, published at Paris in 1545, did not hesitate to write: "It is a common proverb: he who wants the whole, loses the whole. But the Roman Church claims for itself the universal (Dist. 93, 'Diaconi sunt'), whence it is to be feared that she will lose the universal." In another book of the Paris School, written on the dangers of the Church in 1389, the words of Daniel 5:25, "Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin," that is, "God has numbered your kingdom; you are weighed in the balance; your kingdom is divided," etc., were applied to the Roman Church. And Joachim the Abbot, in his notorious prophecies, foretold that Peter, growing old, would again be girded [John 21:18]. The same man did not hesitate to write on Jeremiah chapter 4: "A great eagle with large wings, that is, the Emperor of Germany, will strike the Church, so that she who was once protected by him will be scourged by him, and thus, stripped of help, she will lie open to the plundering of travellers." To the same purpose belongs the vision of Brother Nicholas of Switzerland, which we recited above. Ribera, in his commentary on Rev. 14 and 17, and all who with him think that the Roman Church, at the end of the world, will fall back into heathenism and be prefigured in the Apocalypse as Babylon, frankly confess that "Rome, this harlot city, at the end of the world, is to be laid waste and overthrown." So, according to the ancient prophecy reported by Valerius Probus, marked with these letters, R. R. R. F. F. F., "the kingdom of Rome shall fall by iron, famine and flame." Indeed Viegas, on Rev. 18, asserts that "ten kings will overthrow the Roman empire, and will first begin the war from the city of Rome itself, and will first bring ruin and devastation upon her." Ribera adds that "Rome is to be laid waste to such an extent, and destroyed by the most wretched fire, that she will become a desert and a solitude, and a dwelling of beasts and demons." Finally, Henricus Vechietus of Florence, in Chronology book 7, which he entitled Significance of the Last Things, chapters 26 and 27, discussed very shrewdly and subtly the downfall of Rome; whether his calculation, in which he judged that Rome would be destroyed precisely within one hundred and twenty-six years from 1621, will prove false or not, time will show. The reasoning of the calculation certainly does not appear. Nor does it matter that those who follow Ribera maintain that this downfall impends not on Christian Rome but on Rome again to be heathen. For Rome as it is today, Christian in name only, in fact differs in nothing from a heathen one. And it is enough that these authors vigorously defend the downfall of the last Rome as foretold in the Apocalypse.

units.la: LXIV. Parum certè movet, quòd nonnulli humanarum virium præsidia, & superbissimæ Babylonis, tantis & suis, & Regum aliorúmque sociorum opibus suffultæ, fortunam supra omnem periculi, uti videri illis potest, aleam positam, iniqua lance ponderantes, spes nostras de collapsura ea cœcas & inanem pessundandæ ejus expectationem esse, clamitant. Et profecto, si fortunatum hoc Seculo Babylonicæ prosperitatis cursum; si Euangelicorum fractas vires, dissipata consilia; si dissolutas scopas nostras, aliáque multa profano oculo intueatur & rimetur aliquis, mirum non erit, ei meram næniam, omnium detestatione & odio dignam, videri, quicquid de Hierarchiæ excidio dixerimus.
units.tr: LXIV. It hardly troubles me that some people, weighing on an unfair scale the bulwarks of human strength and the proud Babylon, propped up by its own great resources and by the wealth of kings and other allies, call the outcome a gamble beyond all danger, as it may seem to them, and cry out that our hopes of her downfall are blind and her overthrow is an empty expectation. Indeed, if anyone were to look upon and examine with a profane eye the fortunate course of Babylonian prosperity in this age, the broken strength of the evangelicals, their dissipated plans, our loosened brooms and many other things, he will not be surprised if whatever we have said about the destruction of the hierarchy seems to him mere nonsense, deserving everyone's detestation and hatred.

units.la: Sed Sanctuarium Domini ingressis, alia omnia apparebunt, reputantibus, non tantum summam Babylonis post priorem illum lapsum felicitatem, & extremas Ecclesiæ, rerúmque ejus in aciem novaculæ adductarum, angustias, certissimum imminentis eidem novissimi exci-dii prodromum esse: sed etiam illius executionem in vaticinio ei, qui omnem humanam potentiam suà potentiâ infinitis modis superat & adversùs quem formatum nullum instrumentum prosperatur. ( Esai. liv. 17.) adscribi. Nam uno die venient Babylonis plagæ, & igni illa concremabitur, ὅτι ἰσχυρὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ κρίνων αὐτὸν, quia robustus est Dominus ille Deus, qui judicabit eam, Apoc. xviii. 8. Sub duƈtu ergò & auspiciis Generosi illius Principis exercitus Israëlis, qui Gentes conterit sceptro ferreo, & tanquam vas fictile figuli confringit, Psal. ii. 9. adeóque sacræ illius militiæ primipili, Agni, qui est Dominus Dominantium, & & Rex Regum. Apoc. xvii. 14. negotium conficietur. Cui ergò res hæc ex præsente statu impossibilis videtur, is reputet, Illius hoc opus fore, qui nutu & unâ voculâ omnes causas, occasiones, & dispositiones, quas vult, producere & in actum deducere poterit. Ille, Ille Babylonem judicabit, qui Pharaonem, inermem Israëlitarum manum, cum validissimo Legionum robore persequentem, rubri maris fluctibus obruit: qui Sisaræ ac Moabitarum copias consilio manúque Fœminæ delevit: qui Senacheribum Cœlo exitium minitantem, cum universo exercitu suo, percussoris Angeli unius (quomodo unus etiam Angelus molarem illum Babylonis Lapidem maximo virium robore humo sustollens, cum impetu in profundum maris conjecit) virtute destruxit: qui Antiochum totius Asiæ viribus subnixum per desperatas Macchabæorum copias obtrivit triumphavitque: qui denique superiori Seculo Reformatione Ecclesiæ jam coepta & promota, ipsam Romam, Papam, Cardinales, omnémque Curiam Romanam tradidit in manus Caroli Borbonii, & exercitus ejus, à quibus ex itinere, & velut aliud agentibus contumeliosè habiti sunt, quo vel uno memorabili exemplo haud dubiè Deus demonstrare voluit, omnem illam falsam potestatem Papæ, & auctoritatem Cleri Romani, atque ita omnem factum humanum levi momento à Deo everti, omnémque admirationem sublimitatis illius in vilipendium mutari posse. Illo enim tempore nihil vilius, nihil contemtius, ridiculum magis nihil Papa fuit, qui ab Exercitu Cæsaris, Principis Catholici, uti loquuntur, ita vexatus & illusus est; uti rem totam Sleidanus Lib. vi. narravit. Licet enim irrideri, contemni, ludibrio haberi ab hominibus, per se Divini contemtûs argumentum non sit; quin potiùs ex iis rebus, quibus Deus se tum in Filio suo, tum in Apostolis & Ecclesia sua glorificari voluit: nihilominus contemtus & vilipendium humanum in quibusdam casibus testis & obfes judicii Divini est: nempè quando gloria humana & Majestas, quæ se contra Deum & Ecclesiam effert, contumeliam patitur; inprimis, quando id secundùm prædictionem Scripturæ contingit. In universum enim Scriptura testatur, omne quod inter homines altum est, apud Deum esse abominabile, Luc. xvi. 15. Et pro exaltatione vilitas est filiis hominum, Psal. xii. 9. Effunditque Deus iram in Principes. Psal. cvii. 40. In specie Deus ignominiam & ludibrium ejusmodi Spirituali Tyro comminatur Esai. xxiii. 8, 9. Quis consuluit hoc super Tyro coronatrice (talis Roma est המעטירה Coronatrix, coronas imponens Cæsaribus, Regibus, Principibus & pro lubitu easdem auferens) cujus mercatores sunt Principes, Institores Honorati terræ? Jehova Deus exercituum consuluit illud, ad profanandum celsitudinem omnis decoris, ad vilipendendum omnes honoratos terræ.
units.tr: But those who enter the sanctuary of the Lord will see everything otherwise, if they consider that Babylon's highest happiness after her earlier fall, and the extreme straits of the Church and its affairs brought to the edge of the razor, are not only the most certain forerunner of her final destruction that is now imminent, but that her execution is also ascribed in prophecy to him who surpasses all human power in infinite ways by his own power, and against whom no formed instrument prospers (Isa. 54:17). For in one day shall her plagues come, and she shall be utterly burnt with fire, [ὅτι ἰσχυρὸς κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ κρίνων αὐτὸν] for strong is the Lord God who judgeth her, Rev. 18:8. Therefore the business will be accomplished under the leadership and auspices of that noble Prince, the army of Israel, who breaks the nations with an iron sceptre and dashes them in pieces like a potter's vessel (Ps. 2:9), and so under the chief captain of that sacred army, the Lamb, who is Lord of lords and King of kings (Rev. 17:14). Let him to whom this seems impossible from the present state of things consider that this is the work of him who, by a nod and a single word, can bring about and carry into effect all the causes, occasions and dispositions he wills. He, He alone, will judge Babylon, who overwhelmed Pharaoh with the waves of the Red Sea when he pursued the unarmed hand of the Israelites with the strongest force of his legions; who destroyed the forces of Sisera and the Moabites by the counsel and hand of a woman; who, with his whole army, destroyed Sennacherib, who threatened destruction to heaven, by the power of one destroying angel (just as one angel lifted that great millstone of Babylon from the ground with the greatest force of strength and hurled it with violence into the depths of the sea); who crushed Antiochus, supported by the forces of all Asia, through the desperate troops of the Maccabees, and triumphed; and who, in the last age, when the Reformation of the Church had already begun and was advancing, delivered Rome itself, the Pope, the Cardinals and the whole Roman Curia into the hands of Charles of Bourbon and his army, by whom they were treated with contempt on the march and as if they were distracted, so that by this one memorable example God surely wished to show that all that false power of the Pope and authority of the Roman clergy, and thus every human work, can be overturned by God in a moment, and all admiration of that loftiness turned into contempt. For at that time nothing was baser, nothing more despised, nothing more ridiculous than the Pope, who was thus harassed and mocked by the army of Caesar, the Catholic Prince, as they say; as Sleidanus has related the whole matter in Book 6. For although to be laughed at, despised and made a mockery by men is not in itself a proof of divine contempt, yet, from those things by which God wished to be glorified in his Son, in the Apostles and in his Church, nevertheless human contempt and disdain are in certain cases witness and pledge of divine judgment: namely, when human glory and majesty, which lifts itself up against God and the Church, suffers insult; especially when this happens according to the prediction of Scripture. For in general Scripture testifies that what is exalted among men is abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15). And vileness is for the sons of men in exchange for exaltation (Ps. 12:9). God pours out wrath upon princes (Ps. 107:40). Specifically, God threatens such shame and mockery to the spiritual Tyre (Isa. 23:8-9): Who has purposed this against Tyre the crowner (such is Rome, the Coronatrix, who places crowns on Caesars, kings and princes and removes them at will), whose merchants are princes, whose traders are the honourable of the earth? The Lord of hosts has purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.

units.la: LXV. Gemina est orbis conversio, quæ non parùm hic nostram fidem fulcire potest; una à Gentilismo ad Christianismum; à Papismo ad renovationem Christianismi altera, ardua, difficilis, improvisa æquè, atque arduum, difficile, improvisum, finale Babylonis judicium erit. Quantæ enim res difficultatis laborisque videbatur, Dracone, hoc est, Diabolo in Gentilibus Imperatoribus Ecclesiam infestantibus, imperium adhuc obtinente, Christianam religionem, Judæorum comitiis explosam, Philosophorum judiciis stultitiæ damnatam, Imperatorum edictis ex communi vita relegatam, acerbissimis mundi totius odiis repressam, in publicam lucem splendorémque producere? Produxit illam Deus, & represso Judæo-
units.tr: LXV. The conversion of the world is twofold, and this can greatly strengthen our faith here: one from Gentilism to Christianity; the other, arduous, difficult and unexpected, from Papism to the renewal of Christianity; and just as arduous, difficult and unexpected will be the final judgment of Babylon. For what seemed a matter of great difficulty and labour: to bring the Christian religion into public light and splendour, when the Dragon, that is the Devil, was attacking the Church through the Gentile Emperors while still holding the empire; when the Christian religion had been driven out by the assemblies of the Jews, condemned as folly by the judgments of the philosophers, banished from ordinary life by the edicts of the Emperors, and repressed by the most bitter hatreds of the whole world? God brought it forth, and, with Jewish...

units.la: Gemina orbis conversio improvisa, a Gentilismo ad Christianismum altera, a Papismo ad renovationem Christianismi altera de secuturo Babylonis excidio suffulcire potis est. Judæorum furore, jugulata sapientum ratione, coërcitâ Imperatorum sævitiâ, in omnes Mundi regiones divulgavit. Patrum verò nostrorum memoria, Alexandro VI. Papa & Julio II. Imperii Papalis clavum tenentibus, quàm auribus animisque hominum absurdum dictu visum fuisset, si quis prædixisset, brevi Papatum ingentem conversionem passurum, & Religionem Orthodoxam Cimmeriis Superstitionum tenebris involutam, tanta Pontificum rabie vexatam, tot Doctorum sententiis confossam, tanta suppliciorum diritate laceratam, ex octingentorum plus annorum tetra nocte revocatam, deterso-que situ, atque elutis fœditatis Babylonicæ maculis, Euangelicæ sinceritatis nitori restitutum iri? Quàm ridiculus fuisset, qui hoc ipsum, quod mox magnificentissimè compertum est, & nostris hodieque oculis cernimus, ex Daniele & Apocalypsi prædicere ausus fuisset? Neque valdè fortasse talis derisus, sed potius, ceu alter Stephanus, non quidem lapidatus, sed dentibus dilaceratus esset. Quomodo etiam olim Prophetæ non solùm derisi, sed crudeliter occisi sunt ab iis, quibus imminentem suum & à Deo decretum interitum prædixerunt. Passus tamen est mox Papatus conversionem illam fatalem: restituit Deus & revocavit Ecclesiam per medias Tyrannorum acies, per ignes & tela, remotis obstantium catervis, sibi viam facientem. An ergò gravius nunc erit Deo prædictorum à se Babylonis fatorum fidem exsolvere, fideles ab hostium suorum immanitate, à suppliciorum diritate, à Persecutorum ferro, flamma, tormentis, carceribus, triremibus, ab omnidenique formidinum terrore, prætoriâ benignitatis suæ vindictâ, liberare? An grave Numini negotium reputabimus, Sui cultum Mundo restituere, Ecclesiam suam à tantis molestiis liberare, suæ dignitatis & honoris gravem vem adeò Adversarium, piorum sanguine ebrium, Ecclesiæ lacrymis pastum, omni scelere infamem, commeritis pœnis suis multare?
units.tr: The twofold conversion of the world, unexpected in one case, from Gentilism to Christianity, and in the other from Papism to the renewal of Christianity, is able to strengthen our faith in the coming destruction of Babylon. When the fury of the Jews had been overcome, the reason of the wise had been throttled and the cruelty of the Emperors restrained, he spread it through all regions of the world. And in the memory of our fathers, when Alexander VI and Julius II held the helm of the Papal Empire, how absurd would it have seemed to men's ears and minds if someone had foretold that the Papacy would soon undergo a great conversion, and that the Orthodox Religion, wrapped in the Cimmerian darkness of superstitions for more than eight hundred years, vexed by so much rage of the Pontiffs, pierced by the opinions of so many teachers, torn by such fierce tortures, would be called back from that foul night and, its squalor wiped away and the stains of Babylonian filth washed off, restored to the brightness of evangelical sincerity? How ridiculous would he have been who dared to foretell from Daniel and the Apocalypse that very thing which was soon most magnificently brought about and which we still see with our own eyes today? Perhaps such a man would not have been greatly mocked, but, like another Stephen, would have been torn by teeth, though not stoned. Just as in former times the Prophets were not only mocked but cruelly slain by those whose impending and God-decreed ruin they had foretold. Yet the Papacy soon suffered that fatal conversion: God restored and recalled the Church through the middle of the tyrants' battle lines, making a way for himself through fires and weapons, the crowds of opponents having been removed. Will it therefore now be more difficult for God to fulfil the fates of Babylon he has foretold, to free the faithful from the savagery of their enemies, from the cruelty of tortures, from the sword, flame, tortures, prisons, galleys of the persecutors, and from every terror of fear, by the praetorian vengeance of his kindness? Or shall we think it a grave task for the Deity to restore his worship to the world, to free his Church from so many troubles, and to punish with deserved penalties that adversary, grave to his own dignity and honour, drunk with the blood of the pious, fed on the tears of the Church, infamous for every crime?

units.la: LXVI. Frustrà ergò Roma timorem omnem animo suo excutit, hoc inprimis tempore, quo hostis nemo metuendus ei videtur. Nam gentis Othomanicæ, sic calculum illa subducit, vigor indies marcescit; Hispania devotè servit, Gallia prehensando adulatur, Germania, cujus genius scepticolli isti Jovi semper infestus fuit, per intestinas dissensiones enervatur, & novum Electorem Romanarum partium, mira satorum dispositione, nacta est; denique Britannia & Scotia à Rege, Romæ impensè addicto, regitur. Ad singula fortè Politici, rerum, quæ in mundo geruntur, gnari, reponere aliquid haberent. Ego certus, Ecclesiam non humanis rationibus, sed Divinis consiliis geri; si vel maximè tota Turcia, omnisque Oriens Romano Pontificatui hodiè subderetur, & quicquid præterea in orbe Monarcharum est, beatissimos illos pedes exoscularetur, de ejusdem excidio ne minimum quidem dubitarem, iis, quas ex Prophetia adduxi, rationibus fretus. Quod autem de hostibus objicitur, ad id Jeremias, parium pari ratione habita, respondeat, quando dicit Jerem. LI. 53. Si Babylon cœlum ipsum conscendat, communiátque in sublimi robur suum, ex me tamen ipso venient vastatores ejus, dicit Dominus. Ne etiam, quæsumus, Romani in nostra confusione nimium confidant; meminerintque potius, id ipsum olim Ægyptiorum Ariolos in præcipitium egisse; quando videlicet ab una parte Pharaonis currus militares, ab altera Israëlitarum, inter desertum, Mare rubrum, & Pharaonis præsidia conclusorum, fluctuantem perturbationem intuiti sunt, & Pharao ipse dixit: נכבים הם נארץ, בארץ, Confusi, perplexi hærent in terra, & desertum eos inclusit. Exod. xiv. 3. Quales tum, & quàm fervidas Ariolorum instigantium exhortationes fuisse putamus, quibus Pharaonem & Aulicos ejus ad sumendam de his profugis perditisque (tales enim ab iis habebantur) apostatis vindictam incitárunt, donec eos in exitium suum propulerunt? Ad hoc sanè exemplum Propheta noster perspicuè alluđit, quando uno die venturas Babylonis plagas, viduitatem, luctum, famem, conflagrationem prædixit, atque, ut ab humanorum mediorum omnium consideratione nos avocet, tam disertis verbis subjungit: quia Validus est Dominus, qui eam judicabit, Apoc. xviii. 8. Neque denique assensum nostrum turbent rumores, qui quotidiè ex singulis orbis partibus, confusionis & terroris pleni, ad nos perferuntur. Nam & conrra hoc remedium per os Jeremiæ provisum est, dicentis cap. li. 46, 47. Ne quasso languescat cor vestrum, propter rumores terræ, qui hoc anno tales, & alio anno iterum alii exaudientur, invalescente in terris violentia, & Principe contra Principem insurgente. Ecce enim dies veniunt, quibus visitaturus sum idola Babylonis, ut tota ejus regio confundatur, & interemti ejus in medio illius cadant. An ad præsentem rerum nostrarum faciem quicquam evidentius, vel ad piorum sub eadem tot cum malis & periculis conflictantium consolationem efficacius dici poterat?
units.tr: LXVI. In vain, then, does Rome shake all fear from her mind, especially at this time, when no enemy seems to her to be of concern. For she reckons that the strength of the Ottoman people is wasting away daily; Spain serves devotedly, France flatters by cajoling, Germany, whose genius has always been hostile to that stiff-necked Jove, is weakened by internal dissensions, and by a wonderful arrangement of events has gained a new Elector of the Roman party; finally, Britain and Scotland are ruled by a King who is wholly devoted to Rome. Perhaps the politicians, who know the affairs of the world, would have something to say in reply to each of these points. I am certain that the Church is governed not by human reasons but by divine counsels; and even if all Turkey and the whole East were now subject to the Roman Pontificate, and whatever other monarchs there are in the world were to kiss those most blessed feet, I would not have the least doubt about its destruction, relying on the reasons I have drawn from prophecy. As for what is objected about enemies, let Jeremiah answer it by treating equals on an equal footing, when he says (Jer. 51:53): If Babylon should mount up to heaven and fortify her strength on high, yet from me shall come her destroyers, says the Lord. Let the Romans, I beg, not trust too much in their own security amidst our confusion; let them rather remember that the same thing once drove the soothsayers of Egypt to ruin, when, seeing from one side Pharaoh's military chariots, and from the other the Israelites shut in between the desert, the Red Sea and Pharaoh's garrisons, they saw the wavering confusion, and Pharaoh himself said: [נכבים הם נארץ, בארץ] They are confused, perplexed, hemmed in on the land, and the wilderness has shut them in (Exod. 14:3). What, do we suppose, were the exhortations of those soothsayers who urged them on, and how fervent were they, by which they stirred Pharaoh and his courtiers to take vengeance on those fugitives and apostates (for so they were regarded by them), until they drove them to their own destruction? Our Prophet clearly alludes to this example when he foretells that in one day the plagues of Babylon will come, widowhood, mourning, famine and conflagration, and, so that he may call us away from the consideration of all human means, adds in such plain words: for the Lord who will judge her is strong (Rev. 18:8). Finally, let not rumours that daily reach us from every part of the world, full of confusion and terror, disturb our assent. For against this too a remedy has been provided through the mouth of Jeremiah, who says (Jer. 51:46-47): Let not your heart grow faint, nor fear the rumours that will be heard in the land, one year this report, and another year that, violence increasing in the land and ruler rising against ruler. For behold, days are coming in which I will visit the idols of Babylon, so that all her land shall be confounded, and her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Could anything more evident be said regarding our present state of affairs, or anything more effective as a consolation for the pious who in the same way struggle with so many evils and dangers?

units.la: LXVII. Babylonis finale excidium, Ordinum Regni Babylonici luctus & querela super horribili ejusdem ruina excipiet.
units.tr: LXVII. The final destruction of Babylon will be followed by the lament and complaint of the orders of the Babylonian kingdom over its dreadful ruin.

units.la: Illas verò in triplici differentia Spiritus S. præsentat; Reges nempè terræ, Mercatores terræ, & reliquam Nauticam turbam, quæ mari negotiatur. Reges terræ ii ipsi sunt, qui cum Meretrice hac scortati sunt & lascivierunt, Apoc. xviii. 9. Parùm tamen lachrymabi-
units.tr: The Holy Spirit presents them under a threefold division: the kings of the earth, the merchants of the earth, and the rest of the seafaring crowd who trade by sea. The kings of the earth are those who committed fornication and lived in luxury with this harlot, Rev. 18:9. Yet their weeping will hardly be tearful

units.la: Tom. II. mmmmm lis & pathetica eorum querela erit. Quippe ἀπὸ μακρόθεν procul stabunt, propter metum cruciatus ejus, non ausi ferre ei suppetias, vel efficacem medicinam adhibere laboranti. Quin potius Dei in perfundanda Babylone judicium mirabuntur, dicentes v. 10. Væ, væ, Civitas illa Magna Babylon, Urbs illa Valida, quia in una hora venit judicium tuum. Mirabuntur, subitò adeò excidi potuisse falsam illam Ecclesiam, quæ tam potentes in mundo assertores, & tam validas alteque fixas radices habuit, ut vulgò inexpugnabilis haberetur.
